en: One should indeed offer lamps, new grain, and desirable food for my pleasure. ||41||
In the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, one should offer vehicles— donkeys, camels, mules,
elephants, goats, sheep, carts, and wagons— for my pleasure.
In the month of Pauṣa, one should devoutly give houses, coverings, and so forth, as well as palaces, cities, and the like, along with food endowed with the six flavors. 43.
One should indeed give female and male servants and ornaments for my satisfaction;
whatever is most dear to one, and whatever pure thing can be found in the house, [should be given]. 44.
For the sake of pleasing Puruṣottama, that which fulfills all desires should be given;
he who causes a temple of Śrī Kṛṣṇa to be built shall go to the imperishable realm. 45.
He who gives pleasure groves rich in flowers and fruits shall go to the Imperishable;
he [delivers] eight and twenty generations of his ancestors and descendants.
The builder of a temple for Viṣṇu shall cause himself, along with others, to cross over [to liberation];
and these virtuous ancestors and gods sing this verse.
Will there be someone in our own family who will be a devotee of Kṛṣṇa, who, by building a temple for Hari, will indeed grant us happiness? (48)
May he who anoints the temple with black ointment, and he who performs the sweeping in the shrine—the devotee by whom we have been uplifted—truly be present for us in an unbroken lineage. (49)
May one born in our lineage offer a banner at the temple of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, as well as a lamp, fine incense, flowers, and ointments. (2.69.50)
May he be born in our family and perform the concluding rite for my worship, as well as the fast and the act of giving, with undivided devotion. (51)
Even one burdened with great sins becomes freed from sin by painting the temple of Kṛṣṇa; blessed is the birth of him who belongs to me.
Blessed was the ancient King Manu, who established in this world the supreme Mānavas as constant devotees of Viṣṇu, intent on the highest dharma. ||53||
In the sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpikā,
he caused temples to be built for Śrī Kṛṣṇa and for Nārāyaṇa with great opulence.
He constantly decorated the lamp-stands in the abode of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa with pure and beautiful paintings of five colors. 55.
He joyfully gave golden vessels and indeed vessels for clarified butter; he gave garlands and necklaces of various colors, as well as Vaijayantī wreaths.
And there were divine garlands and necklaces dyed with deep red lac, madder-red, nine-colored, and white pāṭalika flowers. ||57||
Various delightful groves, rich in flowers and abounding in fruit,
entwined with creepers and sprouts, and covered with deodar trees.
He caused enchanting, divine lakes to be constructed, adorned with mountain-like pavilions, and he assigned them all around for the sake of the palace.

The couches were adorned with jewels and occupied by skillful attendants; they possessed seats inlaid with gems and were attended by those knowledgeable in the Gandharva arts and the science of passion.
He caused to be built auspicious, divine structures resembling celestial abodes,
wherein ascetics and celibate students were perpetually honored.
Vedic scholars, the best of Brahmins, and stainless sages; truthful women, virtuous wives, female practitioners of Sāṃkhya and Yoga, and women devoted to Brahman. ||62||
In this manner, devotion to Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa was cultivated by that very Manu together with his wife; and at the end, they both went to the abode of Hari.
In this manner, King Jyāmagha also acted upon the earth like Manu;
he attained supreme devotion to the Supreme Lord and reached the highest state of Brahman.
Therefore, O Rādhikā, you must indeed build a temple for me; worship me with diligence, as well as the virtuous men and women who have taken refuge in me. 65.
O Rādhikā, properly worship those who follow noble conduct, who are speakers of sacred discourse, who bring about the welfare of the world, and who bestow devotion upon me. 66.
With garments, ornaments, jewels, cattle, land, gold, and so forth;
with food, water for drinking and the like, and with massages of the limbs and other such services. ||67||
"Since wealth exists, please satisfy the Lord in every way.
Having been addressed thus, Rādhikā also [went] to the supreme abode of Lord Kṛṣṇa. 68.
He caused a temple, as radiant as the moon, to be built in Goloka,
containing the auspicious image of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
Having established Rādhā [in her seat], she performed service and so forth:
sweeping, smearing [the floor with cow dung], decoration, feeding, and other such duties. (2.69.70)
Rādhikā herself offered sugar and other sweets, as well as lamps, incense, circumambulations, the waving of lights (nīrājana), and the festival celebration.
The large-eyed one performed the cleaning of the vessels in the temple of Kṛṣṇa;
indeed, Rādhā herself sang songs and performed kīrtana.
Thus Rādhā always performed devotion according to the word of her husband;
for if a virtuous woman indeed acts upon the word of her husband, which is like the word of the elders, [she attains the highest state]. (73)
Whether it be ill-spoken or well-spoken, that [speech] which is affectionate becomes like clarified butter for one bitten by the serpent of calamity who is entirely devoid of mantras.

By drinking the nectar of the elders' words and by assenting to what they have said, people indeed bring about the state of being free from poison through those very words, which act as medicine. (75)
The satisfaction that arises in men from drinking soma is not like that which comes from those for whom elders are teachers; they, though living, are indeed dead.
They alone are to be pitied and will be ruined at every step—
those seized by the crocodiles of calamity where elders do not show the way.
Nor are there any deliverers for them; peace is not found for those submerged in an ocean of calamity, sinking amidst the waves of misfortune. (78)
Without the words of the elders, their deliverance is by no means possible;
therefore, one should listen to the words of the elders or carry them out.
He attains success immediately through the repeated blessings of the elders;
O Rādhikā, you must always act in such a way that I may be pleased.
I meditate upon my own fundamental nature, the Supreme Person;
others, such as the men beginning with Kapila, meditate upon me as Kapila. (81)
The manifestations, Vāsudeva and the others, meditate upon Puruṣottama;
and Narāyaṇa, residing in Vikuṇṭha, likewise meditates upon Vāsudeva.
Śrī Viṣṇu meditates upon Nārāyaṇa, and the people meditate upon Viṣṇu;
thus has this meditation been set in motion, handed down through the lineage of gurus.
Viṣṇu resides in the Guru, and the Infinite (bhūman) shines within Viṣṇu; within the Infinite, the Great (bṛhat) shines, and within the Great alone, the Supreme Brahman shines forth. ||84||
Thus, through inquiry into one's own self, one should meditate upon Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa;
one should serve that Supreme Lord, and likewise bow to and worship him. 85.
One should offer everything to this Supreme Self, who is the inner self;
through yoga, the illusory self and the inner self become one with the Supreme Self.
For the individual soul abiding in māyā, the impurities such as desire, anger, and so forth—produced by māyā and consisting of its qualities—arise over a long period of time. (87)
Because it has been brought down from birth to another birth by those [impurities], this nature is said to be defiled; it is pervaded by *māyā* even throughout many successive births. (88)
One conforms oneself to the self through the yoga of the virtuous; one likewise ages [attains maturity] by taking refuge in the Supreme Lord, and thereafter, O Lord, [one ages] through that Master.
Through compassion, one attains the path to liberation characterized by devotion;
by that means, one goes to the Supreme Brahman, just as Jyāmagha did.
O Rādhikā, by reading, hearing, remembering, or even causing others to hear this, both heaven and liberation shall indeed be attained; there is no doubt in this matter. 9.1.
Just as Rādhā, so may a woman attain the good fortune of Kṛṣṇa;
and just as Garuḍa, so may a man attain the state of servitude [to Him]. 92.

Thus ends the sixty-ninth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness and Fruits of Service, Worship, Giving, and Veneration of the Lord," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Rādhikā said: How did King Jyāmagha, though filled with his former nature, later attain liberation through the fruit of his worship? Please tell me that.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Rādhā, to this ancient tale that bestows detachment;
I shall relate the story of Jyāmagha, which arose over many lifetimes.
The son of the sage Dhanurmagha was named Kauśika;
his son was Jāḍyamagha by name, who had the appearance of one who is dull-witted.
He does not speak like a fool, nor does he see like a blind man;
his mother, having placed him under guard at the door of the house with a lamp, [watched over him]. (4)
At that time, Kākākṣī, the Rākṣasī, went to fetch water from the village well; meanwhile, she left the child playing on the swing. || 5 ||
Taking her beautiful, tender child, she gave him to the *svarakṣasa*.
Upon seeing him, the *rākṣasa* asked: "O beloved, what have you brought? (6)
She said, "This boy was brought here by me from Kauśika.
The Rākṣasa replied, "O blessed lady, you have certainly not done well. (7)
The enraged Kauśika will quickly curse us;
therefore, swiftly bring him to his house on a swing.
Alternatively, go and place it right where she goes for the purpose of fetching water;
having seen it there, her mother will take it.
The Rākṣasī, having quickly seized him, went to the pond;
seeing that virtuous woman arrived there, she released the boy before her.
Having obtained a son, that virtuous woman also returned home carrying water;
considering it her good fortune, she caused the worship of the planets to be performed for her son.
And he performed offerings for the pacification of obstacles with sincere devotion,
through the application of the Rākṣasī’s hand and by drinking the milk of the Rākṣasī.
Indeed, the nature of a *rākṣasa* persisted in this child even through touch;
yet, as this boy grew, he received the sacred thread (*yajñasūtra*). (13)
Appointed by his father to the household to study the Vedas, he displayed dullness;
because of his stupidity, he did not recite them, and his father administered a lesson.
Out of fear of being beaten and the like, he fell into a pit on the boundary;
there stood an *āmalakī* tree, which had borne fruit for his nourishment.
Having eaten the āmalaka fruits, he goes to the well and always drinks the pure water; he comes and goes by way of the foot of the tree.
In this well, concealed by trees and creepers and with its roots growing downward,
this boy remains at ease, his movements unnoticed.
Thus nourished, he also ate grains and other produce grown at night;
going outside, he constantly consumed seeds, tubers, fruits, and the like.
Thereupon his father and the others realized that he was either dead or lost;
however, at one time his mother indeed desired sacrificial wood.
He went indeed to that boundary to fetch *āmalaka* wood;
grasping the branches of trees, he made a heap upon the shore. (2.70.20)
Meanwhile, a boy suddenly sneezed at the bottom of the well;
hearing the sneeze of a human being, he approached to see what it was. (21)
Upon seeing her own son, she was filled with extreme joy;
however, the mother, becoming distraught, called out to her son who remained inside the well.
Upon seeing his mother with love, the son’s voice became choked with emotion;
emerging from the well, he prostrated at his mother’s feet with his head.
Having approached her own son and quickly gathered firewood,
she went to her own home accompanied by her son and bowed to her husband.
He related all those actions of his son;
then that Brahmin, having recovered his son, asked him with a joyful heart.
"How did you escape from the house, and how do you still live?
Why do you not speak, my son? Tell me the reason in every way. (26)
Then Jāḍya spoke of his own former history:
"Listen, father, to the cause by which I have resorted to silence. (27)
I shall describe my blindness and my dullness exactly as they are.
Formerly, I was a Brahmin, an astrologer skilled in the interpretation of palm lines. (28)
Through the incidental examination of the lines on the hands of women, I repeatedly fell into delusion and took pleasure in the wives of others. (29)
And once, having been insulted by people with harsh speech,
I died by hanging and subsequently went to the city of Yama.
Therefore, when a thousand years had passed and that transgression was only partially exhausted,
he took birth in the forest as a tiger possessing a human body.
Then the king seized him by the tail and placed him in a cage;
and while he remained bound within that cage, even though he was still in the form of a tiger—
My former knowledge has not perished, nor has my desire increased;
though I am a tiger, I do not kill, nor do I even practice cruelty. (33)
I dwell constantly in the pleasure garden together with the king and the queen;
I stand before the lion throne and follow behind them. (34)
I delighted myself like a child and dwelt in that garden;
thus, as the days passed, I attained youth. (35)
Having become tranquil, I sit near the queen’s bathing pool;
whenever the king and queen have bathed, I then behold them with devotion. (36)
As the queen was bathing and sporting repeatedly in the water, naked, a longing arose in me again and again, born from my former habitual tendencies. (37)
King Sudarśana, having bathed, left the queen in the garden and went to his own city for the sake of royal affairs.
And she, accompanied by her friends, repeatedly delighted me— who was like a tiger, beautiful, auspicious, and protected as if I were her own son.
I wandered again and again in the garden together with them;
at times they would quickly climb onto my back.
Sometimes, standing by her side, I would kiss her thigh with my mouth;
in this way, my desire for the queen grew rapidly. (41)
Then, while all my friends were asleep in their quarters during the night,
I lay upon the side of my bed and thought of the king’s beloved.
In her mind, the god of love increased due to former habit;
likewise, from my touch, the state of passion grew within her as well. (43)
"O Princess, you have been described by me as one endowed with fresh youth; O Queen, you captivate my heart. Tell me, for I have fallen under the power of desire. (44)
She said, "O tiger, beloved of you who possess the body of a beast, how can there be a union of pleasure between us two here among human beings? (45)
Then I said to the queen, "It shall be through skillfulness";
thereupon, she embraced me and proceeded to take her pleasure.
Meanwhile, having been observed by a certain female friend,
she went slowly to the armed doorkeepers and informed them of my very presence.
Having himself heard this news thus reported, the king said:
"I was indeed killed by the king and have gone to the world of Yama. (48)
Then, at the end of a hundred years, I became a white donkey; I was employed by a potter as a beast of burden for people. (49)
There too, my entire previous consciousness appeared to me;
but once, the lords of the earth arrived at the potter's [abode].
Then, beautiful maidens and women remained for two days;
among them, one beautiful young woman stayed at her father's house.
She desired to go to a village situated nearby at a distance of one *krośa*;
her husband said to her, "Go, having mounted this excellent donkey. (52)
"You must arrive tomorrow; you should not stay beyond that time.
Having been addressed thus by her husband, the slender woman mounted a donkey.
As he was proceeding quickly, a river met him halfway;
full of water, she descended from behind me there in order to bathe. (54)
The potter and his caravan also went to the riverbank for the sake of purification; there they saw Ekalā, beautiful in all her limbs, wearing only a single wet cloth. (95)
Having seen her, I went near her under the pretext of drinking water;
then, going up to her as she was bathing, I fell upon her and embraced her out of desire. (56)
Under the influence of my past conditioning, I caused her to touch the linga;
at that time, I was indeed seen by the members of her caravan.
Struck severely with a staff, I fell into the midst of the water;
rising up in an instant out of fear, I fled toward the south.
Then, as I was running away, the rope became very tight around my neck;
due to that noose on my throat, my life came to an end at midnight. (59)
Then I was born again in hell; having been liberated from that, I became a parrot.
Thereafter, in a great forest, I was captured by a wicked Śabara.
Having been placed in a cage and sold there to a merchant's son,
I dwell constantly in that house in the company of young women.
Those young women were always nourishing him with fruits, boiled rice, and other foods.
Once, however, there was a young merchant’s daughter named Candrikā.
She grasped me with both hands and dallied with me again and again with her speech;
placing me upon her breast on the bed, she made me recite a song.
Then, from the touch of her breasts and by the force of my former habitual tendencies,
I flew up and repeatedly touched her in the secret place with a state of passion.
She became enraged that her hips had been wounded by my claws;
she struck me with a slender stick, and I fled from there out of fear.
By fate, her firm waist-string became entangled around my neck;
a tight knot was formed by it, and consequently, I died in an instant. (66)
Having experienced great suffering in the world of Yama, I became a bull;
I lived in the house of a caṇḍāla as a carrier of wooden carts.
Then the husband and wife went into the forest to fetch wood,
while at midday the Cāṇḍāla went to the river to fetch water.
A young Caṇḍālī woman was standing in the shade near a cart;
out of desire and by the force of my former habitual tendencies, I licked her. (69)
Thus, on the riverbank, they were constantly going out and returning for the purpose of gathering wood; then, the rainy season arrived there.
Once, however, the Caṇḍāla became afflicted with fever at home,
while his Caṇḍālī wife went into that forest for the purpose of gathering wood.
Then, having loaded the wood previously gathered onto a cart,
she brought me there to that river to give me water to drink.
I saw her, bathed and endowed with beauty, yet naked;
by the force of past impressions, desire arose within my heart. (73)
Having put on her garments and girded me with a belt, she bound me with a yoke-strap and yoked me to the pole of the cart. ||74||
At that moment, I stood for a brief instant at the front of the yoke;
then, having flown up, I alighted upon her along with the yoke.
Then, she fell far away due to the blow from my forefoot;
as for me, being yoked by the harness, I was dragged along by the downward-sloping cart. ||76||
Then, cast by the two wheels and the two ruts into a pit,
he fell along with the cart into a bottomless hole, helpless.
Bound indeed by the yoke, I then met my death;
and that passionate woman also, having risen slowly, went back to her home.
Then, having been submerged in hell by the command of the King of Dharma, I was born in your house, my dear father; I am entirely one who remembers his former births.
I remember exactly as many births as these today, in their proper sequence;
and because of my former practice, I have consequently experienced extreme sufferings.
In this life, I shall indeed neither speak nor hear, nor desire anything by which sin might arise; that I shall not practice under any circumstances. (81)
The cause of my muteness and deafness is the recollection of my former state;
likewise, even in my dullness, it is consciousness alone that is the cause, and nothing else.
Whether it be evil deeds of terrible form committed through mind, action, or speech,
or even that which is auspicious or inauspicious, whether it be bondage or even death— (83)
Even such things as desire arise through previous habituation;
therefore, one who possesses discernment and understands this is never deluded in that regard.
But when a human being here remembers his former birth, then he will indeed attain cessation from those sins. ||85||
Charity, austerity, study, theft, sin, fame, virtue, wealth, knowledge, and even the burning of fire—all these indeed arise through the power of prior habituation. (86)
Non-violence, devotion to the Lord, steadfastness, tranquility, desire, affliction, suffering, and the attainment of a mate—these indeed arise through the power of prior habituation. (87)
Affection, innate nature, faith, service, learning, arts, wealth, family life, teacher, and disciple—these indeed arise through the power of previous practice. (88)
"Therefore, O father, I am going to the forest for the sake of auspiciousness and to dispel my sins.
Having spoken thus, and having bowed down, Jāḍyamagha then departed for the forest. (89)
Having previously gone to Kurukṣetra and then to Badarikāśrama,
O Rādhikā, he performed various kinds of penance for the removal of his sins.
Then, having met his death at the proper time in the Gaṅgā, he—whose sins were exhausted by austerities and who was an ocean of merit along with his latent impressions—[attained liberation]. ||9.1||
Then, in the city of Śrīnagara in Gaurjara, this son of Raji was born as Jyāmagha,
the righteous and pure son of King Karkamagha.
At that time, the refinements characteristic of the animal species, a nature like that of an ascetic woman, and devotion to Nārāyaṇa were present even in Jyāmagha. (93)
The prince became one who remembers his past lives; he said nothing at all—he did not hear, he did not laugh, nor did he direct his mind toward anything. (94)
Free from pride, he eats his food and likewise drinks water;
free from pride, he wears clothes, ornaments, and decorations as they come. (95)
The kingdom, the enjoyments of the kingdom, wealth, servants, attendants, male slaves, female slaves, elephants, and horses—all these indeed became equal to him. || 96 ||
Even a bed made of flowers appears to him as rough as the bare earth; likewise, food that is sweet, refined, and richly fragrant appears to him as equally coarse. ||97||
Whether it be praise or blame, honor or contempt, salutation or even being treated with disrespect—one who has attained equanimity remains the same toward all of these. (98)
While he was living in this manner, youth arrived;
and his father established him in the householder's life through marriage.
He has no desire to know who his wife is or who his husband is; he has no longing, no volition, and likewise no pleasure or cessation thereof.
And all became equal for her at once; then, during the night, his beloved asked her husband the reason for his indifference.
Then, remembering his wife Rādhikā, he spoke to her with composure:
"Whatever auspicious duty ought to be performed here in this rare human birth," ||| 102 ||

Thus ends the seventieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Persistence of Previous Dispositions and the Examination of Stupidity through the Example of Agha over Six Births," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Rādhikā, to that which Jyāmagha spoke to the beautiful lady—
a knowledge that bestows liberation from everything, after which nothing remains.
Jyāmagha said to his beloved: "Listen, O Goddess, you who are indolent regarding wealth;
Māyā is considered the supreme power of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the enchantress. (2)
Māyā in the form of Śrī Kṛṣṇa is that by which this world is sustained;
by her alone is the entire universe—including gods, asuras, and humans—maintained. (3)
The Lord of Śrī Himself creates, nourishes, and indeed devours;
it is by presiding over portions of Her that the gods have become possessed of power.
By this power, all the lords of the gods, beginning with Brahmā and Īśāna, [exist];
she is the source of the entire universe, primordial nature (prakṛti) consisting of the three qualities (guṇas).
Neither the gods, nor the ancestors, nor humans, nor even Vāsava,
nor any other embodied beings on earth, are able to cross over this illusion.
Blessing him, bowing to him, devoted to him, and taking him as his supreme refuge— one who thus worships Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa crosses over that [ocean of worldly existence].
Once, the supreme devotee Indradyuti,
a brahmin who was ever devoted to Viṣṇu, set his mind upon beholding Māyā.
As he was thus yearning, the supreme form, divine and born from Nārāyaṇa, revealed its own true nature to him at one time.
Having seen her, he bowed his head to the virtuous Satī, the beloved of Nārāyaṇa, and then,
filled with humility, he praised the goddess and questioned her.
"Who are you, O mother, O large-eyed one, auspiciously marked with the signs of Viṣṇu? O compassionate one, tell me now your true identity according to the facts."
Having heard this, Lakṣmī spoke to him: "I am Śrī, the beloved of Śrī Hari;
neither sages nor gods see me, so how could humans? (1-2)
I am the one supreme Māyā whose essence is Nārāyaṇa; I am composed of that.
There is no difference between me and Nārāyaṇa; I am the Supreme Goddess, absorbed in him.
And He is the Lord of All, the Supreme Brahman, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa;
those who serve Puruṣottama are absorbed in Him and are worthy of His grace. (14)
Those who worship the Supreme Lord through knowledge and the yoga of action are His supreme devotees; I do not prevail over them.
By worshipping the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa through all forms of self-surrender and with knowledge, the devotee will certainly attain liberation.
Having heard this, Indradyumna then asked Śrī again:
"Tell me how that Blessed Lord, the Sovereign, is to be known."
Thus addressed, that Māyā touched the Brahmin with both her hands and said,
"O sinless one, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa will speak to you."
Having spoken thus, he vanished within Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa;
that brāhmaṇa remained there in meditative absorption (samādhi) to behold Śrī Hari.
Bestowing grace through that devotion, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa himself appeared— clad in yellow garments, a youth, and the embodiment of the universe.
Indradyuti, beholding Hari, bowed and praised that Lord:
"O Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, O Viṣṇu, O Puruṣottama, O Keśava! (21)
O Lord Śrī Hari, who are without beginning, O Hṛṣīkeśa, salutations to You!
O Soul of the Universe, Creator of the world, O Kṛṣṇa of infinite power, salutations to You! ||22||
O Puruṣottama, whose form is full of infinite divine qualities that are themselves beyond all attributes, who is attainable through knowledge and won by grace—to You, I offer my salutation. 23.
Salutations to you of infinite form, whose nature is supreme bliss;
salutations to you, the Supreme Lord, the Brahman, the Supreme Self. 24.
You are the father of all beings, the mother, the kinsman, the well-wisher, and the friend;
you are the imperishable, supreme abode, pure consciousness alone, the vast void. 25.
Your servants behold you, the Supreme Self—the support of all, unmanifest, infinite, and beyond darkness—by means of the lamp of knowledge. (26)
I take refuge in Him whose form is existence, consciousness, and bliss;
where the Blessed One resides is indeed the supreme abode of Śrī Hari.
O glorious Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, you alone lead me;
grant me peace, grant me Your abode, and let not Your māyā come upon me. (28)
Having spoken thus, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, laughing, repeatedly touched with his own hand that [prince] who was prostrating at his feet. 29.
As soon as he was touched by the Blessed One, he then possessed the divine eye;
through that grace, he came to know the supreme reality exactly as it is.
He said: "By your grace, there has arisen within me, without doubt, eternal knowledge whose sole object is Brahman, which bestows the perfection of bliss. (3.1)
Instruct me here, O Blessed One; how am I to serve you in every way?
And what task must be performed by me, your devotee in this world, O Supreme Lord? (32)
Having heard this from the virtuous devotees, Hari said:
"I alone am to be worshipped through both knowledge and the yoga of devotion. (33)
Having realized me as the supreme reality, the manifestation, and the cause and effect, and having understood my supreme activity, one who seeks liberation should worship me. || 34 ||

Having abandoned all attachments and knowing this world to be my illusory manifestation (māyā), one should meditate upon me alone within one's own self; such a person shall behold me, who am higher than the highest.
Having performed the threefold meditation, O twice-born one, you should always worship me;
therein, one is directed toward my own domain, while the other has the Supreme Brahman as its excellent object.
Distinct from all else, the Blessed One shines in the supreme abode:
the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of Masters, the Sovereign. (37)
The Self-Ruler (Svarāṭ), who possesses all powers, is the cause of all incarnations; therein lies the second contemplation, wherein all that is insentient and sentient constitutes His body.
Everything—both the insentient and the sentient—is pervaded by the glorious Supreme Self;
everything is dependent upon and governed by the glorious Supreme Self. (39)
Within all those principles, the Inner Self shines forth;
He is this very Śrīmat Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Beloved of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Without that [consciousness], not even an atom exists; that which is of its nature is composed of it.
Apart from it, there exists neither the insentient nor even the sentient.
Therefore, everything is its form, and for that very reason, it is the possessor of form.
Just as he remains divine in the divine, so too is he divine even in the insentient.
Unbound, stainless, and unattached, abiding as the inner witness, he shines everywhere—in you, in me, and likewise in all others. ||43||
Thus, having perceived me as the reality in all things, serve me;
then there is the third contemplation, which is one's own nature as Brahman.
The embodied soul should think, "I am myself of the very nature of Brahman. That state of Brahman, which transcends all qualities, proceeds as its own innate form. ||45||
"I am Brahman. The individual self (jīvātman) possesses the state of being a living soul, which is characterized by engagement in action;
yet actions do not exist at all within Brahman, for that [state of Brahman] is indeed the nature of the Self as Brahman. 46.
All action should be performed; by that, one is not smeared by Brahman.
Having meditated in this threefold way, one shall attain the supreme state. ||47||
Even if one is incapable and like a fool, one should take refuge in Hari;
thereafter, with every effort, being fixed upon Him and devoted to Him alone.
One should propitiate the Supreme Brahman; by that, liberation will certainly be attained—[namely] of that glorious Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Supreme Soul. (49)
All sovereignties together are called eternal manifestation;
through the propitiation of the Lord, manifestation is attained by the devotee.
In the unmanifest world of effects, which consists of both the manifest and the unmanifest,
I am the cause— the imperishable Brahman— and I am in every way distinguished.
I am Nārāyaṇa, the inner controller (antaryāmī) there, worshipped by the Lord; I am the author of creation, preservation, and dissolution. Knowing this, worship me. (52)
Therefore, through knowledge and action, you shall attain me by means of yoga.
I am the Lord Nārāyaṇa; formerly I was the Great Virāj.
Then the four-faced Brahmā, the Grandfather, was created by me;
likewise, Rudra and Viṣṇu were created by me from my own body. (54)
Śrī, the power of Viṣṇu, was created—lotus-eyed, beautiful in form, with a gentle countenance, and enchanting to all embodied beings. 55.
Possessing a pure smile, exceedingly serene, with divine luster and great beauty, she wears celestial garlands, garments, and ornaments, and is the abode of majesty.
She is Nārāyaṇī, the Great Māyā, the Vaiṣṇavī who is primordial nature (mūlaprakṛti).
Having seen her, Brahmā then spoke to me again and again.
O Keśava, employ a beautiful woman to delude all beings without exception, so that this vast creation of mine may flourish.
Thus addressed, I then spoke to the goddess Śrī while laughing:
"O Goddess, this entire universe, including gods, asuras, and humans, is yours. (59)
Having deluded them at my command, cast them down into the cycle of existence;
and those who would worship you alone, confine them within you.
Keep far away from those who are devoted to the yoga of knowledge, who are self-controlled, most firmly established in Brahman, exponents of Brahman, free from anger, and dedicated to truth. 6.1.
Keep far away from those Brahmins who have stilled their doubts through the knowledge of the Vedas and Vedānta, and who are devoted to the sacrifice to Brahman (brahmayajña).
Those who worship the Supreme Lord with prayers, burnt offerings, and devotions,
or through Vedic study and ritual sacrifice— avoid them with great effort from afar.
Avoid from afar those pure ones who are endowed with the yoga of devotion, whose minds are offered to the Lord, and who perform the surrender of all things unto me.
Avoid those devotees who have their minds attached to me, who are devoted to meditation on my form, who serve my holy attendants, and who are most righteous. 65.
What is the use of saying more here? Avoid the virtuous men and women who are immersed in my worship; do not delude them by my command.
Thus my beloved Māyā has been impelled by me;
acting according to my command, she does not bind my followers.
My devotee should worship her; one should honor Lakṣmī and Śrī.
She bestows abundant prosperity, nourishment, intelligence, fame, and strength. (68)
When worshipped, the consort of the Blessed One bestows auspicious prosperities;
she grants service to Kṛṣṇa. Therefore, one should worship Lakṣmī. (69)
Without action, the embodied being indeed does not persist by its own nature;
for action arises in two forms: that which is engaged in worldly activity and that which is withdrawn from it.
That which is preceded by knowledge is cessation; that which is otherwise is engagement. By practicing cessation, one attains that supreme state. (71)
Forgiveness, self-restraint, compassion, charity, freedom from greed, renunciation, as well as straightforwardness, absence of envy, and likewise following the sacred fords (tīrthas). ||72||
Truthfulness, contentment, faith, devotion, and restraint of the senses;
the worship of the deities and, especially, the honoring of the virtuous. ||73||
Non-violence, pleasant speech, absence of backbiting, and great humility—this is the dharma for all classes of human beings, and it bestows liberation. ||74||
The realm of Prajāpati is for Brahmins who perform their duties, while the realm of Indra is for Kṣatriyas who act according to righteousness. (75)
The station of the Maruts belongs to the Vaiśyas who abide in their duties;
likewise, the station of the Gandharvas belongs to those of the Śūdra caste who abide in servitude.
That which is the station of the eighty-eight thousand ascetics who have sublimated their vital energy (ūrdhvaretas) is indeed the Vairāja station for those who serve their guru.
The abode of the Seven Sages belongs to those forest-dwellers who live according to dharma; likewise, it belongs to householders who abide in their duties toward Prajāpati.
For ascetics, renunciants, those of sublimated vital energy, those who have renounced,
and for virtuous women who are chaste wives devoted to Brahman, the station of Virāj is declared.
The immortal abode of yogis is that which is the unmanifested state of the Infinite;
but for devotees, it is above that, known as the Void, the supreme imperishable.
The abode of Īśvara consists of bliss, from which those who have surrendered their souls to the Lord Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa never return again. 8.1.
There exists the supreme abode, ruled by the Supreme Lord, which is filled with all things consisting of Brahman and characterized by existence, consciousness, and bliss. ||82||
Listen further, for I shall proclaim another supreme knowledge that bestows liberation;
indeed, it is held that among all the stages of life (āśramas), there is a twofold division within the intermediate state.
The student is of two kinds: the temporary (upakurvāṇa) and the lifelong (naiṣṭhika), both being intent upon Brahman;
he who, having studied the Vedas according to the rules, enters the stage of the householder.
The *upakurvāṇaka* is to be known [as the student], while the *naiṣṭhika* lasts until death;
the *sādhaka* and the *udāsīna* are also mentioned, and the householder (*gṛhastha*) is considered to be of two kinds. ||85||
Devoted to the maintenance of his family, this practitioner shall become a householder;
having discharged the three debts, he should become free from attachment and indifferent.
The forest-dweller (vānaprastha) is considered to be of two kinds: the ascetic (tāpasa) and the seeker of liberation (maukṣika).
The ascetic is one who is devoted to austerity, fire-offerings, sacrifice, and the study of sacred texts. ||87||
Furthermore, among these, the first is established in meditation, devoted to Kṛṣṇa, and seeking liberation;
the second possesses knowledge and is also possessed of devotion. (88)
The monk who possesses discernment between the body and the self proceeds toward knowledge;
delighting in the self and satisfied with the self, this renunciation belongs to the portion of knowledge. 89.
Endowed with right vision, devoted to the service of Kṛṣṇa,
delighting in Kṛṣṇa, and satisfied with Kṛṣṇa— he is indeed a renunciant seeking liberation.
But the yogi is indeed present in all stages of life at all times;
even while at home, he who is unattached and possessed of discernment is the king of yogis. (9.1)
I am Brahman, of the nature of the imperishable and untainted; he, indeed, is the king of yogis.
I have taken refuge in the Supreme Brahman alone; he, indeed, is the king of yogis. (92)
Thus, the yogi devoted to the practice of the path to liberation becomes threefold;
thus indeed has the means to liberation been imparted by me to all creatures.
Brahmā gave all that he had learned to Brahmā; then Brahmā gave it to the sages, his own sons, and by those paths they attained liberation.
These three qualities, which are for the benefit of the world, have been taken up by me alone;
they are mutually attached and indeed subsist upon one another. (95)

And those who belong to the Supreme Lord sport with one another in mutual prostration, through the conjunction of the qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas, which belong to me alone, the Supreme Self. 96.
Three forms have been proclaimed: Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara.
I am Brahmā and Mahādeva; we are not different from the perspective of ultimate reality.
Although I abide as the Inner Controller, having divided myself according to my own will, Mādhava is therefore to be worshipped with every effort in all three ways. 98.
If a twice-born man desires that imperishable state called liberation without delay, he should serve me with devotion through the dharma of his caste and stage of life. 99.
One should worship me with a devoted heart for as long as one lives, according to one's vow, whether one is established in the Vaiṣṇava, Brāhma, or Śāmbhava stage of life.
Bearing those marks, self-restrained, and affectionate toward those devoted to Him, he should meditate upon Me, worship the gods, and be intent upon the supreme knowledge. || 101 ||
But he who has taken refuge in the god Nārāyaṇa as a seeker of protection should wear the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) on his forehead with sandalwood paste and other substances. || 102 ||
Śambhu resides at the top, Viṣṇu in the middle, and Brahmā is established at the base;
he has taken refuge in Brahmā, the supreme lord and seed of the universe.
He should maintain that great bindu located in the middle of the forehead on the brow;
the upward line is Śāmbhavī, and Viṣṇu is established in the center.
That lower line is indeed Brāhmī, and the three deities reside therein;
the devotee who has taken refuge in Śambhu indeed applies the triple mark with ashes.
One should bear on the forehead a mark equal to the moon, occupying half its portion;
Śambhu resides above it, Viṣṇu in the middle, and indeed the Unborn (Aja) below.
From that, this [universe] evolves, consisting of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva;
the forehead of Rudra is like the sun, while that of Viṣṇu is indeed like the moon.
The forehead of Brahmā is always like fire, radiant with the *tilaka*;
indeed, when the *tilaka* is applied, it becomes the very abode of the Lord of the gods.
Having thus borne the supreme mark and having established solitude for yourself, place yourself at the feet of the Lord and attain the eternal state. || 109 ||
Thus, O Rādhikā, Jyāmagha imparted this knowledge, which is rooted in the glorious Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa and endowed with realized wisdom, to his own wife.
Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa Svāmī bestowed upon Purandrayuti this entire liberating knowledge, which is accessible even to those engaged in ritual action.

Thus ends the seventy-first chapter, titled "The Description of how King Jyāmagha told his wife Dhanālasā everything that had been previously said by the Lord to the Brahmin Indradyuti," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Rādhikā, understand this most wonderful knowledge:
the student, the householder, the forest-dweller, and likewise the ascetic. (1)
The stages of life (āśramas) are accomplished through a sequential order, though they may also be attained otherwise for a specific cause;
such a person has produced knowledge and discernment and has reached supreme detachment.
One should go forth into the life of a wandering ascetic from the stage of celibate studentship or from that of the householder as is appropriate;
or, having taken a wife according to the prescribed rule, one should perform various sacrifices.
One should procreate sons according to the Dharma, and when detachment has arisen, one should renounce;
for if, through the force of detachment, one cannot endure remaining in the household. (4)
One should first become a forest-dweller (vānaprastha) and afterwards take recourse to renunciation (saṃnyāsa);
however, one who possesses the force of extreme dispassion should take recourse to renunciation immediately. || 5 ||
Having entered the stage of the forest-dweller (vānaprastha) or even that of renunciation (saṃnyāsa),
he should not return to his home nor enter into union with a wife again.
Detachment is indeed prescribed for all in the matter of renunciation;
however, one who is not detached falls from renunciation—of this there is no doubt.
Or else, one may properly abide in a single stage of life until the end of death;
for he who is devoted to that subject and possesses knowledge of it is fit for immortality.
One who has given away all his possessions for the sake of Dharma, who possesses the knowledge of Brahman, who is tranquil,
and who is endowed with both theoretical and realized knowledge, is fit for becoming one with Brahman.
Having dedicated all actions to Brahman and being free from attachment to desires and the like,
one who performs them with a serene and devoted mind attains that supreme state.
That which is to be given is given by Brahman; indeed, it is Brahman alone that is given.
The gift is given to Brahman; this supreme offering is the sacrifice unto Brahman (brahmārpaṇa). 11.
I am not the doer; Brahman alone performs all this in such a manner. This action is an offering to Brahman; it is absorbed into Brahman.
"May Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa Svāmī satisfy [the deity] with his own action.
Thinking thus, that which is performed is this supreme offering unto Brahman (brahmārpaṇam). 13.
One should also perform the renunciation of fruits unto the Supreme Lord;
thus, the offering of the fruit to Brahman is the unsurpassed dedication.
Whatever action is performed by the wise as a duty, being free from attachment and with the thought "this must be done," that action may even grant liberation. 15.

If the renunciation of the fruits of actions is interpreted as being directed toward Brahman, then one would be bound by that fruit; consequently, there would be an obstruction to liberation. || 16 ||
Through this offering, sin or merit that obstructs liberation—whether pertaining to this life or previous lives—is destroyed, and clarity of mind arises. (17)
From that, there arises the knowledge of the Self, and from that, the knowledge of Brahman is born;
from knowledge conjoined with action, perfect yoga is produced. (18)
Through yoga, one attains the presence of the glorious Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa;
therefore, with every effort, one should remain devoted to whichever stage of life one is in.
One should perform actions for the sake of pleasing the Lord and thereby attain the state of actionlessness;
having attained the realization of Brahman through His grace, one reaches that very state of actionlessness.
Absorbed in the bliss of his own self, which is the Supreme Brahman, he has conquered his senses;
solitary, free from possessiveness, and tranquil, he is like one already liberated even while living.
He beholds the Supreme Self, the Supreme Brahman, the Supreme Lord;
eternally blissful and free from all limiting adjuncts, he attains absorption in Śrī Hari. ||22||

Therefore, O Rādhā, one should practice that disinterested action which consists of offering [to the Lord], for the satisfaction of the Supreme Lord; by that means, one shall go to the supreme state. 23.
The finality thus established bestows eternal perfection;
however, no human being attains perfection by transgressing this.
Thus Jyāmagha also, having reflected upon everything that was for his own benefit,
explained all that knowledge to his wife in accordance with his realization.
Having realized through wisdom that his own beloved wife was indeed the embodiment of Brahman,
he, who is dear to Hari, gave the kingdom to his younger brother, the illustrious Magha.
Jyāmagha, accompanied by his wife, prostrated at the feet of his parents,
embraced his brother, and reported that all was well in every respect.
Having received the blessings of the subjects on the bank of the Sābhramatī river,
he constantly engaged in the company of the virtuous at that hermitage frequented by the righteous.
His brother proclaimed that city as Śrīnagara, together with his own name;
thereafter, Jyāmagha performed a most auspicious Vaiṣṇava sacrifice.
Through his own brother, he caused [the temple] to be built on the bank of the Sābhramatī;
out of devotion to him, the glorious Śrī Narāyaṇa appeared at the time of the fire sacrifice.
Then Acyuta arrived there at the sacrificial pavilion in embodied form;
likewise, Agni himself, Brahmā, Śambhu, and the Tathāgatas arrived in personified forms.
The deities consumed the sacrificial offering presented by Jyāmagha;
and Śrī, being pleased, said to him: "By your devotion, Janārdana [is pleased]."
Being pleased, he indeed gives me permission to remain in your kingdom;
however, I shall not dwell alone in your city.
I have become satisfied by the sacrifice along with my husband and the gods;
therefore, cause a beautiful temple to be built where I may dwell forever. (34)
Having heard this, Jyāmagha, the king of devotees, rejoiced along with his brother;
having spoken thus, he said again, "Go to Kuṅkumavāpikā."
I dwell eternally in that sacred field of Aśvapaṭṭasaraḥ, devoted solely to the service of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. (36)
Furthermore, through the service of that couple, joined with the duty of servitude, there will be a vision of me and my Lord; of this there is no doubt. (37)
Having spoken thus, she vanished from the sight of the gods and men;
the sacrifice reached its completion, and prosperity increased in the city.
Having bowed to his parents and given the sacrificial fee, Śrī Jyāmagha departed from the Sābhramatī river by boat together with his wife.
Śrī Magha caused a seven-storied temple to be built at the place called Nārāyaṇaghaṭṭaka; it was like a cloud to the touch and possessed a spire.
There, Nārāyaṇa, accompanied by Lakṣmī, was first installed by means of Vedic rites; a garden was then offered to this king.
Worship, offerings of food, and festivals of adornment were also arranged;
in this manner, Śrī Magha also served the glorious Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa. (42)
Having enjoyed that kingdom for a hundred thousand years, he went to the supreme abode;
Jyāmagha also returned from the course of the river to the ocean at Stambha.
Then, having visited the holy site of Śrīgopanātha and thereafter,
he abandoned the boat and proceeded by carriage to Kuṅkumavāpikā.
Having seen Aśvapaṭṭasara and beheld the hermitage of Śrī Lomaśa, and having observed the ground rich with divine splendor, he attained supreme bliss. || 45 ||
Having seen the exalted palace of the glorious Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa,
and beholding its peaks kissing the sky and its banners, he spoke with a faltering voice.
Having first prostrated like a staff, he performed a circumambulation of him;
at that moment, a brahmin in the form of a child arrived there.
Delightful is Śrīnivāsa, the vessel of all beauty;
his eyes are like the petals of a lotus, and his fingers are endowed with subtle lines. 48.
Wearing a brilliant gem upon his chest and adorned by a halo of radiance,
he welcomed him while showing him the sacred sites.
He led him to the temple where the Beloved of Śrī resides—
the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, seated upon an elephant throne.
That brahmin revealed himself there and then vanished;
both Jyāmagha and his queen were struck with supreme wonder.
Having obtained the direct vision of the Mānava-nāṭya, and having further obtained the vision of Bālakṛṣṇa there once again; ||52||

Having realized the identity of the two in their essential nature, their inherent disposition, and their virtuous conduct—and likewise regarding even their physical forms—they both attained their life's purpose through that realization of non-duality. (53)
"Oh, what fortune! Oh, what fortune for Jyāmagha and his wife!
For Bālakṛṣṇa himself has then appeared in the form of a young brahmin boy. (54)
He brought him to his own home, and Bālakṛṣṇa vanished;
His grace was attained through the service of merits accumulated over many lifetimes. ||55||
By which means the Blessed One himself came to his own home;
then [he saw] Kṛṣṇa the cowherd and his mother, the virtuous Kambharā. 56.
Thereafter, they beheld the Blessed One with great satisfaction;
having seen Śuka and his beloved, they indeed beheld the entire assembly of gods.
They rejoiced exceedingly and worshipped the Supreme Lord with sandalwood, unbroken rice grains, saffron, ushira root, and water mixed with red lead.
Indeed, those two worshipped him with flowers, *tulasī*, white water lilies, lotuses, and beautiful *kesara* blossoms, as well as with necklaces, ornaments, garments, and various ritual materials.
Then they placed before him offerings such as golden vessels,
as well as bowls of sweet cooked food, betel leaves, water, and so forth.
The two of them gave [the offerings] to Śrī Hari, to his mother, and to his father;
they performed the waving of lights (ārātrika) and prostrated themselves like a staff (daṇḍavat).
Bālakṛṣṇa, however, asked whether his journey had been auspicious, and likewise inquired about his well-being during his absence, his lack of suffering, and his pleasant arrival.
Then Hari led the couple away for the purpose of performing the rites of hospitality;
he caused them to take food, water, betel-leaf, and other such refreshments.
Hari bestowed an independent mansion for their residence,
gave male and female servants to the couple, and provided them with all kinds of articles.
Then, at evening, that king rested by the Aśvasarovara lake;
he went there to bathe according to the prescribed rites, and having bathed, he performed the twilight devotions (sandhyā).
And he performed the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) for the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake, which was endowed with ten million sacred sites (tīrthas), using one hundred and eight wicks.
Having drunk water, he returned to his own palace with his attendants;
the king spent the night happily and, after performing his morning ablutions, [proceeded]. ||67||
Having worshipped his lord Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa, the husband of Śrī,
and having performed the waving of lights (ārātrika) and other rites, he gave gifts of all kinds.
He gave away many gold ornaments, garments, wealth, pearls, and gems;
he fed the brahmins, sages, and noble maidens residing at the sacred ford.
He performed a pilgrimage to all the sacred sites of the gods as well;
having circumambulated the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake, he returned home.
Blessed indeed is the guṇḍraka tree; blessed is the auspicious tintiḍikā;
blessed is the pomegranate tree; and blessed are the two jambu trees. (71)
Blessed is that Badarī where the Blessed One shines resplendent;
blessed is that Kuṅkumavāpī, the most excellent among the best of sacred fords.
Blessed am I, and Jyāmagha is blessed, as is my beloved Dhanālasā, for we have taken refuge in Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the primordial God. (73)
"Indeed, clothing exists for you, for they dwell in the world of Brahmā.
As he was thinking thus, the queen spoke to him with urgency: (74)
"Build here that most magnificent temple shown by Śrī, wherein the Lord Nārāyaṇa may forever receive our worship. (75)
Having heard this, the king reflected for a mere moment: "How vast and lofty must the palace be made! (76)
He beheld a supreme, most excellent, white, and extensive radiance;
there, in its midst, he saw a single vast peak.
Therein, in the center, one should place the auspicious form consisting of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa;
to the left, Rādhā, Śrī, Lakṣmī, Pāravatī, and likewise Prabhā.
And he beheld those wives of divine appearance— Māṇikī,
his father Dakṣa, his mother Santuṣā, and likewise his sister.
He beheld the Blessed One, Śuka, and his beloved kinsmen of the monkey race; he saw this entire circle and beheld his queen as well.
And while he was in service, all of that [instruction] vanished from him;
then the king summoned the preeminent artisan there and spoke to him. (81)
The best of artisans fashioned a painted cloth exactly as described;
then, to the west of the horse-saddle, he built a beautiful temple.
He caused the entire installation to be performed according to the prescribed rites,
and had thirteen images fashioned by the Brahmins.
Having summoned Lomaśa, he had his own palace constructed and received the auspicious initiation endowed with the principles of Sāṃkhya and Yoga.
In his own palace, the great and excellent Vaiṣṇava, together with his wife, worshipped the glorious Kṛṣṇa-Narāyaṇa with devotion. (85)
Through devotion, through vows, through constant austerity, through meditation, and through a state of servitude, he exhausted the karmic residues from his previous births. ||86||
Having become a great devotee of the Lord, he performed everything with sincere devotion;
for the sake of Hari, he practiced the twenty-four principles.
The king offered his consciousness to Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa and employed his very being for the manifestation of Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa. ||88||
Then Śrī Hari appointed rajas for the purpose of creation so that he might be pleased, and tamas for the purpose of dissolution within the elements. 89.

He assigned the principle of Mahat, which is of the nature of intellect (buddhi), to the function of determination; he made the mind (citta) responsible for reflection, and the ego (ahaṃkāra) for self-conceit. ||2.72.90||
His mind was engaged in contemplation; his ears were for hearing the stories of Hari;
his skin protected him from touch; and his eyes were directed toward beholding Him. (9.1)
The tongue is for tasting his grace; the tongue is for his praise; the nose is for the fragrance of his flowers; and speech is for describing his virtues. (92)
He always employed his two hands in service, in attendance, and in ministry;
likewise, he used his two feet for approaching him and for circumambulation. (93)
He provided water for washing the feet upon his taking a seat, and a mark of joy upon his arrival;
he granted him strength for carrying that burden and skill in serving him. (94)
He offered everything pertaining to his body to Śrī Kṛṣṇa, and the queen likewise offered everything to Bālakṛṣṇa. ||95||
She gave everything to Hari— the subtle elements, the objects of the senses, and both the auspicious and the inauspicious— and she herself became his guest.
He likewise offered all his bodily actions to Śrī Kṛṣṇa;
for those who remember Him, there is always worship, salutation, and praise. (97)
Massaging the feet of Viṣṇu, worshiping Him, and even servitude;
friendship, playful sport, humorous speech, laughing, and even joking—[these are the modes of service]. (98)
She always performed all acts of chanting and offering unto the glorious Kṛṣṇa;
and the queen also became a highly fortunate devotee of the Lord. 99.
Sweeping, smearing [the floor], preparing cooked offerings, fetching water, and likewise the washing of garments and so forth—these are [the duties]. (2.72.10)
The washing of the vessels, the fetching of flowers, the stringing of garlands, and likewise the bringing of *tulasī*; || 101 ||
He fanned the breeze with his hands and even rocked the swing; he performed everything, including the spreading of the bed-clothes.
Like a maidservant, she always performed the massaging of Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa’s feet; she then made a complete surrender of herself to him.
Thus, as those two auspicious ones associated with divine merit continued to serve him,
they became cleansed of all impurities through the grace of Bālakṛṣṇa.
And he was initiated by Lomaśa into the supreme Śrī Vaiṣṇava mantra:
"Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord; obeisance. (1.05)
Having received the mantra and worshipped Hari during the bright fortnight of the month of Āṣāḍha,
on the eleventh day at sunrise, one should remain steady for a moment, absorbed in meditation and fire.
Then there appeared a divine, imperishable, and auspicious celestial chariot,
accompanied by its attendants, possessing a splendor equal to ten million suns.
Having cast off their bodies, Jyāmagha and Dhanālasā, assuming divine forms by the command of the attendants, ascended a celestial chariot.
He quickly departed for the imperishable, supreme abode in his celestial chariot, while shouts of "Victory! arose in the palace of Śrī Nārāyaṇa.
Thus, O Rādhikā, those two attained liberation through devotion;
likewise, the reader, the reciter, and the listener shall also go to the state of liberation.

Thus ends the seventy-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Liberation of King Jyāmagha and his wife Dhanālasā through Self-Surrendered Devotion in the Kuṅkumavāpī Lake," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"O Rādhikā, listen to another auspicious wonder of Hari."
In Gaurjara there flows a delightful river known by the name Dhārādhara. || 1 ||
To the south of Tattaṭa lies the auspicious city of Āmoda,
the dwelling place of many eminent merchants, devoted to the service of the gods,
and inhabited by people who are industrious and endowed with wealth.
There, many humans dwelling on the banks of the Dhṛdharā lived as devotees of Śambhu— excellent men devoted solely to the worship of Śambhu—
and others on the shore of the Dhṛdharā were intent upon ritual worship and recitation.
Having beheld Śambhu, they go to and return from the city; there,
on the shore of the Dhṛtadhara river,
is the auspicious Vaiṣṇava temple where Hari Nārāyaṇa, endowed with Śrī, shines resplendent.
Bearing the form of the image, he is honored and worshipped by the people;
he is saluted and served by the Vaiṣṇavas at all times, especially in the early morning.
Pure holy men dwell there in the vicinity of the temple.
Through that association, a Vaiṣṇava merchant named Sudhana also came to be;
having always first bathed and worshipped the deities,
and having bowed to the virtuous Vaiṣṇavas, he would then go to the temple of Śambhu.
It was crowded with excellent gardens, adorned with trees, creepers, and the like;
it shone with noble trees resplendent with fruits, flowers, and other beauties; it was provided with water-pools and beautifully graced by the abundance of crops upon the terraces.

And within that Mahālaya garden, the divine and enchanting Āmodeśvara Liṅga shines forth with the brilliance of pure crystal; it is free from affliction for devotees and bestows peace even by its mere sight. || 11 ||
In his service was the eminent Brahmin, the great seer Varcakāyani,
who was devoted to celibacy, dedicated to the performance of sacrifices and fire-offerings,
subsisting on mere fruit, sleeping in the open air, and possessed of divine vision.
He was a supreme Vaiṣṇava, devoted to the dharma of service toward Śambhu;
he possessed mastery over the Vedas, the Vedāṅgas, and various sciences, and was intent upon sacred stories and narratives.
By means of his vows, he had attained emaciation, and the vessels of his body were dry.
Devoted to the stories of the *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*,
he would daily take refuge in a bower of trees in the garden of Śiva in the evening and narrate the discourse;
the gods, humans, and others would listen to it.
Men, women, birds, and all embodied beings dwelling there—
Sudhana, filled with devotion, goes constantly to hear them.
There, indeed, the learned one [heard of] Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Lord of Śrī,
the son of Śrī Kambharā, in the field of Kuṅkumavāpī in Saurāṣṭra.
The Supreme Brahman as the child Kṛṣṇa, the infant Gopāla-Kṛṣṇa,
endowed with all powers and served by Śrī Rādhā, Ramā, and others.
And he saw the Mahālaya shrine shining near the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake,
as well as the hermitage of Lomaśa and many other sacred fords (tīrthas).
Then, for that merchant Sudhana,
there arose a beautiful vision of the primordial god Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa himself.
Desiring to behold the drama enacted by Mānava, which bestows liberation, she constantly contemplates the beautiful Bālakṛṣṇa day and night. (22)
"Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Master; svāhā!
He received this mantra from that sage, Śrī Varacakāyani. (23)
He recited that supreme mantra and meditated on the form within his heart;
yet, even though he desired to see Satī, he reflected upon the great distance [between them].
Indeed, finding contentment in the worship within his home through offerings and other rites, he constantly worshipped Hari, the beginningless Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa. (25)
He offers the food offering (naivedya) in the morning, at midday, and at the beginning of the night;
he performs the lustration ceremony (ārātrika), as well as hymns of praise (stava) and recitation (jāpa). ||26||
He also performs auspicious festivals with wealth acquired through righteous means;
his wife, sons, grandsons, and others are devotees of Viṣṇu who have taken refuge in Śrī Hari.
For they were devoted to the service of the gods, intent upon the service of the virtuous, dedicated to hearing sacred discourses, and possessed minds whose intellect was offered unto Kṛṣṇa. ||28||
They constantly serve the saintly men and women, O Kṛṣṇa, with wealth and other gifts, as well as with vehicles, carriages, food, and services such as massaging their feet. ||29||
While Sudhana was thus constantly abiding in the house,
Hari himself [resided] within the form of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
Having manifested visibly, he accepts the food and other offerings presented;
then, smiling, he bestows his grace upon that devotee.
Bālakṛṣṇa would thus constantly vanish from his physical form;
once, however, the merchant Sudhana [came] for the sake of his grandson’s wedding.
Having adorned his own army with wealth, ornaments, garments, and the like, accompanied by excellent men, women, and kings, and mounted on vehicles such as chariots and other conveyances; || 33 ||
From Āmoda he went to the city of Kanyānagara, which abounds in Jambu-rivers;
having crossed the river Nāvā and traveled to Jāmbusārasa.
When he had performed the marriage rites and was returning,
twenty notorious thieves were on the bank of the river named Dhṛtadhara.
Those fierce-looking beings, armed with weapons, rushed into the thicket of trees;
those terrible ones then began to strike the drivers of the carts.
They also struck down the protectors of the army with clubs and other weapons, seizing gold, ornaments, silver, as well as garments and the like. (37)
Indeed, those horsemen, acting as thieves, plundered the finest wealth;
they also carried off food and other provisions, and Sudhana became deeply distressed.
The family and the caravan were likewise deprived of their wealth;
the women were stripped of ornaments and bereft of fine garments and finery. (39)
Thus the kinsmen and relatives were overwhelmed with grief;
the great assembly was deprived of its wealth, and the army was shorn of its splendor.
The women of the bride's party and her female friends became overcome with grief and agitation, and even the daughter-in-law was seized by inauspiciousness when the wedding took place. (41)
"The loss of my fortune was surely an omen of future poverty.
Reflecting thus, Sudhana established firmness within his heart.
Supporting himself by his own self, he remembered Bālakṛṣṇaka, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, his own beloved supreme Lord. (43)
With supreme affection, he praised his own chosen deity, the Supreme Person:
"O Lord of Mercy, Ocean of Compassion, Savior from the ocean of worldly existence! (44)
O protector of those who have come for refuge, you previously provided protection for an elephant here within the forest, as well as in the midst of the waters. (45)
By you, protection was afforded to Prahlāda within the circle of the Dānavas;
and by you, protection was afforded to the Maruts within the inner sanctum.
You are the protector and you are the creator, the eternal Supreme Self;
O Lord, ocean of compassion, protect us, protect us from the terror of thieves! 47.
The householders' entire property, their livelihood, gold, silver, ornaments, and so forth, have been seized by thieves; therefore, deliver them from this suffering. (48)
Wealth and property belong to householders; ornaments and possessions belong to women; peace is the wealth of the virtuous; and for the devotees, Lord Hari himself is their wealth. 49.
In this world, no stability exists without wealth;
O Lord, grain, clothing, and worldly affairs all rest upon wealth. (2.73.50)
Even if there are many defects in a substance, its qualities are always the granters of life; therefore, wealth is a constant support. (51)
There too, O Kṛṣṇa, the merchants possessed all their wealth, such as gold ornaments and the like,
and all of that was stolen by thieves.
O Lord, for those devoted to you, this [world] is a place of intense humiliation;
for those lacking devotion, it has become a locus for being objects of ridicule. (53)
O Supreme Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, lift me up from calamities;
make the meaning of Your name "Protector of Devotees" truly realized.
Otherwise, O Janārdana, people will abandon their devotion to you when their hopes are shattered, considering you, the Lord, to be no protector. (55)
Those who are afflicted worship Kṛṣṇa, the remover of affliction, as long as they remain afflicted;
and those who seek wealth worship Kṛṣṇa, the giver of wealth, as long as they seek wealth.
And those who desire to know worship Śrī Hari only as long as there is a desire to know; once He is known, they indeed cease [their seeking]. ||57||
But for those who are intent on their own self-interest, however their rescue might come about, he remains hopeful in some way or another as he clings to you. ||58||
Likewise, O Lord, having fulfilled the desires of Your own devotees, please grant me protection, O Master, so that I may practice devotion. 59.
Having thus entreated him there in the forest, he, being sorrowful, shed tears;
but having heard that entreaty, the Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, Hari, [responded].
Quickly assuming the guise of a Brahmin, he went to where the thieves had gathered;
the thieves were seated together in the shade of a tree on the bank of a river. ||61||
They divided the portions of gold, silver, and wealth;
but while the distribution of ornaments and other items was taking place, a beggar appeared.
Having become a wandering mendicant, Bālakṛṣṇa appeared like a wretched man,
his body covered in dust and clad as if in nothing at all.
Clad only in a loincloth, he went to beg for food;
"I beg for food here; it is pleasing to me who am hungry. (64)
"O fortunate and auspicious merchants, may you grant me [this];
I do not desire wealth, for I require only food. (65)
The thieves said: "There is wealth here; take it, sir!
If it pleases you, then tell us what amount of silver we should give you. (66)
Then the mendicant said: "I have no need for wealth;
for there are many faults in riches that cause suffering and create enmity. (67)
Wealth causes one to abandon righteousness and swiftly incites violence;
indeed, wealth summons sudden calamity.

There is great effort in the acquisition of wealth, great anxiety in its protection, and constant worry about its depletion during enjoyment, along with the afflictions of being stolen by thieves and other such misfortunes. (69)
Therefore, a mendicant who desires happiness should not seek wealth;
you, however, being wealthy, should give food here.
Even one who possesses silver does not find peaceful sleep before him, for he is constantly afraid of separation due to some cause or another. (7.1)
Deprived of wealth, birds become beggars for mere fruit;
having eaten upon the branches, they wander there itself, free from ailment.
Children, having eaten their food, sleep happily upon the ground;
but anxiety devours these others—the elderly, the young, and the wealthy.
Jewels such as pearls and diamonds, though they are by nature stones, indeed serve as invitations to death. (74)
Gold, silver, ornaments, garments, and wealth—whether earthly or celestial—are always causes of anxiety and agitation. (75)
Bound by the notions of "I" and "mine," they produce passion and hatred;
at the end, they manifest as latent tendencies and greed, bestowing birth and death.
"Therefore, I shall not take that wealth, for it is another's property and causes destruction.
O great people, why is such abundant wealth being obtained here? (77)
Thus questioned and addressed with "Go! Go! in anger, they spoke there;
however, one among them took up an iron staff.
And as he rose up to strike the mendicant who stood there like one in distress,
the mendicant vanished from that spot.
Beholding this sovereign power, they were filled with supreme wonder;
yet, struck by illusion, they thought it was either a spirit or a demon.
Just then, a crow arrived and spoke from atop the tree;
standing upon a withered branch, it became an inauspicious omen. ||81||
Then, having indeed divided the gold and wealth among themselves, they proceeded to divide the jewels, such as necklaces and garlands. 82.
Śrī Hari, mounted upon a horse, as did his other royal servants and fifty cavalrymen armed with weapons, proceeded swiftly. (83)
Dressed as royal messengers and the like, they gathered there from all sides, uttering sounds of "shame! and crying out, "Let them be assaulted! (84)
"Let them kill him! Let these men seize him! Let them become thieves!"—saying thus, they then constructed a rampart around him.
Seeing that array of troops, adorned by its cavalrymen, on all sides, the thieves were seized with fear and fled in every direction. (86)
Having instantly cast aside their gold, silver, garments, diamonds, and pearl necklaces,
they were nevertheless unable to find the path and were powerless before the array.
Indeed, they fell into the hands of the soldiers so that they could not escape;
rendered helpless, their hands were bound with ropes and shackles by them. (88)
Some were struck with sticks, some were beaten with whips;
some were struck with clubs, with hands, and with creepers. ||89||
Having been punished by the soldiers, they entreated the Lord,
placing blades of grass between their teeth and resting their heads upon the ground.
Distressed and with faltering hearts, they begged for forgiveness for their faults;
the compassionate Blessed One then instructed them so that they might desist from such faults. They all accepted his teaching and then made a solemn vow.
And from this day forward, we shall never again commit theft. (92)
"O Great King, show forbearance and release them from their bonds"—thus did the Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa address those who were entreating him in this manner. (93)
Having placed water in his hand, he made him take such an oath regarding the act of theft, saying: "Theft must certainly not be committed. (94)
Then, on the delightful and enchanting bank of the Dhṛtadhārā river,
the Blessed One released them and took back the stolen wealth.
Having taken all that gold, silver, jewels, garments, ornaments, and so forth which existed there, Sudhana went to where Tiṣya was staying.
Having approached him along with his assembly, Keśava, together with his cavalry,
gave all the wealth seized from the hands of the thieves to Sudhana.
Sudhana and his caravans rejoiced at the acquisition of wealth;
the king's officers gave all the gold and silver to the caravans. (98)
The soldiers of Hari gave back to each person those ornaments, garments, and so forth, as well as gems, pearls, and diamonds, which had belonged to them. 99.
And Sudhana gave them wealth as a reward; then the commander of the troops said, "There is a dharma that constitutes a reward. (2.73.10)
Always practice devotion to Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, who bestows liberation;
there is no reward here other than that.
Having heard this regarding Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, Sudhana fell into doubt:
"Has the Blessed One himself come here for the sake of protection?
Having thus doubted, he rose and indeed prostrated at his feet.
And others also indeed bowed down, following the example of those who had gone before them.
Accompanied by cavalrymen, the commander of the soldiers led the army across to the other side of the river and rendered it free from fear.
He indeed caused them to reach that beautiful garden of Śaṅkara;
then, at that moment, the soldiers of the commander-in-chief became invisible.
There were no horses, nor royal soldiers, nor likewise any commander of troops;
yet Sudhana and the people there experienced a supreme wonder. (106)
Then Sudhana quickly summoned that lord with all his strength, having indeed let out a great cry that resounded through the sky.
O Hari, O Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa-Svāmin, O upholder of compassion!
Protection has been granted by you in the forest; my fortune increases today because of you.
"I have a desire to see them, O Kṛṣṇa; grant me that vision once again," he said, as he rolled repeatedly upon the ground in a field of dust.
Dancing and clapping his hands, he rolled again in the dust,
having beheld the devotion of Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
Bālakṛṣṇa quickly became possessed of a divine form and great beauty, radiant with a splendor surpassing that of ten million suns, fires, moons, and stars. || 111 ||
Adorned with divine golden ornaments, wearing a divine crown and earrings,
clothed in divine garlands and garments, he was borne by a divine celestial chariot.
His limbs are proportioned to his form, he is resplendent with the Kaustubha and other jewels, and he is served by Śrī, Rādhā, Māṇikī, Pāravatī, Prabhā, and others. || 113 ||
Worshipped by Lalitā, Sujayā, and others who possess the virtues of Mañjulā and Haṃsā, Hari himself became directly visible in this manner. 1.14.
Beheld by Sudhana and the others, he said to them, "Stay here in this celestial chariot," and having placed them in the vimāna, in a mere moment—
Having shown him the Kuṅkumavāpikā field, the temple, his parents, the sage, and all the lakes and holy fords in a mere moment;
Having reached that garden by means of the celestial chariot, he vanished from sight;
Sudhana and the others attained happiness through the grace of the Supreme Lord.
Having attained divine vision and becoming devoted solely to divine worship,
they were all indeed rendered successful by Hari during the bright fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada.
On the eleventh day at midday, on the auspicious bank of the Dhṛtadhārā river,
the Lord then bestowed the supreme abode upon them after some time.
Thus, O Rādhikā, the protection of His devotees was performed by Śrī Hari;
by reading or hearing this, enjoyment and liberation shall certainly be attained.

Thus ends the seventy-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Protection from Thieves and the Divine Vision of the Lord, Granted to the Devotee named Sudhana Residing in Āmodanagara through the Yoga of the Great Sage Varcakāyani, Who Attained the State of Devotion to the Bhāgavata," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Queen of the Rāsa dance, during the festival of the glorious Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa;
in the ninth year, on the eighth lunar day, a gathering of the three worlds took place.
Likewise, the liberated ones and the incarnations, the liberated lords and the sovereign goddesses, the gods, the goddesses, the ancestors, and the sages [all attained liberation]. (2)
The Ārṣyas, those of the lineage of Kaśyapa, the Kāśyapyas, and likewise the Mānavas;
the Nāgas, Daityas and others, trees, creepers, beasts, and birds. || 3 ||
Those born of water and those born of land, the immobile and the mobile, the virtuous men and women, the arts, the rivers, and the oceans all arrived. || 4 ||
The seasons, the Vasus, the mountains, millions of sacred fords (tīrthas), the lords of the directions, kings, and the poor, the blind, the wretched, and others [all came]. || 5 ||
They approached Bālakṛṣṇa and honored him with great respect;
they offered blessings and placed gifts before Hari.
Lomaśa performed auspicious worship, as did the other sages;
and Gopālakṛṣṇaka offered hospitality to those who had arrived.
Kambharā gave sweet foods— eatables, snacks,
and things to be licked— as well as drinks, honey-mixtures, water, and betel nut.
A lustration ceremony was performed by everyone using one hundred wicks,
and the glorious Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Supreme Sovereign, was praised.
Having granted them this favor, and having rested and offered his blessings, he departed;
they, for their part, went by means of their own celestial chariots to their respective regions and to the furthest reaches of the quarters.
Now, listen to a marvel that occurred this evening after the lustration ceremony (nīrājana): what wonder has not happened today on the auspicious northern bank of the Gurjarī? 1.11.
There was a city named Kuśāmbā inhabited by people of the four castes,
where the great seer Kauśikāmba, a mighty sage, resided.
Devoted to meditation on the gods, devoted to sacrifice, and devoted to yogic practice,
he attained the power of moving through space and remained steadfast in the practice of breath-retention (kumbhaka).
He is devoted to the meditation upon the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa;
compassionate toward those who have come for refuge, he bestows the knowledge of liberation.
