Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and those of the lowest castes—
whosoever came to his own hermitage, he instructed them.
"Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Master; svāhā!"—thus he always bestows this mantra upon those who have received initiation as disciples. || 16 ||
Once, however, a low-born man named Tryaṣṭakāru, who was destitute and accompanied by his wife, arrived in the morning to visit the sage.
He was childless and afflicted by dropsy;
his wife, moreover, was overwhelmed with leprosy and deeply distressed.
Indeed, the great sage Kauśikāmbo constantly narrates the Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā in that assembly hall.
Having gone there, the outcaste sat down in the shade of a tree;
right there, he listened with devotion to the story together with his wife.
It was heard there in Saurāṣṭra that Anādikṛṣṇanarāyaṇa, the Lord of the supreme abode, the Master of all, is Śrī Puruṣottama. ||21||
The glorious delighter of the cowherds, the Supreme Brahman and the most excellent of persons, dwells in the form of a child in the sacred field of Aśvapaṭṭasara. ||2||
By the mere act of saluting him, and by the grasping of his name-mantra, diseases, wretchedness, poverty, as well as childlessness and other such conditions [are destroyed]. (23)
Everything indeed goes to dissolution, and good fortune increases;
for one who has come for refuge to Him, the attainment of desired objects occurs swiftly. 24.
Having heard this, when the assembly of listeners had departed at the conclusion of the discourse,
he remained beneath a banyan tree at the edge of the hermitage until midday.
He was indeed reflecting on those words: "How shall I question that sage?
For the sage, through his power of inner knowledge, had already understood the state of his mind.
The resident of Kauśāmbī,
having learned that an outcaste who was a believer, a devotee of Brahman, and desirous of knowledge had come to his hermitage, summoned him.
Sarvamitraka gave him food, water, fruits, and other offerings as he arrived at the sacred ford; he also offered a welcome and performed every act of hospitality. (28)
When he had rested, he questioned that outcaste: "O devotee, tell me from where you have come and how you arrived here; speak what is in your mind."
That devotee, skilled in the eighteen branches of knowledge, spoke while showing humility;
having prostrated like a staff, he said, "May there be victory for the great sage."
May there be security, well-being, and constant happiness for the Sage;
may he live long, O compassionate Knower of Hearts, O God of gods! (3.1)
"O Guru, virtuous ones such as you are the saviors here for sinners;
it is for the purpose of washing away my sins that I have come here. (32)
My task has become fruitful, and likewise my pilgrimage to the supreme sacred site;
through the direct vision of him whose nature is divine, I have attained the fulfillment of all duties.
Through this acquisition of the story, my birth has attained its fulfillment today;
by your grace, my fortune increases this very day. (34)
"I am a sinner and an outcaste, yet I have been delivered by you, O Guru," he said, and repeatedly placed the dust of the hermitage upon his head. (35)
Afterwards, he said to the sage: "If you have permission, I wish to ask about that which delights my mind through the hearing of stories. (36)
The sage said: "Ask with ease; I recognize your desire for liberation.
This is no outcaste at all; he is always pure, consisting of the quality of goodness (sattva). (37)
"And his body was born as that of an outcaste due to his past karma.
Having heard this, the outcaste said: "How did I become such? (38)
How is the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa to be attained?
And what divine duty must I perform here for the sake of achieving liberation? (39)
"For the sake of destroying my childlessness and for the sake of destroying my disease as well— O Lord, please tell me out of compassion what must be performed by me."
Thus questioned, the sage said: "Listen to your former deeds as an outcaste. In the past, you were a brahmin who resided in the seven cities and mountains. (41)
Her name was Devapriyā, and Dyumatī was then your wife;
there was also a temple of Viṣṇu there, containing both Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa.
There, you always performed worship like a servant;
your wife, meanwhile, prepared the kitchen for the purpose of the food offering. ||43||
While you were still impure and wearing soiled garments, and without having bathed for the sake of coolness, both you and your beloved performed my worship and touched me. (44)
Then, without straining the water, she performed the cooking and other rites; and without bathing or washing her clothes, she offered the food oblation. ||45||
She also offered me unfiltered water for my drink;
moreover, O lady, that woman of impure body constantly touched me. (46)
At that time, she did not consider matters such as her menstruation to be of great consequence;
thus, you two have long been consuming the sin born of impurity. (47)
After being in the world of Yama and in the Vaitaraṇī river, you then attained the state of cats;
thereafter, through the service of the gods, you have now come to dwell in the bodies of outcastes. 48.

And by the remainder of your merit, O sinless ones, you have attained the company of the virtuous; this is the result of service rendered in a previous time to your parents, to a deity, or to a guru. (49)
But in another birth, that merit stands ready to bring about one's welfare; everything offered in sacrifice, given as a gift, performed, or chanted over passes on to the next existence. (2.74.50)
Violence, affliction, injury, censure, deceit, trickery, cruelty, deception, and slaughter—all of these return in another birth. (51)
Merit, demerit, intrinsic nature, mental formations, latent impressions, the mind, the sense organs, aversion, and passion indeed pass over into another existence. (52)
Practice, recitation, devotion, service, benevolence toward others, virtuous conduct, observance of vows, and surrender—these indeed carry one over to another state of existence. (53)
Knowledge, discernment, faith, discrimination, worship of the gods, as well as blessings and curses, truly pass over into another existence. (54)
A devoted wife remains bound to her husband as a debt, and likewise a husband to his devoted wife;
even those who have become extreme enemies follow one another into future births. (55)
Fortune, accumulated karma, and the funeral libation offered afterwards—these, along with ancestral rites, austerity, and contentment, surely pass on to another existence. (56)
The service and devotion performed by you both, though mixed with impurity, have now yielded their fruit in the form of this human birth obtained at the end of time. (57)
Consequently, her birth was marked by the defect of impurity and she became an outcaste;
indeed, leprosy is the fruit of a woman's fault, such as menstruating during the ritual period.
Because you offered unstrained water to Mādhava for his drink, this dropsy has arisen within you, which shall remain for you a constant and most grievous suffering. (59)
The fruit of that unconditioned food offering which was presented by you to Hari shall abide with you in this world, and poverty shall pass you by.
From lack of faith, the fruit of evil arises, which is atheism (*nāstikya*);
and because of that atheism, you became devoid of the performance of *śrāddha* and other rites there.
Therefore, O best of the low-born, you remain childless here;
I have related your past history to you, so now listen to what follows here as well.
Even though you are an outcaste, since you perform service to the virtuous, undertake pilgrimages to sacred fords, listen to the sacred narratives, and practice devotional worship; ||63||
By the power of that merit, as well as by the blessings of the guru,
disease, childlessness, poverty, and likewise suffering [shall be removed].
Other afflictions as well will swiftly come to an end through the remembrance of the Lord of Śrī;
quickly take refuge in Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. (65)
The child Kṛṣṇa, the delight of the cowherds, shines in the field of Kuṅkumavāpī, on the bank of the Aśvasaras lake, in the house of Śrī Kambharā. 66.
He is the sustainer of all incarnations and the cause of all causes;
he is the controller of all lords and exists as the inner witness of all. ||67||
He is the bestower of the fruits of all actions and the giver of liberation;
he alone is capable of doing, not doing, or doing otherwise.
He possesses the power of knowledge, the power of action, and the power of cause and effect;
He is the Lord of the powers of Rādhā, Lakṣmī, Prabhā, Pāravatī, and Māṇikī.
The Lord of the Earth, who possesses the graceful gait of a swan adorned with beautiful qualities;
the Lord of Vṛndā, Tulasī, and Padmā; the Master of power, sovereignty, and prosperity.
The Lord of the virtuous, including Nanda, Nārada, Śaṅkara, Sanaka, and others;
the creator, the sustainer, and the destroyer of the worlds; the one who grants liberation to his devotees. ||71||
He is all desires, all tastes, and all fragrances; he is the all-seeing, the bliss of all, the protector of all, the lord of all, and the beloved of the virtuous woman.
The Lord of the virtuous, the friend of the holy, the foremost among renunciants, the teacher of teachers, the eternal supreme reality, the Supreme Brahman, the Ancient One. (73)
The gods devoted to celibacy, as well as renunciants and yogis who are self-controlled, perceive that [Self] through the cessation [of mental activity], for they are wise.
Worship that Lord Bālakṛṣṇa together with your wife every day—the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the glorious Lord and husband. (75)
The primordial form of Manu is indeed known as Pārameśvara;
appearing in age after age, it therefore assumes many forms.
He is the form of compassion and the form of ferocity; he is the form of wisdom, the son of the Bull (Vṛṣa);
he is the form of sacred knowledge, the form of royalty, the ruler, and the ascetic.
Worship that Supreme Person, whether in his manifested form, in his state of dissolution, as the individual soul abiding within, in his essential nature, or in a virtuous form. (78)
Whether as a partial form, a digit-form, or of the nature of possession (āveśa),
or as a manifestation of power (vibhūti), or as the full form— the Supreme Lord is entirely complete.
Whether it be an incarnation of Īśvara, or Viṣṇu, or Mahāviṣṇuka,
or the Imperishable (Akṣara), the Supreme Brahman, the most excellent among the perfect.
Thus, worship this Narayana of beginningless glory in these many ways together with your wife; thereafter, you shall attain liberation.
Come, come; take this water, that nectar of his feet.
Drink it, place it upon your head, and perform the sprinkling over your body. 82.
"May your sins, along with those of your wife, be swiftly destroyed here.
Having spoken thus, he gave her the auspicious water born from the grace of the worship. (83)

His wife, who was afflicted with leprosy, drank [the water] that had been drunk by Tryaṣṭakāru; and through the power of the sage’s self and a fragment of Kṛṣṇa’s grace, she was cured from drinking the water. (84)
Ascites, poverty, leprosy, and childlessness—these four great diseases departed from his body. (85)
Standing at his side, they wept and bowed to that Kauśikāmbaka, saying, "O Brahmin, where shall we go? Grant us our livelihood," thus entreating him.
The sage gave the water-born disease to the Earth, to the plantain tree, and to the bilva tree; he also assigned it in portions for those who drink undrinkable liquids.
He bestowed poverty upon the body of one who was full of craving, upon the greedy, upon one deprived of the bath of giving, upon the addicted, and upon the profligate.
To one who is greedily attached to improper unions, who causes the intermixture of castes, who hates the Dharma, and who commits theft, he granted the state of being afflicted with leprosy. (89)
To those who kill others' offspring and so forth, to those who cause abortions and the like, to those who have been cursed,
and to those who neglect the ancestral śrāddha rites, he ordained childlessness as their punishment.
Having been addressed thus, those four defects departed into such a vessel;
the outcaste became pure, free from disease, and accompanied by his wife. (9.1)
The sage gave him the purifying mantra of the Supreme Lord:
*Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya svāmine svāhā*. (92)
Then, performing his recitation, he remained in the hermitage like a servant;
he performed the sweeping and other duties as was appropriate, and attended to the garden. (93)
Having heard the discourse, his latent impressions of afflictions were completely destroyed;
this occurred during the month of Kārtika, in the lunar fortnight, on the eighth day of the dark half.
The sage indeed celebrated the birth festival of Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa;
there was a divine celestial chariot there, possessing a brilliance equal to a hundred suns.
Where Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa shines resplendent, there the divine attendants and women such as Rādhā and others have also arrived. (96)
They shone brilliantly; therefore, Hari suddenly descended.
The Blessed One himself accepted the great worship performed by the sages.
He gave him a graceful woman with eighteen marks of beauty;
then, having placed the sage in a celestial chariot, he went to Kuṅkumavāpikā.
And Hari, having attained invisibility within the celestial sphere, was beheld by the inhabitants of the sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpikā as he ascended in his aerial chariot. ||99||
He descended from that celestial chariot onto the bank of the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake;
having bathed there in the evening, he then performed the Tryaṣṭakā rite.
His wife also performed her bath in that very lake;
both their bodies fell away, and they became divine, four-armed forms.
At that time, they both became adorned with divine ornaments;
they possessed divine vision, divine movement, and were endowed with divine wisdom.
Quickly, having seen Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa, as well as their mother, their father,
and the sage Lomaśa, they performed extraordinary worship.
They both rejoiced as they traveled by that celestial chariot to Brahma-loka, the supreme abode;
and by the will of Kṛṣṇa, the sage remained there until the conclusion of the month of Kārtika.
Afterwards, by the command of Kṛṣṇa, he went to Kuśāmbī;
while instructing his devotees, he dwelt there for a hundred thousand years in the absence of [Kṛṣṇa].
Every year the sage celebrated the birth festival of Hari;
for what else could Śrī Narāyaṇa have done after going to that sacred ford on the bank of the Nandī river?
Having taken up the water of the river consecrated by the sages,
he bathes and returns in a moment upon a divine celestial chariot.
O Rādhikā, why does the Kauśikāmba holy ford shine even without a river, having arisen from the descent of Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa? 108.
Then the sage went to the supreme abode of the Supreme Lord,
which is beyond the imperishable and even higher than that, and is the refuge of the liberated souls.
Thus, O Rādhā, this wonder of Hari has been told to you;
by reading or hearing this, one shall attain supreme liberation.
The fruit of children, wealth, wives, and the like is liberation, which is most excellent; that has been attained by that devotee—what indeed is the use of children and the rest?

Thus ends the seventy-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of How an Outcaste, a Diseased Man Accompanied by His Wife, Attained the State of Liberation through Devotion to the Lord by means of the Yoga of the Sage Kauśika residing in the city of Kuśāmba on the bank of the Anadyā," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O Rādhikā, I shall likewise relate another marvel concerning Tapatī,
the daughter of the Sun, which occurred long ago on the banks of the Kāmapura river.
There was a Daitya named Santāpana, a lord of the hosts of Daityas;
endowed with great strength, he roamed upon the banks of the Tapatī.
That meat-eater made his dwelling on the Saptapatta mountain;
having gone again and again as far as the distant reaches of the eastern direction, he [seized] children.
Having gone as far as the source of the Tāpī river, they seize even the very fewest [people];
these Daityas, eaters of human flesh, feast together joyfully.
To the east of Bhūśāvālaya, on the bank of the Tāpī, there was a great school;
there lived the sage Hiraṇyakeśaka.
The best among those who know the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda became the most eminent of sages;
at that time, they took up residence in his hermitage, devoted to sacred knowledge and the life of celibate studentship.
There were thousands of Brahmins who were students of the Hiraṇyakeśī school,
and others as well, in the presence of the preceptor named Hiraṇyakeśa.
And those residents of the hermitage, students of the Veda, were going to bathe in the waters of the Tapatī at the time prescribed for Brahmanic rites; there, the Asura Santāpana [was present].
Well-concealed, he would approach and carry off the sons of the brahmins—
always two or five, sometimes six, or even nine or ten.
Among thousands of children, those who perish as infants are not known by those dwelling in the hermitages; indeed, it is not understood where they go at that time.
Where indeed there is no counting, there the exhaustion is not known;
thus, when a great deal of time had passed, five hundred [years] indeed went by.
The offspring of the Brāhmaṇas were brought to destruction by the Rākṣasas,
as were hundreds of others born of the Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra castes.
Thus, when the abundance of youths had come to an end, thereafter the number [of students] engaged in eating and study was perceived by people to have diminished. (13)
Indeed, on the banks of the Tāpī, fools constantly suffer decline;
they sink into the water and are inevitably carried off by crocodiles.
Having fallen into such doubt, they go forth together to bathe;
for those rākṣasas, having become boys, enter among the children.
Those who went far for the sake of purification were taken by them and departed;
they did not return, and then it was indeed realized by the people.
It was not the sea-monsters who carried them away, but rather the Rākṣasas;
moreover, there was exceeding grief for the children in the hermitage. (17)
Then the sage named Hiraṇyakeśa lamented in many ways:
"Alas! My children are lost—more than six hundred in number! (18)
Until this very day, it has not been known what the fate of the ancestors might be, nor what harsh words must be heard from those who are their kinsmen. (19)

"Alas! I have bestowed this meditative power (dhyāna) upon them, yet it has not reached its full limit of efficacy. How can they still live? For they must surely have been slain by the rākṣasas. (2.75.20)
"Alas! It is fate that destroys the weak; they must have been devoured.
Thinking thus, he placed both hands upon his head and wept piteously. (21)
Then other residents of that hermitage wept with great longing;
even those men of pure intellect became dejected within the hermitage.
The sage was born devoid of luster, and grief arose even among the trees;
even the flocks of beasts and birds wept, knowing of his destruction.
The deer and other wild animals did not graze on grass; the parrots did not take fruit; and even the ants did not seize grains from the parched earth.
The creeper did not reach the water, even though it had been placed in the fields;
the wind did not blow pleasantly, nor did the fire blaze within the sacrificial pit.
The peacocks did not utter their cries, and even the sages were like corpses;
the women in the hermitage became lusterless, like widows.
A great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose throughout the region of the hermitage:
"The Daityas, dwelling on the seven-peaked mountain, are carrying off the sons of the brahmins! (27)
They kill and devour us—alas, what misery!—impelled by Time;
oh, there is no protector for us, nor any slayer of these demons. (28)
"Does anyone remain without Kṛṣṇa, or where does Kṛṣṇa stay?
I have previously heard this indeed in the narration near Aśvapaṭṭasara. (29)
The Blessed One himself shines forth in the sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpikā;
this has been heard likewise from the mouth of the sage Kauśika.
Likewise, I have heard from other brahmins that Kṛṣṇa shines forth,
having become a human being in embodied form, the glorious son of the cowherds.
In the *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*, Hari himself is heard;
that Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the beginningless God, shines forth. 32.
"May he indeed provide protection for us from the great calamity of time," [they cried] as the hermitage of Hiraṇyakeśa was thus submerged in grief. (33)
Then the great seer Kauśikāmbaka arrived there,
having perceived through the power of yoga the cries of distress uttered by the sages.
On the full moon day of the month of Pauṣa, at the hermitage of Hiraṇyakeśa,
the sage was received with respect and honored with hospitable offerings such as the madhuparka.
Having been offered a seat, he sat down and asked about the cause of the weeping;
Hiraṇyakeśaka replied that it was because of the Rākṣasas and the young Brahmins.
O Sage, many who were devoted to the study of the Vedas and had gone to bathe on the banks of the Tāpī during the Brahma-muhūrta were seized by Rākṣasas.
Thus, it is known through investigation that six hundred were killed while ten thousand brahmins were indeed living in the preceptor's family. (38)
Thus a great calamity arose for the Asuras: "What shall we do? Where shall we go? What has happened? And where have they gone? (39)
"If such a decline of the Brahmin children proceeds, what will become of this stage of life? Alas, it will surely perish! (2.75.40)
O Yogin, if there exists any means here to prevent destruction and to serve as a cause for the attainment [of truth] by the ignorant, please tell us; we shall put it into practice. (41)
Having spoken thus, the sage Hiraṇyakeśaka ceased;
and Kauśikāmba, remembering Hari, O Rādhikā, spoke to him.
"Do not fall into despair, O Brahmin; I know everything through my yogic power.
Previously, even in my own hermitage, there was a great calamity caused by these very beings."
Indeed, the Rākṣasas and Daityas have been destroyed by me again and again;
yet they are born anew, and they do not depart from those directions.
Dwelling on the Seven-Striped Mountain, they indeed cause disturbances in your hermitage on the banks of the Tāpī, and they even devour human beings. (45)
Having understood that great catastrophe through the power of yoga alone, I remember the Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the God who is without beginning. 46.
We go for refuge to Him who dwells in the field of Kuṅkumavāpī during the spring season and resides in the hearts of all; He will provide protection. 47.
Safety and well-being are within his grasp and are now ours as well;
no one else besides the primordial Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa is capable of this. (48)
"To protect [them] from the cycle of suffering and from calamities in the ocean of existence"—having spoken thus and remembered Śrī Hari, the king of yogis [proceeded] by way of the sky. (49)
Having taken Hiraṇyakeśa with him, he went to Aśvasara,
[the two of them] as radiant as the sun and moon, like two luminous spheres of moonlight.
They descended from the path of the sky onto the edge of Lomaśa’s hermitage;
first bowing to Lomaśa, they then honored one another.
Having bathed in the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake, having gone to Kuṅkumavāpikā, having drunk its water, and having bowed to the deities; ||52||
Yayāti went to the presence of Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa in the temple where the Blessed Lord, the Supreme Ruler, higher than the highest, resides in splendor. (53)
Upon a golden elephant-throne, adorned with jewels and gems,
it was attended by holy fords, sages, gods, Lakṣmī, and others.
Consisting of divine splendor, adorned with divine ornaments, garlands, and garments,
it was worshipped with beautiful fragrances, its lotus-like face serene.
Having beheld Bālakṛṣṇa, the Supreme Brahman, they bowed down repeatedly; filled with tears and the weight of affection, those two gentle ones prostrated themselves like a staff. ||56||
Quickly honored by Hari, they were presented with the madhuparka offering;
having been given seats and questioned comfortably, they sat down near him.
When asked for the reason regarding the scripture, they spoke to the Supreme Lord:
"O protector of Brahmins, cows, the earth, virtuous men, virtuous women, and dharma! (58)
O refuge for the wretched, the distressed, the miserable, the helpless, and the supportless!
Many Brahmins have perished, as well as students and celibate seekers of knowledge. (59)
"Whatever comes into their hands is constantly carried off by the Rākṣasas; O Bālakṛṣṇa, Supreme Brahman, grant us protection from them. (2.75.60)
O Kṛṣṇa, the restoration to life of those who have died shall arise from Your resolve;
act in such a way that they may attain happiness and what is appropriate for them. 6.1
O Protector, inflict the supreme punishment upon the Rākṣasas!
You are the Sustainer, you are the Ordainer, and you are the Unconquerable One, O Supreme among Men. (62)
The bull, sacrifice, the Veda, knowledge, and the Brahmins;
the stages of life, the yogis, and the ascetics—all have their livelihood dependent upon you. (63)
Having heard this, the illustrious Bālakṛṣṇa remembered his own discus, Sudarśana,
as well as the god Śaṅkara, the goddess Pārvatī, and Vīrabhadra.
The science of reviving the dead, the cow of plenty that provides nourishment and bestows life,
the wish-fulfilling creeper, and an aerial chariot that moves through the sky and is eternally imperishable.
Lakṣmī, Siddhi, and Gaṇeśa quickly appeared before him;
they prostrated themselves like a staff before the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
The Lord said: "O Mahādeva, O Gaṇeśa, O Siddhi, O Pārvatī, O Lakṣmī, O Vidyā, O Kalpavallī, O Vīrabhadra, O Sudarśana! (67)
Many fools have been slain by the Rākṣasas such as Santāpana;
thousands of Rākṣasas dwell on Mount Saptapuṭṭaka. (68)
"Those [enemies] must be slain by you today, and the gods on earth (brāhmaṇas) must be protected;
for that purpose, we shall go there equipped with weapons. (69)
"May you all ascend this celestial chariot along with me.
Having been thus addressed, they ascended together with the Lord of Śrī.
Accompanied by Kauśikāmbe and joined by Hiraṇyakeśin,
that celestial chariot, as soon as it was meditated upon, went there through the air.
It performed a flight in the sky above the Seven-Clothed Mountain;
seeing that divine vehicle, the rākṣasas came out.
Armed and capable of traveling through the sky, they sought to seize the divine celestial chariot;
some were as large as mountains, while others had noses like mountain caves.
Some had thumbs as large as palm trees, some had ears like ponds;
some had eyes resembling lightning, and others likewise had nails like the sun.
Others had hair like bamboo, while others had faces like clouds or mist; they assumed many forms and wore various garbs, being masters of illusion.
Ten thousand inhabitants of mountain caves emerged;
seeing them, Śrī Hari quickly blew his most formidable conch shell.
He let out a terrifying roar that announced the battle;
meanwhile, they surrounded him on all sides and let out a loud, mocking laugh.
Ready to support the celestial chariot, they roared with powerful intoxication;
then the Blessed Lord spoke to his beloved, the virtuous Kalpavallī.
"Rouse powerful armies indeed for the sake of battle!
Having heard this, Kalpalatā [sent] ten thousand warriors.
Engaging in battle, the warriors suddenly broke through;
they all emerged from their celestial chariots and surrounded the vicinity of the Rākṣasa.
Indeed, a most terrible battle took place in the sky between the Kālpas and the Rākṣasas;
blinded by the fury of combat, they struck one another for the sake of victory. ||81||
With maces, swords, scimitars, javelins, and iron clubs;
likewise with pillars, trees, stones, pestles, spears, and darts. ||82||
They struck one another with iron shafts, spears, and crescent-headed arrows;
that battle of the Rākṣasas on earth had indeed broken out suddenly.
There, the heads of the rākṣasas fell upon the earth like rain;
the shattered limbs of the daityas fell to the ground like mountain peaks. 84.
Some were deprived of their hands, and others were bereft of their feet; some had their waists severed, while others were split in two, and still others had their shoulders cut off. (85)
Terrible Rākṣasas, slain by their vital breaths, fell upon the earth;
yet from their destroyed bodies, ever-new and fresh ones were born.
Having assembled in the sky, those of great strength fought;
thus indeed did the army of the Rākṣasas increase by the tens of millions.
Then, a terrifying and boundless [darkness] appeared in the sky;
and the Kalpa-warriors, seizing them again and again by the hair with their swords, [struck them]. (88)
Those who have crossed to the other side split them in two and sever them from their trunks;
they fall down headless, yet they rise up and continue to fight. (89)
At the front of the battle, their hands, feet, and other limbs were struck down by the millions by the Kalpalatās, yet they rose again and again in fury.
Flying up into the sky like living beings, they strike the soldiers of the aeon;
yet the warriors of Time, though being struck, do not perish, for they are divine consciousness itself.
Indeed, weapons could not cause any obstruction in them as they moved through the sky; then the Daityas created an illusion that produced mountains. 92.
Mountains appeared in the sky and fell from above with great force upon the celestial chariots, indeed for the purpose of destruction. ||93||
The celestial chariot was indeed divine, as were the gods and the goddesses;
they were all untouchable like the sky, and none were able to overcome them. (94)
Just as a celestial chariot remains steady in the sky while appearing like the sky itself,
so too do mountains fall upon the earth, even though they pervade it entirely.
Having seen it, the Daityas and Rākṣasas attained supreme amazement, saying:
"This celestial chariot is surely not fit to be seized or even destroyed. (96)
Thinking, "These gods and warriors are indeed not fit to be slain," those others, devoid of valor, fled from the battle. (97)
Slain by those iron arrows discharged by warriors skilled in the art of war, their bodies were pierced, their heads split open, and they were deprived of life. ||98||
For even those who have attained their end and have arisen in every way, others still fight out of delusion with inferior soldiers on all sides. (99)
The fire arising from the Kalpalatā reduced them entirely to ashes;
the army of Rākṣasas, consisting of tens of millions upon tens of millions, was turned to ash.
Indeed, five thousand of the root Rākṣasas have perished,
while only five thousand remain who continue to engage in battle.

Thus ends the seventy-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Efforts and Battle Undertaken by Śrī Hari for the Destruction of the Rākṣasas," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*, concerning the destruction of the six hundred boys staying at the hermitage of the sage Hiraṇyakeśin by the Rākṣasas.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Listen then, O Rādhā, to those remaining five thousand demons who were exceedingly powerful and swift.
They engaged in a battle in the sky using trees, stones, and mountains;
and those Rākṣasas then surrounded the celestial chariot on all sides.
Having entered the celestial chariot, they struck Śambhu, Gaṇapati, Sudarśana, and Vīrabhadra with javelins and other weapons.
Then the hero Gaṇeśa, as well as Sudarśana and Śiva,
repeatedly seized the Daityas who were inside the celestial chariot with their tridents.
Vīrabhadra struck down all those who were prostrating before him, and having cast the hosts of living Rākṣasas into his mouth, he chewed them up. || 5 ||
Those who were born from the dead, as well as those of illusory form— Hara reduced them all to ashes with the submarine fires produced by his great *māyā*.
Those four thousand Daityas were thus destroyed and turned to ash.
Then those thousand in number rushed through the path of the sky;
they entered the caves and other recesses of the mountain consisting of seven layers—
the warriors who had arisen from the Kalpa-creeper, following that same sequence.
They entered into caves and other places, and seized them from all sides;
[the enemy] cut Sudarśana, the great discus, at the region of the throat.
Agni, having observed them on all sides, completely reduced them to ashes.

Thus were the great Daityas, who dwelt upon the seven-peaked mountain, slain. Then the wives of the Daityas, accompanied by their children, being terrified, came for refuge to Hari, weeping, for the sake of protecting their lives.
The compassionate Śrī Hari then restrained his own Sudarśana discus from them and granted the gift of life to those deceased Brahmin children who had been devoured by the Rākṣasas.
Then they showed those bones cast into the pit—
belonging to six hundred twice-born men, as well as to a thousand women,
ten thousand men, and birds.
Having looked all around at that great pit extending for a *krośa*, he saw that no count of the bones of the animals and children could be found. (15)
He commanded Lakṣmī, who was present there as the wish-fulfilling creeper (kalpavallī),
and the sciences such as Sañjīvanī, in order to restore him to life.
Then Lakṣmī herself took the auspicious water from the feet of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa into her own imperishable jar made of gold.
Then, seated upon a swan, she departed from her celestial chariot carrying the jar of nectar;
having circled the entire pit, she repeatedly flew through the sky over the bones.
He performed a consecration over it with drops of nectar from that water;
the bones were indeed nourished and then became possessed of life.
Then the Kalpavallī, having taken the juices into an inexhaustible jar,
performed the consecration of that [jar] with drops of nectar-like essence.
By that [process], bodies were produced, endowed with flesh, marrow, and skin—namely, boys, men, women, as well as beasts and birds. ||21||
Indeed, for those embodied beings—more than a hundred thousand—who have died or been devoured, this *saṃjīvanī* lore itself shall restore them to life. (22)
Commanded, she fell in the form of rain upon all embodied beings;
thereafter, the drops of rain, being living entities, entered as conscious souls.
All those born from the bones in the pit arose from their terrible slumber,
possessing bodies according to their own natures and endowed with their respective years of age.
That men and women born from improper wombs, as well as those born from other sources, were endowed with life—this was a great marvel. (25)
All the beasts and birds went toward another forest, bowing again and again to the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. 26.
Then those men and women, boys and girls,
emerged from the pit by way of the uneven terrain and came outside.
Śrī Hari indeed descended his celestial chariot in that region;
he then gave them food and water that brought complete satisfaction.
He gave them garments as well as those things they required;
he bestowed upon them the remembrance of their birthplace, their village, and their kinsmen.
"For those in whom these qualities arise, that [state] indeed becomes manifest.
Thus spoke the Blessed One to the yogin Kauśāmbika. (2.76.30)
"O Sage, bestow upon me from these the supreme Vaiṣṇava mantra.
At his command, Kauśāmbika gave him the mantra of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
"Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord; svāhā!
At that time, Hiraṇyakeśa received that mantra from the sage.
Then the Blessed Lord, having gathered everyone together in the vast celestial chariot, spoke to Śaṅkara: "O Śambhu, these indeed are your own abodes."
"By this very celestial chariot, cause him to arrive in a mere moment.
Śambhu, becoming absorbed in meditation, beheld their respective abodes.
Having produced tens of lakhs of them, all of whom travel through various skies,
he brought them all to that house in a mere moment.
And they became householders, joyful from the acquisition of their own kin;
having heard of that supreme marvel, they thereafter became true Vaiṣṇavas.
The disciples of Hiraṇyakeśa were indeed brought to that hermitage;
thus the hermitage became happy, Vaiṣṇava, and filled with the Blessed One.
Then five thousand Rākṣasa maidens,
having beheld Bālakṛṣṇa and being infatuated by his beauty, chose him as their husband.
The Blessed One accepted those [girls] offered by their mothers;
the sage then recited a mantra over the children and wives of the Rākṣasas to protect them. ||39||
"Oṃ, salutations to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord; svāhā!
Then the Lord himself issued a command to the wives of the asuras.
"From this day forward, no one at all shall commit violence;
having cultivated this field, let them live and dwell here. (41)
"I shall indeed be the giver to you of water, food,
clothing, and wealth," having said this and granted them freedom from fear, he took the girls and entrusted them to him.
Having bathed there in the Tapatī and established that most excellent sacred site (tīrtha),
Śrī Hari proceeded toward the southern direction for the sake of visiting further holy places.
Then, after the Pūrṇā and Ambikā [tīrthas], he performed his ablutions;
thereafter, he indeed wandered over the Sahya mountain by means of his celestial chariot.
Having gone to Mahābaleśvara, he performed his ablutions in the Bhīmā;
then he bathed in the waters of the Tuṅgabhadrā on the Kṛṣṇā.
Having bathed in the ocean at Paścimaghaṭṭaka, he went to Śrīparvata;
then, having beheld Nīlagiri, he proceeded to Elādri.
Having bathed there even in a non-sacred pool, he went to the island of Siṃhala;
having touched the Puṣpanadī there, he performed his ablutions in the Kāverī. (47)
Then, having bathed in the Kaṭu river, he performed the ritual bath at Pannārī;
thereafter, having gone to Droṇācala, he performed the ritual bath in the Kṛṣṇā.
Having bathed in the Kolāra lake, he then went to the Godāvarī;
having bathed there in the Mañjirā, he then went to the Candrāvatī. ||49||
Then, having bathed in the Indrāvatī, he went to the Cilasaras;
then, having bathed in the Mahānadī, he proceeded to the Huhūgalā.
Then, having bathed in the Gaṅgā river, he went to the Brahmaputrā;
after bathing in the Kāñcanagaṅgā, he subsequently bathed in the Kuśī.
Then, having bathed in the Gaṇḍakī, he performed the cow-urine bath;
thereafter, having bathed in the Nandā, and after that in the Yamunā.
Then, having bathed at Cambalā, having bathed again at the Śambhara lake, having bathed in the Śatalājājala, and thereafter having bathed at Rāvi; ||53||
Then, having bathed at Cīnāpāya, he performed his ablutions at Jhela;
then, having bathed at Kābilā, he performed his ablutions at the Sindhu. ||54||
Then, having performed the *luṇī* bath and gone to the Nārāyaṇa lake,
he crossed over the Akhāta and performed the Gomatī bath.
Then, having bathed at Bhadrāvatī, Hari went to Aśvapaṭṭasara,
to the field of Kuṅkumavāpikā, to the hermitage of Lomaśa.
Having bowed to his preceptor, he then set down the celestial chariot;
having gone home, he prostrated before his parents, informed them of what had been done, and spoke to them.
He presented five thousand maidens and fed them, providing them with all necessary articles.
Mādhava established them in the hermitage of Lomaśa,
while Śaṅkara, Gaṇeśa, and Vīrabhadra established them in their own abode.
They departed for Sudarśana, and the celestial chariot vanished;
Lakṣmī and the others remained in their own temple within the sacred field of Śrī Hari.
Having enjoyed their devotion, Bālakṛṣṇa went to his own abode; there, served by all his devotees, he rested happily with Rādhā.
In the month of Māgha, during the dark fortnight on the fourth lunar day, the Supreme Lord,
having protected and restored to life [the world], established sacred fords upon the earth.
The Lord, the giver of life to all beings, came to his own field;
by reciting or hearing this, enjoyment and liberation shall certainly be attained. 63.

Thus ends the seventy-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Restoration to Life of the Disciples of Hiraṇyakeśa Who Were Killed by the Daitya Santāpana, the Destruction of the Daityas, and the Consecration of the Southern Rivers as Holy Tīrthas," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmīnārāyaṇīya-saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Listen, O Rādhā, to another marvel of the Supreme Soul,
who is the protector of devotees, of gods, of saints, of cows, and of those who perform their sacred duties.
In the city of Anaṅgapura, there was once a king named Bṛhadvarcas;
he was constantly devoted to the service of the gods and dedicated to the service of the virtuous.
Devoted to the performance of dharma, dedicated to sacrifices, long sessions, and burnt offerings,
he was perfected in theoretical and practical knowledge, and intent upon discourse and recitation.
He was one who helped the helpless, the wretched, and the poor, and was devoted to the practice of giving;
his wife was a chaste and virtuous woman, entirely dedicated to the service of the righteous.
Constantly devoted to the service of her husband and speaking only of the truth according to the Sāṃkhya philosophy,
she bore three hundred wise sons to that king.
There were also two hundred maidens, all devoted to Kṛṣṇa;
that king would go to the banks of the Tapatī on every festival day.
Having performed the ritual for bathing at the sacred ford (tīrtha), he bestows excellent gifts:
gold, silver, copper, wealth, goods, and rings.
Jewels such as pearls and the like, diamonds, corals and so forth, gems with the color of rubies, elephants, horses, cattle, and other such animals. || 8 ||
Goats and sheep, as well as mounts, vehicles, palanquins, carts, and likewise various celestial chariots and steam-powered carriages. || 9 ||
Vehicles with two wheels, three wheels, or even many wheels, as well as aerial vehicles— these are the most excellent gifts on a festival day.
Furthermore, after the worship, he gives gifts to the Brahmins as is appropriate;
and likewise during a solar eclipse in the month of Phālguna on the banks of the Tapatī.
The king, accompanied by many articles, went there for the purpose of bathing;
at that time, hundreds of thousands of people arrived at Tapatī to bathe as well.
The Brāhmaṇas were village-dwellers who traveled five yojanas [to attend functions]; they performed sacrificial rites and engaged in the teaching of the Vedas. || 13 ||
Those worthy recipients— devoted to austerity, knowledge, vows, and righteousness—
along with their women and children, all came to you for the purpose of bathing.
Having bathed during the solar eclipse, they performed recitations on the riverbank;
and the king began to bestow gifts upon the Brahmins.
He gave elephants, palatial mansions, fields, gardens, jewels,
pearls, diamonds, cows, milch-cows, and likewise buffaloes.
He gave horses, vehicles, food, mung beans, figurines of copper,
a figurine of iron made by himself, and garments of leather.
He gave gold, silver, coins, vehicles, and even mounts;
he gave female and male slaves, goats, sheep, villages, and houses as well.
And black garments, black grains, and black liquids,
as well as black necklaces set with gems and well-strung with black threads.
And he gave the gift of a black man accompanied by ten million coins, making the span of four cubits the limit for the flow [of the water].
Out of greed, those best of brahmins accepted that supreme gift—a great donation laden with weight and endowed with more than a hundred thousand coins. ||21||
Then the Brahmins, numbering one thousand, each took for themselves one elephant,
one horse, one cow, and two bulls.
One milch buffalo, one house for residence, one field, one garden, a gem, and black pearls. (23)
A diamond, a single vehicle, mung beans, a statuette of copper, an iron statuette of one's own, black leather, and likewise a garment. (24)
A black thread, one of black complexion, a male servant, a female servant, a black goat, a black necklace, the city of Madra, and collyrium—these are all called *kṛṣṇā*. (25)
The king gave one hundred thousand black beans, a hundred thousand gold pieces,
and a hundred thousand silver pieces to each individual brahmin.
A thousand greedy brāhmaṇas indeed seized it;
those gods upon earth then bathed again at Tapatī when the sun was purified.
Extremely delighted by the acquisition of the gift and with minds exceedingly serene, they bathed in the water with great affection until they emerged outside. (28)
Thus, due to the fault of that gift, they became black and deformed;
for a fault is incurred by accepting a gift from one who is black-complexioned.
O Rādhikā, listen as I tell you by what means and for what reason there would be fault; indeed, for a king, there is the blemish of injustice in giving an elephant in battle.
Whatever may be sinful, evil, deceitful, or a great transgression—such as the destruction of women and children who are free from fault. (3.1)
The killing of charioteers, animals, draft beasts, and those performing the work of messengers—all that is purified by the gift of an elephant. (32)
This sin shall fall upon the head of the one who accepted the gift of the elephant;
however, for the king who gave the horse, a great merit was produced by the horse-riders.
In battle, the fault lies with the horse for turning back from slaying [the enemy] and so forth;
the fruit belongs to the king, while the recipient of the gift becomes the partaker of the fault. (34)

Furthermore, whatever killing of bulls and other animals occurs in battle and the like, as well as the castration of bulls and other such creatures that may take place during the administration of a kingdom; [these require expiation]. (35)
That sin of the king shall perish and pass upon those who receive the gift;
by the gift of two bulls, those who died in battle as ghosts [are liberated]. (36)
Those who are not heroes, who flee from the rear, and who die having come upon [the enemy] by force—the sin arising from the slaughter of such persons is destroyed for the king once again. (37)
He remains standing right there among those who accepted the two bulls,
until the queen's gift was bestowed and she was lowered onto the noose and the stake.
Whatever sin arises for a king from unjust punishment is incurred when nooses are cast by those wearing black garments who act as executioners. (39)
The sin of the king arising from that killing is destroyed,
and it instead falls upon the one who undertakes the acceptance of the gift of the queen.
And by the gift of houses, there arises for the king merit from his kingdom, from the people on earth, and from such things as palaces constructed by artisans, villages, roads, and so forth. (41)
All the sin of killing incalculable living beings is averted;
O Seizer of Planets, all that becomes attached to you at that very moment. (42)
By the granting of fields and gardens, the infinite sin arising from agriculture—which would otherwise accrue to the king from his subjects—is averted. (43)
That [sin] occurs when one seizes fields, gardens, parks, Brahmins, and so forth;
as does that which arises from digging mines and the like by means of the gift of a black gem. (44)
Whatever sin of governance may accrue to the king, all that shall be averted;
however, O wearer of the jewel, every sin of those who dig for gems shall prevail.
Whatever merit lies in the giving of pearls, in the destruction of sea creatures, in the production of pearls, and in the production of salt; ||46||
Likewise, the sin arising from the killing of creatures such as fish, from the operation of machines, and from the sea and so forth, ceases for the king. (47)
O pearl-catcher, everything becomes exceedingly unbearable;
yet, by the gift of a diamond, whatever sin arises from poison is [removed]. (48)

And the sin arising from poison, medicine, and the like; that produced by the heat of summer; that born from poisonous winds; and that which results in the destruction of living beings—[all these he destroys]. (49)
That [karma] of the king ceases, while that which arises from the slaughter of living beings by means of vehicles and the wheels of those vehicles proceeds against the one who seized them. (2.77.50)
The evil of the king perishes when the chariot-seizer departs;
and by the gift of a masha, whatever affliction from the planets the king may suffer throughout the year [is removed]. //5.1//
The sin arising from the failure to protect the poor, the helpless, and the wretched—
which otherwise falls upon a king— is averted by him, and it passes instead to the one who accepts the māṣa coin.
But by the gift and bestowal of that copper statuette, O King, such sin arising from association with a courtesan is likewise removed. (53)
For one who seizes a wooden doll (puttalī), an inauspicious planetary conjunction occurs that brings terrible suffering, resulting from the gift of an iron doll to the king. 54.
Whatever sin arises from the subjects in the kingdom, born of the sixfold [sources], that accrues to the king; it becomes as if lost upon one who seizes a doll. (55)
Excessive rain, drought, locusts, rats, parrots, and earthquakes—these are declared to be the six calamities. (56)
By the gift of a black antelope skin, the great sin of hunting is averted for the king, and it accrues to the one who receives the skin. (57)
By the gift of black garments, the great sin of the king arising from the slaughter of countless living beings produced by the cloth-weaving machine is destroyed. (58)
Indeed, the sin of one who grasps at the sky perishes,
and by the offering of a black thread, the sin arising from the rope in the kingdom is likewise removed.

Furthermore, whatever sin known as the slaughter of living beings is committed for the sake of wool, for the sake of woolen cloth, or for the sake of silk, that sin shall belong to the king within his realm. (2.77.60)
O Rādhā, by the gift of the thread, all that [misfortune] of the king is averted;
O holder of the thread, when it is given to a Brahmin or others, all that [merit] is fully set in motion.
By the gift of a black man, whatever sin arises from the killing of a child,
as well as that arising from the killing of a fetus, and likewise that arising from a useless killing [is purified].
Whatever evil belongs to the king, all that ceases;
but in the case of the slave and the one who receives the gift, all that proceeds.

By the gift of a maidservant to Kṛṣṇa, may whatever sin has arisen from the killing of a maiden, as well as that arising from the killing of a woman, the killing of a widow, and so forth, be [purified]. (64)
The sin arising from attachment to another's wife is averted for the king;
however, that same sin fully accrues to the Brahmin and others who take a female slave.
Whatever sin arises from the slaughter of goats in the kingdom, whatever sin arises from the eating of goat-flesh,
and whatever sin arises from the consumption of sheep— all that is removed for the king.
And for one who has committed a secret, cruel sin arising from the killing of a Śāli rice plant, [the rite] comes into effect by the offering of a black garland. 67.
And that [misfortune] ceases when the king's garland-bearer departs;
likewise, wealth arises among the subjects through the distribution of black coins and other such gifts. (68)
Whatever sin may arise from the treasury, whatever may arise from the hand [of the king], the evil produced by forcible seizures, and that which is born from the infliction of punishment; ||69||
That [debt] of the king ceases when it goes to one who takes the substance;
however, that which was caused by Saturn for the king is removed by the gift of a black māṣa bean.
The entire suffering transfers to her who accepts that bean;
through the gift of gold, there is the propitiation of the ancestors and the favor of the gods. (71)
By the gift of silver, Lakṣmī becomes composed of pure essence (sattva);
such is the fruit of giving for a king, whereas sin and suffering fall upon the unworthy recipient.
The king departs together with the objects [received], and he turns away from his faults;
however, the recipient is afflicted and becomes deprived of splendor. //73//
If, however, he is not rich in merit, incapable of meditating on Brahman,
and devoid of the power of virtue, he will soon be tormented by sins.
Those with deficient merit are born dark-complexioned from the influence of the planets alone;
or they may be deformed or devoid of knowledge due to the fault of a curse, as is the case with certain people. (75)
Or they are born with disordered minds, afflicted by chronic diseases, with broken limbs, with ruined fortunes, with shattered virility, and likewise with ruined households. (76)
Those who are deprived of happiness and filled with suffering are born as a result of [past] acts of giving and gathering;
therefore, one who wishes to protect their merit should not accept a gift that is more terrible than that. (77)
The hand that stretches out skillfully to receive a gift is the very same that reaches out to bestow merit; it is likewise the hand that extends to take up evil. (78)
Therefore, one who is a treasury of merit should accept gifts;
for the sake of destroying the faults of giving, he should perform acts such as dedicating [the gift] to the deities. //79//
Otherwise, the consumer of sin goes again to a place of experiencing suffering— the realm of Yama, the embodied state, and the womb— from which there is indeed no swift deliverance.
Thus, O Rādhikā, the brāhmaṇas eagerly accepted the gifts;
in an instant, they became dark-complexioned and ugly, like outcastes. (81)
They were born like outcasts, pale and devoid of luster, as if their bodies were made of soot or as if they had been consumed by fire. (82)
Thus born, even after bathing in the Tāpī for a mere moment, this fruit of a terrible gift became indeed difficult to ward off at that time. (83)
But the merit from bathing after an eclipse was not able to save the Brahmins who were exponents of the Veda when they were in the presence of a terrible act of accepting gifts. 84.
Then, having seen those endowed with such evil, the great seer Suratāyana—whose dwelling was made of sandalwood trees and who was an ascetic of extreme austerity—[spoke]. (85)

He was a devotee of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, an exceedingly great Vaiṣṇava, a perfected soul (siddha) endowed with sovereign powers, and one solely devoted to knowledge and meditation. ||86||
He who previously remained established in meditative absorption for a thousand years, over whom tree trunks grew as anthills at their bases; (87)
As the mud was washed away by the force of the water caused by excessive rain, the great sage emerged from his concealment. ||88||
He whose body was bound at the foot of a sandalwood tree remained right there at that root, yet he emerged from his meditative absorption.
Having reached that tree, he dwelt there with his mind fixed on the Blessed One;
and the Blessed One, assuming a physical form, beheld him through his meditative concentration.
Now, in this world, the glorious son of Gopāla resides near Aśvapaṭṭasara, in the sacred field of Kukumavāpī. 91.
The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa Svāmī, the supreme among men, the Lord of Śrī, the Beloved of Kamalā, and the Lord of Haṃsārādhā. 92.
He is the Lord of the virtues of Māṇikī, Pārvatī, Mañjulā, and Prabhāsā;
he is the beloved of the infinite liberated goddesses and of hundreds of millions of billions of virtuous women.
This Bālakṛṣṇa, the son of Kambharāśrī, shines forth;
having known him eternally, one indeed goes every morning for the sake of beholding him. (94)
By means of that samādhi, in a mere moment, he attains Candana;
he worships the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa eternally. ||95||
The compassionate Śrī Hari imparted his own mantra to him:
"Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya svāmine svāhā. (96)
And he remained muttering mantras beneath a sandalwood tree on the riverbank;
at that time, those thousand Brāhmaṇas were seen by him.
Those who had accepted the gift of Kṛṣṇā became possessed of defilement;
filled with grief, they deliberated among themselves for the sake of destroying that fault. ||98||
Having approached that Great Lord of Yoga, the illustrious Suratāyana, they all went to him for refuge and then became tearful-eyed. (99)
Seeking only the pacification of their faults, they entreated him in his presence;
bowing down like a staff, they sat before him as the great ṛṣi meditated upon Śrī Hari.
Then he bestowed knowledge that grants the pacification of sins and provides a basis for spiritual practice,
which leads to the attainment of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.

Thus ends the seventy-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Yoga of the Sage Suratāyana with the Thousand Brahmins who had Attained the Form of Black Monkeys after Accepting Terrible Gifts from King Bṛhadvarcas on the Banks of the Tāpī," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O Rādhā, I shall relate to you that very knowledge which the illustrious Yogīndra, Surataiyan, bestowed upon the Brāhmaṇas.
O Rādhā, that which was previously given by me to the practitioner of the path of sexual union, that very same thing I declare here to you, since it brings about the welfare of the worlds. || 2 ||
The brahminical sage Surataiyana said: "Listen, O brāhmaṇas!
The Lord of the lords of gods is the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa Svāmī. (3)
He who is indeed the manifest Supreme Brahman, the Supreme Self, and the Supreme Lord, shines in the region of Saurāṣṭra within the sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpī.
Endowed with all powers, the destroyer of the sins of the sinful—
seek refuge in that supreme Lord, the Parameśāna, as your highest resort.
Worship that Śrī Kṛṣṇa with unwavering devotion;
he is certainly attained through meditation, the yoga of action, devotion, and knowledge.
O twice-born ones, go for refuge to the illustrious Supreme Lord, who is to be attained;
whatever action consists of charity and dharma, and whatever pertains to the system of castes and stages of life.
O twice-born ones, that supreme Dharma consisting of the knowledge of Brahman which I proclaimed in the past leads to liberation when accompanied by inner knowledge.
When everything is offered and cast into me, the agent is never tainted;
through righteousness, knowledge, and devotion as a servant, one shall manifest the Supreme Brahman.
Having renounced all attachments, they have gone to Him alone for refuge;
established in the divine yoga, they worship Him always with devotion.
Completely liberated from all attachments, peaceful, self-controlled, and free from envy; they are without pride, having surrendered everything to Hari, and exist solely for His sake. || 11 ||
With their minds fixed on Him, their very lives absorbed in Him, and delighting in the discourse of His knowledge,
women and men— whether children or youths— have made all their possessions over to Hari.
The Supreme Lord Hari himself is indeed the remover of their bonds;
they have completely shaken off darkness through that singular knowledge and have become one with Him. 13.
Those who are ever-blissful are not born again in this worldly existence;
O twice-born ones, may you go for refuge to Him through action, mind, and speech.
The yogi must always protect both childhood and the state of being in the womb;
for in either childhood or the womb, there is no latent impression, desire, or thirst. (15)
Striving, thirst, and passion do not exist at all like branches;
likewise, one should remain steadfast in youth as well as in old age. (16)
Just as one who is fast asleep does not attain the fruit of cognition even though he is conscious,
so too, O Brahmins, one should always remain in knowledge, just like a sage.
Just as one whose mind is directed elsewhere has no perception of what is grasped by the senses,
so too the mental activity of a Brahmin whose mind is fixed on Kṛṣṇa leads to liberation.
Just as a child, having taken some earth from the ground, smears it [on his body], does not feel much sorrow or joy regarding that very thing; || 19 ||
Likewise, the wise man, having cast all things—the objects of action and activity—into that Divine Being like a lump of clay, [should remain composed]. (2.78.20)
Even when experiencing [the results], one should neither grieve nor rejoice, nor find fault therein;
for at that time, the experience of those fruits does not proceed with excessive intensity.
In the state of non-experience there is no state of being an enjoyer, and no defilement arises;
that which is the stainlessness of the eternally pure is indeed liberation. (22)
The objects, the body, as well as the senses and the mind, should be understood as distinct; then the Self withdraws from them. (23)
The agent indeed goes to bondage if he becomes attached to those [objects];
one who is unattached does not become attached at all, nor does he go to bondage. ||24||
Just as objects existing in their material form remain far away, they do not exist when they are in contact [with the senses], provided the self does not become attached to them here. (25)
Even though flowers situated in a garden possess honey for the six-legged bee, they do not become attached [to him], nor do they go to the place of that honey. ||26||
In that same way, all those sense-objects do not envelop the knower of the self; therefore, the person (puruṣa) should certainly not be bound.
Having constructed a house with spikes, the Kīṭī dwells in that house;
having dragged the house along, she indeed goes wherever she pleases.
"Before long, both the house and the body will surely go to destruction.
Thinking thus, that ignorant woman led him to her home upon the earth. (29)
Just as that [wind] moves everywhere while bound, so too is the bondage of the body;
the ignorant, being bound, wander about, carrying the body from place to place. (2.78.30)
The suffering and pleasure born thereof arise at every moment;
however, yogis who know its power [subdue] the body through self-restraint.
For even when they depart from one place, they proceed to another world;
indeed, no firm bondage of the body exists for them anywhere. (32)
And having returned there, they may dwell according to their desire;
like birds dwelling upon the branches of a tree for a mere night's stay.
For them, there is no binding by branches; they depart even after leaving that [tree]. Likewise, their dwelling in the body is like that of a bird or one who is liberated.
One should not be born for the sake of bondage, like the sloughed skin of a serpent;
the sense organs always remain dependent upon the body in every way. (35)
Those with mental engagement lead to bondage; those without mental engagement lead to liberation.
The mind should be applied only as long as there is a purpose. (36)
When this which is purposeless must indeed be withdrawn, then the senses would no longer be bound, nor would they grant bondage. (37)
Even when the mind is withdrawn and firmly bound, it does not truly become a binder;
that intellect which is the witness likewise takes refuge in its master and in the Self. (38)
A virtuous woman should never take recourse to her son, nor even to her mind, nor to her sense organs which are like those of a son, nor to servants, nor to sensual objects at any time. (39)
This very absence of reflection therein is the purity of the intellect;
thus, when the stream is obstructed, the Self shines forth by itself. (2.78.40)
Without wound, without blemish, and without stain, he is free from evil;
unattached to the state of fruits, unconditioned, and liberated, he does not partake in suffering.
Where the mind is free from dualities, there the intellect is indeed stainless;
where the mistress of the house is stainless, there the master of the house rejoices.
Always content with his own possessions, he does not desire the wealth of others;
for what reason, then, would sorrow and delusion arise in him? (43)
For the yogi who is always satisfied with the Self and satisfied with bliss,
a state of ultimate contentment arises spontaneously by its very nature.
Therefore, having realized in every way the fullness of bliss belonging to the Supreme Lord, he moves, stays, and rejoices eternally like one who is liberated. (45)
He becomes perfectly attached to that alone and does not desire attachment to anything else; his mental fluctuations are blunted, and his intellect has become characterized by contentment. (46)
For him whose wife is a giver of happiness, liberation resides in his very home;
for him whose wife is a giver of suffering, hell indeed resides in his home. (47)
Therefore, that household-like intellect must be made serene here by all means of purification, through which the King becomes gracious. 48.
One should strive for the Supreme Self in order to attain eternal grace—that state wherein neither action exists, nor does the relationship between the enjoyer and the enjoyed. (49)
Through that yoga, it shall be so, and he will become free from all dread;
submerged in the lake of eternal bliss, what indeed is the use of mud for him?
There was indeed an excellent Brahmin seer named Śvetāśvatara;
his disciple was the grandson of Pṛthu and the son of Śikhaṇḍin. (51)
One named Suśīla, who had relied upon detachment since childhood and was a knower of dharma, resolved to take up renunciation through the power of his good fortune. (52)
Remaining on the slopes of the Himalayas, he indeed performs service to his guru,
staying where the Lord Nara-Nārāyaṇa resides in Dharmavana.
There flows the most meritorious, pure river named Mandākinī,
endowed with groves of lotuses and water-lilies, and frequented by perfected beings and holy men.
Having bathed in her waters and offered libations to the ancestors and the gods,
he worshipped Nārāyaṇa, who is joined with Nara, with beautiful flowers.
Having bowed to his preceptor named Śvetāśvatara, he said at one time:
"Oh, what great fortune is mine! My ascetic penances have borne fruit. (56)
O Lord, you who are like a true guru and a manifest omniscient one to me—grant me knowledge, devotion, dispassion, and renunciation. (57)
Thus addressed, that divine Guru bestowed upon him the supreme renunciation (*sannyāsa*), which is the complete dedication of all actions unto the beginningless Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa. (58)
Then, having offered his complete self-surrender through the nature of *prapatti*,
he was instructed in the great mantra of Kṛṣṇa for the attainment of all perfections.
Oṃ, salutation to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord; Svāhā!
This [mantra] pacifies all sins, is the essence of all things, and bestows supreme liberation. 2.78.60.
He also bestowed upon King Suśīla knowledge and total self-surrender, saying:
"Nārāyaṇa resides in me, and I abide in Nārāyaṇa. (6.1)
"I am Nārāyaṇa," and "I alone am Nārāyaṇa"—
thus the Guru first imparted the knowledge of the abiding state of Brahman.
Then he said: "You are not the body; the body does not possess the form of the senses.
Neither are you the senses, nor the mind, nor the mental faculty, nor even the Great Principle (mahat). (63)
The principle of Mahat is not the Self, nor is the Self ever of the nature of Māyā;
Māyā is not the essential nature of the Self, for your Self is that of the Supreme Lord.
Nārāyaṇa is indeed your self, and you are considered to be Nārāyaṇa;
for Nārāyaṇa is untainted and free from the bonds of karma.
Eternal, pure, enlightened, liberated, and free from illusion—
realizing your own nature to be thus, worship the glorious Supreme Lord.
Perform the morning bath upon your own body, making the Supreme Lord the performer;
clothe your own body, making the Supreme Lord the performer. ||67||
Have ornaments, sandalwood paste, and other offerings prepared for the Supreme Lord, and perform the waving of lights and other rites upon your own body as a representation of Him. 68.
O Supreme Lord, manifest that embodied one within your own body as the sacrificial offering, food, drink, betel-leaf, and fragrant scent.
Offer sandals, shoes, and an umbrella upon your own body; with devotion, surrender all vehicles and conveyances to him, the Supreme Self. (2.78.70)
Bestow upon my body the power for seeing, hearing, touching, tasting, and so forth, as well as for desiring and feeling affection. (71)
Offer to him his lying down, his walking, his livelihood, his awakening, as well as his thinking, his laughing, his weeping, and his agitation. (72)
Offer to the Divine within the body: resting, refining, stumbling, exhilarating, sporting, and the practice of meditation. 73.
Offer to the Lord of Śrī within the body: yawning, melting away, suffering, happiness, purposeful action, reflection, discernment, breathing, and devotion. (74)
Thus, offer that entire collection of actions—whether material, subtle, or consisting of mere atoms; whether arising from the instruments of action or arising from mental cultivation—to that Kṛṣṇa.
Offer this entire collection arising from yourself to the Supreme Lord;
this very renunciation is what is designated by the term "liberation. (76)
And you must not enjoy the fruit of that [action], for it has been offered to Hari.
For one who conducts themselves in this way, all their actions become divine. (77)
Desire, anger, greed, thirst, attachment, pleasure, injury, compassion, cruelty, and impurity—since these are [transcended] through divine dedication to Hari. (78)
This very renunciation is indeed the ultimate Vaiṣṇava path;
neither sin nor merit situated therein obstructs him. (79)
Thus, being of virtuous character, he performed penance at Badarī, worshipping the Lord, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. (2.78.80)
Upon the exhaustion of his lifespan, he, freed from all impurity, attained the supreme abode;
he became four-armed, possessing the divine form of Nārāyaṇa. (81)
In that very same way, O twice-born ones, worship this Nārāyaṇa on the bank of the Tāpī with a Vaiṣṇava sacrifice, so that you may be freed from all affliction.
"Thus, this Blessed One, being pleased, will destroy even [your] sin.
Having been addressed in this way, those brahmins performed a most Vaiṣṇava sacrifice.
There, on the bank of the Tapati river, thick with sandalwood trees,
on the seventh day at the conclusion of the fire sacrifice, a child appeared.
The primordial Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa appeared in person and said to them, "I am pleased; choose a boon, O brāhmaṇas! (85)
Having beheld Mukteśa, who was as radiant as ten million suns, the brahmins bowed to him,
offered hymns of praise, and accepted the gift that destroys all impurities.
"Grant us Your supreme abode and a vision as radiant as a horse- or camel-colored light;
grant us eternal service," they prayed, and then observed silence.
"So be it," said Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the laughing Hari;
and he remembered the two physicians, the sons of Aśvinī, who are the lords who bestow beauty.
And suddenly two sons of the Sun arrived there, possessing beautiful complexions, endowed with youth, and adorned with ornaments and crowns. (89)
Bearing the conch, discus, mace, and lotus, and adorned with the Kaustubha gem, those two,
served by Śrī and Ramā, bowed down to Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
They both paid obeisance to Śrī Hari and said, "Please instruct us; what shall we do here?
Then the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, burdened with compassion, spoke.
"O Brahmins, these have become defiled by accepting gifts from a wicked person;
therefore, provide such a remedy so that they may indeed become free from stain. (92)
Upon hearing this, the two sons of Aśvinī bowed to the Supreme Lord and said:
"O Blessed One, you alone are the master capable of accomplishing everything. (93)
O Supreme Lord, you exist as one who is to be worshipped through your incarnations;
within your resolve lies the state of the great creation, maintenance, and dissolution.
Nevertheless, out of compassion, please cause us to perform service and remember us;
for there is no other superior medicine here than the nectar of your feet. 95.
"Their ugliness and impurities shall be dissolved by fire," having said this, he then [gave] his own water-pot to the two children of Aśvinī.
Having moistened the lotus feet of Śrī Hari with the water of the Tāpī river and washed them,
one should place that water in another pitcher and add the juice of medicinal herbs to it.
They sprinkled only a very small amount and caused the twice-born to drink;
they also sprinkled them, and meanwhile those twice-born [fell]. 98.
From drinking it, they quickly became free from sin and radiant;
their dark complexion vanished, and they then became golden-hued. (99)
By that sprinkling, however, all their deformity was destroyed in an instant;
they became possessed of forms as before, endowed with the power of Brahman.
"With divine countenances like gods, they became exceedingly beautiful," thus Hari instantly consumed their sin.
Having stayed for a moment on the bank of the Tāpī, Hari established a divine holy site (tīrtha);
that most auspicious tīrtha is where these brahmins were purified.
There arose the famous and supreme Aśvinīkumāra-tīrtha, where Śrī Hari indeed stayed, bathed, and performed austerities in the waters.
And that Haritīrtha was born there, which destroys all sins;
likewise, other gods came there to behold it in the water.
And many sacred bathing places (tīrthas) arose there;
indeed, by bathing there, drinking the water, and likewise casting the bones of the deceased, [one attains merit].
Even a man of great sin shall attain liberation by performing this;
furthermore, O Brahmins, by performing the worship of Hari and the worship of the two Kumāras. (106)
They prostrated themselves there on the ground and repeatedly begged for forgiveness;
having then placed the two children of Aśvinī in a state free from blemish, they departed.
Having duly installed Śrī Hari, they indeed went to their homes, O Rādhikā;
thus, in the month of Phālguna, he performed the protection of the brāhmaṇas there.
From reading and hearing this, the destruction of sin will certainly occur;
even by merely hearing it, a human being shall obtain the merit born from bathing in the Tapatī.
The two gods, Aśvinī and Bālaka, departed from there and vanished;
then Śrī Hari arrived at the sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpī in an instant.

Thus ends the seventy-eighth chapter, titled "The Instruction Given by the Sage Suratāyana, the Manifestation of the Lord, the Arrival of the Aśvinīkumāras, the Purification of the Brahmins, and the Clarification of Sannyāsa," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Listen, O Rādhikā; even though the brāhmaṇas had returned to their own homes, they continued to contemplate that Lord with wonder day and night.
That vision which was difficult to obtain has now become easily attained;
therefore, beginning from this very moment, you shall [proceed] by means of the yoga that is the path to supreme bliss.
They behold the Supreme Self, Bālakṛṣṇa, at the very edge of their vision;
they see him constantly in dreams, and it does not cease even in deep sleep.
For once the divine form of the Lord of Ramā has been seen,
it is placed forever within the unfathomable heart and does not depart.
Just as that which has been made firm by long-term practice manifests, this very compassion of his is a manifestation even without practice. (5)
Then, when the auspicious time of the Cāturmāsya arrived, the Brahmins eagerly came to bathe in the waters of the Tāpī at that sacred ford.
They all gathered together and remembered the glorious Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, their own protector and the destroyer of great sins.
Having assembled on the eleventh day of the month of Devaśayana, the brahmins indeed performed the chanting of the names of Nārāyaṇa.
O Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, O Inner Self, O Hari, O Supreme Brahman, O Lord of Śrī, O Master, O Lord of all incarnations, O Bālakṛṣṇa, O son of Gopālakṛṣṇa and Kambharā! || 9 ||

O Lord of Rādhā, Lord of Lakṣmī, Lord of Ramā, Master of Padmā; O Beloved of Prabhā and Lord of Tulasī; O Lord of Vṛndā, Lord of Pārvatī, Lord of Śrī, Beloved of the World, and Lord of Māṇikī! || 2.79.10 ||
O Lord of Haṃsā, O Lord of Mañjulikā, O Lord of Śrī Dayā, O Lord of Śrī Lalitā, O Lord!
O Lord of Ūrjā, O Lord of Śrī Saguṇā, O Lord of Kastūrī, O Lord of Śānti, O Lord of Jayā! || 1 1 ||
Victory to You, the Imperishable, the Supreme Person! Victory to the Lord of the Liberated, the Most Excellent of All!
Victory to the Supreme Lord, the Highest Self! Victory to the Witness, the Best among the Incarnations! 12.
Victory, O Blessed One! Victory, O delighter in the Self! Victory, O one beyond qualities! Victory, O truly desireless one!
O Śrī Bhagavān, destroyer of impurities, always protect your devotees. 13.
Thus they performed their chanting on the southern bank of the Taptī; absorbed in that, they became one with the sounds of the clapping cymbals.
At that moment, a light appeared there, and in its center was a supreme celestial chariot;
therein shone the glorious Bālakṛṣṇa, attended by his devotees.
Together with their sixteen attendants, they all beheld that Supreme Lord,
whose excellent chest shone with rows of necklaces set with precious gems.
Adorned with a crown set with gold, jewels, and gems, he shone with two golden earrings shaped like sea-monsters (makaras). || 17 ||
It was beautifully adorned at its edges with black hair that was fine, tawny, and shimmering;
on its broad forehead, it bore a saffron tilaka mark with the brilliance of fire.
Adorned with two frowning brows that have made their dwelling upon ten million desires, and graced by large eyes whose red corners are as flickering as fish; || 19 ||
Adorned with a halo of radiant light from his gentle smile, and exceedingly beautified by a nose like a full-blown sesame flower; 2.79.20.
Extremely beautiful with its right cheek marked by a black spot, it shone with a multitude of globes illuminated by the radiance of its flowing luster. ||21||
His beard and mustache have fine golden hairs with beautiful lines;
his upper lip is drawn upward in the shape of a bowstring. ||22||
Charming with lower lips beautifully reddened by the abundance of sweet nectar,
and graced with the beauty of a chin and jaw adorned with very fine black spots.
It was uniquely beautiful with a long line shining upon his broad forehead,
and it was exceedingly radiant with a pair of ears as lovely as two circular earrings.
His eyes are a treasure-trove of love, more resplendent than the sun and moon;
his supreme face is the abode of the glory of all beauty and tranquility. (25)
Adorned by two bees resting upon the station of ten million sovereign powers, his teeth—white as jasmine buds and like foam—were utterly enchanting. (26)
His heart was captivated by the corners of his face, which were enriched with broad smiles;
and on his cheeks, he revealed maternal affection through subtle dimples. ||27||
His white eye perceives all other lights that have been eclipsed;
Śambhu resides in his throat, and the conch is situated at the nape of his neck.
On whose chest the Kaustubha gem rests, accompanied by a forest garland, and on whose middle of the throat a black spot shines brilliantly; (29)
