In the hollow of the throat (kaṇṭhakūpa), the wheel of wind (vāyucakra) is situated, supported by the year; it is upon the fold of the throat that the imperishable Brahman shines forth. 2.79.30.
In his heart, he is indeed devoid of worldly qualities; like a *campaka* flower upon a hide, he wears a necklace;
and like a bee, he is known as Śrīnivāsa, for the auspicious clockwise curl (*dakṣāvarta*) shines upon him.
Hari’s two auspicious shoulders are firm like the shoulders of a tiger;
Hari’s two beautiful arms are thick, soft, and resemble the coils of a serpent. (32)
Covered by a cloth as bright as moonlight, his two eyes captivated the heart;
on his belly were two tufts of hair, dark and tawny-hued, thick with fine down.
Upon seeing the devotee of the Seer, affection and devotion are produced;
his two beautiful arms are golden-hued, and the space between his arms has the luster of campaka flowers. (34)
The marks of the conch, discus, mace, and lotus on the upper arms, as well as three lines on the forearms and auspicious marks on the right hand, are favorable. (35)
The fish, trident, iron arrow, banner, svastika, and bow—these beautiful line-marks are indeed present as the eight wheels. (36)
A vajra that destroys enemies is also present;
these two shine brilliantly upon the palms, which have the luster of lotuses. (37)
Her nails shine like moons positioned on a full-moon night; her abdomen is adorned with three folds, and her navel is a treasure-trove of wisdom. (38)
Her hips were enriched with the likeness of the goddess Śrī, and her lingam was the abode of Kāma;
her auspicious waist shone on all sides like a garland of stars. (39)
Her hips were radiant and beautiful, delighting the minds of her friends;
the roots of her thighs were white in color, pervaded by splendor, and exceedingly lovely.
A girdle made of gold is worn around the waist;
rings are for the fingers, and chains are for binding the arms. (41)
In the bracelets, the golden ornaments, on the forearms and the parts of the upper arms,
and in the middle of the thighs, the splendor radiant with the Brahman of syllables proceeds forth.
On the left thigh, below the root, is the mark of Kailaka;
and above the thigh is the mark of Lakṣmī, which is white in color.
The palms of his hands are as broad as a palm-leaf and beautiful, wherein even yogis become bewildered;
Hari’s knees are lovely, rounded, charming, and auspicious. (44)
The shanks were lovely, with the luster of lotuses and adorned with lines of hair;
the thighs were beautiful and cool, possessing the splendor of the root of a plantain tree. (45)
The feet are shaped like tortoises, resembling the interior of a lotus,
endowed with the sixteen marks and the like, and likewise adorned with upward-pointing lines.
The crest, the wish-fulfilling vine, the wheel, and the vehicle as well— ||46||
Saudha, Vṛṣabha, Hastī, Turaga, and likewise Candraka. ||47||
His lotus-feet were marked with the signs of the *garuḍa* and the *haṃsa*, and the upper parts of his feet were beautified by a row of golden hair. (48)
Her pair of arms reached down to her knees, and her toes were long;
possessing a gentle form yet pervaded by splendor, she was indeed divine and auspicious.
Releasing such a gentle smile, the Blessed Lord Hari descended from his celestial chariot into the midst of the brahmins.
The brahmins bowed at his feet and praised the Supreme Lord;
all became exceedingly joyful in their hearts from the mere sight of him.
Then the great sage known as Suratāyana, having approached Śrī Hari from a sandalwood tree, worshipped him with devotion. ||52||
"Oh, may we have such good fortune again that we behold Hari in our home!
Having said this, she then performed a prostration at the feet of Śrī Hari.
All the brahmins, filled with devotion, indeed worshipped him repeatedly;
they were all those who had accomplished their purpose and were experts in the rites of sacred fords.
Standing in his presence, they entreated Śrī Hari most fervently:
"O Lord, grant us a vision of the sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpī. (55)
Thus praised at the Aśvinīkumāra-tīrtha, Hari spoke:
"Having bathed again with me and having ascended the celestial chariot," (56)
"May you, my servants, come together to my field.
Then they bathed with Hari in the Aśvinī-kumāra [tirtha]. (57)
And the foremost among those who travel by way of the celestial path alighted upon that aerial chariot; Hari, having taken them all along with him, traveled indeed by way of the sky.
Accompanied by five thousand brahmins and others, he arrived within a single day,
having crossed the Akhāta and reached the mouth of the Śatruñjita river.
Having bathed them there, he proceeded to Gopanāthaka;
and having caused [a shrine] to be built at that sacred site, he went to Mūlasvarṇapurī.
Having emerged from that sacred bathing place (tīrtha), they then went to Somanātha;
having bathed at the confluence of the Bhadrā and the ocean, they proceeded to Camatkārapura.
Having established a sacred bathing place on the Devikā river, those dwelling in the forest region earnestly entreated [him] to purify that woodland.
The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, having accepted their requests,
[appeared] on the fifth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Śrāvaṇa in the year of Cāndra, on a Sunday.
The Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa himself went to the forest grove,
having purified all his devotees and fed them with the sacred prasāda.
And he gave them the supreme instruction that carries one across the ocean of worldly existence:
"Listen! My devotees are those who offer everything to me without exception."
Indeed, there is never an end to the experience of sins, merits, and so forth;
yet I am Nārāyaṇa for those who offer everything unto me. (66)
I myself perform the purification and lead them to my own abode—whether they be men, women, boys, girls, or even eunuchs. (67)
By even a slight portion of my grace, they quickly become liberated;
therefore, let them worship me with devotion and construct a beautiful temple here.
"Let them install my image and worship me constantly;
for I am the deliverer of you who seek refuge."
Having spoken thus, having pointed out the ground, and having bestowed the nectar of his feet,
he likewise destroyed the diseases of worldly existence as well as the ailments of the sick.
Having purified the forest region with auspicious blessings for men and women,
and having established them in devotion to Himself, He gave them the water from His feet.
Having granted his vision and touch, and having accepted the service of his feet,
he accepted the performed worship and ascended the celestial chariot.
And in a mere moment he went to the auspicious city of Saurāṣṭra,
where dwells the illustrious Lord Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa.
In his own magnificent and vast palace of great splendor, the youthful Hari, possessing a complexion white as milk and overflowing with smiles, shines resplendent as his own sovereign lord. (74)
The Lord, appearing in the form of an image, is to be worshipped and adored by the people of Saurāṣṭra, as well as by yogis, men, and women. (75)
In the Mahālaya temple, which was resplendent with divine golden jars,
he touched his own form as it stood there and addressed his beloved.
Having beheld Lakṣmī, the mother of the worlds, Dharma, Bhakti, Sūrya, Śeṣa, Praśāya, Dattātreya, Śiva, and Brahmā; ||77||
Then Hari, having embraced Hanudāsa and Gaṇadāsa,
departed through the air in a radiant celestial chariot in an instant.
Having established the Kuṃkumavāpikā field and the Aśvapaṭṭa lake there in the sandalwood grove, Mādhava installed a celestial chariot.
He showed them the beautiful hermitage of Lomaśa, situated on the grounds of the celestial chariot,
and had those pilgrims bathe in the waters of the Aśvatīrtha lake.
Having caused the beautiful vision of his preceptor Lomaśa to appear,
he also beheld ten million, a hundred billion, and a hundred trillion Kṛṣṇas.
Having had it constructed, Kṛṣṇa went to his own excellent palace and showed it to his mother, the great and virtuous Śrī Kambharā.
Likewise, the Lord showed his father, the divine and illustrious Gopālakṛṣṇa,
a seven-storied palace and an elephant-throne.
Having offered them hospitality, providing them with food and lodging,
they all then rested after that reception.
In that vast celestial chariot, they spent the night full of eager anticipation;
then, having performed the ritual bath at dawn, they paid homage to the Supreme Lord.
They gave those hundred maidens to Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Soul;
and Keśava protected them in the hermitage of Lomaśa.
Then those followers of other paths, having been honored by him, went to their own homes together with the glorious Nārāyaṇa in a celestial chariot.
Having brought them to those regions, Hari returned again on the sixth day to the divine field of Kuṅkumavāpikā, the abode of the imperishable Lord.
Having thus granted his vision and caused him to perform the pilgrimage, the Compassionate One, by means of a celestial chariot, led him to his own lands. (89)
O Rādhā, the Blessed One has brought about the complete fulfillment of the minds of His devotees;
therefore, the Anādi Puruṣottama is Himself attainable through grace alone. 2.79.90.
Not by vows, nor by gifts, nor by the performance of fire-offerings;
but rather by love for the goal, devotion to the Name, and acts of self-surrender. ||91||
But for those who worship me, I myself remain engaged in their service;
and just as I always abide in your service, O Rādhikā, so do I remain.
O beautiful lady, in Goloka there is no other servant like you for me;
for in the service of a servant, the beloved becomes like a slave. (93)
Likewise, the illustrious Lord also, for the sake of his servants, suddenly becomes a servant himself, ever intent on protecting them. (94)
Worship performed with the body is superior to all other forms of worship;
after that comes mental service, and the worship consisting of material substances is superior even to that. (95)

For service to Rādhikā is incomparable, since it consists of the offering of one's entire being; it should be understood as that which brings about her grace and is practiced with complete conformity to her will. (96)
The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa is pleased with the one who gives;
He indeed bestows the supreme abode which grants eternal bliss at the end. 97.
Wealth, grain, a son, a beloved wife, a husband who increases the family, health, prosperity, fortune, a daughter, a cow, a buffalo, and elephants—[may these be granted]. (98)
He gives horses, female slaves, offspring, male servants, grandsons, and even heavenly realms;
O Rādhā, thus has this wonder of Hari been described to you. 99.
From reading this, from hearing it, from causing others to hear it, and even from remembering it, there shall be enjoyment and liberation in the end; one shall attain the feet of the Blessed One.

Thus ends the seventy-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Arrival of the Five Thousand Brahmins, headed by Suratāyana, at the Kuṅkumavāpī Tīrtha and the Auspicious Instruction," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Rādhā, to this supreme marvel of Hari:
in ancient times, devotees were delivered from suffering on the bank of the Bhīmā river.
In the southern city known as Pauṇḍraka, there was a king named Baleśavarman, a bull among Kṣatriyas and lord of Khaṇḍadharā.
He was a supreme devotee of Viṣṇu, skilled in the practice of yoga,
a disciple of Kapila, and possessed of discernment through the knowledge of Sāṃkhya.
Not far from the bank of the Bhīmā, on a mountain at Kapilāśrama,
he established a meeting for the practice of yoga among the Sāṃkhya practitioners and yogins.
Formerly, in that hermitage, the divine Kapila, who was accomplished in the yoga of sacred fords,
remained right there in that beautiful and auspicious forest for ten years.
Then, on that most auspicious mountain slope—tranquil, solitary, and stainless—that Baleshavarman, having attended upon the sage Kapila, [attained his goal]. (6)
He attained both Sāṃkhya and Yoga, as well as the perfection of supreme sovereignty, the supernatural powers,
invisibility, the ability to assume many forms, birth, and so forth.
Kapila, having thus bestowed such sovereignty, departed for another place;
meanwhile, the king used to come daily to that hermitage to behold him.
Having meditated for a moment on that state and repeatedly recollected the Guru,
he should worship this very seat and then the supreme practitioners of yoga.
Having bowed even to the virtuous ones dwelling in the forest, he goes to his own home;
thus does he, devoted to Sāṃkhya and Yoga, act constantly.
Then once, in order to perform a vow, the king went to the hermitage of Śrī Kapila accompanied by his wife; he resided outside during the month of Kārttika.
Taking refuge in the shade of a tree, he lay upon the ground and subsisted on fruit;
his beloved wife remained devoted to celibacy and observed the kṛcchra vow.
He was devoted to the duty of hospitality, established a continuous distribution of food,
was constantly intent on performing fire-sacrifices, and daily fed a thousand destitute people.
Devoted to the dharma of giving and intent upon the vows at the end of the four-month period, many virtuous ones were there—perfected beings, those striving for perfection, and yogis. (14)
Travelers and forest-dwellers always arrive at his sacred vow;
he gives food to those who seek food and likewise clothing to those who seek clothing.
To those seeking alms-bowls, he gave bowls; to those seeking wealth, he gave wealth;
whatever was desired by whichever petitioner, that very thing he gave to him. (16)
The Lord of Bali indeed grants [his request] and bestows a sacrificial fee upon him who,
in the month of Kārtika, observes the excellent vow and whatever he may pray for.
That indeed should be bestowed upon him, and the word "no" must certainly not be uttered.
There, the king had a son who was twelve years old and exceedingly tender.
The queen, named Śīlavatī, strictly protects her devotion to her husband;
and her son, named Puṇḍraka, indeed practices devotion to Brahmā. || 19 ||
Indeed, three of them became devoted to the service of the virtuous in the worlds;
and there was a great Vaiṣṇava maharṣi named Tārakāyana.
Right there dwells the yogi, devoted to yoga and meditation; a divine ascetic who moves through the air and can assume any form at will. ||21||
He remains as the locus of the eight supernatural powers (siddhis), free from all desires; that sage, having recognized Kuṅkumavāpikā through the yoga of meditation, [attained his goal].
Having gone to the hermitage of Lomaśa, which is directly inhabited by the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, and having beheld Śrī Kṛṣṇa, [he remained there].
And having received from Śrīpati Mādhava the mantra that bestows liberation:
"Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya svāmine svāhā" (Om, salutation to the illustrious Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the Lord; svāhā). ||24||
Remaining within his own hermitage on the inner ground, he constantly recited prayers;
every morning, he would always travel through the sky to the Aśvapaṭṭa lake.
Having beheld Hari, this great seer named Tārakāyana returned once more from the sky to the hermitage on earth.
Then the king descended and went quickly for the sake of a vision;
becoming humble, he questioned the sage who removes the distress of those who bow before him. (27)
"O Sage, where do you always go at dawn, if you are a performer of auspicious deeds? If there is no obstacle, that which I desire to know must be told. (28)
Association with the virtuous is considered always to bestow heaven and likewise liberation; it is held to be the destroyer of suffering and the dispeller of calamities. (29)
Wherever there is the dwelling of yogis, lords, holy men, and the virtuous, there indeed is Nārāyaṇa within the range of perception.
The feet of the virtuous are to be worshipped; the water from their feet is to be drunk as nectar;
their gracious food is to be eaten; and the speech issuing from their mouths is to be accepted. (3.1)
Service to the virtuous is service to Hari; association with the virtuous is indeed association with Hari;
the body of the virtuous is the body of Hari; for the virtuous are truly the very forms of Hari. (32)

The virtuous should always be meditated upon in meditation; the virtuous should always be held within the heart; the virtuous should be served with all kinds of gifts; for in the virtuous, Lord Hari shines forth. (33)
The vision of the virtuous is the vision of Hari; indeed, the touch of the virtuous is the touch of Hari.
Embracing the virtuous is embracing Kṛṣṇa, which destroys all sins. (34)
The dust from the feet of the virtuous should be borne upon the head, the heart, and the face;
the water from the feet of the virtuous should be borne upon the mouth, the head, and the body.
The favor of the virtuous should be sought through one's own person, home, children, and other possessions.
And by the bestowal of wealth and prosperity, and by the total surrender of one's own self in every way. ||36||
The body is impermanent in every respect; even when protected, it perishes.
Therefore, one should always perform service and accept the favor of the virtuous. (37)

Wherever there is a preference for a particular sense organ and its object, and where one's own intensity is greatest, service should indeed be rendered to that sense organ for the satisfaction of both. (38)
The Supreme Self shines manifest within the hearts of the virtuous;
therefore, all auspicious actions arising from the senses and body belong to the good. (39)
The actions of the virtuous are divine, their bodies are always divine, their collection of sense organs is divine, and indeed, the constituent elements of the virtuous are divine. (2.80.40)
The deliberation of the virtuous is divine, and the intellect of the virtuous is always divine;
even their dreaming, sleeping, and pleasure are indeed divine. (41)
When [the Lord] exists, an effect produced by illusion does not exist at all;
likewise, when He exists, merit and demerit reside in the Supreme Lord. (42)
Always free from impurity, divine, and bestowing eternal bliss,
it is a mine of merits for the virtuous, wherein there is indeed not even a trace of sin.
Such a divine one you are, O Sage Tārakāyana;
just as Viṣṇu is, so indeed are you the savior from the ocean of worldly existence. 44.
"Tell them of our meeting; indeed, our fortune is great.
Having spoken thus, the king stood waiting for the words of the sage.
Tārakāyana said to him: "Listen, O King, Lord of Bala!
He who is celebrated in the world as the Blessed One, Puruṣottama. (46)
And the Supreme Brahman exists in the Veda as the Lord who assumes all incarnations;
he who resides in the supreme abode is [present] in Saurāṣṭra in the house of Kambharā. ||47||
In the sacred field of Aśvapaṭṭasara, on the grounds of Kuṅkumavāpikā, that glorious young Gopāla shines resplendent upon the Lomaśa mountain. 48.

There, embodied beings exist who are beloved of Brahmā, numbering in the millions, billions, trillions, and quadrillions; they are all powers (śaktis) and are as numerous as ten million holy fords (tīrthas). 49.
In the human, plant, animal, and elemental creations, wherever the beloved of Brahmā, who long for Brahman, abide; 2.80.50.
The liberated ones, as well as those who have attained their own abodes and dwell in various realms, remain there as yogis, hidden and with their physical forms transformed.
I go daily to see that Lord, the Supreme Self;
having worshipped that God in the morning, I drink from the lotus of His feet.
"Having visited the sacred fords, I shall then come to my seat.
Thus addressed, the king said, "When will I have the sight of him? (53)
"O Brahmin, tell me, 'Will it happen? O virtuous one, have mercy!
The sage said, "Take this mantra and become devoted to its recitation. (54)
"Oṃ, obeisances to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Master; svāhā!
Having thus given this mantra, O Rādhikā, and a garland of tulasī, [he said: 55.
Having bestowed the nectar of Hari’s feet, which is to be served by the great Vaiṣṇavas, the sage departed for his own abode; thereafter, the king, the queen, and their son [followed].
Established in meditation upon that supreme mantra, they remembered Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Svāminārāyaṇa, who is without beginning. ||57||
Then Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa, indeed, in order to test the king,
arrived in the guise of a guest at midday after his meal.
On the seventh day, he was dark-complexioned, wearing an iron bangle,
with red eyes, clad only in a loincloth, like a forest-dweller.
But the king, having looked at him, said: "Come here, O forest-dweller;
take food and water, and then depart as you please. (2.80.60)
Jaṅgamī said: "I never eat what is left over, nor do I eat food cooked by another; how then can you give me food? (6.1)
"I am indeed a forest-dweller, and my food is of the nature of darkness (tāmasa);
however, I never eat that which originates from other living beings. (62)
If you are true to your promise and do not utter the word "no," then give me food, O King, which shall be dear to me and bring me peace. (63)
The king said: "I am able to give you whatever food you desire; tell me what you wish for here, and I shall grant it, for there is nothing that I cannot give. (64)
"Whether it be sattvic, rājasic, or even tāmasic—that which pleases you here [I shall give].
If you do not desire that which arises from another, then tell me what arises from yourself; I shall grant it to you. (65)
Whatever I am able to give, that I shall surely give; this is my vow regarding Kārttikeya.
O forest-dweller, tell me what is to be given if it is obtainable, and I shall give it to you.
The hunter said: "Listen, O King; though I am a meat-eater living in the forest, even during the month of Kārtika, this very vow was observed by me."
"Indeed, I must eat the flesh of the king's son, unasked;
if the king himself should give it, let it be the heart alone and nothing else. (68)
"Such is my vow: blood alone must be drunk as it resides in the heart;
not even water may be drunk, for this is my tamasic vow. (69)
"O King, I do not beg anything from you; the vow I have proclaimed must not be requested, for making a request causes the breaking of the vow. (2.80.70)
Having spoken thus and looking back toward that place from the forest, he then took steps to depart, acting in such a way that he did not appear to be one who had made a formal request.
The queen, having merely looked at the ascetic, said: "Stay, remain steady;
I shall perform the washing of the feet for this guest who is the Supreme Self. (72)
"In another moment, this king will give you your desired food.
Accept this woolen seat and remain here in tranquility. (73)
The woman said: "I have a vow that I must always remain standing during the month of Kārttika;
however, it may be fulfilled if the naked thigh of a young maiden is obtained. (74)
"I must sit upon her thigh, and never otherwise.
Then the queen said to her daughter, "Be seated, daughter, upon this auspicious throne. (75)
There were three daughters of that king, known by the names Kṛṣṇā, Bhīmā, and Tuṅgabhadrā; all three were present there.
Kṛṣṇā, having cast off her garment, gave him her thigh as he desired;
she sat there upon the ground and became absorbed in meditation.
The son said to his father, "O King, quickly pierce my heart and give it to the Supreme Lord as a guest; thus it may lead to liberation. (78)
In an instant, however, the king split his son’s chest from shoulder to hip with his sword, and at that very moment, blood flowed forth.
Then the second daughter, Bhīmā, also, being without her garment,
placed some forest meat there and gave her own thigh to the forest-dweller.
And she ate and drank blood;
meanwhile, Tuṅgabhadrikā, naked, repeatedly massaged the hands and thighs of the forest-dweller.
Then those forest-dwellers repeatedly massaged his face, rubbed his feet with their thighs,
and likewise performed a full-body massage.
Then, as soon as the mendicant rose and attempted to depart, the king spoke these auspicious words for the sake of a gift: ||83||
The woman said: "I have a vow that whenever meat has been eaten, its mother must indeed be accepted as the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), and never anything else. (84)
As soon as she had said, "O forest-dweller," the queen quickly appeared and said, "Here I am, your servant; accept me as your fee, O Lord. (85)
Having made that forest empty of trees, he remained beneath a tree;
for a moment, he sported in the sky without even touching the earth. ||86||
Seeing her held up in the sky, the king then reflected:
"Oh, what supreme good fortune for my son and likewise for his wife! (87)
The great fortune of these maidens is that we have been employed for the sake of Hari;
whether one be a forest-dweller, a forest-recluse, a wanderer in the woods, or even a non-wanderer in the woods. (88)
The inner self, Hari, is satisfied with my impermanent body and so forth;
if [the body] perishes for the sake of another, it becomes fruitful, though it is impermanent. (89)
What greater fortune than this could there be, by which Mādhava is truly satisfied?
I am blessed; I have accomplished my purpose; everything I have done has become fruitful. ||2.80.90||
Having arrived here, the forest-dweller spoke for the sake of my vow:
"The place for the letter 'na' has not indeed appeared in my mouth. (91)
Whether it be my wife, my daughters, or my son—victory be mine!
Blessed are those daughters, and blessed also is my dear son. (92)
My queen here is also blessed; they did not accept [the food] at this vow.
I have been delivered by my family; truly, my family is my salvation. (93)
Having personally accepted this auspicious [food] for the sake of honoring a guest, today, by virtue of my vow, dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa have come into my hand. (94)
"Today the world has been conquered by me through the grace of this guest.
Thinking thus, he became joyful in mind, considering himself truly blessed. (95)
At that moment, the forest, including the trees and other elements, remained as it was even while having enjoyed the Queen;
[the Lord], having abandoned his state as a forest-dweller, stood together with Śrī Lakṣmī Rādhikā. 96.
Then he was seen with two arms, accompanied by Mahālakṣmī;
Mahāviṣṇu held an umbrella over him, and Viṣṇu held a vessel of food for him.
There, devouring the food, the Supreme Lord appeared, endowed with the splendor of ten million Cupids and blazing like ten million suns. (98)
Praised by infinite liberated souls, honored by gods and ancestors, worshipped by lords and incarnations, and adorned with ornaments. (99)
He was seen shining in the supreme abode of the divine ether, served by ten million Brahmā-priyas and worshipped by the Supreme Imperishable.
Seated upon an elephant-throne in the midst of a divine celestial chariot,
he was divine, appearing sixteen years of age, smiling and manifesting love.
He gazed all around at his devotees— the king, his beloved virtuous wife,
and the three maidens— repeatedly enchanting their minds with his intense emotion.
There, in the presence of Śrī Hari, the prince stood,
divine, adorned with celestial ornaments, auspicious, and possessing his former form.
Laughing, Puṇḍraka suddenly approached Hari from the side toward his own father, appearing as pure as one who has just awakened from sleep.
The gods, liberated and empowered, showered a rain of flowers;
the king, with devotion, praised the Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.

Thus ends the eightieth chapter, titled "The Description of King Baleśvara’s Status as a Supreme Bhāgavata through his Union with Lord Kapila in the Second Tretā Cycle of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā; the Arrival of Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa in the Form of a Forest-Dweller for the Purpose of Testing [the King] during the Kārtika Vow through his Union with the Great Sage Tārakāyana; and the King’s Vision of the Lord by Offering His Sons, Daughter, Wife, and Family. || 80 ||
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Listen, O Rādhikā, to how King Baleśvara, with great devotion, praised Mādhava, the Lord of Śrī and the Supreme Lord.
You are the God of gods, eternally the Supreme Self; you abide in the imperishable, supreme abode;
you indeed are the Supreme Brahman and the Supreme Lord.
He who is to be praised alone by the liberated is indeed to be praised by the imperishable. || 2 ||
You are worthy of worship and service because you are the one who descends;
you are to be saluted by all the lords and propitiated by the hosts intent upon your service. (3)
He is worthy of worship even by those whose forms are Viṣṇu, as well as by Maheśa, Brahmā, and other eminent deities;
likewise, he is to be honored by the gods, the ancestors, the guardians of the quarters, human beings, and the perfected ones (siddhas).
He is praised by the Daityas, the foremost Dānavas, the Asuras, and the Rākṣasas;
he is meditated upon by the Nāgas, the Cāraṇas, and all moving living beings; he is protected by the sword and resides within the heart of the sword. 5.
You became Vāmana; you became Narasiṃha; you became Nārāyaṇa; you became the son of Vṛṣa.
You are indeed Viṣṇu in form, and you likewise appeared in the forms of a swan, a fish, and a tortoise.
You are the form of the Boar, you are the form of Kapila; you became the form of Datta and the wielder of the axe;
you are the form of the Sacrifice, the form of Rāma, the form of Kumāra, and the form of the horse-headed one.
Though you possess the form of a celestial sage, you are also the very form of a king; though you are the form of Vyāsa, you are the Lord of Rādhikā.
You are the embodiment of knowledge, the embodiment of Hari, the embodiment of the Master, and the embodiment of the Husband.
You are of concealed form, appearing in the form of a youth; you are in the form of a householder and in the form of a forest-dweller;
you are the very embodiment of the virtuous and the very embodiment of the chaste woman.
You are of the nature of a Brahmin, and you are also a Kshatriya.
You are indeed in the form of a Vaiśya, you are a servant, you possess the beautiful form of the dharma of a devoted wife;
you are affectionate toward those who protect their devotees, O Lord, and you assume the form of the enchantress Mohinī.
You are the supreme pinnacle, you are the refuge of virtues,
and you are favored with divine blessings;
you possess a divine body and you are the ultimate examiner.
For you are our deliverer; protect us! 1.1.
You are the beggar and you are the devourer of your own son;
yet here you are seen as a protector and a living being.
You are both the enjoyed and the enjoyer, and the creator of pleasure.
O Blessed One, you are free from all taints here.
How was it performed, and by whom? Here, O Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, it was indeed performed by you, the radiant one;
that which was offered by me has become fruitful through you. Be gracious toward me here, O you whose form is the universe!
Blessed is Satī, virtuous and dear to you;
blessed also are those three maidens of yours. Blessed is your son, and blessed is Pauṇḍraka.
O Bali, you are blessed; I am your servant.
Blessed is your natural state as a forest-dweller;
blessed is your delight in moving through the sky;
and blessed is your meal upon your son's lap.
Blessed is your son, O King, who is like food to be enjoyed. || 15 ||
Blessed is the Guru, the foremost of yogis and a savior;
blessed is this land on the banks of the Bhīmā;
and blessed is your most divine ritual act.
And blessed is the fortitude of your servants. || 16 ||
The entrustment of the son is most blessed, and the vow of Kumuda is auspicious; the month is blessed,
and you, Anādi Lakṣmīpati Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, are blessed here, as is Kambharāja.
You are the cowherd boy and Bālakṛṣṇa, the Lord of Light and the Lord of Pāravatī;
you are the Lord of Rādhā and the Lord of Māṇikikā, the Lord of Śrī, the Lord of the Earth, and the Lord of Lords. || 18 ||
Lord of swans, Lord of the Mañjus, Lord of the gods, Lord of Māyā, and indeed Lord of the qualified (Saguṇa)—
this form of yours [surpasses] many millions of suns.
Indeed, because one does not look upon it with equanimity for the sake of happiness. || 1.9 ||
It was joined by many who were as radiant as ten million suns, accompanied by numerous incarnations,
and surrounded by lords, sovereigns, ancestors, gods, and others, as well as by Daityas and Nāgas.
He is joined with Lakṣmī, Śrī, and Rādhikā, and likewise joined with Cakrapaviṣṇu;
he is joined with Mahālakṣmī and is likewise well-worshipped by Mahāviṣṇu. ||21||
My eyes are not capable of beholding You here; therefore, make Your form worthy of being seen.
Be gracious, O Lord of the living beings, and make Your own form beautiful like that of a child.
Salutations, salutations to You who deliver [us] from worldly existence; let there be salutations to You who are devoted to Brahman.
To Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa, to Nārāyaṇa—salutations, salutations to You again and again! (23)
Salutations, salutations to you who possess infinite forms, countless mouths, and innumerable eyes;
homage be to the Supreme Lord of incalculable names, the husband of ten million lotus-born maidens.

O Kṛṣṇa, everything has been done and offered to you; act as you please so that you may be pleased. Whatever was to be attained by me, both here and in the hereafter, has already been obtained; nothing remains for me now except this boon.
Having thus praised Rādhikā, the king paused for a moment;
then Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa spoke to the lord of the earth.
O King, he who is seen here is you yourself as Mahāviṣṇu;
and she who sits beside you is this very Śīlavatī, who is Mahālakṣmī.
This Śrī of yours is Bhīmā, Lakṣmī is your daughter Kṛṣṇā, and Rādhikā is Tuṅgabhadrā; indeed, know these to be your three daughters. 28.
"This Viṣṇu here is your son Pauṇḍraka himself;
he is Tāraka, and I am your guru, O King, the Lord who bestows liberation. (29)
Behold me here with these divine eyes granted to you,
endowed with all forms, as well as those which are my own true forms.
Therefore, behold my forms of incarnation within your heart;
O Indra among kings, this son of yours has not died, for he was preserved by my illusory power.
And it was shown by you during the ritual of total surrender for the sake of examination:
"In this vow of Kārtika, one must never say 'no' to anyone who requests [an offering]. (32)
"O King, take back your son according to his true form and as he pleases;
my wife was enjoyed by me, yet this was merely shown for the sake of a test. (33)
The girls were not made naked for the sake of examination;
rather, that was done because I have become pleased, even exceedingly pleased. (34)
"You are my incarnations; that indeed shall be your knowledge. From this day forward, all of you shall always be excellent deities here. (35)
For the sake of upliftment, I have assumed incarnations here on earth in the form of a family for you, through portions and sub-portions of my divine essence. (36)
"By my power, create two forms here—six and six;
let six forms remain here, equal to me, and another six forms likewise. (37)
May the auspicious maidens come and remain there in the field of Kuṅkumavāpī; may they remain at the holy site of Aśvapaṭṭasara. 38.
Having spoken thus, the Lord vanished his own divine form and became Bālakṛṣṇa in person, appearing especially beautiful to behold.
He was full of loveliness, a vessel of all beauty,
a magnet for the eyes, and the very ground for the steadiness of vision.
Resembling the campaka flower and possessing a golden luster, he was clothed in garments as pure as fire;
adorned with ornaments set with excellent gems, he was more beautiful than ten million gods of love. ||41||
Abounding with fresh strength and vigor, his limbs were perfectly firm and filled with vital essence;
he was beautiful in every part of his body, captivating to the mind, and enchanting. ||42||
His beauty is radiant with a gentle smile; he is the bestower of streams of love; he is the treasure-trove of affection to be attained; and he is the ocean of compassion. ||43||
Thus he became like a child, as delicate as the filaments of a lotus,
repeatedly drawing [all hearts] toward him with his two eyes, which were as expansive as white lotuses.
He spoke to that entire family for the purpose of granting a boon;
the king’s desires were fulfilled and the family was indeed satisfied. (45)
"The direct attainment of the Lord has occurred; what other boon remains here?
Having reflected thus, they said, "Employ us as you wish. (46)
Then Hari, smiling, spoke to the three maidens who had taken refuge with him:
"The maiden who is Śrī is indeed the river Bhīmā by name. (47)
"Let my residence be here in this Bhīmā, which is the very embodiment of a sacred ford;
let that Lakṣmī who is the maiden named Kṛṣṇā become the river Kṛṣṇā. (48)
"May my residence here be in this Kṛṣṇā river, which is the very embodiment of a sacred ford;
and may Rādhā become the maiden known as the Tuṅgabhadrā river. (49)
Here, she exists in the form of a sacred ford (tīrtha) and in the form of the Tuṅgabhadrā river;
thus, these three maidens remained established there within the rivers themselves.
Out of compassion, for the sake of performing the task of uplifting the world,
the Lord himself, the founder of the holy order (tīrthakartā), established it in that manner and dwelt together with them.
On the bank of the Bhīmā, Hari shines there as Bhīmākṛṣṇa;
on the bank of the Kṛṣṇā, Hari shines as Nivāsa.
On the banks of the Tuṅgabhadrā, the Lord of the Tuṅgabhadrā shines resplendent;
thus the Blessed One himself created these three delightful sacred sites (tīrtha). 53.
Then he said to the king: "You, however, are the lord of great power;
you are indeed of the nature of Mahāviṣṇu, always equal to Śaṅkara. (54)
Dwell here, O King; you are like a sacred ford, bestowing the fruits of pilgrimage upon me.
You are accompanied by Mahālakṣmī and by your wife Śīlavatī.
Thus, having granted a splendid dwelling to those two, Kṛṣṇa established the holy site of Mahālakṣmīyutamahābaleśvara. (56)
The king and queen remained constantly at Mahābaleśvara;
then Hari himself spoke to his son Puṇḍraka, who was Viṣṇu.
Always assume a divine form and establish a city in Puṇḍraka;
always dwell in Puṇḍrapura as the very embodiment of Viśvasthala.
"And always be the bestower of liberation upon the people who depend on you.
Having thus commanded Viṣṇu to remain in Puṇḍrapura, thereafter—
Having established those various holy places and having entered into each of them,
Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa himself, the Lord of all, especially manifested there.
Having taken those six divine forms which had been assumed by his command,
he then led his guru Tāraka away in his own celestial chariot.
Having summoned Tārakā, he entrusted her to the holy divine hermitage, saying:
"O you who are the very form of a sacred ford, you must remain here at this holy site along with Tāraka."
"My mantra must be given to one who has come for refuge," having said this, he established the Tārakāyana [weapon] upon Tāraka.
Having taken that second form as well onto a divine celestial chariot,
the blessed Lord Hari, being pleased, bestowed blessings upon them all.
Having established seven sacred fords (tīrthas) as the foremost on the surface of the earth,
Mādhava bathed in those various locations within those very tīrthas.
When those seven divine forms indeed came into being, the Leader of the Three Worlds established the most excellent of all sacred fords (tīrthas). //66//
Then, in that divine celestial chariot, Śrī Hari was borne by the gods—
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśa, and the others— as well as by the sages and the ancestors.
The Sādhyas, Siddhas, Vasus, Īśvaras, and the best of men arrived there suddenly and repeatedly uttered cries of "Victory! (68).
They raised shouts of joy and celebrated with unblemished [garlands];
they showered down a rain of flowers and sprinkled sandalwood water.
They honored him with parched grain, gladdened him with hymns of praise,
bowed before him, paid him respect, and showed him hospitality with their very selves.
Having offered various articles, they likewise gave words of praise and said to the venerable Supreme Soul: "O Lord, for Your devotee, [there is nothing] anywhere... (71)
"There is nothing here that you cannot give; the Lord of the Asuras is your witness.
Such a test must never be performed anywhere else."
For one who is unripe, there might indeed be some violation of their vow through illusion;
but for you, O Kṛṣṇa, who are free from illusion, the test must likewise be free from illusion.
"It is possible for one devoid of deceit to overcome that which is difficult to conquer by means of deceitful greed.
Having said this, and having worshipped the Supreme Lord with flower garlands and other offerings, [he departed]. (74)
Then, after once again honoring those seven great liberated ones,
all the other gods and their retinues vanished from sight.
The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa impelled the celestial chariot in the sky, and it quickly arrived, swift as the wind.
In the field of Kuṅkumavāpikā, in the vicinity of Lomaśa’s hermitage,
he shone with a splendor like ten million suns, resplendent with his eight forms.
And having wandered for ten yojanas, he descended in the evening into the midst of a grove of kadamba trees, in a most enchanting garden. (78)
Then those men and women descended upon the earth from all sides;
they ran forward for the sake of a vision and beheld the Supreme Lord.
And the celestial chariot, accompanied by seven divine and highly fortunate devotees,
became invisible to the people in an instant.
Then they uttered cries of victory and prostrated before the auspicious Aṣṭaka; Hari then led his mother toward her father's residence.
Having shown him [the shrine], he then led him to the illustrious Lomaśa,
and afterwards led him to Aśvapaṭṭasara and other sacred fords.
He gave an excellent mansion for his permanent residence to Kudamba,
and he granted a hermitage at the site of Kuṅkumavāpikā to Tāraka.
Śrī Puruṣottama gave everything that was required: honor, food, drink, personal attendants, and objects—all of them divine. (84)
And Hari said to the king: "Indeed, your vow for the month of Kārtika has attained completion in every respect through my yoga."
Fame, giving, a feast of food, water, clothing, wealth and so forth; the recitation of mantras, burnt offerings, service to guests, and subsisting on fruits for a month [are all meritorious]. ||86||
Through a mere fragment of my compassion, everything of yours has reached completion;
O King, there remains nothing further for you to do, nor anything else whatsoever. (87)
Devoted to service here, practice dedication unto me;
thus, the vow of ten million Kārtikas has reached completion for you. (88)
When the Supreme Soul, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, had spoken thus,
the king offered his three daughters there to that beloved wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
In the hermitage of the sage Lomaśa, Śrī Hari sent his daughters— Tārakā, Baleśvarī, and the virtuous Satī.
And there he caused his son Puṇḍraka to perform a ritual bath;
those very places became sacred fords (tīrthas) at the Aśvapaṭṭa lake.
Those divine stars, indeed well-known by their respective names,
then rested themselves in his own exceedingly soft abode.
Then he slept at night, and at dawn on the eighth day of the month of Āṣāḍha,
the birthday of Śrī Hari, Tāraka performed worship.
Mahābaleśvara, the three maidens, and the young girls;
the ṛṣis, munis, siddhas, humans, deities, and so forth. ||94||
On the first day of the tenth year, in the pavilion, all the goddesses, the mistresses, worshipped the Supreme Lord Hari. (95)
The Supreme Person sat upon a great, divine elephant-throne;
the lords, protectors, guardians of the world, and guardians of the kingdom all arrived. 96.
They worshipped him with exceeding love, and Lomaśa performed the ritual of worship; then he offered the evening lamps, and the gods and others presented their offerings.
And the father and mother fed them and performed a hospitable reception for the gods, goddesses, and their families, with great honor, wealth, and other gifts. (98)
Then she arranged an avoidance [of the situation] and held a great festival in the evening;
there were dances and songs by other Vidyādharīs and skilled women. (99)
Their father himself gave them rewards and other gifts;
Hari, however, bestowed blessings, happiness, excellent food, and so forth.
Having thus completed that excellent ten-year festival,
he fed the Brahmins and others residing at Kuṅkumavāpikā.
He gave gifts of jewels and cows to satisfy his supplicants;
having thus celebrated a great festival, the gods and others departed for heaven.
All the other cowherds went to their own respective homes, while Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa also rested comfortably in his own palace.
Lomaśa, accompanied by the maiden, returned to his hermitage after receiving worship;
the honored guests departed for their own lands, praising the festival.
Then, eager for the service of Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa,
there were two divine attendants of Śrī Hari, Hemanta and Bhagavān.
Always remaining in the service of their Lord with their whole being like servants,
they both served Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa with royal honors.
O Rādhā, by reading or hearing of the deeds of the beginningless Kṛṣṇa, enjoyment and liberation will certainly be attained through the majesty of the Beloved of the Goddess of Splendor. 1.07.

Thus ends the eighty-first chapter, titled "The Description of King Baleśvara and his Family’s Praise of Śrī Hari, as well as their Twofold Attainment of Divine Bodies and Other Boons," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Śrī-Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Listen, O Rādhā, I shall proclaim the Pratyakṣa-Puruṣottama,
which was indeed instructed by Viśvāmitra to Jayadhvaja during the sacrifice.
In the lunar dynasty there was a king named Sahasrārjuna;
he possessed a thousand arms, was radiant, and was the foremost among those skilled in the science of archery.
He had five hundred sons, all of whom were great chariot-warriors;
they were skilled in weapons, powerful, heroic, righteous, and worshippers of the gods.
Some worship Rudra, some the Sun, and others Kratu;
others worship Vahni, others Viṣṇu, and still others Satī.
Others worship Aja, while others worship Gaṇeśa and Candraka;
Jayadhvaja is the youngest, he who is indeed the last-born of all.
That wise one became devoted to the Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa Svāmī from time immemorial; he constantly [worshipped] the divine Lord Nārāyaṇa Hari.
"He remains taking refuge in Viṣṇu, the deity who is higher than Brahmā.
To him, the other sons said, "Listen, O righteous younger brother! (7)
"Our father worshipped the god Vahni, Śiva, Datta, and likewise Muni;
worship them here, do not worship Nārāyaṇa. (8)
Jayadhvaja said to them, "In my view, righteousness is supreme.
Kings on this earth have arisen from a portion of Viṣṇu."
The Blessed One, Puruṣottama, is their protector of the kingdom;
Viṣṇu, the unconquered Hari, is the worshipful guardian of the worlds.
Indeed, Śrī Hari is to be worshipped by you in every way;
for Brahmā, whose form is rajas, creates, while Hara, whose nature is tamas, destroys.
The Blessed Viṣṇu, the self of all beings, always nourishes them;
therefore, he is the protector of the kingdoms of the lords of the earth as they rule. 12.
The Blessed Lord Viṣṇu, the supreme sovereign Nārāyaṇa, is to be propitiated;
by means of goodness (sattva), a living being is liberated, for the Blessed Lord Hari is the very essence of goodness.
The quality of *sattva* is always the most excellent, as determined by yogis;
through the purification of all things, the purification of *sattva* clarifies one's fearlessness.
In Viṣṇu, that purity is characterized by sattva, for his mastery is indeed eternal;
in Śambhu, in Vahni, and likewise in Sūrya, it is distinguished by the quality of tamas alone.
In Kratu, Satī, Gaṇeśa, and Aja, rajas is predominant; in Candraka, sattva is predominant; and in Viṣṇu Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of Gods, sattva is especially distinguished.
O brothers, he is always to be honored by you as well;
for Viṣṇu is the nourisher and the ruler, and the duty of kingship resides in him.
One's own duty is conducive to liberation for kings, and no other;
for it always upholds the great power of Nārāyaṇa within them.
Having heard this supreme worship of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, his elder brothers said: "The dharma of our father is the highest virtue. (19)
The fire was propitiated by the father, and likewise the Lord Śambhu was bestowed;
these very ones should be accepted for worship through the duty toward the ancestors, which grants liberation.
Jayadhvaja said to them: "What has been spoken by my elder brothers is appropriate;
the duty toward one's father must be protected, according to what is required and even more so. (21)
But in this sacrifice, in this task which brings together all the gods, who is to be honored and propitiated? To this, Acyuta replied: [22]
"For whatever the bulls among sages, who are the authorities, might say here, that shall indeed be so.
Then the sages, the bulls among progenitors, headed by Vasiṣṭha, were summoned.
When questioned during a dispute over the Dharma, or in a sacrifice consisting of the propitiation of the gods, or at any other time—tell us, which deity is to be propitiated? (24)
I spoke to those sages, Vasiṣṭha and the others, according to the truth:
"Whichever deity is favored by a man, that indeed is his own deity. (25)
However, even now, a deity is worshipped according to specific purposes and desired results;
for there are many deities, and they are indeed the very images of Brahman.
And there exist those who seek different objects; as is the object, so is the deity, according to the force of the task, the force of time, the injunction, and the command. (7)
Due to the demands of business, a servant may be attended upon by a king somewhere;
likewise, a servant may also attend upon another servant for the sake of business.
Even the most excellent serve those who are inferior due to the requirements of their duties;
furthermore, distinct castes exist based on the configuration of the body. (29)
Whatever effect arises from something is discarded for the sake of that [other] thing;
for the sake of excellent and desired fruits, people cultivate crops and consume food. (2.82.30)
Indeed, for the sake of attaining the essence (rasa), they worship the earth and water;
and for the sake of the ripening of essences, they worship the sun and the moon. || 31 ||
For kings, Viṣṇu as well as Purandara is the deity;
for brahmins, Agni, Āditya, Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and Śiva are the deities.
Viṣṇu is always the deity of the gods, and Hara is the deity of the Dānavas;
Soma is said to be the deity of the Gandharvas and the Yakṣas.
For the Vidyādharas, she is Vāgdevī; for the Siddhas, the Lord Hari;
for the Rākṣasas, the god Śaṅkara; and for the Kinnaras, Pārvatī. ||368||
Brahmā is the deity of the sages; Śiva, the ancestors, and the gods [are the deities] of the [other] classes;
as are the Sun, Agni, the Viśvedevas, and likewise Janārdana. ||35||
For women, the goddess Lakṣmī is their deity; a devoted wife is their delight; the husband is their supreme lord, Śambhu; and she is also the very embodiment of the glory of good fortune. (26)
For householders, the gods and goddesses are the deity according to their respective requirements;
for ascetics and students of sacred knowledge, the Supreme Brahman himself is the deity.
For the virtuous, patience is their goddess and character is their deity;
for children, their parents are their deity; and for animals, the protector is their god. (38)
Śaṅkara is the deity of the hosts, the Supreme Lord of devotees;
Vāsudeva is the lord of lords, and water is the divinity of trees. (39)
The Supreme Lord Śrī Parameśvara is the presiding deity and the inner controller of all; He is the medicine for the sick and the punishment for thieves. (2.82.40)
Thus, whether it be insentient or sentient, whatever one's own chosen deity may be, Lord Hari, who exists everywhere, is the deity of all. (41)
Therefore, Jayadhvaja certainly deserves to worship Viṣṇu;
for there is an identity between Rudra and Viṣṇu, and even with Brahmā. (42)
Having understood this, Hari—the Lord of the lords of all lords—is always to be worshipped;
likewise, all his incarnations, such as Vāsudeva and the others, are present therein.

Mahāviṣṇu and others are the Vairājas, who are forms of partial incarnations (aṃśa); or they are manifestations through possession (āveśa), as well as portions (kalā) and divine powers (vibhūti), such as the gods and other beings. ||44||
The gods, goddesses, the Guru, the virtuous, the Brahmins, the cows, and devoted wives attain union with Śrī Hari, the Supreme Soul. (45)
Having spoken thus, all the sages performed his sacrifice;
it was a supreme Vaiṣṇava rite, for which the sacred ceremonies were completed in seven days.
Wherein all the lords, as well as the sages and deities, and all the inhabitants of heaven—the planets, humans, and brahmins—[are gathered]. (47)
They enjoyed various kinds of cooked foods and milk-rice preparations in every way;
they attained supreme satisfaction through the food and drink that was like the nectar of Soma.
At that sacrifice, all the fires and all the Maruts, with great devotion, consumed the offered oblations and other offerings; this brought satisfaction even to the three worlds. 49.
And Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the glorious Puruṣottama, having arisen visibly from the fire, partook of the divine form. (2.82.50)

Thus, when the sacrifice was successfully completed, the act of giving the sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) performed, the remaining oblations offered, and the final purificatory bath (avabhṛtha) concluded; ||21||
All the brahmins and others took their meal in rows;
at that moment, a rakshasa named Videha arrived there.
Terrifying with his fangs, with blazing eyes, and brandishing a trident while making the quarters resound,
mortals fled in fear upon seeing him as he approached from the forest.
Then all the great and powerful sons of Arjuna, being fully prepared,
fought the Dānava with spears, mountain peaks, swords, and mallets.
There, the lords of the earth hurled at him the missiles of Prajāpati, Varuṇa, Rudra, Vāyu, Kubera, Indra, and Agni.
Taking up a spear that shone like the sun and whirling it around, the Dānava brandished it and shattered those weapons on all sides. ||56||
By means of the fire situated within the stake, he drew them all toward him in every way;
then the kings, being fierce, struck him with maces.
As soon as they were touched by it, all the maces shattered like clods of earth against the body of a mountain;
even the lords were unable to move the Dānava with their maces.
Then, having witnessed his prowess, they were overcome with fear and fled;
seeing his extraordinary valor, their enthusiasm was utterly broken.
Then, seeing the flight of the five hundred princes, Jayadhvaja called to mind Nārāyaṇa Hari.
Having meditated for a moment upon the Supreme Person, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa Svāmī, he recited this mantra: "Protect me, protect me, O Supreme Person! (61)
"O Protector of those who have come for refuge, come hither, O Supreme Lord!"—
when thus remembered, the Blessed Śrī Hari himself [appears].
Then Viṣṇu— the victorious, the source of the worlds, the immeasurable, and the one free from all affliction— quickly arrived there, bearing the discus, conch, lotus, and mace as his weapons.
Śrī Hari, the protector of devotees and the supreme primordial ancestor,
gave his own Sudarśana discus to Jayadhvaja.
Having bowed to Śrī Hari, the king took the Sudarśana discus in his hand and then hurled it at the two shoulders of the Rākṣasa Videha.
He quickly struck that head from the shoulder onto the ground;
there the Rākṣasa, whose body was like a mountain, was slain.
Having understood this, the sage Viśvāmitra arrived to see him;
and his brothers, being delighted, praised that banner of victory.
They offered the highest seat to the sage Viśvāmitra;
the sage sat there and then inquired after their welfare.
Jayadhvaja said to the sage: "By your grace, this great Asura Dānava, Videha, has been struck down here by my discus. (69)
"By your words, I have always worshipped Śrī Narāyaṇa;
I have sought refuge in him, and by him, grace has been bestowed upon me. (2.82.70)
Thinking, "I shall perform a sacrifice for the sake of destroying the sin of killing a Rākṣasa," [he asked:
"How and by what ritual procedure is Lord Hari to be worshipped? (71)
Who is this Nārāyaṇa who is to be worshipped here at the sacrifice, and what is his power?
Explain all of this to me; I seek to propitiate that Lord. (72)
Having heard the words of Jayadhvaja, Mani spoke to him—
Jayadhvaja, who was the foremost among the devotees of the Supreme Lord and had sought refuge in Him.
Worship that Supreme Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, who is without beginning, from whom the activity of all beings proceeds, in whom everything exists, and from whom the universe arises. (74)
They say that beyond the supreme syllable of the Yamas is the Lord who dwells in the cave,
the blissful, supreme void situated in the highest abode.
Higher than the highest, the Supreme Brahman, higher even than the supreme Nārāyaṇa.
He is the sovereign of syllables, the bestower of liberation, for he is indeed the Lord of the Liberated.
He who is the cause of thousands of incarnations, the Supreme Person,
who assumes the fourfold manifestation (caturvyūha) and yet remains unmanifest (avyūha), free from all taint (nirañjana).
The supreme Self, the supreme abode, the supreme ether, the supreme state—the imperishable Brahman with three quarters, whom the exponents of Brahman declare. (78)
Vāsudeva is the Lord, the perfected master of yoga, the illustrious Puruṣottama;
from a portion of whom the lords Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara are born. (79)
Vairāja, Mahāviṣṇu, Bhūman, and Kāla are those born from his portions; he who is the Lord of Pradhāna, the Lord of Māyā, and also Puruṣa.
He whose portion is thus the Great Person (Mahāpuruṣa), and who is himself the Supreme Lord among all the Blessed Ones—[he is the one]. 8.1.
That Supreme Person is to be propitiated through self-surrender characterized by renunciation;
therefore, O King, once again appease that sacrifice, the Supreme Lord. (82)
Having spoken thus, the great sage Viśvāmitra ceased;
meanwhile, the sacrifice was commenced by the king there, [dedicated] to the Lord Nārāyaṇa.
Viśvāmitra, together with the Brahmins, performed the sacrificial rites for the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇadeva—the Lord of all, the Supreme Lord, higher than the highest. (84)
When the sacrifice had reached its conclusion, the Lord Hari himself appeared there in person, repeatedly consuming the sacrificial oblation.
"Choose a boon, O Lord of the Earth, whatever dwells in your heart.
Thus Hari spoke, and the king replied: "Your very feet [are the boon I seek]. (86)
"O Compassionate One, lead me to the eternal, supreme, divine abode! Hari said, "What you have requested is indeed correct; let it be so. (87)
Having spoken thus, he vanished from sight; at that moment, four ascetics arrived there, saying, "Give us alms. (88)
The king gave them alms consisting of milk-rice;
they accepted it and ate it, and the king gave them a sacrificial fee.
At that time, those monks were dark-complexioned, coarse, and hairy;
they could assume any form at will, wandered through the forest, and were misshapen.
Having eaten, they then drank water and sat down, taking shelter under a tree;
like four fools, they were indeed tranquil, resembling peaceful clouds.
When the sacrificial rites were perfectly completed, all four of them went together to the Narmadā river for the purpose of the purificatory avabhṛtha bath. ||92||
All the sages, gods, and Vaiṣṇava devotees, as well as the great-souled men, brahmins, the truthful, and the virtuous, had all bathed.
In the lower region, however, those four were dark-complexioned;
by the power of the merit from bathing, they became white-complexioned. (94)
Resplendent like the sun and moon, possessing forms equal to those of Mahendra, with bodies as magnificent as Viṣṇu, they were divine beings like the gods of heaven. (95)
Having seen them, those who had performed the avabhṛtha bath asked them about their lineage;
they each spoke their own names, saying, "This first one is indeed Śrīśaila."
This Nīlagiri is the second, and Elādri is the third;
this Droṇācala is the fourth—we are born from the lineage of Meru.
We are mountains capable of assuming any form at will, desiring here to bathe;
we are steadfast mountains, Vaiṣṇavas longing for the washing away of our sins. (98)
For all those who harm us, whether they dwell in forests or caves, and even the heretics who reside there, commit whatever sins against us. (99)
Having transferred their sins to us, they indeed depart purified;
by those sins we became black in color, but through bathing we have become fair-complexioned.
Thereupon, the Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa himself came here for the sake of receiving his share of the sacrifice and also for the purpose of bathing. || 101 ||
"By the grace of the Vaiṣṇavas, all our sins have been destroyed.
Now we shall depart for our own abodes; salutations be unto you!"
Where the Lord, the illustrious Śrī Bhagavān Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa himself, resides, his devotees bathed in the water; for this is indeed the Narmada Tīrtha.
And Jayadhvaja said to them, "I shall perform the rites of hospitality;
O best of mountains, please take up residence here in my house."
Having spoken thus, O King, at the conclusion of the purificatory bath (avabhṛtha), the monarch, out of great affection, led Rādhikā to dwellings that were like mountains of gold.
All the other great-souled ones, having enjoyed [the festivities] and received worship, departed for their own abodes; Jayadhvaja, however, remained and took rest.
The subjects— including the helpless and the wretched, servants,
male and female slaves, and even insects such as ants— were satisfied by that excessive food.
Whoever listens to this with devotion, causes it to be read, or reads it themselves,
shall attain both worldly enjoyment and liberation through the power of Nārāyaṇa’s grace.

Thus ends the eighty-second chapter, titled "The Description of King Jayadhvaja’s Attainment of Śrī Hari at the Sacrifice through the Power of the Worship of the Supreme Brahman Taught by Viśvāmitra, the Destruction of the Rākṣasa of Videha, and the Avabhṛtha Bath of the Four Mountains," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O Rādhā, in this way that king Jayadhvaja, a great Vaiṣṇava,
[installed] Droṇa, Elā, Nīla, and Śrīśaila— all four— in his own abode.
Having honored them with seats and other offerings, he gave them a most excellent welcome; he provided them with delightful foods, drinks, and various kinds of victuals.
Jayadhvaja also gave objects for enjoyment, pleasing utensils, waters, and even articles for the worship of Śrī Hari.
Those mountains, having accomplished their purpose, questioned Jayadhvaja:
"How are sins destroyed? How is one's true nature restored? (4)
How may one remain forever untainted even when accused of sin? Through the company of whom does liberation arise, and from what comes eternal peace? (5)
What is one's own interest, and what is the interest of others? What activity brings about auspiciousness?
By what action is either dullness or divinity attained? (6)
O Great King, by virtue of even a small portion of the grace of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, you remain as the king of devotees, like one who is omniscient.
"Therefore, tell us that which is the supreme good by which it may be attained.
Having heard this, Jayadhvaja said: "In the forest, the great seers spoke to me: (8)
Many divine beings dwell there who are enriched with higher knowledge; I go for the sake of constantly beholding them and for the attainment of wisdom.
Whatever I have heard from them, whether through the course of conversation or while listening to the narrative of the Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā, [I have retained it].
I shall also relate what I have experienced myself; listen:
at a sacred ford (tīrtha), sins are destroyed, for a tīrtha is both stationary and mobile.
Having rescued the one who has come for refuge from the ocean known as latent impressions (vāsanā),
he dispatches him to the supreme abode of the Supreme Lord.
That sacred site (tīrtha) should be understood in every respect as being either insentient or sentient by nature.
The insentient consists of waters, shrines (caityas), and material objects composed of the elements. || 13 ||
Indeed, those divine holy places (tīrthas), though devoid of qualities, become [efficacious] through divine yoga; they certainly deliver even sinners in every way. 14.
The self is declared to be a great sacred ford (tīrtha), while Kṛṣṇa is the highest of all supreme sacred fords;
the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa is the most excellent of all sacred fords.
Through connection with that sacred ford (tīrtha), all devotees become embodiments of the sacred ford; they all become saviors—saintly men, virtuous women, and yogis.

Those who are devoted to the conduct of Brahman, the conduct of the household, and the conduct of the forest; those who are dispassionate, devoted to renunciation, and devoted to meditation—they are indeed considered to be the true tīrthas of Kṛṣṇa. || 17 ||

The female servants of Kṛṣṇa, the devotees of Kṛṣṇa, as well as the associates of Kṛṣṇa, and all things—whether insentient or sentient—that have attained a connection with Kṛṣṇa are holy places of pilgrimage (tīrthas). || 18 ||

The person enriched with the qualities of Kṛṣṇa, the virtuous woman filled with the grace of Kṛṣṇa, and even beasts, birds, trees, and creepers— indeed, through union with Kṛṣṇa, they are all liberators.
Gardens, village halls, rest-houses for travelers, riverbanks,
lake shores, forest clearings, mountains, and wilderness lands— || 2.83.20 ||
The stationary and the moving beings are all sacred fords (tīrtha) for those yogis devoted to Kṛṣṇa;
so too are villages, cities, market towns, capitals, and even cowherd settlements. (21)
Where Kṛṣṇa shines forth, both the hamlets and the dwellings—all that is indeed a sacred ford (tīrtha), a deliverer that has attained divine status. (22)
That which has been touched by Hari in person becomes a liberating holy site (tīrtha). For as is Hari, so indeed are his virtuous devotees the holy sites themselves.
They constantly ferry people across by means of bestowing knowledge;
having destroyed ignorance, they bestow upon them divine nature. (24)
Having destroyed desire, anger, greed, intoxication, pride, envy, craving, and latent impressions, they perform purification. || 25 ||
Through union with them, the illusion (māyā) is crossed over by people who stand upon the boats that are the virtuous;
the virtuous are the eyes, and the virtuous are also the lamps.
The virtuous are like ships situated in the ocean; they are islands of nectar standing amidst the forest fire.
Indeed, among those overwhelmed by poison, the virtuous are the antidotes who remove the venom.

In this ocean of saṃsāra which is like the Hālāhala poison, the virtuous are indeed like Nīlakaṇṭha; in this ocean of saṃsāra which is like a great sea of disease, they are the very embodiment of Dhanvantari. ||28||
For the virtuous are like showers for those scorched by the fire of sense-objects;
indeed, they are like shears for those bound by the net of latent impressions.
The virtuous are the supreme sacred ford, a sacred ford fashioned by the Supreme Self,
where Nārāyaṇa himself always resides in embodied form.

Those who have renounced the householder's life for the sake of Hari, and have completely abandoned all worldly attachments, are indeed saints whose very form is a sacred pilgrimage site, for they are bound to Śrī Hari.
Hari is the supreme sacred site (tīrtha), and the virtuous are the sacred sites; the virtuous women are likewise sacred sites. Through them, even sinners cross over [to liberation].
These three are the supreme sacred sites, and the fourth is the assembly of Brahmins; the Guru is the sacred site, the best of all sacred sites, and the eternal bestower of liberation.

The mother is the supreme sacred ford, as is the father and likewise the husband; the chaste wife is a sacred ford, the practice of dharma is a sacred ford, and righteous people are indeed sacred fords. (34)

A son is a sacred ford, as is one endowed with righteousness; a daughter is a sacred ford when possessed of virtue; a sister is a sacred ford when joined with dharma; and a wife is a sacred ford if she is faithful.
A righteous family is a sacred ford that delivers others; it is a supreme sacred ford.
A deity is a sacred ford, a temple is a sacred ford, and the nectar of sacred stories is a sacred ford. (36)
The word of the elders is a sacred ford, and the scripture is an eternal ford;
the gift of a cow is the supreme ford, as are the gifts of gold and food. (37)
Truth is a sacred ford, forgiveness is a sacred ford, freedom from passion is a sacred ford, and likewise, freedom from hatred is a sacred ford that produces purity. (38)

Service to Kṛṣṇa is the supreme sacred site (tīrtha), and devotion is likewise the highest sacred site; indeed, the offering of all things to Kṛṣṇa is said to be the most excellent of all sacred sites. (39)
Initiation, mendicancy, and discernment—these three are the sacred fords (tīrtha) through discernment;
thus, indeed, these mountains become sacred fords through their connection with Hari.
What need is there for much speech here? The virtuous are in every way sacred sites; they bestow everything upon living beings seeking dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa.
One who has sought refuge with the virtuous certainly crosses over; of this there is no doubt.
Just as one who has reached a support of wood certainly crosses the ocean of water. 42.
In wood there is only lightness, yet Hari dwells within it;
wherever Hari is, everything that is most dear to one is found there.
The wish-fulfilling creeper is in the hands of the virtuous; the wish-granting gem is in the mouths of the virtuous;
the celestial wish-tree is in the hearts of the virtuous; and the cow of plenty is in the minds of the virtuous. (44)
The supernatural powers, beginning with atomization (aṇimā), roll at the feet of the virtuous;
the lordly powers that bestow happiness truly dwell upon the lips of the virtuous.
Purity resides in the vision of the virtuous, and Dharma dwells even in their speech;
liberation, however, exists in the service of the virtuous, having gone to them for refuge. (46)

Nature (prakṛti) is said to be the habitual tendency toward sense objects; this latent impression (saṃskāra), which resides in the state of stability, is worn away through the practice of devotion to Kṛṣṇa. 47.
"By constantly crying out 'Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa' and 'Nārāyaṇa,' the purificatory rites known as meditative cultivation (bhāvanā) indeed come to be. (48)
Through the yoga of Kṛṣṇa, those divine [powers] destroy the illusory ones;
having destroyed the material [impurities], they purify the interior of the heart. 49.

That illusion is either of the nature of delusion, or ignorance consisting of the notions of "I" and "mine," or it consists of passion and hatred, or it is doubt characterized by falsehood. || 2.83.50 ||
Through the method of true reality, one attains dissolution by the power of Hari;
provided that, until the moment of death is reached, the mind has not failed to dwell upon Kṛṣṇa. (51)
Wherever the mind is fixed upon a woman, a man, a son, wealth, or anything else—that illusion, which is indeed a cause of bondage, perishes through the remembrance of Kṛṣṇa. ||52||
"Thus let the mountains listen, for the yoga of Kṛṣṇa is indeed the deliverer;
the yoga of the virtuous is also a deliverer, by which Māyā is turned back. (53)
Just as iron, through contact with wood, indeed floats upon the water, so too does a sinner, through association with the virtuous, indeed cross over the ocean of existence. //54//
Just as a lotus, by its very nature, is not defiled even by water, so too the wise one endowed with devotion is not defiled even by sin. ||55||
Just as oil thrown into the midst of water floats upon its surface, so the man of knowledge, though situated among the sinful, remains untouched by sin. 56.
Knowledge burns away karmas, and devotion burns away the fruits of karma;
thus, both of these, as well as anything else performed that is other than Kṛṣṇa, are consumed.
O Kṛṣṇa, that self by which [the body] is sustained resides within Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Self;
yet that self remains dissociated from the internal organs. 58.
The internal organ is distinct from that [external] effort;
it cannot perceive [the Self] through the senses, being devoid of power, parched, and separated from its Lord. (59)
Therefore, the senses do not go toward objects that are devoid of darkness;
for sin does not transfer to one who has gone among objects [in this way]. || 2.83.60 ||
When the sense organs become objectless for the yogin, his mind also becomes objectless at all times. ||61||
And the self, being devoid of objects, is considered by Kṛṣṇa alone;
it truly becomes one who has turned away from sin and is going toward liberation. 62.
If, having become thus, his body and senses perform whatever action there may be,
that action would not lead to bondage for the yogin.
Whether it be an action performed according to ritual injunctions, or some [action] devoid of such injunctions;
whether it is recognized in the world, or not recognized at all, being excluded from worldly convention. ||64||
Whether performed with discernment or not performed due to a lack of discernment,
whether sinful or free from sin— regardless of how it appears to worldly perception.
Whatever kind of action a yogi may perform, whether it be of such a nature or otherwise,
it does not result in bondage for him, as it arises spontaneously from his own nature.
He who has no attachment to pleasure and no aversion toward objects of suffering, whose self is free from both joy and dejection—he is not defiled by evil. (67)

For one whose intellect is fixed on the thought, "May I have happiness, may I not have suffering," yet who is devoid of effort—his duty is to remain effortless; for that which is free from striving is never impaired.
For one who has always renounced both the desirable and the undesirable from the perspective of the self,
the subjugation of the three qualities (guṇas) never occurs.

For him, everything—whether the object of enjoyment, the act of enjoying, or the state of being the enjoyer—is of the nature of Kṛṣṇa; and by him, all actions arising from the body and senses are offered unto Kṛṣṇa.
Whether that person's sin or merit has its fruit offered to Kṛṣṇa in such a manner,
he is not tainted in the slightest, even though he may be smeared by all [worldly things].
Thus indeed for one who acts for the sake of Kṛṣṇa, who has accomplished what was to be accomplished, and who is always of a virtuous nature; (72)
Through association with the stainless, liberation—which destroys bondage—shall arise;
for bondage is said to be latent impression (vāsanā), which is characterized by the notions of "I" and "mine. (73)
That which arises from false knowledge—the latent impression whose nature is insentience—is indeed this saṃsāra, this bondage; it perishes through the yoga of Kṛṣṇa.
Through association with the virtuous whose nature is Kṛṣṇa, [ignorance] perishes;
from that, liberation while still living indeed occurs, free from the bondage of the elements. 75.
Free from dualities, free from effort, devoid of thirst, and abandoned of passion, her state is eternally established in the Self and overflowing with perpetual bliss. ||76||
Through union with the eternally peaceful Kṛṣṇa, there is peace in the Imperishable One;
that which is experienced as eternal through the self within the self is established in steadfastness. (77)
That eternal peace arises from Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Lord;
this is supreme liberation, for there is no peace higher than it. (78)
Immersion in the Supreme Self, which is a mass of countless blisses, is indeed the true goal of one's own self; for that is the ultimate purpose.
Liberation is the goal of the world of living beings who desire liberation; it is indeed one's own true interest.
When that goal is known, one should seek it within one's own self; and that self-interest here is liberation.
The self-interest that is momentary and provides pleasure should not be pursued by those seeking liberation;
rather, the self-interest that sustains eternal bliss should be pursued by those seeking liberation. ||81||
Thus, it is by perceiving one's own self-interest that activity bestows auspiciousness;
auspiciousness is merit, which is the heavenly world, the true abode of the Lord.
That which is associated with destruction is said to result from the creative activity of Prakṛti;
liberation is indestructible, auspicious, and consists in taking refuge at the feet of Kṛṣṇa. (83)
The attainment of Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa is the auspiciousness that is the highest of all;
for Kṛṣṇa is divine and eternally abides as he truly is, regardless of how he may appear.
Through actions that are identical with Him, a human being attains a divine state;
for by the grasp of Hari, even the body, the senses, and their functions, though insentient, [become divine]. (85)
Divine states arise and inertness attains divinity;
in this way, even you mountains, through the practice of devotion, become divine. (86)
Abandoning the state of dullness, may you become possessed of divine forms;
[for] the Lord, Master, and Sovereign is the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. ||87||
He resides in the field of Kuṅkumavāpī, near the Aśvasaras lake;
let them practice that yoga and worship Him, and by that, may they attain divinity. (88)
"You shall indeed depart quickly by the power of Nārāyaṇa's grace,"—thus were the mountains addressed by Jayadhvaja. (89)
Four other men, who were peaceful, arrived there;
having bowed to Jayadhvaja and the others, they then stood behind them.
"From where have you come, where are you going, and what is your purpose? They, the Vinatas, replied to him: "Having heard of your sacrifice... (91)
Having arrived here with joy, let us go to Lake Aśvasaras to bathe and to behold the Supreme Lord, Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Master. ||92||
We are going to the site of Kuṅkumavāpikā to wash away the countless sins that have been committed by pilgrims. 93.
This king of holy places is renowned by the name Kolārasara;
indeed, this second one exists by the name Cilasarovara. ||94||
This third one is named Śambhala-saras, the king of holy fords;
I am the fourth, the Person, the Nārāyaṇa-sarovara. ||95||
But today, having gathered together, we went to the divine Mānasa lake on the Golden Mountain in order to see it once again. (96)
Having heard this, we then came here to the sacrifice;
now we shall go to that very place where the Supreme Lord shines forth.
Having heard this, those mountains and King Jayadhvaja also all went through the sky with their families to the city of Hari.
They descended through the sky at the Kuṅkumavāpikā Tīrtha and the Aśvapaṭṭa Sarovara, and they bathed in the Aśva Sarovara.
Then, having seen the sage Śrī Lomaśa who possessed a divine form, they [uttered]:
