"Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord; svāhā! (2.83.100)
Having received the supreme mantra, they went into the presence of Bālakṛṣṇa;
and then, having worshipped Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa according to the prescribed rites, they [proceeded]. (101)
Having drunk the nectar from his feet, they sat respectfully before him and entreated him most earnestly: "Grant us liberation, the supreme state."
Śrī Hari, out of compassion, caused those three forms to be manifested;
he then sent forth the holy places in the forms of liberated devotees.
Indeed, for the sake of purifying embodied beings, he established them there in their respective dwellings in the form of devotees, like [the hermitages] at the Aśvasaras lake.
Having appointed great devotees as his own attendants within his own abode,
he then resided at that holy place, wherefrom the eight sacred sites (tīrthāṣṭaka) originated.
And likewise Kolāṭatīrtha, as well as the excellent Cilatīrtha;
and likewise Śambhalatīrtha, and Nārāyaṇasaraḥ.
Droṇatīrtha, Nīlatīrtha, Śrītīrtha,
and Cailatīrthaka shine with divine forms at the lotus feet of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
O Rādhikā, the Lord, the ocean of compassion, sent those liberated souls in their celestial chariots to the imperishable abode known as Muktanivāsa.
Having thus witnessed that marvel, Jayadhvaja also remained for the month of Mārgaśīrṣa and prayed for the liberation of Hari.
Hari granted him liberation; he then departed by means of a celestial chariot to the imperishable abode, the divine realm filled with eternal bliss.

Thus ends the eighty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Knowledge Bestowed by Jayadhvaja, the Divine Nature and Liberation of Droṇa, Eila, Nīla, and Śrīparvata, as well as Kolāṭa, Cila, Śambhala, Nārāyaṇa, and the Saras, and the Liberation of Jayadhvaja," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmīnārāyaṇīya-saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Rādhikā, listen to this wonder concerning Nārāyaṇa and the sphere of devotion belonging to the wife of Pulastya, the son of Brahmā.
The beloved wife of Pulastya was the auspicious daughter of Tṛṇabindu, named Ilavilā;
by her, Viśravas was indeed born as his son.
He became a knower of many scriptures and was devoted to dharma;
once, however, he questioned Pulastya regarding the virtues (vṛṣas).
"O Lord, tell me, what were the duties of the ages (yugadharmas) like in former times?
Then Pulastya spoke briefly to them all concerning those virtues (vṛṣas).
The Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali constitute the four ages (caturyuga).
In the Kṛta age, meditation and austerity predominate; in the Tretā, knowledge and sacrifice.
In the Dvāpara age, sacrifice alone [is the means], while in the Kali age, charity is the sole [means].
In the Kṛta age, the god Brahmā was omnipresent and accessible everywhere.
In the Tretā age, the sun became possessed of motion and capable of conjunction;
in the Dvāpara age, Viṣṇu himself became a deity and directly possessed of motion.
In the Kali age, the god Rudra manifests in the form of Time itself;
wherever he is present, there is great suffering, for he is the destroyer in the Kali age.
In the Kṛta age, however, there were an equal number of girls and boys;
they existed in balanced pairs, and their way of life was free from greed.
All subjects were always satisfied, possessed of every joy, and established in happiness;
there was no distinction of high or low among the women, for they were all without difference.
Their lifespan, happiness, form, strength, contentment, and intellect were equal; they were free from sorrow, possessed abundant knowledge, and were likewise devoted to solitude.
They were established in meditation, devoted to austerity, and dedicated to the Supreme Brahman;
they always acted without desire and were eternally joyful in mind.
Dwelling on mountains and in the ocean, they are indeed homeless and take refuge upon the earth; their food is produced by mere thought, and they subsist on water born of thought.
Produced by mere volition, possessing divine flavors, and eternally tranquil like lords,
everything was obtainable from their own selves, for they had been surrendered to Brahman.
For in the Kṛta Yuga, people were always overflowing with aesthetic bliss and had fulfilled their life's purpose;
now that four thousand years have passed, the transition [to the next age] has arrived.
At eight hundred years of age, the exhilaration of rasa there is not intense;
passion and amorous play indeed arise only gradually.
When the accomplishment of truth has been exhausted, another accomplishment proceeds;
when the pleasure of the waters has reached its limit, then [it arises] from the sky for those whose nature is like a ram.
The release of rain set in from the thundering clouds;
by that single downpour alone, he was saturated upon the surface of the earth.
The water remained there for twelve months, supporting the land;
therein appeared trees and creepers filled with sap.
Then indeed all objects of enjoyment arose from them;
at that time, the creatures sustained themselves by means of trees and other things known as the Kalpa-tree.
At that time, trees were the dwellings and landmarks for the people;
indeed, all houses were likewise devoid of walls.
All creatures dwelling in the trees, oppressed by passion, greed, and other such afflictions,
occasionally resorted to disputes over what was their own and what belonged to another.
Then the affliction born of passion and greed gained a foothold;
by that, those celestial wish-fulfilling trees (kalpadrumas) of yours subsequently met their destruction. (23)
Then, when those [trees] had perished, the subjects became bewildered and filled with grief;
the wish-fulfilling trees (kalpadrumas) were now bereft of power and yielded fruits only as a result of service.
From the earth, they obtained garments known as bark-cloth, which were the source of seeds and other such things, as well as fruits for food.
Flowers and ornaments were produced from them with great effort;
from those very things, greed arose for them, as well as their food.
In every leaf-cup there is honey, free from bees and of great potency;
from the fruits, sweet juices flow forth in streams.
By means of those [means], the subjects lived, being contented, free from distress, and devoid of wickedness;
then, in the later period of the Tretā age, the subjects were enveloped by greed.
Having forcibly made their own trees level, they especially gathered honey, beeswax, fruits, and other such things. (29)
Thus did passion prevail over the weak when they obtained the honey;
for the trees then observed the partiality shown by the subjects. (2.84.30)
Even trees born from seeds perished along with the honey;
at that time, suffering arose among men due to cold, heat, and rain. (31)
Afflicted by the pairs of opposites (dvandvas), they indeed constructed shelters;
they built house-walls and leaf-huts, contemplating means of livelihood.
But where the waters produced by rain remain in low-lying channels, in stream-beds, in hollows, and in lakes; 33.
There they established their dwellings, subsisting on trees, grain, and other such resources;
then, through the union of water and earth, medicinal herbs came into being.
In some places they ripened without being ploughed and even without being sown; in other places they were sown, and in those places they became possessed of grain and fruit. (35)
There, the trees and shrubs bore flowers and fruits according to the seasons;
yet at the end of the Tretā age, beings became filled with passion and greed, and were possessed by the sense of "I" and "mine."
Because the inevitable destiny had come to pass, the subjects became defiled;
they forcibly seized the grain-enclosures by their sheer power.
Furthermore, out of passion, the subjects forcibly seized trees, shrubs, and medicinal herbs according to their strength,
as well as their own rivers, fields, and mountains.
Even there, powerful Kṣatriyas were formerly born as protectors;
they were indeed appointed by Brahmā for tasks such as the protection of the distressed.
And in the Tretā age, the Unborn One established the system of the castes and stages of life;
for the sake of establishing the boundaries of conduct, he then created the rod of punishment.
At the end of the Tretā age, the Brāhmaṇas, together with the Kṣatriyas, established that system consisting of the performance of sacrifices and the avoidance of injury to animals.
As they guarded it according to their respective capacities, a division of the intellect arose from that:
passion, greed, partiality, conflict, and the plundering of prosperity. (42)
But when the Dvāpara age arrived, all these things indeed began to prevail among the people:
cities, kingdoms, boundaries, fields, and gardens. (43)
O beloved, at that time even the grains ripened on ploughed land;
moreover, there was drought, death, and likewise the afflictions of disease.
Afflictions born of speech, mind, and body arose in every household; and from the time after half of the Tretā age, offspring were produced through sexual union. (45)
In some places, however, O beloved, there were then beings born of mental resolve (saṃkalpa), while in others they did not exist;
indeed, in the Dvāpara age, all beings are born from the seed of desire (kāma).
And those who possess a basis were of false vigor and likewise possessed false fruits;
they were thoroughly pervaded by the power of latent impressions and were devoid of self-vigor. 47.
All subjects, devoid of spiritual accomplishment and afflicted by pride, grew in number;
in the Dvāpara age, there was the sudden onset of sufferings and of death. (48)
Out of fear of that, there arises in them the inquiry into liberation from suffering;
and from such inquiry come dispassion, knowledge, devotion, and final release. 49.
Thus, at that time, the duties of the Dvāpara age arose for the social classes (varṇas),
and likewise the specific duties of the stages of life (āśramas) came into being separately thereafter.
When the Kali age has arrived, characterized by the acquisition of afflictions, the people will be agitated by those very afflictions;
in the Tiṣya age, there will be deceit, malice, and even the slaughter of ascetics.
In the Kali age, people, intoxicated by pride and enveloped in darkness, constantly pursue their goals; moreover, there is the disease of greed and perpetual fear of hunger.
There will be terrible fear of drought and the ruin of countries;
people will be unrighteous and ill-behaved, full of great anger and diminished in luster. (53)
In the Tiṣya age, greedy people of very wicked character speak untruth; they are ruined by improper sacrifices, improper study, improper conduct, and improper scriptures.
Through the ritual faults of the Brahmins, fear arises among the subjects;
for that is not true dharma, nor is it the Vedic dharma, but rather it is merely imagined.
And all subjects, being of a single caste through their commonality of bed, seat, and food, will indeed become devoid of the system of castes and stages of life (varṇāśrama). ||56||
Kings who act like thieves, Brahmins who live off deceit, and gurus who seize the property of their disciples— these indeed flourish in the Kali age.

O Lord of Men, there was the killing of a fetus, the killing of a hero, the killing of a woman, the killing of a virtuous man, the killing of a chaste wife, and the killing of righteousness among the subjects. (58)
In the Kali age, bathing, fire-offerings, recitation, charity, worship of the gods, and remembrance of Hari are abandoned by men who are devoted to desire and greed.
They revile the gods, the virtuous, the bulls of dharma, liberation, and even the Lord of Prosperity; following the path of base conduct, they perform unrighteous deeds.
In the Kali age, people are entirely filled with immoral conduct, heretics, and futile practices; indeed, all people become constant beggars.
The lands are harsh like deserts, and the villages are harsh like outposts;
likewise, the men and women are harsh, devoid of affection, and dependent on others. (62)
There are thieves of grain, thieves of ears of corn, thieves of clothing, and those who strike with violence;
there are thieves who steal from a thief, and yet another who kills the one who steals.

In the Kali age, people will be beset by much suffering, afflicted by disease, prone to ruin, and short-lived; because of their obsession with unrighteousness, the progeny will be pervaded by darkness.
In the Kali age, the distinction between high and low seats, propriety, honorability, right conduct, and the respect due to men and women surely perish. (65)
O Tiṣyaka, under such a king, the subjects become like dancers of deceit;
the twice-born indeed become Śūdras, and the Śūdras likewise become Cāṇḍālas. (66)
But for one who is attached to the food and dwelling that are the objects of enjoyment, all phenomena are indeed one;
there is no distinction between what is drinkable and undrinkable, nor is there the state of being devoid of the enjoyable and the non-enjoyable. (67)

There is no discrimination between truth and falsehood, no transcending of the graspable and the ungraspable, nor any conceptualization of the qualities of worldly existence or of women who conform to one's desires. (68)
Furthermore, those practitioners who follow the ways of rogues are pleasing to delusion;
their chanting of the names of deities with worldly songs is devoid of true dharma.
In the Kali age, knowledge and action are always indeed destroyed;
in this Tiṣya age, there are the stings of insects, mice, and serpents.
All those whose conduct and vows are wicked, who are solely intent upon their own self-interest, indeed delude all people by displaying [false] fruits. (71)
In the Kali age, there will be men who perform rites with mantras, practitioners of malevolent magic, slayers, as well as those who are merciless, deceitful, rogues, and murderers. (72)
Eaters of flesh and drinkers of wine, they were related to me only by birth and connected to me only by outward marks; yet for the sake of wealth, they committed murder against me. (73)

In the Kali age, people will be identical in dress and conduct yet devoid of respectful treatment; they will be betrayers of trust, slayers of friends, and treacherous toward those who have sought their protection.
In the Kali age, there will be those who destroy their homes, those who destroy their families, and those who destroy their own kin;
those who destroy righteousness, those who destroy the righteous, and those who kill their mothers and fathers.

Those who have killed their daughters-in-law, those who have killed their daughters, those who have killed their sisters, and those who have murdered their brothers—those who are devoid of the sixteen and other purificatory rites (saṃskāras) and are excluded from the period of ritual impurity (sūtaka). ||76||

In the Kali age, men and women will be devoid of purity, devoid of ritual bathing, and devoid of vows; they will be without the sacred thread and excluded from the rites of marriage and other ceremonies.

Those who lack the sacred fires, those who lack the sacrificial pavilion and its like, those who are devoid of burnt offerings (homa), those who are bereft of good conduct, and those who are devoid of domestic propriety; ||78||
In the Kali age, all [beings]—whether Rākṣasas, Brāhmaṇas, Yakṣas, Gandharvas, Kinnaras, or gods—consume what is forbidden to eat and become eaters of everything. (79)
In the Kali age, outcastes and Piśācas indeed become equal;
they cause fear for one another and bring about each other's destruction.
Shameless, devoid of modesty, and stripped of all reverence, the youths, maidens, and women indulged in their desires as they pleased. (8.1)
The maidens, adorned with garments revealing their hair, private parts, and navels, as well as the female cutters and the male cutters, [are employed] for secret rites in public view. (82)
In the Kali age, people will have bodies only a cubit in height, clothed in layers of hair, and trees will likewise be only five cubits tall.
There was no king, nor the state of subjects, neither one to be governed nor a ruler;
there were no houses for residence, nor halls for the preparation of food. (84)
There was no one in the house to provide food, nor anyone to provide water to drink;
there was no bed for the woman, nor did the husband dwell in the house. (85)
In the Kali age, yoga performed according to the sequential stages does not indeed endure;
a woman of eight years has a moderate flow, while death occurs at the end of twelve years in the Kali age. (86)
Fifty-five [women], including those who were pregnant, resided there without the village;
at that time, like a female monkey, the woman in childbirth was without a midwife.
Then, on earth, she gives birth to a boy even without sexual intercourse;
at that time, Gaurī lasts for two years, and at the end of those two years, she becomes Rohiṇī.
In three years she becomes a maiden, and at four years she reaches puberty.
From this point onward, she becomes pregnant and gives birth in the sixth month. ||89||
Birth occurs for two years, and the menses appear but once, remaining stable for a moment; death happens in the span of a single ghaṭikā, and life does not endure for long. (2.84.90)
Their offspring roam the earth like young deer;
they are nourished by the essence of grain, while their mothers provide milk from their wings.
In the Kali age, there is no mention of the father's name, nor anywhere the mother's name;
there is the loss of initiation, the loss of the guru, the loss of mantras, and no festivals.
In the Kali age, there is no assembly of gods or men;
in the Kali age, there is no renown of "this is my lineage," nor is there any family bond.
At the end of the Kali age, the word "father" and the word "teacher" will no longer endure;
there will be no king, no royal laws, no punishments, and no ruler.
There is no god, no temple, no tradition, no scripture, nor any ancient vow; there is neither celibacy nor asceticism there, for only the state of being a householder is recognized. (95)

In that time, there was no renunciation, nor indeed virtue or righteousness; neither widowhood nor the state of being husbandless existed, for in the Kali age, righteousness does not exist at all. (96)
In that Kali age, neither goodness nor chastity exists as true dharma;
sensual desire is the supreme dharma, and self-restraint is merely hypocrisy. (97)
Men and women were of equal appearance, equal dress, and equal conduct;
they shared an equal sense of importance and received equal portions from the common store. ||98||
In the Kali age, people whose conduct is shrouded in darkness will have no reckoning of years, nor even a reckoning of numbers, nor indeed any application to the study of knowledge. 99.
For at the end of the Kali age, the Lord, the Sovereign King, manifests;
having utterly destroyed the power of Kali, he establishes the state of Kṛta.
"O wife, thus have I described to you the dharmas in the four ages, and how they all manifest among embodied beings through the conjunction of time. (101)
At the end of the day, the terrestrial sphere (golaka), being indeed struck by the Creator,
becomes diminished in size due to its velocity and its rotation.
At that time, indeed, the days and even the nights undergo shortening;
the ghaṭikās, kalās, kāṣṭhās, months, and divisions of time likewise diminish.
Everything moves toward diminution, and with the exhaustion of the lifespan, it undergoes transformation;
thereafter, decline and dissolution occur at the end of the day.
"O Rādhikā, we shall go to Ailavila; then truth will have its refuge in you. Thus Pulastya spoke to his beloved wife.
Having heard those words regarding the duties of the age, the virtuous Ailavilā said to her husband:
"In what [age] do all the duties of the yugas exist, such that there is a grandson like this? (1.06)
"And I wish to see right here, O Sage, that which rests upon the four yugas.
Pulastya said to his own wife, "So be it."
"By this connection, the Blessed One will also meet with my grandson.
Realizing this gain, the virtuous wife [of Viśravas] [conceived] a son.
She chose him who bestows the yoga of Kṛṣṇa, and thus he became Rāvaṇa; Ailavilā performed penance directed toward Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
The eternal Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Blessed Lord himself,
came to the Sahya mountain to behold the ascetic penance of Ailavila.

Thus ends the eighty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Duties of the Four Yugas as Spoken by Pulastya, the Granting of Boons to Ailavila, and the Practice of Austerity," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Ailavilā, the wife of Pulastya,
performed a difficult penance for the sake of obtaining a son who would possess the virtues of a bull among men throughout the four ages.
The beginningless Śrī Svāminārāyaṇa Kṛṣṇanarāyaṇa,
assuming the form of a brāhmaṇa, was on the peak of the Sahyādri mountain in her hermitage.
Abundantly adorned with matted hair, bark garments, and ashes, and devoted to wearing garlands and reciting prayers,
he approached and stood near a spot shaded by the base of a tree.
Subsisting constantly on roots, tubers, and fruits, and likewise performing the three daily ablutions,
he was like some charming young son of a seer in appearance.
Having arrived, he stays there for a while, and then goes elsewhere to hide;
in one place becoming a parrot, and likewise in another becoming a cuckoo.
Sometimes as a peacock, sometimes as a swan, or even as a deer,
and at other times assuming the form of Agastya, he would watch that asceticism.
In some places he became Viśravas, and in others he took the forms of the wives of Pulastya;
and in some instances, he indeed assumed the forms of the sons of Pulastya.
Lord Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa repeatedly gazes upon her penance.
Rādhikā said: "O Kṛṣṇa, what is the merit of women likewise?"
How indeed did the Blessed Lord, the Master Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, assume various forms in her presence? || 9 ||
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said to Rādhā: "O Brahmā, [teach] your son Pulastya:
'Om, obeisance to Śrī Svāmī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, svāhā! (2.85.10)
Thus he imparted the great mantra; then he, in turn, imparted it to his own beloved, Ailavilā, and she chanted that mantra day and night.
Lord Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, whose heart was drawn by her chanting and who is won over by devotion, appeared before her in that very form.
O Rādhikā, at that time I beheld him in the form of a black deer; wandering about, he was Hari-Kṛṣṇa, my beloved, the Lord of Śrī, the husband.
Beholding the asceticism of Ailavila and hearing his recitation, she shone forth;
for she was indeed the wife of Pulastya, wearing matted hair and bark garments.
The virtuous female ascetic strives to attain the Supreme Lord;
dwelling in the sky, she constructs an altar upon the earth using clay.
Having placed the sacred fire there, she performs her morning worship;
then [she worships] Rudra, Satī, Kṛṣṇa, Lakṣmī, and Aja (Brahmā), the son of Savitṛ.
Having daily worshipped the Sun, Prabhā, Gaṇeśa, and the virtuous goddesses with excellent offerings, she indeed performs a hundred-fold recitation of mantras with a rosary.
Then, having brought fruits and other offerings at midday, he personally presents the food offering (naivedya) along with water to Hari, and remains standing while performing penance.
Having gazed at the sun while standing on one leg, she remains steady;
then, having bathed until evening, she performs the nightly lamp-offering.
At night he performs his worship, chanting "Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa," and after midnight,
he sleeps for only a single ghaṭikā.
Having risen and meditated upon Hari, she performed the worship of Hari in the Brahma-muhūrta,
just as was her daily custom, subsisting on bulbs, roots, and fruits.
Having practiced in that manner for exactly one year, he thereafter subsisted only on water;
from sunrise until sunset, he remained standing constantly.
Thus, remaining steady on her big toe alone, she performed penance for a full year;
thereafter, maintaining that steadiness day and night, she remained fixed in that posture.
Subsisting on air and worshipping Śrī Hari with her heart,
her body then became like wood, as motionless as a log, within a single year.
Where birds perched, there insects built an earthen nest;
thus, in four years, she became covered by an anthill.
In her fifth year, however, the growth of stalks upon her head and the sprouting of grass occurred; she was seen to be no human being.
Then Brahmā, Hara, Viṣṇu, Sūrya, Gaṇapati, and the goddesses, led by Satī, arrived—those who had been moved by the excellence of Satī’s ascetic penance. (27)
The goddesses cleared away the clumps of grass and other debris from the mound of earth,
while Gaṇeśa and Sūrya likewise removed the soil.
There, Brahmā gave auspicious water for sprinkling with his joined palms;
Rudra, moreover, caused the movement of the vital breaths through that sprinkling.
Viṣṇu infused consciousness into her entire body;
thereupon she arose, attained awareness, and bowed before the gods standing in front of her.
"Oṃ, obeisances unto you, Śrī Svāmī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa; svāhā!
Thus spoke the virtuous woman, unperturbed, to her own Lord who was protecting her.
She remembered the Lord of the gods of gods, the glorious Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
The gods said, "Speak, O virtuous lady; what dwells in your mind? (32)
"We shall grant you your desired boon right here; choose today, do not delay.
Thus addressed, she spoke for a boon from Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
I choose [this] alone and nothing else; O gods, may there always be well-being for you!
For you have been constantly honored by me, since that indeed is dharma. (34)
For the sake of protecting and sustaining the world, may there be well-being for you who have come here;
and may there always be well-being and likewise prosperity for you, O goddesses. (35)
Having spoken thus, he offered a welcome with a deeply gratified heart and meditated upon Śrī Svāmī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Lord of Śrī. (36)
At that moment, the illustrious Lord Hari, who had been present there in the form of a tree situated within a pillar, himself manifested from the anthill.
The Lord has two arms, the color of a campaka flower, and is resplendent with golden ornaments; he possesses a divine form, pervaded by the brilliance of ten million times ten million suns. 38.
Richly adorned with divine golden ornaments, resplendent in celestial garments,
and beautified by garlands of divine jewel-strings, he is the beloved of Śrī.
Richly adorned with the splendor of divine bracelets, wearing a divine crown and earrings,
he shone with a divine Kaustubha gem, a girdle, rings, and a staff.
He is worshipped by Rādhā, Ramā, Prabhā, Pārvatī, Haṃsā, and Mañjulā;
he is worshipped by Saguṇā, Māṇikī, Śāntā, Vijayā, and Lalitā. ||41||
Accompanied by his attendants, including Hemanta, Bhagavaddeva, Prakāśakeśava, and others, he remained there as a young man. ||42||
With his limbs proportioned to his form, Hari stood there smiling, holding a betel-roll in his hand and chewing the betel leaf.
Touching her head with both hands and pronouncing a blessing,
he looked toward the gods while requesting a boon for her sake.
Lord Hari was directly beheld by the gods; he was praised with hymns by those chanting the Sāman, and worshipped with supreme devotion; thereafter, the lords of the gods stood [before him]. 45.
That virtuous woman worshipped her husband Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Brahman and the Highest Lord; she offered leaves, flowers, water, and her devotion to the Lord of Śrī.
He requested a boon from him: "O Blessed One, may I have grandsons who are the refuge of the qualities of the four ages, so that through them there may be union with you. (47)

And because of the devotion of your grandson and his family—a devotion unattainable by others—[this has come about] swiftly for you, despite the fault of the age, their own defects, and even their hatred. (48)
Since devotion and constant remembrance [of You] are even greater than affection, liberation for embodied beings does not occur at all without Your yoga. 49.
You are difficult to attain through other means for a long time, yet you are attained swiftly through hatreds;
death at your hands will certainly grant liberation.
"Thus, O Lord, for the sake of my family, I desire this boon; grant it to me. Upon hearing these words, Keśava said, "So be it. (5.1)
Then, by the command of Hari, the gods departed after being duly honored; Ailavilā, having abandoned her ascetic penance, enjoyed the grace of Hari.
Having bathed and performed purification, she partook of water, fruit, juice, and honey.
The virtuous wife of Pulastya questioned her husband Kṛṣṇa.
Ailavilā said:
"O Blessed One, you who know all things, you ought to sever my doubt in this matter;
no one else is capable of resolving the doubts of a woman. (54)

Some [practiced] meditation, others the bull [the vow of celibacy], others solitude as the means for yoga; some practiced celibacy, austerity, devotion to one's husband, and others the vow of a devoted wife.
Truth, renunciation, non-violence, chastity, as well as self-surrender, charity, compassion, and study—these others likewise praise. (56)
Pilgrimage to sacred fords, restraint of the senses, association with the virtuous, total surrender, seeking refuge, dedication to the guru, and dispassion; ||57||
Their knowledge consists of Brahman; tell me, O Lord, what is the highest good?
Or if there exists anything else that is secret, you should speak of that.
Having heard the words of Cailavilā, Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa spoke the supreme divine truth, which bestows the highest good and is higher than the highest. (59)
For the benefit of all living beings, this was set forth by those of old and those even more ancient;
it is inexpressible, containing all hidden meanings—a knowledge excluded by the ignorant.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa Svāmī said: "The most supreme and most secret sacred field (kṣetra), which bestows the highest abode,
is my own field called Akṣara, wherein lies Kuṅkumavāpikā."
Because she is the dwelling place for all embodied beings, she enables them to cross the ocean of saṃsāra;
she is delightful with the Aśvapaṭṭa lake and adorned by the hermitage of Lomaśa.
There, in Ailavila, my devotees dwell, established in my vow;
those great-souled ones have taken refuge in supreme devotion to me.
That which is the best of all holy fords (tīrtha) and the best of all sacred fields (kṣetra),
the best of all places— my field known as the Imperishable (akṣara).
For it is not at all attached to the surface of the earth, but resides in the space of consciousness;
the undivine do not see it, but the liberated see it with their heart.
That place is most dear to me; it is secret and swiftly grants liberation, where my devotees dwell and indeed worship me alone. (66)
The men and women who go there also proceed to my own abode;
having merely seen other dwellings, they enter into me alone.
Whatever is given, recited, performed, endeavored, practiced as austerity, meditated upon, offered in sacrifice, heard, served, fed, or known—all that becomes inexhaustible therein. ||68||
Whatever accumulated sin has been committed over thousands of previous births—
all of it is swiftly brought to total destruction for one who has entered this imperishable field (kṣetra).
Mānavas, however, consist of men, women, and those of mixed castes who are exceedingly sinful; they are born of evil wombs, wicked, and produced from the union of mixed classes. ||2.85.70||
Mlecchas, those born of Caṇḍālas, insects, ants, wild animals, domestic beasts, birds, reptiles, grasses, and trees—[all these are likewise]. ||7 1||
Even creepers born of insentient matter, if they die in this imperishable field, become adorned with the moon as their forehead mark and possess great elephants and other such mounts.
In my beautiful, divine, imperishable state, those who enter find final liberation;
for no one who dies in that imperishable state goes to hell, even if they were a sinner.
Having obtained my grace, they all go to the imperishable state;
what more need be said here regarding the place of Cailavila, which is my own domain? (74)
Knowing that liberation is extremely difficult to attain and that saṃsāra is most terrifying,
even one who has destroyed rebirth through knowledge may dwell in my imperishable abode.
For one who has met with disaster anywhere, this place indeed bestows liberation; through its grace, sin is burned away, and by residing here, one attains divinity. (76)
From the sight of me, liberation arises in my imperishable state;
through union with me, great liberation arises in my supreme state.
Those devoid of merit do not see it, for their eyes are veiled by the film of illusion;
shrouded in darkness, they do not behold my divine, imperishable field.
They indeed repeatedly enter the body that bears feces, urine, and semen;
yet the embodied soul, even when being struck, should enter [the path] despite hundreds of obstacles.
The syllable *akṣara* is the supreme field all around the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake;
he goes to that highest abode, having gone to which one does not grieve.
The supreme field, my own abode, which is free from birth, death, and old age—that has been declared for those who desire liberation and do not die again. 8.1
Neither by gifts, nor by austerities, nor by sacrifices, nor even by knowledge is that supreme goal attained which is obtained in the Imperishable. 82.
They were of various complexions and discolored, such as the Caṇḍālas and others who are loathsome;
their bodies were filled with sins and joined with the most base transgressions. ||83||
For them, the syllable is the potent medicine, the field, and the supreme state;
that imperishable syllable is the highest knowledge, that imperishable syllable is the supreme state. ||84||
That supreme state is the Imperishable; the Imperishable is the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama).
Those who, having taken the lifelong vow of initiation, dwell in that Imperishable.
Having received supreme knowledge from me, they go to my highest abode:
Prabhāsa, Svarṇanagarī, Vastrāpatha, and the Narmadā. ||86||
Nārāyaṇasara, Puṣkara, the Kaurava region, Gaṅgā, Badarikā, Śālagrāma, and also Śrīśaila. ||87||
The Himalaya, Kedāra, Gayā, and Gokarṇa;
the Kṛṣṇā, Godāvarī, Sindhu, Gomatī, and Brahmaputrī. ||88||
Also the Nārāyaṇī river, the Vijñaturīyaka lake, the Tūṅgānīka lake, the Nyāsa lake, and likewise the Caṇḍa lake. ||89||
The river Naṣṭajarā, the Red Sea, and the Blue Ocean;
also Nīparā, Dīnayūpā, and the army; and the great lake Mahābṛhat.
There is also the circular Antārkivartula lake situated one above the other;
likewise Pannāmnī, Kālimā, Yāneśī, and Śvetavāridhi. ||9 1 ||
Mount Uralādi, Lake Mānasa, the Brahma-lake, Bālakṛṣṇa-lake, and likewise Dvikala-lake. ||92||
Also Aṅgaśikṣāṅgikā, Murānadī, Turunadī, Eitānadī, Mikāṅgā, and likewise the river Irāvatī. || 93 ||
And Gaṅgā also, having entered the fire, reached the great lake named Sābhra;
these indeed are the holy places renowned upon the earth. ||94||
They constantly flow toward you at the Aśvapaṭṭa lake;
those who die there do not attain supreme liberation as they do at Akṣara.
In the sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpikā, I, the Supreme Lord, am manifest;
having taken up the Brahma-lake, I abide there eternally. 96.
The Brahmahrada destroys the sins committed over infinite births;
elsewhere, the Gaṅgā, śrāddha, charity, recitation, and vows are easily obtained. (97)
In the sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpikā, all of that is exceedingly difficult to attain—whether one is a sinner, a rogue, or even an unrighteous person. (98)
Having attained that imperishable state, one purifies seven generations of one's lineage;
one should constantly sacrifice, offer oblations, give gifts, and likewise perform worship.
But for the devotee in this imperishable field, the fruit is of infinite quality;
having gone there, those devotees who worship and praise me [attain it].
Those who are completely liberated from all sins should be known as my attendants, except for those [liberated] through sacrifice, knowledge, renunciation, or yoga. || 10.1 ||
That supreme state is attained after a thousand births;
however, those who dwell in the Imperishable attain it in a single birth.
In that regard, I am the yoga, the austerity, the knowledge, and the vow practiced without interruption;
having attained me, there is no further goal for my devotees. (103)
That very secret is considered the most excellent among secrets, bestowing the highest welfare upon those established in knowledge and meditation who desire supreme bliss. 104.
There, in my field consisting of the syllables, I bestow the mantra;
that which is the supreme reality is I, and that field is mine.

Whether the vital breath (asus) departs from the middle of the eyebrows, the middle of the navel, the heart, or even the head—from whichever [place] it goes, one is liberated here into the Imperishable (akṣara). || 106 ||
I, the beginningless Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, dwell herein;
by taking refuge in me, even those of extreme sin attain the supreme goal. 107.
Among all the Nārāyaṇas, I am the supreme lord and the most excellent;
likewise, there are other Nārāyaṇas, as well as Śambhu and others who are indeed Vaiṣṇavas.
All the abodes as well, the millions of liberated ones dwelling in those abodes,
the preeminent lords of the cosmic egg, and the millions of deities beginning with the gods who are the tirthas— [all these were present].
We dwell there in my imperishable field, around Aśvasara; there is Kuṅkumavāpikā, which is of the nature of Brahman, the city of the liberated and the virtuous.
Those whose intellects are impaired by evil do not perceive its divine nature;
for them, it is impossible to behold my imperishable form on the surface of the earth.
Those of meritorious conduct remember this city with their divine eye,
and those perfected in yoga perceive it even while dwelling in another world.
"Let those who desire liberation come to dwell in this place;
for those who die on this path, there is no rebirth. (113)

Whether one is a yogi or not a yogi, whether a sinner or the most virtuous of men—one should not act merely out of the talk of the world, nor from the words of one's father, nor even from the advice of a guru. || 1.14 ||
And one should directly cause the auspicious intellect, which has entered the field of the Imperishable, to ascend;
[one should visit] the abode of Kuṅkumavāpikā and the immersion in the waters of Aśvasaras. 1.15.
O Rādhikā, having thus awakened Cailavilā, the Blessed One became silent for a moment; she too, upon hearing this, was struck with wonder.

Thus ends the eighty-fifth chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Imperishable Syllable as Told by the Lord Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa to Ailavilā," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Listen, O Rādhikā; later Ailavilā spoke to Hari:
"O Blessed One, I have a desire to behold that imperishable abode."
In the month of Caitra, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, having placed her upon Garuḍa, traveled through the sky from the Sahya mountain to the Imperishable Abode (Akṣara).
The sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpikā is divine and designated as imperishable;
it possesses the splendor of the abode of Being-Consciousness-Bliss, and its inhabitants are eternally blissful.
It was pervaded by beings of divine form, frequented by gods, ancestors, and others,
and endowed with the Aśvapaṭṭaka lake mingled with the waters of the ten Brahmahradas.
It was a place where thousands of groups of sages had made their dwelling, brilliantly radiant,
the purifier of purifiers, and the most excellent of all sacred fords (tīrthas).
The supreme bestower of liberation among those that grant liberation, it destroys all sins;
it is adorned with hundreds of thousands of palaces and forest creepers.
It was surrounded by thousands of divine trees and pleasure gardens,
and was fragrant with fruits and flowers from auspicious groves and reservoirs of water.
It was enriched with wish-fulfilling trees and illuminated by the radiance of the *cintāmaṇi* gems;
it was constantly thrived over by sages through their sacrifices, Vedic studies, and devotions.
It was inhabited by beloved guests who had attained the abode of Brahman,
and it was adorned with auspicious marriage-thread ceremonies performed for the beloved consorts of Śrī Hari.
It was endowed with lakes of nectar, frequented by all created beings,
and filled with righteous Vedic scholars skilled in the language of the gods.
It was adorned with a thousand long banners shining with golden staffs,
and it was made resplendent by seven-storied mansions and peaked palaces.
Where men and women fly up by means of celestial chariots,
and where even birds such as parrots, who are conversant with refined Sanskrit, go to heaven.
Even cows, elephants, and other animals speak the Vedic language where the twice-born reside,
and where the blazing sacrificial fires are maintained upon the altar-ground.
Where gifts are bestowed day and night by the guardians of creation, and where hundreds of thousands of pilgrims dwell, destined for liberation. (14)
There were thousands of assembly halls for listeners and speakers,
as well as hundreds and thousands of temples containing images of the gods.
In the sky, there are golden trees appearing like mountain peaks, adorned with beautiful golden jars;
they are seen as the forest groves of householders. (16)
The hermitages of the most excellent sages shine like those of the denizens of heaven, where millions of ascetics dwell all around Aśvasaras. (17)
Where virtuous men perform devotion to Kṛṣṇa for the sake of the worlds, and where virtuous women, beloved of Brahman, are always devoted to the vow of Brahman; (18)
They dwell for the sake of serving Kṛṣṇa, taking refuge in the imperishable field;
they become performers of the sacrifice of knowledge, the sacrifice of Brahman, and the sacrifice of charity.
Sacrifices of service, sacrifices of liberation, and sacrifices of contentment take place there;
and the brahmin-sages dwell there constantly engaged in sacrifices of sacred discourse.
Vow-sacrifices, session-sacrifices, and the established rules for their conclusion;
pilgrimage-sacrifices, and the constant rituals of chanting the names of Hari. (21)
Where the methods for propitiating the gods are practiced constantly, and where embodied beings dwell with divine and pure hearts. (22)
O Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa Svāmin, proclaimer of the Supreme Brahman;
O Kṛṣṇa, son of Gopāla, the joy of Kambharā; O Mādhava! 23.
"O Lord of Śrī, Beloved of Rādhikā, Soul of All, be dear to me!"—worshipping Bālakṛṣṇa in this way, they dwell there. (24)
In the delightful hermitage of Lomaśa, which was presided over by the beloved of Brahmā and others, he saw even animals free from enmity. (25)
The forms dwelling therein, resplendent with abundant brilliance,
were indeed beheld by her as she traveled through that sky seated in the vehicle.
Having performed a circumambulation of the sacred field by means of that celestial chariot,
she descended into the temple of Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa.
Together with Śrīsvāmin, he went toward Śrī Kambharā;
he beheld her, worshipped her, paid homage to her, and bowed down before her. ||28||
Then she went to Gopālakṛṣṇa and bowed at his feet;
thereafter, having approached her Lord who was seated upon an elephant, she accompanied him on his journey.
She served the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Brahman who had assumed a child’s form and exerted himself in his tasks, by massaging His body.
Then, like a maidservant, she massaged the feet of Śrī Hari;
thereafter, she went to the holy sites situated at Aśvasaras and bathed there according to the prescribed rites.
He drank the water from the saffron pond and placed it upon his head;
then, having bowed to Śrī Lomaśa and worshipped him according to the prescribed rites, [he departed]. ||32||
All the maidens who were dear to Brahmā gathered together and went to the temple;
there, Bālakṛṣṇa had Elavilā feed him milk-rice (pāyasa).
He caused them to drink the sweet water that was the nectar of his own feet;
he purified his own devotees and delighted them with his true being.
Then, having beheld that land of the learned,
the virtuous woman, desiring to remain there, constantly prayed to the Supreme Soul for a permanent dwelling.
In the month of Caitra, Hari gave her two identical and auspicious forms;
he then sent Chāyā toward Pulastya.
He always protected Ailavilā, who possessed a divine form, near him;
she was a virtuous woman, observing the vow of Brahma, endowed with the dharma of the righteous, and truly chaste.
Then her boon became fruitful;
Viśravas had four wives who increased his lineage. (38)
Puṣpotkaṭā, Vākā, and Kaikasī, who possessed a divine complexion— Devavarṇinī gave birth to Vaiśravaṇa as her eldest son, a Yakṣa.
Kaikasī gave birth to a son, Rāvaṇa, the lord of the rākṣasas,
as well as Kumbhakarṇa, Śūrpaṇakhā, and Vibhīṣaṇa.
Puṣpotkaṭā also gave birth to auspicious sons for Viśravas:
Mahodara, Prahasta, Mahāpārśva, and Khara. (41)
Kumbhīnasī, Śṛṅgī, and hundreds of other daughters,
as well as Vātāpi, Triśiras, Vidyujjihva, and Dūṣaṇa.
There were also one hundred cruel daughters born of the lineage of Paulastya, as well as ten thousand who possessed the nature of Rākṣasas and likewise took refuge in the dharmas of all the yugas.
They are endowed with austerity, endowed with charity, and endowed with passion;
they are possessed of impurity, and are characterized by both truth and untruth; they are filled with strength and pride.
Furthermore, Hari himself assumes the form of Rāma for the sake of destroying those who rely on the dharma of the Kali age, and from that he slays the rākṣasas.
Having washed away their sins, they attain residence in Vaikuṇṭha,
along with those born in their lineage, through the power of the boon granted by Ailavila.
In age after age, the black discus destroys the powerful Rākṣasas;
O Rādhikā, for me, it is either the discus, or water, or a leaf of Tulasī. ||47||
Or by whomsoever this state has been attained, he becomes liberated—be he a yakṣa, a rākṣasa, a dānava, or even a daitya. (48)
Then Viśravas went to the island of Siṃhala along with his lineage;
there, in the place of austerity where Hari himself dwells, Ailavila performed penance. 49.
He undertook the protection of that [place] and even tested his ascetic power;
that sacred site was the Ailavileya peak of the Sahya mountain range.
It was filled with water, beautified by a water-pool and a spring, purifying, and imbued with the dust from the feet of Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa. ||51||
There, Hari, whose essence is the trunk of the tree, became the bestower of liberation;
indeed, he remained for one year, while Śuka and the others likewise remained for one year each.
Those who assumed the forms of Hari and belonged to his lineage were indeed Vaiṣṇavas;
born of the women of the Sahya mountain and the Sahya-winged [gods], they were the descendants of Hari’s lineage.
Divine beings of celestial form dwell there, endowed with great happiness;
there the purifying trees likewise originate from the lineage of Hari.
Where there is never even a trace of a drought, as on the Sahya mountain;
where there is no forest fire, nor any harm from predatory beasts.
There dwell white elephants with four tusks and great height,
born of the lineage of Hari, who serve as the vehicles of the gods.
And there dwell auspicious śarabhas, born of the lineage of Hari, who are upright, of brilliant white color, possessing two trunks, and belonging to the species of lions. ||57||
There were white, purifying serpents marked with svastikas;
those born of the Harivaṃśa lineage were venomless, and there were white birds of the peacock species.
They exist in divine forms, for they are indeed born from the lineage of Hari;
Sahyādri is in every way the best of holy places, as are its forests. (59)
O Rādhā, for five years these [verses] become sanctified through union with Hari;
by reciting or hearing them, they bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation.

Thus ends the eighty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of Ailavilā’s Arrival at Kuṅkumavāpī, Her Two Forms, and the Residence of the Descendants of Harivaṃśa on the Sahya Mountain," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Listen, O Rādhikā; devotees of Hari accept His true virtues, whereas the wicked, having superimposed faults upon those virtues, accept only His negative qualities.
The son of the Rākṣasa Khara, who was the son of Viśravas,
had a son named Adharmajīva who lived by moving through the sky.
With a crooked waist and a broken back, he has the defect known as "godhā" on his cheek;
he has eyes like matted locks, is always afflicted by asthma, is full of foul odors, and is fond of children. (3)
One who is defiled by sin, whose conduct is excessively wicked, and who betrays trust;
one who strikes his mother with his feet because she has grown old, and one who says "my mother is dead"—these are killers of their mother.
He had the voice of an owl, was black in color, and his hair was like a peacock's tail; he bore a mark on his back, had blunt ears, protruding tusks, and was exceedingly envious.
Causing suffering as soon as he was born, he became a tormentor of children;
once, he went to the bank of a river to play with other boys.
In the dwellings of leather-workers and in the houses of outcastes, as well as in empty child-protection sites, the elder sisters have gone for their task.
There, having beaten the children, she devoured them in that house;
she consumed dog meat, drank liquor, and drank water.
Then, having gathered together, the outcastes forcibly seized and bound him,
and cast him into a foul-smelling pit of alkaline mud.
Covered there by a stone slab within a jar, he remained in that vessel day and night; indeed, in that jar, he acquired the very scent of the jar.
For half a month, while tormented by hunger and thirst, he wandered for the sake of preserving his life, [drinking] water used for washing hides and even the mud from tanneries. (11)
That evildoer, a Rākṣasa by birth who ate the food of a Cāṇḍāla, ate insects produced in a pot. || 12 ||
Dwelling in a leather water-skin and subsisting on leather mud, he is a killer of his mother and a crocodile; who could be more sinful than him? (13)
O Rādhikā, such a person of unrighteous life was a great demon by name;
he was clothed in the dyed garments of the outcaste leather-workers.
Having been expelled, castrated, reviled, beaten, and likewise emasculated,
that wicked man remained on the island of Siṃhala at the edge of the battlefield, subsisting on forest roots.
Sometimes, having seized domestic animals, flocks of birds, or even the children of his own household,
he slaughters them and indeed devours them as well.
Once, Vibhīṣaṇa, the king of devotees and beloved of Hari,
was wandering there while chanting "Rāma," "Kṛṣṇa," and "Nārāyaṇa."
He went along that path to dwell there and to behold the forests;
it was there that he beheld the great Asura Adharmajīva.
She said: "O son, how do you remain here in this desolate place?
Come home; worship Hari, Kṛṣṇa, Nārāyaṇa, for the sake of happiness."
"Do not carry sorrow here in this dry, desolate forest.
Having heard Vibhīṣaṇa, the arrogant one spoke to his father’s eldest brother: ||2.87.20||
Who is Hari? Who is Kṛṣṇa? And who indeed is Nārāyaṇa?
I do not know him; who is he that dwells there, and why do I worship him without reflection? (21)
The devotee Vibhīṣaṇa said: "That Hari is the remover of suffering;
he is the Supreme Brahman himself, divine, and the dweller within the divine syllable."
But the Rākṣasa, who lives by unrighteousness and seizes wealth, said:
"He is a stealer of property, a stealer of women and other such things. (23)
Furthermore, Hari might be some thief who steals the prosperity of others;
for he would indeed be "Kṛṣṇa" (the Black One), meaning a sinful person who performs wicked deeds. (24)
He may become a fisherman dwelling by rivers, traveling neither on land nor in water;
or he may become a servant carrying water, or an attendant to someone else. (25)
Whether dwelling in water, this wind may become a serpent or a fish;
yet another, a great enemy of Brahman, indeed becomes a formidable foe. (26)
He is a certain divine rogue, a master of gambling, and a man of vice;
he delights in dice and snares, and he takes away the coin. (27)
And suppose there were someone of sinful nature living in a gambling house;
Vibhīṣaṇa, however, spoke to him as the Supreme Self, the Supreme Lord. (28)
O son, this very Lord is Puruṣottama, the Lord of lords; he shines as the sovereign of the liberated in the supreme abode.
The Rākṣasa, who lived by unrighteousness, said: "O father, this is not so;
he himself personally takes delight there in that drink born of liquor. (2.87.30)
Greedy for the drinking of intoxicants and the like, he becomes a supreme drunkard;
as a lord, he becomes a creator of suffering for others who are wretched people. (3.1)
He binds many evils and is further enveloped by darkness;
such a person is a doer of evil and is *tāmasa*. He is *Puruṣottama*. 32.
Indeed, she may have the secret mark of a woman, namely the female organ;
that Blessed One would be a woman in disguise, appearing in male attire. (33)
If one who has been struck down by the misfortunes of warriors like me, though he be a lord of lords, were unable to protect himself, [then what need is there for others? 34.
He who becomes the lord of women who have been abandoned by their husbands or driven out from their homes shall be the crest-jewel of adulterers. (35)
O Father, he dwells eternally in another’s abode or house, remaining in the home of another;
or, O Father, he may become a mendicant, deprived even of the door of his own home.
And Vibhīṣaṇa, assuming the form of a military formation, said to him:
"He is the Lord who is the cause of all incarnations and the possessor of all powers. (37)
He is the Lord of Goloka, the Lord of the realm of Vaikuṇṭha, indeed the Supreme Person, accessible to yogis, the inner self, and the bestower of liberation; worship Him. (38)
Rākṣasa, though living by unrighteous means, said: "I think he is a deceiver;
assuming various guises again and again, he acts for the purpose of deluding the world. (39)
In one place he is an actor, in another a cowherd; in one place he is like a prince, and in another he is indeed a Brahmin—a deceiver who possesses various manifestations.
In this world, for all those incarnations who perform lowly deeds, there must be some cause—an agent of low caste, born from an inferior lineage. (41)
O Father, I truly believe that whoever instigates the use of weapons or force against any living beings would indeed be a slayer. (42)
A certain sinner may become a source of great suffering by force;
indeed, he becomes a great [obstacle] within the assembly of cows and bulls in this world. (43)
Or he may be a great bull, or perhaps a bull-driver;
his dwelling may be in a dilapidated place, free from houses, huts, and the like. (44)
For a man who is a supreme enemy in the form of a Rākṣasa may indeed be approached through the seven steps by those endowed with yoga who possess similar character. 45.
Therefore, O father, I truly believe that there is some person who is not a true gentleman, for whom there is a divergence between his desires, his mind, and his inner self. (46)
Therefore, there may be a divergence in speech, whereby one becomes a betrayer of trust;
having completely cut off all liberation for the weak, he brings about their destruction. (47)
I think that some cruel person, a slayer of the weak, is doing this;
for who indeed would resort to such a wicked man, utterly devoid of the highest virtues? 48.
But Vibhīṣaṇa spoke to him—he who was wise, the refuge of virtues, a knower of the Vedas, the author of the Vedic scriptures and other works, and possessed of good character, vows, and the like. (49)

"The refuge of all dharmas, whose actions are virtuous, and who is endowed with peace—such a one who lives by unrighteousness is a demon; moreover, the wise man said that such a person does not exist. (2.87.50)
He does not understand the support, nor does he understand song at all;
he does not understand malevolent spells, nor does he understand illusion at all. (51)
Therefore, O father, he could never truly be a wise man who possesses a rope with the quality [of milk] for the purpose of milking cows. (52)
Therefore, O Father, Gopa, the locus of virtues, should indeed protect the Veda or the sacrificial altar constructed by people at the crossroads of the village. (53)
The potter knows how to fashion that [image] from stones or from clay;
indeed, he must be a skilled artisan, well-versed in the craft of making altars. (54)
For this barber, by means of his weapon, effects the shearing of hair upon the head;
he is indeed one who possesses the sharp-edged tool for cutting the enemy's hair.
Virtue is non-transgression; dharma is the vow consisting of ascetic practices such as the *kṛcchra* penance.
One who devours—that is, consumes—both of these is a destroyer of such dharma. (56)
Moreover, some person might become a mere vessel for the practice of vows and observances;
all phenomena are the nature of sacrificial animals, and one who possesses them becomes a sacrificial animal. (57)
The act of destroying a house is contrary to the duty of virtuous householders;
he who performs such an act would be a renunciant (yati) by his very nature, characterized by renunciation and the like. (58)
Whether he be dull-witted or distracted, let him be alone and filled with tranquility;
and Vibhīṣaṇa said to him: "O son, there is a Brahmin named Mādhava. (59)
He is the wearer of the sacred thread, the quencher of the heat of afflictions, the refuge of the Great Vidyās, and himself the author of the scriptures. (2.87.60)
"This performer of pilgrimages is indeed one and without a second, O Acyuta;
he is a Rākṣasa living by unrighteousness, for he would not be a Brāhmaṇa. (6.1)
But he who seizes a bird like a hunter shall therefore become some hunter, a bird-killer, or a beast. (62)
Mādhava might become one who approaches his mother, or some [man] whose offspring are like cattle—
[such is the state] of him who has no restrainer and likewise no husband.
There might be someone wandering in the forest, deprived of both mother and father;
and from here, a bird arrived in the very vicinity of that sacrifice. (64)
If one holds it for the purpose of eating, he will indeed become a bird-eater;
through afflictions, torments, and excesses, he becomes a destroyer of the world.
Therefore, anyone who causes such confusion would be a murderer;
[one should avoid] great spells, spells of desire, and those that cause eradication or destruction. (66)
O Father, if he knows her to be a woman who causes death or delusion, then he would indeed become an outcaste, a Cāṇḍāla, or a defiled man. (67)
Furthermore, this person is a creator of deception within the scriptures;
for whoever is a deceiver cannot be a true author of scripture. (68)
Wandering alone in the forest and the wilderness, deprived of his family,
he may be solitary and destitute, or perhaps one who has shaved his head at a sacred ford (tīrtha).
Wealth does not diminish when given in charity; rather, O Father, he becomes poor who is devoid of the dharma of the virtuous, being a hypocrite, a slanderer, and a wicked person.
A hidden thief and an increaser of women's fickleness, he is a wearer of disguises who deludes the wives of countless men. (71)
He becomes a maker of invisibility for the gopīs, a performer of perfected mantras, a fulfiller of the desires of amorous women, and a doer of what is otherwise unjust. ||72||
A destroyer of the Dharma and a destroyer of his own family, he is indeed attached to vulgar sights;
he is a mine of defects such as anger and greed, and a treasure-trove of ignorance. (73)
Devoid of conventional conduct, lacking intelligence, and excessively dark in nature, he may be a certain animal-bound soul who abducts girls and is fond of children. (74)
Whether he be such or otherwise, what need have I for him?
I cannot endure his divine or non-divine qualities in any way whatsoever. (75)
O Father, there is no one else for me to meditate upon or to worship;
I am the most excellent among them, and there is no one more excellent than I. (76)
Then Vibhīṣaṇa said: "O son, do not insult him;
he is the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of Śrī Kamalā. (77)
The Lord of all, the Supreme Ruler, the inner witness, and the controller—
he indeed is Hari, who is capable of acting, not acting, or acting otherwise.
He exists in the form of a child; worship Him with your whole being, my son.
Divine qualities reside within Him, each one of which indeed bestows liberation. (79)
Truthfulness, purity, compassion, forbearance, renunciation, contentment, straightforwardness, tranquility, self-control, austerity, equanimity, endurance, detachment, and sacred learning. (2.87.80)
Knowledge, detachment, sovereignty, heroism, splendor, strength, memory, independence, skill, luster, fortitude, and likewise gentleness. ||8.1||
Boldness, humility, good character, endurance, vigor, strength, majesty, profundity, steadfastness, faith, fame, self-respect, and freedom from egoism; ||| 82 ||
Having rendered assistance, non-malice, lack of worldly striving, possessionlessness, friendliness, and omniscience—these qualities exist in the Supreme Self. (83)
The Rākṣasa, living by unrighteous means, said: "I do not think they possess those virtues;
I consider him to be a eunuch, devoid of enthusiasm for action. (84)
Devoid of virtue, wealth, and desire, inactive and powerless, he lives off the fortune of others and covets the prosperity of others. ||85||
I believe that even those who travel on wrong paths exist right there;
therefore, father, you ought not to speak of his virtues to me.
O Rādhikā, in this very manner, this demon who lives by unrighteousness spoke more than a hundred faults regarding Hari to his father.
Then Vibhīṣaṇa, enraged, struck him with a mace;
and Amṛta fled from Siṃhaladvīpa at that moment.
Having become a deceitful man, he came to Saurāṣṭra, to a place on the earth known as Trivaṭa, on the bank of the Śatruñjaya river. (89)
Having established his residence and wearing the garb of an ascetic, that wicked man, a hater of the virtuous, dwelt there while harboring enmity toward Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa. (2.87.90)
Having become a wicked bearer of the banner of Dharma, he deceived many people regarding the primordial Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the glorious Supreme Lord. 91.
Engaging in enmity through his words and instilling atheism in the world,
he arrived at the sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpī with his life already forfeit.
Having gone to the hermitage of Lomaśa, he censured the Supreme Lord;
then Śrī Śaṅkara, having heard this, spoke to his attendant Bhairava. (93)
O Bhairava, by means of these [powers], slay that wicked asura who lives by unrighteousness;
indeed, let the piśācas cast him into hell according to his own deeds.
Thus addressed, Bhairava took up his trident and went with the Piśācas; seizing him alive, he bound him with leather thongs. (95)
Then, in that sacrificial arena upon the ground covered with excrement, the Piśācas cast filth and voided urine. (96)
All [the gods] slew the stubborn asura Mūḍhamāra;
they cut off his limbs and cast him into the waters of the Lāvaṇa ocean.
"Indeed, they were haters of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa;
therefore, by means of a rope-tether, [they were bound] within the tree where the vulture dwells. (98)
They tied him to a branch, and he hung there with his face turned downward;
meanwhile, the excrement of vultures, crows, and other birds fell directly into his mouth.
In this manner, the illustrious Bhairava inflicted punishment upon the asura for two months;
thereafter, overcome by hunger and thirst, he indeed perished from his life-force.
That asura, who lived by unrighteousness, went to the abode of Yama;
there he fell into the Kumbhīpāka hell for a thousand years.
Then, in that very place, Lord Bhairava bathed in the Aśvasarovara lake for the purpose of washing away the sins arising from the defect of contact with him.
Thus, having met his destruction, that asura who lived by unrighteousness and was fond of his son died through his own sin, following the path to an evil rebirth.
O Rādhikā, those who commit offenses against Me have no auspicious destination;
however, if they have sought refuge in Me, then I grant them a destination.
Furthermore, if one has not taken refuge in the Supreme Lord even while dying,
then for him there will certainly be no true happiness, even after hundreds of billions of years.
In the month of Āṣāḍha, that demon-like Rākṣasa, who was a great reviler, died;
then Vibhīṣaṇa heard of the death of Dharmajīva.
Having taken his mother there to Saurāṣṭra by way of the sky,
he returned and requested the supreme lord for a virtuous state of existence.
Hari said in another birth, "He shall find his refuge with me;
having met death at my hand, he shall attain the supreme goal. (108)
Thereafter, the sage Lomaśa gave a mantra to his mother;
he then gave the Śrīpārameśvara mantra to Vibhīṣaṇa.
Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord; Svāhā!
Having stayed for a month, O Rādhikā, those two indeed went to their own abode. (2.87.110)
They both offered their devotion to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Puruṣottama;
and at the end, Vibhīṣaṇa and the celestial woman both became divine beings.

Thus ends the eighty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Atheism of Adharmajīvana, the Son of Khara; His Imputation of Faults to the Qualities of Hari, His Hatred toward Hari, His Evil Fate, and Subsequently the Granting of a Boon for a Good Fate at a Later Time," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Rādhikā, listen again to the divine wonder of Hari:
at Prayāga, during the conjunction of the pitcher (Kumbha-yoga), millions of embodied beings departed [for the next world]. || 1 ||
Mānavas, Nāgas, Daityas, gods, hosts of sages,
ancestors, ascetics, and Siddhas all arrived there during the month of Śrāvaṇa.
Throughout the ten krośas, the city indeed became entirely new;
outside of it, divine trees and creepers dwelt in eager anticipation.
There were also divine sacred fords and divine lakes;
everywhere there were divine rivers, wells, ponds, and oblong pools.
They indeed came there to bathe at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā during the Kumbha Yoga, at the meeting point with the Sarasvatī. || 5 ||
Likewise, in the months of Śrāvaṇa and Bhādrapada, they bathed at the Tīrthaka;
indeed, their own sins were washed away by those pilgrims at Triveṇī.
Then, the virtuous Sanatkumāra, a son of Brahmā and a great renouncer, arrived there in the form of a five-year-old boy.
Seated in a divine, atomic celestial vehicle, resembling ten thousand suns,
he illuminated the entire surface of the earth, the quarters, and the sky on all sides.
The embodied beings, including the gods and others, were filled with wonder and attained great satisfaction;
that celestial chariot of subtle form expanded once again.
There, that yogi of divine form appeared as a child;
he gradually descended to the earth in the vicinity of the imperishable banyan tree.
There the great yogi remained, and he quickly became invisible;
he appeared at the Triveṇī and, remembering Hari, bathed there swiftly.
Becoming invisible, he arrived in an instant at the place where the celestial chariot was;
then, having touched the banyan tree, he bowed down to the one who reclines upon the banyan.
He worshipped with divine flowers and paid homage with Vedic hymns;
meanwhile, having learned of this, the celestial sages, ancestors, and humans arrived there.

Having assembled for the purpose of seeing him, they worshipped him with flowers and other offerings; then, having asked one another whether they had come well and were in good health, they proceeded.
They stood and sat upon the vast surface of the earth and in the heavens;
meanwhile, the sacred fords, rivers, and streams arrived there.
Prayāga in embodied form, as well as lakes, wells, and ponds;
Pūṣā, Kaṭvī, Panārī, Candrāvatī, and Mañjirā. || 16 ||
The Indrāvatī, the Kuśī, the great river Huhūgalī, as well as the Gaṇḍakī, the Kāñcanagaṅgā, the Śatalājā, and the Gogarā. || 17 ||
The Cambalā, Cīnapā, Nandā, Jhelamā, Kābilā, Luṇī, Sindhu, and other rivers, having united, flow toward the son of Brahmā. || 18 ||
Having bowed to Sanatkumāra, the destroyer of sins, the sages asked:
"O Sage, regarding those sins of embodied beings that occur during the twelve-year [cycle]," 19.
But when they have come together among us, they are indeed washed;
all of them remain so for twelve years. ||2.88.20||
"By the occasion of the ritual bath at the Kumbha festival, we shall abandon [our sins] here at Prayāga;
then, freed from sin, we shall attain happiness and peace. (21)
But how, O Sage, may there be the destruction of our sins year after year, so that we may always possess peace? (22)
Show us that place where, by going there month after month, fortnight after fortnight, and likewise on days of terrible sin, the pacification of evil may occur. (23)
O Brahmin, O Lord, show us that place where the burning of great and even greater sins occurs—that scorching spot. (24)
Prayāga, Haridvāra, Puṣkara, and likewise Nāsika—
all these are removers of sin at Kumbha;
yet those who possess such sins go from there to the Śrīkṛṣṇagomatī for the sake of destroying their sins.
Thus was it previously heard from Nārada on the bank of the Godāvarī.
In that regard, O Sage, tell us whether it be Yāma or whatever most excellent and supreme holy site (tīrtha) exists on earth; everything is known within your mind. (27)
Thus questioned, Sanātana Hari himself, the son of Brahmā known as Sanatkumāra, spoke of the sacred fords (tīrthas) in such a manner.
It is the most excellent among the excellent, instantly burning away sins every single day, [including] great sins and extreme sins of all beings existing within the universe. 29.
He who is the Lord of lords, the sovereign Lord of incarnations, the Supreme Soul, the Great Kṛṣṇa, the beginningless Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa. ||2.88.30||
He is the Lord of the Imperishable, the Liberated, and the Supreme Brahman; he is higher than the highest, dwelling in the supreme abode, the Master, and the Sovereign of the Mistress.
Among all the Blessed Ones, there is no Blessed One who is equal to another; indeed, there can be none superior, for therein lies the ultimate limit and the supreme goal. (32)
And this very king of kings, in a mere moment, [manifested] from his own form the Lord of Rādhā, the Lord of Śrī, the Lord of Lakṣmī, and the Lord of Satī.
He revealed his abodes for them to dwell in and granted them their respective domains; he bestowed upon them the perfections of sovereignty as well as his own divine attributes.
This very son of Śrī Kambharā, the delighter of the illustrious Gopāla, first manifested there at the beginning of creation like a child. (35)
He dwells in the field of Kuṅkumavāpī, frequented by the liberated (mukta), served by the Muktānīs, and attended upon by Brahmapriyā. ||36||
It was served by sages such as Lomaśa and others, by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara,
and by the thousand-armed incarnations of Viṣṇu.
There, on the ground known as Akṣara, he was served and worshipped by Vāsudeva and others who have pierced the crown of a hundred thousand [yogīs].
Mādhava sports all around the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake in Kṣetra;
he is present everywhere, even in the vicinity of Lomaśa’s hermitage. (39)
There, the wives of the gods exist in the form of pearl trees and creepers, while the pearls themselves exist in the form of pillars, all desiring to behold [the Lord]. (2.88.40)
Desiring his grace, even the gods have become like ants;
indeed, even swans, sparrows, and other birds roam all around the Aśvasaras lake. (41)
A field extending ten yojanas is considered to be the Imperishable Brahman (akṣarabrahman);
even insects pervaded by its dust attain the supreme goal.
That ground, atom by atom, is divine, auspicious, and bestows liberation;
through union with the Supreme Lord, even the wind grants final release.
Indeed, creepers and trees also purify the worlds,
just as the Blessed One eternally purifies the world of Aśvapaḍṛsara.
One bathes and sports with devotees here, for the Brahma-lake exists in this place;
the Gaṅgā and other excellent holy tirthas reside within its waters and so forth. (45)
The lake called Amṛta, as well as the Virajā, Yamunā, and others,
exist there in that pool, longing for union with Śrī Hari.
In this world, in heaven, in the realm of truth (Satya), in the subterranean realm (Rasātala), or in Vaikuṇṭha and other such places, there are no rivers more purifying than that. 47.
Through its union with Puruṣottama, that lake attained the nature of the Imperishable (Akṣara),
as well as supreme excellence and the power to ward off the heat of sin.
Having gone there daily, one should bathe there even at evening;
by that association, the sins committed during the day are consumed. (49)
Having gone there at dawn, one should perform an ablution;
by that, all the sin arising from the night shall be dissolved for the one who bathes in the Aśvasarovara lake.
At every festival (parvan), embodied beings—whether divine or non-divine—must go there and bathe in that place which removes the impurities of latent tendencies (vāsanā). 51.
Whether every month, or once a year, or during a season, or even at the solstice—one must go there and bathe; for that indeed burns away all evil.
There lies Kuṅkumavāpī, whose water Hari himself always drinks along with the food offerings, as well as [the water] within the pool itself.
This Aśvapaṭṭasara indeed bathes eternally at dawn;
it is this very Kuṅkumavāpī, considered to be the heart of Śrī Hari. (54)
Indeed, there is no holy place superior to that anywhere in the worlds of light, nor is there any in the realms of the gods, nor in the abodes of the Lord and others. (55)
How could it be found on earth except at Kuṅkumavāpikā?
For Kuṅkumavāpikā itself is equal to Kuṅkumavāpikā.
He who is equal to Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa is Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa himself;
she who is equal to the virtuous Kaṃbharāśrī is the virtuous Kaṃbharāśrī herself.
He is equal to Gopālakṛṣṇa; he is indeed Gopālakṛṣṇa himself.
The Imperishable is equal to the Imperishable; there exists nothing superior to that equality. (58)
This is equal to the cosmic egg, for this indeed is the very cosmic egg wherein the beginningless Supreme Brahman, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, truly resides. (59)
Let the rivers there become present; having gone there, let them perform their ablutions at dawn in the divine waters of the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake.
May they drink the water of the Kuṅkuma-vāpī pond, which is the nectar of Hari’s feet;
and may they serve the manifest Bālakṛṣṇa day and night. 6.1.
May the Goddesses dwell there forever in happiness in their primordial forms;
in their active forms, may they sport throughout the lands in the form of water.
Through the yoga of Bālakṛṣṇa, you shall attain true happiness—ineffable, indescribable, and characterized by boundless bliss. (63)
That supreme bliss which resides within the embodied form does not exist even in the imperishable Brahman;
how then could it exist elsewhere? You shall certainly attain that happiness.
By offering oneself with one's whole being in the service of Bālakṛṣṇa,
Hari, being pleased, will surely grant all happiness and his own beloved state.
Wherever there exists even the slightest interval, there is also an interval in bliss;
where there is no interval, there is likewise no interval in bliss. (66)
When the two are united, streams of bliss indeed manifest;
may the best of men be Śrī Kṛṣṇa, and may consciousness be his servant. 67.
O Ānanda, for those two, what talk can there be of suffering?
Their sins dissolve moment by moment through union with Kṛṣṇa. (68)
There, mountains of merits arise moment by moment,
and streams of joys flow forth from every side like oceans.
"By union with Śrī Hari they are born; let them go to serve that very Hari"—as these words were being spoken, from the circle of his body hair (the pores), rivers emerged. (2.88.70)
Indeed, minute black insects emerged from all sides;
they were then asked by those women, "Who are you that have emerged here? ||71||
They said, "We are insects, sinful and of wicked form; having cast off our sins upon you, we truly go to our own home. (72)
We have emerged from your bodies because you remember the lake of horses;
we shall go to other rivers, mountains, and so forth.
"Otherwise, by merely bathing there, our destruction would occur. Having fallen into such fear, they departed from that place and lived elsewhere. (74)
Those who, having remembered Kuṅkumavāpī and Bālakṛṣṇa, the supreme Lord, go toward that imperishable field of Aśvapaṭṭasaraḥ. (75)
When they have made this transition, all sins will quickly perish in every respect;
therefore, desiring to live, we shall go to another place. (76)
Life is better than death, whether through austerity or even through hunger;
for while living, one may at some point inevitably behold auspicious things.
"Human purpose shall also arise, and what is desired shall be obtained again and again.
Having spoken thus, all the rivers then departed from the multitude of streams.
Indeed, by merely hearing of that holy place (tīrtha) from which sins depart far away—a marvel never before seen—what kind of thing must that tīrtha be? (79)
"Therefore, we must go there to serve him and indeed dwell there.
Having thus resolved, they praised the sage again and again. (2.88.80)
They worshipped him with extreme devotion and spoke repeatedly to the sage:
"O venerable Sanatkumāra, lead us indeed to that sacred field."
"Perform a single act of favor for us together with you.
"Om," the sage replied, and at that very moment he went to the sacred fords.
Whatever was on the earth rejoiced exceedingly in every way;
indeed, news of this quickly became manifest among those who had entered the jars. 82.
The venerable Sanatkumāra indeed proceeds toward the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa for the purification of all sins. (84)
Taking all the holy fords along with Kuṅkumavāpikā,
he went to where Bālakṛṣṇa, the Supreme Lord Hari himself, resides.
"Let us go to the field of Aśvapaṭṭasara where the sage Lomaśa resides; having prepared our water-pots, let us indeed depart for the attainment of divinity. (86)
Having thus made this resolution and taken up their requisites,
they then set out for the sacred fords in order to perform the rites of a pilgrimage to those holy sites.
All the rivers situated in every region, all the lakes in every region, the wells located in every region, the ponds, the natural pools, and the oceans; ||88||
All the waterfalls, as well as the tanks, oblong ponds,
and the confluences of rivers and ocean-going streams.
Having beheld the water-tirthas and whatever earth-tirthas there may be,
as well as mountainous regions, thickets, and high elevations.
They came for the purpose of a pilgrimage to forests, excellent wildernesses, river confluences, as well as islands and rivers. (91)
The female companions embraced their male counterparts according to their respective pairs;
