likewise did the mountains, the peaked hills, the gods, and the goddesses.
All the lakes and ponds likewise undertook the journey on foot, as did the holy sites numbering in the hundreds of thousands, and others by the millions as well. (93)
With musical instruments, percussion, flutes, trumpets, cymbals, clay drums, double drums, kettledrums, and pitched wind instruments. ||94||
Accompanied by Tumburu and others, as well as other excellent musicians playing upon lute strings, they sang indeed the praises of Hari.
Having reached the month of Āśvina, they departed comfortably from Prayāga;
on the way, they visited Puṣkara and likewise proceeded to Siddhāśrama.
Having bowed to Satī, who wanders among many [beings], and having visited the mountain Catuṣṭila, as well as the sacred fords (tīrthas), the gods, the Siddhas, and the great seers (maharṣis); ||97||
The Pitṛs, Parvata, and others, indeed assuming divine forms, joyfully arrived at the boundary of the sacred precinct of Kuṅkumavāpī. ||98||
The sages and great seers, accompanied by Sanatkumāra,
as well as other yogis with divine bodies, also arrived.
They took rest in the northern direction from that field, toward the quarter of Śaṅkara;
then they formed a marching array intended to signal a festive assembly.
O Rādhikā, goddesses dwelling in heaven and even celestial nymphs—truthful and virtuous women—arrived, longing to behold the sacred pilgrimage site. || 10 1 ||

Thus ends the eighty-eighth chapter, titled "The Instruction on the Pilgrimage from Prayāga to Kuṅkumavāpī, Surpassing All Other Holy Places through the Majesty of the Aśvapaṭṭasara Lake as Revealed by the Sage Śrī Sanatkumāra," in the second section (Tretā-santāna) of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Rādhikā, in the eastern part of the sacred field known as Kuṅkumavāpī,
there is an auspicious forest of Pārijātaka trees, worthy of being the dwelling place of the immortals.
Then, extending for one yojana,
there is the vast and excellent Kādamba forest situated in the northeast direction, spanning three yojanas in width.
And further to the north, the divine Bhadrā river shines resplendently;
in its various places, Svāmī Kṛṣṇanarāyaṇa bathed. || 3 ||
Having rested well on its bank, bathed, and consumed milk-rice,
that assembly of pilgrims then proceeded along the path while chanting praises of Hari.
In front of him was an elephant moving upon the ground, adorned with various patterns of gold and other ornaments;
it resembled a mountain of red chalk and carried a drum like a rain-cloud.
Carrying her, he indeed goes in front with a roaring sound;
behind him follows the Śarabha named Vairājāvartta.
Carrying two resonant drums upon his back, the personified Elevation (Samucchraya) follows behind him;
and after that, on the back of Māṇikī, is the Banner (Dhvaja), extending for a hundred cubits.
Bearing silken garments adorned with five deities such as gold stars and other ornaments,
the Vindhya mountain moves along, dragging the clouds behind it like banners.
Following that, the sound of conch shells resounded through the ten directions;
produced by the gods and Maruts, it shone forth and was experienced by the inhabitants of heaven.
Thereafter, the Blessed One Vāmana, holding the flowing liquid produced from the excellent minerals, proceeded while making the two worlds resound with laughter.
After that, Śrī Nṛsiṃha himself, roaring in all directions,
proceeds with the splendor of a divine lion’s mane and tawny eyes.
After that, the two Aśvinī deities, both resembling the sun and the moon,
handsome and mounted upon horses, proclaimed their victory.
After that, the powerful Śvetavārāha, white in color and exceedingly handsome, goes for the sake of the holy ford, shaking the ends of the quarters and roaring. (13)
Then the Gandharvas, musicians and experts in instrumental performance,
proceed and play the sounds of *jhaṃkāra*, cymbals, and clay drums.
Vīṇās and mayūrakas, tantryas and jalaniḥsvanakas, prāṇapāśas and gālaśabdas, as well as tālikās and tālapaṭṭakas. || 15 ||
Round drums, kettledrums, bamboo flutes, tongues of flame, trāṭakas, citraghoṣas, śalākās, and likewise rāgiṇīs; || 16 ||
After that, such musical instruments were played;
then indeed the singers of praises and the holy men (puṃtīrthas) proceeded forth.
Then the divine Siddhas, the truthful, the virtuous women, and the virtuous men go forth,
chanting the name of Hari, which is accompanied by music, with their minds fixed on Kṛṣṇa.
Then the ancestors depart with shouts of victory and hymns of praise;
thereafter, indeed, all the deities and the gods who dwell in heaven depart.
Then the sages, established in truth, likewise descended to the earth,
chanting the mantras of the Vedas and the hymns of praise.
Then the Cāraṇas, bards, Gandharvas, and likewise singers proceed with the sounds of musical instruments, proclaiming his name. (21)
After them proceed the kings of the gods and the guardians of the world;
after them follow all the rivers, streams, and springs.
The lakes and ponds flow forth and proclaim it;
then the wives of the sages go, then the goddesses, and then the celestial women. (23)
Chanting the verses concerning Bālakṛṣṇa, filled with love,
they then proceed to the circle of forests, jungles, mountains, sacred sites, and holy fords.
Then the male servants, likewise the female servants, and then the men depart;
such is the continuous flow of the procession, a social gathering extending for the distance of a yojana.
Then a divine rain of flowers fell for a long time;
and having seen that the great holy places were coming toward him, [he rejoiced]. || 26 ||
The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, desiring to offer a welcome,
went forward with great joy, as did Gopālakṛṣṇaka.
The virtuous ones such as Kapila, the great sages such as Lomaśa, the truthful ones such as Rādhā and Ramā, and the Vaiṣṇavas such as Śaṅkara. ||28||
There were also crores, arbudas, and arbudas of Brahmins learned in the Vedas, as well as maidens dear to Brahmā— Kambharāśrī and all the Vallikās.
The sacred bathing place (tīrtha) of Kuṅkumavāpī, as well as other auspicious oblong ponds,
the field of Aśvapaṭṭasara, and the trees of the hermitage.
The guardians of the fields and all the sacred fords on the bank of the Aśvasaras lake, as well as whatever deities dwell there, along with the rivers, streams, and mountains. ||31||
All of them, wearing garlands and provided with honey-mixture (madhuparka) and other offerings,
accompanied by song and instrumental music, went forth to meet the heretics.
Brahmahṛda, Aśvataṭāka, and Kuṅkumavāpikā went ahead by the side of Hari; thereafter, Viraja and the others followed.
Having beheld the temple of Hari and another seven-storied palace made of gold, those great-souled ones arrived.
They prostrated themselves like a staff, casting dust upon their heads;
and overflowing with full enthusiasm, they uttered shouts of victory.
When they had entered the sacred field at a distance of one yojana, they met together,
cast their gaze about, and raised shouts of victory again and again.
Nārāyaṇa, the Blessed Lord himself, personally inquired after their mutual welfare and likewise offered them a welcome as those whose very selves are sacred pilgrimage sites.
"Oh, what fortune! Oh, what fortune! The arrival of sacred pilgrimage sites has come to me!
Having said this, Śrī Hari gave them the madhuparka offering and other honors. (38)
Others gave flower garlands, sandalwood, and floral wreaths; having gathered together, they inquired after his welfare and embraced him as was appropriate. (39)
The followers of other sects and those desiring the sacred ford, intent upon chanting the name of Kṛṣṇa,
arrived near the Kuṅkumavāpī lake as quickly as a swift bird.
The gods, goddesses, and sages, considering it a great fortune, repeatedly rolled upon the dust of the path to the sacred field. ||41||
Some were dancing, others were singing and playing instruments; some placed dust upon their heads and rubbed it over their bodies. 42.
Some bow their heads to Hari, some join their palms in reverence;
some apply the dust from his feet to their chests, while others place it upon their faces. (43)
The Lord Kumāra himself rolled at the feet of Kṛṣṇa;
some, recognizing the greatness [of the Lord], [offered] the dust of the feet of the devotees.
Some sages carry upon their heads the leaves, flowers, stalks, and even the grass of all sacred fords. 45.
Yet they hold it in their mouths and consider themselves to have accomplished their purpose, thinking that water originating from a spring is a destroyer of sin. (46)
Having drunk it drop by drop, some consider their purpose accomplished;
others [consider it so] when they have inhaled the wind that has come into contact with the waters of Lake Aśvasaras. (47)
Then, having drunk from his mouth, some attain supreme bliss again and again;
some remember their own abodes, and others remember those who have descended [as incarnations]. 48.

Those whose hearts are fixed on Him remember at that time the liberated souls, as well as His divine powers and perfections (siddhis), His weapons such as the discus and conch, and likewise His attendants and female servants. 49.
Whatever honors they desire, they quickly bestow upon them along the way;
thus, with musical instruments, hymns of praise, and vehicles filled with love. (2.89.50)
Accompanied by Jayanāda and all the others, they reached the lake known as Aśva;
at that time, the sins of those embodied beings were like thunderbolts.
All those [merits] that are relinquished at sacred fords (tīrtha), though they are indeed innumerable, are surpassed by the sight of Aśvapaṭṭasara and by the sight of Hari. ||52||
Those [sins] which depart far away when a bath is taken at another sacred site are here instantly consumed by fire, so that not even a remnant remains. (53)
All of them were consumed by fire upon the mere sight of Aśvasara;
oh, the great majesty of Kṛṣṇa is now visibly manifest! ||54||
If even the dust, the water, and the leaves of that sacred field burn away all sins, what then need be said of Hari? (55)
Thus praising him, those great-souled ones [reached] the northern bank of the lake, in that exceedingly vast and auspicious region belonging to Śaṅkara.
They rested, bathed, drank the water, and offered salutations;
they performed the rites of the sacred ford, washing away their every sin. (57)
Then, having bathed the beginningless Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa with those waters,
the holy places and others performed their ablutions and drank the water born of his grace.
With divine waters, they became divine in form and liberated in appearance;
thus, having performed the ritual at the Aśvasaras Tīrtha according to the prescribed rules, they departed from there.
They went to the vast Śrī-kuṅkuma-vāpī, which was the very embodiment of light;
they all drank its water and bathed repeatedly in those waters.
Then, by the desire of Hari, those holy places and others attained equality with him (sārṣṭi).
Thereafter, having gone to Brahmahrada, they bathed and drank that water.
Then those great souls attained a state of similarity,
all becoming equal to Balarāma and Kṛṣṇa in their virtues, forms, and prosperity.
Having become fit for liberation and freed from rebirth,
they all then proceeded further to the auspicious hermitage of Lomaśa.
Lomaśa welcomed them with sweet foods, fruits, and water,
and he fed all the distinguished guests who had come from the sacred pilgrimage sites.
He caused [the deities] to be satisfied with foods and refreshments made from the essence of milk brought from the abode of Brahmā,
and he offered them mouth-fresheners.
The gods, sages, ancestors, and humans went to all the sacred fords (tīrthas),
as did the rivers, streams, mountains, and whatever forests and wildernesses there were.
And all those great souls went to the auspicious abode of Bālakṛṣṇa,
which was divine, enriched with divine splendor, and frequented by liberated beings.
It is served by inconceivable and infinite powers, it is the refuge of the Lord, it is always graced by incarnations, and it is auspicious, bestowing liberation through union (sāyujya). 68.
There, in that divine and most excellent Brahma-lake, a pool of water where the beginningless Krishna Narayana had bathed, the Mahimanas plunged in.
Possessing divine bodies and endowed with divine vision, they all indeed beheld their own eternal selves stationed in that supreme, divine, and imperishable abode.
Then those who measure greatness recognized His full majesty;
for here indeed exist sālokya, sārṣṭi, sārūpya, and sāyujya. ||71||
Liberation from sin is found at Anyatīrtha, while Aśvasaras burns away all evil; Kuṅkumavāpī bestows equal status with the gods, and Brahmahrada grants one's true spiritual nature.
Indeed, the divine hermitage of Lomaśa exists here, which bestows the state of living in the same world (sālokya);
and this abode of Bālakṛṣṇa is indeed the giver of liberation through union (sāyujya).
Aho! By the majesty of Kṛṣṇa, indeed each and every one of them increases in extreme power; aho! they are in every way bestowers of liberation.
One should either make one's dwelling here or proceed to the Imperishable;
once the Supreme Brahman has been attained, what sinner would dwell elsewhere? (75)
Speaking thus, they celebrated a great festival at night,
during the month of Kumuda under the moon, on the seventh day of the dark fortnight.
With songs, hymns, dances, devotional worship, and praises,
as well as meditations and listening to sacred narratives, they passed the night in happiness.
Having bathed at dawn in the Aśvasaras lake, they all arrived for the worship of Kṛṣṇa on the eleventh day of birth, the eighth lunar day, during the great festival.
In the vast pavilion constructed by Viśvakarman,
Hari himself shone forth at night upon an elephant-throne in its center.
Other thrones as well as lion-thrones were placed here on all sides;
and upon them sat the lords of lords, the supreme sovereigns.
Likewise, the incarnations, the liberated ones, and other virtuous women;
the virtuous men who possess the nature of Brahman, the gods, the goddesses, and the great seers. ||81||
Brahmā and the other sages, as well as the ancestors and tens of millions of gods, shone forth; and the sacred fords, rivers, streams, and lakes likewise gleamed.
The world-protectors, the guardians of kingdoms, the mountains, the forests, the lands, the wildernesses, the trees, the creepers, the grasses, and likewise the ponds. ||83||
Inanimate and animate entities shone upon their seats;
divine musical instruments were played, and auspicious sounds resounded at that time. (84)
The sound of the Vedas arose and there was a rain of flowers;
Lomaśa, the king of sages, freed from Māyā, worshipped Hari. 85.
He had a *tilaka* and a crescent moon mark applied to the forehead of the Supreme Self;
he placed a crown upon His head and a beautiful garland [around His neck]. (86)
He placed a golden tulasī, as well as one made of flowers and one of jewels, around his neck;
he also offered a handful of flowers and sprouts of dūrvā grass upon his ears.
He placed an excellent *śrīphala* fruit in his hand and offered other fruits before him;
he then applied sandalwood paste to his feet and honored him with unbroken grains of rice (*akṣata*).
She performed the nightly lamp-offering for Hari and bestowed auspicious blessings;
then, the illustrious Queen Kambharā worshipped Bālakṛṣṇa. 89.
The illustrious Gopālakṛṣṇa placed a necklace upon Kṛṣṇa’s neck;
the Lord Śukadeva and Vallabha and others offered garlands.

Hemanta and the Blessed One, as well as Haimī, Upadā, Samuttamā, Santuṣṭā, Amṛtā, Dugdhā, Jīvantī, and the others, offered excellent garlands; they then applied saffron *tilaka* marks and a drop on the forehead of Hari.
Then the lords, the incarnations, the liberated ones, and other goddesses, having worshipped Śrī Hari, performed the ārārtika ceremony. ||92||
The sages devoted to the vow of Brahman, the ancestors, gods, and humans;
the male deities, female deities, rivers, streams, lakes, and even the minor waters. ||93||
The mountains, the unexcavated grounds, the sacred fords, the forests,
and the wildernesses— all these elements worshipped the Supreme Lord.
They offered nightly illuminations, handfuls of flowers, and gifts;
likewise, they presented ornaments, garments, and various articles of utility. (95)
They offered rings, fruits, flowers, gems, diamonds,
vehicles, and divine wish-fulfilling trees during the worship.
Thus, following the worship and the formal dismissal of the assembly, Hari fed all the honored guests who had come with their families.
To all those who were guests and visitors, as well as to embodied beings, he gave pleasing gifts with a sincere heart. (98)
Then, the holy places made this petition before Śrī Hari:
"Having obtained the gain that bestows liberation, who would desire any other gain? (99)
"Therefore, O Ocean of Compassion, grant us liberation and eternal happiness.
Then Hari, out of compassion for them, indeed assumed three forms.
Keśava then sent Mūla, Divya, and likewise Chāyā, along with their attendants (pārṣadas), by means of celestial chariots to their respective abodes in their original forms.
Then, having protected their own divine forms in my presence, they dwelt as they pleased in the sacred field of Aśvapaṭṭasara.
Consisting of sacred fords (tīrtha) and possessing forms, they reside in temples constructed by Viśvakarman; being well-satisfied, they long for the service of Hari. (103)
At that time, the Lord spoke auspicious words for the sake of purifying the world to those shadow-forms of the sacred fords that were present there.
"O Lords of the Tīrthas, your birth upon this earth is solely by my will, indeed for the sake of purifying the worlds; therefore, O Sovereigns, you must go."
One should remain in that very place where one's station lies;
for it was by me that the rivers, streams, and lakes were established here in this world.
Indeed, one must dwell there in that very manner for the burning away of the sins of the sinful;
one should come every year on the anniversary of my birth in every respect.
On the full moon day, during the time of Ekādaśī, in the month of Kumbha, Māgha, and Kārtika;
likewise at the transit of the sun (saṃkrānti), and in the months of Śrāvaṇa and Vaiśākha at Puruṣottama.
Having been addressed thus, those embodied lords of the sacred fords (tīrtheśvaras) bowed down and departed for their own regions; likewise, the great-souled ones (mahīmānas) also departed.
O Rādhikā, having worshipped Hari, the beloved of Brahmā, all those people went from Lomaśa’s hermitage to their respective abodes. 2.89.110.
Even at night, a festival should be celebrated with dancers and singers;
by reading or even hearing this, one shall obtain both worldly enjoyment and liberation. 11.111.

Thus ends the eighty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Arrival of All the Tīrthas, Devas, and Others at Kuṅkumavāpī, and the Festival for the Birthday of Śrī Hari," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā. || 89 ||
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Rādhā, to another wonderful account of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa; I shall relate to you this supreme narrative which protects the world.
In ancient times, the two divine sons of Dharma, Nara and Nārāyaṇa, while on Mount Himālaya at Badarī, meditated upon Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa.

On the eleventh day of the dark fortnight of the month of Kārttika, those two ascetics, longing for a vision of him, meditated upon their own progenitor, the Lord, on the bank of the Gaṅgā at their own hermitage.
On earth, at its western extremity, in Saurāṣṭra,
in the field known as Kunkumavāpī belonging to Ajanābha, Hari resides in the house of Śrī Kambharā.
When will that Supreme Lord, the Highest Brahman, who dwells within you in the form of a child and is the cause of all incarnations, grant his vision?
While the two brothers, who were Nara and Nārāyaṇa in essence, were thus remembering him,
Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa himself appeared in order to fulfill their resolve.
Having addressed his devotees residing in the region of Aśvapaṭṭasaraḥ,
he departed by means of a celestial chariot for the Badarīvana forest on the Golden Mountain.
Having taken Lomaśa along with him and having stationed the remaining ones there,
he spoke for the sake of protection to Hara and the Guardian of the Field (Kṣetrapāla).
On the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika, the two kinsmen worshipped Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa with water, flowers, and fruits.
Dharmabhakti and those sages likewise performed service for them;
even the ascetics performed service to the Lord every day.
Perceiving that Mārgaśīrṣa was the most excellent month for sacrifice, those great sages, the ascetics, performed the Vaiṣṇava sacrifice at Badarī.
Śrī Narāyaṇa constantly gave a leaf-hut as a suitable dwelling for Lomaśa and likewise for Bālakṛṣṇa.
In the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, this great and auspicious festival of sacrifice took place;
there, Lord Hari himself—the Supreme Self and the Supreme Ruler—was present.
Then the Lord of Sacrifice, stationed in the fire, consumed the oblations;

The liberated souls residing in Vaikuṇṭha, as well as those dwelling in other abodes,
arrived at that sacrifice, longing for the grace of Hari.
The great seers, the goddesses, the sacred fords, the ancestors, as well as the Siddhas, Cāraṇas, Gandharvas, the Brahmins, and those who travel through the sky; || 16 ||
Then the devotees, Daityas, and Dānavas arrived at the sacrifice;
for thus did the Blessed Lord, the Supreme Sovereign, shine forth there.
At that very time, in Kārtika, in Surāṣṭra,
the messenger of Śambhu, Mahāmārī, by the command of Śambhu, [arrived] at night.
Standing on the boundary, she protected the field of Aśvapaṭṭasara;
at that time, indeed, she remembered her brother’s son from Siṃhaladvīpa.
Likewise, Kubhīnasī and Śṛṅgī, along with two hundred other rākṣasīs,
were sky-goers, able to assume any form at will, and experts in the web of illusion.
Having learned that the one who lived by unrighteousness had indeed died in Surāṣṭra, they arrived equipped with weapons and missiles in order to avenge their enmity. || 21 ||
Having crossed the lion-infested forests, they traveled through the sky and arrived at Saurāṣṭra on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Kārtika.
On the night before the Festival of Lamps, they descended from the sky,

"Separate these, devour these, lead these away for the sake of the Rākṣasa!

"There is no protector for us here, nor is there any agreement regarding our victory," they said thus, hurrying toward the hermitage of Lomaśa.
Indeed, cruel women who were rākṣasīs descended for the purpose of assault;

Perceiving this sudden conflict and the calamity of war,

In all the maidens' quarters, there arose at night a terrible outcry,

Bhairavī, having taken up a noose and consecrated it with mantras for binding serpents, released it upon the host of Rākṣasīs; the Rākṣasīs were bound within that bond.

Then that Bhairavī, having approached Śambhu while he was asleep,

"Having become free from their bonds, they said to this messenger Bhairavī:

A great artificial army of rākṣasīs was produced;

O Śambhu, if you are pleased, and if a boon is to be granted to us, then let us be filled with hunger and likewise distressed by thirst. (53)

We are all born of darkness, belonging to the realm of tamas, and are intoxicated by battle;

"We desire that very same food and drink if you will give it to us.

"We shall satisfy him with our service as female servants.

Thus ends the ninetieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Lord’s Journey to Badarī, the Arrival of the Rākṣasīs at Kuṅkumavāpī, the Destruction of the Rākṣasīs by Mahāmārī, and Subsequently His Pervasiveness for the Purpose of Consuming Sinful Beings," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā. || 90 ||
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O virtuous Rādhikā, listen; having gone to Śrī Badarī, the twice-born, the truthful, the chaste women, and likewise the saintly ones bathed in the waters of the river by way of the sky.
Having performed their ablutions in the Gaṅgā, they gathered together and chanted the names of Hari; thus they went to where Nārāyaṇa was.
Having bowed to Nara and Nārāyaṇa, and having repeatedly saluted the circle of great sages, they were honored with hospitality and received a welcome and worship there. (3)
Having accepted the madhuparka offering from Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa,
they went to the leaf-hut where Lomaśa was also staying, after having inquired about his location.
Lomasha, seeing the devotees who had arrived with sorrowful minds,
quickly asked after their welfare and the purpose of their coming.
Having offered him a seat and likewise having beheld the sage Lomaśa and performed worship, they all spoke to him.
"Therefore, we shall indeed explain the reason for our departure here," having said this to Śrī Hari, who was staying in the leaf-hut, Lomaśa—
Having gone quickly inside the house and announced the arrival of his kinsmen,
he took Hari— who was filled with affection— and went outside together with him.
Then those pilgrims prostrated themselves like a staff before the glorious Lord Hari, who had arrived at the courtyard of the hall on the slopes of Śrī Badarī.
Out of love, Hari inquired after their welfare, their welcome, and their well-being;

By that Mahāmārī Bhairavī, who acts as the protector of the frontiers, countless rākṣasīs of Siṃhaladvīpa were slain. (1)
Those maidens who had arrived at the site of the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake for the purpose of battle,

Likewise, during that great plague at night, Śambhu himself then [appeared] for her sake.
Being pleased, he spoke for the sake of granting a boon; she then requested:
"O Great Māyā, those born from me who engage in battle and are afflicted by hunger—" || 14 ||
"O Śiva, we desire that he be a consumer of human flesh.
When this was said by Śambhu, it was not deemed appropriate; thereupon Bhairavī spoke.
We shall certainly not accept food from those who have taken refuge in Śrī Hari, nor from those sinful ones who abandon the devotees of Śiva and the devotees of Hari. || 16 ||
Those who are nihilists, devoid of dharma, and indeed enemies of the gods;

"Men and women who are devoid of bathing, worship, recitation, and devotion—we shall indeed devour them here, from ten yojanas outside. (18)
"So be it," said Hara; and then tens of millions upon tens of millions of Mahāmārīs swiftly devoured the people—both children and the elderly—to their hearts' content.
Pregnant women, old women, young women, and even young men—

There were people living like crows, devoid of family ties;
some had become half-homes, and others were even without lineage.
But this calamity, O Lord, proceeds having gained strength;

There is indeed no counting those who have died, nor do even their bearers meet again; the wilderness has become a city, and villages have become forests.
"O Lord, come quickly and protect us from that destruction!
Having spoken thus, they all wept; and the compassionate one, overcome by pity, [acted].
Having arisen from that state, he then quickly called to mind Nārāyaṇa;

"Even these devotees shall be devoured; therefore, for their protection, I must go quickly to that Surāṣṭraka along with these devotees. (32)

I have constantly remembered the Blessed One for the sake of worship during Kārttika;

May they also receive this mantra from me alone. (76)
"Let them make all men hear this in their very ears!
Thus addressed, all those women, swift as thought, seized him firmly in an instant.

Having all achieved their purpose, the men and women, numbering in the tens of millions, were restored to life by Hari and then departed for their own homes. 84.
Then those goddesses, the Rādhikās and even the Mahāmāryas, chose from Mādhava—
the illustrious Bālakṛṣṇa— service to his own feet.
Hari then gave them a dwelling in the forest of Saurāṣṭra, saying:
"May you become bael trees (*badarī*) of divine form. (86)
In the fields and even in the forests, there are indeed few who live long;
they are possessed of two thorns and are joined with the thorns of darkness (tamas).
May those who are completely covered by the dust of my feet in Saurāṣṭra obtain a reward equal to that of serving my feet, and may they remain so until the end of the kalpa. (88)
"In the form of Rāma, I shall devour your fruits;
moreover, women of the Śabara caste here will also give you fruits. (89)
Thus, having been made into devotees on the surface of the earth, they became the forms of *stambas*;
those *kṣudrikās* and *badarīs* were quickly born as long-lived beings.
Śrī Hari welcomed Nara, Nārāyaṇa, and the other sages who were devoted to dharma; Lomaśa was their mother and father. (91)
Lord Hari provided lodging for them in his own golden palace,
and the Master gave food and sacrificial offerings to the ascetics.
Then they all rested there, and at dawn they bathed in the Aśvasaras lake;
thereafter, they all went to behold the hermitage of the venerable Lomaśa.
It is vast, of divine form, radiant with the beloved consorts of Brahmā;
there is no illusion (māyā) therein, and it is auspicious, equal to the divine syllable (akṣara). ||94||
Then, having performed the ritual for the sacred ford and taken up the worship,
and having met with the deities of the ford, you two assumed two forms.
Then, having assumed the form of sacred fords (tīrtha) and obtained the command of Hari, they all departed for the venerable Badarīvana.
The sacred ford of Dharma, the sacred ford of devotion, the supreme sacred ford of Manu, the sacred ford of Nārāyaṇa, and likewise the auspicious sacred ford of the Ṛṣis. ||97||
Thus, Badarītīrtha came into being at Aśvasaras;
indeed, O Rādhikā, a great miracle occurred there. 98.
Bestowing both worldly enjoyment and liberation, and removing death through mere remembrance,
he indeed made the world Vaiṣṇava for the sake of protecting Kanyā.

Thus ends the ninety-first chapter, titled "The Description of how, during the destruction of many human beings by great plagues in the second period of the Tretā-yuga within the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā, the assembly of virtuous women, saints, and brahmin sages went to Badarī, informed the Lord, and caused Hari to arrive; and how Hari restored the deceased living beings of the world to life," etc. || 91 ||
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Rādhikā; Vāsudeva, Saṃkarṣaṇa, and the others—these three lords of lords—questioned [him] regarding the knowledge that awakens one to Brahman. || 1 ||
O elder brother, tell me how knowledge produces devotion in individual souls and the Lord;
who is the Self, what is liberation, and what is the cause of worldly existence?
What is saṃsāra, and likewise, what is Brahman that is higher than even that?
You know all this, O Blessed Lord, for you know every supreme secret.
O Nārāyaṇa, you are yourself the ancient, inconceivable Puruṣa manifest before our eyes;
for there is no other knower of you than you, O Supreme Person.
Having spoken thus, Aniruddha, Pradyumna,
and Saṃkarṣaṇa meditated within their respective hearts upon that certain Supreme Person, the Lord.
Then they beheld Śrī Hari, the Supreme Person,
who had abandoned his supreme causal form known as Vāsudeva.
[He saw] the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the supreme Brahman, Hari,
resplendent, served by the liberated ones, divine and wonderful.
He whose chest bears the Śrīvatsa mark, who is lovely and adorned with a halo of light,
who wields all weapons— the Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa endowed with wisdom.
He is the refuge of eternal bliss, qualities, sovereignty, prosperity, power, and happiness;
he has two arms, and his lotus feet are served by millions of liberated souls.
Laughing and causing others to laugh, as beautiful as ten million gods of love,
a youth endowed with divine splendor, and enchanting to all of creation.
Brilliant, endowed with a gentle disposition, and possessing long eyes—
the Supreme Lord seated upon his divine elephant-throne in the highest abode.
Then they beheld the imperishable abode of Brahman, which is devoid of all boundaries; and they beheld ten million beautiful beings known as the Imperishable (Akṣara).
Then they quickly beheld Goloka, inhabited by cowherds, adorned by hosts of gopīs, and presided over by Śrī Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa. || 13 ||
Then they beheld the beautiful Vaikuṇṭha, which is like unto Brahmā,
the abode of Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa, and inhabited by ten million attendants.
Then they beheld the divine and beautiful Kailāsa, the abode of Sadāśiva and Śivā, as well as the radiant realm of the Infinite (Bhūman) known as Amṛta.
Then, while Vāsudeva was their elder brother, they beheld Viṣṇu’s Vaikuṇṭha, the Ocean of Milk,
Śvetadvīpa, and Badarī.
In each respective place, they beheld the form of Hari exactly as it was;
for in Vāsudeva, they indeed saw the entire illusory creation.
Then the creation vanished; at the end of that moment, they beheld there a divine mass of light, situated exactly as the land of Saurāṣṭra had been.
Therein is the field named Aśvapaṭṭasara, which is brilliantly radiant;
there also is the Kuṅkumavāpī and the hermitage of the venerable Lomaśa.
All that is the supreme abode, resplendent with divine pearls and other jewels,
pervaded by the beloveds of Brahmā, and presided over by the Sāṃkhya-yoginīs.
It is permeated by the devotion of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, and it is graced by the divine Śrī Kambharā Lakṣmī and Gopāla Kṛṣṇa. ||21||
It is resorted to by Prabhā, Pāravatī, Lakṣmī, Māṇikī, Rādhikā, Mañjulā, Saguṇā, Haṃsā, Vijayā, and Lalitā. ||22||
It is perfumed by one hundred and twelve beloved ones, empowered by infinite millions of lotus-born beings, and possesses divine majesty. (23)
They beheld the palaces adorned with divine jars;
they also saw this great palace of Anādikṛṣṇa.
In that supreme, divine realm which is the support of His own self, the Blessed Lord Himself—Nārāyaṇa Bālakṛṣṇa, possessing the splendor of a youth—resides. (25)
The Supreme Person, the illustrious Parameśvara, is the highest among the Nārāyaṇas; and Śrī Puruṣottama is the supreme among all lords, manifest before our eyes. ||26||
He who is the cause of the multitude of incarnations and the one who is the incarnation himself; he who is the Kṛṣṇa of all Kṛṣṇas and the Lord who creates the manifestations of the Vyūhas.
O Rādhā, they beheld that Hari, Vāsudeva,
in the form of Hari, shining brilliantly upon a pure throne of gold and ivory.
Having seen that Vāsudeva who exists within all this, from whom this entire world is non-different, they attained supreme bliss. 29.
Then, in another moment, they saw everything dissolved before them;
they beheld Vāsudeva and their minds became tranquil. Having thus caused them to attain direct realization, he then [proceeded].
Vāsudeva spoke this secret, eternal knowledge,
which neither the gods nor the twice-born sacrificers fully understand.
Having known that Supreme Lord, the great seers who have become one with Brahman do not enter into saṃsāra again, just as those of old who dwelt in the abode of Brahman.
This self is possessed of bliss, translucent, pure, subtle, and eternal;
yet within it dwells that which is the innermost of all, higher than the highest. (33)
He is the Inner Controller, He is the Puruṣa, He is Prāṇa, known as the Lord;
from Him the universe is born, and into His abode it is dissolved. (34)
Grasping his illusory power through its reflection, he creates various bodies;
yet for him there is no bondage, nor is there the state of being bound, for he does not depend upon the qualities of illusion.
Just as the identity of light and darkness is not possible, so too there can be no relation of oneness between the phenomenal world and the Supreme Self. (36)
Just as in the world shadow and sunlight are mutually distinct, so too, from the perspective of ultimate reality, the phenomenal world and the Puruṣa are separate. //37//
The self is pure, eternally awakened, and by its very nature liberated;
it is the supreme self, utterly pure, omniscient, and perfectly established in itself. ||38||
Free from modification and beyond dualities, ever overflowing with bliss, the Self and its Inner Self are united, possessing divine and auspicious qualities. (39)
The two friends are eternally united, the seers and the controllers;
the Self enjoys the action performed, while the Inner Ruler remains devoid of enjoyment.
Having thus regulated [the fruits of action], He bestows the result upon the merchant (the individual soul) at the proper time;
yet men [think]: "I am the doer; I am happy, I am miserable, I am thin, and I am fat. (41)
Through egoism, by the power of ignorance, it becomes the enjoyer of that [object];
due to ignorance or distorted knowledge, it becomes joined with the mind. (42)
Having repeatedly joined the unstable mind with the association of the material qualities (guṇas), he indeed makes his own self rich in its inherent nature. 43.
Through the lack of discrimination regarding the ego, one who considers "I am the doer" and is thus defiled surely forgets his own self, which is the imperishable Brahman. (44)
One who perceives a self in what is not-self is the abode where all suffering dwells;
therein, passion, hatred, and the like, born of delusion, also take their place. (45)
Through those defects, he experiences merit and demerit according to their inherent nature;
however, upon the destruction of delusion and the disappearance of defects, he is free from conceptual proliferation (niṣprapañcaka).
One remains established in the divine Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, having offered himself to Him;
through union with Being-Consciousness-Bliss (saccidānanda), he is forever possessed of Being-Consciousness-Bliss.
He exists by the grace of the Supreme Lord, just as the Lord [exists];
indeed, just as the sky is never soiled by contact with smoke. 48.
Likewise, untainted by mental defects and designated as the Imperishable (akṣara),
free from limiting adjuncts (upādhi), pure, and stainless in essence, it shines forth.
Having abandoned the object of knowledge, and then having abandoned both cognition and the mental impressions of cognition, one becomes the self-luminous Self, just like Nārāyaṇa himself. (2.92.50)
Therefore, the Self—which is imperishable, pure, eternal, and devoted to Śrī Hari—should be worshipped, reflected upon, and heard about by those seeking liberation. ||5 1 ||
When the Supreme Brahman shines within oneself at all times and in all places, then it manifests spontaneously to the faithful devotee. (52)
When one perceives the entire range of effects within oneself alone, and perceives one's own self within the range of effects, then one attains Hari. ||53||
When one established in samādhi perceives nothing as being separate, and the self has become one with the Supreme, then it becomes liberated. ||54||
When his mental states dissolve into the Supreme Hari,
then, having become immortal, he attains liberation at the station of Hari.
When everything that exists as distinct is perceived within that very [Self],
and likewise its expansion [is seen therein], then one possesses the fitness for Brahman.
When he perceives both the self and the absolute Self alone, then his attainment of Brahman occurs and his worldly illusion ceases. ||57||
When there is the realization of the Self as the Brahman-Self, which is the sole remedy for birth, old age, suffering, and disease, then this [Self] is eternal and auspicious. 58.
Just as rivers and streams reach oneness with the ocean,
so too does the self reach oneness with the Imperishable and with the Supreme Brahman.
Then one should proceed; there would be the direct perception of that which is not beyond the senses.
That non-duality of distinction is thoroughly established by the Vedas. ||2.92.60||
That consciousness, known as upāsanā, bestows the supreme good;
wherever it arises, there is neither the phenomenal world nor latent impressions.
Wherever ignorance exists, there also exist delusion and latent impressions;
therefore, having abandoned delusion and burnt away all latent impressions, [one should remain]. ||62||
Having become Brahman, which is the perfect transcendence of all that is heard, the wise one should cross over;
indeed, having firmly accomplished spiritual knowledge, devotion to the Blessed One, and yoga.
Having meditated upon the form of Brahman, one shall attain the supreme Hari.
This unmanifest Self is I; this is Brahman, the abode for the devotee. (64)
This supreme Lord is devoted to Brahman; He is the Imperishable Puruṣottama.
That Hari, the Supreme Lord, is the non-duality that transcends all distinctions.
He possesses all tastes, all forms, and all fragrances; he is undecaying and immortal.
His hands and feet are everywhere; he is the self of all and faces every direction.
He is the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, who, though existing as the inner controller, is without hands or feet; yet he is swift-moving, a grasper, and is established within all things.
Though without eyes, he sees; though devoid of ears, he hears.
I know this Puruṣa, the ancient Supreme Lord.
And [he saw] the auspicious Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Lord of Śrī, the son of Kambharāśrī, who resides even in the supreme abode, as well as that Naranārāyaṇa.
The sages who possess his grace behold him as Vāsudeva, Hara, Viṣṇu, Hari, and the one dwelling within all.
The ascetics do not see it at all; rather, His servants behold it—that sovereignty of the one whose form is stainless, which is called the Imperishable (Akṣara) and devoid of qualities (Nirguṇa).
The lay devotees, who perceive the subtle reality and so forth, clearly behold that which even the gods do not understand, being deluded by his illusory power.
What need is there to speak of the world of living beings? Listen to me, O brothers:
Aniruddha, in you resides the supreme sovereignty over all creation.
That which exists within you, Pradyumna— the sovereignty of nourishment— is born from but a ten-millionth part of that very imperishable Brahman.
That should be understood as arising from but a ten-millionth part of the imperishable Brahman;
O Saṃkarṣaṇa, the sovereignty over dissolution likewise resides in you.
That which is to be understood from the syllable is born from but a ten-millionth part of Brahman;
and that sovereignty which resides in me—namely, dwelling and sporting—is likewise [derived from it]. //76//
That which was attained by Hari is indeed the meaning to be understood as the Imperishable (akṣara); therein, within that Imperishable whose nature is non-duality, there is the qualification "I. (77)
This indeed is non-duality with distinction; it exists as the imperishable Brahman.
That alone is the one imperishable, and there is nothing else equal to it, designated as the Imperishable.
But where the qualified, the Imperishable, is subsumed within the non-dual Śrī Paramātman, that Supreme Lord is the Non-dualism of Qualified Non-duality (viśeṣādvaitādvaita). ||79||
That which transcends Māyā is the Imperishable (akṣara), and beyond that is the Supreme Lord;
indeed, having abandoned Māyā, living beings go to that state, the Imperishable.
Those practitioners of devotion who have transcended all Māyā, which takes the form of the entire universe, enter [Him] and attain union with Him. ||81||
They attain the abode of the Imperishable; therein is my supreme station.
For them there is no returning again, whether by the power of the Lord or through Māyā. 82.
This is the instruction of that Lord Hari, Kṛṣṇa, the master of the imperishable, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, [bestowed] through His grace. 83.
It should be given to his sons, disciples, and virtuous men, and to the wife of a Brahmin;
it must not be given to others who are unworthy recipients, for that would be as unwholesome as unwholesome food.
Thus, O Rādhikā, this knowledge has been revealed to you by me,
which was previously proclaimed by Vāsudeva to his younger brothers.

Thus ends the ninety-second chapter, titled "The Exposition," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*, concerning Vāsudeva’s attainment of that state through the knowledge of the Supreme Brahman and the specific non-dualism of Advaita as taught in the *Gītā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O Rādhikā, Śrī Vāsudeva spoke to Saṃkarṣaṇa and the others concerning the Supreme Soul, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
The son named Kāla, who possesses the power called *sthitisthāpaka* (elasticity), brings about dissolution;
he takes away everything, including even the imbalance of *māyā*.
Then this Māyā, the agitator, causes agitation and,
through union with the Great Puruṣa, brings forth an uneven state.
Māyā, Kāla, and Puruṣa are the powers (śaktis) of the Supreme Lord;
from them all this has arisen, therefore they are of the nature of Brahman.
That which is born from it is the form of Brahman, and the entire world is indeed its body;
for in all that [exists], there truly resides this imperishable Brahman.
The hands, feet, eyes, ears, face, head, and navel—from these [limbs] it exists, pervading everything; that indeed is the Imperishable (akṣara).
It manifests as the quality of all the senses, is endowed with divine faculties,
is the support of all, is great bliss, and its sphere transcends all means of valid cognition.
Devoid of all comparison, the abode of all, the supreme nectar;
undivided yet existing in divided forms, eternal, constant, and imperishable.
The supreme light is devoid of qualities, free from conceptual construction, and limitless;
it is the self of all beings, abiding both within and without.
There dwells the omnipresent, peaceful Supreme Lord, whose very self is that [reality];
by him this entire universe is pervaded, permeated by the liberated souls who have realized the Lord.
By His will, I was born as Vāsudeva, the Supreme Lord;
from me, you three forms alone were produced, like sparks from a fire.
From him came Bhūman, then Mahāviṣṇu, then Virāṭ the creator of the universe; from him came the great sages, the gods, and the entire world of moving and non-moving beings. || 12 ||
The Mother of the World is Mahāmāyā, whose fundamental form is Will;
she is known as Amṛtā, Doṣakartṛ, Pāragā, and likewise Pūrikā.

That which is accepted as *prakṛti*—the enchanting and beloved one, like a mistress—produces the entire world, beginning with the Great Principle (*mahat*) and ending with the specific elements (*viśeṣa*). 14.
But that person who has fallen into delusion [thinks]: "He is the Self, the individual soul, the Lord;
He is my friend through the agency of ego, and my close kinsman through the principle of the Great One (mahat-tattva). (15)
One who places trust in the mind leads only to the acquisition of further birth;
for one who has no desire for material nature, delusion does not exist.
There is indeed no friendship in the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra), nor kinship in the principle of the Great One (mahattattva);
nor is there trust in the mind (mānasa)—these do not conduce to the attainment of liberation.
For these—māyā, time, and the person—are indeed his benefactors, existing in a state of conformity with him; even these are his benefactors.
They cause him to attain the divine imperishable state, for whom the Supreme Lord—the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa who dwells in the supreme abode—is the beloved. 19.
Through union with that, however, divine forms arise for this devotee,
as well as knowledge, will, and action, along with the mental states of pleasure, pain, and so forth.
The sheaths of dharma and adharma, as well as the mind, ego, intellect, and sensation, arise; likewise do pure being, passion, and impurity, all appearing in divine forms.
The subtle elements, the group of sense organs, the six sheaths, and the five gross elements—all these transformations arise from the divine friction [of consciousness]. (22)
Their actions, their conduct, their efforts, and even their livelihood—all this becomes divine, bestows liberation, and is the attributeless Brahman. ||23||
Time is not the master here, he who indeed creates and destroys living beings;
all are under the control of Time, yet Time itself is under the control of the devotee.
In devotion, one should worship the Imperishable within the Imperishable—the omniscient one who is dear to his Master.
There is nothing higher than the Omniscient One; by worshipping him, one is liberated. ||25||
In this world, there is nothing—whether stationary or moving—that is eternal, except for the glorious Supreme Self, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Puruṣottama. (26)
Neither by various austerities, nor by charity, nor by sacrifice can this [Supreme] be known by embodied beings, except through supreme devotion directed toward Him.
Śrī Hari dwells within all beings on every side;
though He is the witness of all, the worlds do not know Him, even though they are under the supreme Lord. 28.
He in whom all this exists, and who abides within all—He is the Ordainer and the Disposer, Time, Fire, and the one whose face is turned in every direction. (29)
The sages of the quality of passion (rājasa), the ancestors, the gods, Brahmā, Virāṭ, as well as Bhūman and others who are devoted to that [state], do not perceive him.
In some way or another, I know that Protector, but my understanding of his meaning is inferior to that;
since even those liberated ones do not reach the end or the ineffable state, what then can be said of others? (31)
Māṇikī, though she is constantly pervading his body, does not know it at all;
so what need is there to speak of her knowing the other Śaktis? 32.
The Vedas constantly proclaim that one Supreme Lord;
the Brahmins, who have mastered the Vedas, worship Him with various sacrifices.
Those established in yoga meditate and strive to perceive the further shore;
yet, without his grace, they do not see it at all, even with a piece of wood.
He alone is the enjoyer of all oblations and the bestower of their fruits;
he is the embodiment of all gods, the soul of all, and the abode of all that is auspicious. (35)
Only the wise and the virtuous behold Him through His compassion;
He is ever present for those who constantly worship Him. (36)
To them he grants that state of bliss, the supreme station;
whether they be of high, middling, or even low birth from sinful wombs. ||37||
Through devotion to him they are liberated when they have attained union with him;
his devotees do not perish, nor do they ever go to a low state.
For the virtuous, established on that path, indeed cause him to practice yoga;
the fool who reviles them reviles Bālakṛṣṇa himself.
He who worships them with devotion worships that Lord;
[offering] a leaf, a flower, a fruit, water, food, clothing, or even a liquid. (2.93.40)
He who gives to him with devotion shall always be dear to him;
for he [gives] first indeed for the sake of destroying the suffering of the class of devotees. (41)
He manifested his Śakti, Rādhikā, from his left side;
requested by her, Kṛṣṇa indeed became present in the imperishable abode (Akṣaradhāman).
He resided in Goloka for the purpose of accepting her devotion, and indeed, for the sake of bestowing prosperity upon his assembly of devotees. 43.
Requested in such a manner, Nārāyaṇa manifested his power, Śrī Lakṣmī, from his own chest, and thus he became Vaikuṇṭha.
He indeed remembered the creation as it was before for the sake of prior arrangement;
he manifested the supreme Prakṛti, his power, from his loins. (45)
Requested by her, that Blessed One, Vāsudeva—who is unmanifest, rests in the imperishable, and bestows consciousness upon primordial nature—became "I" (the individual self). 46.
Therefore, the great creation was requested by him, characterized by birth, stability, and end;
and from his own body, you three also came into being.
Aniruddha, Pradyumna, and Saṃkarṣaṇa—possessing supreme majesty—are the manifestations of the glorious Supreme Lord who perform the functions of the qualities (guṇas). 48.
Therefore, that logic (nyāya), which is abundant and born from his heart, was requested by him;
it shines forth in the immortal abode of the lords who establish justice.
Requested by him, that illusory transformation which is the cause of the sprout was released;
from his frown, that Puruṣa was born.
Then this Puruṣa sports with Māyā through Prakṛti;
from that, the pair known as the Mahat and Buddhi is born. (51)
And the man who is served by her is her beloved, the delighter of his consort;
both the Pradhāna and the Puruṣa are always known as the body of Hari. 52.
From those two, that which is called the ego-principle (ahaṅkāra) was born as the Tattva;
he indeed became Mahāviṣṇu, attended by Śrī, for the purpose of creation.
From him was born the one called Virāj, and from him the gods, Hara and the others;
through them, by way of the lineage of the ancestors, Hari indeed caused the Vedas to reach [the world].
That very Supreme Lord, shining in the highest abode,
assumed the form of Nara and Nārāyaṇa for the sake of performing austerities.
For the sake of peace for the world of living beings, for the destruction of suffering as well, and for the pacification of the Asuras, the Lord of Lakṣmī [resided] in the Ocean of Milk. (56)
In Śvēdhāma, the Beloved of Ramā shines forth as a mere partial manifestation;
he is the supreme preceptor of yogis, the virtuous, and noble women. (57)
He is the protector of the righteous and the slayer of those who hate the Vedas;
he is the destroyer of the magic of illusionists—he is the Supreme Lord. (58)
When that supreme power, Māyā, is celebrated as Vidya, she is Māyā; but when she is Avidyā, she is indeed considered the inferior power.
And he shall destroy that illusion, for Mādhava is the bestower of liberation;
Śrī Kṛṣṇa is the impeller and the withdrawer of all powers.
He is the foundation of all things and the repository of immortality;
he is the singular power of Keśava, the imperishable Brahman, and the supreme abode.
There is another vast power which indeed sustains the universe;
His state as the inner controller (antaryāmitā) therein is precisely that other power.
He who propitiates the Lord through the two wings of knowledge and devotion indeed goes to the abode of Hari, having transcended all sin.
Transcending all powers, he who performs what is pleasing to me approaches me;
through my worship, some men even become Narāyaṇas.
Accumulated through my manifestations, they deliver embodied beings;
by the power of his grace, some become lords of the worlds and Viṣṇus.
Some are Hara and others, while some are Brahmā, Īśvara, and the rest;
among all of them, the Blessed One is the impeller and the one who causes their cessation.
He is this very Brahmā, the self-existent one with faces on all sides for those who know Brahman;
he is the ancient, imperishable Lord Hari, the master of illusion.
For yogis, this Śambhu exists; for women, the Goddess born of the Lord of Mountains;
among the Ādityas, he is Viṣṇu; and among the Vasus, he is Pāvaka.
Among the Rudras he is Śaṅkara; among winged creatures, he is Garuḍa;
among lordly elephants, he is Airāvata; and among wielders of weapons, he is Rāma.
Among the sages he is Vasiṣṭha, and among the gods he is Śatakratu;
among artisans he is Viśvakarman, and among the enemies of the gods he is Prahlāda.
Among the sages he is Vyāsa, and among the hosts he is Vināyaka;
among heroes he is Vīrabhadra, and among the perfected ones he is the sage Kapila.
Of mountains, this Meru is the foremost; of constellations, the moon;
of weapons, the thunderbolt; and of vows, truth alone is supreme. (72)
He is Ananta among the serpent-beings, and he is the son of Agni among the commanders of armies;
he is the householder among the stages of life, and he is Truth itself among the ages.
Kubera is the sovereign of all yakṣas, Nirṛti of all rākṣasas;
Dakṣa is the lord of the Prajāpatis, and the lion is the king of beasts. (74)
Of the Vedas, he is the Sāmaveda; of those to be chanted, he is this Praṇava;
of hymns, he is the Puruṣasūkta; and of those possessing wisdom, he is indeed Manu. (75)
Among sciences, it is the science of the Self; among principles, it is indeed consciousness;
among goals, this is liberation alone; and among bonds, it is latent impression (vāsanā). //76//
Among the wives of the twice-born, he is the chaste Kambharā; among virtuous women, he is Satī;
and among all prosperities, that Puruṣottama has the form of Mahālakṣmī.
In this way, one should indeed meditate upon Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa in every place;
by that, the Lord Nārāyaṇa bears fruit there in every respect. (78)
And he exists in all worlds in the form of an image, O younger brothers;
likewise, the venerable Supreme Lord exists in the form of the Preceptor. ||79||
He alone is the one of virtuous form, he is the divine body, he is the purifier; Mādhava is indeed the father and he is also the mother.
He alone is the best of men, possessing the form of a father and the form of a husband;
for these eight are indeed gurus, saviors, and divinely inspired. (81)
Indeed, no repayment whatsoever exists for them;
one should always do what is pleasing to them through action, mind, and speech. (82)
These very beings are essentially the beginningless and glorious Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa;
those who worship them with this realization attain the supreme goal. ||83||
Thus, this very one is the manifest Supreme Brahman, the primordial Śrī Puruṣottama, the teacher of all incarnations, the Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa. (84)
The Blessed One, who transcends the syllable, the inner witness, and the Lord of lords, has descended and dwells in the house of Śrī Kambharā in the form of a child. 85.
That glorious Gopālabāla dwells in a golden palace near the hermitage of Lomaśa, in Akṣarakṣetra at Aśvasarasa.
In the sacred place known as Kuṅkumavāpī, upon this earth with its divine form,
he dwells in human form, served by the beloved of Brahmā.
Out of compassion, for the sake of liberating living beings and for the protection of the universe, Mādhava—though beyond the human state—exists in human form. (88)

By good fortune, he who exists as the visible form of you—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa—who are the very embodiments of their portions, has become an object of our sight, though he was previously beyond the range of our vision. (89)
Having spoken thus, the Lord Vāsudeva paused for a moment; all three of them then meditated in their hearts upon Acyuta, who is both divine and human.

Thus ends the ninety-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Means for Attaining the Lord and His Glorious Powers," in the Vāsudeva-gītā, within the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Rādhikā; awakened by the words of Vāsudeva, those three, possessing knowledge of His majesty, [beheld] that egg which was born before the universe.
At previous festivals, we went for the sake of beholding Kṛṣṇa.
Now, for the purpose of seeing that [state], those endowed with knowledge of its majesty [should proceed]. ||2||
"O You who possess the form of a child, we wish to go along with you, desiring to behold Your unique divine play and being delighted by the knowledge thereof. (3)
Thus addressed by his brothers, the Lord Hari Vāsudeva went from that world to the interior of the cosmic egg along with his brothers.
From the worlds of Vāsudeva, atoms resembling those of the Vairāja world arose,
and having become so, they entered the worlds of the Vairājas from there as well.
Having become exceedingly subtle, they then entered the world of truth (satyaloka);
from there, becoming even more minute, they ascended to heaven.
Becoming even more minute than that, they entered the world of men,
where previously the form of Śrī Vāsudeva had indeed resided in his own abode.
Of that hair, a portion equal to the highest unit of measurement (pārārdhya) resides here on the human plane;
and even of that, by a ten-millionth part, they have taken up human bodies.
And those four, known as the Vyūhas, resplendent with brilliance,
became like children in the sky above the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake.
Extremely radiant celestial swans arrived in their vimānas;
there, Vāsudeva appeared four-armed and exceedingly brilliant.
He possessed the conch, discus, mace, and lotus as his weapons and was radiant with a crown;
the other three were two-armed, bearing the discus and mace as their arms.
The youths were of divine form, auspicious, and equal to Vāsudeva;
they resembled many suns and were adorned with golden earrings.
Wearing forest garlands and the Kaustubha gem, they were graced by crowns.
Possessing divine bodies, they shine with the power and sovereignty of divine accomplishments.
Those whose pores possess the radiant splendors of ten billion gods— such are they in their celestial chariots.
Standing in the sky at evening, they appeared as if it were midday;
all the subjects of Saurāṣṭra, seeing this, thought it was still day. (15)
The Lord himself reflected upon those exceedingly vast splendors:
"He travels through the sky in a celestial chariot from one region to another for the sake of wandering. (16)
Or rather, they reasoned that just as the gods frequently come for the purpose of worshipping Hari, so too might these [beings] have arrived. || 17 ||
Then, at that time, the Bhāgavata subjects of Kuṅkumavāpī went out quickly from their own homes for the sake of a vision [of the Lord]. || 18 ||
At that moment, a beautiful celestial chariot descended from the sky onto the bank of the Aśvapaṭṭa lake, in the vicinity of Lomaśa’s hermitage.
Those four dark-hued Vyūhas emerged from the celestial chariot,
their forms like the ocean of nectar pervaded by the brilliance of ten million moons.
Having waded slowly through the waters of the Aśvapaṭṭa lake on foot,
they, in human form, bathed and proceeded to the hermitage of Lomaśa.
The sage performed hospitable reception, including a welcome and honors;
he offered the madhuparka and performed worship with sandalwood and other offerings.

Having understood the true nature of the celestial array through his divine vision, the sage Lomaśa prostrated himself like a staff; thereafter, he performed the ritual waving of lights for the various arrays.
Then the sages, dear to Brahmā, offered their salutations;
rising up and bowing to those sages, they went to the abode of Bālakṛṣṇa.
Then Bālakṛṣṇa informed his parents of the arrival of the military array;
full of enthusiasm, the parents quickly went there for the sake of honor.
But upon hearing this, other gods, sages, and even lords, as well as sacred fords, collections of essential truths, virtuous ones, holy women, and great seers [were moved]. (26)
And they went to honor those who were there in their arrayed forms, repeatedly [saluting them] with unbroken grains, sandalwood, flowers, and shouts of "Victory! (jaya).
Having been nourished and honored, they went to the abode of Bālakṛṣṇa;
then Bālakṛṣṇa assumed his own form and departed for his celestial realm.
Into whose form the multitudes of Vāsudevas attain dissolution, even the lords of ten million Golokas and Vaikuṇṭhas attain dissolution. (29)
Hari, the beginningless Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, assumed such a divine form while seated upon a celestial elephant-throne in that supreme abode.
Adorned by hosts of liberated souls numbering ten million, he shone with his form established therein;
at that moment, all other eyes abandoned their respective manifestations and were instantly fixed upon Śrī Hari.
Indeed, being defeated by the splendor of Hari, they could not prevail;
with the lotuses of their eyes closed in defeat, the gods and others then departed from there.
Then all the armies returned to their respective places, and Hari likewise [dismissed his own forces];
meanwhile, the two parents affectionately welcomed him on the courtyard of their home.
Accompanied by their lords, they entered the palace of Bālakṛṣṇa; they bowed down and paid homage to their beloved Lord, who was seated upon the elephant-throne.
Having prostrated themselves on the ground like a staff, they joyfully performed worship;
Vāsudeva placed a divine crown upon the head of Hari.
Saṃkarṣaṇa applied sandalwood paste and the essence of oil to his forehead;
Pradyumna offered him a tilaka-mark, a moon-shaped ornament, and the essence of fragrance.
She applied lovely collyrium and other cosmetics to her eyes, and placed earrings, clusters of flowers, ear-ornaments, and crest-jewels upon her ears.
Vāsudeva placed auspicious golden garlands around his neck,
as well as necklaces adorned with diamonds, rubies, and pearls, and set with the Kaustubha gem.
Saṃkarṣaṇa gave beautiful bracelets, as well as chains,
signets, rings, and likewise bracelets for the forearms.
Aniruddha gave him a girdle with beautiful golden bells,
as well as two divine, soft sandals, two fly-whisks, and a parasol.
And Saṃkarṣaṇa gave him a golden staff adorned with jewels, a turban for his hand,
and a fragrant bundle of flowers, leaves, and other items.
And Pradyumna offered a beautiful golden platter filled with sweet food like nectar, and stocked with fruits, seeds, and other delicacies. || 42 ||
Aniruddha offered him a drink of nectar as well as betel-leaf;
then the Lord Vāsudeva himself performed the waving of lights (ārātrika).
The lords performed circumambulations and prostrations like a staff;
those supreme lords offered handfuls of flowers and praised Kṛṣṇa.
You are the beginningless Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the glorious Puruṣottama, shining in the supreme abode with two arms, served by the imperishable ones. ||45||
Served by those liberated through him and by those liberated themselves, you are the Supreme Lord, the Supreme Brahman, the Supreme Self, the transcendent Blessed One, the Sovereign. ||46||
Released from you, they shine forth; they dissolve into your body;
and they abide in your presence, exceedingly delighted by your bliss. (47)
Innumerable beings in the state of Brahmā, beloved of Brahmā and equal to you, exist;
they are indeed the powers of sovereignty born from your own body. (48)
Even those liberated ones, whose forms are Brahman, perform service unto you;
we ourselves—your emanations, incarnations, and lords—are born from you. (4.9)
Likewise, the Īśvarīs, Māyā, the Puruṣas, the years, the Kālas, as well as the Vairājas, the Vaiṣṇavas, the Brāhmaṇas, and the Śāmbhavas. || 2.94.50 ||
From the various forms of your body, the great seers, the ancestors, the sages, the perfected ones, and the virtuous practitioners of yoga have indeed arisen. ||51||
Satī, Sāvitrī, those who observe the vows of Sāṃkhya and Yoga, beloved wives, chaste women, likewise the wife devoted to her husband, Lakṣmī, and Nārāyaṇa. ||52||
The Pitṛs, those clad in celestial raiment, Nara, and likewise Nārāyaṇa;
those dwelling in Pātāla, those in the subterranean abodes, and Śeṣa-Nārāyaṇa in the milk-ocean.
Śrī, Līlā, Bhū, Satī, Padmā, Gaṅgā, Prabhā, Sarasvatī, Māṇikyā, Saguṇā, Premā, Pāravatī, and Mañjulā. (54)
Vibhūti, Rādhikā, Sītāmṛtā, Santoṣikā, Ramā, Haṃsā, Duḥkhahālakṣmī, Dayā, Jayā, and Tulasī. (55)
Haimī, Śāntā, Sāvitrī, and Vṛndā—these are indeed the Śaktis;
likewise Campā, Lalitā, Kastūrī, Ojasvatī, and others.
Kapila, Datta, Īśāna, Nṛsiṃha, Vāmana, Hari, Haṃsa, Matsya, Kūrma, Varāha, and also Jiṣṇu. (57)
Hari, Pṛthu, Gopāla, Haṃsa, Ṛṣabha, the Lord (Īśitā), Rāma, Paraśurāma, Bala, and the venerable Śuka. ||58||
Vallabha, Hemanta, and Devaprakāśa—these, as well as Yajña and the Kumārayogas, are all manifestations of your own portions. 59.
The principles, the consciousness of the principles, the qualities, powers, flavors, and so forth—
O Blessed One, all these are Your portions, and You alone are woven through them.
Everything is thus woven in you; you alone are the supreme Lord.
We are eager to behold the Child for the sake of obtaining a vision of you. 61.
"O Lord, we have attained the vision [of you] and our purpose is fulfilled," they said;
having spoken thus, they bowed down, offered a handful of flowers, and remained in a state of happiness.
Then Bālakṛṣṇa, Vāsudeva, spoke to Rādhā in order to request that boon from her: "May you always have your dwelling at my feet."
"O Lord, ocean of compassion, grant [our request] and completely fulfill our desire!
"So be it," the Lord said, and he created two bodies for them.
The second primary form, as well as the fourfold manifestation (vyūha), resided at Kuṅkumavāpī and Vyūhatīrtha respectively.
By the command of Śrī Hari, it then went to that white island (Śvetadvīpa);
from there it went to Satyaloka, and from there to the unmanifest abode (Avyākṛtadhāma).
Thus, O Rādhikā, those great lords known as Vāsudeva and the others are the rulers of the emanations and the masters of the individual souls, standing before Śrī Hari.
They always made their residence at the Aśvapaṭṭa lake;
on the bank of that sacred water was their most auspicious temple. (68)
And the place called Vāsudevālaya was constructed by Viśvakarman;
there, by the command of Śrī Hari, those brothers shine resplendent.
Within the crown disciple of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa,
Svayaṃprakāśa, those known as the Vyūhas remain merged.
The four Blessed Ones are the very embodiment of consciousness; He is the manifestation of the Vyūha itself, the self-luminous Lord. (71)
Vāsudeva himself dwells there, endowed with fourfold qualities;
and men behold him as divine, four-armed, and self-luminous.
Those who shall worship Him will obtain the merit resulting from the manifestation of the cosmic array;
listen, O Rādhikā, to Vāsudeva, who is self-luminous. (73)
And his beloved wives always go there every morning for the purpose of worship;
indeed, the wife of Vāsudeva is Lakṣmī, while she who is Hariṇī is Mā. (74)
Sunandā, the wife of Saṃkarṣaṇa, was a great virtuous woman;
she was the beloved and the intellect of Pradyumna, and the nourisher of all.
O Rādhikā, those four women of excellent character indeed always travel in a celestial chariot of fourfold splendor belonging to Aniruddha.
Behold, this auspicious moment has arrived for their departure;
at that very instant, their celestial chariot emerged before Rādhikā.
Upon seeing them, Rādhikā descended from her celestial chariot;
Rādhikā, for her part, rose up, bowed, and embraced them with deep emotion.
With a serene mind, she offered him a welcome, as well as the honey-mixture (madhuparka) and a seat;
she performed worship, extended full hospitality, and completed all the rites.
She also inquired after their welfare, as she did for Rādhikā.
Rādhā said, "O dear ones, where is your journey taking you? It will soon be morning."
They said to us: "The Lord Śrīśa, known by the name Svayaṃprakāśa, the Blessed One who is an avatāra from the Vyūha, resides at Aśvasarovara. (81)
The great lord (Mahāprabhu) is a disciple of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa;
indeed, there are four portions of our husbands present therein. (82)
He dwells among human beings, endowed with the vow of celibacy from childhood; we indeed go there daily for the purpose of worshipping him. ||83||
"O Rādhā, because you remembered us, we have come here filled with joy.
Having spoken thus to Rādhikā, they, being eager, worshipped her. (84)
They indeed gave all the articles of adornment to Rādhikā;
then, having received her command, they quickly departed for Lake Aśvasaras.
Hariṇī, Sunandā, Dhī, and Suśīlā—these [four] worshipped their respective portions with flowers, unbroken grains of rice, and sandalwood paste. ||86||
Having drunk the water from the husband's big toe and having fed him, she then performed the waving of lights (ārātrika) and other rites,
and received his grace.
Having massaged her feet, and then having bowed to the glorious Śrī Kaṃbharā, offered worship with joined palms, and received her auspicious words. (88)
Then they went toward the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa; having worshipped the Supreme Lord of Lords, they bowed down and praised him again and again. (89)
Having performed the nightly lamp-offering for Hari, they stood there and meditated upon Hari for a moment.
The Lord said, "I am pleased; choose whatever boon you desire."
Then they said to us, "We shall dwell here in such a way that our devotion to our husbands may be protected while serving in both places. (91)
"O Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, always fulfill my desires!
"So be it," Hari replied, assuming two forms.
The Lord established four forms of the Tīrtha at Vyūhatīrtha and caused them to reside within the images in the temple. (93)
Just as the service of self-luminous [beings] occurs through their own divine forms, so indeed was it performed by them when Nārāyaṇa had been created. //94//
Then, having received the command, the other primary forms indeed departed for the unmanifest abode (avyākṛta-dhāma) which is the resort of Vāsudeva and the others. 95.
O Rādhikā, thus has the wickedness of yours come before my eyes, as well as the wonderful sovereignty of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa. (96)
What shall I say of the majesty of that Supreme Lord, by the chanting of whose qualities both worldly enjoyment and liberation are eternally secured? (97)
Where sovereign powers always abide with divine forms, and where even the lords of lords dwell with divine forms. (98)
Where the incarnations of Hari abide in divine forms, and where all the lords of creation and the gods dwell in divine forms. (99)
There, the beloved of Brahmā dwell in liberated states with divine forms,
for the sake of attaining the grace of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
The greatness of that sacred field cannot be described;
on the full moon day of the month of Jyeṣṭha, that Vyūhatīrtha became a lake.
And on the second day of the month of Āṣāḍha, the four holy sites of Śrīcatuṣṭaya and Svayaṃprakāśatīrtha became sanctifying at that time.

Thus ends the ninety-fourth chapter, titled "The Arrival at the Kuṅkumavāpī Tīrtha by the Four Vyūhas and the Four Śrīs, and the Description of the Svayaṃprakāśa Tīrtha, the Vyūhacatuṣṭaya Tīrtha, and Others," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen to another marvel of Śrī Hari, the Supreme Soul:
through the union of Rādhā and the eleven devotees, the land was perfectly protected. (1)
Indeed, while the southern region known as Uṣṇālaya was being attacked,
there in that arsenal of weapons during the battle, by means of the terrible ocean winds—
When the calamity had arisen, the region was buried in the midst of sands,
while its surroundings were overwhelmed and inundated by the waters of the ocean.
It was covered by rain in the month of Bhādrapada and destroyed;
thereafter, it was [restored] by the Lord Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
Listen to this most meritorious story concerning Rakṣita, who protected his devotee;
in the great region of Uṣṇālaya, the great sage Agastya [once lived] in the east.
In former times, Agastya traveled through the sky to purify that land,
traversing many regions and even crossing over the ocean.
He went to that great region on the mountain named Hemaśāla;
from there, he traveled through the sky to Bālācala and then to Mount Rāvāsana.
Dārāliṅga Mountain, Maṣīgrīva Mountain, Bhekadānaka,
likewise Śālavīna Mountain, and then Grāmācala.
Having gone to Mount Ācāla, as well as Mount Divādi,
and then to Mount Cāṭa, he arrived at Hemaśālaka.
Having beheld his auspicious valley, which was covered with trees, creepers, and grasses, and made rich with fruits and flowers by the excellent rains, he dwelt there for a year.
One should remember the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa day and night:
*Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya svāmine svāhā*. (1.1)
Dwelling on the Hemashalacala mountain, he always recites the mantra; Lopamudra, devoted to her husband, likewise recites that very mantra.
Accompanied by her, the sage would constantly travel through the sky to make those rivers sacred; he went daily to bathe at the banks of various streams.
He bathed repeatedly in the Murā river, the Turu river, and the Aita river;
likewise, he bathed in the Gośaṅku river and also in the Bālā river at times.
He bathed in the Marcāśanā river, as well as in Lake Māka,
Bālāsarovara, Māṅgī lake, and the waters of Śvānikā.
He bathed in the Kuvana lake, as well as in the Lābharuci lake,
and likewise in the Jhinku river, the Rinku river, and the Phinku river.
He bathed in the Uttuṅga lake, as well as in the Āra lake;
he bathed in the Turū lake and also in the lake named Grāgi.
The sage bathed in the Maurī river, the Turā river, and likewise the Bhurā river,
as well as in the Kavindumānā river and the Gaurānara lake.
Then, at Kāruliṅgī, Dāruliṅgī, and Cāruliṅgī-sarit, as well as at the rivers Kvīlpī, Laviṅgā, and Pāvanā. (19)
The sage Agastya indeed bathed in the Mīcalā, the Philañcā,
the Ghelī river, the Helī river, and also in the Vitūrīyā stream.
Having bathed in the Phījarā river, the Cāpagā, and even in the mountain cascades,
the virtuous Lopāmudrā performed worship and the adoration of those deities.
The lakes and rivers also brought about the humiliation of Agastya;
then, in those regions, here and there upon the banks of the rivers— || 22 ||
In a certain mountainous region and on the bank of a certain lake,
there were Brahmins who were fierce ascetics, devotees of Viṣṇu, and worshippers of the Sun.
Upon seeing this Agastya of renowned prowess, all of you, O Vāsanta,
with delighted hearts, joyfully offered him a welcome and other courtesies.
Hemaśālāyana, Bālāyana, Rāvāsanāyana, Dārāliṅgāyana, and the ascetic Bhekadāneya; ||25||
And the great seer Masigrīva, as well as Śālavanāyana;
the seer Ācāla, as well as Grāmāyana and Vāṭāyana. ||26||
Thousands of ascetics who knew the Veda, such as Divāṅgāyana and others, as well as other Brahmins residing in hermitages and forests, were present. || 27 ||
Ascetics devoted to great renunciation, wise women, truthful and virtuous wives, and those dedicated to the meditation on the Self all dwell there. (28)

Agastya, however, bestowed upon them the supreme knowledge of the Lord (Pārameśvara-vijñāna)—[the knowledge] of the Supreme Brahman, which transcends the imperishable and shines in the highest abode. ||29||
He who is served by infinite liberated souls, known by the name Śrī Puruṣottama,
who is the Supreme Self and the Inner Self, and who is even more dark than Kṛṣṇa.
From Vāsudeva came Mahāvāsudeva, the illustrious Supreme Lord,
the Blessed One and Sovereign, endowed with divine sovereignty, majesty, and other such powers.
He is the controller of time and illusion, the teacher of the manifestations of his emanations;
the Lord of lords among lords, and the bestower of divine power upon the gods. ||32||
He is the protector of the sages and the ancestors, abiding within their hearts;
he is the inner witness of gods, humans, and nāgas, higher than the highest.
He is beloved and dear to all Brahmas, the bestower of light upon all abodes,
the sustainer of all incarnations, the witness of all, and the stainless one.
You are self-luminous, possessed of boundless splendor, more beautiful than the ultimate Kāmadeva;
You are of divine form, to be known through the Vedas, and to be realized by yogis within the inner self. 35.
He is to be known by those with the eye of the heart, yet unknowable by external functions; inaccessible to those veiled by illusion, but accessible to those endowed with devotion.
Though situated at a great distance or even in extreme proximity, Hari is the friend who bestows happiness; he is the giver of all, eternally blissful, and the bestower of all joy. (37)
The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of Rādhā and Ramā, the husband of Prabhā, Pāravatī, Haṃsā, Mañjulā, and Saguṇā. || 38 ||
