The Lord of Lakṣmī, Śrī, and Māṇikī; the true master who is cherished by his devotees; the chief of sages, full of compassion; though not a child, he assumes the form of a child. 39.
And he resides in the region of Surāṣṭra, in the district of Ajanābha,
on the shore of the Aśvapaṭṭa lake, in the field of Akṣara that bestows liberation.
In his own residence, the divine city known as Kuṅkumavāpī, that glorious young Gopāla was the son of Kambharāśrī. 41.
He who is the Supreme Brahman himself exists today as the child-Brahmā;
and he who is the inner self now indeed exists externally as the child-self.
He bestows the fruit of yoga upon yogins, is the object of the wisdom of the knowers, dwells in the minds of the liberated, and is the upholder of truth for virtuous women. ||43||
He is the fire-form of sacrifices, the consumer of oblations;
he is the Lord who exists as the very form of faith, sustaining the ascetic life of those devoted to austerity.

For those of virtuous nature, it is the essence of dharma; for political strategies, it is the expansion of justice; for noble deeds, it is hospitality toward guests; and for devotees, it is the sphere of propitiating the Lord. ||45||
He who is formless and possesses an infinite form shines as a child;
out of compassion, he is an ocean of mercy, bestowing liberation even upon sinners. (46)
By whose influence even insentient principles, whether they be created or uncreated, become sentient and divine. ||47||
The unliberated attain liberation, the sinful become pure, and those who have not achieved perfection reach perfection—through whose meditation they go to final release. (48)
By his majesty, the unvirtuous become virtuous;
and by his mere remembrance, those who are deceitful become empty of deceit.
Impurities are destroyed even by the mere sight of his form;
once he has been seen, nothing further remains to be done.
Nothing remains to be attained; indeed, he exists as a child today.
O Brahmins, accept that mantra which bestows liberation and grants all perfections. 51.
Thus addressed, O Rādhikā, the brāhmaṇas received the supreme mantra:
"Oṃ, obeisances to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Master; svāhā! (52)
They constantly chanted prayers and indeed meditated upon Him of divine form;
within their hearts, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa shone forth clearly.
A youth of divine form, as beautiful as ten million gods of love,
they then constantly enjoyed themselves through the worship prescribed by Agastya.
Desiring liberation, they performed the eightfold devotion to Śrī Hari;
thus, hundreds of thousands of Brahmins worship Hari in this manner.
Then, through the power of Agastya, on that land which was the abode of weapons,
they became devoted to the Great Lord in the great region of Uṣṇālaya.
At the end of the rainy season, the king of sages, Agastya, having visited all the sacred fords in every direction,
traveled through the air together with Lopāmudrā to the Aśvasārasa lake.
He became established there in that sacred field known as Śrī-kuṅkumavāpī. Then, in the month of Bhādrapada, a great planet appeared there in the sky during the night.
With his crest-flames extending for a thousand yojanas,
he indeed rises daily as a portent foreboding the calamity of the land.
The comet Dhūmaketu, the destroyer of the world, brings great terror;
upon seeing it, all living beings are overwhelmed by the fear of destruction.
O Bālakṛṣṇa, they both became and were devoted to the Supreme Person;
they performed devotion toward Him consisting of various forms of worship. ||61||
Then, at the end of the month of Bhādra, on the full moon day, at the very break of dawn, a flooding of the waters of the ocean indeed occurred all around. ||62||
The tides, which bring fear and cause the destruction of all lands,
were agitated by exceedingly fierce winds together with rains.
The earth surrounding the continent of Uṣṇālaya was indeed submerged by the waters of the ocean for a portion of a yojana in extent, like at the time of universal dissolution.
Villages, hamlets, market towns, dwellings, and extensive cowherd settlements—
extending for as many yojanas as there are from the ocean to its limit.
Then, during the dissolution by water, the trees, creepers, forest regions, gardens, and groves were destroyed by the forceful surges of the ocean's tide.
He seized the moorings for ships, embankments, cultivated lands, roads for the protection of travelers, and the houses situated on the heads of the earth (mountain peaks). 67.
The sites of business were destroyed by the forceful currents of the flood; all the structures supporting the aerial chariots were swept away by the surging waters. (68)
Likewise, all the river mouths, as well as the dwellings of living beings, cattle, birds, and other things—even the mines—have gone to destruction. (69)
When the water had thus subsided, a great cry of "Alas!
Alas! arose; then even the rivers were agitated, and the lakes as well were tossed in turmoil.
The rivers, lakes, and waters flowed everywhere across the fields; those regions, along with their inhabitants, were destroyed by the overflowing floods. (71)
On land there was water, and in water there was land; everything became inverted.
Due to excessive rain and violent winds, embodied beings met their destruction.
Embodied beings are no longer seen on the mountains or dwelling in the forests;
instead, the corpses of men and birds are visible amidst the currents of water. (73)
And numerous beasts, such as reptiles and deer, are seen by the thousands being swept away by the waves. (74)
Trees and the branches of trees are seen in the waters of the flood;
houses and leaf-huts float amidst the waters of dissolution. (75)
Rivers, lakes, other ponds, and even wells appeared filled with water, resembling the ocean or large excavated reservoirs. ||76||
When the cause of destruction, the deluge of waters, had thus arisen,
the sands lying on the battlefield were then swept away by violent winds.
Then those [visions] appeared in the sky just like clouds;
their eyes, filled with sand, fell into blindness. (78)
With their eyes struck by the sand, those embodied beings do not see one another there at all; blinded by the dust, they are buffeted by the wind.
By the force of the wind, trees, houses, creepers, and even the coverings of pavilions were cast into the sky.
Ceilings, canopies, garments, and birds alike were cast with great force by the wind, both upon the water and onto the land.
The houses were utterly shattered, as were the trees, the leaf-huts, the dwellings, the hermitages, the mansions, the palaces, and the huts; all perished. (82)
The villages were indeed covered beneath sands by showers of sand;
thus, having risen up from the battlefield, there was a shower of sand.
The trees, groves, gardens, people, birds, animals, and even the ascetics had their bodies covered with sand. (84)
Those who were buried within the sand and placed inside the earth instantly became breathless; thousands of millions of them died. (85)
The sages and seers, dwelling both on the mountains and upon the earth,
beheld that most fierce Upacchava and remained restrained in meditative absorption.
Having drawn back the vital breaths through the channels, they sat in the practice of *kuṃbhaka* and other yogic techniques,
and remembered the Blessed Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa within their hearts.
Distraught, they wept, trembled, and cried out with choked voices;
the children wailed "Alas! Alas! and cried out, "O Mother! O Father! (88)
Lamenting, the men called out to their wives from the riverbank;
the wives, in turn, called out excessively to their children and their father.
There were also the cries and roars of beasts and birds, as well as of camels, elephants, lions, and fires. (2.95.90)
Then, during the violent storm, those who bore the suffering were repeatedly overwhelmed;
they could neither be heard nor protected, where even self-preservation was difficult to achieve. (9.1)
In that regard, by whom or where can others be protected without Hari?
For those who have become morsels of food in the jaws of Time, who here is their protector? (92)
Mountains, battlefields, rivers, and lakes;
forests, highlands, wildernesses, and cultivated lands—93.
Then, on the night of the full moon of Bhādrapada and on the first day [of the new moon], the entire surface of the earth was oppressed by violent winds. ||94||
In the evening, those subjects died as if by death, though without the great portents;
at that time, the stainless great sages, headed by Hemaśālāyana, [were present].
Beholding the unappeased force of the wind and the dissolution caused by the waters and the air,
they remembered Bālakṛṣṇa for the sake of attaining peace within meditative absorption alone.
The ocean of compassion, the protector of devotees, the treasure-house of mercy, who disregards all sins and protects those who have come for refuge. (97)
The Lord who protects the elephant, the Black One who guards the womb, the Protector during the dissolution of the universe, the Master who guards against illusion. 98.
To Hari, the protector of the vital breaths, the beloved, the performer of all protections;
to the divine Lord who protects children, the husband who effects the preservation of creation. ||99||
In yoga, one should meditate upon the Supreme Lord Nārāyaṇa, the Master who provides protection,
the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the life-sustainer of all embodied beings.
But when the dissolution had set in, the eleven sages remembered [the Lord] within their hearts;
they all praised Him mentally for the sake of protecting the world.
For the sake of pacifying violent winds, for the sake of pacifying rain, for the sake of pacifying showers of sand, and for the protection of living beings. (102)
O Rādhikā, when destruction was imminent, the great sages praised the Supreme Lord, the highest of the high, the compassionate Bālakṛṣṇa.

Thus ends the ninety-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of Agastya’s Departure and the Recollection of Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa by the Assembly of Sages Thereupon when Dissolution Occurred Due to the Turbulence of the Stormy Wind and Ocean Waters," in the Uṣṇālaya-khaṇḍa of the second section (Tretāyantāna) of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Listen, O Rādhikā; the child Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Lord, having arrived when thus praised, protected her and granted her life. || 1 ||
In every land, those living beings who had taken refuge in Agastya remembered their preceptor, whose nature is that of Brahman, as they were facing death.
They praised Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Lord, and the Supreme Brahman:
"O Blessed One, if we have been created here by you for the sake of destruction," (3)
Why do you not come here yourself in person and bring about our destruction?
For destruction at your hands would lead to our liberation and be for our ultimate welfare. (4)
By you, birth was bestowed; by you, Agastya was appointed as my preceptor.
O Lord of Compassion, you dwell thus upon my tongue and in my mind.
Thus, O Lord, these people are living beings who have been rendered lifeless by you;
their very lives, which constitute their death, truly remain in your hand. (6)
Life, vitality, and movement—all are under your control;
so how is it that here there is wind and rain, as well as showers of sand? (7)
Death, which brings about miserable rebirths through floods and cosmic dissolutions,
does not even behold the presence of the yogi Agastya at its end.
In this case of sudden death, this formidable realm of the hungry ghosts will become the domain of the Ender; how can such a thing be pleasing to you? (9)
You are the protector of those who have come for refuge, the one worthy of being sought as a shelter, and the remover of suffering;
O Lord, why do you not come for the sake of destroying the misery of death?

Foolish men and women whose wisdom has not yet arisen, pregnant women suffering from the pangs of pregnancy, and those dwelling in dependence upon the elderly—all these die in the womb, struck by the sand. (11)
O Lord, they die even in the waters without seeing you;
is it that the name Hari does not belong to you, or are you indeed Nārāyaṇa? (19)
In this matter, O Kṛṣṇa, what has been made black by you, you who are [already] black? Alas, O Janārdana, you have been stifled by the suppression of your own breath! 13.
O Janārdana, why are you celebrated here for deeds that are like those of the wind?
O compassionate Kṛṣṇa, how is it that you cut off compassion in a time of calamity?
How can you, who are non-violent, tolerate violence? Are you devoid of virtue?
For if a father were to witness the suffering being born to his offspring, [he would surely prevent it]. (15)
A human being strives for the sake of destroying suffering even at the cost of his own life;
yet you, though not a human, remain here—does fatherhood not exist in you? (16)
Why do you not deliver us from this misery? O Lord, why are you not the destroyer of suffering? And how is it, O Hari, that this death of your devotees has occurred so suddenly?
"O Lord, why are we not devoted to you? What offense have we committed against you?
Is this the fruit of our devotion to you—nothing less than death and destruction? (18)
How can such sin remain in one who is devoted to you, since the fruit of it is sudden destruction, for the ground of the dead is indeed the earth? (19)
On one side, let the ocean overflow; on the other, let there be the downpour of clouds.
On one side, let there be a rain of sand; likewise, on the other, let there be a violent whirlwind.
There is destruction on all sides by the waters of the ocean, ruin from above by rains, slaughter from the flanks by sands, and annihilation on every side by the blows of the wind.
Sacrificial offering, pressing, the restraint of breath, as well as crushing, harming, becoming a mass of refuse, beating, confinement, and so forth. (22)
Everything that exists here is complete, and there is no other world such as the realm of Yama;
how then, O Lord, can there be calamities for your devotees on this earth? (23)
O Lord, tell us why you sacrifice your life in this untimely dance;
protect, protect us, O ocean of compassion, and ward off the ocean of water! 24.
Save us, save us from the calamities of battle; save us from rain, water, and the like!
O Agastya, O Guru, protect us, and protect those who have died while taking refuge in you.
"Protect, protect, O Guru! Protect, O Kṛṣṇa! Protect, O Lord Nārāyaṇa!
Thus they prayed, seeking protection for the subjects in that manner. (26)
O Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, O Hari, protection was formerly afforded by you to the earth in the form of the Boar, and again in the form of Pṛthu. ||27||
In the form of a fish, he placed the worlds upon a boat in the water;
and in the form of Narahari, he provided protection for Prahlāda.
Indeed, through the forms of Pradyumna and others, the worlds are protected;
and in the form of Jiṣṇu, you always provide protection for the gods. (29)
Even while assuming the form of a virtuous being, you grant fearlessness to all living creatures;
indeed, O Hari, you are the protector of all, for everything created has been created by you.
You are the dwelling place of all living beings; O Treasure of Compassion, grant us protection!
You provide protection for the seed in the earth, and you likewise provide protection for the sprout. ||31||
You provide protection for the leaf, for the stalk, and for the knot;
likewise, you provide protection for the stem, the pod, the flower, the grain, and even the fruit. (32)
Furthermore, O Lord of the worlds, you provide protection for seeds;
you are the bestower of protection in water, on land, in the sky, in wind, and in fire.
Thus, you shine forth as the deliverer of those in hell;
the children of Śāva, Dīna, and Mahākālī have been well protected by you.
In the past, you warded off the curse that would have turned her into a Rākṣasī;
you, O Blessed Lord, are always the protector of the sages. (35)
The twice-born Devāyana was raised by you from a caṇḍāla womb;
the son of a brahmin who had gone to the abode of Yama was brought back to life by you. (36)
O Lord, in former times Moñjāmbikā was protected by you in the ocean;
and O Kṛṣṇa, the protection of the sage Brakadāna was performed by you at Arava. (37)
Protection was indeed afforded by you to King Udayana when he was submerged in water;
Vasumedha, along with his family, was likewise rescued by you from the depths of the water. (38)
Protection was granted to the devotee named Sudhana from the thieves;
protection was granted to the disciples of Hiraṇyakeśin when they were being destroyed by Rākṣasas. ||39||
The worlds, who had died from the great pestilence, have been restored to life by you;
likewise, protect and give life to these people from these great portents.
Lord of the syllables, Lord of liberation, Lord of the abode, Sovereign of power;
Lord of the lords of lords, Lord of the world, Lord of Māyā, Supreme Lord. 41.
O Ātmeśvara, Mahākāleśvara, Saṃkarṣaṇeśvara, Rudreśa, and Sarvavighneśa, protect us who have come to you for refuge! 42.
We are as if dead or fallen at your feet;
whether it be life or death, do as you please.
Death that grants liberation is the most excellent, whether it be natural or caused by external signs;
indeed, it may be of any kind whatsoever, or may occur through whatever means.
On the sovereign throne of Brahmā, death is like that of a denizen of hell;
yet for one who is destitute and without protection, the supreme path bestows liberation. 45.
Whether it be from you, or from your devotees, or from virtuous women of the Brahmin caste—
if their sight should occur during the movement of the vital breaths, that alone is auspicious and bestows liberation.
Whether it be the grace of the breath-control practice, or of water, or of fruit—only that person who attains it possesses the fortune that bestows the path to liberation. (47)
Indeed, at the time of death, neither the sight of you, nor the remembrance of you, nor even the chanting of your name shall ever occur for the wicked, nor even for the virtuous. (48)
If we are your devotees and you remain our teacher, and if you possess the power to deliver us, then grant us protection. (49)
What is the use of killing those who are already dead, or of protection that is fruitless like a barren hope? Let whatever may be, let it be; we shall desist from this excessive prolixity.
Having thus offered this praise according to her intellect, O Rādhikā, all creatures have sought refuge in every way with you in the face of death. (51)
Then the primordial Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa himself, accompanied by Śrī, as well as the great devotee Agastya, who was equal to Brahmā in his power, [arrived]. || 52 ||
And Śaṅkara was accompanied by Lopāmudrā, as was Pārvatī;
and Aśvinī-bālaka was likewise joined by Sañjīvanī and others. ||53||
They went swiftly by celestial chariot toward Hemaśālāyana,
to that great mountain Hemaśāla where he shines within a cave.
With his body covered by sands, the lord of yogis remembers the Lord;
in this same way, those eleven devotees, the lords of yogis, indeed remember him. 55.
Having himself made that celestial chariot stable in the atmosphere,
Hari personally surveyed that region, the land of Khaṇḍa, which was being oppressed by the earth.
Then the Blessed One, impelled by compassion, quickly [covered] the ground where the sites had been lost and destroyed with water and sand, as well as with a fierce wind.
In a single great breath, he drank them up in a mere moment;
the storm wind went to its destruction, and Rudra indeed seized the clouds.
The clouds have vanished, and the sky has become stainless and free from affliction;
the sage Agastya, the king of munis, drank the ocean in a single moment with his cupped palms.
When all the water had dried up everywhere in that hot abode,
the virtuous Lopāmudrā then called upon the auspicious Earth.
There, the Earth, in the form of a maiden and endowed with humility, arrived;
she bowed down to Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa, Agastya, Satī, Bhava, and Śivā.
And seeking his command, Lopāmudrā quickly said to him:
"Become as you were before, like the former land prior to the storm."
Wherein were villages, cities, market towns, and hamlets;
where there were cowherd settlements and city dwellers, and where the subjects lived as they had been.
"In that manner, you must naturally level the surface of the earth.
Thus commanded, the Earth immediately became sentient.
In every region where your subjects indeed resided, she became in every way a provider of space for the protection of the planets hidden within the earth's womb.
Then the Blessed One gave this command to the gods and the Maruts:
"Let all the sand that has been newly gathered be carried away quickly. (66)
Wherever there may be a living being situated beneath the sand,
let all those places indeed be made uncovered.
Thus addressed, all the Maruts, assuming the forms of whirlwinds, then gathered up the sands from the entire earth through the sky in a very short time.
And Kṛṣṇa Narāyaṇa said to the Puruṣa of the fire-element (tejastattva):
"Quickly dry up all the moist lands within that space. (69)
"Let those who were hidden and those who are dead be brought out!"—
thus the fires and all the gods performed that task with reverence.
In the ocean and in rivers, in streams and in lakes, on mountains, in valleys, in caves, in the womb, in mud, in forests, and upon the earth. ||71||
In a pit, in a dug-out trench, in a pond, in a forest, in a city, in a house, in a hall, in a bower, in a garden-plot, in a grove, and in a courtyard. ||72||
Whether at the edge of a palace, in the middle of a palace, at a gateway, or within clay;
in the midst of water, within a stone, or wherever it may be most inaccessible—(73)
On dry land, on every piece of ground, in the water, in wooden troughs, and wherever there are human beings, animals, birds, or other embodied beings worthy of being counted; ||74||
Men, women, youths, children, and likewise young girls;
whether old or even decrepit, as well as cows, buffaloes, and so forth—75.
Having dispatched the messengers of Yama in an instant, they are perceived everywhere as having completely surrendered their lives. (76)
They searched most thoroughly for all of them— whether living or dead, those established in meditative absorption or those who had fainted— throughout every location.
Then Śambhu dispatched his own messengers in all directions—
ten million Gaṇas endowed with the juices of the Sañjīvanī herb— to act with speed.
The boy Aśvinī, having caused [them] to hear the mantras,
gave them the juices of the Sañjīvanī and the Sandhinī plants, as well as their potent essences.
Then Rudra, known as Prāṇa, restored life even to those who were dead;
indeed, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa bestowed consciousness upon them.
Within two ghaṭikās, that entire region of the hot abode became inhabited by living beings who enjoyed happiness, just as before. ||81||
Then, in another moment, Śrī restored his prosperity to its former state; and Lopāmudrā, Satī, Pārvatī, Śrī, and the circle of female companions did likewise.
Then, having repeatedly gathered those householders who were separated and wherever they might have been, I brought them to their dwellings in the village.

The hosts of supernatural powers (siddhis), numbering in the tens of millions, as well as their various capacities, were all subject to Lopāmudrā and the others; at that time, they were her male and female servants.
And by the command of the virtuous ones, having gone with the speed of thought to the region of Uṣṇālaya from all sides, he brought them forth by means of his powers of sovereignty.
Just as the families had previously been situated there, they restored them to those very places and, full of zeal, brought them happiness.
Thus, by his own majesty, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the ocean of compassion, rendered the great region of Uṣṇālaya free from all affliction. (87)
He restored them all to life and brought them back to their respective abodes—
the humans, birds, and animals that were worthy of living, as well as his own self.
Then, indeed, the ocean, the wind, and the clouds, oppressed by fear, came there to seek refuge in Śrī Hari for the sake of forgiveness. (89)
There, Hari granted them the gift of fearlessness and spoke thus:
"May they never indeed bring about the dissolution of the sovereign of the whole earth."
"Wherever My devotees reside, there no calamity shall occur.
Having spoken thus to them, Śrī Hari said to the ocean: "By you, at any time... (91)
One must never act without observing the proper time; one must by no means travel across the land after having transgressed the prescribed hour. 92.
However, for all oceans, as well as for famous lakes—whether they are natural or artificial—this rule is prescribed. (93)
Likewise, having crossed over their locations by means of sands, one must never go upon the ground, nor indeed anywhere by means of winds. (94)
The sands on the surface of the earth must not be carried away by the wind;
leaving the shores behind, one must never go further ahead.
One must certainly abide by the rule in battle and on the fields of combat;
this boundary is established here and must never be transgressed.
May the clouds grant abundance; may they never be turbulent anywhere;
and having regard for the clouds, may all things turn out otherwise than this nowhere at any time. (97)
Thus was the boundary established there by Mādhava;
likewise, even regarding the conjunction of the planets in the sky, it was thus ordained.
From that time forward, the principles (tattvas) indeed exist on the surface of the earth in accordance with the rules, providing only happiness and being entirely free from calamities. 99.
Then, having thus caused the protection of the country to be performed and having made the necessary arrangements,
the vehicle of Śrī Hari descended from the sky onto the surface of the earth.
O Rādhikā, in the midst of the forest of the mountain named Hemaśālā,
there dwells the living disciple, the sage Hemaśālāyana.

Thus ends the ninety-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Prayer of the People and Great Sages of the Region of Uṣṭrālaya, the Lord’s Departure, the Pacification of the Calamity, and the Granting of Life to All," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O Rādhikā, then all those hosts of celestial beings (vaimānika-gaṇas), numbering indeed billions upon billions, were the servants of Anādi-Bāla-Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
Śaṅkara, the king of sages Agastya, and the goddesses also took leave of their own Lord and descended at the site of Hemaśālāyana.
Hemaśālāyana welcomed them upon seeing Agastya, his preceptor Śambhu, as well as Kṛṣṇa Narāyaṇa. || 3 ||
He attained supreme joy and welcomed him;
falling prostrate on the ground like a staff, he cried out, "Victory to Kṛṣṇa! || 4 ||
Then she offered them seats, the honey-mixture (madhuparka), water for the feet (pādya), and the respectful offering (arghya);
she danced before those compassionate protectors. || 5 ||
Seeing that devotee dancing, Śrī Hari rejoiced;
the Lord, overflowing with affection, placed his feet upon the chest of the devotee.
He placed his hands upon the head [of Hemaśālāyana] and embraced him again and again;
he then quickly bestowed divine vision upon Hemaśālāyana.
Hemaśāla, with his divine vision, beheld the abode of the camel;
indeed, the entire surface of the earth all around was well-protected.
Seeing that humans, birds, and even conscious animals had indeed been restored to life, he attained great joy.
Then he remembered the ten Vaiṣṇava sages; for the sake of seeing Hari there, they were instantly remembered and arrived.
By way of the path of the sky, auspicious Vaiṣṇava yogins, shining like the moon, descended into the hermitage of Hemaśālāyana.
All of them wore garlands of *tulasī* and were chanting the name of Śrī Hari;
they beheld their guru Agastya as the primordial Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
Filled with joy, they bowed to Śaṅkara, the physician of happiness, and the Mothers; they all honored them with mental offerings.
Hemaśālāyana, Bālāyana, Rāvāsanastathā, Dārāliṅgāyana, and he who bears the name Bhekadāneyana. (14)
Maṣīgrīvāyana, Śālavanāyana, the sage Ācāla, Grāmāyana, and Vāṭāyana as well; || 15 ||
These eleven great sages, beginning with Diva and ending with Liṅgālaya, were solely devoted to their beloved Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. || 16 ||
And those most excellent and highly fortunate devotees rejoiced greatly upon seeing their beloved deity Bālakṛṣṇa, as well as Agastya and their preceptor.
They prostrated themselves like staffs before those who had granted them the gift of life;
then Keśava spoke to the great ṛṣis as they were seated upon their thrones.
Is all well in every respect with the dwellings and other facilities? Is there also well-being regarding your ascetic practice, as well as for the embodied beings there? (19)
Is all well with all living beings among the subjects and others? Is there welfare for the lands, and is there happiness for the ascetics? (2.97.20)
Is there perhaps happiness for the male and female devotees? Is there perhaps well-being for all the castes throughout the lands? (21)
Having asked this, the venerable Lord Svāmiparameśvara fell silent;
then Agastya spoke: "Does there exist any sacred field (kṣetra) here?"
Śaṅkara likewise inquired after the welfare of those ascetics, the subjects, the disciples, and the men and women.
Satya also questioned them, and then all those great sages spoke in turn of their exceedingly terrible afflictions.
There was a dissolution that brought great suffering, as well as the destruction of their own [people], the re-emergence [of others], and likewise the devastation of the regions. (25)
"Furthermore, O Blessed One, by the sight of you, Hemaśālāyana has understood both the destruction and the protection of living beings. (26)
"It is well with you today that your arrival has occurred in this region;
for this region was formerly submerged by the ocean. (27)
Indeed, a great calamity was subsequently wrought all around by violent gales;
many living beings were destroyed by the wind-rain and the downpour of water. ||28||
And you were remembered by the great sages within the womb of the earth through their excavations;
having come here, this terrestrial globe has been protected by you. (29)
Beyond this, nothing else is found that is so highly skillful or secure as the granting of fearlessness to living beings which has been ordained by your honors. (2.97.30)
O Hari, in this sudden dissolution, who other than the illustrious Supreme Lord would be capable of granting life to those who have died?
O Lord, that stretch of land extending for a yojana near the ocean was submerged on all sides by the waters of the sea and destroyed.
Then, O Hari, that water was drunk by Agastya with his own cupped hands; and there, by that physician, the living beings were restored to life.
All is well with you; what else could be more auspicious, O Lord, than this:
that the regions of the earth where the people were oppressed are now covered with sand? (34)
O Hari, by the grace of the Maruts, all those who had died were delivered;
all those separated—both family members and servants—were reunited.
O Hari, O Kṛṣṇa, by your command the waters were dried up by Rudra, and the fortunes were restored to their former state by the Śrī-mothers. (36)
"O Kṛṣṇa, this land has been protected; those who were dead have been restored to life.
Indeed, all are well; what happiness could there be beyond this? (37)
Oh, what fortune! Oh, what happiness! Oh, what security! For those who have the Supreme Lord as their protector—what deity could there be beyond this? (38)
Oh, what merit! Oh, what heaven! Oh, such is the state of Brahmā! For in their abode Kṛṣṇa himself has come, the bestower of liberation. (39)
The Supreme Lord, who removes all sins, bestows all merit, and grants all bliss, has been attained; nothing remains to be attained.
O Supreme Lord, what need is there for further speech? All happiness proceeds [from you].
O Omniscient One, you know everything; indeed, may all that is auspicious be in our hands. 41.
You are the restrainer of the ocean, of battle, and even of the wind;
by you, acting as its cause, the oceans and other elements have been restrained.
Furthermore, there shall indeed be no destruction of living beings here in this cosmic egg;
welfare and great happiness have been established—what more than this could be desired? (43)
Then, having spoken thus to the sages, the seer Hemaśālāyana said:
"O noble lady, listen to my release from this great suffering. (44)
Hemaśālāyana said:
"O Lord, while I was among the rows of trees on the bank of the Bālā river, I was submerged in water by excessive rain and driven toward the ocean. (45)
But when he was submerged in that water, he then ascended by force into the air and arrived at Mount Hemaśālā by way of the path. ||46||
A rain of sand occurred, in which I was once again submerged;
thereafter, I entered into meditative absorption and remembered you, my Guru.
O Lord, I was nearly dead, buried beneath a bed of sand;
yet you came and rescued me, as did my preceptor. (48)
Bālāyana said:
"When I had gone to bathe in the waters of the ocean, at that moment, there arose terrifying waves of the sea such as I had never seen before. (49)
Drawn into the midst of the water along with the waters toward the earth,
he arrived at the bank of the river Bālā by that time.
Covered by showers of sand, I became enveloped within the sand;
having fixed my vital breaths in the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), I remained established in meditative absorption (samādhi).
Thus have I been rescued and restored to life by you who have come here;
O Kṛṣṇa, without your arrival, my destruction on this earth was considered imminent.
Rāvāsana said: "On the bank of the Gośaṅku river, I was indeed in meditative absorption;
I do not know what happened to me when I returned to the waking state. (53)
Then I realized that there, oppressed by the earth within the sand, I was inside the womb of the earth; I remembered Kṛṣṇa Agastika.
O ocean of compassion, I have been protected by you who have come here;
I have emerged from the earth with my life restored, like one awakened from sleep. (55)
Dārāliṅgāyana said:
While I was dwelling in the forest of Mount Dārāliṅga, chanting the name of Hari, a branch of a tree there was broken off by the wind and cast far away. (56)
"Cast down by the branch, my body was broken and I died;
I know not what happened after that, O Lord, until I arose restored to health. (57)
While awake, I obtained cool water and a drink;
thereafter, I reported the disaster, for I was indeed protected by you.
Bhekadāneya said:
"I was on Mount Bhekadāna, taking refuge in a hollow tree;
by a gale, my leaf-hut was uprooted and carried into the sky. (59)
Then I fell asleep within my hut upon a wooden floor;
together with my leaf-hut, I was cast from the sky onto the mountain.
On an inaccessible peak, I perished from falling into the sky; I do not know by whom I was brought back to life—by you, or perhaps by Hari? (61)
Remembering you, I have come here; be victorious, O Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa!
When death has arrived, who other than you is there to protect me? (62)
Maṣīgrīva said:
"I went from the edge of the battlefield to the southern forest;
that wilderness was seen by me as submerged in water in an instant. (63)
In the water, I was seized by a crocodile and devoured;
I do not know how I subsequently came back to life through your grace. (64)
In that case, there exists a cause for survival even after having been eaten;
likewise, O Lord, you were certainly brought back to life by the physician Śārṅgin.
Śālavanāyana said: "While I was worshipping you, the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama), on Mount Śālavana,
I was uprooted from my place by a whirlwind and carried five yojanas away."
Then, having fallen from the sky, I sank into the ocean and died;
at that time, I remembered you, O Ocean of Compassion, crying out, "Save me! Save me! (67).
I saw you there indeed grasping me with your own hand;
I was protected, rescued, and established here by you.
The sage Ācāla said:
"Once, while I was performing the agnihotra sacrifice, a fierce fire broke out due to a gust of wind;
then a forest, overwhelmed by a wildfire, began to burn from its very wood."
I was burned in the forest and there I was reduced to ashes;
at that time, I remembered Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Lord.
I am Agasti, the divine Guru, the protector, and the Lord of the universe; born from the sacred ash, I have been restored to new life by you.
Nourished by the astrologers and well-joined with consciousness, I have arrived here through your grace by means of aerial power. (72)
Grāmāyana said:
"I was staying there on the mountain behind the village, remembering Hari;
while I was bathing and performing worship, there was a roar. (73)
A terrifying earthquake occurred, and at that moment, as I was trembling, I fell from the peak of the mountain. (74)
Carried far away by a whirlwind, he was placed upon a cloud in the sky;
having died on the cloud from extreme cold, I know not what happened after that.
Or how have you attained this life? Such is your compassion; O Kṛṣṇa, you protect your devotee even in the midst of the sky. (76)
Vātāyana said: "I was cast into the sky by a whirlwind and, being whirled about with extreme speed, I was thrown into a certain forest where I saw a rutting elephant. (77)
"By him, being exceedingly hungry, I was both seized and devoured;
therefore, O Keśava, I do not know why my life remains—I do not understand this. (78)
Divādiṅgāyana said:
Between the mountains Divādi and Diṅkā, on the bank of the Kavindu, there was once ocean water that had arrived from the east. (79)
There flows the Kavindumanadī, overflowing with ocean water;
I indeed sank there, and the water receded far away.
Then a mountain made of sand rose even upon my head;
while I remained there established in meditative absorption, that mountain was removed by you. (81)
Then, O Lord, remaining within my own body, I regained consciousness;
at that moment, I beheld a most radiant celestial chariot in the sky.
Having seen that [being] approaching from a great distance, resembling the sun, I was protected by you, O Kṛṣṇa, and brought back to life from the jaws of death. (83)
O Lord, without compassion, a living being indeed cannot survive here;
O Kṛṣṇa, it was by you that the people who had died in this land were restored to life.
Furthermore, who is capable of undoing that which has been duly ordained?
Protection was repeatedly provided by Agastya and again by Śaṅkara. (85)
By the boy Aśvinī, the subjects here were rendered conscious;
the regions were filled with prosperity and made to flourish once again. 86.
O Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the beasts and birds have been protected by you;
blessed is this land of Astrālaya, also known as Uṣṇālaya. (87)
Though it was like a dwelling for camels, it has been made like a celestial abode;
having come here, you have purified us, protected us, and delivered us. (88)
When the eleven sages had thus addressed Rādhikā, Śrī Hari said: "Indeed, by your devotion, you have been delivered by me."
Indeed, for the sake of my devotees alone, I bestow all things;
for it was for the sake of the female cakravāka that I caused the water to flow swiftly over the mountain.
In the past, having flooded the surrounding lands, I brought water and gave it to drink;
for the sake of my devotees, I abandoned Lakṣmī, who is hostile to my devotees.
For the sake of my devotee, everything is given by me and he is protected;
for the sake of one individual, I provide protection for countless embodied beings.
For the sake of one [devotee], I bring about the destruction of countless embodied beings;
for the sake of a devotee I do everything, but never for the sake of one who is not a devotee. (93)
But those who are not devotees do not obtain even a portion by the side of the devotees;
this land has been uplifted for the sake of you, my devotees. (94)
And in the past, out of extreme devotion to a female cat, I protected her kittens even amidst a mass of blazing frying pans. 95.
Whatever kind of affection anyone may have, I always grant them a corresponding degree of devotion; my vow in this world is the protection of those who are devoted.
Through chanting, remembering, touching, seeing, and even bowing; through worship, the state of being a friend, and even through hearing—the highest [merit is attained]. (97)
The offering of oneself out of affection is pleasing to me;
for one who has nothing whatsoever that cannot be given for my sake in this world. (98)
For his sake, O twice-born ones, I have renounced everything here and in the hereafter; for your sake, I have provided all protection. (99)
Having spoken thus, the Blessed Supreme Lord ceased;
O Rādhikā, Bālakṛṣṇa, and you, their minds became steady.
For a moment they meditated on his external form, and then on that Hari within;
immersed in an ocean of bliss, they rested for a moment.

Thus ends the ninety-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Descent of Lord Hari’s Celestial Vehicle at the Hermitage of Hemaśālāyana in the Land of Uṣṭrālaya, and the Narration of the Account of His Own Protection," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā. || 97 ||
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Then, after a moment, all the yogīs questioned the Supreme Lord as to how Rādhikā had been protected like a female cakravāka bird.
Just as Lakṣmī, though beloved, was formerly abandoned by the Supreme Self,
and just as Hari formerly protected the offspring of a female cat.
Who were they, how did they become devotees, and what was the nature of their protection?
What kind of merit did they possess that Mādhava provided them with such guardianship? || 3 ||
Śrī Hemaśālāyana said:
"What kind of devotion to you was born from a previous birth for this female ruddy goose?
How did such affection arise for your sake? Cut through our doubt regarding these animals. (4)
Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa said: O brāhmaṇas, listen to this story concerning a cakravākī bird from ancient times.
This one named Sanatsujāta was the mind-born son of Brahmā.
He was a knower of the truth of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, devoted solely to the path of devotion,
dedicated to celibacy, and a teacher of the knowledge of Brahman.
Possessing unimpeded movement throughout the fourteen worlds,
that observer of vows wandered upon the earth in the form of a youth, desiring to visit sacred pilgrimage sites.
Once, he whose face was like the full moon, who was gentle and adorned by a halo of splendor, went to the Nārāyaṇa lake to bathe on its bank.
The sage was covered with bark garments whose parts were proportionate to his own form;
yet his limbs were robust and well-nourished, and he blazed with the radiant beauty of passion.
He was captivating to women, adorned with extreme patience and gentleness,
possessed of a serene mind, and solely devoted to meditation upon the One Lord.
Casting off his bark garments and wearing only a loincloth,
he descended into the waters of the Nārāyaṇa lake.
Having plunged into the water and recited the Mother of the Vedas, he goes to the bank;
again he enters the midst of the water, and again he stands upon the bank. || 12 ||
Meditating upon Hari and chanting the Gāyatrī, he goes again into the midst of the water;
having bathed with ease, he bows to the Sun and immerses himself in the water.
Having come outside, he remained in meditation for the duration of one ghaṭikā;
meanwhile, Urvaśī, the daughter of Nārāyaṇa, arrived there from the Himalayas.
She arrived of her own accord accompanied by many female companions;
she was born from the thigh and was bestowed upon Mahendra.
From that very day onward, she would come to Badarī every fortnight on the first and fifteenth days of the lunar month for the purpose of seeing her father.
In Badarī, she beheld the auspicious vision of her father Nārāyaṇa,
and then proceeded to the Nārāyaṇa-sarovara lake for the sake of visiting the holy sites.
The great devotee of Viṣṇu, the daughter of Viṣṇu, the goddess who is a supreme Bhāgavatī, and the one with hair like a host of Apsarases, arrived there. 18.
O fortunate one, fickleness is indeed the natural disposition of apsarases toward men;
thus, through such a fickle nature, even she, though devoted, yearned for a youth.
Beholding him alone, radiant with splendor and his limbs beautiful to the sight, she was brought under the sway of the god of love.
Standing before him, she entreated that sage Sanatsujāta for dalliance;
having assumed the form of a young maiden, she danced with many expressions of emotion.
He performed a song with seven rhythmic beats and joyfully sang a little melody;
during his dance, he whirled many times like a wheel.
Displaying her own fickleness by making circular gestures with her hands,
she captivated the sage with her speech, accompanied by a dance of her eyebrows.
The sage heard her voice and watched her dancing;
she too regarded the charming sage and danced even more intensely.
With gestures of amorous allure, movements of her limbs, and glances full of love and affection, she enchanted the sage; indeed, the sage laughed repeatedly.
Just as she, afflicted with fever, desired to touch the sage, the discerning brahmin Sanatkumāra, the sage, [perceived her]. || 26 ||
Then the Holder of the True Dharma rose up and said, "Do not touch me!
Laughing, he went a great distance and sat down in another spot.
Then, having come under his power, she went to the bank of that very lake and once again performed a captivating dance.
Looking at that sage again and again and desiring him as her suitor, she approached him with the wish to sport;
yet, having come close, she indeed became steady.
The sage said: "O handmaid, why indeed do you behave here like a servant?
You who are the daughter of Nārāyaṇa himself, you feel no shame at being touched."
"I am indeed the son of Brahmā; you are but the daughter of a son’s son.
I alone am one who observes the vow of Brahman; do not exert yourself in vain. (3.1)
Bathe in the delightful waters of the sacred ford, in the Nārāyaṇa lake; O daughter, do not bring upon yourself such mental anguish at this place in vain.
Thus addressed, she, despondent and filled with the distress of grief,
spoke to that youth with a mind that had abandoned all sense of propriety.
"O Brahmin, we are Apsarases who bestow all common enjoyments;
we are highly esteemed by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śambhu, and the gods. (34)
Therefore, O yogin, you must never look upon me here as a daughter;
for all [of us] are daughters of Nārāyaṇa and likewise beloved of Nārāyaṇa. (35)
Lakṣmī, born from the body of Nārāyaṇa, is the beloved of Nārāyaṇa;
Rādhā, born from the body of Kṛṣṇa, is the lover of Kṛṣṇa.
Gāyatrī, the beloved of Brahmā, was born in the lineage of Aja;
she is the daughter of Dakṣa, the son of Aja, and the wife of Dharma and the other gods. (37)
In the creation of the gods there is no obstruction; therefore, I have approached you.
By you, laughter and creative contemplation have been shown, which awaken the experience of delight.
"Therefore, accept [this], O best of Brahmins; otherwise, I shall quickly curse you.
Having said this, she threw herself onto the lap of Sanatsujāta. (39)
But the seer Sanatsujāta, out of fear of a curse or because of his failure in the vow of Brahman, said nothing at all to her.
But then, having performed yoga and instantly drawn up his vital breaths,
he went to the aperture of Brahma (brahmarandhra) in meditative absorption and dwelt there at ease.
And seeing that beloved sage devoid of desire, who remained established within himself like a cat’s behavior that provides no satisfaction, Urvaśī— (42)
Then he quickly cursed him: "O King of rogues, become a cat!
For you have no regard for the value of a woman, even though she is devoted to you in every way. (43)
He does not know the suffering of a woman, yet he increases his desire for women;
having kindled a fire, he stands at a distance watching it burn.
But for such a eunuch, there is indeed the fitness for birth as a female cat;
let her be a pitiless cat, experiencing suffering. (45)
Just as you shall come to know what the suffering of women is like through the various forms of desire,
so may you, who are now deprived of your cat, become a female cat dwelling in a frying pan.
Having thus incurred this curse, the sage became a female cat;
yet, possessing the memory of his former births, he remained right there on the bank of the Nārāyaṇa lake.
Having arisen from samādhi, he immediately looked at his own body;
he then perceived that it had attained the state of a female cat and was seized by anger. (48)
Then, as Urvaśī was bathing and delighting in her circular dance, he said to her with playful words:
"You cause even those like me to fall into delusion. (49)
Having failed to obtain what you desired, you, being full of fault, curse one who is free from fault;
therefore, you shall indeed be in a waterless place, possessed by thirst. ||2.98.50||
Be insatiable like a maidservant, and like a ruddy goose afflicted by love;
be separated from your mate like a ruddy goose, and abandoned by your circle of friends. (51)
Thus cursed, Urvaśī was born in that very place in an instant as a cakravākī bird, richly variegated, possessing wings, and belonging to the species of birds.
Then her other friends quickly left her and went through the path of the sky to heaven and to Mahendra; there they told them exactly what had happened.
Since desire in saṃsāra brings about many sufferings and is a defect,
it is not reckoned as a virtue by the wise, even though it is a treasure-trove of bliss.
Then Indra, overcome with grief, went to the illustrious Parameṣṭhin and related the account; Brahmā, too, was seized with sorrow.
Those two went to Viṣṇu, the deliverer from that [curse], in the form of Nara and Nārāyaṇa at Badarīvana, for the sake of liberation from the curse. (56)
They both bowed down, paid homage, and worshipped Hari;
Nārāyaṇa himself, having bowed to Brahmā, the supreme lord, [did the same].
Having offered the madhuparka and extended a welcome, he spoke: "O Grandfather, is all well in every respect with your subjects? (58)
Brahmā said: "O Hari, there is always well-being for all creatures;
why then do you perform penance here, and how could there be any ill for them? (59)
But that daughter of Urvaśī who was bestowed upon Indra—Sanatsujāta is my son, a lord of yogis and a knower of Sāṃkhya and Yoga. ||2.98.60||
These two, having fallen into the state of animals due to the power of a curse,
were our two sons— excellent Vaiṣṇavas who were devoted to us both.
And a female ruddy goose and a female cat were born in the region of Kaccha on the shore of Lake Nārāyaṇa, having been laid down by one another through desire. (62)
O Lord, may you two possess the memory of past births, and O compassionate Blessed One, please ordain that which shall lead to our liberation. (63)
"The ruler is capable of doing, not doing, or doing otherwise.
Having heard this, the Blessed One then reflected and spoke to the Creator.
"I shall effect their deliverance within a very short time;
however, due to the curse, they will experience some suffering while in their animal state. (65)
For one who remembers me through devotion to me by virtue of the nature of remembering past births,
I shall manifest a sign for the sake of liberation from the womb of animals.
"Having gone quickly to their presence, I shall grant the release of those two who are devoted;
there shall be no further suffering for long, so cast away your anxiety, O Grandfather. (67)
When this was said, Mahendra and the Grandfather (Brahmā) became pleased;
having worshipped Nārāyaṇa and bowed to the lake of Nārāyaṇa, [they departed].
And they both arrived at that shore where the maidservant and the cat were;
having seen Mahendra and the Creator, those two remembered their former births.
They quickly came to their side and wept out of sorrow;
once they had been comforted by the two of them, the release from the curse was announced.
"In a very short time, the Blessed One will grant you liberation from the curse;
indeed, perform the worship of your Lord, the beginningless Nārāyaṇa. (71)
For the wise there is no grief at all, because the bodies that come and perish are merely common objects of enjoyment for embodied beings. (72)
In that state, consciousness alone remains, which is the knowledge that destroys suffering.
That which is suffering for the ignorant is indeed happiness for the wise. 73.
For those who possess discernment, all things are suffering due to the transformations of objects, the three kinds of torments, and various mental impressions.
Youth is entirely wicked and a source of suffering because of its pursuit of desire;
with craving as its companion, even one who is happy shall encounter misery. (75)
If there were no suffering in saṃsāra, what would distinguish it from liberation?
Therefore, saṃsāra is indeed suffering, while liberation is said to be happiness. (76)
In the realm of illusion, suffering is always mixed with pleasure and continues to increase;
when craving is exhausted, there is great bliss, and illusion no longer causes affliction. //77//
A wise person should abandon craving if they desire their own happiness; for the destruction of craving is not even equal to a fraction of ten million supreme sensual pleasures. (78)
The enjoyment of sense objects increases new craving;
craving is the defect of sense objects, for its fruit is indeed extreme suffering. (79)
For the wise, however, the enjoyment of sense objects leads to cessation; when desire is destroyed, the supreme fruit is happiness that assists toward liberation. (2.98.80)
For yogis and men of knowledge, even such enjoyments do not cause bondage;
on the contrary, they indeed serve to turn back the thirst born of [wrong] perception. (81)
For when that [intellect] is endowed with knowledge, it comes to rest at the end of thirst and non-satisfaction;
however, if it is possessed of a state of delusion, thirst increases its craving. (82)
Ignorance is indeed destroyed by knowledge, and the guru is the cause of that knowledge.
The attainment of a guru comes through the accumulation of merit, and merit is gained by listening to the scriptures and other such means. (83)
Hearing the scriptures and so forth arise from faiths; faith arises from the desire for liberation and so forth; and the desire for liberation proceeds solely from the compassion of Hari. (84)
The grace of Hari, however, comes from worship, service, remembrance, and so forth.
He is the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa Svāmī, the Supreme Lord;
he is indeed to be heard, reflected upon, and meditated upon with longing.
Having gone to him for refuge, they cross over the oceans of suffering. ||86||
In every way, one should offer everything to him with one's whole being;
love and devotion should always be practiced toward him alone, for they lead to the end of worldly existence. 87.
If we were His [servants], He too would always be ours;
for the Lord of devotees honors the devotee, and the Lord of devotees honors His follower. (88)
Through union with the ocean of bliss, the river shall attain happiness;
through union with the milk-ocean, the water of the stream shall become milk. ||89||
There is no illusion in the Supreme Lord, nor is there suffering or even thirst;
indeed, there are no defects whatsoever in Kṛṣṇa, Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Sovereign.
Divine qualities, free from limitation and surpassing excellence, exist in the Great Kṛṣṇa; indeed, the devotees attain them. 9.1.
And let the Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa be remembered by you both;
He Himself will, in a short time, grant liberation from the curse. (92)
Having manifested a sign, he will come here of his own accord;
even while in the state of an animal, he will perform a bath at this very sacred ford and remember Hari.
Bowing even with the head, offering fruits, leaves, and so forth, and even the mere chanting of the Name—this must never be abandoned. (94)
If such devotion arises even in the state of an animal, that gain would be most excellent, even compared to a human body. (95)
Without devotion, the state of being a bound soul (paśu) is equal even among the gods;
what distinction is there in being a god if devotion is not present? (96)
Even for one established in sovereignty, the tongue’s capacity to perceive flavors is equal; indeed, the power of all the senses is the same for both a pauper and a king. (97)
Indeed, what has been fashioned by me is equal; no distinction exists here.
For the body is indeed equal, and the sense organs are also equal. (98)
Their tastes are equal and their satisfaction is likewise equal in every respect; bestowed upon all embodied beings, there is no distinction here. (99)
Devotion to Hari alone, when practiced here, is preeminent;
therefore, through such devotion, your deliverance shall soon come to pass.
"Let us go to our own abode; may there be well-being for you through your devotion.
Having spoken thus, both Mahendra and Brahmā were honored by them.
Having touched his feet with great affection, the maidservant and the cat bowed and offered him their salutations; then, by way of the sky, they departed for their own celestial realm.
For both of them, by their father’s command, worship the illustrious Narayana;
day and night they chant the names of their Lord, the Consort of Sri and Rama.
Thus did the sages speak there at the Nārāyaṇa lake;
for indeed, because of your curse, they both became beasts and birds.
Having spoken thus to Rādhikā, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Lord,
rested for a moment and drank the auspicious water offered by His devotee.

Thus ends the ninety-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Previous Births of Cakravākī and Mārjārikā as Asked by Hemaśālāyana in the Land of Uṣṭrālaya," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Listen, O Rādhikā; afterwards, Śrī Hari related that story of how the beginningless Śrī Narāyaṇa performed the deliverance. || 1 ||
Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa said: O sage Hemaśālāyana, listen now to a further narrative concerning her who was once a female cat on the shore of Nārāyaṇasara.
Having encountered the fear of wolves and other predators,
she went to a nearby village where cowherds who were devotees of Śrī Hari resided.
Those men and women who are Vaiṣṇavas worship the Supreme Lord;
there she indeed wanders constantly, afflicted by hunger, seeking alms.
Having obtained food with great effort through theft, he may indeed subsist by it;
or else, he simply continues to commit theft at all times.
Out of fear of dogs, she sleeps at night upon a heap of *pulaka* grass,
or on a heap of straw, or on a heap situated on the roof of the house.
Having obtained it somehow or other, she makes her living from leftovers;
where there is no longer even the species of cat, there this one remains alone.
Without a man, the young woman, having reached her season, dwells in distress; then, like a female cat, she is tormented day and night by the burning of desire.
On account of that very curse, she does not obtain a cat;
the villages are much farther from Kheṭa, so it is not possible to go there.
In the midst of wild beasts, she remained right there out of fear;
thus she was tormented by the burning fire of desire until the limit of eight years had passed.
In the ninth year, there was excessive rain on the earth;
by the force of that flood, a certain cat [was carried] from a great distance.
Being carried by the waves upon the waters of the lake,
he reached the edge of the lake alive, having clung to the branch of a tree.
Carried by the water with a swift,
curved current, the cat together with the branch was brought to the bank, and the branch came to rest upon the shore.
When he had dissolved into the water, that cat then went very slowly toward the village where that female cat was located.
Having united with him, she became pregnant;
she remained in the house of the potter, in the midst of fodder and straw.
Pregnant, she gave birth at the full term to five boys;
she then placed them upon a heap of grass on another spot of ground.
Then she protected her own children in another place;
subsequently, she protected them at the site of uncooked grain, amidst a heap of unbaked vessels.
Having hidden the children in raw clay pots within a fire-pit prepared by a potter for the purpose of baking, she went outside.
Later, for the sake of obtaining his own food, the potter set fire [to the kiln];
she, seeing that very smoke rising for the purpose of cooking the alms-bowl, [was filled with grief].
Arriving there quickly, she saw fire at her mouth;
her offspring stood behind her, and there was no path for escape.
The fire there grew in intensity, blazing with garlands of flames;
she too, out of fear of the dog, remained there on the side amidst the withered grass.
Suguptā and the young Cārudattā weep for the fire;
indeed, there is truly no means found to protect the lives of these children.
The potter was not there; who indeed would hear her wailing as she, filled with affection for her offspring, sought to protect her child? (23)
She remembered the Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, who is without beginning;
she praised Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Lord, with imagined feelings of devotion.
The fire was surrounded on all sides by the hollows of the vessels,
while the offspring of those vessels stood in their midst upon that ground.
The fire blazed upward and did not reach the ground at all;
with great devotion, Mārjārikā muttered, "O Kṛṣṇa, O Hari, O Lord! (26)
O Kṛṣṇa, protect my children with effort, who have been brought here auspiciously;
O Lord Nārāyaṇa, protect those who are innocent and devoid of worldly knowledge. 27.
"If I am devoted to you, O Lord, protect my children;
for by you protection was granted to the one in the womb and to his father within the waters."
May that Lord by whom [the world] is protected guard my children—O Nārāyaṇa, O Hari, O Kṛṣṇa, O Master, O Śrīman, O Supreme Person! (29)
May he by whom I was formerly brought forth protect my children—
He who makes his dwelling in fire, in water, on earth, in the sky, and in the wind.
May that God who is eternally pervasive within the heart, the left vessel, the pit, the frying pan, and the hearth, protect my children. (3.1)
O Hare Kṛṣṇa! O Lord Kṛṣṇa! Protect these boys;
protect well my dear ones, who are but small and without a protector, even more so than my own life-breath. ||32||
"I shall perform one hundred thousand recitations for the sake of your very satisfaction;
O Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, Teacher of the World, protect my children! (33)
"O protector of those who have come for refuge, please protect my young ones!
Thus she entreated her as she stood in the courtyard of the potter. (34)
Having approached the Tulasī plant, he prostrated himself ten times like a staff;
and considering the tree to be Hari himself, he performed fifty circumambulations.
O Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, O Consort of Śrī, O Consort of Kamalā!
Protect me, O Lord of Rādhā, O Lord of Brahman, O Lord of the liberated, O Sovereign! 36.
O Lord of Pārvatī, O Radiant One, O Lord of the Swan, who acts with grace;
O Witness of the Self of the Lord of Attributes, protect my children, O Hara! 37.
O Self of the self, ocean of compassion, Lord of Lakṣmī, Lord of Victory, bestower of nectar to the gods, O Acyuta, Lord of Peace, protect me! 38.
O Lord of Śrī, O Lord of the Earth, O Lord of Badrī, O sinless Lord of Līlā, O Lord of Prosperity, O Lord of the Imperishable, O Lord of Power—protect these children! 39.
O Lord of Goloka, O Lord of Haimī, O Lord of Lalitā!
O dweller in the abyss, O you whose mouth is the womb, protect us, O Lord of the Lord of Fire! 2.99.40
O Hṛṣīkeśa, Lord of Maheśa, Lord of the beloved of Brahmā, remover of fear!
O Īśvara, who dwells in the imperishable field, protect my children for me. 41.
May the god Vahni protect the children; O omnipresent one, may their burning be stilled.
Under your protection, may my children possess bodies of nectar. 42.
Where there is no other refuge, you, O Guru, are that refuge; you are the deliverer and the one worthy of seeking shelter. O Lord, protect these children! 43.
Thus repeatedly entreating Tulasī,
the female cat bowed down, took some of her leaves, and went to the place where the fire was located.
He offered the leaves to the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, whose body is fire, saying:
"O Agni, protect my children, who are the very fruit of my old age. (45)
Having spoken thus and offered salutations, he performed a circumambulation;
for there is no other means here for protection than the remembrance of Hari.
In this manner, with her mind, speech, and actions, that female cat worshipped the Supreme Lord, Śrī Puruṣottama, with leaves. 47.
And she remained constantly muttering prayers near the fire of the frying pan, clinging to the hope for life while worshipping the Lord of the Universe. 48.
Then, while she remained thus by his side, no man approached;
not even a guardian was seen, and so, filled with despair, she took refuge in Hari.
At that moment, she heard the words of the children from within the bakery;
filled with hope for life, her mind became serene.
And the fire, rising above the upper part of the frying pan,
increases on all sides with flames that are blue, green, and tawny.
The fire, fierce with its red and variegated flames and possessing white roots,
pervaded the smithy on all sides and in every direction.
Internally and externally, on the sides, in the middle, and even at the base— in every respect—
there were unbaked and baked vessels, and they remained so day and night.
Afflicted by hunger and thirst, that female cat heard her own young ones crying out as they played, likewise hungry.
One said, "O elder brother, when will mother return? Hunger afflicts me greatly; please call for mother. (55)
The eldest brother said, "A fire remains, blocking the paths on all sides;
how can our mother come? Remember the Supreme Lord Śrī Parameśvara. (56)
He who provided protection for the womb shall provide protection here;
the Blessed One will restore life by giving food with devotion. (57)
Seeing the fire, hot and exceedingly fierce, intensified by garlands of flames—how could a mother come here? Remember Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa. (58)
This is the compassion of the Blessed One that we live;
for here, in this cool cave, protection has been provided by Hari.
Fire does not arrive here, even though there is a collection of fuel;
see how the flame does not burn and the smoke produces no fuming.
"Come, come; let us go outside quickly from this smokeless, hollow fire.
This fire appears cold to me, O younger brother, and it does not burn."
Saying, "Let us go toward our mother," they departed swiftly;
emerging from the midst of the fire with their body hairs unburnt, they went to her.
All the children, having emerged from the frying pan, went to their mother;
filled with joy yet overcome by hunger, they drank their mother’s excellent milk.
The mother showed affection and licked him again and again;
they told the mother that the frying pan was a cool place of refuge.
Having drunk milk and taken leave, they entered the frying-pan again;
going beneath the surface of the frying-pan, they rested happily and with joy. (65)
That fire which indeed cooks unbaked jars and other such objects by means of burning,
and that fire which, having consumed fuel, grass, and the like, even reduces them to ashes.
This very same [fire], for the sake of the kitten, became perfectly cool; at that time, it truly became devoid of burning by the power of Kṛṣṇa’s grace. (67)
And the female cat, having observed this and being herself free from fear, went toward the opening of the frying pan to enter its surface. (68)
The fire was likewise so hot and so intensely burning when touched;
I attained supreme wonder and remembered Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. (69)
Oh, how great is the majesty of the Lord! For that which is indeed a single thing becomes for one a source of happiness, yet for another it truly becomes a source of suffering. (2.99.70)
This [fire], which is the burner of all, became a burner on his side;
this was certainly by the Supreme Soul, Śrī Nara-Nārāyaṇa. ||71||
My children have been protected here, and they are being protected again and again;
this is the greatness of my devotion—the taking of refuge by these children. (72)
Whatever great merit from previous lives I may possess, by that power these children play in the midst of fire as if in their own home. (73)
Then, having understood the most perfect greatness of Kṛṣṇa, Mārjārī worshipped Śrī Hari, the Supreme Lord, with exceeding devotion. 74.
Tormented by hunger and thirst, and having made a firm resolve, she thought:
"I must not go elsewhere; Hari will provide me with food. (75)
Thinking, "He is my protector and will protect me from the foolish," she recited: *Oṃ hare acyuta*. (76)
"Kṛṣṇa, Govinda, Gopāla, Nārāyaṇa, Narāyaṇa"—thus he muttered his inhalations and exhalations with his speech, mind, and heart. (77)
And Hari’s consort sat down near the oil-presser;
two days passed, yet she neither rose nor departed. (78)
Kṛṣṇa, the divine Nārāyaṇa, the supreme among men, the one who leads men to the goal—having understood his firm resolve and his devotion that transcends the highest, [he spoke]. (79)
He who protects those who have come for refuge assumed the form of a potter;
at the Śrāddha ceremony performed in the month of Bhādrapada, he likewise consumed the milk-preparation and the *pūrikā* cakes.
Holding [the vessel] in his hand, he arrived and gave it to the ancestors;
he gave it to the crows in the sky, and he gave it to the cow.
He gave [the food] to the spirits and also gave some to the female cat;
meanwhile, those children emerged from the fire-heater.
He made them drink milk cooked for the śrāddha rite, which bestows happiness;
having drunk it, they entered there upon the comfortable surface of the frying pan.
Thus addressed by that potter, other potters were summoned:
"Let them see indeed whether cats truly live within the midst of fire. (84)
Having said this, he showed the children to the potters;
and the superintendent of the frying-pan makers also beheld them and was struck with wonder.
Raw vessels are baked, yet the children are not burned;
this is indeed a supreme marvel that has become manifest therein. (86)
Crowds of people arrived to see the sons of the oil-presser;
they worshipped the god Agni and gave food to the female cat. (87)
They gave milk to the children; and those children, having come outside and drunk it, would enter again and again through the hollow of the frying pan. 88.
Having observed this, those people, protected by Hari, reached this certainty:
"These people live and do not cause harm, for he is indeed the protector of the distressed. (89)
Then the Lord himself, the creator of the pot, after the pacification of the fire,
removed the ashes and all other materials from the pots and vessels in every way.
He even made the ground empty where the young girls were stationed;
for there he clearly beheld the footprints of the venerable Bhagavat. ||9.1||
There, a potter constructed an altar for the feet of the Blessed One, and that place indeed became famous as the sacred site known as Mārjārarakṣā. || 92 ||
That yogi Nārāyaṇa, by whom the children were protected, also then shone resplendent right there in the midst of them all. (93)
Others do not know that Lord in His form as a potter;
then, at that time, this Blessed One, Badrinārāyaṇa himself— ||94||
Out of compassion, he revealed his own four-armed form;
seeing Hari, the potters, filled with faith, worshipped him. (95)
Mārjārikā beheld that glorious Nārāyaṇa, Hari;
instantly, she attained the remembrance [of Him] in the form of Sanatsujāta.
He experienced manifold grief arising from the birth of the kittens and other such things, thinking:
"Where am I, Sanatsujāta, and where have I come to this state of being a cat? (97)
"Today Nārāyaṇa himself has come for the sake of destroying the curse"—
thinking thus, having attained true detachment, he did not bow to Hari, Nārāyaṇa.
Nārāyaṇa also, quickly emerging from that animal body,
assumed the form of Sanatkumāra, the very self of Brahmā’s son.
The children were protected and raised by potters;
under their influence, they indeed became forest-dwellers and subsequently turned into cats.
Then the god Nārāyaṇa and Sanatsujāta went to the lake to bathe; the potters followed after them.
At that time, the gods released a rain of flowers from the sky onto the lake.
Indeed, it was there that Nārāyaṇa himself bathed, and thereafter the gods [did so as well].
And the auspicious holy site known as Nārāyaṇasaras has been proclaimed;
it provides protection, grants liberation, and bestows [the state of] Nārāyaṇa.
Accompanied by Sanatsujāta, the Lord Nārāyaṇa, having bathed,
went to his own vast abode at Śrī Badarī on the Golden Mountain.
The sage Sanatsujāta, having bathed in the waters of the triple-pathed river (Ganges) and bowed to Nārāyaṇa, then departed for Satyaloka in an instant.
"The village was given the name Mārjārapura by the people.
Thus did Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa speak to the sage Hemāyana.
O Rādhā, he likewise told the story of the protection of the cat’s offspring;
after pausing for a moment, they attained a most great joy.

Thus ends the ninety-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Protection of the Kittens from the Great Kiln-Fire of the Potter by Nārāyaṇa and the Liberation of Mārjārikā from Her Curse," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Rādhikā; the Lord, the beginningless Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, narrated this story to the Ṛṣi Hemāyana through the female ruddy goose.
By the curse of Sanatsujāta, Urvaśī, the daughter of Nārāyaṇa,
became a female cakravāka bird on the shore of the Nārāyaṇa lake.
Remembering her past births, she constantly meditated upon sacred fords;
she would fly far away, traveling continually from village to village.
Having eaten grains at midday and rested beneath a tree, he flies far into the distance through the air before returning by evening.
Thus, though she desired the sacred fords, she remained fixed in a state of detachment;
slowly leaving the region of Kaccha, she crossed the ditch with speed.
Having come from the land of Ānarta toward Camatkārapura,
she bathed in the lake and beheld Hāṭakeśvara.
He went to Somanātha and, having seen it, proceeded to Akṣarakṣetra;
there, having bowed to the illustrious Kambharā-Lakṣmī and having worshipped Bālakṛṣṇa, he stayed.
Having gone to Siddhasarasvatī, she went to Puṣkara at Arbuda;
having bowed to Brahmā there, she arrived at Gaṅgādvāra.
Then, having visited Kurukṣetra and the river Pragaṇḍakī, and having paid homage to Śālagrāma and prostrated before Śālādri; || 9 ||
For the sake of beholding Paśupati, he flew up into the sky;
then, in the atmosphere above the valley near the vicinity of the Himālaya mountain, [he remained].
As she was flying over a region of the earth in the vicinity of the Nīpa forest,
she saw a certain maiden on the bank of the Gaṇḍakī with her gaze directed downward.
With a face like the moon, exceedingly fair, and a body radiant like the sun,
though only eight years of age, she was on all sides equal to Kamalā in the beauty of her form.
Rich with a luster like that of a land-lotus, her eyes were as long as lotus petals;
her body was permeated with fragrance, and she was divine like Nārāyaṇī herself.
Holding the beloved Lord of Śrī in her heart and "Hari, obeisance! on her tongue, she stands as if looking all around while clutching the Cloud (Kṛṣṇa) at her waist.
With hands adorned with jeweled bracelets, a beautiful necklace bound with gems upon her neck, her waist encircled by a girdle, and her forearms richly decorated with chains.
Her feet were adorned with anklets, her nose was pierced by a nose-ring,
her beautiful ears were graced with earrings, and she was decorated with garments and jewels glowing like fire.
O Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa Viṣṇu, O Supreme Brahman, O Lord Hari! She is exceedingly beautiful, enriched with a luster like that of a golden campaka flower. 17.
"O Blessed One, Supreme Person, when will you grant me your vision?"—
thus she was seen speaking these words in a secluded place.
But the female ruddy goose (cakravākī), recognizing her as one worthy of trust,
descended from the sky to the side of the illustrious tree.
And in order to attract her, he sang with very sweet words;
indeed, having heard that song sung by the Apsarā, the maiden—
She beheld upon a tree a small female bird skilled in song;
within that song was the sentiment: "When will Kṛṣṇa meet me? (2.1)
"I am the daughter of Nārāyaṇa; when I shall attain Mādhava, then he too, the Great Kṛṣṇa, will meet you—do not grieve.
O friend, you are seen to be separated just as I am."
Who are you, appearing in the form of a maiden? Tell me your former state as a human being.
Having heard this sentiment expressed by the singer, the maiden was greatly delighted and said:
"Tell me, O maidservant, who are you that possess the body of a bird? (24)
"Come, O lady of excellent vows; you awaken me with the language of the gods.
Are you Kṛṣṇa, or a messenger of Kṛṣṇa, or are you Kṛṣṇā herself who stands here? (25)
"Come here, stay by my side, and tell me of auspicious blessings;
I shall listen to your auspicious words, for Hari will remove my suffering. (26)
Thus addressed, she descended from the tree onto the ground in her presence;
she beheld a gentle form at her feet, like the feet of Śrī.
He also smelled her feet and drank the water offered by her;
he sat down near her as she was seated on the riverbank.
Questioned for the sake of familiarity, she spoke of the fruit born of a curse:
"I am Urvaśī, the daughter of Hari, [fallen] due to the curse of Sanatsujāta. (29)
Even as an Apsaras I shall become exposed, and indeed I shall become a female ruddy goose,
when I behold Nārāyaṇa himself.
"Then I shall be released from the curse and become Urvaśī once again.
Having spoken thus, that maidservant repeatedly [addressed] the maiden.
With his whole being, he gazed upon her who was equal in splendor to Lakṣmī and adorned with auspicious marks.
Upon her heart, he beheld the dark mark of Kṛṣṇa, like that of a female ruddy goose; above her feet, he saw the line of the tilaka-mark known as the puṇḍra;
on her hips, the line of Bāṇa; and on her forehead, the shape of a crown.
On his right cheek and forehead she beheld a red mark;
on his chest, the line of Viṣṇu, and likewise a mace upon his left arm.
On his left thigh he saw a sandal, and on his chest the Vaijayantī garland;
in his hand, however, he beheld a beautiful lotus and the mark of an elephant.
On the right foot, there are the marks of a conch, a boat, a celestial chariot,
a mace, a fish, a mountain peak, a large fish, and a betel vine.
On the left foot, there is a barley-corn line, a temple, and an umbrella;
likewise, an upward line, a lotus, a banner, a goad, and a jar.
He has hands like the kumuda lily, the bilva fruit, the land-lotus, and the moon;
his ten palms are perfectly full, and his fingers are marked with golden lines. (38)
On the forehead, he drew a golden necklace, a golden line, and a dot;
on the chin, a dot; and on the upper part of the right breast, the lines of the hand.
A wheel on her left breast, a necklace at her throat, a golden ornament on her chest,
