and a banner, a fish, a flute, and a swastika on her right hand.
He likewise beheld a bow, a fish, and a water-pot in his hand;
he also beheld a rampart and an archway in his right hand. ||41||
Upon his hood he beheld a most beautiful plow-sign;
on his feet, a horse, an elephant, a tree, a sacrificial post, an arrow, and a lance;
and on his hand, the lines of a beautiful garland, the line of a lamp, and a fly-whisk.
She displayed the mountain, the earring, the altar, and the discus;
she attained supreme wonder, considering it to be the glory of the Supreme Lord (Pārameśvarī),
for no other such thing could be seen except for the glory belonging to Nārāyaṇa.
"None of these signs exist except for Kamalā," he decided, and having so resolved, he asked her name, family, and other details. (45)
Having heard this, the female cakravāka spoke to her daughter according to the facts:
"Daughter, what can I say to you in this matter? Destiny is indeed always all-powerful. (46)
I am indeed the wife of Nārāyaṇa and your mother;
by name I am Lakṣmī, the eternal beloved of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
As the half-bodied consort, I always dwell in the realm known as Mahāvaikuṇṭha;
never do I go far away, leaving Nārāyaṇa.
"Nārāyaṇa, however, leaves me behind and goes far away for the sake of his devotees;
if I were an obstacle to the devotion of Hari's devotees in his presence. (49)

"For the sake of your devotion, O child, I have been sent from the abode of Vaikuṇṭha by your father. The Lord Śrī Bhagavān, who is dear to His devotees, having abandoned that supreme Vaikuṇṭha and become a follower of His devotees,
has arrived here in this universe."
I have come to this earth to search for him. ||51||
Having manifested her power in an unmanifested state, she took the form of a human woman;
my father was Śaṅkara, known as Śivarāja, on the bank of the Gaṇḍakī.
Hara, the lord of Kailāsa, exists in a form created by his own will;
he is a great devotee of the Lord, a worshiper of Śrī Gopāla, and possessed of dispassion.
Satī, the daughter of Dakṣa, his wife Jānakī, and the beloved of Hara—she too, a human being by her own will, shines resplendent in the house of Śambhu. (14)
Those two parents of mine were created by me as excellent Vaiṣṇavas of the mind;
they indeed reside on the bank of the Gaṇḍakī at the place named Kailāsadhāma.
This most magnificent city is situated within a mountain valley;
here, Satī and Śiva shine forth in human form. (56)
In the city of his own kingdom, within a garden resembling Mount Kailāsa, he took recourse to the duty of a warrior (kṣatradharma) for the sake of protecting the world. ||57||
Those two, whose true nature is unknown to the world, were born from a king who knows all;
for in their illustrious home dwells Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa under his control.
Every morning, Hari regularly comes there to the house of worship;
having accepted the worship offered by Satī and Śambhu, he enters into a state of absorption.
Therefore, for the very purpose of worshipping Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa,
I have come from the garden to fetch water for the sake of the ancestors and the gods.
"By good fortune, my daughter, you have been seen by me here after being separated for a long time.
Come to my home; dwell here in my cage."
"You should conduct yourself according to the nature of a bird so that they do not recognize you at all;
I shall protect you in every way when the time arrives, my dear son. (62)
By the will of Nārāyaṇa, liberation from the curse will occur quickly;
nearby here, not far away, are many forests.
"We two shall indeed dwell here and behold Nārāyaṇa;
there is no fear here from Hari due to his yoga, nor likewise anywhere from the yoga of Śiva. (64)
"O daughter, through my yoga and likewise through the yoga of Satī, the kingdom shall be free from fear, and the city named Kailāsadhāma shall also be free from fear. (65)
Everything indeed proceeds properly and auspiciously;
moreover, your father Nārāyaṇa knows me as well.
He always remains as if ignorant and does not awaken Śambhu;
yet he alone, being affectionate, will deliver him when the time has arrived.
Or else, we shall perform our penance in secret for the sake of its elevation;
then it will bestow the fruit of penance known as "one's own grace. (68)
Having thus heard the words spoken by the daughter of Śiva,
the daughter of Nārāyaṇa, Cakravākī Urvaśī, spoke to her:
"O Mother, by the sight of you today, my sorrow has indeed vanished."
For in whatever state one may be, the mother’s lap indeed bestows peace.
"By good fortune, I have today obtained and beheld you, O most venerable one.
Whatever you tell me, O Mother, that I shall do exactly so."
The mother’s word is the Veda; it is dharma, charity, austerity, and the vow.
Indeed, for a maiden, all these are considered fruitful only through the mother’s word. (72)
"You are the remover of my suffering, O Mother, and I am your daughter.
For the sake of destroying the pain of separation from Kṛṣṇa, I shall strive through austerities and other means.
Indeed, for a daughter, service to her mother is the supreme and highest virtue. (73)

Before her daughter's marriage, the mother is everything to the daughter; thereafter, the mother desires her daughter's happiness for as long as she lives. Indeed, there exists no other living being equal to a daughter for a mother.
Through the merit accumulated over a hundred births, a mother becomes possessed of a daughter;
through the merit arising from a thousand births, that daughter becomes a servant to her mother.
A daughter inherits her mother’s wealth, while a son inherits his father’s wealth;
a son is the helper of his father, and a daughter is the helper of her mother. (77)
Even though she has a son, a mother is considered barren without a daughter;
[this applies] day and night, whether at bathing, cooking, eating, or within the house and garden. (78)
In bed and on a journey, a daughter is a companion in solitude;
just as a cow with her calf becomes more beloved, so does she become most dear. (79)

Likewise, a mother accompanied by her daughter is considered highly honorable and esteemed in the world; the daughter is the support of the mother, and the mother is the support of the daughter. (2.100.80)
Therefore, a mother is always served by her daughter as the bestower of welfare;
the mother is the supreme sacred ford (tīrtha), the mother is Sarasvatī herself. 8.1
The mother Lakṣmī is ever the nourisher, the savior, and the protector;
she indeed instructs even her own daughter, who exists for the sake of others, in the noble arts. (82)
She protects her beloved like her own self and constantly gives everything;
in hardship she experiences hardship, and in happiness she experiences happiness—such a mother no other can find. (83)
Having experienced hardship and considering her daughter to be weak, the Mother—who indeed bestows strength—always provides refuge; no other is like her. 84.
Bodhi is the mother, as is Sāvitrī; Svāhā and Svadhā are likewise mothers.
Brāhmī is the Great Power (Mahāśakti), the mother who is most venerable of all. ||85||
The word of a mother is always considered most auspicious and the best omen;
she is eternally composed of blessings, like a stream of clarified butter.
The motherland, the mother tongue, and the mother's milk are praised; the Mother, who is the land of the Triveṇī and the Savior, is likewise praised. (87)
The mother’s milk is considered the Gaṅgā, the mother’s lap is the Yamunā river, and the mother herself is declared to be the triad of sacred fords; the mother’s word is the Sarasvatī. (88)
The water from a mother’s feet is meritorious, purifying, and the destroyer of sins;
the touch of a mother is like the touch of nectar, providing nourishment even in the absence of food. (89)
And eating the remnants of the mother’s food is like the grace of the Supreme Lord;
since a daughter consists of the mother’s blood-essence, the mother is therefore praised. (2.100.90)
Indeed, from the mother's body the daughter's body is produced;
therefore, the mother is equal to Brahmā, the cause of the flow of creation. 9.1
Indeed, the sight of him yields even greater fruit than the sight of Brahman;
and indeed, the remembrance of him bestows even greater happiness than the remembrance of Brahman. (92)
Service to her, attendance upon her, and the carrying out of her commands—even these are considered superior to the study of the Vedas and are held to bestow the world of Brahmā. (93)
By that daughter, her own mother was satisfied through service and the like; she was likewise delighted by compliance in thought, deed, and speech.
For her, there is no fear born of illusion, the god of death, karma, Yama, and the like;
nor is there sudden fear, nor any fear arising from disease and so forth. 95.
For her, there is no fear of the three realms, nor fear of thieves and the like;
likewise, she has no fear of obstacles, nor fear of hungry ghosts (preta) and so forth. ||96||
What is the use of saying more in this matter? There is no fear of birth and death [for one who honors her].
A mother is ten times more venerable than a father, owing to her bearing the child in the womb, giving birth, and nourishing it. 97.
The guru is the mother; Hari is the mother; the progenitor is the mother; and she is the abode of Brahman.
The mother is heaven; the mother is the home; indeed, the mother is the eternal state.
Beasts and birds alike, whether children or having reached old age,
and even the young, utter "moṃ moṃ moṃ" when they encounter distress.
Affection for one's mother and affection for Brahman are such that there is indeed no liberation superior to them;
upon seeing her daughter in a dream, joy arises in the mother.
"Today my daughter has been seen by me," saying this, he remembers her constantly;
for Tāriṇī is the mother's daughter who accomplishes all tasks. (101)
By serving her mother [inappropriately], she would always be devoid of fortune;
through the distress of the mother's heart, the daughter's fortune perishes. 102.
Bringing water for household tasks, cooking food,
removing refuse and the like, as well as cleaning the vessels;
likewise, making up the beds and so forth, and washing the clothes.
I authorize the dyeing [of garments] and the protection of the household, its purification, and so forth. || 104 ||
The preparation of grains and other ingredients, the cleaning of spices and such, the protection of household goods, and appropriate service—these are the duties of the members of the family. (105)
Performing worship of the gods and the like, churning curd, buttermilk, and so forth, serving cows, cattle, and the like, and massaging the body of one's mother. 106.
Grooming her mother's hair, massaging her feet, and so forth—
such a range of activities is performed by the daughter toward her mother, who is her Brahman.
Having prepared [the offerings] again and again, the daughter, endowed with devotion and possessed of faith, should present them;
through the merit of her vow to her mother, she shall attain dharma, artha, kāma, and liberation.
The daughter obtains victory and eternal prosperity;
indeed, she is born in this world as one equal to ten million Brahmās, like Nārāyaṇī herself.
What more need I say here? My mother has been served; she has served the eternal Brahman and attained heaven while on earth.
Thus did the daughter Cakravākī, who was Lakṣmī herself— the destroyer of sorrow and possessed of knowledge of her own majesty— speak to her mother, Rādhikā.
The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa spoke this story there on the mountain named Hemaśālā to the sage Hemāyana.

Thus ends the one hundredth chapter, titled "The Description of Cakravākī’s Meeting with Her Mother Lakṣmī on the Banks of the Gaṇḍakī and the Narration of the Greatness of the Mother," during her pilgrimage in the second section, the Tretā-saṃtāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Rādhikā, that female cakravāka bird questioned her mother again: "Tell me here, for what reason have you been abandoned by Hari? (1)
Thus questioned, her mother Lakṣmī spoke to her daughter:
"Śrī Kṛṣṇa has told the nectar of a story to Hemaśālāyana. (2)
Listen, I shall tell you this for the sake of your devotion: even the Lord himself abandons Lakṣmī; what then need be said of anyone else? (3)
In the world of Mahāvaikuṇṭha, the supreme lord Śrī Nārāyaṇa is constantly served with devotion by the inhabitants of Mahāvaikuṇṭha.
Just as she was devoted to Lakṣmī, so too were all others with even greater feelings of devotion;
indeed, the female companion named Kṛṣṇā surpassed Lakṣmī herself in her service.
In her own home, that beautiful woman constantly protects Nārāyaṇa;
she herself performs his bathing and anoints him with fragrant unguents.
With thorough massages of the limbs, along with shaving and other such services,
as well as with garments, ornaments, and decorations, that female friend adorns her.
With worship, food, drink, and the like; with beds, furnishings, and so forth; and with constant varieties of laughter and jests, as well as various forms of service.
Through many varieties of love and through constant offerings of everything day and night,
Kṛṣṇikā was never for even a moment separated from Him, as if He were her own body.
Even while constantly crying out "Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa" during her state of separation,
she serves her beloved husband Nārāyaṇa-Kṛṣṇa with three bodies.
In this way, her two brothers, the two attendants Jayacandra and Kāka,
offered their entire ritual practice to Hari.
They were eternally possessed of great devotion and were solely devoted to Nārāyaṇa;
they found all happiness in Hari and could not endure even a moment without Kṛṣṇa.
And those two ascetics were devoted to their rosaries and dear to Hari;
their senses and internal faculties were fully absorbed in Kṛṣṇa.
Endowed with the ninefold devotion, devoted to the yoga of meditation,
and possessing the disposition of offering their very selves, those two worship the Supreme Lord.
Kṛṣṇa dwells wherever his brother resides;
Kṛṣṇa himself, as an eternal youth, always dwells in that house.
Their father, Dhenupāla, the lord of cowherds, was always like a cowherd himself, absorbed in the service of Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. (16)
Just as he was one whose very self was the form of Kṛṣṇa through acts of self-surrender,
so too did he abide in love for Hari, devoted to every form of service.
Then once, those four came to their own residence to present various offerings to Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa.
Then Nārāyaṇa, in an invisible form, comes together with them into the inner chamber of that divine, most magnificent palace.
On His bed, Śrī Narāyaṇa is served by Śrī Mahālakṣmī;
receiving the loving service of Mahālakṣmī, He remains utterly absorbed in Her.
Mahālakṣmī, immersed in love and united with the body of Nārāyaṇa, became his beloved, submerged in the great ocean of bliss of the Supreme Brahman. ||21||
Out of a desire for long-term service and a longing for eternal bliss with Hari,
she became free from any wish for separation and was endowed with the embrace of the illustrious Hari.
At that time, those four excellent female attendants, having gathered their offerings, quickly came to the door. (23)
O Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, O Viṣṇu, O Supreme Lord Keśava,
O Hṛṣīkeśa, grant Your vision to Your devotees within their hearts.
Thus they uttered the word "bhakta" (devotee) with full devotion;
and the Blessed One, hearing that word "bhakta," left his bed.
Rising quickly, he immediately commanded the gatekeeper to admit him, and then he left his own bed, which was overflowing with great comfort. (26)
Even though her beloved husband had departed, that devoted wife, though pained by separation from the joy of Nārāyaṇa himself, did not say anything to her maidservant. ||27||
"Keśava will soon arrive and delight me," thinking thus, she remained steady upon her bed, filled with anxious thought. (28)
Then the beloved Lord Nārāyaṇa, taking his devotees with him,
entered and sat upon the throne situated within the house, joined by them.
Nārāyaṇa summoned his own Lakṣmī to a beautiful seat;
Lakṣmī, her face radiant with joy, was addressed by Nārāyaṇa.
Then she quickly approached Hari at his throne;
together with Śrī Hari, Lakṣmī sat down upon the seat. ||3 1||
Then, having brought them, they offered with true devotion all those various gifts they had gathered: foods, drinks, and delicacies—saying, "These four [are yours]. (32)
The materials for the sentiment of love included garments, ornaments, and beautiful garlands;
numerous strings of necklaces and rows of pearl ornaments set in vessels.
They presented to Nārāyaṇa objects rich with the fragrance of flowers and fruits, endowed with excellent flavors, and worthy of Lakṣmī’s adornment.
There they gave [offerings] to Lakṣmī and worshipped her with extreme devotion;
they stood [before her], offered hymns of praise, and then became absorbed in meditation.
When they had performed worship and offered gifts, yet did not rise even after a long time,
Lakṣmī quickly became enraged toward those obstacles.
And she does not manifest her inner anger outwardly;
for even though she is capable of speaking, she cannot do so without the will of Hari directed toward them.
She was unable to rise, for there was no one capable of doing so except Nārāyaṇa;
filled with wrath, she thought only: "When will these devotees depart? (38)
When indeed shall I again attain Nārāyaṇa in the blissful sleep? Meanwhile, those devotees remain absorbed in meditation, having fixed Hari before them in their contemplation.
While Śrī Satī and Hari remained there for a long time,
they both arrived from Kailāsa to behold the glorious Nārāyaṇa.
Thinking, "One obstacle has passed away, but for now a second has not yet arrived," Śrī remained firmly and helplessly by the side of Kṛṣṇa. (41)
Śaṅkara was likewise a great devotee of the Lord and the best among devotees, and Satī too was a great devotee; who then could transgress them? (42)
Nārāyaṇa himself, rising quickly from his lion-throne, embraced Śambhu and offered him a welcome. ||43||
Then Satī and Śambhu respectfully performed the welcoming rites for Lakṣmī,
and they both carried out the worship of Lord Hari with great devotion.
Seated upon a beautiful throne offered by Satī,
Śambhu, a devotee of the Lord, performed many kinds of dances before the Goddess of Fortune.
Hara danced for a long time out of sheer love in the presence of Śrī Hari;
Hari’s mind was so captivated by him there that he perceived nothing else.
Lakṣmī, agitated by her longing for the bliss of the touch of Nārāyaṇa, swiftly desires the end of the dance and a state of solitude. ||47||
Hari is subject to the power of devotion; he neither merely remembers nor merely looks upon Lakṣmī.
With his mind fixed on his devotees, he does not permit them to depart elsewhere.
Then, abandoning all composure, [he attacked] those who wasted time in vain:
Śaṅkara, Satī, Dhenukā, Pāla, Jaya, and Candraka.
She cursed her friend Kṛṣṇā, saying, "May humans come to be where there will be no doubt that you shall experience the fruit of obstacles. (2.101.50)
They are immersed in untimely dancing and are practitioners of untimely meditation;
for they cause me obstacles precisely because they disregard the proper time.
"May those who possess bodies in the world of men encounter obstacles," having said this, he repeatedly took Śrī Hari by the hand. (52)
"O Kṛṣṇa, please come to our home and rest for a moment;
O Lord, such hosts of devotees as these are rare indeed here. (53)
Yet they exist without regard for time; those affectionate devotees come again and again, and indeed they do not understand the [Lord's] inner mind. 54.
Come within, O Hari, and bring peace;
for you who have remained seated here for a long time, your fatigue will become great. (55)
Thus Ramā made this persistent effort to lead Nārāyaṇa away;
but Śaṅkara and the other devotees, having heard this, were struck with supreme wonder.
Due to the curse of Lakṣmī, they became dejected-faced and as if devoid of luster;
having bowed to Nārāyaṇa and quickly perceiving that Lakṣmī was distressed, [they acted].
Then they departed quickly from their own abode, from the presence of Śrī Hari,
and descended into the world of mortals while the gatekeepers were looking on.
A great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose there among the inhabitants of Vaikuṇṭha;
the news spread everywhere throughout every region of Vaikuṇṭha.
By the curse of Lakṣmī, four virtuous women from the Kṛṣṇā river fell into the world of mortals for the sake of Hari,
like those who are ignorant of the proper time and are as if inert.
Therefore, a moment should never be spent in vain by those who possess splendor;
one must never go into the presence of great beings at an improper time.
One must never create an obstacle for a married couple when they are in a private place;
for such a person shall become a destroyer of happiness and an enjoyer of misery, whether he be a great man or even a lord of the earth.
"The one who creates obstacles shall surely perish by the obstacle; indeed, he who created an obstacle for the couple!
Thus there was a cry of "Alas! Alas! among the gods and even among men. (63)
A virtuous king named Śaṅkara Śivarāja reigned in the city of Kailāsadhāma on the Himālayas, on the bank of the Gaṇḍakī.
In the house of Kṛṣṇasiṃha, a son was born who was mind-born like a celestial being;
he was a great divine lord, endowed with supreme sovereignty and possessing a luster like that of Arjuna.
And Satī was born as the daughter of the lord of the city of Ṣaṇmāṇḍavya; she became the goddess Jānakī, equal to Śivā in name and in her virtues. 66.
Satī and Śambhu, both remembering their former births, grew up like gods;
they were united once more by the rite of marriage, like speech and its meaning joined together.
Thus, at a most opportune time, those two residents of Kailāsa were united on the bank of the river at the base of the Gaṇḍakī on the snowy mountain.
In their own kingdom, in the city whose abode is Kailāsa, they attained sovereignty;
then there were the friends Kṛṣṇā, Dhenupāla, Candra, and Jaya.
They descended upon the city of Kailāsa-dhāma on the Himalayan mountain;
there, Śivarāja’s younger brother became the cowherd.
Kṛṣṇā was the virtuous daughter of that Śivarāja;
Candrāditya was his younger brother, and Jayakumāra was his younger brother.
Due to the occurrence of a common curse, the family became one;
all were devoted to Brahman, established in Brahman, and always intent upon Kṛṣṇa. ||72||
Devoted to meditation, yoga, and austerity, they possess knowledge of the Dharma and are free from passion;
they are constantly engaged in the sacrifice of Brahman, are of the nature of Brahman, and are free from deceit.
Endowed with all the marks, they were not recognized as such by men;
they were always great devotees of the Lord, whose duty was the protection of their subjects. (74)
Constantly engaged in the service of Kṛṣṇa, they were as intent upon it as if in Vaikuṇṭha;
they roamed through the regions of Nīpālaya and the snowy mountains.
They exist with divine forms through the perfections of natural yoga;
they exist in human forms through actions such as those resulting from curses. ||76||
When they fell due to the curse, Hari was then in their hearts;
the Lord became sorrowful because of the suffering of his devotees, yet he remained devoted to Śrī.
Since Hari is known as the essence of all beings, he was unable to say anything else;
he endured all the suffering of his devotees and indeed maintained silence for a moment.
Although Śaṅkara and the others were capable of cursing Lakṣmī in the presence of Hari,
nevertheless, being devoted as his servants, they did not curse that Ramā at that time.
"The mother who belongs to the worlds has cursed us—who are obstacles—to being deprived of the touch of Hari; his followers considered that to be appropriate. (2.101.80)
Thinking thus, and perceiving it to be the will of Hari determined by their chosen deity, they accepted it as a source of happiness, even though it was in the form of a punishment from the Lord. (81)
Faith in Śrī Hari, the granting of boons by Him, the words of Hari, the entrusting of one's self to Hari, and the state of total dependence upon Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Lord. (82)
Even though they possessed great wealth and even though they were endowed with sovereign power in every respect,
they served Hari day and night.
The intellect of devotees alone remains steady even in great calamities;
and for them, this intellect becomes firmly established in the glorious Supreme Self. (84)
Even if everything were to perish, may the Blessed One not depart from my mind;
for that which is favorability toward Hari is indeed true favorability.
Whatever hostility there may be toward Hari is indeed hostility itself;
for this is the duty of a servant for those who have surrendered, since it cannot be otherwise.
Thinking thus, Śambhu and the others could not endure the words of Śrī;
for she is indeed Satī, the devotee of Viṣṇu, Rudrāṇī, the bringer of dissolution. (87)
How could she endure the curse if she were not indeed devoted to Hari?
For she knows Lakṣmī to be her mother, and she is dear to her preceptor. (88)
One should always pay homage to the wife of the guru and never provoke her to anger;
for the wife of the guru carries out his command without hesitation. (89)
She too must be protected to the best of one's ability; the word "no" must certainly not be uttered.
Herein dwells Nārāyaṇa, the Lord Kṛṣṇa, who is beloved by his master.
The Guru is the venerable speaker of the Vedas, and his beloved wife must certainly not be disparaged;
for Satī knows everything arising from the interruption of their pleasure. 9.1.
Since there is suffering in every kalpa, she did not cast a curse;
for thus, O Rādhikā, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa is indeed the remover of distress.
He told the cause of the curse to the one named Hemaśālāyana;
Lakṣmī related her own domestic history to the female cakravāka bird.

Thus ends the one hundred and first chapter, titled “The Description of the Descent of the Six—Kṛṣṇa, Dhenu-pāla, Candra, Āditya, Jayāditya, and others—who were servants [of the Lord], as well as Satī and Śaṅkara, into the world of mortals due to the breaking of the pleasure of Lakṣmī’s reclining with Nārāyaṇa and her subsequent curse,” in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-nārāyaṇīya-saṃhitā*, concerning the time when the Blessed Lord was reclining upon Lakṣmī in Mahāvaikuṇṭha.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Rādhikā, to what occurred in Vaikuṇṭha following the curse; I shall relate to you what took place between Kamalā and Kṛṣṇa.
That which the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa spoke to the sage Hemāyana, and likewise that which the maiden spoke to the female ruddy geese; || 2 ||
I shall tell you all of that; listen with a one-pointed mind.
Having heard the curse, Hari Nārāyaṇa Kṛṣṇa Janārdana—
Then Kṛṣṇa, his very soul pained by the suffering of his devotee, did not speak to Kamalā,
but reflected for himself upon what was both just and auspicious.
Oh, how wonderful is the diversity of manifestation, having reached a state beyond comparison!
May I forever satisfy this Lakṣmī who dwells within my heart. (5)
"I shall indeed distance myself for a moment; yet she remains unsatiated with my great joy and speaks as if she were restless. (6)
For the sake of my devotees, that virtuous lady cannot endure even a moment;
she cannot endure separation from me, nor can she endure delay for long.
I always grant happiness to Śrī just as I do to myself;
just as separation from Śrī is not desired by me, so too is it for my devotees.
This is indeed the nature of women: if their own purpose is not fulfilled, they become like strangers in an instant and yield only evil fruit.
Even though Lakṣmī is not a devotee, she should never be abandoned;
for she is my most excellent devotee, exceedingly devoted to me, my wife, and my own dear friend.
Śaṅkara was also a devotee, as were his devoted Satī and Kṛṣṇikā; likewise Jaya, Candra, and Dhenupāla, and thereafter Ramā, the most excellent of devotees.
Nevertheless, for the sake of showing affection toward my most excellent devotees,
my devotees are always exceedingly dear to me, even more so than Lakṣmī.
Even if Lakṣmī, though dear to me, were to cause suffering to my devotees, I would abandon her for the sake of my devotees; Lakṣmī herself is the very example of this.
In this matter, however, I shall provide an illustration;
let the fruit of my curse and that of Lakṣmī be seen as an example. (14)
"And so that my instruction may be true to its purpose, he shall never again act in this way";
having reflected thus, the Blessed One brought forth his grief. (15)
Afflicted by the suffering of his devotee, he himself became sorrowful; he did not speak, nor did he look upon him. Having become as if mindless, he did not even smile in the slightest.
Looking upward with his mind, he shines forth greatly agitated,
just as one would at the death of a mother or the loss of a wife.
Just as grief is experienced at the loss of an only son, so too is it contemplated [regarding others],
thinking that in another moment he will leave the house and go away somewhere.
Just as one might become broken-hearted upon the loss of all one's possessions,
so too is Nārāyaṇa seen to have attained a state of dispassion.
Just as one who has conquered the collection of senses, subdued the internal organ and so forth,
and stands on the far shore of Māyā, so did Nārāyaṇa become.
Lakṣmī, filled with various amorous gestures and expressions, laughed repeatedly; taking his hand in her own, she pressed him close and kissed him again and again.
Having dragged Nārāyaṇa, he desired to lead him into the interior of his house;
however, at that time, Nārāyaṇa was like a corpse or like a block of stone.
Due to the grief for his devotee, the Supreme Lord became as if insentient;
indeed, He who is the refuge and the giver of happiness to His own devotees remains in that house. (23)
"If misfortune caused by a curse should arise in the home of my devotees, what would be the purpose of my dwelling there? Having reflected thus, he spoke to her. (24)
"Do not touch me here, O fair-thighed one; do not cause me vain distress.
I have no desire for that house where my devotees are cursed. (25)
O virtuous lady, because of you, my bed is no longer pleasant;
for the great devotees have been cursed—what indeed could be more painful than this? (26)
Guests are always to be honored, and among them, those who are devoted to me;
those who have surrendered all their possessions for my sake are always to be worshipped and honored by me. (27)
O Lakṣmī, for the sake of my devotees I am always turning the rosary;
and for the sake of my devotees I descend into the worlds at all times.
I am Nara-Nārāyaṇa as an ascetic for the sake of my devotees;
and I am Nārāyaṇa in the immortal field (Akṣara-kṣetra) on the White Island (Śveta-bhūmi) in the Ocean of Milk. 29.
In Goloka, in Vaikuṇṭha, in the unmanifest, and in the abode of immortality—
wherever my devotees dwell, there I abide, O lotus-born one.
I dwell in the homes of my devotees, sporting together with my devotees;
Vaikuṇṭha is my abode, for nothing else is pleasing to me.
If my abode were the cause for the attainment of suffering by my devotees, then indeed the name "Vaikuṇṭha" would lose its true meaning. ||32||
If that abode of Mine, renowned as divine and bestowing eternal bliss, were to grant suffering and rebirth, what then would its "Vikuṇṭha" (imperishable) nature be? ||33||
Even there, the curse of Śaṅkara, the God of gods who is dear to me, and of my devoted wife Satī, resulted in my birth as a human being. (34)
What could be more grievous than this, a most intense suffering that brings ill repute upon Kṛṣṇā, upon your friend, and upon both Jayacandra and Karka? (35)
And likewise the downfall of the attendant Dhenupāla—O beloved, how is it that your mind is thus engaged in such an untimely dance? (36)
She spoke what was improper, being opposed to the devotion of her devotees;
yet you have never done such a thing, for you have always acted rightly toward Śaṅkara.
What should I do here in a house filled with hostile women?
Even sweet and delicious food becomes like poison without [the presence of] Bhakta. (38)
A drink rich in coolness and fragrance acts like fire without food;
and gentle silk clothing acts like an arrow without food. (39)
Ornaments such as gold and jewels become like fish without a devotee; fragrant oils, garments, and the like become like mud without a devotee. (2.102.40)
All happiness within my heart blazes like fire because of the power of the curse;
O Lakṣmī, without Śambhu, I am consumed by this.
That curse of mine was a curse from my devotee, and that curse of yours was likewise from me;
because we share the nature of being half-bodies and half-limbs, it causes suffering—of this there is no doubt.
"You do not know the supreme greatness of my devotees;
Sanatkumāra knows the exalted majesty of devotion. (43)
If my eyes do not see my devotees who have approached me, I shall always remove them by taking them out from their sockets. 44.
If my head does not bow to this devotee of yoga, I shall cut it from my neck and cast it far away; of this there is no doubt. (45)
If my two ears were not to hear the words of my devotees, I would cut them off at the root and cast them far away; of this there is no doubt.
O Lotus-born One, if my nose does not perceive the fragrance of food at all, then I shall cut it off by its very root and cast it far away.
If the tongue never sings the songs of the devotee, or if the palate does not savor the nectar offered by the devotee; ||48||
Then, having pulled it out from its root, I shall forever abandon my tongue, if my lips do not receive the betel and other offerings given by my devotees. (49)
If my teeth do not chew that which is offered by my devotees,
then I shall indeed cut off my lips and teeth with weapons and cast them away.
If my two hands are not useful for the service of my own devotees, I shall cut them off at the root; I would abandon them like pieces of wood. (51)
If my chest were not useful for embracing devotees, then I would rather tear out my chest and cast it forever into a pit. (52)
If devotees were ever to dwell within my heart, I would indeed draw out that heart along with its blood and utterly destroy it. (53)
If my stomach is not permitted to digest the food offered by my devotees, I shall quickly tear it all apart and cast it away; of this there is no doubt. (54)
If the touch of my devotees is indeed not pleasing to you, I shall quickly tear this body from my frame and cast it into the great fire. (55)
If my vigor, strength, and virility do not bring happiness to my devotees, then I shall destroy all of that and make myself impotent. (56)
If these thighs are not even for the purpose of seating devotees, then, for the sake of my devotees, I shall indeed become a headless trunk (kabandha). (57)
If my feet do not indeed go toward my devotees, then I shall surely cut them off with an axe and become footless. (58)
If my body were not born for the sake of the happiness of my devotees, then having kindled a fire, I would surely reduce it to ashes. (59)
Furthermore, if the qualities such as intellect and the rest do not depend upon me,
then having abandoned the qualities, I dwell quality-less in the dense forest.
What is the use of much speaking to you in this matter? If you persist in obstructing devotion, causing distress to devotees, and creating obstacles to devotion.
Whether she causes suffering to my devotees or opposes the peace of my devotees, I abandon you; O Rati, what else indeed would I not abandon?
"I renounce everything, my entire being, for the sake of my devotees; I have no desire for this myself.
Know, O Lotus-born One, that when my devotee perishes, everything of mine perishes. (63)
Know that when my devotee is protected, everything is protected by me.
Oh, where indeed will the illustrious Śaṅkara become a mere human being? (64)
Alas! Where will his virtuous and beloved human wife be?
Alas! Where will his beloved dark-complexioned maidservant or devotee be born? (65)
"Alas! Even Dhenu-pāla, Jaya, and Candrarama shall, by your curse, come to exist on the earth in a place of misery. (66)
As long as I do not know the state of these living beings, I shall find no joy;
therefore, I have no happiness until I go where they also are.
Having spoken thus, he abandoned Kamalā, abandoned Śrīkamalākara,
and abandoned the beautiful throne, the palace, and the radiant abode.
Having completely abandoned Vaikuṇṭha and having forsaken his abode of affection,
Hari departed with a heavy heart, even leaving Garuḍa behind.
Without looking back, he proceeded through the universe to the surface of the earth;
there he did not see Lakṣmī, his most beloved life-breath, who was wailing piteously.
As she cried out, "O Lord! O Lord!", Śrī Hari went to the surface of the earth—becoming invisible with his unmanifest body—there upon this ground produced by jewels.
Indeed, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the glorious Puruṣottama, descended into the field of Aśvapaṭṭasara, which is a field of imperishable merit. 72.
Then, the Supreme Brahman, who transcends the imperishable and is the ordainer of all incarnations,
[resided] in the field named Kuṅkumavāpī, in the house of the illustrious Kaṃbhārī.
She descended into the home of the illustrious Gopālakṛṣṇa, which was endowed with divine prosperity,
for the purpose of Nārāyaṇa’s arrival.
Having arrived and attained dissolution in the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Person (Śrī Puruṣottama), he remained near the Aśvasaras lake.
Then, by the command of the beginningless Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa,
he assumed a disguised form on earth and set out toward the north for the purpose of searching.
In the region situated at the base of the Himalayas, in the district of Nīpālaya, and within the kingdom of Kailāsadhāma, [he saw] the prince Śivarāja. ||77||
Having sought out his devotee Śaṅkara, he remained there beyond the range of perception;
thereafter, to search for Satī, he went to the city of Ṣaṇmāṇḍavya.
There, she became a maiden by the name of Jānakī;
and there also dwells Nārāyaṇa, invisible and fond of his attendants.
From their marriage were born Kṛṣṇā and Jaya, as well as Candraka;
Dhenupāla, the brother of Śivarāja, was also established there.
And the Lord Nārāyaṇa dwells together with his devotees;
remaining unmanifest, he eats, rejoices, and acts with them incessantly.
In one place he comes to the sacred field of Akshara, and in another to Ashvasarovara;
there, in the temple of Shiva-Raja, he remains with devotion.
Thus, having renounced Lakṣmī for the sake of his devotees alone, the Blessed One came into the universe and made his dwelling among his devotees. 83.
Then Lakṣmī, who dwells in Vaikuṇṭha, having realized [the situation], abandoned her own [form];
and Nārāyaṇa, having left Vaikuṇṭha, his throne, and his abode, [departed]. ||84||
He went for the sake of a long journey and for the sake of his devotees while in his human existence;
there, in that house which was like a void, he grieved in many ways and wept.
She praised him in many ways with her voice and spoke of her own faults:
"I am indeed the fickle Lakṣmī, who follows after the defects of suffering. (86)
Always the cause of pride and other such vices, providing no assistance to the wretched, my dwelling in the house of evildoers is considered by me in many ways to be sinful. (87)

It is the abode of faults such as violence and falsehood, and it nourishes unrighteousness; it is the locus of deceit, hypocrisy, and sensual enjoyment, as well as the place where the venerable are insulted. (88)
The loss of morality, the loss of purity, thirst, passion, excessive greed, theft, violence, and abuse—these are the faults rooted in pride. (89)
Fickle, unstable in any one place, and causing mental distress, I am ever-moving and take away everything; yet, O abode of compassion, [you remain so]. (2.102.90)
The Blessed One, impelled by supreme compassion, protects me within his own heart;
devoted to mercy, he does not even enjoy his own pleasures without me.
Having given everything to me, Kṛṣṇa himself has departed from his home;
what kind of straightforwardness is this, that he does not grant me any sorrow? (92)
He does not despise me as insignificant; he endures my lack of discipline.
Dependent upon my devotion, he always protects me, his devotee, even though I am impure. (93)
"My devotion to my husband was not perfect; nevertheless, the Blessed One himself, becoming devoted to his wife, has protected me even more than he did for himself. (94)
"He does not eat without me, nor indeed does he drink even water;
wherever cooked food is prepared by another without me, that is indeed [unacceptable]. (95)
Keśava neither sees, nor grasps, nor eats at all;
when my entry among the cooks occurs, then Hari [will do so]. 96.
Hari partakes of the food offering only when it is obtained from a trusted person, and never otherwise;
likewise for clothing, jewels, water, vessels, betel, food, and collyrium. (97)
Ornaments, sandalwood paste, gold, a vehicle, a mount, lordship, a seat, a bed, objects, and gifts—these are the offerings; their fruit is surrender. (98)
"Having offered all my food to him, this lord of mine has indeed eaten it;
oh, when considered with discernment, Kṛṣṇa is the best, for he remains steadfast in his vow toward his wife. (99)
"Though fickle, she is a vessel of affection; I, a devoted wife, am not like her.
Alas! All my good fortune is indeed fruitless without my beloved."
In Vaikuṇṭha, all riches and every kind of object for enjoyment are fruitless;
there are male and female servants, gardens, celestial chariots, and grounds for pleasure groves. (101)
Palaces, mansions, pinnacle-vessels, elephants, horses, chariots, and cows—
indeed, ornaments, garments, and the drinking of nectar are all fruitless without a beloved.
My beloved has departed from my home solely because of my own fault.
"Alas! How is it that I have not died? Why do I not become a corpse? (10.3)
"Without my beloved, I am as if dead, since life is fruitless without him"—thus did she lament, O Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa. (104)
"O Lord, without you, Vaikuṇṭha is like a cremation ground to me.
Having said this, she fell down near the lion-throne.
Having fainted for a moment, she rose up again with speed and, crying out "O beloved! O beloved!", she came to the door.
Fainting, she fell once more onto the ground, powerless;
meanwhile, her friends arrived, crying out, "What is this? What is this?"
Though they reasoned it through, they could not accept the undesirable outcome; they were deeply grieved by that sorrow, and remained distressed by the winds and the sprinkling of water.
Dispelling her fainting fit with offerings of flowers and other means, they asked: "Why has this suffering come upon you at such an untimely hour?"
Lakṣmī said: "Hari has gone somewhere; for a long time he has departed from Vaikuṇṭha, leaving me and all his devotees, O Nārāyaṇa."
O Rādhikā, upon hearing these words, which were like a thunderbolt falling from the sky, Lakṣmī and they too fell into a most intense swoon at hearing such an undesirable thing.

Thus ends the one hundred and second chapter, titled "The Description of Śrī Nārāyaṇa’s Departure from Vaikuṇṭha after Abandoning Kamalā, Following the Curse of Śrī Lakṣmī upon Śambhu and Others," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Rādhikā, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa related this account to the sage Hemāyana, as well as to the maiden and the female cakravāka birds.
Upon hearing that Vaikuṇṭha and everything within it had been deprived of Kṛṣṇa, Lakṣmī, her companions, and all else became filled with grief in an instant.
Then all the women residing in Vaikuṇṭha fainted;
[Brahmā] dispelled their fainting with breezes, sandalwood water, and [other] fragrant liquids.
Then, in another moment, Lakṣmī fainted;
remembering her separation from Śrī Hari, she wept again in many ways.
"I shall neither eat nor drink; I will die without that Hari.
For the attainment of the Blessed One through a woman's body is always difficult to achieve. (5)
"I have indeed attained that eternal union with Hari;
for if I do not obtain Hari, I shall bring about the destruction of my body. (6)
"I shall perform severe penance; I will go toward the surface of the earth.
Wherever my Lord dwells upon the earth, there my death is preferable. (7)
O Lord of lords, O Hari, O beloved Kṛṣṇa, O Lord Nārāyaṇa, I shall renounce whatever is hostile to Kṛṣṇa, including my mind, hands, feet, and so forth.
"Having abandoned me, your wicked maidservant, where have you gone? Tell me quickly!
O Hari, without you, this hearing of yours acts like a piercing thorn in my ear."
Without seeing you here, O Hari, my vision burns like a flame of fire;
without hearing your praise here, O Lord, it feels as if scorched by poison.
O Lord, without you, even touch here feels like a disease to my sense of smell;
O Hari, without you, every taste seems like vomit to me.
O Lord, without you, the nose perceives fragrance as if it were a scorpion; without you, eating and drinking feel like a constriction of the throat.
O Lord, without you, even a beautiful seat appears like a spear;
O Hari, without you, flower garlands and the like seem like venomous serpents and spears.
O Viṣṇu, without you, all aesthetic delight appears to me like a demon;
O Lord, without Hari, even Vaikuṇṭha appears to me like a hollow pit.
To me, this moment in its form as an instant becomes like an eon without you;
the cool breeze, O Kṛṣṇa, acts like the heat of the sun's rays when separated from you.
Without the Lord, everything—water, land, and home—becomes empty;
even beautiful clothing becomes like a tiger, and likewise, ornaments become like lions.
My good fortune, my mass of hair, and everything else have become like those of a widow; the happiness I once enjoyed now seems like the void of space without you. (17)
Without you, everything—the body, material possessions, and so forth—leads to ruin;
and even your own existence, without your wife, becomes like that of an atheist.
O Śrī Narāyaṇa, what is the use of saying much more here?
Without you, I shall not remain anywhere alone; I will fall after you upon the earth.
O Lord Kṛṣṇa Govinda Nārāyaṇa, O Supreme among Men!
O You whose form is beloved by Śrī Kṛṣṇa, protect me, O Master, in Your presence.
My life has departed; where are you, and where are your devotees, Hara and the others?
Wherever you go, this Lakṣmī, your wife, shall go with you.
I do not know where you, who are omnipresent, have gone;
O Janārdana, here I now fly upon your back.
"Do with me as you wish, for I am your devotee falling [at your feet].
Having spoken thus, Lakṣmī fell from Vaikuṇṭha, bowing her head toward the ground.
A great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose in Vaikuṇṭha and throughout all creations;
indeed, Lakṣmī fell from all the worlds like [the world] at the time of dissolution.
Brahmā and the other gods swiftly seized the splendor falling from Satī, as if it were a cluster of delicate flowers; yet they did not do so with haste.
No harm whatsoever occurred from the fall; thus the lords received her, and hundreds of thousands of female and male servants descended along with Lakṣmī. ||26||
In the world of truth (Satyaloka), you were held aloft in the canopy by the gods and others in the sky;
you were honored, consoled, and worshipped with all manner of objects. ||27||
Having been fed, given drink, and seated upon their thrones,
they were all indeed struck down by the illusory wind and became overwhelmed by delusion.
And they forgot that suffering born of separation from Nārāyaṇa;
the female companions were honored by Sāvitrī, and the male companions were honored by Brahmā. (29)
After they had rested, they were asked, "For what reason did you fall?
Then Lakṣmī, remembering once again her separation from Nārāyaṇa, [spoke].
She wept for a moment and sought to know about Nārāyaṇa: where he was staying, his current condition, and how their union might come to pass.
Brahmā himself said: "Nārāyaṇa is present today at the Aśvasarovara lake and in the field of Kuṅkumavāpī in Saurāṣṭra."
Having internalized his own form within the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Person (Śrī Puruṣottama), he shines forth as non-different from Him. 33.
Moreover, Nārāyaṇa, who is your eternal master and beloved, Mādhava, goes to the region of Nīpālaya for the sake of his devotees; O Ramā, [I am there too]. 34.
In the city named Kailāsadhāma, at the source of the Gaṇḍakī river,
there shines one who is a portion of Śaṅkara in the form of a king.
His wife, ever-auspicious and named Jānakī, was formerly Satī;
by your curse, she has now become a human woman. (36)
That husband of Jānakī is Śambhu, known by the name Śivarāja;
his daughter is your friend Kṛṣṇā, the maiden Kṛṣṇā. (37)
By your curse, his daughter has been born this very day, as have two sons named Jayāditya and Candrāditya. (38)
The great hero Dhenupāla, likewise the younger brother of Śivarāja, a highly devoted bhakta and a friend, resides in the abode of Kailāsa. (39)
She who was the wife of Śivarāja, the lord of Ṣaṇmāṇḍavyapura,
that daughter, the goddess Jānakī, worships the glorious Narāyaṇa.
Thus, O Lotus-born One, these young men have indeed been born on the slope of the mountain on the bank of the Gaṇḍakī by your curse. (41)
Go wherever your mind desires to go; remember Hari there—either on the shore of the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake or on the bank of the Śrīgaṇḍakī river. (42)
"Your beloved husband will be Nārāyaṇa himself,"—having been addressed thus by Brahmā, Kamalā then rejoiced. (73)
Immediately, her left limbs throbbed again and again, and there were also auspicious omens from thousands of male and female servants. (44)
And they repeatedly became proclaimers of the attainment of the Imperishable.
Thus indeed were Lakṣmī, the male servants, and the female servants addressed by Brahmā. (45)
Having paid homage to Sāvitrī and Brahmā Parameṣṭhin,
and having received worship, they departed and went to Kuṅkumavāpikā.
They descended from the sky near the Aśvapaṭṭa lake,
beholding an excellent palace with a golden pitcher and a banner.
Practicing the vision of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, he is the Supreme Brahman, the beginningless Śrī Puruṣottama who transcends even the Imperishable (Akṣara). ||48||
Having learned of their entire situation, he offered them a respectful welcome;
honored by him, they dwelt there for the sake of attaining the glorious Lord of Vaikuṇṭha. 49.
However, the four-armed Nārāyaṇa himself is not seen there,
nor is Lakṣmī herself, along with Mahālakṣmī, the glorious Kaṃbhārī Śrī.
She is constantly served, protected, and likewise propitiated; and all her female attendants are protected with great devotion as if they were her own. (5.1)
The servants and the residents of Vaikuṇṭha are protected by Janaka;
thus all remained there, yet he himself was four-armed.
At that time, Śrī Puruṣottama did not come within the range of their vision;
they prayed most fervently again and again for the sake of a sight of him. (53)
Having come together, they performed ascetic practices while subsisting on air alone;
thereafter, for two months, they likewise performed a sacrifice to Viṣṇu.
Nārāyaṇa became pleased and, with a gracious countenance, spoke to them who were accompanied by Ramā; he was four-armed and the dweller of Vaikuṇṭha. (55)
"O my devotees who dwell in Vaikuṇṭha, go indeed to the Gaṇḍakī river, to the region of Nīpālaya, and likewise to Vihāra and Kosala. (56)
I go daily to the palace of Śivarāja, having come under the power of service, where the boys Kṛṣṇa, Jaya, and Candra reside. (57)
Where Satī, the daughter of Dakṣa, became Jānakī, the consort of Śiva,
there dwells a human being who is her younger brother, a cowherd.
"Indeed, these humans are wandering about due to your curse, O Lakṣmī;
therefore, O beloved, you too shall become a human there, a daughter of Śiva. (569)
"O human maiden, experience the painful fruit of bestowing this curse;
these attendants of mine, who dwell in various sacred fords, shall become your slaves. (2.103.60)
May all men, free from sin, be seekers of my service in due time among kings and brahmins here upon this earth. (6.1)
"May you all possess the power to assume any form at will and remember your past lives;
once the fault of the curse has been removed, I shall then reunite with you."
When this Lakṣmī, her nature purified by asceticism, beholds me on Mount Himālaya together with my daughter Cakravākī. ||62||
"The liberation of my daughter, Urvaśī Cakravākī, will come about;
on a peak of the Himalayas, she shall give water to her thirsty daughter. (64)
Having caused her to drink and having satisfied her, thereafter my supreme vision shall be granted;
for when the auspicious time has arrived, my marriage with Lakṣmī shall take place.
When [this] shall be accomplished in the great garden of the kingdom of Kāśī,
then indeed you, my attendants, and even my female servants shall be there.
And at my wedding, there will be an audience for all of you;
thereafter, I shall lead you to my own eternal abode.
Having spoken thus, the Blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa vanished from sight within the eternal Lord Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. (68)
And Lakṣmī and the others, the inhabitants of Vaikuṇṭha, having taken leave of their mother Kaṃbhārā, their father, and the glorious Lord Gopālakṛṣṇa—
Leaving behind the region of Aśvapaṭṭasara and the river Śrīgaṇḍakī,
they went to the Nīpālaya district, the abode of the illustrious Śaṅkara.
And having beheld from the sky the city named Kailāsadhāma,
they descended at the palace of King Śiva, who was accompanied by the illustrious Jānakī.
By means of his yogic vision, Śivarāja perceived them as they truly were:
the attendants accompanied by Lakṣmī, as well as the female servants.
They welcomed him with joy, and Jānakī rejoiced;
Kṛṣṇā also rejoiced there, as did Jaya and Candraka.
The cowherd also rejoiced upon learning that the residents of Vaikuṇṭha had arrived,
and he offered them a welcome, a seat, water, the honey-mixture, fruit, and leaves.
Śiva and the other gods provided and gave him excellent food, honor, a palace, beds suitable for royalty, and dwellings. (75)
Vehicles, mounts, objects of enjoyment, all utensils, and items for eating, drinking, and touching—these are [to be provided] according to the royal custom. (76)
The Lord Śrī Śaṅkara bestowed [blessings] upon those great souls;
they became guests and were satisfied by the service of Śaṅkara.
And there, having risen in the morning, everyone constantly awaits the sight of the god Nārāyaṇa as he arrives. (78)
In order to accept the worship performed by Śaṅkara and others in the temple of Śaṅkara,
Hari himself goes there in the morning after having received his own worship at the shrine.
These arrogant ones never behold him;
therefore, Lakṣmī herself remained there in the royal palace of Śiva as his daughter.
She desired to become so out of a longing for a morning audience;
by the mere power of her resolve, she became the daughter of King Śiva. (8.1)

A human woman possessing divine and excellent qualities, remembering her past births and possessing supreme knowledge, a maiden endowed with all auspicious marks, she is Ramā, the dweller of Vaikuṇṭha. (82)
She who was wronged by Nārāyaṇa became a maiden;
suffering in the house of Satī and Śambhu, she remained there to experience the fruit of her curse. (83)
Then that sorrowful woman was addressed by Hara with the name Lakṣmī,
and she was also constantly called Satyā by her sister Kṛṣṇā.
At the time of Lakṣmī’s manifestation, a rain of flowers was showered from the sky by the inhabitants of Vaikuṇṭha as well as those of Kailāsa. (85)
There was likewise a rain of sandalwood and a rain of wealth;
there were cries of "Victory! and blessings, as well as the sounding of musical instruments and great festivities.
There was dancing by the Apsarases and auspicious rites by the goddesses;
there were gifts by King Śiva and also the sacramental rites performed by the twice-born.
Likewise, all other various festivals were established by Śiva and the others;
however, Lakṣmī, being of human form, did not wish to manifest herself. ||88||
For the sake of gaining the favor of her husband, that princess remained there as a deceptive mortal woman;
yet she always behaved like the daughter of a sage. (89)
Subsisting on the fruits of her ascetic vows, she was a servant of Nārāyaṇa; born as the daughter of Śiva’s family, she was therefore always like a member of that family.
She serves the beloved Nārāyaṇa, the resident of Vaikuṇṭha;
for the sake of serving Nārāyaṇa, his dear wife fetches water.
He gives them food, drink, fragrant betel, and performs the lustration rite (nīrājana) for them; he drinks the nectar from their feet. ||92||
The maiden Ramā constantly massages his feet and daily entreats Janārdana for the sake of the removal of the curse. (93)
Once, for the sake of her marriage and likewise for her swift departure to Vaikuṇṭha, Hari said to her: "O beautiful lady, perform penance."
"Your desire shall be fulfilled by him together with the female ruddy goose.
Having been told this, that maiden then [departed] together with the female ruddy goose.
Having gathered together, she went to the Himalaya to accomplish her ascetic success;
meanwhile, other male and female servants remained in the region of Nīpālaya.
In the monastery, as well as in Kosala and the field of Avimukta, and in the house of their beloved fathers, they all manifested themselves. 97.
And all those supreme devotees of the Lord became rememberers of their past births;
they were Vaiṣṇavas, possessed of spiritual perfection, and likewise able to assume any form at will.
Divine and possessing divine dwellings, moving in celestial garments, they were happy and endowed with all perfections, just like those residing in Vaikuṇṭha. ||99||
The Supreme Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa related this entire story to Hemaśālāyana, just as the maiden had told it to Urvaśī.
Thus, O Rādhikā, everything occurred by the will of Nārāyaṇa;
neither time, nor karma, nor even prārabdha was the cause here. (10.1)

Thus ends the one hundred and third chapter, titled "The Description of Lakṣmī’s Arrival from Vaikuṇṭha to Satyaloka with her male and female servants, followed by their arrival at the Aśvapaṭṭa lake, and then the manifestation of Lakṣmī in the palace of King Śiva in the region of Nīpālaya, as well as the manifestation of the male and female servants in various separate locations," in the second section (Tretā-santāna) of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O Rādhikā, thereafter Hemaśālāyana asked Nārāyaṇa, "What kind of austerity was performed by the daughter of Śaṅkara?"
The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa spoke this reply to Cakravākī, the daughter of King Śiva, on the bank of the Śrī Gaṇḍakī river. || 2 ||
He spoke with supreme affection: "O daughter, come to my home.
Thus addressed, the daughter Urvaśī went indeed to her mother's house.
In that exceedingly beautiful royal palace, she remains well-established as if protected;
yet, in the presence of people, she does not say anything at all.
In secluded places, she engages in various conversations with her mother-in-law by the river,
in the garden, in the grove, in the field, in the palace, and in the assembly hall.
In the kitchen, on the bed, in the granary, in the kitchen-chamber, in the bathhouse, in the assembly hall, and likewise in the temple of the master; || 6 ||
Thus, in all other places as well, Urvaśī always remains accompanied by her shadow;
due to the cause of the curse, she spends her days together with that shadow.
Indeed, through the true devotion of Śivarāja and the devotion of Jaya, as well as through the excellent devotion of Kṛṣṇā, Candra, and Dhenupa; || 8 ||
Nārāyaṇa himself, eternally possessing the form of a divine youth,
being pleased, goes to that house and departs after receiving worship.
He eats the offered food, drinks the sweet water, and accepts the betel leaf as well as the garments, ornaments, and decorations. (2.104.10)
He ate everything with devotion that was given by his daughter Lakṣmī,
as well as that which had been secretly offered by Urvaśī to her father.
The Lord, the Master, accepts all of that with extreme devotion;
thus, as it is constantly being accepted, the beloved becomes exceedingly beautiful.
Immersed and overcome by love, she offered auspicious prayers in solitude for the sake of her own marriage and also for the destruction of the curse. (13)
Then, for the sake of the liberation of Kṛṣṇa and the others, Nārāyaṇa said:
"O fair-thighed one, do not proceed with such haste; it is not very far from here, just a moment's distance."
Having spoken thus, the illustrious Nārāyaṇa then vanished from sight;
that maiden Urvaśī then said, "Hari is attained through austerity."
Thus the Blessed One said: "Nārāyaṇa, your father, told me:
'Tell me, what kind of austerity is to be performed, and where must one go—to the Himālaya? (16)
"O daughter, tell me, has there ever been seen by you such a place where no calamities exist? Show me that place. (17)
Daityas, rākṣasas, and dānavas who are enemies of Hari,
as well as those who are enemies of Śambhu, roam about in the forest day and night.
For women, there is great hardship in performing penance in a desolate place;
in that regard, you remain as a female ruddy goose, and you always have fear of hawks.
"I am a maiden fit for marriage, yet I have fear of the Daityas and others; may I achieve the perfection of my penance without obstacles for the sake of pleasing Hari. (2.104.20)
"Tell me, daughter, if you know of such a place upon the mountain," she said;
thus addressed, Urvaśī replied, "O Mother, as vast as the Himalaya is... (21)
While wandering about together with the gods, I have seen certain tracts there where human beings dwell.
Those troughs are situated on the side, interspersed with forest groves;
there is a region known as Bhūtāyana where the progeny of Śaṅkarī dwell.
This is the region of Nīpālaka, where the offspring are indeed Pārvatī;
likewise, there is the region of Badarī, where the offspring are Nārāyaṇī.
Likewise is the land of Trivarta, where the subjects are born from the three gods;

He offered the madhuparka and nectar and other gifts, and rejoiced exceedingly; thus, by the desire of Hari, this family made their dwelling there.
Everything happens in due time according to Kṛṣṇa’s will:
the Vaiṣṇavas, the male attendants, and whatever other female attendants there may be.
They were of human descent and were honored by the kings of Kāśī;
being honored by Śambhu as well, they dwelt in royal palaces.
They were constantly remembering the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa,
as well as Nara-Nārāyaṇa and Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa.
The goddesses remained there, remembering Lakṣmī and the female ascetic;
and Rādhikā, Urvaśī, and Lakṣmī likewise remembered their families.
Released from the curse of her existence as a female ruddy goose, the maiden— equal to Ramā and enriched with the beauty of Urvaśī’s form— did not bow to her own father, Hari.

Thus, in the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, in the second section, the *Tretā-santāna*, while the vital breaths of Lakṣmī and Cakravākī were circulating through the water consecrated by Nārāyaṇa during their ascetic penance, the female ruddy goose (Cakravākī) chose to drink water upon the mountain peak and subsequently sought liberation. Hari, having submerged the region with rains, provided water upon the peak; having drunk it, she was released from her curse. Out of fear of the rains, the family of King Śiva and the attendants (*pārṣadas*) of Vaikuṇṭha, who had assumed human forms, came to Kāśī and settled on the banks of the Varaṇā.
The one hundred and fifth chapter, titled "The Description of Dwelling in the Mango Grove and Receiving Hospitality from Śambhu within the Palaces of the King of Kāśī."
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Rādhikā, in this manner Hari related this narrative to the sage Ayanarṣi concerning the female ruddy goose who was seeking water.
That celestial beauty Urvaśī was indeed liberated from her curse;
she bowed down to her father Nārāyaṇa and to her mother Ramā.
Since she had previously gone to the world of Indra and been entrusted to him,
Lakṣmī then indeed spoke to her own beloved.
Hanumān protected me while I was established in austerity along with my daughter;
O Lord, a boon should be granted by you to that Hanumān.
Thus addressed, Śrī Hari said, "Hanumān, choose what you desire.
The lord of monkeys chose that his name should always have its meaning made literal.
"By your grace, may I possess the nature of a monkey so that I may drink incessantly the eternal bliss from the form of Nārāyaṇa"— may this be my purpose.
May there be unwavering devotion toward you, Nārāyaṇa;
wherever there is the story of Nārāyaṇa, there lies the very life of my breaths.
The nectar of the stories of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, and also the nectar of the stories from the Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā. (8)
Wherever that may be, let my presence truly be there;
and wherever those devotees sing, let my abode be there as well.
Wherever your abode may be, there, at its door,
let my presence remain eternally for the sake of service, acting as a protector of your devotees.
Then Hanumān, the king of devotees, offered this prayer;
Hari replied, "So be it," and gave him a string of pearls.
She gave him the two sandals and a garland of unfading flowers;
Lakṣmī also granted Hanumān the status of a family deity.
Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa said to Hanumān: "Dwell in my presence at the sacred field of Aśvapaṭṭasara, well-protecting the land. (13)
Hanumān caused a magnificent palace to be built for Lakṣmī upon the mountain;
there he performed worship of Lakṣmī together with Nārāyaṇa.
Then, having taken Lakṣmī from there by means of a celestial chariot, Hari went to Kāśikā,
where indeed Śivarāja and others dwell.
Having brought him down from the celestial chariot, he granted a boon for the sake of marriage:
"I shall return in twelve years; then your end of the curse will come to pass."
"Wait for me for that long, and tell this to King Śiva:
'I shall come and perform the marriage; everything will turn out auspiciously.'"
Having spoken thus and having made her aware of his fierce austerity, the Lord Śrī Narāyaṇa became visible there on the bank of the Varaṇā. 18.
Hari traveled by means of his celestial chariot to the Aśvapaṭṭa lake,
and Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa spoke thus to Hemaśālāyana.
"Having married Lakṣmī, he will liberate Śambhu and others from their curse";
thinking thus, Hari formerly abandoned Lakṣmī for the sake of his own devotees. (2.106.20)
Hemaśālāyana and the others, having heard that, attained supreme joy.
Then all the sages [arrived] there at the camel-pens, at every place.

In order to repeatedly bring about the contact with the feet of the beginningless Śrī Hari, as well as His touch, and furthermore to sanctify it and establish its status as a sacred ford (tīrtha), [He remains there]. 22.
Having worshipped him, they made this request: "In order to sanctify the surface of the earth, as well as that region of the Uṣṇālaya and its people, please make it a sacred ford (tīrtha). (23)
O Blessed One, Lord of the Gods of gods, by the placement of Your own feet and by Your bathing, sitting, and wandering, [You have sanctified] the mountains, lakes, and rivers.
"May sacred fords, as well as our homes and forests, become holy shrines for us.
"So be it," Hari replied, and then [they ascended] into a divine celestial chariot.
And they all ascended the mountain named Hemaśāla,
having first gazed all around at the house of the lord of Hemaśālā.
Having purified themselves by applying the touch arising from his feet and having received worship performed with gold, they then proceeded to the Bālā river.
Having bathed there and purified themselves, and having beheld Bālāditya as well,
they bathed in the waters of the Gośaṅku and proceeded to Mount Rāva.
Then, having purified the entire mountain with their feet,
they [visited] the Marcāśanā river, as well as the Surānadī and the Turūnadī.
Having purified the Aita river and made it a sacred ford by means of immersion, and having bathed in the lake known as Mākamānasa as well as in the Bālāsaras; ||2.106.30||
Then, having bathed in the Śvāna river and visited the Dārāliṅga mountain,
he performed a most purifying pilgrimage on foot and bathed in the Kuvans lake.
Having seen the stream Lābharuci and the southern forest, he bathed in the Turu lake amidst the waters of the Gaurī river. (32)
Having bathed at Prāggiri and having bathed at Ārasarovara, and likewise having purified Maṣīgrīva mountain with his feet; ||33||
Having bathed in the Utuṅga lake and beheld the battle from the sky,
he then sanctified Mount Mekadāna with his feet.
And having gone further north from there, having performed a ritual immersion in the Vitūrīya river, and having bathed and drunk that water at Delyā and Ghelyā; (35)
Having gone to Śālavīnaśaila and having purified that place,
they then [proceeded] to the Rinku river, the Jhinku river, and the Phinku river.
Having bathed at Grāmaśaila and having purified himself by descending into the waters of the Kāruliṅga river and then the Dāruliṅga river; ||37||
Having bathed repeatedly in the waters of the Cāruliṅga and the Murā river,
and having bathed in the Turā and Murā rivers, they proceeded to Mount Ālā.
Having purified themselves with their feet, they went toward Mount Diṅpa;
then, having bathed in the waters of the Kuvindūmā river at Kiṇḍīcā, [they proceeded].
They bathed in the purifying waters of the Kvīlpīnā and Laviṅgā rivers;
then, having bathed in the Miccalā river and beheld Mount Cāṭa.
Having purified themselves and crossed over the Uttara river, they went to the west;
then, having bathed in the Phijarā and purified those subjects, [they proceeded].
The servants of Hari accepted the worship offered by the subjects;
they were fed, honored, and saluted again and again. (42)
Agastya and likewise Śambhu, Lopāmudrā and Ramā, Pārvatī and the son of Aśvinī, as well as their attendants. ||43||
Then, those who were the protectors of the people dwelling in the hot regions bestowed very abundant blessings upon those subjects.
They gave to them the auspicious, great Vaiṣṇava mantra that bestows liberation:
"Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya svāmine svāhā. (45)
They also gave him tulasī necklaces as well as rosaries for chanting;
thereafter, they granted him refuge, and a great cry of victory arose.
Then, having gone to the capital city, they performed a Vaiṣṇava sacrifice;
the sages residing there became the officiating priests at that time.
Agastya became Brahmā, and Rudra remained in the place of Rudra;
the Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa stayed in the place of the principal deity. 48.
The Hotṛ was Homāyana, the Udgātṛ was Balāyana, the Āharta was Maṣīgrīva, and the Pratihartṛ was Ravāsana. ||49||
The others indeed became the Hotṛ priests, while the great king Dakṣa, the sovereign of the land of Uṣṇālaya, became the Sacrificer. (2.106.50)
The mind-born son of Dakṣa, who is saluted by gods and daityas, [removes] whatever sins there may be caused by regional calamities and obstacles. (51)
"May all obstacles be withdrawn, and may they not arise for us again"—thinking thus, all those brahmins acted according to the king's command. (52)
The embodied gods performed the Vaiṣṇava sacrifice and were satisfied;
the Brāhmaṇas there also performed the *puraścaraṇa* rite. ||53||
Some [recite] the Puruṣasūkta, others the Viṣṇusūkta;
likewise, others [recite] the Nārāyaṇasūkta and the Śrīsūkta.
Others [prefer] the Lakṣmīsūkta; others, the Devīsūkta; others, the Rudrādhyāya; and others, the Sāvitrī of Savitṛ. (55)
Others were reciting the Gaṇeśa-stotra, and others were chanting the sections of the Sāmaveda;
in this manner, they then performed the recitations of the various Vedas.
King Dakṣajaṅgha, from the commencement of his sacrifices, always gives gifts at dawn and his subjects always enjoy them. (57)
Every day, sweet foods were given to boys, girls, and others, as well as to the poor, the helpless, the destitute, the lame, the blind, the wretched, and so forth. ||58||
Having completed the sacrifice for half a fortnight,
they then performed the concluding bath (avabhṛtha) near the capital city of King Dakṣaja-vangara.
To the south of the auspicious city named Uṣṇādattāṅga, at the confluence of the Ārasa lake and the Phiṅkū river, they performed [the rites]. || 2.106.60 ||
Then, on the sixth day of the bright fortnight, the Brāhmaṇas and others residing there made their departure by means of celestial chariots and went to their own respective regions.
The king, who was devoted to Nārāyaṇa, became joyful;
he prayed to Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa to construct a magnificent temple.
"So be it," Hari replied; and there, in the capital of the king, the monarch caused a most excellent and lofty palace to be constructed. (63)
On the full moon day of the month of Āśvina, the great sage Agastya, a knower of the Vedas, installed the Lord Hari, Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, according to Vedic injunctions.
The king indeed showed devotion to him, the delight of Kambharā;
then he, together with his subjects, his family, and the brahmins, set out.
A pious and pure Vaiṣṇava should go to see the holy field of Aśvapaṭṭasara, the city of Śrī Hari, and the sacred site of Kuṅkumavāpikā.
Hari said, "So be it," and with a hundred celestial chariots,
he [took] those subjects consisting of ten thousand men and women.
Having taken [him], he traveled by way of the sky to the hermitage of Lomaśa;
and Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa also went along with him.
In his own celestial chariot, together with his own celestial attendants,
the throngs of devotees from Uṣṭrālaya also arrived.
On the third day of the dark fortnight of the month of Ūrja, they arrived at Akṣarakṣetra;
honored with welcomes and other courtesies, they stayed there for five days.
All the holy fords (tīrthas) performed [this] and heard the nectar-like discourse of the *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*, which bestows eternal liberation. 71.
On the eighth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Ūrja, during the Brāhma-muhūrta,
they bathed in the Aśvasarovara lake and celebrated the festival of Anādikṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
On the occasion of his twelfth birthday,
the Lord Śrīkānta performed worship and other rites there in a golden pavilion that had been constructed.
It was graced by gods, goddesses, Satī, virtuous women, and great sages,
and it was presided over by lords and their consorts within its vast expanse.
Seated upon a divine elephant-throne, resplendent with hosts of Apsaras and adorned by the Pitṛs, Gandharvas, and Vidyādharas, he shone forth; the lords of sages offered him worship. (76)
The lords bestowed their blessings and performed the ārātrika ceremony;
the people offered gifts and presented auspicious parched grain and ceremonial lamps.
There arose singing, as well as dancing accompanied by musical instruments, and hymns of praise by celestial bards that proclaimed divine gains. (77)
And there, honored by the maidens who are dear to Brahmā,
the divine Lord shone forth, magnified by those whose speech consists of the ancient lore.
There, the illustrious Gopālakṛṣṇa bestowed gifts;
at night, ten thousand devotees gathered at the camel-shed.
Placing Lomaśa, Agastya, and Hemaśālāyana at their head,
they celebrated a festival for the occasion of the Lord’s birth.
Having seated the Lord upon a beautiful elephant-throne, they all bowed to their mother and father and worshipped them in due order. ||81||
They worshipped Bālakṛṣṇa with various kinds of offerings;
they placed a divine crown upon the head of Bālakṛṣṇa.
They hung upon their crowns and at the sides of their ears desirable crests, bound with the finest essence of the seven precious gems and gold.
They poured fragrant oil and unguents such as *attara* upon their hair; having made a sectarian mark (*puṇḍraka*) on the forehead, they placed a dot of saffron in its center. (84)
Having applied collyrium to their eyes, they placed earrings upon their ears;
they gave them golden ear-ornaments and floral decorations, and applied rouge to their lips.
On the two shoulders [he wore] a royal armor made of gold and adorned with jewels;
a jacket of the *nāṭa* type, made of silk and embroidered with gold. (86)
The two long, auspicious banners, rich with gold, jewels, and gems, were like lamps and moons;
they shone like the sun and moon, emitting a radiant luster. (87)
Hanging from her two shoulders, they rested upon her chest over her breasts;
joined by a golden girdle at her waist, they were radiant with rays of light.
They placed two [gems], each worth more than a hundred thousand lakhs, upon Kṛṣṇa’s chest;
they set the sword above the crown, its hilt adorned with pearls. (81)
In its center, it was adorned with fine diamonds set within a halo of radiant light;
at its edge, it was endowed with a shimmering brilliance flowing from a row of golden stars.
They gave him well-set jewels fastened with golden chains upon his neck, cheeks, forehead, chin, and forearms.
They placed golden necklaces, flower garlands, and excellent wreaths of *tulasī* upon their necks, and likewise they placed bracelets and anklets upon their arms.
They indeed gave him bracelets, armlets, and rings;
Mādhava wore golden staffs and golden necklaces.
And below the waist, he wore golden garments with a sun-colored border;
his thighs were richly adorned with golden girdles, studded with gems and pearls like stars. (94)
The feet were adorned with anklets set with gold and jewels, variegated and richly decorated with the seven netherworlds (pātālas) and many colors. 95.
Those best of devotees indeed gave golden sandals for his feet, adorned with lion-heads on the big toes and embellished in the middle with elephant figures. 96.
Adorned with swans on its two sides, graced by Garuḍa at the rear, resembling Śeṣa at the front, and beautified by a tortoise in the middle. ||97||
And they indeed applied red-dye to their nails, which were radiant with rows of pearl necklaces on all sides, as well as to the palms of their hands and the soles of their feet.
They gave him betel-leaf rich with fragrance mixed with lime-powder, as well as an upper garment of great cloth, resplendent like the seven heavens. ||99||
They gave him a golden umbrella, rich with divine sights, resembling the Imperishable, possessing thirty-two ribs, and resplendent with all its ornaments.
In Cāmara, it shone with the splendor of the sun, moon, fire, and lightning;
there they offered a canopy resembling Truth itself upon a jeweled staff.
They gave a single, vast, divine celestial chariot, richly adorned with images of all the worlds, endowed with splendor, and furnished with wish-fulfilling creepers. 102.
Then the king gave golden vessels and jeweled bowls; he offered an ārātrika lamp accompanied by a thousand excellent wicks and other offerings.
For the sake of ten million maidens, he gave ornaments to the beloved of Brahmā,
as well as infinite jewels, gems, and other articles.
Afterwards, he joyfully offered the supreme worship and performed the lustration ceremony (nīrājana);
then musical instruments were sounded and dances took place.
The hymns of the great seers, the songs of the celestial nymphs, and the melodious voices of maidens are heard, bestowing auspiciousness. (106)
