"Aha! Who is this killer who has arrived today in my hermitage?
He is wicked, a source of terror to the animals, devoid of restraint, and most cruel."
"Whoever here has slain the faultless gavaya with arrows while it was breathing"—
thus indeed did the best of sages reflect.
Just then, the king, mounted on his horse, arrived there by that path and beheld a beautiful brahmin wearing a garland and possessing matted hair and a beard.
He likewise saw a wild ox that had fallen while taking its steps;
with a gentle mind, he [reflected] on the circumstances of that hermitage.
Tormented and seeing that his rear was being attacked, the king indeed turned back;
having tethered his horse at the foot of a tree, he approached on foot and,
filled with fear, quickly fell at the feet of the seer.
Then the sage said to him: "O wicked one, how was the animal killed? (74)
By you, a hunter, one who was innocent and lived in the forest has been killed;
you appear to be a wicked king, for you perform cruel deeds. (75)
O lord of men, you whose deeds are as cruel as a hunter's— do you not feel shame to commit such wicked acts even within the hermitages of sages?
By my arrow, those deer dwelling in my hermitage have been struck down.
And this gavaya that is here will surely die a moment later. (77)
When the arrow has reached the point of drawing, his life-breath does not remain.
Behold, O wicked one, your own son; why indeed do you not kill him yourself? 78.
"Hunting is certainly not suitable for you among creatures who trust the sages;
the deer near my hermitage are like my own sons. (79)
Out of fear of you, and desiring to save their lives, they fled;
they were struck down by an arrow from a deer near my hermitage. (2.116.80)
"O King of beasts, you have lived in the forest for a very difficult time;
henceforth, you shall never again inflict such punishment or carry out any execution. (8.1)
Thus addressed by the seer, the king right there became a śarabha;
having abandoned his human form, he assumed the form of a beast. (82)
Thus was King Samīraṇa cursed by the sage;
having become that animal, the Śarabha, he then departed from the hermitage.
At that time, being exceedingly afraid of the sage’s fault and his wrath, he did not even speak to request release from the curse right then and there.
Quickly abandoning that hermitage, he entered the lion forest;
submerged in sorrow upon sorrow, he found no happiness anywhere.
Remembering his past lives, he constantly and repeatedly wanders through the forest, thinking only of how to bring an end to his own suffering.
The king's servants, having learned of that event, were indeed terrified; perceiving that their own lives were in danger, they fled quickly to their homes. (87)
And then, by the sage himself, a handful of mantra-consecrated flowers was cast toward the Gavaya together with Sandhinī; by that means, his restoration to life was accomplished.
Then the king, having wandered through that forest for the sake of ending the curse,
arrived at Pārṣṇigṛha and requested liberation.
The sage said: "In the great forest, at the Pātālīya lake, Mount Raivata will arrive and make it his own dwelling."
There indeed, the Lord Dattātreya, the great master,
was personally present upon a peak that was devoid of people, inaccessible, and traversing the sky.
When he himself performs great and fierce austerity,
then that Blessed One must indeed be attended by you while staying there in a mountain valley.
Having been seen and propitiated by you, he will lead you out of compassion;
the son of Atri shall remain there at the sacred field known as Kuṅkumavāpī.
Then, on the western shore of Aśvapaṭṭasara, he propitiated Hari—the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa—through ascetic penance. 94.
By the grace of Dattātreya, you beheld the beginningless Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa and drank the water of his favor from his feet. 95.
"You shall be swiftly released from my curse, of this there is no doubt.
Thus addressed, that royal sage, possessing a body, [spoke] to Śarabha.
From there, he went to the forest near the great lake;
then, after some time, Mount Raivata arrived at that place. 97.
Right there, the venerable Atri’s son was performing austerities;
on that very peak, Śarabha saw him engaged in silent recitation. 98.
The compassionate Lord Dattātreya, having taken him with him, has arrived at that house at the Aśvapaṭṭa lake. 99.
And for the very purpose of his release from the curse, there remains an invisible holy site named Dattātreyatīrtha here at this Aśvasarovara.
For that place is indeed purifying, existing for the purpose of destroying curses and sins;
having gone there, Śarabha [worshipped] the beginningless Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa. || 101 ||
Having beheld and drunk the water from his feet, he obtained liberation from the curse; thereafter, by the power of that sacred ford (tīrtha), he regained his auspicious royal form.
Having assumed a divine form here, he went to the auspicious, imperishable world;
thus, O Rādhikā, the excellent Aśvasarovara is always [holy]. 1.03.
In the evening, having drunk water and the water from Hari’s feet, that śarabha attained the supreme,
divine, and eternal liberation of Brahmā.
From reading and hearing this, there shall be both enjoyment and liberation;
for those with desires, there shall be the increase of their lineage and even release from suffering.

Thus ends the one hundred and sixteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Lord’s Thirteenth Birthday Festival, King Samīraṇa’s Transformation into a Śarabha in the Forest due to the Curse of the Sage Pārṣṇigṛha While Hunting, His Liberation at the Kuṅkumavāpī Site through Dattātreya on Mount Raivata, and the Dattātreya Tīrtha at Aśvapaṭṭasara," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Rādhikā, to another [account] concerning the sacred site known as Vārāha,
which formerly existed at the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake of Kuṅkumāvāpī.
The glorious Lord of syllables, the Sovereign of all, the Supreme Person,
the Supreme Brahman himself, when he began creation from his own form.
As he contemplated the principles (tattvas), fire was born from his mouth;
it was divine, released from the divine syllable, and bore a divine, liberated form.
Then he became two-armed, white in color, and possessed of a cool touch; this very one became an auspicious, beautiful form consisting of radiant splendor.
Then the Blessed One perceived that he was about to create the fire consisting of the ultimate reality;
and the Fire-god, having understood his intention, stood before Hari at that time.
And Hari gave him this command: "Go;
whenever the lords and others are being created by me, you shall always be their principle of splendor (tejas)."
Having thus formed this hope, he entered Mahāmāyā;
then, in the form of an embryo, Māyā experienced agitation like a blazing fire.
In whatever way that Māyā, consisting of the three qualities (guṇas),
though subtle and by nature in a state of equilibrium, repeatedly underwent agitation.
In that manner, the fiery effect of Māyā receded,
while that portion consisting of Tamas increased by the will of Hari.
Through Māyā, the aggregate of the principles (tattvas) became Vairāja;
having attained a state of heat therein, he indeed became the great fire whose nature is warmth.
The Lord named Vahni emerged from his mouth;
having taken recourse to the syllable *vaṃ*, the Vairāja, he [uttered] *haṃ* at the jaw from the path of the mouth. (11)
The god emerged from it and became known as Vahni;
he was divine, with a bright face, a radiant complexion, and full of brilliance.
Having relinquished his state as Brahmā and attained the state of Īśvara,
Vairāja [entrusted] that fire, his own son in the form of Puruṣa.
He said to his sons who were fit for creation, "Create sons equal to yourselves.
Placing the command upon his head with the word "Om," Vahni reflected.
"May my sons indeed be worthy of creation, possessing my own nature; born from mere volition, may they be purifiers like the wind. (15)
Three Pavis were produced; the Pavi that is the Vajra is of lightning.
This son was offered to Indra by Brahmā Parameṣṭhin.
Known as Pāvaka, he was entrusted by the worlds with the task of cooking;
Pavamāna, endowed with great flames, is exceedingly fickle.
"Being swift-moving and destructive, this burner is also exceedingly fierce";
when the people realized this, they no longer took it.
Enraged, this one went to the forest for the sake of food;
that one of great strength wandered through the great forests and other such places.
Thus, while wandering himself through the region of Saurāṣṭra, Pavamāna searched for food but, finding none, became exceedingly distressed.
Extremely tormented by hunger, he set the tiger-infested forest ablaze;
the forest became terrifying, completely enveloped in garlands of flames.
Being consumed by fire, it was difficult to enter and impossible to exit from any side;
there, beasts, birds, and other creatures, wild animals, and reptiles [were gathered]. (22)
There, in that dense thicket of trees, pervaded by masses of grass and creepers, and with a ground surface where the earth was invisible, they were consumed by fire.
All the deer fled, as did the birds blinded by the smoke; so too did the wild animals and those of bestial nature, including the weak, the young, and the children. (24)
Thousands of streams of vital breaths, incapable and overwhelmed by fire,
were burnt there and indeed died by the son of Fire, Pavamāna.
The trees were burnt along with the living creepers, and they were reduced to ashes;
what need is there to count the grasses, the vines, and the shrubs?
The treetops appeared like mountains of fire,
and the elevated regions of the forest ground were likewise composed of fire at that time.
Then the mountains with their few peaks, along with the trees, forests, and the sky,
were consumed by fire, as the mountains became like flaming mouths.
Thus, when cruelty had fully set in for the destruction of those dwelling in the forest, and a pervasive fire had arisen accompanied by the wind; || 2.9 ||
Even on the riverbank, when the trees were about to be consumed by fire,
the hermitage of the seer Picchala was overwhelmed by the force of the conflagration.
The seer Picchala, who had been established in asceticism for many years, remained steadfast in his penance.
Meditating upon the god Nārāyaṇa in the form of the white boar.
They performed most terrible austerities in the forest among the forest-dwellers,
at that hermitage where cows that grant all desires roam.
The cowherds stood there on the bank and even took refuge under the trees;
then, driven by the force of the fire, they fled toward the waters of the river.
To protect their lives, the cowherds fell and plunged into the waters.
Then this great seer, Picchala by name, the lord of the twice-born,
beholding the cruel deed of Pavamāna,
became himself filled with compassion and spoke to Pavamāna.
"O Vahni, O you who are exceedingly cruel and more than a great predator!
Afflicted by hunger, [I have come] to this forest and likewise to my hermitage,
[seeking] cows, cattle, living beings, flocks of birds, and reptiles."
You burn me though I am without fault, and yet you do not release this wretched man. || 37 ||
It is indeed true that one who is hungry becomes evil-minded;
yet how is it that you, disregarding all bounds of propriety, destroy everything by force? (38)
Behold, even the offspring of birds and other creatures, though devoid of feet and wings, are being burned before your very eyes;
yet you feel not even a trace of compassion.
How have you come to such cruelty that you find no peace at all?
Even mountains and the heights of the earth have been scorched by your power.
Having obtained his own food, he indeed burnt all other provisions;
my forest has been brought to ruin, for all living beings have perished. (41)
"Therefore, I shall curse you here as the one who causes destruction; of this there is no doubt.
Thus was the sage Picchala tormented by Vahni, O Rādhikā. (42)
Pavamāna uttered a curse: "May you quickly meet with destruction!
Having said this, he released the water held in his hand onto the ground. (43)
To that same extent, the flames of the fire became feeble;
its power to burn was destroyed, and its power to cook came to an end.
Likewise, the capacity of the taste for eating is dissolved in another moment;
the whiteness of fire is destroyed, and its heat has likewise gone into dissolution. ||45||
Then the naturally increasing [element] itself underwent diminution;
the state of smoke increased, and the coals became lusterless and black. (46)
Then the wooden brushes became lusterless and black;
indeed, without any effort, the fire was extinguished due to the cause of the curse. 47.
All the juices, seeds, and beasts and birds that were consumed emerged from the stomach of Pavamāna uncooked. 48.
His belly became distended, his luster faded, and his breath grew faint;
deprived of the power of his feet, he reached the brink of death. (49)
Devoid of the flames [of passion] and devoid of the activity of the senses, he became one;
having obtained the fruit of his karma, he grieved in many ways and wept.
"What should be done? Where should one go? How might the curse imposed by the great sage be revoked? And how might he become propitiated?"—thus he reflected. (51)
Then this Pavamāna, free from pride, went toward that ṛṣi,
prostrating himself like a staff with his heart, mind, and speech.
Desiring liberation from suffering, he praised him who was in the form of Brahmā:
"O holy one, you are indeed compassionate, whereas I am merciless and violent. (55)
"O virtuous one, you are devoted to truth; no truth exists in me.
You are always sinless, whereas I am most sinful and a giver of suffering. (54)
I am indeed discontented and greedy, whereas you are contented and not a hunter; I am intent on possessions, while you are dispassionate and free from attachments.
I am indeed the scorcher of living beings, whereas you are an ascetic who does not scorch;
you are eternally established in Brahman, while I am deluded by the nature of illusion.
I am indeed devoid of forgiveness, yet forgiveness always resides in you; I possess not even a trace of supernatural powers, while you are here the very locus of all accomplishments.
For the destruction of the sins of the sinful, I am not capable as you are;
you abide in the form of a sacred ford (tīrtha), whereas I neither am a ford nor do I cross over one.
I am the individual soul (jīva) characterized by ignorance, while you are always the locus of knowledge;
you possess the body of Brahman, whereas I possess the body of Māyā. (59)
"You are the bestower of divine liberation, while I am the giver of birth and the destroyer;
you abide as the giver of peace, whereas I am the giver of agitation."
Constantly contemplating the supreme, gentle Brahman, you remain here capable of effecting the very deliverance of wretched embodied beings. (61)
O Great-minded One, grant forgiveness for these offenses committed out of ignorance;
you are the one capable of restoring to life that which has been set ablaze by me. (62)
Shining with ascetic power, revive the wilderness—
its beasts, its multitudes of living beings, its birds, and its trees.
O ascetic, deliver me along with the living beings, such as the reptiles;
may I once again become a vessel for the curses of the virtuous and a vessel for their satisfaction. (64)
O virtuous one, I have received the training; do not bring about my death!
I have reached the presence of Death; O remover of distress, restore me to life! 65.
The saintliness of virtuous devotees of Kṛṣṇa consists precisely in this:
that having forgiven the offenses of the living being, they bestow virtues upon him.
The scorpion attaches its sting, yet the virtuous man does not cast it off;
the mouse gnaws at the wing, yet the swan does not cast it off. (67)
Guardians provide protection even for wicked embodied beings;
O best of Brahmins, restore me to life, for the virtuous have forgiveness as their very essence.
"I shall never again commit such an offense;
truly, truly, truly, I fall at your feet. (69)
Thus, O Rādhā, Pavamāna, having fallen there in the forest, repeatedly praised that sage Picchala from his heart.
Then, through his meditative absorption, the great seer understood that hymn of praise;
filled with compassion and becoming gracious, he immediately rose from his seat. (71)
The refuge of auspiciousness went quickly to Pavamāna as he was praising him.
"O Pavamāna, may there be auspiciousness for you; do not grieve, O son of Vahni. (71)
If you, the god who is the son of Agni, do not act thus, I shall indeed restore you to life; let not the embodied beings be consumed by fire.
Having spoken thus, he took water in his hand, consecrated it with mantras from the vessel,
and as soon as he had taken it, he sprinkled it over the Pavamāna fire.
Pavamāna became empowered; he stood up and bowed down, and then, filled with splendor, he prostrated himself like a staff before that sage.
And Pavamāna said to him, "O Lord, grant me release from the curse.
The sage replied, "I have given you the power to travel through the sky."
By which [paths] one reaches the mountain named Śrīśaila, where dwells the glorious Boar, the bestower of liberation and the protector of the life-force of the earth. ||77||
"The boar, the creator of all protection, shall provide you with protection.
Having been told this, Pavamāna went with reverence to Śrīśaila.
Standing near the anthill, he remembered him at that very moment;
O Rādhikā, the Lord then rose up from that anthill.
Then the Lord, white in color and beautiful, bowed to Pavamāna and said to the son of Agni, "Be happy."
Then Anala asked him the reason for his coming there;
he then related the entire cause, including the curse.
"O Viṣṇu, perform my complete extraction," so said Vibhāvasu;
[granting] splendor, power, strength, form, divinity, and likewise pervasiveness. (82)
"O Supreme Lord, may you first bestow these qualities upon me here";
thus addressed, the illustrious Varāha spoke to that Pavamāna.
Come, O Pavamāna, come with me to Surāṣṭraka, to the sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpikā, and to the Aśvapaṭṭa lake. (84)
He who is the sustainer of all incarnations, the manifest Lord, the supreme among men, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the glorious Puruṣottama. ||85||
He shines in the field of the Imperishable; he will bestow all that upon you—he will grant you liberation and the state of lordship, everything he possesses. ||86||
Having spoken thus, he suddenly led Śrīvarāha by the path of the sky to the ground of the Imperishable (Akṣarabhūmikā) and likewise to Lake Aśvasaras.
He quickly summoned him for the purpose of showing him to Hari;
having led him there, the glorious Lord, the Blessed Varāha, departed.
Pavamāna prostrated himself on the ground before him with devotion;
then Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa raised the son of Vahni up.
Having sat down upon the seat, he embraced his lap against his chest;
he offered the lion-throne to that Boar, who was his own self.
Having understood that cause, the Lord Hari, assuming the guise of a human being, granted his grace for the sake of lifting the sage's curse. (91)
Pavamāna enjoyed that clarity as the fruit of immortality and drank the water;
indeed, for as long as he did so, he was endowed with all excellent qualities.
The Soul of the Universe, the locus of his former attributes as before, entered [his body];
liberated from all curses, he became exceedingly joyful and happy. ||93||
He worshipped Varāha as well as Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa;
thereafter, through his union with Hari, Pavamāna became the very embodiment of a sacred ford (tīrtha).
By the command of the Lord Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa himself, Varāha also took up residence at the sacred ford (tīrtha) in the lake. ||95||
Thus, that Vārāha-tīrtha came into being there eternally;
the Lord Varāha, the sovereign, dwells there, joined by Pavamāna.
Those people who perform their ablutions there shall become free from disease through the power of Hari and by being sprinkled with the waters of the sacred fords.
Through its recitation and exposition, they shall attain liberation and worldly enjoyment, as well as divine status; moreover, there shall always be health and what is dear.
O Rādhikā, the Blessed One spoke thus to you, who had assumed the form of a boar,
on the morning of the full moon day of the month of Phālguna, at the Pavamāna ceremony.
He gave a dwelling on the sacrificial ground, as well as in the forest and in great waters;
indeed, he gave a dwelling in the rain and in the water to Pavamāna.
And Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa granted him a dwelling within the womb of the earth;
he indeed bestowed fearlessness upon him and likewise granted him the status of a Vaiṣṇava.
One should also wear a necklace of tulasī beads, as well as a tilaka and a forehead mark [of the same], while reciting:
"Oṃ namo śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya svāmine svāhā. (102)
Having thus imparted the mantra and having prostrated before Hari at the sacred ford, Pavamānaka performed worship and departed for the lake to dwell there.
Varāha also accepted the hospitality offered in every way;
O Rādhikā, he took up residence in that great holy place (tīrtha) of Vārāha.

Thus ends the one hundred and seventeenth chapter, titled "The Description of Pavamāna’s Journey toward Aśvapaṭṭasarovara after Assuming the Form of the Lord Varāha for the Purpose of Reversing the Curse Given by the Sage Picchala, the Liberation from the Curse through Hari’s Yoga, and the Exposition of Varāha-tīrtha, Pavamāna-tīrtha, and Others," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Rādhikā, listen to another auspicious wonder of Hari,
which is supreme, provides protection to devotees, and destroys sins and afflictions.
In Jayanagara in Saurāṣṭra, there was a twice-born man named Santāraṇa,
who was devoted to the Vedas and dharma, and fully intent upon the performance of worship.
He was devoted to the six duties: reciting the sacred narratives, proclaiming the virtues [of the Lord], listening to the stories of Viṣṇu, remembering Him, and serving His feet.
He was a great devotee of the Lord, solely intent on the worship of Kṛṣṇa through secret salutation, service, friendship, and self-surrender.
Every morning, the twice-born man himself would rise and go to the riverbank; having bathed in the Bhadrā and performed the twilight prayers and salutations, he would remain there.
Having personally carried a water-pot upon his head with devotion, he performed the worship of the Śālagrāma with flowers and other offerings brought by himself.
While the worship was being performed, that twice-born man always used well-ground sandalwood and other offerings, and his wife was devoted to her husband.
Indeed, the collection known as Taraṇī, when offered with sincere devotion, bestows water, flowers, fruits, clothing, ornaments, ghee, and so forth. (8)
His daughter, Taralikā, being a maiden,
always used to rise quickly every day before the time for worship.
Having bathed, having bowed to her own parents, and having prostrated before the Lord with great devotion,
the virtuous woman quickly prepared the hearth together with the fire.
Having cooked milk-based preparations and *pūrikās*,
she offers this excellent oblation to Kṛṣṇa Viṣṇu with extreme devotion.
The second daughter, named Kumudā, always at dawn,
having milked her own cow, would offer the milk for worship.
Having prepared the essence of milk and other offerings, he constantly gives them during worship; his son Vinoda likewise does so, taking refuge in the celestial flowering trees. (13)
One indeed performs service such as the sprinkling of water, the washing of vessels, incense, lamps, the offering of water, and so forth. (14)
He always remains by his father's side, staying in his proper place;
and his second son is indeed the Vaiṣṇava sage Vasantarṣi.
One performs the gift of air by means of a fan during acts of worship and the like; one also removes flies with sugar and a leaf of *tulasī*. (16)
He indeed bestows fruits according to their needs and provides service as required;
then, after the worship, everyone performs a hymn of praise to the Lord.
They circumambulate him and prostrate like a staff, offering handfuls of flowers;
they also seek forgiveness and then dance with joy.
They play excellent musical instruments, proclaim songs,
and always sing with various rhythms, measures, and dances.
Having thus worshipped the Lord of Ramā, her eternal husband,
she then distributed and bestowed the prasāda upon her devotees.
Those householders partake of sugar-rice, water, and other offerings;
likewise, they perform worship according to the prescribed rites at midday and in the evening. (21)
But for the sake of their livelihood, they strive each day for even a slight necessity;
while time was passing in this manner, the Blessed One, the Supreme Person, [appeared].
Once,
during the night of the Ekādaśī vow in the dark fortnight of the month of Āṣāḍha, he became visibly manifest through his supreme devotion alone.
He wore a beautiful, excellent golden crown,
adorned with the tips of the finest peacock feathers and embellished with jewels and gems.
Wearing beautiful earring-shaped earrings in the form of sea-monsters upon his ears, and bearing a saffron tilaka in the center of his forehead that resembled a beautiful crescent moon. (25)
With a face of gentle smile, his mind captivated by a divine radiance,
he wears the excellent Kaustubha gem and garlands of Tulasī leaves around his neck.
Wearing golden garlands and necklaces, he had a golden girdle around his waist, as well as golden bracelets on his arms and on his forearms. (27)
On his hand were beautiful golden bracelets and finger-rings,
as well as a staff made of gold, inlaid with pearls, rubies, and diamonds.
Wearing sandals fashioned from beautiful gold,
Hari appeared by chance, resplendent in his yellow garment.
Standing in the midst of a circle of light, honored by hosts of male and female servants,
He is the youthful Emperor of kings, served by Rādhā, Ramā, and the others.
Then, having made his devotees invisible, the self-effulgent Lord himself became a youth—the form of Bālakṛṣṇa, the illustrious Great Emperor of Emperors. ||3 1||
The youthful Lord Kṛṣṇa, the Sovereign himself, bestowed the mantra:
"Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya ravāmine svāhā. (32)
And the Lord placed his hand upon her head and vanished there;
thus, from that day forward, she began the daily worship at dawn.
During the worship, the glorious Great King Keśava always comes—the youthful Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, attended by Śrī and Bhū. (34)
The Lord indeed accepts all the ritual offerings presented during worship in the months of Śrāvaṇa, Bhādrapada, and likewise Āśvina.
Accepting their sincere worship, Hari said to them:
"On the eighth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Kārttika, there shall be a great festival for my birth on the shore of the Aśvasarasa lake, upon the ground known as Akṣara. (36)
Thinking, "It will happen," you must come to my house.
The lords of the three worlds will come to my abode together with their parents, daughters, and sons, in order to worship me. (38)
Having spoken thus to those devotees, the Blessed One then vanished;
thereafter, those devotees became eager for a pilgrimage to sacred sites.
On the sixth day, having prepared his provisions for the journey and secured the house with locks,
he took auspicious gifts and set forth on foot.
On the seventh day, at evening itself, they reached Lake Tvaśvasaras,
and having seen Kuṅkumavāpī as well as the hermitage of Śrī Lomaśa.
The sages, the virtuous people, the gods, the many temples,
the guardians of the fields, the protectors of the sacred sites, the city, the gardens and so forth,
the various pleasure groves, and the forests of divine trees. ||42||
Sacrificial halls, storytelling halls, dharma-halls, and great assembly halls; ||43||
Having seen the glorious Kambharā-Lakṣmī and likewise Śrī-Gopāla Hari,
and having beheld the divine earth and the maidens who are the beloveds of Brahmā,
as well as the most celestial palanquins and the liberated souls in their mansions on all sides; ||44||
They attained the most wonderful and marvelous Supreme Lord. ||45||
Having bowed to and worshipped the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, those people were then honored and fed by that Nārāyaṇa. (46)
They spent the night in a magnificent palace within the great mansion; overwhelmed with love, they kept vigil throughout the night on the seventh day.
They beheld celestial chariots arriving through the path of the sky, in which the liberated souls of the Imperishable One as well as the residents of Goloka were seated. 48.
Likewise, the liberated inhabitants of Vaikuṇṭha and Vairāja who dwell in the nectar-like realm,
as well as the lords such as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa, the ancestors,
the sages, the celestial gods, and the deities residing on Mount Meru.
The guardians of the directions, the protectors of the worlds, and stainless human beings;
the perfected ones (siddhas), virtuous women, chaste noble ladies, and even the female practitioners of Sāṃkhya and Yoga;
likewise the rivers, streams, sacred fords, oceans, and the seasons.
The months, the virtues, the forest regions, the asuras dwelling in the netherworld,
the divine devotees, as well as the Daityas, Dānavas, Cāraṇas, and others,
and those kings who are established there as divine devotees— [all these reside] in them.
Such celestial chariots, resembling the sun and the moon,
resplendent and auspicious, resounded with the songs of hosts of maidens and the loud sounds of musical instruments; they descended from the sky without delay.
In the vicinity of Kuṅkumavāpī in that sacred field, there were indeed thousands of them;
their splendors and radiances then resembled ten million moons.
In the sky, on the earth, in the city, and in every direction, there was not even a particle of dust nor any darkness; for that place was like a mass of light. (56)
The primordial Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Blessed One and Master, as well as the one known as Gopālakṛṣṇa, are his father and mother Kambharā. (57)
And Santoshā was his sister, and the venerable Śuka was his brother;
likewise, Vallabha and the venerable Hemantaka were also there.
The two charming swan-maidens, their attendants, and the circle of their friends offered a welcome, a place to stay, respectful water, and the honey-mixture, providing them with comfort. (59)
Then, at the hour of Brahmā, the great seers recited the Vedas;
at that time, auspicious musical instruments were sounded on all sides.
The sages made it their place of worship, and the virtuous practiced meditation;
even the people of great renown went to the lake to bathe.
The twice-born Santāraṇa was his [son], and his wife was Taraṇī;
they had Tarala, Kumudā, Vinoda, and Vasantaka.
Remembering their family and Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, they all then went to bathe in the waters of the Aśvapaṭṭa lake.
Taking the boat, they looked for the Śabara standing on the shore;
desiring to sport upon the ocean, they boarded the vessel.
Having paid the toll, they sat down, and the boatman set the boat in motion;
when the boat had gone more than a *krośa* into the middle of the water, [he said]: 65.
Then other boats were boarded by men by the hundreds,
both in the middle of the lake and along its banks on all sides.
At that time, they indeed dwelt happily upon the great ocean in that ship, as if in a lake, by their own free will.
Suddenly encountering a violent impact, the boat instantly became crooked and turned its face downward;
out of fear of that, those on board were then suddenly thrown into turmoil. (68)
They fled to one side and fell into the midst of the water;
the boat too, filled with water, sank in the middle of the stream.
For at that time, there was no means whatsoever to rescue them,
neither by means of a great ship nor even by smaller boats.
Suddenly, they were all searched for there by the fishermen;
however, at that very moment, six of them sank into the bottomless water.
They do not know even a fraction of the means for crossing over; for that reason, though submerged in the very depths of the lake, they do not come into the hands of the fishermen.
They sank into its depths and drank the water in abundance;
they then remembered Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Lord.
Those who were subject to the noose of death praised Hari with their minds within the water that has no support, [praising him] as the remover of suffering and the provider of protection.
And he who, as a boar, lifted up the earth submerged in water;
and he who, as a crocodile, seized the great ship situated upon the water. (75)
Lord Hari, the Protector, who bore the great mountain submerged in water upon his back,
and who protected his devoted elephant when it was submerged in the water.
The Blessed One protected the merchant who was submerged in water;
he also protected the great region of Uṣṭrālaya which was submerged in water. ||77||
He who in former times protected King Udayana when he was submerged in water,
and he who protected Māñji and Ambikā when they were submerged in the ocean.
And in this manner, the Lord protected others who were submerged in water in many ways,
O Nārāyaṇa, if you consider your own devotees to be truthful.
Then, O Kṛṣṇa, deliver us out of the midst of the waters through Your compassion;
death is forever subject to You, and time is likewise Your morsel.
Water and the restraint of breath are always under your power;
you abide as the inner self, the remover of untimely death.
O Lord of Gods, remove our sorrows if you indeed intend to protect us;
you are the boat, you are the Great Breath, you are the individual soul, and you are life itself.
In the midst of the waters, you alone were indeed the giver of life to Prahlāda;
there is no time for praise now, as my life-breaths are being stifled by the water. (83)
The heart and the self attain stability, and it ascends to the crown of the head;
for a moment it remains poised in the midst of death, and there is nothing beyond that. (84)
Thus, O Rādhikā, they were utterly overwhelmed in the midst of the water;
having offered praise and surrender, they went for refuge to the son of Śrī Kambharā. (85)
The omniscient Blessed One, the Lord of Śrī, Bālakṛṣṇa, with great haste,
assumed the form of a tortoise, an excellent and massive shell.
Suddenly placing six of them upon his back,
the Blessed One brought them across the water where there was no boat, right onto the surface of the water.
The Lord, assuming the form of a child, suddenly touched the fainting girl and the water with both hands and instantly warded them off.
The water they had drunk dissolved by the mere touch of their hands; their fainting fit also vanished, and they became radiant once more. (89)
They saw the great bestower of well-being standing nearby upon the tortoise,
and likewise they saw the child who was the protector of Gopāla-Kṛṣṇa.
Seeing Kṛṣṇa assuming a divine form, they attained supreme peace;
indeed, those six were seen by the searching people upon the tortoise.
"Protected by the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa," they then suddenly climbed onto the back of the tortoise on the boat. (92)
The boatmen indeed seized them, and the tortoise vanished from sight;
for he was the Blessed Lord himself, bearing the conch, discus, mace, and lotus.
For a moment, everyone saw the man as a tortoise within the water;
then, he was seen by the people thus having attained dissolution into Bālakṛṣṇa. ||94||
Having gathered them all together by boat and brought them to the shore, they left them there;
the people marveled at this wonderful feat, which was the very essence of Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa’s miraculous power. 95.
Having found Kṛṣṇa as their protector, they then devoted themselves to him with true feeling;
thereafter, they proceeded to the pavilion to perform the birth-festival worship.
The liberated lords, gods, goddesses, and embodied beings arrived; they performed worship with all kinds of articles and offered the waving of lamps (*ārātrika*).
They presented offerings and likewise bestowed blessings;
Śrīgopāla then fed all the honored guests in every way.
Having given many gifts and considering their service to be supreme, he dismissed all the lords of the earth, and they departed. 99.
Then the Brahmin Santāraṇa, knowing that Bālakṛṣṇa had reached the age of sixteen,
joyfully gave him his two daughters.
The Blessed One, the Lord of Śrī, accepted the two jewels of maidens; and the two maidens became fulfilled by obtaining a husband. || 10.1 ||
And at the hermitage of Lomaśa, Hari, the Mādhava, entrusted both maidens to Lomaśa along with the beloved wives of Brahmā to protect them.
Then Santāraṇa, together with his wife and sons, having performed the worship and the birth festival for Śrī Hari, felt his desires fulfilled upon seeing [the Lord]. || 103 ||
Having received her command, that brāhmaṇa went to the city of Jayanta;
O Rādhikā, that auspicious great tīrtha is named Santāraṇa.
Where indeed the Lord himself appeared as a tortoise, he shines upon the shore and within the temple; by bathing there, one is delivered from the cycle of worldly existence. 105.
By reciting or even by hearing it, he would deliver one from the torment of sin;
through the mere remembrance of this Lord, liberation would occur—how much more so, O Lord, through his direct service?

Thus ends the one hundred and eighteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Rescue of the Brahmins Submerged in Water by Assuming the Form of a Tortoise at the Morning of the Aṣṭamī of the Fourteen-Year-Old Bālakṛṣṇa at Aśvapaṭṭasara Lake," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Listen, O Rādhā, to another wonder concerning a devotee of Hari named Devāyatana, a resident of Saurāṣṭra, my dear.
In the village named Samādhiyāna, there was a devotee named Devāyatana, a preeminent member of the Ābhīra caste, who possessed a virtuous refuge. || 2 ||
Constantly devoted to daily bathing and taking refuge in the beginningless Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, he would cry out:
"O Hari! O Kṛṣṇa! O Master! O Hari Nārāyaṇa, O Lord! (3)
Śrī Gopāla, Hare Kṛṣṇa, Kambharāśrī Rame Sati, Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, Śrī Puruṣottama. || 4 ||
O Lord of the Imperishable, O Consort of Prabhā, Māṇikī, and Pārvatī; O Lord of the virtuous, O Master of the abode of liberation, Bālakṛṣṇa, Hare, Hare! 5.
In this manner, he constantly performed recitations on the riverbank,
upon the sands, in the water, under trees, and on the ground.
Whether in a house, a field, a garden, a grove, or even in a forest,
he then remembers that Supreme Lord Kṛṣṇa during all his activities.
Always [one should be mindful] while eating, sleeping, traveling, walking, and sitting;
likewise during yawning, hunger, bathing, purification, and in the abode of laziness.
At the crossroads, in the assembly hall, at festivals for one's clan or family, during childbirth, in matters of grief, and even on occasions of joy—at all such times—(one should act). || 9 ||
"Hare Kṛṣṇa, Hare Svāmin!"— thus, preceded by the clapping of hands,
let there be the constant chanting of the names of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
With faith, he indeed performs worship after his bath,
and he performs it for the form of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
Filled with the love of devotion, he indeed offers to the Blessed One the nightly lamp and the food offering adorned with fruits, rice, and water. (12)
In the village and the country, the people called him by the name Devāyatārṣi;
and once, while Devāyatārṣi was seated at the foot of a tree, [he spoke].
Taking a ripe, sweet ṭimburu fruit that bestows happiness,
he indeed remembered Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa in order to offer it.
The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, brought under control by devotion,
arrived at the site of the Tumburu tree where that king of devotees was located.
Then, having approached while wearing the dress of a young cowherd and smiling,
he [offered] *tumburu* fruits from his hands into the temple of the god.
Having gathered ripe and sweet fruits, he ate their delicious juice;
the devotee and the sage at the temple offered him beautiful fruits.
He enjoys the grace bestowed by Kṛṣṇa, dances, and praises Him;
absorbed in Him and immersed in His form, he possesses divine vision and a divine body.
Free from all bonds and possessing the power to traverse the sky, Bālakṛṣṇa, having eaten fruits, went to the river for water. || 19 ||
Devāyana also went after him toward the river for water;
with his senses, life-breaths, and body drawn away by Kṛṣṇa, he followed along the enclosure.
Having leaped over mountains, forest trees, and other obstacles after Hari,
he proceeded by way of the sky with his body free from all obstruction.
He arrived at the sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpī and the Aśvasarovara lake,
having fixed his gaze upon Śrī Hari within the lake through the practice of meditation.
He bathed by means of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s yoga and by means of steps within the water;
forgetting his body, he was submerged in the water in an instant through divine play.
Indeed, his body remained standing right in the midst of the water, yet it was not turbid;
having drunk the water himself, he became divine and stood truly above the water.
Chanting "Hare Kṛṣṇa, Hare Rām" thus on the outer bank, he emerged with a divine body and remained there for a moment. 25.
Then, a deliberation occurred to him that would save his life:
"If I cause [this] to be done among the subjects with a divine body... (26)
"By worshipping and chanting the praises of Viṣṇu, living beings shall attain liberation"—having reflected thus, one should worship Śrī Hari, Hari. (27)
Then, having made the forest-dwelling tiger his [vehicle], he thereafter went to the lion-forest;
from there, having gone to Saṃyamanī, the city of Yama, he proclaimed [his arrival]. ||28||
Hare Kṛṣṇa, Hare Svāmin, Hare Nārāyaṇa Prabhu! Śrī Gopāla, Hare Kṛṣṇa, Kaṃbharāśrī, Hare Vibhu! (19)
O Bālakṛṣṇa, O Lord of Ramā, Rādhā, Lakṣmī, and Pārvatī; O Lord of Kamalā, O Lord of Prabhā and Māṇikī, O Lord Nārāyaṇa! 2.119.30.
Thus he performed worship by proclaiming the chanting of the Name;
hearing this, those standing in the fetters of Yama were freed from their bonds and released.
Suddenly they became pure, freed from the torment of sin; fit for liberation, possessing divine bodies, they were embodied beings worthy of Vaikuṇṭha. ||3 2||
Having acquired meritorious bodies and having repeatedly heard the name of Hari,
they paid homage to Dharmarāja and went to the eternal Brahman.
Devāyana also, having wandered through all the lands of the Yāmyas and having repeatedly caused the name of Bālakṛṣṇa, Hari, to be heard, [attained his goal].
Having kindled the sins of the sinner, he sent him to his own abode;
and the messengers of Yama, beholding this great marvel, [reported it] to Yama.
Hurrying, they went forth and reported the unfavorable news:
"O mighty-armed King Yama, the prisons for sinners [are overflowing]. (36)
But some, having approached and proclaimed the name of Hari, cause the empty vessels to be filled; yet those sinners go to the world of Brahmā.
Possessing meritorious bodies, meritorious forms, and meritorious souls, they are indeed capable of traveling through the sky by means of a divine vehicle; thus they proceed.
He does not take account here of us, who have been appointed as his staff-bearers;

This saṃsāra is most sinful, a giver of suffering, and enveloped by karmas;

"O devotee, you have not done what is appropriate; perform the chanting of Hari's names!

Having realized that, one attains the state beyond death; there is no other path.

The constant liberation of the wretched, the helpless, the poor, and the powerless,

For even a single human being here, if he were to deliver another from this state by means of the Name, [that merit would suffice].

"Let [this] indeed be given by you to them, and from this day forward, let there be no longer [any state of] servitude."
May Citragupta and the others, beginning with Śravaṇa, proceed toward liberation.

May they cleanse the machines; grant liberation to the sinners!

"By the power of Hari's name, I shall liberate everyone from all suffering, there is no doubt;

"By this worship of Hari here, I shall make myself free from sin;

Having spoken thus and bowed to Yama, while worshipping Hari Nārāyaṇa and holding Bālakṛṣṇa within his heart, he went to the pits of the sinners.
O Hare Kṛṣṇa, O Lord Hari, O Nārāyaṇa, O Master!
O Bālakṛṣṇa, O Hare Kṛṣṇa, O Lord of Śrī, O Lord of Pārvatī! ||72||
O Supreme Brahman, O Imperishable One beyond the syllable, O Lord of Māṇikī, O Lord of Ramā, O Kṛṣṇa, Lord of Rādhā and Lakṣmī, O Lord of Prabhā, protect me, a sinner! 73.
Thus making sounds with his palms and likewise from his throat,

"The syllable is the supreme abode, from which those who have gone do not return"—such was the wonderful realization perceived by the people at that time. (99)

By the fourteen worlds as well as by the inhabitants of the celestial realms, Kṛṣṇa—who bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation—is praised; being all-powerful, what is there that he cannot do? 2.119.100.

He to whom everything belongs, in whom everything resides, and who holds everything under his control; from whom everything arises—he who is indeed the Teacher—what, O Rādhikā, can he not accomplish? (101)

Thus ends the one hundred and nineteenth chapter, titled "The Description of How Devāyatana, the Devotee of the Sages, Liberated All the Messengers of Yama by Chanting the Names of Śrī Hari in the City of Yama," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Rādhikā; later, honored by the inhabitants of the world of Yama, you, being a devotee of the abode of the gods, shall receive worship offered by Yama.
From there, he went alone toward the southern direction by means of his celestial chariot;

It was adorned with palaces belonging to the Nirṛtas and Rākṣasas,
and it was encircled by a rampart extending for a hundred thousand yojanas.
It was filled with halls of false magic and sorcery, augmented by supernatural powers,

Then the king of devotees beheld that [city], frequented by the great gods, situated in the sky, shining like the sun.
The chanting of Hari’s names, accompanied by long vowels and rhythmic beats (tāla), such as:
"Hare Kṛṣṇa, Hare Svāmin, Hare Nārāyaṇa, O Lord! (6)
O Bālakṛṣṇa, O Harekṛṣṇa, O Supreme Brahman, O Lord of Ramā;

Thus, moving through the sky over the city of Nairṛta and chanting his names,

And the Nairṛtas and the worlds of living beings, having heard that auspicious speech again and again, became sinless; and the hosts of Rākṣasas assumed divine forms.
Deprived of their demonic nature and possessing bodies like those of divine attendants,

Then they departed by the power of their devotion alone, on vehicles produced from wish-fulfilling creepers,
on elephant-rides, and on celestial chariots offered by the gods.
Some call it the Imperishable (akṣara), the world of Brahmā, or likewise Vaikuṇṭha;

Having become attendants according to their desire, they went to their respective abodes by means of hearing the name of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. || 15 ||
Having become oceans of great merit, they indeed went to the eternal Brahman;
then, from that region, he [departed] through the sky toward the city of Varuṇa.
Chanting the names of Hari, he proceeded toward the west,

Wandering through the sky in his celestial chariot in every direction, he beheld her and repeatedly caused the people to hear the verses composed by Vālmīki.
And all those divine beings, having heard the name of Manu,
traveled to the abode of the Lord by means of vehicles fashioned from the wish-fulfilling vines.
Men and women, possessing divine bodies and entirely celestial forms,

Then, from that place, the devotee Devāyana traveled through the sky to the city of Vāyu, repeatedly chanting the name of Hari.
All the deities of the winds and the creations of the Maruts likewise,

But his celestial chariot, wandering through the sky, made the inhabitants of the entire city of Pracetasa hear the cry: "Hare! Hare! as they stood there.

Chanting the name of Hari, he beheld from the path of the sky that host of Yakṣas traveling upon her, as he himself wandered with his celestial chariot following after them.
He caused the Yakṣas to hear the names of the Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa— Hare, Brahmā, and Parabrahmā— and he made them liberated souls.
The sins of the meritorious yakṣas have come to an end, and their merits have increased by the power of hearing the name of Nārāyaṇa. (29)
Then, having become possessed of divine bodies and liberated from their former bodies on all sides,

Then Devāyana, a devotee, went toward the direction protected by Īśāna; there he beheld the city ruled by Īśa.

Yoginīs and yogins as well, ascetics free from passion, Vetālīs, Kūṣmāṇḍīs, Kṛtyās, and hosts of Pūtanās; ||36||

It was surrounded on all sides by the abodes of the hosts of gods led by Ketu, and by the temples of all the *siddhis* as well as the excellent mansions of the Vasus.
It was endowed with the abodes of the treasures, the dwellings of the seven sages,
the great palaces of the Kṛttikās, and the mansions of the quarters.
It was endowed with the abodes of the Rudras, the Suns, and the Kāmas; and it was joined with the temples of the Manus, the Kalās, and the lunar days (Tithis). ||53||
With the dwellings of the Maruts, the Vālakhilyas, and the Āruṇas, as well as the abodes of the goddesses, the Apsarases, and the Brahma-lakes; ||54||
It was adorned on all sides by well-arranged groves of the trees of paradise (kalpavṛkṣas) representing the principles of reality (tattvas),

It was attended by charioteers, Magadhan people, and bards;

Having beheld that preeminent capital city, which was filled with the deities to be propitiated, the Viśvedevas, the Siddhas, and kings, and was most abundantly adorned; ||57||
Delighted with great intensity upon reaching that city, which was beautiful because it was inhabited by various classes of beings, the sage Devāyana became eager.

"O Hari-Kṛṣṇa! O Hare-Svāmin! O Hare-Nārāyaṇa, O Lord! (59)

Thus chanting his names in many ways and playing the cymbals,

O Rādhikā, the king of devotees, Devāyatana, the foremost of the Sāttvatas,
liberated the gods who dwell in the city of Mahendra.
Having rendered them possessed of divine bodies, liberated from their physical forms, and fit for the celestial realm,

Vaikuṇṭha, Amṛta, Avyākṛta, Goloka, and Akṣara—the supreme abode, the fit dwelling for the liberated, and the beloved of Kṛṣṇa. (69)
It is the supreme abode, endowed with devotion to Dharma, presided over by the Supreme Lord, the Master of All, and served by the Supreme Ishvara.
The gods are of many kinds, as are the goddesses; they possess divine bodies and have four arms, two arms, eight hands, or likewise sixteen arms.
Having repeatedly assumed various names and having heard them, they went to the abode of Hari;

Devoted to the temple of the gods, he then went to Agnipurī,
where countless crores of distinct fires dwell.
And there are the fires of the womb, the fires for cooking, the digestive fires,
as well as the fires of heat, the fires for oblations, and the fires of poison.
Likewise, there are the fires of anxiety, the divine fires, the funeral pyre fires, the forest fires, the hosts of cold fires, and the fires of indigestion. ||75||
The fires of the pretas and the fires in the form of the mouths of the gods, as well as Pāvaka, Pavamāna, Pavi, and those born in the cremation ground; ||76||

The fires of the jars, the all-consuming fires, the sacrificial fires that consume the oblations, those in the form of the submarine fire (vaḍavānala), as well as the fires of the clouds and so forth—[all these are within him]. ||77||
There are also the fires of the seasons, as well as the cruel and the gentle groups;
there are the fires of the pits and the fires of living beings, belonging to various distinct classes.
White, red, black, blue, yellow, and greenish-yellow;
tawny, seven-tongued, and many-tongued—these are the burners. (79)
Beholding them all, the Lord of Devotees, stationed in his celestial chariot in the sky,
loudly proclaimed the names of Hari in many ways.
He caused Manu to hear [the mantra]: "Hare Kṛṣṇa, Hare Kṛṣṇa, Hare, Hare;
Bālakṛṣṇa, Supreme Brahman, Lord of Māṇikī-Rādhikā. (81)
O Yajñanārāyaṇa, beloved of Kṛṣṇa, Lord of Śrī Satī!
O Supreme Lord, Lord of Gods, Hari, Lord of the Abode of Liberation! 82.
O Prabhākānta, Ramākānta, Kamalākānta, Mādhava! O Lord of Śrī, Bhū, and Līlā; O Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, Lord of Satī! ||83||
O Lakṣmīnātha, O Lord of the wretched, O Lord of the beloved of Brahmā, O Sovereign of Pārvatī and Lalitā, O Protector of the splendors of Vṛndāvana! ||84||
O Lord of all fires, O Viṣṇu, O Mahāviṣṇu, O Nārāyaṇa! O Cause of all incarnations, O Lord of Śrī, O Delighter of the cowherds! ||85||
Thus did Bhaktarāja, known as Devāyatana, proclaim [the name] of Hari while reciting it together with those who were beating cymbals. (86)
Having wandered all around the city of Lakṣāyatā, which was auspicious, he,
being devoted, made offerings to all the fires and the progeny of the fires with divine oblations.
By the power of chanting His names, having fashioned and offered to Hari images with two arms, four beautiful arms, or many arms, one should give the mantra of Hari.
Oṃ, salutations to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord; Svāhā!
May Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa be my refuge at all times. (89)
Out of fear of Time, Illusion, evil karma, enemies, Yama, and treacherous friends,
he bore the signs of the trident, fish, banner, bow, wheel, and the svastika.
"I am Brahmā, an eternal devotee of Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa;
the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa is my Lord and my husband. (91)
"I am a devotee of Kṛṣṇa’s beloved; Śrī Hari is my refuge"—having given these mantras to them and having thus caused them to attain liberation, [he departed].
Having seated the Vaiṣṇavas and those fit for the divine abode within celestial chariots,
he sent them to the immortal realm of Vaikuṇṭha.
Proclaiming shouts of victory, they went to the unmanifest Goloka and the supreme abode of the Imperishable, the realm of Hari.
Thus, O Rādhikā, the devotee named Devāyatana, who was a knower of the Self of Śrī Hari, became a bringer of liberation in ancient times. 95.
For he indeed liberated all those creatures from the abodes of the eight guardians of the directions and sent them forth to liberation.
By the power of devotion to the chanting of the names of Śrī Hari alone,
he bestowed the sacred mantras upon all and established them as auspicious Vaiṣṇavas.
He caused those regions to be named after him;
indeed, there has never been, nor will there ever be, a sage equal to Devāyana.
For in the first creation, this devotee was born with a body like that of Kṛṣṇa;
then, from that direction, this devotee arrived, seated upon a celestial chariot.
Filled with joy, he arrived at the sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpī;
having bowed down to the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, he stood before Him.
Bālakṛṣṇa, having risen, embraced that devotee;
he placed his feet upon the devotee's heart and likewise his hands upon his head.
On the first day of the bright fortnight of the month of Kārttika, the Lord Hari fed Prasāda to him and placed a necklace around his neck. 102.
He gave him a reward and likewise lodging in his own home;
he then took rest there until the full moon day of the month of Kārttika.
O Rādhikā, by reading this, my devotee shall partake in wonders;
and by teaching it, causing it to be heard, or even by listening to it, one shall become a possessor of liberation. 104.

Thus ends the one hundred and twentieth chapter, titled "The Description of how Bālakṛṣṇa, being pleased by the devotion of the sage Devāyatana, became subject to his will and protected him from the water; and how, by causing the name of Śrī Hari to be heard by the subjects of the eight guardians of the quarters, He brought about their liberation," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O Rāseśvarī, O Great Goddess Rādhā, O Moonlight of Goloka,
listen now to the supreme narrative concerning the abode of the gods.
Attaining liberation through the power of the Supreme Brahman, he indeed performs actions equal to that of the Supreme Brahman according to His command. || 2 ||
On the first day of the dark fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa spoke with respect to his devotee who was worshipping him with many offerings.
I alone am Bālakṛṣṇa, the Supreme Brahman, higher than the highest;
the Supreme Lord, the sovereign and master of all Nārāyaṇas.
O best of devotees, all Nārāyaṇas always manifest from me;
in all creations, my incarnations are innumerable.
My forms are innumerable, consisting of qualities and sovereign powers;
through their union, I bring about the supreme welfare of living beings.
My devotees, my attendants, and even the truthful ones who possess divine nature are dear to me;
they manifest in the worlds and deliver embodied beings.
O lord of devotees, you are always liberated for me; you truly are my abode within my heart. You are my dwelling place, and the work of me is performed by you.
The living beings belonging to Yama and the gods of Īśvara have been delivered by you;
nevertheless, go now to this world of earth, to the region beyond Kiṃpuruṣa.
On the further shore beyond the Himalayas, for the sake of the welfare of the subjects,
he crossed the Sindhu river and the mountain, and thereafter reached the Indukuśa.
And the Kaśyapāyana ocean, as well as the river Urulā, the mountain Urula, and also the Kārusamudra. || 1 1 ||
Trimura, Dvīpakalpa, and also the region of Tandrā; the region of Śāntalāri, and the districts of Kāmacāṭaka;
Stenāvāsa, Parvata, as well as Śaila and Prabhānula.
And likewise, the lake Dvikala and the mountain Samāna are equal.
The region of Kīragarjana, the territories of Śibirāja, the areas of the Obīna river, and the lands along the Yāneśī river. || 14 ||
Go to the river Bīṇā, to the Piṅga country, and to Raśanābhū; indeed, go to the northern regions known as Raśanā, which belong to Kiṃpuruṣa.
O King of Devotees, make all the people there Vaiṣṇavas;
cause them to perform worship, recite the mantra, and chant the names [of the Lord] incessantly.
The great celestial chariot was wondrous and filled with great marvels,
endowed with the wish-fulfilling creeper, the wish-fulfilling tree, and the thought-gem.
"Take this and set forth thus with diligence to uplift the living beings;
I shall even grant you my assistance in the form of Pradyumna. (18)
Having spoken thus and having given him a magnificent celestial chariot, the Blessed One likewise dispatched Pradyumna during the dark fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa.
But by the path already described, the king, devoted to the temples of the gods,
beheld Indukuśa and rejoiced repeatedly in his heart.
And he performed worship with loud cries of: "Bālakṛṣṇa! Hare! Hare!
Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, O Lord! Śrīmad-Gopālanandana! (21)
O Supreme Brahman, Hari-Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, Lord of Śrī;
O Rādhā-Kṛṣṇa, Prabhā-Kṛṣṇa, Māṇikī-Kṛṣṇa, Mādhava! ||22||
O Lord Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa, O Nārāyaṇa, O Narāyaṇa!
Victory to you, O Lord of the liberated, O Lord of the virtuous, O Lord of Śrī Pārvatī! ||23||
O upholder of all incarnations, victory to you, O Śrī Kṛṣṇa-vallabha!
O beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, O Śrī Puruṣottama! 24.
Hare Kṛṣṇa, Hare Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa, Hare, Hare!
O Lord Hare, Rāma-Kṛṣṇa, Lord of Sītā, Lord of the virtuous wife! ||255||
Rāma-Kṛṣṇa, Hare-Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa-Rāma-Janārdana;
O son of Kaṃbhārī, glorious Gopāla-Bāla Keśava! 26.
O Sun of the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake, O Moon of the Akṣarakṣetra field, O glorious Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa residing in Kuṅkumavāpī, be victorious! 27.
Hare Kṛṣṇa, Hare Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa Kṛṣṇa, Hare Hare!
O beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, O Śrī Parameśvara! ||28||
O Lord of the beloved of Brahmā, O Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa, Hare, Hare!
O Lord of Padmā, O Lord of Kamalā, O Lord of Śrītulasī! ||29||
O Lord of Vṛndā, O Lord of the self, Kṛṣṇa, Hare, Hare! O Beloved of Bhārgavī, O Beloved of Lalitā, O Lord of the gopīs, Hare! 2.121.30.
Thus chanting the names, roaring repeatedly, making all the directions resound, and proclaiming them to the subjects again and again; (3.1)
He traveled ahead by celestial chariot to the ocean where Kaśyapa’s son resided,
and there he proclaimed his message to the people in the eastern regions.
Again and again, from the path of the sky, he caused the chanting of Hari’s names to be heard throughout the regions east of the Ūrulā river.
From Mount Uruḷā, proclaiming the name of Hari, he caused the eastern regions from the Karu ocean and the southeastern lands to hear it. (34)
He went to Trimura and Dvīpakalpa, and among the people there,
he caused his name to be heard by those subjects who were enduring the cold of the snow.
Then indeed [he went to] the regions of Śāntalāri, Kāmacāṭaka,
the mountain that is the abode of thieves, and the lake Dvikala.
He went to Mount Prabhālunagiri, as well as the mountain Samāna, the Bālakṛṣṇa lake, and the land of Kīragarjana. (37)
[He conquered] the regions of Śibi and Rājapura, the river Obīṃyāneśakī, Bīnā, the regions of Piṅga, and the entire land of Raśanā. ||38||
Having wandered again and again through the regions of Rāśīyāna,
he indeed caused all the people to hear the names of Hari.
Seven times he gave his discus, like a heap among heaps,
to the people of the aforementioned regions, upon the earth, mountains, battlefields, and waters.

By means of his celestial chariot, he traveled through forests, jungles, the Himalayas, the continents, and the lands of the subcontinents, bestowing the discus and causing the proclamation of his fame.
Let them worship Bālakṛṣṇa and Harikṛṣṇa as the Supreme Brahman here;
let them indeed hold the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa within their hearts. 42.
Let them always hear with their ears this delightful story which destroys the heat of sin, and let them always behold it with their eyes. 42.
Let men take the tulasī garland from his very neck;
let them eat his prasāda and drink that auspicious water. (44)
And let them always chant the names of Bālakṛṣṇa;
let them touch his feet and smell his fragrance. (45)
Let them worship Hari daily, the glorious young cowherd boy;
let them remember Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa and offer hymns of praise to him. 46.
Let them take refuge in that Kṛṣṇa for the sake of liberation;
let his feet, which bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation, be fully served. 47.
Let the form of Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa indeed be held within the heart;
for that Supreme Person exists as the very nature of the Supreme Brahman. (48)
In the city of Kambharāgṛha in Saurāṣṭra resides Śrīpati Puruṣottama;
alas, O people, at the destruction of the body, nothing at all comes along with one! 49.
Everything here remains just as it is, yet it is perishable and illusory;
therefore, having abandoned that bondage, let them worship the Supreme Lord.
I am indeed a devotee of that very Nārāyaṇa himself;
let them here chant His names and remember the Lord Hari, the goal.
Let men and women remember Brahmadhāmeśvara, Sādhupati, Śrīmāṇikīpati, Muktanātha, and Ātmanātha. ||52||
This human body is indeed difficult to obtain, and the [right] state of existence is difficult to attain; by means of this body, liberation is achieved through auspicious spiritual practices. (53)
O Lord of Hara, O Hari-Kṛṣṇa, O Bāla-Kṛṣṇa, O Janārdana!
O son of Dharma, O Hari, O supreme Brahman, O Śrī Parameśvara! (54)
O Lord of Rādhā, Ramā, and Satī; O Lord of Prabhā and Pāravatī; O Beloved of Lakṣmī, Śrī, and Maṅgalā; O Lord of Śrījayā and Lalitā! ||55||
O Blessed One, Lord of all worlds, Sovereign of all Nārāyaṇas;
O Lord of incarnations, Lord of the abode, Lord of reality, O Lord Hari! 56.
"By thus proclaiming this very thing, indeed, both enjoyment and liberation shall be yours.
O Rādhikā, that king of devotees repeated these words seven times over and over again. (57)
He caused the recitation [of his glory] to be heard in the regions of Rāśiyāna;
and the people, having heard it and seen the divine, bliss-bestowing celestial chariot, [were filled with wonder]. (58)
Having attained a state of supreme wonder, men from the young to the old came together outside to behold him in the sky. (59)
They gaze upon him in many ways and likewise proclaim Hari:
"Bālakṛṣṇa! Hare Kṛṣṇa! O Lord Kṛṣṇa! Kṛṣṇa! Hare! Hare! (2.121.60)
They praise a devoted teacher as a temple of the gods, like the Lord himself;
"O Blessed One! You are our mother, father, and kinsman, the giver of the name! (61)

A husband, a wife, a dear friend, a giver of the names of Hari, a son, a daughter, a companion, and one who causes others to hear the names of Hari—he indeed becomes such through the names of Hari. (62)
But those sons and others who do not indeed awaken devotion here are merely seekers of their own self-interest in this world, bearing the name in name only. (63)
For embodied beings whose merit is exhausted, a human body is difficult to obtain;
therefore, that wise person must attain the imperishable, undecaying abode.
Those men who obstruct devotion to the Supreme Lord are not true kinsmen nor are they worthy of honor; for it is those who bestow devotion who are indeed kinsmen. 65.
May that powerful deity who dwells in his celestial chariot and manifests devotion to Kṛṣṇa come here to this place, to our home. (56)
"O Divine One, we shall offer our devotion to Bālakṛṣṇa;
O Lord, having ascended to our homes, please purify our dwellings. (67)
Thus, all those people from the region of Rāśiyāna,
having heard and heard the name of Hari again and again, prayed with great reverence.
Then, there were twelve preeminent sages who were foremost;
dwelling in separate locations, they were detached and possessed knowledge of the three periods of time.
O Rādhikā, having perceived that the celestial chariot of Hari was adorned with devotion,
they approached the chariot by way of the sky.
The great seer Meṣāyana, Vṛṣabhāyana the king of yogis, the ṛṣi named Mithunāyana, and the ascetic Karkāyana; ||7 1||
Likewise, there is Siṃhāyana, Kanyāyana, Tulāyana,
the sage named Vṛścikāyana, and the sage Dhanāyana.
The sage known as Makarāyana, the sage Kuṃbhāyana, and the sage Mīnāyana—all were devoted to yoga. ||73||
Having found their places in the regions of Rāśiyāna, all those great sages dwelt separately, devoted entirely to meditation upon Brahman. ||74||
Furthermore, those devoted to the knowledge of Brahman and established in meditative absorption, having understood through yoga the abode of the gods as revealed by Hari, [attain their goal]. (75)
Overwhelmed with joy, they came through the sky in celestial chariots to behold you, who were awakening the people in the world with the auspicious chanting of the glories of Śrī Hari.
First, those sages, in the form of devotees,
bowed down according to worldly custom and were honored by the devotee.
They were saluted, honored, praised, and thanked with words of blessing; they were seated by the devotee and questioned regarding each of their desired objects. (78)
And when questioned for the sake of familiarity, they declared their own origin:
"We are all brothers; indeed, we are sons of Rudra, born from Rudra. (79)
When Brahmā first created that which was produced from his forehead,
Rudra was born as a fierce son and appointed for the sake of growth.
By him, indeed, innumerable Rudras were manifested over the course of many eons;
they were seen by Brahmā to be cruel, destructive, and contemptuous.
Indeed, for the sake of their destruction, Brahmā spoke to Rudra;
and when Rudra carried out the destruction of all of them, [the world was restored].
Then we twelve sons of Rudra were seized with fear;
the Rudras themselves, having assumed their own forms within the water, [remained there]. (83)
In thickets, in caves, in pits, and in mountain clefts, as was appropriate, those desiring to live remained hidden, having entered a state of concealment. (84)
At the end of many thousands of years, Brahmā performed penance;
at the conclusion of the destruction of Rudra’s creation, he brought forth Dundubhi and the others.
Then indeed the attendants residing in the temple, then Sanaka and the others,
then the lords of yoga, and then the circle of great sages.
Then Brahmā created the royal sages and the ancestral deities;
from Kaśyapa, the Sun, the Moon, and other auspicious beings were then born.
We have established our self-luminosity in the assemblies of the gods;
likewise, the great sages were honored by Brahmā and the deities. ||88||
The yogins, who are beneficial for the purpose of creation in the world of humans, were appointed by Brahmā together with the gods after they had reached a consensus. (89)
"O Rāṃ! We respectfully attain Lakṣmī, prosperity, wealth, and splendor;
we also give, and because of that, we are indeed joyful multitudes. (2.121.90)
Appointed for the purpose of bestowing fruits upon those who have performed actions, we remain wherever we are; therefore, they are our regions. (91)
"We are these Rāśiyas; indeed, we are designated as Rāśis, carrying out the command of Brahmā Parameṣṭhin. (92)
Wandering through the region of Dhruva, may we dwell here forever;
may all the nine planets, including the sun and the moon, grant us their assistance. ||92||
But for us, the entire circle of creation is cooked together;
we, those sages who are the sons of Rudra, dwell here. (94)
Indeed, those who remained after the creation of Rudra bestow the fruits of actions according to their merit;
thereafter, Brahmā bestowed upon us the Sarasvata castes separately. 95.
Aja gave the *alaivarṇaka* flowers to Meṣa;
then Brahmā gave the *vavauvarṇaka* flowers to Vṛṣabha. (96)
Then Brahmā gave the syllables *ka* and *cha* to Mithuna;
the Grandfather gave the two syllables *ḍa* and *ha* to Karkāyana.
The Grandfather bestowed the letter *ma* and the letter *ṭa* upon Siṃhāyana;
the Unborn One bestowed the letters *pa*, *ṭha*, and *ṇa* upon Kanyāyana. (98)
The Grandfather then gave the two syllables *ra* and *ta* to Tulāyana;
thereafter, Brahmā gave the two syllables *na* and *ya* to Vṛścika. 99.
Then the Unborn One (Aja) bestowed the letters Bha, Ma, Pha, and Dha upon Dhanāyana;
thereafter, Brahmā gave the letters Kha, Ja, and Va to Makara.
The Grandfather (Brahmā) gave the letters *ga* and *śa* to Kuṃbhāyana;
the Unborn (Brahmā) gave the letters *da*, *ca*, *jha*, and *ya* to Mīnāyana.

Indeed, the Unborn One ordained those respective letters which indicate the karma of the individual soul; for whatever embodied being is born under a particular yoga with the Moon and other planets, [those letters reveal their destiny].
"By means of names assigned according to their respective castes, their karma and lifespan shall come to pass;
this was ordained by the supreme Brahmā for the sake of maintaining the flow of worldly order."
"We, the fierce ones, have always been appointed for the sake of assisting creation;
today indeed we have accomplished our purpose by being devoted to Nārāyaṇa."
"You have arrived here for the sake of the welfare of the world;
formerly, we were likewise [present] in the form of rams and other animals, remaining concealed."
"However, those names were assumed by us for the sake of livelihood;
in reality, we are divine, fierce beings, the grandsons of Brahmā.
Come to our home, O devotee, and receive rest in every way."
We shall repeatedly perform the chanting of the glories of Śrī Hari once again.
Thus addressed, the king of devotees, the sage Devāyatana, rejoiced;
he then said "Om," O Rādhā, and caused the celestial chariot to descend.

Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-first chapter, titled "The Arrival of the Great Sages Beginning with Mēṣāyana," in the *Kiṃpuruṣa-khaṇḍa* of the second section, the *Tretā-santāna*, within the *Śrī-Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*, concerning the region of Rāśiyāna and the dispatch of the sage Devāyatana to instruct the people in the chanting of the names of Hari.

Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O Rādhikā, by the permission of the great sages beginning with Meṣa, this celestial chariot belongs to the king who is liberated from the abodes of the gods and is a devotee of the Lord.
On the southern bank of the lake named Dvikalā,
the sage Karkāyana indeed descended into the waters in the form of a chameleon.
He made his dwelling in the lake and descended upon its bank;
then the people raised cries of "Victory! Victory to the celestial chariot! (3).
"Victory to the god seated in his celestial chariot! Victory to Pradyumna, the Lord!"—thus did the men and women cry out, accompanied by shouts of "Victory! (4).
They honored him with parched grain, flowers, perfumes, and unbroken rice;
they joined him with benedictions and beheld the gateway to the divine.
They likewise worshipped Pradyumna and Karka at the temple of the deity;
they all prostrated at his feet and drank the water from his feet.
They considered themselves blessed and fortunate, crying out, "Hare! Hare!
Hare Kṛṣṇa! O Lord Hare! Bālakṛṣṇa! Hare! Hare! (7)
There, Karkarṣi gave instruction regarding the chanting of the name of Hari to the king named Tharkūṭastha.
The king accepted the mantra, as well as that Tulasī garland;
he caused him to dwell in a beautiful palace located in the northern part of Tharkūṭa.
He performed a great worship of the deity and the sage in that royal palace,
which served as a temple for the deity.
[He saw] Meṣa and the other twelve Ṛṣis who were related to the king,
as well as Rājñī, Cārumakāvā, and Bākṛkalāsikā.
Then he also imparted the name-mantra of Trilūnā Maṅgalā:
"O Hare Kṛṣṇa! O Hare Svāmin! O Hare Nārāyaṇa, O Lord! (1-2)
O Bālakṛṣṇa, son of Kambharāśrī, delight of Gopāla—may Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa be my refuge forever. 13.
Oṃ, salutation to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord; svāhā!
[I seek refuge] from the fear of Time, Māyā, sinful karma, Yama, and the wicked-hearted. || 14 ||
Bearing the trident, fish, banner, bow, discus, and the svastika, I am Brahmā; I am an eternal devotee of Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. (15)
The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa is my Lord and my husband;
I am a devotee of Kṛṣṇa’s beloved, and Śrī Hari is my refuge. 16.
Thus he then bestowed the mantras upon the deity's abode;
thereafter, he gave the recitation of the mantras to all the subjects.
Having thus made them Vaiṣṇavas and being honored by those present,
he ascended the celestial chariot along with the sages and the royal family members.
And together with the king and the queens,
he made them hear the proclamation of his name as they stood on the uppermost floor of the palace.
Having bestowed mantras for the sake of progeny, he caused Vāyāna to descend; then,
having received the honors offered by him, he went to the small Alpasāras lake,
descended from his vehicle, and proceeded along the Irātrī-Īśāna river.
And having descended, they all bathed in the abode of the sage Makara;
likewise, they caused the subjects to bathe in the lake and in the river.
The sage Devatāyatana gave them the name-mantras;
having received the supreme worship performed by them, he then [proceeded] toward the west.
Having gone to Bālakṛṣṇa-saras, they descended upon the bank of that lake;
at the confluence on the southern side of the Bālikā river, they performed their ritual ablutions.
The sage Mīna led him to his own home and honored the circle of devotees;
then, ascending a celestial chariot, he worshipped Pradyumna.
Causing the names of Kṛṣṇa and the mantras of Śrī Hari to be heard by all creatures,
Devāyatanaka made the subjects truly Vaiṣṇava.
Having received the worship offered by him, they all departed toward the west;
indeed, they descended from their celestial chariots in the regions of Kīra and Garjana.
Having gone to the dwellings of the Vṛścikarṣis and having granted his own vision,
Devāyana imparted the *mantras* to the people of that region.
Having caused King Kīragarjana, along with his family, to hear the auspicious Manu and having made him a Vaiṣṇava, he took him away in a celestial chariot.
Having accepted the great worship performed by the people, the deity,
accompanied by the king, his family, and others, proceeded to the confluence of the Sīrā and the Nandī rivers.
In the Urule lake, he caused his own celestial chariot to descend,
proclaiming his name to all the subjects there at that lake.
Then he bathed them and gave them the mantras along with the kīrtanas;
and the sage named Mithunāyana assumed a dual form.

He brought Pradyumna and the others, who were situated in their own abodes within the glorious celestial chariot, to his residence; he worshipped them with supreme devotion and ascended the chariot himself.
Then they all set out toward the confluence of the Āmuṇā river,
while the sage proclaimed [the message] to the subjects living in the regions beyond that point.
He caused those subjects to hear the mantras of Hare Kṛṣṇa and Bāla Kṛṣṇa;
having made them Vaiṣṇavas, he ascended the celestial chariot.
Then, having gone to the auspicious eastern shore of the ocean of hair and sin,
they descended from their celestial chariot and bathed in that sea.
Having consoled the subjects there and causing them to hear the chanting of his name,
he then indeed bestowed mantras upon them at that temple of the deity.
Having ascended the celestial chariot, he went to the assembly of Uru;
there, all the supreme lords were honored by the sage Kumbha.
Devāyana caused them to wander through his own residence for the sake of purification,
and he had the subjects recite the name-mantras.
After giving those [teachings] to them, the sage later traveled by celestial chariot to Mount Apa,
and also to the river named Urula-trivalā.
Then they bathed at the confluence of the Irāvatī, the Śatadrū, and the Vitastā;
and the sage [bathed] at the temple of the deity in that region.
Then the king of sages indeed caused the name of Hari to be heard and bestowed the names of the Manus upon the subjects as commanded by Siṃharṣi. 41.
By them Pradyumna was honored, and Devāyana was also honored;
all the others too were honored by means of a celestial chariot in that northern region.
Proclaiming the name of Hari, which destroys the contact with the three powers of delusion,
they descended from their celestial chariot and bathed there in the great waters.
Then the great sage Dhanāyana and the subjects as well worshipped those people seated in the celestial chariot with supreme devotion. 44.
Having repeatedly honored the temple of Hari, he gave names and mantras to the subjects, and [bestowed them] upon the king residing there. (45)
Having caused the *Vīrajāra*, the name-mantra, and likewise the *manus* to be heard, and having caused the sons, daughters, their wives, and those *manus* to be heard as well; ||46||
Having taken them together in the celestial chariot, he went to the confluence of the Ogha and the ocean;
they descended from the chariot and bathed at the confluence of the Ogha and the ocean.
Making the people hear the name of Hari, we beheld the subjects;
thereafter, the sage Devāyana gave the mantra to them.
On that very mountain named Corula, the sage Kanyāyana took them all in his aerial chariot to his own abode and honored them.
Having accepted his worship, he then departed toward the eastern direction;
and at the confluence of the Trāsa and Sāgara rivers, they descended from their celestial chariot.
