The protection of the subjects must be performed, and compassion should be shown toward the subjects and others—toward the poor and the helpless, toward women, toward the virtuous, and toward the elderly and so forth. (24)
One should perform service to others that brings happiness to oneself and others;
one must never inflict pain upon others, except in accordance with the laws of war. (25)
"You must always provide protection for those living beings who have taken refuge [in you].
Whoever bears the name of the Blessed One upon his lips is worthy of honor and must certainly not be punished. (26)
Vaiṣṇavas are to be honored in every way with gifts, marks of respect, and worthy objects, as well as through humility, speech, and service characterized by the duty of a servant.
An association with those of sattva-nature should indeed be formed through the heart;
however, an association with those of rajas-nature should be formed only slightly through the body. (28)
One should indeed associate with those characterized by tamas in a manner that appears false, so that the kingdom may not perish and one may not suffer personal bondage. (29)
One should always act in such a way that obstacles do not arise;
indeed, one must place trust in all respects in virtuous devotees of the Lord.
One should trust the queen, the son, or the chief minister only with caution;
one should not consider them as one's own until they have been thoroughly tested.
One should not trust those who are greedy and intent solely on their own self-interest in matters of sovereignty;
rather, one should trust with devotion those people who are free from desire and established on the path of the virtuous.
One should not meet anyone alone, for a deserted place is indeed a source of fear;
nor should one accept food without first [offering it] to another.
If someone were to offer something drinkable or touchable, one would not take it without reflecting;
for inanimate objects that are to be enjoyed cannot be used without their being transferred to another. (34)
One should never, even for one's own sake, consume so much as a grain of it;
even a brother or a son must be regarded with such mindfulness.
Subjects must not be provoked to agitation, nor should embodied beings be harmed; one should never trust a person who bows down while casting sidelong glances with a flickering gaze.
He should never dwell in an empty house without his weapon, nor should he ever dwell there;
he should never dwell with a maidservant, nor even with a queen in a secluded place.
One should certainly not have many wives, nor should one resort to sexual union with a female slave;
one should not approach [a woman] except for the sake of dharma or for the purpose of procreation. || 38 ||
Having become fearless, one should not sleep, but should protect virtuous people;
one should never indulge in sensual desire in a place of dharma.
One should certainly not apply knowledge to the place of desire, nor should one apply longing to the place of dispassion and austerity. (2.127.40)
One should employ spies in the territories of others, as well as within one's own kingdom, in the home, and on the ground;
one should also employ spies born of righteousness within the kingdom of the body, the senses, and so forth. (4.1)
One should carry out one's duties having made discernment the primary concern;
if the principal [minister] becomes dejected, one should strive to prevent the obstruction of affairs. ||42||
Having obtained experience from an elder, one should practice that which grants peace and is eternal;
one should not rely upon a newborn infant even in a great matter. ||43||
For the sake of liberation, one should resort to that which is beneficial, whether it be small or great;
one should cast away a wisdom that causes exhaustion, like a she-wolf.
One should well perfume the peaceful and humble intellect as if it were a virtuous woman;
and one should protect even a dull-witted person like a pillar in a place of calamity. (45)
A king should protect even a learned man who is intent on the acts of an assassin; furthermore, he should not wander alone in the forest or while hunting. 46.
One should not trust one's own people at a reservoir, a well, or similar places;
rather, having placed the family priest at the forefront, one should traverse the forest accompanied by an army.
In that regard as well, one should always place a forest-knower at the head;
one should not go into the forest during the rainy season, nor during a festival or a time of upheaval.
Even at night, he should examine the welfare of his subjects by means of a disguise,
[fearing] the barber, the weaver, the tax-collector, the flatterer, and the thief.
Having personally assumed that form, he might at times become a great lord;
having understood every circumstance, he should act for the happiness of his subjects.
First, one should dispatch one's own servants, such as barbers and others, in those respective forms;
thereafter, having assumed those same forms oneself, one should go, and not otherwise. (5.1)
Having become a woman, at the time for Brahmanical rites, she went to the water-source with her own maidservants who were fetching water to fetch water herself. (52)
And he should ascertain from them, as well as through news, what is beneficial for the subjects, as well as the livelihood and other needs of his own servants, dependents, and wives. (53)
Having understood the sufferings of the wretched, the helpless, and the poor, he should destroy them;
likewise, he should eliminate atheism, deceit, and crookedness.
Through discourses and through the application of punishment, he should discipline the wicked subjects;
being devoted to compassion, he should provide widows with food, clothing, and shelter. (55)

The king should cause the gift of knowledge to be bestowed and cause the knowledge of the precepts to be imparted; he should always cause the knowledge of the arts and the sciences of craftsmanship to flourish. (56)
One should not cause the scrotum of men or humans to be cut open;
nor should one cause women to perform tasks such as guarding children for others' households.
One should cause the protection, nourishment, and education of children to be carried out through the mother;
one must never, under any circumstances, obstruct the menstrual flow by means of a royal edict.
One should not alter the seasonal flow of menses, fruits, flowers, and so forth by means of medicinal drugs;
nor should one cause a human being—who is dependent on others—to be led away like a beast. (59)
One should never kill a person who is free from desire, purposeless, inactive, an obstacle, or unfit for yoga. (2.127.60)
One should indeed entrust the doctrine of liberation (mokṣadharma) to such a person for their benefit,
and for the welfare of the worlds, one should entrust them with the tasks of the gods.
One should never treat the human state as something difficult to attain, like chaff;
one should achieve new blossoming and never allow that blossoming to perish. (6.2)
One should cause agriculture to flourish, which is the supreme form of all developments; one should also cause craftsmanship to flourish, as well as authentic knowledge.
One should develop, according to one's strength, the alchemical (rāsāyana), the tantric, the mechanical, the mantra-based, as well as the divine and the aerial methods.
One should never cause a portion that bestows excellence to become mixed with inferiority;
rather, one should place a portion that bestows excellence into what is already inferior, thereby granting it prosperity. 65.
One should indeed expand the authentic [perception] of hearing from afar, seeing, and so forth;
one should expand the path for entering the earth and other such feats like a yogi. //66//
One should cause the movement toward water, fire, the atmosphere, the directions, and so forth to expand;
likewise, one should never suppress the movement toward the supreme egg (the cosmic source).
He should convene an excellent assembly of sages, ancestors, gods, and others, as well as Daityas, humans, and Rākṣasas, for the purpose of mutual acquaintance.
Therefore, the king himself should perform the Sarvamedha sacrifice;
by that, he shall gain familiarity with all those who dwell in the world.
The king should not practice the omission of the proper sequence of honors, such as worship and veneration;
rather, he should in every way increase the state of venerability of his gurus.
One should protect the treasures of all things as if they were the treasures of heaven;
one should act in such a way that all subjects rejoice like the gods. (71)
Just as I, the Supreme Lord, am the bestower of happiness upon my subjects, so too,
O Queen, do I, following the duties of a king, always provide you with a dwelling.
Therefore, the king, being of my own nature, should protect his subjects like his own children;
he should then cause them to attain virtue, wealth, pleasure, and liberation.
One should never cause subjects to fall from the worship of the Supreme Lord;
for falling results in the loss of liberation, while rising results in the non-abandonment of liberation.

Having determined that the primary object of meditation is indeed the state of being human, one should practice virtue so that there may be no lapse in devotion; thus one should cultivate that which is to be meditated upon.
Without that, the designation "king" on earth would become the designation "paramour";
therefore, you who are named Tharkūṭarāja, become filled with the bliss of *thurā*. (76)
But if you should violate the Dharma spoken by me, suffering will surely arise for you at some time;
therefore, being vigilant, you must thoroughly protect my teachings. (77)
Devotion to Hari and auspicious association with the virtuous—these two essentials one should practice by all means; for such a king makes his royal purpose truly fruitful. (78)
The protection of subjects in this world and the granting of liberation in the next, as well as the granting of one's own liberation, must be performed by one who follows the duty of a king. (79)
The governance of those who act contrary to the duties of protection, the encouragement of those devoted to divine dharma, and the assistance of those seeking the welfare of others. (2.127.80)
One who follows the dharma of a king must contemplate liberation as his object of meditation;
those endowed with wisdom should be appointed to the administration of the kingdom.
The king must achieve the fruit of his human body, which is liberation;
for by performing the consecration of that which is impermanent, one will certainly not obtain a permanent fruit.
Having ruled the kingdom according to the prescribed law, he should practice the teaching of liberation;
then, having entrusted the kingdom to his sons and others, he should depart for the forest.
Even if ordination is not desired, one should nevertheless prioritize, above all else, actions consisting of service within the duties of the king. (84)
Victory over a foreign kingdom is not considered a certain victory;
victory over the realm of Brahman is considered a certain victory. 85.
Lying down upon the body, senses, and so forth is not a permanent happiness;
lying down within the latent impressions (vāsanā) is said to be the truly permanent happiness. ||86||

When the memory of things enjoyed has dissolved and the mental impression (saṃskāra) has reached a state of dissolution, a happiness born from the destruction of craving arises, equal to the bliss of the Self. ||87||
That kingdom of Brahmā, the great sovereignty, is to be attained by a ruler—a realm that is neither finite, nor subject to seizure, and never a source of agitation. (88)
A merchant should engage in such business as increases his prosperity; however, a person seeking success must abandon any enterprise that leads to loss. (89)
One should practice that which leads to attaining a kingdom superior to one's current kingdom;
however, one should not perform that which, upon the destruction of the kingdom, bestows the state of a denizen of hell.
Merit, the supreme station of the virtuous, heaven, my lotus feet, enjoyment, and union with my own form—these indeed are to be attained by the Vaiṣṇavas. (91)
Suffering, the bondage of sovereignty, hell, the multitude of latent impressions (vāsanās),
negligence, laziness, and death— these must indeed be abandoned by the Vaiṣṇavas.
My sovereignty shall be the attainment of the Imperishable; my family shall be the circle of the liberated. My palace itself shall be the abode of the liberated within the realm of the Imperishable.
That kingdom which is my empire, let that kingdom be his;
I give my kingdom to him who is devoted to me and offers himself to me.
"O King, serve me with devotion alone, always like a maidservant serving her master;
I shall grant you liberation at the proper time, so practice devotion toward me here on earth."
"Build for me a beautiful temple and install me as the Lord, together with Rādhā, Lakṣmī, Ramā, Brahmavidyā, Śrī, and Māṇikī. (96)
"Continue the unbroken flow of my worship;
remaining in the form of the image, I shall accept your service."
Thus did Śrī Bālakṛṣṇasvāmī Śrī Puruṣottama instruct the householder named Tharkūṭa, O Rādhikā. 98.
The king, however, had a very great temple constructed; having installed that image there, he served it like a servant. || 99 ||
The Lord Śrī Bhagavān Prabhū, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa,
at the end of the Pratipad night, in the morning, [appeared] at the place known as Tharkūṭa.
He said, "For the sake of the third sacrifice in the kingdom of Vīrajāra, you must go this very morning; I shall go with you. (101)
Having spoken thus, on the second day at the very dawn, Hari himself,
along with the king and queen, [sent] his own fifty auspicious daughters.

Having accepted those [gifts] offered according to the prescribed rite, as well as the marriage portion (yautaka), and having received the worship and bestowed auspicious blessings, they departed. || 103 ||
By means of a celestial chariot, she quickly went from Prajādi to meet the Lord of the Night (Śiva) and beheld various regions provided with pavilions.

Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Deliverance of the Preta, and the Instruction on Royal Policy and True Dharma to King Tharkūṭastha," in the second section, the Tretā Cycle, of the glorious *Lakṣmīnārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Listen, O Rādhikā; the Supreme Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa has arrived in the sky upon a most radiant celestial chariot.
A white radiance, like the light of ten million moons,
appeared upon the earth, in all directions and intermediate points, at the confluence of the two rivers.
"Victory to you, Mādhava! Tens of millions of humans, gods, and sages [proclaim]:
Victory, Kṛṣṇa! Victory, O Lord! Victory, Bālakṛṣṇa! Victory, O Master! (3)
"May the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa be ever victorious! Thus, with great joy, they uttered shouts of victory with open throats. (4)
With palms joined in reverence, they spoke and gazed with unblinking eyes,
while Kṛṣṇa’s celestial chariot circled five times.
Having bestowed his auspicious sight upon the people while still in the sky, he descended to the earth in that beautiful vehicle which moves at will.
At the junction of the Irā and Triśauṣikā rivers, in the most beautiful Middle Country,
fifty yojanas from the lovely pavilion.
On the bank of the Irātrīśā river, Kṛṣṇa descended from his celestial chariot,
as did Śrīgopāla, the illustrious Kaṃbharā, and the kings as well.
Lomaśa and the maidens also came out from the celestial chariot;
they were honored by the people with parched grain, unbroken rice, and flowers.
Then the glorious Lord, having bathed in the waters of the Irāvatī and Śānadī rivers,
and having looked upon the pavilion, the sacrificial pit, the altar, and the rest, went to his own dwelling.
Then, honored and served by the king, the royal family, Vīrajarā, and the others, Kṛṣṇa rested in the palace.
Then, having bathed in the morning, Bālakṛṣṇa went to the sacrificial ground on the third day of the dark fortnight of Pauṣa, which was graced by gods, sages, and ancestors.
He beheld the sacrificial altars, the fire-pits, and golden slabs,
as well as countless materials for the performance of the sacrifice, which were beyond human calculation.
Then, on the sacrificial ground, Hari beheld ten million brahmin-sages and deities there in the pavilion at their own seats for the purpose of choosing [a bride].
Thus the king, the lover of his heroic daughter, sat down accompanied by his beloved;
and Lomaśa arrived for the sake of the sacrifice, and indeed he came.
Likewise, Brahmā, who is devoted to his wife, and the great Vaiṣṇava Vasiṣṭha sat upon their respective seats; at that time, auspicious songs were sung.
The learned brahmins, filled with joy, sang the Sāmaveda,
and the goddesses there sang songs that announced auspiciousness.
Indeed, musical instruments and various kinds of drums were sounded; the binding of bracelets and the recitation of benedictions and other such rites proceeded.
The installation of the deity of the ancillary parts (Aṅgadeva) and the worship for the removal of obstacles took place;
indeed, there was the worship of the principal vessel and the worship of the ritual materials.
Then, in the sky, the worship of the God of gods and his Goddess began;
at that moment, the gods and others arrived for the purpose of raining down sandalwood paste and other offerings. (2.128.20)
And as soon as the god Vahni was established in the sacrificial vessel,
those gods, beginning with Brahmā, who possessed embodied forms, then raised a cry.
Lomaśa and Vasiṣṭha began the seasonal rites;
there the mantras were recited and the oblations were offered.
With fire-like faces, they are the incarnations of the liberated souls of the Supreme Brahman;
they have become the twice-born among gods, celestial sages, ṛṣis, lords, and ancestors.
Those whose faces are fire indeed attain satisfaction and consume the sacrificial offerings;
there is also the creation of living beings, the creation of Brahmā, and the creation of Īśvara.
O Rādhikā, all those who were created there were satisfied by the consumption of countless offerings, just as they had been in the previous sacrifice.
Inanimate beings and stationary objects, as well as sentient beings capable of assuming forms at will;
sacred fords, mountains, rivers, insects, moths, and birds—[all these were present]. ||26||
Indeed, all the bodies of the Blessed One were satisfied there at that great sacrifice;
so too was the Lord Nārāyaṇa, the beloved of the primordial Lakṣmī, in that Vaiṣṇava rite.
The Lord Hari, the inner self of all, is the foremost among those who are never satiated;
thus indeed are these seven days, consisting of the vow of the festival of satisfaction.
On the ninth day, the dismissal of the sacrifice took place with the ritual sites for the gods;
there was a suspension of that rite, and the sacrificial fees were devoid of the Aṅka mark.
And for all of them, fresh foods should be cooked daily as appropriate, being wholesome for embodied beings.
Then Bāla, the Lord of Śrī, Puruṣottama,
was born from the union of Oghavī and Irāvatī at the supreme Avabhṛtha bath.
He performed [the rites] together with all the sacrificial priests and ten million people;
at that time, all the sacred fords (tīrthas) there became manifest in embodied form.
All the Muktatīrthas as well as the Brahmatīrthas were likewise present.
Those which are the bathing-places for descents and those which are the bathing-places of the liberated; || 33 ||
All the black pilgrimage sites (kṛṣṇatīrthas), as well as those belonging to Nārāyaṇa,
and likewise those of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśa, the ancestors, and the yogins.
And of the sages, the gods, the twice-born, and the virtuous;
of the chaste goddesses, the world-protectors, and the ascetics. (35)
At that time, I dwelt at the confluence of the Ovyā and Irātri rivers, where the holy places of virtuous women and virtuous men exist in embodied form.
There, one should perform ablutions starting from the third day of the dark fortnight of Pauṣa until the ninth; this seven-day period bestows the merit of a sacrifice.
Thus spoke the great king at that time during the avabhṛtha bath: "O Rādhikā, I was then standing by the side of that Hari, bathing again and again. (38)
Nārāyaṇa himself, the lord of Lakṣmī, was also present there by his side;
he heard what was said by Hari and repeated it again and again.
Indeed, by all the Nārāyaṇas, by all the Kṛṣṇas here, by all the Vāsudevas who are incarnations, and by millions of Lords; ||| 2.128.40 ||
One should dwell here even in the form of a sacred ford (tīrtha) for the welfare of men;
and Rādhā, Lakṣmī, and other goddesses should likewise always reside here.
"Indeed, you must always remain together with your respective consorts in the form of sacred fords (tīrtha).
Thus did the gods [speak] there at the confluence, the sacred ford of the sacrifice.
And at night, during the three periods of twilight, and in water and the like—whether in ponds, in parts of wells, or even in oblong lakes—in every way [one should avoid it]. (43)
O beloved, by the command of Śrī Hari, we all dwell there in ponds, on sacrificial grounds, and in various places.
Hari spoke again there: "By bathing here, indeed, the mountains of sin of those who commit extremely heinous crimes shall go to destruction. (45)
The sons, grandsons, and family members shall become partakers of merit;
they shall be prosperous householders, enjoyers of pleasures, free from disease, and long-lived. (46)
Whenever people come together anywhere and bathe here, drink the water, or touch these waters; ||47||
Even those residing in other lands who remember the sacred ford of Kratu, I shall grant them both worldly enjoyment and liberation; of this there is no doubt. (48)

Bathing, giving gifts, austerity, burnt offerings, rendering assistance to others, and so forth; likewise, constructing temples for the gods, building almshouses for the righteous, and planting trees. ||49||
And those people who shall cause the gift of knowledge, the giving away of a maiden, and the distribution of medicinal herbs and grain to be performed, their merit shall be infinite. (2.128.50)

The laboratory for alchemy, the observatory for the planets, the laboratory for piercing gems, the hall for sacrificial vessels, the hall of the virtuous, the hall for sacred discourses, the laboratory for mechanical devices, and the temple of Śiva; || 51 ||
He established a food hall, sacrificial sessions, a water hall, a dairy,
a maternity home, and even a hall of knowledge for those who frequented it.
Those people who shall cause a service hall, as well as houses for feeding guests and so forth, and a hall for the spirits to be built at the site of the sacrifice; //53//
"I shall grant them both enjoyment and liberation; of this there is no doubt.
Thus did Śrī Hari speak, O Rādhikā, at the site of the avabhṛtha bath.
He himself bathed by repeatedly immersing himself in the waters;
he was bathed with handfuls of water by everyone, and everyone was likewise bathed by him.
Having been bathed repeatedly with showers from my joined palms during the final purificatory rite, this pleasing water has been held by me for your sake. (56)
"Drink from the jar the unattainable, purifying nectar of the Supreme Lord.
Saying "I shall drink," Rādhā drank the nectar from the feet of Śrī Hari. (57)
Nārāyaṇa gave [the water] to Lakṣmī, and she too drank the water;
thus, O Rādhā, the Supreme Lord completed the purificatory bath (avabhṛtha).
Having gone outside and put on his garments, ornaments, and so forth,
Hari proceeded to his own seat situated within the pavilion.
Then, having obtained a moment's rest, the Blessed One caused a beautiful assembly hall to be constructed for the inhabitants of all the worlds in the evening.
King Vīrajāra performed worship with devotion;
by the command of Śrī Hari, he worshipped Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. (61)
And Vāsudeva, the Infinite, the Vairāja, the Supreme Lord;
Viṣṇu, Śiva, Āryamāṇa, Sanatkumāra, and the others.
Likewise, all those beloved of Brahmā— Indra, Sūrya, the Prajāpatis,
Vasiṣṭha, Gālava, Patnīvrata, and the sage Devāyata.
The king worshipped Śrī Gopāla, as well as Kambharā, Śrī Rādhā, Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, and other goddesses worthy of worship. 64.
Then he presented various offerings there for worship;
he asked for forgiveness and said, "May my service be forgiven for its deficiencies."
I have been purified by his very grace; the circle of the earth has been purified.
Having come here, the lords have proclaimed my fame throughout the quarters of the world. (66)
Blessed is the king known as Jāra, who has attained true heroism, since I am in every way his paramour, yet my state of being a paramour has been destroyed by him. (67)
And what indeed could be a greater fortune for me than this, that I have obtained the feet of Kṛṣṇa here in my own home? (68)
Today my kingdom has become meaningful, my enjoyments have also become meaningful, and my family has become meaningful through the nectar of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s feet. (69)
Today my subjects have become meaningful, as have the men and women;
even this lifespan has become meaningful, since here resides the Supreme Person.
All my wealth, including my elephants, horses, and palanquins, has become meaningful today;
indeed, everything of mine has become meaningful now that the Supreme Person is here.
I am blessed, my mother is blessed, and this family of a hundred members is blessed,
since in our lineage and in our home dwells Kṛṣṇa, who is the glory of all incarnations.
The attainment of Śrī Hari here results from merit accumulated over ten million births; that attainment has arisen solely through His grace—how can I describe such good fortune? (73)
The river Obī is blessed, and likewise the auspicious river Irātriśā is blessed;
the Tribalā also is blessed, for in its waters dwells Puruṣottama.
Blessed indeed are the sages who dwell in whose house Puruṣottama resides;
blessed are the trees, the creepers, the shrubs, and the multitudes of grasses as well. (75)
Fortunate indeed are the beasts and birds whose dwelling is Puruṣottama, for today Nārāyaṇas and Kṛṣṇas have arrived at his home. (76)
Liberation is theirs, victory is theirs, and the wealth of good fortune is theirs; all prosperity is always theirs in whose home Puruṣottama dwells. (77)
Blessed is King Śibi, and blessed is King Ṭharkūṭaka;
blessed is King Vīrarāja, in whose house Puruṣottama dwells. (78)
Blessed are those who dwell in the netherworld, and blessed are those who dwell upon the mountains;
blessed are the maidens and the youths who have the vision of Kṛṣṇa.
Let all those remaining human beings who desire liberation receive from us this mantra that bestows liberation, from Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Lord.
Having spoken thus, the king prostrated himself like a staff before Śrī Puruṣottama;
he also prostrated like a staff before the assembly hall and rolled eagerly upon the dust.
Hari placed both his feet upon his head;
he also placed his feet upon his heart, and then gave him an embrace.
Hari himself gave the king the Puṣpahāra temple,
and his four queens worshipped the Supreme Lord.
The sons and daughters likewise worshipped Kṛṣṇa with great devotion;
and the subjects also worshipped Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Person.
Men and women, as well as local dignitaries and guests, offered worship to the venerable Lord Svāmī Parameśvara. 85.
Śrī Hari took his own crown from his head and gave it to the king;
then, for the sake of the mantra, the subjects arrived by the millions. 86.
Hari gave them mantras preceded by the remembrance of His names:
"Oṃ, obeisances to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa; obeisances to the Lord. (87)
May Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa be my refuge at all times, from the fear of time, māyā, sinful karma, enemies, Yama, and treacherous hearts. (88)
Bearing the trident, fish, banner, bow, discus, and svastika, I am Brahmā; I am the eternal devotee of Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. (89)
The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa is my Lord and my husband;
Bāla Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Brahman, is indeed my eternal husband.
May he be my father, my venerable one, my well-wisher, my friend, my protector, and my guardian;
may I indeed be his body, and may he truly be my embodied self.
"Śrī Kṛṣṇavallabhasvāmī, Śrī Hari, is my refuge"—thus did the glorious Bālakṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa give these mantras. 92.
He indeed caused his own people to provide pleasant drinking water, and he granted them a vision [of himself] while stationed in a divine abode together with great liberated souls and others. (93)
The Lord Bālakṛṣṇa himself gave [his own nature] to his people;
the people took refuge in Kṛṣṇa, the supreme Lord Nārāyaṇa. 94.
At the conclusion of the assembly, the Blessed One, having fed the people who had arrived, rested for a moment; and everyone rested throughout the night until morning.
Having bathed, Hari said to the people, the sages, the gods, and others:
"Let everyone indeed go quickly for the purpose of performing the fourth sacrifice. (96)

In this kingdom, which is like a boat on the ocean joined to a mooring and possesses the power of the senses as its earth, let them quickly bring about the fitness for the commencement of the sacrifice. (97)
"We shall indeed come on the morning of the eleventh day";
thus were the gods, sages, ancestors, and humans commanded by Hari. 98.
All the sacrificial priests went to the confluence of the Ālana and the ocean;
Bālakṛṣṇa remained at the abode of Vīrajārā, as requested by him.
Attended by the queens, the king, and the princes and others,
Hari dwelt happily with his family, finding delight in his mind.
But the king, having learned that his hundred daughters were infatuated with Kṛṣṇa,
gave them to Kṛṣṇa out of devotion, with the approval of the queen.
Then, having obtained Śrī Puruṣottama as their husband, the hundred maidens felt they had accomplished their purpose; the king and the others became happy.
O Rādhikā, all the queens, having obtained Kṛṣṇa as their son-in-law,
considered themselves to have fulfilled their purpose and to be worthy recipients of merit at all times.

Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Performance of the Third Viṣṇu Sacrifice at the Confluence of the Obīrā and Trīśā Rivers during the Reign of King Vīrajāra, the Bestowal of Mantras and Other Gifts, and the Greatness of the Tīrtha," in the second section, the Tretā Cycle, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Rādhikā, to the wonder that occurred there in the king’s palace.
A certain king, adorned with a crown, [arrived] by way of the sky. || 1 ||
His four arms were beautifully adorned with a conch, a discus, a mace, and a lotus;
he bore a most divine tilaka upon his forehead and a mark made of sandalwood paste.
Clad in garments pure as fire, holding a garland of tulasī in his hand,
golden-hued with a serene countenance, and adorned with a sword at his waist.
Wearing the attire of a king and accompanied by many others similar to himself, he was adorned with a parasol and chowries, and his splendor was increased by shouts of "Victory! (jaya).
May Bālakṛṣṇa be victorious here, and may this devotee of his also be victorious;
and may there be victory for us, who have taken refuge in him, at every step today.
Oh, what a worthy recipient is the Supreme Brahman! The donor himself is the ageless Vīra;
for by the merit arising from his majesty, he has attained the supreme state of having four arms.
This king has arrived here, and we, his servants, have been rescued;
O King, Vīrajāra has performed a virtuous deed, and may he live eternally.
Having spoken thus, he who was in the guise of a king bowed repeatedly to Hari;
all the other servants, who were four-armed, likewise prostrated themselves.
Having touched the feet of Śrī Hari and performed the ritual purification with the water used for washing His feet, they placed that water upon their own heads.
All of them, chanting "Victory to Kṛṣṇa! offered libations to Rādhikā;
they worshipped Śrī Svāmī Śrī Rameśvara with divine necklaces and other offerings.
O Rādhā, Vīrajārā and the others remained there for that long;
indeed, all those girls and the rest were also in the dwelling of Bālakṛṣṇa.
Then the queens and the king’s servants, filled with supreme joy and having attained an incomparable wonder, made this inquiry: ||| 1-2 ||
"Who is this, and from where has he come—the king who possesses four arms?
Let us offer him a welcome here," they said, and then they offered him a throne.
They offered him the guest-water (arghya), the honey-mixture (madhuparka), sweet food, sweet water, betel-leaf, and due honors, each according to the proper custom.
With great devotion, they, whose minds were fixed on the Supreme, accepted [the offerings];
and Śrī Hari, abandoning his state of silence, [inquired after] their welfare and other matters.
He questioned him, who was devoted to the divine, and rejoiced again and again;
then the king, the lover of Vīrā, questioned Hari at that time.
"O Blessed One, from where do these great devotees of the Lord come, even though they follow the Great King? We wish to know this. (17)
Where is the kingdom, and where is this earth of theirs? How are they renowned, and for what purpose do they exist? Grant the realization [of truth] to us who are devoted to your service. (18)
Thus addressed, the Blessed Kṛṣṇa then said to that king:
"Speak, O King, your own history exactly as it is to those who desire to know it."
Having thus received that command there, the king, being well-pleased, related the entire account to them all; listen to it, O Rādhikā. (1.129.20)
I was the king named Śūrajāra, the lord of men here;
and these ministers were then the sons of Vīrajāra, my father. (2.1)
I ruled the kingdom according to dharma, always protecting the subjects;
having become a servant of the people, I performed the guardianship of the realm. ||22||
I performed meritorious acts of giving that bestow heaven and are filled with happiness;
I protected the helpless and others, and I fed them daily at a sacrificial feast.
I honored the virtuous, I always worshipped the ancestors and guests, I served cows and other animals, and I repeatedly gladdened all living beings. (24)
I caused excellent trees to be planted which provide benefit to living beings;
if, year after year, food remains even when the year has passed. (25)
And after the cooking was finished, all of that was offered by me to those who requested it;
Brahmins were fed daily, and the truthful ones were exceedingly honored. (26)
The village deities and others were honored and welcomed as those who had come for refuge;
and by the giving of material goods, I brought about the destruction of the suffering of the distressed. (27)
By giving medicine to the sick, I brought about health and happiness;
likewise, I gave gifts of houses, elephants, fields, and so forth. (28)
I performed and announced everything that was for the sake of virtue; by that merit, having ruled the kingdom and having entrusted it to my son, [I attained this state]. (29)
Having met my end, I left my own queen and ascended to heaven;
there, in the world of the Sun, I dwell resplendent.
Belonging to the lineage of Hiraṇyadeva and endowed with every happiness,
these were formerly my servants, solely engaged in meritorious deeds.
Having died, those who were companions in my religious duties have come to heaven;
born from the lineage of Hiraṇya, they dwell with me as gods. (3.2)
Even there, my kingdom indeed extends for many yojanas;
some of these principal ministers of mine are present there as well.
O Prabhākara, all the servants and some of the messengers are happy, full of joy, and overflowing with great bliss.
We have indeed heard that a sacrifice was performed there by the gods and others; here, moreover, an excellent Vaiṣṇava sacrifice has been accomplished by our son and the deities.
The Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the primordial Śrī Puruṣottama, has arrived for the sake of the welfare of the world. (36)
To that God of gods, the sovereign lord of all, a hundred maidens have indeed been offered today by my son for worship. (37)
By that gift, my family has been purified and attained divinity;
we have all reached heaven through the merit of giving away our daughter. (38)
Having dissolved away, all those who were four-armed have now become two-armed;
these Vaiṣṇava attendants have today become yogis of the abode.
Possessing forms equal to Viṣṇu’s and having gone to the abode of Viṣṇu,
these auspicious ones are endowed with all sovereign powers and possess a splendor exceeding ten million suns.
"By giving away his daughter, our son has secured our liberation;
for the gift of a daughter to a worthy recipient at a sacred site yields merit greater than that of a hundred lineages. (41)
Since it is directly perceived that this indeed delivers one's ancestors,
therefore, having become four-armed and having beheld Hari, [one should perform this].
"We have come here from the solar realm to tell you this: we shall go to the divine abode of Hari, which is known as the Imperishable (Akṣara). (43)
They have come with great composure to behold Śrī Hari, to enjoy his grace, to receive his command, and to request permission to enter his abode. (44)
Having spoken thus, they desisted; Hari granted them grace, and the maidens and others beheld him in his own divine form as their grandfather.
Greatly rejoiced, they prostrated themselves, and Hari granted them his grace;
with joyful hearts, they ate and drank the nectar of his feet.
Then Śrī Hari indeed spoke to Śūrajārā and the others:
"My devotees, the Sāttvatas, go indeed to my auspicious abode. (47)
Only householders who have received the mantra are indeed fit to go there;
otherwise, there is no way to enter my abode by any means whatsoever.
Thus addressed, they then received the mantras from the mouth of Bālakṛṣṇa:
"Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Master; svāhā! (49)
May Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa be my refuge at all times,
from the fear of Time, Māyā, sinful karma, the god of death, and the wicked-hearted.
Bearing the trident, fish, banner, bow, discus, and the svastika, Bālakṛṣṇa, who transcends the imperishable Supreme Brahman, is my Lord. 51.
I am Brahmā, an eternal devotee of Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa;
the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa is my Lord and my husband. (52)
Bālakṛṣṇa is the Supreme Brahman; he is indeed my eternal Lord. May he be my father, kinsman, well-wisher, friend, protector, and guardian. (53)
"Śrī Kṛṣṇavallabhasvāmī, Śrī Hari, is my refuge.
These mantras Śrī Svāmī Śrī Rameśvara gave to them. 54.
Then they became liberated from the syllables (akṣara) and thus fit to depart;
then King Vīrajāra [addressed] that family as "father."
Having understood this, she performed worship for him and requested his forgiveness;
then the queen, the king's mother, named Devavarūthinī— (56)
Knowing that her husband was liberated, divine, capable of traveling anywhere, and imperishable, the aged and devoted wife,
a true satī, prostrated at the feet of her husband there.
The widow shed tears and, desiring to go along with Manomatī, spoke with humility: "What sin of mine is there for which this has happened? (58)
"I remain a widow in this body; O King, take me with you!
Since the Blessed Lord himself dwells as the son-in-law in his house, there is no end to that merit; I am not merely your beloved, but his mother. (59)
"How is it that I, an aged woman, have not become divine, while my husband has?
Therefore, O King, make a perpetual request on my behalf."
"Act quickly so that I may go with you to liberation.
Having heard this, King Śūrapati then entreated Śrī Hari.
Having prostrated there like a staff for the sake of the kingdom and out of a desire for liberation, the Blessed Lord Śrī Hari said: "O King, your heart's desire shall be fulfilled."
Likewise, the resolve of the queen has indeed been fulfilled; of this there is no doubt.
For in this month known as Pauṣa, there are indeed sacrificial rites to be performed.
Having seen those [omens], you should then proceed; that is my imperishable abode.
Let your beloved remain here for as long as it takes to obtain the vision [of me]. 64.
On the full moon day of the bright fortnight of Pauṣa, let my queen ascend my celestial chariot, served by my attendants, and go to my imperishable abode. (65)
And may you, O Four-armed One, remain steady here together with your faces;
on the full-moon day, having taken the four-armed Queen along with you—
"However, you must go to my imperishable abode, which is overflowing with my mantras.
Having spoken thus to Rādhikā, the Lord Bālakṛṣṇa himself then [departed]. (67)
Out of compassion, he bestowed mantras upon the queen for the attainment of divinity;
though the queen possessed a physical body, she then became divine.
Just as King Caturbhuja was, so too was she four-armed;
she became fit for residence in Vaikuṇṭha, just as the king was.
O Rādhikā, even regarding the bestowal of the mantra, they shall remain in this world until the full moon of the month of Caitra, by the will of Hari.
When they go to the imperishable state on the full moon day,
then, having become two-armed, those auspicious ones become equal to those liberated from the syllable (akṣara).
They shall go to the supreme abode, the imperishable, through the grace of the illustrious Lord;
likewise, Hari himself [will lead] Śūra, Śūradevī, and the heroic Bhatyas.
Having commanded them to remain for the sake of the sacrifice, Hari fed them with nectar and made them drink his own holy water from his feet.
And he caused Śūrajāraka to dwell in his own palace,
awakening him with various words that bestow liberation.
O King, wherever there is a man or a woman, there is the latent impression of worldly existence;
O King, wherever there is Hari and I, there is the realization of the Imperishable.
O King, wherever my saints are, there I am, O Supreme Person;
and wherever those dear to Brahmā are, there is my imperishable abode.
Even Māyā attains divinity in every way through my yoga;
she becomes liberated and takes the form of the Imperishable—what then need be said of others? (77)
Although all these granddaughters of yours appear as women, they are nonetheless transformations of the bodies of elemental beings through my yogic power. (78)
All shall become liberated, free from illusion, and identical with my own nature;
O King, many indeed have attained divinity in the past by worshipping me.
Just as the women were liberated, so too did men become liberated;
through my yoga, many men became like Nārāyaṇa.
There were many Nārāyaṇas, and there were indeed many who were also Nārāyaṇas;
likewise, there were many supreme persons (pum-uttama) who were Nārāyaṇas. ||8.1||
Indeed, many Puruṣottamas have appeared;
they bear the name Puruṣottama within the teaching of Puruṣottama. (82)
Devotees of Puruṣottama dwell in his abode, accompanied by him;
they are like Puruṣottama himself in their qualities, virtues, and powers. (83)
Then, by means of their sovereign powers and the splendor of their forms, those supreme persons [declared]:
"I am the Supreme Person among these Supreme Persons. (84)
For he is the director of all; thus, he is the Supreme among the Supreme Persons.
There is no one equal to me, so what need is there to mention another? (85)
Such as I am, I have indeed arrived in your kingdom as the son of you;
my kingdom is the true kingdom, for that which is on earth is not mine, being indeed false.
Bliss in truth is great bliss; it is not of illusion, for it is not false.
Here, my happiness is true happiness, not material, because the latter is false. (87)
I am indeed the family, not the physical body, for that reason;
though the body is called by that name and appears transformed, it is not truly transformed through my union.
That which is called "false" by name is indeed untrue; for that which is unstable apart from me is not truly false when united with me. (89)
That which is devoid of me should be avoided, while that which is endowed with me must indeed be accepted;
for everything else is empty without me, whereas that which is joined with me fulfills all needs.
Without me, everything is dissolution; joined with me, it becomes prosperous. Whatever is defilement without me, that very thing, when joined with me, becomes like me. (9.1)
"All my devotees are like me; therefore, they are the supreme among men.
Knowing me thus, worship me and become like that.
Having spoken thus, the glorious Hari granted his own vision right there to Śūrajāra, the most excellent among the most excellent of men. 93.
With divine vision, Śūrajāra beheld the Supreme Lord,
the Puruṣottama, who is served by Ananta, Parameśa, and others.
Then he rejoiced and realized the greatness of Śrī Hari;
thereafter, Hari concealed his divine nature and appeared like a human being.
In a mere moment he became gracious and said to Vīraka:
"Take rest, O Indra among kings; you must indeed depart quickly at dawn."
On the eleventh day of the fourth month, for the sake of glory,
he began that sacrifice at the confluence of the ocean on the eleventh day of the dark fortnight of the month of Pauṣa.
"I shall perform the full [rite] on the second day of the bright fortnight of Pauṣa"—having been addressed thus, Vīrajāra, Śūrajāra, and others likewise [responded]. (98)
They rested with ease, and Hari likewise took his rest;
at night, the blessed Lord Hari slept, attended by the maidens.
On the morning of the eleventh day, having risen quickly and performed his worship,
he became composed and traveled by celestial chariot, attended by the royal family.
Accompanied by his parents and flourishing with his subjects,
he went in an instant to the sacrificial ground in the kingdom of King Śaktyakṣi.
Then, having whirled the vast surface of the earth around in his aerial chariot, he gazed repeatedly at the sky from the vessel that was like a boat upon the ocean.

Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of Liberation through the Bestowal of an Imperishable Divine Body Consisting of a Golden Person upon the Great King Śūrajāra—the Father of King Vīrajāra—who Possessed a Divine Celestial Form along with His Family," in the second section, the *Tretā-santāna*, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Listen, O Rādhikā; having seen the vast surface of the earth in the sky, well-prepared for the sake of sacrifice by King Śaktyakṣi, [he descended]. || 1 ||
The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa Svāmī, the supreme among persons,
dwells on the western bank of the Ālanaukā river until the end of time.
Having observed a beautiful pavilion on the ground for fifty krośas as far as the northern shore of the ocean, he brought down a celestial chariot.
Then a white light, like ten million suns, appeared in the sky;
at that time, shouts of victory, hymns of praise, and sounds of joy arose.
Then there arose hymns of praise from the cane-clad bards accompanied by shouts of victory,
while various musical instruments were sounded on all sides.
All of them, filled with intense enthusiasm, ran toward that celestial chariot to see the Lord Bālakṛṣṇa and to offer him congratulations with garlands and other gifts.
The king and the people went forth to honor him with flower garlands and other offerings as he descended from his celestial chariot amidst a great throng of men and women.
With joyful faces, they eagerly celebrated Bālakṛṣṇa;
with delight, they offered a welcome with parched grain, unbroken rice, and flowers.
Then the glorious Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Supreme Person, went to bathe at the confluence of the river and the ocean thereafter.
Having arrived quickly at the sacrifice, the Lord shone resplendent upon a golden throne offered by the king, while the virtuous ones awaited him in the midst of the assembly.
The sages headed by Lomaśa, the lords of the gods headed by Brahmā and Indra, the Brahmins headed by Patnīvrata, and likewise the Nārāyaṇas who are liberated; || 11 ||
Gaṇeśa and the other deities of the sacrifice, as well as the goddesses and the Mothers,
along with all the gods of creation and others, shone resplendently in the magnificent pavilion.

The recitation of benedictions, purification of the body, binding of the forearm and so forth, the consecration of the deities of the limbs, and the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) of the principal deity. || 13 ||
The installation of the sacred fire, the oblations, and so forth occurred just as in previous rites; likewise, the sounds of the Vedas and songs arose according to the prescribed order. || 14 ||
The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Person (Śrī Puruṣottama), whose mouth is Agni, consumes the oblation offered by the king along with various materials. 15.
That seven-day period is born as the Vaiṣṇava season,
during which embodied beings dwelling in the three worlds are satisfied by eating directly before their eyes.
The liberated ones, the lords, the incarnations, the goddesses, the gods and others;
the female deities, the goddesses of the gods, and the guardians of the directions and the protectors of the worlds. || 17 ||
The gods of sacrifice, the gods of the worlds, and likewise the deities of the sacred fields;
humans, those dwelling in the world of Vāyu, those situated in the waters, and even those dwelling at the bottom. 18.
Trees, those who drink the wind, and likewise living beings who drink coldness;
sacred fords, the virtuous, sages, ancestors, Daityas, and Dānavas.
The Rākṣasas and even the tamasic living beings, both stationary and moving,
became satiated by the sacrificial offerings and the enjoyment of sweet foods.
And there, nothing whatsoever was lacking, thanks to the wish-fulfilling trees, jewels, and creepers;
there were foods such as edibles and chewables produced [magically], as well as the milk of the wish-granting cows.
Abundant sacrificial fees consisting of gold and jewels were presented;
indeed, the gifts of food, clothing, and ornaments were truly endless.
There, King Śaktyakṣi bestowed [the gifts] in the presence of Hari,
and thereafter a seven-day exemption was granted on the second lunar day.
And the final purificatory bath (avabhṛtha) was performed at the midpoint and at the conclusion when [the rivers] met in the ocean,
as well as in the waters of the Anāvara ocean mixed with the water of the *ālana* boat.
And at the Anāvarā river, as well as at Ālanaukā and Sarit, there were then gifts of elephants, horses, camels, goats, and cattle. (25)
Vehicles, mounts, fields, orchards, and lands, as well as houses endowed with prosperity, were likewise bestowed by the king upon the brahmins. (26)
At that time, gifts of daughters were given to the destitute, as well as gifts of food,
and various acts of charity involving gold, silver, and ornaments were bestowed.
Devoted to the temple of the gods, he spoke of its greatness:
"O Rādhikā, listen to the auspiciousness of the avabhṛtha bath compared to all others. (28)
By descending into the entire sacrifice so that it may reach completion without obstacle, there is a final rite; that accumulation consists of the *bhṛtha* offering.
Whatever deficiency occurs in a sacrifice, such as the abandonment [of rites] or the causing of pain to living beings—
whatever misconduct exists there, all that is destroyed by the *bhṛtha* bath.
That bath in which all evil— whether born of impurity, or arising from speech, body, or mind— is indeed destroyed, is called *bhṛtha*.
Indeed, upon the recitation of mantras, or even during the offering of oblations in a sacrifice,
whatever sin arises from greed and the like— all that fear perishes.
The failure to satisfy those who come with hope by providing water, food, and sacrificial fees—
even if it results in a sin as small as an atom or a mere speck— that sin is destroyed by that ritual fee (dakṣiṇā).
If a creature should suddenly fall into the fire while the fuel is being kindled,
even its subtle association with wood causes that sin to perish through the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
Furthermore, if there is purity in the preparation of the vessels and the oblations, [the rite is successful].
That sin would not be complete, and it is indeed destroyed by that sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā). || 35 ||
If that which is most dear to the gods is not gathered together, there is indeed a deficiency in the oblation;
yet even so, sin is destroyed by that *bhṛtha* offering.

That state of being burnt in fire which belongs to seeds capable of producing sprouts is indeed the destruction of the sin consisting of the destruction of seeds; therefore, that [fire] is the *bhṛtha*. (37)
Even that which has fallen from the sky by the beaks of vultures and other birds, or whatever else is impure, is purified; that sin is destroyed by the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā). || 38 ||
When there is an invocation of innumerable deities at some sacrifice, one who does not exhale [during the rite] destroys that evil; that is the *bhṛtha* (concluding oblation).
Even at the time of reciting the mantra, surely, as the syllables emerge from the mouth, drops of spittle fly out; by that, evil is instantly destroyed. (2.130.40)
When Brahmins possessed of lust, anger, and other such defects are chosen for a sacrifice,
whatever sin arises from that association is surely destroyed by the *bhṛtha* offering.
If a bad dream should occur during the patron’s anxiety, or if there is illness, birth-impurity, or sin, that is indeed destroyed by the *bhṛtha* offering. (42)
Furthermore, when an undesirable expenditure occurs or a sudden,
severe expense arises, the sin born of the contraction of one's spending is indeed destroyed by that sacrificial fee (bhṛtha).
In some cases, there may be the destruction of those who cause obstacles to the sacrifice;
at that time, the sin resulting from such violence is indeed destroyed by that *bhṛtha* (concluding oblation).

The secondary status of expiatory rites and the like, the secondary status of celibacy and the like, and the secondary status of the ritual section (karmakāṇḍa) and the like—that sin perishes as the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā). ||45||
The merit that arises constantly at every sacrifice, individually within each of its constituent parts and so forth—all that merit combined together forms a mountain of merit. ||46||
If indeed some harm should arise for the sacrificer, he should perform the *bhṛtha* oblation for its destruction;
for sometimes, due to the power of time, there may be a lack of auspiciousness during the sacrifice. (47)
When the sacrifice has been completed, that evil born of it is indeed destroyed by the *bhṛtha* offering.
This applies whether the slighting of the gods and so forth was done unknowingly, or even if such slighting of those worthy of worship was done knowingly. (48)
The sin of honoring those who are unworthy of honor is indeed destroyed by that sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā). ||49||
Varuṇa is eternally the witness, the presiding deity of the waters;
in heaven he bestows prosperity, for he is essentially Nārāyaṇa himself. (2.130.50)
All the gods reside with the sacrificer, and the goddesses with the sacrificer's wife;
at the time of the ritual bath, they dwell indeed in the *bhṛtha*—the sacred ford that is the soul of all.

The venerable Hari resides in the teacher; the incarnations dwell among those who perform sacrifices; the lords abide in the officiating priests; and the sacrificial bath is the holy ford that comprises all things.

The sacred fords (*tīrthas*) are among those who recite prayers, the principles (*tattvas*) are among those performing rituals, and the sages (*ṛṣis*) are among those providing assistance; the all-pervading bath (*bhṛtha-tīrtha*) is [the goal].
Barley sprouts should be offered to the high-souled Varuṇa.
Then, the five limbs beginning with clarified butter (ghṛta) should be offered into the water.
The five nectars (pañcāmṛta) offered there are indeed obtained again in heaven;
the Lord of Waters (Jaleśvara) is to be worshipped with the sixteen secondary substances (upasuvastu) and others.
There dwells Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of the Imperishable, the Supreme Person;
bathing in the water and bathing in Hari bestow great merit as a concluding purificatory rite (avabhṛtha).

Where there is sacrifice, a feast of food, the recitation of the Vedas, the nectar of sacred discourse, the ritual bath (avabhṛtha), and immersion—that is considered the eternal sacred ford (tīrtha). //57//
Rivers, streams, ponds, lakes, as well as oblong pools, natural pools, and excavated reservoirs— indeed, all sacred bathing places were purified by the avabhṛtha bath.
At the moment of the Avabhṛtha bath, the purifying water should be taken up in vessels;
for when offered into the mouth of a mortal at the time of death, it indeed bestows liberation. ||99||
For the sake of destroying the sins of sinners, the sacrificial deities and others always bathe at the site of the avabhṛtha ceremony and remain there indeed.
But even for any deceased embodied being whatsoever, if even a small portion of their bone, leaf, or limb falls into the avabhṛtha [concluding bath], [they attain liberation].
Whether situated in the next world, or as a departed spirit (preta) gone to the realm of Yama, or even from there to an evil destination,
he goes to the eternal abode of Śrī Hari.
Evil deeds perish and mountains of merit arise for one who bathes at the site of the final purificatory rite; the worlds of the hereafter bestow happiness upon such a bather.
In the world of Avabhṛthasthalī, there is the month of Śrī Puruṣottama, and the three images of Bālakṛṣṇa, which are the most excellent bestowers of liberation. ||64||
In this world, the virtuous Vaiṣṇavas are indeed known as Sāṃkhyayogins; the three *saṃhitās*—the *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā* and the others—are the three forms of Hari. (656)
Brahmapriyā, Brahmamuktā, and Brahmakekumavāpikā—
these three are indeed the sacred bathing places (tīrthas) of Brahmā, which constitute the final purificatory baths of all sacrifices.
In his heart, there is always the constant remembrance of Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa;
in his hand is a garland of tulasī, and upon his neck as well is a tulasī wreath.
These three grant the abode of the Imperishable (akṣara) by means of mere faith:
the tilaka on the forehead, the moon [mark], and the drawing of the discus and other symbols on the arms. (68)
The three— namely, the name of Śrī Hari on the tongue,
Vaiṣṇavas in the house, and Tulasī in the garden— are the destroyers of Yama.

Even among animals, he whose three cows cross to the further shore of existence, he whose wife is devoted to her husband, and he who possesses compassion for the true guru—[these are the ones who attain liberation]. (2.130.70)

He who possesses knowledge of the scriptures coupled with devotion, and by whom his entire physical body has been offered to Hari-Kṛṣṇa, is one who has reached the further shore of the ocean of worldly existence.
Peaceful in conduct and free from worldly desire, these three bestow a state of stainless purity:
he for whom the night dwells with Hari, and he for whom the morning is spent in His worship. (72)
And at midday, during the portion of knowledge, he indeed becomes liberated here while still possessing a form,
through association with the virtuous, through the yoga of sacrifice, and through yoga that brings Śārṅgin (Viṣṇu) within one's direct perception.
Neither a man nor a woman is born superior to another once they have performed the *avabhṛtha* bath;
[for all] the ritual bath at the conclusion of a sacrifice, the bath with sesame seeds, and the bath with *āmalaka* fruits are equal. (74)
By recollecting the sacred fords (tīrthas), one should perform [the rite]; it becomes superior even to the final purificatory bath (avabhṛtha).
Likewise, at the time of death, there is the sacrificial ground as well as Nārāyaṇa Hari.
It is recorded that virtuous men and women obtain a fruit even greater than that [of ordinary merit]:
namely, what is gained by the gift of ten million maidens and by a thousand sacrifices. ||76||
The fruit that is obtained from a thousand fields of grain is attained through the avabhṛtha bath,
as well as through the Cāturmāsya vows and the study of the Vedas.
Whatever fruit is obtained on earth through a thousand years of austerity or by the gift of a thousand cows, that same fruit shall be attained from the avabhṛtha bath.
By pilgrimages to all sacred fords, by service to one's father and mother, by service to one's husband, by service to cows, and by service to the gods; ||79||
Whatever fruit is obtained by residing in a divine sacred field and likewise by the service of Tulasī, that same fruit shall be gained by serving the feet of a saintly person.
Even a man or woman devoid of intelligence should worship Hari after hearing this narrative;
one should constantly serve the virtuous, for through their power even liberation may be attained. (8.1)
He who possesses no wealth, nor land, nor even a garden, and whose livelihood consists merely of manual labor, as well as service and slavery; ||82||
Therefore, one should indeed serve the temple of Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa by means of sweeping, smearing, and washing with water. ||83||
By removing refuse and the like, by the crafting of flower garlands and such, by handicrafts, and by the constant washing of clothes and other items; (84)
By washing the bowls, by scrubbing the walls, by removing cobwebs, and by clearing away dust; ||85||
And by the arrangement of objects, by the act of lighting lamps at the crossroads, by the task of opening the gates, and by the sounding of musical instruments; ||86||

And by means of kīrtana with rhythmic beats and the like, by the recounting of his qualities, by shouts of "Victory! and "Hare!", and by devotional acts such as the use of rosaries and so forth; ||87||
By bringing forth vessels, by the purification of grains, by the fetching of water, and by hymns of praise and circumambulations; ||88||
By prostrations like a staff, by the grasping of his qualities, and by divine states of being filled with love that serve to delight the mind; ||89||
The temple of Śrī Kṛṣṇa should also be served by bringing clay; this may be done by a woman, by a man, or by either one, according to their ability. (2.130.90)

Whatever may be possible according to one's strength, according to what can be accomplished, and according to what is appropriate—that should be the manner of service rendered to the temple, even by the virtuous. (9.1)
Thus, that great devotee of the Lord who serves as a servant is indeed purifying and superior to all ritual ablutions (avabhṛtha). ||92||
"Come then for the final ablution," thus instructed the sage Devāyatana; thereafter, Śrī Puruṣottama became silent. 93.
And he said: "I am pleased with the great many offerings presented here by the king in this sacrifice;
I am also pleased by his service. May the king be ever victorious in this world! (94)
Then the king fell at the feet of the Supreme Lord, Śrī Hari;
a golden necklace was then placed by Hari around his neck.
The king honored all the guests with gifts and other offerings; having received their blessings, he then granted them leave to depart. (96)
The people returned to their own dwellings and rested for a moment;
the king then fed the embodied beings of the three worlds.
There he gave sacrificial fees, and all embodied beings were gratified;
during the night, the people and the celestial sages held a great festival.
Indeed, for the sake of pleasing the Blessed One with communal singing and dancing, they then went to sleep; and having risen in the morning, they performed their daily rites.
Having performed [the rites] there in that assembly, they were then honored by Śrī Hari with the presentation of priceless offerings, including the deities and others.
Then, having been fed by Hari, they were all commanded:
"In order to perform the fifth sacrifice, you must go this very evening."
On the shore of the ocean in the land of King Kālima, on the earth,
the commencement of the sacrifice shall take place on the fifth day of the bright fortnight of Pauṣa.
"I shall come there on the fourth day, specifically at evening.
Having said this, the Blessed One bestowed the Manus upon those worlds who seek liberation.
May Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa be my refuge at all times—men, women, and others alike—who desire liberation and have taken shelter in the kingdom of Śakti. 104.
Oṃ, salutation to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord; svāhā!
[I seek refuge] from the fear of Time, Māyā, evil karma, enemies, Yama, and wicked-hearted beings. 1.05
Bearing the trident, fish, banner, bow, discus, and svastika, I am Brahmā; I am the eternal devotee of Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. (1.06)
The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa is my Lord and my husband;
Bālakṛṣṇa, the Supreme Brahman, is indeed my eternal husband.
May He be my father, kinsman, well-wisher, friend, protector, and nourisher;
may Śrī Hari, the beloved Lord of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, be my refuge. 108.
Hari himself bestowed these mantras upon those seeking liberation;
then, being thus commanded, they all proceeded there for the sake of the Pañcama sacrifice.
For the sake of a sacrifice, on the bank of the Kālī river within the kingdom of King Kālīma, Śrī Hari was served there by King Śaktyakṣi and Rādhikā. (2.130.110)
The beloved Lord stayed for two days, delighting the eager king,
and out of compassion bestowed spiritual knowledge upon the king and the others.

Thus ends the one hundred and thirtieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Performance of the Fourth Viṣṇu Sacrifice in the Kingdom of King Śaktyakṣi, the Greatness of the Manifestation of the Purpose of the Concluding Bath (Avabhṛtha), and so forth," in the second section, the Tretā-saṃtāna, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Listen, O Rādhikā; at dawn on the third lunar day, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa spoke these beneficial words to the lord of the earth named Śaktyakṣi.
The sacrifice has been performed by you perfectly; all embodied beings have been satisfied.
I, Śrī Hari myself, am pleased; nothing further remains to be gratified.
When Śrī Hari Kṛṣṇa is satisfied, all embodied beings become satisfied;
for the Lord, the indwelling soul of all, who resides within my heart, is satisfied.
"Tell me your desire here; I shall grant you the most excellent of boons.
I am pleased with your devotion; I give you whatever is wished for in your mind."
Thus addressed, the king said: "Always dwell here in this palace;
I shall have a beautiful golden temple constructed for you out of gold."
"Therefore, for my own welfare, dwell there forever like an image;
Hari replied, 'So be it,' and said, 'I shall dwell in your temple.'"
"Install there my beautiful golden image,
accompanied by Rādhā, Lakṣmī, Ramā, Brahmavidyā, Śrī, and Māṇikī."
Dwelling always within your form, I shall perform service and other duties;
being devoted to your affection, I shall remain there just as if you were present in person.
Just as I always abide as the inner self within the hearts of people, so shall I dwell as the inner self within this image, remaining within its range of perception.
Just as [I am] in the great field of the Imperishable (Akṣara-kṣetra) and in the abode known as the Imperishable (Akṣara-dhāman),
so shall I become the object of perception here in Kuṅkumavāpī.

That divine form of mine which serves as the inner controller (antaryāmin) for the purpose of being worshipped, possesses a power dependent upon the will of the devotee; it is considered the source of ultimate welfare for all the worlds. 1.1.11.
"In this first age, fashion my form to a height of seven tālas,
so that humans shall indeed be tall."
Just as there is indeed a decline of embodied beings during the times of other ages,
so too is my form approved by them according to the essence of their minds.
Just as it should be well-proportioned for worship, travel, dwelling, and mounting a chariot, so should it be made; it must not exceed the measurement of a man.
A single measure cannot apply to humans across different times;
it is determined that one's own [measure] is seven spans for oneself alone. (15)
Just as the body becomes long, so too does the arm become long;
and just like the arm, his fingers likewise become long at that time.
The finger is likewise long according to the proportions of that particular body;
it is short like a child's finger in childhood, and becomes long like a youth's finger in youth, and so forth.
And today I am in your house, measured by my own fingers; I am fifty-six and a half cubits in height and possess a beautiful form. (18)
He had the luster of a golden campaka flower, was as tall as his knees,
possessed eyes reaching to his ears, and was endowed with curved eyebrows.
He was resplendent with a row of teeth resembling jasmine buds;
he bore a broad tilaka upon his forehead, and his body was endowed with fullness.
O King, my auspicious form must be fashioned by you with a broad and elevated chest, and adorned with well-developed thighs and arms. (21)
On my right side indeed are Lakṣmī, Brahmavidyā, and Ramā;
Lakṣmī is sixty finger-breadths [in height], and Brahmavidyā is fifty-seven.
Then, from Ramā, there were indeed three daughters, forty-four finger-breadths in height;
they were all radiant, with the luster of gold, and sixteen years of age. (23)
Now, on my left side are Rādhā, Māṇikī, and Śrī;
Rādhā is considered to be sixty finger-breadths [in height], while Māṇikī is fifty-seven. (24)
The third [line] is Śrī, richly endowed with great beauty, measuring fifty-four finger-breadths;
it should be measured by my own fingers and fashioned so as to be adorned by the moon. (25)
Beautiful, with slender waists, holding vessels for worship and other implements in their hands,
they were all radiant, possessing the luster of gold, and sixteen years of age.
Richly endowed with all auspicious beauty, with every limb perfectly formed,
they were robust, possessed of cheerful countenances, and adorned with ornaments of liquid substances.
I, Hari, four-armed and endowed with the conch, discus, mace, lotus, śrīvatsa mark, and kaustubha gem, must be installed by you in the center.
Beautiful, eighteen years of age, and bearing the royal insignia, he must be made complete in all the marks upon his body; it must not be otherwise.
"O King, having thus established me, perform my worship perpetually in the middle temple, and then in the right temple."
Establish me, along with my father and mother, before Bālakṛṣṇa, who is dark as a rain cloud and beautiful in his twelve-year form.
Behold! Here shines my father, the illustrious Gopālakṛṣṇa;
here shines my mother, Kaṃbharā-Lakṣmī. Look! (32)
Likewise, fashion the three forms through the medium of artistic skill;
then, construct a beautiful bed for me in my left chamber.
"Adorned with the splendor of golden balls and equipped with all necessary implements, have an elephant and a garuḍa fashioned near the central temple. (34)
Indeed, place those two auspicious feet of mine in the center of the excellent palace at the foremost point, specifically within the small pavilion at the crossroads. (35)
O Indra among kings, install my attendant at the city gate—he who is devoted to the temple of the God and is known by the name Raṇaṅgama. (36)
And having made those two excellent auspicious ones equipped with all weapons, appoint Hemanta and Vasanta as the gatekeepers. (37)
Make them self-luminous, as luminous as the sky, and serve as their illuminators;
place those who produce the sound of victory upon the excellent frontal sections of the temple. (38)
Likewise, place the auspicious Lord Santoṣa, Śuka,
and Vallabha together with the arghya vessels upon the side-sections.
Construct the twelve zodiac signs above the temple;
let those auspicious ascetics be images of the sages and devotees of Viṣṇu.
There were one hundred and forty principal wives dear to Brahmā;
for all my wives and for the men as well, [there were] separately. (41)
In the form of a *rāsa*, cause [the assembly] to enter the circular palace situated in the center and above;
taking up musical instruments, place the circle in the middle. 42.
Whether by the craft of artisans or by the knowledge of the Caitras,
I am in their midst, with twenty-four wives on each side— two hundred in total.
Thus, O King, always practice gentle service;
there I shall become your range of perception and I will dwell here, of this there is no doubt.
Then the king said to Kṛṣṇa, out of a desire for his divine vision:
"Grant me your divine vision while you are indeed established in the palace. (45)
Indeed, having seen that beautiful [scene] together with his six wives, as well as the forms of the ancestors and the *rāsa* dance, I likewise prepare a bed. (46)
Thus addressed, O Rādhikā, the Blessed Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa immediately showed himself, as well as his statues and temples. 47.
The Blessed One, of auspicious form, was pervaded by a splendor like that of many millions of suns; he was accompanied by his sixteen-year-old wives.
Having indeed displayed his own forms residing in the divine abode,
he gratified the king as well as the king's family.
The sixty princesses, as well as the hundred princes and the queen,
were struck with wonder upon seeing Puruṣottama directly before their eyes.
Then the king, perceiving that the minds of the maidens were drawn toward Hari for the sake of obtaining him as their husband,
and the queen likewise understanding that to be so, [acted accordingly].
He gave sixty young maidens to Śrī Hari;
having obtained Hari as their husband, they all indeed became fulfilled.
Having obtained Hari as their son-in-law, the king and queen attained great joy;
they then considered themselves especially fulfilled. 53.
Overwhelmed with love, the maidens performed the worship of Śrī Hari;
eager and longing, they offered the garland of choice upon Hari’s neck. (54)
There they served Hari with food and other offerings with great devotion; the king also gave him an unexpected and abundant amount of divine wedding gifts.
He also gave necklaces made of divine jewels and other gems numbering in the millions and billions,
as well as sixty excellent divine female slaves.
Then the king presented four-tusked white elephants,
as well as a divine chariot of great speed, [drawn] by a thousand men.
He bestowed the land as a gift for the purpose of establishing a convent for the girls;
and Śrī Hari, having thus obtained the gift, dwelt there in happiness.
Having performed the fourth [rite] there, she said to the lord of men at evening:
"In the evening, you must go to the land of Kālimā for the sake of the fifth sacrifice. (59)
"Come, O King, with your family to the sacrifice along with me.
Thus addressed, the lord of the earth prepared himself together with his servants.
While Hari was drinking water,
there arrived a certain Piśācī of wretched appearance, accompanied by a hundred servants.
At that time, she wept profusely there in the presence of Śrī Hari;
the Blessed Lord Śrī Hari said, "Who are you, and why do you weep? (62)
"What is your sorrow? Who are your friends? Tell me; I shall bring you happiness.
Then, overcome with shame, she did not say anything at all.
Just then, Śaktyakṣi arrived there before Hari;
seeing him, she wept again, wailing repeatedly.
Having seen her, the king asked, "Who are you, and why do you weep?
At that moment, she assumed for an instant the form she had held in her previous birth.
The king’s eldest sister, a young maiden, died;
through the fault of the poison of latent tendencies, she became a piśācī.
And she said to the king: "Without my sacred thread, I have become sickly; though still in the bloom of youth, I am on the verge of death before my marriage. (67)
With a heart possessed by latent impressions and through craving for a man, I quickly attained the state of a preta; indeed, I dwell here in this forest.
And whatever other maidens possess hearts filled with latent desires, they too meet their death; these are the women who exist [in this state]. (69)
"For my friends are indeed Piśācinīs, the wives of Piśācas;
our husbands are Piśācas who, having eaten the remnants of the sacrifice," || 2.131.70 ||
Having shaken off their sins, they have attained liberation, heaven, or that supreme state;
whereas we, being devoid of such grace, remain here in our very homes.
Due to the suppression of the Piśācas, they did not assemble here at the sacrifice;
nor was even a sight of the beautiful sacrificial rite obtained. (72)
If our state as Piśācīs has not perished during such a sacrifice, then those Piśācas have attained liberation while we, wretched and inauspicious women, remain behind. (73)
The weak have no strength without a protector, O Immutable One;
being deprived of both children and husbands, they have therefore come here. (74)
"O King, O brother Hari-Kṛṣṇa, do what is auspicious out of a desire for liberation.
I am your sister, as are these daughters of the subjects who have died. (75)
Therefore, we have come for refuge to the God of gods for the sake of liberation;
grant us great liberation so that suffering may truly never exist for us. (76)
The king said: "By what karma were these female piśācas produced? Tell me this, and may there be well-being for you from that. (77)
And the sister said to the king, "Listen to the origin of the Piśācikā:
there is a girl who dwells in her father’s house, merciless and exceedingly wrathful. (78)
And she who excessively incites quarrels shall become a female piśāca after death;
having disregarded her own mother, she is independent and a destroyer of virtuous conduct. 79.
And that female piśāca, submerged in evil karma, having died, was devoted to secret sins and devoid of merit and dharma. (2.131.80)

There is no one more devoted to serving her mother than she who is devoted to the worship of Kṛṣṇa; there is no one who cleanses the home more than she who is devoted to the worship of Kṛṣṇa. She who is devoted to the worship of Kṛṣṇa cannot be a female ghost, even if she has died. (81)
Just as a mother, sister, brother’s wife, or even a wife who has been provoked to anger, if she becomes a malevolent spirit (piśācinī), she may cause the family to become defiled and perish. 82.
One who is devoid of bathing and worship, likewise possessed by menstrual impurity, impure, or having sexual intercourse with a beast, shall become a *piśācinī* upon death. (83)
She who commits suicide, she who destroys her family, and she who kills her father and others—upon death, she becomes a female demon (piśācinī). //84//
That girl who, under the sway of anger, repeatedly strikes children,
and who commits theft in the house, shall become a dead Piśācinī.
She who kills living beings in their hair or on their clothes, and who, even though aware of it, does so at the hearth—she shall become a female Piśāca spirit. (86)
She who kills mice, cats, or other living beings, or who causes the death of calves, shall become a female Piśāca spirit after she dies. (87)
She who does not cause milk to be given to the children of the chief queen, or even gives buttermilk to that mother—she shall become a female Piśāca demon. (88)
She who harms birds and animals, she who kills living beings, she who is wanton, she who is unchaste, as well as she who is lustful and a courtesan; ||89||
One who consumes liquor and meat becomes a destroyer of embryos and indeed a female Piśāca;
likewise, if she dies in water or by fire, she remains afflicted by hunger and thirst.
