If she dies submerged in the earth or in a cave and the like, she becomes a *piśācinī*.
She who dies without having been consecrated—whether she be intact or even wounded—[becomes such]. (9.1)
"Devoid of devotion and possessed by passion, she becomes a female ghost (piśācinī) upon death;
thus, indeed, these women have become female ghosts due to such faults. (92)
O Indra among kings, perform the redemption through the granting of Hari’s grace;
for you have performed a sacrifice here, and likewise, the gift of a maiden has been made.
By that merit, may our physical sin be destroyed;
but our mental sin shall go to destruction through your grace—grant this to us.
"Then Lord Hari, the master and lord of all living beings, shall grant liberation.
Thus, O Rādhikā, was the king himself entreated by them. 95.
He gave them the grace of Hari and water that had touched his feet;
they drank and ate it out of love at that very moment. 96.
Then they became possessed of divine forms, like the goddesses of the Lord of the Gods;
those pure maidens fell at the feet of Hari.
Śrī Hari, immersed in compassion, bestowed his own mantras from his own mouth:
"Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya svāmine svāhā. (98)
May Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa be my refuge at all times, from the fear of time, māyā, sinful karma, enemies, Yama, and wicked-hearted beings. 99.
Bearing the trident, fish, banner, bow, discus, and the svastika, I am Brahmā; I am an eternal devotee of Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. 2.131.100.
The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa is my Lord and my husband;
Bālakṛṣṇa, the Supreme Brahman, is indeed my eternal husband.
May He be my father, kinsman, well-wisher, friend, protector, and guardian;
may Śrī Hari, the beloved Lord of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, be my refuge. 1.02
Having thus bestowed these mantras and given him the sacred thread,
he showed him all his paternal kinsmen and his own family.
As soon as Śrī Hari sent all of them away with a message,
they all became infatuated with Hari and did not wish to go according to that message.
Abandoning their handsome and beloved husband Śrī Puruṣottama,
they chose Harikṛṣṇa, Bālakṛṣṇa, and Narāyaṇa.
Those maidens, numbering in the hundreds, as well as the princesses,
held garlands in their hands, their faces resembling ten million moons.
Then all of them, beautiful and exceedingly radiant, sixteen years of age,
out of love and with the desire for marriage, placed [garlands] around the lovely neck of Kṛṣṇa.
"Out of a desire to please them all, Hari accepted every one of them.
O Rādhikā, having thus taken them into his own celestial chariot, he departed.
Having taken the princess, she then quickly traveled by way of the sky at evening toward the land of Kālimā as a swift retort to the challenge.
"O Rādhikā, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa is the giver of the auspicious marriage-thread; thus indeed is Kṛṣṇasvāmī, the beginningless Supreme Person. (2.131.110)
Then, purifying the hearts of his devotees from the sky,
he went to the kingdom of King Kālimāśa and beheld the earth.
By reading or hearing this, one shall become a partaker of the fruit of liberation;
and whoever causes it to be read or heard, he too shall obtain the fruit of liberation.

Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Dispatching of the Celestial Sages for the Fifth Sacrifice after the Sacrifice [of King Śaktyakṣi], the Offering of Sixty Maidens by the King to Hari, the Causes of Becoming Piśācīs, and the Liberation of One Hundred and One Piśācinīs," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Listen, O Rādhikā; the Lord Nārāyaṇa-Nārāyaṇa beheld from the sky in his celestial chariot the land of King Āśan, which was dark with the hue of Kālī.
During the conjunction with the Kālimā ocean, he beheld a vast pavilion,
fifty yojanas in length, extending as far as the auspicious Yānā river.

By means of that celestial chariot, there was indeed illumination everywhere— over the surface of the earth as well as in the cardinal and intermediate directions— with a splendor equal to ten million suns.
Then musical instruments were sounded and shouts of victory arose from men,
gods, and embodied beings who are lords.
Then the spectators also quickly ran toward that auspicious ground,
which was worthy of the descent from the celestial chariot, carrying parched grain, unbroken rice, and flowers.
On the shore of the ocean, Kṛṣṇa brought down the celestial chariot;
he himself descended from it, and then the king and the others followed.
Then all those beloved of Brahmā descended from their celestial chariots;
they were honored with gifts of necklaces and other offerings, and their prosperity was increased with parched grain and unbroken rice.
Then all those born together with Śrī Kṛṣṇa were honored by the subjects with shouts of victory and welcomed with prostrations as they were beheld by the people.
They were seated upon thrones and honored with offerings of honey-mixture (madhuparka);
they were gratified with drinks of water and the like, and likewise fed with sweet foods.
Likewise, they were rested at night and massaged so that they were comfortable; and they were put to sleep in palaces upon priceless beds and the like.
Then King Kālimāśa, together with his family,
duly served and paid homage to Kṛṣṇa and his family as was appropriate.
At dawn, Hari was awakened by the songs of instrumental music and the like;
listening to the praises of the bards, he performed his dental cleansing.
Nārāyaṇeśvara bathed with fragrant water and other substances;
having donned a pair of garments, he put on ornaments.
The kings and others performed the worship of Śrī Hari with the splendors of their royal power;
likewise, the beloved wives of Brahmā performed the supreme worship of the Lord.
On the fifth day, at an auspicious time, he went to the sacrificial pavilion;
he saw that everything was ready and had it prepared by Lomaśa.
Likewise, by means of his vow as a devoted husband, he then caused King Kālimāśa to undertake the commencement of the sacrifice and to perform the formal resolve (saṃkalpa) for the rite.
He had his forearms bound following the recitation of benedictions,
and he engaged the Brahmins and sages in the purpose of the mantras through chanting, fire-offerings, singing, and other rites.
He chose as his bridegrooms the gods and lords, those who are not lords, the dwellers of heaven, sages, virtuous men, chaste women, noble ladies, and divine maidens. (18)
She chose the principles of the sacred fords (tīrthas), the sons of Diti, the offspring of Kaśyapa, and those worthy ones who were deities embodied in visible form.
At the site of the principal deity, the glorious Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa was present; Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and the others were also visibly manifest as the presiding deities of that place.
There, the guardians of the directions, the mothers, the guardians of the house, the guardians of the field, the planets, and other dark forces each remained in their respective places. ||21||
They too were present there, stationed in their proper places as objects of perception:
the Vasus, the Ādityas, the two Aśvins, and those born of the Sādhyas and Siddhas.
The Brahmins learned in the Vedas, those of the sages' lineage, the gods, and likewise the ancestors;
the seers, the lords, and also the goddesses and their hosts.
Gaṇeśa and his attendants, the supernatural powers (siddhis), the infinite multitudes of liberated souls, all the incarnations, and the consorts of those incarnations; ||24||
At the sacrifice, they appeared in visible form and shone resplendent in their respective places;
even the four Vedas themselves then became embodied.

Likewise, the Ṛg-verses became manifest as mantras possessing form, and the fires likewise took on embodied forms as the personifications of the sacrificial offerings (havya) and ancestral oblations (kavya). || 26 ||
In that supreme Vaiṣṇava sacrifice, all the spheres of perception indeed became present there as rituals, procedures, and embodied forms. ||27||

The ritual injunctions and their applications, the most excellent recipients, the embodied forms, the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles and other implements personified, the *darbha* grass and other materials, as well as rice and barley grains; ||28||
Wheat, wild rice, juices, and honey-sugar—
indeed, all these appeared then, manifest in physical form.
At that time, the sacrificial fuel, the mandalas, the places for installation, the altars, the fire-pits, the protective enclosures, the ritual sections, and so forth, all became embodied forms.
O Rādhā, where Hari himself resides, joined with all bodies, what deficiency can there be regarding food, enjoyments, activities, and the like? 31.
Then, when the worship of Gaṇeśa had taken place, the worship of Rudra and others was performed,
and the worship of the Mātṛkās and so forth had been completed, Śrī Hari himself [appeared].
Then, according to the prescribed ritual, he had the fire established in the sacrificial pit with the measurement of a royal cubit;
at that time, the Vedas uttered their sounds.
Then Agni appeared visibly within the sacrificial pit, shining in the midst of the flames;
and the offering of oblations, accompanied by mantras, proceeded as desired into the fire. (34)
Once the rites for the gods, sages, and ancestors were completed, even the consumption of food and such— beginning with sweet foods, water, and betel— was discontinued.
At night, where discourses and other such activities performed by the Sāttvatas take place, the daily rites are then resumed, beginning with the fire-oblation (havana) and so forth. ||36||
Thus the seven-day sacrifice proceeded as a great festival;
indeed, it was completed on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Pauṣa.
At midday, after the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) had been given, the final oblation was likewise performed;
and even at the conclusion, the Fire-god remained unsatiated by the countless *śrīphala* fruits.
Then indeed Śrī Hari fed the liberated souls (muktas) in every way,
as well as the beloveds of Brahmā, the incarnations, and those who are dear to the incarnations.
And [he saw] the inhabitants of each abode, male and female attendants,
lords and mistresses, Nārāyaṇas and Nārāyaṇīs.

The principles (tattvas), primordial māyā, Brahmā and the others, the forms of the Vyūha, the ancestors, the gods, the Siddhas, the Sādhyas, the sages, the ascetics, and the practitioners of yoga. ||41||

The virtuous men and women, those who have taken refuge in Sāṃkhya and Yoga, the celestial and divine beings, human beings, the guardians of the quarters, and the planets, lunar mansions, and stars. ||42||
The Brahmins residing within the body, as well as those belonging to the various castes and stages of life (āśramas), the trees, creepers, clusters of grass, and the rivers, streams, and lakes; 43.
[He saw] lakes, excavated ponds, oceans, islands, caves, and mountains;
and the inhabitants of the worlds, from the nether regions upward, dwelling in water, on land, or in the air. (44)
Keśava fed all those who had gathered—the lords of the earth dwelling in the subterranean realms and those situated in the cavities of the ground—down to even the insects and moths. 45.
There is no one—whether fasting or dull-witted, whether stationary or even sentient beings equal to the insentient, or even the wise or the powerful—who is not [subject to this]. (46)
Whether they were of the nature of goodness (sāttvika), passion (rājasa), or even darkness (tāmasa), Hari then fed them all, saying, "They are my own sons. (47)
Having been given water to drink and other refreshments, and being gratified with sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā),
they all, together with the illustrious Hari, then took their rest.
Then the illustrious Lord Hari went to perform the final purificatory bath (avabhṛtha), preceded by the sounding of musical instruments, amidst the waters of the Kālindī and the ocean. 49.
Accompanied by songs, all the goddesses indeed went for the purificatory bath (avabhṛtha);
Kālī entered the water, as did others who were in their vehicles within the water.
Then, at the final purificatory bath (avabhṛtha) at the conclusion of the sacrifice, other guests bathed there in the waters of the ocean as well as in wells, tanks, and lakes.
Having remembered the supreme Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, who is without beginning, the beloved, the bestower of peace, and who shines eternally within hearts. (52)
To the Lord who bestows liberation and salvation, the Lord of the lords of Nārāyaṇa, the Sovereign of the abode of Brahman, the glorious Bālakṛṣṇa, Hari, the Master; ||53||
And there the king bestowed gifts of treasuries, camels, and horses;
of elephants, swans, and garuḍas; and of palaces, vehicles, and carriages.
Gold, silver, rubies, diamonds, and pearls;
houses, household utensils, gardens, forests, and groves.
Kālimakeśvara gave away fields, worthy recipients, and all kinds of food;
he bestowed every manner of great gift.
Having thus performed the concluding ablution (avabhṛtha), they returned to their own abode;
in the evening, he provided various kinds of foods and drinks.
King Kālimeśa, addressed by Bālakṛṣṇa, was filled with happiness;
at night, Lakṣmī Mahālakṣmī, in the form of a maiden, [related] the story of Hari.
Seated upon the throne of Vyāsa, she recited the beautiful Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā in the assembly at the command of Bāla-Kṛṣṇa. (5.9)
The rivers and goddesses who are the wives of the ocean, having arrived there,
purified that Mahālakṣmī, and thereafter Śrī Kambharā-satī.
With various objects such as jewels, with captivating necklaces,
and even with divine garments and ornaments, one performs auspicious worship.
Then the forest goddesses,
all the wives of the sacrificers, and likewise the wives of the gods, also performed the *ārātrika* lamp-offering ceremony.
Then the wives of the Pitṛs, the wives of the Siddhas, the wives of the Īśas, as well as the Śris,
the wives of Brahmā, and the wives of the Dhāmas, performed worship.
They joyfully performed the worship of Kambharā, the mother of Hari, who is Lakṣmī;
and the goddesses residing in all of creation performed auspicious worship.
He offered an excuse for both his conversation and his worship by means of various names,
[addressing him as] the Lord of Śrī, the son of the cowherd of Śrī, and the cause of all incarnations.
To Kṛṣṇa, the son of Yaśodā, Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of Ramā, the Lord of all desires, the Lord of Rādhā, and the Lord of Śrīmāṇikī. ||66||
We worship Bālakṛṣṇa, the beloved lord of Brahmapriyā, the husband of Lakṣmī, the protector of the virtuous, and the master of the goddess of Brahman-knowledge. 67.
In this manner, all the members of the assembly performed a delightful recitation;
then, following the acceptance of the favor, they did so for the sake of obtaining rest.
They performed the night-rituals and recounted stories; then they went to their own dwellings and all took sleep, as if it were a state of wakefulness.
Having performed his daily rites on the twelfth lunar day, the king came for the purpose of worship;
he worshipped Bālakṛṣṇa, his own self, with devotion.
They also worshipped the queens with one hundred and eight substances;
twenty queens performed a great waving of lights (ārātrika).
And then, those two hundred maidens were enchanted by Hari,
the Lord of divine form, who was more beautiful than millions upon millions of Cupids.
They indeed chose him, placing the bridegroom’s garland around his neck;
all those queens and maidens there offered it to him. (73)
Śrī Hari accepted those [gifts] for the Supreme Soul, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa; the king also gave them as a wedding dowry.
He gave him a celestial chariot one yojana in length, four-tusked elephants, and Garuḍas as mounts— winged beings capable of traveling through the sky.
At that time, he gave away natural lamps, jewels, male servants, and female servants;
and the son of Kambharā took two hundred of each. (76)
Having obtained that enchanting Supreme Lord as their husband, all the maidens rejoiced exceedingly; nothing further remained to be attained.
Thus, after the sacrifice and following the worship on the twelfth day, Kṛṣṇa placed his own feet upon the king’s heart and his hands upon his head.
Hari also gave a beautiful flower necklace to the queen,
and he gave necklaces set with diamonds to all the other queens as well.
He desired to grant his own vision, which reveals the Supreme Lord;
immediately and suddenly, a circle of light manifested.
Indeed, streams of splendor issue forth from all sides of Śrī Hari;
they pervade the sky like the radiance of ten million billion suns. (8.1)
Then Hari indeed bestowed upon all of them, both men and women, their eyes united together— a divine vision, the Sudarśana, capable of enduring his splendor.
Then the royal family as well as the subjects likewise beheld the Lord Śrī Parameśa, the all-pervading one who transcends the supreme syllable (Parākṣara). 83.
It is frequented by those devoted to various abodes, such as the Brahma-world and others,
as well as by incarnations of the Lord, gods, perfected beings, and humans.
He is the youth of beautiful form, dark and handsome, the remover of lust and pride, the beloved one served by Rādhā and Lakṣmī. ||85||
Two-armed, beautiful, dark-complexioned, the enchanting Bālakṛṣṇa, in the full bloom of youth and endowed with all powers. ||86||
The Lord wore a crown of peacock feathers and was adorned with golden earrings; his lofty chest shone with the Kaustubha gem and a radiant necklace. 87.
Adorned with golden ornaments, holding a flute, with a face slightly tilted,
he then has four arms beautified by the conch, discus, mace, and lotus.
Then, having seen him with two arms, attended by his own daughters and others, established in his own kingdom, residing in a palace, and shining resplendently in their presence; ||89||
Seeing this, they all quickly abandoned their meditative absorption;
they beheld Śrī Hari before them and were struck with wonder at that marvel.
The queens considered themselves to be the king's subjects because he had perfected his self;
then other kings indeed arrived for the purpose of seeing him.
Ruling over the five kingdoms together with their queens, they worshipped the Lord Hari most intensely, as did the great sages thereafter.
The virtuous, gods, mortals, Daityas, and even the lords of devotees,
as well as those dwelling in all the worlds, having arrived, worshipped Acyuta.
The inhabitants of the regions of Rāśiyāna and of Śibirājya, as well as the people of other islands, also worshipped the Lord of Lords. (94)
The subjects resembling the Cāṭakas of Kāma, who were devoted to Ālāyuta, and the people of the eastern lands, worshipped the Supreme Lord. ||95||
Also those born from the spray of the waves, those born from the wind of their wings, the inhabitants of Māloṣṭha Island, and the inhabitants of Sphuṭākṣa Island. ||96||
Those dwelling on the island of Thurāyasa, those residing in Kūṭalāna, those living on the island of Svairanārī, and those inhabiting Kṣemīyāna. ||97||
In this way, other beings as well worshipped the Supreme Lord.
O Rādhā, there was a certain saintly man named Lālāsana who dwelt in the midst of the eastern ocean. 98.
Standing on the island, he traveled by way of the sky to see Kṛṣṇa;
having fallen at his feet, he begged for food from Hari. (99)
Hari gave him excellent payasa, pūrikās, and other foods;
that best of virtuous men ate them, while at that moment drums resounded in the heavens.
The sounds of conchs resounded naturally, and having drunk water, he released a belch indicative of his satisfaction. || 101 ||
At that moment, all the musical instruments were sounded spontaneously; though not being played by anyone, they resounded incessantly—this was a most wonderful marvel.
Then, having been seen by the people, King Kālimeśa said:
"O Bālakṛṣṇa! O Hari, my Lord! O Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, my Master! (103)
"What is this that arises so suddenly? Cease the musical instruments! O Kṛṣṇa, fear arises within me upon hearing these unexpected roars. (104)
Hari said, "There is no fear; this virtuous one is the foremost of my devotees.
He has been performing penance for many kalpas upon a seat of foam in the midst of the ocean."
He sat upon his yogic seat with his consort, having realized that I had arrived here;
when he ate, the sacrifice reached completion, and thus five sacrifices were performed by me.
When one person of sattvic nature is satisfied, indeed the three worlds are satisfied;
he is the very embodiment of existence, consciousness, and bliss, signaling the conclusion of the sacrifice.
"Joy prevails for me; indeed, the musical instruments are sounding with delight.
Having spoken thus, that Hari silenced the sound of the instruments.
Having eaten well, the naked ascetic went to the Lalāsana island;
by reciting or hearing this, both enjoyment and liberation will certainly be attained. 109.
Even insentient things offer honor to those whose minds are solely devoted to Kṛṣṇa;
all elements of reality do so, just as musical instruments played in harmony.

Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Fifth Viṣṇu Sacrifice, the Concluding Bath, the Feast, the Narrative, the Worship, the Gift of Two Hundred Maidens, the Divine Vision, the Worship Performed by the Subjects from Many Islands, the Feast at the Seat of Sādhulāla, and the Natural Sounds of Conchs and Drums," in the second section (Tretā-santāna) of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, concerning the kingdom of King Kālimeśa at the confluence of the Kālimā and the ocean.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Listen, O Rādhikā; I am Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the Lord himself.
On the twelfth lunar day, at the conclusion of the Vaiśvadeva ritual, having fed those engaged in the sacrifice— || 1 ||
After having fed all embodied beings, he indeed attained rest;
and in the evening, he prepared a great assembly hall within the sacrificial pavilion.
And in an instant, he was seen in the assembly seated upon a red lotus,
wearing all saffron-colored garments and bearing a garland of tulasī.
His limbs were proportioned to his form, just as the syllables are arranged by the dweller [of the heart];
he was indeed the very nature of great liberation, manifested through the vow of Brahman.
Chanting the name of Japan, may Kṛṣṇa Bālakṛṣṇa be victorious here;
may the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of the virtuous, be victorious! (5)
Victory to you, O Lord Bālakṛṣṇa, O Supreme Self; salutations be unto you!
Victory to you, O son of Śrī Kambharā; victory to you, O delighter of the cowherds!
This land has been purified by the performance of sacrifice and made sacred to Viṣṇu;
blessed are those men in the world for whom you have appeared here in person.
Blessed are those women and all those men in whose home dwells the Supreme Person;
blessed am I, the king of yogis, who am blissful in truth and consciousness even while sitting upon a stool of saliva.
"Since I have attained Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Supreme Lord,
O Refuge, grant me the mantra as well as the Bhāgavata initiation."
"Grant me the imperishable abode, your station at the end of death.
Thus addressed, the Blessed One bestowed upon him the Vaiṣṇava initiation.
O Rādhikā, for the yogi who dwells on the island and seeks liberation,
the Blessed One caused a pavilion made of plantain trees to be constructed there.
It was enriched with the splendor of leaf-shaped arches, adorned with altars and water-pots,
provided with sacrificial pits, furnished with canopies, and graced by offerings of cow-products and other oblations.
Hari also caused purification with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) for him;
he brought about the purification of the body of that devotee who was seated in the dance posture (lāsāsana).
Then Hari, whose forest-dwelling is in the north, first gave water into the hand of him who faced the east, for the fulfillment of his resolve.
Having proclaimed the place, time, and other details, and having released the water onto the ground,
Hari then caused its sprinkling upon the head.
The ocean of mercy gave him that mantra of refuge into his right ear:
"May Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa be my refuge at all times. (16)
Having first imparted the mantra,
he gave him the protective mantra for fear of Time, Māyā, evil karma, enemies, Yama, and treacherous-hearted beings.
Having first imparted the mantra "Śūlamīnadhvajadhanuścakrasvastikavānava," he then gave the mantra for offering.
Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Master; svāhā!
Bālakṛṣṇa, the Supreme Brahman, is indeed my eternal Lord. (1.9)
"May he be my father, kinsman, well-wisher, friend, protector, and guardian"—
having thus imparted these mantras and having caused [the disciple] to apply the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍraka), [the preceptor should proceed].
And Hari placed a double-strand garland of tulasī around his neck, [saying]:
"Wine, meat, adultery, and theft must never be committed under any circumstances."
And thus Mādhava caused him to hear these restraints (yamās);
he then bestowed upon him assistance, dispassion, knowledge, and devotion.

"Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of Śrī, the Supreme Person, has declared that the company of the virtuous must always be sought, for it bestows liberation; thus he spoke to him regarding the observances that grant release. (23)
"Service to the guru, service to Hari, service to one's parents, and service to one's family members—
this is what should be performed," the Blessed Lord Puruṣottama said to him.

On this earth, there is no one at all who is to be feared or to be propitiated; rather, the truthful and virtuous women are always to be saluted, for they are indeed the powers of the Supreme Lord. 25.
Having thus instructed him, Śrī Puruṣottama then directed him to observe a fast for the purpose of bestowing the great initiation (mahādīkṣā).
At that place of fasting, he likewise caused the gift of a cow to be performed;
thus, for the sake of purifying his body, he observed the proper rite of fasting.
Lord Hari himself caused the Nāndī-śrāddha and the Svastyayana rites to be performed;
in the pavilion, he had a Sarvatobhadra mandala fashioned, beautifully adorned with grains.
And in its center he had a golden pitcher fashioned,
and he had eight pitchers placed in the eight directions, filled with water, jewels, and fruits.
And he established them upon the jars, clad in garments of young sprouts;
and having placed an auspicious vessel filled with sesame seeds, he set there the image of Hari.
Having placed her upon a pedestal made of precious gems, he worshipped her with a golden image,
accompanied by Rādhā, Lakṣmī, Brahmavidyā, Ramā, Śrī, and Māṇikī.
Then, in the jars placed in the eight directions: Satī and Śaṅkara in the east, Bhāskara and Saṃjñā in the south, and Gaṇeśvara in the west.
And [he should worship] Siddhi and Buddhi; in the north, Śrī Narāyaṇa;
in the southeast, the Caturvyūha; and in the southwest, Garuḍa and the Elephant.
In the northwest he established Hanumān, and in the northeast the host of Brahmapriyās;
Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Supreme Lord, installed them himself. (34)

Having caused the recitation of benedictions (*svastivāca*), the *vṛddhi-śrāddha*, and thereafter the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*), as well as the invocation (*āvāhana*) and other rites for the ancillary deities; || 35 ||
Having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the Mātṛkās, he worshipped Acyuta with the sixteen services (upacāras), as well as with mantras and Vedic hymns. ||36||
Then he established the god of fire in the sacrificial pit to the south;
he caused the Vaiṣṇava caru to be cooked and worshipped Hari.
Then he caused the oblation of fuel-sticks, clarified butter, and sacrificial porridge to be performed;
he had it performed with mantras for the offering of one hundred and eight [units].
He offered one oblation each to the deities of the limbs,
and then, having performed the final full oblation (pūrṇāhuti), he conducted the great lustration ceremony (mahānīrājana).
Then Kṛṣṇa, facing north, seated his disciple facing east, and caused him to offer auspicious handfuls of flowers to Hari.
He gave him divine saffron-colored garments as well as an upper cloth, a sacred thread, and the four marks beginning with the discus. ||41||
Then he gave the mantra, which bestows the state of Brahman, together with its meaning, three times into the right ear of that Lālāyana.
I am Brahmā, an eternal devotee of Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa;
the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa is my Lord and my husband. (42)

"Śrī Kṛṣṇavallabhasvāmī, Śrī Hari, is my refuge"—thus he gave him the mantra; thereafter, for the sake of worship, he indeed gave him his own golden image accompanied by the six beloveds for the purpose of attaining liberation. 44.
He bestowed the liberating knowledge that reveals existence, consciousness, and bliss:
"The Self is indeed of the nature of Brahman, radiant with existence, consciousness, and bliss. (45)
Therein, O sage, you should meditate upon me, Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Brahman, within your heart;
from this day forward, as one who has surrendered his self, you shall indeed be equal to me. 46.
Thus addressed, that sage rose and prostrated himself like a staff upon the ground at the feet of Śrī Kṛṣṇa as the fee for the initiation rite.
He offered a leaf, a flower, a fruit, water, and his very heart;
Hari bestowed upon him auspicious blessings that grant liberation.
O devotee, by my grace, your desire has borne fruit here;
and by serving me, you shall attain supreme happiness in both worlds. 49.
May he who possesses supreme devotion to Kṛṣṇa and to his guru, the beloved of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, attain the fulfillment of the goals of human life; may that be yours through my grace.
Then Śrī Hari himself performed the dismissal of the gods;
thereafter, Hari said to him, "Worship me, Nārāyaṇa."
O Sage, grant me instruction gathered from my service;
by this rite, bestow initiation upon me who am desirous of liberation.
You, whose name is Saccidānanda and who wear the saffron robes, are my preceptor; please accept my command for the initiation of these people. 53.
Make all women, men, animals, birds, grasses, and so forth— those who remember their past births and can assume any form at will— purified by initiation.
"I am Nārāyaṇa-Kṛṣṇa, the Lord indeed of all embodied beings;
let everyone constantly worship me, the husband who is Hari, the Supreme Brahman. (55)
O virtuous one, propagate my devotion among every person on earth—from children, youths, and the elderly, to men, women, and eunuchs. (56)
Thus addressed in that assembly, Saccidānanda, the king of yogis,
bowed to Svāmī Bālakṛṣṇa and gave instruction to the people.
She bestows the divine knowledge of Īśvara and even washes away all sins;
such is the great and virtuous will of Hari, known by the name Dīkṣā. 58.
Since the Brahmaputrī bestows the abode of Brahmā and grants liberation, she—whether common or extraordinary—should be taken up by people for their welfare. (59)
Hari does not eat the food or water offered by one who is uninitiated;
however, Śrī Hari never abandons even a leaf offered by one who is initiated.
The consecrated king of devotees, Hari himself, is the supreme sacred ford;
all sacred fords reside there within the toes of his feet.
All the deities and even all the lords dwell eternally within the body of one who is initiated; therefore, one should indeed become initiated.
The fruit of serving one who has been initiated is liberation;
the merit born from touching one who has been initiated destroys even great sins and the like.
The food of one who has been initiated is purifying, and so too is his water;
dwelling together with one who has been initiated bestows liberation and grants the divine abode. (64)
For one who has been initiated, however, association with the virtuous is equal to association with the Blessed Lord;
all the ritual acts of the initiated are divine, consisting essentially of offerings unto Hari.
Indeed, the merits of all sacrifices reside in one who is initiated;
by drinking the water used for the initiation-rite's bath, the ancestors are satisfied.
The seers, sages, perfected ones, yogis, and likewise ascetics,
as well as the virtuous whose conduct is that of Brahman, indeed bow down to the initiated one.
Whatever house an initiated person enters becomes like a divine abode;
she who serves the initiated one should indeed be known as a woman endowed with merit.
He who serves one who has been initiated becomes an attendant of Hari;
the Earth constantly prays before Hari for the sake of the initiated. (69)
I am indeed purified by the feet of those who have received the initiation of the virtuous;
merely by the bath of one initiated, the water becomes a sacred ford (tīrtha).
I am indeed Sādhulālāsana; I speak the truth repeatedly.
By the initiation of Hari, I have truly become known as Saccidānanda.
Even from childhood, one should be accepted as having taken refuge in the mantra;
where Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the provider of shelter for such a person, resides, there is truly no fear at all.
Therefore, the mantra for protection should indeed be grasped from childhood itself,
[for it guards] against time, the bondage of illusion, sin, and the bondage of karma.

From enemies, from the suffering of Yama, from evil companions, and from whatever fear arises therefrom—Mādhava, whose symbols are the trident, the fish, and so forth, shall indeed protect one from that. (74)
In whose hand there is the mark of a trident, the mark of a fish, the sign of a banner, the sign of a bow, the mark of a wheel, the sign of a svastika, and a thunderbolt; ||75||
Therein, the divine trident indeed destroys the fear of Death;
likewise, the divine fish destroys the fear of illusion and bondage.
Likewise, the divine banner-mark always destroys the fear of sin;
and the divine bow-mark likewise strikes down the dread of karma.
The great and divine wheel-mark destroys enemies and their fear;
likewise, the divine svastika-mark destroys the dread of Yama.
This very divine vajra destroys fear from the heart;
it belongs to him whose hand, bearing the seven marks, even touches his body. (79)
In his body, however, even the possibility of the aforementioned fears does not arise;
therefore, one should indeed take up the mantra of surrender preceded by knowledge.
Oṃ! I always offer salutations to the one named Hari; I have become dedicated to the offering of all things to my Lord, Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. ||81||
From this day forward, I belong to no one else;
from this very day, O Hari, I shall become a slave, a servant, and a wretched handmaid, remaining under his sole control.
Thus, in this manner, my entire being, known as the gift of self, is offered there;
just as clarified butter is poured into the fire, so am I offered into Hari.
"From this day forward, I have no separate existence apart from Śrī Kṛṣṇa, my Beloved;
having realized this in my own being, I regard Śrī Hari as I do my own body and my own self. (84)
Likewise, it should be known that Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa is eternally the husband, the father, and the kinsman here within the Supreme Brahman. (85)
Friendship, as well as the state of being a friend, and likewise the state of being a protector and a guardian—these should be known as eternal in Kṛṣṇa. (86)
Thus, when such knowledge of non-offering has become mature and firm, then one should receive the auspicious and excellent initiation that bestows the state of Brahman. (87)
Since I am of the nature of Brahman, I am certainly not the body, senses, and so forth;
for I am the eternal devotee who performs loving service to Hari. (88)
The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa alone is my everything:
my husband, my protector, my enjoyer, my master, and my controller. (89)
The inner self, the supreme self, and the external self are mine alone;
the sensory self, the bodily self, and the physical self are mine alone.
Thus, I am never devoid of Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa;
I am always immersed in His form, possessing His qualities, and being a portion of Him.
Thus, indeed, having realized one's own nature as Brahman, goodness will bear fruit;
for in the supreme syllable, one shall find the eternal bliss of Śrī Hari. ||92||
Thus, by swiftly receiving initiation, embodied beings become divine;
therefore, the supreme and perfect initiation of Hari should be received by those possessed of knowledge. 93.
Therefore, others should receive either the initiation of protection (*rakṣiṇī-dīkṣā*) or the initiation of refuge (*śaraṇī-dīkṣā*).
Without such initiation, human beings must not remain here. 94.
The place, the time, and the auspicious company should never be abandoned when the Supreme Lord, who bestows liberation, has become gracious and reached one's home. (95)
The fool who does not abandon deceit suffers loss at every step;
for a human body, the supreme means for attaining liberation, is difficult to obtain. (96)
Having attained that [state], one should not even strive for liberation here, for such a person is a destroyer of the self.
Therefore, men must not destroy the self, even though it is fit for liberation.
Let them receive the excellent initiation, or another as is appropriate for their fitness, just as this venerable Lord himself has granted it to me. (98)
Having spoken thus, that king of yogis, whose nature is existence, consciousness, and bliss, fell silent;
and hundreds of thousands of men, having heard him, arrived for the sake of initiation. (99)
Bālakṛṣṇa granted them refuge and protection,
as well as the mantra of surrender and the Brahma-mantra to those who possessed knowledge.
Divided by five thousand, they then indeed became holy men,
gurus of the living beings of the world and truly the bringers of liberation.
Commanded for the purpose of instruction in regions such as Rāśiyāna and others,
those beloved of Hari departed for various lands at the command of Hari.
O Rādhā, Hari rested at the end of the assembly hall;
indeed, having proceeded to the dwellings, the embodied beings also took their rest. 103.

Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-third chapter, titled "The Description of how Śrī Hari, having bestowed the Vaiṣṇava initiation upon the saintly Sādhulālāsana-yogin, subsequently gave the initiation of a female devotee (sādhavī) to five thousand others," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Rādhikā; the Lord, the beginningless Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, having bathed at dawn on the thirteenth lunar day, summoned the king.
That king went quickly to the great king Kālimeśa;
having bowed to Hari and performed worship well, he sat down before Hari.
The Blessed One said: "O King, at the conclusion of the meal today, give to all a gift known as the *vidāyā* upon the dismissal of the festival."
Thus addressed, that great king quickly brought everything under his control;
he caused various foods to be brought and gathered excellent wealth.
Diamonds, rubies, and gems; gold, silver, and signet rings;
ornaments, decorations, and garments; cows, celestial chariots, and vehicles.
At midday, he caused Śrī Hari to be honored with gifts for all the great lords of the earth, and he joyfully presented them with sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) and fed them.

The king fed the powers, the attendants, the male servants, the female servants, and the subordinates— those who are liberated, those who are partially liberated, and the manifestations of the imperishable syllable Brahman.
The servants, the male incarnations, and the female incarnations—Rādhā, Lakṣmī, and all others, as well as Vāsudeva and the rest—were all well-fed. (8)
Bhūmi, Viṣṇu, Mahāviṣṇu, Vairāja, Śambhu, and their attendants; Māyā and Tatpuruṣa—these are the abodes and the inhabitants thereof.
The Vairājas, the sages and seers belonging to Satyaloka, as well as the Siddhas, the virtuous ones, the ancestors, and the celestial deities; || 2.134.10 ||
The guardians of the quarters, the protectors of the worlds, the inhabitants of Mount Meru, as well as the Maruts and the Viśvedevas residing in the Bhuvarloka; || 11 ||
The Vasus, Cāraṇas, Sādhyas, treasures (Nidhis), human groups, the lords of the Gaṇas, courtesans, as well as Bhūtas, Pretas, and the Mothers; || 12 ||
The Daityas, Dānavas, Rakṣasas, and Asuras were created from his devotion;
likewise the Sūryas, Rudras, planets, stars, and the Kāśyapa constellations.
Trees, creepers, clumps of grass, bamboos, bulbous roots, fruit-bearing trees, rivers, streams, oceans, lakes, waterfalls, and so forth. || 14 ||
Ponds, wells, tanks, and dug-out reservoirs as well as the oceans;
sacred fords, mountains, forests, and groves. || 15 ||
Insects, moths, and reptiles dwelling in the netherworld; others as well from various regions, and even insentient elements—(all these were drawn forth). || 16 ||
Then, by the power of Hari’s yoga, all the sacrifices, the sacrificial fires, the vessels, and the excellent liquid offerings were personified and worshipped by the king.
Likewise, they were honored and fed by all the kings; they were gratified with sacrificial fees and assigned to positions such as those of ministers. || 18 ||
The groups of servants and laborers who were engaged in the sacrificial rites—the Bhaṭṭas, the Bandins, the Sūtas, the Bhāṭas, the Cāraṇas, and the Guhyakas—[all attended]. (19)
Gandharvas, dancers, masters of the dramatic arts, actors, and singers; as well as female dancers, female singers, goddesses, hosts of apsaras, and others. ||2.134.20||
There were also foot-massagers, servants performing service,
attendants, washers, sweepers, and even those who carried away [the refuse].
The Kvaṇakas, Mālinas, Tvaṣṭṛs, weavers, washermen, dyers, and artisans skilled in the fine arts; ||22||
Likewise, there were others such as lamp-bearers and cane-bearers, as well as those who proclaimed victory, guards of the horses, and protectors of the palaces and gardens. (23)
Cowherds, householders, and guardians of forests and wilderness,
as well as protectors of vehicles and mounts— millions of such men were there.
Likewise, there were courtesans, as well as eunuchs and jesters;
those of many forms who frequented the stage, as well as jesters and storytellers. ||25||
The courtiers, experts in the arts of the assembly, performers of amorous gestures and expressions, as well as those who produce displays and those who cause fire-explosions; || 26 ||

Those who possess knowledge of lightning, those who operate machines, those who transport water and so forth, as well as others who are artisans of visible works and those who perform various types of labor. (27)
All those men and women were honored by the kings;
they were gratified with sacrificial fees and with articles of reward.
With garments, clothes, wealth, and the like; with ornaments, utensils, and so forth; with materials such as gold and silver, as well as with jewels, necklaces, and the like. (29)
The mendicants, the wretched, the destitute, and those burdened by poverty were fed, satisfied, and repeatedly gladdened.
Men and women who were virtuous and chaste, righteous men free from passion, homeless ascetics, and guests dwelling in the forest. ||3 1||
There are also beings of many species who remember their past births and are not born from a womb;
likewise, there are others who are indolent, as well as those characterized by passion (rājasa) and darkness (tāmasa).
By the command of Acyuta, all were satisfied with every kind of gift;
by the kings, they were gratified there at that festival with all manner of donations.
Then, in the afternoon, they also performed the worship of Hari at Rādhā’s [abode], and they requested leave; Hari granted them leave. (34)
Having performed the lustration ceremony for Śrīpati Bālakṛṣṇa, the supreme among men,
and having received the command of the Supreme Lord, they considered themselves to have fulfilled their purpose.
Having offered forgiveness to the king for the failure of his service,
he requested blessings [for himself] by means of celestial chariots, personal vehicles, and chariots.
According to their sovereignty, according to their prosperity, and according to their destination,
they went to their respective homes and worlds by means of aerial chariots traveling through the paths of the wind and portions of the earth.
And likewise by means of Garuḍas, elephants, horses, swans, lions, and the like; by fires, rays, as well as by volitions and supernatural powers (siddhis). ||38||
They proceeded by means of meditative concentration, as well as through sovereign powers characterized by various forms,
by means of the cultivation of invisibility, and likewise through the dissolution of sovereign powers and other such states.
Thus, on the thirteenth day, those who were honored by all went to their homes, accompanied by the powers of creation and the manifestations of the reality of the Self.
Accompanied by ten million times a hundred billion daughters of the beloved of Brahmā, Hari departed for his own worlds and regions, with the sole exception of the Saurāṣṭra territory. 41.

Together with the sages beginning with Lomaśa, as well as the lords of the sacred sites such as Aśvapaṭṭatīrtha, the guardians of the field (kṣetrapas), the incarnations and others, and likewise his two parents.
Together with devotees, servants, family members, Vaiṣṇavas, and sages; along with virtuous women, holy men, and all the maidens as well. ||43||
Together with the people dwelling in Akṣara-dhāma and the fields, along with the Sāttvatas and the Devāyanas and others, Śrī Hari [remained] until the full moon.
The Compassionate One dwelt in the palace of King Kālimeśa for the welfare and the satisfaction of Kālimeśa’s family. (45)
All the royal households dwelt there until the full moon;
I, Kṛṣṇa, and likewise Nārāyaṇa remained there by the will of that Lord.
Together with you, Lakṣmī, we have dwelt until the full moon;
thus indeed, O Rādhikā, have we performed the duty of hospitality.
Having attained rest during the night, Śrī Puruṣottama himself,
Hari, bathed at dawn on the fourteenth day and summoned the kings.
In the assembly of kings, he taught his own heart’s secret to the members of the court:
"Let all the Vaiṣṇavas, the kings, and their families listen! (49)
There is a king who is a refuge of righteousness, and I dwell within that king;
indeed, the powers of the guardians of the quarters have been deposited by me in the monarch.
With all their subjects dependent upon the king, they protect the auspicious virtues:
non-stealing, non-violence, celibacy, and likewise justice.
Truthfulness, protection [of others], and service to one's mother and father;
likewise, the wife is dependent on the husband, and the husband is dependent on the wife. (52)
Just as servants are dependent on their master, and the protector is dependent on his servants,
so do they abide in their conduct out of fear of the king and out of fear of punishment.
Therefore, the king is my form and he abides by my teaching;
indeed, it is by the king that Dharma is protected, and likewise Artha is also protected.
The king performs sacrifices and festivals for the welfare of his subjects,
as well as food-donations for the gods and temples with vast heaps of wealth.
The king who is a devotee of the Bhagavat performs devotion himself and causes it to be performed throughout the kingdom; he also delivers his subjects. ||56||
Therefore, by you kings on this earth, proclamations of devotion to Hari should be made everywhere through messengers and even by means of drums.
And may all creatures be devoted to Hari, well-initiated, entirely belonging to Viṣṇu, and taking refuge in Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa. (58)
Let them take up the auspicious, purifying Vaiṣṇava sacred thread;
let them also receive initiation, the mantra, and the name of Hari, which grants final liberation.
And let them observe the vow on the auspicious Janmāṣṭamī in the month of Kārtika,
and likewise the vow of Ekādaśī with great devotion during the dark fortnight.
In this place, let them perform pilgrimages on the days of sacrifice,
and let them also chant the sacred names day and night.
Let them also perform various festivals together with the assembled Vaiṣṇavas, as well as the recitation of sacred narratives and other such rites for the subjects.
"Let them perform worship and other rites for Śrī Hari during the Cāturmāsya; let them cause such proclamations to be made throughout their respective kingdoms. (63)
Thus commanded, the five principal kings and others likewise [departed],
as did King Śibi Deva and King Tharkūṭastha.
King Vīrajāra, King Śaktyakṣi, King Kālimāśa, and likewise other regional rulers. ||65||
Placing their hope in his head, they bowed to Śrī Puruṣottama;
and having said, "We shall do so," they issued a proclamation through their most excellent messengers.
They caused [the festival] to be performed extensively throughout their respective kingdoms;
and Śrī Hari fed everyone in his own palace.
Indeed, at the word of King Kālimāśa, [the Lord] manifested his grace in many ways;
then, in the evening, he ascended a celestial chariot and went to the house of the sage Lālāyana.
The illustrious Blessed One went to the island situated in the eastern ocean;
having performed that act of grace, he returned by way of the sky-path.
At night, Kālimāśa’s royal palace indeed attained rest,
along with the virtuous sage Lālāyana, who is known as Saccidānanda.
Śrī Hari said to the initiated one: "Go to the Northern Kurus, and from your island, [go] to the eastern regions together with Keṇāṭa Island."
"Proclaim my devotion throughout the regions of the immortals.
Having spoken thus, that ascetic also departed for the Kuru lands of Kenāṭaka.
Endowed with manifold powers through the yoga of the path of the sky,
Hari then attained rest once again during the night.
On the day of the full moon, having risen in the morning and bathed, he became absorbed in meditation;
at that moment, O Rādhā, a great wonder occurred there before Hari.
Then the celestial chariot, joined with those liberated from the imperishable abode and blazing brilliantly,
arrived instantly and came to rest steadily in the presence of Śrī Hari.
The attendants, descending from that celestial chariot, worshiped Puruṣottama and Rādhikā, and spoke, being devoted with supreme bhakti. (76)
By your command, for the sake of the liberation of Śūrajāra as well as that of his wife,
named Devavarūthinī, [act] for the sake of their release.
Remembering exactly as we promised, we have come together;
O Kṛṣṇa, command us, for we are devoted to serving you accordingly. (78)
Then, having bestowed blessings upon King Kālimeśa Śakti, he related all of that to the illustrious Hari.
Accompanied by Vīrajāra and joined by Śūrajāra and others,
Śrī Harivīrajāra established his kingdom on the bank of the river Cobīnā.
Then Hari arrived in his magnificent celestial chariot, attended by his own retinue,
toward Śūrajāra and the army of the gods.
Leading them to the divine, imperishable, and eternal abode of liberation, the Blessed Lord then quickly reached Bālakṛṣṇa-sarovara. 82.
He returned again to his own palace in Śibi by means of that celestial chariot;
having received the command of Hari, Tharkūṭastha went to his own kingdom. ||83||
Then a marvel occurred there: sixteen maidens arrived, all possessing divine forms, bearing tridents, and having three eyes. (84)
Likewise, those four Kumāras are also leaders with tridents;
they are divine, endowed with the arts of yoga, and possessed of great sovereignty and other such qualities. ||85||
Then other divine men arrived there—four white ones with tridents for eyes, restless, tall, and stout. ||86||
And five other men, dark-complexioned, bearing tridents, three-eyed, of divine form, tall and lean, arrived. ||87||
A certain person arrived, though he was alone, weak, and unarmed; despite his harsh appearance, he was happy, free from anxiety, and even fickle. (88)
Thus, having assembled together, these thirty fell prostrate like staffs at the feet of Kṛṣṇa in the presence of Hari, filled with devotion. (89)
"We are blessed, we are blessed! We have been uplifted by the Supreme Soul.
Having said this, they worshipped the Supreme Lord with many jewels and other offerings.
Honored by Śibi, they performed the *ārārtrika* and other rites;
then, being questioned—"Who are you, who possess the forms of gods?"—they sat down. (9.1)
They said: "We were created by Rudra in the past as his own sons;
we have remained hidden here during the destruction of Rudra's creation."
Today we always abide purified by you, O Supreme Self;
grant us the Vaiṣṇava mantras, O glorious Supreme Lord.
Thus entreated, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa granted the Manvantaras;
therein were those maidens who were the fierce daughters. (94)
Uruḷā, Bālikā, Irātriśā, Obī, Māniśī, Bīnā, Tribalā, Trāsā, Tuṅgāsikā, and Anāvarā. ||95||
The Ālanaukā, the Uṣṭrīyāskā, the Anādirā, the Anāṃśukā, and the Kālimā— these were the Vaiṣṇavī [weapons] that appeared at that time.
And there were also four youths; hear their names, O Rādhikā:
Bālakṛśa, Dvikala, Alpamātra, and Yurālaka. (97)
Having received those mantras, they too became auspicious Vaiṣṇavas;
there were others as well, long-bodied men—listen to their names, O Rādhikā. (98)
Akṣodha, Kāraka, Kaśyapāya, and Dviriṅgaka also received the mantras, and they too then became Vaiṣṇavas. (99)
And there were five other men; hear their names, O Rādhikā: Ūrula, Samāna, Stenāvāsa, and Prabhāluna.
Even those who were rushing toward him seized the Vaiṣṇava men;
and then, even that single weak person became a Vaiṣṇava.
He was named Śivaraṇa, and at that time he received the mantras;
all became Vaiṣṇavas, servants of Śrī Hari.
Having received the command, those maidens went to the land in the form of rivers,
and the four youths indeed went in the form of lakes.
And four men also went forth in the form of oceans,
and these five men likewise went forth in the form of mountains.
Then one [being], harsh and weak, went forth with the form of a battle;
meanwhile, the stars always dwelt there in the form of sacred fords (tīrtha) for embodied beings.
Seeing that, the family of Śibi Deva was indeed filled with wonder;
by reading or hearing this, one obtains the fruit of those respective holy places (tīrthas). || 106 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Honoring of All the Great Beings, the Proclamation of Vaiṣṇavism, the Dispatching of the Abode of Saccidānanda to Uttarakuru, the Liberation of the Couple Śūra and Jārā, the Transformation of the Thirty Sons of Raudrī and Rudra into Vaiṣṇavas, and those Sacred Fords," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇī Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Listen, O Rādhikā; I am Kṛṣṇa, the supreme Lord Nārāyaṇa.
Having stayed in the palace of Śibi and having accepted the service rendered by him, [I have come here]. || 1 ||
Having passed the night, on the first day of the month of Māgha at dawn, having performed the daily and divine rites, and having instructed him in the excellent duties of the Sāttvatas; || 2 ||
Having received the great worship offered, as well as food, gifts, and so forth,
he should gratify and propitiate everyone with auspicious benedictions.
[He addressed] Devāyatanaka, Bhakta, as well as Śrīlomaśa and the others, all those beloved by Brahmā who dwell in the Akṣara-kṣetra. || 4 ||
The guardians of the fields, the deities of the sacred fords, the family members, the attendants and others,
as well as his mother, father, brothers, and sisters-in-law.
He also placed his sister, her friend, and the maidens presented by the king,
as well as his own people from Saurāṣṭra, upon new celestial chariots.
Having seated himself in his own celestial chariot, he traveled along the path of the sky;
passing beyond Indukuśa and crossing over Sindhuvyoma.
Having gone to Badarikāśrama and beheld Nara and Nārāyaṇa,
and having seen the sages and ascetics, he then proceeded to Śrī Kāśikā.
On the bank of the Varaṇā, [he saw] his own Lakṣmī, the virtuous Satī, the daughter of Śiva;
likewise Śivarāja, Kṛṣṇā, Candra, Jaya, and Jānakī.
Having seen them all, they gathered together and bathed in the waters of the Gaṅgā;
then, having beheld Viśveśa and all the gods, they worshipped them in every way.
Accompanied by all his celestial chariots, Śrī Hari, the Supreme Person,
arrived with Rādhikā at his own auspicious Aśvapaṭṭa-kṣetra.
The Tīrthaṅkaras, honored by their subjects and those seeking victory, ascend celestial chariots; that imperishable realm, however, is reached for seven cycles of time.
Having wandered about and beheld the Kuṅkumavāpī as well as the garden groves,
he then informed everyone of his arrival in the west.
Then they descended into the great garden, having attained stability,
and were honored by the people with flowers, unbroken grains of rice, and parched grain.
All of them emerged from their celestial chariots, repeatedly bidding farewell and bestowing upon him well-being,
prosperity, and health, as well as garlands and other gifts.
Having honored and embraced them, the people departed for their respective homes;
Hari, however, settled his own people in palatial mansions worthy of residence.
He fed them quickly, and they likewise rested;
then he sent forth all the maidens together with those dear to Brahmā.
In the beautiful hermitage of Lomaśa, which was always free from illusion, the supreme sage Lomaśa, who was liberated through divine means, protected them all. 18.
The sages, the deities and others, and the guardians of the field dwelling there,
having eaten and returned to their own abodes, attained rest.
Hari, together with his family, ate and attained rest;
then, on the morning of the second day, having performed his daily obligatory rites.
With devotion, he fed the Mahīmānas of Surāṣṭra,
as well as the Kanthādharas and others, including the Raṇaṅgamas and their like.
The brahmins, those devoted to their vows and observances, and even the virtuous great sages,
having received the command of Hari, departed for their own villages in all directions.
With a gracious mind, Hari said to Devāyatanaka:
"O devotee, you have performed everything pertaining to the Vaiṣṇava kingdom. (23)
Such a great task as this does not arise without a devotee;
indeed, men, women, and even eunuchs have been purified [by him]. (24)
"I am pleased; tell me what may be given to you, for there is indeed nothing that I do not possess. Listen, I shall give you everything that dwells within your mind. (25)
Having spoken thus, Śrī Hari drew him close and embraced him with his own chest; for a moment, he placed his hands upon the head of that [devotee].
Śrī Puruṣottama placed His divine feet upon the heart;
O Rādhikā, this devotee Devāyana has his every desire fulfilled.
Then that king of devotees chose [this boon]: "I shall indeed become your servant wherever you, Hari himself in his supreme form, may reside. (28)
And the nature of the descent [of the Lord] occurs in the divine, celestial, and human realms;
it may be known as a manifestation (vibhava), or a formal emanation (vyūha), or a partial incarnation (aṃśaka). ||29||
Whether in the form of an image, or possessing a form manifested through the power of divine possession, or in the form of Śakti, or in the form of a deity— wherever you, O Blessed One, reside.
"Let my home be wherever you are; dwell forever in my house," [the devotee said].
And Hari replied, "You are blessed, for I shall dwell daily in the house that is your very self."
Just as I dwell in happiness, so may you become my home; for you are conscious, of the nature of liberation, and the embodiment of existence, consciousness, and bliss. 32.
Likewise, become my temple in the form of an effect;
I shall always dwell within that temple throughout the entire cycle of creation. (33)
May this palace indeed become worthy of being a palace;
wherever I am, let it everywhere become a temple for the gods.
Endowed with manifold powers and assuming various forms, become like an insentient object in your visible form, while you remain the presiding deity over it. (35)
May you become the presiding deity of all the celestial palaces, magnified by Tvaṣṭṛ; for you shall be exceedingly beautiful and truly lovely for all embodied beings.
"And I shall show you forms consisting of divine abodes," having said this to him, the Blessed One [manifested] that body of divine abodes.
He showed him the auspicious temple endowed with peaks;
thereafter, he remained in his own form as well as in the temple of the deity.
He showed him such a divine temple in every part:
the altar, the courtyard, the base, the pedestal, and likewise the upper chamber.
The pinnacle, the lotus-stone, the pitcher, and the banner; likewise, the pavilion at the front, the elephant-throne, and the circumambulation.
Then, within his own true form, Hari repeatedly placed everything that constitutes a temple of the deity into that very temple of the deity. 41.
He manifested pure knowledge and likewise bestowed divine [vision] upon him;
having attained knowledge, Devāyatanaka realized the nature of his own abode. || 42 ||
Having accomplished his purpose, he became humble; he possessed a dual form, was liberated in nature, and was exceedingly beautiful as the abode of the gods. ||43||
In the field of Kuṅkumavāpikā, a divine temple came into being;
that palace, measuring a thousand cubits, appeared in the sky. 44.
Indeed, the Blessed One made his own auspicious abode such that even the jars, accompanied by banners, would constantly bathe with the waters of the clouds. (45)
Having understood this, the ṛṣis, the siddhas, the goddesses, and the deities—
both those born from water and those born from land, as well as those produced from the four sources— [acted accordingly].
The lords and those headed by Īśvara, as well as sentient principles, trees, creepers, forms, Garuḍas, elephants, and horses [all arise]. (47)

The yoginīs and the flowering creepers, the tree trunks and likewise those seeking liberation, those dwelling in the forest and those dwelling in the sky, as well as other yogins residing in palaces—[all these were present]. (48)
Having understood that the temple was the very embodiment of the abode of the gods,
and desiring to dwell there, they came into the presence of Hari.
Desiring service to Śrī Hari with their very bodies and filled with the spirit of devotion,
they indeed worshipped Hari and prayed to him most fervently.
O Lord of Compassion, ocean of mercy, soul of all, protector of all, you who grant refuge to all—grant me a dwelling in your own abode. (51)
You are known as the one who is affectionate toward devotees; your entire body belongs to them.
Without you, the dwelling of the worlds cannot be conducive to happiness.
Devoted to the temple of the deity, through devotion he became your abode;
by your grace, we too are your servants, dwelling in your abode. (53)
"O Soul of the Universe, grant us that by which we may become [liberated]; please bestow it upon us.
To them spoke the Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa, the ultimate refuge of all that is auspicious. (54)
Considering that which is difficult to attain as easily attained, you have indeed requested this here;
my abode truly becomes yours, where I dwell in a threefold manner.
The Imperishable is the supreme Brahman, the abode of liberation, my own dwelling;
wherever that Imperishable Brahman exists, there indeed do I dwell.
For this is indeed the dwelling place of those who are liberated, of those who have reached the further shore of illusion, of the knowers of Brahman, and of the yogis; it is never for others.

Wherein the ancient Sādhyas, the gods who dwell there eternally, having abandoned the state of individual souls (jīva-bhāva) and having relinquished the state of [limited] lordship (īśa-bhāva), [reside]. ||58||
Having burned away the latent impressions of illusory karma, those intent on my propitiation and devoted to meditation upon me have washed away all causes for rebirth. (59)
Pure, consisting of consciousness and bliss, having taken refuge in me and seeking my purpose, those who are intent on self-restraint toward my form go to the imperishable Brahman.

Those divine beings who have arisen from a mere fraction of my compassion and whose essence is identical to mine— they, being absorbed in a state of non-duality with me, attain my imperishable Brahman.

For those who are greedy for the transformations of illusion, whose essence consists of the desired flavors of illusion, who are possessed of the illusory sense of "I," and who are characterized by the nature of illusion. ||62||
For those who always strive for the sake of passion through efforts to achieve their own ends,
and who are devoid of meditation upon Me, there is no place whatsoever in Brahman.
For those devoid of devotion to me, likewise for those who do not know my path,
and for those who are destitute of my mantras and so forth, there is no place whatsoever in Brahman.
Thus, this supreme state has been declared by me; it is my imperishable [nature].
But that other, second state is my heart for the virtuous.
In that abode of consciousness where I always dwell—
therein reside my liberated ones, the great liberated ones, and even the imperishable Brahman.
We always dwell in the hearts of the liberated and the virtuous who live here;
indeed, we all reside together within the hearts of the righteous.
Therein indeed there is no latent impression (vāsanā), nor is there any transformation of illusion (māyā);
therein there is nothing at all apart from Me, and therefore I dwell there.
My form, which eternally dwells in the abode of the divine syllable, shines there in the hearts of the virtuous, endowed with devotion and righteousness. (69)
My lineage of Dharma exists in embodied form, consisting of divine qualities;
those qualities shine there, always indeed within the hearts of the virtuous.
Faith, tranquility, compassion, intelligence, contentment, nourishment, as well as progress; modesty, friendliness, forbearance, wisdom, form, action, and excellence. ||71||
Those who love the Dharma always dwell in the hearts of the virtuous:
knowledge, dispassion, sovereignty, fearlessness, austerity, and uprightness. (72)
Truth, security, happiness, purity, steadfastness, fortitude, gentleness, self-restraint, renunciation, faith, contentment, and mindfulness; ||73||
Self-restraint, sacrifice, tranquility, yoga, cessation of worldly activity, worship, serenity, auspicious splendor, Vedic study, humility, and joy—[these constitute the path]. 74.
Meditation, equanimity, the knowledge of Brahman, attainment, capability, effort, and the forms of devotion such as hearing reside in the hearts of the virtuous. (75)
There I always dwell, peaceful and with a serene heart;
you are my eternal abode, and residence there is difficult for others to attain. (76)
For those who have not been liberated, who are devoid of my mantra,
or who lack devotion to me, there is never any dwelling among my true devotees.
Those virtuous ones whose dwelling is indeed in the Imperishable (akṣara) and whose dwelling is in the heart—they alone are always worthy of a beautiful residence in my divine abode. (78)
Then this temple of the deity, which was the best of dwellings, became today like a divine abode; though appearing inert, it became conscious.
If you desire to dwell there in the temple, that inert shrine, then accept my mantras and become my devotees. (2.135.80)
"Except for my devotees, the Sāttvatas, no others shall be able to remain here.
This Lomaśa, the best of sages, will impart the mantras to you. (8.1)
"Let the Vaiṣṇavas come here and then dwell in my house.
Having been addressed thus by Śrī Hari, the deities and other embodied beings then [responded]. (82)
Having bowed down, honored, and worshipped him, they departed with the permission of the venerable Lomaśa;
Lomaśa, for his part, bestowed mantras upon them and made them Vaiṣṇavas.
Then they went to the abode of the gods, the temple of the deity;
they bowed to the temple and fell at the feet of Hari.
By the command of Hari, those Vaiṣṇavas who were residing in the temple became initiated for that purpose; then the temple spoke: ||85||
O Blessed One, the gods are fickle and so too are embodied beings;
for they are always possessed by fear when a time of calamity arrives. (86)
If, having perceived the assault of the Asuras, they were not to flee;
if, leaving [the city] at intervals, they were to go to another place rather than [simply fleeing] in the midst [of the attack]. (87)
If they should make a vow to dwell there permanently in your presence, then you must grant them residence; carry out this injunction. (88)
Having heard those auspicious words of Devālaya— which were beneficial, wholesome, and true— Bālakṛṣṇa then spoke as he was being entreated.
If you believe what the temple deity says to be true, then take oaths right here; only then will I grant you residence.
As long as the temple remains—whether it be dilapidated or reduced to mere walls—and as long as the deity also remains, so long should one reside in that temple. (91)
When a deity, having left its place in a temple, rises up for all time, then one may approach; otherwise, one must not. ||92||
Thus, indeed, I then made this vow here:
"I shall always take up residence in a temple of the gods, in a divine abode. (93)
Thus addressed, they made an uninterrupted vow:
"As long as the temple stands, and as long as the deity remains. (94)
"You must certainly remain here even during this great period of calamity.
Having said this, he drank water that was pleasing to the eye, even though it was on the ground. (95)
Having released the water from their feet onto Hari, the gods and others were cursed thus; they attained their residence in Mahālaya.
For those Vaiṣṇavas are indeed worthy of dwelling in the temple, the abode of Hari;
therefore, as long as the temple remains, so too does that Lord remain there.
O Rādhikā, as long as the limbs of the temple remain, they shall indeed always endure, O Rādhikā, even though they are broken and shattered. (98)
Therefore, the restoration of a dilapidated temple is beneficial for human beings;
those portions of the deities who have become manifest grant their assistance and bring happiness. 99.
Having thus attained such clarity, the sage Devāyatanaka attained the nature of a divine abode,
and likewise the gods attained their dwelling place.
Out of compassion for Śrī Hari, one should indeed bow down to those [images] even from afar;
for just as I always dwell within a Śālagrāma stone, even when it is broken into pieces.
Even when a temple is broken or decayed, as long as it still contains an image—
even if it is merely a small shrine— I indeed continue to dwell within it.
Indeed, he shall dwell [in heaven] as long as he bears my command upon his head;
by reciting or hearing this, the fruit of a temple-dwelling shall be attained. (103)

Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of Śrī Hari’s Threefold Abode—His Arrival at Reaching the Field of Aśvapaṭṭasaraḥ in the Second Tretā Cycle of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*; His Residence in the Imperishable Abode (*akṣaradhāman*), within the hearts of the virtuous, and in the form of the temple; the nature of the temple-sage (*devāyatana-ṛṣi*); and the stability and other qualities of the deities who are limbs of the temple. || 135 ||
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Rādhikā; then Devāyatana, the king of devotees, again questioned Śrī Hari regarding the construction of a temple in order to know it. || 1 ||
For the benefit of the world, in order to know the measurement of the limbs,
and indeed to understand all the internal measurements of the temple.
O Blessed One, Lord of the Gods of gods, please explain how the various limbs and the primary parts of the temple arise, as well as the banners for the deities.
By which means I may know my own limbs and where the deities reside,
as well as these internal [powers] that shall dwell within my body.
Having thus understood the true nature of this [deity] and of Prāsādaka,
other excellent Prāsādas shall arise as his kinsmen.
When artisans, who are masters of craft, shall fashion palaces of manifold forms by means of their own intellects, that will be even more excellent than before.
Therefore, O Hari-Kṛṣṇa, speak of the analysis of the components of the temple,
which is the root of the extensive science of architecture and which brings benefit to the dwellers of heaven.
Thus questioned, Harikṛṣṇa spoke briefly to that sage Devāyatanaka, whose own form was characterized by lines and marks.
A finger-breadth (aṅgula) is traditionally defined as being measured by seven barley-corns;
twenty-four finger-breadths are indeed proclaimed to be one cubit (hasta).
This hand is known as "Gaja" (the Elephant) when located on a temple of the gods,
as well as upon an image, a linga, a pedestal, or a pavilion.
And for royal palaces, as well as for great long-term residences, one should measure out a long mansion on the ground using this very cubit. || 11 ||
The measurement should also be taken for the temple of the deity, the pavilion, the exterior of the walls,
the spire, and the sanctuary within the divine abode.
Whatever the number of cubits for the length of the ground may be, that should be multiplied by the number of cubits for its width. || 12 ||
The number produced by dividing the count of hands by the count of eight [fingers] shall be the remaining number; this is renowned as being named after the *ayana*. (14)
A single mark is for the banner, while five marks are for the bull;
seven in number are for the elephant—these are the best types for a temple.
A banner brings the acquisition of wealth; a bull bestows riches and grain;
and an elephant grants auspiciousness—these are considered [auspicious] when placed at the beginning of a house or similar location. (16)
In the palace, in the image, in the linga, on the earth, in the pavilion, on the pedestal, on the lion-throne, on the altar, in the sacrificial pit, and in the banner and the fly-whisk; (17)
On a parasol, in a well, a pond, or a tank; in a well, on a divine throne, or in the sky; likewise on an ornament, a pedestal, a necklace, or a crown. (18)
A banner made of iron is in every way the best and should be accepted by one who knows the arts of craftsmanship;
however, in the remaining three cases, a lion-made banner is considered auspicious for a lion-throne.
In a temple, a flagstaff made of iron is indeed the best; there is no doubt about this.
However, a staff made of wood from a bull or an elephant must not be accepted in a temple.
If the Dhvaja (Banner) does not occur, then the Gaja (Elephant) is taken there;
the Lord of the East is Dhvaja, while that of the West is Vṛṣa (Bull).
There is a northern elephant from the southern direction;
one should multiply the length of the field by its width, and then [multiply] that [result]. (22)
One should divide that number by twenty-seven; whatever remainder remains, the asterism of the house shall correspond to that numerical value.
Having divided the lunar mansion by the number eight, the remainder is designated as the expenditure (vyaya); if that [remainder] is less than the income (āya), it is so.
That which is known as the "Human" (Nara) yoga is the most excellent, bestowing wealth, grain, and so forth;
the "Rākṣasa" yoga involves excessive expenditure, while the "Piśāca" yoga is neutral. ||25||
Those two should always be understood as inauspicious, for the human expenditure (nara-vyaya) indeed bestows gain;
the eight expenditures should also be known, while the remaining one is named "Peaceful" (śānta). (26)
The expenditure that yields fruit should be given equally with the Dhvaja [day];
the second type of expenditure, the Pauro, should be given equally with the Siṃha [day]. ||27||
Śriyānanda should be given together with Vṛṣāya as the fifth;
likewise, Śrīvatsa and Vyaya should be given together with Gajāya. (28)
They are proclaimed as the guardians of the field (kṣetrapāla); when worshipped, they destroy obstacles.
Temples made of jewels, gems, gold, and other materials are dear to the deities. (29)
Auspicious temples should be constructed on the banks of rivers, in cities, at sacred fords (tīrtha), in perfected hermitages (siddhāśrama), in mountain caves, in gardens, and by ponds.
The excellent palaces facing the city always bestow happiness;
and within them as well as outside them, the deities always bestow happiness. (3.1)
Śrī, Kubera, and Gaṇeśa always bestow happiness at the gateway;
likewise, Vaiṣṇavas dwelling within one's own home truly bestow happiness. (32)
At night, having placed a lamp upon the earth aligned with the Pole Star (Dhruvatāraka),
the wise man should draw a line of perfect alignment using a plumb-line.
That northern direction is pure; having fixed it with stakes, one should establish a boundary and level the ground with stone fragments.
One should place the tortoise-stone (kūrmaśilā) at the edge of a rock or at the edge of water;
one must not perform an excavation in that direction where the serpent’s mouth is located.
Indeed, a single square should be made for the sixty-four quadrants;
having formed it as an equal-angled quadrangle, one should do so in both directions.
There, one should write the eight days beginning with Sunday in sequence;
just as the Sun moves within the four corners, so should one write it.
In that body, within the square of Mars, there is the great Nāgamukha;
indeed, his body is considered to be in the square of Saturn and the square of Mars.
The tail should likewise be placed gradually in the row within the nāgāsya square;
however, no excavation whatsoever should ever be made in the region of the body.
When the sun is in Virgo, Libra, or Scorpio, the face [of the temple] should be toward the east;
likewise, during the months of Bhādrapada and Kārttika, the face should always be toward the east.
Then there should be a *tri-koṇa* in the south, a *tri-koṇa* in the west, and a *tri-koṇa* in the north; one should not cause a pit to be dug there.
It is considered auspicious to excavate on both sides of the two "bellies" as prescribed;
however, if there is no "elephant's mouth" in the east, one should perform the excavation in the northwest.
If [the opening] is on the south, one should perform the excavation with the face of a serpent toward the northeast;
if it is on the west, one should perform the excavation with the face of a naga toward the southeast.
If [the opening] is in the north, one should not have the mouth of the serpent [face] toward the south;
in all temples, one should perform the excavation in the left side of the belly. 44.
In a palace measuring one *gaja*, the tortoise is four finger-breadths [in height];
from there, up to ten *gajas*, the *pratihastaka* is two finger-breadths [per *gaja*].
One should increase the tortoise [in size]; that which is suitable is considered the tortoise-stone (kūrmaśilā).
From ten [aṅgulas] up to twenty, one should increase it by one aṅgula at a time.
One should take twenty-five finger-breadths for the elephant and half a finger-breadth [for the rest];
this is known as the "Brick-Tortoise" (iṣṭakākūrma) in the case of bricks used in a temple. ||47||
In temples and other structures made of stone, there is indeed a tortoise of stone;
one should fashion a lotus on the lower part of the tortoise-stone, measuring one-eighth of its size.
