One that is one cubit long, eight finger-breadths high, and square in shape should be placed upon a stone building; it is called "Svasthā" (the Stable One) and provides assistance. 49.

In the case of brick-built palaces, however, having made the tortoise [pattern] on the bricks according to a measurement of half a finger-breadth, the tortoise-stone (kūrmaśilā) should be placed; in its thickness, it shall be a bestower of stability.
Then, nine square compartments should indeed be made upon the tortoise-stone;
in the compartment situated in the southeast (Agni), the water-sign is seen, while the fish is in the south.
In the southwest, there is the sight of a frog; in the west, the sight of a crocodile;
in the northwest, the mouth of a predator; and in the north, the sight of a conch shell.
In the northeast, there is the sight of a serpent; in the east, the sight of a jar;
and in the ninth central portion, a tortoise must indeed be made—such is the established rule.
Nandā, Bhadrā, Jayā, Riktā, as well as Ajitā, Aparājitā, Śuklā, Saubhāginī, and Dharaṇī is considered the ninth. (54)
A tortoise should be fashioned on one hand [of the image], measuring half a finger-breadth in the temple;
it is considered excellent if made of gold or silver. (55)
Subsequently, this tortoise should be increased by half a finger-breadth at each successive hand-unit up to fifteen hand-units. ||56||
From fifteen to thirty-one cubits, an increase of one-fourth of an *aṅgula* per cubit is always prescribed for the tortoise [pedestal]. //57//
From thirty-one up to fifty,
however, an increase of one cord each is assigned to the tortoise-shaped [mandala].
Then he, together with a tortoise, should be bathed with milk, curd, ghee, honey, and sugar;
thereafter, he is to be installed, for he is indeed named Dharaṇī.
The petals must not be made at all; rather, they should be made free of gaps.
In the center, there should be a void space, devoid of any divisions.
It should be worshipped with jewels and covered with corals;
and those auspicious stones, such as Nanda and others, located in the eight directions, should be treated accordingly.
In a palace of one cubit [in height], a stone slab of seven aṅgulas is prescribed;
from that point up to five cubits, those stone slabs are prescribed to be two aṅgulas [thick] each.
Therefore, for a [liṅga] of ten cubits, those stones are considered to be three finger-breadths [in thickness];
for one of twenty cubits, they are three-quarters of four finger-breadths.
Up to fifty elephants [in height], nine stones should be made with sides measuring four and a quarter *aṅgulas*, having equal angles and a thickness of one-fourth [of the side]. 64.
Upon the stones, one should cause the Śakti to be placed in the southeast corner;
the Daṇḍa in the south, and the Khaḍga in the southwest.
In the west, one should place the noose, and likewise the goad in the northwest;
in the north, one should place the mace, and the trident in the northeast.
One should place a vajra in the east, and outside of them [the other directions] as follows:
red, dark-blue, cloud-colored (grey), pale-yellow, and white garments.
One should cover [the site] with green, white, and yellow cloth in sequence.
Within the excavation, beneath the stone slab, nine caskets of treasure should be placed.
Śaṅkha, Padma, Mahāpadma, Makara, Kunda, Nālaka, Kacchapa, Mukunda, and Kharva are the nine treasures (nidhis). 69.
Either from the northeast or from the southeast corner, the eight foundation stones (śilā) are placed on the right;
in the center is the tortoise-stone (kūrmaśilā), followed by Vedic hymns and auspicious songs.
First, Nandā should be established, then the other, Dharaṇī;
the interior of the eight stones, being provided with space, should be protected like a sealed vessel. (7.1)
Having fashioned small bowls on all sides, they should be placed upon it like a *puṭa* [or layered vessel];
however, the navel-stalk of the earth should be left with space above that.
One should bring [the image] as far as the lion-throne, for that bestows happiness;
during the installation of the tortoise and the installation of the stone, [an offering] cooked in ghee is prescribed. (73)
One should offer sweet food to the deities and sweet cakes to the guardians of the directions;
one should give divine clothing, accompanied by a *śrīphala* fruit, to the artisan.
One should offer food and a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to a Vedic Brahmin. The base of the palaces is considered to be the *jagatī*, which is the altar (*vedikā*). (75)
The temple of the deity and its base (jagatī) may be as many-sided as desired—quadrangular, octagonal, circular, or oblong. ||76||
A vedikā in the form of a palace is indeed highly praised;
the vedikā, the jagatī, and the pradakṣiṇā are thus considered effective. ||77||
The jagatī (pedestal) should be made six times the height of the prāsāda (temple); this is considered auspicious.
However, for the temples of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara, it should be seven times [the height].
It is considered by some to be twice, four times, or even five times [the size of the previous];
the world-mountain with three circumferences is the best, while that with two circumferences is middling. (79)
In the temple of Viṣṇu, the lowest [tier] has one whorl,
while the second whorled tier is reduced by one-third of the total height.
The third enclosure should be less by a division of that height;
thus, the total height of the enclosures should be made according to three parts.
They may have four corners, twelve corners, twenty corners, twenty-eight corners, or thirty-six corners; these are indeed the most excellent. ||82||
If the palace is twelve cubits in length, then the terrace is considered to have a height equal to half that measure. (83)
When the length is twenty-two [units], the height is considered to be one-third of that;
when the length is thirty-two [units], the height is considered to be one-fourth. ||84||
When the length is fifty [units], even in the fourth [section], there is a four-part division;
when the height is equal [to that], it always brings about the absence of obstacles. (85)
First, the parts of the height of the Jagatī should be made equal;
then, there should be twenty-eight [parts], and the *jāḍyakuṃbha* is one-third [of that]. 86.

The pericarp (karṇikā) should be made with two parts; on the three-part [base], the stalk-band (sarapaṭṭikā) should be made, provided with lotus petals; the plinth (khuraka) is considered to be two parts. ||87||
The *kuṃbha* shall consist of seven parts, and the *kalaśa* shall consist of three parts;
the *antarapatrī* shall be one part, and the *kapotālī* shall be produced from three parts. 88.
The *puṣpakaṇṭha* should be made as four parts; these grant happiness.
Indeed, in the projection, the *puṣpakaṇṭha* is taken as four parts. (89)
And likewise, a jar for dross (jāḍyakuṃbha) is taken as the fourth part;
indeed, starting from the east among the pericarp-petals, one proceeds in a clockwise direction.
Excellent and auspicious images of the eight guardians of the directions should be installed;
the stone slabs supporting the temple should be long, thick, and without gaps.

The foundations should be established firmly with fine lime and other materials, free from any gaps or voids; above the base platform (jagatī) and the wall (dāśikā), there should then be the entablature (bhīṭa).
Having constructed a terrace for the elephant's palace, four finger-breadths in height,
one should then proceed up to a limit of fifty elephants.

Each successive *bhīṭa* (moulding) should be half a finger-breadth higher than the one below; furthermore, there may be one, two, or three *bhīṭas* stacked one above the other according to measurement.
They must be constructed in every respect with measurements reduced by one-fourth;
the projection (nikāsa) as well shall be one-fourth, according to the measure of their respective heights.
Having divided the *bhīṭa* into three parts, one should fashion *puṣpaka-cippikās* in the uppermost portion; one should then place the pedestal (*pīṭha*) upon the *bhīṭa*.
In a palace that is one cubit [in height], the pedestal should indeed be twelve finger-breadths;
from that point, for every additional cubit up to five cubits, it should increase by five finger-breadths.
From that point, the increase up to ten [years] is by a measure of four finger-breadths;
thereafter, the increase up to twenty [years] is considered auspicious at three finger-breadths.
The increase reaches up to thirty-six [fingers], measured at one and a half fingers;
the height decreases by a quarter [of a finger] until it reaches fifty elephants. (99)
An increase in the height of the pedestal (pīṭha) exceeding one-fifth [of the total height] is considered auspicious and excellent.
Furthermore, there are twenty-one divisions to be made in the height of the temple (prāsāda).
The height of the pedestal (pīṭha) may be up to five parts of the base, as desired;
it may be of the Śubhada, Sarvatobhadra, Padma, or Vasundhara type. || 10.1 ||
The lion, the void, the garuḍa, the swan, and the bull constitute the pedestal;
thus the pedestal is ninefold, for the pedestal is that which supports the temple.
Beyond that, fifty-three parts should be made for the height of the pedestal (pīṭha);
then, according to the rule, twenty-two parts are to be assigned as the projection (nirgama).
In the *jāḍyakubha* there are nine parts, while in the *karṇaka* there are seven parts;
it should be understood that when combined with the *andhārī*, there are likewise seven parts.
Likewise, the *grāsapaṭṭikā* (the band for the mouth) is considered to be accompanied by six *chajjikas*.
The elephant-hair rug (*hastistara*) is [applied] in the twelfth part, and the horse-hair rug (*vājistara*) in the tenth part.
In the eighth part, a man should be depicted as a beautiful sight;
or else, there may be a horse-stallion or even a stallion that is the mount of the principal deity.
Indeed, by the power of the tip of the *karṇaka*, there is an emergence of five parts;
for the jar of dullness (*jāḍyakuṃbha*) should be made with a *karṇaka* of three and a half parts.
The intermediate part shall be half a unit, and beyond that, four units; then the *chajjikā*, the pair of *yugma*, and the *grāsapaṭṭī* should be made beautifully and excellently.
The elephant-passage should be one-fourth [the width] of the horse-passage;
indeed, the male-passage should be made with one part, while the female-passage should be two parts.
In the intervals between the stars, as well as above,
the pericarp (karṇikā) and the filaments (chajjikā) should be fashioned, O Rādhikā, for they create great beauty.

Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-sixth chapter, titled "The Specification and Measurement of the Components of the Temple, Beginning from the Excavation and Ending with the Pedestal and Cornice," in the section on the construction of temples in the form of palaces, within the second part, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmīnārāyaṇīya-saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Then Nārāyaṇa spoke to the sage Devāyatanaka:
"Listen, O Rādhikā, to the matter of the maṇḍova and other structures exactly as they are."
Above the corner line of the palace, the *maṇḍovara* is prescribed;
*maṇḍovara*, *udayinī*, and *ubhiṇī* are synonymous terms.
The height of the temple should indeed be five cubits, starting from one cubit;
its length should be made equal to that, for such a proportion bestows auspiciousness.
Up to a length of ten cubits, it should be fourteen finger-breadths in height for each cubit;
beyond that, it may extend up to thirty cubits.
Beyond that, a platform twelve finger-breadths high should be made;
up to fifty cubits [in length], the height of the archway is considered to be nine finger-breadths.
The sections of the maṇḍovara should be constructed by the artisan such that the maṇḍavāraka consists of one hundred and forty-four parts.
These are considered to extend from the top of the pedestal (pīṭha) to the top of the dome (śikhara).
The cornice (khuraka) occupies five parts, and likewise, the pitcher (kumbhaka) occupies twenty.
In eight parts, the pitcher (kalaśa) and the intervening space are two and a half [parts] each;
in eight parts, the pigeon-cornice (kapotikā), and the pedestal (mañcikā) consists of nine parts.
The shank is produced from thirty-five parts; the emergence [of the knee] is in fifteen;
the *bharaṇī* is eight parts, and the *śirāvaṭṭī* is ten parts.
The *kapotālī* consists of eight parts with an interval of two and a half;
the covering is thirteen parts, and the projection is ten parts.
The *khuraka* is five parts in height, with its projection being two parts;
the *antarapatra* is half a part, and the *karṇaka* is two parts.
The *vāpī-skandha* consists of one and a half parts, while the *kaṇakottama* is one part;
the tip of the *kaṇaka* should be made beautiful with two fillets (*paṭṭikā*) for a pleasing appearance.
The *paṭṭikā* should project out by one part, and the *bodhi* should not exceed that;
the *kaṇaka* should have a projection of one and a quarter parts. || 13 ||
The emergence of the apaskandha from the great row of the kumbhaka should be performed up to the ears; now, indeed, listen to the kumbhaka.
The height of the *kumbhaka* there is twenty parts;
it is divided into sections, with the *skandhapaṭṭa* being half a part and the *cippikā* being one part.
The shoulder-band should be made very graceful, circular, with variegated leaf-patterns, and beautiful, so that the sight upon it is indeed lovely. (16)
One should cause the *cippikā* to be adorned with lotus petals;
in the eastern, middle, and western sections of the pitcher, one should place Brahmā, Hari, and Hara.
Images should be established according to their forms, worthy of being seen, and accompanied by their weapons;
they should possess the auspicious beauty of the three junctions of the day, as well as various paintings.
One should indeed fashion the shoulder-band (skandhapaṭṭa) as it appears [in the model], beautiful to the mind;
the nostrils are to be placed upon the petals of the pratirathikā, which is named after the ears.
In the corners and in the central inner sanctum, auspicious images should be fashioned;
on the pillars, an archway should be constructed resembling a lotus petal.
Thus, adorned with lotus stalks and the like, possessing an excellent form, this kumbhaka, having a variegated appearance, is considered the most excellent. 21.
Above the *kuṃbha*, a very beautiful *kalaśa* should be made, consisting of eight parts;
its middle portion should be made very ornate, consisting of six parts. || 22 ||

It should be fashioned in the form of a rounded base, and above that, an auspicious *cippikā* (a small knob or finial) should be made; on one side, a beautiful *paṭṭabandha* (a ribbon-like band) should also be fashioned. ||23||
It should be fashioned endowed with jewels within two and a half parts;
an intermediate space should be fashioned, adorned with divine flowers and the like.
Then, the *kapotālī* (dove-cornice), which brings auspiciousness, should be made one-eighth [of the width];
the *skandhapaṭṭī* (shoulder-band) half a part; and the *skandha* (shoulder) two and a quarter parts. ||25||
The face-band (mukhapaṭṭī) occupies one part, and the ear-band (karṇapaṭṭikā) two parts;
the auspicious projection of the shoulder (skandhasyanirgama) consists of two and a half parts. ||26||
The shoulder-band (skandhapaṭṭa) should be made half a part in width and joined to the neck-band (galatā);
the face-band (mukhapaṭṭī) should also be made, and below it, at the front, the gagārakas.
The two faces facing forward should be four finger-breadths wide, symmetrical, and considered beautiful; the upper shoulder, moreover, should be fashioned with an inner recess for the petal.
Above the interior of the *kapotālī* (dove-cot), a *ṭhagārikā* (balcony) should be constructed;
above the *kapotālī*, a *mañcikā* (pedestal) consisting of nine parts should be made.
Then follows the inner petal (antarapatraka) measuring one and a quarter parts;
the *kāmarūpa* measures three-quarters of a part, and the fillet (*paṭṭikā*) is one-quarter of a part.

The shoulder-piece (skandha) consists of two parts, and the face-band (mukhapaṭṭī) follows that; likewise, the ear-piece (karṇaka) is one and a quarter [parts], and the shoulder-piece is also one and a quarter. ||3.1||
The leaf-pattern should be one and a quarter units, and the fillet (kaṇa) likewise one and a half parts;
the beautiful and auspicious *nirvāṇa-ṭṭikā* should be made at the foot.
Gagārakas should be made with openings for the sūtras at the kapotālī;
the jaṅghās and stambhas should be rich in projections, and below them should be circular lumbikas. ||33||

Above that, the shanks (jaṅghikā) should be made, occupying thirty-five auspicious parts; they should be provided with spherical pillars (golastaṃbhī) and endowed with the nose-ornament (nāsāphala) and the nose (nāsā). ||34||
At all the principal entrances, four-pillared pavilions should be constructed,
adorned with elephants, lions, garuḍas, crocodiles, and horses.
In the ears are the eight guardians of the directions in clockwise order starting from the east;
dancing Rudra is in the southeast, and the slayer of Andhaka is in the south. (36)
The goddess Caṇḍanāśakarī with fanged face is likewise in the north;
in the Pratiratha [sections] are the Sūtra-deities as well as the lords of the directions. (37)
The lords of sages, established in austerity, should be placed along the watercourses;
and windows should be made in the auspicious sections, provided with exits.
Adorned with five pillars, canopies, and decorative marks, they are beautifully graced by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Mahādeva, and are most pleasing to behold. (39)
Above the small pillars of the windows, they were adorned with semi-spherical arches;
on the lower walls (jaṅghā), there were either figures of couples or likewise groups of birds.
Or likewise, the *mañjarī* and *parya* [styles] should be made so beautiful that the *bharaṇī* is eight parts in height, possessing a metrical form shaped like a sphere.
The exit, the neck-band, and the shoulder-ornament should be circular;
it must not be made with uneven petals at the exit. ||42||
The *kāmarūpa* is three-quarters [of that], and the shoulder-band (*skandhapaṭṭikā*) should be one-quarter;
the *cippikā* is half a part, and likewise the *kaṇaka* is one-and-a-quarter parts. ||43||
The band, the interval, and the foot are always prescribed as one unit each;
the shoulder should be made two units, and the ear-lotus half a unit.
The band, the interval, and the foot are likewise considered to be one part each;
the shoulder is half a part, and the fillet (vartana) is three-quarters of a part. ||45||
The inner leaf should be made half the size [of the outer leaf] to bestow desired results;
auspicious sprouts should be fashioned on all the side-branches of the nose. (46)
Moreover, those aśoka sprouts indeed grant all desires; they have their stalks bound upon golden [bases] and take the form of tamāla leaves. ||47||
And above the Bharaṇī [constellation], in the northern sector, the Pralīnin [deities] should be fashioned;
and in the tenth part, the auspicious Śirāvaṭṭi should be made elevated. 48.
In that [structure], auspicious load-figures (bhāraputtalikā) should be made in three parts;
the shoulder should be one-quarter less, and likewise the ear-part should be one-quarter less.
In the middle, there should be half a part; likewise, a band (paṭṭaka) should be placed within that interval.
A circular head-piece (śirāvaṭī), provided with a central cord (tantra), should be made to occupy five parts.
It should be adorned with pearls and endowed with diamonds;
above that, a row of pigeons (kapotālī) should be well-proportioned, measuring one quarter-part (pādabhāga).
The intermediate space, however, must indeed be made to measure two and a half parts;
therein, the covering should be made according to the thirteenth part.
The shoulder-band is half a part, and the shoulder itself is three parts;
the face-band is half a part, and the height of the pediment is four parts. ||53||
The *daṇḍikā* is one part, and the *antarāla* is four parts;
the *kaṇaka* is one and a quarter parts, and the *skandha* is also two parts. (54)
The shoulder-band (skandha-paṭṭī) measures one-quarter part and fulfills all desires;
the eaves-projection (kapota), which is slightly smaller, is considered to be one-tenth part. ||55||
The lower part of the trunk is indeed four parts; the wrist-joint is one and a half parts;
the tip of the penis is half a part; this [liṅga] shall be the bestower of all desires. || 56 ||
The *kāmarūpa* is one part; the shoulder-band (*skandha-paṭṭikā*) is one-quarter of a part;
the *cippikā* is also half a part; and the face-band (*mukha-paṭṭikā*) is one-quarter of a part. ||57||
The *kaṇaka* is two parts, and the *daṇḍaka* is half a part;
at the location of the wrist (*maṇibandha*), the *sārilambana* is three parts.
The loss is one-tenth, while the revenue is one-sixth;
for the water-course, the revenue is one-sixth and the entry [of water] is also one-sixth. ||59||
The sixteenth part of that portion shall consist of the width and length of the palm;
when established in this manner, the temple will indeed be firm and grant long life. ||2.137.60||
All the stationary parts, beginning with the *kuṃbha*, have equal threads at their projections;
likewise, the projection of the pedestal (*pīṭha*) on the exterior is the same as that of the covering (*ācchādaka*).
The measurement of the *kumbha* (pitcher) and the length of the temple should be understood by the artisan as appropriate according to the primary *nāsikā* (nose/face). 62.
The emergence of the phalanges of the minor limbs (upāṅgas) should be understood by a craftsman of beautiful workmanship as being three, five, seven, and nine [units] outside [the main body]. 63.
Karṇa, Pratiratha, Karṇikā, Nandikā, Uparatha, Bhadra, and Subhadra are [the names] at the exit. 64.
It should be made such that it extends beyond the boundary of the base;
indeed, seven *nāsikas* should be fashioned within the six-part division of the *bhadra*.
The first [section] consists of eight parts, the second is one-tenth [of a part],
the third is also eight parts, and at the end there are four and a half.
The auspicious half [of the site] should indeed be one-sixth, while the full [portion] should be one-twelfth;
the site for the temple should be made octagonal.
In the case of stone walls, the thickness of the foundation is always considered to be one foot;
furthermore, it should be understood that for stone walls, this may extend up to six parts [of the total height]. //68//
A wall made of wood for a palace is considered to consist of seven parts;
a wall made of gold, silver, and so forth, as well as one made of rubies and the like, consists of ten parts.
A circumambulatory path (bhramaṇī) should also be constructed, measuring one-tenth of the temple's size;
from the center of the circumambulatory path and its corners, the lines should be led upward according to that sequence.
In a palace of fifty elephants, the upper gallery should be circular like that of the Bhadra type;
the pavilion (maṇḍapa) should also be circular and supported by pillars.
The lamp-shrine should be constructed in the southern portion of the temple;
likewise, the pillar-base should be made half the width of the temple's breadth.
Above that, a very beautiful śukanāsa (gargoyle) should indeed be fashioned;
the entrance should be made in the east, west, or north, but not in the south.
The door of the Gajaprāsādaka temple shall be sixteen finger-breadths in height;
it extends as far as four elephants, with sixteen [finger-breadths] for each cubit.
In a [stūpa] measuring eight cubits, the height should be increased by three finger-breadths;
up to fifty cubits, it should be increased by two finger-breadths for every additional cubit.
The width of the door is always auspicious when it is half of its length;
if one-sixteenth part of the height is added to that half, it is likewise excellent. (76)
That indeed shall be the most excellent door, bestowing all prosperity and happiness;
in a palace of celestial chariots and various flowers, the *nāgara* style is auspicious. (77)
The Vaiṣṇava door should indeed be made with nine branches;
a banner should be placed at the door according to the measurement-line of the temple.
One should divide the door-jambs according to the proportions of the base;
indeed, in a nine-part [structure], there should be nine jambs, while in a three-part [structure], they should be auspiciously arranged.
For the sake of purifying the defects of income, even the shortening and increasing [of dimensions] are approved;
the door-keepers should be made very beautiful in the middle section.
Subtle creepers are also considered to be beautiful upon the side-branches.
At a height of one-fourth the length of the branch, two auspicious door-keepers are prescribed.
On the left is the Yamunā and on the right the Gaṅgā; likewise, both Gandharva women and Gandharvas should be depicted together with musical instruments. 82.
In the Navaśākhaka [temple], elephants, Garuḍas, swans, horses, and attendants—or whichever deities are appropriate—should be fashioned. (83)
There, eleven parts of the branch (śākhā) should be made as its length;
two form-pillars (rūpastambha) should also be made, measuring two parts each and joined with corner-projections (koṇikā).
In that case, a projection measuring one and three-quarter parts is auspicious;
the first [projection] is the leaf-branch (patraśākhā), and the second is the Gandharva. 85.
The third is Rūpastambhā, while Aśākhā is indeed the fourth;
Gandharvā is the fifth, and Rūpastambha is the sixth. ||86||
The seventh is the Rūpa branch, and the eighth is indeed the Khalva branch; the ninth is the Siṃha branch, or whatever else is desired and beautiful. ||87||

The expansion of the branch-cases (śākhāpeṭaka) is five times the width of the entrance; the image of the deity to be installed should be on the northern beam (uttaraṅga), joined with the deities of the branches (śākhideva).
Alternatively, Lord Gaṇeśa, the gods together with their retinues, and the goddesses who are the beloveds of Brahmā should also be depicted on the northern side. (89)
With a cord from the root-ear, the Udumbara [mark] should be made equal to the Kumbha;
five jewels should be placed beneath the layer.
In the middle third of the doorway, the *mandārikā* is prescribed;
it is shaped like a half-moon and is joined with lotus stalks and petals. ||91||
Beneath the lotus stalk is the jar of dullness (*jāḍyakuṃbha*), and the *kaṇālī* is the pedestal for the ear;
on both sides of the stalk are the corner-pieces (*koṇikā*), and at the opening of the two jaws is the *grāsa*. (92)
Beside the Udumbara tree, there should be sesamum seeds in the form of branches;
the auspicious [pillar] should be made to the height of an Udumbara tree, being one-quarter less than the water-pot.
The height of the half-moon [arch] should always be equal to the *khuraka* (pedestal);
its projection, however, should be half as long as the width of the door. //94//
On two parts of the half-moon, at the half-and-half portion,
the planets Mars and Mercury are to be fashioned on both sides, beautiful and well-formed.
Between the moon and the planet Mars, there should be a conch shell together with a campaka creeper;
upon the moon, a lotus should also be made, for that indeed bestows prosperity and is beautiful. 96.
"O Rādhikā, thus everything within you has been revealed;
Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa has declared you to be the abode of the gods. (97)

Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Dome, the Water-Pot, the *Chajju*, the Nasā-maṇḍapa, the Door, the Udumbara, and so forth," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmīnārāyaṇīya-saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Listen, O Rādhikā; I shall tell you what the beginningless Śrī Hari, the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama), spoke to His devotee Devāyatanaka. 1.
An auspicious pavilion should be constructed according to the dimensions of the temple; its central axis should be established by a cord extending from the corner of the temple's base.
The four-pillared pavilion and the spire should likewise be constructed;
it may be enclosed or open, having either one door or three doors.
A pavilion should be well-constructed at the top of the palace in the temple of the deity;
to the north, south, and east of the pavilion, there should be four small chambers.
A dance pavilion (nṛtyamaṇḍapa) should be constructed, and gate-towers (balāṇaka) should also be built;
indeed, one that measures one and a half parts in length is considered beautiful for a temple (prāsāda).
It should be provided with four pillars and made twice as large, very great;
above the pavilion, there should be a dome (dhūmmaṭa) possessing an elongated and long measurement.
It should indeed be made tall and shaped like a hemisphere;
the pavilion (maṇḍapa) is best when it has eight parts and is enclosed by walls.
It is enriched with stairs and arches, with water-spouts shaped like the mouths of sea-monsters (makaras);
the windows are provided with lattices, or they are considered to be without lattices.
The base, the plinth, the waist-band, the pedestal, and so forth,
should be constructed in the main temple exactly as they are, and they should follow the same single measuring line in the pavilion as well.
The projections of the petals are considered to be half a petal in width and one-quarter of a petal in depth;
having divided the pavilion into nine parts, four of those parts [are used for this].
The central hall should be taken as the basis, and the ground for the performance must indeed be fashioned; it should be variegated, beautiful, and composed of squares.
A pavilion provided with sixty-four pillars is always dear to me;
twenty-one steps should be constructed at the front of the pavilion.
Adorned with jewels and featuring forms of elephants, horses, and Garuḍas, beautiful side-chambers should be constructed on the sides, possessing appropriate width and splendor. (13)
Nine beautiful quadrangular pavilions should be constructed on all sides;
they should be auspicious, enriched with the splendor of many canopies and endowed with variegated beauty.
Indeed, this pavilion named Akṣarabrahma is very dear to me;
it should be constructed with an even number of pillars, never with an odd number.
The pavilion (maṇḍapa) should be understood as being shaped like a *kādamba* flower, or like a lotus, or even having the form of the sun's face; it may also be lunar in nature or resemble a rainbow.
The *jagatī* and the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) are considered to have an extension according to the measurement of the *bhadra*;
the *jagatī* at the gateway (*pratolī*) is also considered to have an extension like that of the *bhadra*.
The door-keepers (pratihāras) should be fashioned at the front of the principal image, on both its sides,
extending from above the human pedestal up to the top of the bharaṇī moulding.
Thereafter, fifteen squares (padas) are to be made;
one part is considered the Rājasena, and two parts are the Vedicā.
The pillar consists of four parts, with its capital (paṭa) situated at half a part;
the fillet (bharaṇa) is half a part, and the sacrificial vessel (caru) is likewise one part.
One and a half parts shall be the *pāṭa*, and after that the *chādyaka*;
likewise, the *kammānikās* should be fashioned, along with beautiful arches (*toraṇas*) and other such ornaments.
To the east of the theater pavilion, pavilions for dancing should be constructed;
likewise, pavilions for storytelling and pavilions for fire-offerings (homa) should be made.
For the concluding ceremony (udyāpana), pavilions and dance-halls (rāsamaṇḍapas) should be constructed;
however, the piercing of the site (vāstuvedha) must certainly not be performed, nor indeed the piercing of the pillars (staṃbhavedha). || 23 ||
The thickness of the pillar should be ten parts at its base, increasing up to fourteen parts;
this is relative to the thickness of the temple and follows the solidity of the stone.
In a palace of one cubit [in height], the pillar shall be four finger-breadths;
in one of two cubits, seven finger-breadths; and in one of three cubits, nine finger-breadths. (25)
Then, for a twelve-cubit [structure], there is an increase of two fingers per cubit,
and up to sixteen cubits, there is an increase of two and a quarter fingers.
The increase in finger-widths continues until forty cubits;
up to fifty cubits, it increases by three-quarters of a finger-width.
The pillars at the summit are adorned with svastikas and eight-sided bhadras;
likewise, the base-pillars are enriched with figures, leaves, and beautiful creepers, as well as bhadras.
In the supporting structure, there should be rafters joined with creepers and accompanied by kinnaras;
my residence must indeed be made as an excellent seven-peaked edifice.
At its front, the *kolikā* is to be understood; at its front, the *gūḍhamaṇḍapa*;
then the *nṛtyamaṇḍapa*, and then the maṇḍapa known as the *sabhā*.
Then indeed the Rūpacokī, and then the Sopānakas;
fifty-six on the right side and fifty-six on the left. (3.1)
Temples for my wives must be constructed on all sides; I shall reside in the central temple, and my six wives in the surrounding ones. (32)
In the pavilions and domes, seven terraces each should be constructed, beautifully adorned with Rāsa-dance arenas, archways, altars, and other features. (33)
In the west is the chariot-house, in the south the monastic cells,
in the north the kitchen, and in the east the armory.
In the northwest is the storehouse, while in the southeast is the kitchen;
in the northeast is the flower hall, and in the southwest is the utensil room. (35)

In the west, a water-house (jalaśālā) should be built, and above it, a recitation hall (vācanālaya); furthermore, the various residences should be constructed with due regard for the surrounding temples. ||36||
In one-third of the height of the door, two parts should be occupied by lattices;
likewise, windows should be made, either short or extending to the top. (37)
Above the pavilion is an octagon, and above that, a sixteen-sided figure;
above that is the dome (ghūmmaṭa) and the sphere (gola), with a height equal to half the length [of the base].
Having divided the height into sixty parts, in the first [of these], the *karṇas* and *dardarikās* are seven parts in both height and projection. (39)
The neck of the *rūpaka* is considered to be one-fourth [of the total height] and provided with a projection of two parts;
sixteen Vidyādharas and twenty-four elephants are to be fashioned.
The emergence [of the deities] in the seventh part is considered to be by way of the vastness of the Vidyādharas;
above that are those of variegated forms, namely the female dancers performing their rhythmic dances. 41.
The first [sections] are six and a half parts; the second are six parts;
then the *kola*s are five parts, plus four and a half *gavālaka*s.
The canopy over the central dome was adorned with figures performing music, singing, dancing, and other arts, which shone with the splendor of wonderful tales.
The interiors were adorned with various paintings of the world of living beings, the world of the lords, the world of Brahmā, and so forth;
and the canopies were the color of the sun, studded with jewels.
The first section of six parts should be decorated with ornaments;
those same [sections] from the second onwards are increased by four parts each.
Twenty-five [deities] adorned with ornaments should be fashioned in sequence;
in the first [set], five bells should be made that are exceedingly beautiful.
From the second [square] onwards, they should be made by increasing by four;
thereafter, on the left and right, in the half of Bhadra and the half of Rakṣā, there is the nine-bell [pattern].
In the half-portion extending over the width of the *rathikā*, bells and pinnacles (*kūṭas*) should be fashioned above the *rathikā*; thereafter, the pinnacle-vase (*kalaśa*) should be placed.
The first bell should be fashioned, adorned with five kalaśas; likewise, further beautiful bells should be made in a single series extending forward. (49)
At intervals of one, two, three, four, five, six, or seven paces,
there shall be a quadrangular platform for the deity of the palace and for the vehicle.
The vehicle-seat should be fashioned as something very beautiful and auspicious;
it consists of nine parts of the deity’s form, from the feet up to the crest. (51)
The height of the vehicle should be made up to five, six, or seven parts;
or else, it should be equal to the two eyes of the vehicle, and the heights of the secret organ, the navel, and the breasts [should be proportioned accordingly].
The two lines should be equal, and likewise the height of the vehicle;
or rather, the vehicle should have its lines level with the feet, the waist, and the knees.
The height of the Śiva-liṅga’s base (vāha) should be equal to the height of the water-receptacle;
the height of the Sun’s base (sūryavāha) is considered by the Lord to be equal to the line of Skanda (skandharekhā). 54.

Around the principal temple, there should be temples equal in number to the central chambers (garbhas). Having established the central chamber, one should then construct [the others], but one must not cause a piercing of the navel (nābhivedha). ||55||
The palaces of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva are situated to the east and west;
the gods facing toward the city are always auspicious and bringers of well-being. (56)
When turned away from the city, all these auspicious deities—the nine planets, Gaṇeśa, Bhairava, Caṇḍī, and Nakulīśa—destroy it. (57)
The Mothers and Kubera are auspicious when facing south;
Hanumān faces the southwest (nairṛtya), and no other deity [is so directed]. (58)
The best image is one-third the height of the interior of the temple;
that which is less by one-tenth is proclaimed as the middling. (59)
The smallest [door] is reduced by one-fifth and is shaped like a svastika;
it is positioned at one part above the top of the nine parts that constitute the height of the door.
When one-eighth remains, it is considered auspicious with a height of four parts;
likewise, a lion-throne (siṃhāsana) measuring four parts is also prescribed.
Alternatively, among the thirty-two parts of the height of the door itself,
having omitted the upper four, [the measurement is] in twenty-eight parts.
The lion-throne and the image are prescribed for the fourteenth [day];
the lion-throne for the thirteenth, and the form is recorded for the fifteenth.
The lion-throne is prescribed for the fifteenth [part], and the image for the thirteenth;
if the lion-throne is in the twelfth, then the image is in the sixteenth part.
In a temple of one cubit, the image should be eleven finger-breadths;
it should be increased by ten finger-breadths for each cubit up to four cubits.
It should be increased by two finger-breadths up to ten cubits;
it should be increased by half a finger-breadth until it reaches a limit of fifty finger-breadths.
The medium [form] is diminished by one-tenth [of its size], and the smallest is diminished by one-tenth of that;
the form is dormant within the inner chamber, occupying five out of seven parts.
Two parts are to be avoided; [the remaining area] situated where one rests provides comfort, excluding two sections of the interior of the palace and the section of the doorway. 68.
In the remaining section, five parts should be made, each equal to half a seat;
in the first part, which is attached to the wall, the seating for the Yakṣas and others is to be placed. (69)
In the second division, indeed, shall be the seats of all the gods;
and in the third division, indeed, shall be the seats of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Hara.
In the northeast, at the fifth part [of the measurement], the seat of Śiva (śivāsana) should be one barley-corn (yava) in size;
indeed, for all temples, the division is considered to be measured from the inner sanctum (garbha).
Indeed, from the middle portion of the womb, the seats of the deities are arranged in sequence:
they are square, rectangular, and likewise oblong-circular.
One should fashion the wall-maṇḍalas according to what is appropriate,
either as circular or even as octagonal, numbering exactly twenty-eight.
Śiva is in the center, while Viśvasṛj is in the second maṇḍala;
Nakulīśa is in the third, and Sāvitrī is considered to be in the fourth. (74)
Rudra is the form in the fifth, while Svāmī Kārtika is in the sixth;
Brahmā is in the seventh, and Vāsudeva is in the eighth maṇḍala.
Janārdana [is worshipped] in the ninth, the Viśvedevas in the tenth;
Agni in the eleventh, and likewise the Sun-god in the twelfth.
Durgā is honored in the thirteenth [chapter], and Vighneśa in the fourteenth;
the nine planets in the fifteenth, and the Mother-deities in the sixteenth.
In the seventeenth [chapter], the Gaṇas are also [described]; Bhairava is held to be in the eighteenth;
the Kṣetrapālas in the nineteenth; and the King of Yakṣas in the twentieth.
Hanūmān is in the twenty-first [year], Bhaga likewise in the twenty-second;
the other gods are in the twenty-third, and Daityaka in the twenty-fourth.
In the twenty-fifth [year] there is a Rākṣasa, but in the twenty-sixth a Piśāca;
in the twenty-seventh is the class of Bhūtas, and in the twenty-eighth it is indeed empty.
The deities, served by their respective wives, servants, maidservants, family members, and devotees, should always be installed in their own abodes according to what is appropriate. 81.
And likewise, the elephant-throne, the lion-throne, or the swan-throne;
or a celestial chariot (vimāna) to be borne by liberated beings, or one with a parasol—the most excellent of the excellent.
Just as the Śaivaliṅga is, so too is the pedestal (yoni-kāsana);
the yoni should be made with eighteen parts according to its height.
The *kaṇa* should be one and a half parts, and the first fillet (*paṭṭikā*) half a part;
the second fillet is equal [to the first], and the shoulder (*skandha*) is known to be three parts. ||84||
Another band is half a part, while the intermediate leaf is one and a half parts;
another band is half a part, and the corner is two parts. ||85||
Another band is half a part, while the leaf is one and a half parts;
another band is half a part, and the shoulder is three parts.
There should be two bands, each measuring one and a half parts;
then the *karṇaka* measures one and a half parts, after which the appearance of the *liṅga* is revealed.
Whatever material the liṅga may be made of, it is considered to be of that same material for its base (yoni).
It may be square, circular, with a girdle, or having many corners. ||88||
The thickness of the liṅga should be measured with a thread, for that constitutes its circumference;
the pedestal should be made as long as the thread and indeed wide as well. (89)

The sūtra should be divided into three parts; it is considered that the yoni occupies two parts, while the Śivaliṅga occupies one part in height—this should always be understood by the wise. (2.138.90)
The water-channel is considered to extend from the *liṅga* to its exit, measured by a cord;
the length of the cord is exactly twice [the height of] the *yoni-liṅga*, and not more. ||91||
The entry of the *liṅga* is desired from the top of the head when it is either incomplete or fully complete;
or indeed, the entry of the *liṅga* from above occurs when it is completely full from the *koṣṭha*.
The water-channel should fall into the secret Caṇḍamukha on the north or the left;
for many deities, the channel should indeed be on the plinth (jagatī) in the four directions.
The door-frame should be divided into six parts, and the auspicious gaze of Lakṣmī, Nārāyaṇa, and others should always be placed in the fifth [part]. 94.
In the third part of the form of Śiva, and likewise for the illustrious Śeṣaśāyin,
one should divide the door-jamb into eight parts and then further divide one of those parts into eight.
Thus, there are exactly sixty-four divisions in that regard in every respect; the vision of the gods occurs in a single division, but not in a pair—this is the determination. (96)
Among the thirty-two divisions, the aspect of the deity (devadṛṣṭi) is prescribed for the odd ones;
the even divisions are strictly forbidden for the purpose of the deity's aspect, as they cause loss.
Through the ripening of the fault of wrong views, there is the destruction of one's station and the loss of wealth;
whatever is struck down by the fault of wrong views does not grow again. (98)
With an upward gaze there is loss of wealth; with a downward gaze, loss of enjoyment;
an even gaze bestows happiness at all times, as is appropriate. 99.
Among the sixty-four divisions, the first consists of the Ādi-tattva;
creation is the third tattva, and the eighth is in the fifth, while the sacrifice (iṣṭi) is in the seventh.
Longevity is considered to reach one hundred thousand years in the ninth and eleventh [stages];
likewise, one is considered wise in the thirteenth and learned in the fifteenth.
The principle of peace (śāntitattva) is unmanifest in the seventeenth [chapter], and likewise in the nineteenth;
it is both manifest and unmanifest in the twenty-first, while in the twenty-third it is manifest alone.
In the twenty-fifth [pillar] is Śeṣanāga; in the twenty-seventh lies Hari;
in the twenty-ninth is Garuḍa; and in the thirty-first are the Mothers.
Kubera is in the thirty-third [chapter], Varāhaka in the thirty-fifth;
Umā and Rudra are indeed in the thirty-seventh, while Buddhaka is in the thirty-ninth.
Then, in the forty-first and the forty-third [years], there were those three other great sages: Durvāsas, Nārada, and Agastya. || 105 ||
In the forty-fifth [chapter], Śrī Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa and others [are described];
in the forty-seventh, Dhātṛ, and thereafter the deities.
In the forty-ninth [digit] is Śāradā and Gaṇeśa;
and in the fifty-first digit is Brahmā seated upon a lotus throne.
In the fifty-third [chapter], there is the accomplishment (siddhi) of Hara and other such [accomplishments];
in the fifty-fifth, the unborn Viṣṇu, Sūrya, and the dispassionate ones.
In the fifty-seventh [chapter], Śukrācārya is described as he was in the past;
and in the fifty-ninth, Caṇḍikā and other goddesses are described.
In the sixty-first [chapter], the gods beginning with Bhairava are proclaimed;
in the sixty-third, those beginning with Vetālaka; beyond that, however, there is only emptiness.
The gaze [of the deity] should be directed toward the feet or the waist of the image, while for the vehicle it is likewise;
through such installation in the proper place, the four aims of human life are attained.
O Rādhikā, when things are contrary, the fruit indeed becomes contrary;
thus Kṣayakṛt spoke to the sage Devāyatanaka regarding Śrī Hari. 11.2.

Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Measurement of the Temple, the Pavilion, the Dhūmaṭa, the Throne, and the Respective Parts of the Deities and Others," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Listen, O Rādhā, to that which was told by Hari to the deity;
I shall relate to you that Śikharādya in brief. (1)
Now, I shall describe in brief the various auspicious types of *prāsāda-śikhara* (temple spires) along with their divisions and their variegated structural arrangements.
It has many peaks, many turrets, and many parapets;
it possesses many auspicious windows and is indeed multiform and eternal.
That householder’s dwelling has many altars and many seats, with many climbing vines and falling leaves; it has many lines, many wonders, and many corners.

It has seven stories, a hundred stories, and a pinnacle; it possesses many rooms for children, terminates with a moon-chamber (candraśālā), has many finials (kalaśas), and is like a forest-dweller’s hermitage.
It may have one horn, or be hornless, or belong to a noble species; likewise, it may be long-bodied, globular, or whatever form is desired.
In its width it should be one-fourth [of the base], while in length it should be one-fifth;
at the top, there should be three kalaśas joined with lions and hanging globes.
The right and left portions of the hanging globes (lambagola) have a width of one and a half units;
the emergence from the forehead constitutes the eight-fold auspicious hanging globe.
A single egg-shaped pinnacle (golashikhara) on the ear [of the temple], and rows of egg-shaped pinnacles starting from one-fourth and increasing by twelve up to one hundred and twelve.
Upon seeing the terraces, there are indeed peaks;
for above even a single terrace, there are many peaks.
Above the covering (chādya) there should be a projection (prahāra), and on that peak, another peak higher still;
indeed, peaks numbering one, two, or three are formed by means of a single line alone.
A line of wall-ornamentation (śṛṅgabhitti-rekhā) within the interior of the womb is not at all praised;
however, that which is broad and expansive on the exterior bestows all happiness. 12.
The upward extension of the horn-line (śṛṅgarekhā) should indeed be taken as one and a quarter or one and a half units in relation to its length; it must never be less than that.
A bell should be placed upon the upper part of the shoulder-projection; it is auspicious and bestows fruit.
One should again provide a portion for the prongs, and there, further prongs should be fashioned.
Beautiful images accompanied by musical instruments are considered appropriate at the base of the pinnacle (śṛṅga);
likewise, beautiful śṛṅgikas are likewise [placed] on the sides of the pinnacle and above the pinnacle. || 15 ||
The broad-crested [ornaments] should be made, either nine or with equal lines;
from the base of the first broad crest up to the limit of the shoulder of the subsequent broad [section]. 16.
Thirteen parts are to be made; having formed the first horn from seven parts, one should then crush the second, large horn.
Thus, indeed, nine parts are to be made from the base of the *mṛdya* upwards;
having divided the base of the line into ten parts, there shall be six parts above.
The shoulder (skandha) should be made beautiful, neither exceeding its proportions nor being defective; it should not be less than five parts, so that it remains truly pleasing to behold.
If the flagstaff enters at the root or the trunk, it causes the destruction of the master;
and for every finger-breadth [of deviation], the seat of the flagstaff is outside [the intended position]. (2.139.20)
A window should be placed on the first pinnacle, a *māḍha* (pavilion) on the second,
and it is considered auspicious to have a lion-base extending up to the third summit.
Up to the fourth head, he is called Śukasiṃha;
or alternatively, up to the ninth, there are other divine forms.
The deities should be placed in the windows, while Śuka and Hari are to be stationed at the front of the three [shrines];
Bhadra is to be established [therein], and by that, all happiness arising from the spire shall be attained.
From the *chādya* up to the end of the *skandha*, there are indeed twenty-one sections;
between the ninth and the thirteenth [sections] are the lions and the *śukanāsas*.
In that [measurement], five auspicious śukanāsas (gargoyle-noses) are to be made;
from one to nine kolīs in length according to the measuring line, they are considered to be like lions. 25.
One should construct the pillars in the pavilion according to the dimensions of the central sanctum;
the bell should be made equal to the *śukanāsa* or otherwise slightly smaller.
One should indeed provide as many castor-oil plants as there are horns, humps, and minor limbs;
and on the ears, which have nine corners, one should place a tilaka that is an ornament of white plaster.
Alternatively, the intermediate spaces between the parts should be made auspicious according to their number;
or else, from the commencement of the foundation stone up to the pinnacle, in the case of the total height. ||28||
The sections should be made twenty in number; for when divided into eight parts, the upper story (maṇḍovara) is excellent;
with two and a half times eight [parts] it is middling, and with nine it is the lowest.

The emergence of the pinnacle (śikhara) is said to be directly above the mandovara; likewise, it is [placed] at the second, third, or fourth part among the ten divisions of the temple (prāsāda). (2.139.30)
The emergence of the *śṛṅga* (ornamental pinnacle) is always prescribed at one-quarter, one-half, or one-third [of the height].
Having divided the summit and the base into ten parts each, [the proportions follow] from there.
Two parts each for the two ears, and one and a half parts each for the two *paḍhārakas*;
the *bhadraka* should be made as three parts, and likewise at the top of the *bandhana*.
The nine divisions (navāṃśas) should be constructed; two parts each have two corners, while the two side-panels (paḍharas) are each one and a half parts.
Then, the auspicious central portion (bhadraka) is two parts.
The pinnacle should be one and a quarter times the width of the ear, or one and a half times the width;
between two ears measuring one and a quarter [karṇas], there should be twenty-five lines.
From the rising point to the middle of the ears, there are twenty-five lines;
from eight onwards up to sixty-eight, there are sixteen lines. (35)
In the fivefold state above, there are five; thus, there are twenty-five.
The increase of parts constitutes a *kalā*; by that, such divisions are formed. (36)
Starting from eight and ending at sixty-eight, there are sixteen [units] with an increase of four;
likewise, they extend upwards in the sequence of eight, twelve, sixteen, and twenty.
Alternatively, eighteen [lines] extend upwards and sixteen likewise;
thus, there are indeed two hundred and fifty-six lines.
From the three sections, there is an increase of sections up to eighteen;
each one has eight parts, and by that, there are sixteen equal divisions.
The first [layer] consists of twenty-four parts, the second twenty-seven, and the third thirty; in each of those cases, there are sixteen [parts]. (2.139.40)

Having taken a cord four times the length [of the base], one should form a circle like the interior of a lotus bud from the center line; the height of the dome should be one and a quarter times its diameter.
Five parts, six, seven, eight, twelve, and then sixteen; now, O Rādhikā, I shall indeed describe the *dhvajapuruṣa*. 42.
Starting from the line of the horn (śṛṅga-rekhā) up to the height of the binding (bandhana), one should divide [the space] into six parts;
then, in the sixth part, there should be four units.
Excluding the upper portion,
the remaining three parts should be made into the base for the banner on the right side of the *pratiratha*.
Alternatively, starting from the line, having made two parts up to the end of the shoulder of the prong,
and having divided the upper part into three portions, [one uses] half of that.
A support for the lineage should be fashioned; on his left hand, a banner should be placed, and a flagstaff should be provided on the right.
On the southern side of the palace roof, on a pedestal,
the flagstaff should be erected in the south-eastern direction of one facing east.
In the northeast, at the shoulder-region of the west-facing temple, between the two rows of pillars in the middle, stands the flag-bearer. ||48||
The *paḍharāva* should be made circular and of *āmalasāraka* wood; its beautiful height should be half of its width. ||49||
There, at the top, there are four parts of its height; the neck is three-quarters of that, and the *alasa* part is one-and-a-quarter [parts]. (2.139.50)
The moonlight [candrikā] is one part, and the jhāṃjharī is also one part; thereafter, I shall describe the measurement of the pitcher (kalaśa) in brief. ||51||
In the lotus-bud there are seven parts, and its neck is one part; the *āmalasāra* is proclaimed to have a height of one and a half parts. (52)
The five petals are three-quarters [of the width], and the *jhāṃjharī* is likewise three-quarters;
the auspicious pitcher (*kalaśa*) has a height of three parts and a width of two parts.
The pinnacle (kalaśa) is one-eighth of the length of the temple's spire;
when increased by one-sixteenth, that pitcher is considered excellent in its width.
Increased by one-thirty-second part, that indeed is considered the middle [measurement];
or else, it is one-fifth of the diameter of the line at the base. //55//
The length of the pitcher (kalaśa) should be made beautiful;
or else, it should be one-fourth of the length of the *āmalasāra* [pillar]. (56)
The length that exists in one part is proclaimed to be the measure of the *kalaśa*;
the fourth part should be increased, and from that, the height should be one and a half [parts]. (57)
The height shall be nine parts and the thickness likewise six parts; by these measurements according to the measuring-line, the pitcher (kalaśa) grants all desires. 58.
The neck and the pedestal, however, occupy one part each; likewise, the dome occupies three parts.
Each of the two ear-ornaments occupies one part, and the *ḍoḍala* occupies three parts.
The tip of the ḍoḍala should be one part, the thickness at its base two parts,
the karṇikā three parts, and the chajjī four parts.
The neck is two parts, the half-pedestal is likewise two parts,
the full pedestal is four parts, and the dome (aṇḍa) has a height of six parts.
The golden pitcher-banner, the best among all excellent things,
is proclaimed as the stainless essence of the temple and the abode of the Jīva.
There, the person within the palace is considered the deity of the temple;
that person is to be established as the inner self endowed with consciousness. (63)
In a palace of one cubit, the person is half a finger-breadth;
up to fifty cubits, one should increase it by half a finger-breadth for each successive unit.
His bed is indeed silver; in his right hand is a lotus, and in his left a banner with three pennants, which is held as if against his chest.
The portion for the banner and flagstaff is situated upon the shoulder;
on the *āmalasāraka* is a vessel of ghee made of either copper or gold. (66)
Likewise, the Sthāpanīya [image] should be established; it is considered auspicious when it is a golden man lying upon a silver couch. ||67||
On each of the four legs of the couch, there shall indeed be four jars,
joined with gold and jewels, and adorned with the signs of those treasures.
The names are Śaṅkha, Padma, Mahāpadma, and Makara;
listen as I describe the measurement of the flagstaff. (6.9)

The flagstaff should be made hanging down from the pinnacle of the palace; its length should be exactly equal to the width of the palace, according to the measurement for the eldest [class]. (2.139.70)
The medium [size] is reduced by one-tenth, and the smallest is reduced by one-fifth;
or else, it extends from the top of the *jagatī* up to the very top of the *ghaṭa*.
Of the height, there are three parts; among them, one part constitutes the long staff.
That is considered the largest [size], while the medium is held to be reduced by one-eighth.
The smallest [measure] is said to be diminished by one-sixth in every respect;
alternatively, that which is equal in measure to a line is called the smallest. (73)
If it increases by one-twelfth, then it becomes the middle [type];
furthermore, that *daṇḍaka* becomes the best when it increases by one-sixth.
The boundary for the corners of the temple is considered to be seven cubits;
the boundary for the measurement of the inner sanctum (garbha) shall be twenty-five cubits.
The limit for the measurement of the lines is considered to be fifty cubits; by that same limit, the length of the flagstaff from its base is also determined. (76)
In a palace measuring one cubit, the staff shall be one-quarter of an angula;
thereafter, for each subsequent cubit, one should maintain an increase in width of half an angula.
A measurement up to fifty cubits in thickness is considered auspicious;
it may be made of bamboo, *añjana* wood, *mādhuka* wood, or *śaiṃśapeya* wood. (78)
It should be made of Khadira wood, circular, provided with a series of steps, joined at a single joint, and endowed with a number of knots equal to twice [the height]. ||79||
The *markaṭī* and *pāṭalī* [types of brackets] have a projection equal to one-sixth of the length of the staff;
they are as wide as half that length and as thick as one-third of that width. (2.139.80)
It is equipped with small bells and tinkling bells, beautifully adorned with *kāṅgarīs*;
and the height of the pinnacle (*kalaśa*) is five parts of the length of the *markaṭī*. ||8 1||
Below the monkey, there should be a crescent moon; on its two sides, the syllables *sa* and *ga*;
and above the staff itself, a water-pot with a tip of *kuśa* grass should be placed. (82)
The banner should hang like a staff, its length being one-eighth of that [staff],
and it should be beautifully adorned with three or five cloth strips of various forms.
On the right shoulder [of the deity], at Paṇḍharāya, the flagstaff should be situated;
on the right side behind the temple, it is auspicious at Paṇḍhara.
The *kalāba* (vessel) in the form of a support for the flagstaff is considered auspicious;
its length should be made six parts of the measure of the *mitti*. ||85||
The kalaśa is considered auspicious when its height is equal to that of the bell; and this applies for as many cubits as there are in the width of the temple. 86.
The width of the pit for the staff should be equal to the measurement of those same finger-breadths;
however, in a four-faced temple, the installation of the staff takes place in the northeast.
If one observes a *pāṭalikā* tree slightly toward the northeast on the staff, there will arise an increase in the kingdom, an increase in one's position, and happiness for the subjects. ||88||
Rākṣasas desire to dwell in a great mansion that is devoid of a banner;
however, by the gift of a banner, the deities as well as the ancestors are satisfied. (89)
The merit of ten horse-sacrifices shall deliver a hundred generations of one's lineage;
in the restoration of what is dilapidated, one should follow the original plan and not abandon the layout of the temple.

When a superior material is used in place of the previous material, the collapse of a dilapidated structure is auspicious, provided it occurs during a favorable conjunction of an excellent muhūrta and other such factors. (9.1)

The act of causing a fall [of an image] using elephants or bulls made of gold or silver belongs to another deity; one should not offer a dilapidated or similar object into the temple of a different deity.
Shaking an established deity causes the destruction of merit;
this applies to householders, but not to virtuous ascetics or celibate students. (93)
The re-establishment of the image is considered to be performed at an auspicious moment by means of a bribe;
and the bribe for an elephant or a horse consists of a silver coin or a diamond. 94.
The door panels should be aligned along a straight line, and one should not cause a break in their row;
all stone foundations and other supports should be considered properly aligned according to the same straight line. //95//
Beautiful side-streets and great gate-towers (gopuras) should be constructed;
likewise, a pillar of fame (kīrtistambha) and such things as perforated mechanical devices (vedhayanttra) should be made. ||96||
Thus did Nārāyaṇa speak to his own devotee Rādhikā, and he spoke those same words to Lakṣmī, the devotee of the abode of the gods.

Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-ninth chapter, titled "The Detailed Description of the Specific Features such as the Pinnacle, the Lotus-Bud, the Finial Vase, and the Banner of the Temple," in the second section, the Tretā-saṃtāna, of the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O Rādhikā, listen to what Hari told Devāyatanā regarding the temple, its beautiful structure resembling Mount Meru, and its various divisions.
Indeed, in divine palaces, there may be as many as one hundred golden eggs,
or even one thousand, that are found within them.
The king of palaces is indeed Meru, considered the refuge of all the gods;
this palace is celebrated as being named Akṣara and Goloka. || 3 ||
Known as Vaikuṇṭha, the Unmanifest (Avyākṛta), the Immortal (Amṛta), and the Golden (Hiraṇmaya); also the Son of Fire (Vāhneya), the Vairāja, the Infinite (Bhūman), and the Vaiṣṇava. || 4 ||
Kailāsa, Vaiśāla, Śvetadvīpa, Mandara, the one named Sarvatobhadra, as well as Śrīvatsa and Svastika. || 5 ||
The Haima, Haṃsa, Gāruḍa, Gaja, Vṛṣabha,
Mandira, and the one known as Brāhma— these are the twenty-five types [of temples].
The king of mountains, Meru, is proclaimed to be circular with infinite peaks;
it has thousands of facets, is imperishable, and is filled with infinite abodes.
Goloka is held to be endowed with nine hundred and ninety pillars,
while that which is celebrated by the name Vaikuṇṭha is described as being in every respect adorned with mountain peaks.
In every respect, that which is rich in smoke is proclaimed as "the unmanifest" (avyākṛta);
in every respect, that which is rich in the mere house is proclaimed as "immortal" (amṛta). || 9 ||
In every respect, Karmānikāḍhya is proclaimed to be golden;
in every respect, Vāhneya is proclaimed to be the support of the quarters.
In every respect, that which is rich in the splendor of elephants is proclaimed as the Vairāja;
in every respect, that which is rich in the splendor of horses and so forth is proclaimed as the Bhūmāsaudha. || 11 ||
One who is pervaded by female servants and messengers of Viṣṇu is called a Vaiṣṇava;
however, that which is pervaded in every way by the hosts [of attendants] is proclaimed as Kailāsa.
Vaiśālī is indeed proclaimed to be entirely pervaded by sages; Śvetadvīpa is said to be entirely pervaded by ascetics. (13)
The *sarvabhadra* is quadrangular; the *śrīvatsaka* is like the *śrīyantra*;
the *svasti* is equal to the *svastika*; and the *haimaka* consists of many sections.
Bahuhamsa, Hamsaka, Garudadhya, and Garuda; Pancapada is called Gaja, and Catuṣpada is named Vṛṣa. || 15 ||
The Śatapāda and the Mandira, as well as the Daśapāda and the Brāhmaka—these indeed are the primary [types], distinguished by various subdivisions of their limbs. (16)
Distinguished by various crafts, various forms, and various visible appearances,
[they exist] according to intellect, according to power, according to the world, and according to pleasure.
Indeed, palaces belonging to those who travel in celestial chariots arise in many ways, produced by the intellect of craftsmanship and devoid of human effort.
As many as there are embodied beings, so many shall be such abodes;
moreover, other palaces of manifold forms will also come into being.
It has eight floor sections and five *caṇḍa* elements; it is the *kesarī*.
It is the *sarvatobhadra* with nine *aṇḍas*, for it indeed possesses eight *tila* elements on its base.
The palace named Nandana is joined with thirteen *aṇḍas*;
the mansion Nandiśālika is recorded as having seventeen *aṇḍas*.
There, ten *talabhāga*s constitute four *tilaka*s;
and ten *talabhāga*s plus one [additional] part constitute the *nandiśa* egg. 22.
With twelve sections of floor-levels, twenty-five tiers, and adorned with eight tilakas, it is called the Mandira [temple]. (23)
That which consists of fourteen parts for the base, nineteen sections, and twenty-four dots is called Śrīvatsa. || 24 ||
The *Amṛtodbhava* is said to have fourteen parts for its floors, thirty-three auspicious *bhāṇḍakas*, and sixteen excellent *tilakas*.
[Another version] has fourteen parts for its floors and thirty-seven auspicious *bhāṇḍakas*.
And Himavat is proclaimed as being endowed with twelve tilakas. ||26||
Having fourteen parts for its height and eight *tilakas*,
with forty-one *daṇḍas* [in width], that is called Hemakūṭa.
The sixteen parts of the floor and the four *tilaka*s [are described];
that which has forty-five *daṇḍas* is celebrated as Kailāsa. (28)
With forty-nine cubits for the pillars and sixteen for the floor sections, that temple is celebrated by the name Pṛthvīvijaya. ||29||
The Indranīlaka palace has sixteen square units, eight tilakas, and fifty-three daṇḍakas. (2.140.30)
With sixteen parts of a *tala* for the *tilaka*s and likewise eight [parts], and with a staff of fifty-seven [units], that is called Mahānīla. (3.1)
That mountain has sixteen parts of a *tala* and sixty-one *aṇḍas*;
likewise, it has eighteen parts of a *tala* and sixty-five *aṇḍas*.
Forty-four *tilas* are called a *ratnakūṭa*;
likewise, eighteen parts of a *tala* and forty *tilas* [constitute another measure]. ||33||
The great and auspicious [temple] called Vaidūrya is said to have sixty-nine eggs (aṇḍakas);
it consists of eighteen parts for the floors and is endowed with thirty-six tilakas.
The great and auspicious Padmarāga is said to consist of seventy-three eggs;
it has eighteen parts at its base and likewise thirty-two *tilakas*.
The temple has seventy-seven egg-shaped sections, for it is indeed made of vajra;
it consists of eighteen parts of storeys and twenty-eight *sattilas*.
And that which consists of eighty-one parts is called the "radiant crown";
it has eighteen parts of sesame and twenty-four with sesame. (37)
This [mandala] consisting of eighty-five squares is called Airāvata;
it has twenty-two sections for the floors and likewise four tilakas. (38)
The temple named Rājahaṃsa is said to consist of eighty-nine cells;
it has twenty-two sections on its floors and is likewise adorned with eight tilakas.
That auspicious temple named Garuḍa is said to consist of ninety-three egg-shaped units;
it has twenty-two sections for the floors and four decorative tilakas.
This bull is said to consist of ninety-seven eggs;
likewise, one possessing one hundred eggs has twenty-two parts of a sesame seed.
This is called the Meru palace, for it is the locus of all beauty;
it has a square base, consists of a single block, and is named Tilaka. (42)
The Gaurī-tilaka is square, consisting of eight segments and one egg-cell (aṇḍa), with eight parts at its base and possessing four tilakas and one egg-cell. 43.
The Rudratilaka temple is to be known as the most excellent, bringing happiness;
it has eight parts at its base, four tilakas, and five aṇḍakas. ||44||
That temple, known by the name Śrītilaka, is also auspicious;
it has eight sections on the ground floor as well as four tilakas.
The spire known as Haritilaka is considered to consist of nine eggs;
that same [spire], when consisting of thirteen eggs, is called Lakṣmītilaka.
Having a base of ten parts, supported by twelve *tilakas*, and possessing nineteen *aṇḍakas*, that is called the *bhūtilaka*. ||47||
That same [surface], known as Rambhātīla, measures thirty-three daṇḍas;
it is twenty-four tilakas long and twelve bhāgas wide. 48.
The Mandiratilaka is considered to have thirty-seven sections (aṇḍakas), twelve floor-divisions, and twenty tilakas. 49.
The *pañcacatvāriṃśadaṇḍa* is considered to have a golden tilaka;
it has twenty-four tilakas and measures twelve parts of a *tala*.
The Kailāsatilaka is considered to have forty-nine sections (daṇḍas), with twelve parts for the floors and endowed with twenty tilakas. 51.
The Pṛthivītilaka is considered to have fifty-seven sections (daṇḍas),
while the Tilaka has thirty-six and the Talabhāgaka has twenty-eight.
That which is called the triple world (tribhuvana) is said to consist of sixty-five eggs;
that same [world] consists of sixty-nine eggs and is composed of sapphire and sesame seeds.
With twenty-eight *tilakas* and thirty-two parts for the stories, it is proclaimed as having seventy-three *aṇḍakas*; this is considered the *sarvāṅgatilaka*.
It has twenty-four tilakas, thirty-two talabhāgas, and seventy-seven aṇḍakas; it is known by the name Suravallabha.
This auspicious *siṃhatilaka* design, consisting of twenty-five eggs and eight parts at its base with four sesame seeds, has been fashioned by artisans. 56.
With twelve *tilakas* and seventy-seven eggs, and measuring ten *talas*, that *tilaka* known as Makaradhvaja is considered auspicious. (57)
Adorned with one hundred and forty-five eggs, its floor consists of ten parts and eight *tilas*; it is named Maṅgala.
It consists of one hundred and seventeen eggs (aṇḍakas) and four sesame seeds (tilas); its ten-layered base portion is indeed called Tilakākṣa.
That very same [structure], known as Padmatila, consists of forty-nine pillars;
it has one hundred and sixty-five pillars and twelve parts of the floor-area.
The twenty-fourth *tilaka* is called the *somatilaka*;
it contains one hundred and eighty-nine *aṇḍakas* and indeed twelve *talas*.
The auspicious system known as Vijaya consists of twenty tilakas;
it is a beautiful arrangement of four hundred and twenty-five aṇḍakas.
In this twenty-fourth [chapter], the *Trailokyanam*, there are twelve *tilakas*;
in the thirty-second, there are portions of thirty-two *talas* and four *tilakas*. (63)
That which is known as Ṛṣabha consists of three thousand three hundred and seven eggs,
and it possesses two hundred and sixty-nine eggs.
The Ajita palace is said to have twelve floor-sections;
it has one hundred and thirteen chambers and eighteen stories.
The temple named Svayambhū is said to bestow happiness;
it possesses one hundred and seventy-seven small shrines and is of auspicious form.
The section consisting of eighteen stories is named Abhinandana;
the section consisting of fourteen stories has fifty-seven pillars. ||67||
He who is named Sumati should indeed be known as the bestower of all peace;
his [measurements] are twenty parts of a *tala*, and two hundred and nine *aṇḍas*. 68.
That temple is known by the name Padmavallabha;
it has ten sections on its floor and measures fifty-seven *daṇḍas*.
This temple is celebrated as Supārśvavallabha;
it shall have two hundred and twenty-nine eggs (aṇḍakas).
The temple named Śītala has thirty-two storeys;
it has twenty-four storeys and is endowed with twelve tilakas. ||71||
That which consists of forty-nine daṇḍas is called a portion of Śrī;
it possesses twenty-four tilas and twenty-four *sattilas*. ||72||
That which consists of thirty-three sections is called Śītalā;
it has eighteen horizontal divisions and is endowed with twelve tilakas. ||73||
This [mandala] consisting of seventeen eggs is called by its own name;
it has twenty-two parts for the floors and is endowed with sixteen *tilakas*.
Vasupūjya possesses two hundred and fifty-seven *aṇḍas*, consists of twenty-four layers, and has seventy-seven *kāṇḍakas*. (75)
This temple, named Vimala, shall possess auspicious characteristics;
it shall consist of twenty stories and measure five hundred and three [units] on each side.
That temple of Anantamāyā, which consists of eggs, is said to have twenty-eight storeys and be endowed with twelve tilakas. (77)
Two hundred and twenty-five eggs—this is called the Dharma; and likewise, there are one hundred and eighty-nine parts consisting of twelve stories. (78)
This beautiful temple named Śānta is considered excellent;
it consists of eight floor-sections and is endowed with twenty tilakas.
This [structure] consisting of sixty-nine eggs is called Kanthādhara;
likewise, that which consists of twenty-one eggs has eight parts at its base.
That beautiful temple named Kamalakanda should have twelve storeys and likewise eight decorative tilakas. ||81||
This [mandala] named Mahendra consists of one hundred and eighty-one squares;
it has fourteen sections for the stories and eight tilakas therein. 82.
This [mandala] named Mānasatuṣṭi consists of eighty-five squares;
it has twenty-six parts for the tiers (tala) and is endowed with sixteen tilakas. ||83||
Sumati indeed had seven thousand three hundred and forty eggs;
twenty-two were the portions of the base, and they consisted of forty sesame seeds each. (84)
This one named Nemi has one hundred and ninety-three *caṇḍakas*, twenty-six sections of floors (*talabhāga*), and eight *tilakas*. (85)
That mountain named Pārśva indeed consists of one hundred and thirteen egg-like structures;
it has twenty-four divisions of floors and measures two hundred and twenty-one [yojanas]. (86)
He whose [body] consists of eggs is to be known as the one named Vīra, the bringer of auspiciousness;
he has a single limb, a single palace, is square, and possesses a single egg. (87)
There are those with three parts and three temples, as well as those with five parts and five [temples];
likewise, there are those with seven parts and seven temples, and those with nine parts and nine [temples]. (88)
Possessing various forms of peaks and endowed with the creative ingenuity of artisans, that which is square and has a single dome is indeed called the Vairāja. 89.
The region called Nandana consists of thirteen quadrants; that which consists of twenty-nine quadrants is called Śrīnandana. (2.140.90)
That which has six parts of the base and twenty-five sections is named Mandira;
that which has twenty-nine sections is called Malaya. (91)
That which has thirty-three pillars is called Vimāna;
while Viśālaka has thirty-seven pillars and eight tilakas. ||92||
The Trailokyabhūṣaṇa is considered to have forty-one daṇḍas;
the Talāṣṭāṃśa has forty-five daṇḍas. (93)
Endowed with four *tilakas*, he is considered to be named Mahendra;
indeed, through the increase of his *aṇḍas*, there are seven varieties of him. (94)
That which has ten parts at its base, forty-one *daṇḍas*, and is endowed with sixteen *tilakas* is called Mahīdhara. (95)
"O Rādhikā, this [type of pinnacle] also becomes manifold through the various divisions of the *tilaka* and *kāṇḍa*; thus he then described those varieties of *śikhara*s to him. (96)

Thus ends the one hundred and fortieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Nature of Temples Made of Meru-like Materials, Alphabetic Materials, and Other Various Materials," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Rādhikā, to how Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa spoke; I shall describe to you exactly as it is the devotee Devāyatanaka. (1)
Containing one thousand and one eggs and endowed with seventy-two layers,
this very one named Jyeṣṭha-Meru is considered the most excellent among all.
When the field has been made square and divided into seventy-two parts,
the wall consists of four and a half parts, and the *abhrāntikā* (the space between the wall and the plinth) consists of three and a half parts.
Then, one should divide the square field into ten parts;
one part is to be made for the circumambulatory path (bhramaṇī), and one part is considered for the wall (bhitti).
Each corner consists of two parts, and likewise each *pratiratha* (re-entrant) is one and a half parts; the *bhadra* (frontal projection) consists of three parts, and this is equal in all directions.
Then, one should again divide the square plot into eight parts;
therein, a corner consists of two parts, and a *bhadra* consists of two parts.
Thus, there are three kinds of Meru palaces on earth:
those with seventy-two stories, beginning with Kaṇa and ending with Bhadrakānta.
In that [mandala of] Bodhi, there are six pairs, six pairs, six pairs, and six pairs;
having encircled it up to the ears, the arrangement of the limbs and so forth is joined.
There are eight parts for the half-bhadra, and six parts in the projection;
