above the bhadra are the gavākṣas, as well as the taṅgas and rathikas.
Likewise, five "great-horned" (uruśṛṅga) [pitches] are to be planted in every way;
in the corner, however, are the Sarvatobhadra, the Nandīśa, and the Pṛthivījaya.
These firm-natured ones are established one above the other in succession:
Navāṇḍa, Bhadraka, and Nandīśa, which consists of twenty-one eggs (aṇḍas).
The conquest of the earth is esteemed at forty-nine sections;
likewise, there are the Keśarī and Bhadraka divisions within the square section equal to the ear.
The Nandīśāla should be provided there with five egg-shaped projections (aṇḍakas) and a lion;
the Bhadra has seventeen egg-shaped projections and nine egg-shaped projections.
Then, above the Nandikās situated on the left and right of Bhadra,
there are Keśarī, Keśarī, Śrīvatsa, and likewise Śrīvatsāṇḍaka.
There, one [panel] should have a single pillar and a śrīvatsa; the others, however, are as before.
Then, above the nandikas situated on the left and right of the corner: || 15 ||
Keśarī, Keśarī, Śrīvatsa, Śrīvatsāṇḍaka, and likewise Nandika— these six are to be understood there, whether they be small or indeed large.
The Dhruva should be placed upon the Nandika situated on the left and right ears;
it must be given as a lion (keśarī) and never otherwise. || 17 ||
In the Bhadra [type of temple], however, having made the nose (nāsikā), there is the Śrīvatsa-kāṇḍaka;
and on the left and right ears of the Bhadra, there is the pratikarṇa.
In this manner, eight subsidiary limbs (pratyaṅga) are to be offered in each of the four [directions];
thus, there are indeed thirty-two subsidiary limbs in the four directions.
Thereafter, in the building of seventy-two parts, lines for the seventy-four-fold pinnacle should be drawn.
And thus there exists one [world-system] endowed with a thousand eggs,
known as Jyeṣṭha-Meru, which is the dwelling place of the Supreme Brahman.
I shall describe the central Meru, the field which is square,
divided into sixty-four parts, extending from the center to the corners.
One should divide it by seven, two, three, four, six, two, four, and six.
This [mandala] has seven parts; its auspicious expanse is three parts, and this is the auspicious [Bhadra] division.
The first *nandikā* consists of two parts, while the other consists of three parts;
the *pratikarṇa* is four parts, and the *prātirāthaka* is six parts. ||24||
The *pratikarṇa* is one-fourth [of the side], and the corner (*koṇa*) is likewise produced from six parts;
thus it should be done in the four directions, and the circular sweep (*bhramaṇī*) is considered to consist of six parts.
The walls consist of six-sixths [of the total] and the lines are twenty parts;
these are the Keśarī, Sarvatobhadra, Nandana, and Nandaśālika [mandalas]. (26)
The thirteen [deities] beginning with Aṇḍanandana are to be established in order in the corners;
two Śrīvatsas and Keśarīs are situated in each corner (karṇa) respectively.
The Śrīvatsa, the Keśarī, and likewise the Sarvatobhadra—these three ornaments of the temple should be placed upon the pedestal. (28)
One should place the Śrīvatsa and the Keśarin upon the Nandikā;
the second Nandikā should be fashioned, adorned with two Śrīvatsas. (29)
On the *paḍhara*, the *pratirathaka*, the *karṇa*, and likewise on the *nandika*,
as well as on half of those, on the left and right sides, each minor limb (*pratyaṅga*) should be assigned.
The eggs (aṇḍaka) and the measurement of the peaks are to be understood as before;
this central Meru consists of five hundred and five eggs. (3.1)
Accompanied by the Munividyādharasiṃha, Gajaghaṇṭaka, and Kūṭaka,
as well as the Varālikās and Saṃvaraṇas, he is the one who dwells in Śiva.
The central Meru is said to have sixty-four terraces and five hundred and five eggs; now I shall describe the smallest.
In a field made square and divided into fifty-five parts,
the arrangement should be performed in sequence by means of six, three, three, six, three, and six [parts].
Starting from the *bhadra* and extending to the edge of the ear, there is half a *bhadra* and six parts;
with two parts for the projection (*nirgama*), the *nandikā* likewise consists of three parts.
The second [line] is three parts, and the *paḍhara* possesses six parts;
the third is the *nandikā*, enriched by three parts, while there are six corner sections (*koṇaka*).
Upon their exit, they should be treated with equanimity; thereafter follows the application of the limbs of the ritual action.
The wall is four and a half parts, and the circumambulatory path (bhramaṇī) is likewise extended.
On the *nāmana* (the central part), however, the lines are fixed like the central Meru;
and on each *pratiratha* and at each corner, there are three *śṛṅgas* (projections) each.
Only those known as *keśarin* should be placed above and around;
on the *nandikā* and at each ear, there should be three *śrīvatsas*.
Having made the nose beautiful, two Śrīvatsa marks should be fashioned;
likewise, four thigh-crests (ūruśṛṅga) should be made on each limb, on the left and right sides. (2.141.40)
Meru, the smallest [of the mountain ranges], consists of two hundred and ninety-three eggs;
it is adorned with hosts of Vidyādharas and others, and is indeed beloved by the gods. (41)
Now, even that which is named Mandira is called Merumandira;
this is when the field has been made square and divided into thirty-eight parts.
The *bhadra* shall consist of four parts, and its projection shall be two parts;
the *nandikā* shall be one part, and the second likewise two parts.
The *paḍha* consists of five parts, and likewise another part consists of two;
then there is the *nandikā*, and the corner (*koṇa*) likewise consists of five parts. ||44||
All these petals are equal; that wall is considered to be three and a half [units].
The circumambulatory path (bhramaṇī) is also considered to be three and a half [units] and equal in all four directions.
The ground floor of the central temple is considered to consist of twelve parts;
it should be constructed in all four directions, with three lions at each corner.
Then, above the six lines, one *śrīvatsa* should be made;
furthermore, three *śrīvatsas* and one *tilaka* must also be fashioned.
In the Sarvanandika and Urdhva types, there should likewise be three egg-shaped projections (aṇḍakas) for each of the Śrīvatsas; in the Bhadraka type, four horns (śṛṅgas) are to be made.
One should likewise place the secondary limbs on the right and left sides as appropriate;
furthermore, one should install the forms within the twelve divisions above the lines.
With thirty-eight parts for the terraces and likewise eight for the tilakas,
this Meru is thus considered to consist of eighty-five sections.
The circle of the cosmic egg (aṇḍamaṇḍala) consists of thirty-eight parts of a tale (tala), sixty-four tilas, and one hundred and forty-nine [additional units]. 51.
This temple, known as Lakṣmīkoṭara, is called Meru;
it possesses twenty-four tilakas and thirty-six storey-sections.
Kailāsameruka consists of one hundred and nineteen eggs, is adorned with seventy-two tilakas, and possesses eighteen parts for its floors. ||53||
That [work] named Pañcānana consists of one hundred and sixty-one sections (aṇḍa), twenty-four tilakas, and seventy-seven kāṇḍas. (54)
That Meru-vimāna is said to consist of twenty-six parts of *tilas* on its upper level;
however, on its base level, it measures one hundred and sixty-four *tilas*.
Consisting of thirty-six parts and measuring two hundred and nine sections, this mountain named Gandhamādana is considered a palatial structure of Meru. (56)
It has twenty-six parts for the floor and twenty *tilakas*;
it consists of one hundred and twenty-five *aṇḍas* and is free from corners. 57.
And likewise on the base, there are one hundred and thirty-six *tilakas*;
and for that [base], there are one hundred and thirty-two parts, as well as five. (58)
There were forty *caṇḍakas* known as mountain palaces,
eighty-four *tilakas*, and [a structure] consisting of eighteen stories.
Meru is named Tilaka and consists of twenty-one eggs;
it has ninety-two Tilakas and one hundred and nine eggs.
Meru, the peak of Candraśekhara, consists of thirty-four parts of *tilas*;
it has fifty-six *tilakas* and seventy-three sections (*kāṇḍas*). ||61||
It consists of twenty-eight sections (talas), is named Mandiratilaka, contains thirty-three daṇḍakas, and is endowed with sixteen tilakas. ||62||
And that very Saubhāgyameru consists of twelve parts;
therein, indeed, are forty-nine cosmic eggs (aṇḍas).
Where there are forty-eight *tilakas* and twenty-two divisions of the floor-levels, that is indeed the beautiful Mount Meru. (64)
There are twenty parts of *tala*, thirty-six *tilaka*s, forty-nine *aṇḍa*s, and exactly one hundred [units]. 65.
This auspicious temple, known by the name Śrītilaka, is highly esteemed;
it consists of one hundred and fifty-seven aṇḍakas.
With forty *tilakas* and twenty-eight *sattalas*, that temple known as Viśāla is indeed to be understood as one that bestows auspiciousness. (67)
It has a single egg, forty-four sesame-marks, and twelve divisions of floors; indeed, it is like a mountain peak.
Having forty *tilakas* and fifty-seven *daṇḍakas*, and possessing twenty-two *talas*, he is called Nandivardhana. (6.9)
Thus have all the palaces and my abodes been described;
now I shall speak of the images exactly as they are conceived by me.
The stone should be dense, free from fissures, soft, fragrant, sweet, endowed with luster, beautiful to behold, and suitable for an image. (71)
Stainless gold, bronze, and so forth, as well as any mark made of iron,
and likewise various strange deformities on an image, are terrifying.
Resembling a bee, a pigeon, a white water-lily, mung beans, or lentils;
pale-white, or possessing the luster of ghee or a lotus—the stone is auspicious for all images. (73)
An image less than twelve finger-breadths in height is considered suitable for worship in a home;
from twelve finger-breadths up to nine cubits, it may be worshipped in a temple.
A statue ten *gaja* in height may be worshipped even without a temple;
however, within a quadrangular courtyard (*catuṣkī*), it may extend up to forty-five *gaja*. (75)
An image made of the eight metals, of stone, of jewels, of choice wood, or even of coral and other materials, bestows auspiciousness. (76)
An image that was installed by gods or men more than a hundred years ago is to be worshipped even if it is broken or cracked; any other such image brings about faults.
Even if they are mutilated, deities at sacred fords and in forests must indeed be worshipped, for they grant fruits; but never elsewhere.
A vessel made of precious gems, one made of base metals, or one smeared with unguents that is difficult to repair—if it is fit for restoration, it may then be worshipped. (79)
An image made of wood or stone that is broken is not considered fit for restoration;
it should never be fashioned with extra limbs or missing limbs. (2.141.80)

Images made of wood, plaster, stone, or ivory, as well as those fashioned from glass and other materials, which exceed the prescribed measurements or belong to the retinues of deities, should not be worshipped in the home. (81)
Where the gods engage in roaring, weeping, laughing, opening and closing their eyes, and displaying cruelty, there is great danger. (82)
When the stone that has been laid upon the earth is buried outside,
one should cause it to be positioned with its head directed toward the south or the west, keeping those directions in mind.
The crocodile-faced bird occupies one part; likewise, [the next] two parts belong to the left;
the elephants and others occupy three parts, and the kinnaras occupy four parts. 84.
The auspicious gods Vṛṣa should be made as five parts by the artisan;
Gaṇeśa, Vāmana, and Kroḍa—these are considered to be six parts. (85)
The bull, the boar, and the man should each be made with seven parts;
Pārvatī, Śakti, and likewise the other goddesses should have eight parts. 86.
The other Asuras are nine parts; Śiva and Saṃkarṣaṇa are ten parts;
Caṇḍī, Bhūta, Hanumān, and Kārtika are eleven parts.
The Vaitālas occupy twelve degrees, the Rākṣasas thirteen degrees, the Daityas fourteen degrees, and Bhṛgu fifteen degrees. ||88||
The cruel deities, beginning with Devikā, are always considered to be sixteen parts.
Gaṇeśa, mounted upon a mouse, holds a tusk and an axe;
he has the face of an elephant, bears a lotus and a sweetmeat (modaka), and is adorned with serpents. ||89||
Its mouth is two parts, and likewise its belly is two parts.
The hips are four finger-breadths [in width], from the hips to the knees seven finger-breadths;
the knees are three finger-breadths, and likewise the shanks are seven finger-breadths.
The measurement for the three-limbed [image] is indeed three finger-breadths; now listen as I describe the measurement for the six-part form and the seven-part standard. (92)
The hairline consists of three parts, and the face likewise consists of one part;
the neck is three finger-breadths, and the wing is ten and a half finger-breadths.
The belly is said to be nine finger-breadths, while the space between the navel and the genitals is indeed seven and a half finger-breadths;
the two thighs together measure eighteen finger-breadths.
The knee is three finger-breadths, the shank eighteen finger-breadths, and the foot should be understood as three finger-breadths;
thus the body is seven spans in height.
The face is eight tālas; likewise, the hairline is three aṅgulas;
the neck should be known as three aṅgulas, and the heart is nine aṅgulas.
The navel is measured at twelve finger-breadths, the pubic region at nine finger-breadths;
the thigh is considered to be twenty-one finger-breadths, and the knee three finger-breadths.
The shank is twenty-one finger-breadths and the foot likewise three finger-breadths;
this form, augmented by eight spans (vitasti), is declared for the excellent artisan.
Likewise, I shall describe the nine tālas: the hairline is three aṅgulas;
the face should be known as twelve aṅgulas, and the neck is three aṅgulas. (99)
The heart is ten finger-breadths [in width], the navel twelve finger-breadths;
the abdomen is four finger-breadths, and the secret organ is eight finger-breadths in extent.
The thigh is twenty-four finger-breadths long, the knee is four [finger-breadths], the shank is twenty-four finger-breadths, and the foot is four [finger-breadths]. || 101 ||
The width of the space between the breasts is said to be twelve finger-breadths;
likewise, from the breast to the belly, it should be four finger-breadths in length and beautiful.
An opening of one finger-breadth between the belly and the arms is considered auspicious;
the forearm from the shoulder to the elbow is seven fingers in girth when well-developed. (103)
Then the forearm is sixteen finger-breadths in length and ten in width;
the extension of the forearm is three finger-breadths, and the palm of the hand is likewise [three].
The [upper] part should be twelve finger-breadths in length and five finger-breadths in width;
the middle part should be fourteen finger-breadths long, and the waist likewise. (105)
The root of the thigh is twenty-four finger-breadths, and the shank and forearm are each ten and one [eleven] finger-breadths long;
furthermore, they are four finger-breadths in width.
The length of the foot is fourteen finger-breadths, and the beauty of the toes is likewise; from the armpit to the region of the breast, it extends four finger-breadths upward.
The upper portion of the abdomen above the navel is considered to be eight aṅgulas;
likewise, the neck is eight parts, and the foot is six parts in length—such is the measurement.
Thus, O Rādhikā, although pride arises in many ways,
it occurs exactly according to the age and as Lord Hari has declared for each respective deity.

Thus ends the one hundred and forty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Measurements, Proportions, and Other Details of the Supreme, Middle, and Lowest Meru Temples, as well as the Images of Gaṇeśa and Others," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā. || 141 ||
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Listen, O Rādhikā; I shall describe to you other forms of the Divine, which the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa spoke to His devotee.
One should discard in water an image whose limbs or minor parts are broken;
however, one should not discard it if only its nails, ornaments, garlands, or weapons are damaged.

Indeed, the four-faced creator of the universe [is so called] because of the fourfold division beginning with the Ṛgveda, because of the divisions beginning with the Satya Yuga, and because of the distinctions among the castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇa.
The lotus-seated one, possessing a beard, holds in his right hand a rosary above the wrist, as well as a sacrificial ladle, a sacred thread, and a water-pot.
She holds a rosary, a book, a lotus, and a water-pot;
indeed, this four-faced Sāvitrī brings joy to those learned in the Vedas.
The Ṛgveda is white in color, has two arms, and the face of a donkey;
he holds a rosary and a water-vessel, and is devoted to the private recitation of the Vedas.
He has the face of a goat, is yellow in color, and holds a rosary of beads;
in his left hand he carries a goad, and he is the bestower of prosperity and the bringer of auspiciousness.
The Sāmaveda has the luster of the petals of a blue lotus and the face of a horse;
he holds a rosary in his right hand and a conch shell in his left. || 8 ||
The Veda known as Atharvaṇa is white-complexioned with the face of a monkey;
bearing a rosary and the Khaṭvāṅga staff, he is indeed the bestower of victory.
Viśvakarman has four arms; he holds a rosary, a thread, an elephant, and a water-pot;
he has three eyes and is mounted upon a swan.
Holding the *sudarśana* discus in the right hand and a lotus in the left hand—this is proclaimed to be the form of the Sun known by the name Viṣṇu. (1.1)
Endowed with all the primary marks, adorned with every ornament,
having two arms and a single garment, his hand holds a white lotus.
A circular orb of light, situated in the center and clad in red garments,
joined with seven-faced horses on a chariot yoked with Aruṇa.
Viṣṇu, Gaṇeśa, Sūrya, Śakti, and Rudra are the deities; they should be understood as the fivefold abode (pañcāyatana) and are auspicious everywhere. || 14 ||
There, a nine-part image of Nārāyaṇa should indeed be fashioned,
holding a conch, a lotus, a mace, and a discus, and adorned with a crown.
Hari bears the conch, the discus, the lotus, and likewise the mace;
Kṛṣṇa holds the Pāñcajanya, the mace, the lotus, and the Sudarśana.
Garuḍa is green in form, with a nose shaped like that of an owl;
he has four arms, round eyes and face, and is endowed with a pair of wings. || 17 ||

With thighs, knees, and feet like those of a vulture, golden in color and endowed with all artistic perfections, he should hold a parasol and a pitcher while performing the añjali gesture with reverence.
The left foot is bent at the front, while the other foot is placed behind, resting upon the earth with the knee; thus he is established in the Garuḍa posture. || 19 ||
Umāmaheśvara holds a trident and likewise a mātuliṅga in his right hand,
while he is embraced by her in his left.
The lord of serpents sat with the goddess Pārvatī of auspicious countenance upon his own lap; the hand of Umā, resting upon the shoulder of the other [the serpent], was exceedingly beautiful. (21)
In his other hand he holds a mirror, and likewise a bull stands below him;
he is accompanied by Kumāra, Gaṇeśa, Bhṛṅgī, Raṭa, and others.
One should depict Umā with two arms, and Lakṣmī as resting upon Nārāyaṇa;
Hari is seated upon Garuḍa, equipped with his own weapons.
The right hand should be placed around the neck, while the left hand holds a lotus;
Hari’s left hand rests auspiciously upon the side of Lakṣmī’s abdomen.
She who beautifully holds a trident-line, a drinking vessel, a peacock, and an elephant is proclaimed as Mahālakṣmī. 25.
Above the eight-petaled lotus, Lakṣmī is seated upon a lion-throne;
she sits like Vināyaka, adorned with auspicious ornaments. (26)
The two hands of the Goddess should be raised, holding lotuses;
she holds a jar of nectar in her left hand and a citron in her right. (27)
She has one face and four arms, is resplendent with a crown, endowed with a halo of light, and adorned with earrings and a crest-jewel. ||28||
The Mahāvidyā is proclaimed as being enriched with dice, a lotus, a lute, and knots;
Sarasvatī, when endowed with excellent dice, a lotus, and knots, brings auspiciousness. (29)
A man whose reflection is fixed upon a wall is entirely inauspicious;
a flagstaff should never be erected within a house or a temple.
When the sun is in Uttarā, the installation and other rites of the deities are most excellent;
likewise are the consecration, the formal establishment, the entry, the worship, and so forth. (3.1)
Likewise, at the top of the palace and in the northeast, there should be pavilions supported by elephants;
in the intermediate spaces, there should be three, five, seven, nine, or eleven [pillars].

Having first purified the earth by means of burning, digging, and the pouring of water, and having caused the proclamation of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) and worshipped the Tortoise (Kūrma), [one should proceed]. //33//
After worshipping Śeṣanāga and the Earth as well,
one should thereafter prepare the eastern direction for the sake of the pavilion, according to the prescribed method.
Having made a circle with a cord, one should plant a stake in the center;
one should determine the directions by means of the two lines [drawn] for the times of sunrise and sunset. (35)
It may measure eighteen, twelve, sixteen, or eighteen cubits;
it may be provided with pillars starting from sixteen, or even twenty cubits in length.
It should be one *vitasti* in height and width, or else equal in height and width to an elephant;
when a second pavilion is to be constructed, it should follow the measurements of the first pavilion.
Having set aside a space measuring one cubit, another pavilion should be constructed;
and within that pavilion, which is divided into nine parts, the altar shall occupy the central portion.
The central altar (vedikā) is considered to be one-third of the pavilion's size;
it measures exactly two cubits plus eight finger-breadths.
The four gates should be made beautiful and radiant with archways and other ornaments; now listen as I describe the banners to you. (2.142.40)
Eight banners are to be erected in order starting from the east, measuring two, two, eight, five, five, and five *gavyūtis* in length respectively. (41)
That which is yellow in the east and variegated with elephants is called Indradhvaja;
that in the southeast is red, has a thief's face, is variegated, and has Agni as its presiding deity. (42)
In the south is Kṛṣṇa, rich in buffaloes; he is called Yamadhvaja.
In the southwest is the blue-colored Rākṣasa-dhvaja, who is variegated. ||43||
In the west is the white-colored Varuṇa, who has the face of a crocodile;
in the northwest is the green one with a deer, who is called Vāyu, bearing the wind-banner.
In the north is Kubera, white in color and having the elephant as his emblem;
in the northeast is [Iśāna], white in color and possessing a banner marked with a variegated bull.
Having placed them upon the tops of bamboo poles ten cubits long, one should indeed plant those bamboos in the ground for the sake of stability. 46.
In the middle part of the pavilion, there was a [platform] seven cubits long, or even three cubits wide, beautiful with a network of small bells. ||47||
A beautiful banner, richly decorated with various colors and adorned with yak-tail whisks (cāmara), should be offered;
it is considered auspicious when it is very firm and ten cubits in length from the top of its bamboo pole. 48.
Seven cubits in length and one cubit in width for each, triangular in shape, endowed with their respective weapons, and extending along the bamboo pole. (49)
The vajra, śakti, staff, sword, noose, goad, mace, and likewise the trident—these are to be understood as the weapons in their respective order. (2.142.50)
And banners endowed with the previously mentioned excellence should be placed on all sides;
the ninth banner, white in color, is in the center between the northeast and the east.
Having worshipped it with flowers and other offerings, one should plant it at the heads of the staffs;
I shall now describe the procedure for the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) on the ground within the pavilion.
Beginning from ten cubits up to sixteen cubits in measure,
one should construct an altar in the center of the pavilion, as well as a sacrificial pit and other auspicious pits.
One should indeed construct five, eight, or nine [circles] in the sequence starting from the east;
a four-cornered [figure] in the east, and likewise a triangle-shaped one in the southeast (Agni).
One should draw a half-moon in the south, a triangle in the southwest,
a circle in the west, and a hexagon in the northwest.
In the north, for the Mistress (Īśinī), there is an eight-cornered [altar] resembling an eight-petalled lotus;
it may be circular or square, located in the middle between the east and the northeast.
This preceptor, named Kuṇḍa, possesses sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) for the guardians of the directions and so forth;
or else he may construct five pits, with that one in the east being square.
It is shaped like a half-moon on the right, circular on the west, lotus-shaped on the north, and either circular or [otherwise] in the northeast. 58.
And it should be made square through the differentiation of its various forms; for if only one is desired, that is indeed considered to be square. (59)
That [fire-pit] must indeed be made in the west, the north, or the northeast;
all the fire-pits are to be at a distance of one and a quarter elephant-lengths from the altar.
Alternatively, they are considered to be at the end of the interval comprising one-fourth of the altar;
for Brahmins it is square, but for Kṣatriyas it is circular.
That [mark] of the Vaiśyas is indeed a half-moon; that of the Śūdras is triangular. Alternatively, it may be square for all, or else circular.
The sacrificial pit for women is indeed considered auspicious in every respect;
it should be one cubit in measure and provided with a girdle and a yoni. ||63||
Ten thousand oblations (homāyuta) are for a pit one cubit in measure; fifty thousand (lakṣārdha) for a two-cubit pit;
one hundred thousand (lakṣahoma) for a three-cubit pit; and ten million (daśalakṣa) for a four-cubit pit.
For a five-cubit [mandala], thirty lakhs; for a six-cornered one, fifty million (five hundred lakhs);
for a seven-cubit one, eighty lakhs; and for an eight-cubit one, ten million homas.
For fifty oblations, one should make [the vessel] twenty-one finger-breadths;
likewise, for a hundred oblations, it should be twenty-two and a half finger-breadths.
For the purpose of offering with the hands, it is considered to be one cubit in measure;
for ten thousand oblations, it is two cubits, and for a hundred thousand, it consists of four cubits.
For the purpose of a *daśalakṣa* [homa], it should be six cubits;
for the purpose of a *koṭi-homa*, however, it should be eight, ten, or sixteen cubits.
Sesame and ghee are declared to be the subtle oblation; grapes, barley, and the like are the middling; and wood-apple, coconut, sacrificial fuel, and so forth are the gross.
The sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) must correspond to the nature of the substance used;
alternatively, one may increase the measurement of the pit by one cubit for each hundred thousand [repetitions].
One should have a sacrificial pit constructed measuring ten cubits in extent for up to one million oblations;
or else, a pit of seven cubits may suffice for the purpose of fifty thousand oblations.
For a fire-offering of one million oblations, a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) measuring five cubits is prescribed;
for the purpose of an offering of twenty lakhs, a pit six cubits long is considered appropriate.
For the purpose of performing half a lakh oblations, the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) should be three cubits in size;
its depth is considered equal to the area of the field, and its girdle (mekhalā) is likewise equal.
Even without a girdle, the levelness of the depth is proclaimed;
in a twenty-four-fold division, the twelve-fold part constitutes the neck of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
These girdles may be one, two, three, or two, three, or five;
then, on the eightfold division of the site, one should dig a foundation five parts deep. ||75||
In the upper third, three girdles (mekhalā) should be fashioned according to the rule:
the uppermost is considered to be four finger-breadths [in width], and the middle one three finger-breadths.
The base (mekhalā), provided with two parts and sloping downwards, is considered to bring auspiciousness.
It should be square, measuring one cubit [in length] and four finger-breadths in height. ||77||
The sacrificial altar (sthaṇḍila) or the homa-vedi may also be one finger-breadth in height;
on a spacious altar, it may extend by one, two, or three cubits.
Furthermore, O twice-born ones, the maṇḍala named Sarvatobhadraka should indeed be constructed with eight, thirty-two, or even sixty-four deities.
The Vedic officiating priests, who are conversant with ritual procedures, are to be consecrated with mantras.
The bathing pavilion should be located in the northern third of the main pavilion.
There, on a sacrificial mound, on a mountain, or on sand provided with shade,
the images should be bathed with the five products of the cow and with decoctions.
One should bathe them, adorned with bark garments, with the waters of a hundred jars,
accompanied by Vedic mantras, musical instruments, songs, and auspicious recitations.
One should cover the deities beneath the pavilion on the side of the altar with cloth;
one should place the balance upon the altar and set it down starting from the north.
One should place the water-pot (kalaśa) at the region of the head and the water-strainer (kamaṇḍalu) at the position of the feet;
the fan (vyajana) at the region of the back and the mirror (darpaṇa) on the left side.
Diamond, vaidūrya, pearl, as well as sapphire, beautiful blue [stone], topaz, gomeda, and coral, according to the sequence of the directions starting from the east. (85)
One should offer the metals— gold, silver, copper, bell-metal, brass,
lead, tin, and iron— in order, starting from the east.
Vajra, vahnīśikhā, sahadevī, tulasī leaves, indravāruṇikā, śaṅkhāvalī, and likewise udyāvalī; ||87||
One should quickly place the medicinal herbs according to the previous sequence,
as well as barley, rice, millet, javarī, and sesame seeds.
One should offer *akṣaka*, *mudgaka*, and *godhūmaka* grains in order, starting from the east;
and there should be a great festival with dancing, singing, food offerings, the waving of lamps (*ārātrika*), and so forth. (89)
One should also perform the rite of consecration through the placement of mantras on the limbs (aṅganyāsa) and other such methods;
then one should give the garments, ornaments, and so forth offered to the deity to the artisan.
One should offer everything dedicated to the sacrifice to the one in the form of the preceptor;
one should cause the installations of the deities in the temple to be performed upon each of its individual parts.
One should worship Vārāha on the stone of the donkey, Nāga at the water-channel,
Jaladeva on the water-jars, and likewise the Asuras on the neck of the flower-vessel.
One should place Nandinī in the jar of dullness (jāḍyakuṃbha), Viṣṇu in the two pericarp petals,
Gaṇeśa on the elephant-throne, and likewise the Aśvins on the horse-throne.
One should worship the mountains on Narapīṭha, the earth on Kṣuraka, the three junctions (sandhyās) on Bhadrakumbha, and likewise Pārvatī on Kalaśa. ||94||
One should worship the Gandharvas in the Kapotālī, Sarasvatī on the Mañcikā, the guardians of the quarters (Dikpālas) on the Jaṅghā, and the deity Indra at the Udgama. 95.
One should know Sāvitrī in Bharaṇī, the Devikās in Śirāvaṭī,
Vidyādharī in Puṣpakaṇṭha, and the Suras in Ayantarālaka;
Parjanya in Kūṭacchādya, and the Sun and Moon in the two Śākhas.
One should place the three deities on the northern beam and likewise the Yakṣa on the Udumbara post. ||97||
The son of the Aśvins [is worshipped] in the Śaṅkhāvaṭa; Śeṣa in Kolyā; the Earth on the pedestal;
the mountain deities on the pillar; and the deities of the sky in the Ghūmmaṭa. ||98||
In the center, one should worship the principal deity, and on the upper tube, the river Jāhnavī;
on the broad peaks of the pinnacle, one should worship Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Hara, and Īśvara.
One should worship five deities beginning with Indra in the palace, three lords of the gods on the roof, the god Īśvara on the pinnacle, and Indra alone upon the water-pot.
On the neck is Amara, on the amalasaraka pearl is Niśācara;
on the lotus petal is Padmākṣa, and on the water-pot is Sadāśiva. || 10.1 ||
One should install the deity Aghora on the left of the covered area and Tatpuruṣa on the right; furthermore, one should establish Bhairava in the temple which is divided into five parts.
The daughters of Brahmā should first gaze upon the deity once he is installed;
thereafter, other virtuous men and women who are free from passion may behold him.
Then, indeed, those following the rules of domestic life should request from the architect that the sacrificer obtain merit through the propitiation of the gods.
The architect should say, "O Master, may you be free from decay.
One should give the architect and the craftsmen offerings, gifts, and other honors. (105)
One should celebrate a great festival with feasts and the like, as well as with narrations and other such activities;
thus, O Rādhikā, I have described to you this ritual according to the opinion of Hari. (106)

Thus ends the one hundred and forty-second chapter, titled "The Demonstration of the Consecration, the Measurement of the Images of Brahmā, the Vedas, the Gods, and the Goddesses, and the Mandapa, Kuṇḍa, and Concise Consecration Rituals," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Listen, O Rādhikā; I am Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Lord.
I shall tell you of that Vāstu which is the body of the abode of the gods. || 1 ||
The installation of the tortoise-stone and the setting up of the door-frames and so forth; the installation of the lotus-stone and the entry of the flag-man. || 2 ||
The installation of the bell, as well as the installation of the banner,
and the consecration of the deity— these are considered the seven auspicious days.
Indeed, the worship of the site (vāstupūjā) must be performed again and again in each respective case;
I shall now declare to you those fourteen rites of pacification (śāntikarma). || 4 ||

In the excavation of the ground, in the gift of the tortoise, in the gift of the stone, in the cord, in the gift of the door, in the gift of the hoof, in the gift of the jar, and in the enclosure; || 5 ||
On Mount Pādma, at Śukanāsa, at Dhvajapuṃs, and at Ghaṇṭaka,
as well as at Kalaśa and during the installation of the flagstaff (dhvajadāna), these indeed are the established opinions.
Once, however, the Supreme Brahman assumed a visible form;
from that, a splendor arose, shining like ten million infinite suns.
Then the Lord, the master of yogis, who possesses the nature of withdrawal, manifested; at that moment, a drop of sweat appeared upon his forehead.
When that terrifying form of the embodied Puruṣa appeared,
it was then cast face-down upon the earth by the gods who had become Brahmās.
Of that Puruṣa who was the dwelling, his feet, calves, and knees were then located in the southwest (Nairṛta), and likewise his head was in the northeast (Īśāna).
His right elbow then became the fire-god Agni, and his left the wind-god Vāyu;
thus, forty-five gods came to reside within his body. (11)
Accompanied by all the gods, he who has received worship shall be the giver of happiness;
even that which is divided into sixty-four parts and is square is worshipped.
That square, divided into eighty-one parts, is worshipped;
and that square, joined with a hundred parts, is also worshipped. || 13 ||
Eight deities dwell in each of its eight pillars;
and from one elephant, fifty elephants are prescribed as its constituent parts.
Having prepared thirty-two mandalas, one should worship them on all sides with jewels,
gold, silver, coral, and even fruits.
One should draw a diagram of sixty-four or one hundred squares on the site,
using either flour or unbroken grains, and having prepared it, one should present the bali offering.
I shall show you the site-plan consisting of sixty-four squares; listen to me as I describe it. When the field has been made square and divided into eight parts [on each side], || 17 ||
In the center is Brahmā; in the eastern quarter is Aryaman;
likewise, in the south is Vaivasvata, and in the west is the host of Maitra.
And Pṛthvīdhara is in the north; likewise, when [the northeast] is divided into two, there are Āpa and Āpavatsa;
and likewise, when [the southeast] is divided into two, there is Agni.
Sāvitra and Savitṛ are likewise situated in the southwest (Nairṛta) in two divisions;
and Indra and Jaya are similarly established in the northwest (Vāyu), also divided into two.
Furthermore, Rudra and Rājayakṣman are to be established;
listen now as I describe how they are to be placed on all sides in a clockwise sequence. 21.
In the northeast are Īśa and Diti; Parjanya is at the right ear;
Jayas and Indra are on the shoulder; and then Sūrya, Satya, and Bhṛśa.
Ākāśa and Agni, then the two fires, Pūṣan and Vitatha;
thereafter Gṛhakṣata, Yama, Gandharva, and Bhṛṅga. || 23 ||
Mṛgapitṛ and Āveka are in the south-west; then Nandika, Sugrīva, Puṣpadanta, and likewise Varuṇa and Asura [are in the west]. (24)
And Śeṣa; thus, from that [direction], Pāpa and Roga are situated in the wind (northwest).
Then there are Nāga, Mukhya, Bhallāṭa, and Kubera. (25)
Śaila and Aditi—thus the last one is situated on the left shoulder.
These indeed are to be worshipped in the sixty-four-fold division. (26)
In the division into eighty-one parts, however, there are not two deities each in the corner;
rather, there shall be only one deity in each. I shall explain that to you as follows. (27)
Īśa, Parjanyaka, Jaya, Indra, Sūryaka, Satya, Bhṛśa, Ākāśa, Agni, Pūṣan, and Vitatha; || 28 ||
Gṛhakṣata, Yama, Gandharva, Bhaṅga, Mṛga, Pitṛ, Nandī, Sugrīvaka, Pūṣya, Varuṇa, and Asura. ||29||
Śeṣa, Pāpa, Roga, the principal Nāga, Bhallāṭaka, Kubera, as well as Śaila, Aditi, and Diti.
Carakī is outside in the northeast;
Vidārikā is outside in the southeast; Pūtanā is outside in the southwest; and the wicked one is considered to be outside in the northwest. (3.1)
When the square field has been divided into nine parts,
Brahmā occupies the central nine squares, while Āryamā and the others occupy six squares each.
In the corners, those situated in the middle of the squares are proclaimed to occupy two squares;
those on all sides are to be known as occupying one square each—the deities in the eighty-one-square grid.
Alternatively, O Rādhikā, listen as I describe the site-plan consisting of one hundred squares;
when the field has been made square and divided into ten parts.
All the outer corners are empty; the deities are situated on the right side.
In the center is Brahmā, occupying one-sixteenth part, while Aryamā and the others occupy six parts each. ||35||
The Āpādya deities, consisting of two groups, should always be established and worshipped as auspicious;
Īśa is located on the head, and Parjanya is always situated in the right ear.
Jaya is on the shoulder; Indra, Sūrya, Satya, Bhṛśa, and Ambara are on the arm;
Sāvitra is on the hand; and Savitṛ, Agni, and the others ending with Pitṛ are on the foot. 37.
Nandī and other disease-afflicting spirits reside on the left foot;
Maitra resides on the left thigh, and Vivasvān on the right thigh.
Indra is proclaimed to be in the secret place, and Jayanta in the region of the anus;
likewise, Rudra and Rājayakṣman are considered to be in the left hand. (39)
Nāga, Mukhya, Bhallāṭa, Kubera, Śailaka, and Aditi—these are the serpents of the left arm; Diti, however, is on the left ear.
Āpa is in the throat, Āpavatsa in the heart; Aryamā is considered to be in the side;
likewise, Pṛthvīdhara is considered to be in the right and left sides. ||41||
Carakī is in the northeast, Cipicchā is considered to be outside in the east,
Vidārikā is in the southeast, and likewise the guardians of the directions (dikpālas) are in the south.
In the southwest, Pūtanā is proclaimed; in the west, Skanda himself;
in the northwest, the wicked Rākṣasī; and likewise in the north, Kubera. (43)
Thus, the deities within the body of the site (vāstu) are considered to be givers of auspiciousness when worshipped.
To the north or in the northeast of the temple, one should prepare an altar measuring two cubits.
Having placed a silken cloth there, one should spread a white garment over it;
then, having fashioned an unbroken svastika there, one should place a yellow garment upon it.
Having spread an eight-petaled lotus, one should perform [the rite] there with unbroken grains (akṣata); then, having spread a yellow cloth and over that a red cloth, one should act there.
Having drawn the lines of the site with a golden needle or with barley-flour paste,
one should place a water-pitcher in the center at the Brahma-sthala.
O Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Virajā, Godāvarī, Sarasvatī, Narmadā, Sindhu, and Kāverī—be present in this water! 48.
Viṣṇu shines at the front, Śiva in the middle, and Brahmā at the base;
the Mothers are all around, and within the belly are the oceans and tens of millions of sacred fords.
All the Vedas are in the form of leaves, and the earth is in the form of jewels;
the fruits are within the Bilva fruit. May you sit here; I establish you—be firm! 2.143.50.
Oṃ, salutations to Śrī Siddhi; Oṃ, repeated salutations to Śrī Brahmā.
Oṃ, remain upon the beautiful Śrī Brahmāsana; salutations to the Śrī Guru. ||5 1||
Oṃ, salutations to you, Vāsudeva; O Viśvakarman, let there be salutation to you!
Indeed, the pure materials for worship have been sprinkled with water.
Everything becomes pure through the remembrance of Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
Oṃ Klīṃ, salutations to Siddhi; come here and remain firm in this place. (5.3)
Oblation to Omaryaman; come here and be firm in this place. Oblation to Vivasvat; come here and be firm in this place. ||54||
Oṃ, obeisance to Mitra; Oṃ, O Pṛthvīdhara, be firm!
Oṃ, obeisance to Ṛddhi; come hither and be firm in this place. ||55||
Obeisance to Āpā and Apāvatī; come both of you, remaining steadfast.
Obeisance to Sāvitrī and Savitṛ; Oṃ, come both of you, remaining steadfast. (56)
Oṃ, salutations to Indrajaya; Oṃ, come hither, remain firm! Oṃ, salutations to Rudra and Yakṣman; come hither, remain firm! ||57||
Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ! Homage to Īśa; come here and remain firm!
To Parjanya, Jaya, Indra, and Sūrya—oṃ, homage! ||58||
Salutations to Satya and salutations intensely to Ākāśa; Oṃ, salutations!
Come hither, come together with me, and remain firm in your own place. ||59||
Oṃ klīṃ, obeisance to Agni; come hither, remain firm in this place!
Obeisance to Pūṣan, to Virocana, and to Gṛhakṣata; Oṃ, obeisance! (2.143.60)
Oṃ, homage to Yama; homage to the Gandharva Bhṛṅga; Oṃ, homage!
Oṃ, homage to the Deer; come hither, be firm in this place! ||61||
Oṃ klīṃ śrīṃ! Salutations to the ancestors; come and remain steadfast!
Salutations to the gatekeeper Sugrīva; be firm! ||62||
Salutation to Puṣpadanta and Varuṇa; be firm! Om, salutation to Asura, Śeṣa, and Pāpa; be firm! (63)
Oṃ klīṃ śrīṃ! Obeisance to Rogā; come here and remain firm.
Oṃ! And to Nāga, to Mukhya, and to Bhallāṭa—remain firm! ||64||
Homage to Soma, to Śaila, to Ādityā, and homage to Diti;
O firm one, om, homage to Cipicchā! Come here and be firm. (655)
Oṃ, salutation to Vidārī, Jambhā, and Pūtanā;
Oṃ, salutation here to Skandā, the sinful Rākṣasī, and Yama. ||66||
Oṃ, salutations to Carakī; come here and remain firm in this place!
Oṃ, salutations again and again to the illustrious Great Lord of Gaṇas. ||27||
Salutations again and again to the chosen deities and to the family deities; salutations again and again to the deities of the site and the local spirits, and to all others.
Salutations again and again to these deities, who are preeminent and rich in ritual action;
for the sake of accomplishing my desired goal in this eon, year, month, and day. (69)
I shall perform the worship of the deity Āḍhyavāstudeva; salutations!
Having bathed the deity with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and water, [I shall apply] the sacred thread (brahmasūtra).
Garment, ornament, flower garland, incense, lamp, food offering,
and likewise the oblation for the eight [deities], as well as water for sipping and betel leaf.
One should perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana), circumambulation, prostrations like a staff, and so forth;
then one should mutter the mantra: "Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ kuru kuru svāhā. (72)
One should recite "Namaḥ oṃ vāstudevāya" twenty-one times. Then:
"Oṃ, obeisance to Hetukabhairava in the east; and then in the south... (73)
Salutation to Ādivaitālabhairava in the west, and salutation to Kālabhairava in the north. ||74||
Homage to Ekapādabhairava; Om, and also to Ūrdhvakeśa.
Homage be to Svacchandabhairava; and also to Āgneyaka. (75)
Salutation to Tripurāntaka Bhairava in the southwest;
salutation to Agnijihvaka Bhairava in the northwest. (76)
Salutation to Vāyu-deva, and salutation to Īśāna and Īśānaka;
salutation to Oṃ in Pātāla, and salutation again and again to Viṣṇu. ||77||
Having offered the *arghya* and requested forgiveness, one should then bow to the Vāstu deity,
as well as to the guardians of the directions (*dikpālas*), the guardians of the field (*kṣetrapālas*), Gaṇeśa, and Caṇḍikā.
Then one should perform worship; thereafter, one should carry out all the rites beginning with the installation (pratiṣṭhā).
Oṃ Āṃ Īṃ Klīṃ, obeisance to Mahendra; be firm in your place! ||79||
Oṃ hrīṃ hroṃ hrāṃ, accept the offering together with the guardians of the field; svāhā to Indra! Oṃ hrīṃ hroṃ hrāṃ, salutations to Agni; remain firm in this place. ||2.143.80||
Oṃ *krauṃ* *krauṃ* *krū*, together with the guardians of the field (*kṣetrapāla*s), accept, accept this offering (*bali*) for Agni, *svāhā*.
Oṃ *krauṃ* *krauṃ* *krū*, obeisance to Kālamūrti; be firm here. (8.1)
Oṃ aiṃ kṣoṃ kṣīṃ, accept, accept the offering together with the guardians of the field (kṣetrapālas); obeisance, svāhā! Obeisance to Death; remain firm in this place. 82.
Oṃ śrāṃ śrīṃ śrūṃ vaṃ viṃ, accept, accept the offering together with the guardians of the field (kṣetrapālas); obeisance, svāhā! Obeisance to Varuṇa; be firm. ||83||
O guardians of the field, together with them, accept, accept this offering! *Namaḥ svāhā*.
Oṃ aiṃ, obeisance to the Lord of the Universe; be firm in your place! ||84||
Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ, together with the guardians of the field (kṣetrapālas), accept, accept the offering! Homage, svāhā!
Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ, homage to Kubera; remain firm in your place! 85.
Oṃ klīṃ klīṃ klūṃ, accept, accept the offering together with the guardians of the field; obeisance, svāhā!
Oṃ klīṃ klīṃ klūṃ, obeisance to the Sustainer of the Universe; be firm! ||86||
Oṃ, together with the guardians of the field (kṣetrapālas), accept, accept the offering! Homage, svāhā!
Oṃ vrāṃ vrīṃ vrūṃ, homage to Brahmā; be firm in this place! ||87||
Oṃ! Accept, accept the offering together with the guardians of the field (kṣetrapālas); homage, svāhā!
Oṃ śrāṃ śrīṃ, homage to the Lord of Śrī; be firm in this place! ||88||
"O guardians of the field, together with them, accept, accept the offering! Homage! Svāhā!
Having thus performed the worship, one should thereafter carry out the rite of consecration.
Indeed, performed in the months of Māgha and Phālguna, it bestows wealth, long life, and health;
however, in Jyeṣṭha and Vaiśākha, the consecration destroys wealth and sons.
When the sun is in its southern course (dakṣiṇāyana), one should likewise install the Vārāha, the Mātṛkās,
Bhairava, Vāmana, Devī, and Nṛsiṃha.
In Śrāvaṇa, one should worship the Liṅga of Śaṅkara; in Āśvina, the Mother of the World (Jagadambikā);
in Mārgaśīrṣa, Hari Nārāyaṇa; and in Pauṣa, all the gods.
On Saturdays, Sundays, Mondays, Wednesdays, Thursdays,
and Fridays, the raising of the door should be performed by dividing [the measurement] into eight parts and omitting the eighth part.
One should again fashion three parts from the seven-part self-branch;
two parts shall be the image—this is the definitive conclusion for all [types] known as the *lamba*.
Having divided the door into nine parts, one should set aside one part;
having divided eight parts into three, the image is considered to be two parts. 95.
From one elephant up to four elephants, there is an increase of six *aṅgulas* for each elephant;
then, from ten elephants onwards, the increase is three *aṅgulas* for each elephant.
The increase [in height] shall be by one *aṅgula* up to a limit of fifty *gaja*s;
herein, the measurement of the temple is considered excellent when there is an increase of twenty parts.
The *kolī* is also said to be the largest according to the measurement of the temple's purpose;
thus, O Devatāyana, you remain in such a state. (98)
The temple is indeed my own form; listen now to its meaningful significance.
The palace is the form of the deity, and the foundation stones are known as his feet.
The shank is to be understood as the *jagatī* meter; the knees are indeed known as the pillars.
The thigh is to be understood as the *karmānikā*; the penis is the area below the *kuṃbha*.
The channel (praṇāla) is considered the region of the anus, and the water-pot (ghūmmaṭa) is held to be the belly;
the place of the deity (devasthāna) is equal to the navel, and the pedestal (pīṭhikā) is held to be the heart. || 101 ||
The image itself is the living being; the pinnacle is the chest, the pure essence is the neck, and the śukanāsa is the nose. (10.2)
The lamp is the eye, the window is the ear, the shoulder is the body-protector;
the jar is the head, the banners are the hair, and the elements are the constituent parts. 103.
In this case, the flesh and fat are the plaster; the earth and liquids are the bones; and all the stones constitute the cloth made of powdered rags. (104)
"O king of devotees, know your own body to be thus a temple of the gods.
Thus did Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa speak to him, O Rādhikā.

Thus ends the one hundred and forty-third chapter, titled "Description of the Installation of the Vāstu-puruṣa, His Deities, and Others," in the section on the Pratiṣṭhā festival within the second part, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmīnārāyaṇīya-saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Rādhikā, listen now to the procedure for installation and other rites,
which the primordial deity Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa has spoken.
The patron, having bathed at dawn and handed over the materials for worship into the hand of the preceptor, accompanied by women and auspiciously married ladies, [proceeds]. || 2 ||
The temple, having reached the ground in front of the pavilion in the eastern direction,
[the officiant] should wash his feet and sit down upon a seat.
Then, having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) and likewise breath control (prāṇāyāma),
with his topknot tied and accompanied by his wife, he should then meditate upon Gaṇapati.
Facing either east or north, having proclaimed the place and time,
for the sake of pleasing the Supreme Lord and for the successful accomplishment of the rite of installation.
One should perform the worship of Gaṇeśa, beginning with the formal selection of the preceptor (ācārya);
one should then carry out the washing of his feet and the worship of his feet.
Having worshipped him with moon-like eyes, flowers, and other offerings, one should indeed bow down before that deity in his beautiful palace for the sake of accomplishing one's purpose. (7)
For the sake of accomplishing the consecration and for the successful completion of the work of the pavilion and other rites,
I choose you, a devotee of the illustrious Hari, as my preceptor.
The preceptor, who is learned in all matters, should say, "I am chosen," and the sacrificer should tie the preceptor's marriage-thread bracelet.
Having performed the worship of the preceptor, one should then invoke the Earth:
"Come, O Vasudhā, source of all auspiciousness; be firm here."
Come, O bestower of boons, O Sustainer, O giver of auspiciousness in this sacrifice!
Om! May Mahī and Dyauḥ, and Pṛthivī, sprinkle this sacrifice for us. || 11 ||
"Fill us with nourishments endowed with all flavors, O You who are beheld!
Having thus invoked the Earth and remembered all the deities, || 1-2 ||
"Oṃ, may all the gods rejoice here; Oṃ, be established!
Having thus established the ground and joined his palms in *añjali*, he should pray. || 13 ||
Accept your share of the sacrifice; I bow to you, please forgive me.
The pavilion and other structures for the ritual will be erected over you for the sake of the sacrifice.
Having thus brought her to existence and paid homage to her, one should sprinkle her with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Having performed this with green kuśa grass, one should sprinkle her again and speak as follows.
Om! This Viṣṇu strode across; in three places he planted his step. His footprint is gathered in the dust. Svāhā! We invoke you. 16.
Oṃ! May Mitra be auspicious to us, may Varuṇa be auspicious, and may Aryaman be auspicious to us.
May Indra and Bṛhaspati be auspicious to us, and may Viṣṇu of the wide stride be auspicious to us. 17.
Oṃ, by the impulse of the god Savitṛ, and likewise by the arms and hands of the Aśvins, and by the speech of Pūṣan who delights in the waters. (18)
Having said, "I consecrate you with the sovereignty of Agni; you are sprinkled, O Earth," and having taken white mustard seeds in his hand, he [performs the rite].
Facing the northeast, he should then scatter [the offerings] in all directions:
"Oṃ! Whatever beings or Rākṣasas dwell anywhere... (2.144.20).
May all of them depart from the site of Viṣṇu’s sacrifice;
may the bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, and others likewise withdraw to a distance. (21)
May those beings depart who are situated upon the earth;
may those beings who create obstacles go away by the command of Hara. 22.
Having spoken thus, having scattered white mustard seeds everywhere,
and having sprinkled [the ground] with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), one should offer the arghya water to the Earth as follows.
Having taken auspicious water containing perfumes, dūrvā grass, fruits, flowers, and barley in a copper vessel, and wearing a pair of white garments; (24)
Facing north, with the *arghya* in hand and palms joined in reverence, one should offer the *arghya*, saying:
"O Mother of the World, accept this *arghya*; be gracious at all times. (25)
Having thus worshipped the Earth and performed the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi),
and having worshipped Vāstu upon the auspicious seat (bhadrapīṭha), one should accomplish the eastern direction.
On this very earth, one should worship Gaṇeśa as well as the venerable Guru with mental offerings, and meditate upon the family deity.
Having given a sacrificial fee to the Brahmin and having satisfied the artisan,
one should indeed construct a pavilion sixteen cubits in size and twelve-fold in its nature.
Having constructed there a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) as previously described and according to the specifications, measuring ten cubits, eight cubits, or according to the available space.
Then, in all four corners of the *uttaravedi*,
in the northeast corner, there is a pedestal for the planets (*grahapīṭha*) measuring thirty-four finger-breadths.
In the southeast (Agni), the Mātṛpīṭha is one cubit [in area] and twelve aṅgulas in height;
in the southwest (Nairṛta), the Vāstupīṭha is also one cubit [in area] and twelve [aṅgulas] in height.
And in the northwest (Vāyu), one should fashion the seat for the Yoginīs and Kṣetrapālas, measuring one cubit,
or twelve finger-breadths in height, or as is appropriate.
Furthermore, when a stream of ghee eight cubits in length has been prepared on the previously established ground, the installation of beautiful stones is also performed.
Then a beautiful wall made of bricks should be constructed,
and the square pavilion should be adorned with arches and banners.
Having constructed the pavilion in the manner previously described, and having likewise prepared another pavilion for the purpose of the ablution, one should then construct three altars.
Having prepared the pavilions as appropriate on the first day, the most meritorious sacrificer should indeed subsist on sacrificial food (haviṣya). || 36 ||
Having slept on the ground at night, remaining celibate and full of sattva,
he should then bathe in the waters of a sacred ford (tīrtha) on the morning of the day of the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana).
For the sake of liberation through expiation, one should offer a "sin-cow" (pāpadhenu).
Today, on this day, there is fitness for the work of the temple of the God. (38)
Thinking, "May it be mine," for the sake of gain and likewise for the removal of sins, one should offer [the gift] with the words:
"I give this cow of sin to the Brāhmaṇa. (39)
Having bathed again with the waters of sacred fords, which contain all medicinal herbs and are mixed with the five products of the cow, while employing the Varuṇa mantras; ||| 2.144.40 ||
Oṃ! You are the embodiment of Varuṇa, for you are the deity arisen from Varuṇa;
you are the abode of Varuṇa, so bestow long life and prosperity upon me. ||41||
"Let your nooses indeed go far away; let them not fall upon the sacrifice.
Free from nooses, I shall offer the oblation to the deities; ordain that. (42)
Having bathed thus, wearing a white cloth and anointed with fragrant unguents, he—
being exceedingly pure, wearing white garlands and garments, and accompanied by his wife— [proceeded].
The patron, having gathered all the necessary materials from the site of the artisans,
should bring forth the divine [image] in a clockwise direction accompanied by beautiful songs.
Accompanied by the sounds of musical instruments, auspicious songs of women,
and the recitation of peace-mantras, they arrived in the vicinity of the pavilion.
Having entered through the western gate and taken his seat,
the sacrificer then [approaches] the deity near the southern gate.
Thereafter, he should sit facing east upon the auspicious seat in the western direction with the tips of the darbha grass pointing eastward; or, he may sit facing north together with his wife.
One should have the sacrificial materials and requisites placed on the right side.
I shall describe the various requisites in brief, according to the tradition. 48.
One should offer one hundred and eight fuel-sticks of each kind:
*arka*, *udumbara*, *pippala*, *vaṭa*, and *tūla*. (49)
Apāmārga, Palāśa, and Āmalakī—the trees of sacrifice;
Candana, Śiṃśapā, Bilva, and Pippalī—the trees of sacrifice.
One should collect such sesame seeds as are available from the trees,
and one should preserve three auspicious seats, flower garlands, and blossoms.
Saffron, sandalwood paste, musk, camphor, agallochum, guggulu incense, an incense burner, and a mirror. ||52||
A bell, sandals, the ārātrika lamp, offerings of grain, oblations, milk-rice, various kinds of food and edibles, sacrificial offerings, and fruits. ||53||
Areca nuts, betel leaf, clarified butter, sesame seeds, barley, unbroken grains, sugar, the finest fruits, and bilva fruits as well. ||54||
Grapes, plantains, and even fresh saffron and other such items;
four seats for each fire-pit (kuṇḍa), as well as a large and small sacrificial ladle (sruk-sruva). ||55||
The seats should likewise be beautiful, adorned with three threads smeared with saffron, as well as white woolen thread, for the attainment of the Sarvatobhadra [mandala]. (56)
The colors white, red, blue, yellow, and black, as well as the bathing jars and the five types of sprouts. (57)
There were ten banners made of excellent plantain trunks;
their flagstaffs were of bamboo, and likewise, there was one central banner.
Diamond, pearl, lapis lazuli, conch shell, crystal, topaz, sapphire, and emerald—these are the eight precious gems. (59)
Realgar, yellow orpiment, mica, and black collyrium;
likewise, honey, ferrous sulfate, gold pyrite, and red ochre.
One should protect all those eight grains for the sake of the sacrificial rite:
barley, wheat, wild rice, mung beans, millet, and mustard seeds. (61)
One should deposit this eightfold collection of seeds, namely sesame, rice, gold, silver, copper, lead, tin, and iron. 62.
One should protect the dye, the style, and the eight metals for the sake of the sacrificial rite;
likewise, the vessel for the madhuparka should be made of gold or copper.
One should likewise preserve the argha vessel, a golden probe, and [the five gems]:
gold, diamond, sapphire, ruby, and pearl. (64)
One should place those precious jars at one's own side:
sixteen door-jars and eight jars for the world-protectors.
One should protect the four altar-pitchers, the site-pitcher,
the pitchers equal in number to the sacrificial pits, and likewise the pitcher of sleep.
Eighty-one jars for the ceremonial bath (snapana), as many shallow bowls (śarāva) as well,
two jars for the thousand-fold stream (dhārāsahasra), and earth from the royal palace (rājasthāna).
Also earth from a stable for horses, as well as clay from an anthill,
earth from a confluence of rivers, earth from the two riverbanks, and earth from a boar’s track.
One should protect [the site] with eight types of earth: earth from a royal gate and the following: *mūrvā*, *māṃsī*, *vacā*, *kuṣṭha*, *śaileya*, and *haridrā*. (69)
One should also preserve dāruharidrā, ginger, campaka, mustā, and all medicinal herbs, as well as the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), each separately.
Likewise, one should protect these seven grains: rice, barley, sesame, wheat, śyāmāka, nivāra, and mung beans.
A bed with its furnishings, a white parasol, two chowries,
a variegated canopy, and indeed three fine silk cloths.

The materials for the selection of the officiating priests (ṛtvij) consist of substances for anointing the body, cow’s ghee, water from a cow’s horn, water from a sacred ford (tīrtha), and rice-husk water (kambuka). ||73||
One should preserve garments to be given to artisans, as well as fragrant oil, a vessel for eye-salve, and vermilion. (74)
One should protect garlands made of fresh mango leaves, golden images of the deity,
coconuts, and other such items within the sacrificial pavilion.
Having placed all these well-prepared materials upon his own right side,
and having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) and breath control (prāṇāyāma), [he should proceed].
Having taken water, darbha grass, and so forth in his right hand, [he should say]:
"Om, may the lotus-eyed Lord Nārāyaṇa, Hari, purify [me]. (77)
Having spoken thus, and having sprinkled all the ritual materials as well as himself,
he should remember Gaṇeśa and the other deities and then perform this following formal resolve (saṃkalpa).

In this world-system, at this place, in the presence of a Brahmin, in such-and-such a year, on such-and-such a month, fortnight, lunar day, and day of the week, for the sake of the destruction of all sins. (79)
I have come for the sake of uplifting my ancestors, for the attainment of prosperity and long life,
for the excellent acquisition of enjoyment and liberation, and for the arrival of the gods at this sacred image.
According to my ability, I shall perform the consecration of Śrī Hari or another deity, as well as the worship of Śrī Gaṇeśa and others known as the preliminary rites for that [consecration]. (8.1)
The recitation of auspicious and meritorious days, as well as the worship of the Mātṛkās, the Nāndī-śrāddha, the selection of the preceptor (ācārya), and the honoring of the Brahmins. ||82||
Having made the formal resolve (saṃkalpa), "I shall perform [this]," one should pour water upon the ground. [The mantras are:
"Sumukha," "Ekadanta," "Kapila," and "Gajakarṇaka. (83)
Lambodara, Vikaṭa, Vighnanāśa, Vināyaka, Dhūmraketu, Gaṇādhyakṣa, Bhālacandra, and Gajānana. ||84||
One should indeed recite these twelve names of my form, together with the elephant-faced one, the trident-bearing host, and those joined by their wives and sons. (85)
One should meditate on Gaṇeśa as serene and armed for the warding off of obstacles;
having thus meditated upon Gaṇeśa, one should worship him with many offerings.
O Heramba, come, come here; may you be endowed with the attainment of a hundred thousandfold fortune.
O Lord of Siddhi and Buddhi, come, accompanied by all your weapons! 87.
I invoke you for the sake of worship and for the protection of my sacrifice;
come, take your place firmly upon this golden seat, and protect us. 88.
We invoke the Lord of the hosts, the beloved Lord, and likewise the Lord of treasures; O Śrī Kṛṣṇa, you are indeed Śaṅkara. 89.
I am born as the one who sustains the womb; you too are born as the one who sustains the womb. I invoke Gaṇanāyaka, who is endowed with both accomplishment and wisdom.
I establish you here; please accept this golden seat.
Accept also the water for washing the feet, which is fragrant, pure, and auspicious.
Accept this arghya water contained in a copper vessel, which brings about success;
O Leader of the Gaṇas, accept this ācamana water from the sacred ford.
Accept this bath of milk, and accept this bath of curd;
accept also the bath of clarified butter, and accept the bath of honey.
Accept this bath with sugar-candy, and likewise accept the fragrant unguent;
O Lord of the Gaṇas, perform your bath with pure water from the sacred fords.
Wear these garments and accept the sacred thread, O Lord;
please accept the sandalwood paste, the unbroken rice grains, and the beautiful flowers. (95)
May you accept these beautiful sprouts of *durvā* grass, incense, a lamp filled with ghee, and an offering of sweets such as *laḍḍukas*. (96)
"O God, please accept these fruits, water for sipping, water, and betel; please accept this sacrificial fee and this ritual waving of lights."
Please accept this handful of flowers; I perform circumambulation around you.
Having received this special water offering accompanied by fruit, be a granter of boons here.
Salutations to you who have the trunk of an elephant; salutations to you in the form of Kṛṣṇa.
O Lord, make all my undertakings, such as sacrifices and other rites, free from obstacles.
"By this worship, may the Lord of the Gaṇas, together with his limbs [attendants], be pleased with me.
Having thus performed the worship, one should then perform the recitation for the auspicious day (puṇyāhavācana).
Thus, O Rādhikā, Hari—the beginningless Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa—spoke to the devotee Devāyatanaka; that has indeed been related to you.
From reciting, hearing, or worshipping this, one obtains the fruit;
the undertaking of the listener and the speaker becomes free from obstacles and endowed with its result.

Thus ends the one hundred and forty-fourth chapter, titled "Description of the Selection of the Preceptor, the Gathering of Sacrificial Materials, the Worship of Gaṇeśa, and Other Rites," in the section on the Festival for the Installation of the Image within the second book, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Furthermore, O Rādhikā, I shall now describe before you the ritual for the installation of the water-pot and other rites, as Śrī Hari spoke them to the sage Devāyana.
Then, holding in both his hands a water-filled jar adorned with fruits, jewels, and other ornaments, he placed it on the ground before his head.
Sitting with the right knee bent and the left on the ground,
and supporting [the image] with his right hand, he should install it on the ground according to the prescribed rite.
Then the sacrificer should have the Brahmins recite the *puṇyāha* (day of merit) formula;
and the gods on earth (the Brahmins) gave their response to the words of the sacrificer.
"May it be an auspicious day for me; may you have long life," we say, and likewise, "May the waters be auspicious," and "May there be goodwill. (5)
May there be freedom from injury and misfortune; likewise, may there be auspiciousness and well-being.
May the fragrances protect you, and may the unbroken grains (akṣata) protect you; may there be long life.
May the flowers protect me, and may there indeed be beauty; may there be success. May the betel-leaves protect me, and may there be sovereignty; may the sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇās) protect me.
May there be manifold wealth, may there be prosperity, and may there be great fame; may there be knowledge, humility, riches, and the like, as well as long life. (8)
May you possess many sons and the like, and may your life be long; may there always be peace, nourishment, and contentment for the sacrificer.
Having uttered this, they should sprinkle [the water] upon the head of the patron:
"May we hear what is auspicious with our ears; may we see what is auspicious with our eyes. (2.145.10)
May we always attain that body which is worthy of praise and beneficial to the gods;
may the gods bring about our welfare, and may all enemies be turned back. (11)
May there always be friendship with the gods, and likewise a lifespan free from the constraints of time;
may there be abundant wealth, and may Savitṛ protect us from all sides.
May Candra, Āyu, and Amṛta—the excellent deities—bestow [these] upon him;
may the Vasus, as givers of gold, truly belong to this sacrificer.
Thus, may you, who are a vessel for blessings, prosper as the patron;
with concentrated minds, may we be gracious and bringers of peace. 14.
May there be nourishment, contentment, and growth; may there be long life free from obstacles. May there be health, auspicious activity, and success in all undertakings. (15)

May you always possess an abundance of knowledge regarding the Vedas, Shastras, and Samhitas; may there be prosperity in wealth, grain, sons, and grandsons, as well as the attainment of all desired riches.
May there be the destruction of misfortune; may disease and evil remain far away;
may all that is inauspicious be destroyed for you, and may every auspicious thing be realized.
May there always be freedom from obstacles for you in future undertakings;
and may all your subsequent actions be auspicious and fruitful. (18)
May the lunar days and other auspicious factors always be favorable to you through this sprinkling of water;
may all the presiding deities of the lunar days and other periods be pleased by this libation.
May the lunar day (tithi) and the astrological moment (karana) be pleased, as well as Durga and Panchalika;
may the Vishvedevas be pleased, and may the hosts of Maruts be pleased.
May the Mothers of Umā be pleased; may those who have but one husband be pleased;
may all the gods be pleased; and may those whose form is the Vedas be pleased. (21)
May the Brahmins be pleased; may Brahmā and Śaradā-Śrī be pleased;
may Faith and Intelligence be well-pleased, and may Kātyāyanī be pleased. ||22||
May Māheśvarī be pleased, and may Ṛddhikarī be pleased;
may Siddhikarī be pleased, and may Puṣṭikarī be pleased. ||23||
May Tuṣṭikarī be pleased; may the family deities be pleased;
and may the two Blessed Lords, Vighna and Vināyaka, likewise be pleased. (24)
May the village deities be pleased; those who were your adversaries have been slain, the haters of Brahman have been slain, and likewise the givers of obstacles have been slain.
May all enemies be slain, and may those of terrible form be pacified;
may the heaps of sins be pacified, and may your mental afflictions be pacified. (26)
May your auspicious deeds increase, may the waters be favorable to you, and may they be auspicious for you.
May the oblations be auspicious, and may both night and day be auspicious. (27)
May the rain-cloud pour as it pleases, may the plants be laden with fruit, may you have security and prosperity, and may the household deities be pleased. (28)
May the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa be pleased;
likewise, may Parjanya be pleased, and may the Lord Kārtika be pleased. (29)

May the time be auspicious for Brahmā, and may every day be a holy day (puṇyāha) for you, always bringing about auspicious deeds. May there be a truly holy day for you for the rite of the installation of the deity.
May the gods of gods purify me; may they purify my mind and intellect.
May all beings purify me; O Jātavedas, do thou purify me. 3.1
And when the earth has been lifted up, let them proclaim auspiciousness for me;
O Brahmins, let them proclaim for me auspiciousness and great supernatural power. 32.
"May they proclaim for me the power of the sacrifice, my light, the nectar, and heaven;
may they indeed proclaim well-being and prosperity, and let the Brahmins say, 'So be it'. (33)
May Indra of far-reaching fame grant us well-being; may Pūṣan, the knower of all, grant us well-being;
may Tārkṣya with unimpaired wheels grant us well-being; may Bṛhaspati bestow well-being upon us. 34.
May Haripriyā Svastimatī grant well-being at all times.
Om! May Śrī and Lakṣmī, the two wives of Nārāyaṇa, be yours. (35)
In this way, let the declarations for the auspicious day (*puṇyāhavācana*) of the venerable scholars be fulfilled;
thereafter, the rite of consecration (*abhiṣeka*) [is performed] with the water from the pitcher into the vessel. (36)
And four Brahmins, holding *dūrvā* grass, mango sprouts, and other items, should sprinkle the patron with the mantra, "May they purify you. (37)
May the divine beings purify me; may the sacred fords and oceans purify me;
O Jātavedas, may these five rivers purify me as I stand at the sacrifice.
I consecrate you with sovereignty, you who abide in sacrifice through speech;
I consecrate you with healing medicine, with splendor, and with the luster of sacred knowledge.
I consecrate you with the power of Indra; may the sacrifice of Indra abide in you.
O divine Savitṛ, drive away all difficulties. (2.145.40)
In this sacrifice for Makha, pour upon us all that which is auspicious.
Oṃ! May the heavens be peace, may the intermediate space be peace, and may the internal self be peace unto you. 41.
By this recitation, may Prajāpati indeed be pleased here;
thus, O Rādhikā, after the declaration of the auspicious day (puṇyāha-vācana). ||42||
One should perform the worship of the Mātṛkās on a beautiful pedestal in the southeast corner,
either upon heaps of unbroken rice grains or upon betel nuts.
Gaurī, Padmā, Śacī, Medhā, Sāvitrī, Vijayā, Jayā, Devasenā, Svadhā, Svāhā, the Mothers, and the Mothers of the World. ||44||
Hṛṣṭi, Puṣṭi, Tuṣṭi, one's own family deity (kuladevatā), and Gaṇeśa—these sixteen indeed should be fully worshipped during a rite for prosperity. 45.
Rādhā, Lakṣmī, Māṇikī, Brahmavidyā, Ramā, Rati, Suguṇā, Mañjulā, Haṃsā, Lalitā, Kambharā, and Satī. (46)
Santoṣā, Kamalā, Durgā, and Śāradā—these sixteen are worthy of worship. Om, salutation to Gaṇeśa; I invoke the Lord of the Gaṇas. ||47||
Oṃ, salutations to Gaurī; I invoke Gaurī, salutations to you.
Oṃ, salutations to Padmā; I invoke Padmā, salutations to you. ||48||
Oṃ, salutations to Śacī; I invoke Śacī, salutations to you.
Oṃ, salutations to Medhā; I invoke Medhā, salutations to you. ||49||
Oṃ, salutations to Sāvitrī; I invoke Sāvitrī. Salutations to Vijayā; I invoke Vijayā, salutations.
Oṃ, obeisance to Jayā; I invoke you, Jayā, obeisance to you! Obeisance to Śrī Devasenā; I also invoke Senā. ||51||
Oṃ, salutation to Svadhā; I invoke Svadhā, salutation to you.
Oṃ, salutation to Svāhā; I invoke Svāhā, salutation to you. ||52||
Oṃ, salutations to the Mothers; I indeed invoke the Mothers, salutations!
Salutations to the Mothers of the World; salutations, I invoke them. ||53||
Salutations to Hṛṣṭi, I invoke her; likewise, salutations to Puṣṭi, I invoke her;
salutations to Tuṣṭi, I invoke her. ||54||
Salutation to the glorious family goddess; I invoke her, and let there be salutation to you!
Oṃ, salutation to Rādhā; I invoke her and bow down to her repeatedly. (55)
Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Lakṣmī; I invoke her and I bow to her. Oṃ, obeisance to Māṇikī; I invoke her and I bow to her. ||66||
Oṃ, salutations to Brahmavidyā; I invoke her and bow to her. Salutations to Ramāratī; I invoke her, and salutations again and again to her. ||57||
Oṃ, I invoke Śrī; obeisance again and again to the Goddess Śrī. Oṃ, I invoke Suguṇā; obeisance again and again to her. ||58||
Homage to Mañjulā; I invoke her, homage again and again to her.
Homage to Haṃsā; I invoke her, and let there be homage to her as well. ||99||
Salutations to Lalitā; I invoke her, salutations again and again to her. Salutations to Kambharā; I invoke her, and let there be salutations to her as well.
Oṃ, salutation to Satyā; I invoke her, and salutations again and again to her. Salutation to Santuṣā; I invoke her, and salutations again and again to her. ||6 1||
Salutation to Kamalā; I invoke her, salutation again and again to her. Om, salutation to Durgā; I invoke her, salutation again and again to her. ||62||
"Salutation to Śāradā; I invoke her, and salutation be to her.
Having thus invoked and established her, one should worship her with ritual offerings (upacāras). ||63||
May the gods be pleased by this worship; may the goddesses, the Mothers, be satisfied.
And I offer a stream of clarified butter upon the head of the Mother residing in the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, Vaiṣṇavī, as well as Vārāhī, Indrāṇī, and Cāmuṇḍā [were worshipped] with a stream of ghee. 65.
May they be satisfied by the continuous stream and likewise grant boons;
one should worship them with water for the feet and other offerings, for the divine streams bestow strength.
Likewise, one should worship the other sixteen goddesses with a stream of clarified butter,
and perform the Nāndī-śrāddha in due order, beginning with the ritual rinsing of the mouth (ācamana).
Having restrained the vital breaths (prāṇāyāma) and then determined the time and place,
one should proceed with the materials for the rites of installation of this deity.
"I shall perform the Nāndī-śrāddha for the removal of obstacles and other impediments.
O Viśvedevas, known as Satya and Vasu, who possess the faces of joy (nāndīmukhas)! (69)
Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ! This is for you: water for the feet, water for washing the feet, and the rinsing of the feet; may there be prosperity for the mother and grandmother.
And these [ancestors] who are the great-grandmothers are the Nāndīmukhīs;
"Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ, this is for you: water for the feet and for washing the feet. (71)
May there be the washing of feet and prosperity for the father, the grandfather, and the great-grandfather; these indeed are the ones who are called Nāndīmukhas.
Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ! This water for your feet, for washing the feet, and for rinsing the feet; may there be increase for all of you thereafter. (73)
The maternal grandfather, the great-grandfather, and the great-great-grandfather, together with their wives—those who are Nāndīmukhas, whoever they may be. (74)
Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ! This water for the feet, this washing of the feet, and this rinsing of the feet—may there be prosperity—and I offer you a seat. (75)
