May all the followers of Indra, being well-disposed, partake of the offering.
O Agni, come from the southeast; protect the sacrifice; homage be unto you! (68)
Guard the direction, consume the offering, and bring prosperity to the sacrificer;
may all the followers of Agni, being well-disposed, partake of the offering. (69)
"O Yama, come from the south; O Nairṛta, come from the southwest;
O Varuṇa, come from the west; O Lord of Wind, come from the northwest. (2.154.70)
Come from the north, O Kubera; come from the northeast, O Īśvara!
Protect the direction, consume the offering, and bring prosperity to the sacrificer. ||71||
May all those respective followers, being happy, consume the offering.
O Brahman, come between the *īps* (the vowels); O Anantarāṭ, come indeed between the *nips* (the consonants). //72//
Protect the direction and consume the offering along with your attendants;
bring about the prosperity of the sacrificer and the success of the sacrifice. (73)
Now, O Kṣetrapāla, accept this offering and always protect the sacrifice; together with your followers, bring prosperity to the patron and grant him happiness.
Having said, "Eat curds, beans, and so forth," one should scatter rice grains; then, at the crossroads, one should say: "May the spirits take the offering from the winnowing basket."

A woman who performs a sacrifice at a crossroads [is known as] a *makhī*; she uses ground black gram, curd-rice, turmeric, and the like as collyrium, vermilion, fragrant substances, red flowers, and so forth.
While reciting the mantras, one should place a winnowing basket honored with perfumes and flowers, [saying]:
"May those gods—the Ādityas and the Vasus—accept this offering. (77)
The Maruts, the Aśvins, the Rudras, the Suparṇas, the Pannagas, the Grahas, the Jṛmbhakas, the Siddhas, the Gandharvas, the Mālas, the Vidyādharas, and the Nagas. ||78||
Asuras, Yātudhānas, Piśācas, hosts of Ḍākinīs, Śaktis, Yakṣas, Vetālas, and those who are Vighnas and Vināyakas; ||79||
May the bhūtas, pretas, kūṣmāṇḍas, śākinīs, and mātṛs likewise be satisfied by this offering, which takes the form of the grace of the sacrifice.
May they not create obstacles for the sacrificer, nor disease, suffering, or anything undesirable;
may they not become adversaries to his family. ||81||
May all be satisfied and may they grant protection for my sacrifice to the deities, the ancestors, the spirits, and along with all living beings. (82)
I offer this oblation with reverence to those who dwell in these places;
to all beings in the three worlds, whether stationary or moving. (83)
Gods, dānavas, gandharvas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and pannagas;
kimpuruṣas and kinnaras, as well as the sādhyas, the virtuous, and those who practice virtue. ||84||

The sages, the seers, the cows, and even the mothers of the gods—these descendants of Kaśyapa belong to his lineage; they are characterized by the qualities of passion (rājasa), darkness (tāmasa), and purity (sita). 85.
May these embodied ones provide protection for me at this sacrifice;
may the Yamas and Yāmyas, whose nature is both manifest and unmanifest, move about for my peace. (86)
And to all these [deities], "Svāhā" and the offering (bali)— "Oṃ, obeisance"—
having thus performed these and the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), one should proceed to purification in the vicinity of the pavilion.
"Having rested, the teacher should then perform the duties regarding the sacrificial post.
Thus, O Rādhā, that ritual pertaining to Brahmā which was spoken by the Lord has been told to you by me. (88)

Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-fourth chapter, titled "The Worship and Offering of Balis by Viṣṇu, the World-Guardians, and the Elemental Beings to the Two Supreme Lords, Kambharā and Her Consort, who are satisfied by the One Hundred and Forty Paravidyās beginning with Rādhikā," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Then the Blessed Lord spoke: "O Rādhikā, I shall describe to you the ritual of erecting the sacrificial post (yūpa) and other such rites, which are like the body of a divine temple."
The preceptor, having left a space measuring three feet from the eastern side of the previous sacrificial pit or from the pavilion, and beyond that—
One should prepare the site for the sacrificial post (yūpa) either in a temple or in a Śānaka [sanctuary],
having set aside a plot of land measuring sixteen or ten cubits.
One should prepare the site for the sacrificial post (yūpa) and perform its worship; thereafter, having dug a hole in the wood measuring one aratni in depth.
One should indeed offer praise to the sacrificial post (yūpa): "O Post, you were fashioned of old;
you are the auspicious deity consisting of the sacrificial portion, the protector of the temple."
"Having performed worship with an offering of flowers, make us firm and grant us inspiration.
Having thus worshipped, he then [prepared] the sacrificial post (yūpa) smeared with turmeric oil.
Having bathed [the sacrificial post] with the waters from the *śānti* jar and having anointed it with clarified butter,

and having worshipped it with flower garlands and other offerings, one should then tie a *poṭalī* (cloth bundle) to it. Then, the sacrificer, tying the *yūpa* together with *dūrvā* grass, *guggulu*, mustard seeds, nimba leaves, and *gorocanā*, should recite the mantra.
Oṃ! When the Dākṣāyaṇas, being well-disposed, bound the gold upon Śatānīka, that I bind upon myself for a life of a hundred autumns, so that I may reach old age with my full span of years. 9.
"Oṃ! Young, well-clothed, and girt about, he becomes more excellent as he is born;
the wise poets, seeking the gods with their minds through sacred study, draw him up.
Having thus wrapped [the sacrificial post] with a cloth, the sacrificer should then cause it to be suspended. 2.155.10.

Oṃ! May the approval of those who hew the sacrificial post, those who carry the sacrificial post, those who carve the top-ring for the horse’s post, and those who prepare the cooking-vessel for the steed, further us. 11.
Having raised [the post] with the mantra "Oṃ, rise up, O Lord of the Forest," and having cast unbroken rice grains,
flowers, and darbha grass into the pit, he should sprinkle it with water.
One should install the deity of the sacrificial post with the mantra "oṃ dhruvāsīti," [saying]:
"Be well-established, long-lasting, firm, the giver of longevity, and the giver of happiness."
Oṃ! You are firm; may this sacrificer be firm in this sacrificial session through offspring and cattle.
May Heaven and Earth be filled with clarified butter. You are the canopy of Indra, the shade for all people. 14.
Thus, having filled the pit with earth and making it firm so that it does not shift, [one recites]:
"At every sacrifice, with every song, for the sake of skill, [we offer] to Agni... (RV 6.48.1).
"I shall praise Jātavedas, who spreads forth the nectar of immortality, like a beloved friend.
Having spoken thus, he should offer water at the base of the sacrificial post, which has been smeared with saffron. (16)
Having prepared incense, lamps, flowers, perfumes, food offerings, and excellent fruits,
and having worshipped with sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇās), one should construct an auspicious mandala under that lunar mansion.
One should prepare a sacrificial altar (sthaṇḍila) one cubit in size for the sake of the deity of the sacrificial post (yūpa),
having spread a white cloth over it in the manner of twenty-five squares.
Having fashioned a beautiful pavilion with six lines each running east-west and north-south to form excellent squares, one should worship the deities with grains of rice.
One should worship Brahmā in the central cell, and likewise Soma in the north; one should worship Śiva in the northeast, Indra in the east, and Agni in the southeast. || 2.155.20 ||
One should worship Yama in the south and Nairṛti in the southwest;
one should likewise worship Varuṇa in the west and Vāyu in the northwest.
The sacrificer should worship the eight Vasus in the space between Vāyu and Soma,
and the eleven Rudra deities in the space between Soma and Īśāna.
Between Īśāna and the East, one should worship the twelve Āditya deities;
and in the interval between Indra and Agni, one should worship the two Aśvin deities.
One should worship the seven Mothers in the middle between the southeast and the south;
and one should worship Gaṇeśa in the middle between the south and the southwest.
One should worship the Nāgas and the Bhūtas between Varuṇa and Nirṛti; one should worship the Yakṣas and the Rākṣasas in the interval between Varuṇa and Vāyu. || 25 ||

Starting from the northeast and proceeding clockwise, one should place Brahmā in the center, Sādhya in the northeast, Vṛṣabhadhvaja (Śiva) in the east, Nārāyaṇa in the southeast, and the Pitṛs in the south.
Having established the eight deities— Yama, Mṛtyu, the Diseases, the Maruts, and Citragupta— one should thereafter worship them.
One should indeed worship the earth at the base of Brahmā’s feet;
one should perform the consecration while reciting their respective names.
Oṃ, to those innumerable thousands of Rudras who indeed dwell upon the earth—to them, whose bows are drawn to a distance of a thousand yojanas, we pay homage. || 29 ||
Oṃ! O Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Sarasvatī, Śatadrū, and Vitastā, accept this my hymn of praise, along with the Asiknī,
the Mahatī, the Vedasmṛti, and the two Ārjīkīyas.
Listen indeed to the blessings uttered by me.
Oṃ! To this son of Brahmā, Irāvati, Sāla,
Candra, Menakāṅga, Aṅgaśikṣāṅga, Corala,
Balo, Dīnāp, Kaṅga, Nīpa, and Nāyija— [I offer this].
Narāyaṇi, meke, cārthe, kaliṅgini, and ime. ||3 1 ||
Oṃ, one for me, three for me, three for me,
five for me, five for me,
seven for me, seven for me.
Nine for me and nine for me; eleven for me and eleven for me;
thirteen for me and thirteen for me.
Fifteen for me and fifteen for me,
seventeen for me and seventeen for me,
nineteen for me and nineteen for me.
Twenty-one for me and twenty-one for me;
twenty-three for me and twenty-three for me;
twenty-five for me and twenty-five for me.
Twenty-seven for me and twenty-seven for me; nineteen for me and nineteen for me;
thirty-one for me and thirty-one for me.
And thirty-three for me, and thirty-three for me;
may they be prepared through sacrifice. ||32||
Four for me and eight for me, and eight for me;
twelve for me and twelve for me,
sixteen for me and sixteen for me.
Twenty for me and twenty for me;
twenty-four for me and twenty-four for me;
twenty-eight for me and twenty-eight for me.
And thirty-two for me, and thirty-two for me;
and thirty-six for me, and thirty-six for me;
and forty for me, and forty for me.
May my forty-four and my forty-four, and my forty-eight and my forty-eight, be made perfect through sacrifice. 33.
Oṃ! Those who roam through the sacred fords, carrying spears in their hands and wearing quivers—we place our weapons a thousand yojanas away from them; we pay homage to that [power]. 34.
Having thus consecrated the sacrificial post (yūpa), one should perform the ritual placement of the post: "Obeisance to Brahman" on the head of the post, and then "Obeisance to the eyes. (35)
Salutation to Sūrya and Śaśin; salutation to Keśava in the heart; salutation to Agni in the navel, and likewise to these [deities] in the hips, the private parts, and the thighs. (36)
I bow to the eleven Rudras; salutations to Meru at the shanks, and I bow again to the Nāgadevas at the feet.
Oṃ! You who dwell here, givers of the kingdom, grant the kingdom to me, svāhā! You who dwell here, givers of the kingdom, grant the kingdom to so-and-so!
You who are full of vigor, givers of the kingdom, grant the kingdom to me!
Svāhā! You are full of vigor, givers of kingship; grant the kingdom to that person.
O Waters, you are flowing around, givers of kingship; grant the kingdom to me, svāhā! O Waters, you are encompassing, givers of kingship; grant the kingdom to me.
Lord of the waters, you are the giver of sovereignty; grant me sovereignty, svāhā! Lord of the waters, you are the giver of sovereignty; grant sovereignty to [Name]!
You are the embryo of the waters, the giver of sovereignty; grant me sovereignty!
"svāhā! You are the womb of the waters, the giver of kingdoms; grant a kingdom to such-and-such a person.
You are those whose skin is like the sun"—with these words, [he places it] on the crest-lock (śikhā).
"Oṃ, you who have eyes on all sides and faces on all sides..."
"With arms everywhere and feet on every side, the one God, generating heaven and earth, fans them with his arms and wings," [this is recited] over the two eyes. (3.9)
"Oṃ, salutation to Vārāha"—thus, salutations again and again to the two nostrils.
"Oṃ, I place Agni at the forefront as the messenger; I invoke him who carries the oblations;
may he bring the gods here"—thus, salutations again and again to the mouth. 2.155.40.
Oṃ, the blue-necked, white-throated Rudras have taken refuge in heaven;
may their weapons perish at a distance of a thousand yojanas—thus [he recites] over the neck.
Oṃ, "May there be strength in my arms," and likewise "Salutations, salutations" over the two arms.
Oṃ! For the heart thee, for the mind thee, for the sky thee, for the sun thee!
May this sacrifice go upward; may the *hotṛ*-offering reach the gods in heaven—thus [he says] over the heart.
Oṃ! From the ocean the honeyed wave has arisen; through the *upāṃśu* [cup], it has attained immortality.
That which is the secret name of clarified butter is "the tongue of the gods" and "the navel of immortality," [so it is said] in the belly. 43.
Oṃ vāmadya savituḥ—thus [he places] on the two hips; *namo namaḥ*.
Oṃ nābhir me cittam vijñānam, pāyur me ’pacitir bhasat. || 44 ||
"Ānanda and Nandana are my testicles; Bhaga and Saubhāgya are my private parts;
through my two shanks and feet, I am Dharma, established as the king of the people"—thus [he should touch] the two shanks. 45.
"Oṃ, this cow has stepped forth; she has settled before her mother and before her father, reaching toward heaven.
With these words, [one should offer] salutations again and again at your two feet.
Having thus performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) upon the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) and worshipped it with the fivefold offerings (*pañcopacāra*), [one should proceed].

One should offer worship and a sacrificial oblation (bali) to the sacrificial post (yūpa), saying: "This is my oblation to the sacrificial post. "Come, come, O Banner of Dharma, Lord of Sacrifice, you who consist of the Three Vedas and whose body is the Veda!
May you grant protection to the divine sacrifice and the ritual; accept this oblation, salutations, salutations to you! (48)
Oṃ *somaparvata*: with this, one should encircle [the object] with a thread smeared with saffron.
Oṃ *parvatasya*: [one should worship] the mountains, Varuṇa, and the guardians of the directions. (49)
Having worshipped the sacrificial post with perfumes and other offerings and meditated upon it, one should recite [the mantra] while facing north;
[otherwise], by cutting the root or striking the ground, one incurs sin and other faults.
Having removed [the wood] from the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), it is always pure when touched by all the posts.
*Oṃ*: "The medicinal herbs (*oṣadhīḥ*) which were born of old, three ages (*triyugam*) before the gods... (51)
"I have indeed entered into a hundred and seven abodes; having thus made the sacrificial post a garland of flowers for my bride, I shall circumambulate it. (52)
Having embraced his entire family closely, he should pay obeisance to them.

A sacrificial post made of *pālāśa* wood is prescribed for a Brāhmaṇa, while that of *naiyyagrodha* is for a king (Kṣatriya). The post of a Vaiśya should be made of *bailva* wood, and for a Śūdra, it is traditionally recorded as being of *audumbara* wood.
It should reach the head of a Brahmin and the neck of a Kṣatriya. ||54||
The [altar] for a Vaiśya should be the size of the chest, and for a Śūdra, it should be the size of the navel;
at a distance of one foot toward the east, one should bow to Nārāyaṇa. ||55||
Then, in the evening, the formal acceptance (adhivāsana) must indeed be performed for the principal deity;
the preceptor, the patron, the officiating priest, and likewise the virtuous woman [should perform it].
They should go to the workshop of the artisans, and one should place the pitcher before the deity;
there, one should invoke the sacred fords—the Gaṅgā, Yamunā, and Sarasvatī.
The Cerāvatī, the Brahmaputrā, the Nārāyaṇī, and the Gaṇḍakī;
the oceans, the lakes, the sacred fields, and the Aśvasaras lake.
One should invoke Puṣkara, Bālakṛṣṇa, Mānasa, and Badarīvana into the water-pot; by the command of Brahmā, let them enter.
On the four sides of the water-pot, however, [one should say]: "Oṃ, salutation to Indra;
salutation to Yama, to Varuṇa, and to Kubera. (2.155.60)
I worship with perfumes and other offerings, and likewise perform fire-oblations (homa),
for the purpose of warding off defects in the image and the stone.
For the sake of removing the sin arising from the destruction of living beings during the performance of a rite or similar occasions,
one should prepare a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) suitable for an image and perform the consecration of the elements (bhūtasaṃskṛti).
Having established the fire, one should perform the oblation with sesame seeds, clarified butter, and so forth;
and having offered the Āghāra and Ājyabhāga portions, one should likewise offer them with the mantra of the deity.
Having offered two hundred oblations of clarified butter as well as the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti), one should pray:
"O you who exist in the form of the deity's image, may you always be endowed with prosperity."
Having cleansed with kuśa grass and applied honey and clarified butter, the destruction of the wound must be performed; furthermore, a bath with pure clay should be undertaken.
One should perform the consecration by sprinkling cow dung, cow urine, ashes, and milk individually,
interspersed with water at each interval.

Having worshipped with perfumes and other offerings, including white flowers, and having bathed [the image] with water from the pitcher, the patron [should give] garments and other gifts to the artisan.
Then the preceptor, having inspected the image from all sides,
should place [the offering] made of white wool and other materials into the right hand of the deity.
Then, one should tie a cord measuring one span (vitasti), provided with all medicinal herbs and *manas* fruit, around the image using the root mantra.
One should place her, adorned with ornaments, upon the chariot accompanied by songs and instrumental music;
Brahmā, reciting the Vedic mantras, should cause her to ascend the chariot.
Oṃ! Standing in the chariot, the skillful charioteer leads the horses forward to wherever he desires;
one should praise the greatness of the reins, which control the mind.
Afterwards, the reins restrain them. ||7.1||
Having led her to a river, a lake, or a pool, one should perform the consecration;
then one should perform the recitation for an auspicious day and likewise the pronouncement of blessings.
Oṃ! May auspicious intentions come to us from every side—intentions that are undeceivable, unimpeded, and victorious.
May the gods be ever-present for our prosperity, our protectors day by day, guarding us with tireless care. (73)
May the auspicious favor of the gods who walk uprightly come to us;
may the bounty of the gods turn toward us.
We have approached the friendship of the gods; O gods, [protect] us!
May they increase your lifespan so that you may live. || 74 ||
Oṃ! We invoke for our protection that Īśāna, the Lord of all that moves and stands, who quickens the intellect;
may he, as Pūṣan, be present with us for the attainment of wisdom.
For our prosperity, he is the protector and guardian, undeceivable for our well-being.

Having recited these and other verses for the recitation of peace (śāntipāṭha), and having sprinkled the riverbank with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), one should set down the substances for worship and so forth.
And having clothed its form, the sacrificer, facing north and having proclaimed the place and time, should consecrate it in the waters with the mantra. (77)
I shall perform the worship here of Varuṇa, Gaṇeśa, the Mothers, Kṣetrapāla, and the rest; then, reciting "gaṇānāṃ tvā," I shall proceed.
Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ! O Gaṇeśa, come here and remain;
together with Siddhi and Buddhi, I worship you and I bow to you. (79)
"I offer this oblation of lamp-oil and black-gram rice to you;
likewise, one should worship the Mothers of Water in the water and present the oblation. (2.155.80)
Salutations to Matsyā and Kacchapī; salutations to Kūrmī and Vārāhī.
Salutations and full worship to Dadurī, Śiśumāri, and Īśvarī. (8.1)
And upon the lines that have not been destroyed, one should worship the Mothers of Life:
"Homage to the Fish, the Tortoise, the Crocodile, the Alligator, and the Water-snake. (82)

One should offer salutations to Dadhryā and Jalī, as well as worship with perfumes and other offerings; likewise, one should perform the worship of the sixty-four Yoginīs in the water with saffron and other substances.
In the northwest, a person should worship Kṣetrapāla with saffron and other offerings, [reciting]:
"Oṃ Bhūr Bhuvaḥ Svaḥ! O Kṣetrapāla, come here and stay!
Accept this saffron, lamp, and the offering of black gram, curd, and rice."
Then one should perform the water-worship with "Oṃ,
obeisance to the waters" (adbhyaḥ) and likewise "obeisance to the oceans, the lakes, the sacred fords, and the rivers.
Having cast scents and unbroken rice grains into the water, one should also worship Varuṇa.
"O Bhūr-bhuvaḥ-svaḥ, O Varuṇa, come here and remain here!
Accept this offering of black-gram and rice; salutations again and again to Varuṇa.
Holding the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) in his hand, he should cast them into the water while reciting those mantras.
One should pray to Jaladeva and protect the image within the water. ||88||
For seven nights, five nights, three nights, one night, or even for a single watch;
[he should give] gold to the teacher and abundant sacrificial fees to the others.
One should offer the image at the Brahma-hour, when two ghaṭikās have elapsed;
having removed it from the water, bathed it on the bank, and worshipped it with excellent substances.
Arise, O Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, Lord of Rādhā and Ramā!
Arise, O Brahmaṇaspati; seeking you, we offer our worship. 91.
"May the Maruts, the givers of good gifts, approach; O Indra, may you be the foremost among them.
Having raised her with these mantras, she was adorned with all ornaments. (92)
Having placed [the deity] upon the chariot with instrumental music and songs, one should lead him along the path to the residence;
having led him from the workshop to the water, one should proceed to the right of the temple pavilion.
Having caused [the deity] to be circumambulated, one should then lead him to the bathing pavilion;
there, the Lord should be seated facing east upon a throne on the auspicious altar.
One should establish [the deity] with auspicious mantras and then perform the ritual bathing;
that which Hari spoke to the goddess has been told by me to you, O Rādhā. (95)

Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Installation of the Sacrificial Post, the Worship of the Deities and Others, the Immersion of the Image in Water, the Procession through the City, and the Bringing of the Pavilion," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Then the Blessed Lord spoke to Devāyatanaka: "O Rādhā, I shall tell you everything regarding the procedure for bathing and so forth."
The Guru, having prepared three altars in the hall for the bath—
one after another— and having gathered the materials for the ritual ablution, [proceeds].
Having performed this and having sprinkled the ground and the altars with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya),
one should then [worship] with unbroken grains (akṣata) upon the southern altar made of sand.
Having drawn a svastika and prepared an auspicious seat,
one should thereafter place six water-pots upon the altar.
Likewise, five others filled with water and rich with sprouts [should be prepared],
using earth, sprouts, bark of trees, astringent decoctions, cow’s urine, and cow dung.
Then, having filled them with ashes, scented water, and [other substances], one should place the jars designated for the five deities in the manner of a northward-facing row.
Having placed the eleven jars— the last being the *sthapati-kalaśa*—
to the west of the altar, one should place them upon the eight jars on the *uttaravedi* at the auspicious seat (*bhadrapīṭha*).
Having placed milk, curd, ghee, wine, sugarcane juice, dūrvā-grass water, and darbha-grass water around [the vessel] in the previous order.
One should arrange those eight jars with the *hiraṇyagarbha* and other mantras;
thereafter, ten others on the western altar should be arranged in sequence with clay.
With cow urine, cow dung, ashes, and the five products of the cow (pañcagavya),
along with milk, curd, ghee, honey, and sugar.
Furthermore, fourteen jars should be placed there;
others, filled with pure water, as well as thirty-five jars [should be arranged]. (11)
Among those, five should be placed [in the cups] together with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta),
then five together with the five waters, and finally five containing the decoctions of leaves.
Again, one should worship in sequence with flowers, fruits, golden water,
water from the horns of cows, and grains from a vessel with a thousand holes.
It should be prepared with all medicinal herbs, the five sprouts, and dūrvā grass, as well as the nine gems; it should be made without distinction for ten [deities].
It should be filled with clear water and adorned with sprouts of the *kadamba* and other trees;
having invoked the world-protectors (*lokapāla*) therein, one should hold the vessel while inhaling its fragrance.

The leaf of the *kādamba*, the leaf of the *śālmalī*, that born of the *jāmbava* and the *aśoka*, as well as the leaf of the *plakṣa*, the petal of the *udumbara*, and likewise the leaf of the *vaṭa*. || 16 ||
The bilva leaf, the betel leaf, the palāśa leaf, as well as other items, fine cloth, and fragrant substances. (17)
Barley powder mixed with oil for the purpose of anointment, as well as other fragrant powders such as those of *āmalakī* and auspicious substances like *jaṭāmāṃsī*.
One should place everything there, both upon the altar and within the jars;
and the jar known as the Antyasthapati, filled with water from sacred fords (tīrtha).
Having performed [this] in the presence of the deity, one should invoke the sacred fords (tīrthas) into the water:
"O Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Sarasvatī, and likewise Irāvatī! (2.156.20)
O Menakāṅgī, O Brahmaputrī, O Nārāyaṇī, likewise O Urulā, O Kaṅgī, O Nāyī, O Vālge, and O Maki, you who possess the Kāruliṅga! 21.
At Dīnāp, Nīpa, and likewise at Artha, as well as at the Narmadā, Gaṇḍakī, and Harī; at Svarṇarekhā, Puṣkara, Mānasa, and Aśvapaṭṭaka. || 22 ||
May Bālakṛṣṇa, as well as Nārāyaṇa, the lake, the oceans, and the sacred fords (tīrthas)—all auspicious ones—enter into this jar. ||23||
Then the patron should indeed bathe the deity with water accompanied by Vedic mantras,
and he should bestow a reward upon the artisans.
Then the preceptor should offer oblations (bali) consisting of white mustard seeds, ghee,
and milk-rice to the guardians of the directions in all directions, starting from the east and proceeding outward.
One should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) and offer an oblation to Indra in the east:
"I offer this to the direction; protect it and bring about prosperity for the sacrificer. (26)
In the southeast, I offer this oblation to Agni together with his limbs; salutations!
In the south, I offer this oblation to the god Yama; salutations! (27)
In the southwest, I offer this oblation to Nirṛti; obeisance! In the west, I likewise offer this oblation to Varuṇa; obeisance! (28)
To Vāyu in the north-western direction, I offer this oblation; salutations to you! And to Kubera in the north, I offer this oblation; salutations! ||29||
"I offer this oblation, salutations, to the Lord God Īśāna.
Having offered the oblation and sipped water for purification, one should bathe the deity according to the prescribed rite.
One should cleanse with clay using the mantra "agnirmūrdhā," with decoctions using "yajñāya," with cow's urine using the Gāyatrī, and with cow dung using "gandha."
Then, after that, one should bathe [the deity] with ashes while reciting the *mānastoka* mantra, with scented water using the *gāyatrī*, and with the five-deity jars.
With the first [mantra] beginning with "namaḥ śiva," with the second "haṃsa," with the third "yāta," and with the fourth belonging to Viṣṇu; || 33 ||
Then, with the fifth [mantra], "Brahmā," one should indeed worship [the deity] with pure water,
flowers, unbroken rice, and so forth, and clothe it with a silken garment.
And on the second altar, having placed a throne (bhadrāsana) and having spread out kusha grass with its tips pointing eastward, he should place the deity there.
Facing north, the Great Teacher, having first encircled the image with a saffron thread, [should then perform the rite] with the Hiraṇyagarbha mantra.
In a vessel, one should mix honey and ghee while reciting the mantra beginning with "madhuvātā";
then, one should take a golden probe smeared with that honey and ghee.
Oṃ, the wonderful array of the gods has risen—the eye of Mitra, Varuṇa, and Agni.
Oṃ, Agni is light, light is Agni; svāhā!
The Sun is light, light is the Sun; Svāhā! || 38 ||
Oṃ, Agni is splendor, light is splendor, svāhā! Sūrya is splendor, light is splendor, svāhā! Light is Sūrya, Sūrya is light, svāhā!
One should fashion [the mark] on the eyes of the image. ||39||
Oṃ! Moving through the dark expanse, establishing both the immortal and the mortal, the divine Savitṛ comes upon his golden chariot, beholding all worlds. 2.156.40.
With this [mantra], one should form the pupils in the two lotus-petals;
at the time of opening the eyes, one must not look directly at the face of the deity. (41)
One should show a mirror, gold, food, milk-rice, and fruits;
when this is done, the gaze of the deity becomes gentle and auspicious. (42)
The artisan should draw the lines with a blade according to the prescribed rule;
the preceptor, having sprinkled [the site] with honey and having sprinkled it with ghee while reciting the mantra, [should proceed].
One should bathe [the image] with clay and cow dung for the removal of defects caused by weapons;
one should then present a golden vessel, a probe, and so forth, as well as garments and other items, to the artisan.
Having also given the gift of a cow to the preceptor, one should perform the oblation in the sacrificial pit;
then, having offered the bali-oblation to the guardians of the directions, [one should honor] four auspicious Brahmins.
Having fed them and bestowed gifts such as the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), one should dismiss them;
thus, having performed the application of collyrium to the eyes, one should proclaim the place and the time.
One should perform the great ablution for the God, the Supreme Self;
reciting the mantra, one should raise the image from the auspicious seat (bhadrāsana).
Oṃ! Arise, O Brahmaṇaspati; we, seeking the gods, entreat you. May the Maruts, the bounteous givers, come forward; O Indra, be present with us. 48.
Having raised [the deity] with the mantra *bhadraṃ karṇebhiḥ*,
one should place him upon an auspicious seat in the northern direction on the altar and provide a footstool.
One should bathe [the deity] with four jars using the "Oṃ Samudre" mantras;
having worshipped with curd, dūrvā grass, unbroken rice, and other offerings, one should perform the ārārtika ceremony.
Salutations to you, O Goddess worthy of worship, Sovereign of the gods, Prakṛti of Viśvakarman!
O Mother who sustains the entire world through your power, salutations, salutations unto you! 5.1
In you I worship the Lord Nārāyaṇa, the highest of the high;
O you who have destroyed all defects, may you always be endowed with prosperity. (52)
Then, while tying a thread made of powdered [substances] measuring one span (vitasti) onto the right hand,
one should bind it with the "Iti-mantras" and likewise offer prostrations.
One should bathe [the image] with four jars using the *idamāpa* mantras;
then with clay using the *agnirmūrdhā* mantra, and thereafter with pure water.
With cow dung, cow urine, ashes, pure water, with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), with pure water, milk, and pure water. ||55||
One should bathe [the deity] with curd or even pure water, with honey and water, or with sugar and water; thereafter, one should wipe [the image]. 56.
The performer of the bath should recite the mantras of the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and anoint [the image] with fragrant oil, saying "To the Sacrifice" (yajñāya). ||57||
Oṃ! May the waters purify me from mental impurity—just as one released from a pillar, or one who has sweated and bathed is freed from dirt, or as clarified butter is purified by a strainer. (58)
Having rubbed [the body] with powders of barley, rice, wheat, lentils, and bilva,
one should smear it with yakṣakardama while reciting "Oṃ yāta."
Two parts of musk, three parts of saffron, one part of camphor,
and three parts of sandalwood— this is called *yakṣakardama*.
Having smeared [the image] with *jaṭāmāṃsī*, one should bathe it with two jars while reciting the two mantras "mā nas toke" and "pra tad viṣṇu. (6.1)
Having bathed [the deity] separately with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) using their respective mantras—reciting "pañcanadyaḥ" and so on—and then indeed with pure water; ||62||
And with scented water, with the decoction of the five leaves, with the jar of medicinal herbs, and with water containing white flowers. ||63||
Reciting the mantra "hiraṇyeta," one should [sprinkle] with the water from the peace-pot (śāntighaṭa), the water from the fruit-pot (phalaghaṭa),
or even the water from the golden pot.
Then, with water from the Śṛṅga [mountain], then with water from the Dhanya [mountain], with pitchers having a thousand streams, and with water containing all medicinal herbs; ||65||
Then, one should bathe [the deity] with water from leaves, water from dūrvā grass, precious gems,
water from sacred fords (tīrtha), and jars filled with ocean water.
Then with alkaline water and with water from a jar of milk;
then with a jar of curd, with ghee, and then indeed with sugarcane juice. ||67||
Then with water from the celestial ocean (Suroda), then indeed with sweet water (Svādūda),
and then also with coconut water, using the jars of the world-protectors (Lokapālas).
With a pitcher of Kadamba leaves, with water from a pitcher of Śālmalī flowers, with a pitcher of Jambū leaves, or with water from Aśoka leaves; ||69||
With water and the sprouts of the *plakṣa* tree, with a vessel of *cūta* leaves, and also with water from *vaṭa* leaves and water from *bilva* leaves. || 2.156.70 ||
Having bathed [the image] even with a leaf of the betel vine (*nāgavallī*), a sprout of the *pālāśa* tree, or the water from a *rudrākṣa* bead, one should wipe it clean.
One should invoke the deity with mantras: "Come here and remain firm;
accept this portion of the sacrifice, O Supreme Lord, salutations be unto you. (72)
One should offer water for the feet in a golden vessel, as well as the auspicious arghya offering;
likewise, one should provide water for sipping, sandalwood paste and the like, and a sacred thread.
With the mantra "vedāhametaṃ," he wears the lower garment; likewise, with "yuvā suvāsāḥ," the upper garment;
with "vedāha," the upper shawl; and with "idaṃ viṣṇuḥ," the beautiful flower-garland. (74)
Then, with the mantra "dhūrasi," he offers incense; with "candramā," the lamp;
with "annapate," the food offering (naivedya); and [with the appropriate mantras] the rubbing of the hands and the water for sipping (ācamana).
Having offered betel-leaf, fruit, and a handful of flowers with the mantra "yajñena," one should present all things, such as vessels and garments, to the artisan.
One should perform the consecration of the food in a corner of the pavilion;
indeed, the deities are to be seated upon the seven peaks of grain.
Having placed the Lord of Gods upon the bed, one should perform the ritual consecration (adhivāsana);
then, one should feed twelve Brahmins and others, saying, "May [the Lord] be pleased."
Then, having performed the gift of a cow, having placed the couch in the south-facing front of the temple and in a corner, and having offered praise to the deity, one should raise it up.
One should also place [the deity] upon the chariot and, proceeding clockwise from the temple,
bring [it] to the sacrificial ground and seat [it] at the western gate.
Having placed him facing east upon the five seats of the central altar, one should offer the *madhuparka* with the mantra beginning "Puruṣa evedaṃ... (RV 10.90.2).
Thereafter, one should offer water for the feet (pādya), the respectful oblation (arghya), and the honey-mixture (madhuparka) with the appropriate mantras.
Then, upon a heap of grain on the central altar, one should place a wooden bed with its head facing east.
Having spread white garments, one should draw a svastika with unbroken grains;
having spread kuśa grass with its tips pointing eastward, one should perform worship starting from the east.
Salutation to Viṣṇu in the east, and to Madhusūdana in the south;
to Trivikrama in the west, and to Vāmana in the north. (84)
In the southeast, [one should worship] Śrīdhara; in the southwest, Ṛṣikeśa;
in the northwest, Padmanābha; and in the northeast, Dāmodara. ||85||
Saying "I pay homage; I worship," he should then circumambulate them three times, having placed the deity upon the bed with three silk garments.
Having covered the region of the head, one should place the sleep-pitcher;
one should install it, together with gold and a cloth, with the mantra of the goddess Āpaḥ.
One should establish [the image] with the mantra "āpo asmān mātaraḥ" and so forth;
then, one should anoint it with honey and ghee while reciting "āpyāyasva. ||88||
One should smear [the image] with oil and mustard seeds while reciting the mantra "yā te rudra," worship it with perfumes and other offerings, and present a white garment.
With the mantra "bṛhaspate," one should place the bracelet on the hand;
with "viśvataḥ," one should touch the feet, the navel, the chest, and the head. (2.156.90)
In front [are placed] the two sandals, and likewise the two jars for peace on the two sides;
on the right, the umbrella and the two fans, and likewise a seat in front.
Then one should place a bell, food, water, a mirror, and so forth;
and all around, one should construct three enclosures with ashes, *darbha* grass, and sesame seeds.
Having prepared the offering outside the pavilion, he should present the bali to the world-protectors;
having offered the bali in the directions, he should return to the sacrificial pit and perform the fire-oblation.
Oṃ, obeisance to the supreme Viṣṇu, the Self; Svāhā! This [offering] is for Viṣṇu.
One should perform one hundred and eight oblations with sesame seeds, barley, and other such materials. (94)
One should perform the ritual placements (nyāsa) as follows: *yaṃ* on the two feet, *ūṃ* on the heart, and *maṃ* on the forehead; in this manner, one should offer the *praṇava* into the image.
One should place the vyāhṛtis: *bhūḥ* on the two feet, *bhuvaḥ* in the heart, and *svaḥ* on the forehead;
*aṃ* on the palate, *āṃ* in the mouth, *iṃ* in the right eye, and *īṃ* in the left eye.
Uṃ on the right [cheek], Ūṃ on the left ear, Kaṃ on the right cheek,
Ṛṃ on the left cheek, and likewise Laṃ on the right nostril.
Lūṃ on the left nostril-petal; Eṃ on the upper lip; likewise Aiṃ on the lower lip; Oṃ on the upper teeth; and Auṃ on the lower teeth. ||98||
Aṃ on the forehead; aḥ on the tongue; yaṃ on the skin; raṃ on the two eyes;
laṃ on the nose; vaṃ on the teeth; śaṃ on the two ears; and ṣaṃ on the belly. (99)
One should place *saṃ* on both hands, *haṃ* at the heart, *kṣaṃ* at the navel, and likewise *laṃ* at the genitals;
then *pa, pha, ba, bha, ma* on the right arm, and *ta, tha, da, dha, na* on the left.
One should perform the Mātṛkā-nyāsa by placing ṭaṃ ṭhaṃ ḍaṃ ḍhaṃ ṇaṃ on the right shank, caṃ chaṃ jaṃ jhaṃ ñaṃ on the left [shank], and kaṃ khaṃ gaṃ ghaṃ ṅaṃ on the fingers. 101.
Oṃ, to Ravi and Candra for the two eyes; likewise to Bhauma for the heart;
to Budha for the shoulder; and likewise to Bṛhaspati for the tongue. (10.2)
To Śukra on the penis, to Śanaiścara on the forehead,
to Rāhu on the feet, and likewise to Ketu on the hair.
He should place [the mantras] for Rohiṇī on the heart, for Mṛgaśiras on the head,
for Ārdrā on the hair, and for Punarvasu on the forehead.
One should likewise perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) upon the mouth for Puṣyā, upon the nostrils for Āśleṣā, and upon the rows of teeth for Maghā.
To the right ear, [offerings] for Pūrvā-phalgunī;
to the left ear, for Uttarā-phalgunī; and likewise to both hands, for Hasta.
To Citrā, [one should assign] the right arm; to Svātī, the left arm;
and to Viśākhā and Anurādhā, the two breasts on the right side.
In the right side of the abdomen for the Jyeṣṭhās, and likewise for Mūla in the left side of the abdomen;
then for Pūrvāṣāḍhā on the hips and the two sides, and likewise for the Liṅga.
From Uttarāṣāḍhā alone [he fashioned] the testicles, for Śravaṇā the ears, for Dhaniṣṭhā likewise the eyes, and from Śatabhiṣā alone [the rest]. || 109 ||
Salutations likewise to Pūrvābhādrapadā and Uttarābhādrapadā for the two thighs;
to Revatī and Aśvinī for the navel; salutations indeed to Dhruva;
to the Seven Sages (Saptarṣis) in the region of the throat; and salutations to the Mothers (Mātṛkās) at the waist.
Salutations to the Viṣṇupadas in the two feet, to the stars in the pores of the skin,
and to the Nāgavīthī, Aṅgavīthī, and Vanamālā.
"Kaustubhe, Agastimunaye, Namaḥ Grahebhyaḥ"—thus Hari spoke of the various types of nyāsa to Rādhā, and they have also been declared by me to you. || 112 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Installation of the Bathing Jar, the Offerings to the Guardians of the Quarters, the Golden Rod, Eye-Collyrium, the Bath with Many Pots, the Leaf-Bath, Worship, Ornaments, Food-Offerings, Homa, the Nyāsa of the Praṇava, the Nyāsa of the Mātṛkās, the Nyāsa of the Constellations, and so forth," in the second section, the Tretā-Santāna, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Rādhā, to those methods of formal surrender (nyāsa) which the Blessed Lord himself has declared;
I shall indeed explain them, along with the ritual procedures, for the installation of a deity in an image.
Salutation to Caitra upon the head, and likewise to Vaiśākha on the face;
salutation to Jyeṣṭha in the heart, and to Āṣāḍha and Śrāvaṇa on the two breasts.
To Bhādrapada, [he offers] on the abdomen; to Āśvina, on the hips;
to Kārtika and Mārgaśīrṣa, on the thighs; and to Pauṣa and Māgha, on the shanks.
To Phalguna, [he offers worship] at the two feet; to Vatsara, on the right upper arm; and to Saṃvat, Paridhāvin, and Vatsara, he says "namas" at the four arms.
In the joints from the mountains, in the linga from the seasons, in the bones from day and night, and in the body hairs from the moments and so forth. || 5 ||
Salutations to Tretā placed in the mouth, to Dvāpara and Kali in the heart and the two hips respectively,
and to the Manus in the feet and the arms.
Salutations again and again to Parārdha in the shanks;
salutations to Mahākalpa in the body, and to the two Ayanas in the feet. || 7 ||
Salutation, salutation to Viṣuvat in the fingers, and to Kāla in the mouth;
to the Brāhmaṇa in the arms, and to the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya in the thighs.
Salutation to the Śūdras at the feet; salutation to the mixed castes (saṃkara) at the tips of the feet;
salutation to the hair-bearing [beings] at the joints; and likewise, salutation to the cows at the mouth.
Salutation to goats and sheep; salutation everywhere to the hands and to all cattle; salutation to the clouds in his hair, and salutation to the mist in his body hairs.
Salutation to the rivers on the limbs; salutation to the oceans on the belly.
Salutation to the Ṛgveda on the head; salutation to the Yajurveda on the right arm.
Salutations to the Sāmas and Upaniṣads on the left arm; salutations to the Ākhyānas in the heart, to the Jaṅghās in the shanks, and salutations to the Atharvans at the navel.
Salutations to the Kalpasūtras at the feet; salutations to Vyākaraṇa at the face;
salutations to the Ūhas at the region of the throat; and salutations to Nirukta at the heart.
To Chanda and Jyotis, the two elemental beings, [he assigned] the eyes;
to Āyurveda, the right arm; and to Dhanurveda, the left.
Salutation to Yoga in the heart, to Nīti in the feet, and to Tantra in the lips; salutation to Dyu in the head, and salutation to the Sun and Moon in the eyes.
Salutation to Anila (the wind) in the nose; salutation again and again to Vyoman (the ether) in the navel;
salutation to the oceans in the bladder; and salutation to Pṛthvī (the earth) in the feet. || 16 ||
Salutations again and again to Hiraṇmaya in the head, to Kṛṣṇa in the mass of hair,
to Rudra on the forehead, and to Yama on the frown.
Salutation to the Aśvins in the two ears, and to Vaiśvānara in the mouth;
salutation to the Maruts in the nose, and salutation to the Vasus in the throat.
Salutations to the Rudras in the teeth, and to Sarasvatī, the embodiment of speech;
salutations to Indra in the right arm, and to Valaya in the left.
To Prahlāda on the right breast, to Viśvakarman on the left;
to Nārada on the right side of the belly, and to Ananta and the others on the left.
Salutation to Varuṇa for the two hands, and to Mitra for the two feet;
salutation to the Viśvedevas in the middle of the thighs, and to the Pitṛs in the middle of the knees.
From the sacrifices [he created] the calves, from the Rākṣasas the two ankles,
from the Piśācas the right foot, and from the Asuras the left foot.
To the Vidyādharas at the two feet, to the Grahas likewise on the soles, to the Guhyakas at the anus, and to the Pūtanas and others on the nails. ||23||
To the Gandharvas on the two lips, to Skanda on the sides of the hips, to Gaṇeśa on the sides of the hips, and salutations to Matsya on the head. (24)
Salutation to Kūrma at the feet; salutation to Nṛsiṃha on the forehead;
salutation to Vārāha at the shanks, and salutation to Vāmana on the face. (25)
Salutation to Paraśurāma in the heart; salutation to Rāma in the arms; to Kṛṣṇa in the navel; to Buddha in the intellect; and to Kalki in the knees.
To Keśava on the head, to Nārāyaṇa on the face,
to Mādhava on the neck, and to Govinda on the two arms.
Salutation to Viṣṇu at the heart, to Madhusūdana at the back;
salutation to Trivikrama at the waist, and to Vāmana at the belly. (28)
Salutations again and again to Śrīdhara and Hṛṣīkeśa for the two calves;
to Padmanābha for the two ankles, and to Dāmodara for the two feet. ||29||
Salutations to Aśvamedha on the crown of the head; to Naramedha on the forehead;
to Rājasūya on the face; and to Gomedha on the throat.
Homage to Hṛd in the heart, to Dvādaśabhuja in the region of the navel,
to Sarvajit on the right hip, and to Sarvamedhin on the left.
"Salutation to Agniṣṭoma on the penis; salutation to Atirātra on the two testicles;
salutation to Āptoryāma on the two thighs; and salutation to Ṣoḍaśin on the two knees. (32)
Salutation also to Utathya in the left thigh,
and to Vājapeya and Atirātra-agniṣṭoma in the right arm.

He should offer to the Cāturmāsya sacrifice on the left [side], to the Sautrāmaṇi in the two hands, to the animal sacrifices and the iṣṭis on the fingers themselves, and to the Darśa-Pūrṇamāsa sacrifices in the two eyes.
To all the *iṣṭis*, [he offers] at the hair-pores with *vaṣaṭ* and *svāhā*;
at the breast, and at the toes of the feet, [he offers] to the five great sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajña*). || 35 ||
Salutation to the Āhavanīya fire in the mouth, to the Dakṣiṇa fire in the heart,
to the Gārhapatya fire in the navel, and to the Vedi altar in the region above that.
Salutation to Hari for his ornaments during the Pravargya rite, for his feet during the Soma pressings, for his arms during the fuel-offerings, and for his hair during the Darbha grass rites. (37)
Salutations again and again to Dharma at the head and to Jñāna at the heart; salutations indeed to Vairāgya at the secret place and to Aiśvarya at the feet.
Salutation to Khaṅga on the head, salutation to Śārṅga on the crown;
to Mūśala on the right arm and to Hala on the left arm. (39)
Salutations again and again to the navel, the belly, the back, and the discus;
to the conch at the genitals, to the testicles, and to the mace at the knees and shanks.
Salutation to Padmā and Lakṣmī at the feet and ankles; salutation to Sarasvatī on the forehead; salutation to Rati on the face; salutation again and again to her in the secret place.

Salutation to the neck for the sake of joy; salutation to the quarters for the sake of fame; salutation to the heart for the sake of peace; salutation to the belly for the sake of contentment; and salutation indeed everywhere for the sake of nourishment. ||42||
Salutations again and again to Śrīvatsa on the right and left breasts;
salutations to the Kaustubha gem on the chest and to the forest garland on the neck. ||43||
Oṃ at the two feet, naṃ at the two knees, moṃ at the secret place, bhaṃ at the navel,
gaṃ at the heart, vaṃ at the throat, teṃ at the face, and namaḥ at the two eyes.
Suṃ on the forehead, deṃ on the head, vāṃ on the right side, and yaṃ on the left;
aṃ in the [right] ear, nāṃ on the crest-lock, diṃ on the forehead, and śrīṃ in the middle of the eyebrows. ||45||
Kaṃ in the mouth, ṣṇaṃ in the middle of the throat, nāṃ in the two arms, rāṃ within the heart,
yaṃ on the breast, ṇāṃ in the belly, yaṃ at the navel, and paṃ on the hips.

One should repeatedly offer salutations to Śrī Hari, saying "Oṃ" to the secret place, "Yaṃ" to the testicles, "Naṃ" to the two thighs, "Maṃ" to the two knees, "Visargaḥ" to the two feet, and "Namaḥ" to Śrī Hari. (47)
Śrīṃ: Rādhikā in the heart; Lakṣmī on the left arm; Ramā on the right arm;
Brahmavidyā in the heart; and Māṇikī on the [right] arm. (48)
I bow to the forms of Hari, beginning with Parā-vidyā and ending with Kṛṣṇā; salutations to Kaṃbharā, who brings satisfaction, and to the two eyes of Hari. (49)
Having performed all the ritual placements (nyāsa) in this manner, one should then perform the placement of the vital breath (jīvanyāsa);
having meditated upon the splendor [of the deity] within the image, as well as the intellect, the senses, and the mind.
Having joined the vital breaths, the ego, and the subtle elements together to produce the state of a body,
and having brought about the state of a person therein, one indeed contemplates the Witness.
Or one should deposit the three principles (*tattva*), or one should deposit the five principles (*pañcatattva*).
"Salutation to the deity Brahmā, the principle of the self (*ātmatattva*), at the feet;
salutation to the deity Viṣṇu, the principle of knowledge (*vidyātattva*), at the heart."
Salutation to the head for the divine Śiva, the principle of auspiciousness. ||5 3||
To the principle of Brahman (brahmatattva), [offer] at the head; to the principle of Māyā (māyātattva), at the throat;
to the principle of Īśa (īśatattva), at the heart; and to the principle of the individual soul (jīvatattva), at the two feet.
Salutations to the Inner Controller (Antaryāmin), the reality within, who dwells in all bodies.
[Salutations] to his two big toes, to his two ankles, and likewise to his two shanks.
Place *tuṃ* on the two knees, *vaṃ* likewise on the two thighs, *reṃ* on the anus, *ṇiṃ* on the testicles, *yaṃ* on the hips, *bhaṃ* on the navel, *gaṃ* on the belly, and *deṃ* on the breasts. 56.
Vaṃ at the heart, syaṃ at the throat, dhīṃ at the mouth, and mam at the palate;
hiṃ at the nose, dhiṃ at the eyes, yoṃ at the eyebrows, and yom at the forehead. (57)
*Pūrve* in the east, *naḥ* in the south, *ca* in the west, *uṃ* in the north, *dam* on the head, and *tatsavitur* everywhere; this is the heart-mantra of Hari. ||18||
We meditate upon the most excellent splendor of the divine; may he who impels our intellects [bestow it] upon our head, our hair, our two eyes, and our neck. (899)
Oṃ nāṃ on the two big toes; rāṃ on the two ankles; yaṃ on the two shanks; ṇāṃ on the two knees;
yaṃ likewise on the two thighs; viṃ on the anus; and ghmakam on the testicles.
Heṃ at the waist, vāṃ at the navel, suṃ at the belly and the breast, dem;
vāṃ at the heart, yaṃ at the throat, dhīṃ at the mouth, and mam at the palate.
Hiṃ is on the nose, tat on the two eyes, no on the eyebrows, viṃ on the forehead, ṣṇuṃ on the nostrils, praṃ on the crest-lock, coṃ on the mind, and daṃ on the body.
And that form of Hari which I contemplate within myself as his universal embodiment, I know it as Nārāyaṇa in the heart and likewise upon the head. (63)
And for the armor-mantra, "We meditate upon Vāsudeva"; for the eyes, "May Viṣṇu impel that [knowledge] within us"; and for the weapon-mantra, "May he impel that. (68)
One should worship Agni at the two feet with "agnim īḷe," the two ankles with "iṣe tvā" and "namaḥ," the two knees with "śanno devī," and the two thighs with "suparṇo 'si. ||65||
"May there be well-being for us" on the belly; "O long-lived one" indeed on the heart;
"Prosperity and Fortune are yours" on the throat; and "The Protector" on the face. (66)
With the mantra "Tryambakam," one should offer salutations again and again to the two breasts and the two eyes;
with "Mūrdhānam," one offers salutation to the head, saying, "Salutation to you, O Nārāyaṇa. (67)
Oṃ, salutation to Keśava on the head; salutation to Nārāyaṇa on the face;
moṃ, salutation to Mādhava on the neck; and bhaṃ, salutation to Govinda on the throat. (68)
Gaṃ to Viṣṇu on the back; vaṃ to Madhusūdana in the belly;
teṃ to Trivikrama on the hips; and vāṃ to Vāmana in the shanks.
*Suṃ* at the secret place for Śrīdhara; *Deṃ* at the ankle for Hṛṣīkeśa;
*Vāṃ* at the left foot for Padmanābha; and *Yam* at the right for Dāmodara.
Huṃ, salutation to the heart; salutation to Viṣṇu on the head;
likewise, salutation to Brahmā at the crest-lock, and salutation to Dhruva for the armor. ||71||
"Obeisance to the Discus-bearer for the eyes; *namaḥ astrāya phaṭ* [obeisance to the weapon]; obeisance to the Discus-bearer for the feet;
*sahasraśīrṣā* (the thousand-headed) for the shanks; *puruṣa eva* for the calves. (72)
"Knowing it to be of such extent—from the knees, the thighs, and upwards from the feet;
from that [part] comes Irāṭ in the testicles, and from that sacrifice [comes] Kaṭisthala. (73)
From that sacrifice, from its very center, horses were produced; from its heart-region, that fame was born; and likewise from its two breasts and its two arms, Puruṣa emerged. (74)
"From this [Puruṣa] came the Brāhmaṇa," thus [it was said] regarding his mouth; "the moon from his eyes," regarding his two eyes;
"from his navel, the ears, and the two worlds," regarding the verse beginning with "yat puruṣa. (75)
The mantra "saptāsyāsan" is on the forehead; "yajñena" is on the head;
"adbhyaḥ" is on the heart; and "vedāham" is on the head.
One should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of Prajāpati on the crest-lock, and likewise of the deity on the armor; one should place the Brāhma-ṛc on the two eyes, and Śrī as the weapon. ||77||
And one should also invoke sleep with the mantra: "O Enchantress, come and stay by the command of Nārāyaṇa, who is asleep upon the serpent-couch. (78)
O Goddess, you are indeed the foundation; accept this worship and offering. Come, O Sāvitrī, embodiment of the sacred syllable, you who dwell within the range of our vision! 79.
O Goddess, enter the nostrils; longing, enter the throat.
This arghya is offered by me; please accept this worship.
In this manner, having worshipped Nidrā (Sleep) in the sleep-pitcher, and having offered bali-oblations to the world-protectors and others, one should then worship the bed. ||81||
One should cause Viṣṇu to enter the twelve-spoked, excellent wheel of the Sarvatobhadra [maṇḍala], and Kṛṣṇa into the eight-petaled lotus, by means of the root mantra. ||82||
One should worship the heart in the pericarp with "Obeisance to the Lake" (hrade namaḥ), and one should worship the head on the eastern petal with "Obeisance to Viṣṇu" (viṣṇave namaḥ). || 83 ||
One should worship the *śikhā* on the right petal with "Salutation to Brahmā," and one should worship the western *kavaca* with "Salutation indeed to Dhruva. ||858||
In the north, one should worship with the mantra "Astram Phaṭ" and say "Salutation to the Wielder of the Discus" (Cakriṇe Namaḥ).
Likewise, in the southeast, one should worship Śambhu with "Salutation to Śambhu" and worship Gāyatrī. One should worship Sāvitrī as Vijayā in the northeastern petal.
And in the southwest, one should offer salutations with "Salutation to the One whose Form is Light" (Jyotirūpāya) and "Salutation, Salutation" (Namo Namaḥ).
"Salutation to the one in the form of a discus, and the tawny weapon is for Vāyu.
Having thus performed the inner enclosure (garbhāvaraṇa) on the spokes according to the previous sequence, [one proceeds].
Keśava, Nārāyaṇa, Mādhava, and Govinda;
likewise Viṣṇu, Madhusūdana, Trivikrama, and Vāmana. ||88||
One should worship Śrīdhara, Hṛṣīkeśa, Padmanābha, and Damodara; these are the twelve forms, and that indeed constitutes the second enclosure.
And furthermore, in the east, there is a sword, a discus,
a beautiful conch, a lotus, a plow, the Śārṅga bow, and likewise the one who is the lord of the forms of fire.
One should worship the fierce Ugra, as well as Ārka, who has the sacrificer as his presiding form;
thereafter, one should worship the lords of that third enclosure.
Salutation indeed to Pṛthvī and to her lord, Vāsudeva;
salutation indeed to Jala on the right and to its lord, Saṃkarṣaṇa. || 92 ||
In the west, salutations again and again to Agni, the Lord, and to Pradyumna;
in the north, salutations indeed again and again to Vāyu and to Aniruddha. || 93 ||
"Salutation to my own form, and salutation again and again to Nārāyaṇa.
Having worshipped Indra and the other deities, one should clothe the Lord with garments. || 94 ||
Having offered praise, presented a handful of flowers, and scattered them over the pavilion and other areas,
one should write the word "svasti" upon the mandala with flowers and other substances, and [invoke] the three deities.
The world-protectors, the Vasus, the Rudras, the Ādityas, the Viśvedevas, the Sādhyas, the hosts of Maruts, and the Gandharvas and Apsarases—these [he worshipped]. 96.

Having offered salutations to the hosts of ancestors, the excellent holy places, Skanda, Durgā, and the others, as well as the guardians of the fields and the attendants, one should worship them. ||97||
The preceptor, having approached the sacrificial pit, [should take] eight hundred fuel-sticks indeed produced from the Palāśa, Udumbara, Aśvattha, and Apāmārga trees.
Whether three thousand, six thousand, eight thousand, or even twelve thousand [disciples], he should protect them while they are near the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa). ||99||
One should offer oblations with mantras for pacification and nourishment according to their respective proportions:
"Oṃ! May the wind blow auspiciously for us; may the sun shine auspiciously for us. (2.157.10)
May the divine Parjanya, thundering for our benefit, pour down rain upon us.
May the divine waters be for our aid and for our drink. 101.
Oṃ! He is nourishing and all-pervading like the earth, vast as the ground, a source of enjoyment like a mountain, and a bringer of bliss like the waters.

Furthermore, he is a majesty that is not submerged, a consecrated creation, and a flowing stream like the ocean; he is the giver of the kadamba fruit, the increaser of victory, the dispeller of disease, the finder of wealth, and the promoter of prosperity. 102.
Then, one should offer oblations into the fire in the eastern pit with sesame seeds and barley,
or else with *palāśa* wood-sacrificial sticks, one hundred and eight times.
One should offer oblations into the southern sacrificial pit with the mantra "iṣe tvā," and likewise, one should offer oblations into the western pit with "oṃ agne."
One should likewise offer oblations into the northern pit with the mantra "śanno devī," and one should offer oblations into the southeast direction with the mantra ending in "vauṣaṭ."
One should likewise offer oblations with the Gāyatrī mantra into the Nairṛta pit; with the Jātavedas mantra into the Vāyavya pit; and with "Namo Brahmaṇe" into the Īśāna pit.

Then, with the mantra "mūrdhānaṃ divaḥ," they should offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti); at that time, it is prescribed that the falling of the oblations should be directed into the peace-pot (śāntighaṭa).
Thus Hari spoke to Rādha regarding the body of the temple;
everything that has been told to you by me is a bestowing of fruit even through its mere hearing.

Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Embodiment [of the Lord], the Months, Seasons, Yugas, Varṇas, Vedas, Vasus, Directions, Guardians of the Quarters, Kṣetrapālas, Divine Incarnations, Sacrifices, Fire, Weapons, Ornaments, Beloveds, Tattvas, Root Mantras, the Two Gāyatrīs, the Arpaṇa-mantra, the Puruṣasūkta-nyāsa, Worship, Offering of Bali, and Homa," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen then, O Rādhā, to the great oblations and the final offering which Śrī Hari spoke of there; I shall describe the ritual procedure for you here.
With the mantra "Syonā pṛthivī," [he offers] to the Earth; with "Aghorebhyaḥ" and "Śambhave," to Śambhu;
with "Indrāya," to Indra; with "Mahendrāya," to Mahendra; and with "Agnim dūtam," to Agni.
To Agni, the Lord of Animals, and to Agni, come hither!
You are the sword for the sacrificer; [I offer] to that Indra who is the embodiment of Rudra. || 3 ||
One should offer "yāmāya" to Yama himself; "udutyaṃ" to the form of Sūrya; and "ā vo rudrāya" and "asunvantam" to Nirṛti. || 4 ||
"Āpo hi ṣṭhā" is for the deity of water; "vibhūḥ" is for Bhava;
"imaṃ me varuṇāya" is for Varuṇa; and "vāta ā vātu" is for the form of Vāyu. || 5 ||
"To Īśāna, that Lord; and to Vāyu, [the mantra] beginning with 'ā noni';
to Soma, to Sūrya, and to Indra, the Great God. (6)
One should offer oblations consecrated by mantras to Hari with "ādipragna," to Bhīma with "mṛgo na bhīmaḥ," and to Īśāna with "abhityam. || 7 ||
In a single sacrificial pit, the great master should perform oblations with the names of all [the deities];
he should offer eight thousand or, alternatively, one hundred and eight oblations.
Then, having offered the *pūrṇāhuti*, one should touch the two ears of the deity— specifically the right ear— and thereafter offer eight oblations of clarified butter.
And one should perform the oblation with the root mantra a hundred times or more;
having offered curd into the *yāma* fire-pit, one should then touch the navel of the deity.
Having offered milk into the western pit (kuṇḍaka), one should touch the heart of Hari;
having offered honey into the northern pit, one should touch the head of Hari.
Having offered into the Varuṇa fire-pit the four substances beginning with ghee mixed together,
and having performed the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti), one should touch all the limbs of Hari.

Having performed the ritual of placement (nyāsa) upon the image and having worshipped the tortoise-stone (kūrmaśilā), as well as the Brahma-stone, the pedestal (piṇḍikā), the vehicles, and the attendants; 13.
One should worship the attendant deities and their retinues; one should consecrate those attendants of Viṣṇu, beginning with Caṇḍaprabha, on the left side.
Having anointed it with honey and ghee and washed it with water, one should worship it;
then, having covered it with a cloth, one should perform the ritual placement of mantras (nyāsa) upon the image.
Wherever Viṣṇu is to be installed according to the rite for the image and the pedestal,
[one should perform the placement] with "Oṃ Ghaṃ Ṅaṃ Paṃ Bhaṃ Phaṃ, obeisance to Lakṣmī" at the heart and the head.

Having thus performed the placement (nyāsa) on the pedestal with "śikhāyai," "kavacāya," "netrābhyām," "huṃ phaṭ svāhā," and "namama," one should likewise perform the five-limbed placement there as well.
One should install the embodied form with mantras, and indeed, one should worship the embodied form with mantras:
"Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ hrāṃ kṣaḥ, salutations to the illustrious Supreme Brahman, the sustainer of all. (18)

"Oṃ hrāṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ, salutation to Subhagā, the bearer of divine splendor. Having thus performed the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana), one should perform the preliminary consecration of the temple near the new [image], using a mandala of eighty-one squares.
Having made seven heaps of the seven grains with unbroken rice at each of the steps.
Having prepared eighty-one auspicious and new jars filled with water,
and having brought them there, one should place the middle one among the nine groups of nine.
Having ascertained their respective chambers, one should place the jars within them according to the sequence beginning with the center and the east;
then, indeed, twelve sprouts should be placed in the central jar.
The śamī, udumbara, aśvattha, palāśa, aśoka, campaka, kadamba, plakṣa, nyagrodha, āmra, bilva, and arjuna trees; ||23||
Their leaves should be taken and offered with the mantra "Namas somāya. Then, into the eastern jar, one should place lotus fibers, yellow pigment (rocanā), and sprouts of dūrvā grass.
Likewise, one should offer blades of *darbha* grass, white and yellow mustard seeds, red sandalwood, *jātī* flowers, and *nandāvarta* flowers. (25)
Then, one should place seven substances into the fire-pitcher as follows:
barley, rice, sesame, gold, silver, and earth from a riverbank. (26)
Having said "Namaḥ," one should cast cow-dung that has not touched the ground;
then, one should duly place eight [substances] into the southern jar as follows.
One should add sahadevī, viṣṇukrāntā, bhṛṅgarāja, mahauṣadhī,
śamī, śatāvarī, guḍūcī, and śyāmāka.
Then, in the pitcher of the Nairṛtya direction, [one should place] plantain, betel nut, coconut, wood-apple, nāriṅga, and citron. ||29||
Having uttered "Salutation to Badara and Āmalaka," one should cast them [into the water];
then, one should take the consecrated five products of the cow (pañcagavya) into the northern jar.
In the pitcher located in the northwest, one should place the five astringents (kaṣāya-pañcaka) derived from the Śamī, Udumbara, Aśvattha, Nyagrodha, and Kapāśa trees.
In a northern jar, one should place śaṅkhapuṣpī, sahadevī, balā, as well as śatāvarī, kumārī, guḍūcī, and vacā. ||32||
One should place the eight roots, including the tigress-form,
and one should place the seven types of earth beginning with that from an anthill in the pitcher of Īśa.
O Jātavedas, bring to me Lakṣmī, who is golden-hued, tawny, adorned with garlands of gold and silver, moon-like, and made of gold. 34.
With this mantra, one should consecrate the central jars;
then, having filled the remaining ones with scented water and likewise consecrated them, [one proceeds]. ||35||
Having wrapped [the structure] inside, outside, below, and above with threads while reciting the root mantra,
one should sprinkle the temple, including its pinnacle, with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Then, one should smear the top of the anthill with clay using the mantra "mūrdhānaṃ divaḥ," and subsequently with the mantra "samudrād ūrmī."
One should then bathe [the deity] with the *īśāna* mudrā using the *kuṃbhaka* breath-retention, and with the *yajñāyajña* mantra using the *kaṣāya* *kuṃbhaka*. || 38 ||
One should bathe [the deity] with the Vāyavya mantra using milk, according to the verse beginning "payaḥ pṛthivyām";
thereafter, one should bathe [him] with a jar of pañcagavya using the Vāruṇa mantra.
Then, with the pitcher of *nairṛta* fruits while reciting "yāḥ phalinī," and with the pitcher of the eight *mūla* herbs situated in the north while reciting "haṃsaḥ śuciṣad."
With the mantra "viṣṇorarāṭam asi" and the pitcher located in the east, and with the mantra "somo rājā" and the pitcher located in the southeast; ||41||

With the mantra "viśvataśceti" and the *kumbhaka* performed while standing facing south, and with the mantra "namo'stu sarpebhyah" and the *kumbhaka* performed while standing facing the center. ||42||
Then, one should bathe the pinnacle with eight [verses] in the preceding order:
"Oṃ, O Waters, carry away this, whatever is impure and whatever is foul. (43)
Whatever falsehood I have uttered through treachery, and whatever I have sworn falsely in my fearlessness—may the Waters and Pavamāna release me from that sin. 44.

"Oṃ! Be purified for the divine rite, for the sacrifice to the gods; whatever impurities have clung to you while you were flowing, those I now purify for you. Having sprinkled [the image] with this mantra, having wound it with thread, and having bathed it, one should meditate upon the temple as having the form of a deity and perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa). ||45||
Oṃ Hrīṃ! O inconceivable one who embodies all the gods, whose form is radiant with all jewels!
As long as the moon and the sun endure, remain firm here. 46.
Then one should likewise install the horn-vessel and the banners;
having performed the fire-oblation (homa) with sesame seeds and other materials for the pedestal and the deities of the vehicle.
Then, having worshipped four cows facing north at the eastern gate, [one recites]:
"Oṃ, we know Nārāyaṇa; we meditate upon Vāsudeva. (48)
Having milked the cow with the mantra "tanno viṣṇuḥ pracodayāt," and having cooked the milk-rice (pāyasa) and the sacrificial oblation (caru), he should offer them to Nārāyaṇa.
Having fed ten Brahmins, one should recite, "May Viṣṇu be pleased.
One should give cows to the Great Preceptor and golden rings to the officiating priests (ṛtvij).
Having given the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), one should hold a great festival at night;
the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) may last for seven, five, three, or one night, or it may conclude with the offering of oblations (bali).
Then the Guru, having gone outside, should meditate upon the deity of the temple:
"The feet are said to be the foundation stone (pādaśilā), and the shanks are said to be above the feet. (52)
The womb is to be known as the belly, and the hips as the hip-girdle;
the pillars are to be understood as the arms, and the bell is proclaimed to be the tongue. (53)
The life-breath (prāṇa) is to be known as its lamp, while the downward breath (apāna) is the exit of the water;
the navel is its seat of Brahman, and the heart-lotus is considered its pedestal (piṇḍikā). ||54||
This image is that very person; the foot is likewise the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra), the light is the eye, and what is above that is proclaimed to be his primordial nature (prakṛti). 55.
The image itself is Nalakuṃbha; the lower opening is the penis, the śukanāsā is its nose, and the window is said to be its ear. (56)
Its shoulder is the dove-niche (kapotapāli), and its neck is the amalasaraka;
the pitcher (kalaśa) should be known as the head, and the marrow-impregnated juice is beneficial. //57//
One should know that the fat is the earth; the flesh is said to be the plastering;
the bones are its stones, and the sinews are remembered as the wooden stakes and so forth. (818)
The eyes are its peaks and the hair is proclaimed to be its banners;
thus the sacrificer should meditate upon the temple as having the form of a man.
One should worship it with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, and likewise encircle it with a thread;
one should provide a cloth for the thread and then perform a salutation.
Having thus performed the consecration, the preceptor, having bathed in the morning, arrives at the pavilion along with the image-protectors, the gatekeepers, and the deities.
Having worshipped the deities of the site (vāstudeva) and offered one hundred and eight oblations into the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa),
he should then offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) with the mantra "vāstoṣpate" and the root mantra.
Having offered the bali-oblation to the guardians of the directions, one should then bow to the deity;
thereafter, one should sprinkle the patron with the water from the jars located to the north of the pavilion.
One should satisfy the preceptor, the Brahmins, the architects, and others with sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) and other gifts;
then, having specified the place and time, one should perform the consecration ceremony (utsarga) of the temple.
Having declared, "I offer this temple, which inspires serene joy, for the pleasure of the God," he then scattered *kuśa* grass as an intermediary.
Having bowed to the Lord, one should feed Brahmins and other virtuous men and women,
together with the image-guardians (mūrtipas), for the sake of the ritual of the immovable image.
Having consecrated the divine support (devādhārā), the tortoise stone (kūrmaśilā),
as well as the Brahma-stone (brahmaśilā) and the pedestal (piṇḍikā), the preceptor should circumambulate them clockwise.
Having brought the temple, while reciting the mantra "trātāram indrakam," one should indeed destroy the obstacles with the weapon-mantra "astrāya phaṭ. (68)

Having sprinkled the auspicious dwelling with streams of water mixed with flowers, one should then indeed scratch [the ground] with a blade of *darbha* grass while reciting "Oṃ ca mahām̐ indreṇa. (69)
Having properly sprinkled with water from the *astra-mantra* the middle of the temple door,
one should [draw a line] half a barley-corn wide toward the south-eastern or northern direction.
Having placed the tortoise-stone, consecrated by bathing and other rites, along with the five gems, into a bright golden tortoise with the syllable Om (praṇava), [he should proceed].
Having brought [the materials] facing the door and having deposited jewels there,
[he should do so] either together with thirty-six or forty-five pits.
One should place the consecrated Brahma-stone and worship it with:
"Oṃ, salutations! O Pervasive One, O Firm, O Immovable, O Eternal One, grant us peace! (73)
One should worship according to one's desire with the mantra "Oṃ śrīṃ laṃ svāhā," [saying]:
"You alone are the power of the seat; remain here forever, O Stone! (74)
Salutation to the path of phonemes (varṇādhvan), salutation to the path of words (padādhvan), salutation to the path of mantras (mantrādhvan);
salutation to the path of worlds (bhuvanādhvan), salutation to the path of principles (tattvādhvan), and salutation to the path of the manifest (sakalādhvan). ||75||
Having meditated upon [the deity] as having ascended the level path, one should then cause the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be made;
then, having offered one hundred and eight oblations into the cavity of the Brahma-stone (*brahmaśilā*).

One should perform the placement of jewels with the right hand, together with gold, on a stone surface free from cavities; however, if there is a cavity, one should do so on a stone portion that includes the cavity.
Reciting the Dhruva-sūkta, he placed the *piṇḍikā* on the eastern face of the temple, with its northern drain facing east and its southern drain facing north.
One should consecrate the pedestal with the mantra of Devapatnī;
then, having recited the Śrīsūkta and the Tejas-sūkta, one should install Ramā there.
One should perform the ritual placements of the principles (tattvanyāsa), saying: "Obeisance indeed to the principle of the self (ātmatattva);
obeisance again and again to the sovereign power of the activity of the principle of the self."

Salutation to the principle of knowledge (vidyātattva) and salutation again and again to the power of knowledge (jñānaśakti); salutation to the principle of Śiva (śivatattva) and salutation again and again to the power of will (icchāśakti). ||81||

One should install the forms and formless ones, as well as the world-protectors, within each respective principle; and one should offer salutation to the foundational power (ādhāraśakti) and the seat of Ananta together with Agni.
Having fashioned and worshipped her, one should pray to that Suśaktikā:
"O you who are the substratum of all worlds, I establish you here. (83)
"Remain firm in this temple as long as the earth endures"—
having thus prayed, one should place the Praṇava and the sixteen vowels outside of that.
Having arranged the various offerings all around and placed them within the hollows, one should then set down gems and other such items on the outer perimeter, as well as barley and rice grains.
Niṣpāva beans, sesame, māṣa beans, priyaṅgu, and nīvāraka grains; likewise, śāli rice, white mustard, diamonds, pearls, and conch shells.
Vaiḍūrya, crystal, puṣparāga, indranīla, and padmarāga; moonstone, realgar, yellow orpiment, and antimony. (87)
Janaka, sīsaka, saurāṣṭrī, rocanā, and gairika;
mercury, gold, silver, copper, iron, and tin. ||88||
Lead, bell-metal, brass, or even various types of steel;
likewise, white sandalwood, red sandalwood, agallochum, and arjunaka. ||89||
One should place uśīra, vaiṣṇavī, sahadevī, and lakṣmaṇā;
in the absence of seeds, one should offer barley, and in the absence of gems, one should offer a diamond.
In the absence of the [proper] mineral element, one should use yellow orpiment; in the absence of copper, gold;
in the absence of the medicinal herb, Sahadevī; thereafter, the attainment [of the goal] follows.
In the east, "trātāram indra" (RV 8.50.1); in the southeast, "agnim īḷe" (RV 1.1.1);
in the south, "yamāya tvā" (VS 39.16); and in the southwest, "asunvantam" (RV 7.104.1).
In the west, he recites "pañcanadya"; in the northwest, "vāyo yeti";
in the north, "oṃ vayaṃ ca"; and in the northeast, "tamīśāna. ||93||
Having thus performed the placement of the jewels, one should likewise place the golden figures of the Earth, Sumeru, and the Tortoise, as well as the vehicle, all facing toward the doors.

Having placed mercury in the middle of the cavity, having stabilized the gems and other substances with guggulu resins, and having smeared the cavity with milk-rice (pāyasa), [one should proceed]. ||95||
Having smeared it with honey and covered it with a cloth, one should say "Hūṃ," then veil it with the armor-mantra (Kavaca), and subsequently utter "Phaṭ" for the weapon-mantra (Astra). ||96||
May Manojūti be pleased; having consecrated the temple and offered the bali-oblation to Indra and the other deities, [one should proceed] outside the temple.
Having sprinkled the ground while circumambulating it clockwise with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya),
one should then sweep it with tufts of darbha grass in the eight directions.
Then, eight square sand-platforms, each measuring three spans in size, should be prepared starting from the northeast (īśāna) corner. 99.
Having placed water-filled jars, adorned with fine flowers, sprouts, and excellent fruits,
and wrapped with threads upon the sacrificial mound, one performs the consecration of the ground.
