Then, having prepared the fire and brought it forth, one should offer one hundred and eight oblations of *palāśa* fuel-sticks, and subsequently offer oblations of clarified butter with the *gāyatrī* mantra.
One should sprinkle water from eight jars consecrated with the root mantra upon the head of the deity, and then perform the binding of the directions with "huṃ phaṭ."
One should pray to him: "Awaken, O God of gods, Lord of the world!
Salutations to you, O Vāsudeva, the infinite one who dwells upon the earth, once awakened! (103)
O Rādhā, having offered the arghya consisting of rice, sesame, kuśa grass, milk, water, and so forth, placed within a conch, one should raise the Lord with the mantra. 104.

Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Pūrṇāhuti, Nyāsas, Adhivāsana, Water from the Pitcher, the Bath on the Summit, the Cooking of the Caru, Meditation on the Temple as having the Form of the Person, Worship, the Kūrma-śilā, Brahma-śilā, the Piṇḍikā, the Jewels, the Arghya for the Deity," and so forth, in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Then, O Rādhā, the awakening of Hari by means of the mantra has been proclaimed;
likewise, all that ritual section (karmakāṇḍa) and the immovable image have been described. || 1 ||
I shall relate that which Hari spoke to the body of the temple: "Oṃ! Arise, O Brahmaṇaspati; we, seeking the gods, pray to you. (2)
Having raised [the deity] with the mantra, "May the Maruts, the bounteous givers, come near; O Indra, be swift with them," one should cause him to sit upon the chariot. || 3 ||
Oṃ! Standing in the chariot, the skillful charioteer leads the horses forward wherever he desires. Admire the greatness of the reins; the traces follow behind at the mind's command. || 4 ||
Thus, on the chariot of the deity, the preceptor himself should sit in the front part,
while the sacrificer, together with his family, should sit in the rear part.
And for the sake of protection, the guardians of the forms of Pārśva and Payomūrti [accompanied him] with auspicious sounds,
the resonance of musical instruments, and [the blessings] of the palace, the village, and the city.
Having performed a circumambulation and brought [the image] from the chariot to the temple,
he set it down and positioned it facing the door of the shrine.
Having offered the arghya water, one should then place the deity in the temple;
the patron and the preceptor should cause the deity to be installed upon the pedestal (piṇḍikā).
At an auspicious moment and a favorable conjunction, while being gazed upon by benefic planets,
he meditated upon the Lord of Lords and placed the lotus in the cavity.
"Remain steadfast for as long as you dwell upon this earth.
Having spoken thus, he firmly and securely fixed the Lord together with Śakti.
One should install Mahālakṣmī on Viṣṇu’s left side so that she does not move; with the mantra "viśvataścakṣuruta," one should place the hand upon the head of the deity.
Having performed [the ritual] and meditated, the sacrificer should then properly perform the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* (consecration of the vital breaths).
For the mantra of *prāṇapratiṣṭhā*, the sages Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva are the seers (*ṛṣis*).
The Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas are the meters; the deity is the vital breath of the ritual action;
"Āṃ" is the seed-syllable and "Krauṃ" is the power; thus is the application in the Pratiṣṭhā rite.
Salutation to Brahmā and the others on the head; salutation to the Ṛgveda and the others on the face; salutation to Prāṇa in the hearts; and salutation to the secret seed-syllable *Āṃ*.
"Krauṃ, obeisance to Śakti; and on the feet and the body, obeisance, obeisance. Thereafter, one should perform the seed-syllable nyāsas for the purpose of the arrival of the vital breaths. (15)
Oṃ kaṃ khaṃ gaṃ ghaṃ ṅaṃ āṃ! To the self consisting of earth, water, fire, air, and ether: Oṃ, salutation to the heart.
Oṃ caṃ chaṃ jaṃ jhaṃ ñaṃ iṃ! To the self consisting of sound, touch, form, taste, and smell:
Īṃ, svāhā to the head. || 16 ||
Oṃ ṭaṃ ṭhaṃ ḍaṃ ḍhaṃ ṇaṃ oṃ; to the essence of the ear, skin, eye, tongue, and nose, aṃ, to the tuft (śikhā), vaṣaṭ!
Oṃ taṃ thaṃ daṃ dhaṃ naṃ eṃ; to the essence of speech, hands, feet, anus, and genitals, aiṃ, to the armor (kavaca), hūṃ! 17.
Oṃ paṃ phaṃ baṃ bhaṃ maṃ oṃ, to the self of speech, grasping, movement, excretion, and pleasure, oṃ, to the three eyes, vauṣaṭ!
Oṃ yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ haṃ laṃ kṣaṃ aṃ, to the self of mind, intellect, ego, and consciousness, aḥ, to the weapon, phaṭ! || 18 ||
Then, having touched the deity: *oṃ āṃ hrīṃ krauṃ yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ haṃ saḥ*, the breath of the deity is here, its breaths are here.
*oṃ āṃ hrīṃ krauṃ yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ haṃ saḥ*, the life-force (*jīva*) of the deity is stationed here. (19)
Oṃ āṃ hrīṃ krauṃ yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ haṃ saḥ, may the all the senses of the deity be here.
Oṃ āṃ hrīṃ krauṃ yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ haṃ saḥ, may the speech, mind, eyes, ears, nose, and vital breaths of the deity abide here; svāhā!
Then, having placed his thumb upon the heart of the image, he should recite: "May the vital breaths of this [image] be established; may the vital breaths of this [image] move;
may no one whatsoever cause harm to the divinity of this image. (21)
Having restrained [the breath] with the *praṇava* and meditated upon it as being endowed with life,
while reciting "Firm is the heaven," he should whisper the *gāyatrī* mantra into the ear.
Having worshipped with the Puruṣasūkta and bowed thereafter,
and having touched his feet, navel, and head, he should mutter "May I prosper right here" three times.
Welcome to you, O Hari-Kṛṣṇa! Be firm for our welfare;
as long as the earth exists, so long should you remain here, O compassionate one. (24)
Endowed with all splendor and equipped with the conch, discus, and mace, I establish the wielder of the discus here as the God, the Supreme Lord. (25)
One should recite the mantras known as the *Pauruṣa-sūkta* according to the prescribed rule:
"O Blessed One, by which form all that is moving and unmoving is pervaded. (26)
"Be established in the image with that distinguished form.
Having said this, he should then install the deities of its retinue. (27)
In the eastern pit, one should offer with the heart-mantra; in the southern, with the head-mantra;
in the western, with the crest-mantra; and in the northern, with the armor-mantra.
One should offer twenty-one oblations into the guru’s fire-pit with the Netra-mantras;
having offered into the eastern pit with the Astra-mantra, one should then offer with the weapon-mantras.
And having offered the oblation, he should pray: "Dwell here always for the sake of protecting the world;
let there be no cessation of progeny in this [place], and may the sacrificer prosper."
"May the kingdom of the virtuous be prosperous; may they enjoy inexhaustible happiness.
Having thus prayed, O Aṅgada, one should install the deities in their respective shrines.
One should offer the arghya, pādya, ācamana, and the seat, saying "namaḥ";
then, having worshipped with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and water, [one should say] "svāhā. ||32||
Having bathed [the image], one should recite the Puruṣasūkta and likewise offer prayers;
one should touch the feet, the navel, the head, and the chest, saying: "Be the bestower of liberation. (33)
O Lord, may your ritual of worship—whether performed with knowledge or without knowledge—be complete for you;
by the grace of Hari Kṛṣṇa, Ādikṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. (34)
One should give gifts, perform the lustration rite (nīrājana) with musical instruments, and offer hymns of praise;
for the sake of destroying the dense clouds of occasional impurities, one should perform the oblation of atonement (prāyaścitta-homa).
With *śamī* leaves, *palāśa* leaves, sesame seeds, and so forth, one should perform [the rite] consisting of one hundred and eight [offerings];
and to the preceptor, one should give a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) consisting of wealth, cows, jewels, land, and houses.
One should perform the homa again for the pacification of the arrival of what is prohibited:
"Oṃ, for stability, be firm; svāhā! And may you be established here. (37)
Become immeasurable, awakened, eternal, and all-pervading;
for the sake of universal peace, perform here one hundred and eight oblations.
Oṃ, svāhā to Prajāpati; this is for Prajāpati, may it be mine. Oṃ, svāhā to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt; this is for Agni Sviṣṭakṛt, may it be mine. ||39||
Having offered the oblation, performed the consumption of the remnants, the sipping of water, and the giving of the vessel,
I indeed give this full vessel, dedicated to Prajāpati, to you, O Brahmin.
And one should perform the loosening of the Brahma-knot with the Sumitri mantra:
"Oṃ, may the waters and plants be friendly to us. (41)
Having wiped the head of the sacrificer with water purified by the two strainers (pavitra), he should then cast the two strainers into the fire.
Uttering the mantra "durmitri," one should indeed overturn the *praṇītā* vessel;
then, having lifted it outside toward the northeast and poured clarified butter (*ājya*) into it, [one should discard it]. //43//
And one should offer oblations with the hand itself, reciting the mantra again and again:
"Oṃ, O you who know the path of the gods, having found the path, come to the path. (44)
"O Lord of the Mind, this sacrifice for the gods; Svāhā! O Vāta, place it; Svāhā!
Then, having uttered the location, the time, and the officiating priests [he should offer]. 45.

They should perform the fire-oblation (homa) in their respective fire-pits, concluding with the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti). The patron (yajamāna), together with his wife, should touch the right shoulder of the preceptor (guru).
Having placed betel leaves, areca nuts, unbroken grains, ghee, and bilva fruits into the *sruva* ladle, one should offer them with the respective mantras. ||47||
Oṃ! From the ocean a wave, rich in sweetness, has arisen; through the Upāṃśu [graha], it has attained immortality.
That which is the secret name of clarified butter is the tongue of the gods, the navel of immortality. 48.
Let us proclaim our names at this sacrifice; may you sustain me with a stream of clarified butter through our salutations.
May the Brahman hear the hymn being recited; the four-horned bull has bellowed this. 49.
The gods discovered the threefold clarified butter hidden by the Paṇis within the cow:
Indra alone produced one part, Sūrya produced another, and from Vena they fashioned the third by their own inherent power.
These flow from the ocean within the heart; they were not seen by the enemy who possesses a hundredfold thunderbolt. I behold the streams of clarified butter;
in their midst stands the golden reed.
The streams flow rightly, like milch-cows, being purified within the heart by the mind;
these waves of clarified butter surge forth like wild beasts fleeing from a swift arrow.
Like swift birds on the path of the ocean, the mighty streams fly forth, overtaking the wind;
the streams of clarified butter, swelling with their waves, break through the barriers like a ruddy stallion. 53.
The auspicious women, with their youth fully matured, smiling as they approached Agni; he,
rejoicing, [received] the streams of clarified butter like continuous fuel-sticks.
Jātavedas desires it. ||54||
Like a maiden choosing her bridegroom, I gaze upon your anointed form as you are being anointed;
where the Soma is pressed, where the sacrifice is performed, there the streams of clarified butter flow around it. 55.
Flow toward our excellent praise in the race for cattle; bestow auspicious riches upon us!
Lead this sacrifice of ours to the gods; the streams of clarified butter flow sweetly. 56.
Oṃ, I offer consciousness with mind and clarified butter, so that the gods, who increase the cosmic order through the Vīna-homa, may come hither;
I offer it for the Lord of the entire world.
To Viśvakarman, who is invincible for all time, [be] the oblation. ||57||
Seven are your fuel-sticks, O Agni, seven your tongues, seven the Ṛṣis, and seven your beloved abodes;
seven hotṛ-priests worship you in seven ways.
Fill the seven wombs with clarified butter; svāhā! ||58||
May the Ādityas, Rudras, and Vasus kindle you again; may the Brahmins, O leader of wealth, [kindle you] again with sacrifices.
Expanding yourself with clarified butter, cause the desires of the sacrificer to become true. (59)
Thou art the purifier of wealth, with a hundred streams; thou art the purifier of wealth, with a thousand streams.
May the god Savitṛ purify thee with the purifier of wealth.
With the hundred-streamed [soma] as the milking-stone, he milked the cow of plenty.
O full ladle, fly away; well-filled, fly back again!
Like two merchants bargaining over goods, let us exchange food and strength, O Śatakratu! Svāhā!
This salutation is to Agni Vaiśvānara, to the Vasus, Rudras, and Ādityas,
to Śatakratu, and to the Waters;
this [salutation] is to the three Lords, the divine incarnations.
To the Supreme Brahman from the Śaktis, Svāhā! Adoration! ||62||
Thus one should perform the *pūrṇāhuti* and offer what remains in the *sruva* ladle;
thereafter, one should perform the rite of bestowing the triple life-span (*tryāyuṣa*) through ritual placement (*nyāsa*).
On the forehead, [place] "The triple life-span of Jamadagni; Om, salutations, salutations.
On the neck, [place] "And the triple life-span of Kaśyapa; Om, salutations, salutations. (64)
That which is the triple life-span among the gods, [is located] at the base of the arms; salutations again and again!
May that triple life-span be ours; thus, salutations to you, Kṛṣṇa, in the heart. (65)
Having thus offered the *pūrṇāhuti*, one should present the sacrificial offering (*bali*) to Īśāna,
and one should sprinkle the water from the *śāntighaṭa* upon the patron.
Together with his family, [he should perform the rite] with Vedic mantras, using *kuśa* grass, *dūrvā* grass, and mango sprouts:
"Oṃ, you waters are indeed the source of our happiness; grant us strength. (67)
For the great battle to behold, for the peace of the sacrificer—may you cause us here to partake of that most auspicious sap of yours. 68.
Like longing mothers, for the prosperity of the sacrificer—unto him whose abode you quicken, we come gladly unto you. (69)
O Waters, bring us forth for the satisfaction of the sacrificer;
may they be for our health, for our abundance of essence, and for our long life. 2.159.70

O Bhaga, bringer of fortune, O Bhaga whose gifts are true, O Bhaga, lift up our inspired wisdom for us! O Bhaga, bringer of fortune, cause us to be born with cattle and horses; O Bhaga, may we be possessed of heroes through those who bring good fortune.
O Waters, carry away this defilement and whatever impurity there is; whatever malice, falsehood, or treacherous oath I have uttered. (72)
May the Waters and Pavamāna release me from that sin. Om! May the divine beings purify me; may they purify my thoughts with the mind. ||73||
May all beings purify themselves; O Jātavedas, purify me!
Increase, O Soma, and let virile power come to me from every side. (74)
Be present at the gathering of strength for the sacrificer;
bring forth your grace for great prosperity and for the increase of his descendants, including his great-grandsons.
Oṃ! May there be milk on the earth, milk in the plants, milk in the sky, and milk in the atmosphere;
may the quarters of space be full of milk for me. May milk be present in my house, not in the forest. 76.
Oṃ! At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins and the hands of Pūṣan,
I place you— the fourth of Sarasvatī’s speech— into the three worlds.
O Bṛhaspati, I consecrate you with sovereign power. ||77||
Oṃ! At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, with the fourth vessel of Sarasvatī’s speech, I consecrate you, O Agni, with sovereign power. 78.

Oṃ. At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins and the hands of Pūṣan, I sprinkle you with the healing medicine of the Aśvins for the sake of splendor and the luster of sacred knowledge. 79.
With the healing power of Sarasvatī, I consecrate you for vigor and the enjoyment of food;
with the sensory power of Indra, I consecrate you for strength, prosperity, and glory. 2.159.80.
It is made of *pālāśa* wood; with it he consecrates him for the sake of the Brahman.
The *pālāśa* is indeed the Brahman; thus, by means of the Brahman, he consecrates him. 8.1.
The Sāman is indeed the essence of all the Vedas;
he thus consecrates him with the essence of all the Vedas.
When he offers the *devakalpa* oblations, the *kalpas* are indeed the vital breaths (*prāṇas*).
The vital breaths are indeed immortality; he thus consecrates him with immortality itself. ||82||
For long life, for strength, for splendor, for good offspring, and for power— live, moreover, for a hundred autumns!
May the sky be peace, may the atmosphere be peace, may the earth be peace.
Peace is the waters; peace is the herbs; peace is [all]. ||83||
The trees are peace; the Viśvedevas are peace; Brahman is peace.
All is peace; peace indeed is peace.
May that peace be mine; the Supreme Brahman is peace, O images.
Peace is dear to Brahman; peace alone is peace. ||84||
The Supreme Brahman is the imperishable Brahman; Goloka is Kṛṣṇa and Rādhikā;
this is Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa, as well as the creation consisting of the gods and so forth. (85)
May the creation of living beings, the powers, the goddesses, the truths, and the virtuous ones consecrate you; may they also grant well-being and peace. 86.
Then the sacrificer should indeed give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the preceptor:
a village, a herd of cattle, land, or vehicles such as elephants and horses.
I give you male and female servants, canopies and the like, vehicles, garments, ornaments, gold, silver, and so forth, as the sacrificial fees at the conclusion of the sacrifice.
O Brahmin, with water containing cow-tail hair, tulasī, sesame seeds, and a pair of kuśa blades, one should pray: "O Sacrifice, may you be the bestower of eternal heaven. (89)
Today my wealth, my birth, and all my prosperity have become fruitful;
I have given according to my ability—be pleased, O bestower of merit!
Whatever has been done by me, whether through knowledge or through ignorance, if it was deficient in any way—may all that become complete through your grace; please forgive me.
And the teacher should say with devotion, desiring the Supreme Person:
"May what was deficient attain completeness; may everything bestow its full fruit. (92)
May all that which was deficient in substance, deficient in action, deficient in ritual procedure, or born of negligence—may all that become complete through the grace of Śrī Hari unto you. 9.3.
Oṃ! May Indra of far-reaching fame grant us well-being; may Pūṣan, the knower of all, grant us well-being;
may Tārkṣya with his unbroken wheel grant us well-being; may Bṛhaspati bestow well-being upon us. 94.
Oṃ Śrīḥ! May splendor, longevity, and health be bestowed; may he who shines forth be honored.
May there be grain, wealth, cattle, the gain of many sons, and a long life of a hundred years. || 95 ||
May the Ādityas, the Rudras, and the Vasus kindle you again;
may the Brahmins, O leader of wealth, [kindle you] again with sacrifices.
Increase your body with clarified butter; may [your words] be true.
May the desires of the sacrificer be fulfilled. || 96 ||
May the meanings of the mantras be fruitful; may your desires be fulfilled. May there be the destruction of the intellects of your enemies, and may there be the prosperity of your friends. (97)
One should also ask the gods for forgiveness, saying, "May they always be gracious," and having fully worshipped the fire, one should dismiss it while offering words of apology. (98)
"Go, O Blessed One, first to your own place from the center of the sacrificial pit;
taking the oblation, quickly give it to the gods and be gracious to me. (99)
Go, go, O best of gods, to your own abode, O Supreme Lord;
O Consumer of Oblations, go to where Brahmā and the other gods are.
May all the hosts of gods depart, taking my offering, for the sake of fulfilling their desired wishes and for the purpose of returning again. (101)
In all installations, one should offer unbroken grains and a handful of beautiful flowers;
this alone constitutes the consecration festival, even if it lacks faith, ritual materials, and the like.
Through the grace of Brahmā and Viṣṇu, may my ritual be most perfect;
through those Brāhmaṇas, may the entire sacrifice be complete in every way.
They should speak without interruption and receive more from that;
they should also take food and speak again thereafter. (104)
I bow to Lord Hari, by whose remembrance and utterance of His name any deficiency in austerity, worship, ritual acts, and so forth, immediately attains completeness.
Whatever ritual act may fail among the sacrificial rites due to negligence, let that indeed become complete through the remembrance of Śrī Hari; so may it be.
Salutations to Him whose essence is sacrifice, who is offered oblations with four, and again with four, with two, with five, and once more with two.
Having provided a great feast and bestowed great gifts,
and having performed a supreme, grand festival, the patron then partook of the meal.
Having fed everyone, he should then present gifts;
he should also perform the purificatory bath (avabhṛtha) in a river, the ocean, or a lake.
Then all the gods arrive at the sacred fords for the avabhṛtha bath;
thereafter, the avabhṛtha rite is performed for the sake of destroying all evil deeds.
Thus, O Rādhikā, this procedure for installation has been told to you,
just as it was spoken by the Blessed One for the sake of a divine sanctuary.

Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-ninth chapter, titled "The Installation of the Deity upon the Lion Throne in the Piṇḍikā, the Prāṇapratiṣṭhā Nyāsas, the Invocation of the Life-force (Jīvāvāhana), the Ārārtika, the Homa, the Offering of the Pūrṇāhuti, the Benedictions, Peace-chants, and the Recitation of Auspiciousness; the Farewell of the Deities, and the Final Bath of Completion," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Now, O Rādhikā, I shall indeed speak that which was spoken by the Supreme Soul regarding the ritual procedure for the hoisting of the banner with its golden pinnacle.
Having prepared a svastika maṇḍala on the northern side of the pavilion itself, the preceptor, together with the officiating priests, the patron, and others, [should proceed].
Having gone to that hut where the artisans had fashioned the assembly of water-pots,
he bathed the supreme pitcher with five jars.

Having installed [the deity] with the mantras beginning with "manojūtiḥ," and likewise having offered the bali-oblation to the world-protectors (lokapālas), one should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) and sprinkle [the area] with oil-based substances.
Having worshipped [the image] with sandalwood paste and other offerings, having encircled it with a triple-thread cord, and having mounted it upon the chariot,
one should lead it to the bathing pavilion while reciting propitiatory chants and other rites.

Having placed [the image] upon a seat known as the Svastika or the Bhadra, one should recite the "Puṇyāha" formula before it, while consecrating ghee with the mantra "ghṛtam ghṛta... and indeed with ghee offerings.
Having rubbed [the body] with a paste of barley, lentils, and turmeric,
and having washed it with warm water, one should smear it with clay from an anthill.
Having bathed [the image] with scented water and likewise with four jars of pure water,
one should worship it with perfumes and flowers.
Having covered [the image] with cloths, one should recite the mantras for the rite of peace (śāntipāṭha). Then, rising with the Svasti mantra, one should circumambulate the pavilion clockwise.
Having brought him in and entered through the western gate, he should seat him upon an auspicious throne in the presence of the deity, and then worship him with perfumes and other offerings.
Having filled [the vessels] with various kinds of food, both solid and soft, and having recited the Viśvataḥ-śruti mantra,
the preceptor should perform the *saṃkalīkaraṇa* rite separately in each of his own fire-pits.
Having performed one hundred and eight oblations with honey, milk, clarified butter, and curd, and having then poured the remnants into the peace-vessel (śāntikalaśa), [one should proceed].
Then, with that water, he should gradually touch the feet, the navel, the heart, and the eyes; thereafter, having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the Puruṣasūkta upon the pitcher.
Having worshipped the water-pot and offered the sacrificial oblation (bali) as well as the temple,
he then ascended it and washed his limbs with fragrant waters.
Having performed the ritual placements (nyāsa) accompanied by the sounds of musical instruments upon the roof of that palace,
and having brought the water-pot (kalaśa), he should then rest for a moment.
One should offer [the vessel] upon auspicious ground at a favorable moment with the twelve-syllable mantra:
"Oṃ, smell the jar; may the gods enter it, O Earth, and the drops. (16)

Having installed [the image] with the mantra: "Oṃ, return again with vigor; may you, the milch-cow, yield a thousandfold, flowing with broad streams of milk; may wealth enter into me again," one should wrap it with a cloth.
Having uttered "streṇa huṃ phaṭ svāhā," one should then pay homage. || 17 ||
The artisan, having firmly stabilized them, should likewise bathe the golden discus, the lotus, the trident, and the weapon with water.
Having worshipped with perfumes and flowers, descended below, and prostrated,
one should give gifts of clothing, ornaments, silver, and so forth, according to one's ability.
And one should likewise provide food and other necessities for the poor, the helpless,
and the virtuous, as well as for Brahmins, teachers, their families, chaste women, and celibate students.
Then, in the vicinity of the water-pot (kalaśa), a pillar of pride (mānastaṃbha) of extreme firmness [is to be placed];
and there, a flagstaff (dhvajastaṃbha) should also be installed according to the prescribed rite.
The pillar of honor (mānastaṃbha) is indeed considered to be made of the essence of wood, born of the essence of stone, or even of iron; it is richly adorned with śiṃśapā wood and copper plates. 22.
The staff, the pitcher, and the banner should be made circular, horn-shaped, long, or larger as appropriate, according to the measurements of the craft.
In the three hundred and ninth chapter, their measurement was described;
here, however, only their worship and the declaration of their fruits are intended.
In this worship, the mantras for the banners of the pavilion should be understood;
both the worship and the fire-oblation are intended to be performed according to the procedure pertaining to that [pavilion]. (25)
The banner is indeed the emblem of the Supreme Lord and a sign common to all deities;
upon seeing it, even wicked beings come to abide by his command. (26)
For the virtuous there shall be a disposition of devotion, and likewise fear for the asuras;
moreover, a temple devoid of a banner must never be constructed anywhere on earth.
For ten thousand years, the donor is glorified in heaven;
by the weapon of shaking the banner, the donor’s sin is destroyed. (28)
In whatever village, city, kingdom, or realm this banner stands, there is no untimely death, nor is there misfortune, even among those who commit evil deeds. (29)
There, there is no fear of calamities, nor diseases, nor afflictions;
there are no adversities there, but rather abundance of food and a bountiful harvest of crops.
The rain-clouds pour forth at their proper time, the milk-yielding cows abound with milk, and those who offer salutations to the banner become possessed of merit. (3.1)
The sight of the banner, as well as that of the pitcher and the pinnacle, is entirely auspicious and bestows merit. (32)

The pacification of the sins of sinners occurs through the sight of the flag and other such items; indeed, this happens in relation to the temple, the image, the altar, the sacrificial pit, the flag, and the water-pot. (33)
For as many thousands of years as there are atoms [in those realms],
they indeed rejoice in the eternal heaven and in liberation.
"The sacrificer and all others [attain their goals] through the grace of the God; therefore, I shall describe the installation of the mobile image in brief, as it is. (35)
Having constructed a pavilion and a sacrificial pit along with an altar in a pure place,
one should then bring the image into the pavilion on the day of the consecration ceremony.
Having seated himself on a seat, restrained his breath, and marked the day,
he should then perform the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) for the sake of the consecration and worship Gaṇeśa.
One should likewise have the Puṇyāhavācana and the worship of the Mātṛkās performed;
then, having performed the Nāndīśrāddha and having chosen the preceptor (guru) and the officiating priests (ṛtvij),
one should honor four of them, and the preceptor should perform the installation of the pavilion (maṇḍapa).
The installation of the fire, the worship of the site, and the sacrifice to the planets. ||3||
Then, one should invoke Brahmā and the other deities in the Sarvatobhadra [mandala]; one should worship them, establish them, and then offer a sacrificial oblation (caru) made of wild rice (naivāra).
Having cooked the oblations and performed the *grahahoma* at the conclusion of the *ājyabhāga* offerings,
one should offer one hundred and eight fuel-sticks (*samidh*) each, made of *pālāśa* wood and other suitable varieties.

Alternatively, one should offer oblations for each respective deity using the mantras of the world-protectors (lokapālas) and so forth, or one may perform the clarified butter (ājya) oblation with the vyāhṛtis. ||42||
Having offered ten oblations each of fuel-sticks, sesame seeds, and clarified butter to the installed deities, as well as one hundred and eight oblations to Sviṣṭakṛt; ||43||
One should offer oblations with the mantras of the principal deities and bow to the Lord;
one should say, "Welcome, O Lord of all gods! We have indeed made you welcome here. (44)
Having raised [the image] with the *sumantra* mantras saying "Arise!", and having placed it upon the altar,
one should bathe it with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and the five nectars (*amṛta*) while reciting the mantras.

Having performed the anointing with ghee, the rubbing with unguents, and so forth, as well as the ceremonial bathing with jars and the like, and having seated him upon the pedestal on all sides, [one should proceed]. ||46||
Having placed water-jars and having scattered fragrant flowers and unbroken grains of rice,
one should place seven types of earth in the first jar and auspicious sprouts in the others.
In the third [vessel] are the seven grains and kusha grass;
in the fourth, water for pacification; in the fifth, the five jewels and fruits.
One should throw flowers into water flowing down a slope on the sixth day, and likewise barley grains;
on the seventh day one should throw [them], and on the eighth day indeed, water from a confluence.
Having carefully placed all the medicinal herbs there, he should do so with the mantras beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā," as well as with the "hiraṇyavarṇā" mantras and the "pavamāna" hymns.

Having bathed [the image] and offered two garments and a sacred thread, one should worship it with perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, and lamps made of flour, performing the lustration ceremony (nīrājana). ||51||
Having placed honey and clarified butter in a golden vessel, one should then draw lines on the right and left eyes with a golden probe while reciting the mantras.
Oṃ, the wondrous array of the gods has risen—the eye of Mitra, Varuṇa, and Agni.
Oṃ, you are splendor; you are radiance; you are immortality; you are the name of the abodes.
You are the beloved, unassailable place of sacrifice for the gods. 53.
One should anoint the image with the mantra "añjanti tvāmadhvaram";
furthermore, one may also anoint it with honey, ghee, and sugar.
One should apply collyrium with the mantra "devasya tvā savituḥ" and show him various kinds of food, both solid and soft, as well as mirrors; however, he should not gaze at them. ||55||
Having given the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the twice-born and others, he should offer praise;
then, having placed food endowed with five colors into a bamboo vessel over a fire, [he should proceed].
One should perform the lustration ceremony for the deity with food at a crossroads for Rudra, saying:
"Oṃ, obeisance to Rudra, svāhā; may the rite indeed be auspicious. (57)

Having offered the bali-oblation upon an aśvattha leaf with the words "Salutation to the beings," and having sipped water (ācamana), one should worship the deities of the mandala within the central mandala.
Having said, "May you be firmly established," and having seated the deity, one should worship him;
one should offer ten oblations of sesame and clarified butter into the sacrificial pit while reciting the names of the deities.
Having offered a handful of flowers and bowed from the north of the mandala,
one should prepare a bed upon a swastika-patterned couch and rise with these mantras.
Having sat upon the bed while reciting the Sahasra-sūkta,
one should perform the ritual depositions (nyāsa), saying "Salutation to the Self of Puruṣa" at the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra).

Salutation to the self of vital breath in the mouth; salutation to the one whose form is primordial nature (prakṛti) in the throat; salutation to the principle of intellect (buddhi-tattva) in the heart; salutation to the ego-principle (ahaṃkāra) in the belly. ||62||

Salutation to the principle of mind (manas-tattva) and the secret place (gupta), and to the principle of consciousness (citta) at the feet; salutation to the principle of taste (rasa-tattva) at the bladder and to the principle of smell (gandha-tattva) at the nose.
To the principle of sound, indeed, in the ears; to the principle of touch, in the body;
to the principle of form, in the eyes; and to the principle of taste, in the tongue. (64)
Salutation to the principle of speech in the mouth; salutation to the principle of the hands in the two hands;
salutation to the principle of the feet in the feet; salutation to the principle of the anus in the anus.
Having offered salutation to the Earth, one should say "Salutation" to the Upastha;
to the Water element at the genitals, and to the Fire element at the heart. (66)
Salutations again and again to the wind-principle in the sense of smell, to the space-principle in the ether, to the quality-principle in the physical form, and to the instruments of perception.
Having performed the ritual assignments (nyāsa) with the Pauruṣa Sūkta, he should then say,
"May you sleep in comfort," and thus cause the Lord to lie down upon the bed.

Having performed worship, one should perform the consecration (adhivāsa) and offer oblations to the deity; there, one should offer all kinds of food to Brahmā, ghee-rice to Indra, and water to the wielder of the thunderbolt (Vajrin).
One should offer food with clarified butter to Agni and food made of mung beans to Yama;
one should present food of black rice together with ghee to Nirṛti.
To Varuṇa, rice cooked with fresh butter; to Vāyu, barley-rice;
to Kubera, food made of priyaṅgu seeds; and to Īśāna, milk-rice (pāyasa). ||71||
One should offer milk-rice (pāyasa) to all, as well as an oblation of wild rice (naivāra-caru);
having set it forth, one should present the bali-offering to the deities of the maṇḍala.

Then he should pass the night; having risen in the morning, he should cook the sacrificial porridge (caru) with the root mantras, and after sprinkling it with ghee, [recite] one hundred and eight [times].
Having indeed offered oblations with the root mantra, as well as by the names of the deities:
"Svāhā to Agni, to Soma, and to the one whose form is Dhanvantari. (74)
Svāhā to Kuhū and to Anumati; svāhā to the Lord of Creatures (Prajāpati); svāhā to Agni, who is the Supreme Being (Parameṣṭhin) in essence;
svāhā to Soma; svāhā to Agni; svāhā to Food (Anna) and to Agni.
Svāhā to Agni, the lord of food; and svāhā to Prajāpati. ||76||
Svāhā to the Viśvedevas, and svāhā to all beings!
Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ, svāhā to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt; obeisance. ||77||
At sunrise, having placed the Guru upon the altar facing the Deity,
[he should offer] gems, flowers, and so forth, as well as roots, fruits, and medicinal herbs.
Having displayed it and taken the water of peace in a copper vessel,
one should consecrate it ten times with the mantra of the principal deity.
Having consecrated the deity upon the head, one should cause him to rise with the words "Oṃ, arise!
One should then recite the mantra beginning with "viśvataścakṣuḥ" and bow down again and again.
Salutations again and again to Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa; salutations to the guardians of the quarters;
salutations to the Vasus, and salutations again and again to the Rudras and Ādityas. ||81||
Salutations again and again to the Aśvins, to the Maruts, and to Kubera;
salutations to the great rivers, to Agni and Soma, and to Heaven and Earth. ||82||
Salutations to Indra and Agni, to Dhanvantari, and to the Lord of All;
salutations to Brahmā, to the Viśvedevas, and to the Supreme Brahman. ||82||
Having thus recited the mantra and consecrated the patron, one should meditate upon the deity;
then, having offered a handful of flowers to the established deity— ||84||
Having installed the deity within the image with the Puruṣasūkta, the Gāyatrī, the Vyāhṛtis, and other mantras, thereafter—
One should perform the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* (the ritual installation of life-force), O Rādhikā; listen to it as follows:
for this mantra known as *prāṇapratiṣṭhā*, there are three sages (*ṛṣis*). (86)
The deities are the three Vedas and the meters; likewise, the body consists of ritual action and the self.
The deity is named Prāṇa, the seed-syllable is "Āṃ," and the application of power is "Krauṃ. ||87||
Likewise, in the rite of Prāṇapratiṣṭhā: "Salutation to the sages on the head;
salutation to the meters in the mouth; and salutation to the deity in the heart. (88)
Oṃ, salutation to the seed-syllable Āṃ at the secret place; Krauṃ, salutation to Śakti at the feet.
Oṃ Kaṃ Khaṃ Gaṃ Ghaṃ Ṅaṃ Āṃ, salutation to the heart for the five elements, Āṃ. ||89||
Oṃ caṃ chaṃ jaṃ jhaṃ ñaṃ īṃ, obeisance to the subtle elements (tanmātras); īṃ ca ke svāhā.
Oṃ ṭaṃ ṭhaṃ ḍaṃ ḍhaṃ ṇaṃ oṃ, obeisance to those who produce knowledge; oṃ śikhāyai vauṣaṭ. ||2.160.90||
Oṃ taṃ thaṃ daṃ dhaṃ naṃ eṃ, obeisance to the performers of action; eṃ, to the armor, hūṃ!
Oṃ paṃ phaṃ baṃ bhaṃ maṃ auṃ, obeisance to the actions; auṃ, to the three eyes, vauṣaṭ! 9.1.
Oṃ yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ haṃ laṃ kṣaṃ oṃ. Oṃ, salutations to those within; Aḥ, to the weapon, phaṭ! Having thus performed the ritual placements (nyāsa) upon oneself and the deity,
Having touched the deity, one should then recite the mantra. ||92||
Oṃ āṃ hrīṃ krauṃ yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ haṃ saḥ | The vital breaths (*prāṇāḥ*) of the deity are here as its vital breaths. Oṃ āṃ hrīṃ krauṃ yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ śaṃ ṣaṃ haṃ saḥ.
The life-force of the god remains here. ||93||
Oṃ āṃ hrīṃ krauṃ yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ haṃ saḥ!
May all the sense organs of the deity [be established here].
Oṃ āṃ hrīṃ krauṃ yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ haṃ saḥ! May the internal faculties and the vital breaths of the deity abide here. (94)
"Having come here for well-being, may he indeed remain for a long time, Svāhā!
Having touched the heart [of the image] with the thumb, one should recite [the mantra] over the image as prescribed. || 96 ||
May her vital breaths be firmly established; may her vital breaths move within her.
May no one whatsoever cause harm to this deity-like image. (96)
Having restrained [the breath] with the *praṇava* and meditated upon it as being endowed with life,
one should mutter the verse "Oṃ dhruvā dyauḥ" and the *gāyatrī* mantra into the ear.
Having touched [the deity's] feet, navel, and head with the Puruṣasūkta hymns, [one says]:
"Welcome, O Supreme Lord; we perform [this rite]; remain firm for a long time. (98)
O Lord of Gods, as long as the moon, the earth, and the sun remain unimpeded, so long should you remain here out of compassion for your devotees. (99)
Having worshipped with the Pauruṣa Sūkta and the sixteen Upasvastu offerings, he should release the bracelet and the ornaments and weapons from the image.
Having meditated upon the vehicle and the retinue, and having displayed the mudrā, one should worship with the root mantra and recite it one hundred and eight times. || 10.1 ||

Having offered praise and prostrated, and having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), he should complete the rite ending with the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering and the final full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), and then bestow the gift of a cow as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
Having performed the Ārātrika festival and the meal at the conclusion of the food offering,
and having caused the people to eat, he himself should conclude the ritual.
"In this way, one should indeed cause a movable installation to be performed for a movable image during the month of Mādhava.
Thus spoke the Blessed One concerning the body of a temple.
The procedure for the restoration of a temple whose paint and other features have decayed is considered to be as follows in brief:
it should be auspicious, with its entrance facing west and its vestibule to the south.
Then, having constructed a pavilion with a single archway in the center,
one should prepare a circular or square altar on the western side.
To the north, there should be the site-altar (vāstupīṭha) as well as a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) made of sand;
having proclaimed the place and the time, this is for the purification of defects arising from decay.
One should reflect, "I shall perform the rite for the purpose of extraction.
Then follows the worship of Gaṇeśa, the recitation of the benediction (svastivācana), and the worship of the Mothers (mātṛkā).
Then, having performed the Nāndī-śrāddha, having chosen and honored the preceptor, and thereafter the consecration of the pavilion as well as the worship of Vāstu; || 109 ||
Having assigned the gods to the Sarvatobhadra [mandala], one should then worship that seat upon the pedestal: "Come, O God of Gods! Salutations to you, Vyāpakeśvara! (2.160.110)
Hṛdayāya namaḥ svāhā; śirase śikhāyai vaṣaṭ;
kavacāya huṃ; astrāya phaṭ to the all-pervading wielder of the Śārṅga bow. || 111 ||
One should worship with the root mantra and recite it one hundred and eight times;
having established the fire and performed the oblations up to the portion of clarified butter (ājyabhāga), one should present the bali offering.
Having worshipped the worn-out deity with the *praṇava*, one should then pray:
"O God of gods, you who are worn out, broken, whose skin is decayed, and whose form is decrepit."
I shall extract the decayed limb here; please be patient and have mercy.
You may go to your approved place, whether it be at the side of the image or within the syllable.
After the restoration of the dilapidated [shrine], proceed indeed toward the arrival [of the deity];
perform the waving of lamps (ārātrika), the meal offering, worship, and the offering of water for drinking.
Having led everything away and carried it elsewhere to another place out of compassion,
O Viṣṇu, go now to your own desired abode, accompanied by all the gods.
Having spoken thus, one should offer [the image] while forming a *añjali* with flowers and unbroken grains (*akṣata*);
then, having again performed the installation of life-force (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*) and other rites, one should worship it.
One should feed Brāhmaṇas and others during rites for the restoration of what is dilapidated;
such a person who increases the prosperity of a temple attains both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Thus, O Rādhikā, has Hari, the beginningless Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, been described by me to you as having a body like that of a temple deity. Thus have I spoken to you. 1.19.
From hearing this, from reciting it, and from the construction of a temple,
one shall obtain the fruit of the Uddhāra sacrifice as well as the fruit of consecration.

Thus ends the one hundred and sixtieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Ascension of the Vessel, the Erection of the Staff of Pride, the Ritual for the Installation of the Mobile Form, the Restoration of the Decayed, and Other Matters," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Rādhikā, that divine devotee, the sage Devāyatanaka, having heard this and being filled with wonder, worshipped Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. || 1 ||
Having performed the supreme *ārārtrika* rite, he was immersed in love and attained great perfection;
then, by the will of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa himself, [he became so]. || 2 ||
He became a divine palace, endowed with a thousand pitchers,
possessed of all auspicious marks, and complete in every limb.
He is endowed with all forms of service, even when manifest in bodily form;
yet he also exists apart from that, even while assuming a liberated state.
That palace became renowned and was worshipped by the gods and others;
seeing it, Indra set his mind upon constructing one equal to it.
Having summoned Viśvakarman, he showed him that creation and then gave him the command to build a magnificent palace in Amarāvatī.
Having thoroughly practiced [his art] upon the ground where the letters were formed of saffron, Viśvakarman then went to heaven and fashioned the peak with its thousand pitchers.
He installed the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the glorious Puruṣottama,
together with his six wives amidst great festivities.
Then, indeed, palaces were constructed throughout all the worlds;
in them, there exists everywhere the divine Adhyātmika Devāyana.
In this way, humans, gods residing in the netherworld (pātāla), and inhabitants of Satyaloka come to behold that divine temple. (2.161.10)
Having beheld the Kuṃkumavāpikā sacred field adorned with temples,
men and women rejoice and rest in great happiness.
Having heard that the temple was beautiful to behold, people from the community of Kapardin came from as far as the ocean, eager to see it.
Even the fisherman Dhanamitra, situated on the shore of the western ocean,
heard [the news] and, accompanied by his family, went out from his house to see [him].
Having seen the auspicious Vastrāpatha on the road, he went to the goddess Turī, who was stationed there in embodied form, beautiful and situated amidst a cluster of tree-shadows. 14.
She was seated upon a palace on the bank of the Jīvantikā river,
situated in the midst of a mango grove, attended by wood-gatherers and others.
Having beheld that beloved of Hari, who bestows refuge upon forest-dwellers, who grants peace, who dwells in the forest, and who stands upon the back of an elephant with four arms; 16.
Having approached her— who was a partial incarnation of Lakṣmī, abundant in goodness (sattva), and worshipped with fruits, flowers, and other offerings—
he stood near her, bowing with great devotion and an abundance of wealth.
He bathed in the river and in the lake at the foot of a mango tree on the ground,
and thereafter he set down all his travel requisites.
Having taken cool water, campaka flowers, and the finest ripe fruits of immortality along with tulasī; || 19 ||
He went indeed to the temple to worship the goddess named Turī Lakṣmī;
together with his family, he prostrated himself in the presence of that deity.
He offered a hymn of praise according to the prescribed rites for the protection of the forest-dwellers,
and worshipped with supreme devotion using fruits, flowers, water, and other offerings.
"O Mother! O Mother Mahālakṣmī, O great chaste lady!
That which was given by me in the forest has been taken home today; salutations be to you! (22)
Be gracious for the sake of our journey and burn away my impurity;
O beloved of Hari, you are the purifier of fishermen—lift me up! 23.
"I do not know how to perform worship, for I am low-born and indeed impure;
yet, considering my heart to be offered pure, please accept this nectar. (24)
Grant me wisdom and likewise devotion; grant me liberation worthy of me, and bestow upon me, together with my retinue, that which is most auspicious.
Having spoken thus and bowing repeatedly, he swept the temple;
having removed the dry leaves and having cleared away the dust and other debris.
He washed the temple and likewise the woolen cloth with water;
he bathed [the deity] with waters and performed a circumambulation. ||27||
Taking many fresh leaves and flowers,
she fashioned an archway and a garland, and offered them as an act of worship.
Having observed that very place to be a peaceful refuge, he stayed there for the night;
and seeing forest-grown food such as fruits, he remained there during the following day as well.
On the third day as well, he remained there and obtained great rest;
every daily task and the excellent worship for the Goddess were performed just as if in his own home.
In the forest, he performs purification, service, and so forth with devotion;
for at night, his family members indeed perform their worship aloud.
Having kindled the fire to dispel the cold,
they gathered together in the temple of that goddess and took hold of it as well.
Thus, O Rādhikā, having passed the night,
on the following day she took various kinds of flowers and garments.
Having prepared only flowers, they offer them to Lakṣmī:
a crown, blossoms for the ears, ear-ornaments, and a beautiful bodice.
Having fashioned a skirt, a girdle, a garland, a cluster of flowers, a waist-belt, as well as sandals and a small bell, they offer them [to him]. (35)
Having brought fragrant, sweet, and delicious honey well-situated upon trees, they offer it to the Goddess, along with many other flavorful foods. ||36||
Having gathered the auspicious wood of sandal from within the forest, they prepare incense rich in fragrance and serve it with devotion. (37)
"O Śrī Hari Kṛṣṇa, O Mother Lakṣmī, obeisances unto you!
Thus they constantly perform [their worship] in the midst of the forest, within the house of the flute.
Lakṣmī, who is of the nature of the fourth state (turya), though invisible, accepted his worship; being virtuous, she became gracious through the service rendered according to her own nature.
Although she remained in her physical form, she took up the nectar, honey, and fruits;
she drank the cool water and wore those garlands.
He took up the flower-garments and accepted the incense with devotion;
he received all the service performed by the devotees in the forest as it reached his very form.
Thus, even though he was a fisherman with a large family and great wealth, he obtained security and prosperity in the forest by virtue of his journey to the sacred fords. ||42||
With a stainless inner heart, he dwelt joyfully for fifteen days in that temple within the forest, near Turyā.
Through the perfection of daily worship and other rites, he acquired abundant merit;
by the grace of the goddess Lakṣmī, he attained purity in many ways.
On the night of the full moon of the bright fortnight of Pauṣa, when the moon was positioned at the head [of the zodiac],
he performed a recitation accompanied by a mṛdaṅga drum along with his family members.
In that spotless and tranquil royal assembly hall, which was adorned with forest trees and other features, and filled with a cool luster like a bed of nectar, during the portion of the night; 46.
He sang a song together with his wife, daughters, and sons;
hearing that sweet melody directly, Turī herself became manifest before him.
Richly adorned with the beauty of form, her limbs and members were exceedingly beautiful;
she was virtuous, with a serene countenance, holding a lotus in her hand. (48)
Adorned with jewels and gold ornaments, wearing divine garments and the like, she is radiant with a beauty that surpasses the luster of ten million full moons of autumn. 49.
Seated upon the back of the white elephant, that enchanting lady said to him, "Receive a boon here; I am pleased with you."
O devotee, you have made your dwelling here in my forest grove; you have performed service in many ways, as if it were your own home. (51)
Choose a boon—blessings be upon you—speak as you desire and I shall grant it;
even for the single act of sweeping my house here, [I shall fulfill your wish]. (52)
Poverty shall perish and one shall attain the divine heaven, by lighting a lamp even once in my abode for a long duration. (53)
The fruit of offering Tulasī to my head even once shall be the attainment of the worlds of the Sun for a thousand yugas. (54)
I grant him the status of a universal monarch (cakravartin) along with lasting prosperity;
by offering garlands of flowers and the like, I bestow upon him golden ornaments.
By offering fruits even once,
I indeed bestow the eternal nectar, heaven, and the resplendent station of Indra.
By offering water even once, I grant the realm of Varuṇa;
by the surrender of oneself, I grant one's entire being and the eternal abode.
The Blessed Lord Śrī Narāyaṇa, who is manifest and beginningless, is my master;
I bestow upon this high-souled devotee of mine the prosperity that belongs to Him.
I accept what is offered to me and then offer it to my Lord;
being devoted to His service, I always consume that which is His grace.
The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the glorious Puruṣottama, the opulent and gracious Lord, becomes manifest through my service. 2.161.60.
Just as I am dear to him, and as Māṇikī is dear to him, so too is my devotee dear to me; the husband gives abundantly to him.
"O Dhanamjaya, you are pure because I am pleased with you;
choose whatever is in your mind, for I shall grant it according to your husband's desire. (62)
Thus addressed by Rādhikā, Dhanamjaya, within a moment, attained supreme wonder, experienced bliss, and reached the highest joy. (63)
Before his mother, he chose servitude for one joined with a family;
he did not desire wealth, nor kingdom, nor sovereign power. (64)
You are blessed, O Dhanamada; you shall have everything at your disposal.
Yet, in this world, such sincere service toward one's master is difficult to find. (65)
Indeed, throughout millions of cycles of existence, servants long for the state of servitude;
for countless slaves to their own self-interest exist within the three worlds. (66)
Those who grant the heart’s desire are indeed rare; therefore, become for me here one who grants the heart’s desire.
For in the state of granting the heart’s desire, the perfections and sovereign powers always abide.
In servitude to the false, those who steal away one's passion remain as mere afflictions;
therefore, in this matter, one must surely practice a service that delights the heart.
Just as I, the lotus-born, am here the servant of Nārāyaṇa,
so too is the virtuous Pārvatī here the servant of Śiva.
Sūryadāsī and Prabhā are the maidservants of Hari, as is Padmāvatī;
and just as Māṇikī is a maidservant, so too is Rādhā, the victorious maidservant of Hari.
And just as Mañjulā, Haṃsā, and Suguṇā are the maidservants of Hari; and Lalitā, Akṣarabrahma, and Garuḍa are likewise His servants. (71)
Therefore, O Lord, perform service in such a way that the monkey Hanumān may become your servant, as well as Hemantaka and Vasanta. (72)
"In every kalpa, these indeed become the servants of Hari;
therefore, obtain service unto me and my husband, Śrī Puruṣottama. (73)
The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the son of Śrī Kaṃbhārā, exists there in human form wherever you go. (74)
In the field of Kuṅkumavāpikā, in the vicinity of Lomaśa’s hermitage, within the temple mansion, the Lord of Śrī shines resplendent there. (75)
There, even millions of lotuses like me shine forth, filled with bliss through service to this one who possesses all heroic power. (76)
O devotee, serve that beautiful and auspicious field named Kuṅkumavāpikā; all the abundance of fruits of your service shall be granted to you. 77.
"Take these forest flowers and various fruits;
offer them there to my husband and speak words of salutation on my behalf. (78)
By his command, I abide here on the western boundary of the field in the form of Turī, while Kamalā herself is the guardian of the field (kṣetrapā). ||79||
Indeed, I shall always serve Kṛṣṇa with my invisible form;
go quickly to Mānasa, and your desire will be fulfilled there.
Having spoken thus, that Turī-lakṣmī dissolved into the image;
meanwhile, Dhanameda, intoxicated with joy, was in the dark fortnight of the month of Māgha.
Accompanied by his family, he joyfully went to the Kuṅkumavāpī lake on that day;
beholding again and again the gardens and forests, he attained great delight. (82)
Having repeatedly beheld the hermitage of Lomaśa, which has its abode in the sky, and having gazed upon those dear to Brahmā and observed the Aśvasaras lake; 83.
Having beheld many hundreds of thousands of palaces and temples of the gods,
and having seen divine sacred fords, he rejoiced at the loss of his wealth.
At every stage, he prostrated like a staff along with his family;
then, to behold Mahālaya, whose beauty was revealed by Lakṣmī, he went there. ||85||
Therein shines the Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, who is beginningless, resplendent with a crown and ornaments possessing the brilliance of ten million suns. ||86||
The Blessed One Śrī Hari, whose limbs are perfectly proportioned, is served by lotuses and other offerings; he is the manifest deity served by gods, liberated souls, and others. (87)
Some prostrated like a staff before Kṛṣṇa, while others offered lamps made of reeds;
he himself worshipped him with flowers, fruits, and heartfelt devotions. (88)
He drank the water for washing the feet and held the image in his heart;
having received hospitable treatment, including a welcome and other honors. (89)
Having obtained food, he took rest;
then, in the evening, he went to the bank of Lake Aśvasaras to perform his ritual ablutions at the holy fords.
And at night he dwelt at the foot of a banyan tree on the bank;
by the very nature of his birth, he preferred to reside upon the shore. (91)
At night he performed worship and the chanting of the names of Hari;
in the morning, by his natural disposition, he saw Rohita fish.
At that time, he set his mind on wearing those [robes] which were richly adorned with the mark of the wheel;
having gone to the bank, he cast the corded thread into the waters. (93)
Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa himself, Lord Hari, assuming the form of a fish, took a hook in his mouth and came under its control. ||94||
Through the transformation of his body, the fish attained vast proportions;
in an instant, he became Padmavat, bearing the conch, the discus, and the mace.
Upon beholding that magnificent form, the devotee then felt shame;
Hari said, "O fisherman, abandon your own nature and take refuge in me. (96)
Through the benedictions of Lakṣmī and by a fragment of your grace, I have attained this;
accept my service, go, and bring the sage Lomaśa.
Become a Vaiṣṇava, stay here, and likewise perform service for me,
just as you have seen my four-armed form in the shape of a fish here.
"This is my Matsya-tīrtha; possessing the form of the Fish Incarnation, I have come within the range of your vision for your sake—worship Him. (99)
Fishermen, the heirs of fish, indeed become devoted to fish;
in the form of a fish, I shall grant you liberation—worship me.
Having assumed the form of a fish here beneath the banyan tree, worship me;
this sacred site of my Fish Incarnation is the destroyer of sins.
On the shore of the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake, there shall be an auspicious place that bestows heaven and liberation;
it will especially grant lordship to the fishermen.
Having spoken thus to Rādhikā, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa vanished;
Dhanamitra then quickly went from there to the hermitage of Lomaśa.
He attained the mantra, the tulasī, the garland, and the state of being a servant of Viṣṇu:
"Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya pataye svāhā. (104)
Having thus reached the shore of the lake, he arrived together with his family;
having constructed a leaf-hut beneath a banyan tree, he dwelt there continuously.
Then, having fashioned an image of Matsya, he worshipped Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa;
and indeed, O Rādhā, in a very short time he attained eternal liberation.
Led by the foremost of divine attendants and accompanied by his family,
he went to the imperishable world after bathing at the Matsya-tīrtha, Aśvasārasa.
O Rādhikā, even fishermen who go there and perform such acts as bathing will attain liberation equal to that [of the sages].
On the new moon day of the month of Māgha, I manifested there in the form of a fish;
by reading or hearing this, one shall obtain the fruit of visiting the Matsya-tīrtha.
A mortal shall obtain enjoyment and liberation, heaven, sons, wealth, and so forth;
whatever is most desired, he shall obtain all of it through a mere fragment of Kṛṣṇa’s grace.

Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Liberation and the Matsya-tīrtha of Dhanamēdhadhi, the Fisherman, following his vision of the Fish-incarnation in Kuṅkumavāpī through the blessing of the goddess Turī," in the second section (Tretā-santāna) of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Rādhā, on the full-moon day of the month of Māgha, another miracle occurred.
I shall relate it to you in brief; listen to that which bestows knowledge. || 1 ||
In the western region of Pāñcāla, there was a supreme devotee of Viṣṇu named Śatoḍhu, a leader among those born of the Viṣṭi caste. || 2 ||
The group of servants was under his control and became carriers of his palanquin;
they also performed the task of carrying the vehicles of kings and merchants. ||3||
Those performing the work of *viṣṭi* travel together with those seeking to journey to distant lands,
as well as to the other sacred field of Soma.
Gopakṣetra, Camatkārapura, Siddhapura, as well as Māthura-kṣetra and Puṣpakara-kṣetra; || 5 ||
They go to Vārāṇasī, the Narmadā, the Godāvarī, and the Gomatī;
likewise, they go to the Svarṇarekhā and the Aśvapaṭṭa-tīrtha.
Once, he and Śatodhu heard a Vaiṣṇava discourse stating that for one who is childless, there is no way to attain a higher state by any means whatsoever.
That story remained in the heart of Śataudha, who was childless;
he too, observing perpetual silence, urged her toward the goal of obtaining a son.
Having recited the mantra over his rosary, he worshipped and propitiated Bhuvaneśvarī, who resides in the Śamī tree on the riverbank,
alone night after night.
He always remained at the foot of a śamī tree near his own village,
offering incense, lamps, śamī leaves, food offerings, chickpeas, and so forth.
Having thus offered the oblation, he indeed performs the hundred-fold recitation of the garland-mantra, while muttering:
"O Mistress of the World, O Mistress of the World, O Mistress of the World! (11)
"Grant me a son," he prayed, and then he departed for his home;
in this manner, he performed auspicious penance for the duration of a year.
During the rains, the cold season, and the heat, even when there was an excess of cold,
he never at any time suffered a breach of his vow, owing to his intense faith.
Through the quality of forbearance, he fulfilled his vow;
at the end of the year, on the final day of Navarātra, that Bhuvaneśī [appeared].
She appeared before the devotee and said to him, "I am pleased.
The devotee, for his part, beheld her divine and beautiful form, which was the very limit of splendor.

One should meditate upon the auspicious Satī, who has three eyes, bears a trident, is white in complexion, possesses a serene countenance, is seated upon a lion, and has raised one hand for the purpose of granting boons. (16)
He prostrated, uttered cries of "Victory!", and danced;
he said, "O Mother, today my heart's desire has borne fruit and blossomed beautifully."
She who is the direct sustainer of the worlds has come within my sight;
indeed, with but little austerity, I have obtained a great fruit.
What can I do, such as worship and the like, since my vehicle has been offered by myself?
I have fallen at your feet; my mind is fixed upon you.
For those beings for whom she acts as mother, protector, and nourisher in every way, all suffering is utterly destroyed. (2.162.20)
"All my suffering has indeed vanished, like that of one born for service.
Having said this, he offered an excellent oblation, worship, and likewise gifts.
That gracious Bhuvaneśī spoke to the person who had prostrated:
"Choose a boon quickly, O devotee; what is it that dwells in your mind? (22)
"I grant you [boons] quickly; O giver of boons, there is nothing that cannot be given to you.
Thus addressed, Śatodhu was overcome by the power of the goddess.
Maintaining silence and using her hands and gestures, she chose the auspicious boy for her womb; placing her hands [over her belly], she indicated her son by the sign of silence.
The goddess said, "So be it; you shall have a son who is mute.
Having spoken thus, she known as Śatoḍhurī vanished from sight.
Having bowed to the goddess Śamī and circumambulated her repeatedly, he requested her forgiveness, performed the final worship, and then departed for his home. ||26||
He told his wife the entire story concerning the one called Mūkaputra;
and she too, having heard it, attained the joy of a son, the joy of Mūka.
Then, born at the end of the rainy season, the boy grew like the moon through the power of the Goddess, though he was mute and devoid of speech. (28)
Refined by various activities and awakened by consciousnesses, he—who was like a thread for the continuity of his parents' lineage—generated great joy for them. (29)
Indeed, it is the very absence of his voice that constitutes the cause for grief here;
for once, the father, Śreṣṭhi Pravāhaṇa, took the form of a *viṣṭi* laborer.
Having then gone on a pilgrimage to the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake,
he heard an auspicious story at night in the hermitage of Lomaśa.
The Lord of Gods, being well-pleased, grants sight to the blind man who seeks the *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*, which accomplishes all goals. (32)
When entreated, the Blessed Lord grants ears to the deaf;
by bestowing feet upon the lame, Hari makes him happy.
By simply granting his severed hands, Janārdana makes his devotee happy;
he indeed renders one afflicted with leprosy free from that disease.
The Lord of Śrī indeed endows the poor with prosperity;
that very Hari is this Svāmī Kṛṣṇa Narāyaṇa, who fulfills all desires. (35)
The son of Gopāla and Kambharā certainly fulfills the desires of the devotee who, having made his permanent residence at the holy site, worships this Hari. (36)
"Everything for him shall be accomplished; his effort will not be in vain.
Having heard this story on the shore of the lake, Śataudhu [acted accordingly]. (37)
And then, during that night, the Lord Bālakṛṣṇa,
possessing a divine form, fell asleep in the presence of Śatoda.
Having arrived, he said to you, "O devotee, your anxiety will be far removed;
a son named Voḍhu will come here and perform penance. (39)
His own voice shall here itself become sprouted;
go home, and then, taking your son, go to the Aśva-sarovara lake.
"Come here, so that your mind may bear fruit in this regard.
Having spoken thus, the Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa vanished. (41)
Having awakened, he reflected upon that great wonder:
"Truly, the fruit of the sacred field has been realized merely by coming to this holy place. (42)
"I shall indeed perform that auspicious act exactly as I saw it in my dream"; having thus resolved, he established a sacred bathing place (tīrtha) together with his companions.
Having brought the merchant and those seated in the palanquin to his house, he went to his own home and spoke everything to his wife exactly as it had happened. ||44||
For the sake of my son’s attainment of success in the autumnal season, I consider residence at the Aśvapaṭṭa lake appropriate, by the grace of Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. (45)
Having spoken thus and obtained his wife's consent, he took his son along with Śatoḍhu and his wife to the Aśvapaṭṭa lake.
There, at the onset of night, the great mute Voḍhu— who had been mute since birth—
fell asleep and then beheld a dream concerning the manifestation of speech through ascetic penance.
Having recognized her parents in the morning through their gestures and having understood the splendor of her dream,
she herself gradually performed austerities like an ascetic for the sake of her husband.
First, he went there to the great hermitage of Lomaśa;
there, according to the prescribed rite, he received the mantra for consuming the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
She performed the purification of her body and wore a garland of *tulasī*;
she recited: "Oṃ namo śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya svāmine svāhā. (2.162.50)
Constantly chanting that mantra which is dear to Śrī Kṛṣṇa, he went to the temple to see Him, and having bowed down to Śrī Puruṣottama, [he remained there]. (51)
Having drunk the water from his feet, he approached the shore of the lake;
having prostrated at the feet of his parents, he took refuge beneath an *āmalakī* tree. (52)
Seated upon the earth on a seat of kusha grass,
he performed japa with his rosary while meditating upon the glorious Krishna Narayana.
Having withdrawn all his mental activities within and established himself in austerity,
he performed penance for the sake of the Goddess of Speech on the bank of the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake.
Having fashioned a very small sand image of Bālakṛṣṇa,
he performed its worship three times a day with all the ritual offerings.
He performed the recitation of the rosary, while his mind was fixed on the thought, "Grant me speech";
he constantly gathered ten thousand leaves from the Tulasī grove.
He would daily offer tulasī leaves himself for the worship of Bālakṛṣṇa; he spent that month subsisting only on them. ||57||
In the second month, he subsisted on wild fruits; and in the third month, he became one who ate only leaves from the forest.
In the fourth [month] he subsists on a diet of bulbous roots;
in the fifth, on water alone; and in the sixth, he lives on air.
In the seventh [birth], he became a bubble of foam lying upon the water;
having reflected within the water, he thought, "Shall I perish, or shall I speak? (2.162.60)
"I offer myself here to Hari for the sake of liberation"—
having thus resolved, he thereafter became a dweller in the waters.
Indeed, he knows only the mere chanting of names and nothing else;
yet all mental chanting and even supreme austerity unto the end of life [are included therein].
Having understood this, Bālakṛṣṇa was pleased with the boy;
"This one is performing severe penance for the sake of carrying the autumnal meaning. (63)
"Having renounced all his possessions for my sake and being intent on death, this devotee must indeed be gratified by me with the gift of speech upon this earth. (64)
I am the protector of those who have come for refuge and the savior of my devotees; I am indeed attainable through grace, and by grace I satisfy him.
Having reflected thus, the Blessed One, Anādi-Śrī-Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, who is filled with grace for his devotees, assumed the form of Kapila.
Wearing the garb of a holy man with tawny matted hair, he carried a sacred thread over his shoulder,
held a water-pot in his hand, and a supporting bowl at his waist.
Wearing a deerskin and a crystal rosary, holding a water-pot,
that auspicious youth shone with a body resplendent with streams of splendor.
His body was covered with ashes, adorned only by a loincloth;
he was handsome, possessed of a tranquil form, and bore a golden line upon his heart.
His hands are marked with the signs of a fish, a trident, a bow, a svastika, and a banner;
his left thigh is resplendent with the auspicious marks of Lakṣmī and the moon.
The Blessed One, though appearing in the guise of a holy man, was resplendent with divine perfections;
suddenly, he appeared via the path of the sky from the midst of a circle of light.
He descended into the water and remained perfectly steady before his devotee;
though the Lord has no support, he became the support for the water in order to carry him.
Having lifted him up with his right hand and set him down on the bank of the lake,
he wiped his eyes, opened them, and bestowed his own vision upon him.
He said: "Why indeed do you remain here in the water? What do you desire?
Speak, and I shall grant it all to you; I have been well-pleased by your asceticism. (74)
I indeed become one who offers myself to you, who have no other;
you have become one who has no other than me, and I become one who has no other than you. (75)
"Speak quickly; ask for a boon here, and I shall grant whatever you desire.
Having said this, the Blessed One, the ocean of compassion, became silent. (76)
Then the carrier, having attained composure, beheld Śrī Hari, who was endowed with splendor, wearing the dress of a holy man, bestowing boons, and possessing a beautiful form. ||77||
Overwhelmed by excessive joy, he rose and fell at [Viṣṇu's] feet;
he then began to lick the soles of Hari’s feet.
He placed the feet of the Blessed One upon his heart and experienced momentary bliss;
he placed [the feet] upon his head with his lotus-like hands and prostrated himself like a staff.
Overwhelmed by an excess of affection, he shed tears from his eyes;
then, his hair standing on end, he moved the Supreme Lord with a mental disposition,
showing his tongue through that gesture.
O ocean of compassion, there is no voice [to speak]; grant me a voice and show me mercy. ||8 1 ||
Thus she made Mādhava understand everything through her gestures alone;
she showed him her tongue, which was tawny, reddish-brown, and black.
The Blessed One, the savior of the distressed, smilingly touched with his fingers that tongue which she had displayed, doing so joyfully with his hand. (83)
Having drawn out a small amount of water from his water-pot (kamaṇḍalu), he poured it there;
that [water], white in color, the locus of all knowledge, and dissolved therein, [was offered]. (84)
Where Sarasvatī herself was present in person within the water, there indeed arose the knowledge of Brahman as well as the specialized wisdom of Sāṃkhya. (85)
The Vedas possess all-encompassing knowledge and the vision of reality;
thus, under the very guise of water, they have revealed the demonstration of truth. (86)
At that moment, by the grace of Hari, the divine speech—the celestial voice, the well-refined Gīrvāṇavāk—manifested upon the tongue of Voḍhu. (87)
He, who was proficient in the Bṛhadbrahmaṇyayana and occupied the divine seat of a brahmin, offered various hymns of praise to Hari, the bearer of the Veda.
May the Lord of Śrī, the abode of all, whose feet are cherished by the Īśanīs, whose divine self manifests as partial incarnations, and who is worshipped with innumerable virtues, protect us. (89)
May the Lord of ten million forms, who is served by all, grant me prosperity;
may he, the heart of the Vedas, the expansion of speech, the sovereign of autumn, and the Supreme Person, provide for my sustenance.
The Lord of Sarasvatī, Piṅgala, protect me! He who is the Indra of Indras, beyond the reach of speech, and the revealer of the Self through the differentiation of bodies. ||91||
May Kapila, whose form is distinct from the portion of primordial nature, always protect me—
he who is the sacrifice, the knower of all that is born, and the tree of Brahman for the perfected seers.
May Kṛṣṇa Sāmba, the pillar of his own companions, protect [us];
may he protect the gross and the subtle, the rays, and the flowing stream. 93.
May He protect me—He whose manifestations are the fulfillers [of all], whose glories are heard, from whom all life arises as a sprout, and who is distinguished as the essence of all. 94.
To that divine God, from whom this ancient and active world is born again and again from its foundation, let us worship with oblation and with our heart. 95.
May I worship that Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, known as Kaṃbhṛta, Kāmbhareya, and Kapila; may there be peace at His feet. 96.
Having thus offered praise, O Rādhikā, he fell at the feet of Kṛṣṇa;
there, the Lord known as Kapila quickly vanished.
Then, having entered the consciousness of the charioteer, he became a divine ṛṣi, a wise and auspicious expounder of the principles of Sāṃkhya, Yoga, and other systems. (98)
The sacred ford where he beheld the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa in the form of Kapila—that very place is indeed a sacred ford (tīrtha). 99.
Born from the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake, it was auspicious and bestows knowledge;
there, it granted the ultimate realization of reality to the people who bore it.
Having carried the beautiful-limbed image of Hari in the form of Kapila to the hermitage and installed it on the bank of the lake, Voḍhu worshipped it daily.
Then the beautiful temple of Kāpileya came into being;
on the full moon day of Māgha, there was knowledge, speech, and vision for the bearer.
There he attained the abode of Śrī Hari and dwelt for a long time;
then, O Rādhikā, at the end of a yuga, the cowherd attained liberation.
Having bathed there and heard the sacred narrative, one shall attain knowledge of Brahman; one shall undoubtedly attain both worldly success and the supreme perfection. || 104 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Carriers' Vision of Śrī Hari in the Form of Kapila at the Aśvapaṭṭa Lake and Their Attainment of the Siddhi of Sāṃkhya Knowledge and Speech," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, concerning the son named Mūka who was obtained through the penance of the carriers of the palanquin and their subsequent vision of Śrī Hari as Kapila and attainment of perfection.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Rādhikā, to another auspicious wonder of Hari;
I shall relate to you [the marvel] of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
In the sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpikā, in the city of Kāmyaka,
there lived a farmer named Dyuviśrāma who was a devotee of the Lord.
He does not know the ritual action according to the Dharma, nor does he know worship at all; he knows neither the procedure prescribed in the scriptures nor the rites for the gods. || 3 ||
He indeed knows the supreme task of protecting cows and rearing bulls,
and he also knows the most excellent practice of agriculture.

Bathing with the dust from the feet of cows, performing the twilight prayers while offering mouthfuls of grass to the cows, chanting the Gāyatrī mantra using the names of cows, and worshiping through the protection of cows—[these constitute the daily rites]. || 5 ||
The Vaiśvadeva offering is one's own meal; self-study is indeed agriculture; the fire-oblation is the preparation of bread; and the libation is the nourishing of the crops. || 6 ||
Thus his ritual section proceeds with agricultural work;
he knows nothing else at all, yet his mind remains pure.
Neither theft, nor a livelihood based on falsehood, nor malice, nor the harming of living beings,
nor any act of deception exists anywhere in his heart.
One who is stainless, serves the elderly, partakes in the merit of tending cows, and observes vows—should such a guest arrive at the field or the enclosure, he is to be honored. || 9 ||
