There are as many powers (śaktis) and other perfected beings (siddhas) as there are, and all those lords (īśvaras) are likewise adorned by their respective powers and so forth. ||22||

There are as many Maheśas and others, as many inhabitants of the cosmic egg (aṇḍa), as well as gods and demons, sentient and insentient beings, and all things consisting of substance, quality, action, and so forth. (23)
The Vedas, the sciences, the sacred fords, the principles, and the expansions of dharma—there are as many of these as there are beings born from the earth and those dwelling in all the heavens. (24)

Those residing in the cavities, those in the mixed states, as well as those who are distinct and those who are combined—all of them, consisting of the Supreme Brahman and endowed with the three qualities, arrived there. ||25||
That vision of all the abodes of creation which is indeed difficult to obtain, becomes easily accessible here at this sacrifice through the power of Nārāyaṇa’s grace. 26.
O Rādhā, what more need be said? At that time, Hari was capable of acting otherwise;
he is established as both the doer and the non-doer, for no other power is like his.
All causal complexes (sāmagrī) are attracted according to the nature of the attractor;
since the attractor here is the Supreme Brahman, how indeed could there not be an attraction of all things? 28.
I am unable to describe how the subjects were drawn to the sacrifice;
indeed, they had never before been seen by me drawn in such a manner during any other sacrifice. (29)
They come to you from the festival with hymns of praise, instrumental music, and dances;
and while singing of the Supreme Brahman, they even address us as well—how wonderful! (2.168.30)
Thus, while everyone was indeed departing from all sides,
the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa set forth.

Together with sages and ascetics, as well as the guardians of the sacred field (kṣetrapālas) and others, along with the holy places (tīrthas) of the Saurāṣṭra region and the householders among the subjects. ||32||
Accompanied by all those beloved of Brahmā, numbering in the hundreds of billions, trillions, and quadrillions,
as well as his devotees and his family, he ascended the celestial chariot.
Likewise, millions of other devotees ascended by way of the celestial path upon thousands of celestial chariots and raised shouts of victory.
Then the virtuous ones, the perfected ones, and the truthful ones followed after Hari;
the entire sky resounded with the roar of celestial chariots and musical instruments. (35)
At the forefront, the Vedas proceed in embodied form, resonant with the chanting of mantras;
Śāradā and the other goddesses, bearing canes, sing praises of his virtues.
Then indeed the wise go to celestial instruments and divine chariots;
thereafter, the sounds of victory arise from the tinkling of the moon’s banner and other ornaments.
Then there were the countless beloved wives of Brahmā released from there;
then the celestial chariot of Kṛṣṇa, and then the men who were its guardians. ||38||
Then all the attendants, followed by the subjects born in the land of Surāṣṭra and the guardians of the field (kṣetrapālas), arrived at the sacrifice at that time.
Does the Himalaya itself travel through the sky, or does it come of its own accord from heaven and travel upon the northern part of the earth? || 2.168.40 ||
"Do the oceans, rich with the splendor of jewels, perhaps go to heaven?"—such indeed was the vision of Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa in the sky. 41.
Then, on the third day, after midday, the Blessed One himself became distinct from the caravan of travelers setting out on their journey. (42)
When exactly ten ghaṭikās had passed, the sacrificial smoke reached the sky;
at that time, shouts of victory arose in the atmosphere, both in the air and upon the ground. 43.
Millions upon millions of bubbles emerged for the spectators to behold,
and the sky became pervaded by a most extraordinary radiance.
There, the sun, fire, and other such elements were dissolved and no longer within the range of perception; indeed, at that time, the eyes of the world-beings were not even capable of seeing.
By the grace of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa alone, and through the splendor of Śrī Hari, everything then indeed became composed of light. 46.
Even all the black rocks shone like jewels;
even the dark surface of the earth then became as radiant as the moon. (47)
Then even the body hairs and the hair on the head became golden-colored;
even the crows, bees, swans, and cuckoos appeared like [golden] swans. ||48||
Then even the sky became blue like the lunar surface,
and even the inner spaces of the worlds became as bright as Brahman.
But that material body then became divine, for it had become like the Imperishable;
even the distinction between the principles of heaven, earth, and space had gone to dissolution.
All seven forms became white in color;
even the dark (tāmasa) nature of Māyā turned into the quality of goodness (sattva). 51.
Furthermore, at that time, all collections of things became composed of Brahman;
even the villages and houses were then equal to the abode of Brahmā.
By the splendor of Bālakṛṣṇa, everything became permeated with Brahman;
the subjects, kings, and great sages [were filled] with divine offerings, worship, and the like. ||53||
To welcome Rādhikā, they stood there full of eagerness, uttering cries of "Victory! and adorning the portraits.
With palms joined in reverence, bearing offerings, full of devotion, their faces moist with affection, their lotus-eyes blossoming, and their hearts overflowing with love. (55)
Then the women appeared with infants held within their wombs, and the men with severed heads held in their hands; they stood with their movements suspended upward and their faces turned upwards.
The primordial Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Blessed One,
withdrew that fierce splendor and descended from the sky.
The Lord became visible to all and became visible even to those with coarse vision;
at that time, a rain of flowers released by the gods fell from the sky.
An auspicious rain of sandalwood and likewise of unbroken grains occurred;
at that time, a rain of gold, silver, and diamonds fell from the sky. (59)
Kṛṣṇa descended slowly by the stairs of the constructed gateway;
he was then seated upon the vehicle of the four-tusked elephant Arjuna.
All the kings presented necklaces and clusters of gold and jewels;
they prostrated like staffs, while the queens and princesses offered their congratulations.

He repeatedly honored the Blessed One with unbroken grains and other offerings, with sprouts, sandalwood, and flowers, with lotuses known as *netrapuṭa*, and with hands joined in the *añjali* gesture that destroys suffering.
They honored him with the hems of their garments, with ritual services, with hands in the svastika gesture, with hearts full of love, and with prostrations. (63)
And with shouts of victory, parched grain, flowers, and waters from sacred fords.
The subjects caused Hari, Bālakṛṣṇa, Nārāyaṇa, to grow.
With fans, chowries, umbrellas, and fragrant, cool waters infused with sandalwood,
the merchants joyfully brought comfort to Kṛṣṇa.
They nourished Bālakṛṣṇa with coconuts, sugar, saffron, lotus stalks, auspicious fruits, and other such items.
Then the Lord, resplendent upon a golden chariot with a hundred wheels and a divine throne,
accepted the offerings presented by the people.
Kṛṣṇa indeed honored some of his subjects with a glance, with the corners of his eyes, with smiles, with his hands, and with various other gestures.
Then, with smiling faces and many forms, Hari out of compassion granted his own vision to everyone from all sides for a long time.
As it was in front, so it was behind; as it was on the sides, so it was above; even so it was seen in all eyes and in all hearts. (2.168.70)
Out of grace, he gives garlands of flowers to some, and to others, clusters of gems such as diamonds, pearls, and the like. (71)
The great king, the supreme lord, indeed gives pleasing fruits, betel leaves, areca nuts, and the like. (72)
He indeed offers coconuts, garments, and whatever has arrived for the worship—gifts intended as a welcome—as pleasing offerings. (73)
Having granted his vision everywhere throughout the hundred *krośas*,
Hari returned to his dwelling at night by means of an elephant vehicle.
Then all the members of the caravan drank water and so forth, took their meal,
and rested in suitable dwellings that had been provided for them.
Hari, together with his family and accompanied by Brahmapriyā,
himself enjoyed [the kingdom] for one hundred and forty-six years.
He drank [the elixir], attained peace, and then entered a sleep consisting of yoga;
attended by male and female servants, he remained thus until dawn.
At night, in various places there,
the great sages performed kīrtanas and narrated stories interspersed with accounts of past events.
Then, in the assembly of kings, the bards recounted the expansions of various lineages and historical narratives filled with past events. 79.
The virtuous and those possessing knowledge, who bestow the methods for liberation, engaged in discourse;
and women, their minds fixed on Kṛṣṇa, sang songs with passionate melodies.
The young maidens, having formed a *rāsa* circle, wander in circles; they sing to the sounds of clapping hands and the jingling of their anklets and waist-bells. ||81||
Dancing girls perform their dances on the stage amidst a crowd of wealthy patrons;
musicians skilled in their craft play their instruments and take their delight.
Actors perform a dance and display their skill;
poets, immersed in composition, are then seen proclaiming it. (83)
The Mallas engage in battles for the delight of the people; various displays are seen, as well as creations and further transformations of those creations. (84)
Magical illusions are displayed, fashioned by those skilled in the arts;
there are also humorous performances and jests in halls of laughter. (85)
Forms in the shape of fire are manifested by the skilled artisans of lightning-fire using sparks of fire, as well as thundering sounds in the sky. (86)
Through applications of fire, playful displays are cast even into the sky;
there arise roars in the firmament and the variegated appearance of exploding substances. (87)
Assuming many forms, they are manifested through their own skills;
then the jesters and actors delight the people.
And there were the combats of bulls, buffaloes, and arrogant rāṇḍiyas, as well as those of elephants, bears, and monkeys. (89)
O Rādhikā, at that time, during the night, I appeared in the form of a festival;
pairs of musical instruments were played, and there were repeated sounds of "tūpa."
Then the notes of the lutes of Muru and the others arose, and the songs of the Apsarases and maidens resounded everywhere. (91)
There on earth, even the Vedic sounds of the sages became like the jests of eunuchs and the playthings of dolls. (92)
Then there occurred the applications of the Gāruḍī spells,
and in certain places, various compositions of the network of ritual manuals (kalpa).
In the rāsa dance, the pastimes performed by Kṛṣṇa, adorned by the multitude of gopīs, occurred in various places there, captivating the mind through the different varieties of devotion. (94)
In some places, those who know them perform the sports of Rāmāditya and Narāditya, and in other places, they manifest the wonders of Bālakṛṣṇa. (95)
Thus, O Rādhā, at that time during the night, there were indeed festivals of joy for the people dwelling on the earth, as well as for others, according to their desires. 96.
Then, in every place, songs of the glory of the illustrious Gopālakṛṣṇa and the illustrious Śrī Kambharā were sung by the women. 97.
The sacred field of Kuṃkumavāpikā and Surāṣṭra, which is accessible even to the unborn (Aja), are then praised with words of benediction in all songs. 98.
At that time, the sons of Gaṅgā, the young princes, as well as the kings and the sages devoted to Brahman, were praised in songs. (99)
The confluence of the two rivers, as well as the Sudarśana Tīrtha and the Śatakrośa Yajña-tīrtha, are praised on all sides, O Rādhikā. (2.168.10)
In this way, that third night passed away in great comfort;
then, at dawn on the fourth day, Kṛṣṇa abandoned his sleep.
Auspicious musical instruments were sounded on all sides,
while the bards, chroniclers, and panegyrists sang songs of his glory.
O Rādhikā, Śrī Hari, hearing auspicious sounds, abandoned his sleep; the entire sacred field for a distance of a hundred krośas became fully awakened.

Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-eighth chapter, titled "The Announcement of the Auspicious Sacrificial Invitation, the Arrival of All Inhabitants of the Created World, and the Description of Śrī Hari’s Journey to the Sacrificial Ground by Air-chariots along with His Family and the People of Saurāṣṭra, as well as Their Welcome, Wandering, Resting, and Entertainment," in the second section on the Tretā Age of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Rādhikā, having risen in the morning, the Blessed One performed his bath,
as well as meditation, recitation, fire-offerings, Vedic study, and libations.
Then he performed the worship of his own form, the beholding and salutation of his father, and the sight of holy men and virtuous women.
Having drunk a small amount of the milk-nectar and in order to inspect the sacrificial ground,
he mounted his elephant and departed from his own abode.
Carrying his elephant Sapakṣa, which moved through all terrains as if through the sky,
he surveyed the auspicious ground while holding the Sudarśana discus.
Seeing the altar constructed by Viśvakarman right where it had been hidden, revealed, and brought forth, he was delighted and returned to that place.
Hari praised Īśāna, the god who is all-seeing,
as well as Bhakta, Devāyana, Viśvakarman, Kapila, and the others.
Then Hari praised the preceptor of the gods, Gaṇeśa and the others,
as well as all the millions of male and female servants who had provided the necessary materials.
Then Hari praised all the protectors of the earth, and the Blessed One repeatedly praised all the principles (tattvas). || 8 ||
Then the kings, sages, the truthful, the virtuous, the attendants and others,
as well as the beloveds of Brahmā and the rest, performed worship to Hari.
Having bowed down to Lomaśa and the others, Hari obtained rest in the palace;
in the morning, the Lord caused drinks and foods to be served to everyone.
Rasaśālās (alchemical laboratories) were established and foodstuffs were distributed; appropriate and desired items were given to everyone for their complete satisfaction. || 11 ||
Beginning from morning, food, drink, and whatever else is required are given continuously,
in a constant flow, until the break of dawn.
Just as there are certain principles, and as bodies are of such a nature, and as their respective wholesome regimens are, so do the creepers provide them. (1.3)
Jewels, cows, and even wish-fulfilling trees; pearls and other such things, as well as supernatural powers (siddhis) such as Śrī, Ramā, and others.
Then, the infinite divine powers, sovereignities, and qualities indeed offer all things worthy of being desired or enjoyed to everyone.
They provide these people with their desired food in every house; indeed, they provide everything that is needed, even more than that.
O Rādhā, having seen the high regard for Gāṅgeya, why have you fallen into such indignation? Do you not remember how you were pacified by me through skillful means?
You were fed and worshipped by Gaṅgā, who massaged your feet;
you were adorned with her braided hair, and at that time, you indeed became pleased.
On the fourth day, O Rādhikā, millions of humans arrived there on celestial chariots as distinguished guests during that day.
Then, sixteen hundred thousand men came from the regions of Rāśiyāna, and one hundred thousand men arrived from the land of Prāgjyotiṣa.
Ten hundred thousand also arrived from the eastern regions;
a hundred thousand people came from the land of Brahmā, and one hundred thousand from the land of camels.
From Ājanābha came ten million people; from Abrikta, ten million people;
and from the reddish region of Uttarā, a hundred thousand people also arrived. (22)
At that time, there were forty million human beings there,
as well as others from the worlds of the three realms of existence.
There is no counting the number of embodied beings who have arrived, whether they dwell on the earth, in water, in air, or in the intermediate space. (24)
In the clouds, on the mountain, in the caves, in the sky, and in all the elements,
they were fashioned by Viśvakarman, the seer of subtle things.
Then those possessed of spiritual power, having become minute, having become pervasive, and even having become merged,
remain here at this sacrifice with their minds fixed on Hari.
Then, through the dwelling within the inner state, there occurred a complete immersion of all [beings] into the supreme Brahman, even in the imperishable abode. ||27||
All have merged into the supreme, imperishable, and directly resplendent abode;
there is no wonder here, O Rādhā, because Hari is the refuge of all. 28.
He is capable of causing all created things to enter into a single atom; He is able to manifest vastness within a very small space. (29)
I do not find the end of His activities; who else is capable of knowing them?
He alone is capable of displaying creations within an atom and kalpas within a single moment. (2.169.30)
He alone is worthy to satisfy those born in the three worlds with a mere mouthful of water,
and to grant them satisfaction by the consumption of a single grain of food.
In Mādhava, nothing is impossible, nor inconceivable, nor unthinkable, nor unachievable;
for all this [universe] formerly arose from the mere glance of his form.
By whose will there is again a decrease, and at the end, one shall go back to that very place;
who am I, who are you, and likewise who are the others—the four-armed Nārāyaṇas? (33)
Indeed, we were once possessed of power before that form;
enough with these excessive words, for Hari is the support of all.
He made everyone happy at the sacrifice through honors and other such means.
Then, on the fourth lunar day, when the sun was in the middle of the sky, that illustrious Bālakṛṣṇa—
In the pavilion, Bālakṛṣṇa, assuming ten million forms, bestowed mantras upon the kings and the common people; he was present everywhere.
Then, having sat down upon a grass mat at each dwelling, the Lord caused the mantras to be heard with water poured into the ears of those who had taken their meal. (37)
May Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa be my refuge at all times.
Oṃ, salutations to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord; Svāhā! || 38 ||
Out of fear of Time, Illusion, evil karma, enemies, Yama, and treacherous friends,
one should bear the trident, fish, banner, bow, wheel, and svastika.
I am Brahmā, an eternal devotee of Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa;
the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa is my Lord and my husband.
Bālakṛṣṇa is the Supreme Brahman; he is indeed my eternal Lord. May he be my father, kinsman, well-wisher, friend, protector, and guardian. (41)
"Śrī Kṛṣṇa is my beloved; Kṛṣṇa is my master and indeed my husband. Thus is the mantra of refuge and the mantra of surrender, which provides protection. (42)
The Supreme Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa [bestowed] upon Manu the state of Brahman, the mantra that proclaims his sovereignty, and his entire being as Manu. ||43||
Having observed everyone—men and women, young and old—according to their respective capacities, he caused them to hear the teachings that fulfilled their goals and made many people truly human. 44.
Then, O people, those who were initiated took their meal;
and in the evening, Lomaśa indeed performed the narration of the *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā* and then conducted the *nīrājana* ceremony for Hari.
And there, O Rādhā, festivals arose during the night following the meal;
they brought happiness to everyone, while [the others] rested during the latter part of the night. (46)
And on the fifth day, at dawn during the Brāhma-muhūrta, Śrī Hari himself bathed at the confluence of the two rivers; thereafter, everyone else bathed as well. 47.
Then, having performed the daily rites and completed the worship of the deities and other ceremonies,
Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa quickly arrived at the sacrificial pavilion.
The kings and all the subjects, as well as the sages and ascetics, the ritual assistants, the officiating priests, the chanters, and others, all assembled there. (49)
And then the sounds of musical instruments became auspiciously indicative, as if saying,
"Let the Brahmins perform the ritual portion of the sacrifice."
The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa informed the twice-born ones; the brahmins and others performed auspicious rites with Vedic mantras in resonant voices. (51)
There, the preceptor Lomaśa proclaimed the proper place and time;
and the Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, having performed the remembrance of Gaṇeśa, [proceeded].
Having bowed to his guru, the venerable Lomaśa, he performed the formal selection of the preceptor;
he made the binding upon the forearm and performed the invocation of the Earth.
He performed the sprinkling of the ground with the five products of the cow using kusa grass,
and he scattered white mustard seeds for the purpose of driving away malevolent spirits and other obstacles.
Having thus worshipped the ground, he performed the rite of atonement;
having performed the ceremonial sipping of water (ācamana) and breath-control (prāṇāyāma), he carried out the formal worship.
He performed the *puṇyāhavācana* ceremony for Gaṇeśa, who is his own self, using sixteen auspicious items, as well as the installation of the ritual water-pot (*kalaśa*).
There, the Brahmins who were knowers of the Vedas bestowed their blessings;
then those twice-born ones recited peace-chants and performed the ritual sprinkling with water.
They sang benedictory hymns and performed the consecration of Kṛṣṇa;
they worshipped the Mothers and performed the Nāndī-śrāddha rite.
Then the Supreme Lord performed the giving of the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā),
as well as the formal selection of each individual officiating priest (ācārya) and the selection of the Brahmā priest.
He performed the selection of the officiating priests, the selection of the gatekeepers, and the selection of the reciters;
thereafter, he worshipped them.
Then, having worshipped the earth, he performed the protection of the quarters;
thereafter, having sprinkled the sacrificial materials with water, he recited the Svasti mantras.
He performed the worship of the pavilion and the worship of Vāstu;
he carried out the entire ritual honoring of the Vāstu deity according to the prescribed injunctions.

He performed the installation of the water-pot (kalaśa), the offering of fruits, medicinal herbs, and earth, as well as the presentation of the *darbha* grass strainers and the invocation of the sacred waters (*tīrtha*).
Then the Supreme Lord performed the rite of rescuing the fire, worshipped all the deities,
and uttered the mantras for the installation of life-force (prāṇapratiṣṭhā).
Hari worshipped the Yoginīs and the Kṣetrapālas according to the prescribed rite;
he performed the adoration of the deities of the sacred seats (pīṭhas), offered the sacrificial oblation (bali), and prostrated himself.
He performed the worship of the pavilion and indeed offered worship to Brahmā;
likewise, he also performed the worship of the deities of the pavilion.
The worship of the sixteen pillars and so forth, the external worship of the deities and others, the thorough worship of the deities of the branches, and likewise the worship of the banners. ||67||
He performed the worship of all the jars and the worship of the Vedas;
he also performed the worship of the sacrificial pits in all the altars and fire-pits.
In the center of the sacrificial pit, he performed the worship of Viśvakarman;
there he also performed the worship of the girdle and likewise the worship of the gods.
He performed the worship of the womb, the worship of the throat, and the worship of the navel;
he also performed the worship of the Vāstupuruṣa and the ritual installation of the sacred fire.
He performed the worship of the nine planets and the worship of the presiding deities;
he performed the worship of the secondary deities and the worship of the serpents.
He performed the worship of Gaṇeśa and the bhūtas, which is worthy of the world-protectors;
he likewise performed the worship of the guardians of the directions and the worship of the Goddess Śrī.
Hari likewise performed the worship of the deities installed in the mandala,
as well as the worship of the water-pots and the worship of the fifty-six deities.
He performed the worship of the ṛṣis, the worship of the ancestors, and the worship of the siddhas;
he offered honors to the time of death and performed the worship of the rivers and the ocean.
He performed the worship of Śailāyudha and the propitiation of the Ṛṣi’s wife;
having established the water-pot (kalaśa), he carried out the worship of Varuṇa.
The virtuous Harī worshipped all the twenty-four incarnations beginning with Vāsudeva, as well as their lords and their chaste wives.
All the attendants of the three gods, all those dwelling in every abode,
including all those consisting of the creation of Brahmā as well as those consisting of the creation of Īśa.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa honored all those embodied beings who dwell within the fourteen worlds, including all those composed of the creation of living souls. ||78||
Kṛṣṇa indeed honored all— the dull-witted and the divine, the conscious and the teachers, the female and male servants, and those born from the four wombs.
And at each sacrificial pit, the kings likewise performed worship;
they carried out everything exactly as it had been instructed by their respective great sages and preceptors.
The Supreme Lord performed the renunciation of material substance into the fire of the sacrificial pit;
he performed the sprinkling with the *prokṣaṇī* water and likewise carried out the oblation of clarified butter (*ājya*). ||8 1 ||
Having placed the sacrificial oblation (caru) into the fire and established it in that place,
he performed the offering of fuel-sticks and gave oblations of clarified butter with the dipping-spoon (sruva).
He performed the oblation in this manner: "Svāhā to the god [Name]!
as well as to the creation of Brahmā, the creation of Īśvara, and the creation of the individual soul (jīva).
The Lord offered many oblations even to the deities of the sacrifice;
he offered invocations to the deities of the sacrificial pits, pavilions, and sites; and Kṛṣṇa offered invocations to Satī, Sāvitrī, the female attendants, and the Śaktis.
And Kṛṣṇa offered oblations to the liberated Yoginīs, also known as the beloveds of Brahmā, who pervade all limbs and bestow spiritual accomplishments (siddhis). 85.
He offered an invocation to the Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, and the Aśvinikumāras; he also offered oblations to his own [deities] together with their respective incarnations. (86)
Hari offered oblations of the nature of nectar for the sake of satisfaction;
then he performed the installation of the sacrificial post and worshipped the deities of the post.
He sprinkled the sacrificial post and indeed offered an oblation for the post;
thereafter, Hari caused the worship of the sleep-vessel to be performed.
To those living beings invited to the sacrifice, Hari gave their share;
he provided milk-rice, ghee, milk, fruits, and juices. (89)
Just as oblations consisting of sacrificial offerings fell into the fire in the sacrifice by the thousands and tens of thousands, so too did they fall from all sides.
By the grace of Hari, all living beings become satisfied, as do the rice, barley, wild grains, and other foods fit for sages. 9.1.
Dates are succulent, and grains possess a sweet flavor;
the medicinal herbs serve as sacrificial fuel, and the fruits are full of juice.
Offerings of sugar and other such sweet foods were presented; fires of every kind arrived and brought about satisfaction. 93.
There are embodied beings whose faces are fire, and others whose faces are Brahman; likewise, there are those whose faces are Kṛṣṇa, and others whose faces are the virtuous.
There are the Śaktis who have Satī as their chief, those who have Devikā as their chief, those who have Svāhā as their chief, and others who have Lakṣmī and Śrī as their chiefs. ||95||
And all those whose mouths were filled with food attained satisfaction; the principles of both the insentient and the sentient were satiated by various sacrificial offerings. 96.
Afterwards, he offered the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) and then performed the ārārtrika rite;
thereafter, he granted rest to all beings, beginning with the gods.
Thus, indeed, in all twenty-seven types of sacrificial pits (kuṇḍakas), the seers performed worship, the offering of oblations (bali), and the burnt offerings (homa). ||98||
And likewise, by the kings and their pairs who were desirous of performing the sacrifice,
the right to the sacrificial offering was accepted at the ritual according to the command of Bālakṛṣṇa.
In return for their hospitality, even greater gifts were indeed offered;
for they were exceedingly fond of fruits, juices, and grains as food.
The wielder of the Śārṅga bow bestows upon all living beings their respective foods;
and the most delicious edibles produced by the wish-fulfilling gem of the Kalpa are likewise bestowed.
Thus was the beautiful and auspicious fifth oblation completed;
thereafter, [he offered it] for all those [beings] numbering in the tens of millions, billions, trillions, and so forth, like lotuses.
He fed the liberated souls, the liberated abodes, the incarnations and their beloved consorts, as well as the male and female attendants with nectar.
And there were divine sweet foods and infinite drinks,
all kinds of edibles and eatables, as well as auspicious things to be licked.
The Blessed One fed those who were dear to Brahmā, as well as devoted, virtuous, and chaste women, and many young maidens who were beloved by Hari.
Mādhava fed the lords and non-lords, Māyā and the family of Māyā, and the twenty-four principles.
Mādhava fed those residing in the worlds of the eight enclosures who serve Brahmā, Īśa, and Viṣṇu, as well as the male and female servants of the three gods.
All the goddesses of the three divine realms, virgins preeminent in their celibacy—the goddesses, the maidens, the yoginīs, and the virtuous ones of Sāṃkhya and Yoga—[were there]. || 108 ||
He caused all the goddesses in the form of lunar days, such as Ekādaśī and others, as well as the hosts of Apsarases, to partake of a feast.
The Blessed One, the beloved of Kṛṣṇa, caused them all to feast together—
those residing on Meru, those in Satyaloka, and those situated in Mahar, Jana, and Tapoloka.

The ṛṣis, the ancestors, and likewise the ṛṣis of the ancestors, as well as the maternal ancestors; the gods dwelling in heaven and the goddesses, as well as those situated in the Bhuvarloka. || 11.1 ||
Mādhava fed the men and groups of women dwelling on earth, as well as those born from a womb, from an egg, from sweat, and from sprouts.
Mādhava fed the sacred fords, forest rivers, mountains, oceans, and so forth, even down to the insects and moths.
The sons of Brahmā, those born of passion (rājasa), those born of darkness (tāmasa) from all castes,
those produced through both dharma and adharma, the Kāśyapas, and those born of the Sun and the Moon.
He [saw] the Rākṣasas dwelling in Pātāla, as well as Yakṣas, Gandharvas, Kinnaras,
the seven classes of Bhūtas, and the Pretas residing in the abode of Yama.
Furthermore, what man fed the bards of Magadha, the heralds, the minstrels, the Cāraṇas of Śūdra birth, and the Vidyādharas who dwell in the forests? 1.16
Mādhava fed cruel beings, as well as ḍākinīs, śākinīs, and others, along with cāṇḍālas, śvapacas, and animals.
Mādhava fed the serpents, the nāgas, the flocks of birds, the kuṣmāṇḍas, the pravināyakas, the daityas, the gods, and the asuras.
Both the insentient and the sentient, all mixed together as the container and the contained,
indeed enjoyed the auspicious sacrificial portion of the rite, which was pleasing and beautiful.
Having consumed all that is born of the three creations— eternal and transient, stationary and moving—
he indeed attained eternal, perfect satisfaction through the grace of the sacrifice.
"Rādhā and all my beloveds have attained satisfaction born of my grace.
Thus, O Rādhikā, the sacrificial rites took place on this first day.

Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Worship of the Earth, the Worship of the Deities of the Vāstu, the Fire-pits, and the Pavilions, the Worship of Beings Created by Brahmā, the Lord, and the Jīva, the Oblation, the Offering of the Great Final Oblation (Mahāpūrṇāhuti), the Distribution of Food, and so forth," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Rādhikā, likewise on the sixth, seventh, eighth,
ninth, and tenth lunar days, they were gratified by Hari during the sacrifice.
On the eleventh day, as many embodied beings as were gratified according to the prescribed rites—
whether gross or subtle, indeed all those who bear names— became bodiless.

Those who are insentient and those born of sentient beings, those designated as substances and those called qualities, those called actions, and likewise the gods and the lords of their respective principles (tattvas)—[all these are manifestations of Him]. || 3 ||
All the inhabitants of every world, as well as all householders— both the stationary and the moving, women, men, and eunuchs— were thus gratified.
Indeed, there is nothing at all remaining of the food;
in this same way, this Vaiṣṇava sacrifice of all desired offerings was performed by Hari.
Every week, inhabitants of the worlds and their dwellers come constantly;
having obtained a vision [of the deity], men and women depart by the tens of millions and hundreds of billions.
But in the sky, the crowding of celestial chariots does not cease;
as many gods as there are dwelling in heaven and other realms, they all remain in the sky.
There are as many Mānavas on the earth, as many in the mountains and other such places,
as many among the trees, and as many in the rivers.
There were as many men on the boats, on the riverbanks and so forth,
as there were in the pavilions, the halls, the palaces, and even in the mountain caves.
In the groves, at the carts and other places, and even among the vehicles,
men were looking about here and there, observing only other men.
And the dwellings of the various realms are perceived here and there;
and the inhabitants of the worlds and the non-worlds are seen here and there. (11)
At that time, the dwellings on the surface of the earth were seen everywhere;
and during the seven-day sacrifice, a constant increase in the arrival of people was observed.
They became the source of gold, silver, diamonds, and gems in the form of ornaments;
of all beautiful jewels, and of the wish-fulfilling trees and horned animals.
Mountains of possessions arose, consisting of millions of vehicles and conveyances;
there were mountain ranges of garments, riches, foods, and objects of enjoyment. || 14 ||
At that time, there were peaks of pearls, mountains of sweet foods,
and mountain-treasure-houses of articles for enjoyment.
There were rivers of milk-rice and oceans of products derived from cows;
and treasures of various goods were offered within the sacrifice.
Kubera, Vasava, Indra, Meru, Bṛhaspati,
and Viṣṇu, beholding the splendor of the sacrifice, became bowed down with shame.
Beholding the greatness of Aṇṇapūrṇā, which belongs to the Supreme Lord,
Lakṣmī and Śrī became bowed down with shame at that sacrifice.
Immeasurable, inconceivable, non-manifest, and beyond thought—
whatever the knower of reality desires, that very thing appears before him at that very moment.
O Rādhikā, this is the power of Hari, Bālakṛṣṇa,
even there [in that place] for those who are afflicted with leprosy, the poor, the maimed, and the suffering.
Blindness, leprosy, poverty, and physical deformity have gone to destruction;
what was undesirable has met its end, and indeed, that which was desired has been attained. (21)
In this sacrifice of the Supreme Lord, everything was like heaven;
even the Siddhas, beholding this, were struck with supreme wonder. (22)
All sovereign powers became bowed down with shame,
and even Māyā fell into delusion at that marvel of Hari.
Indeed, millions, billions, and hundreds of millions of men come at every moment to behold Bālakṛṣṇa,
and a great crowd gathers.
Then the people, longing for a vision of him, fall into despair;
yet he, having understood their supreme disposition and recognized the fatigue of their journey, [acts accordingly].
Recognizing their state of despair, the Lord, who is compassionate toward His devotees,
became manifest everywhere before His devotees as their inner self.
He is seen in the form of ten million [manifestations] before one's eyes at every spot—
just as he exists in the pavilion and just as he is upon the sacrificial seat.
And such [a form] was he before the other sacrificial pits and at the seats for the oblations;
such was he in countless palaces and in the pavilions. || 28 ||
Such [beings] were on the banks of rivers, in boats, and even in vehicles;
likewise in celestial chariots, in trees, and in forests and wildernesses. || 29 ||
Among the devotees, within the groups of devotees, on the paths, in the streets and so forth,
in the halls, in the attic rooms, and in the kitchens— such was he.
Such [a person] was found in dwellings of great honor, in places for guests,
in dining halls, on mountains, and even in gardens.
Such [a state] is found in chariots, in parts of carts, and even in horses, elephants, and so forth; it is seen in theatrical performances on stage and even in deep caverns.
Whether in water, on land, or in the sky; in oceans, in lakes, and even in rivers;
and in deserts and difficult terrains—Hari is seen everywhere.
With a face of gentle smiles, radiant, adorned with all ornaments, wearing yellow garments, and serene, Bālakṛṣṇa is beheld. 34.
The Lord, bearing divine marks and possessing a bow, a banner, and a trident, is seen adorned with the fish, the svastika, the wheel, and other such signs. (35)
With dark, curling locks of hair, eyes as broad as lotus petals,
his chest adorned with the beauty of the Kaustubha gem, he was attended by Lakṣmī.
Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, bearing the luster of ten million suns, is beheld;
thus is the vision of Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa in every direction. (37)
Then, during that seven-day sacrifice before the devotees,
Rādhikā accepted the worship performed by children, the elderly, and others.
He takes and gives food and joy;
he delights in the company of donkeys and delights in virtuous women. (39)
He sports in all the worlds, assuming every form;
having seen such a marvel, O Rādhā, I am filled with wonder.
Then Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of Vaikuṇṭha, said to me:
"Behold, O Kṛṣṇa, this great wonder that has reached its ultimate limit."
Bālakṛṣṇa shines indeed as a counterpart to every form;
for there is truly no place where Bālakṛṣṇa is not present. ||42||
For those people who come toward the sacrifice without knowing the way, he becomes a person before them and arises as a guide of the path. (43)
But that brahmin storyteller, appearing before those whose minds were uneasy, would indeed recount an ancient, delightful story that was truly captivating. (44)
Approaching them with an unwell body while disguised as a physician, he gives them auspicious medicine that brings about health. (45)
O Rādhikā, a marvelous wonder was seen by me there:
among worlds numbering in the millions, billions, and trillions, not a single person had abandoned their body.
Nowhere indeed does any destruction occur without cause, nor is anyone there who suffers;
nor is there any person with a family who is separated from their own kin. (47)
During that crush, no one’s ornaments and such were lost; nor did anyone there experience bodily friction or the rubbing of feet. (48)
Neither was the vehicle broken, nor did anything disappear;
and there was not a single person who had not seen Bālakṛṣṇa. (49)
Not a single embodied being remained who had not completed his sacrificial rites;
nor was there anyone on the earth who had not received a welcome or lacked honor.
At that time, there was no one whose desires were not yet fulfilled, nor was there anyone who had not obtained the Brahma-mantra. (51)
Oh, the sovereign power of the Lord! Even Īśāna was deluded;
Vāsudeva and the other members of the vyūha were struck with wonder upon seeing this marvel.
They became bowed with shame and were deprived of their pride in their own strength;
"Oh, the power of Lord Bālakṛṣṇa at this sacrifice! (53)
Mahāviṣṇu, shaking his head, spoke thus to Bhūmā:
"O Pārvatī, look at the wonder of your husband's [power]! (54)
Kaṃbharā said to Kamalā, "Behold the majesty of my son!
Kamalā, overflowing with joy toward her husband, held herself in high esteem.
In the place of Kṛṣṇa, as well as in the place of Nārāyaṇa during his auspicious deeds, Hari himself remains as the agent; this is indeed a great marvel to me. (56)
"O Rādhikā, truly, by the attainment of Kṛṣṇa here,
those sons of Gaṅgā, the oceans, have been made low by you in this performance of the sacred ford."
Today, Ketumāla has become meaningful in its own sense through the grace of Hari;
indeed, from this day forward, he has become like a banner (ketu) among all the worlds. Moreover, he shall always remain like a banner upon the garlands of the cosmic eggs (brahmāṇḍas). ||58||
"Purified by the constant sacrifice associated with Bālakṛṣṇa, this place shall become equal to Śvetadvīpa in its supreme sovereignty;
this great, purifying region shall become a bestower of liberation. (59)
The living beings who meet their death here—even subtle creatures such as insects and even embodied souls who are sinners—shall attain supreme liberation. (2.170.60)
Even those people who merely remember this sacrifice in the form of all-desired offerings,
their sins shall be destroyed and liberation will come into the palm of their hands.
Even those who have gone to distant lands will bow to the earth upon remembering [it];
there is no doubt that they will obtain the merit born of a sacrifice.
Even if they should cry out "Nīpa" and perform the *prapīṭhikā* [preliminary rite], there shall be the destruction of their sins and the fruit born of bathing shall accrue to them. (63)
The person who shall proclaim the twenty-seven sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) will attain worldly enjoyment, liberation, great satisfaction, prosperity, and so forth. ||64||
He will even take up the dust from the ground between us;
whether on his head or upon his body, he shall become a pure soul.
Furthermore, whoever shall go to that land on foot with faith, desiring to visit the sacred sites (tīrtha), shall obtain at every step the fruit of a sacrifice. ||66||
If any person shall dwell for even a week or a single day at the confluence,
his heaven shall indeed be eternal.
Even if a man or a woman performs this seven-day vow for a single day with fruits and other offerings, they shall obtain the fruit of universal sovereignty.
Furthermore, he who lights a lamp even on the surface of a leaf and offers it to a deity at a sacred ford shall attain the abode of the Sun.
Furthermore, he who shall give milk-rice to the poor and the helpless will indeed reach the world of the Moon and become a consumer of nectar.
Or perhaps a garment, or an ornament, or sandals, or two bracelets;
or a parasol, or a fly-whisk, or a fan, or even a towel. (71)
Whoever here gives a bowl, a water-pot, a granary, or even a protective amulet, as well as a loincloth to an ascetic, shall attain the station of Indra.
One who attains liberation should worship Pārvatī, Lakṣmī, Prabhā, Śrī, and Rādhikā, together with Bālakṛṣṇa, here at Māṇikyā.
One should give morsels of food here to the cows and auspicious grains to the birds;
one should also give food to people here, and such a person shall partake in liberation.
One should offer water, one should offer fruit, and one should present leaves, flowers, and milk;
that man who does so here at this confluence on the ground of sacrifice shall partake in heaven. (75)
Those who here, with sincere devotion, shall offer a bed, a bolster, or a couch, will go to the great heaven by the power of their great merit. (76)
There, attendants will provide seats, grass mats, and even small couches;
they will become worthy of the Brahma-seat, of this there is no doubt. (77)
Those men who shall perform sacrifices here on this sacrificial ground will indeed go to the supreme abode of the conscious ether (cidākāśa). ||78||
The gift of elephants, the gift of horses, and also the gift of donkeys; as well as the gift of swans, cuckoos, peacocks, and parrots—[these are the gifts]. (79)
Those who shall here perform the gift of bulls, celestial chariots, vehicles, or likewise [gifts] of their own minds, they shall go to the abode of Brahmā.
The gift of a daughter, the gift of land, and the gift of a son are most excellent;
so too are the gift of a house, the gift of a field, and the gift of a garden. ||8 1 ||
Those people who shall perform the gift of trees, creepers,
and pillars here will go to the immortal heaven, which is endowed with the nectar of all flavors.
They will offer gifts of wood, gifts of stones and the like, gifts of clods of earth, and gifts of minerals; thus they shall attain the circle of fire.
Those who give curd, milk, and other such things will go to the lunar orb;
those who give household utensils, however, will go to the abode of Brahmā.
Those who bestow kingdoms shall attain the realm of Vairāja here;
for those who give gold and silver, there shall be a journey to Goloka. (85)
They will be givers of the gift of knowledge, worthy of worship by the gods;
they will be providers of the means for cultivation, like Kuberas. (86)

Those who have mastered the training in the arts and crafts will become pierced [in their realization]; yet, even after carrying this water-pot to another land, not even a single drop [will be lost]. (87)
If they should give it to anyone else, it would grant liberation to both;
furthermore, in this water, the feathers and bones of animals and birds shall fall away. (88)
Those from whose mouths even at the time of death water falls [into the mouth of a dying person] shall be liberated from all sins and go to the supreme state. (89)
Whether it be liberation from the body or even whose bones fall into the water, they shall all attain liberation, O Rādhikā; there is no doubt in this matter.
Such is this sacred ground, circular for a hundred yojanas, situated between two rivers, purifying and beyond description. (91)
If anyone receives Vaiṣṇava initiation at the site of sacrifice, he shall become a divine four-armed attendant in Vaikuṇṭha. (92)
A woman who possesses initiation becomes divine, four-armed, and beloved of Hari;
she is eternally liberated, and for her no further rebirth exists.
Those people who cause the narrative of the Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā to be heard and those who listen to it are, in this world, people destined for liberation. ||94||
One should give food to virtuous women and to chaste women here in every way;
one should give food to holy men, and the donor shall attain liberation. (95)
Those who perform penance here through the observances of fasting shall be known as pure and established in Brahman; seeking the meaning of the divine syllable, they are liberated. ||96||
O Rādhikā, what more need I say to you? For there [dwells] Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, as well as other Nārāyaṇas, incarnations, lords, and gods. 97.
The ancestors, the seers, the perfected ones, the truthful, the virtuous, the lords of ascetics, the yoginīs, the classes of Arhats, the sacred fords, and the stars. ||98||
Having arrived, they stayed; they drank the water of the rivers, ate forest produce, and touched [the ground] at every spot. 99.
Merely by remembering His divine play, people become partakers of liberation;
and by reciting or hearing this, one shall certainly attain both worldly enjoyment and liberation.

Thus ends the one hundred and seventieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Offerings Presented at the Seven-Day Sacrifice (*saptāhayajña*) in the Second Section on the Tretā Age of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā, including Bālakṛṣṇa’s assumption of ten million lotus-forms and the majesty of the gift of the sacrificial ground and other offerings."
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Rādhikā, there, in that assembly of people at night, the auspicious narration of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā takes place eternally. || 1 ||
The Lord Sanatkumāra himself recites it as the Master; Vyāsa Śvetakṛṣṇāyana also analyzes the narrative.
And because it belongs to Śvetavyāsa by name, it is called Śvetāsana;
that place is the very embodiment of a sacred ford (tīrtha), always bestowing both knowledge and realized wisdom.
And at that very spot where the great seer Yavakrīta, the son of Gaṅgā,
having consumed a mouthful of salt water, performed most severe penance.
That supreme and purifying holy site (tīrtha), known as Kṣārakavala, became established there on that ground; it is renowned as always bestowing liberation.
By that name, even that region extending for a hundred yojanas—
from the shore of the Black Ocean as far as the Nistārā river— [became known].
Yavakrīta became renowned, taking his refuge at the bank of the Niṣṭhāpara river;
that great ṛṣi Yavakrīta was devoted to the performance of Vedic rites.
On the eleventh day, at midday, he spoke to Bālakṛṣṇa:
"O Hari, at this very moment of Abhijit, please offer the final oblations."
Having heard that, Lomaśa, with the consent of the illustrious Hari,
offered the final oblations (pūrṇāhuti) there into the fire whose essence is the Supreme Brahman.
Having placed betel leaves, areca nuts, unbroken grains of rice, ghee,
and bilva fruits into the *sruva* ladle, Hari offered the final oblations (*pūrṇāhuti*).
Having heard the mantras beginning with "oṃ samudra" as they were recited by the sages, and having been prompted by the verses beginning with "pūrṇā darvi," he offered the full oblations.
This [obeisance] is to Agni Vaiśvānara, to the Vasus, Rudras, and Ādityas,
to Śatakratu, and to the Waters;
this [obeisance] is to the Lords of the three heavens, to the incarnations, and to the Śaktis.
To the Supreme Brahman, Svāhā! Salutations! || 12 ||
This is for the seven who dwell on the upper floors and the four who dwell on the ground— both the insentient and the sentient— svāhā!
This is for the seven musical notes and those situated in the eight enclosures.
To the abodes ending with Īśāna, svāhā! Adoration! || 13 ||
And this [offering] with Svāhā to Brahman, and Svāhā to the Supreme Brahman;
and to the One, the Non-dual, and to Me—Svāhā! Om! Salutation! 14.
Having spoken thus, Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa offered great final oblations (mahāpūrṇāhuti),
consisting of countless bilva fruits and thousands of streams of clarified butter.
He offered sandalwood fuel and great oblations of sweet substances;
the beginningless Lord himself appeared visibly within the circle of fire.
Laughing, he took up the oblations with particular distinction every day;
likewise, he took up those offered as pairs in all the sacrificial pits.
Then the Lord gave countless golden sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇās),
as well as various gems such as jewels, pearls, diamonds, and the like.
Having thus offered the final oblations (pūrṇāhuti), the brahmins who had mastered the Vedas bestowed blessings upon the sacrificer there with sacred mantras.

"O Brahmins, with the waters from the *śāntighaṭa* jars, along with *kuśa* grass, *dūrvā* grass, and mango sprouts, and reciting the hymns beginning with 'punantu,' let us sprinkle [him]," so they spoke. (2.171.20)
Then the Brahmins on all sides uttered words of peace;
furthermore, having received their sacrificial fees, they then sang benedictions.
The Brahmins gave the gods, beginning with Agni, their respective places; then, having attained fulfillment, they spoke these pleasant words.
Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa bestowed upon them all the grace of sacrifice, which brings about the cessation of suffering, increases through the lotus-line, and is imperishable. ||23||
And Mādhava, assuming ten billion forms, bestowed [his grace] everywhere;
indeed, at that time, no one remained without the favor of the sacrificial oblation (caru).
In the intermediate space, in the atmosphere, in the sky, in water, on land, in the forest, on the earth, in a cave, in a remote region, in the wilderness, in a tree, and on a mountain; ||25||
In a celestial chariot, a vehicle, a carriage, a boat, and even upon a mountain peak,
Kṛṣṇa, assuming countless forms, bestowed the grace of the sacrificial oblation (caru).
Then, indeed, he fed all those who were honored by the earth— the great guests,
the great liberated ones, the liberated ones, the abodes, and the possessors of abodes.
And likewise [he saw] Brahmapriyā, Muktānī, Rādhā, Ramā, and others,
as well as all the incarnations of Nārāyaṇa and the glorious Supreme Lords.
The Vyūhas, the Prakṛtipālas, the Kālapuruṣas and Īśvaras, the Vairājas, those known as Bhūmans, and likewise the hosts of Mahāviṣṇu. ||29||
He likewise [honored] the lords who guard the three deities, as well as their wives, female servants,
male attendants, and female attendants on all sides.
The Blessed One fed those born of the creation of Brahmā and those born of the creation of Īśa,
as well as the Siddhas, Ṛṣis, Sādhus, Pitṛs, and virtuous women.

All the gods and goddesses dwelling in the five heavens along with their families, as well as the hosts of celibate students, the guardians of the quarters, and the protectors of the worlds—[he saw them all]. ||32||
And the thirty-three deities dwelling in the Bhuvarloka, as well as the four classes of living beings situated in the Bhūrloka—both the insentient and the sentient. ||33||
Mādhava fed all the hosts of gods and demons, as well as the descendants of Kaśyapa and human beings, even those residing in the seven netherworlds.

The Blessed One indeed caused those created by Brahmā— the moving and stationary beings, along with their qualities, actions, and their dependencies, as well as that upon which they depend— to partake in the sacrifice.
Today I am the Blessed One, and I feed even one devoid of merit;
on this Ekādaśī day, everything for me is indeed fruitful. (36)
"May all of you eat everything touched by me with devotion, for today, by my will alone, this meal shall indeed become a sacred vow. (37)
Thus spoke the Blessed One; and then Bālakṛṣṇa, O Rādhikā, having fed everyone, himself likewise ate together with his father. 38.
Together with his brothers and his family, he took his meal;
so too did his mother, his other mothers, and his well-pleased sister. (39)
Then all those beloved of Brahmā enjoyed the family feast;
and having received betel-leaf, all the lords took their rest.
Then musical instruments were played and songs were sung;
indeed, everyone became diligent for the purpose of the ritual bath at the conclusion of the sacrifice.
In the union of Niṣṭhā and Parāprapīṭhā reside infinite beings:
gods, liberated souls, lords, incarnations, and all powers. 42.
The ṛṣis dwelling in the three worlds, as well as the truthful and the virtuous,
all departed toward the Blessed One, the Lord of the lords of all lords.
Accompanied by the great sages and celebrated by them,
he went on foot to the riverbank for the sake of the avabhṛtha bath, being praised with Vedic mantras.
And the Lord Bālakṛṣṇanārāyaṇa remained at the confluence;
the ancient Lomaśa then caused him to make a solemn resolve (saṃkalpa). 45.
In the four-faced Brahmāṇḍa, at the commencement of creation when the end of the Kṛta age had arrived, during the first cycle, in the glorious Kāmbharīya Nārāyaṇa. || 46 ||
And in this present fourteenth year on this earth,
while He who has descended here exists in His form as the primordial Man.
On the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Śrāvaṇa, on a Sunday,
at the confluence of the Niṣṭhā and Aparā rivers, this indeed concludes the sacrifice.
The bath, which is of the nature of the *avabhṛtha* (concluding purificatory rite), is the cleanser of all sins;
it possesses the power to wash away the inevitable impurities incurred during the sacrifice. 49.
It bestows all merit and wards off all unknown sins,
even when an offering is made as small as a minute creature, a seed, a piece of wood, a grain of dust, a flower, or a mere filament.
In the fire-offering, in the purification of the ground, in the construction of the pavilion, on the site of the alchemical laboratory, at the hearth, at the mortar, and at the water-jar; ||51||
Whether it be grinding in a mortar, sweeping, or even the breaking of leaf-plates, whatever ill-conduct or transgression has occurred— whatever at all has come to pass.
The Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa performed a purificatory bath for him to bring about his destruction,
for the sake of completing the sacrificial rite and to ensure the favor of the gods.
For the sake of nourishing the supreme *apūrva*, I, endowed with the threefold creation, now perform this bath consisting of the final purificatory immersion (*avabhṛtha*); *oṃ namaḥ*. (54)
Having thus formed this firm resolve, O Rādhikā, the Blessed Lord, the Supreme Person, submerged himself in that water and did not emerge again.
Then, having remembered the three worlds, he performed the libation (tarpaṇa) as an ancillary rite of the bath;
thereafter, he indeed massaged his body with sesame paste.
With the powder of *āmalaka* fruit, with clay from a sacred ford (*tīrtha*), with ashes,
with the powder of sacrificial earth, with turmeric powder,
with sandalwood, with musk, and likewise with barley flour and other such substances. ||57||
Likewise, with powders of five colors, with all medicinal herbs, and also with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), as well as with gold and water from sacred fords (tīrtha). ||58||
Then, according to the ritual for the consecration of the door of Brahmā’s water-vessel,
he rubbed together all the powders and performed the avabhṛtha bath.
When the great king had bathed, then the oceans were there:
the Brahma-lake, the ocean of nectar, and the vast waters of Virajā.
The waters of the Nārā, as well as rivers, streams, lakes, and oblong ponds;
the water of the sky, the clouds, and the divine white water—[all these are the source]. ||61||
The great sacred ford of Varuṇa and likewise the Mahābhūtajala,
along with all the sacred fords together with their presiding deities, arrived there.
They indeed caused the Blessed One to tremble excessively by means of their stream [of power];
for they were liberated, having descended from their abodes as both male and female incarnations.
The Śaktis, the Īśvaras, the Īśvarīs, and likewise the beloveds of Brahmā; the Pitṛs, the lords of the gods of gods, the Ṛṣis, the Siddhas, and the Sādhus. ||64||
The stages of life, all the social classes, men, women, and eunuchs; those born from a womb, those born from an egg, those born from a sprout, and those born from sweat. ||65||
The Daityas, Dānavas, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and likewise the Vahnis;
those consisting of earth, water, fire, and those whose bodies are air. 66.
Those dwelling in the vault of the sky, both sentient and insentient,
all bathed there in that holy water of the avabhṛtha rite.
In that divine union, possessing divine qualities yet free from attributes, and performing divine deeds,
a beautiful rain of flowers and sandalwood then fell there.
Then the divine preceptors, the purifiers who dwell in the imperishable syllable of the Supreme Brahman, spoke from the sky: "May they purify us! (69)
May the devotees stationed in every abode,
the incarnations of the Lord of Devotees, His attendants, and likewise the Lords, purify us.
May the sovereign goddesses, the great truths, and the lords of the gods purify us;
may the great seers purify the sacrificer and those who perform the sacrifice. ||71||
"O gods, let the god Mahānārāyaṇa, who is pure by his very nature,
purify you and these sacred fords that have come here for the ritual bath."
Gaṅgā, Cerāvatī, Menakāṅgī, Brahmaputrikā, Aṅgaśikṣāṅgikā, Harāṅgahā, and likewise Āyūrikā. ||73||
Bīnā, Yāneśvarī, Caubī, Sindhu, Coralikā, Valgu, Niṣṭhā, Aparā, Dīnā, and Dinapā—these are the foremost rivers. (74)
Nārāyaṇī, Naṣṭajarā, Karmāṅgī, Jāmbujā, Nadī, Murā, Kāruliṅgā, Parīṇā, and Āmajānikā. (75)
The Miśrasurī, the Mahākāñjī, the Yūkāsanā, and the Saridvarā—may these and other great rivers purify the performer of the sacrifice. (76)
Aśvapaṭṭa, Puṣkara, Mānasa, the lake Nārāyaṇa, the Pampā lake, Indradyumna lake, and the great lake of Brahmā; 77.
The lake Śambhula, the lake Cilasa, the lake Kolāraka, the lake Mākamāna, the lake Bāla, and the lake Māṅgira; ||78||
The lake of delight in gain, the lake of the forest, the lake of speech,
the lake of the mountain, the lake of the swift wind, and likewise the lake of the essence of the earth.
And the lake Suśīla, as well as the auspicious Mīnakaṅūsa lake, the Bālakṛṣṇa lake, and also the Dvikala lake. (2.171.80)
And there is the Yugala lake, as well as the Tryaṅgi and Narasarovara lakes;
also the Phulamaṇḍa lake and likewise the Lurāsa lake. ||8 1 ||
Also Maśakelasaras, as well as Jayeśānasaras;
Udvaśa-saras, and likewise Yoniga-saras. ||82||
Leṇḍuga and Sara, Pāyūśa and Sarovara, Tūnāya and Rukmavāsa, Āvāla and Rudanphala. ||82||
Also Viśturīyasaras, as well as Ālavārta-saras; Itivarta-saras, Kimvāsa-saras, and Tuṅgayānika. ||84||
The lake Mādhura, the lake Vāgviyāla, the lake Nyāsajayātmaka, the lake Śirova, the one named Caṇḍa, and likewise the lake Grātavīra. 85.
Also Grātaślavasara, Arthavāsa-saras, Vinipāra-saras, and likewise Suparīyāraka. ||86||
Also Klinnavārisaras, the lake named Īśa, as well as the Śoṇabhadra river and the Ghargharā river. ||87||
May all the oceans here also purify embodied beings;
may the celestial rivers purify them, and may tens of millions of sacred fords purify them.
May Meru, Mandara mountain, Himādri, Yūrala, Kārukarmā, Patatkāya, and Raivata mountain purify you! (89)
And thus, throughout the hundred-krośa expanse of rivers and ocean waters,
all the kings who were performing sacrifices bathed during their rites.
In each of those places, there was a single divine man, radiant as the sun,
who had arisen from the confluence of the two rivers like Hari himself.
Holding in his hand a golden vessel containing sandalwood paste and unbroken grains of rice, as well as a flower garland and a crown, he approached Bālakṛṣṇa. ||92||
He worshipped according to the prescribed rites and applied a tilaka-mark upon the forehead of Hari with fresh unbroken rice grains and a paste of saffron and sandalwood.
He placed the crown upon the head of Kṛṣṇa and a garland around His neck;
he prostrated himself there like a staff and spoke to Bālakṛṣṇa.
In a voice as deep as the roar of clouds, while all were listening, he said:
"I am the Puruṣa who performs the final ablution; I am the eternal son of Yama."
This Vaiṣṇava sacrifice, which fulfills all desires, is now complete, bestowing full merit;
today I have attained nourishment through the arrival of all sacred fords here.
For those who perform their ritual bath here every year, the state of liberation shall certainly become eternal through a fraction of Nārāyaṇa’s grace. (97)
May all beings be happy, filled with glory, wealth, and prosperity; may they be replete with health, family, and the various flavors of enjoyable things. (98)
May the yogins and those who seek security also become possessors of spiritual accomplishments; and may all the men and women who have gathered here at this sacrifice likewise attain them.
"May they be like Hari, experiencing the joy brought by both worldly enjoyment and liberation"—
having spoken thus, O Rādhikā, he indeed drank the water of the avabhṛtha bath.
At that moment, a maiden arose from the water, radiant as the moon,
beautiful, endowed with all splendor, well-nourished, and as lovely as a campaka flower.
She was worthy, serene, and pleasant-faced; like Lakṣmī herself, she was adorned with ornaments and held in her hand a vessel filled with materials fit for worship.
She worshipped the Supreme Lord Bālakṛṣṇa with unbroken grains and other offerings;
upon seeing her, even millions of humans, gods, demons, sages, and embodied ancestors were struck with wonder. (103)
Having bowed to and worshipped Bālakṛṣṇa Hari, she said:
"I am eternal satisfaction (Tṛpti) and I am the daughter of Havya;
my birth here at this sacrifice from all the sacrificial offerings is meritorious."
O maiden, I am well-pleased, and I have been born through auspicious blessings;
I unite you here, sirs, may you be happy forever.
"Those who grant me good fortune shall themselves become highly fortunate.
Then Śrī Hari said to her, "O maiden, ask for a boon.
The maiden replied, "Grant me a boon; indeed, let the ritual bath (*avabhṛtha*) be my boon."
Śrī Hari, having reflected immediately upon the avabhṛtha bath at the time of giving, [acted].
Having summoned that prince and taken the young boy by the hand,
he entreated him for the sake of the maiden who was seeking him.
The Lord, the master who knows the ritual rules, gave the gift to the maiden according to the prescribed rite;
the blessed Lord bestowed the gift of a son upon the maiden.
The prince also presented a necklace of jewels to the princess;
thus, having received the gift of the prince according to the marriage rite, she— || 111 ||
The maiden became possessed of good fortune, and the prince became fortunate;
from that time forth, the gift of a maiden has been considered supreme in Ketumāla.
The woman is the principal one, and the son is dependent on the woman;
indeed, the glory of the man lies solely in his subordination to the woman. 113.
The performance of the purificatory bath (avabhṛtha) and the perpetual entrustment [of the kingdom] to the queen—
indeed, that entire female sovereignty exists through her majesty.
Having thus performed the festival known as Naradāna at the confluence during their immersion in the waters, they emerged from the water.
While all those who had come for the bath were still there, the two couples,
performing a dance with joyful hearts, vanished into the midst of the water.
Thus those seeking the sacrifice beheld this great wonder;
and at that time, humans and others gave gifts by the millions.
Just as it had been arranged for the millions of maidens,
the girls then obtained the Kumāras, who were of excellent form.
There, millions were born, adorned with good fortune and prosperity;
thus indeed was the gift of a maiden performed at that first marriage.
That [merit] was always present there; it is an eternal ordinance that the gift of land, houses, cows, and gold should be made together with one's sons. 2.171.1–20.
The ancestors, filled with joy, indeed gave [gifts] to their daughters-in-law;
and thus, having performed the purificatory bath (avabhṛtha) and having given gifts by the millions, [they departed]. || 121 ||
They all went to their respective places and rested in their dwellings;
and then the sounds of musical instruments subsided into silence.
Thus, O Rādhikā, this great marvel has been related to you;
by hearing, reading, remembering, or even causing others to hear this, [one attains the highest goal].
Having obtained the fruit of the avabhṛtha bath and the fruit born from the gift of a youth,
one shall attain worldly enjoyment as well as liberation, and obtain eternal good fortune.

Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-first chapter, titled "The Description of How Lord Hari Manifested in Person and Accepted the Great Final Oblations (*mahā-pūrṇāhuti*), the Feasts for All, the Concluding Bath (*avabhṛtha-snāna*), the Manifestation of the Youth (*kumāra*) as the Concluding Bath Itself, the Manifestation of the Maiden (*kumārī*) as Satiety, the Bestowal of the Youth named Avabhṛtha upon the Maiden who requested him as her husband, the Gifts of the Youth during the Marriage Rite, the Great Gifts (*mahādāna*), and Their Resting in Their Respective Places," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*. || 171 ||
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Rādhikā, for the Kumārikās alone in the land called Ketumāla, the best fruit indeed arises from the giving away of young girls to young men. || 1 ||
In that matter, the woman is independent; for the prince, she is his own mistress during the night.
There, the wife’s word is paramount; the wife’s command is supreme.
For the wife is indeed the sustainer of splendor, while the husband is merely the provider of seed;
the field is the most excellent and primary factor. (3)
The field (kṣetra) is indeed the protector, the nourisher, the progenitor, and the controller; it is stable, endowed with all authorities, and the indicator of the lineage. || 4 ||
Through the offering of the final purificatory bath (avabhṛtha), the supreme dharma of bestowing a maiden in marriage was established there from that time onward by the will of Bālakṛṣṇa. || 5 ||
Then the glorious Bālakṛṣṇa, the supreme Lord and Master himself, personally instructed Gāṅgeya and the others in the ritual for giving away the cows to the young princes.
And on a sacrificial ground, or in a temple, or in the house of a guru; or in a place adorned with musical instruments and the like, resounding with sounds, and filled with assemblies.
On an auspicious day, during a favorable weekday, at dawn on the day of the propitiation ceremony,
he should go forth, taking the girl along with her family and having her beautifully adorned.
Then she was beautifully attired, radiant with appropriate ornaments, in the full bloom of youth,
her face visible to all, dressed in variegated garments, and accompanied by an umbrella.
Having bowed to the Teacher of Dharma seated upon the great lion throne,
she was presented with a garland of flowers by her mother and received the benediction bestowed by the Guru.

The teacher should cause her to hear the teachings on dharma, interspersed with principles of statecraft and other subjects, while she is honored by other spectators, friends, well-wishers, and so forth. (11)
At that time, the family of the prince, accompanied by his friends and well-wishers, arrived there together with him.
Having seated the well-adorned youth beside the girl,
the preceptor should then offer flowers, garlands, and other gifts, as well as pronounce blessings.
One who possesses devotion to the Dharma should cause those two to hear the mantras of the Supreme Lord;
then, in the temple, the Guru should worship both of them with flowers and other offerings.
One should personally place flower garlands on their two necks separately;
one should offer clusters of fragrant substances and so forth, and two garlands of flowers upon their hands.
The bridegroom and the bride should place a garland upon each other's necks;
then the preceptor should place the hand of the youth into the hand of the maiden.
Then the young maiden should take the hand of her husband;
thereafter, the young maiden should place her own hand in the hand of the youth.
The youth should take hold of him while looking upon him with affection;
then they should perform mutual kissing of the hands and so forth. (18)
Holding each other's hands, they performed a dance;
then they both bowed down to the Supreme Lord and likewise to the Guru.
Then, they should give two green parrots to the two [deities],
and upon the neck of each bird, they should place fragrant substances and other auspicious items.
May you both be happy and long-lived;
may you be blessed with the fruit of sons, daughters, and the like, and be filled with the treasure of love.
Upon receiving this blessing, they should bow to the book of Dharma;
thereafter, there should be dancing before the Guru, which they should behold performed by pairs.
The two should take their meal together while remaining in each other's company;
having received betel and other such items, they should be joined by the Guru’s benediction.
Having risen, they may go as they please to the maiden's house, or at the maiden's command, they may then go to the bridegroom's house. (24)
A prince should not frequent a house that is independent, or one provided for his residence through the acquisition of fame, nor should he act in violation of the command of a maiden. (25)
That bride is the eternal mistress and indeed the controller of her husband;
the groom should in every way remain dependent upon her will and her mind. (26)
In this manner, the gift of a young man to a young woman in a temple is considered valid when accompanied by a festival, a feast, and items such as necklaces and bracelets.
It was beautifully adorned with singing, dancing, instrumental music, and the like;
for in this rite, no sacrificial procedure involving fire or the presence of a deity as witness is required.
This method is free from bondage and allows one to dwell in whatever house one desires, provided there is no injury to love; otherwise, it is merely a natural coincidence. (29)
At that time, the man must indeed be abandoned by the woman;
furthermore, a second [man] must be taken by the independent woman. (2.172.30)
Thus, O Rādhikā, regarding the giving of a daughter in marriage,
this ritual for bringing a virtuous woman under one's control was indeed proclaimed in Ketumāla.
Then the glorious Bālakṛṣṇa took rest during the night;
indeed, millions of marriages were performed there on that twelfth day.
In the sacrificial pavilion, the gift-offering was performed according to the marriage rite;
and at midday, after having fed all the honored guests, [the ceremony concluded]. (33)
Having bid them farewell, Hari himself bestowed many gifts upon them;
all those presents that were brought there were produced from his grace.
Having made them and perceived them as such, Kṛṣṇa gave them; all embodied beings accepted them, as did the liberated ones and the divine incarnations of Nārāyaṇa. (35)
The lords and the goddesses, the liberated ones and likewise the Śaktis, the principles (tattvas) and those who know the principles, and the truthful celibates (brahmacārins). || 36 ||
The virtuous, the ancestors, the gods, the sages who resemble deities, kings, humans, divine Gandharvas, and other offspring of the gods; || 37 ||

The world-protectors, the guardians of the quarters, the forests, the lands of pilgrimage sites, those dwelling in the netherworld, those living in the waters, those dwelling in the sky, and those established upon the earth; ||38||
Then those who were present at the sacrifice— both the insentient and the sentient beings, as well as the great lords— received their respective portions.
Then, by the command of Śrī Hari, they all, having worshipped the Supreme Lord,
departed for their own abodes by means of celestial chariots and vehicles.
Then the subjects of Saurāṣṭra, all the maidens dear to Brahmā, and the family of Śrī Hari also went along the path of the celestial chariots. 41.
The sages, headed by Lomaśa, as well as Nīlaka, Karṇa, Vṛka, and others—
all of them, being requested by the kings, remained there at the site of the sacrifice.

The deities of the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake, the guardians of the field (kṣetrapālas), the primary deities and others, Īśāna, the royal preceptors, and the sacrificial teachers—all these are born from that [lake]. (43)
And the Gāṅgeyas, whose subjects were of such-and-such [names], dwelt there at that confluence for the sake of obtaining a vision of Hari, in order to lead Hari to their own abodes. 44.
Having eaten at night, they then took rest, and in the morning Hari arose and performed his ritual bathing and worship according to the rules.
On the thirteenth day, at midday,
the king, the sovereign, having joined his palms in reverence, fed the men and prayed to Mādhava.
"O Kṛṣṇa, make my home pure by the placement of your feet. "So be it," Hari replied; then the one whose banner bears the dolphin followed him. 47.
The king indeed commanded his chief officers for the sake of Svāgata's arrival;
they, being eager, brought forth well-prepared celestial chariots.
Then Pradhāna and the others undertook the exclusion from the sacrifice,
and likewise they took charge of protecting the remaining ritual materials.
The classes of kings, as well as the subjects and the merchants, took with them the pillars, cloths, pavilions, and vessels from the ocean of vehicles to their respective abodes. (2.172.50)
Requested there by the kings and entreated by the merchants,
the Lord respectfully desired to sanctify their respective countries and homes.
Hari said, "So be it," upholding his own and his subjects' desire:
"I shall come to all your abodes for your happiness. (52)
"Therefore, let all the kings depart from here to their own abodes;
but let the preceptors remain with me, established as my own kin. (53)
"Wait for my arrival in due order on the following day;
I shall come to your homes by way of circumambulation."
Having been addressed thus, all the kings, saluted by King Urala, ascended their celestial chariots and departed for their own kingdoms. (55)
Śrī Hari and the others traveled through the sky to the capital city that bestows liberation, known as Mokṣaka-pattana, which was adorned with manifold and most worthy splendors. (56)
The gate-towers were made of gold and silver, and the archways as well, shining with a brilliance equal to the light of the sun and moon, and were most beautiful. 57.
The royal highways were beautified with artificial garden flowers, with decorative festoons and the like, with pillars made of plantain trunks, and with lotus petals. (58)

With water-pitchers, welcoming gestures and the like, with variegated banners representing sacrificial rites, with beautiful verses of glory, and adorned with stage-curtains and other decorations; ||59||
The palaces were adorned with banners and turrets,
while the paths and streets were sprinkled with fragrant waters.
The royal highways were made auspicious with fragrant flowers and unguents,
and were provided with signet rings indicating victory, welcome, honor, and other such greetings.
It was beautiful, spacious, and highly esteemed, equipped with all kinds of mechanical devices;
it was ten yojanas in circumference and filled with prosperity and other such riches.
The city was adorned by people whose complexions were like white campaka flowers,
and it was delightful and captivating with its trees, creepers, houses, and gardens.
Amidst the sounds of many musical instruments and the thundering roar of the bursting of trumpets,
Bālakṛṣṇa, his pride raised by the royal armies, entered that city.
Having descended from the celestial chariot and standing upon his four-tusked elephant,
the Blessed One shone there, honored by tens of millions of people.
Richly adorned with the splendor of parasols and chowries, he was repeatedly gazed upon with cries of victory, honor, and love by the king and queen from within their elephant.
Honored, saluted, and bowed to repeatedly on the royal highway,
Hari proceeded toward the king’s palace, showing his favor to them.
The god descended slowly, accompanied by his mother and father,
joined by householders and great sages, in the auspicious courtyard.
