Then, upon the ground in front of the royal palace, which was like a great garden,
the beloveds of Brahmā as well as Īśāna and the others descended.
From the celestial chariots, along the path of the sky, he led Puruṣottama to the great divine royal palace, a beautiful refuge within the magnificent garden.
The prince Ūrukīrti and King Coralaketu honored him in many ways with devotion, offering water, food, and honey-mixture (madhuparka).
With sandalwood, unbroken rice, perfumes, and the like, with musk and fragrant essences, with vessels made of much gold, and with ornaments rich in jewels; ||72||
He worshipped Hari with an abundance of various divine articles;
then he performed the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) and offered ten million gold coins.
He gave gifts before Hari and placed jeweled necklaces around his neck;
then, having washed his feet, he drank water along with his family. (74)
A hundred sons, ten daughters, as well as other young girls, two wives, and even the female slaves drank the water born of that grace. (75)
Then all the royal yogis, along with their families— and especially the thirty daughters of the king— considered themselves to have accomplished their purpose.
Having obtained Śrī Hari, they rejoiced; they always desired the Lord with their minds.
And the great sage Yavakrīta worshipped the Supreme Lord.
Hari gave the wealth offered by the king and other riches to the great sage;
and Kṛṣṇa, being entreated by the maidens, acted according to the duty of bestowing a son.
By the will of Kṛṣṇa, the giving away of the princes took place in the royal palace;
having obtained Hari there, the maidens had their desires fulfilled. (79)
Having bowed down to their fathers, elders, and maternal relatives, and having obtained their permission,
they set their minds upon staying forever together with Śrī Hari.
Having indeed received Vaiṣṇava mantras, those maidens were purified;
with their hearts sanctified, they always remained in the midst of the beloveds of Brahmā.
There, service was performed by the king, as well as by the queen and others, by the attendants, by the chief ministers and merchants, and even by male and female servants. (82)
With foods, gifts of drink, massages, and acts of pleasing,
they took Hari even into the city and honored the Lord, the merchant.
Before dawn, having brought the beautiful Śrī Hari, Bālakṛṣṇa, the Supreme Lord, from the merchant’s own residence, those possessed of great devotion worshipped Him. (84)
They joyfully offered many dedications and performed self-surrender;
all those men and women became exclusively devoted bhaktas.
All were indeed supreme Vaiṣṇavas and servants of Bālakṛṣṇa;
eager for liberation, they took refuge in Bālakṛṣṇa. ||86||
In that city, which was illuminated on all sides by the light of lightning,
the Blessed One, Acyuta, wandered about together with his family.
Then, together with the great sages and the circle of Īśāna,
he reached his own abode in the city at dawn and indeed obtained a brief rest.
Having taken up yogic sleep and abandoned it at sunrise,
he arose, performed his own meditation, and carried out his ablutions.
Honored with warm water, sandalwood paste, and other offerings, and likewise massaged by the queen and other devoted women, the Creator of the World bathed.
Then, having performed his worship and the twilight rites, and having taken his meal, the great king returned from the assembly hall. ||9.1||
Worshipped by all beings, Lord Hari shines and triumphs;
Śrī Hari, the beloved of Kṛṣṇa, resplends with the honors of kings.
At that time, men with blackened bodies, deformed, emaciated, and filled with sorrow, arrived there in that assembly hall. 93.
Having prostrated before Hari, they said: "O Lord, grant us liberation!
We are people living here in the Uraśa region, having no other recourse. (94)
And having heard that their ancestors of the royal lineage possessed minds imbued with latent impressions (vāsanā), the Blessed One had them drink water. 95.
But those who were born before the kings, having abandoned their intense impurity, became possessed of divine bodies, four-armed, and traveled in celestial chariots. 96.
Being led by the attendants, they went to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu;
seeing this, the king experienced a most great and supreme wonder. (97)
Having bowed, he considered himself to have accomplished his purpose, even regarding his own liberation;
yet, for the sake of final liberation, he entreated the glorious Kṛṣṇa-Narāyaṇa.
"So be it," the Lord said; "when the time arrives, there shall be liberation for you along with your family"—thus he granted that boon at that time. (99)
Then, O Rādhikā, having obtained leave on the thirteenth day,
Hari was honored by the king and dispatched from there.
Adorned with necklaces and other ornaments, the illustrious Lord,
eager to depart and honored by his subjects, gave instructions to everyone in the evening.

Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Marriage Rite of Kumāra and Dānavī, the Farewell of the Great Honorees, the Lord’s Arrival at Mokṣikā, the Capital City of Uralaketu, His Wandering Through the City and Worship, and the Liberation of the King’s Ancestors," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Listen, O Rādhikā, to how the Blessed Lord bestowed knowledge upon the great-souled Yavakrīta, the son of Gaṅgā, who was a seer. || 1 ||
For the sake of the king, the royal family, and the subjects as well,
he offered what was auspicious for the purpose of preserving the lineage, making known his own status as a disciple.
Let Yavakrīta, Uśanas, the queens, and likewise these subjects,
listen to my words which are indeed centered upon Kṛṣṇa as their root.
I am the Blessed Lord, the Supreme Brahman, higher than the highest;
the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the illustrious Puruṣottama. (4)
But in the supreme, divine abode beyond the syllable (akṣara),
I dwell, shining brilliantly, possessing a divine form, attended by liberated beings who are themselves divine.
I indeed repeatedly bestow the knowledge of my own true nature upon devotees known as *muktas*, and likewise, in some cases, upon *muktānīs*.
In some places [he was worshipped] by the beloveds of Brahmā; in some places for Rādhā and Śrī;
in some places for Lakṣmī and Ramā; and likewise in some places for Māṇikya.
And to Ramā, to Jayā, and likewise to Lalitā; to Padmāvatī, to Mahālakṣmī, and likewise in some places to the attendants.
In some places [the worship is] from weapons, from ornaments, and likewise from qualities;
in some places from sovereign powers and from energies, and also from devotees.
I bestow the knowledge of my own true nature upon the one who serves me;
that indeed is declared to be the tradition (sampradāya), which is of the essence of knowledge and grants liberation.
And let them know in every way: "I am the supreme Brahman.
Today, I bestow upon you here that which is in every respect most excellent.
That which has been given by me in person must be accepted and always held within the heart;
from me, incarnations such as Kṛṣṇa and others are born constantly by the millions.
The twenty-four incarnations and likewise others by the thousands are all born from me; they are indeed endowed with my sovereign power.
Likewise, all the Nārāyaṇas are born from my own nature;
the manifestations (vyūhas) such as Vāsudeva and the others are born from my form.
But Bhūmā and the others, as well as all the lords such as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśa, and so forth—they are all indeed my portions; they become my partial manifestations. || 15 ||
Rādhā, Ramā, and all others are my various powers (praśaktis).
Goloka, Vaikuṇṭha, and the immortal abode—
these are my imperishable regions (akṣara-pradeśas), my peripheral dwellings.
The abode of the Imperishable, belonging to the Lord of all, is devoid of all human [limitations];
all other abodes of mine are possessed of human [attributes]. (17)
Just as branch-towns surround a great city,
so indeed do those branch-dwellings surround that great abode.
I am the sovereign of all incarnations; all [others] are merely joined with a portion of me.
Such indeed is my supreme state as the controller of those who exist in this manner.
Even beyond the great abode of the Imperishable (Akṣara), there is a supreme and most excellent abode;
and all around my own form, that most excellent abode of mine shines forth.
And from that supreme abode, the splendor which issued forth before [all] is called the imperishable, vast abode within all cognitions. || 21 ||
Therefore, my abode is to be realized as the imperishable, supreme, and vast;
for the imperishable is declared to be the vast, while other abodes exist within its boundary.
From that very syllable (akṣara) they abide, and from it arise millions of Lords (īśvara);
from that indeed the eight veils (āvaraṇas) become defiled.
Then the worlds of the cosmic egg always fly away like atoms;
and I always abide within all of them as the inner controller.
Whoever I am here, that same Bālakṛṣṇa, the Supreme Lord, I am there;
all those who have attained union with Me here go to the supreme abode.
I am always of one single form, endowed with all sovereignty and other perfections;
yet people, having diverse perspectives, always perceive me through their own particular views as if I were like themselves.
The gods see like gods; men see like mortals;
the Siddhas see like Siddhas, and likewise the Rishis see like Rishis. (27)
The ancestors are like fathers, and likewise the lords are like the Supreme Lord;
the incarnations are like themselves, and likewise the liberated ones are equal to the Liberated One.
Brahmā sees me as Brahmā, and those possessed of illusion see me as an illusion; likewise, the great liberated ones always see me as themselves, just as they see their own selves.
I am infinite and boundless in form, and I am immeasurable in every respect— at all times, by my essential nature, my inherent being, my qualities, and my manifestations.
There is no end to my divine forms; how then could there be an end to my manifestations?
Since there is no limit to me, how then could there be a measure for me at that time?
I am possessed of bliss; by me all living beings live.
Where there is bliss, there I am. Knowing this, one should worship me. ||32||
Whether a man or a woman, one shall thereby attain liberation;
for this city is indeed called Mokṣikā, having been honored by me upon my arrival.
Through my knowledge, this [devotion] grants liberation to the worlds dwelling [in saṃsāra];
it [leads them] to me by means of the body, the senses, the dispositions, and the internal organs.
Those people who worship me, who am situated within, cross over [the ocean of existence]—whether they are always engaged in ritual action (karmakāṇḍa), or in bodily, or even mental [action]. 35.

Even in that which is perceived by the senses, my manifestation alone is considered the giver of liberation; for my sake, everything—whether devoid of qualities (nirguṇa), divine, or pertaining to the objects of the senses—is indeed [liberating].
Thus, I consider both the insentient and the sentient to be my body;
in that [body] I am always present, and I remain distinct from it. (37)
I am in the hearth, likewise in the wood, in the fire, in the frying pan, and in the skull-cup; I am in the flour, in the cake, in the cutter, and also in the eater. (38)
I am in the stomach and the belly, in every transformation and even in strength; I am in the bodily constituents, in the embryo and so forth, and I am in childhood and also in youth. (39)
Indeed, I dwell in old age and in the corpse, in the state of becoming ashes; again, I dwell in the eater and the eaten, in the seed and the tree, and in the axe.
In cutting, in the cutter, in the state of being split, and also in sacrificial fuel;
likewise, in every case, I am in destruction, in nourishment, and in birth. (41)
Without me, not even an atom exists; everything is presided over by me.
Knowing this, one should always worship my form in all its various manifestations. (42)
Then, having attained the state beyond the qualities (nirguṇya), it becomes fit for my own nature;
this knowledge was [revealed] by me in the past at the time of creation in the supreme abode. ||43||
It was certainly offered by me to my goddess Māṇikyā, who is her vehicle;
she, in turn, gave it to Lakṣmī, the destroyer of suffering, and she gave it to Śambhu.
To the one whose nature is that of Śivarāja, it was given by Śiva to his own wife Satī; she, in turn, offered it in ancient times to her son Gaṇeśa. 45.
To her [Buddhi] for the sake of awakening, and likewise to Siddhi for the sake of perfection; from those two comes that supreme knowledge.
To Padmāvatī and to Ramā, and from those two comes Hiraṇyagarbha.
And by him, it was propagated in many ways through numerous branches to many disciples; thus it exists today within the various lineages of the tradition. ||47||
Indeed, obstacles may even arise as destroyers of the tradition;
yet knowledge must not be overcome by them, provided I am remembered within [the heart]. 48.
Therefore, the tradition must be preserved by disciples and their own disciples through body, mind, intellect, wealth, knowledge, and excellent dwellings. (49)
In this matter, for the sake of the descent of knowledge alone, the scripture is always required,
as are the Vedas and the Saṃhitā which enlightens one regarding the meaning of all the Vedas.
This *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā* should always be protected within the heart;
its expounder, my guru, should be held as my own form for the sake of worship. (5.1)
The guru is indeed initiated and knows the Saṃhitā, for he is identical with Me;
he should always make known the meaning of the Saṃhitā to people by means of stories.
One should perform the modes of my worship and so forth exactly as they have been written down;
for the purpose of worship, a stable image of me should be installed in a beautiful temple. (53)
Together with Rādhā, Ramā, Lakṣmī, Śrī, and Māṇikī;
together with Padmāvatī, Ramā, Gaṅgā, and Virajā. ||54||
Together with Sarasvatī, Durgā, Bhavānī, Brahmapriyā, and others, as well as Jayā, Padmā, Vṛndā, Tulasī, and Haṃsā. ||55||
She should be established together with Mañjulā, Sadguṇā, and Lalitā;
and with the goddess Muktā, Haimī, Śānti, or Campā. (56)
For the sake of the continuous flow of its worship, the king should offer land, villages, and so forth according to the prescribed rule, while those possessed of wealth should offer riches. (57)
For the sake of bestowing my supreme knowledge upon others, large schools and educational institutions that grant awakening must indeed be established;
teachers must be appointed, and they shall also be worshippers in my temple. (58)
And the dissemination of these books must be carried out among human beings, as well as among the gods, in other worlds, and in all the nether regions (pātālas) in every way. (59)
In each respective place, one should carry out the dissemination of the portions of the Saṃhitās;
in this way, the tradition proceeds in its form of six limbs.
Knowledge is the scripture, the teacher is the embodiment [of the deity], and the assembly of disciples is the temple.
Knowledge is said to be the supreme mantra, as well as its name, worship, and so forth. (6.1)
Another [form] is knowledge manifold, mixed with worldly convention;
it consists of the scriptures, the Vedas, the Saṃhitās, the words of the Guru, and the speech of Hari. (62)
The Guru is indeed a Vaiṣṇava who imparts knowledge, mantras, scriptures, and so forth;
and I myself am his form, the Supreme Lord, accompanied by my consort.
The noble one, the beloved of Kṛṣṇa, together with his liberated devotees and his consorts;
all my incarnations and my manifestations that accomplish tasks [are present]. 64.

The portions (aṃśas), the digits (kalās), the manifestations (āveśas), and those possessing their own forms (vibhūtisvarūpiṇas); the complete ones (pūrṇas), the worshippers, the devotees, and others who are Nārāyaṇas. (65)
One should cause a temple to be built— possessing either a hundred or a thousand pinnacle-pots (kalaśas)— made of gold, divine, fashioned from jewels, and firmly constructed.
Indeed, the groups of disciples shall become practitioners through the reception and observance of mantras; likewise, householders, men, women, and servants [shall do so]. (67)
Children, youths, and the elderly; those with wives and those who are widowed; girls and boys; the learned and those devoid of knowledge;
kings, subjects, and leaders; and those most devoted to Brahman who are free from passion—[all these were present]. (68)
The virtuous renunciants, as well as the ascetics practicing yoga; ||69||
Even those men who are eunuchs, whoever they may be among my followers, let them always worship me with a heart full of devotion and free from deceit. ||2.173.70||
If those free from thirst, passion, hatred, anger, malice, and envy were to worship me, then the tradition would become eternal. (71)
If those who have taken refuge [in the tradition] are faultless, the lineage shall attain illumination; but if those who have taken refuge are faulty, the lineage shall fall into blindness. (72)
Where there is no teacher who is a realized Buddha, who is eternally contented and free from desire, and who is endowed with restraints and observances—that tradition perishes. //73//
Where there is no teacher who is renounced, dispassionate, self-controlled, learned in the scriptures, and virtuous in conduct, that tradition perishes. //74//
Where there is no guru who is a knower, a giver of knowledge, and a destroyer of ignorance,
and who pervades all the scriptures— that tradition perishes.
Where the teacher is a thief of wealth, addicted to vice, and likewise untruthful; where he is intent solely on his own interests and remains silent—there the tradition perishes. (76)
Where the guru is devoid of compassion and regards those who have taken refuge in him as strangers, casting his disciples into suffering, that lineage perishes. //77//
Where the teacher is a destroyer of Dharma, an atheist, a rogue, and a swindler; where he is an abode of faults and a seeker of sensual pleasures—that tradition perishes. (78)
Where the guru is a consumer of all things, a hoard of craving, greed, and the like,
and whose belly is never filled, that lineage perishes.
Where those who are protectors are devourers, where saviors are mere mockers, and where betrayers of trust are held as the best—such a tradition perishes. (2.173.80)
Where those devoted to ritual action—who are like heretics, thieves, and plunderers—stand at the forefront as leaders, that tradition perishes. (8.1)
Where the members of the assembly, the judges who decide legal cases, the mediators, the extortionists, and the consumers [of bribes] exist together, that tradition perishes. ||82||
Where men are violent, engaged in injustice, contentious, antagonistic, and afflicted by suffering, there the tradition perishes. (83)
Where people who betray their guru, who perceive faults where none exist, who are devoid of devotion, and who are slanderers reside, that tradition perishes. (84)
Lacking discernment, lacking foresight, devoid of love, and transgressing the worship of those worthy of honor—such a tradition perishes. 85.
Where there is a tradition that delights in acts of violence, consumes the property of the gods,
and disregards the honor of the guru, that tradition perishes.
When those with wrong views, evil intentions, and minds obsessed by bad associations plunder the houses of others, that tradition perishes.
Where people indeed perceive faults in virtues and cannot endure the excellence of others, that tradition perishes; such is the teaching of Yama.
When the effect is non-existent [in the cause], when speech is false, when there is injustice at every step, and when there is contempt for the great—then that tradition perishes. (89)
Where there is no image of mine, nor any temple of mine, nor my Saṃhitā scripture, that tradition perishes. (2.173.90)
I have no constant discourse, nor do I possess pure disciples; my servants are not pure, and thus that tradition perishes. (9.1)
Where householders are the gurus and millions of renunciants are the disciples;
where the gurus indulge in women—that tradition perishes. (92)
If all enjoyments and luxuries reside only with the gurus, and there is no portion for renunciation therein, that tradition perishes. //93//
There is a great flaw behind the Guru, a demonic disposition in his heart, and blindness caused by grasping at appearances before him; thus, that tradition perishes. (94)
If that which men and women sigh for—the very traditions—is its own support, then that tradition perishes. 95.
Where there is neither learning nor a school, where there is no wonder, and where there are no accomplished masters, that tradition perishes. //96//
Where the disciples are merely gluttons, consuming the food of the Dharma for their own sake,
and devoid of fear of the gods, that tradition perishes.
In speech one thing, in appearance another, and yet another in the heart of a man—where such a tradition exists, that fire of action perishes. (98)
Where there is atheism regarding knowledge and action, and the display of false sovereignty, and where giving away after having first taken back occurs, that tradition perishes. 99.
O Lord of Creatures, where there are no sacred sciences, scriptures, teachers, or deities, and no temples exist, the destruction of the tradition occurs swiftly. (2.173.10)
Therefore, the mantras have been given by me; let them be given to the group of disciples.
Let them establish and worship the Vidyās, the Śāstras, the Gurus, and the Devas. || 101 ||
Having spoken thus and bestowed his blessings, he caused him to ascend the celestial chariot amidst joyful shouts of victory, the sounds of musical instruments, and the resonant blasts of trumpets.
Accompanied by his caravan and together with the sky, he went to the kingdom of Krathaka,
at the request of the sage Romāyana and King Krathaka.
Then, seeing Hari departing into the sky, O Rādhikā, the subjects cried out, "Please come back! You must protect us! Grant us your vision! (104)

Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-third chapter, titled "The Description of how Hari Bestowed the Knowledge of His Own Nature and Eternal Wisdom upon the Royal Sage Uralaketu, the Great Sage Yavakrīta, and Their Subjects," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Listen, O Rādhikā; I am the supreme Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, in the capital city of Krathaka, which bears the name Oṃkāreṣṭā.
While the city was being adorned and resounded with the humming of bees named Kṛṣṇa,
there were the Ṛṣi Romāyaṇa and King Krathaka.
Having shown him the various decorated green grounds,
he caused the celestial chariot to descend into the garden crowded with people.
When the Blessed One descended from his celestial chariot and entered the royal palace, a rain of flowers and consecrated rice fell.
Musical instruments were sounded according to the royal custom by those with sweet and pleasant voices;
well-composed songs were sung, and shouts of victory likewise arose.
The entire family of Śrī Hari— the beloved wives of Brahmā and the great sages—
descended from their celestial chariot onto the king’s residence, which was richly adorned with gold.
It was brilliantly illuminated by the light of lightning, filled with fragrant scents,
delightful with every necessary provision, and attended by male and female servants.
Amidst a great crush of attendants, chief ministers, royal family members, and the common folk, Kṛṣṇa entered the palace.
At the time of his entrance, he was honored with a welcome,
with prostrations and salutations, with affectionate glances, and with excellent auspicious parched grains.
By the king, the queen, the princes, the princesses, and the brothers and kinsmen,
Śrī Hari was [worshipped] with water and even with cool breezes.
Honored for a mere moment with fruits, juices, and excellent drinks,
all those people of his caravan, including his family members, were likewise honored.
The Supreme Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa was delighted by flower garlands, clusters of blossoms, and the sprinkling of fragrant liquids. 1–2.
Having rested for a moment in this manner, awakened by Romāyana,
Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa proceeded to the royal assembly hall.
Even at night, it shone just like day by means of lamps,
as well as by the rays of jewels that produced the effect of moonbeams.
It was vast, with deities stationed upon its wall-surfaces all around, rich with the visible splendors of gardens, and possessed of bodies as beautiful as those in heaven. || 15 ||
Having entered the assembly hall, Hari sat upon an elephant-throne,
which was enriched with the splendor of gold and diamonds and adorned with a royal umbrella and chowries.
Others, including his father and the rest, also sat down on suitable seats;
the Blessed One [inquired] after the welfare and the abundance of happiness of all the worlds.
He inquired after their health, and the people became happy;
the king and the royal family, having washed the feet of Hari, [honored him]. (18)
Then they all drank the pleasing water, which was fragrant with sandalwood,
flower garlands, and the like, as well as with golden necklaces.
The subjects worshipped the Supreme Lord with diamonds and pearls;
likewise, the principal citizens and the merchant-chiefs offered their worship.
O Lord, we have been made to fulfill our purpose by the visions of the sacred scriptures;
the holy city has been sanctified by the Blessed Śrī Hari. (21)
"Having attained rest today, grant us your vision tomorrow morning";
having spoken thus and offered their salutations, all the subjects departed. (22)
Then all the attendants quickly brought the dwellings;
and Śrī Hari, together with his family, [entered] the most beautiful royal palace.
For the sake of rest, Kṛṣṇa went with King Kratha and the ṛṣi; when a bed was shown to him, Kṛṣṇa lay down and fell fast asleep.
Having partaken of milk and other refreshments, the great ones rested;
O Rādhikā, the king, however, went to his own palace for the sake of rest.
On the morning of the fourteenth day, the glorious Lord, the Master,
having been awakened by auspicious sounds, heard his own stainless fame.
Having meditated upon himself, he then performed his daily rites in their entirety;
meanwhile, Lomaśa and other subjects likewise assembled for the purpose of seeing him.
King Krathaka, the queen, the daughters, and the sons all arrived, eager with every requisite for the worship of Hari. (28)
They washed his feet with milk and drank that water;
and they honored him with garments, ornaments, decorations, diamonds, and pearls.
They worshipped Hari with sandalwood, unbroken rice, flowers, and jewels,
and likewise satisfied their mother and father, who were as dear to them as Śuka and his beloved wife.
The daughters, who were dear to Brahmā, worshipped Lomaśa and the others;
then they performed the *ārātrika* ceremony and prostrated themselves while circumambulating [the sages]. || 31 ||
Then, having placed various offerings before him with devotion, the king spoke to Hari-Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the Teacher of the World. ||32||
My kingdom has been purified, and even my own abode has been sanctified;
my family here has also been purified. O Blessed One, dwell here forever.
"O ocean of mercy, I am yours along with my family.
And the Blessed One, who is always present in embodied form, spoke to the king.
"O King, I shall dwell in your house as if always before your very eyes;
build a temple for me and establish me here as your Lord. (35)

And the king asked Hari: "When indeed should the temple be constructed? What is the proper time—such as the auspicious moment (muhūrta) and so forth—and what are the days, lunar mansions (nakṣatra), and zodiac signs? (36)

For in auspicious undertakings such as the construction of temples and other virtuous works, the times for your installation are of the utmost importance; therefore, O Lord, tell me about them here. (37)
Hari said: "O King, whenever the Blessed One dwells upon the earth, having indeed assumed a human form, then his command must be obeyed. (38)
Whether by night or by day, at twilight or even during a period of birth-impurity; at an improper time, or likewise in an undesirable situation, or even when filled with grief and affliction—(39)
Whatever the time may be, it is considered auspicious according to that view;
for all times are dependent on Hari, and by His will they are indeed auspicious.
Every kind of place is indeed auspicious when it is resorted to by Hari;
and so too are the words of those who are capable and equal to Kṛṣṇa. 41.
At whatever time they are obtained, that time is indeed entirely auspicious; however, I shall tell you their natural excellence—listen now to their temporal superiority. (42)
Years, months, as well as fortnights, weeks, days, and nights;
constellations, planets, weekdays, four ghaṭīs, and a muhūrta. 43.
The yogas and lunar days have been determined for the sake of establishing worldly practice;
O King, listen now as I first describe those that are to be avoided, each according to its proper nature. (44)

One should indeed avoid those yogas produced by inauspicious lunar days, asterisms, and weekdays for auspicious rites; likewise, one should avoid the *vyatīpāta* and other such [inauspicious] conjunctions,
as well as unfavorable yogas, the *bhadrā* period, the new moon, and the sun’s transit (*saṃkrānti*).
One should avoid one's birth asterism, the lunar day of birth, and the month of birth. ||46||
One should avoid both the increase and the decrease of the lunar day (tithi) for auspicious rites, as well as those [lunar days] currently occupied or previously occupied by malefic planets. 47.
One should also avoid those lunar mansions that are designated for enjoyment in auspicious rites; one must likewise avoid a mansion affected by portents or pierced by malefic planets. 48.
One should avoid that *ṛta* which has been defiled by a malefic planet;
furthermore, one should avoid the asterism of a solar or lunar eclipse for a period of six months.
One should avoid the lunar mansion of an "half-bite" for a period of three months;
one should avoid the lunar mansion of a "quarter-bite" for a period of one month.
Three days prior to an eclipse should be avoided, and seven days after it one should likewise avoid;
when the sun sets eclipsed, three days before should be avoided, and when it rises eclipsed, three days afterwards.
One should avoid [the practice] for three days prior to and after a full eclipse;
likewise, one day at the end of the month and two ghaṭīs at the end of a lunar mansion.
One should avoid the single ghaṭikā at the end of a lunar day (tithi), as well as the half-ghaṭikā at the end of the ascendant (lagna),
and the poisonous hour (viṣanāḍī) of the constellations (nakṣatra) in auspicious rites.
One should avoid the fault of *pāta*, as well as the *ekārgala* and the day of combustion (*dagdhadina*), and also the time of the sun's transit (*saṃkrānti*) during auspicious rites. //54//
When the lord of the ascendant is situated in the house of an enemy or of death, one should avoid midday, midnight, and the junctions of the twilights. (55)
One should avoid an intercalary month, as well as the setting of Venus and Jupiter;
one should also avoid the childhood and old age periods of Venus and Jupiter. ||56||
One should avoid the setting of the lord of the birth sign, mental distress, birth-impurity, the mother's menses, the onset of disease, portents, and other calamities during auspicious rites.
When Jupiter is situated in Leo, one should avoid marriage, shaving, religious vows, journeys, initiation, and consecrations; for these activities will encounter obstacles therein. (58)

A lunar mansion that has been occupied by a malefic planet, or is currently being occupied, or is about to be occupied, should indeed be accepted for all undertakings as it brings about success. ||59||
However, a lunar mansion conjoined with Rāhu must indeed be avoided in auspicious rites;
likewise, a lunar mansion afflicted by a planet when it is being traversed by the Sun [is to be avoided]. (2.174.60)
If it should be consumed by the Moon, then it will bestow auspicious results;
a lunar mansion (nakṣatra) struck by an eclipse will become auspicious at the end of six months.
In the case of two eclipses within a single month, the first lunar day is pure until the commencement of the second eclipse; however, the other [lunar day] remains pure for six months.
A well dug in Caitra brings sorrow; in Vaiśākha, it is remembered as bestowing wealth;
in Jyeṣṭha, it causes affliction by malevolent planets; and in Āṣāḍha, it leads to the destruction of cattle.
In Śrāvaṇa it brings increase of wealth; in Bhādrapada, however, it makes one empty-handed;
in Āśvina it shall cause affliction; and in Kārttika it results in the loss of servants.
In Mārgaśīrṣa it bestows wealth; in Pauṣa, it grants the fulfillment of desires;
in Māgha, it brings fear of fire; and in Phālguna, it is considered to bestow prosperity.
The commencement of a house, when the Sun is situated in Aries, bestows all auspiciousness;
when in Taurus, it causes an increase in wealth; and when in Gemini, it brings about death. (66)
If situated in Cancer, it bestows auspiciousness; if in Leo, it increases fear;
if in Virgo, it causes disease; and if in Libra, it shall grant happiness. ||67||
When [the Sun] is situated in Scorpio, there is an increase of wealth; when in Sagittarius, there is great loss;
when in Capricorn, there will be acquisition of wealth; and when in Aquarius, it is considered a source of jewels. (68)
If [the moon] is situated in Pisces, it will bring fear; therefore, one should undertake an enterprise after due consideration.
Furthermore, the installation of deities in the months of Māgha and Phālguna likewise bestows wealth.
She indeed bestows long life and health upon her husband and brings him fame;
however, she occurring in Caitra should be understood as being entirely fraught with danger and disease.
In Vaiśākha and likewise in Jyeṣṭha, she bestows wealth, sons, and other blessings;
so too, when the sun is in its southern course, [the worship of] Vārāha and the Mātṛkās [yields the same].
One should comfortably install Bhairava, Vāmana, Durgā, and Nṛsiṃha;
in Śrāvaṇa, the Śivaliṅga, and in Āśvina, Jagadambikā.
In the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, one should install Hari, Viṣṇu, Nārāyaṇa, and me, the Lord;
but in the month of Pauṣa, one should install all the deities.
Singing, agriculture, painting, festivals, and houses; clothing, ornaments, decorations, and the like; craftsmanship and the arts—these are his constant occupations. (74)

On the eleventh, the first, or the sixth lunar day—on these auspicious dates known as Nandā—one should cause [the text] to be performed, have it taught, or study it oneself; this shall bring about good fortune. (75)
Marriage, the investiture of the sacred thread, journeys, wearing ornaments and the like, manual crafts, training in the arts, and the driving of elephants, chariots, and horses; ||76||
Listen as I describe how the installation during the invocation may grant success:
on the second, the seventh, the twelfth, or on an auspicious lunar day (tithi). ||77||
The maintenance and practice of military forces, warfare, and weapons; as well as expeditions, festivals, the construction of houses, medical practices, and various occupations. (78)
Listen likewise to [the rites] on the third, the eighth, and the thirteenth lunar days of the Jayā cycle; these should be performed as they bestow all accomplishments. (79)
Listen: the slaying of enemies, their binding, as well as the administration of poison, and the employment of weapons and fire should be performed on the lunar day known as Riktā.
Success is achieved on the fourth, the ninth, and the fourteenth [lunar days]. On a *riktā* day, an auspicious rite must never be performed. (8.1)

Listen: royal consecration, a military expedition, marriage, the investiture of the sacred thread, rites for peace, and rites for prosperity—these are to be performed on the lunar day known as Pūrṇā. 82.
On the fifth, the tenth, and indeed on the full moon day, it bestows accomplishment;
by performing it in this manner, the success of the task becomes certain. (83)
The second, the fifth, the third, the seventh, as well as the tenth, the eleventh, the first of the dark fortnight, and the thirteenth. (84)
Indeed, these full-moon lunar days (pūrṇimā) bring auspiciousness in all undertakings; other lunar days, however, are never considered to be givers of auspiciousness in any respect. (85)
The fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, the first day of the bright fortnight, and the day known as Darśa—these lunar days should be avoided for auspicious undertakings, as they bring fear. (86)
The Sun, the Moon, Mars, Buddha (Mercury), Jupiter, Venus, and Saturn—these are the seven days that have been ordained. (87)
Jupiter, the Moon, Mercury, and Venus are auspicious planets for auspicious actions; whereas the Sun, Saturn, and Mars are malefic planets for malefic actions.
By their very nature, the Sun is stable, the Moon is mobile, Mars is fierce, Mercury is even, Jupiter is light, Venus is mild, and Saturn is sharp. (89)
On Sunday, the installation of a deity bestows splendor and power;
on Monday, it brings security; on Tuesday, it causes fire and burning.
In Mercury, it bestows desired results; in Jupiter, it grants stability;
in Venus, it bestows joy; and in Saturn, it dwells within one's imagination.
The royal consecration, auspicious rites, the construction of vehicles and mounts, the mobilization of the army, the accomplishment of mantras, and the discharge of missiles and weapons; ||92||
The administration of medicine, fighting, trade and commerce, arson, serving [others], and even the work of a goldsmith; ||93||
Indeed, wearing ornaments on a Sunday is auspicious;
furthermore, on a Monday, one should wear conch shells, pearls, and silver.
The fashioning of ornaments, as well as the wearing of jewelry, the study of the science of music, the performance of sacrificial rites, and the practice of agriculture; ||95||
Eating, sexual intercourse, the preparation of sugarcane juice products, and the excellent undertaking of water channels, wells, and reservoirs. ||6||
Furthermore, on a Tuesday, there is a sense of division as well as falsehood;
there is also theft, deceit, and even injury by poison, weapons, or fire. (97)
The collection of taxes and fines, and the wearing of gold and coral—these auspicious activities are thus prescribed for Tuesday. 98.
Furthermore, on Wednesday, one should study, engage in trade, the arts and so forth, establish relationships, enter service, perform physical exercise, and chant the Vedas. (99)

The commencement of writing this treatise is considered auspicious through these rites; likewise, performing sacrifices on a Thursday, as well as acts of righteousness and honoring [the teacher], are likewise auspicious. (2.174.100)
Auspicious rites, nourishing ceremonies, learning, journeys, the construction of houses, medicine, and adornment—indeed, all auspicious deeds should be performed. (101)
In the period of Venus (Śukra), there is singing, association with women, and the wearing of jewels;
likewise, the preparation of beds and couches, and the wearing of garments, ornaments, and the like.
Festivals, the purchase and sale of land, agriculture, trade activities, and the protection of the treasury—these are the auspicious effects during the period of Śukra. (103)
On Saturday, one may enter a house, receive the initiation of mantras that is most excellent,
take elephants and so forth, and likewise determine upon service.
The use of weapons, speaking untruths, and even theft— these,
as well as firm undertakings and indeed auspicious deeds, should be performed during the period of Saturn.
Rohiṇī, Aśvinī, Mṛgaśiras, Puṣya, Hasta, the three Uttarās, Revatī, Śravaṇa, Dhaniṣṭhā, and Punarvasu. (106)
Anurādhā and likewise Svātī—these asterisms are indeed auspicious; all auspicious undertakings are accomplished under these lunar mansions. (107)
The three eastern constellations, Viśākhā, Jyeṣṭhā, Ārdrā, Mūla,
and Śatabhiṣaj— in these, the activity shall be common (sādhāraṇa).
Bharaṇī, Kṛttikā, Maghā, and likewise Āśleṣā— in these lunar mansions,
however, that most fierce and wicked deed should be performed.
Thus, O Rādhikā, the Lord Anādi-Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa then spoke to Kratha in the presence of the sage Romāyana.

Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of How Hari, having gone to Oṃkāreṣṭā in the capital city of Krathaka during the second Tretā cycle of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, accepted worship, rested, and when questioned by the king on the morning of the fourteenth day, spoke regarding the auspicious times and other factors for the construction of temples and so forth."

Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Listen, O Rādhikā, to what the Blessed Lord himself later declared regarding the auspicious and inauspicious effects of actions specifically according to the lunar mansions (nakṣatras). || 1 ||
Since Rohiṇī and the three Uttaras are considered to be fixed (dhruva),
one should construct temples, dig village ponds, and perform the consecration of kings under them.
Therefore, one should have all stable works performed under these [asterisms], for they are stable;
Mṛga, Citrā, Anurādhā, and Revatī are known as the "mild" (mṛdu) ones.
Therefore, one should cultivate a friendly disposition toward them, as well as sing songs and take delight;
one should always wear auspicious ornaments and garments that grant happiness.
Puṣya, Aśvinī, Abhijit, and Hasta are declared to be light and swift;
therein, one should engage in the knowledge of ornaments and medicinal herbs, travel, craftsmanship, and pleasure. (5)
Jyeṣṭhā, Ārdrā, Mūla, and Āśleṣā are said to be sharp and fierce;
therein [are performed] piercing, killing, binding, and the accomplishment of mantras, spirits, and so forth.
The three asterisms beginning with Śravaṇa, Svāti, and the latter half of Punarvasu are movable (cala).
Under these, one should undertake the mounting of horses and elephants, the construction of gardens and the like, and so forth.
Bharaṇī, Maghā, and the two Pūrvās are declared to be cruel and fierce;
therein one should effect the cutting off and destruction of poison, weapons, fire, enemies, and the like.
Viśākhā and Kṛttikā are also considered mixed or common;
the release of a bull, fire rituals, and miscellaneous rites succeed under these.
If Jupiter is in Puṣya, or in the three Uttarās, or in Rohiṇī, Mṛgaśiras, Śravaṇa, Āśleṣā, or Pūrvāṣāḍhā; ||| 2.175.10 ||
If the Guru or one devoted to him should undertake the construction of a house, it shall bestow sons, grant a kingdom, and likewise provide all forms of happiness. || 11 ||
If Aśvinī, Citrā, Śatabhiṣā, or Ārdrā are occupied by Venus, or if Venus is situated immediately after them, the commencement of a house brings the gift of wealth and food. (12)
If Mars is in Revatī, Puṣya, Hasta, Pūrvāṣāḍhā, Maghā,
or Mūla, or if Mars is situated immediately after that [asterism], then it is an auspicious time for building a house.
An undertaking begun under Rohiṇī, Aśvinī, Uttarāphālgunī, Citrā, or Hastā will either be consumed by fire or cause suffering to one's sons. (14)
Or, if one is devoted to Mercury, the commencement of a house built then bestows sons.
[The asterisms] known as the two Bhādras (Pūrvā and Uttarā), Anurādhā, Svātī, Jyeṣṭhā, and Bharaṇī— || 15 ||
Or if Saturn is predominant, and if the commencement of a house occurs there under Saturn, then without a doubt that house will become an abode for spirits and rākṣasas. || 16 ||
If the sun or the moon should be in Kṛttikā at that time,
the house begun will immediately turn into ashes from fire.
Even when the Moon and the stars are joined with or pierced by malefic planets,
and even when the strength of the Moon and the stars is deficient, rites may indeed be performed under the Puṣya asterism.
All auspicious things will indeed be accomplished; of this there is no doubt.
Having reflected thus, O Kratha, the digging of the pit and other such tasks must be performed.
And I shall declare to you the twenty-seven names of the yogas:
Viṣkumbha, Prīti, Āyuṣmān, Saubhāgya, and likewise Śobhana.
Atigaṇḍa, Sukarman, Dhṛti, Śūla, Gaṇḍaka, Vṛddhi, Dhruva, Vyāghāta, Harṣaṇa, and likewise Vajraka. ||21||
Siddhi, Vyatīpāta, Varīyān, Parigha, Śiva, Siddha, Sādhyā, Śubha, Śukla, Brahmā, Aindra, and Vaidhṛti. ||22||
Just as their names are, so indeed are they considered to be fruitful and meaningful;
one should avoid Vaidhṛti and Vyatīpāta in every way for auspicious acts.
In the case of Vajra and Vikumbha, the first three ghaṭikās must be abandoned;
in the case of Parigha, half [of its duration] is to be avoided, and in the case of Śūla, five ghaṭikās.
In the Gaṇḍa and Atigaṇḍa yogas, six ghaṭikās must be avoided; in Vyāghāta, nine ghaṭikās are to be shunned for auspicious undertakings, as they constitute the first quarter of an adverse yoga.
Now I shall tell you the karaṇas: kiṣṭughna, bava, bālava, kaulava, taittila, and likewise gara. ||26||
Merchants, forced labor, birds, quadrupeds, and elephants [should be undertaken] on the Bava karana;
rites for prosperity and the duties of the twice-born on the Balava karana. (27)
In Kaulava, one should perform acts related to women and friends; in Taitila, what is pleasing to one's wife; in Gara, the sowing of seeds; and in Vaṇija, one should engage in trade. (28)
Burning, falling, and similar acts are not auspicious during the Viṣṭi yoga; one should not move about then.
During Śakuni, however, one may administer medicine, perform mantra-sādhana, and carry out rites for nourishment (pauṣṭika).
One should perform rites for the kingdom under the asterism Govipra; rites for the ancestors under Catuṣpada; rites for good fortune under Dāruṇa; and auspicious rites under Kistughna and Magala.
On the eleventh and fourth days of the bright fortnight, Bhadrā is considered to occur in the afternoon;
on the eighth and the full moon day, Bhadrā is held to occur in the forenoon.
On the third and tenth days of the dark fortnight, Bhadrā occurs in the afternoon;
likewise, on the seventh and fourteenth days, Bhadrā occurs in the forenoon.
That Bhadrā lasts for five ghaṭīs in the mouth and one ghaṭī in the throat;
it lasts for ten ghaṭīs in the heart and five ghaṭīs in the navel.
At the hips, Bhadrā lasts for six ghaṭikās; at the tail, it lasts for three ghaṭikās.
Thus, through these thirty divisions, there are likewise six limbs of Bhadrā.
The results of these limbs in their respective undertakings are as follows:
the destruction of the task, death, the loss of fortune, the dissolution of the intellect, and strife. (35)

Therefore, the *viṣṭi* yoga must be avoided; furthermore, one should avoid eating when it falls on a Monday, Wednesday, Friday, or Thursday, provided these days coincide with a lunar mansion belonging to a deity or a sage. (36)
Bhadra is auspicious and highly beneficial; it accomplishes all undertakings.
When born in the first half of the lunar day, Bhadra occurs at night; when born in the latter half, it occurs during the day. (37)
Indeed, one should never consider faults when a necessary task must always be performed, provided that the Moon is situated in Aries, Taurus, Gemini, Scorpio, or Cancer. (38)
Bhadrā indeed dwells in heaven; she is always considered auspicious when the moon is in Libra, Virgo, or Capricorn. (39)
Bhadrā resides in Pātāla, and she too is always considered auspicious when the moon is situated in Aquarius, Pisces, Cancer, or Leo.
Bhadra exists in the world of men; she should be avoided in auspicious rites.
Vyatīpāta, Vaidhṛti, Bhadrā, and Bhauma [are inauspicious] during the afternoon. 41.
All auspicious [planets] as well as even malefic stars are considered auspicious when the Moon is situated in the birth ascendant; in such a case, the fruit that arises is prosperity. (42)
In the second house-position, there shall never be happiness at any time;
in the third, there is gain of wealth; and in the fourth, the onset of disease. ||43||
In the fifth [year], there is the destruction of one's undertakings; in the sixth, a great acquisition of wealth;
in the seventh, honor from the king; and in the eighth, death is certain.
In the ninth, however, fear is to be known; in the tenth, the success of one's undertakings.
In the eleventh [house], there is the acquisition of wealth; in the twelfth, various calamities. ||45||
In the bright fortnight, the second, fifth, and ninth lunar days are auspicious; in the dark fortnight, those nights when the stars are powerful should be accepted, for they bestow good fortune. (46)
Having made a four-cornered enclosure, a long nine-sectioned one, and a wide three-sectioned one, [there are] twenty-seven [sections]. 47.
In the first group of nine squares, the numbers one through nine should be placed in order;
likewise, in the second group of nine, the numbers ten, eleven, and eighteen should be placed in order.
In the third group of nine, the nineteenth and twenty-seventh [verses] are likewise;
having thus given [these], there is birth, prosperity, and likewise adversity within that group of nine.
Kṣema, Carma, Sadhana, Nidhana, Maitrī, and Mitratā—these are the names; she is to be known as Tārā, the birth-star consisting of ninefold nature. (2.175.50)
In the first group of nine it is that [nature], but in the second it consists of action;
in the third group of nine it is always declared to be the "placing" (ādhānā).
In each of the three groups of nine, the first, the second, and the eighth stars are proclaimed to yield middling results. ||52||
The second, fifth, and seventh stars are indeed considered inferior;
the fourth, sixth, and ninth stars are excellent and bestow fruit. (53)
An inauspicious moon, an inauspicious lunar day, and likewise an inauspicious asterism—
by overcoming these, a star situated in the sixth, fourth, or ninth house yields its fruit.
In journeys, battles, and marriages, the birth asterism (janmatārā) is not auspicious; however, it is auspicious for other virtuous undertakings as well as for entering a new home. 55.
When the Moon is in Aries, Leo, or Sagittarius, it is always situated in the East;
when it is in Taurus, Capricorn, or Virgo, the Moon is considered to be in the South. (56)
The moon is considered to be in the west during Aquarius, Libra, and Gemini;
the moon indeed resides in the north during Cancer, Pisces, and Scorpio. (57)
The Moon brings gain of wealth when in front, prosperity and happiness when in the south, death when in the west, and loss of wealth when in the north. 58.

The asterism of the instrument, the day of the week, the solar transit, the lunar day, the *kulika*, and the four-hour period (*prahara*) consisting of four *ghaṭīs*—these are the conjunctions of Mars, Saturn, and the Sun. (59)
The moon, when facing forward, removes Rāhu, Ketu, and other defects;
even though the moon is situated in a single zodiac sign, it exists in all directions.
In the east there are seventeen ghaṭīs; in the south, fifteen;
in the west, twenty-one; and in the north, sixteen ghaṭīs.
Furthermore, there are seventeen [ghaṭīs] in the east, fourteen in the south,
twenty in the west, and likewise fifteen ghaṭīs in the north.
Even when situated in a single zodiac sign, he bestows the results pertaining to each respective direction;
indeed, Jupiter is considered powerful during festivals and weddings.
In matters concerning the king, the strength of the Sun is desired everywhere;
however, the strength of Mars is required for battle, and Mercury is powerful during the study of knowledge.
The strength of Venus is for journeys, and the strength of Saturn is for initiation;
the strength of the Moon yields full results in all undertakings. (65)
On the eleventh day the Guru [Jupiter] is present, on the sixth day Bhauma [Mars], and on the thirteenth day Śukra [Venus];
on the ninth, eighth, or first day, the Sun shall be the day-lord.
On the second, ninth, and tenth lunar days, when Monday occurs, one should recognize that as the Siddhi-yoga, which brings success to all undertakings. (67)
Nandā occurs on Friday and Wednesday, Bhadrā on Saturday, Riktā on Tuesday, and Jayā on Thursday;
Pūrṇā becomes Siddhi, which, when employed as a yoga, grants success in one's undertakings.
On Sunday, Hasta; on Monday, Mṛga; on Thursday, Puṣya; and on Tuesday, Aśvinī.
Anurādhā on Wednesday, Revatī and Rohiṇī on Friday, and [Puṣya] on Saturday. ||69||
The Amṛtasiddhi yoga brings about the accomplishment of all undertakings and purposes;
however, if it occurs on the fifth lunar day (Pañcamī) when conjoined with the Hasta nakṣatra and the Sun, it is not auspicious.

Even if the sixth lunar day is joined with the Mṛgaśirā constellation and the Moon, it is not auspicious; and even if the seventh lunar day is joined with the Aśvinī constellation and Mars, it is not auspicious either.
On the eighth lunar day, Anurādhā joined with Mercury is not auspicious;
likewise, on the ninth day, Puṣya joined with Jupiter does not bring good fortune.
Although that Amṛtasiddhi must be abandoned for auspicious rites, other Amṛtasiddhi yogas accomplish all undertakings. (73)
In a marriage ceremony, one should carefully avoid Jupiter and Puṣya; in an entry ceremony, Mars and Aśvinī; and in a journey, Saturn and Rohiṇī.
On a day falling on any one of the weekdays of Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, or Saturday, and on any one of the lunar dates (tithis) of the first, fifth, sixth, tenth, or eleventh. ||75||
Under any one of Anurādhā, Rohiṇī, Punarvasu, or Maghā;
or under any one of Hasta, Viśākhā, Mūla, Śravaṇa, or Pūrvabhādrapadā. (76)
On an auspicious lunar mansion, the Kumāra-yoga is most excellent and brings about all accomplishments, occurring on any day of the week—Sunday, Tuesday, Wednesday, or Friday. (77)
On any one of the twenty-second, seventh, twelfth, or fifteenth lunar days, and under any one of the asterisms Bharaṇī, Mṛgaśiras, Puṣya, Pūrvaphalgunī, or Citrā; ||78||

If any one of the asterisms Anurādhā, Pūrvāṣāḍhā, Dhaniṣṭhā, or Uttarābhādrapadā occurs [in conjunction with the moon], it is indeed a Rājayoga, which is excellent and accomplishes the goals of one's undertakings. ||79||
When Jupiter and Saturn are within four, eight, or nine [degrees] of each other, or on either the thirteenth or fourteenth lunar day (tithi), [one should avoid it]. (2.175.80)
On any one of the asterisms Kārttikā, Ārdrā, Śravaṇa, Uttarāphālgunī, or Svātī;
or on any one of Jyeṣṭhā, Uttarāṣāḍhā, Śatatārakā, or Revatī. (8–1)
In the asterism of Ṛkṣa, the conjunction with a *sthavira* (elder) planet is excellent and accomplishes one's goals,
provided it occurs when Mars, Jupiter, or Saturn is in either the seventh, second, or twelfth house.
The Dvipuṣkara yoga occurring in any one of the asterisms Mūla, Citrā, or Dhaniṣṭhā is declared to be excellent; it bestows success in undertakings and brings happiness when beginning a task. (83)
When Mars, Jupiter, or Saturn is in any one of the second, seventh, or twelfth [houses], and when the Moon is in any one of Kṛttikā, Punarvasu, or Uttaraphalgunī; ||84||
In any of the asterisms Viśākhā, Pūrvabhādrapadā, or Uttarāṣāḍhā, there occurs the Tripuṣkara yoga, which accomplishes the purpose of all undertakings. ||85||

On the fifth lunar day, when the sun is in Hasta, there is an inauspicious conjunction of death; on the sixth lunar day, when the moon is in Mṛgaśīrṣa, there is an inauspicious conjunction of death. ||86||
On a Tuesday, under the asterism Aśvinī, on the seventh lunar day, there is an inauspicious conjunction of death;
on a Wednesday, under Anurādhā, on the eighth lunar day, there is an inauspicious conjunction of death. ||87||
On the ninth lunar day when the moon is in the Puṣya constellation and Jupiter is present, there is indeed an inauspicious conjunction with death;
on the twelfth lunar day when the sun is in Ārdrā, there is an inauspicious conjunction with weakness.
On the eleventh lunar day, when the moon is in Mṛgaśīrṣa and in conjunction with the Sāma constellation, the Abalā yoga is also impure.
On a Wednesday, when the moon is in either of the two [Punarvasu or Puṣya] and in Rohiṇī, the Abalā yoga is inauspicious.
On a Saturday in the asterism Kṛttikā, there is the "Eveless Conjunction" (abalāyoga), which is also impure;
on a Sunday in the asterism Kṛttikā, on the twelfth lunar day, there occurs the "Poisonous Conjunction" (viṣayogaka).

On the seventh lunar day of the asterism Śatabhiṣā, when it falls on a Tuesday, there is an inauspicious Viṣa-yoga. On the second lunar day of Āśleṣā, when it falls on a Saturday, there is an inauspicious Viṣa-yoga.
And on the asterism Bharaṇī, when it falls on a Sunday, a Dagdha-yoga is always considered inauspicious.
Furthermore, when the moon is in Citrā, the yoga is always considered inauspicious and burnt. ||92||
In Maṅgala (Mars) and Uttarāṣāḍhā, the burnt yoga is always inauspicious;
in Dhaniṣṭhā, when Mercury is present, the burnt yoga is always considered inauspicious. (93)
The *dagdha* yoga with Uttarā-phalgunī in relation to Jupiter is always inauspicious;
likewise, it is *dagdha* with Jyeṣṭhā in relation to Venus, and also when conjoined with Revatī in relation to Saturn. (94)
The "burnt" (dagdha) asterism should always be understood as inauspicious, for it causes the failure of one's undertakings;
likewise, when the sun is in Maghā, the Yamaghaṇṭa yoga is also inauspicious.
In Viśākhā with the Moon, he is [the Yama-ghaṇṭa]; in Ārdrā with Mars, he is likewise;
in Mūla with Mercury, he is the Yamaghaṇṭa; and in Kṛttikā with Jupiter, he is that same one. (96)
That Yamaghaṇṭa occurring on the Rohiṇī nakṣatra with Venus, or on the Hasta nakṣatra with Saturn, must always be avoided; it never bestows auspiciousness.
When the moon is in the fourth, sixth, thirteenth, twentieth, or ninth lunar mansion from the sun’s mansion, it is the Ravi-yoga, which bestows all auspiciousness. ||98||
"O Rādhikā, the Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, who is without beginning, is the destroyer of the multitude of manifold defects and is always the bestower of auspiciousness. (99)
He said to Krathaka: "Everything that has been spoken by me to you is likewise a giver of knowledge regarding auspicious times and a bringer of results for one's undertakings. (2.175.10)

Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of Auspicious and Inauspicious Actions and Their Results in the Lunar Mansions, the Bhadrā-cakra, the Results of the Moon, the Strength of the Stars, the Moon’s Motion, the Siddhi-yoga-cakra, Auspicious and Inauspicious Yogas, and the Strengths of the Sun and Other Planets," in the second section, the Tretā-saṃtāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Listen, O Rādhikā, to the twenty-eight yogas beginning with Ānanda, which the Blessed Lord spoke to Kratha; I shall now declare them to you. (1)
Likewise, when the Moon is conjoined with Aśvinī, Puṣya, or Mṛgaśīrṣa;
and when Mars is conjoined with Āśleṣā; and when Mercury is conjoined with Hastā. || 2 ||
When Venus is situated in Anurādhā and Saturn is in Śatabhiṣaj, while Jupiter is in Uttarāṣāḍhā, it is the Ānanda Yoga, which bestows success.
When the Sun is conjoined with Bharaṇī, when the Moon is conjoined with Ārdrā, when Mars is conjoined with Maghā, and likewise when Mercury is conjoined with Citrā; || 4 ||
When Jupiter is conjoined with Jyeṣṭhā, Venus is joined with Abhijit,
and Saturn is situated in Pūrvabhādrapadā, that configuration is known as Kāladaṇḍaka.
Since death is the result, one must therefore avoid [these] in all ritual actions whatsoever;
however, when the Sun is conjoined with Kṛttikā and the Moon is situated in Punarvasu, [it is auspicious].
When Mars is situated in Pūrvaphalgunī, when Mercury is likewise joined with Svātī, when Jupiter is joined with Mūla, when Venus is in Śravaṇa, and when Saturn [is in the same]; || 7 ||
In Uttarābhādrapadā, there is the Dhūmrākṣa yoga, which yields the fruit of unhappiness;
one ghaṭikā at its commencement must be avoided, after which it bestows happiness.
On Sunday, Rohiṇī; on Monday, Puṣya;
then on Tuesday, Uttarāphālgunī; and likewise on Wednesday, Viśākhā.
Pūrvāṣāḍhā when Jupiter is present, Dhaniṣṭhā likewise when Venus is present,
and Revatī when Saturn is present— this is the Prajāpati yoga, which bestows good fortune.
If the Sun is in Mṛgaśirā, the Moon in Āśleṣā, Mars in Hastaka, Mercury in Anurādhā, and Jupiter likewise in Uttarāṣāḍhā; || 11 ||
When Śatatārakā (Pūrvabhādrapadā) occurs with Venus, or Aśvinī with Saturn, that is the Saumya Yoga which bestows good fortune; it should be avoided for five ghaṭikās.
Ārdrā is for the Sun, Maghā for the Moon, Citrā for Mars,
Jyeṣṭhā for Mercury, Abhijit for Jupiter, and Pūrvābhādrapadā for Venus.
On Saturday, when the moon is in Bharaṇī, that is the Dhvāṅkṣa yoga, which causes the destruction of wealth;
likewise on Sunday in Punarvasu, and on Monday in Pūrvāphālgunī. (14)
When Mars is in Svāti, Mūla in Mercury, Śravaṇa likewise in Jupiter, Uttarabhādrapadā in Venus, and Kṛttikā when Saturn is present; || 15 ||
The Dhvaja-yoga indeed bestows happiness and grants victory in all undertakings.
Puṣya and Uttarā-phālgunī on Sunday, and likewise on Monday and Tuesday; || 16 ||
Viśākhā on Wednesday, Pūrvāṣāḍhā on Thursday, Dhaniṣṭhā on Friday, and Rohiṇī on Saturday—this auspicious Śrīvatsa yoga brings happiness. (17)
In the case of the Sun, Anurādhā is for embracing; on Monday, Hasta;
on Wednesday, Uttarāṣāḍhā; and on Thursday, Śatabhiṣaj. (18)
When Venus is in Aśvinī and Saturn is in Mṛga, it is the Vajra yoga, which brings about destruction;
it should be avoided for five ghaṭikās, though in some cases it may occasionally bestow auspicious results.
If the Sun is in Maghā, the Moon in Citrā, Mars in Jyeṣṭhā, Mercury in Abhijit, Jupiter in Pūrvābhādrapadā, and Venus in Bharaṇī; 2.176.20.
The conjunction known as Mudgara, occurring on a Saturday with the Ārdrā nakṣatra, causes the destruction of wealth;
it should be avoided for five ghaṭikās, though it may occasionally be auspicious. (21)
When the Sun is in Pūrvāphālgunī, Svāti in the Moon, Mūla in Mars, Śravaṇa in Mercury, and Uttarābhādrapadā in Jupiter; ||22||
When Kṛttikā falls on a Friday and Punarvasu on a Saturday,
that is indeed declared to be the Chatra Yoga, which always bestows honor upon kings.
When Uttarāphālgunī coincides with Sunday, Viśākhā with Monday, Pūrvāṣāḍhā with Tuesday, and Dhaniṣṭhā on Wednesday; || 24 ||
When Revatī occurs on a Thursday or Friday, Rohiṇī on a Saturday, or Puṣya on a Saturday, that is indeed declared to be the Mitrayoga, which bestows nourishment in all undertakings. (25)
On Sunday, Hasta and Anurādhā;
on Monday and Tuesday, Uttarāṣāḍhā; and on Wednesday, Śatabhiṣaj. (26)
Aśvinī with Jupiter, Mṛgaśīrṣa with Venus, and Āśleṣā with Saturn—this yoga is indeed called Mānasa, which bestows happiness in all undertakings. ||27||
When the Sun is in Citrā and the Moon in Abhijit; when Mars is in Pūrvābhādrapadā and Mercury in Bharaṇī; and when Jupiter is in Ārdrā and Venus in [Punarvasu]. (28)
When Maghā is joined with Saturday, it is the Padma-yoga, which brings the acquisition of wealth;
however, the first four ghaṭikās must be avoided, as it is thereafter considered to bestow happiness. (29)
When Svāti, Mūla, and Indrā (Jyeṣṭhā) fall on Sunday; Śravaṇa on Tuesday; Uttarābhādrapadā on Wednesday; and likewise Kṛttikā on Thursday.
When Venus is in the asterism of Śravaṇā and Saturn is in Pūrvaphalgunī, there occurs the Lambuka yoga;
it causes the loss of wealth and must be avoided for exactly four ghaṭikās.
When Viśākhā falls on Sunday, Pūrvāṣāḍhā on Monday, Dhaniṣṭhā on Tuesday, Revatī on Wednesday, and Rohiṇī on Thursday; ||32||
When Puṣya coincides with Venus and Uttarāphālgunī with Saturn, that is the yoga of portents (utpātayoga), which must be avoided because it results in the destruction of life. ||33||
Anurādhā is [assigned] to the Sun, Uttarāṣāḍhā likewise to Mercury, Śatabhiṣaj to Mars, Āśleṣā to Mercury, and Mṛgaśīrṣa to Jupiter. (34)
Āśleṣā with Venus and Hasta with Saturn constitute a yoga of death;
it should always be avoided, for it is indeed full of the fruit of death. (35)
Jyeṣṭhā is for the Sun, Abhijit for the Moon, Pūrvabhadrapadā for Mars; Bharaṇī for Mercury, Ārdrā for Jupiter, and Maghā for Venus and Saturn. (36)
That Kaṇayoga with Citrā is troublesome and should be avoided for two ghaṭīs.
Mūla is [inauspicious] on Sunday, Śravaṇa on Monday, and Uttarābhādrapadā on Tuesday.
Kṛttikā with Mercury, Vasu with Jupiter, Pūrvaphālgunī with Venus, and Svātī with Saturn constitute Siddha-yoga; its fruit shall be the accomplishment of one's undertakings. ||38||
Pūrvāṣāḍhā on Sunday, Dhaniṣṭhā and Revatī on Monday, Rohiṇī on Wednesday, Puṣya on Thursday, and Uttarāphālgunī on Friday. (39)
When Saturn is in Viśākhā, that is an auspicious conjunction which brings about welfare;
when the Sun is in Uttarāṣāḍhā, and the Moon is in Śatabhiṣaj (Śatatārā).
Aśvinī on Tuesday, Mṛgaśirā on Wednesday, Āśleṣā on Thursday, Hasta on Friday, and likewise Anurādhā on Saturday. (41)
That is the yoga of Amṛtasiddhi, which brings about prosperity such as royal splendor and the like;
it occurs when the sun is in Abhijit or Pūrvābhādrapadā, and likewise when the moon is in those same asterisms.
Bharaṇī with Mars, Ārdrā with Mercury, Maghā with Jupiter, Citrā with Venus, and Jyeṣṭhā with Saturn—this is called the Mūlaśalya yoga. ||43||
That which lasts for four ghaṭikās causes the loss of wealth; it must certainly be avoided.
[This applies when] the Sun is in Śravaṇā and the Moon is likewise in Uttarābhādrapadā.
Kṛttikā on Tuesday, Punarvasu on Wednesday, Pūrvāphālgunī on Thursday, Svāti on Friday, and likewise Mūla on Saturday. (45)
The Gadayoga causes destruction; it lasts for seven ghaṭīs and must be avoided.
Dhaniṣṭhā occurs on Sunday, Revatī on Monday, and Rohiṇī on Tuesday.
Puṣya with Mercury, Uttarāphālgunī with Jupiter, Viśākhā with Venus, and Pūrvāṣāḍhā with Saturn constitute the Mātaṅga yoga. (47)
He is considered a bestower of family prosperity and a performer of auspicious deeds at all times.
Śatatārā occurs on Sunday, Aśvinī on Monday, and Mṛgaśirā on Tuesday. (48)
Āśleṣā with Mercury, Hasta with Jupiter, Anurādhā with Venus, and Uttarāṣāḍhā with Saturn—this indeed is the Rākṣasī yoga. (49)
It brings great suffering and must always be avoided in auspicious rites;
likewise, Pūrvābhādrapadā when the sun is in it, and Bharaṇī when the moon is in it.
Ārdrā with Mars, Maghā with Mercury, Citrā with Jupiter, and Jyeṣṭhā with Venus or Śravaṇa constitute the Carayoga, which causes the failure of one's undertaking. ||51||
That period of three ghaṭikās is indeed to be avoided; thereafter, it may occasionally bring profit.
When the sun is in Uttarā-bhādrapadā, and likewise when the moon is in Kṛttikā.
Punarvasu on Tuesday, Pūrvāphālgunī on Wednesday, Svāti on Thursday, Mūla on Friday, and likewise Śravaṇa on Saturday. (53)
The Sthirayoga causes great undertakings and increases everything;
it occurs when the Sun is in Revatī, the Moon in Rohiṇī, and Mars in Puṣya.
Uttarāphālgunī on Wednesday, Viśākhā likewise on Thursday, Pūrvāṣāḍhā on Friday, and Dhaniṣṭhā when it falls on Saturday; ||55||
That yoga known as Vardhamāna, which has the ascendant as its maker, is always auspicious:
on the first lunar day when the Sun or Venus is present, and on the second lunar day when the Moon or Mercury is present. 56.
The third lunar day on Tuesday, the fourth on Saturday, the fifth on Thursday, the sixth on Tuesday or Friday, and likewise the seventh on Wednesday. (57)
The eighth and ninth lunar days are auspicious when they fall on a Sunday, a Saturday, or a Tuesday;
likewise, the tenth day is auspicious when it falls on a Thursday or a Monday. (58)
The eleventh lunar day falls on a Thursday or Friday; the twelfth on a Wednesday;
the thirteenth on a Tuesday or Saturday; and the fourteenth on a Saturday. (59)
If the fifteenth lunar day (pañcadaśī) falls on a Thursday (gurau), it is the Siddhiyoga, which brings auspiciousness.
Now, I shall describe to you twelve other inauspicious yogas. (2.176.60)
Hutāśana, Dagdha, Viṣa, and likewise Krakaca; Saṃvarta, Caturthīgṛha, Mṛtyu, and Vajrapātaka. ||6 1||
Likewise, Kālamukha and Jvālāmukha are to be avoided; these are inauspicious.
On the sixth day is the Moon, on the seventh is Mars, and on the eighth day is Mercury.
On the ninth day, Jupiter and Venus [are unfavorable]; on the tenth and eleventh, Saturn;
and on the twelfth, the Sun—this conjunction with fire is always inauspicious. (63)
On the third day Mercury, on the fifth Mars, on the sixth Jupiter, on the eighth and ninth Venus, and on the eleventh indeed Saturn; and [on the twelfth] the Moon. (64)
When the twelfth lunar day falls on a Sunday, it is always considered the inauspicious *dagdhayoga*.
Mercury is [the lord] on the second, the Sun on the fourth, and the Moon on the sixth. (65)
When Saturn and Mars are on the seventh day, Jupiter likewise on the eighth,
and Venus on the ninth, that is a "poisonous" conjunction (viṣayoga) which brings great fear.
On the sixth day Saturn, on the seventh Venus, likewise Jupiter on the eighth,
Mercury on the ninth, and likewise Mars on the tenth.
When the moon is on the eleventh lunar day and the sun likewise on the twelfth, that yoga is indeed called Krakaca; it is considered inauspicious in every respect. (68)
If Mercury is in the first house and the Sun in the seventh, it is the inauspicious Saṃvarta yoga;
likewise, if Saturn is in the first, Venus in the second, and Jupiter in the third. (69)
On the fourth day Mercury, on the fifth Mars, on the sixth the Moon, and on the seventh the Sun;
the conjunction with the house of the fourth day is inauspicious.
In the first [house], Jupiter and Mars; in the second, Venus and Jupiter;
in the third, Mercury and Venus; and in the fourth, Venus and Jupiter. ||71||
On the fifth day, it is Saturn; on the sixth, likewise Jupiter and the Sun;
on the seventh, the Sun, Moon, Jupiter, and Venus; and on the eighth, Mercury. (72)
The ninth [tithi] falls on Friday and Saturday; after that, the tenth;
on the eleventh day are Sunday and Tuesday; and on the twelfth are Monday and Jupiter.
On the thirteenth day, Mercury and the Moon [form a yoga]; likewise, Saturn on the fifteenth;
and Mercury, Venus, and the Sun on the fourteenth constitute the Mṛtyu (Death) Yoga. ||74||
This inauspicious death-inducing [asterism] must always be avoided;
however, Anurādhā on the second day and the three Uttarās on the third [are auspicious]. (75)
On the fifth day, however, is Maghā; on the sixth, Rohiṇī follows thereafter;
Hasta and Mūla are on the seventh, and Pūrvābhādrapadā on the eighth.
If Kṛttikā occurs on the ninth lunar day, Rohiṇī on the eleventh,
and Citrā or Svāti on the thirteenth, that conjunction is known as Vajrapātaka.
It certainly causes suffering equal to a thunderbolt strike during undertakings on the third lunar day of Anurādhā and on the fourth lunar day of the three Uttarās. (78)
On the fifth lunar day with Maghā, on the eighth with Rohiṇī, and on the ninth with Kṛttikā—this is the yoga known as Kālamukha, which always yields inauspicious results. (79)
On the first lunar day, Mūla; on the fifth day, Bharaṇī;
on the eighth, Kṛttikā; on the ninth, Rohiṇī; and on the tenth, Āśleṣā.
And that Jvālāmukha yoga is always inauspicious, causing constant agitation;
it occurs on the seventh lunar day with the asterism Bharaṇī, on the ninth with Puṣya, and on the tenth with Āśleṣā.
On the thirteenth day, Citrikā occurs, for that is indeed an inauspicious conjunction;
on the first [tithi] there is the Sun and Mars, and on the second, Venus and the Moon.
On the third day Mercury, on the fourth Jupiter, on the fifth Saturn, on the sixth the Sun and Mars, and on the seventh Venus and the Moon. (83)
The Moon on the eighth and ninth, Jupiter on the tenth, Saturn on the eleventh, and the Sun, Mars, the Moon, and Venus on the twelfth. (84)
Mercury in the thirteenth, Jupiter in the fourteenth, and Saturn in the full [fortnight]—these are declared to be inauspicious yogas that obstruct all undertakings. (85)
At the junction of the constellations Jyeṣṭhā and Mūla, as well as that of Revatī and Aśvinī, and within the interval between Āśleṣā and Maghā, there is a period of four ghaṭīs.
Two ghaṭīs before and two ghaṭīs after [the junction] constitute the Gaṇḍānta yoga;
that too must be avoided in auspicious undertakings, for the Gaṇḍaka yields undesirable results.
Between the fifth and sixth [tithis],
at the junction of the full moon and the first day of the lunar fortnight, and between the tenth and eleventh, there is a *gaṇḍānta* lasting for two *ghaṭikās*.
Two ghaṭikās at the end of the ninth [tithi], one ghaṭī at the end of the fifth,
and half a ghaṭikā at the end of the fourth— this is also known as the gaṇḍānta, which should be avoided.
The interval between Cancer and Leo, the interval between Pisces and Aries,
and the middle of Scorpio and Sagittarius are known as the *gaṇḍānta* (critical junctions) measured in *ghaṭīs*.
From the Sun to Saturn, these Muhūrtas are respectively fourteen, twelve, ten, eight, six, four, two, and one. (91)
Those forms of the Kulika-yoga should be avoided in auspicious rites;
from Mercury to Mars, those very same figures constitute the Muhūrta-numbers.
Gradually, those [muhūrtas] consisting of the conjunction of thorns (kaṇṭaka-yoga) are also to be abandoned;
from the teacher (Guru) up to Mercury (Budha), the numerical values of the muhūrtas are indeed those very same ones.

In due order, that very yoga known as Kālavelā must be avoided; likewise, those same Muhūrta-numbers from Śukra up to Guru [are to be avoided]. Yamaghaṇṭa, indeed, should be avoided in succession for the most excellent rites.
The Kulikas and others have been described for the day; now listen to those for the night. ||95||
From Sunday to Saturday, these muhūrtas are respectively thirteen, eleven, nine, seven, five, three, and one. (96)
Those forms of the Kulika-yoga should be abandoned in auspicious rites;
from Mercury to Mars, those very same [planetary] figures constitute the "thorn" (kaṇṭaka).
From Jupiter to Mercury, those *tens* (units) are the *kālavelikās*;
from Venus to Jupiter, those *tens*, however, are the *yamaghaṇṭakas*. ||98||
These [periods] must be avoided at all times during auspicious rites in the latter part of the night; indeed, the fourteenth muhūrta of the sun is to be avoided for evil deeds. 99.
Likewise, for the Moon, the ninth and twelfth [houses] are indeed to be avoided as they are unfavorable;
for Mars, the seventh is to be avoided at night and the fourth during the day. (2.176.10)
In Mercury, the eighth; in Jupiter, the sixth and twelfth should also be avoided;
in Venus, the fourth and ninth; and in Saturn, the first and second. (10.1)
These indeed are the evil moments that must be avoided during auspicious rites;
however, when the Moon is auspicious, all of them become weak and proclaim good fortune. (102)
In the conjunction of accomplishment (siddhi-yoga), even bad yogas are powerless and become indicators of success;
this occurs when the sun is at the center of the sky during the muhūrta called Abhijit.
The two-ghaṭī period known as Jayamuhūrta destroys all defects;
any undertaking begun therein brings victory—of this there is no doubt.
Then, a staff seven finger-breadths long should be placed upon the ground.
Its shadow should be observed, just as that which is called the "shadow of accomplishment" (siddhacchāyā).
On Sunday it is eleven finger-breadths long; on Monday, eight and a half finger-breadths;
on Tuesday, nine finger-breadths long; and on Wednesday, eight finger-breadths long.
When it is made by the Sun, [the shadow] is seven fingers long for Jupiter, eight and a half fingers long for Venus, and likewise eight and a half fingers long for Saturn. (107)
That Muhūrta called Siddhicchāyā makes even the inauspicious [planets] auspicious—the asterism, lunar day, day, lunar mansion, moon, planet, and so forth. (108)
"Only after deliberating upon these aforementioned points should auspicious works such as the digging of wells be undertaken.
Thus did Śrī Hari speak then to King Krathaka, O Rādhā. (109)

Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of Malefic Yogas Born from the Twenty-Eight Lunar Days, Weekdays, and Asterisms Beginning with Ānanda, as Well as the Three Types of Gaṇḍānta Yogas, Kulikā and Other Malefic Muhūrtas, Abhijit, and Chāyā-muhūrta," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmīnārāyaṇīya-saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Listen, O Rādhikā, to how Hari spoke to Kratha regarding the higher planets and other matters; I shall relate that as well as other relevant information. 1.
The Sun is the lord of Aries, the Moon of Taurus, and likewise Mars of Capricorn;
Mercury is the lord of Virgo, and indeed Jupiter is the lord of the sign Cancer. (2)
Indra (Jupiter) is in Pisces and Saturn is in Libra; indeed, these two are situated in their exaltations.
Furthermore, the Sun is in Libra and the Moon is likewise in Scorpio.
Mars is indeed the lord of Cancer, and Mercury is likewise the lord of Pisces;
Jupiter is the lord of Capricorn, Venus of Virgo, and Saturn resides in Aries.
These, situated in their debilitated positions, should be understood as not at all bestowing happiness;
for Virgo is the domicile of Rāhu, while Gemini is its period of exaltation.
The bow should be understood as its debilitated position, and its result is likewise;
[this applies] when the ascendant is of dual or fixed nature, excluding the eighth and twelfth houses. (6)
If auspicious planets are situated in other houses, and if malefic planets are situated in the eleventh and the sixth houses; || 7 ||
The commencement of houses, mansions, and palaces is auspicious there, provided Jupiter and the Sun are in the ascendant and Mercury is in the sixth or seventh house. (8)

If Venus is in the fourth house and Saturn is in the third, then if one should undertake the construction of a house or similar undertaking, that [house] will indeed have a lifespan of a hundred years. || 9 ||
If Venus is in the ascendant, the Sun in the third house, Mars in the sixth, and Jupiter also in the fifth, one may build a house; that house will indeed grant a lifespan of two hundred years.
If the Sun is in the eleventh house, Venus in the ascendant, and Mercury in the tenth house,
and one constructs a house or similar structure there, it will indeed last for a hundred years.
If one constructs a house when Jupiter is in the fourth house, Saturn and Mars are in the eleventh,
and the Moon is in the tenth, that house will indeed grant a lifespan of eighty years.
If Venus is in its exaltation or in the ascendant, or Jupiter is in the ascendant or the fourth house, and Saturn is in its exaltation or in the eleventh house, that house bestows prosperity. (1-3)
If Cancer and the Moon are in the ascendant, and Jupiter is in a quadrant, while the other planets are in their exaltation signs or in their friendly signs; || 14 ||
