Through that conjunction, the house built shall become eternal and a bestower of prosperity, provided that Venus is situated in the ascendant of the sign of Pisces. (15)
If Jupiter is situated in the fourth house, and Saturn is in the eleventh house, [then... (16)
A house begun under these [planets] bestows prosperity and long life;
however, all planets are not auspicious when situated in the twelfth or eighth house. (17)
Malefic planets situated in the ascendant, the trines, or the tenth house are not auspicious;
nor is the Moon in the ascendant conjoined with Mercury auspicious. (18)
The Moon situated in the eighth house is neither auspicious nor inauspicious;
even if all the planets should be in their debilitation degrees, [the result] is determined therein.
Indeed, the house shall be destitute of wealth, and no undertaking whatsoever should be undertaken there;
moreover, some single planet [is situated] in the ninth division (navamāṃśaka) of a malefic planet.
If the lord of the ascendant is likewise situated in the tenth or the seventh house, yet remains weak, then that is the house [of the planet]. 21.
That [result] will certainly occur within a year once it has passed into the hands of another;
so too for whichever planet is the lord of the ascendant, the lord of the birth [sign], or the lord of the [current] sign. (22)
Likewise, if the Moon, Jupiter, and Venus have not set, and if they are situated in their exaltation, their own signs, or their own degrees; ||23||
A house begun at that time always becomes a bestower of happiness and prosperity;
furthermore, if at the time of consecration the Sun is in the Lagna or the Kuṇḍalī.

If [the planets] should be situated in the places of strength—the third, sixth, tenth, and eleventh—and likewise the Moon should also be in those aforementioned positions, [then it is auspicious]. ||25||
In the signs of Sagittarius, Taurus, Libra, and Aries, such a person will be excellent;
likewise, Mars and Saturn in the third house, and the benefics in the eleventh and sixth houses [bring similar results]. (26)
If Mercury and Jupiter are auspiciously situated in the twelfth, eighth, or other [favorable] houses, and Venus is in the first, second, third, fourth, fifth, or ninth house; ||27||
He who is situated in the tenth or eleventh house is indeed most excellent;
whereas the malefic planets are the Sun, Mars, Saturn, Rāhu, and Ketu. (28)

If they [the malefics] should be in the first, eighth, fifth, and seventh houses, and likewise the benefic planets should be so placed, and the Moon should likewise be in the eighth or the first house; ||29||
In the sixth and eighth houses, these planets become Kuṇḍalis and must be abandoned;
however, the consecration of the deity Sūrya in Leo ascendant is considered auspicious.
For Hara, it is in Gemini; for Viṣṇu and myself, in Virgo;
for Brahmā, in Aquarius; and for the minor deities, in a movable sign.
Likewise, the installation of the Yoginīs is considered appropriate when the ascendant (lagna) is indeed movable;
however, for the Goddesses, a stable installation is best when the ascendant is of dual nature.
When the ascendant is fixed (sthira), the installation of all deities is considered most excellent;
however, if the Moon is in the first house during the installation or the ear-ornament rite, it brings death.
In the second house, however, the Moon bestows an increase of grain;
but in the third house, which represents valor, the Moon indeed becomes a giver of suffering.
The Moon situated in the fifth house causes the destruction of one's lineage and progeny;
in the sixth house it bestows fear from enemies, and in the seventh house the Moon brings suffering. (35)
In the eighth house, the Moon bestows death and causes obstacles; in the ninth, it is the Moon itself;
in the tenth, it bestows strength; and situated in the eleventh, the Moon bestows wealth. (36)
The Moon situated in the twelfth house causes expenditure; indeed, the Moon is like an earring.
Even if the Moon is auspicious, it becomes malefic if it is located in the seventh place from a malefic planet.
Likewise, one who is joined with malefic planets is impure;
similarly, one who is weak and situated among malefic planets is also impure. ||38||
If [the Moon] is in its sign of debilitation and also in a division belonging to Saturn, it will be inauspicious;
however, if it is conjoined with or aspected by Jupiter, it will become auspicious. ||39||

It may be situated in its own sign, or in its exaltation, or it may be auspicious; it may be located in the ninth-part (navāṃśa) of an auspicious planet, or in the ninth-part of its own or a very friendly planet. ||2.177.40||
Even if it (the Moon) should be inauspicious, it becomes auspicious when situated in the first, fourth, seventh, or tenth house from the Moon. ||41||
If the planet should be malefic, then by that same sequence these following configurations are inauspicious:
Āpīḍā, Saṃpīḍā, Bhṛgu, and likewise Vartitā. ||42||
In that case, once the task is completed, there would be the destruction of four things: oneself, one's relative, one's wife, and one's merit; therefore, one should not undertake such a task.
If there is a malefic planet even in that zodiac sign where the Moon is located, then a conjunction occurs which is a defect and must be avoided in auspicious rites. //44//

When the Moon is conjoined with Mercury or Jupiter, there is indeed no fault arising from the conjunction; nor are there any defects produced by the year, solstice, season, month, asterism, fortnight, or the "burnt" day (dagdhāha). //45//

The defects arising from the conjunctions of Andhaka, Kāṇa, and others, as well as those produced by the Navāṃśas of Saturn, Mars, and the Moon, are destroyed when Jupiter, Mercury, and Venus occupy angles or trines. (46)

All defects arising from the *kunavāṃśas*, planetary positions, the six-fold divisions (*ṣaḍvarga*), the *kṣaṇa* periods, and the ascendant—all these vanish by the power of the Moon when it is in the eleventh house. (47)

If Jupiter is in the Lagna in its Vargottama division, or if the Moon and Sun are in the eleventh house, or if Jupiter is in a quadrant or a trine, then by that strength all defects are destroyed. 48.
Having abandoned the seventh house, Mercury in a quadrant or a trine destroys even a hundred faults; Venus does so for two hundred among those same positions.
Among those, the Guru destroys a hundred thousand faults; the undertaking shall become auspicious.
This occurs if the lord of the ascendant is situated either in the ascendant itself or in its ninth-part (navāṃśa). || 2.177.50 ||
Whether in the eleventh house or in a quadrant, it destroys all defects;
moreover, when the strength of the ascendant is excellent, malefic planetary combinations never cause harm. (51)
Having counted from the first day of the bright fortnight according to the number of the lunar day (tithi), from Sunday according to the number of the weekday,
and from Aśvinī according to the number of the lunar mansion (nakṣatra).
Then, having combined those numerical values, they should be divided by four;
if one remains as the remainder, the earth is situated [there], which brings strife at the commencement of a house.
If two remain as the remainder, the Earth is seated; if three remain as the remainder, she is auspicious;
and if zero remains as the remainder, she is awake—at the commencement of building a house, she bestows undesirable results.
Having thus surveyed everything here, O Kratha, construct a magnificent palace for my sake, so that I may obtain offerings, service, and the like. (55)
Having spoken thus, the Lord, the Supreme Ruler beloved of Kṛṣṇa, became silent;
Krathaka, holding those words in his heart, worshipped the Supreme Lord.
Likewise, other people with their hair standing on end worshipped,
and full of eagerness, they paraded Hari through that city.
With auspicious vehicles, mounts, musical instruments, and the like, along with welcoming words and infinite offerings, they worshipped the Imperishable One.
There, Hari gave everything to the high-souled Romāyana;
and he bestowed a gracious gift upon the king and his family.
Having purified the city as well as the mansions of the wealthy merchants,
he returned to the royal palace and partook of a meal.
Then all those daughters of the king took their food;
however, the five divine ones who knew the Self grasped the hand of Hari.
The gift of the prince took place at midday;
thereafter, they departed from the kingdom together with the prince, just as [the gods] did with Hari.
All the sages, headed by Lomaśa, who were dear to Hari and likewise dear to Brahmā, departed in their celestial chariots after receiving leave.
And they were dispatched by the king, preceded by royal honors;
thereafter, they were entreated by King Pṛthu of Kṛpāsthalādri.
Accompanied by King Pṛthu, as well as the sage Kṛpāsthala,
and joined by the subjects, Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa traveled through the sky.
By way of the divine vehicle, they beheld from the sky the royal capital of Jarasthalī, O Rādhikā, which was adorned by the forest.
Seeing her standing on the bank of the river Pṛthā, rich with the beauty of the welcome ceremonies performed,
the subjects raised a proclamation of victory for the celestial chariot.

Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Results of High and Low Planets, the Results of Planets Situated in the Ascendant Chart at Pratiṣṭhāna, the Results of the Moon, Yogas such as Āpīḍa, the Defect of Conjunction (Yuti-doṣa), the Strength of the Ascendant, the Examination of 'the Earth is Asleep' and so forth, and thereafter the Wandering through the City, the Worship, the Farewell, and the Arrival at Jarasthalī, the Capital of King Pṛthu," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Goddess Rādhikā, my beloved of dear life and beautiful form;
Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa departed for Jarasthalī by means of a celestial chariot.
At that time, Hari, seated upon his celestial chariot, welcomed the family of King Pṛthu and caused Acyuta to descend from it.
Making the air resound with the sounds of musical instruments, shouts of victory, the bursting of mechanical devices,
and the booming of kettledrums, ḍaṃkaka drums, and vigalīs.
Receiving the worship of the necklace, the king stood nearby on the ground in a great garden on the bank of the Pṛthā, resplendent with royal palaces.
The Lord descended from the vast expanse of the sky onto the broad earth;
the King himself presented necklaces to Śrīśa, the Supreme Soul.
Then Kṛpī gave necklaces to Kaṃbharā for the sake of Śrī;
her young daughters saw those necklaces upon the neck of the beloved of Brahmā.
All twenty of them, as well as others, performed worship;
and likewise, the hundred princes worshipped the sages.
Having welcomed him and inquired after his welfare, the king,
accompanied by the assembly and the people, seated Hari upon a divine throne situated within the royal court.
And Hariśca then inquired after the welfare and well-being of all the people;
on the evening of the fourteenth day, he caused Hari to be paraded through the city.
Then, having gone to the riverbank, Śrī Hari performed his evening prayers at night together with the sages; thereafter, he partook of a meal.
Having obtained rest during the night, he woke up quickly in the morning;
having performed his daily worship and other rites, he was honored by the king in the assembly hall.
The Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa himself gave this instruction:
"O King, during the rainy season, clouds arise and then pass away into dissolution. (1.2)
In this same way, all beings are born and they enter [into dissolution];
whether today, tomorrow, the day after, or even further than that, their separation occurs.
There is no doubt that for those who have come together in a collective,
bodies will develop within the womb and attain nourishment once outside.
Indeed, once old age has arisen, it laughs at the very destruction [of the senses], for the mind is unstable, fickle, and deceptive. (15)
In the same way, the body should also be understood; there is no distinction here.
A human being [should consider]: "When and where will this ever become separated? (16)
He will not be able to determine [the truth], and even though protected, he will lose his kingdom, his lineage, his family, his kinsmen, his subjects, and his servants. (17)
Women have offspring according to their past karma;
the attainment of the Blessed One by these beings arises through great merits.
O King, there is no end to your merit, nor even to that of your family,
since today the great sages have taken up residence in your home along with me.
Great is the good fortune of those subjects who have indeed obtained my sight;
today your kingdom has become meritorious, having taken on the very nature of a sacred pilgrimage site.
Having thus bowed to Śrī Hari, who was instructing him there, the king himself questioned Śrī Hari regarding his own previous births and other matters.
"Who was I in the past, O Kṛṣṇa? Who are these my kinsmen? And what is all my family and my progeny? Tell me, O Mādhava. (22)
Thus questioned, Hari said: "Listen, O King, to your own story.
In a former kalpa, you were a sage named Cāraṇyaka."
Eating wild fruits and always dwelling at the base of a tree,
he should remain near his hermitage where the eight great roads meet.
Men travel along the path to and from your hermitage, resting for a moment after eating the fruits given by you. (25)
Having drunk the water and bowed to you, they depart as they please;
there, service is rendered to them by you through fruits and waters. (26)
By providing seats and other such things for their support, you caused them to perform your own service for a long time and repeatedly; yet you never, in any way, allowed them to do so. (27)
Since you possess knowledge, you must by no means incur debt;
indeed, one should give to all, but never accept even so much as a speck of dust.
In the same way, a debt arises for them through receiving and giving;
however, with this human body, one should never incur a debt at all.
The debtor undergoes rebirth; of this there is no doubt.
Through service, liberation is born; through service, heaven is attained.
By means of services, having obtained blessings, they become long-lived;
whatever was given in the past is certainly received later through the power of discipline.
Therefore, one should give according to one's ability; one should give repeatedly with faith to a man, a woman, or any living being whatsoever, even to oneself.
Thinking thus, you gave [the gift], and many souls were propitiated;
at that time, twenty-five sages came to dwell in your hermitage.
Your servants are equal to you, all devoted to service;
likewise, by all of you, women, men, and others who are helpless [must be protected]. (34)
Having served you and provided a refuge, these foolish forest-dwellers have come, having seen the happiness in your hermitage and observed your service. (35)
The poor and the helpless likewise lived there continuously, always remaining under the command of the twenty-six Brahmins. (36)
They indeed serve all who arrive and thereby acquire merit;
for all those servants serve with their desires fulfilled.
The sages, residing in hermitages and living like householders, became the foundation; that circle of humans reached a population of more than a thousand. (38)
That [consciousness], indeed, exists dependent upon twenty-six [factors], like a servant and so forth;
and by means of them, it is said to engage in the discourse of consciousness regarding the transition to the next world. (39)
And you, O compassionate Brahmins, who have been requested to lead us forward—
you must not depart from us, O imperishable ones.
"O Brahmins, whether it be heaven or liberation, we must certainly go after leading [you] there;
thus, out of compassion, these words were offered to those who had sought refuge: 'So be it. (41)
This compassion of yours has turned into a form of bondage for you; however, the virtuous should practice auspicious compassion that removes the suffering of living beings. 42.
But one should not act in such a way where even for oneself there would be bondage;
yet you have indeed acted so as to bring about bondage for yourselves. (43)
In that regard, you twenty-six [disciples] were indeed previously established as forms of merit by means of the storehouses of merit consisting of service to others. (44)

Likewise, when the thousand-fold [universe] has reached its end, and that mandala has dissolved—whether in the daily dissolution, the occasional dissolution, or when the evening [dissolution] arrives unexpectedly—[the same applies]. ||45||
Having all abandoned their bodies, they departed from here for the heavenly world;
then, having gone to Maharloka itself, they remained for the night of Brahmā.
Having dissolved [the world], they are created again; having resorted to heaven, they become deities—the fourteen Manus as well as the twelve Suns.
When that kalpa had passed, those who were formerly his servants were all born there as inhabitants of heaven, taking refuge in happiness. 48.
Thus they came into being, and their family was established;
a full kalpa passed away through the merits of service previously acquired.
Then, in heaven, within the creation of the gods, I myself became the Lord,
the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the beloved of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
In the form of the King of Kings, I have been the bestower of the turban-consecration upon all your joints in various places.
At that time, I was indeed the ruler of the Sūryas and the Manus;
and I was entreated by you all through your service for the sake of liberation.
Having reflected upon my merit, I prayed, "May liberation come for you after one more birth"; and the words "So be it" were granted.
Karma is not exhausted even after the passing of ten million eons unless it has been experienced;
moreover, what remains from the enjoyments of heaven must be experienced upon the earth. (54)
For that [consciousness] has indeed come to you for the sake of enjoyment upon the ground of the self that experiences karma;
and when the aeon is exhausted, it returns again at the time of creation solely for the sake of auspicious enjoyment.
O sirs, you were indeed born together with your families here;
and Bhava was the Araṇyaka, and from him the third Manu arose.
The first was Coraḷaketu, the second was Krathaka Manu, and the fourth was Uṣṭrālarāja; such were the Manus in that Kalpa.
This Haṃkāra was the fifth; the sixth was Jayakāṣṭhala;
Tīrāṇa was the seventh, and Alvīnara was the eighth. (58)
Jinavardhi was the ninth; the tenth was Alpaketuka;
the eleventh was Jayakṛṣṇa; and the twelfth was Yajñaśānaka. ||59||
The thirteenth was Indurāya, and the fourteenth was Gaṇaka;
these indeed were the Manus who were the lords of the earth here.
Then there were twelve suns; Mudrāṇḍa became the first, Līnorṇa the second, and Vṛhaccharas the third.
The fourth is Balalīna, the fifth is Varasiṃhaka;
the sixth is Rāyagāmalaka, and the seventh is Phenatantuka. ||62||
The eighth was Stokahoma; the ninth was Kāṣṭhayānaka;
the tenth was King Kolaka; and the eleventh was Aṅgarājaka. ||63||
In ancient times, Śākuntarāja also became the twelfth sun;
thus, these suns are my own forms as the Lord of the Kings of Kings.
Through my own entry [into them], you twenty-six have indeed become kings here, as Manus, Suns, and auspicious refuges.
From that, there arose for you the yoga of the Lord of the Kings of Kings;
then, on the following day, the yoga of Vāmana occurred again in heaven.
Through the great power of my supreme merit, you have once again attained union with me, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, here on this earth.
All those who were without a protector—women, men, boys, girls, and servants—your family members, then resided in heaven. (68)
Furthermore, though you have been born on this earth as householders,
I have indeed granted to all of you the range of sacrificial gain.
Because you have asked, I have indeed related your previous birth to you;
I know all of that, for it has been forgotten by you.

But as for the service you rendered to embodied beings in the forest with forest-dwelling provisions, by the merit of that, having enjoyed the kingdoms of Manu and the realms of the Sun, [you shall attain liberation]. ||71||
Indeed, by means of my yoga, my merit, and my ancient power, they have now been born here as kings for the sake of experiencing the remainder of their karma. (72)
O Gāṅgeya and great sages, you have also acquired the power of the saṃskāras and holy sites such as Kṛpāsthala while residing in this region. (73)
Having been served in every way with love and likewise having received blessings,
I, for my part, remembered everything there once again as it was in the past.
I dispatched Vṛkāyana and Nīlakaṇṭha for the sake of the sacrifice,
and likewise Lomaśa and other sages for the sake of awakening and liberation.
I have come here myself, remembering you who are devoted to me, as well as all these subjects who formerly were before you. (76)
Those people who have eaten the sacrificial grains and the fruits offered as guests—verily, those meritorious beings become your devotees in your various regions. (77)
I consider their fortune to be supreme, since they have been united with the Blessed One;
for the Blessed One, the creator of all beings, cannot be attained by those of meager merit.
The virtuous who know Brahman are not obtained by those of little merit;
nor are kinsmen devoted with sincere affection obtained by those of little merit. ||79||
A family that serves Hari cannot be obtained by one of meager merit; nor can a virtuous wife, devoted servants, and sons who are faithful and obedient to his commands. (2.178.80)
The daughters were endowed with devotion toward Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Self;
they were righteous, truthful in their vows, and bringers of contentment. ||8 1 ||
Servants who grant prosperity, who provide assistance in religious duties, and who share in one's suffering—these do not meet with those of little merit. (82)
Worldly happiness is obtained through meritorious deeds for a finite duration,
whereas the bliss of the Supreme Brahman is obtained through the dharma of service to Hari.
It is incalculable and infinite, never consumed;
it is neither diminished nor subject to transformation, for that bliss is devoid of suffering. (84)
O King, the fulfillment of a human being's purpose lies in the dedication to Brahman;
that has been accomplished by you kings during this great festival of sacrifice. (85)
"O you, you have become ones who have accomplished their purpose here by taking refuge in me;
I am pleased and I am honored by all your dispositions in this great sacrifice. (86)
Today I have been established in your house, which is eternally purifying; honor me with a spirit of love and cause this beautiful mansion to be built. (87)
Establish me there as the two-armed Supreme Lord, in whatever form was seen or obtained, beautiful in appearance and joined with Māṇikī. (88)
Always serve that divine being endowed with Lakṣmī, who sits upon an elephant-throne and measures forty-five finger-breadths in height. 89.
Likewise, having established me upon the great throne, endowed with the two glorious lotuses and joined by Ramā, worship me eternally and obtain happiness.
Having thus given instructions, received honors, and fed the people, he himself ate and appointed many [disciples] who were devoted to his own mantra. (91)
Having obtained a brief rest at midday from the circles of kings, Śrī Hari was then honored by the chief ministers and others at the end of the watch. ||92||
Requested in many ways by King Uṣṭrālaka and entreated by the sage Yugaśāva, the Supreme Lord indeed desired [to act].
That great kingdom was like a camel for him to traverse after midday;
meanwhile, King Pṛthu had twenty daughters at that time. (94)
Having gathered together with their mothers, they approached for the purpose of worship,
holding in their hands garlands of choice flowers, unbroken grains of rice, and vessels of fragrant perfumes.
At that very moment, O Rādhikā, the bridal garland was offered by twenty [of her companions] around the neck of Hari in the form of a svayaṃvara.
They took Hari’s hand according to the rite for giving a maiden in marriage;
filled with longing, they all gazed upon Hari with love.
Having bowed down to their father, their mothers, and the circle of elders, and having received blessings in every way, those beloved of Brahmā then became [ready for departure]. 98.
A festival was quickly celebrated by everyone through the offering of garlands and other gifts; then the celestial chariots, fully prepared for departure, arrived.
Twenty maidens indeed desired to go with Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa upon the celestial chariot of Śrī Hari, as they were in every way beloved by Him.
Others, having closed their eyes, set forth, all having ascended the celestial chariot;
likewise, the entire family of Hari and other great sages did the same.
Then musical instruments were indeed played that bring auspiciousness to hear,
songs were sung, and hymns of praise arose.
Thus honored by the ritual of the *ārārtrika* offering, as well as with handfuls of flowers and other rites,
Śrī Hari quickly rose from that spot into the sky.
Accompanied by shouts of victory, the sounds of machines, and cries of joy from the Lord,
his celestial chariot and other vehicles moved easily ahead in the sky.
"O Lord, out of compassion, please do not abandon us, your subjects, here once again.
Thus they spoke with many words, satisfying the Supreme Lord.
In a mere moment, O Rādhikā, celestial chariots then [descended] from the sky;
by the path indicated by Yugaśāva, they reached the kingdom of Uṣṭrāla.
Having arrived at the bank of the Dinapā river, Hari saw the city of Viyānikā; O Rādhikā, from the sky he beheld the beautifully adorned kingdom.

Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of Hari’s Arrival at King Pṛthu’s Capital, Jarasthalī, and His Bestowing of Blessings; His Statement Regarding the Former Kalpa’s Status as Sages, Manus, and Suns of Twenty-six Kings; and His Departure for the Kingdom of Uṣṭrāla on the Full Moon Day," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Listen, O Rādhikā; King Uṣṭrāla was the lord of the city of Viyānā, and his younger brother was likewise a king of devotees.
The gentle lord of the city of Guḍākeśī was named Haṃkāraka;
likewise, his third brother was named Jayakāṣṭhala.
The king of the city of Prayāga was righteous and possessed auspicious intentions; he was the family preceptor of the three kings and a protector of the age.
At that time, the entire retinue of kings, other kinsmen, well-wishers,
merchants, and all the subjects came for the sake of welcoming Hari.
On the bank of the Dīnapāsarit river, beautifully adorned by a great garden,
in a place not far from the city called Viyāna.
For the purpose of welcoming Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Supreme Soul,
they were provided with banners, flags, insignia, and musical instruments such as drums.
They were equipped with vehicles, carriages, carts, celestial chariots, and wagons; they bore flower garlands, unbroken grains, ritual substances, sandalwood, and fragrances.
Accompanied by the royal armies and the circles of subjects who had arranged their own services,
they were indeed intent upon that [task], awaiting the auspicious arrival in the sky.
They beheld celestial chariots and many other chariots equal to the sun in brilliance;
and with their exceedingly great splendors, they raised shouts of victory.
They displayed banners of welcome in the sky;
then musical instruments were sounded and the roar of mechanical engines arose. (2.179.10)
To signal the descent of the celestial chariot, the heralds gave their notice;
all the subjects sang cries of victory mingled with hymns of praise. (11)
O Hare-Kṛṣṇa, O Bāla-Kṛṣṇa, O Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa! O Supreme Brahman, O Consort of Ramā, O Consort of Rādhā, O pervasive Hari! 12.
In this manner, the chanting was performed by hundreds of thousands of those possessed of great pride;
indeed, both the riverbank and the sky were filled with the resonant sound of that chanting.
Then the subjects, like oceans overflowing their shores, gathered to behold the Lord,
the Sovereign of the Lords of Lords, who was like the full moon.
In the vast Mahodyāna grove, the vehicle of Hari alighted;
then all the other vehicles descended there from the sky.
The three kings and their ministers welcomed him with respect;
likewise, all the subjects then offered a auspicious welcome to Hari.
The elder brother offered a necklace of jewels around Hari’s neck;
then the second brother placed a string of diamonds upon Hari’s throat.
With the third [offering], a necklace of ocean pearls was presented;
and then the queens offered a golden garland to Hari.
Flower garlands were offered around their necks by their sons, daughters, and others;
Hari was honored and worshipped with flowers, unbroken rice grains, sandalwood paste, and other offerings.
He was honored by the subjects, by those wealthy with riches, and by the assembly of ministers;
likewise, Śrī Hari honored his parents, as well as his brothers and sister.
Then all the queens and members of the royal household worshipped the sages, the great sages, the devotees, and the female attendants who were dear to Brahmā. ||21||
Having bowed to the royal family seated upon the elephant-throne,
and having prostrated like a staff, he washed their feet and partook of that nectar of the feet.
Then the king and others, as well as the principal subjects, drank [the water] in succession;
thus, having offered a warm welcome and having caused the milk-rice (pāyasa) to be prepared, [they partook].
They caused drinks and fruit-eatables to be distributed throughout the entire city, accompanied by royal splendor, armies, and various kinds of musical instruments. (24)
Eagerly chanting praises and singing his names, they paraded him about; and a magnificent, spacious elephant-vehicle moved forward at the head of the procession.
At the city gate, he was honored by young maidens with flowers, unbroken grains of rice,
parched grain, water-pitchers, and likewise with hands joined in salutation that dispel all suffering.
On the main road, Hari was honored by wealthy merchants stationed in their shops;
and at the crossroads, he was sprinkled with pearls by throngs of women.
By all the subjects in every way, with sandalwood waters, flowers, unbroken rice grains and the like, coconuts, fruits, and saffron. ||28||
Hari was worshipped and honored with sugar candies and flower garlands;
he was venerated by the city women on all the royal highways.
Beheld in many ways, the Lord, who is delightful to the maidens, was then known as the lovely Kumāra, whose true form is beyond description. 2.179.30.
To young women he appeared as a charming youth, well-known as their lord;
to the elderly he appeared in the form of a child, and was then regarded by them like a son.
Then he was known as the manifest Lord to be attained by widows;
he was known as the true essence of virtuous women and the protector of the helpless.
He is the teacher of the youths, the ruler of the young, and the one who is the very form of the goal for the aged; thus is the Supreme Lord known. (33)
That Hari is known as the Lord of his devotees who are vessels of love;
he is the beautiful form for those who behold him, and the embodiment of Brahman for yogis. (34)
Then Acyuta, bearing the conch, discus, and other emblems, awakened the sages;
and the Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, who is without beginning, awakened the virtuous ones as well. (31)
"Thus, by wandering through the city and manifesting his form, the Supreme Lord appeared with two arms, becoming known to all the worlds. (36)
Having drawn the hearts of the people toward him, he went to his own royal palace;
there he rested for a moment, and Lomaśa gave him instruction.
O King, this is Nārāyaṇa himself, Śrī Puruṣottama, who has appeared for the sake of you, the suns among kings, as well as for the sake of the Manus of former ages. (38)
The Lord, who is directly subservient to His devotees, has come here upon remembering them;
[all acts such as] sacrifice, fire-oblation, chanting, rotating the rosary, worship, and austerity [are complete]. (39)
Knowledge, charity, and service shine forth directly in Kṛṣṇa;
Kṛṣṇa is the refuge of all dharmas and is himself the treasury of all merit.
For those with whom he has personally met in the form of a human sage,
their service shall bring about the delight of Kṛṣṇa.
Just as one serves a husband, a wife, an aged mother, a teacher, an elder, or those worthy of honor, so too should one serve Hari. (42)

The divine form has been directly realized, which bestows the four goals of human existence; there, both the duty of the householder and the duty of the ascetic exist where true devotion is found. 43.
While both of them dwell eternally in that very Supreme Lord, they must offer themselves with their whole being to the Supreme Lord, who is higher than the highest. (44)
The Blessed One, the true worthy recipient, is encountered only through millions of merits.
Wealth is momentary, the mind is momentary, the body is momentary, and riches are momentary. (45)
That Blessed One, the Supreme Person, is to be accomplished in a single moment;
what is the use of kingdom, wealth, family, or people? (46)
What is the use of fortune or prosperity? What is the use of honor or learning?
What is the use of a field, a wife, women, sons, daughters, and so forth? (47)
What is the use of vehicles and celestial palaces? What is the use of fame or even renown?
What is the use of physical vigor, a handsome form, or bodily strength? (48)
If, in this birth, the beginningless Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa has not been gratified by one's disposition, service, offering, or even devotion; ||49||
One's own self is to be given, for everything belonging to oneself must indeed be offered therein;
both enjoyment and liberation are to be acquired through the offering of all things unto Acyuta.
By you kings, a great and auspicious sacrifice was performed here;
this child Śrī Kambharā-Bālaka-Kṛṣṇa has been fully gratified. ||51||
"You have indeed accomplished all that was to be done; every auspicious state has been attained. No further duty remains, since he has been so thoroughly propitiated. (52)
Having spoken thus, Lomaśa then ceased;
the king, placing the feet of Śrī Hari upon his head, set them down there. ||53||
The queen, the princes, and the princesses placed [the command] in their hearts;
having received the order, they all departed, and Hari attained rest.
Having arranged for food and other necessities, they all went to sleep;
then, having risen in the morning and performed their daily rites, Hari [proceeded].
The great sage, honored by the assembly of sages, sat upon a beautiful seat;
at that moment, the king, the queen, their daughters, and their sons arrived.
Uṣṭrāla, Haṃkāra, and Jayakāṣṭhala also entreated the Lord most earnestly for the sake of dwelling there for a long time.
Hari said: "Today, indeed, the fruitfulness of your birth has been realized through my vision and worship; it was earned by me through my graciousness. (58)
"O sinless ones, you must always do whatever it takes for me to be fully satisfied; there is absolutely no time remaining for me to dwell here any longer. (59)
There is a need to go to the kingdom of Haṃkāra’s Ālaya, and there is also a need to go to the kingdom of Jayakāṣṭhala. ||2.179.60||
"Here my gain has been secured; I am satisfied with this honor, thinking that the touch of his feet upon the ground shall become the touch of royalty within my palace. (6.1)
I shall fulfill your desire this very day; let it be held in mind.
Having drunk milk this morning, you shall travel by means of celestial chariots. (62)
Everyone must go first to that kingdom which is the abode of the ego;
there, at midday, they shall have their meal and likewise wander through the city. (63)
Having performed the ritual placement of the feet and other preliminary rites, one should indeed proceed to that temple in the kingdom of Jayakāṣṭhalara only after midday.
Having wandered through that city and purified his dwelling there,
he then took his meal at night and rested for the remainder of the night.
"At the time of dawn, we must go to the kingdom of Ālvīnara; therefore, act in accordance with that plan and show favor. (66)
My command must be observed in every way; happiness is found right there.
Even in a very short time, I shall grant you happiness beyond all counting. (67)
Having thus heard the command of Hari, those three brothers,
being pleased with the words of the Lord, acted accordingly with great respect.
O Rādhikā, at that time, the Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, having received the worship of Uṣṭra and being prepared for his departure, [was addressed].
The five daughters of Uṣṭrāla performed worship with great reverence;
ten daughters took the hand of Hari, desiring him as their husband.
Rejoicing there with their parents according to the marriage rites, they reached Hari and met eagerly within the circle of the beloveds of Brahmā.
Having then accepted those blessings, they set out;
and the maidens of the mountain king likewise departed together with Hari as he had set forth.
Then, having ascended their celestial chariots, they set out swiftly through the sky toward the capital city of Guḍākeśin, which was ruled by King Haṅkāra.
In a mere moment they arrived, hearing the proclamation of victory,
which was made auspicious by those who had gone ahead and announced it.
[He saw] the city of Guḍākeśī, situated on the bank of the river Dīnapāyā, beautifully adorned and endowed with magnificent gardens. ||75||
It was adorned with gate-towers and other such structures, with arches, pinnacle-pots,
and the like, and decorated with painted festoons, svastikas, and banners bearing emblems.
It was swept clean, sprinkled with perfumed waters, and made to resound with the music of instruments;
and the citizens, having come out from the city, raised a great clamor to welcome him.
Haṃkāra, together with his family and his younger brother, went forward first;
accompanied by his army, he offered a welcome with Jayadhvaja and the others.
Then, following its indications, the young bull of the Yugas brought that celestial chariot down from the sky near the sage’s palace.
And other celestial chariots descended from the sky at that time;
then there arose the sounds of trumpets, along with cries of victory and hymns of praise.
Then Hari quickly descended from his celestial chariot to the surface of the earth;
at that time, King Haṃkāraka was also there with his family.
Indeed, [the Lord] was celebrated with shouts of victory and honored with sandalwood paste and other offerings;
having washed the feet of Hari, the king and others drank the water. ||82||
Then, having placed Śrī Kṛṣṇa upon the horse-carriage,
the king led him toward the city along that royal highway with great festivity.
Bowing to Hari at every place, the subjects honored him with devotion;
they presented offerings, sought his audience, and performed salutations and other rites. (84)
The ministers, having led him to their own homes, performed the ritual of waving lamps for the Lord;
the subjects, having led him to their respective homes, worshipped the Supreme Lord.
Having thus purified the city of Guḍākeśī, they all then proceeded to the royal palace; at that time, Hari descended from his golden chariot.
Having descended quickly and bathed, he performed the midday rites;
having offered food to the deity, he himself [provided for] all his own dependents. (87)
Having fed him, he himself ate and then rested for a moment;
having made the king well-pleased and having bestowed auspicious blessings upon him, [he departed]. (88)
At the time following midday, Hari, desiring to depart with his retinue by means of a celestial chariot, was entreated by the queen, the princesses, and the others. (89)
Then, having been honored by the king, he took the hands of five maidens; at that time, he was also commanded by Kṛṣṇa’s mother.
They had accomplished their purpose and their family was filled with joy;
those five, beloved of Brahmā, closed their eyes, assuming divine forms.
Then, having taken leave of the king, the queen, and their subjects,
Hari ascended his celestial chariot and, together with his retinue, departed for the sky.
Then musical instruments were sounded and shouts of victory arose;
having granted his audience, he quickly departed for the city of Prayāga.
Then, in the evening, the Lord reached the beautiful capital city of King Jayakāṣṭhala, a source of auspicious refuge, which was endowed with magnificent gardens.
King Jaya, having gone forward with his subjects, offered a welcome accompanied by the sounds of musical instruments and well-adorned banners and armies. (95)
Having seen the beautiful city named Prayāga at evening,
he then descended from the celestial chariot to the earth through the path described by Yugasāva.
Then the Lord of Lords, Śrī Hari, beloved of Kṛṣṇa, caused [them] to descend;
and the celestial chariots descended into the vicinity of the palace. 97.
Having washed the feet of Hari with water, the king indeed drank [the water from them];
having offered a welcome with necklaces, garlands, and other gifts, he gave him excellent water. 98.
Having caused all his troops to drink sweet waters, the king, accompanied by his army,
joyfully led Kṛṣṇa on a tour through his own city.
The Supreme Lord, honored by the subjects and the leading classes,
purified the ground of the city with his footsteps and the granting of his vision.
Having arrived at the royal palace, he then took his meal and other refreshments;
after feeding everyone, he rested at the onset of night.
Pleased by the songs of those royal singers, the Supreme Lord granted them offerings and diamonds as rewards.
Having slept at night, Hari then woke up at dawn to the sounds of musical instruments;
thereafter, Mādhava quickly performed his daily rites during the Brahma-muhūrta.
The subjects, having assembled, presented offerings before Hari;
he bestowed all of that upon the three brothers for the sake of Yugaśāva.
Then the queen Vaiṣṇavī, accompanied by her five daughters,
arrived for the purpose of worship, and having worshipped him along with those five maidens.
Overcome by delusion, they seized Hari, thinking him to be their own beloved;
having wedded the Supreme Lord according to the rite for bestowing a maiden upon a youth.
Having accomplished their purpose, they were born and indeed drank the milk;
they caused the Blessed One, the head of the household, to drink it excessively.
And Mādhava caused the king, all his subjects, all the sages beginning with the gods, and likewise those dear to Brahmā, to drink [the nectar]. 108.
The eternal Supreme Soul caused her to drink milk and other nourishment;
then Kṛṣṇa, intending to depart, bestowed his blessings upon her.
Then, having been quickly prepared by his subjects and others, he was dispatched;
at first, he swiftly ascended the divine celestial chariot.
Others also quickly ascended their own celestial chariots,
and then they set forth with shouts of victory and auspicious sounds.
The king of the Valgurāya regions was named Tīraṇa;
likewise, the sage Valgurāya lived with his family and household.
Having previously mounted his celestial chariot, he then departed together with Hari;
and from the sky, Hari beheld the regions of Valgurāya.
Then, from the sky, he beheld the beautiful capital of Tīrās, situated on the delightful bank of the river Sevikā.
And Rādhikā, seated in the celestial chariot, heard the sounds of auspiciousness—the shouts of victory, the noise of trumpets, and the cries of "Victory! uttered by the people.

Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Travel by Celestial Carriages to the Capitals of King Haṃkāra of Uṣṭrālaya and King Jayakāṣṭhala, Their Wandering Through the Cities, Their Worship, and the Departure at Dawn on the First Lunar Day toward the Capital of Tīrāṇā," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Then, O Rādhikā, the glorious Lord Hari, together with the sage Valgurāya and King Tīraṇa, ascended His own celestial chariot.
He brought them down to the earth by the path he had shown;
thereafter, the other celestial chariots descended behind him.
Then there arose the sounds of "Victory! and the blaring of musical instruments, as well as the cries of joy from the women and the sweet, melodious voices of the children.
At that time, cries of "Welcome! arose from the people on all sides;
there was a rain of flowers, a rain of unbroken grains, and even a shower of sandalwood powder.
At that time, when Hari indeed went forth from the celestial chariot,
the other great-souled ones also descended from their vimānas.
There, King named Tīrāṇa did not bow at the feet of Hari;
nor did the royal household bow at the feet of Hari.
Having washed their feet, all the members of the household partook of the drink; they wore golden necklaces and jeweled necklaces adorned with pearls and gems.
They all placed [the garland] upon the neck of Hari, the Supreme Brahman and the Supreme Self;
they offered a welcome with flower garlands and uttered cries of "Victory! (jaya).
Then the king seated Hari upon a chariot drawn by seven white horses, and likewise the others upon horse-drawn vehicles.
Honored by the royal armies and worshipped by the foremost among men,
the beloved of Śrī Kṛṣṇa shone forth, enriched by the splendor of the parasol and chowries.
In the city named Tīrāṇa,
the king indeed caused Śrī Hari, accompanied by his caravan, to be paraded with great honor.
All the subjects worshipped him exceedingly at every spot,
and having granted an audience until midday, he returned to the royal palace.
The Lord reached the palace of Indra, which was equal to the assembly hall of the gods;
having rested for a moment, he then performed his ablutions and other rites.
The king provided everything, including the drinking of milk;
and Hari, having been honored, also fed the members of his family.
The Lord, the Master Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, personally partook of the food along with all the honored sages, the devotees dear to Brahmā, and his own servants. || 15 ||
Then the king and the others obtained the auspicious grace of Śrī Hari;
and after midday, they all established a grove.
The king, together with his family, massaged Kṛṣṇa’s feet;
he performed the rubbing of the body and obtained the fruit of service.
Then, in the evening, that assembly hall became vast,
wherein hundreds of thousands of men sat in the presence of Hari.
Women and men sat down and stood around him on all sides;
then the king honored that Supreme Lord with offerings.
The king sat upon his throne and, filled with humility, asked:
"O Kṛṣṇa, how is it that while the kingdom is being governed by you, no bondage or calamity approaches?"
I know that through attaining you, my bonds have been severed;
nevertheless, because of the state of being bound [to existence], may there be no further bondage. (21)
"O Great King, instruct your family in this way; speak words that grant peace.
Upon hearing this, the Blessed One spoke in the assembly while everyone was listening.
I shall declare to you that which leads to the shore of the ocean of existence, so that there may never be bondage for you anywhere in the midst of it. (23)
All this is food for the vital breath (prāṇa), but never for the Self (ātman);
everything, both stationary and moving, is the nourishment of the vital breath alone. (24)
When the vital breath (prāṇa) remains, the dependence upon the principles (tattvas) persists within the body;
for the vital breath is indeed the effect of primordial nature (prakṛti), and when the vital breath has departed, there is no thirst [for existence].
Realizing this, the wise person should engage in eating and enjoyment without longing;
one should not behave like a greedy person, for there is no bondage for one who is free from passion.
Just as one who has climbed a great tree and taken its honey abandons the tree right there after having eaten that honey; ||27||
"After that, one abandons the impurity; thereafter, the body will be cast off.
Having reflected in this manner, he who conducts himself accordingly is not bound. (28)
Just as a person, agitated by hundreds of hopes, might fall upon a great path and, becoming despondent, fail to obtain the fruit; ||29||
Having remembered all this and understood it thus, the wise person, perceiving the world as unstable, is not bound;
for even a powerful man yields to gentleness in times of adversity.
One should conduct oneself with gentleness even toward a deceptive person so as not to be bound by them,
just as one who is overcome by old age or one who has fallen into the hands of a child.
One who acts in such a manner surely abandons the hope for objects of enjoyment and is not bound;
even mountains and trees are practitioners of perpetual renunciation.
Having abandoned the sense of "mine," they live without possessions;
one who governs a kingdom with such a disposition remains untainted and is not bound. //33//
All aquatic creatures are intent solely on sustaining themselves;
they do not engage in possessiveness, and thus their way of life is not bound by attachment.
Listen also to this history which brings benefit to ascetics:
in ancient times, certain Vaiṣṇava twice-born men, having abandoned their homes, [went forth]. (35)
The wise ones, devoted to the life of celibacy, came to the forest; for they were like ascetics, handsome, and even though their hair had not yet grown, they were already so.
Indra, assuming the form of a bird and becoming compassionate, spoke: "Oh, sirs! Out of childishness, you have indeed resorted to the path of renunciation. (37)
"How did you come to leave the life of a householder, O sinless ones? What was the cause for your renunciation?
Having heard this, the sages said: "To one who is free from desire, the entire world is but a blade of grass. (38)
Whether in the state of a householder or in the forest, no such bondage exists for him;
we, indeed, being free from desire, have therefore taken recourse to the path of the forest.
For it is better indeed not to touch mud at all than to wash it off;
for one who has already come into contact with mud, there is certainly a need for water.
Cleansing by means of knowledge, which is of the nature of water, is considered superior;
or rather, the state of being dried up through the application of heat is considered superior. (41)
Kardama, having become like a saw, would himself resort to separation;
for there is the worship of Hari, which takes the form of heat and is purifying.
Furthermore, even the state of dryness brought about by the wind is considered supreme;
for by relying on the Guru as the wind, the mire of ignorance is destroyed. (43)
Therefore, by firmly embracing the knowledge of that Great Guru, the True One, or the Supreme Lord, the wise person shall destroy Māyā. 44.
Performing all this very action—whether worldly or Vedic—a human being attains perfection through the state of non-action (naiṣkarmya). ||45||
"O bird, this is a meritorious field of accomplishment that bestows the fruits of one's actions;
it [purifies] the lineages of gods, the lineages of ancestors, the lineages of Brahmā, and virtuous people. (46)
Only that action which is performed in accordance with tradition yields fruit for men;
we abide by relying upon the Vedic lineage of Brahmans. (47)
If the life of a householder were joined with austerity, it would be conducive to granting liberation;
however, that [household life] is indeed a house of obstacles, and therefore we are peaceful. (48)
When one lacks strength, one should resort to the simple path of the self;
the great path belongs to the strong, and the life of a householder to those with great fervor. (49)
"We are not capable of bearing the burdens of household life; therefore, we have taken refuge in the dharma of the virtuous, wherein ultimate welfare is certain. (2.180.50)
"In both doubt and certainty, one should abandon the first [doubt] and rely upon certainty.
Having heard these words of the sages, the king of birds himself—
Though submerged in water and yet possessing an excess of contact with water, he spoke to them of those household duties that are both difficult and most excellent.
Even though he has fallen into the fire, he possesses an abundance of the state of being unburnt;
even though he stands within the nature of desire, he is devoid of any portion of longing. ||53||
Only someone rare in this world may be both capable and possessed of merit;
if such a person is a householder, he attains the highest good. (54)
By the renunciation of even one's own self, a person attains auspiciousness;
by means of household duties, a person becomes a creator of immeasurable merit.
Just as all rivers find rest in the ocean, so do all beings find rest in the home of a householder. (56)
Indeed, the high-souled yogis, though full of renunciation and free from desire,
take refuge in the fruitful trees that stand within the domain of domestic life.
In that domestic dharma, the rendering of assistance to others arises;
indeed, one who possesses the domestic dharma provides shelter for guests, just as birds provide shelter in their home.

Having acquired wealth through the duties of a householder by means of policy, truth, and reason, the householder enjoys it only after distributing it among his family members and the mendicants dependent upon him. 59.
Remembering the king, guests, the destitute, and even ants and other small creatures, the householder always eats after giving to them as is appropriate.
For the gods are satisfied in the morning, guests and mendicants at midday, thereafter the ancestors, and finally, indeed, the small creatures. (61)
All embodied beings eat food cooked by the householder;
therefore, the householder is a consumer of *vighasa* (remnants), for he takes only after having given, and not otherwise.
To consume evil for the sake of filling one's own belly alone is called *ghasa* (gluttony);
but where others also find satisfaction, that evil consumption has ceased.

Sacrifice, charity, austerity, fire-offering, and the study of sacred texts—when these six are performed as offerings to the Lord, that indeed constitutes the state of eating the remains of a sacrifice (vighasāśitva). 64.
Indeed, among all dharmas, the eating of remnants (vighasa) is the most excellent;
by observing that dharma, one shall acquire the highest welfare.
For them, this world bestows enjoyments, and even heaven brings about supreme happiness;
moreover, when the fruit exceeds even that, there shall be the highest bliss.
The supreme state is to be attained through the practice of total surrender;
indeed, there is nothing else so excellent as this stage of the householder on the field of action.
"O ascetics, I have attained the status of Lord of the Gods through my own deeds;
formerly, even Sūrya, Candra, and all the others were eaters of sacrificial remnants. (68)
But now they dwell in heaven as eaters of the remains of sacrificial offerings;
Hari himself, residing in Vaikuṇṭha, shines forth as an eater of the remains of sacrificial offerings.
Likewise, in Goloka, Kṛṣṇa shines as one who eats the remains of offerings;
so too does the four-armed Vāsudeva Viṣṇu, who partakes of the remnants of sacrificial food.
Hara, Brahmā, Vasiṣṭha, and the others are indeed eaters of the remains (vighasāśins);
though they abide on the path of enjoyment, they remain free from the pairs of opposites (dvandva).
Those whose dharma is the dedication of all to the Lord shall go to the supreme state;
thus indeed do the ascetics, subsisting on the remains of offerings, attain Brahman.
Dividing the food into portions every morning and evening, he should distribute it among his family, guests, beggars, the Supreme Lord, the gods, living beings, his father, and his kinsmen.
Toward a protectorless dependent or servant, as well as toward a helpless dog and the like; likewise toward a woman, a cow, a beggar who has arrived, and even toward one's own teacher. (74)

Having divided all food and other provisions according to what is appropriate and in accordance with dharma among the male servants, female servants, laborers, dependents, and the physical bodies [of the deceased], ||75||
Those who eat what remains [of the offerings] are eaters of vighasa;
having become teachers of the world, they are born as eternal eaters. //76//
And having attained the great sovereignty of the celestial realm for eternal years,
they go, by virtue of merit offered to the Lord, to the state from which there is no return.
Therefore, those who eat the remains of the sacrificial offering become liberated from bondage;
many, by relying on the duties of householders, have gone to that state. (78)
Therefore, O sirs, let even fools be eaters of the remains of offerings;
the Brahmins, the Seven Sages, and others know this to be true austerity. (79)
Having been addressed thus and having heard those words endowed with righteousness,
those lords of ascetics abandoned the stage of renunciation and took up the life of a householder.
The great sages, subsisting on the remains of sacrificial offerings, offered everything to Kṛṣṇa; from that time forth, they all took refuge in the dharma of self-surrender.
In ancient times, those who were richly endowed with wives, sons, and family members attained Brahman at the end;
therefore, O King, although the duty of householdership is difficult, it brings happiness.
Rich in the merit of helping others, always attaining the service of the virtuous, and bestowing the fruits of serving the Supreme Lord and the like—he is therefore the most excellent one. (83)
May you always subsist on the remains of food (vighasa) along with those who depend upon you;
and in all activities of the senses, may you meditate upon me, Kṛṣṇa, repeatedly.
"By my power, no bondage shall ever befall you;
by my power, O King, there shall always be peace for you. (85)
"Protect my image here and offer everything to me;
O King, I shall lead you, who are devoted to no other, to the abode of Brahman."
Whosoever among the people here are devoted to the dharma of surrender unto me,
I am their deliverer from the ocean of the bondage of karma.
Having spoken thus, the Blessed One ceased there;
those subjects worshipped the Supreme Self and received the mantras with reverence. (88)
"From that day forward, all of them became observers of the vow of eating only the remnants of offerings (vighasāśi-vrata).
Having thus concluded the assembly, O Rādhikā, the Blessed One then departed.
He performed his ablutions, twilight prayers, and other rites, followed by his meal;
then all those honored guests, having eaten, rested.
The king, together with his family, attended upon the sleeping Hari;
then, at dawn, Śrī Hari awoke to the sounds of musical instruments.
Having performed his daily rites, he came and sat upon the lion-throne;
meanwhile, the king and all the others approached in order to worship Hari.
Indeed, many footprints were left by King Tīrāṇaka;
likewise, his queens and daughters arrived with their hands [bearing those marks]. 93.
Holding the vessels for worship, they worshipped the Supreme Lord;
and the six maidens, O Rādhikā, took the hand of Śrī Hari.
Having received the gift of the prince, they then felt their purpose was fulfilled;
then, having attained rest and performed their meals and other duties, [they remained]. (95)
Requested by King Alvinara and eager to depart, Hari—who is worshipped by the sages of the Lord of Mountains—then became ready. 96.
Then musical instruments were played and songs were sung; hearing shouts of victory and receiving honors and other marks of respect, [he proceeded]. (97)
Then Hari ascended his own celestial chariot, and others likewise mounted their chariots;
at that time, they traveled along the path of the sky.
Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa and the others were likewise honored with auspicious sounds, the noise of mechanical instruments, and benedictions.
They set out with great speed in their celestial chariots and, in a mere moment,
reached the excellent kingdom situated by the ocean, known as Girīśa.
Hearing the shouts of victory and looking about, Hari became pleased;
Alvinara went before him and stood there to offer a welcome.
"Harir is coming, O Great King!"— thus the subjects, filled with eager anticipation,
were ready upon the surface of the earth to behold him and offer him a welcome.
Gazing toward the sky with eager anticipation, the women and men held unbroken grains of rice, flowers, and other offerings in their hands, and they performed a hymn of praise. 103.

Thus ends the one hundred and eightieth chapter, titled "The Description of how Hari, having gone to the kingdom of King Tīrāṇa in the second section on the Tretā Age within the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*, wandered through the city of Tīrāṇā in the guise of a welcome party accompanied by his army, partook of food and other offerings, and in the evening assembly instructed on the duty of eating the remains of a sacrifice (*vighasāśitva*), spoke of liberation from bondage, rested at night, and in the morning, having performed worship, eaten, and prepared himself, arrived at the kingdom of Alvīnara on the second lunar day."
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Listen, O Gopī Rādhikā; together with Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the Lord [will take] birth as Alavīnara on the second day of the dark fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada.
Instructed by the sage Girīśa to go to the appointed place,
he joyfully brought his celestial chariot down from the sky while observing the subjects waiting for him.
Then other celestial chariots descended from the sky onto the grounds of the garden in the vicinity of Arthaśrī and King Dhanya.
Likewise, the sage Girīśa and King Alvinara, together with their families,
offered a welcome with musical instruments, worshipful offerings, garlands, and sandalwood paste.
As Hari was descending from the celestial chariot onto the courtyard by means of a constructed staircase and ladder, the people placed golden necklaces around his neck.
Then there arose shouts of "Victory!",
the sounds of those bearing canes, and the fame-recording words of the *sūtas*, *māgadhas*, bards, and *cāraṇas*.
Then there occurred an excellent hearing of the verses produced by the voice,
accompanied by flowers, unbroken rice grains, parched grain, gold coins, and other such offerings.
At that time, the people performed the worship of Kṛṣṇa with wheat;
the king, having led Hari along with his family into the royal palace, [honored him]. (8)
The king, accompanied by his sons, daughters, and others, offered water for drinking and betel-leaf, and he also performed the washing of their feet.
Together with his family, he partook of the nectar of [the sage's] feet;
thereafter, he offered milk to everyone there.
Accompanied by his army, he quickly brought a golden chariot with horses for the sake of Hari, in order to travel through the city.
The Blessed One shone there with joy together with his two parents,
as well as his brothers, other sages, Brahmapriya, and the rest.
Then they sat down in vehicles, palanquins, chariots, and elephant-machines, while musical instruments were played along with shouts of victory.
The army, rich in every splendor, set out toward the city;
it reached the royal highway in the city known as Arthaśrī.
He was repeatedly honored, praised, seen face-to-face, and touched by the ministers, royal officers, guild-leaders, and the subjects; he was their manifest Lord. (15)
Having been saluted with offerings and thoroughly propitiated, the Blessed One then wandered again all around the city. (16)
Having arrived at the garden and the royal palace, he took rest upon his own seat;
and others who had become weary also bathed and found repose.
Then they rested in their own abode and enjoyed themselves happily;
indeed, with great reverence, they partook of many kinds of cooked foods.
O Rādhā, that was a marvel; listen, for I shall tell it to you.
A great Rākṣasa, who lived in the vicinity of Krītadvipa, was indeed very dear to him in matters of wealth. (19)
He had indeed come for the purpose of testing and observing the strength of Hari;
first, he [placed] stones resembling sweetmeats among the sweetmeats.
Smeared with ghee, they were placed in the food by one in the form of a server;
Hari quickly perceived them all as stones by His own will.
Having abandoned their state as mountains, they indeed attained the state of sweet food;
having witnessed that marvel there, he then performed an investigation.
Listen further, O Rādhā: he indeed took the form of a bed;
having displayed a beautiful ball upon a lovely couch. (23)
For the sake of Śrī Hari, he secretly prepared a bed of spikes below;
and Hari, full of reverence, ascended that bed of spikes.
Then the spikes became golden flowers and filaments;
having experienced that wonder there as well, the Rākṣasa departed from that place.
Then the Blessed One also performed a third test, having had sandals treated with poison prepared.
Having put on his sandals and established himself in the form of nectar,
the Lord remained there in that palace, moving about with ease in every direction.
Furthermore, that Rākṣasa performed a fourth test:
he placed a divine golden throne in the assembly hall and set fire to it.
Then Hari, having gone to that assembly hall and touched that fiery seat,
made it cool once again, even though it was made of gold.
Then that Rākṣasa, having attained supreme wonder and being freed from his human form,
requested Kṛṣṇa for his own liberation so that he might return to his own home.
Hari said to the Rākṣasa, "So be it," and as soon as he placed his two feet upon the Rākṣasa's head, he became a god.
That divine realm named Tuṣita, which always grants residence in heaven, was then questioned by the people, and he too told them his own story. (32)
"I am a god named Tuṣita; having come here to wander upon the earth as I pleased, I beheld Sundarī here. (33)
In the past, at the shore of the ocean, she who was desired for her beauty was insulted by me; she then suddenly pronounced a curse upon me.
"O you of wicked conduct, intent on violating maidens, become a Rākṣasa!
I, however, have immediately become a Rākṣasa, dwelling upon purchased ground. (35)
"O Blessed One, by your touch I am now freed from the curse;
O God Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, Lord of the Universe, I have become a god once again. (36)
"If I have his command, I shall go from this place to my own home.
Hari said, "Go to the Kurus situated in the northern direction. (37)
Lālāyana was previously sent by me after meditating upon the nature of Being-Consciousness-Bliss;
having searched for him, give me news of him. (38)
"Accept these mantras, O God, and depart at my command.
Having spoken thus, he bestowed the mantras upon him and sent the deity away. (39)
To indicate the northern regions by means of the sky, Hari himself came to the sage in the western region of Ketumāla.
"At the end of this month, the Blessed One will certainly come here as well.
Having gone to the shore of the Pālipāraka lake, he spoke thus to that sage. (41)
Situated on the eastern bank, joined by the Śeṣa forest and the river Ānandī,
the sage rejoiced exceedingly upon hearing of the arrival of his own Lord.
Then the Sage offered a great welcome to Tuṣita;
together with Tuṣita, the Sage quickly proceeded to the northern regions. (43)
Then, eager for the arrival of Kṛṣṇa, he told the people; meanwhile, two [of them] wandered everywhere through the villages and towns in all directions. 44.
Then the Lords respectfully gave the name-mantras to the subjects;
thereafter, the illustrious Lord [resided] in the abode of Rādhā and Akrūra.
At night, Mādhava prepared a very large assembly hall there;
being honored and worshipped, he gave instruction to the subjects.
Whether they be subjects, the royal class, ascetics, or householders, if they perform their appropriate duties and offer them unto Me, [they attain perfection]. (47)
There shall be no bondage for them regarding either those actions or their fruit;
I am the bestower of their fruit, and I indeed bring about their state of actionlessness.
Those who offer wealth acquired through righteous means in sacrifices,
being self-realized practitioners, they are indeed renunciants belonging to the stage of life of renunciation (tyāgāśramin).
They do not call renunciation "renunciation"; rather, freedom from bondage is called renunciation.
It belongs to that person who, having embraced equanimity, dwells like a tree.
If he does nothing at all, he is indeed called *tāmasa*;
but if his dwelling were in the Lord, he would attain freedom from the qualities (*nirguṇya*). ||51||
Performing all actions repeatedly with a desire for pleasure, yet not remembering the Lord therein—those indeed are rajasic deeds. 52.
The renunciation of actions for the sake of pleasure is considered to be rajasic.
[But] performing all actions while focused on me, Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Beyond, [is sattvic]. (53)

And that action which one offers up with all one's possessions, out of a desire for pleasure or a desire for its fruit—that action is characterized by *sattva*; and renunciation (*tyāga*) is likewise characterized by *sattva*. (54)
If a person, having abandoned the desire for fruits, offers everything to me, then all that—though connected with me and intended for my sake—becomes devoid of qualities (nirguṇa). ||55||
Just as the action corresponds to its qualities, so the householder is bound;
if the action were devoid of qualities, he would be liberated and not bound. //56//
On one side are other stages of life, and on the other side is the householder stage;
he who follows both the duty of the householder and the dark duty (of asceticism) becomes a practitioner of the stage beyond qualities (nirguṇāśramī).
May all action renounced in me grant its fruit to my very self;
[may there be] tranquility, self-restraint, as well as fortitude, truth, purity, and likewise uprightness. (58)
Sacrifice, fortitude, and righteousness do not attain any separation from this;
action performed out of egoism is devoid of my remembrance.
The gatekeeper of Yama swiftly places the noose of death around one's neck;
therefore, casting aside pride, perform actions dedicated to Me alone.
"Even while remaining in the householder's state, I shall accomplish the goal of liberation, which has been placed within me;
for in the past, Brahmā created all beings by my command. (61)
For the sake of maintaining the continuity of karma, for my own worship,
and likewise for the purpose of sacrifice, one may [take] shrubs, trees, and medicinal herbs.
Juices, fruits, leaves, sacrificial materials, and oblations—all these are intended for the sake of sacrifice;
indeed, the householder's life joined with a wife is always considered fit for performing sacrifice.
A pair of gods and goddesses is indeed highly praised for the purpose of worship;
having obtained such [an image], those householders who are endowed with wealth, grain, and flavors [should perform it]. (64)
If they do not sacrifice to the gods, they indeed consume sin;
however, for the wise and the virtuous, the sacrifice of knowledge and the propitiation of holy beings constitute their sacrifices.
For sages, the sacrifice is the private recitation of sacred texts; for kings, it is the sacrifice of material goods;
for those who rule over agriculture, it is the sacrifice of food; and for yogis, it is the sacrifice of meditation.
Service is the sacrifice for servants; the service of women is their ritual;
the words of the father are the Veda for sons; and indeed, the Veda is for those practicing celibacy.
For householders, sacrifices consist of giving; for ascetics, they consist of austerity.
Thus, sacrifices become manifold according to one's fitness.
For all people, however, sacrifices of devotion to Hari are free from bondage;
therefore, having beheld me as being absorbed in Him, sacrifices should be performed according to what is appropriate.
"Being pleased by these offerings, I shall grant you liberation; of this there is no doubt. Indeed, horses, elephants, cows, and other such things must be given by kings. (2.181.70)
Male and female servants adorned with ornaments, as well as villages and districts, gardens, houses, fields, and various types of groves. (71)
That fruit is declared to be eternal, especially for kings;
however, those kings who do not give and who provide no refuge partake in sin.
They are the eaters of faults alone, never of pleasures;
for they have neither performed the great sacrifices nor offered libations and other rites of satisfaction. (73)
If one proceeds on the path without bathing in sacred fords and without having propitiated the Supreme Lord,
he indeed returns again.
Like a scattered cloud, it goes to dissolution and perishes;
the two-syllabled [word] is death, while the three-syllabled is Brahman and the immortal.
"Mine" is indeed death, while "not mine" is eternal immortality;
both of these always reside either upon one's own head or in one's heart. (76)
In this regard, having abandoned what is harmful and attained that which is supreme, this path practiced by the virtuous should always be followed by you, O embodied beings. (77)
Having obtained a kingdom, a good family, wealth, and likewise prosperity, if one does not worship the Lord in sacrifice, that indeed is fruitless for him. (78)
For one who has not propitiated the gods, who lives solely for his own sake, and who possesses a sense of "mine" regarding wealth and other possessions, death does not spare even his topknot. (79)
Death releases those by whom that witness of all beings, existing both externally and internally, has been propitiated here with offerings.
Even if the mind is prosperous and filled with enjoyments, if it remains fixed in craving, that mind is said to be impotent; it does not find the kingdom of Brahman.
A eunuch does not enjoy the land of Brahman nor the wealth of devotion;
indeed, there is no worship of the gods or auspicious rites in the abode of a eunuch.
Therefore, one should never exhibit weakness in the worship of the Supreme Lord;
Hari should always be served by the elders, for others indeed follow them.
Since those who rely on the madness of worldly prosperity become perpetually intoxicated, one should therefore abandon madness, which arises from illusion, passion, and the like. (84)
Lord Kṛṣṇa, the beginningless Nārāyaṇa, is always to be worshipped;
just as a sacrifice was performed [in the past], so should it be performed at all times in the home. (85)
"The Brahma-yajña must always be performed; I shall grant liberation, of this there is no doubt.
Having said this, the Lord then bestowed the mantras upon the subjects. (86)
Then, O Rādhikā, there was a departure from the assembly;
having rested at night, the Blessed One then performed his morning rites.
Requested by King Jinavardhana and also entreated by Iṣṭalavarṣin, he indeed desired to depart quickly for the kingdom of Iṣṭāli.
The king, together with his family, brought offerings such as food and other honors;
then Kṛṣṇa, the performer of deeds for his devotees, accepted them without any hesitation.
After that, all the others belonging to Hari’s caravan also accepted [the gifts];
and the queen, together with her five daughters, worshipped Hari.
There, all five maidens took the hand of Śrī Hari;
according to the marriage rite, Kṛṣṇa gave his own hand to them.
Having received worship and words of blessing, Hari became ready to depart,
accompanied by the five maidens, including Brahmapriyā, who were devoted to their son.
They went forth together with Śrī Hari and sat down in the celestial chariot;
having received leave, the Blessed One ascended into the vehicle.
At that time, all others indeed ascended their celestial chariots;
then musical instruments were played and shouts of victory arose.
O Hare, Kṛṣṇa, Hari, Nārāyaṇa, Lord! All the subjects then chanted Your names as celestial chariots appeared in the sky. 95.
Moving over the water in the direction indicated by the Lord of the Desired Portion (iṣṭalavaprada),
they crossed the Vārdhikhāḍī river and then reached Rāmapurī.
In the past, on the western bank of the Khāḍikā, King Jinavardhana, accompanied by his family, descended from his celestial chariot to welcome [him]. (97)
Then the great sage Iṣṭalava and all the subjects were on the bank near the garden to welcome the Lord Hari. (98)
Upon merely beholding the celestial chariots, the sounds of victory,
the cries of "Long live!", the praises of the subjects, and likewise the sounds of hymns of glorification were heard.
Thus, O Rādhikā, the entire kingdom became intent on welcoming [them];
the earth there was crowded together and became like an ocean of people. (2.181.10)

Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-first chapter, titled "The Description of how Hari, on the second day of the dark fortnight of Bhādrapada in the Tretā-yuga, went to the kingdom of Alvinara, wandered through the city of Arthaśrī, ate, granted liberation to the Rākṣasa, sent the Tuṣita-deva to Uttarakuru, gave instruction in the assembly hall, accepted worship, rested, and after breakfast in the morning set out toward the capital of King Jinavardhin," in the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*, within the second section, the *Tretā-santāna*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Listen, O Rādhikā; Hari, the beginningless Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, having been instructed by his beloved consort, arrived at the appointed place with his own celestial chariot.
He brought it down into a vast, auspicious expanse of ground within a garden,
situated on the bank of the river Trivarā and thick with fine trees.
In the vicinity of the city of Rāmapurī, which resounded with the music of instruments,
King Jinavardhana was present together with his ministers, princes, and kinsmen.
There, the subjects offered a grand welcome to Hari;
they placed flower-garlands and necklaces of gold enriched with diamonds around His neck.
And as the illustrious Hari was descending from his celestial chariot to the outside,
all the subjects honored him with sandalwood paste, parched grain, unbroken rice, flowers, and other offerings.
With shouts of victory, cries of joy, and prostrations,
they honored their parents, all their kinsmen, their sister, and their elders and sages.
And all those dear to Brahmā honored him with pearl necklaces and sandalwood paste;
then, he [mounted] a golden elephant-vehicle accompanied by his army.
King Jinavardhaka caused Hari to mount [the elephant],
and he caused all the great lords to mount upon many [elephants].
Upon vehicles, celestial chariots, carriages, and even carts,
they celebrated Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa with the resounding joy of musical instruments and hymns of praise.
He caused Hari to be paraded everywhere throughout the city of Rāmapurī;
on all the royal highways, Hari was honored by the common people.
Having thus granted his vision with fruits, flowers, unbroken grains of rice, silver, gold coins, garments, and other such things, he returned to the royal palace.
Nourished by the people, the Supreme Lord shone forth;
with a heart full of joy, he convened an assembly in the evening.
