Then Hari, for the sake of performing what was pleasing for the ten million humans, drank water and instructed the subjects.
Seated there upon a divine throne with a serene disposition,
they were performers of the Lord’s work and those who took refuge at the feet of the Blessed One.
Those endowed with meditation on the Blessed One attain the supreme goal—those who serve the virtuous or take refuge at the feet of the virtuous. (15)
Those who travel upon the path of the virtuous attain the supreme goal;
for riches born of the earth ultimately dissolve back into the earth.
If those [gifts] were for the sake of the virtuous, for the sake of Viṣṇu, and bestowers of liberation, then the earth would give food and the clouds would even give water. (17)
Fire indeed performs cooking, and the wind produces dryness;
having thus provided all these, as well as beds and objects of enjoyment, they remain.
Human beings surely give for the sake of humans; they offer wealth to the Lord.
But without such offering to the Supreme Lord, riches are indeed calamities.
They indeed become female denizens of hell, even at the end, being the bestowers of hell;
therefore, those riches which have been given by living beings out of extreme reverence [must not be misused].
All those [offerings] should indeed be offered to Hari at that time, for they truly grant liberation;
by him even the ocean was made, and by him the earth was fashioned.
By that god, the crops were made to yield grain;
by him the body was fashioned, and by him the seed was created.
That which is of the same nature as that [Self]—whether it be what has been done, what is to be enjoyed, or what is given—is equal;
all this which has been given must be offered to Him, the Supreme Self. (23)
That very Blessed One dwells here upon this earth for the sake of the world and for the welfare of embodied beings; he is visible to the eyes and bestows happiness. (24)
Having understood this with effort—that he is to be served and propitiated—those people who, knowing it thus, shall perform service unto me; ||25||
I shall indeed lift them out from the ocean of birth and worldly existence;
I am the dispenser of punishment, for punishment has been ordained by me.
Since embodied beings indeed require a support for their staffs and bowls, let them rely on me alone here in every way as the one who provides that staff. (27)

Whosoever among kings has been struck by me with punishment is always subject to my will; and whomever I have appointed as the wielder of the rod of punishment is the chastiser of those who act wrongly.
Punishment governs all subjects; righteous punishment protects them.
Punishment remains awake while others sleep, bringing about dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa. (29)
Grain, wealth, women, sons, servants, daughters, and gardens;
dharma, justice, and the bounds of social order—all these are maintained through the fear of punishment. (2.182.30)
Out of fear of their mother’s punishment, children do not engage in quarrels;
out of fear of the king’s punishment, some sinners do not commit evil.
For the wicked do not resort to injustice out of fear of punishment from the gods, nor even out of fear of Yama’s rod or fear of the next world. (32)
Moreover, in this world, subjects are restrained by mutual fear;
thus, through this natural order, the world is established in dharma out of fear.
Out of fear of punishment alone, all beings do not devour one another;
there is the royal punishment, the punishment of dharma, and likewise the other, the punishment of Yama. (34)
The gods have the rod of punishment as their primary means; they protect the various classes of beings.
If beings were without the rod of punishment, they would sink into great darkness.
The staff indeed subdues even those who are unsubdued and ill-behaved;
I possess the staff of command, for my command is indeed Vedic.
Those who go without abandoning her reach the further shore of punishment;
for I am the leader of all creations, as well as their ruler and protector. (37)
Entering into kings, I abide and act within their governance; likewise, assuming the form of a restrainer, I govern all subjects as well as all monarchs.
Wherever my rod of punishment proceeds, ever uplifted,
there the subjects do not become deluded and do not lead others astray from the path of righteousness.
Humans, beasts, winged creatures, and even insects and flies—fearing the rod alone, these remain established on the path of their respective duties. (2.182.40)
No one who is not afraid performs sacrifice; no one who is not afraid desires to give;
and no person who is not afraid desires to abide by an agreement. (41)
Rudra, Skanda, Mahendra, Vahni, Varuṇa, Yama, Kāla, Vāyu, Kubera, Ravi, Mṛtyu, and likewise Śani. ||42||
The Vasus, Maruts, Sādhyas, Viśvedevas, and Rākṣasas—
even these have fallen into fear and abide by the restraint of the rod.
Thus these creatures, being terrified, bow down to them again and again;
for were there no fear in the world, they would destroy one another. (44)
Out of fear of the rod alone, everyone proceeds according to dharma;
it is for the joy of the four castes and for the protection of sound policy. (45)
Fear of punishment has been ordained always to protect both dharma and artha;
thereafter, liberation from those two shall accrue to him who takes refuge in my form. (46)
If beasts of prey and other wild animals of different species did not fear the Dharma, then cruel lions and others dwelling in the forest would devour their own kin. (47)
Furthermore, men would gather together and forcibly devour one another; universal ruin would ensue, and the boundaries of ethical conduct would be shattered. (48)
A maiden should not perform the duties of a religious stage of life, nor should she long for marriage;
a young woman should not resort to a lover, and a servant girl should not carry out orders. (49)
A man should not abide by a religious observance or moral conduct without the fear of dharma;
for both heaven and this world of men are established upon dharma. (2.182.50)
And Dharma, when accompanied by devotion, leads to the state of being devoid of qualities;
for nothing is absolutely possessed of qualities, nor is anything absolutely devoid of qualities. (51)
Both the good and the bad are seen everywhere in all the worlds;
having investigated thoroughly, that which is good should be performed, and that which is not good should be abandoned. (52)
The assembly of the virtuous is auspicious; may I always have refuge in Śrī Hari.
Through the rite of total surrender, my meeting with Him must be accomplished.
For those people who have placed their trust in me, Kṛṣṇa, the invincible teacher,
shall indeed never be afflicted by the fear of time, illusion, or other such forces.
Therefore, let the subjects protect the Bhāgavata dharma;
my command, which takes the form of punishment, shall be a source of happiness and free from fear. (55)
May all people here be fearless and established in their desired goals;
may there be well-being for you while Jinavardha remains supported by his desired portion. (56)
Having spoken thus, the Blessed One, the Supreme Person, ceased;
then they performed the lustration ceremony and the worship of Śrī Hari.
The king and others were intensely eager for their parents and kinsmen;
the queen and others performed worship for the women, beginning with Brahma’s beloved consort.
And they deposited all their possessions—gold, silver, and diamonds;
ornaments, garments, gems, vessels, and pearls. (59)
They took up jewels, various utensils, and sacred mantras; all the men and women who remained did so.
Then Śrī Hari made his departure from the assembly;
thereafter, he and all the others partook of milk-bread and other foods in every way.
The subjects, filled with great honor, partook of the food and accepted the favor;
then the king and others returned to their own places, and thereafter Hari departed.
He fell asleep during the night, and having risen in the morning,
he meditated in his heart upon his own supreme form and heard auspicious sounds.
Having performed his daily rites,
when the king had become well-disposed, he brought vessels of cooked food, milk, and other offerings.
They offered it to Hari, and the guests partook of the food;
then, at the time of midday, having eaten, they took their rest.
When Hari had finished eating, the queen and the seven maidens indeed came to serve him,
offering garlands of flowers and other gifts.
They wore various ornaments upon the Lord;
having adorned Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the beautiful Nārāyaṇa. ||67||
The seven maidens took his hand through the rite of marriage;
having obtained the beloved Śrī Kṛṣṇa, they became fulfilled. 68.
The Vaiṣṇava women, filled with joy, gathered among the beloved wives of Brahmā; then, O Rādhā, they all indeed worshipped the divine couple.
And then a great wonder occurred; listen, I shall tell it to you:
a certain wretched person, like one without a protector, came before Hari.
Crying out, he said, "O Blessed One, some rākṣasa indeed carried off my young son and my only daughter during the night. (7.1)
Other Rākṣasas carry off sons and daughters of the people;
they kill men as well, and they even follow behind them.
Seizing them on the mountain, those Rākṣasas carry off both the old and the young;
therefore, O Great King, O Nārāyaṇa, Supreme Lord, protect us! (73)
"O Lord of Mercy, have mercy upon all the people of the mountains!
Thus addressed, Śrī Hari quickly became ready, O Rādhā. 74.
Having placed his subtle Sudarśana disc, resembling a ring, upon his finger, he,
endowed with concealed splendor, quickly endeavored to go to that place.
Meanwhile, King Jinavardhana, equipped with weapons and prepared for battle alongside Hari, was intent on protecting the distressed.
Just then, the king named Alpaketuka,
the lord of the kingdom of Alpaparvata, arrived there and, having bowed to Hari, spoke at that time.
"O Śrī Parameśvara, please sanctify my kingdom";
likewise, the great sage Āpyāyana also made this request of the Lord.
"So be it," Hari said, and likewise he commanded Udantaka to provide protection for the Rākṣasa Anātha, whose deeds were cruel.
And having heard that, Alpaketu, prepared with his weapons,
sat upon his celestial chariot in order to slay that bull among the Rākṣasas.
Then all the armies, equipped with weapons, missiles, and machines, quickly ascended into the sky in celestial chariots for the purpose of battle. ||8 1 ||
The Lord, honored by the king, the queen, and the subjects as well,
was about to go to the house of Alpa-ketu, intending to slay the Rākṣasa.
Having recognized this, he accepted the offerings presented to Śrī Hari;
then, having bestowed a gracious gift upon all, he gave them auspicious blessings. (83)
Having heard the sounds of clarionets and the thundering of battle drums,
and having taken up flower garlands, she ascended into the middle of the carriage.
Then all the other groups of guests and merchant caravans,
having ascended their celestial chariots, uttered shouts of victory for Hari.
Even a person without a protector became a spectator in the black celestial chariot, as the vehicles proceeded along the path shown by him. (86)
In a mere instant, they reached that mountain, and from the eastern half of Khāḍikā, they also reached the long mountain in the west. (87)
It was difficult to traverse due to thorny forests, boulders, and crags, as well as because it was the dwelling place of predatory beasts and, in particular, of Rākṣasas.
Especially by those obstacles consisting of mountains enveloped in garlands of flames and mountain juices, there is a great cavern upon the plateau of the mountain in the sky. (89)
In front were the Rākṣasas, beneath whom the trees had their banners cast down;
they were terrifying, naked, and even eaters of livestock and meat.
Furthermore, there were those who ate human flesh, naked and terrifying,
equipped with weapons made of bone, and likewise skilled in the weapons of mantra-weaving.
Seated in his celestial chariot, Hari, who is devoted to the helpless, showed him that direction;
upon seeing it, he recognized it as the abode of the Rākṣasas.
Although Kṛṣṇa, who assumes the human dance, knows everything, he nevertheless said:
"Then a great and terrible battle will take place. (93)
"But these terrible Rākṣasas cannot be slain here without Rudra Śaṅkara," he said, and having spoken thus, he addressed Īśāna.
O Rudra, O Rudra of mighty arms, O lord of the gods, you are indeed always here with me for the purpose of fighting and for my protection. 95.
"You have been protected by my side; your task has now presented itself.
Assume a fierce and great form and destroy these great asuras! ||96||
"Kill these! O Lord known as Īśa, may you, the god Īśāna, be successful!"—thus [spoke he] to Hara, the lord of the Kṣetrapālas, who was situated in his own celestial chariot.
Having addressed Mahārudra, the great king urged him toward battle;
meanwhile, Rudra Maheśāna abandoned his state of tranquility.
He assumed a terrifying form resembling a mountain;
meanwhile, in the sky, Hari [held] celestial chariots that resembled wheels. 99.
Having caused the military array to be formed,
King Jinavarddhi and likewise King Alpaketu ensured that everything was made completely secure.
They gave the command for the sounding of musical instruments to announce the battle and its roar;
the war-drums were beaten, and the heroes became red-eyed with rage.
Then conchs, kettledrums, and trumpets were sounded on all sides,
and shouts of victory for the heroes arose for the sake of battle.
At that time, ten thousand Rākṣasas belonging to Mārīca appeared;
and Śarva, having suddenly perceived those sounds of battle, [acted accordingly].
Having prepared themselves, they all set out from the city of Mārīśā; traveling through the path of the sky, they reached a deep ravine and were filled with wonder.
Desiring victory in the great battle, they were as if deprived of their vision;
at that time, O Rādhikā, Rudra’s cow-faced companion bellowed loudly.

Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-second chapter, titled "The Description of how Hari, having purified Rāmapurī in the kingdom of King Jinavardhin during the second period of the Tretā-yuga according to the *Śrī-Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*, instructed him, partook of food, rested, and received worship, and then departed for Mount Apināda along with Vidāya for the purpose of destroying the people-destroying Rākṣasa. || 182 ||
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Listen, O Rādhikā; having heard the war-drums, the Rākṣasas made terrifying sounds of "kilakila" and the cracking of their thigh-bones. || 1 ||
Making the earth tremble and causing the quarters of the sky to resound,
they let out loud bursts of laughter, firmly resolved for battle.
Seizing javelins, spears, swords, scimitars, mallets, clubs, stones,
sarja trees, and rocks, they took them up in the sky.
Ten thousand in number, they all rose up for the purpose of battle, bearing mountain-like forms and equipped with missiles and weapons.
Let them kill, devour, and chew those who dwell in celestial palaces;
let them bind and crush them, or even deprive them of their lives. || 5 ||
Let them cut off my hands, feet, and other limbs; let them strike down my heads;
let them devour human bodies; and let them carry away these maidens. (6)
Let them set the vehicles ablaze, let them shatter the machines, let them crush the heads [of the enemies], and let them seize the celestial chariots! || 7 ||
Thus, those many-talking Rākṣasas, resembling an army,
having gathered all around in the sky, then ascended upwards with their projectiles.
They created a terrifying shower of stones and arrows;
they unleashed a rain of iron shafts and a scorching downpour of balls.
Then Hari quickly remembered both the ocean and the moon;
they both arrived in embodied form and bowed down.
Hari said, "Extinguish this fire quickly with waters that are like nectar"; they both did so joyfully for the sake of the globes.
The ocean rained down vapors laden with water;
there, the moon, brought by fire, caused the nectar to flow like rain.
Then King Jinavardhin, Cālpaketu,
and Mahābala struck the rākṣasas with hundreds of thousands of iron arrows.
Cut through in two by crescent-shaped and broad-headed arrows,
those rākṣasas fell upon the earth, flinging their hands and feet into the water again and again.
Then the royal armies stationed on the ground, as well as those in the sky with their catapults, abandoned their lives while wailing in that mountain fastness.
They indeed kill the rākṣasas and cast them down while still alive;
having seen such a terrible slaughter, they cause corruption in the mantras.
Then those rākṣasīs, numbering one hundred thousand, quickly emerged from the cave and flew up into the sky.
By means of Rākṣasas created through mantras and arisen from falsehood, bearing swords,
they caused these two kings to fall from the sky to the earth.
They caused the armies to be slain by means of artificial Rākṣasas;
thus, the crushing of the human armies took place.
Then, seeing the two kings dying, a cry of "Alas! Alas! arose everywhere among the celestial chariots; Kṛṣṇa and Narāyaṇa departed in haste.
Having descended from the celestial chariot with the speed of the wind onto the mountain,
and having supported himself with both arms, he returned once more to his own chariot.
Mādhava restored the two kings to life by the touch of his hand;
he commanded the Moon and caused nectar to be distributed everywhere.
"Quickly restore to life those who have died among the armies of men! Candra then acted with such speed that the troops indeed returned to life.
Then, in order to destroy the artificial armies of the Rākṣasas,
he produced from his matted locks an illusion that deluded the enemy.
The god Īśāna released an illusory army;
she went forth, assuming the form of a Rākṣasī, and became an innumerable host of counter-Rākṣasīs.
Then Śaṅkara devoured all the Rākṣasas,
having manifested his own Durgā from his left side and dispatched her.
Having bowed to Śaṅkara, Durgā assumed ten million forms for the sake of destroying the rākṣasīs,
appearing beautiful with eighteen hands.
Mounted upon lions, bearing many weapons, and possessing great strength and prowess, she descended from the sky in every form at that very moment. 28.
Having seized each Rākṣasī by the neck, he led them to the abode of Yama;
at that time, a great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose within the circle of the Rākṣasas.
Amidst the celestial chariots, the armies, and the men, cries of joy arose;
seeing the deed accomplished by Durgā, the Supreme Lord rejoiced.
The maidens, headed by Brahmapriyā, rejoiced, having attained their long-cherished desire;
meanwhile, the Rākṣasas beheld their wives departing for the abode of Yama.
Exceedingly enraged and distressed, they rushed swiftly toward the army of Durgā; indeed, for the sake of destroying the women, they charged from the sky toward Durgā herself.
Śaṅkara said to his own attendants, the Kṣetrapālas:
"Seize each one of the Rākṣasas individually by the throat quickly as they travel through the path of the sky."
Then the guardians of the fields (kṣetrapālas) seized the backs of the rākṣasas through the air;
having reached them again and again, they seized them by the throat and indeed slew them.
With his feet, with a mace, with a club, and likewise with spears and other weapons;
with his fists, by striking the knees, and by blows from the elbows. ||35||
The lords killed those who had broken bones and were carrying heavy burdens;
some they slew with weapons, such as swords, spears, javelins, and arrows.
The attendants of Īśāna deprived the Rākṣasas of their lives;
five thousand Rākṣasas who fought as human warriors lay dead.
Then hundreds of thousands of rākṣasīs were slain and perished; as for those remaining, having reflected upon it, [they thought], "What purpose indeed is there for us in life? (38)
"Since we must die anyway among these hostile clans," having reflected thus, they all prepared themselves completely for the sky. (39)
They indeed fashioned various nets of illusion;
they also created countless delusive and illusory devices.
Just as the celestial chariots and the armies of the Vaimānika gods met their destruction right there in the sky, so too did they act in vain.
The great king of the Rākṣasas, devoted to the net of illusions, was named Mārīcaśārdūla; his eyes were copper-red with rage as he bit his lip.
Then, disregarding Mahārudra, Nārāyaṇa, and Satī, he discharged illusory mantras from his teeth, tongue, and lips.
Perceiving that the human army was powerful or of such a kind,
he released the magical spells of the Rākṣasas, who were born of other [powers].
Having first protected five thousand [beings] with his own shadow, he then released these terrifying *śālabhañjī* mantras. (45)
Indeed, an ocean of locusts then arose in the sky, by whose weight the celestial chariots were pressed down. 46.
And all the warriors, covered by locusts resembling a rain of clouds in the form of locusts, could not see one another at that time. (47)
And for its destruction, Rudra indeed discharged his weapon;
then, innumerable birds known as *kilahas* appeared in the sky. 48.
Locusts from every direction devoured them in the sky;
and the leaders among the Rākṣasas, seeing the swarms of Karburīs, [rushed forward]. (49)
He set his mind upon the destruction of those women who were prone to quarreling;
by means of his illusory power, he fashioned nets of hawks with arrows.
Then, having become hamsas equal in number to the śyenās and in body, they devoured them in the sky. ||5 1||
Fierce [demons], some resembling celestial chariots and others having bodies like mountains, struck the vimānas with the strength of their wings. 52.
Possessing various forms of grossness, they shattered [the enemies] on all sides;
the broken celestial chariots were cast down and fell from the sky. ||53||
While such diverse slaughter was thus occurring,
Hari himself then commanded the god Vāyu for the sake of providing sustenance.
The Lord of Winds sustained even the shattered celestial chariots in the sky,
while Viśvakarman, as was remembered, arrived there.
By means of his craft and labor, he quickly joined the broken parts together;
having fashioned the vehicles according to their proper arrangement, he presented them to the Supreme Lord.
He made [the enemy] very dejected and remained right there on the battlefield;
then Rudra, by means of fire-mantras, [created] birds known as "fires."
He swiftly produced millions upon millions of arrows;
fierce fire-birds and hawks devoured them. (58)
Impelled by Rudra, they rushed to devour even the Rākṣasas;
however, the Rākṣasas there vanished for a moment through their illusory power (māyā).
Then they unleashed fierce serpents of virulent poison;
having mounted their winged vehicles, they would go and bite those who were situated in their celestial chariots.
Rudra, by means of the Garuḍa-mantra,
produced thousands of crores of Garuḍas, the devourers who bring about the destruction of the Nāgas.
The Garuḍas pursued them and indeed devoured them;
then, for the sake of destroying the Garuḍas, the Rākṣasa unleashed fire.
Agni, Mahāgni, and Ālāmaya appeared in the sky;
at that very moment, Rudra opened his third eye.
The fire of dissolution that arose there drew in the false fire produced by the Rākṣasa and indeed consumed it within its own exceedingly terrible form.
Then the fire was quickly extinguished, bringing fear to the Rākṣasas;
they remained hidden beneath the trees at the edge of the thicket, with their arrows and shafts ready.
Having resolved that they must fight,
the hosts of Rudra released bhalla-missiles from the path of the sky, while the Kṣetrapālas did so from all sides.
Then they unleashed a rain of arrows to slay the foremost of the Rākṣasas;
and when those Rākṣasas reached a state where their very lives were in peril, [the monkeys acted].
Then, with mantras over stones, they released many arrows;
at that moment, boulders as large as crags appeared in the sky.
Flying up again and again into the sky, they indeed struck down the celestial chariots;
having perceived that action of Rudra, he released the Vajra weapon.
All the rocks, having been reduced to powder, were carried away by the wind in all directions;
then the Daityas vanished and released massive clouds.
Then, by means of the wind-weapon (vāyvastra), Rudra caused the clouds to dissolve;
thereafter, those Rākṣasas who remained alive out of the dead fled in fear toward the ocean.
Just as they rushed forward to enter, Śaṅkara, the benefactor of the world,
released his attendants (gaṇas) in order to hold them back from behind.
Then, having turned back, the Daityas again engaged in battle with the Gaṇas;
at that time, Rudra then released his trident, which strikes fear into the worlds.
Whirling with speed and emitting fire in every direction,
that lord of Mārīśa slew those Daityas and then vanished from sight.
Then, assuming an illusory form, he placed that very trident of fire into his mouth while everyone was looking on.
Seeing that supreme marvel, Śaṅkara and the other Gaṇas were likewise struck with wonder;
and having observed that extraordinary feat of the Rākṣasa, Nārāyaṇa—
They praised this world-terrifying deed of the Asura;
then, beholding Śambhu, Hari quickly released his discus from his hand.
When a wheel resembling a ring emerged from the finger,
it quickly released fire and grew into something most terrifying.
It had a thousand spokes, was equal to the sun, red in color, and possessed great velocity;
it made all the directions resound and set the forests ablaze.
Reducing the mountain to ashes, he swiftly devoured the Rākṣasas;
by his force, the earth and the circle of the wind were shaken.
The oceans indeed trembled and became rigid, rising beyond their usual limits;
the celestial chariots in the sky momentarily lost their stability and levelness.
The hearts of all embodied beings trembled and they abandoned their fortitude; then a cry of "Alas! Alas! arose, and the weak fainted for a moment. (82)
In that moment of extreme velocity, all beings were indeed rendered unconscious;
the Rākṣasas became paralyzed once they recognized the Sudarśana discus.
In that very moment, the wheel indeed tore asunder their heads;
the remaining Rākṣasas were slain, and even Māriṣeśa was destroyed.
Then their bodies fell upon the earth like massive boulders;
thereafter, he took up his discus and his trident, which protects the hosts.
That most terrible [weapon], resembling a circle of fire, having attained extreme velocity, did not quickly attain pacification. ||86||
He gradually withdrew from the mountain ranges and forest expanses;
at that time, there were many extensive regions of the mountain's terrain. (87)
Then, consumed by the fire of the [inner] wheels, they attained the state of rasa;
though rich with the ashes of white crystal, they became like black gems. 88.
The beloved regions, which were like gold in color, became yellowed and scorched by the fire of the wheel, reduced to the state of stone and mountain ash. (89)
Furthermore, just as beautiful jewels may become stones,
so too stones produced from mercury throughout their entirety become of the nature of non-mercury.
From the friction of the wheels, the joints produced a rustling sound;
those regions, whose bodies were fit for artistic work, underwent a transformation.
He indeed assumed a peaceful form and took on the appearance of his attendants;
he also bore the trident and the form of the Gaṇas, as well as the three-eyed aspect.
Having summoned the hosts of men stationed in the forest, both of them bestowed courage upon them and proclaimed their victory. || 93 ||
At that moment, victory trumpets resounded on all sides, and a rain of flowers was showered from the sky by the gods and other beings. (94)
The kettledrums resounded, as did the conchs and trumpets;
indeed, joy entered the army of Manu in embodied form.
Indeed, even among all the hosts of gods in the celestial palaces,
as well as within the hearts of both kings, joy could not be contained.
Shouts of victory arose from great joy within the celestial chariots;
then the discus, the trident, and the two attendants likewise descended upon the mountain.
They went to the entrance of the cave, the dwelling place of the Rākṣasas;
having gone inside, they beheld it enveloped in darkness. 98.
Having spread its own light even into that abyss, it [reveals] the heaps of remaining bones of the men and women who have been devoured there. (99)
Seeing that the two attendants had fallen into distress, the two who were full of compassion went forward and then looked back at that place once more.
Two hundred and one thousand maidens and women who had been abducted by the Rākṣasas wept at that time.
Both of them reported the occurrences concerning the rākṣasas,
saying that there was a city within the forest amidst a grove of trees.
In that place where many people— men, women, children, and even infants— had been seized and held captive, they remained within a wooden trough, their forms rendered invisible.
Having quickly brought all of them out from that cave,
the two of them went to the city as it had previously been made by the Rākṣasas.
There, many youths were seen standing in fetters; others, though freed from their bonds, were confined within the walls of the fortress.
Many men and women were to be eaten by the Rākṣasas in succession;
seeing more than a thousand [victims], the two of them liberated them.
Then the discus remained there, while the trident went toward Hari and Hara;
at that time, Nārāyaṇa and Hara related the entire account.
Quickly abandoning the celestial chariot, they went swiftly to the city;
though weeping, they were filled with joy upon seeing Lord Hari and Hara.
And those subjects, released from their bonds, bowed down to him again and again;
there Hari consoled all the subjects like a father.
The son and the daughter of Anātha also bowed down to Hara,
the Supreme Lord, and wept again and again.
O Rādhikā, Hari indeed granted them fortitude and fearlessness;
to Śaṅkara, Hari spoke words that bring happiness for the sake of their deliverance. || 111 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Battle of the Rākṣasas with the Two Kings and Their Armies, the Battle of the Rākṣasīs with Durgā, the Destruction of the Rākṣasas by Rudra, the Protection of the Subjects Held in Shackles, and the Transformation of the Mountain into a Stone of Liquid Essence through the Splendor of Sudarśana," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Listen, O Rādhikā; I am Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Lord.
I spoke to Rudra, who is capable of lifting [the earth] and is the slayer of the Rākṣasas. || 1 ||
O Śambhu, grant a mantra to this childless woman and her son;
then, O Viṣṇu, grant two sons to that childless man.
Śambhu quickly gave the mantra to both Bālā and Bālaka;
although he was without a protector, he received the mantra of Śambhu and became a Vaiṣṇava.
Then that young girl, considering Kṛṣṇa to be a suitable protector and bridegroom,
obtained her father's permission and took Kṛṣṇa’s hand right there.
Having observed this, he then released and protected two hundred and one thousand young women from the abyss.
Having recognized their own beloved Nārāyaṇa as the Supreme Lord, all those goddesses,
who were white in complexion, [perceived] the Lord as their worthy consort.
And there in the forest, independent and impelled by merit, they took hold of Hari’s hand as its protector with auspicious marriage rites performed at their hearts' desire.
Śambhu first gave the Vaiṣṇava mantra to all of them;
he then established all those beloved wives of Brahmā in the sky.
Mādhava placed all the men and women situated in the prison upon his own feet with his head, and he made them independent.
Kṛṣṇa removed their sufferings and caused them to receive the mantra from Śambhu;
they then became Vaiṣṇavas and took refuge in Śrī Narāyaṇa.
And to those subjects who were besieged by Rākṣasas in the city of Mārīśāna,
Hara gave Vaiṣṇava mantras and thus delivered them.
Then, having wandered through that most beautiful city at every spot,
the Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa sanctified everything.
Requested by all of them and honored by their hearts, Kṛṣṇa was repeatedly entreated to remain right there for the night.
Having seen that state of meditation, he quickly descended his celestial chariot then in the vast Araṇyaka forest, in the vicinity of the city of Mārīśā.
At the onset of night, Hari himself caused all of them to take up residence on the ground beneath trees and had them eat their meal during the night.
And there he caused a most excellent festival for Vijaya to be celebrated,
with singers, dancers, musical instruments, and joyful hymns of praise.
Then he passed the night with plays, stories, and narratives;
meanwhile, all those warriors on his own side who had died in battle [were honored].
Śrī Hari quickly brought them all back to life by means of his yogic power;
they all regained their state as living beings, along with their vital breaths and bodies.
Having recovered their health, they returned that very night to the abode of Hari;
indeed, even those whose bones lay in the thickets or who had perished in the forest arrived there.
And at that time, they fell down in the vicinity of the city;
there, by means of his yogic power, the Blessed One recalled those embodied beings.
All who had died became alive again by the will of Kṛṣṇa, whose resolve is truth;
restored to health, they gathered there during the night. ||21||
Indeed, many men and women, as well as boys and young children,
were seen in their dwellings in the morning with entirely new appearances.
In this manner, at the end of the night, Śrī Hari restored a hundred thousand men to life out of compassion; and Śambhu bestowed a mantra upon them.
Then they became true Vaiṣṇavas and drank the water from the feet of Hari;
though they were people from different lands, they remembered their own native soil.
Some went to their own countries, while others indeed remained there;
then the Blessed Lord spoke to the high-souled Lomaśa.
"Indeed, this kingdom is to be surrendered to King Jinavardhana;
O Guru, bestow upon him the crown according to the ritual of consecration. (26)
"Apply a *tilaka* on his forehead; he shall become king here.
Then Jinavarddhi said, "That should indeed be given to the victor. (27)
"O Śrī Parameśvara, that kingdom must be given to Īśāna;
likewise, Alpaketu and the other great sages shall do so. (28)
Then Hari spoke to Śambhu, having forcibly seated him upon a golden throne and having applied unbroken grains of rice and saffron to his forehead like the moon.
With his own right hand, the Lord Śrī Mahādeva placed a crown upon her;
thus Mārīśā became the queen of Īśāna.
O Rādhā, he gradually resettled the city upon the foothills of the mountainous land,
adorning it with groves and gardens.
This very Lord Īśāna, the benefactor Śaṅkara, assumed a second form;
he was accompanied by Durgā as well as by his attendants.
At the command of Hari and requested by the subjects, he established his own residence;
thus this very one became the presiding deity, the Lord, the Supreme Ishvara.
He is indeed the destroyer of the Rākṣasas who possess white and fair progeny;
he is the god who destroys all defects, and he is forever the bestower of liberation and happiness. (34)
On that day, Śaṅkara said to the son of Gaṅgā:
"Only after I have secured the stability of your kingdom will I give this city to you. (35)
"Take this garland and offer it with a handful of water in the presence of Hari";
having been addressed thus there in the morning, he took up the garland. (36)
In the morning, Hari, having stationed the attendants of Śambhu as guards there,
[took leave of] Śambhu, Durgā, the wives of Brahmā, the great sages, and his own family.
On the fifth day of the dark fortnight of Bhādrapada, the Blessed One, having assembled the people, instructed them regarding the performance of the milk-drinking rite. (38)
Time is indeed a Rākṣasa, just as the Rākṣasa who appeared here was slain along with his entire lineage by Śaṅkara, my devotee.
Likewise, by relying on me alone, even the demon Kāla is destroyed by my devotees who have attained a state of liberated being; of this there is no doubt.
Let them practice devotion to me, and likewise let them worship Īśāna;
let them indeed take refuge in Śambhu, their chosen deity, who provides great protection. 41.
Let them also worship Mahādevī, Satī, Durgā, and Vaiṣṇavī;
for tomorrow is indeed Sunday, and the Sun is the presiding deity.
For the sake of destroying all defects, she who bestows light was propitiated by me here on a Sunday, accompanied by Śaṅkara and others.
The terrible Rākṣasas, who devour and bestow suffering, have been struck down;
likewise, you too must destroy those faults that grant sin, O Ravi. (44)
All [afflictions] such as desire and anger must be restrained; the bull [dharma] is to be protected when the sun [of time] shines.
Disease arises in two ways: either physical or mental. (45)
Physical disease arises from mental [afflictions], and bodily-born [disease] also arises from the mental;
for these two arise from one another, as do desire, anger, and the rest. (46)
The humors (doṣas) are indeed declared to be diseases; they should be abandoned on the day of the Sun.
Sattva, rajas, and tamas are the three qualities (guṇas) of the mind. ||47||
On Sunday, those three who possess universal forms should not be joined with [worldly] attachment;
sorrow is overcome by joy, and joy is overcome by sorrow. (48)
But by means of the quality of darkness (tamas), joy and sorrow are oppressed;
having understood this wheel of qualities, one should suppress it while the sun of spiritual power shines.
Discontent, negligence, intoxication, passion,
excessive greed, avarice, delusion, arrogance, and agitation— these indeed are the Rākṣasas.
One possessed by these evils would never find relief even in the sun;
people are not able to fill the pit called the belly in a single day. (51)
The wise man, considering it thus, should not fill that [breath] during the sun;
for it should not be filled, just as a fire blazes when kindled and is extinguished when unkindled.
When the Lord himself is devoid of the desire for food, he indeed becomes tranquil;
yet for the sake of his own belly, the world produces much sacrificial residue.
On Sunday, one should be a conqueror of the belly and a victor over all evils; human desires and enjoyments are likewise to be conquered on the day of the Sun. (54)
People who possess no worldly enjoyments go to the unsurpassed state when the sun [is present];
likewise, yoga, security, and renunciation should always be performed toward the Sun, who is Hari.
For the sake of a single belly, a tiger consumes a great deal of prey;
other dull-witted and greedy creatures, such as deer and the like, subsist upon him.
Having reflected thus, one should avoid fruitless accumulations of obstacles during the Sun's [transit];
for people who subsist on leaves, fruits, or eat but a single meal a day, [these obstacles are avoided] during the Sun's [transit]. 57.
Even a king who might rule this entire earth in its completeness does not truly excel a man who is devoted to the Sun and intent on renunciation. ||58||
On the day of the Sun (Sunday), auspicious resolutions should be made without undertaking new worldly activities;
those who are free from meat do not grieve, and indeed, meat must be abandoned on the day of the Sun.
The path of the ancestors and the path of the gods may be attained from Śaṅkara by the great sages through austerity, celibacy, and devotion. (2.184.60)
Having cast off their bodies, they go at the end to the stainless world of Brahmā;
one should always abandon worldly gain, which is a bond-making action, like [casting off] a garment in the sun.
Therefore, O Hari, one who is liberated and remains attached attains that supreme state;
having ascended the clarity of wisdom, whatever is to be abandoned must indeed be relinquished. 62.
If the worship of Īśāna is to be undertaken by one who possesses vision and sound intelligence,
then within this body composed of the six sheaths, the Sun indeed stands as the seventh, distinct [from the others].
He who perceives that deity as his own self truly sees;
from that very state, he gradually attains the supreme Brahman.
The self-controlled, the peaceful, and the patient attain the state of the wise when the sun is present;
likewise, there is the invocation of Īśāna and the worship of Durgā during the time of the sun.
Worship of the Guru and worship of Hari must be performed by devoted human beings;
on that day, one should remain unattached, free from worldly ties, and liberated from bondage.
He who is equal toward both enemy and friend will certainly be liberated;
those who follow such dharma, or who are devoted to charity and austerity, [attain the same].
Endowed with the quality of benevolence, free from desire, anger, and other such passions,
they were dedicated to the protection of their subjects and remained steadfast in the vows of Sūrya and Īśāna.
Devoted to honoring your gurus and elders, you shall attain the worlds you desire;
may there be well-being for you, and may there always be happiness for those who dwell with the Sun.
Having spoken thus, Śrī Hari, after reflecting and observing silence,
said to Alpaketu that he should go to his city of Jīvanīpurī.
"Let others also be prepared; we shall indeed eat there as well.
Then King Jinavarddhi, having bowed to Hari, spoke thus.
Īśāna, as well as Durgā and the sage Āpyāyana, having eaten here in the city and wandered about, thereafter, O Blessed One... [72]
"Having purified the surface of the earth, you must then depart from here.
The compassionate Lord said, "O Rādhikā, let it be so. (73)
Cooked foods had already been prepared there by the local people;
at midday, everyone took their meal according to the desire of Īśāna.
Then Durgā, Satī, and the wives of Brahmā indeed partook of food,
having rested for a moment in vehicles, mounts, and celestial chariots.
Having prepared themselves and reached the sky, Kṛṣṇa, Nārāyaṇa, and the others quickly entered the celestial chariot after receiving the worship offered by those men.
Then, many excellent musical instruments were sounded profusely;
indeed, shouts of victory and the sounds of trumpets arose on all sides. ||77||
Having protected the royal army there, King Jinarddhika granted leave to Śambhu, Durgā, Nārāyaṇa, and the others.
They departed together with King Alpa-ketu in vehicles,
and their celestial chariots traveled along the path shown by Alpa-ketu.
And the great ṛṣi Āpyāyana arrived together with him in a celestial chariot;
they passed beyond Mount Apiyāna and crossed over the northern mountain.
And those stationed in their celestial chariots beheld the exceedingly beautiful one known as Alpa;
and Alpaketu was the first to go forward with his chariot. ||8 1 ||
Sāpyāyana, accompanied by his army and attendants, quickly went to his own city of Jīvanī with offerings such as garlands and honors for the sake of a welcome.
Accompanied by the queen, her sons, daughters, and others, he stood before him;
then, at his command, the musicians quickly sounded their instruments. (83)
The people uttered shouts of victory, those bearing whisks offered words of praise, and the artisans made the sounds of their machines—all indicating a welcome. (84)
Seeing the golden celestial chariot in the sky, the men bowed down,
as did the women dwelling on the mountains and the people living in the houses upon the earth.
Beholding Hari’s celestial chariot, blazing with splendor and adorned with a banner—
extraordinary, perfectly equipped, and resplendent with an excellence of divinity.
It was enriched with many garlands, arches, and the like made of pearls, diamonds, and precious stones;
it was radiant with the rays of the splendor inherent in its form, resembling the sun.
It was preceded by swans, Garuḍas, elephants, and horses with rubies for manes,
as well as by lions and śarabhas, all appearing in embodied forms.
It was adorned on its sides by many other vehicles and celestial chariots,
and from behind, it resounded with the shouts of victory from gods, goddesses, and their retinues.
Adorned with flowers, unbroken rice, garlands, and well-nourished growths,
it was cooled below by moon-like jewels that possessed the radiance of the cool-rayed moon.
Its center was beautifully adorned with gardens featuring rows of kalpa-trees and their flowers;
it shone with wall panels enriched by ornaments set with wish-fulfilling gems (cintāmaṇi). ||9.1||
It was exceedingly beautiful with peaks adorned by the splendor of golden jars,
and it displayed variegated svastika patterns fashioned by the auspicious Kamalā.
Adorned with divine fans, parasols, and radiant chowries, and resounded with the cries of "Victory! from staff-bearers and pearl necklaces, he proceeded toward the eastern quarter. 93.
"May the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa be ever victorious!"—thus indicating his devotion to Mādhava with words of golden hue. (94)
Beholding such a beautiful celestial mansion, they bowed in the sky;
and by the path shown by the king, they descended upon the vast and auspicious earth. (95)
The infallible Hari brought down his own celestial chariot,
and other chariots as well descended to the surface of the earth.

The subjects offered a welcome with shouts of "Victory! and prostrated themselves like well-disciplined staffs; standing at a distance, they scattered parched grain and other offerings there upon the celestial chariot.
Others scattered flowers, some scattered unbroken grains of rice,
and others scattered perfumes, garlands, and so forth upon the celestial chariot.
Thus, O Rādhikā, on the fifth day of the month of Bhādrapada, Nārāyaṇa reached the city of Jīvanī, which was surrounded by forests. 99.
King Alpaketu, the queen, their daughters, sons,
and others were waiting outside at the front of the celestial chariot for the arrival of Hari.
All of them, with steady eyes and filled with great joy, were watching right there at the gate, wondering when Mādhava would indeed come outside.

Thus, in the *Śrī-Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*, within the second section, the *Tretā-Santāna*, [described is] the taking of the hand of Hari by one thousand two hundred and two maidens following the destruction of the Rākṣasas for the sake of rescuing the orphaned children; the restoration to life of the deceased from the bones killed by the Rākṣasas; the establishment of the kingdom of Īśāna; the majesty of Sunday (*ravivāra*); the worship, blessings, and rest at night; and, after the morning meal on the fifth day of the dark fortnight of Bhādrapada, [the journey] toward the city of King Alpaketu.
The one hundred and eighty-fourth chapter, titled "The Determination of Going and Other [Actions]."
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Then, O Rādhā, this Blessed One, casting his gaze toward the city of Jīvanī from the celestial chariot, quickly descended outside of it. || 1 ||
Then King Alpaketu, the sage Āpyāyana, and others likewise placed auspicious necklaces upon the necks of the young Kṛṣṇa.
They placed upon his head clusters of flowers— golden, made of silk, emerald, and set with gems— as well as fragrant blossoms held in their hands.
They honored him by offering unbroken grains (akṣata) and bowed at his feet;
likewise, Īśāna and the other lords, as well as the sages, were all honored by everyone.
Then the ancestors, together with their families, were highly honored with words of welcome;
having washed their feet, those devotees of Hari drank the water.
They seated Hari upon a golden, elephant-drawn palanquin;
the others, however, were placed upon auspicious carriages, mounts, and chariots. 6.
Having seated them in palanquins and celestial chariots amidst auspicious sounds,
the king and others, overwhelmed with love, paraded them through the city.
And by the ministers, the kings and others, the merchants, the officials, the subjects, and likewise by women and men of all castes. || 8 ||
He was honored and worshipped on the main road, at the crossroads,
in the courtyard, at the junction of paths, and in the circular area of the market stalls.
Hari was repeatedly propitiated by all of them with a welcome and with priceless offerings, such as all kinds of requisites.
Nārāyaṇa was worshipped with fruits, flowers, and auspicious offerings;
having thus beheld that city and granted his vision,
he returned to his dwelling and partook of water.
Hari quickly sat down in the assembly hall and gave his instructions.
Where the Blessed Lord resides in person, where the virtuous have taken refuge in Hari,
and where devotees dwell— that region is called divine.
Indeed, that place is beyond the material qualities (nirguṇa) and bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Blessed is this Ketumāla, and blessed are the kings dwelling on its banks.
Blessed are those cities where my feet have come;
blessed are you, the subjects here, who have attained the state of being Vaiṣṇavas.
Being a Vaiṣṇava, association with the virtuous, the grace of the Supreme Lord, devotion to one's chosen deity, and service to the holy—these are indeed difficult to attain. (16)
For those among whom these have assembled, nothing remains to be attained;
even the inhabitants of the celestial realms desire this pentad. (17)
For those whose character is devoted to austerity and the study of sacred texts, there exist eternal worlds;
wise ones who have no enemies have attained supreme liberation through devotion. (18)
Turning away from sense objects, those seeking liberation go to the supreme state through devotion; endowed with devotion, they attain an indescribable goal.
But it has been said that for those who do not possess the five [faculties], there is only the mundane;
having split open the trunk of a plantain tree, no core is to be found. (2.185.20)
Therefore, having obtained those five [faculties], having set the goal of the highest good,
and having restrained the thirst of the mind, one should cast off the continuity of karma.
But he who is attached to the Supreme Lord, following the path of the virtuous, should meditate on the God dwelling within; he shall indeed attain the highest good.
Those who are devoted to ritual action, immersed in sacrifice, charity, and the practice of service,
and who, having beheld me, renounce [all else], are considered by me to be destined for my world.
For those who possess renunciation, contentment, worship of the Lord, the destruction of longing, and the dissolution of pride and the like, there is indeed eternal happiness. (24)
In this regard, there is a four-stepped ladder that grants the world of Brahmā:
the sacrifice of discourse, the lineage of sages, and the knowledge of those who perceive reality. (25)
The ladder of action is prescribed for householders, while the ladder of austerity is considered for the virtuous;
if worldly endeavor is rich with sense-objects, then non-endeavor is superior.
In worldly striving there are many faults that bring about both destruction and birth;
by such striving the self is defiled, and thereby one's spiritual welfare perishes.
He who acquires what is unworthy here and abandons what is worthy in every way will, at the end, be utterly forsaken by both and thus become blind. (28)
Having reflected thus, especially by householders among men, even a sacrifice of action should be performed according to the rules, and even a sacrifice of wealth with genuine riches. (29)
Nārāyaṇa and I myself must be sought after and worshipped;
in ancient times, Indra became the king of the gods through various sacrifices.
Having offered himself as an oblation in the great sacrifice, that Mahādeva became the God of gods; pervading and supporting all worlds, he attained the state of the Sovereign Lord.
Āvikṣita and the Maruts, through devotion, attained Śrī— who serves at the sacrifice and bestows all things— and he also went to my own abode.
In this way, other performers of ritual action in previous kalpas and in other ages,
having engaged in sacrifices of action, attained heaven along with their wealth.
In the sacrifice of action, one attains Vaiṣṇavahood, association with the virtuous, and the pleasing of Hari; indeed, service to the virtuous occurs—thus one should perform such a sacrifice.
If one is free from desire and perfectly contented, he attains the eternal Brahman;
for contentment is indeed the supreme heaven, and satisfaction is the highest bliss. ||35||
Nothing whatsoever is praised anywhere as a happiness superior to contentment;
having withdrawn all desires, the embodied soul finds delight within its own self alone. (36)
He has no fear from anywhere, nor does anyone have any fear of him;
for when he becomes a seer of the Self, he is himself devoid of desire and anger.
Free from malice toward all beings and devoid of all desires, having offered everything to Hari, he attains Brahman. ||38||
For those beings whose activity flows toward passion, their course remains there; but for those dedicated to Hari, it is eternal. (39)
Some praise conciliation, while other people praise effort;
others praise meditation, and still others praise a virtuous refuge. (2.185.40)
Some praise sacrifice, while others praise renunciation;
some praise giving, and others accept gifts.
Those who are peaceful, having attained a state of silence, worship the Supreme Lord;
those who are not peaceful desire sovereignty—wherein both are equal in their respective scales.
Having reflected upon this, the wise should resort to that auspicious means which bestows happiness, follows its natural course, and grants the highest good. (43)
Living without harming living beings is the means for attaining the state of the virtuous;
that indeed is declared to be the path of the good, wherein the self is not bound at all.
If that king were always to conduct himself in his kingdom by the path of non-malice, through truthfulness, sharing, self-restraint, and likewise compassion; ||45||

Through modesty, through generosity, through extreme devotion to the gods, through the protection of subjects, through self-mastery, and through a mind that regards the pleasant and unpleasant as equal; ||46||
By subsisting on the remnants of the sacrifice and by showing favor to the virtuous,
both this world and the next shall become for him a source of the most excellent fruits.
Thus, for those who are devoted to the Dharma, who always resort to the service of the virtuous,
and who fight here solely for the sake of protecting their subjects and for the cause of righteousness— 48.
Beyond heaven, there shall be a supreme, auspicious state, the highest goal;
there dwell the ancient Rudras, Vasus, Ādityas, and world-protectors. (49)
The Sādhyas, the Maruts, and all the Viśveśa gods, having performed such dharma through meritorious deeds, attained the supreme heaven; from that [state], they became human beings here.
Relying upon such a dharma, let them indeed go to the supreme goal;
for the gods, the ancestors, and likewise the guests always depend upon the householder. (51)
Virtuous servants and human beings constantly depend upon him, as do birds, cattle, and all living beings who have taken refuge in him. (52)
Austerity, sacrifice, as well as knowledge, living on alms, restraint of the senses, meditation, solitude, contentment, wisdom, and service. (53)
O Kṛṣṇa, those duties of the brahmin which belong to the householder must always be offered by me unto You:
sacrifice, learning, exertion, the acquisition of wealth, and the wielding of the rod of punishment.
O Kṛṣṇa, the state of severity, conduct, knowledge, procreation, and giving— those duties of kingship which belong to the householder— should always be offered by me unto You.

The acquisition of wealth, enterprise, charity, protection, and so forth, as well as the cultivation of crops and other such duties, are the dharmas of the Vaiśya; these should be offered to me, the Lord. (56)
Service, endurance, obedience to commands, eating the remnants of food, and the state of servitude—these are the duties of a Śūdra; these too must be offered to me, Mādhava. (57)
Devotion to one's husband, service to the teacher, the maintenance of the household and so forth, and the protection of offspring—these duties of women must be offered by me to my Lord. (58)
Study, play, expansion, delight, jesting, and daring—these are the qualities of children, which I offer to my Lord. (59)
Desire, strength, the pursuit of self-interest, victory, lack of reflection, acquisition, and union—these are the duties of youth; they should be offered to me, their Lord.
Chattering, trembling, dependence on others, incapacity, ferocity, laziness, and insults—these are the characteristics of those who have increased their passion for me. (6.1)
Beating, endurance of suffering, poverty, being like an animal, punishment, harshness, and insults—these are the wretched conditions that exist when I am the master. (62)
Laughter, pleasure, dalliance, affection, servitude, severity, bondage, and hopelessness—these feminine qualities are indeed offered by me unto my Lord. (63)
For those who live in this manner, having dedicated their minds to me alone,
I surely effect their deliverance even as they are sinking in the ocean of death.
Formerly, there were two sages born of the brahminical order named Śaṅkha and Likhita;
they were brothers who lived in separate dwellings.
Once, Likhita came to the hermitage of Śaṅkhapālita along the Bāhudā river, which was always endowed with trees bearing flowers and fruit.
At that time, Śaṅkha was not in the hermitage, for he had gone into the forest;
however, Likhita indeed caused the ripe fruits to fall.
While he was eating right there, Śaṅkha arrived;
he said to his brother, "You have indeed eaten the property belonging to another without asking permission."
"The fruits have fallen here of their own accord; your virtue is not compromised here.
By taking these fruits yourself, you have committed no act of theft. (69)
"Go, approach the king, and report the act of theft.
He also went quickly to the monarch and reported that deed.
"I have committed theft; grant me the expiation for it.
King Sudyumna said, "If you consider me to be a king," (71)
"O Brahmin, then receive my permission; choose something other than punishment.
Although addressed thus, the king of sages chose nothing else.
Then the king had the hands of the sage cut off;
having received his punishment, the brahmin departed and went to his brother.
Śaṅkha said to him: "O most righteous brother, go to the Bāhudā river;
satisfy the sages, the ancestors, and the gods according to the prescribed rites. (74)
Then once again, at another time, you must certainly never set your mind upon unrighteousness;
having received the command of Śaṅkha, Likhita went to the Bāhudā river. (75)
Having plunged into the holy river and offered the fruit of his atonement to me,
the Brahmin proceeded to offer the water libation.
At that moment, his two hands appeared before me as he offered himself;
then, having performed the ritual libation of water, he forever surrendered everything unto me.
Having realized the greatness of *arpaṇa*, which destroys all sins, that brahmin performed it here in this land of action continuously. ||78||
The punishment which the king has inflicted was also assigned to me by him;
and the delivery of water and other offerings was likewise assigned to me by the written document. (79)
And likewise, the command of Śaṅkha was entrusted by him to me;
thus, through this complete surrender, they have been purified by my power.
There is no fault of speech for Śaṅkha, no fault of punishment for the king, nor likewise any fault of the hand for the scribe, because [the document] was delivered by me. (81)
Thus, those men who, having remembered me and having surrendered themselves to me, eat and live free from affliction—they are my dependents. (82)
"Free from the bonds of karma, they indeed come to me alone at the end;
so shall you all, O groups of kings and groups of subjects, in every respect. (83)
Having made the offering of everything to me and having worshipped me, go to my abode;
at the end, when your life-breaths depart, I shall appear before you within the range of your vision.
"I shall lead my devotees by means of a celestial chariot to my supreme abode;
therefore, perform worship of me and always honor me. (85)
"Make my foundation firm; I shall lead you to my supreme abode.
Having said this, the Blessed One spoke to the high-souled Lomaśa.
"Give mantras to the subjects, and let the people receive food.
Thus addressed, he gave mantras that deliver those who have come for refuge. (87)
Then all the subjects went to their respective homes; thereafter Hari took his meal with Rādhikā, and everyone else also partook of their meals. ||88||
Having found rest at night and rising quickly in the morning, Kṛṣṇa, having performed his daily rites, sat down upon his own seat. (89)
Then the king requested Hari to allow him to drink milk and so forth; and Hari partook of a meal of milk.
He took betel-leaf and desired to depart;
others as well, having already consumed their breakfast of milk and other foods, did likewise early in the morning.
Then the queen, together with her daughter, became ready to go;
she arrived for the purpose of worship and worshipped the Supreme Lord. 92.
The seven daughters and maidens took the hand of Hari;
having thus performed the offering of tribute, they obtained their beloved, the Supreme Lord.
Having received the garland of choice and other honors, they then felt their purpose was fulfilled;
those seven, having united with the beloveds of Brahmā, ascended that celestial chariot.
Then the king ascended [the mountain] and worshipped Hari with devotion;
having bid farewell to his subjects, they gave gifts, and the king presented royal offerings. ||95||
Then musical instruments indicative of the departure were indeed played;
thereafter, the Lord ascended the palanquins and celestial chariots.
He ascended his own celestial chariot together with his family, with Śambhu,
and also with the sage Iṣṭajara, who was full of devotion.
Then Hari, being requested by the king named Jayakṛṣṇavana,
increased Alpaketu and the others with his blessings in the sky.
By means of his celestial chariot, he made his way to Jayakṛṣṇa’s excellent kingdom,
passing over Alpādri and reaching the land that was his own desired refuge in old age.
Harikṛṣṇa and others, whose vehicles were the sky, reached the atmosphere;
they arrived at the sources of the rivers beginning with the Rāhunā.
Formerly, King Ṛṣi and Yayu made the surface of the earth ready for the arrival [of Hari]; there they welcomed Hari with musical instruments and other offerings.
O Rādhikā, upon seeing the city of Vārāṇasī— spacious, radiant, and adorned— the Lord Hari then rejoiced.

Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of Śrī Hari’s wandering in the city of Jīvanī belonging to Alpaketu, His worship, His instruction in the assembly by means of the example of Śaṅkha and Likhita, His meal, His rest at night, His arrival on the sixth day in the city of Varaṇā in the kingdom of King Jayakṛṣṇavana after breakfast, and so forth," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O Rādhā, from the sky the Lord beheld the city of Prāvaraṇā;
by the path indicated by the king, he caused the celestial chariot to descend.
Furthermore, other celestial chariots descended after that;
many musical instruments were played, and shouts of victory arose. || 2 ||
There were shouts of victory and cries of joy from the subjects, yet they did not cease;
for King Śrī Hari himself had gone out with his gold-seizing guards.
He worshipped him with flower garlands, clusters of blossoms, unbroken grains of rice, and other offerings;
the king’s servants, the merchants, and the subjects all offered him a welcome.
With prostrations, shouts of victory, and auspicious hymns of praise,
the subjects displayed their enthusiasm and showed their honor.
Having washed the feet of Śrī Hari with water, he drank the nectar;
the king, together with his family and subjects, drank that nectar.
They performed the worship of Īśāna and likewise of the others according to their respective rank;
the queen also performed the worship of Brahmapriyā and the other ladies in the same manner.
Having caused all the armies, adorned with ornaments, to mount their elephant-vehicles in every respect, the Blessed One himself ascended his elephant-vehicle. || 8 ||
In the city, with instrumental music and songs, the king joyfully paraded Kṛṣṇa along the great highway and at all the junctions of the streets, celebrating Hari.
In the royal palace, in the residence of the servants, in the house of the chief minister,
and in the homes of other subjects, they led the people and performed acts of worship.
Having made the city pure, at midday the Blessed One returned to his own abode; he performed his ablutions and took rest.
Then, seeing that everyone was exhausted, the king indeed had auspicious foods prepared, including abundant and exquisite delicacies.
The Blessed One ate, and others then partook of their meal;
having rested for a moment, the Lord Hari held an assembly in the evening.
There, Bālakṛṣṇa himself gave this instruction:
"Virtue and vice are always joined as the two paths for embodied beings. (14)
In due time, whether it be evil or merit, it bestows both suffering and happiness;
yet, for you, your merit has borne fruit in that I have come here. (15)
My yoga and my service—this indeed bears the fruit of great merit;
a mantra bears fruit in due time, and medicine bears fruit in due time. || 16 ||
Rain falls in due season, trees bear fruit in their time,
the moon waxes at its appointed hour, and even the rivers swell at the proper time.
But when the time has arrived, prosperity comes of its own accord;
and a seed sown at the proper time sprouts when the season comes. (18)
In due time there is decay, and likewise in due time the loss of sap even in trees;
for the succession brought about by Time touches all embodied beings. (19)
Having reflected thus, the wise person should take refuge in the Supreme Lord at the proper time;
for now, this most auspicious moment exists for you.
"Indeed, a union with me, Nārāyaṇa, has arisen for you here;
yet those who, having obtained such as me in person, remain elsewhere [are truly lost]. (21)
Foolish and devoid of wisdom, they suffer loss at every step due to the arising of thirst and greed, having abandoned the Supreme Lord.
And those who remain in other realms through their impulses are partakers of suffering;
for them, the fruit is suffering born of the affliction of craving, and nothing else.
Or rather, if a happiness that is momentary and followed by suffering were to be obtained—wherein suffering follows happiness and happiness follows suffering—[it would not be worth pursuing]. (24)
For pleasure indeed ends in suffering, and suffering indeed ends in pleasure;
therefore, one who desires eternal happiness should abandon both of these. (25)
Whatever cause may give rise to grief, distress, or fainting and the like, a wise person should abandon that here and acquire eternal happiness. (26)
In this world, every pleasure is invariably accompanied by suffering and is indeed illusory;
for there is no end to sufferings, as they arise ever more and more. (27)
Therefore, indeed, for those wandering in saṃsāra, suffering always arrives mixed with happiness, both through its alternating states and through its inclusion within them. (28)

Having reflected thus for a moment, one should abandon that which is fleeting, involves great exertion, and causes distress; instead, one should strive to acquire the bliss known as happiness, which is stable and eternal. (29)
Indeed, through service, austerity, devotion, and single-minded righteousness, as well as by charity and self-restraint, they attain eternal happiness. (2.186.30)
Contentment is indeed the highest heaven; contentment is the supreme happiness.
Satisfaction is the nectar of immortality; through satisfaction, indeed, comes the highest perfection.
The individual soul, resting in Nārāyaṇa, always possesses the power of Nārāyaṇa;
he never fears anyone else, nor do any fear him.
Then, one attains Brahman, experiencing joy produced by me everywhere,
when one does not harbor any evil intention toward anything whatsoever.
Then, through mind, action, and speech, one attains Brahman—
he by whom pride and delusion have been destroyed, as well as attachments and falsehoods.
Having taken refuge in me as his support, he attains nirvāṇa,
realizing that all accumulations end in exhaustion and that all elevations end in a fall.
A wise person should take refuge in me, for union ends in separation, life ends in death, and even pleasure ends in suffering. (36)
Whether it be happiness or suffering, it arises only in succession;
yet it swiftly carries away the consciousness of the embodied being who stands on the shore. (37)
Thinking, "I am indeed well-born, I am accomplished, and I am truly great," the mind becomes thus intoxicated and even loses its mindfulness. (38)
One whose memory is lost considers the seizing of others' property to be virtuous;
the King, Yama, therefore punishes him who has transgressed the bounds of propriety.
Therefore, having deliberated and investigated, the wise man should administer medicine, or else seek refuge in the virtuous or in the glorious Nārāyaṇa. (2.186.40)
Otherwise, the occurrence of suffering, prosperity, and delusion—the experience of the undesirable—would be impossible; for a fourth [type of experience] does not exist for him. (41)
For old age and death are the devourers of all beings, like two wolves;
no one can escape them, not even the sovereign of the universe, Brahmā himself. ||42||
There is no avoiding suffering once it has arisen;
likewise, one should understand that pleasure is not found to exist with absolute certainty. (43)
In this cycle of existence, desired objects do not come about as one wishes;
rather, they present themselves and persist in ways that are always contrary to one's intent. (44)
Union with those who are unpleasant and separation from those who are very dear—these two are considered to be the causes of gain and loss, and the givers of happiness and suffering. (45)
Origination, growth, and end—these are all established in time; fragrance, form, taste, and touch exist in time and pass away in time. (46)
The seat, the bed, the vehicle, the celestial chariot, the drink, the collyrium, the food, and even the act of rising—these are born and they perish. (87)
Even physicians are sick; the strong are powerless before women;
even the wealthy are eunuchs—how wondrous is the reversal of karma! 48.
Birth in a noble family, great prowess, health, beauty, honesty, good fortune, and enjoyments—these are obtained through abundant merit. (49)
Even though these exist, if there is no devotion to Kṛṣṇa, they are fruitless;
for the poor have many sons even when they do not desire them.
There is no son for the wealthy; the workings of karma are diverse.
Likewise, the wise suffer from disease and distress, while the poor suffer from hunger. (5.1)
Calamity always befalls the wealthy man, and fever the king;
since such is the nature of each, their actions and efforts are truly strange.
A wealthy youth dies, while one who has lived for a hundred years is destitute;
those with nothing live long, whereas the prosperous are short-lived. (53)
The power of enjoyment resides in the wealthy, not in the poor; the digestive fire is excessive in the rich, yet the mind for action is absent. The workings of karma are truly wondrous! (54)
Having reflected upon this, the wise person should practice what is for his own ultimate welfare;
neither medicines, nor indeed mantras, nor fire-offerings, nor even recitations [can help]. (55)
Pride and the prosperity of pride do not protect one whose death has arrived;
just as a tree and a log might come together by chance in a flood. (56)
Having come together, they depart; such is the meeting of living beings.
This applies to those who possess kingdoms, sons, and women, as well as those who are destitute and dependent on the food of others. (57)

Whether they be lords or paupers, Time acts equally toward them all; likewise toward those who have mastered the sciences and those who are blind, toward those who exert effort and those who do not. (58)
Whether they are devoted or undevoted, time acts equally toward them;
it does not distinguish between that which has been enjoyed and that which has not, nor between that which is protected and that which is disregarded.
Whether one has been wronged or has acted wrongly, time treats them all equally;
for thousands of mothers and fathers, and tens of thousands of sons and wives, have passed away.
Countless riches and kingdoms have been enjoyed and then abandoned throughout various births;
having encountered them again in this cycle of existence, to whom do they belong, and to whom do we belong? (6.1)
No one will belong to him, nor does he belong to anyone;
this collection of wife, kin, and friends is merely encountered on the road. (62)
"Where have I come from, and where shall I go? Who am I, and what is established here?
How much time remains certain for me?"—thus one should reflect again and again. (63)

In this impermanent life, which is a dwelling in suffering and outwardly appears as happiness yet is impure, this coming together on the path—mother, brother, son, and beloved—is indeed merely a temporary meeting. (64)
The world is constantly sinking into the deep ocean of time, which has old age and death as its great crocodiles; yet no one perceives this.
Even those who study Ayurveda and are defeated by disease,
and even those who drink medicinal decoctions, do not transcend death.
Even those who drink elixirs become overwhelmed by old age;
even ascetics, donors, and performers of sacrifices do not remain for long.
Even those with divine bodies, though dwelling in the sky, decay over time;
for indeed, the days that pass away for living beings never return.

Indeed, even a person who has established firm resolve, being utterly helpless and excessively prone to craving, is carried away by time and space—which are infinite and frequented by all the worlds. (69)
Either the body approaches the soul, or the soul approaches the body, like a traveler;
just as travelers and kinsmen, having approached one another, depart. (2.186.70)
In this world, one can never find perfect companionship with anyone, even with one's own body; what then need be said of another? (7.1)
Where have those former performers of ritual acts gone, such as our grandfathers and others?
We do not see them, nor do they see us. (72)
Devoured by the Piśācinī through her illusory power, they have reached the place of digestion;
fallen asleep in a bottomless pit, they do not emerge again. (73)
Therefore, having reflected upon time, action, and deceptive illusion, as well as the body which inspires trust and the separation of those who are united; (74)
One's own instability, the devouring of time, and the world’s sudden transience—let them all take refuge in me, the Blessed One, as their protector from the noose of Time. (75)
In this yoga, there shall be no further death for you, nor the devouring by the serpent of Time;
in my abode, there shall be no destruction of the perfection of your happiness. (76)
Those whose pride has been subdued, whose minds are fixed on Me, who have offered the objects of the senses to Me, and whose wisdom is established in My true nature— they go to My eternal bliss.
Knowledge is said to be truly nectar if it results in awakening;
service is my food if it is endowed with faith. (78)
If my attainment is indeed endowed with greatness, then the total surrender of that [attainment] unto Me bestows eternal bliss. (79)
Reflecting thus, let devotees—both men and women—in every way offer all their various actions unto me, Kṛṣṇa, day and night. (2.186.80)

Having brought about the absence of qualities in this [soul] through the relinquishing of fruits, I shall grant the attainment of a fruit whose nature is myself, which is designated as "liberation. ||8.1||
Having spoken thus, O Rādhā, the Blessed One then ceased; thereafter, the people indeed worshipped Bālakṛṣṇa with supreme devotion in due order. 82.
With sandalwood, flowers, unbroken grains of rice, fragrant garlands, *puṣpasāra* perfumes, *rasasāra* essences, and garments of great value; ||83||
Then the people, having honored him with ornaments, fruits, seeds, pearls, gems, diamonds, and various kinds of gifts, [proceeded]. (84)
They performed the nightly lamp-offering and likewise offered praises of homage;
then the king, the queen, and the royal family did the same. (85)
Having indeed brought the assembly to a conclusion, Hari’s family members escorted Hari to his own residence and fed him there. (86)
Devoted to the service of the king, they fed the great sages, those of high honor, and others who were dear to Brahmā to their heart's content.
Then the queen herself spoke to her own most beautiful daughter, who was truly peerless:
"Take hold of Kṛṣṇa’s hand alone, indeed. (88)
She too, being full of desire, quickly took hold of Kṛṣṇa’s hand and placed a golden garland inlaid with jewels upon the neck of Śrī Hari. (89)
Hari even placed a garland made of flowers around her neck;
thus, according to the marriage rites, he wedded Mādhava to the princess.
Then the king held that festival, and after that,
having rested during the night, the Blessed One himself [addressed] the subjects in the morning.
And he caused Manu to hear his own [mantra], which bestows the state of a Vaiṣṇava;
then, having performed his daily rites, the king set his mind on departing.
He fed all the great lords of the earth on every side with milk-based foods for Hari according to the prescribed rite, and then he gave them their leave to depart.
Then, with vehicles, mounts, and armies, with the sounds of musical instruments and shouts of victory, and with joyful offerings of flowers and unbroken rice grains, he granted him leave to depart.
Celestial chariots appeared in the sky and people from all sides took their seats; Hari, having ascended his own chariot, set it in motion for the purpose of traveling.
Having crossed the river of the Rāhus in the sky, their celestial chariots indeed proceeded swiftly toward the regions inhabited by jackals and mustard seeds.
There, King Pariśāna and the sage Pherunasa likewise descended quickly to the earth,
placing their celestial chariot in front of them.
To welcome Hari, the king dispatched an auspicious army;
he caused the sounds of musical instruments, shouts of victory, and the bursting of firecrackers to resound.
Then the subjects, filled with an abundance of joy and equipped with parched grain, unbroken rice, flowers, and other offerings, respectfully awaited the celestial chariots in the sky. 99.
Then Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa indeed beheld beautiful grounds on the lovely bank of the Senā river, and the auspicious city of Parīśā.
It was resplendent with prosperity, making even the earth below heaven appear beautiful;
it was adorned with gardens and gleaming palaces of golden hue.
