O Rādhikā, it was a vast city inhabited by men equal to gods and graced by beautiful women who were like you.
Following the path shown by the king, Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa slowly descended the aerial chariot in the great garden at the royal palace.

Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of Hari’s Journey to the Kingdom of King Parīśāna in the Region of the Sages of Pheruna on the Sixth Day, Following His Descent from the Celestial Car, His Wandering through the City of Varaṇā, Receiving Worship and Instruction, Taking Food and Rest at Night, Performing His Morning Rites, and Consuming Milk and Other Foods," in the second section (Tretā-santāna) of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*, concerning the reign of the royal sage Jayakṛṣṇa.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Sovereign of the Lord of Goloka, Bālakṛṣṇa emerged from the midst of the celestial chariot.
At that time, he beheld a wondrous throng of more than a hundred thousand people. || 1 ||
Just as the eyes of all those belonging to the species of the *cakora* bird function toward the circle of light from the moon,
so too [do the eyes] of all those who perform the rites of welcome [function toward you].
His gaze was fixed upon the Supreme Lord, the bestower of boons. || 2 ||
Just as peacocks, upon seeing a cloud, become utterly absorbed in their cries of joy,
so too do living beings upon seeing Śrī Hari.
Then they indeed became immersed in the sound of victory. || 3 ||
Just as the flocks of cātaka birds rejoice exceedingly when there is rain from a cloud,
so too do they rejoice exceedingly at the fruit that is dark as a cloud.
The flocks of birds were delighted by the welcome. || 4 ||
Just as children, upon obtaining sweet sugar-candy, become filled with excessive joy,
so too did the subjects, having obtained the Lord whose face was like the nectar of their own desires, then become filled with excessive joy.

Just as a virtuous woman rejoices upon finding her beloved husband, who is exceedingly handsome and from whom she has long been separated, so do all creatures rejoice upon finding Him, the Supreme Beloved, the Infallible.
Having obtained that which is never separated [from them], they were filled with joy. || 6 ||
Just as moths, deluded, are drawn toward and rush into a fire of extreme brilliance upon seeing it,
so too do the limbs of living beings [rush] toward the blazing Lord.
O enchanting one, having looked [at them], they fall as they are pulled away.
Just as the oceans in the worlds rush toward the full moon upon seeing it at night,
so too do they rush toward the Imperishable Lord upon seeing Him in His fullness.
Even millions of living beings rush toward him.
Just as iron pieces naturally gravitate toward a magnet,
so too do worldly beings gravitate toward one who is beloved by the world.
By their very nature, they go toward the child-like Hari. || 9 ||
Just as rivers flow toward the ocean, and just as hearts go toward that which is desired,
so do the hearts of all beings go toward Kṛṣṇa.
For they had come from all directions. || 2.187.10 ||
Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa, endowed with immeasurable splendor, became like the midday sun;
his subjects were of very white complexion and exceedingly beautiful.
They became like fully blossomed lotuses. || 11 ||
Then the celestial chariot, presided over by Hari,
became a garden of flowers with hundreds of thousands of lotuses;
it appeared like the peak of Mount Mandara, filled with the whirling fragrance of various kinds of exquisite blossoms.
Then Hari indeed became a flowering tree,
beautiful with clusters formed by the mixture of all medicinal herbs,
as if from the cavern of his own mouth.
Emerging with a splendor released from syllables. || 1.3 ||
Wearing upon his own head that most excellent crown— which was held by Acyuta, adorned with imperishable diamonds, gold, rubies, and fine pearls, and joined with a pair of swords— [he shone].
He shone resplendently, remaining exactly as he was, like the Lord of Day.
Possessing a naturally born, innumerable web of rays,
with a halo of facial splendor all around,
he stands like a thousand moons risen together.
It also extends the mindfulness of non-differentiation. || 15 ||
With a broad forehead adorned by a tilaka and two upward-pointing white streaks of saffron,
her face proclaims to the people the two paths of the Lord of the Gods and the Abode of the Imperishable.
O beloved, your eyes are large, enchanting, exceedingly tremulous, and most lovely with their weight of love;
they shower forth infinite affection and awaken the consciousness of Hari’s distinct limbs. (17)
At that time, Hari’s lower lips, red as coral and filled with joyful, gentle smiles,
captivated the hearts of women.
[He is] through all states of being, as well as through minds and selves. || 18 ||
The two [breasts] of Hari are perfectly round, touched by the hue of saffron, elevated, radiant with beauty,
full of bliss, and as brilliant as jewels.
They were soft, level, heart-pleasing, and auspicious. || 19 ||
His left hand, holding a cluster of flowers, was then raised high as he granted boons;
his right hand became the bestower of fearlessness, enriched with the bow, banner, svastika, trident, fish, and arrow.
Adorned with beautiful flower garlands of fresh and diverse patterns that grace their broad chests,
they display the face of Śrī upon their breasts, which has come into contact with the Kaustubha gem.

Their two shoulders were firm, adorned with flower garlands and likewise graced by beautiful earrings; and upon the surface of their arms, which shone like the banks of the Pārāvatī river with the luster of jewels, they displayed the marks of Rādhā’s embrace.
Then, Hari’s belly, covered with divine flowers and garlands, reveals [the path] to the people:
"O you who are joined in devotion, enter my chest above me by means of the ladder that is the necklace. (23)
His two feet, served by countless maidservants, shone like land-lotuses; they were constantly bowed to by floods of people, bestowing nothing else upon those who offered even a little.
Then Hari was honored by kings as a sovereign emperor,
by subjects as their king, by disciples as their teacher, by the virtuous as a holy man, and by women as a beloved.
He is the giver to the wretched and the ancient one among poets. ||25||
He is attained as the subtle one by devotees,
as the supreme actor in the attire of a dancer by those who love form,
as the beloved by virtuous wives, and as the Vedic one by the sages.
He is captivating to the mind and desired by all people. || 26 ||
On the path of the stairs, Hari descended slowly while smiling, as the Lord rained down a shower of flowers;
he was honored by the people with handfuls of unbroken rice from the city women and made to hear shouts of "Victory!", his desires having been fulfilled.
Repeatedly pointing to his own birthmarks,
he descended from the steps;
the king, in turn, offered him soft silken garments.
He spread it out by the sequence of placing his feet upon it. ||28||
There was a chariot made of beautiful gold, its poles topped with a hundred golden jars,
possessing eight wheels and exceeding speed.
It was joined by seven elephants, each four cubits in height. ||29||
In the midst [of it], surrounded on all sides by celestial maidens who offered garlands,
with their beautiful faces beaming toward their beloveds.
Adorned with ornaments, it was like a celestial flower-chariot.
King Pariśānaka quickly led that Lord Hari, together with his family,
and caused the Lord of lords to mount the chariot.
He seated him upon a golden elephant-throne.
He worshipped with various and diverse necklaces,
with the finest fragrant sandalwood,
with parched grain and unbroken rice, and with cool, sweet-smelling waters.
With golden ornaments and priceless garments. ||32||
And the king gave him an excellent Suravāla garment made of fine silk, as well as a superior golden waist-cloth;
likewise, he gave him a brilliant bodice of the same kind, the finest sort, fit to be worn by a great sovereign.
And he gave him a noble crown adorned with rows of gems set with diamonds, along with earrings;
he also gave ornaments fashioned from gold.
The Blessed One, the Supreme Lord, sustained them all. ||34||
Together with his family, he drank the water washed from the feet of Śrī Hari and placed it upon his head; Hari,
for his part, gave him a beautiful garland that had been around His own neck.
And he presented a cluster of flowers to the king as a sign of his own favor. ||35||
But were the people, with their complexions fairer than a hundred thousand [leaves], then truly become Sugatas from the abode of the gods—
possessing the splendor of the moon's luster and white in color?
They had beautiful tawny eyes and slender, tall bodies. ||36||
And there were fair maidens, young women,
and even aged ones whose bodies were slightly concealed;
they shared the same passion and held variegated parasols.
And they have disheveled hair and tawny eyes. ||37||
Their garments were closely clinging, their luster was soft and reddish, their foot-protectors were visible due to the very slight turning of their heels,
and the coloring of their fine inner garments was clearly seen at the edges.
The Gaurīs, though previously pale, became exceedingly joyful.
At that time, great kettledrums resounded, along with lutes, cymbals, and peacock-drums,
as well as the sounds of harps and flutes.
Likewise, lutes, bards, and musical instruments. ||3 9 ||
For at that time, there arose shouts of victory all around,
as well as many proclamations of his glorious qualities,
even though they were mingled with the sound of a thousand throats.
Then there were also songs and hymns of praise. ||2.187.40||

Thousands of sounds, produced by mechanical *bandhūkī* instruments, formed into stūpas, and created by the piercing of spheres (*golaka*), became auspicious and pleasant to hear; having attained the resonance of *Oṃ*, they awakened the Supreme Lord. (41)
Great shouts raised by the vast armies and sounds of exultation went forth toward Kakutstha;
there were the roars of elephants and the neighing of horses.
Those who had gone to the Veda spread out in the intermediate directions. ||42||
Following the procession of elephants,
hundreds and thousands of vehicles,
equal to celestial chariots and beautifully adorned, arrived slowly, occupied by the followers of Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa.
With excellent banners, flags, and canopies, with numerous golden-peaked jars,
and with most divine archways on all sides;
The chariots, yoked with great seers, shone brilliantly.
With a mass of radiance shining above, their complexions excellent, dear to Brahmā, and possessing lovely golden splendor,
they shine resplendently in golden vehicles.
They lead one's mind toward Goloka and Vaikuṇṭha. ||45||
Then those people, both men and women, who had come to behold him, were truly bewildered by Hari,
whose limbs were so exceedingly beautiful and perfectly proportioned to his form.
Indeed, among the cowherd boys, [there was] Kāmbharēya. ||46||

Then that cavalry force indeed became a league in length, crowded with the trampling of people, [and filled] with many elephants, horses, female elephants, bulls, swans, pragaṇḍas, garuḍas, and gaveyakas. (47)

With excellent chariots, celestial palaces, and horse-drawn carriages, with those traveling on foot and those accompanied by tears, [he was followed] by virtuous kings, princes, and all the subjects residing in the city. ||48||
Accompanied by sages, true gurus, Sāṃkhya and Yoga practitioners, devoted wives, those in the highest stages of life,
the sons of Gaṅgā, the Raudra hosts, and others, as well as the cavalry and the army, she truly shines with splendor. (49)
Having heard and recognized the Lord of Lords while staying within the city, the men and even the playful women abandoned all their activities in great agitation.
They go out from their houses to see Hari.
Their minds intensely eager for the sight of him,
they formed a dense line at the edge of the main road,
their bodies pressed against one another.
They gazed [upon him] with upturned eyes. ||5 1 ||
Even though they were situated on a distant path,
having heard the loud sound of musical instruments,
their eyes were fixed with the hope of Hari’s arrival.
With their hands joined in reverence, they stood upright and bowed down. ||52||
Resplendent with the emblems of sovereignty, such as a golden parasol and beautiful whisks,
he beheld the city of wondrous and abundant splendor.
Well-prepared and filled with all flavors. ||53||
And with the main roads and crossroads sprinkled with fragrant waters and the ichor of elephants,
and made exceedingly beautiful with auspicious golden jars, plantain pillars, and leaves of mango trees and other fruits. (54)
With flowers and consecrated rice, with artificial gateways, with very high and secure main gates,
and likewise with lofty mansions of many stories;
[It was] exceedingly beautiful with its garden sections. ||55||
In every house, it was adorned with flowering creepers and fragrant trees in full leaf,
as well as with clusters of flowers rich in beauty whose roots were situated in water-vessels, and with excellent gardens abundant with grain.
It possessed lakes, a central main thoroughfare, pleasure gardens, monasteries, lecture halls, and grounds for dancers and the like, provided with spectacles and entertainments. (57)
It was exceedingly well-endowed with infinite schools of arts, desirable schools of medicine, Avantika schools of alchemy, and schools of the true Dharma. (58)
Possessing the splendor of countless halls of learning, halls of music,
and halls for the company of the virtuous, it was filled with the joy of cherished delights.
[It was] filled with the constant sound of workshops for mechanical devices and the like. ||99||

By those skilled in the piercing of constellations, those skilled in the piercing of clouds, those skilled in the piercing of the ocean, and those skilled in the piercing of planets; by those skilled in the piercing of foreign lands, those skilled in the piercing of time, those skilled in the piercing of wind, and those skilled in the piercing of the principles of equality.
It is provided with heating apparatuses along with cooling apparatuses, equipped with ghaṭī-vedha machines,
and furnished with lightning-veins, mercury-veins, as well as veins for the vowels and other veins for demonstration. ||61||
Accompanied by chariot-piercings, cart-piercings,
body-piercings, earth-piercings,
and water-end-piercings, it was exceedingly beautiful.
He beheld that city, which was the abode of consciousness.
It was constantly filled with throngs of celestial chariots resounding with noise,
and occupied by beautiful women;
its lofty, magnificent halls reached toward the very edge of the sky.
And he beheld that other city in the sky. ||63||
It was adorned with aguru incense and lamps, with banners and flags that inspired longing,
with water-spouting fountains and pipes, and with loud sounds that captivated the heart.

The Blessed One beheld the place named Pariśā, which resounded with the distant cries of cranes and was illuminated here and there by lamps like stars, while the Mānasa lake was being drained at various spots.
And it was adorned with the temples of celestial nymphs. ||65||
As he entered that [palace], his limbs were most enchanting,
resembling the full moon and endowed with fresh youth;
[he was attended] by a golden parasol and two chowries.
And the subjects beheld him thus honored.
Then, having ascended the palaces, the women,
filled with agitation and abandoning all other activities,
crowded the windows with their garments and ornaments disarrayed.
With steady eyes, they beheld their supreme beloved.

In various places, Śrīpati, the Lord of Lords, was honored by circles of women on the balconies of the mansions with unbroken grains, flowers, and sandalwood; he accepted that which was offered from their hearts.

In that very manner, the merchants, casting their eyes upon the forefront of the marketplace, then paid him honor and reverence with offerings of women, fresh fruits, dried fruits, seeds, desirable coins, and garments and other such things. (69)
Then the Brahmins, with unbroken grains, sandalwood paste, and other offerings, with flower garlands and salutations,
made her auspicious by means of Vedic mantras; and filled with joy, they sang the Sāman chants aloud.
The wealthy classes [are satisfied] by gifts of wealth;
the poor people by gifts of mental solace;
and devoted followers by the offering of their devotion.
Then they performed a welcoming reception for Hari. ||71||
The king, accompanied by his army, caused the Lord to wander all around the city, as far as its boundaries;
and upon merely beholding the city, Hari [delivered] the command.
He offered praise for the city of Pariśāna. ||72||
Having sanctified with his feet the ground made exceedingly pure by visiting the king’s palace, the hut of the great seer, and the mansions of the leading merchants and others, he—
Kṛṣṇa made the city Sutīrtha.
Having wandered thus, the sovereign of kings turned back toward the royal palace;
having arrived, he descended from his vehicle and entered the palace.
He took refuge [in him] for the sake of his desired peace.
He drank water, attained peace for a moment,
and then entered the assembly hall where a high throne had been prepared for the king.
At that time, Acyuta became resplendent.
Then the Lord of the high and the low, whose purpose is the preservation and upliftment of the world, gave instruction to the people, beginning with the kings;
thereafter, all the subjects sat in silence.
O Rādhā, they are like cakora birds whose minds are fixed on the moon. || 76 ||
The functions of their senses fixed their minds upon Hari, who is the beloved of all, the bestower of splendor upon his own devotees,
who eternally showers nectar, and whose conduct is ever virtuous.
To her own beloved, the dear consort of Kṛṣṇa. ||77||

Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Crowding of the Subjects, the Splendor of Hari, the Ascending of the Elephant Vehicle, the Attracting of the Subjects, the Wandering through the City of Parīśāna, and the Arrival at the Royal Palace," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O Rādhikā, I shall relate to you that which Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa instructed the assembly in the city of Parīśāna. || 1 ||
Hari said: "In this worldly existence, death is indeed certain;
the body is transitory, the vital breaths are transitory, and riches are transitory. (2)
All unions are transitory, and even the entire universe is transitory;
for all beings are indeed transitory, while the Self alone shall go beyond them.
Having attained such a transient state, one of firm intellect should not seek it again;
for eternal liberation is to be obtained by means of the permanent self.
The king, who was honored by the foremost of rulers and by gods and great sages,
was strengthened by words of auspiciousness and joined with blessings.
And Marutta, the son of Avikṣita, was indeed a great devotee of the Lord,
for whom Indra, Varuṇa, and the others, led by Bṛhaspati, [performed his sacrifice].
The gods, the creators of the universe, came to the sacrifice of the high-souled King,
while he ruled the earth, which yielded crops even without being ploughed.
At whose sacrifice the Viśvedevas were then the members of the assembly,
the Maruts the servers, and the Sādhyas likewise the virtuous attendants.
At that time, I was the embodied enjoyer in the sacrificial fire;
having made his kingdom devoted to me and having made himself intent upon me, he [ruled].
He went to my imperishable abode; likewise, kings here must perform their duty.
There was a king named Suhotra who was a devotee of the Lord (Bhāgavata).
In that year, Maghavan rained down gold;
the earth became true to its name "Vasumatī" (the possessor of wealth), and then the rivers carried away the gold.
Indra rained down crocodiles, tortoises, and various aquatic creatures made of gold; the sovereign presented them all to the Brahmins. || 11 ||
"I am Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa; having worshipped me well in all worthy recipients, that guest, having become [my devotee], went to my supreme abode. (13)
King Bṛhadratha of Aṅga was indeed a great devotee of the Lord,
who gave away a thousand times a thousand white horses as gifts.
And a thousand times a thousand maidens adorned with gold,
and a thousand times a thousand elephants of the supreme *padminī* breed.
A hundred times a hundred thousand bulls adorned with golden garlands, and thousands of gold coins as a counterweight for the scales. 16.
Performing sacrifices during the extended ritual and throughout the seven Soma-offerings, he bestowed sacrificial fees even upon mendicant Brahmins.
Having made me well-pleased and having worshipped me in the sacrifice, the king became a great devotee of the Lord and, at the end, went to my abode.
And King Śibi Auśīnara was a great devotee of the Lord,
who covered this entire earth with gold.
In this [world], he gave away everything— including cattle, horses, elephants, and gayals—
in charity, which then became multiplied by countless qualities.
Having attained serenity here through me and becoming a great devotee of the Lord,
Śibi worshipped me and went to my eternal, imperishable abode.
Bhagīratha brought the Gaṅgā for the sake of delivering his ancestors;
having become a great devotee of the Blessed One, he went to my imperishable abode.
Dilīpa performed the Vaiṣṇava sacrifice for my gratification;
he offered a thousand golden elephants as the sacrificial fee.
Upon that golden sacrificial post, which had a golden crest-ring,
six thousand celestial Gandharvas danced in seven ways.
Having propitiated Me, the Supreme Brahman, through devotion and service to the virtuous,
he went to my imperishable and eternal abode, from which there is no return.
Māndhātā, the son of Yuvanāśva, was a great devotee of the Blessed One who became king;
Indra himself served as his nourisher, and he ruled over the entire earth.
He performed a hundred horse-sacrifices as well as a hundred royal consecrations;
and he gave golden Rohita fish to the Brahmins.
Having fully gratified me in sacrifices and having cultivated supreme devotion toward me,
he attained my imperishable abode and became forever one who has accomplished his purpose.
And Yayāti, the son of Nahuṣa, became a king devoted to me;
having caused a sacrificial pit to be constructed by means of throwing a clod of earth, he indeed worshipped me. (29)
He performed a thousand sacrifices as well as a hundred Vājapeyas;
he gave as gifts three excellent golden mountains for my sake.
Having gone to the forest and propitiated me, Kṛṣṇa, he attained the Imperishable. And Ambarīṣa, the son of Nābhāga, became a great devotee of the Lord.

He who, having performed a sacrifice with a thousand times a thousand kings who had each performed ten thousand sacrifices, offered everything as an oblation unto me while the sacrifice was being spread out. ||32||
The Sudarśana discus was entrusted by me for his protection;
at the end, having propitiated me, the Supreme Lord, he attained the imperishable abode.
And there was a great devotee of the Lord, King Śaśabindu;
having given away his kingdom and all his possessions in sacrifice, he departed for the forest. (34)
Having propitiated me, he went to my imperishable, eternal, and stable abode.
King Gaya became preeminent, a most fortunate and pure devotee of the Lord.
For a hundred years, that king subsisted on the remnants of sacrificial offerings;
Agni, being pleased, granted him a boon consisting of devotion to Hari.
He performed the horse sacrifice for a thousand years;
having fashioned the earth out of gold, he bestowed it as a gift upon the twice-born.
He gave away as many cows as there are grains of sand in the Ganges;
and having propitiated me, at the end of his life, he went to my imperishable state.
Rantideva was a king and a great devotee of the Lord;
upon seeing me as a guest, he gave water even to a Puṣkasa.
In his house, thousands of tens of millions of Brahmins were fed;
having propitiated me, he attained my abode, the imperishable state.
And the king named Sagara, having performed a thousand horse-sacrifices and having given away all his possessions, worshipped me and went to the imperishable state. 41.
I was Pṛthu in person, and he too, having performed my worship, entered into my own form; let the kings do likewise.
The royal sage Rukmāṅgada and his son Dharmāṅgada, having propitiated me, went to my supreme, imperishable abode. ||43||
In the house of Rukmāṅgada was a maiden, the enchanting beloved of the Creator;
she became his wife in the form of a consort, and she is declared to be the lunar day (tithi) of the Creator.
And King Sudyumna, having meditated upon me as Nārāyaṇa, attained my eternal and imperishable abode through devotion; indeed, such shall be your offspring.
Indradyumna became a king, the sovereign among devotees of Puruṣottama;
having propitiated Me, he indeed went to My eternal, imperishable abode. 46.
Puṇḍarīka was my king, a great devotee of the Lord; through devotion, he attained the imperishable abode, the eternal, supreme station. 47.
Prahlāda, Bali, Bāṇa, and the kings dwelling in Pātāla—though they are merely subjects—they please me day and night with their devotion. (48)
The great king Udayana, as well as Raṇaṅgama, Citraketu, and Nanda—these are my devotees (bhāgavatas). 49.
Kanṭhādhara, Bhadrāśva, Lakṣmaṇa, Mucukundaka, Viśāla, Prajāpāla, Durjaya, and likewise Aśvaśiras. (2.188.50)
Camatkāra, Satyasandha, Amitrajit, King Kalaśa, Puṇyanidhi, Suyaśas, and likewise the king of Pañcāla. ||5 1 ||
Also Alarka, Toṇḍa, Nābhi, Ṛtadhvaja, Ranti, Vedaśravas, and Nandasāvarṇi.
Nimi, Dhruva, as well as Dharmadhvaja, Kuśadhvaja,
Dṛḍhadhanvan, Divodāsa, Ānarta, Raivata, and others.
These and many other kings, indeed my devotees of Viṣṇu,
having attained my state which is difficult to reach, have truly become perfected.
Accompanied by their subjects, many of them proceeded to the supreme Vaikuṇṭha;
for the protection of subjects is the duty of kings, coupled with devotion to Hari.
Obedience to the king's command is the duty [of the subjects], and devotion to Hari is the duty [of the king];
thus, those desiring righteousness should provide mutual assistance to one another. (56)
"By the mere succession of my remembrance, they shall be awakened as partakers of liberation;
for it is the person appointed by me who performs both the good and the evil. (57)
One should personally be a stream of the virtuous, and not a stream that carries away the unvirtuous;
having reflected with the vision of knowledge, one should do what is right and nothing else. (58)
In all actions, goodness consists in dedication to me; this is my view.
That which is dedicated to me becomes good; that which is separate from me is not good at all. ||59||

One should not commit an act that causes injury to others, nor ever be intent on causing distress; one should not do what brings about one's own ruin, nor should one do what is censured by the world. (2.188.60)
Thus should the wise one conduct himself, having indeed cast everything into me;
then, having attained supreme peace, he shall abide at the end in the imperishable Supreme.
Men and women are indeed bound by their actions; they do not exist without action.
And whatever activity is innate, that too casts [the agent] into the Lord.
Just as wood—whether dry, moist, or otherwise—when cast into a fire, will surely be reduced to ashes, either quickly or after a long time; of this there is no doubt.
Likewise, whatever action—whether auspicious or otherwise—one might cast upon me, the Supreme Lord, I am capable of reducing it to ashes; indeed, I can even liberate one from the bondage of karma.

Alternatively, because one obtains the fruit of action through that [offering] as its material cause, and for the reason that "one shall obtain" [the result], one should offer it to me, the Lord. (61)
Nevertheless, the person, through the operation of ignorance, acts with a sense of ego as the agent of both auspicious and inauspicious deeds, and becomes the enjoyer of their results as well.
Indeed, everything consisting of the threads of karma, bound together in succession and resulting in the qualities of pleasure and pain, falls apart when cast upon me.
For one who, at the commencement of an action, is permeated by the state of that [action], would be overcome by it; but when one is established in me, one is not overcome.
Consequently, all impurity is entirely exhausted within me alone;
for that [impurity], there is no expiation, nor does it have any further experience.
Failing to perform prescribed duties and likewise practicing what is forbidden,
the embodied soul becomes liable for expiation if it is devoid of dedication unto Me.
A person should never perform improper acts; for instance, the abandonment of one's own duty and the pursuit of the duties of another. (71)
One should never abandon one who has come for refuge, nor withhold ornaments and such from a servant, nor misappropriate the property of another, nor engage in dispute with one's father. (72)
A young and beloved husband should never abandon his wife,
nor should a young and beloved wife ever abandon her husband.
It is always considered that one should provide for those who depend on one;
one should serve the elderly and offer assistance to the distressed. (74)
One should never speak untruth, nor harsh words filled with deceit; one should never commit violence against living beings, but remain devoted to compassion. (75)
One should provide relief from hunger and thirst to the animals that depend on him;
one should perform acts of service for others and always feed the virtuous. (76)
One should practice service to the virtuous and service to me at all times;
one should make oneself happy and never lead oneself into agitation.
One should never, under any circumstances, cause distress to others through idle talk, falsehoods, lies, and the like;
rather, one should constantly perform the congregational chanting of Hari’s names with both speech and heart. (78)
One should always perform meditation on Hari, which bestows liberation and destroys sins;
one should perform auspicious deeds and desist from those that are inauspicious. (79)
One should constantly give wealth and other gifts, for by that one is released from sin.
The conduct of the virtuous (*śiṣṭācāra*), applied according to place, time, and other circumstances, is the supreme dharma;
it alone should be practiced here by one who desires happiness both in this world and after death.
One should perform the recitation of mantras (japa), fire offerings (homa), fasting, and other such rites in a sacred place of the gods.
The vision of the Divine bestows knowledge that purifies the self;
a wise person who is subject to the law of death should never be possessed by pride. 82.
Having honored the gods, the ṛṣis, humans, the ancestors, the domestic deities, and Hari as well, the householder is entitled to eat. ||83||
Acting thus, neither the king nor the subjects, nor the virtuous, nor women, nor the poor, nor the common crowds shall be defiled; let them all act accordingly in every way. (84)
Constantly uttering my name, remembering me at every moment for even an instant, and performing all actions while dedicating them to me, one is not stained by sin. (85)
"Let them always act thus, remembering me and offering everything unto me;
I shall liberate all my Vaiṣṇavas who are devoted to me. (86)
May there be well-being for you all—O kings, members of royal families, subjects, lords of subjects, and especially for the poor. (87)
May there be well-being for those who are weak and for those who have performed deeds for my sake;
may there always be well-being indeed, and may Hari bestow peace upon you.
Having spoken thus to Rādhikā, Bālakṛṣṇa, the beloved of Śrī Kṛṣṇa,
then remained silent for a moment in the assembly of the learned.
And the king performed worship with countless pearls and diamonds, with necklaces and other ornaments, garments and other finery, and fragrant substances such as sandalwood.
The queen, the princesses, the princes, the chief ministers, and the subjects also performed a great *ārārtrika* ceremony. ||9 1 ||
Having performed prostrations and hymns of praise, and having offered pleasing gifts,
Hari then presented the royal maidens with tribute.
Then twenty-one young women of charming minds took the hand of Hari according to the marriage rite. (93)
Immediately after the hand-grasping ceremony, the king quickly held a great festival at night,
having fed the honored guests, including Hari and the newly arrived visitors.
He caused a delightful entertainment to be performed with dance, song, and the arts;
at night, all the guests attained the highest rest.
The young maidens, however, served their beloved with intense devotion;
then, having risen in the morning, the Blessed One performed his own meditation.
The king also came for the sake of worshipping Kṛṣṇa and worshipped him;
thus, O Rādhā, this great festival of the Supreme Lord indeed took place. (97)
Then, in the city of Pariśāna, the subjects presented gifts;
King Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa then accepted those parting gifts. 98.
Lomaśa caused all the subjects to perform the drinking of milk and other rites with devotion,
and he indeed bestowed the Tāraka mantra upon the people.
Then Hari became ready to go to Mount Parīkha;
however, King Indurāya strongly urged him to stay.
Then musical instruments were played as Hari ascended his celestial chariot;
others also mounted their chariots there by the king's command.
And they traveled by way of the sky to the kingdom of Indurāya;
Hari gazed upon the earth, filled with mountains.
To welcome him, Indurāya, accompanied by his family, went out before him;
at that time, the sounds of trumpets for his honor resounded on all sides. || 103 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-eighth chapter, titled "The Bestowal of Instruction upon Parīśāna, Prajā, and Others; Their Worship; and the Arrival in the Morning on the Seventh Day in the Kingdom of Parījara by Means of Celestial Vehicles," in the second section, the Tretā-saṃtāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmīnārāyaṇīya-saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O Rādhikā, Śrī Hari gazed all around at the splendor arising from his own mountain, as well as that produced by the trees from the very sky.
To the west of that, having beheld the auspicious city named Vāyūnā situated there, the people gathered in order to see it. || 2 ||
To welcome the king who had arrived before him,
he caused the celestial chariot to descend along the path shown by the monarch.
Then all the celestial chariots descended from the sky into that most beautiful garden, which was like a forest and stood before the royal palace. || 4 ||
Bālakṛṣṇa descended from his celestial chariot toward his own courtyard;
the king then placed necklaces made of fine gold around Kṛṣṇa’s neck.
He then offered a welcome to the others as well, according to their merit;
and upon hearing the sound, Hari attained a state of great joy.
Having crossed over, he then found rest in the royal palace;
having washed his feet, the king and others drank the nectar of his feet.
The king fed the great monarch, his family members, the great sages, and the wives of the Brahmins with various kinds of sweet foods and other delicacies.
He hospitably fed all the other great kings with devotion;
and at midday, Hari obtained rest thereafter.
The king said to his great army, "O Suśṛṅgārya,
go to the city of Vāyūnāya for the purpose of granting me an audience with Hari."
"O Lord, I desire to wander with my army along with you.
"So be it," Hari replied, [placing him] upon a most splendid elephant-throne.
Then he sat down upon Ambālikā, the daughter of Kānaka;
after that, the others likewise sat down upon their respective mounts.
Various excellent musical instruments and diverse types of drums were sounded;
then there arose the bursting sounds of mechanical devices and the cries of those bestowing honor.
The women of the household, both those with golden complexions and those who were dark as a tawny deer, honored the Lord of Īśa within their own courtyards and other areas,
increasing his glory with parched grain, flowers, unbroken rice, and other offerings.
They offered fruits and other gifts, worshipped him, and gazed upon him for a long time;
then those subjects considered themselves to have fulfilled their purpose. 15.
Having thus wandered through the city, Hari went to the royal palace;
the king and queen performed a great worship with many articles.
He presented to Śrī Hari royal gifts consisting of golden and silver vessels, coins, diamonds and other gems, as well as garments and ornaments. (17)
Then, by the queen's command, having beheld the lovely Hari, the two maidens joyfully took the hand of Bālakṛṣṇa.
There, the festival proceeded perfectly according to the rites of marriage;
out of compassion, the king beheld his son-in-law as four-armed.
Though situated on a mountain, he, who was himself without joints, praised with supreme affection the one who holds the conch, discus, mace, and lotus, and whose face is compassion itself.
Devoid of the veil of ignorance and free from the qualities of māyā, protect me from the phenomena of composite existence and lead me to Your imperishable abode. 21.
You are the beginningless and endless Supreme Brahman, Bālakṛṣṇa, Nārāyaṇa;
you are Harikṛṣṇa, you are Bhava, you are Nara, and you are Nārāyaṇa. 22.
The ṛṣis, the ancestors, the siddhas, the gods, the gandharvas, the dānavas,
the pannagas, the rākṣasas, and the yakṣas do not know him in his true essence.
Even yogis, the virtuous, the truthful, the wise, and the lords of ascetics do not know that Lord of Gods; how then could this Blessed One [be known]? ||14||
Let there be my salutation to him; protect me from the ocean of saṃsāra! Salutations again and again to you, in whom the birth, growth, and destruction of beings reside. (25)
O Soul of the Universe, O Soul of Viśvakarman, O You who possess the eyes and other senses of Viśvakarman;
grant me freedom from action even amidst actions, and protect me from the ocean. 26.
I bow to the Supreme Lord Viṣṇu, the thousand-rayed one, the Lord whose eyes are everywhere, and whose hands, feet, and other limbs are infinite.

I bow to You, the Supreme Lord, who exists as Hari—subtler than the subtle, greater than the great, and eternally present even within the greatest; the most venerable, the most excellent, and the highest of all. 28.
I bow to you, the Supreme Lord, the Ancient Person, the Brahman who has transcended all actions such as the past and future, and who is beyond the range of the senses and the intellect. 29.
I bow to You, the supreme Lord, the eternal treasure-house of the universe, self-born, the Lord of the world, the Lord of all, and golden-hued. ||2.189.30||
Salutations to you who radiate heat even while being cool, and salutations to you for the sake of illumination;
salutations to you who are the primordial sound (*svara*), the reality of the ultimate meaning, and whose form is song.
You are the syllable Om, you are the incarnation, you are the manifestation, and you are the four-armed one; you are the Infinite, you are Mahāviṣṇu, you are Virāṭ, and you are the abode of Kamalā.
You are action, the instrument, the agent, and likewise the object; you are the doer, the seer, the witness, Mahākāla, and the devourer—salutations to you!
Salutations to you who possess all forms, who are peaceful, and who are the son of Kambharā;
salutations to you, Bālakṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa, and the son of Gopālā. ||34||
Salutations to the one who pacifies all sins, who removes all suffering, who is the form of the soul’s provisions for the journey, and who is the inner controller of all. ||35||
"My home has been made pure by my lord, the beloved of Kṛṣṇa;
and my family, who were submerged, have been rescued by you after taking hold of me. (36)
Salutations to you in all the worlds; salutations to you in all souls.
O Bālakṛṣṇa, Mahākṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇeśvara, let there be salutation to you! (37)
Having spoken thus, King Indurāya offered obeisances to Rādhikā;
then the beginningless Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa addressed him with auspicious words.
O King, having observed your supreme and steadfast devotion toward me,
I have shown you here a small portion of my divine form.
"When he took the hands of these two daughters of mine, what indeed arose in your minds? 'Who could this man possibly be? (2.189.40)
Out of compassion, you have shown me this four-armed form of yours to dispel that doubt; meditate upon it always within your heart. (41)
Having spoken thus, he withdrew his form and was then born as a human being;
the king fell at his feet and held those feet to his heart.
With tears in his eyes, he also entreated him, saying: "Grant me forgiveness!
The entire world belongs to you alone; what then of these two girls? (43)
Having spoken thus, the king then performed a great festival according to the prescribed rites; he fed everyone and honored them with devotion. ||44||
And Hari also instructed him:
"O King, everything that is performed as action results in either success or failure; thus it becomes free from bondage. (45)
But that action, having me as its support, passes away, for it accomplishes my own desired end;
otherwise, an action supported by my power would yield a different result.

The worship of the deities, the twice-born, and spiritual preceptors, as well as the honoring of virtuous people and likewise the honoring of one's parents, indeed brings about freedom from debt. (47)
The duty of kings is exertion; through that, the divine is produced.
When both arise together, they bestow prosperity as well as liberation.
Human effort is the first thing to be undertaken; thereafter, one may rely upon destiny.
Without initiative or exertion, one shall never enjoy the fruit of success anywhere. (49)
If both human effort and destiny are attained through truth,
that shall grant certain success and bring happiness both in this world and after death.
A person who is rich in virtue, self-control, and gentleness shall be attended by prosperity;
one should contemplate the Supreme Brahman as the cause of one's own happiness. (51)
One must never harm the cause itself, for by doing so, one’s own self is destroyed;
from water comes fire, from a Brāhmaṇa comes a Kṣatriya, and from stone comes a clod of earth.
If that which has arisen goes to destroy its own cause, it perishes;
for the self, knowledge, action, and karma have all arisen before Hari. 5.3
If he does not worship Hari, that destroyer of his own self becomes a slayer of Hari; for one intent on harming Kṛṣṇa, destruction shall come like fire.
Therefore, I must always be protected, upheld, and honored with reverence; I must be remembered and worshipped, for I shall grant liberation from bondage. ||55||
Those seeking liberation should avoid these vices in vain:
eating, drinking, sleeping, and engaging in jesting. (56)
If this passion, which is constantly attached and exceeds what is required, were indeed cast upon me, it would not be called a vice. (57)
That vice which is merely for the sake of subsistence is not called a calamity;
however, gambling and the like, being both improper and useless, are considered true misfortunes.
But that which is the constant abode of calamities, followed by suffering and grief—how could a human being find his own true happiness therein? (99)
Therefore, having reflected upon its worthlessness, one should abandon that which is inherently corrupting;
for if subjects conduct themselves in this manner, they will follow the path of excellence.
Then Dharma shall be present there, endowed with devotion and faith;
and where Dharma is, there I dwell perpetually.
Or, being visibly present within my heart, I protect those who have taken refuge in me;
like a mother protecting her children, I protect him who is endowed with righteousness.
Therefore, let all my subjects and others, endowed with righteousness, worship me;
I shall deliver them from the ocean of desire—of this there is no doubt.
"Let them install my image here for the sake of constant viewing;
as for me, I shall go today to bathe in the auspicious waters of Indirā."
"May it be well with you; may there be happiness, and may there always be health free from disease.
Having spoken thus, Kṛṣṇa then rose from his seat. 65.
The king quickly prepared all the vehicles, including those that travel through the sky, and the monarch granted them leave to depart.
"Having bathed in the great river Indirā, one must certainly go to Supānarāṣṭraka by evening"— this was the firm resolve of Hari.
Having prepared themselves, they ascended the celestial chariot, and others as well;
having mounted their vehicles and ascended the celestial chariots, they came to be in the sky.
The king, the queen, their household, and the subjects implored him for forgiveness;
likewise, there were the sounds of musical instruments for his departure and songs. (69)
Then shouts of victory, cries of joy, and cries of "Long live! arose, together with Supāna the sage and King Mudrāṇḍa.
Requested by Sahastha, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa went before him;
honored by multitudes of joined palms, he arrived at the bank of the Indirā.
Then, having descended from the vehicle onto a spacious area, Hari bathed there, and all [the others] likewise bathed; for that place indeed became a sacred ford (tīrtha).
There, the Blessed Lord gave a gift to the sage Supāna;
at that time, the devotees drank the nectar-like water used for Hari’s bath.
Where Hari bathed, there were many Vetālas;
all of them, produced by their past actions, indeed met their destruction there.
All of them, though fair-complexioned, arrived bereft of splendor; suffering in human form, they reported their miserable state. ||75||
Formerly, we were plunderers who used force, wicked men devoid of compassion, and thieves who oppressed the subjects; now, by our own sins, we have died here.
Afflicted by cold and violent winds, and tormented by hunger and thirst,
we have become Vetālas here and dwell upon the riverbank.
"O Lord of Gods, grant us deliverance; we have come to you for refuge.
Thus addressed, the Blessed Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa [poured] nectar-water.
He gave it to them for the purpose of drinking; they drank it, freed from sin, and at that very moment, having acquired merit, they possessed divine bodies like the gods.
They became gods and goddesses, worthy of heaven and possessed of auspicious limbs;
the compassionate Blessed One spoke thus to the high-souled Lomaśa.
"O Vaiṣṇavas, lead them here; thereafter they shall become [your] followers.
Lomaśa then quickly caused them to hear the mantra of Hari. 81.
"Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Master; svāhā!
Having heard this mantra, those Vaiṣṇavas, possessing divine forms, offered their salutations. ||82||
Hari spoke to Īśānadeva and his own dependents:
"O Śambhu, send them to Kailāsa; let them be your attendants there."
Thus addressed, Śaṅkara quickly dispatched them all—
Hari and every person there— through the sky to the realm of Kailāsa.
Having ascended their celestial chariots, they went to the kingdom of Supāna,
to the auspicious city of Madriṭa on the bank of the river called Dūra.
In that vast city of Lakṣaśāla, which was surrounded on all sides by many gardens,
exceedingly prosperous, and resembling heaven, they beheld the splendor of the sky.
Adorned in many ways and sprinkled with fragrant waters,
the city shone brilliantly with its archways and excellent cow-stalls.
By the king's command, the army then encamped on the riverbank in a great garden for the evening, in order to welcome Nārāyaṇa and please him. 88.
Then the king brought his celestial chariot down from there;
the sage, the king, and the subjects also stood before him for the purpose of welcoming him. (89)
Then musical instruments were played and shouts of victory arose; thereafter there were the sounds of machines, the clamor of people, and the sounds of stūpas.
Following the path shown by the king, Śrī Hari brought his own celestial chariot down into the great garden near the royal palace. ||9 1 ||
Other celestial chariots also descended from the sky at that time,
O Rādhikā, amidst sounds of joy and showers of parched grain, unbroken rice, flowers, and other offerings.
Then the subjects, the king, and others greatly increased [their offerings];
they uttered cries of "Victory! to the Lord of the countless principles (tattvas) and his presiding deities. 93.

Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Worship and Feeding of Hari in the Palace in the Kingdom of Indurāya, the Wandering through the City of Vāyūnāna, the Instruction, the Farewell on the Seventh Day, the Evening Bath in the Indirā River, the Deliverance of the Vetāla, and the Arrival in the Kingdom of King Mudrāṇḍa," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Rādhikā; at that time in the month of Mādhava, King Mudrāṇḍa offered flower-garlands and golden necklaces and worshipped [Me]. || 1 ||
Then he dressed Hari in a most splendid royal costume and endeavored to lead him about the city of Madriṭā in the evening. || 2 ||
There, the lion among kings honored all the great lords;
and Supānārṣi applied a tilaka-mark and a crescent moon to Hari.
Afterwards, the king gave water for drinking to all those on the mounts; he then stationed them with musical instruments and caused auspicious sounds to resound.
Hari [mounted] a new, bright chariot covered with blankets and deerskins, yoked to sixteen white, excellent horses possessing the characteristics of celestial steeds.
Likewise, he was accompanied by a single, magnificent, and pale-white bull,
while being praised by bards and honored by great seers.
He ascended a chariot resplendent with gold, gems, and pearls;
Maudgalya’s son Trigrasaṇḍaka took up the reins.
And the sage Gavākṣa held the parasol;
that great white parasol was being held over the middle of the chariot.
He shone like the moon accompanied by stars because of his beautiful earrings;
meanwhile, two sages joyfully took up the fly-whisks for him.
The great sage Supāna and the great sage Mitra were both observers of mighty vows;
they possessed a splendor equal to the rays of the moon and were exceedingly long and beautiful.
O Rādhā, Kṛṣṇa’s parents, brothers, and sister were then seen standing upon the chariot, all equal to the gods. || 11 ||
Mounting a bright chariot yoked with the finest horses,
Rudra, the Lord, attended by his hosts, followed behind.
Mounting an excellent golden chariot yoked with very large horses,
Lomaśa himself followed Rudra as his preceptor.
Both Vṛkāyana and Nīlakarṇa set out with Pītaratha,
while Yayāti departed on a chariot yoked with dark-blue horses.
Then all those thousands of women dear to Brahmā, beautifully adorned, departed from there on human carriages as well as various other vehicles.
All the sages of the Gaṅgā lineage, as well as other maidens, princesses, and queens, followed along on excellent chariots and other vehicles. || 16 ||
Then numerous chariots, elephants accompanied by camels and bulls,
infantrymen, and horsemen followed closely behind.
Then the panegyrists, bards, genealogists, and minstrels likewise went along with the subjects, singing well-spoken verses.
Then, however, the vision of Viṣṇu became incomparable happiness—an unsurpassed experience on earth of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. (19)
Upon the entry of Hari into Madriṭā,
the city and its royal highways were adorned in many ways by the city-dwellers.
The royal highway was adorned with white garlands and banners, and it was thoroughly perfumed with incense.
Likewise, the city was made beautiful by fragrant powders, various flowers, priyaṅgu blossoms, and closely interwoven garlands of flowers. (22)
At the entrance, new and auspicious jars filled with water were placed;
white, beautiful, and bright flowers were scattered here and there.
Just as the gates themselves were adorned with decorative festoons,
so too did he enter the city that had been thus beautified.
At the time of Hari’s entry there, thousands upon thousands of city-dwellers gathered, desiring to behold him. ||25||
The royal highway, with its squares beautifully decorated, shone intensely,
like the swelling of the ocean at moonrise due to the arrival of incoming and outgoing tides.
An unexpected prosperity came upon the people along the royal roads;
the houses by the royal roads were entirely adorned with jewels. (27)
The breasts of the fair women seemed to tremble under their weight;
those women praised the son of Kambharā, the Lord of Śrī.
These blessed women, dear to Brahmā, who had obtained Puruṣottama as their husband,
likewise praised the religious observances and vows of Gaurī.
O Rādhikā, the city resounded with words of praise for them, cries of joy, shouts of victory, and hymns of glorification.
At every street, at every crossroads,
at every square, at every marketplace, and at every palace, the subjects worshipped the Lord.
Having wandered through the city along the royal highway, Hari then approached the decorated and resplendent royal palace.
There, all the subjects, both citizens and country-folk, spoke words pleasant to the ear: "By good fortune you have arrived, O Mādhava! (33)
In this matter, your grace and your vision are considered auspicious;
otherwise, O Kṛṣṇa, how could there be a vision of you without [great] fortune? (34)
Thus, gratified by auspicious rites at the gate of the royal palace,
Hari descended from his vehicle and entered the royal residence.
The king, the great sages, the queen,
and the maidens honored the beloved of Kṛṣṇa with perfumes, garlands, and necklaces of jewels.
With *sumana* flowers, sweetmeats, jewels, and abundant gold, with various kinds of offerings and diverse gifts according to their desires. || 37 ||
Knowing that very moment to be opportune, fifteen princesses, fallen under the sway of the noose of delusion, took hold of Hari’s hand.
Then there arose the proclamation of a holy day (*puṇyāha-ghoṣa*) and likewise the chanting of names,
which produced joy for friends and was meritorious and pleasant to the ear.
Likewise, the sound of kettledrums and the delightful blare of conchs arose,
along with the auspicious sound of those proclaiming victory.
Having heard this, the illustrious Bālakṛṣṇa, with a joyful heart,
then sat down upon a supreme throne situated within his golden royal palace.
In the assembly, he gave many instructions to the king:
"If a king should become addicted to vices, he is despised by the people. (42)
He who causes distress to the world hates it and finds no happiness;
rather, having relinquished his own personal preference, he should practice what is for the welfare of the world. (43)
A king who brings about the welfare of the world should never abandon his composure;
indeed, excessive joking with his servants must not be indulged in by the monarch. 44.
Out of rivalry, those who live off the king treat him with contempt;
they do not remain in their proper place, but rather transgress his commands.
When sent on an errand, they do not go; they reveal secrets;
they beg for what should not be asked for, and they eat foods that ought not to be eaten. (46)
They cry out, they burn with rage, and they cause tasks to be destroyed;
they practice deception and indeed sometimes seize by the hair. (47)
They accomplish their own deeds through forged signatures and letters;
they conspire with the women's guards and assume identical appearances.
They even vomit and spit in the presence of kings;
being shameless in the vicinity of the monarch, they destroy his reputation as well. (49)
They cause King Rājavāha to mount horses, elephants, chariots, and the like;
and even in the assembly hall, they speak of the king as being ignorant.
When the king is angry, they laugh and cause his secret counsel to leak;
they make public what was hidden and they transgress his commands. ||5.1||
They even show contempt and revile us in our very presence;
they say, "The king is indeed in our fist," and they speak thus of the worlds as well. (52)
Therefore, one should not be overly mild even when joyful in the company of servants and others;
rather, one should always exert effort, which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation. (53)
A king is so called because he delights the worlds; for the duty of a ruler is indeed to bring delight, as well as the protection of truth and the protection of legal proceedings. (54)
One must practice the protection of patience and not deviate from the royal path;
a self-possessed man who remains vigilant in his human endeavors deserves kingship.
Indeed, men and all dharmas must be protected by the king;
the elderly should be served, and the virtuous should be honored.
The king should give to the virtuous and take from the wicked for the sake of dharma;
furthermore, the king should honor the learned and their virtuous deeds in every way.
The king should protect the learned, those who know political ethics, those skilled in the scriptures, storytellers, upholders of dharma, and teachers of the Supreme Lord. (58)
The king should honor his gurus and worship them with abundant gifts;
he should constantly revere the virtuous, feed them, and listen to sacred narratives. ||59||
The king himself should cause temples to be built, establish a continuous system of worship, and daily sacrifice to his beloved deities with devotion. (2.190.60)
He should offer for the sake of dharma a tenth part, a twentieth part, a hundredth part, or even a fifth part, from his royal authority, wealth, and grain.
The king should protect sacred fords and likewise cause sacrifices to be performed;
he should protect cows, Brahmins, women, the destitute, children, ascetics, and those who have sought his refuge.
One should constantly give gifts after having honored one's teachers and fellow men;
one should always pay homage to the elderly and receive their blessings therefrom.
One should constantly remember the Blessed One during one's activities in the morning and evening;
this will not produce any fear, nor will it cause the destruction of one's lifespan.
One should never perform any act that causes the destruction of merit;
one should always subsist on the remains of offerings (vighasa) and be devoted to the Brahma-yajña.
One should perceive the highest parental affection for one's offspring;
regarding me, Hari, as being present in all of them, one should worship them accordingly.
A king should never engage in harmful acts in vain, even for the sake of his own interests;
rather, he should always undertake virtuous deeds in this world with sincere devotion.
One should provide assistance in meritorious deeds and perform them oneself;
one should cause the virtuous to dwell in the kingdom and serve them with supreme reverence. (68)
The king, remaining constantly on his throne, should cause the Blessed One and the devotees to wander through the city and other places, and he should arrange for the presentation of garlands.
One should maintain one's own family and others in righteousness, in their duties, and in acts of devotion;
as well as perform bathing, meditation, recitation, fire-offerings, libations, and the presentation of offerings.
If the king himself practices giving, righteousness, devotion, and service, and conducts himself in this manner, he is liberated and not bound. (71)
In whom there is never any deceit, hypocrisy, or illusion toward the virtuous; in whose home there are discourses on wisdom, devotion, and the worship of the Divine. (72)
And he who follows the path of the virtuous and conducts himself as one who has renounced, may indeed become a partaker of liberation somewhere through service to the Lord of Lords. (73)
As is the king, so is dharma; as is dharma, so are the subjects.
A king who desires liberation must protect the dark dharma with great effort. (74)
The family, kinsmen, friends, and others, including all subjects, remain entirely established in their own Bhāgavata dharma. (75)
"As the king is, so shall the subjects conduct themselves according to the Sātvata dharma;
therefore, O King, let all the subjects also practice the Sātvata way. (76)
"I shall uplift those who have taken refuge in Me with the most excellent devotion that grants liberation"—having said this, O Rādhikā, Bālakṛṣṇa indeed became silent. (77)
The king, his subjects, and all others indeed accepted those words;
even those who were devoid of mantras accepted the Lord's counsel.
They took up necklaces, vessels, and the chanting of the Lord's names;
then King Mudrāṇḍaka dismissed the assembly.
The great sages, Hari, the family members, and the lords beginning with Īśāna, as well as Brahmā, Priyā, and others, prepared the foods.
Having obtained rest at night, and having performed rising, bathing, and so forth, one should then perform the daily worship as well as the drinking of milk and other such rites. ||81||
Hari became ready to go toward the regions of Pūrtagaṇḍa;
then the king requested Śrī Hari to go to Śaivālapattana.
To go to that supreme place situated on the bank of the river Gavadaka-vitāna,
Hari said, "So be it," amidst shouts of victory and songs of praise.
Having accepted the worship, he ascended his own celestial chariot;
others sat down quickly, and Mudrāṇḍaka also did so at that very moment.
Having ascended his celestial chariot, he went ahead to achieve a successful welcome;
and other chariots also moved toward the city of Śaivāla. (85)
In an instant they reached that place, the vicinity of Gavādakavita;
their celestial chariots descended upon the bank of the Gavādakavita. (86)
In his own palace, the king honored Kṛṣṇa and all [the others] with devotion;
the monarch worshipped Hari with garden fruits, flowers, and other offerings. (87)
Then he performed the *ārārtrika* rite and caused the Lord to circumambulate the city;
having thus purified the town, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa indeed [departed]. 88.
Having consumed milk, fruits, and other offerings, and having received all the worship performed by the king and others, as well as by the subjects, and having bestowed blessings upon them; ||89||
Desiring to go quickly with him at that same speed, Acyuta departed;
meanwhile, a king named Gaṇḍa arrived there to take Kṛṣṇa away.
Then Hari, together with Pūrtagaṇḍarṣi, prepared himself;
having ascended the celestial chariot quickly and having bestowed words of blessing, [he departed]. ||91||
Hearing the sounds of victory, Hari proceeded toward the river Gavādayānikā;
having crossed the regions along the river, he traversed through the sky.
Having reached the river Trigirā, King Gaṇḍaka indeed descended first,
together with the sage Pūrtagaṇḍa, for the purpose of welcoming him.
O Rādhikā, having gone to the auspicious city of Līśavana, which was adorned and filled with armies, he offered a welcome in the garden. 94.

Thus ends the one hundred and ninetieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Wandering in the City of Madrid, the Arrival at the Royal Palace, the Worship, the Instruction, the Meal, the Departure after the Morning Rites on the Morning of the Eighth Day following the Night, and the Journey toward the City of Līśavana belonging to King Gaṇḍaka in the Regions of the Pūrta Gaṇḍarṣis," in the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, within the second section, the *Tretā-santāna*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Listen, O Rādhikā; King Gaṇḍaka was a sage who had fulfilled his vows, as were his queen, his daughters, his sons, and others as well. || 1 ||
Relatives and groups of ministers stood before him to welcome him;
then the aerial chariot of Hari descended from the sky into the royal garden.
Other celestial chariots also descended from all sides;
at that time, musical instruments were played, and the sounds of trumpets arose.
Songs were sung and shouts of victory arose,
along with the most excellent sounds of kettledrums, flutes, and drums.
Making the ten directions resound with the sounds of the citizens' overwhelming joy,
Hari rose from his palanquin and came outside to meet the procession.
The king, the sages, and the householders nourished him with flowers and other offerings; they offered a welcome with necklaces, excellent unbroken grains, and parched rice.
King Vyāsa likewise seated Harikṛṣṇa upon an elephant,
and the others upon suitable mounts and excellent vehicles as was appropriate.
He placed the Lord of Gods upon a palanquin and other vehicles, as well as on carts and carriages, and brought Him to the city of Līśavana accompanied by the sounds of musical instruments.
Full of enthusiasm, he caused them to circulate;
the subjects offered their worship with great respect, seeking his audience and honoring his feet with many gifts.
Then, having beheld the beauty of the seashore,
the Blessed One arrived at the excellent royal palace together with his family.
The beloved of Kṛṣṇa was honored by the king, the queen,
and the maidens with sandalwood, the essence of fragrance, flowers, and auspicious garments.
The leaders performed the worship of Śrī Hari with cooling offerings, powdered garments, jewels, ornaments and the like, as well as various substances and fruits. || 12 ||
Then the nine young daughters of Gaṇḍa quickly took the hand of Hari in marriage according to the rites of wedding.
And by good fortune, the king indeed became one who had accomplished his purpose;
he celebrated that great festival with worship and honors. (14)
The king caused a meal filled with cooked food to be served;
there, the lord of the earth had dancing and singing performed. || 15 ||
The king bestowed many riches upon Kṛṣṇa;
then the Blessed One gave them to the sage Pūrṇagaṇḍa.
Having eaten, they attained rest through the chewing of betel and drinks;
the King himself delighted the honored guests with draughts of milk.
Then, in the evening, in the assembly hall, Bālakṛṣṇa directly instructed the subjects in many ways with words of peace.
Whether in a kingdom, in a garden, in a house, or even in a forest,
the embodied soul who is devoted to internal conduct and possesses discernment attains peace.
Having thoroughly severed the thread of craving and abandoned the pursuit of worldly enjoyments,
he who remains well-established in the state of the Self attains peace.
He whose striving has ceased and whose mark has attained the state of being markless,
and whose tongue is devoid of relish— he attains peace.
He for whom sounds are but portions of space, touches like forest fires,
and forms like leprosy, attains peace.
Whichever woman is a taker of life for a man, and whichever man is a Rākṣasa for a woman,
he attains peace indeed through the mental renunciation of her.
He whose elements are in the form of impurity, whose family behaves like monkeys,
and whose servants are like consumption, indeed attains peace.
He whose disciples are like enemies, whose sons are intent on devouring him,
and whose body is always diseased— he indeed attains peace.
He for whom dispassion prevails, for whom the sphere of passion is painful and the sphere of affection is not favorable, indeed attains peace.
One who possesses discernment attains peace amidst great enjoyments and great suffering;
for I am not the body, nor is there anything to be enjoyed by me, nor am I an enjoyer like a wretched man. || 27 ||
One who possesses such discernment does not attain peace by being dependent on the dull-witted, nor in the delightful regions of rivers, nor in forest gardens, nor in a palace. (28)
In temples, at sacred fords, or in solitary places, one should abide in peace whenever and wherever there are no enemies, neither external nor internal. (29)
Whether they are adventitious or permanent, it then attains peace;
for just as one whose pain has been cured falls under the power of sleep and no longer feels the suffering,
so too the individual soul (jīvātman), though struck by the world, does not suffer when it has entered the chariot.
A living being whose latent impressions have been destroyed attains the company of the virtuous. ||3.1||
If one is devoted to serving the virtuous, one attains auspicious peace;
one should adopt the qualities of the good and practice the conduct of the good. (3.2)
One should always avoid what is ungraspable and strive for what is graspable and auspicious;
the embodied being should calm the waves of the mind and become peaceful. 33.
Through the grace of the Guru, one should abandon conceptual constructions, doubts, and delusions;
and through one's own discernment, one should abandon logic, causal arguments, and disputes. (34)
Having recognized sources of distress and causes of forest fires, one should avoid them from afar;
having thoroughly considered the future, one should live free from calamity.
Having taken refuge in Hari, one should dedicate the fruit thereof to Him;
he who undertakes an action after meditating on Hari and perceiving Me as the agent [should do so likewise]. (36)
With a state of mind permeated by me, one should perform what is beneficial and bestows welfare;
one should especially practice that which brings about the highest good for oneself or for another. 37.
One should contemplate the richness of wealth through the treasury of knowledge and discernment;
endowed with non-possessiveness and contented, one brings about supreme peace. ||38||
Having reflected thus constantly, the king, the queen, and the subjects should conduct themselves for the sake of perfect peace, relying upon mutual benefit. (39)
One should perform service to the subjects and protection for one another with the king's protection,
regarding them with the thought of oneself and the thought of one's own son, thereby bestowing perfect peace.
Bṛhaspati the large-eyed, Kāvya, Prācetasa, Bharadvāja, Mahendra, and Gauraśiras Manu; ||41||
These very exponents of Brahman always praise one another’s protection of the Dharma, which is promoted by kings in every eon. (42)
Giving, constant service to the virtuous, as well as the gathering of the virtuous;
skillfulness, truthfulness, straightforwardness, and likewise impartial consideration on all sides. ||43||
The rescue of those who are sinking, the promotion of those of noble birth, the non-abandonment of the virtuous, and service even to the wise—[these are the duties]. //44//
One should observe enemies, friends, and those who are neutral, whether they be outsiders or one's own kin;
one should always follow the path of policy and dharma, and avoid the ignoble.

Exertion is entirely appropriate in worldly affairs, in devotion to Hari, in the pursuit of knowledge, in liberation, in renunciation, and in dispassion; these are the duties devoted to protection. 46.
They must always be protected by the king and by the subjects who desire immortality;
through industrious effort, the gods, joined by Mahendra, attained immortality.
Indeed, for one devoid of exertion, protection recedes far away;
therefore, one should always practice righteous exertion and perform virtuous deeds. (48)
Even if there should be a failure in this duty of protection for an embodied being,
that too is a vast merit for him, since I myself am indeed the protector.
I am the protection, I am the protector, and I alone am that which is to be protected;
I am always the provider of protection, and I protect—of this there is no doubt.
I never protect those who are cruel-natured and devoid of guardians;
for on this earth, the class of kings exists as my own form to provide protection. (51)
"Therefore, my dharma is protection; let it be upheld by the people," Śrī Kṛṣṇa, Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Self, said as he was being addressed thus. (52)
O Rādhikā, King Gaṇḍaka questioned Śrī Narāyaṇa:
"How, why, and when indeed was the title 'King' bestowed upon you by you? (53)
Even though there is equality in physical existence, equality in the nature of the sense faculties, equality in pleasure and pain, equality in transformation, and equality in bodily form; ||54||

In those who possess equal semen, bone, and marrow; who are equally endowed with flesh and other bodily constituents; who have equal vital breaths and bodies; and who are alike in their birth and death—(55)
And even though such is the case for each individual, how is it that kingship ascends to one alone?
How is it that one alone [rules] those who are distinguished, as well as the brave and the wise? (56)
The possessor of existence presides over and protects the earth alone;
likewise, by the grace of that one alone, the entire world becomes gracious.
In one [instance], the entire kingdom bows down as before a god;
O Blessed One, how is it that even when there is equality, this [other instance] transcends kingship? (58)
"O most excellent one, tell me now what the reason is for this.
Having heard this, Hari spoke to Rādhā about the story arising from the king's decree. (59)
In the beginning, during the Kṛta Yuga, there was here neither kingdom nor one who protects the kingdom;
there was no king, nor was there punishment, nor anyone deserving of punishment, nor anyone who inflicted punishment.
By means of truthful dharmas, the people protected one another according to the Brahmanic way;
there were wish-fulfilling trees, wish-fulfilling creepers, the thought-gem, and the cow that grants all desires.
By that [means], all subjects then became happy and dependent upon their own selves;
but then, in the course of time and at the end of the age, the powers [of the senses] were indeed subject to conceptual construction.
When they had reached a state of depletion, ownership was then established:
"This is mine and this is the wish-fulfilling tree; this is not yours"—thus was it disputed.
Thus, at that time, possessiveness and delusion entered living beings;
and their thoughts, taking the form of mental constructs, became fruitless.
Through the obsession with the faults of craving, they destroyed the true Dharma;
having fallen under the power of greed, they grasped at what was not yet attained.
Another great evil, desire, took hold among living beings;
passion, which brings about what is undesirable, indeed touched those people who were devoted to desire.

Deluded by that, they did not understand what ought to be done and what ought not to be done; thus, approaching those who should not be approached arose, as did the speaking of what should not be spoken. (67)
He determined what was edible and inedible, as well as what was defiling and non-defiling;
when the world of men had fallen into confusion, the state of Brahman indeed perished.
Upon the destruction of the Brahmins, there was the destruction of Dharma; consequently, the gods were struck with fear.
They went to their father, the unborn one (Aja), and, being deeply distressed, spoke to him after propitiating him. (69)
O Brahmin, in this world of men, the Brahman has indeed dissolved into truth;
dharma has gone to destruction, and for that reason we have been deprived of the Svāhā-call.
"We have now reached a state of exhaustion and have become equal to ordinary men;
therefore, O Grandfather, contemplate here that which is our ultimate welfare. (71)
Brahmā said: "I am contemplating for you that which is beneficial and removes fear.
Then, at the beginning of the Tretā age, Brahmā [bestowed] virtue, wealth, and desire.

He established the fourfold aims of life, including liberation, as well as the Dharma with its distinct virtues, and the religious observances consisting of the forms of Dharma devised for protection through punishment and other means.
He created sacrifices and other rites mixed with the fruits of action,
as well as objects in the form of wealth, such as fields, gardens, houses, and the like.

He created the various forms of wealth and prosperity, as well as the rules that define ownership and other rights, and the seasons, which can take any form at will and are interconnected with one another.
Out of delusion, he established rules regarding their respective objects of enjoyment;
yet he taught the dharma of liberation, which is of the nature of Sāma, and the dedication of all to me, Mādhava.

Because it is not determined that even the dedication of the three aims of life (trivarga) alone grants liberation, and because many other various modes are likewise not determined [as the sole means]. (77)
Śaṅkara, this very Īśānaka, formerly received that policy;
and that scripture spoken by Śaṅkara then became known as the Vaiśālākṣa.
Indra therefore took up that very Bāhudantaka;
Bṛhaspati wrote this down, and so it became known as the Bārhaspatya.
From him was born the work of Uśanas, from which political science (nīti) was set forth;
then the gods petitioned Viṣṇu regarding one who would be a knower of the treatise on political science.
Then Nārāyaṇa and I gave him a mind-born son;
his son was Virajas, and Kīrtimān was his son.
His son was Kardama, named Anaṅga, who was highly intelligent, a protector of the subjects, virtuous, and expert in the science of governance. ||82||
His son was Aṅga, who, having married Sunīthikā, the daughter of Mṛtyu,
begot a single son, the cruel Vena.
The great seers slew that hateful Vena with the tips of their sacred mantras;
the seers then churned the right thigh born from Vena’s body.
They produced the Niṣāda, and from that the Niṣādas came into being;
then those great seers again churned his right hand.
Then I became Pṛthu by name, bearing weapons and clad in armor;
being a knower of the science of polity, I attained the title of "King. (86)
Together with the gods, I caused the earth to be leveled; by my resolve, the entire prosperity of the kingdom was renewed. (87)
In the first cycle of the Yugas, the kingdom was indeed established by me;
the earth was milked for the sake of the subjects, and the subjects were protected with the rod of punishment. ||88||
Because of his delighting [the people], they called him "Rājā Pṛthu" on earth;
because of protecting [them] from injury (kṣata-trāṇa), I became a Kṣatriya, even though I was a twice-born (dvija). (89)
I alone established the earth and established the kingdom; there, as the eternal Viṣṇu, I applied the principles of statecraft.
Then, from the forehead of Malla, a beautiful golden lotus was born;
from that, the goddess Śrī, Kamalā, the wife of Dharma, came into being. ||9.1||
In his kingdom, Śrī took the form of wealth, granting both desires and liberation;
for when Vaiṣṇavī Śrī dwells in a kingdom, she is indeed the giver of liberation.
Thus, from that time forward,
both gods and kings were called equal to the wise, because these rulers are portions of myself.
Thus, O Queen, I have set aside that which is designated as kingship, the very state of being preeminent;
therefore, both the king and the subjects should regard me as residing within their own selves. (94)
They are to be worshipped, saluted, and offered with supreme devotion;
for those who have dedicated themselves to me shall attain me alone—of this there is no doubt. (95)
Those kings who, abandoning me, consider themselves their own masters, will surely go to ruin; their royal lineages will become diminished and impoverished. 96.
Having thus understood this definitive conclusion, let people worship me, Janārdana, the eternal Lord of the kings of kings, while establishing themselves in the four aims of human life. 97.
"Only in me," Hari said to Rādhikā and the assembly;
they all accepted those very words, bowed, and then departed. (98)
