Hari reached his own residence and took his meal in the royal palace;
the other great men also took their meals with due respect.
Then they all found rest, and having slept during the night,
those princesses, O Rādhikā, served that beloved of Kṛṣṇa.

Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Journey to the Capital City of Gaṇḍaka, the Wandering through the City of Līśavana, the Worship, the Meal, the Instruction, and the Resting at Night," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O Rādhikā, on the morning of the ninth lunar day, the Lord was awakened by auspicious sounds of musical instruments and by the words of bards, chroniclers, and panegyrists.
Likewise, they all remained awake and performed their daily rites;
the king, having brought milk and other foods, offered them to Hari.
Everyone drank milk and partook of food as was appropriate;
there, the Lord Śrī Hari bestowed blessings upon the king.
Then Hari bestowed blessings and honors upon the people;
thereafter, he became ready to depart, having dissolved the entire kingdom within his matted locks.
King Līnorṇa arrived there and requested [the boon] from Acyuta;
then the Lord spoke together with the sage who subsisted on fruits.
There, King Gaṇḍaka gave him many parting gifts;
honored by all, Hari ascended an excellent celestial chariot.
Likewise, others also then ascended, hearing the sound of the cries for victory from the subjects; all of them urged on their birds that travel through the sky.
Having crossed the Khāḍikā river, they went to the city of Vāruṇī;
meanwhile, King Līnorṇa had previously descended to his own city.
He offered a welcome to Hari along with the fruit-eating sage;
then, by the path shown by the king, he brought down the celestial chariot.
Then Hari and the others descended from the sky in their vehicles;
the sound of musical instruments and songs pervaded every direction.
Descending from his carriage onto a magnificent golden palanquin presented by the king, Hari shone amidst the sounds of victory.
The Supreme Lord, having been duly honored by the king with garlands and other offerings,
sported in the western quarter together with his family and all his attendants.
Accompanied by the royal army and honored by the citizens, the Blessed One arrived at the vast palace, the king’s residence.
Then he rested, bathed, and took his meal;
others also ate, and thereafter the queen [ate] before Hari.
Having arrived for the sake of worship accompanied by four maidens,
the maiden, having obtained her beloved Hari, joyfully performed the taking of his hand in marriage.
Then the queen offered worship and a dowry according to the prescribed rites;
thereafter, having rested, the Blessed One quickly became ready for his journey.
Having ascertained the king's intention, the lord made everyone ready;
indeed, he presented the entire kingdom, extending to the borders of Khāḍiga, before King Bṛhacchara.
Requested by the sage Vallījīvana, Hari departed;
meanwhile, King Bṛhacchara descended ahead to his own city.
He brought Śrī Hari, who was adorned with the name Dhīvara, along with him;
in the city, within a beautiful palace, he worshipped the Supreme Lord.
The king, the queen, and the subjects offered a welcome;
then, with pure devotion, the two maidens took the hand of Hari in marriage.
King Hari, having accomplished his purpose, passed the night;
at dawn, adorned by his army, he wandered about the city.
Having granted an audience to the subjects and having purified that city,
the Lord prepared to depart after partaking of milk and other refreshments.
Then, having heard that his lord had departed quickly, the King of Paścimasamudra arrived there in haste with his celestial chariots to lead him back. || 23 ||
The King of Aṅga, having bowed to Hari, the Supreme Lord, made his request;
Hari said, "So be it," and immediately became ready.
Other celestial chariots as well became well-prepared at that time;
having crossed the Khāḍī river, the Blessed One proceeded to the city of Milinda.
Honored by the king according to his power with musical instruments, troops, and panegyrics, and gratified with worship and the presentation of gifts, he was paraded through the city.
At midday, he caused all human beings to take their meal;
in the evening, having placed them all in celestial chariots, he showed them the various continents.
Having again surveyed everything, Hari returned to Milinda and gave him instruction augmented by the principles of statecraft.
The subjects of Dvilīnā and likewise those of Sukautukīprajā,
having arrived there along with their children, heard the instruction.
On the tenth night, in an assembly of hundreds of thousands of people,
O Rādhikā, he taught that which is beneficial and brings about liberation.
This Īśāna is the Supreme Brahman; he should always be honored by people.
Indeed, supreme devotion must be offered to Īśāna, who is my very self.
Indeed, one must not speak untruth, nor should one even take an oath in that matter;
rather, Sunday must be observed for the propitiation of Hara.
Parents should always be served; violence should never be committed;
theft must be avoided; and false testimony must be shunned even in a court of law. (33)
One must never desire the wealth, clothing, or other such desirable things belonging to others; one must not kill another living being, nor should anything belonging to another be taken. (34)
One must never betray the trust of anyone at any time;
nor should one ever, under any circumstances, destroy the dharma of the subjects. (35)
Having thus protected the dharmas, the king shall attain heaven;
[by practicing] truthful speech, freedom from anger, forgiveness, and impartiality. (36)
Delighting only in one's own wife, purity, avoidance of malice, straightforwardness, and the maintenance of dependents—these should always be practiced by all people. (37)
The classes of Brahmins adopted the ancient dharma of self-restraint,
the study of sacred texts, the practice of yoga, austerity, and the protection of progeny.
One should always maintain and protect speech that is friendly and beneficial;
by conducting oneself in this manner, a brahmin shall eternally attain heaven.
A Kṣatriya, however, may give gifts, study the Vedas, and perform sacrifices;
he shall protect his subjects and exert his prowess against those who act unjustly.
The primary duty of the kṣatriya class is the warding off of robbers;
furthermore, giving gifts, study, and sacrifice bring happiness to kings. (41)
And by abiding in his own duty through these [means], the king should indeed cause all [his subjects] to abide [in theirs];
thus established in dharma, the king is called a lord of kṣatriyas.
Furthermore, others who are engaged in agricultural work or various occupations should employ their wealth in giving, study, and sacrifice. ||43||
One should indeed protect all cattle with the affection one has for a son;
by the protection of cattle, the Vaiśya shall attain supreme happiness. ||44||
In ancient times, Prajāpati, having created the animals, gave them to the Vaiśya;
he gave all subjects to the King, and he gave the autumnal [knowledge] to the Brahmins.
Taking one-seventh for his livelihood, he may live in every way;
if he is a Kṣatriya, then by offering that to me, he shall attain liberation. ||46||
By performing service, servitude, slavery, attendance, and even acting as messengers, groups of servants may indeed attain great happiness. (47)
Service is the wish-fulfilling creeper; service is the wish-granting tree; service is considered to be the cow of plenty and the jewel that fulfills all desires. (48)
Through service, a lion, a king, a guru, and the planets come under one's control;
through servitude, a master, a husband, a virtuous wife, and subjects become submissive. (49)
Through service, enemies, the hateful, the ignorant, and the wicked are brought under control; a person devoted to attendance wins over even those who restrain others. (2.192.50)
The kingdom of kings and so forth does not indeed exist apart from the one who pleases;
therefore, one should attain everything that is filled with jewels through service. 5.1
Parasols, head-wraps, ornaments, sandals, fans, and so forth, as well as garments and excellent food, are given to the attendant. (52)
One who is childless must be maintained; likewise, the aged and the infirm must be maintained.
Furthermore, according to dharma, the male and female slaves and the group of servants must be supported by you.
Sacrifice is the worship of Brahmins; sacrifice for kings is through wealth;
for Vaiśyas, sacrifice is the act of supporting others; and for servants, sacrifice is faith.
Among all sacrifices, faith is the foremost sacrifice and is exceedingly difficult to perform;
faith is the supreme deity, by which Mādhava is pleased.
Those whose nature is faith are performers of action who are enriched with all fruits;
therefore, the sacrifice of faith is prescribed in all worlds.
Where that which is called faith is the supreme deity, there the deity resides; having entrusted the accomplishment of the task and the attainment of mastery to Me, it is brought to fulfillment. (57)
Whether he be a thief, or a sinner, or even the worst of evildoers—if he desires to perform a sacrifice, he is indeed virtuous, for such is his intent. (58)

Therefore, one should always perform sacrifice, whether toward a deity or even toward a sentient being, or toward a poor person, a group of the helpless, or a dependent who has been rescued through faith. (59)
It is certain that one should sacrifice in every way, at all times, and with all means;
for there is nothing else equal to sacrifice as a supreme bestower of fruits and happiness.
Or he may be devoted to the life of celibacy, not practicing the duties of a householder;
by offering oblations into the Brahman alone, he attains the Supreme Brahman. 6.1.
Or rather, even one who performs worldly actions, provided he possesses the dharma of being devoted to me and practices dharma while taking refuge in me, is liberated even from bondage.
Or else, having accomplished his purpose through the vision of knowledge, he may dwell even in the forest;
such a performer of action, ever devoted to Me, attains equality with the Imperishable.
If an ascetic, having relied upon my teachings and their virtuous nature, becomes free from dualities, he attains me and is prepared for my own state of being.
Whether one subsists on alms, remains free from possessions, and is self-possessed,
or whether one is engaged in action or even devoid of action, such a person is fit for attaining my state of being.
Sleeping in moderation, eating in moderation, being free from desire, and without a fixed abode, a sage who lives on whatever is obtained may attain me. (66)
Free from desire, he is declared to be like Brahman; satisfied, he is the refuge of perfect bliss; devoid of enjoyment and free from worldly activity, he attains equality with the Imperishable.
The householder should cross over illusion by means of illusion; having cast all illusions, even those consisting of illusory women, into me, he is then liberated from bondage.
Content with his own wife, satisfied, free from deceit and crookedness, devoted to the worship of the gods, truthful, self-controlled, and likewise one who makes proper divisions [of wealth]. ||69||
He was devoted to forgiveness and compassion, a giver to all as was appropriate,
upright, honoring guests, and supporting those who sought his protection.
Whoever should perform it, cause it to be performed, or even practice it himself shall partake in liberation;
having attained pure fruit in heaven, he shall rejoice for eternal years. (71)
And at the end of the body, one shall undoubtedly attain inexhaustible and infinite desires existing everywhere—those centered on me, provided they have been offered unto me. (72)
Whatever one performs here in such a manner, he shall obtain a corresponding result;
first, by making another's property the means for an act of service during the festival. (73)
Then one should perform the bodily rite, followed by the internal one, and then the innate (naija) rite;
thereafter, one should perform the supreme (pārameśa) rite, which wards off all defects.
Whether it be a king or even a common subject who conducts himself in this manner,
he attains a black sapphire threaded upon all the strings [of the world], like Mount Meru.
Therefore, having constantly surrendered themselves to the Supreme Lord, people should remain free from dualities and free from ritual actions in order to attain the state of Brahman. (76)
One who performs my rites, rests in me, offers oblations to me, and has me as their supreme goal—I deliver them from the depths of the ocean of death; of this there is no doubt.
Having worshipped all the ancestors, the gods, and the sages who have taken refuge [in him],
as well as Hari who dwells within, one shall go at the end to the abode of Hari.
Whether not acting, or acting otherwise, or acting at all, one who has taken refuge in me reaches the further shore of the ocean of countless karma through my yoga.
Let them always worship me at dawn; let them remember me during their ritual acts and other duties;
and having placed me within their hearts at the end, let them proceed to my imperishable state.
Having spoken thus, O Rādhikā, the Blessed One himself became silent;
so too did the king of the capital city of Milinda, his subjects, and the others.
Having attained the Dharma—which is blended with higher cognitions and capable of destroying bondage—all those [beings] joyfully accepted the teachings then imparted by him. (82)
And there Lomaśa gave to them the mantra of Hari as well:
"Oṃ namo śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya svāmine svāhā. (83)
Then the subjects and the king honored the Lord with gold and silver coins, as well as with offerings and garments. (84)
[He worshipped] the Supreme Lord with ornaments, sandalwood paste and the like, unbroken grains, flower garlands, and various articles suitable for offering. 85.
With a gracious heart toward those subjects and the kings, Hari bestowed his blessings: "May you possess the most excellent fame! (86)
Possessing the best kingdoms, the best virtues, and devoted to the highest justice, they were intent upon devotion to me alone, the Supreme Lord. (87)
Having spoken thus, Hari rested in his own dwelling;
the people, who had realized their true selves, went to their own homes. 88.
The King of Aṅga gave food offerings to the glorious Supreme Soul, and he also fed all the honored devotees who had taken refuge in Hari. (89)
He worshipped Īśāna and also paid homage to Lomaśa;
having honored the family of Hari, the king took his meal.
The queen named Raṅgarajā was the wife of Cāṅgarāja;
she was fair-complexioned, possessed of a gracious heart, and had eleven daughters. (91)
Taking flower garlands, golden necklaces, sandalwood paste, and unbroken grains of rice fragrant with perfume, she came into the presence of Bālakṛṣṇa to worship him.
With affection, she worshipped the feet of Hari and washed them with water;
Gaurī and all those eleven maidens likewise drank that water.
Beholding the beloved Lord, the beginningless Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa, they took him by the hand according to the marriage rite. 94.
They placed necklaces around his neck, and Hari gave them to them as well;
that great festival took place, and the king became one who had fulfilled his purpose.
Then they fell asleep and rested comfortably through the night; and when the Blessed One perceived that the night had passed and heard the auspicious sounds, he [arose]. (96)
When Hari, having performed his daily rites, quickly became composed once more,
at that moment the King and the virtuous Queen brought forth auspicious milk.
The Blessed One accepted that fruit, his own self, food, and so forth;
and the sages, eager for the welfare of the family dear to Brahmā, took those [other items]. || 98 ||
Thereafter, they took fruits and betel leaves;
having received due honor at that very moment, they also accepted their leave.
Hari and the others, having questioned the king, quickly ascended their prepared celestial chariots,
hearing the sounds of trumpets from the path of the sky.
Then, as words such as "without cause" circulated before him, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa thus proceeded ahead, O Rādhikā. (101)
From the sky, Kṛṣṇa beheld the surface of the earth, which was exceedingly beautiful, with its kings and kingdoms subdued by his power and its sages rendered silent by old age.
Then the king, accompanied by the great sage Jarāmauna, went on foot upon the ground, humbly following behind for the sake of welcoming Hari.
O Rādhikā, on the eleventh day of the dark fortnight of Śrāvaṇa, at the second watch of the night,
musical instruments were then sounded and shouts of victory arose.
Then, on this earth, mechanical sounds, garlands of names, and objects of worship appeared;
and in due course, celestial chariots emerged according to the path shown by the King. 105.
They descended into the great garden in the presence of Vālīnā,
within the capital city of Viśālā, which was crowded with hundreds of thousands of people.

Thus, in the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā, in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, [is described] the arrival at the kingdom of Līnorṇa by Hari, his wandering in the city of Vāruṇī, his worship, his meal, and his departure; then his arrival at the kingdom of King Bṛhacchara and his wandering in the city of Dhīvarā; then his journey toward the city of Milinda belonging to the King of Aṅga, his wandering there, his giving of instruction, his meal, and his rest at night for two watches on the eleventh day of the dark fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada.
The one hundred and ninety-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Departure of King Balalīna and His Kingdom," etc.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Rādhā; then the king [saw] the Blessed Lord Bālakṛṣṇa descending from the celestial chariot and placed a garland of flowers around His neck.
She placed a necklace of jewels around his neck and a cluster of flowers in his hand;
the queen, for her part, applied saffron paste along with unbroken grains of rice and a mark of the moon.
The maidens washed the feet of Kṛṣṇa and drank the nectar;
likewise did the king’s family, the ministers, the chief officials, and the subjects.
There they respectfully welcomed Śrī Hari with offerings of worship,
and the king gave fragrant water for Hari to drink.
The king also caused all other people to drink water, and he seated Hari upon a golden elephant-vehicle. || 5 ||
He seated his family members in elephant-vehicles, the great sages in those drawn by bulls and horses, and others in beautiful, covered carriages.
Then the king seated his beloved Brahmins upon divine silk palanquins,
and thereafter the monarch himself mounted a vehicle drawn by elephants.
In the city of Vālīnā, the king, together with his army, paraded the Lord Hari through the royal highway,
the other streets, and the squares.
First, indeed, the sound of the bell goes upon the back of the camel;
then the excellent horse proceeds, accompanied by its banner and its driver.
Then the great elephant proceeds, awakened by the sound of kettledrums;
those decorated steeds shine like deities.
Then the divine chariot, adorned with mechanical dolls,
proceeds for the sake of the subjects' worship of Kṛṣṇa, in order to bestow flower garlands and other offerings.
Then there was a large, golden palanquin, mechanically driven,
wherein the assembly of Jhāñjhapa, Khājā, and others were eager for the kīrtana.
Wherever there were horsemen making a clamor and bearing banners with the marks of birds,
thither went the great elephant, wherever the princes were.
Then camel-caravans proceed to where the principal subjects dwell;
thereafter, people dressed as lions go forth, sounding musical instruments. (14)
Then seven elephants, resounding with the cries of tigers and other beasts,
proceed as the mounts of the Brahman-sages.
Then, pairs of horse-riders, dressed in golden attire and bearing weapons,
proceed in groups accompanied by musical instruments, carrying drums and kettledrums.
Then the drum-bearers proceed, and after them the silk-banner carriers;
then follow the hosts of Śambhu by the hundreds, along with their servants and attendants.
Then thousands of servants indeed [prepared] excellent vehicles for the king, as well as other musical instruments with sweet, pleasant, and excellent sounds. (18)
These beloveds of Brahmā first awaken the people and then depart;
thereafter, among all the vehicles, the Gaurīs, adorned with ornaments, set out.
Then Kṛṣṇa’s family, beautifully adorned, proceeds upon elephants;
thereafter, Īṣānadeva shines resplendent upon the back of an elephant.
Then the queen, the king’s mother, shines resplendent in a golden palanquin;
after her follow all the young princes, and beyond them, the princesses.
Then the king, highly adorned, shone amidst the elephant-riders;
the great monarch, endowed with strength, was honored by Śrī Kṛṣṇa. ||22||
In an elephant carriage near Bālakṛṣṇa, he shone at the front;
holding a parasol and attended on both sides by two chowrie-bearers, he stood firm.
Behind them, great horsemen and elephant-riders advance;
then follow women clad in gold, uttering auspicious sounds. (24)
Then all the female guards, carrying pitchers upon their heads filled with fruits, leaves, and water, proceed intent on singing; after them follow the male protectors.
Then, at the end, those who operate mechanical devices indeed depart;
and the fair-complexioned women, beloved by the people, also depart then in great throngs.
At that time, the royal highways were crowded with people;
so too were the crossroads, the upper chambers, the houses, the palaces, and the watchtowers.
The crossroads, the junctions of the streets, the paths along the sides, the courtyards, the houses, and the terraces of the city gates—[all these were filled with people]. (28)

The tree branches, the difficult-to-access parts, the walls, the house-enclosures, the corners, the elbows, those that are turned upward, those with weight in the middle, and those filled with water [are the locations for the snake]. ||29||
The heights, the dilapidated portions, the ground above the mounds,
the garden plots, the roadways, and the foundations of the side walls.
Everything was crowded with men desiring a sight;
the city was trampled by ten million people seeking a vision.
Just as that city named Indrāvatī shone like heaven, so too did its courtyards,
adorned with clusters of flowers, appear like artificial gardens.
The gateways of the streets were adorned with ornamental towers and the like,
and all the market squares were beautified with arched gateways.
The edges of the pathways were beautified by groves of plantain trees,
and the dwellings were adorned with colored streaks, svastikas, and other auspicious designs.
The sky above the road was beautified with small flags and banners;
the well-constructed platforms were likewise adorned with arches and festoons.
The door-frames were beautifully adorned with water-pots and bilva fruits;
the courtyards were graced by fair-complexioned maidens.
The windows were graced by the lotus-faces of deer-eyed women,
and the white-colored mansions were beautifully adorned with balconies.
The peaks, the domes, the stupas, and the spires—all the pinnacle-turrets were adorned with beautiful, auspicious banners. (38)
Resounding with shouts of victory, the sounds of musical instruments, the rumbling of lutes, and beautiful songs,
this city of Vālganikā became filled with thunderous noise in the ten directions.
At the city gate, Kṛṣṇa was honored by the guards and the chief officials;
thereafter, he was honored by the troops and the royal people who stood before him.
He was honored by guild-leaders, those of noble families, merchants, and likewise by those established in their positions;
he was worshipped by all classes, as well as by women and men. (41)
With offerings such as fruits and the like, grains and the like, ornaments and the like, garments, woolen blankets and the like, necklaces, and garlands made of gold; ||42||
With unbroken grains of rice, saffron, jewels, diamonds, necklaces, and flowers, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa was honored with exceeding devotion. (43)
Having wandered thus through the city, he arrived at the royal palace;
the king honored Hari with offerings of ten million jewels.
On the eleventh day, Hari performed the worship of the vow at night and kept a vigil in the assembly hall,
accompanied by the exposition of dharma.
He organized a festival filled with the chanting of Kṛṣṇa’s glories; and Rādhikā and the great devotees respectfully performed the restorative rites.
And Hari instructed all those who were awake and observing the vigil:
"While a man remains awake and established in his vow, there is no fault arising from sleep. (47)
This fruit of keeping vigil does not fail to reach one who has broken a vow;
the vow becomes complete, and the state of darkness is restrained.
Even by force, devotion to Hari may become a source of satisfaction;
when Śrī Hari is pleased, the entire human birth becomes fruitful. (49)
For that purpose, indeed, a vow must be observed with vigilance in this world;
whichever lunar day remains at sunrise, that alone is the Ekādaśī for one seeking the fruit of the vow.
Considering the rising of the sun, Ekādaśī should always be observed;

likewise, my Janmāṣṭamī is on the morning when the eighth lunar day occurs at sunrise. In the dark fortnight of Kārttika, it should always be accepted as occurring after the full moon of the autumn season.
In this manner, other lunar days as well are to be accepted when they coincide with sunrise. ||52||

Human beings may achieve success by relying upon either a lunar mansion (nakṣatra) or a day (vāsara), but that is certainly not my primary view; for I hold that the lunar day (tithi) is what matters at the time of sunrise.
The vow should be performed on that very day where the specific lunar date (tithi) falls;
there is no such thing as the "loss" of a tithi, though it is considered "lost" when the moon rises during its waning.
The existence of a lunar day (tithi) is certain at either moonrise or sunrise;
however, for a festive rite performed at night, the lunar day is considered to be that which ends at moonrise.
But for the performance of festive rites during the day, the lunar day (tithi) is considered to begin at sunrise;
likewise, those vows must be observed by my power in every respect. (56)
The full lunar days (Pūrṇakās) become givers of merit; there is no doubt in this matter.
Even the deluding Brahmajā, when associated with me, is not a source of loss. 57.
Thus, having understood my command, the supreme vows must always be performed by my devotees; for my command is the bestower of fruits. (58)

At whatever time there is a festival, birth, or dissolution of a deity or other such being, the lunar day (tithi) that exists at that very moment is always auspicious for a religious vow (vrata). //59//
The rising of the sun, the rising of the moon, or the rising of the stars should be understood as merely secondary (gauṇa) in that regard; day and night are the primary (mukhya) moments.
If men, abandoning this, should perform other vows,
there will undoubtedly arise conflicting opinions regarding them.
Indeed, those [actions] will surely become causes for the breaking of one's vows;
therefore, one should always seize the opportune moment during a vow or any festive occasion.
By that means, indeed, dharma increases, and never otherwise;
merit increases through faith, especially when joined with the proper time.
From that point on, it increases even further by the power of the worthy recipient;
for I am the worthy recipient, the Supreme Brahman, who is to be served—this is the great vow. (64)
Service to one's mother, father, and teacher is the supreme vow;
service to the preceptor and the virtuous is a great vow that bestows merit. (65)
One should devotedly cause public service centers, water-stations, wells, and auspicious beds to be established; for such acts of charity bestow merit. ||66||
Non-violence, truthfulness, freedom from anger, right livelihood, charity, protection, service to the elderly, and the maintenance of one's wife and children constitute his vow. (67)
One who desires prosperity should give sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) in the performance of sacrifices;
one should perform cooked sacrifices (pākayajña) and grain sacrifices (kaṇayajña), which bestow prosperity.
For one who constantly honors the Arhats by sharing with them in every way, that very vow will indeed grant heaven; there is no doubt about this. (69)
But in this case, for one who rescues kinsmen, relatives, and friends from distress, this vow shall indeed always yield merit that bestows heaven; it is the supreme vow.

For one who performs all forms of hospitality, heaven is certain; of this there is no doubt—provided he performs the sacrifice to the ancestors, the sacrifice to the spirits, and the honoring of guests and so forth. (71)
For one who performs the sacrifice to the gods, heaven is certain; of this there is no doubt.
Furthermore, there is always the undertaking of initiation and the honoring of the learned.
The remembrance of the gods, the protection of those who have come for refuge, conduct free from crookedness, and the vow of celibacy—this bestows heaven. (73)
For an embodied being who acts with compassion toward all living creatures and is devoted to their protection, this vow shall become a bestower of heaven.
For one who offers a welcome and other courtesies to those who have arrived, who performs appropriate services, who honors them with humility, this vow shall bestow the heavenly realm. (75)
For one who remains under the control of the family, as well as under the words of the virtuous and the words of the scriptures,
the vow shall become the bestower of liberation.
Wherever that bull may be situated within the hermitage, his vow consisting of dharma leads surely to heaven; of this there is no doubt. (77)
For one who conducts themselves in the world by disregarding pride of status, pride of lineage, pride of age, and honoring only those worthy of their virtues, heaven is assured.
Having observed the laws of the country, the laws of kinship, and the laws of the people, he conducts himself accordingly; this is his supreme vow. (79)
Even a householder who is not greedy regarding prosperity, sense-objects, wealth,
the body, or anything pertaining to the body, his vow shall be equal to that of a saintly person.

For virtuous people, even while in the householder stage of life, become dwellers of Dharma—delighting in Dharma, devoted to Dharma, providing assistance through Dharma, and indeed abiding in Dharma. ||8.1||
And that embodied being who always behaves toward all creatures in the world as he would toward himself, removing the suffering of others, obtains happiness in this very life. (82)

Those who possess the arising of Dharma, the vigor of Dharma, and are protectors of the sacrificial rites of the Dharma-guardians—relying upon the Dharma of renunciation—they indeed swiftly cross the ocean of existence. (83)
When his worldly intention, though difficult to overcome, has been eradicated from its very root,
the embodied soul, having attained the state of pure being, then partakes of Brahman.
Therefore, all my volitions must be surrendered to me, the Lord;
my very self must be offered, and liberation shall be granted as my abode. (85)
Having spoken thus, Bālakṛṣṇa, the Supreme Lord, ceased;
and the king likewise worshipped the deity Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa. (86)
Having performed his morning bath and other rites, and having completed the worship and other ceremonies, he worshipped Maheśa, the Lord of Satī, with the utmost devotion. ||87||
The king caused the breaking of the fast to be celebrated with sweet foods and other delicacies;
meanwhile, Śrī Hari, having completed his fast, attained rest.
Meanwhile, Queen Śrīratīśā, accompanied by the requisites for worship,
arrived together with forty fair-complexioned maidens.
He worshipped the Supreme Soul and then drank the nectar of His feet;
thereafter, forty maidens took the hand of Hari in marriage.
Then, by the king's command, musical instruments were played and songs were sung;
together with the Gaurīs, there was a festival accompanied by dance.
The king was born, and he considered his own purpose fulfilled;
the king then gave gifts and wedding dowry to the wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
Having received all those pearl necklaces, golden ornaments, blankets, garments, and fine cloths, Hari then quickly departed at the king's command.
The king quickly prepared to depart; he fed Acyuta and all his honored guests with milk-rice and other delicacies. (94)
Then the army, which bestows honor, became ready for the expedition; the musical instruments were sounded and a roar of victory was raised. 95.
Then all the celestial chariots appeared in the sky; the great king, honored on all sides by his subjects, ascended one of them. (96)
Thus, having been exhorted by the sages for the sake of protection, they all mounted [the chariot],
and they were then invited by King Varasiṃha.
Possessing the power of movement through the sky and hearing the shouts of victory, they proceeded toward the kingdom of Hari, that excellent lion. 98.
Formerly, King Varasiṃha, accompanied by sages,
prepared his army in front of him and stood ready to welcome the host of Hari.
On the bank of the Viṣṇutulyā river, on the shore of the city of Vāśīlā,
the army beheld the aerial chariot of Hari and offered a welcome.
With the sounds of various musical instruments, the thundering of mechanical devices,
and the songs of fair women, the sky indeed became filled with sound.
By the path shown by the King, the celestial chariot descended to the earth,
and indeed other chariots of Hari also arrived.
A rain of flowers was showered upon the celestial chariot by the people;
O Rādhikā, the multitude became overwhelmed with emotion at the sight.

Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-third chapter, titled "The Description of Lord Hari’s Arrival at the City of Vālīna, His Worship, the Vigil, the Instruction on the Vow, the Breaking of the Fast on the Twelfth Day, and the Subsequent Departure for the City of Vāśīlā," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Rādhikā, on the broad and circular bank of the Viṣṇutulyā river,
Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa descended from his celestial chariot into the garden.
The king placed a garland of flowers around the neck of Nārāyaṇa;
the sage gave him necklaces, and the queen and the other principal ladies presented him with wreaths.
With beautiful flowers, with his offspring, and with unbroken grains and other offerings, the king placed [these] in the hand of the Lord who is dear to Śrī Kṛṣṇa. || 3 ||
Then, even while dressed, he offered fragrant water containing sandalwood and other perfumes;
thereafter, the king and the others washed their feet and drank the nectar.
King Varasiṃha placed Kṛṣṇa upon a mechanical carriage,
his family upon a long wagon, and the great sages upon vehicles drawn by horses.
The king seated Brahmapriyā upon elephant-vehicles,
and Śambhu, who is honored by millions of worlds, upon a beautiful chariot drawn by deer.
Then, with musical instruments that signaled the honors due to the army,
the king settled Hari and caused him to wander through the city of Vāśīlā.
Then the royal family worshipped Kṛṣṇa at the city gate,
and the principal householders worshipped Kṛṣṇa in the square.
The merchants stationed at the front of their shops and at the crossroads,
as well as all the subjects on the great highway, worshipped the beloved of Kṛṣṇa.
At that time, fair-complexioned women ascended to their own dwellings;
gazing at Hari, they showered flowers upon Hari.
Then, having attained the fruit of their wide eyes and with their minds drawn by his gaze, the beautiful women spoke to one another, filled with joy and having reached a state of peace.
Having beheld this Hari, who is most beautiful to look upon, whose vision is bestowed by the impulse of compassion, and whose sight is unattainable even for embodied beings, the woman— |||
Make your own birth fruitful; do not delay.
"The mind that is excessively greedy for sense objects and lacks self-control does not attain a state of stability;
thus, by demonstrating this very greed and lack of control, Mādhava himself has indeed become a woman. (1.3)

Place this pair of lotus feet within your mind— feet upon which the crowns of the lords of gods, kings, and sovereigns rest as their crest-jewels, which serve as the seat for yogis, which are praised by the virtuous, and which are supported by Kamalā. 14.
He who, in His supreme abode, possesses a beautiful and divine form,
is described by the Vedas as the locus of all virtues;
He is completely filled with sovereign power, prosperity, beauty, and excellent qualities.
Now, O Mānasā, envelop this one with your splendor.
Indeed, you weak women shall never again obtain this beautiful one, who is endowed with abundant luster, whose body is well-nourished, and who is the refuge of the planets.
Therefore, this [mind] should always be restrained within one's own heart. || 16 ||
The lotus-face, which destroys manifold afflictions, is charming with its measured, gentle, and beloved smiles;
it bestows liberation upon this earth and grants liberation in the world beyond.
Let this [work], which brings happiness like the full moon amidst the poison [of worldly existence], be drunk in. || 17 ||
This Supreme Person swiftly draws away the heart, as well as the collection of senses and consciousness;
having recognized him here as the beloved, eternal Lord, [one should take refuge in him].
May they meet in the heart; having met, let them be enjoyed. || 18 ||
Let this one, who has come forth from his abiding within the heart,
be worshipped with flowers and the weight of mental offerings; let him be honored with the presentation of jewels, gems, and diamonds.
Embraced by her friend, let him be united with you and enjoyed. || 19 ||
Thus, Kṛṣṇa, whose fame was sung everywhere, having wandered through the city,
arrived at the royal palace, where he was saluted by the citizens.
The king quickly worshipped the feet of Hari with sandalwood paste, unbroken grains, and flowers; then Hari sat upon the throne.
As he sat down, the people showered him with flower garlands and blossoms;
with hearts overflowing with love, they gazed upon him with steady eyes.
There, a very grand assembly was convened by the illustrious Supreme Lord, and he then gave instruction for the sake of the welfare of the people. (23)
The Blessed One, the Supreme Lord who shines in the supreme imperishable, comes indeed out of compassion for the protection of His own subjects. 24.
The subjects, who are like daughters to the Blessed One, must be protected like a mother; they must be nourished, made happy, and led to the imperishable state. 25.
I am the sustainer of all incarnations, the beloved of the illustrious Lord Kṛṣṇa; having crushed Māyā, I abide here in this world within the range of your vision.
The Lord of Kāṃbhareya, the Lord of Rādhikā, the husband of Lakṣmī and Padmāvatī,
the Lord of Māṇikī, the Master of Ramā, he himself is the delight of the cowherds.
He is the beloved of those dear to Brahmā, the Lord and Master of all creation;
he is the husband of Lalitā, who is victorious and as charming as a swan amidst the lotuses of excellent virtues.
Wherever my dwelling may be even in this world, let that place consist of His divine abode; by the residence of Nārāyaṇa, the earth shall become like Vaikuṇṭha.
"O Blessed One, this birth is the cause for my divine nature and divine state;
likewise, devotion to you is the cause for my acquisition of a virtuous land and other such things. (2.194.30)
If the king should indeed be devoted [to dharma], then the Kṛta Yuga would prevail there;
for a king endowed with policy and righteousness truly brings about the Kṛta age. ||3 1 ||
There, indeed, among all the social classes, no thought arises that is contrary to dharma;
for the welfare and prosperity of the subjects prevail at all times. (32)
All sacred rites are performed by the twice-born,
and all seasons become exceedingly pleasant and free from disease.
Human beings become gracious in heart, mind, and speech;
diseases do not arise, nor is anyone born with a short lifespan. ||34||
There, no men were miserable, nor were there women without husbands;
even the earth, without being ploughed, produced crops of its own accord. (35)
The medicinal herbs indeed bear fruit through the essence of the earth, bestowing happiness;
even their bark, leaves, fruits, and roots become potent. (36)
In every household, there shall be only righteousness, happiness, and contentment; in every person, there shall be trust, happiness, and never any cause for agitation. (37)
In this way, when a king endowed with righteousness abandons a portion of his time for the sake of truth, that very act becomes a portion of his own righteousness. (38)
And here, among human beings in various places, the Tretā age has arrived;
its inauspicious portion is a fourth part, and it causes suffering to that same extent. (39)
Then the earth shall yield crops when ploughed and grant a third part as its fruit;
everything shall yield a third part as its fruit, while in the fourth part it shall be worthless.
When the king— the cause of the Tretā age— is absent, everything— be it happiness, the means to achieve it, or even the objects to be obtained— does not bear fruit, for nothing remains complete.
When the king indeed abandons half of his duty and his policy,
then the Dvāpara age has arrived for the king and proceeds in this manner among the subjects.
In the cloud, the forest, the season, the tree, the sap, and the cows, it proceeds;
at that time, two parts are considered inauspicious and two parts are considered auspicious. 43.
Everything bears fruit—whether external or internal, one's own or another's, divine or non-divine. (44)
Whether for one's own sake or for the sake of others, it bears fruit in every way;
half the earth yields crops, while the other half is enriched by grain. (45)
When the king abandons even one-third of the Dharma on this earth, then [Dharma] becomes quartered in the seasons, the tastes, the people, the trees, the duties, and the fruits. (46)
One should understand that there is fruitlessness in three parts, and even in the [remaining] part there is no certainty;
when the king conducts himself in this way, then the Kali age (Tiṣya) prevails.
Through lack of discipline, the subjects suffer, and then people become devoted to unrighteousness;
indeed, the minds of all human beings fall away from their own duty. 48.
In the Kali age, unrighteousness is powerful in every house and among every person;
monks possess all castes, and servants belong to all castes. (49)
In this world, which is filled with the intermixture of castes, there is indeed no security or prosperity anywhere;
virtuous deeds are not found, so how could there be any Vedic discourse?
All the seasons become unpleasant, and people fall ill;
they remain constantly imagining victory in what is untrue. (51)
The physical forms, voices, and minds of human beings decline;
new diseases arise there, and people die after a very short time. (52)
For the most part, many people become widowed and destitute;
generally, such offspring are indeed contemptible, being utterly devoid of happiness and peace. (53)
In one region the rain-god pours down rain, while in another he causes drought;
in some places there is a harvest arising from grain, and in others the destruction of sprouts.
O Queen, when the *rasas* (flavors/virtues) have reached depletion and the Age of Strife (*kali*) arises,
kings become destroyers of their subjects' protection and possess treasuries of strife.
The king is indeed the creator of the Kṛta age, as well as of the Tretā and Dvāpara; the king alone is the cause for the transition between the ages, being the creator of even the Kali age.
By performing what has already been done, a king enjoys the highest heaven;
by initiating the Tretā age, a king enjoys three parts of heaven.
By winning half [of the kingdom] during the Dvāpara age, the king attains happiness;
but by initiating the Kali age, he encounters suffering and the destruction of his kingdom. ||58||
Thus, in the Kali age, the king who is indeed like a Rākṣasa experiences only sin;
consequently, he goes to hell and dwells there for many years.
He consumes the impurity of his subjects; he also experiences boundless suffering, as well as sin, ill repute, and a succession of miseries. (2.194.60)
Therefore, a king should always conduct himself according to the eternal law, as did Manu and the other ancient sages;
he should practice the dharmas without delusion and cultivate affection free from bondage.
One should act out of compassion for those who are truly distressed, even if it means acting without greed for the sake of gain;
one should speak kindly not out of sycophancy, and one should exert effort without boasting.
One should not give to an unworthy recipient, nor should one be profound yet not a river; one may associate with all, even the ignoble, but one should never accept anything through improper means.
He should not behave improperly anywhere, nor should he perform actions that cause suffering;
he should not speak of wealth to the wicked, nor should he speak of his own virtues.
One should not take from the poor, nor should one seek shelter with the wicked;
one should not inflict punishment without deliberation, nor should one disclose a secret.
One should not bestow [favor] upon the wicked, nor place trust in those who do harm;
one should also be free from envy toward one's own wives and children.

One should not indulge excessively in women; one should eat what is wholesome and avoid what is unwholesome; one should honor those worthy of respect and serve one's gurus with sincere devotion. ||67||
One should worship the gods with devotion if one desires blameless prosperity;
one should exercise skill as required and practice gentleness according to the occasion.
One should conciliate to gain their affection, favor them for the sake of prosperity, and strike only after having ascertained the truth; having done so, one should not grieve afterwards.
One should not give way to anger, nor indeed should one adopt excessive mildness;
one should constantly serve the virtuous for the sake of peace and liberation.
For the sake of concentration, the king should constantly serve wise men;
thus, having risen early in the morning, he should cultivate his intellect in solitude.
And one should serve the inner self, which reveals reality as it is;
for through forty qualities, a king attains his royal status just as a god attains divinity.
Therefore, one ought to be endowed with statesmanship so as to bring about prosperity;
O King, you should always and in every way remember me as a witness within your heart.
Therefore, one should perform everything; I am the bestower of the Satya Yuga, and I am the savior of one who has set out upon the path of unrighteousness.
I am Janārdana, the one who shall lift up those submerged in the mire of doubt;
I am the liberator of those who have fallen into the snare of unrighteous actions.
And because I am one who goes to the further shore while others have not yet reached it, I am indeed always the one to be served; therefore, I am the refuge. //76//
Whether it be the king, the subjects, a son, or a daughter, even those engaged in the performance of duties would never reach the end of the detailed exposition of dharma.
When a matter that must always be practiced is doubtful and its conclusion is uncertain,
O best of gods, those established in dharma and learned in the scriptures should be consulted.
Having risen, taken hold of his feet, and paid homage, one should report matters concerning one's business, as well as the recollection of Nārāyaṇa. (79)
Men are devoted to one who is a protector, a giver, constant in righteousness, unwearied, and free from desire and hatred. (2.194.80)
For indeed, all beings follow him who has me as his supreme goal, who serves the virtuous, who exerts effort for my sake, and who has surrendered everything to me. 8.1.
Therefore, both the king and the subjects should act according to the etymological meaning [of their names];
in this way, there will be happiness in this world, and a favorable rebirth in the next. (82)
Whether he be a king, a subject, or anyone else whatsoever who possesses a body here,
if he constantly worships me, the giver of bodies, he shall be happy and no other.
He by whom dharma, wealth, pleasure, and liberation have been directed toward me, Mādhava, becomes truly united with me through innate nature. (84)
In this way, let all perform actions dedicated to me;
enjoyment and liberation will surely follow—there is no need for deliberation on this matter. (85)
Having spoken thus, the Blessed Kṛṣṇa then imparted his own mantra;
thereafter, the Lord, who grants satisfaction to the minds of all, became silent.
The queen and the princesses worshipped the Supreme Lord;
at that very moment, five maidens respectfully took his hand.
Having obtained their beloved and attained supreme bliss, the five Gaurīs were fulfilled;
the king rejoiced exceedingly, and the queen considered her purpose accomplished.
The people performed the worship of Hari, and the dismissal of the assembly took place;
having partaken of food, Hari attained rest in his abode. (89)
All those who were honored attained profound rest;
the Blessed One spent the night protecting the sage.
Having provided the necessary materials such as gifts and other requisites, the king then became ready to depart with his army and musical instruments; he bestowed a great farewell gift upon him.
Then, in the morning, after Hari had performed his daily rites, the king honored him with garlands of flowers and provided him with milk and other offerings, followed by a most magnificent worship.
He performed the rite of lights and then drank the nectar of [the Lord's] feet;
with his chest adorned by rows of necklaces, Hari ascended to a celestial chariot.
All those of great majesty ascended into the sky-going celestial chariots; then, musical instruments were sounded there in abundance.
From there, they went by means of supernatural powers to the kingdom of Rājagṛha;
and King Rājagṛha as well as the sage Lāṭavāya [welcomed them]. (95)
Having gone before the royal family and the city, which was exceedingly beautiful, there was a welcome for Śrī Hari, accompanied by a military splendor that caused great wonder. (96)
Seeing the celestial chariot of Kṛṣṇa then arrived in the sky, they all made sounds with shouts, hymns, musical instruments, flowers, and so forth. 97.
They raised shouts of victory and caused the sound of musical instruments to resound;
all the women also sang sweet songs. 98.
Thus, on a site endowed with honor and prosperity, beautified by gardens, on the bank of a river lacking two [of the five], in the vicinity of the city of Rīgā, Hari [resided]. (99)
He brought down the celestial chariot by the path shown by the king;
and other celestial chariots also descended from the sky at that time.
O Rādhikā, the people gazed at Kṛṣṇa with steady eyes; they honored him with flowers and celebrated him with the sounds of songs and shouts of victory. 101.

Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of Lord Hari’s wandering, worship, instruction on the Yugas, dining, and resting in the city of Vāśīlā belonging to King Varasiṃha, followed by his departure for the kingdom of Rāyagāmala on the thirteenth day before midday after falling asleep," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Rādhikā, Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa descended from the celestial chariot;
King Rāyagāmalan offered flower garlands around His neck.
The queen washed the feet of the Supreme Soul,
and the maidens and the royal family worshipped the Imperishable One.
Then the king also offered perfumes, unbroken grains of rice, flower garlands, and fragrant sandalwood, as well as necklaces and clusters of jewels, to that Lord Hari.
He seated him upon an excellent, four-tusked white elephant, which was beautiful, adorned with the splendor of a bridegroom, decorated with ornaments, and exceedingly auspicious.
The people gazed upon Kṛṣṇa as he stood upon the high [palanquin];
the princes held the umbrella over his head as well as the fly-whisks.
He placed all the other great deities upon carts;
the king paraded the Lord of Lords through the royal highway of the city.
Having bowed to Hari, the Rigvedic sages worshipped him with the most excellent of offerings:
fruits, jewels, garments and the like, gold, silver, and woolen blankets.
With flower garlands, diamonds, and other priceless objects,
[he should worship] at the city gate, the crossroads, the assembly place, the marketplace, and along the road.
In the courtyard, people honored him in every way with excellent offerings;
auspicious women increased his prosperity with unbroken rice, parched grain, lotuses, and filaments.
With heartfelt meditations, glances of pure mind,
and through the intellect, they offered a welcome from all sides with hymns and songs of praise.
The exceedingly radiant Kṛṣṇa went to the excellent royal palace;
five princesses then respectfully took hold of Kṛṣṇa’s hand.
Then the queen, filled with joy, worshipped the Lord of Gods, her son-in-law;
the fortunate lady gave various gifts and performed worship.
There, indeed, he gave five maidens to Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa;
and the king, feeling his purpose fulfilled, celebrated an auspicious festival.
Then Hari went everywhere to the principal palaces, the houses of the subjects, and the mansions, gardens, and residences of the merchants.
The Blessed Lord Śrī Hari, the Sovereign, was worshipped everywhere there,
as were Īśāna, the wives of Brahmā, the Gaurīs, and likewise the great sages.
In that city, everyone was joyfully honored by the citizens;
the family of Kṛṣṇa was worshipped by the Gaurīs with offerings of sincere devotion.
Then Hari, resplendent with his army, returned to his own abode;
he drank water and held a council there.
And Rādhikā’s beloved instructed the people:
"Dharma must always be observed by devotees; through it, wealth is produced. (18)
A person intent solely on wealth perishes before long;
likewise, wealth that is given away or deposited in an improper place is lost. (19)
Even that which is employed for the purpose of violence leads only to sin;
for it either inflicts injury upon oneself or makes one a perpetrator of violence.
The udder of the Dharma truly exists; one should never cut it.
If the udder is severed, one who seeks milk will not obtain it.
A person possessed of discernment should take this milk for the sake of the udder;
by serving the milch cow, the most excellent milk is obtained perpetually.
Thus, one who enjoys the earth through proper means obtains its fruit; likewise, by enjoying a virtuous cow, his own body, and righteousness, he obtains their fruit.
A man of discernment, regarding her as a milch-cow, should protect grain, gold, and that earth, and he should always protect righteousness, considering it likewise a milch-cow. (24)
The protection of living beings is dharma; compassion is considered its supreme form.
Indeed, by means of the dharma of compassion, the practitioner crosses the shoreless ocean. 25.
One must provide protection for those who are afraid; the fruit of such protection is easily obtained, for it consists of a residence in heaven for ten thousand years. (26)
Whatever worlds one conquers through well-performed sacrifice, through sacred study, and through the drinking of soma,
a wise man, practicing dharma, conquers those very same worlds out of compassion.
The gods and the ancestors, being virtuous, live by the duty of giving;
other beings live by the duty of compassion and the life of a householder.
In shade, in water, and in the wind, there is pleasure when it is hot;
in fire, in clothing, and in the sun, there is pleasure when it is cold. (29)
The mind delights in sound, touch, taste, form, and smell;
it finds coolness in heat, perceives the beautiful as excellent, and seeks that which is pleasant within the heart.
In cold, one should obtain warmth; that which is black in form always bestows happiness when attained.
One who is not attached to those enjoyments attains supreme bliss. ||3 1||
For those born in cold regions, other [practices] are beneficial, as are others for those dwelling in heat;
and for those living in hot places, the fruit arising from bathing is that which bestows auspiciousness. (32)
For those residing in cold regions, the fruit resulting from sacrifices and gifts shall be even greater than that.
The gift of wealth is considered to bestow nourishment for the satisfaction of the body. (33)
Wealth here is indeed twofold: that in the form of riches bestows happiness, while the supreme goal in the form of liberation bestows eternal bliss. (34)
The fruit for one who bestows fearlessness is the most supreme of all;
indeed, there is no gift equal to the gift of life, and the gift of liberation is superior even to that. (35)
I am indeed Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa, the beloved of Svāmī Śrī Kṛṣṇavallabha;
I bestow the gift of liberation, the gift of life, wealth, and more.
This [giving] is divided into three types: superior, middling, and inferior.
The gift that bestows liberation is the supreme gift; it should be given in every way on this earth. (37)
That gift which bestows eternal bliss must indeed be accepted;
by accepting another [unworthy] gift, disease arises, but it is destroyed by the giving of that which grants liberation.
In the granting of liberation, the gift of Brahman indeed makes one become Brahman;
for the tree of Brahman, when protected, truly yields honey and gold.
In the realm of creation, there is no gift superior to the gift of Brahman;
the gift of liberation is the gift of Brahman, and I am Brahman, and I give myself.
I am Dharma, and I am the embodiment of Artha; I am Liberation, and I am also the giver of liberation.
When propitiated, I grant the very self of liberation to one who seeks it.
He who kills a woman, or the Veda, or kills a virtuous person out of cruelty—
by the sins he commits, he is born as a pauper.
The Lord Rudradeva, the all-pervading soul, the Rudra who is my very form and the Supreme Controller, destroys the wicked and sinful while protecting the virtuous. (42)
The Self (Ātman) is declared to be Rudra’s own; when it spontaneously destroys evil, it shall eliminate sin, hatred, deceit, and the like, as well as self-destruction and other such faults. ||44||
Self-destruction is the destruction of liberation; one should never commit it.
One should always be intent on one's own true welfare, seeking liberation through union with Me. 45.
One should not conceive of the existence of a body; one should abandon the state of mixture.
Even if the wet is burned by the dry, it is so only if they are mixed together.
If the self were mixed with the body, it would even be born as one who suffers;
however, one who possesses discernment can never be mixed with evildoers in any way.
Attachment and aversion, which are forms of evil, must be abandoned by one who desires liberation;
negligence and delusion, which are also evil, must be abandoned by one who desires prosperity. 48.

The world of merit is heaven itself, where the self is happy; this is considered the celestial realm. The world of sin is hell here, where the self is miserable; this is considered the downward path. ||49||
The earth sustains both the virtuous and the wicked alike;
likewise, the sun imparts its heat equally to both the virtuous and the wicked. (2.195.50)
Water indeed brings satisfaction to both the virtuous and the unvirtuous;
the wind provides equally life-force and touch to all embodied beings.
Water purifies everyone equally, both the virtuous and the non-virtuous;
this is so in this world, yet there is a distinction in the world of results.
For one who possesses merit, cool water approaches there;
for one devoid of merit, the water does not even come within the range of vision. (53)
For the sake of the meritorious, the earth is provided with soft carpets; for the sake of the meritless, the earth is filled with thorns and gravel. (54)
For one who has performed meritorious deeds, the wind is cool and touched by fragrance;
for one who has performed no merit, the wind is fierce with poison and exceedingly terrible.
Just as the sun provides warmth according to the merit of a person,
so the sun becomes a burner that reduces one to ashes for the sake of one who lacks merit.
And thus, in this world rich with fruits, there always exists such an interval:
the world of merit, where there is honey and meat, where one eats ghee, and is adorned with gold ornaments. (57)
The eater of nectar rejoices, freed from old age and death;
whereas the world of the wicked is hell, a place of darkness, suffering, and intense torment.
He who, pervaded by hunger and thirst, a vessel of sorrow, and fallen under the power of momentary death, desires to go to that world, is indeed one who has strayed from discernment. (19)
Indeed, he who desires to go to the world of merit,
or to the eternal and supreme world known as my abode, the Imperishable (Akṣara), must possess discernment.
The wise man who desires to go there is indeed the best among those seeking liberation;
that Brāhmaṇa, through his daily worship, attains that world.
Even a Kṣatriya who is constantly charitable, performs sacrifices, protects others, and honors the worthy goes [to that realm];
and even a Vaiśya who is industrious, helpful, and righteous goes there as well. ||62||
Even a Śūdra who serves, is devoted, is contented, and eats only the remnants [of offerings] goes [to that state];
in each such case, my devotion-constituted contemplation is prescribed. (63)

For that person who, being self-restrained, carries out the command of the guru without faltering, accomplishment certainly comes to pass through the power of the guru; of this there is no doubt. (64)
The task to be performed is specifically both small and essential, by which the embodied being swiftly attains accomplishment that bestows the highest good. (65)
Those for whom the Blessed Lord is to be protected, and for whom His glorification is to be protected—my devotees, as well as they, are to be protected; they are always to be protected by me. (56)
Those whose leaders are devoted, who are virtuous, and for whom I am the supreme Brahman, as well as the daughters of those devotees in their homes—they must always be protected by me. (67)
They have no fear of time, nor of karma, nor of illusion, nor of Yama;
I am always worshipped both in the house of women and within their hearts. (68)
The king should always protect the virtuous, for they, when protected, protect him in turn;
their blessing shall be a bestower of splendor and a destroyer of bondage.
Whether they be virtuous ascetics or householders, they should desire their own welfare through charity, austerity, sacrifice, devotion, self-restraint, and service. (2.195.70)
He who establishes others on the further shore where there is no shore, and who provides a boat where there is no boat;
by relying upon him, people find happiness in this most terrible cycle of existence. (71)
Whether he be a renunciant or a householder, a man or a woman, one should worship that saintly person, regarding him as a kinsman who delivers one from saṃsāra. ||72||
One should likewise worship the Supreme Lord, the virtuous one, the Guru who bestows knowledge, and the sovereign;
and one should honor the chaste and virtuous wife, for the Guru is indeed the giver of liberation. (73)
What is the use of those bulls that cannot carry burdens, or of a cow that yields no milk?
What benefit is there from a barren wife, and what purpose is served by a king who does not protect? (74)
What use have I for that wealth or for this body, since I cannot serve the holy man?
What use is a withered kingdom, or prosperity seized by bandits? (75)

What is the use of that which is devoid of essence and fit only for enjoyment? Of what value is a birth that does not grant liberation? It is like an elephant made of wood, or like a tiger made of leather. (76)
Like a eunuch, like a saline field, like one devoid of discernment, like the thundering of clouds, and like a kingdom bereft of strength. (77)
Just as a vow without charity, a devotee devoid of affection, and a guru empty of knowledge and so forth—all these are likewise useless. (78)
Everything endowed with that is fruitful and bestows liberation; everything devoid of it is fruitless.
Where there is no attainment of the Self, that is indeed called a loss.
The attainment of the Self is the supreme gain; it is the surrender to the Supreme Self.
Through that, the attainment of liberation occurs, for that is indeed considered the attainment of Truth.
May people always serve the virtuous and constantly worship me;
may they protect their own dharma and also proceed to my abode. 8.1
"May there be well-being for you all in this world and in the next.
Having spoken thus, the king then ceased speaking and honored that Lord. 82.
The subjects honored him with great respect and many offerings;
then the queen, accompanied by her daughter, performed worship to Śrī Hari.
The three maidens, devoted to their husband, took the hand of Hari;
having obtained Śrī Puruṣottama, they made their birth meaningful.
The king gave food to Hari and his family, as well as to the great dignitaries; thereafter, the monarch himself ate. 85.
Accompanied by his subjects, he celebrated a very great festival at night;
he caused dances to be performed along with instrumental music, devotional songs, and other such arts.
Having obtained a sumptuous meal at night, Hari and the others rested;
then they rose in the morning to the sounds of musical instruments and auspicious chants.
Having completed their daily rites, Viṣṇu and the others then became ready to depart;
there, Hari quickly granted the mantra requested by the subjects.
King Śrī Hari gave much gold as a wedding gift; he also presented various offerings, and Hari likewise gave wealth at that time. (89)
The king offered Lātavāya Ṛṣi appropriate worship and then granted him leave to depart after he had finished drinking milk.
Mounting his celestial chariot while hearing the shouts of victory, Hari quickly ascended into the sky accompanied by his entire family.
At that time, all other vehicles were suspended in the sky;
the king, together with his army, paid him the honors appropriate for the occasion.
Then King Phenatantu and the sage Phālanāda both arrived to bring the Lord of the virtuous back to their own kingdom. (93)
Requested by Hari with great honor, he then quickly departed through the sky after bestowing blessings upon all.
Then other celestial chariots also quickly traveled through the sky,
having crossed over Khāḍikā and the great kingdom of Phenatantu.
On the bank of the river Tūrṇanayā, at its charming confluence, lies the city named Trinayā; nearby, within the circle of its gardens— || 96 ||
The king went forward and honored the army;
then, by the path shown by the king, Hari [mounted] his own celestial chariot.
He brought down [the chariot] into the garden near the royal palace;
likewise, other celestial vehicles descended from the sky at that time. (98)
Then musical instruments were sounded, shouts of victory arose, and a rain of flowers fell from the vicinity of the celestial chariots of the people. 99.
The Gaurī women sang songs of praise for Rādhikā,
while the King offered them a most excellent welcome with excellent mechanical fluids.

Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Wandering, Worship, Teaching, Feasting, Resting, and Passing the Night in the City of Rigā in the Kingdom of Rāyagāmalā within the Second Section on the Tretā Age of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā," following the drinking of milk and other substances on the morning of the fourteenth lunar day, and the subsequent journey toward the kingdom of King Phenatantu.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Rādhā; then the glorious Bālakṛṣṇa, the Supreme Lord, descended from his aerial chariot onto a beautiful and auspicious horse-drawn vehicle.
It shone brilliantly, enriched with the splendor of gold, provided with a parasol and chowries,
and equipped with a woolen, variegated rug and a footstool.
King Phenatantu worshipped Kṛṣṇa with flower garlands,
celestial necklaces, sandalwood paste, and other priceless, excellent objects.
Then the queen, the royal family, the sage Phālanāda,
and the subjects as well, worshipped the Lord of Śrī, the husband of Gaurī.
Accompanied by his army, the king, increasing the welcome reception,
caused Hari indeed to be paraded all around the city of Trinayana.
The chief ministers honored him at the city gate of the capital;
the king’s servants did so on the royal highway, and the merchants did so at the crossroads and other such places.
In every marketplace, the people— the buyers and sellers—
adorned [the deity] with sandalwood, saffron, divine flowers, and ornaments made of bilva fruits.
Then, at every spot, the fair-complexioned women greatly celebrated [the occasion];
they bowed down and honored Acyuta with offerings of unbroken rice and parched grain.
At that time, they obtained the fruit of procreation through the sight of Hari;
and by beholding Kṛṣṇa, the fair-complexioned women attained the gain of long, wide eyes.
At that time, the entire city of Trinayana was crowded with people;
for the purpose of seeing Hari, they abandoned all other activities.

In this manner, Mādhava granted his vision to all people throughout every region without exception; then, duly honored, he departed for the royal palace. There, the Blessed Lord himself gave instruction to the subjects.
Shining brilliantly upon a golden throne, he was exceedingly resplendent.
The mind, which is constantly dependent on the latent impressions of saṃsāra, must be conquered;
likewise, the senses must especially be conquered from their objects. (13)
Embodied beings must constantly turn away from sense objects;
they should not engage in vain thoughts, having abandoned the Supreme Lord. 14.
A day should not be spent in vain without devotion to the Blessed One;
life should not be spent in vain without service to the holy ones. 15.
People should not exert themselves in vain without the company of the virtuous;
nor should their speech ever be rendered fruitless except through the chanting of my glories. 1.6.
One's physical life should not be spent in vain without offering [all actions] unto Me;
likewise, the night should certainly not be passed fruitlessly without meditating upon Me, Hari.
Wealth must not be spent in vain except for my temple and such;
one's self must not be employed in vain except for me, the Supreme Lord. (18)
All that illusion would be in vain if I were not present there;
likewise, everything would be in vain wherever I am not worshipped. (1.9)
When I, Kṛṣṇa, am worshipped, everything becomes worshipped;
for when even a small amount of wealth is offered to me, all wealth is thereby offered, since I am beyond all qualities (nirguṇa).
Devotees who possess human bodies should always remain free from the qualities of material nature (nirguṇa);
they should be characterized by freedom from malice, absence of pride, modesty, endurance, self-control, and tranquility. (21)

Truthfulness, fortitude, mindfulness, self-control, cessation [of worldly activity], and freedom from greed—these qualities, when offered to Kṛṣṇa, lead me to the state beyond all qualities (nirguṇya). ||22||
Through that, liberation shall indeed occur; and I, the bestower of liberation, am devoid of qualities (nirguṇa), yet I am filled with all sovereign powers, wonders, and divine attributes.
Having established the state beyond the three qualities (nirguṇya) within my devotee, I deliver him; of this there is no doubt.
Non-violence, truthful speech, kindness, self-restraint, and compassion—[these are the means]. (24)
This is declared to be the great austerity; by it I am always pleased.
Indeed, the drying up of the mind is far superior to the drying up of the body. (25)
In my view, service consisting of the drying up of the mind is the highest form of servitude;
abiding by one's command is, for me, superior to all else. (26)
A person who obeys my command is always near to me, even if far away; one who does not obey my command is far from me, even if close at hand—this is my conviction.
Therefore, the expectations of one's teacher, parents, Hari, one's wife, husband, and the circle of venerable persons who possess specialized knowledge must always be fulfilled. (28)
Indeed, the Vedas were composed by me, as were those commands and injunctions;
they are repeatedly remembered by the sages for the welfare of embodied beings. (29)
These [duties] are taught to the subjects, and they abide following them;
those who do so indeed attain liberation after having experienced many heavens. (2.196.30)
One should honor and worship the sages both through speech and through action;
one should do what is pleasing to them and never perform anything that is displeasing.
The sages and the virtuous ones are divine; they are indeed my very forms.
In every respect, they are treasuries of virtues, identical with my own nature, and bestowers of liberation. 32.
Neither fault nor virtue can be discerned among them;
he who thus constantly conducts himself within the circle of the assembly of the virtuous and the good. (33)
Wherever he may be situated, he is here conceived for the sake of long-lasting glory;
having gone to the highest heaven, my abode, he is indeed so conceived.
This world is a place of calamities, bestowing misfortune at every moment;
yet through the attainment of the knowledge of yoga by the virtuous, those calamities dissolve away. (35)
Calamities are of two kinds: external and internal;
all of them manifest constantly, whether by oneself or through another. (36)
Those who are internal indeed exist by virtue of their own performed actions; whereas those who are external arise from other causes and may even exist without [one's] own action. //37//
The internal [ministers] proceed by means of forbearance, wisdom, and perseverance;
the external ones proceed by conciliation, compliance, and gifts. (38)

One should constantly give food according to one's ability, as well as gifts of material goods; likewise, one should practice straightforwardness, gentleness, great forbearance, and such acts as honoring [the worthy]. (39)
It is considered that the benediction of the virtuous brings about clarity of mind, wards off external calamities, and destroys all misfortunes. (2.196.40)
Taking refuge in Śrī Hari is considered the bestower of all happiness;
for there, where I am well-worshipped by devotees, protected, and sustained, I am the ocean of bliss. (41)
There is not even a trace of distress where I am an ocean of happiness.
Where I am not present, there thieves and evildoers slay the lord of the city;
they slaughter the subjects and destroy the authority of the virtuous when there is no protector.
Formerly, there was a sage named Kākalata who dwelt among the trees;
he instructed a crow in living together with humans.
Many crows, moreover, stayed upon his tree as if in a cage.
Through association, he mastered the science of crows after a long time;
and gradually, through incidental contact, he came to know the entire art of speech.
He discerns auspicious omens and recognizes inauspicious ones as well. (45–46)
Having placed crows in a cage, he wandered through the city;
he went to the vicinity of the dwelling in the city of Kosala, repeatedly speaking to people as one who perceives fortune and seeks news. (47)
"Study the science of the crow; my crows announce [the future].
I know what is yet to come, what has passed, and what is present.
Thus he wandered for four months through the city, from house to house.
He observed the wicked deeds of all the king's servants;
all those royal attendants were seizing wealth through unjust means.
They consume liquor and meat, they commit theft, and being devoid of virtue, all these subjects are merciless and oppress one another in secret. (51)
Those followers even desired to kill the king for the sake of obtaining the kingdom;
having learned all this through the speech of a crow, he went to the monarch. (52)
He told the king, "I am omniscient," and he spoke of the conduct of servants and so forth;
even at the king's command, the crow spoke to the minister.
"This substance was stolen from there, and this other thing was done by you here;
this royal treasury has been plundered and ruined by you. (54)
"Moreover, these followers of yours are also treasure-seizers;
thus this crow declares, and what I have spoken is the truth. (55)
The king, having seized them all, demanded the treasury wealth;
all that was produced by the subjects was true, and nothing false was spoken.
Thereafter, those chief ministers and others were punished by that king;
the other servants, for their part, became filled with fear of the punishment known as "the crow's cry. ||57||
While the brahmin was sleeping at night, they pierced a crow with arrows;
then other crows emerged from that cage whose bars had been broken.
Having observed a dead crow, the Brahmin went before the king and said:
"O King, I beg for your welfare and likewise for your safety. (59)
"By your command, I spoke the truth regarding that which was uttered by the crow;
furthermore, your servants were punished, and others have now become afraid because of this."
"Those wicked servants of yours, acting as enemies, have killed my crow;
this state of mine has come about because there is no powerful king here. (6.1)
"The crow's property has been destroyed here by me, and other crows have likewise departed;
from you, indeed, nothing has been obtained other than the fear for my life. (62)
For kings have many friends and likewise many enemies;
for one who is addicted to the company of kings, destruction comes first.
Indeed, constant vigilance must be maintained by the king;
for when the king is negligent, he who places his trust in him perishes. (64)
For a king may indeed stumble through negligence, and when he has stumbled, there is no life [for his subjects].
A wise man should serve the king, truly thinking, "I am as good as dead."

From ill-spoken words, from improper instruction, from an unstable state, from a poorly maintained posture, from sitting wrongly, from walking improperly, and from gestures and movements of the limbs; ||6||
A wise man should proceed with caution in the presence of a king,
for like an enraged Vaiśvānara fire, the king might consume him.
Therefore, I shall not dwell here; for my sake alone, O King, understand my supreme [desire] to go where no king is found. (68)
In that case, calamities arise among the subjects themselves, incited by the wicked,
where the king is weak, lacks vision, is ignorant, and devoid of discrimination.
Even there, heavy calamities surely befall the subjects;
likewise, in your kingdom, servants remain intent only on taking. (2.196.70)
