Those who desire the non-existence of living beings, who destroy and steal from them, or who seek eternal sovereignty through the destruction of existence—[they are the enemies]. (7.1)
Out of fear of them, O King, I shall go to another refuge, just as a crow, though struck by their aimed arrow, did when it died. (72)
"Whether it be me or you, let us not fall under the power of Bāṇa.
Having resolved thus—"Shall I survive? Shall he survive?"—I have crossed over [the danger] by means of the gift to the crows. (73)
Your wicked river of sovereignty, which bestows death, is filled with many crocodiles, large fish, and sharks, and is teeming with swarms of *timiṃgila* monsters. (74)
Your kingdom is indeed dense and filled with darkness;
it is not possible even for you to place trust in this, so how could it be for me? (71)
Therefore, there is no auspicious dwelling here where slaughter indeed reigns supreme;
for in this place, the virtuous are slain while evildoers are protected.
It is not fitting for one who desires his own welfare to remain here for long; this kingdom is like a honeyed precipice, and its enjoyment is like food mixed with poison. (77)
O King, purify that [body] which is surrounded by venomous serpents, devoured separately by the wicked, and joined by dogs, vultures, and jackals.
Nourished by you, appointed to the kingdom by you, and protected by you,
even these followers of yours seek to kill you, aiming their intent solely at you.
"For your sake, my crow was killed by those evil-minded ones;
therefore, O Great King, I am departing, for there is no other reason."
"One who seeks security must break away from all those who are malicious toward him.
Having been told this, the king spoke to the truth-telling Kāka. (8.1)
"I shall provide you protection with the greatest hospitality;
I will satisfy you, O Kākapālin. Dwell further in my house. (8.2)
As the king was speaking thus, the crow said to him:
"O King, do not commit such a rash act, nor exert such haste here."
But seize each one individually with a strong rod and weaken them; then, according to their respective faults, strike down each man. (84)
Victory will be yours if you act in this way, but not otherwise if you act impulsively;
for many sharp and sturdy thorns indeed cause injury to an elephant.
For many weak men, when united, can harm a powerful king;
likewise, many invisible defects destroy the master of the body. (86)
"Therefore, enemies must indeed be destroyed one by one, just like individual defects.
When this was said, the king acted accordingly and slew them in succession.
Having cleared his kingdom of enemies, the illustrious lord of Kosala subsequently ruled the earth, having made it beautiful through virtuous deeds. 88.

Having performed vows, austerities, and the rites of pilgrimage, and having rendered service to his guru and to the virtuous, he performed divine worship and went to the abode that is the source of happiness. (89)
Likewise, in the city of the body, there is indeed a king named Kauśala;
this self exists there, afflicted by the anger and other passions of the chief robbers.
The Guru, like a crow, having led away the crows of the scriptures along with the lord of the city, repeatedly declares the wickedness of anger and the other passions. (91)
The defects, which are destroyers of the scriptures, are exceedingly firm and powerful;
acting in concert, they seek to kill the self that is situated within illusion.
Having understood this, the king himself should cultivate his own inner strength; his faults must be destroyed gradually and subtly by means of that very strength. (93)
Then, in a kingdom free from thorns, one should perform service to Śrī Kṛṣṇa;
by that, there shall be great bliss and the sovereignty of liberation in this very world.
Thus, O Rādhikā, Hari, the beginningless Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, having instructed her in this manner, became silent and bestowed upon her the Vaiṣṇava mantra.
Then, in the assembly hall, the two maidens, having honored the King together with the King [Śrīhari], took the hand of the most beloved Śrīhari. (96)
When the two had attained their purpose by obtaining a husband through the rites of marriage,
the king, Hari, and all the subjects indeed honored them.
Then the king had various kinds of food prepared;
everyone rested in the evening and held a great festival during the night.
Having risen early in the morning, the Blessed One, the Supreme Lord, took up his plow and gave away everything he possessed as a gift in every respect.
Having performed his daily rites and drunk milk, he set his mind on departing;
meanwhile, King Stokahoma approached to take Kṛṣṇa with him.
Having taken leave of Phenatantu, Hari quickly became ready;
accepting the worship offered by Rājadattā, he ascended his celestial chariot.
Then all the other great gods, traveling in their celestial chariots,
arrived with the sounding of musical instruments and shouts of victory.
Pervading the sky and all directions with the offspring they had produced, shouts of joy arose everywhere; hearing them, Śrī Hari proceeded on his way.
Having abandoned a small kingdom with a king, a sweet-faced realm,
and a coastal region by the sea, he beheld a land of great fortune.
The king indeed went forward there to welcome Hari;
the sage named Svādana also came forward from the sky.

Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of King Phenatantu’s Arrival, Wandering, Worship, Instruction, Feeding, and Resting in the City of Trinayana, as well as His Return to the Kingdom of King Stokahoma after the Night and the Morning Consumption of Milk on the New Moon of the Dark Fortnight of Bhādra," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Śrī-Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O Rādhikā, the sage Svādana and King Stokahoma descended from the sky into a vast and magnificent garden.
They went quickly to the vicinity of Umāpuri for the purpose of welcoming [him];
taking their army with them, they remained in the garden awaiting him. || 2 ||
Following the path shown by the king, he brought down his celestial chariot; Hari and the others likewise brought their chariots down into that garden.
Then musical instruments were played, and shouts of victory arose; there were cries of joy from the people, and songs of praise were sung at that time.
The celestial chariot was adorned with fruits, flowers, and other offerings by the subjects. || 4 ||
Honored with parched grain, unbroken rice, and other offerings, and welcomed with words of greeting,
Śrī Hari emerged from the middle of the celestial chariot and stepped outside.
The king indeed worshipped [him] with devotion by means of golden flower-crests,
necklaces made of jewels, clusters of flowers, and sandalwood waters.
With various excellent fragrances and by washing his feet, he,
together with his family, also drank the water from his feet.
Then the king, accompanied by Pradhāna and the others as well as the subjects, honored the parents of Hari.
The queen worshipped all the supreme goddesses who are dear to Brahmā;
the king worshipped Lord Īśāna, and the daughter worshipped Gaurī.
Then the king, the seer among great seers, honored Hari, the Lord;
he caused him to be seated upon a golden, jewel-adorned palanquin like Śeṣa.
The king seated others on new carts, which were enriched by the beauty of a thousand hoods and drawn by sixty men.
Then, while all the quarters resounded with the blare of trumpets, songs of glory,
and beautiful melodies, Hari was graced by a magnificent welcome.
He wandered through Umāpurī, purifying every spot,
and was honored at the city gate by royal officials with ornaments of precious gems.
Then, in the middle of the city, on the great highway, in the courtyards of the houses, and everywhere among the subjects, there were the best of servants and merchants.
Honored and having bestowed his own vision [upon them], Kṛṣṇa departed;
then, having received worship, he went to his own residence together with his army. || 15 ||
Prompted by the king, he arrived and drank water and so forth;
his family likewise drank water and so forth, as did others as well.
Then, having partaken of water and other refreshments in the assembly hall, Kṛṣṇa sat upon the royal throne and began to instruct them.
The subjects must always act for the sake of the Supreme Lord;
the kings must always act for the sake of the indwelling witness within the subjects. (18)
One must always maintain both [states] for the sake of mutual internalization;
being composed, let them worship me within me in both the Virāj and the Ātman.
By that, your victory shall be attained both in this world and in liberation;
one should always honor the virtuous and abandon all rivalry therein.
One should not abandon the Dharma out of desire, fear, greed, or anger;
likewise, one should be free from pride, truthful in speech, and self-controlled.
For one who conducts himself in this manner, there arises eternal prosperity:
splendor, fortitude, patience, purity, devotion, stability, and steadfastness. (22)
Relying upon these qualities, one should indeed conduct oneself for the sake of liberation;
for he is one whose wisdom is perfected, who is intelligent, wise, and a seer of the Self in all. ||23||
One who is purified by all good deeds, wise regarding himself and others, whose soul is friendly toward all, and who is free from passion, deserves to go to my world. (24)
One who speaks the truth, is endowed with virtuous conduct, is modest, remembers the Veda, is contented, and is devoted to the vow of truth, deserves to go to the world of Brahmā. (25)
A person practicing consoling speech, adorned with virtues in every word, shall obtain happiness everywhere throughout all creations. (26)
"Sāma" is declared to be my praise, and it is also that very same thing as consolation;
even the consolation of people is indeed my own, residing within their hearts. (27)
I am constantly pleased by conciliatory words, praise, and service; for a single word of conciliation always brings happiness to all living beings. (28)
For I dwell upon the tongue of that well-performed conciliation which is gentle and sweet when properly practiced. (29)
Through pure conduct, I dwell within his heart;
through both [conduct and purity], I come into his presence and become as if within his range of perception.
"I indeed exist eternally in that way; I surely perform what is auspicious for him. Thus I always abide among righteous people. (3.1)
And wherever righteous people have made their own dwelling, there I dwell in secret for the sake of protecting them. (32)
One should perform sacrifices with those rituals, and one should give gifts to those worthy of charity;
one must protect the helpless, and one must not do anything that obstructs the Dharma.
The righteous must indeed provide for the welfare, security, and livelihood of the miserable, the helpless, the elderly, women, and likewise those who serve others.
In the hermitages, clothing, vessels, and food must be provided at the proper time by those subjects, as well as by the king and the merchant guild leader. (35)

One who desires his own welfare should indeed honor with beds, seats, and food that virtuous man who renounces all objects for the sake of others, who bestows liberation, and who is well-versed in the scriptures. (36)
Even bandits and murderers place their trust in such a person:
in the Guru who is pure, who destroys sin, who is virtuous, and who bestows liberation. (37)
Those dwelling in the forest, as well as wild animals—even lions, cruel beasts, and the like—place their trust in a virtuous person who brings about all that is most auspicious. (38)
They find peace right where there is the dwelling of the virtuous; even the seasons become characterized by goodness through association with the virtuous. (39)
Beings endowed with goodness are born in the presence of the virtuous,
because I myself dwell daily within the hearts of the virtuous.
From serving them, my auspicious service is produced;
for that which arises from the very service of those who are worthy is the fruit of service itself. (41)
One who seeks dharma and yearns for liberation should constantly serve the virtuous, according to the place, the time, their intellect, and their strength. (42)
One should pursue that which brings security in such a way that one's own welfare is enhanced;
likewise, one should perform actions so that the virtuous person may be satisfied. (43)
Those virtuous men who favor living beings and instruct them in the duties of the bull and so forth, must always be protected in the kingdom by a wise king. (44)
A wealthy person should always honor with drink, clothing, and food that virtuous man who governs the subjects and auspiciously upholds the law of Dharma. (45)
Generally, a wealthy man who is righteous should honor those engaged in asceticism;
an intelligent man should always protect virtuous persons within his own city. (46)
Those virtuous ones who maintain truthfulness, straightforwardness, freedom from anger, devotion, righteousness, and detachment are considered to be the bringers of security to the kingdom. 47.
"What is my flaw? To what am I attached? What means of practice should I perform?
From where might a fault seize me?"—thus should the wise man reflect. (48)
The king should indeed protect the virtuous, for they remove all faults;
the king exists for the sake of dharma and for the purpose of protecting the world. (49)
If a king practices righteousness, he is fit for divinity;
if a king practices unrighteousness, he is fit for hell. ||2.197.50||
Living beings abide in Dharma, and Dharma abides in kings;
that king who governs it well is considered a protector. (51)
The king who is supremely righteous is called a virtuous dharma;
for those who abide in their own duty, the accomplishment of their goals is clearly seen. (52)
The world follows that very same auspicious Dharma;
for the virtuous who are established in Dharma, there is no sense of "this is mine."
Having observed the welfare of the world on all sides, the virtuous sages created that great being, thinking, "This shall indeed become Dharma. (54)
That king in whom the Dharma shines forth is considered a protector;
when the Dharma prospers, all living beings prosper in happiness. (55)
When that [the king] diminishes, [virtues] perish; therefore, one should protect Dharma.
For Dharma was created by the Self-Existent One for the sake of the prosperity of all beings. (56)
Dharma prevails through the virtuous; therefore, the virtuous must be protected.
Since the virtuous are the source of Dharma, one should always honor them. (57)

From one who is intoxicated, from one who is negligent, from one who is immature, from one who is insane, from one who is addicted to vices, from one who is deceitful, from one who is dishonest, from one who is a rogue, from one who is lustful, and from one who is essentially a gambler; ||58||
For the virtuous are always far away because they are stainless;
yet they rescue those who have sunk [in the ocean of existence] and lead even me to liberation. 59.
Therefore, virtuous people must indeed be protected, honored, and served;
one should avoid excessive attachment, pride, hypocrisy, and anger. (2.197.60)
The Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali are the fourfold cycle of ages;
all these are dependent upon the king, for the king alone is said to be the age.
That best of kings who is righteous in soul is said to be the Kṛta Yuga;
when the king becomes unrighteous in soul, the virtuous indeed depart.
Even calamities will surely arise throughout that kingdom;
when the king has become unrighteous, all living beings perish.
He who has no teacher in the Dharma, who does not consult the virtuous,
and who does not see the further shore for himself, does not enjoy happiness for long.
A king who prioritizes righteousness among all duties, who himself abides in the dharma of the virtuous, and who holds righteousness as his primary concern, enjoys imperishable happiness. (65)
Therefore, both by the subjects and by the king, one should always abide in the armor of dharma and in the company of the virtuous, whereby both worldly enjoyment and liberation are attained.
Having spoken thus to Śrī Hari, Kṛṣṇa then indeed ceased;
the king honored him, and the subjects honored him with great respect.
Then, having fulfilled her mother’s command, the daughter of Stokahoma took hold of the hand of that glorious Bālakṛṣṇa.
Having performed her religious duties, Gaurī celebrated the royal festival;
she fed Hari, her family, and the honored guests.
Then everyone rested; the subjects went to their respective dwellings, while at night the king caused great festivities such as dances to be performed.
Then they took their meal and thereafter rested;
in the morning, the Blessed One arose, performed his daily rites, and was well-honored.
Having drunk the milk and other refreshments, Acyuta was ready to depart;
the illustrious king, together with his army, presented him with gifts.
He also gave him a parting gift, and at that time the sounds of trumpets arose;
Hari, having ascended his celestial chariot, listened to the auspicious shouts of victory.
Accompanied by the songs of fair women and all the inhabitants of celestial chariots,
he proceeded swiftly through the sky toward King Kāṣṭhāyana.
The kingdom, extending as far as the ocean and vast in its extent, was free from the rain of arrows;
it was situated near the city of Tunnayāma and abounded with trees.
In the garden, King Kāṣṭhāyana likewise went ahead,
and the sage Nārada also went forth to welcome Hari.
Thus, O Rādhikā, the king stood at the front accompanied by his army;
likewise, all the subjects arrived for the purpose of honoring Kṛṣṇa.

Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Offering of a Small Oblation, the Descent of Hari in Umāpurī, His Wandering, Worship, Teaching, Eating, Resting at Night, and the Arrival of King Kāṣṭhayāna from his Kingdom on the Morning of the First Day of the Bright Fortnight of Bhādrapada," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Then, O Rādhā, King Kāṣṭhāyana commanded Bālakṛṣṇa, Lord Hari, who was accompanied by his chariot, to descend from the celestial vehicle.
Hari brought his celestial chariot down from the sky into the garden;
at that time, other celestial chariots also descended from the heavens.
The military instruments were sounded and shouts of victory then arose; Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, celebrated by the people, rejoiced.
Worshipped with sandalwood paste, unbroken grains, flowers, necklaces, and other offerings,
the Lord was honored by the king, by the subjects, and also by the sage.
Filled with serenity, that beloved of Kṛṣṇa indeed came out from the celestial chariot, granting fearlessness with his hand out of love.
The great king Kāṣṭhayāna placed a necklace of Hari,
enriched with the value of ten million diamonds, around his neck, and worshipped his feet with sandalwood paste.
He drank water arising from that grace and honored his family as well;
filled with joy, he placed Kṛṣṇa upon the chariot drawn by dark horses.
Then Rātri held the umbrella, and the two Kumāras held the auspicious chowries;
at that time, the shouts of victory were proclaimed with splendors.
The Lord was honored with white flower garlands and unbroken grains;
then indeed, the other great lords were placed upon auspicious vehicles.
Then the king properly seated Him upon various high and low thrones;
the monarch caused Śrī Hari to wander through the city of Tunnavāya.
The Supreme Lord was worshipped by the king in the middle of the city gate,
and honored with five principal lamps in the nīrājana ceremony.
Honored by the guild-leaders in the central courtyard of the city,
he was also honored by the common people at the market stalls with offerings of fruit and coins.
And in every house, the Sustainer of Life was worshipped by the Gaurīs;
thus indeed did the Blessed One himself wander through the entire city.
He returned to his own residence, the palace in the royal garden;
there, the Blessed One himself presided over a delightful assembly for the people. (14)
Having received worship from the subjects, he taught them what is beneficial:
"The ocean of worldly existence always bestows cold, heat, and other such conditions. (15)
When one is sinking, the wicked—like crocodiles with their claws and teeth—seize them;
indeed, the virtuous become like boats for the purpose of crossing over.
Holding them by the hand, they deliver those submerged in the ocean of worldly existence;
I, the Blessed One, the bestower of liberation, dwell eternally in the hearts of those [who hold me]. 17.
Those virtuous and steadfast ones are worthy of worship, for they are considered by me to be my very heart;
through the side of the virtuous, there shall be victory, both in this world and in the ultimate sense. (18)
For victory joined with unrighteousness is indeed unstable and leads away from heaven;
it surely causes even the victor to sink into the terrible mire of saṃsāra.

But he who, by the destruction of dharma, by the violation of established order, and by the transgression of the words of the virtuous, should bring about happiness therein— [he is a fool]. (2.198.20)
He whose people are serene, whose guests are honored with worship, and whose family is content—Nārāyaṇa indeed dwells in his house. (21)
In whose house virtuous people, elders, teachers, and other venerable ones, as well as the truthful, are honored, there I dwell. (22)
By the suppression of the wicked, by the gathering together of the virtuous,
and through devotion, sacrifice, charity, and service, I am always brought under control.
He who fights for the sake of the virtuous, for the sake of liberation, or for the sake of Hari—
having offered himself as a sacrificial post— is one whose fame is the infinite sacrificial fee.
He who has renounced pride and other such traits for my sake, and who is initiated for my sake—
he indeed enjoys all his desires, which yield every object of need inexhaustibly.
Having abandoned the wicked, one should always practice the company of the virtuous;
one should recognize the wicked through their dispositions and by signs that fall within the range of indirect perception.
He speaks of faults behind one's back and finds fault with one's good qualities;
or, when these qualities are being praised by others, he remains silent with his face turned away. (27)
He sighs frequently, bites his lips, and shakes his head; being dejected in mind, he speaks perversely. (28)
He acts perversely when out of sight, but does not speak [harshly] in one's presence;
having spoken separately, he crushes [the matter], saying "this is not so" again and again. (29)
On the seat, in the bed, or in the vehicle, he behaves in a contrary manner; in whatever situation that occurs, his wickedness is to be recognized through living with him. (2.198.3)
To feel distress when one's friend is distressed, and joy when one's friend is joyful—this much is the definition of a friend;
the opposite, however, should always be understood as the characteristic of a wicked enemy. (3.1)
The virtuous, who are true friends and excellent companions, desiring one's own welfare, destroy sin and bestow liberation; they should be especially served. ||32||
One should also personally conduct oneself with discernment in his presence;
indeed, one should cultivate discernment within the heart regarding impermanent things. (33)
All this is impermanent, produced from the ego-sense of "mine";
whatever name and form exists, all that does not exist in the ultimate sense. (34)

Thus, one who possesses discernment is never distressed when things are lost, nor does he remain filled with joy when they are obtained; for since all things are transitory, what is there to celebrate? (35)
Even when fallen into calamity, the man of discernment does not suffer;
for he understands that what has passed is past, what is yet to come has not arrived, and only that which is present truly exists. (36)
Everything passes away as if laughing; all that shall not be. One who has thus known what is to be known is no longer subject to sorrow.
Knowing that what has come must perish, who indeed would suffer?
Having understood that everything has its root in sorrow, one should abandon sorrow. (38)
Where indeed have the elders gone—those such as fathers, grandfathers, and so forth? Knowing that none of them remain permanent, who indeed would grieve? ||39||
Then children, those of middle age, and the elderly shall live long lives;
they will die at the ages of one hundred thousand, one million, or ten million years—of this there is no doubt.
Nevertheless, embodied beings do not relinquish their great craving;
having reflected thus and abandoned it, one should do what is beneficial for oneself. (41)
The future does not belong to me, and the past no longer exists for me;
that which is on my forehead [the present] does not truly exist. Therefore, one should always be virtuous.
Even those who are not wealthy live, and kings do likewise;
there is an abundance of disease among kings, whereas it is not so among the non-wealthy; therefore, the poor man is happy.
Thinking thus, one should not grieve, for time is indeed equal toward all:
some are enjoyers, others are acquirers, and still others are lost in anxiety.
Having seen this regarding all enjoyments in this world, one should not grieve;
for it is a fixed law that what was given by another in the past shall be obtained by oneself.
They desire what is not given and long for it even without effort;
such people, whose enjoyments are base, never reproach their own unborn nature. (46)
But one who is possessed of envy and pride then experiences agitation;
for this reason, suffering persists even more intensely in the manifest state.
The fortune of another is to be endured, provided it does not exist upon one's own forehead;
or else, one should strive for its sake, since prosperity bears fruit only through effort. (48)
Elsewhere as well, those who are skillful always enjoy existing prosperity;
for Fortune indeed vibrates toward the one who is industrious and radiant. 49.
Having produced prosperity, sons, grandsons, daughters, and even the earth—all things to be enjoyed by others—they themselves indeed abandon them. (2.198.50)
Desiring objects that are undesirable, dependent on others, and fraught with calamities,
one should abandon such volitions and become happy like a virtuous person who has renounced all grasping.
Indeed, misfortunes take the form of benefits, and benefits take the form of misfortunes;
these occur according to one's destiny, so a wise person should not place trust in them.
For some, even total ruin occurs for the sake of wealth alone.
For some, even great gain leads only to misfortune.
Ignorant and infinitely greedy, he becomes attached, considering this to be happiness;
delighting in his prosperity, he later regards nothing else as superior.
But when prosperity is lost without cause, one's undertakings perish;
then, with his desires shattered, he becomes disillusioned with wealth. (55)
Some on this earth, born of noble lineage, practice the Dharma indeed, desiring happiness in the next world, yet they become weary of worldly existence. (56)
Some, overwhelmed by great greed, merely amass wealth;
for they consider the purpose of human life to be nothing other than wealth for the sake of living. (57)
Having recognized their wretchedness, having recognized their lack of wisdom, and seeing that they have, out of delusion, fixed their gaze upon material wealth while life is unstable. (58)
Beholding men devoid of knowledge who perform fruitless austerities and are cast into blinding darkness—who indeed would set his mind on falsehood? (59)
Restrain the senses from these objects; restrain your own mind as well; and by means of discernment, restrain your speech too from these sense-objects. (2.198.60)
If you are the ones who negate [existence], then victory will be yours;
one who is satiated with wisdom regarding phenomena that last but a moment does not grieve.
One who is content with little, gentle, self-controlled, and devoted to the way of Brahman does not grieve;
but one who has fallen into a cruel and most sinful mode of life is not released from sorrow.
Even one who subsists on roots and fruits finds delight in the lonely forest;
restrained in speech, devoted to Me, and offering everything, such a person lives in happiness.
Having restrained his desires through wise reflection, the householder may become happy;
he delights alone in the forests and finds contentment in that which belongs to the forest alone.
Satisfied as a great person, he finds contentment in his very own self;
for one who conducts himself rightly, all suffering resides in another.
Having abandoned hypocrisy, desire, anger, joy, and likewise fear,
and having served the virtuous with one's body and other means, one should acquire eternal happiness.
Service to the virtuous is considered the supreme merit, superior to all other merits;
one whose character is meritorious undoubtedly attains the highest goal. (67)
The honoring of mother, father, and teachers is highly esteemed by me;
a man engaged in this in this world enjoys great fame and the higher realms. (68)
Whatever they may authorize you to do when they have been duly honored—
whether it be consistent with dharma or contrary to dharma— that must indeed be performed by sons and others.
And one should not practice any other dharma without being authorized by them;
whatever they authorize, that is dharma—this is the settled conclusion. (2.198.70)
These very three are considered to be the three worlds and the three fires;
those established in that doctrine—the three Vedas and the three stages of life—truly prevail.
The father is indeed the Gārhapatya fire, the mother is the Dakṣiṇa fire, and the teacher is the Āhavanīya fire;
this triad of fires is most venerable.
By being vigilant regarding these three, one shall indeed conquer the three worlds:
by the service of the father, this world; and by the service of the mother, likewise heaven.
One may conquer the world of Brahmā by serving one's gurus; of this there is no doubt.
One should constantly attend upon them, for that indeed is the highest merit.
All the worlds are honored by him by whom these three are honored;
but for him by whom these are not honored, all his ritual actions are fruitless.
For one who is constantly disrespectful toward these three gurus,
neither this world nor the next will lead to his well-being.
Neither in this world nor in the next does his fame spread; nor does any other auspicious result arise for him in either place. ||77||
For a teacher of good conduct is indeed superior to ten śrotriyas;
and here, an upādhyāya is said to be superior to ten such teachers. ||78||
A father is superior to ten teachers in every respect;
a mother is even more excellent than ten fathers, for she is equal to the entire earth. (79)
As the mother is declared to be the guru, there is no guru equal to a mother; the guru is always more venerable than both father and mother. (2.198.80)
For both mother and father are the givers of birth and the creators of the body;
the teacher, however, is divine, the bestower of knowledge, and likewise the creator of divine kinship. (8.1)
But that birth which is joined with a guru is divine, free from old age and death;
for a mother, a father, and a guru are always inviolable by their children and others.
The sages and the gods, together with the ancestors, are pleased when the gurus are honored; therefore, the guru is most worthy of honor. (83)
One should never treat a guru with contempt on account of any conduct whatsoever;
for neither mother, nor father, nor likewise the guru deserve such disregard. (84)
One should not obstruct their work, but should always treat them with respect;
for there is the sin of killing an embryo (bhrūṇahatyā) in one who treats them with contempt. //85//

For these four—those who betray a friend, those who are ungrateful, those who kill their wives, and those who murder their gurus—there is no atonement, for they are the greatest of great sinners. (86)
The virtuous devotees of Śrī Hari, who are renunciants and auspicious spiritual masters, are to be worshipped, saluted, and fed from all sides. (87)
When these, which constitute the very essence of dharma, are practiced here, all sacrifices are accomplished for those who are content; of this there is no doubt.
Thus, having always worshipped and propitiated the gurus and me, O people, you shall indeed obtain worldly enjoyment and liberation here through my grace. (89)
Having spoken thus, O King, the Blessed Lord ceased speaking;
then the monarch, full of reverence, worshipped Śrī Hari with the nīrājana ceremony and other offerings.
Then all the subjects worshipped him with many offerings;
the queen also performed worship, as did the princess Kumudvatī.
Then, according to the marriage rites, he took Hara’s hand;
the king held a great festival and celebrated the occasion.
Then the king fed Hari and his guests;
having rested and passed the night, he performed his morning rites at dawn.
Having drunk milk and other refreshments and performed his worship, Hari became ready to depart for the kingdom of King Kolaka; he then ascended his celestial chariot.
Then everyone ascended,
and Kṛṣṇa, together with the sage Lepana, rose into the sky amidst shouts of victory.
Honored by the people at that time, they went quickly to the site of the plastering;
meanwhile, the king, out of extreme devotion, went ahead for the sake of accomplishing a welcome reception.

Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of King Kāṣṭhayāna’s wandering through the city of Tunnavāyāpurī, his worship of Śrī Hari, the offering of food, and his departure at dawn for the kingdom of King Kolaka," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Rādhikā; the glorious Bālakṛṣṇa, Hari himself, beheld from the earth the king of Leperāṣṭra together with his army.
The Blessed One, beloved of Kṛṣṇa, arrived by the path shown by the king at his own vast and magnificent garden, which stood ready to welcome him.
He brought the celestial chariot down from the sky to the earth, upon the shore of the city of Muramāṣapura,
in a vast, delightful, and most beautiful region.
Other celestial chariots also descended nearby;
at that time, musical instruments were played and shouts of victory arose.
There were songs from the fair-complexioned women and shouts of joy from the subjects;
and from his celestial chariot, Hari quickly descended outside there.
The Lord was then honored by the king, the subjects, the queen, and the great sage.
With necklaces, beautiful crests, flowers, sandalwood, unbroken grains of rice, and other offerings,
the other great lords there were also honored by the subjects. Having seated Hari in a palanquin, the king placed the others upon elephants and other mounts.
Out of great respect, he caused the royal lineage, the leading merchants, and even the learned scholars to circumambulate the city of Muramāṣā; likewise,
men and women [circumambulated] at the gateways and other locations along the royal highway and at major junctions.
And at the crossroads and in the halls, they worshipped with great reverence,
offering many gifts such as ornaments of gold and jewels,
various divine decorations, woolen blankets, and wealth.
At every place, they performed the lustration rite and worship;
the fair-complexioned women honored Kṛṣṇa, the Lord, with flowers and other offerings.
Having thus wandered through the city, he arrived at the royal palace;
having assembled the people, the Blessed One, the benefactor, spoke to them. (12)
The eternal Supreme Lord, whose nature is truth, consciousness, and bliss, is indeed to be worshipped and adored by human beings who desire liberation. || 13 ||
Truth is the supreme vow; it is most excellent, for there is nothing higher than truth.
Even if this truth would lead to one's own ruin, it must never be spoken.
The proclamation of Dharma was made for the sake of non-violence toward all beings;
they say Dharma is so called because of its upholding, for by Dharma all creatures are sustained. (15)
That which is joined with upholding [the precepts] is Dharma; this is the certainty.
That which is joined with non-violence is Dharma; this is the certainty.
When there is violence, even if one speaks the truth, falsehood is established as Dharma.
Even in falsehood and in violence, there is the established rule that this is dharma.

Whether in truth or in falsehood, whether in violence or silence, the established rule is that dharma consists in the protection of living beings; for truth is considered to be Brahman, remaining as the remainder after the protection of life.

Wealth should not be disclosed to thieves, for truth is no ornament there; one should not speak the truth to them—this is the settled rule of dharma. If release can be achieved by remaining silent, one should not speak at all.
Or, if one must certainly utter speech, it should be very little and mixed with falsehood. ||2.199.20||
In that case, even a falsehood would be righteous and conducive to the highest good;
indeed, an oath should be uttered if one is thereby released from thieves.
In a life-threatening situation or at a marriage, such a falsehood is said to be the truth.

For the sake of protecting wealth or for the preservation of another's life, untruth becomes truth; such is the hidden essence of dharma. One must not speak untruth to the virtuous, for they are the saviors of embodied beings.
Among those, falsehood is always sinful; therefore, one should speak that which is purified by truth.
Truth is indeed the very nature of Brahman, and it is considered the most excellent vow.
One should practice truth and righteousness through deed, mind, and speech;
for one whose vow is truth, sufferings never approach.
One who has a self-controlled mind and is free from craving crosses over even the difficult fortress of suffering;
one who is devoid of hypocrisy and deceitful conduct and is a restrainer of the sense objects [also does so]. 26.
One who is non-violent and free from excessive speech crosses over even the difficult pass of suffering;
likewise, one who is a giver, free from the state of begging, and a worshiper of guests. (27)
One who is free from malice, who serves his mother, father, teacher, and virtuous people,
and who is devoid of sin and lives by righteous conduct, crosses even the difficult fortress of suffering.
One who is firm in truth, a remover of the suffering of others, pure, steadfast, and free from deceit,
crosses even the difficult fortress of misery.
The ascetic, possessing the luster of Brahman, peaceful, transcending all beings,
free from fear and bestowing fearlessness, crosses even the difficult passage of suffering.
Possessing equal vision toward all things and likewise increasing the prosperity of others, and having turned away from vulgar objects, he crosses over even the difficult fortress of suffering. (31)
One who is intent on bowing to all the gods, who constantly listens to the stories of Kṛṣṇa,
and who is full of faith with a tranquil mind, crosses even the difficult pass of suffering.
Free from pride, yet honoring those worthy of honor, he worships the gods, sages, and ancestors;
devoid of anger and pacifying the anger of others, he indeed crosses over the difficult passage of suffering.
One who has conquered the tongue, conquered the genitals, and even conquered Nārāyaṇa;
one who has conquered thirst and conquered worldly conduct, crosses over even the fortress of suffering.
Therein I am Janārdana, with eyes as red as lotuses and clad in yellow garments;
I am his kinsman, brother, friend, and relative, the bestower of happiness. (35)
I am Kāmbhareya, Bālakṛṣṇa, the cowherd boy Acyuta;
I abide there as the benefactor, present in the heart of my devotee.
He who takes refuge in me—wherein I, the beloved of Brahmā, the charming one, and the Lord of Śrī, reside—he crosses over the difficult fortress of suffering. (37)
I am Truth, I am the embodiment of Truth, and I am the destroyer of all sufferings;
by knowing me and taking refuge in me, they too cross over the difficult fortress of suffering.
"Therefore, worship me constantly; you shall attain me alone in my abode.
Having said this, the Blessed One gave the mantra to the one seeking refuge. (39)
Then, for the sake of the king and his subjects, the king worshipped Hari;
and Rādhā, together with her daughter, then worshipped Kṛṣṇa.
A certain maiden took that beloved of Kṛṣṇa by the hand with deep devotion;
having obtained him through the rites of marriage, she indeed became one who had fulfilled her life's purpose.
Having dismissed the assembly of the great-souled ones,
that king fed them various foods and delicious fruits.
The king celebrated a most auspicious festival for Arjuna during the month of Bhādra;
thereafter, they rested on the night of the third lunar day.
Having all performed their morning ablutions, they partook of a meal of milk-rice;
at that moment, the daughters of Gaṅgā arrived to solicit Hari.
Having paid homage to Nārāyaṇa, those maidens chose a boon from Bālakṛṣṇa, that they might become the best of rivers, sanctifying the earth as sacred fords (tīrthas). 45.
"Bathe, O Nārāyaṇa, beloved of Kṛṣṇa, Lord of Śrī, in the water! Through your immersion, we all shall become identical with sacred fords. (46)
Hari said, "So be it," and assuming manifold forms, he went quickly out of compassion to bathe in the rivers. ||47||
Just as he who assumes many forms appears in rivers and oceans, so too does Kṛṣṇa shine with a single form in the presence of kings. 48.
The great king named Kolaka, by means of the divine vision granted to him,
perceives everything right there, even while remaining within a bean pod.
Hari bathed then in the Nīparā and likewise in the Nistārā; he performed his ablutions in the Pṛthā, the Dinapā, and the Sevikā.
He performed his ablutions in the river Trivarā when it was eclipsed by Rāhu;
he performed his ablutions in the Indirā when it had become turbid with cow dung. ||51||
He performed his ablutions in the river Gavādya at Trigirā;
he performed his ablutions in the rivers Dūrā, Gurūṇā, and Mitrā.
In the army of Lava-vāra, he likewise caused it to float when it was split in two;
and in the river Sthāyin, which was full of curiosity and had little danger, he acted in the same way.
Having immersed himself in the great river Prapīṭhā, which is equal to Viṣṇu in its vastness,
he saw those who were tormented by the lack of water during their observances on the banks of the river Pāyupaśyakā.

One should perform a bath even in a lake that has a foul-smelling excrement-like source; likewise, one should immerse oneself in a river that possesses three channels and is free from defects, even if it is only five cubits wide.
He also performed ablutions at Kāmā, Volgā, and Donā,
as well as at Ājavābdhi, Śvetavārddhi, Kṛṣṇābdhi, and Kāśyapeyaka.
Then, at the confluence of the three rivers, the Lord,
the creator of all beings, assuming forty forms, bathed simultaneously.
Having fashioned those maidens and the lakes as sacred fords (tīrtha), and having likewise established the secondary maidens (upakanyā) there as his own spiritual manifestations; ||58||
Kṛṣṇa quickly vanished and went to Kolaka’s abode;
there, Kolaka came to realize the greatness of Kṛṣṇa.
The Supreme Self, higher than the highest, having descended through successive incarnations,
became this very Lord Nārāyaṇa, my son-in-law in person.
"I have indeed accomplished all that was to be done; O Blessed One, dwell here forever in my abode, which is worthy of you. Show me your grace, O Janārdana. (61)
While they were thus occupied with these matters, midday arrived;
so too did Yavakrīta and all the other great sages dwelling on the banks of the Ganges.
Then, being summoned by Hari for the purpose of seeing him, they arrived;
having bowed down, they sat near Bālakṛṣṇa.
Then Lomaśa and others, as well as the Vṛkāyanas and Nīlakaṇṭhaka, Īśāna and other attendants (pārṣadas) were likewise remembered as his hosts.
They all arrived in the presence of the king of the Kolas at his palace.
Hari said, "The task concerning Ketumāla has been accomplished in every respect."
All the regions have been traversed; all the kings have taken refuge in devotion; the subjects have become devoted and multiplied; and sacred pilgrimage sites have also been established.
The sages also became satisfied by those gifts and other offerings;
likewise, I made the beloved wives of Brahmā and the Gaurīs full of happiness. (67)
The mountains here have been purified, and everything has consequently become complete;
now one must go to where the circle of sages is said to be.
"O sages, you virtuous great seers are indeed my authority.
Having said this, Bālakṛṣṇa awaited the words of the ṛṣis. (69)
At that moment, indeed, a rain of flowers fell from the sky along with shouts of "Victory! for the virtuous one known as Saccidānanda.
The great seer Lālāyana, who had previously come from the north, departed;
later, on the full moon day of the month of Pauṣa, the deity Tuṣita also departed.
Both of them, seated upon their excellent celestial chariots, arrived at the abode of Kola;
worshipping Bālakṛṣṇa, they uttered shouts of victory.
May he who makes Ketumāla a sacred ford conquer the waters of the imperishable abode—Hare Kṛṣṇa, Bālakṛṣṇa Svāmī Śrīkṛṣṇavallabha! 73.
O Kāmbhareya, Lord of the power of Brahman, son of Gopāla!
Prosper here, remain for a long time, and make the lands pure. (74)
Speaking thus, the two of them slowly brought down the sun-like celestial chariot into the garden of the king’s palace. (75)
Those two sages, the preeminent among the Sātvatas, descended from the celestial chariot,
adorned with flower garlands, their hearts overflowing with devotion and their minds supremely fixed upon Kṛṣṇa.
Having approached Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa who was nearby, they both bowed down and worshipped the Supreme Lord with prostrations like a staff, as well as with flower garlands and other offerings.
With tearful eyes, ears dripping [with ichor], and their limbs covered in horripilation,
they sat down near the two seats by the command of Hari.
Hari rose and placed his feet upon their chests;
he laid his hands upon their heads and embraced them with both arms.
He inquired after their welfare and the expansion of their devotional activities; they both replied that, by his grace, their well-being and security were proceeding successfully.
O Lord, by your grace, why have the Aṭa and Cāmarī regions been perfumed by those seeking liberation and are awaiting your arrival?
Having come there, you must indeed perform the purifying sacrifice of Viṣṇu.
Those subjects born in the land of Amarīka must be purified.
Both the kings and the subjects, as well as the great sages who have gone there, await your arrival; therefore, bring fulfillment to those subjects.
Thus entreated, the illustrious Hari questioned Lomaśa, Śaṅkara, and the great sages: "Tell me, what ought to be done?
They all replied, "O Lord, do as Lālāyana requests."
Thus it must indeed be done in this matter, since you are our savior.
Yavakrīta, Nīlakaṇṭha, Vṛkāyana, Lomaśa, and all of us, the sons of Gaṅgā, [follow] Śaṅkara and the others according to their directions. (86)
"We shall do so, without doubt, for the sake of delivering the world.
When this reply had been given, the Blessed One, who assumes the dance of a man, [spoke].
"Let it be so," said the deity Tuṣitadevata to Lālāyana; and there, at that time, the sage named Hārita spoke to Hari. (88)
O Hari, I am going first to my disciples in the eastern regions;
make those known as Garima, who have been lost, and those who are neutral, into purifiers.
Having spoken thus and placed the command upon his head, he departed from the celestial chariot before them;
he then prepared the regions known as Garima for their reception.
In the city of Aparāntikā, King Dinamāna,
having lost his own preceptor’s disciple, prepared various auspicious and festive ornaments for the sake of welcoming Hari. ||9 1 ||
Then King Kolaka [honored] the supreme lord, the sages, and the virtuous women. ||92||
He satisfied the great ones with supreme foods and meals;
he honored them in many ways and by all means through offerings.
He requested the Lord to remain in his own abode for one night;
Hari said, "So be it," and the king celebrated a great festival during the night.
He caused an auspicious performance to be held with displays of dance and wrestling; then, after the night's sleep had ended, Hari quickly performed his morning rites in the morning.
The king quickly prepared to depart and offered honors;
he was honored by his army and honored by his subjects as well.
He ascended the celestial chariot, and others likewise ascended their own.
Hearing of his fame, glory, and other virtues, the Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa,
together with the Gāṅgeyas and Naijikas, swiftly traversed the ocean by way of the sky and went to the earth, Garima. ||97-98||
Then, from the sky, he beheld those regions that had been traversed by Hārita;
there stood the sage Hārita and King Dinamānārka,
positioned before the city of Aparāntikā, to welcome him.
Beholding those two by their banner-signs, he regained his composure in the sky.
Beholding the welcome offered by the army, the Lord Hari,
Bālakṛṣṇa, rejoiced while remaining in the sky, O Rādhikā.

Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of King Kolaka’s Third Journey to Śrī Hari in the City of Muramāṣa, His Worship, Instruction, and Feeding; His Simultaneous Bathing in the Waters of the Ganges by Assuming Many Forms at the Request of the Daughters of Gaṅgā, Making Them Holy Tīrthas, and Resting at Night before Departing for the Realm of King Arka on the Fourth Day of the Bright Half of Bhādrapada," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O Rādhā, in these lost lands, amidst vast forests of extreme cold inhabited by very few people, this Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa resides.
In the city of Aparāntikā, near the ocean,
his own celestial chariot swiftly descended from the sky like the sun at the end of the day.
Having seen Hārita Ṛṣi standing on the surface of the earth along the path he had shown, he slowly brought him down.
Other celestial chariots also descended from the sky at that time;
the king, accompanied by his army, offered a grand welcome to the Supreme Soul.
The queen, the minister, and the subjects likewise practiced [devotion];
meanwhile, the king heard that Śrīmat Bālakṛṣṇa Hari was traveling in a celestial chariot.
Having approached nearby, he beheld and attained a state of wonder at that lovely one of beautiful form, whose splendor was never seen before.
Having first beheld that divine vision, he became steady for a moment,
absorbed in the form of Śrī Hari within the celestial chariot, like one possessed of deep meditative absorption (samādhi).
As soon as they were born, the queen, the princes,
and the princesses all beheld Bālakṛṣṇa and entered into a state of meditative absorption.
They beheld a splendor equal to ten million lightning flashes facing every direction;
and there they saw the Lords, beginning with Virāṭ, who were even higher than those.
After that, they beheld the supreme abode of Goloka,
the most excellent world, inhabited by millions of hosts of cowherds.
There, having beheld Kṛṣṇa, the youthful Kṛṣṇa, they once again beheld Śrī Puruṣottama stationed in the supreme abode known as Akṣara.
He beheld Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of all lords, who is served by the liberated ones and others, seated in the midst of the liberated souls together with the beloved of Brahmā.
Then their meditative absorption was lost, and they arose from it within their celestial chariots;
filled with intense devotion, they beheld Bālakṛṣṇa in their own kingdom.
The king and the royal family members attained a state of supreme wonder;
they worshipped the celestial chariot with necklaces, sandalwood paste, perfumes, and other offerings.
Just then, Hari, clad in radiant garments, emerged from the chariot.
Charming with all-encompassing loveliness, beauty, brilliance, and laughter,
the Gaurīs and Hārītīs caused Acyuta to prosper.
With parched grain, unbroken rice, flowers, songs, prostrations, and other offerings, the subjects bowed down to the Lord of Fortune, the beloved of Kṛṣṇa. || 16 ||
The king, taking Hari’s hand with his own,
seated him upon a golden chariot adorned with garlands and other ornaments, which was positioned outside the mechanical device.
The king’s family also sat upon this chariot;
the king held the umbrella, and the queen held the fly-whisk.
The maidens held chowries and the youths carried the staff;
on other chariots were the parents of Hari and his entire family.
The king seated Śambhu in another chariot, the circle of sages in the others, and Kṛṣṇa’s beloved wives in the guarded vehicles.
With such a grand welcome, preceded by the sound of musical instruments and echoing with the noise of trumpets, she led the Lord into the city.
Indeed, great enthusiasm arose among the subjects at that time from the sight of the new [incarnation];
Hari repeatedly drew the hearts of the people toward himself. ||22||
On whichever limb of Hari’s body his eye happened to be fixed at that time,
there it became surely attached, steady, unwinking, and stable out of bliss.
Some, beholding his lotus-face, cast aside their meditative concentration which was the means for [attaining] liberation;
and there, seeing the Lord who is exceedingly heart-pleasing, they attained a tranquility that transcends all measure. (24)

Some women, their minds bewildered upon seeing his eyes— which were fixed on her with passion, wide, and drawn back with great intensity— attained a state of stillness and partook of the supreme drink of nectar.

Those women whose hearts were utterly captivated upon beholding his lips, which possessed the luster of a large, deep-red bimba fruit, became filled with longing and their hearts were seized by desire. (26)
Some women, whose conduct was driven by desire for his limbs— the most beautiful in the world— and who possessed divine insight,
offered to him both their minds and their entire bodies.
Beholding him, some female devotees thought, "May this supreme Lord lead us to his own imperishable state," and thus they were then completely captivated.
Rādhikā, Kamalagārā, Māsatī, Māṇikī, and others—these powers of Brahmā born from the lotus-born one, who are indeed fair-complexioned—worship him day and night in many ways. (29)
Abandoning this transient body, let us worship Him who is joined with this world;
for in Him alone does eternal happiness exist—therefore, perform the full adoration of His abode.
The Blessed One has arrived here at this ocean-surrounded cool abode out of his grace;
therefore, through action, mind, recitation, and service, worship your own Lord.
What kind of radiant halo indeed surrounds his face here on all sides, since his body possesses a heart-captivating splendor that flows forth with the brilliance of ten million moons? (32)

One whose feet are not served by even a single liberated being, nor whose body is massaged by ten million slaves—such a person cannot be attained even by those rich in abundant merit; therefore, one must not forget that he is the True One (the Buddha). //33//
From the very beginning, human beings and the masses have never desired such a thing in their hearts;
yet here, this very Lord of Umā has appeared as the trustworthy one, and by taking refuge in that Supreme Lord, one attains supreme happiness.
Let them not abandon this assembly, which is easily accessible, most beautiful, and possessed of great virtues;
let them honor it with their hearts as if with flowers and worship it with the offering of all their own possessions. //35//
Thus, O Rādhikā, having beheld Lord Bālakṛṣṇa, all those women were captivated; they spoke and drank in the Lord with their senses of bliss. 36.
The king was at the city gate, the chief ministers likewise on the main road; the market-keepers were in the markets, and the women were at the openings of the streets. (37)
In the courtyards, the maidens; on the ground beside the people, on the riverbanks, and in the squares—all the subjects worshipped the Supreme Lord. (38)
They worshipped the Imperishable One with parched grains, excellent fruits, flowers, saffron, and unbroken rice;
also with garments, sandalwood paste, and fragrant perfumes. (39)
And the subjects, having paraded other ocean-borne jewel necklaces through the city of Āvikā, presented them to that supreme lord.
Having worshipped [the deity] and brought it home, each attained a sense of fulfillment;
thereafter, Hari went to his own residence, the temple of the sun that measures the day.
The sage Hārīta arrived and, having bowed to the Supreme Lord, said:
"Exquisite foods are available; please partake of them. (42)
O Hare-Kṛṣṇa, feed others and satisfy them with milk-pudding and other delicacies;
then, ascending the celestial chariot, look upon the earth with a sense of weightiness. ||43||
"One must go everywhere, purifying by the mere sight [of you].
Having been told this, the Blessed One quickly consumed the milk-rice and other offerings. (44)
Having dismissed everyone from the royal palace, King Śaṅkara quickly caused all those honored guests to be fed.
Accompanied by the sage and a limited number of attendants, Kṛṣṇa ascended his own celestial chariot and departed into the northern sky.
Having observed the region of the Vāśṛṅga mountain, as well as the surrounding terrain—the Phudrikta, Vilaya, Kāñcana, and Ārṣuka regions—[he proceeded]. 47.
Having observed the land of Hāyana and seeing other boatmen, the Blessed One descended from the sky. 48.
The queen rested in the royal palace and came for the purpose of worship;
having worshipped Hari, her two daughters then [worshipped] Hari.
While the two maidens remained with steady eyes, absorbed in happiness, they beheld Hari; they gazed upon him and, offering their garlands, chose him as their husband.
The Blessed One took her hand as she offered it with great devotion;
thereafter, the king held a celebration that night, following the meal.
He worshipped Gaṇeśa with dūrvā grass, sweetmeat balls, and saffron;
the king caused dances to be performed and likewise had musical instruments played.
He worshipped the auspicious form of Gaṇeśa with vermilion and sang verses and hymns during that festival.
When the maiden had been won back, they both served Kṛṣṇa most excellently.
The night passed, and at dawn, having performed his ablutions and excellent worship, [he arose].
Then Bālakṛṣṇa became ready to go to the lands of the Aṭakas and the regions of the immortals after drinking his milk.

On the fifth day, at the time of *saṃgava*, during the most auspicious bright fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada, the king then bestowed a leave of departure along with many jewels and other gifts. (56)
Hari presented that wealth and other gifts to the sage Hārita;
there, the king, accompanied by his army, bestowed great honor upon him.
At that time, there arose shouts of victory, shouts of glory, and songs, filled with sweetness and performed by the Gaurīs and the Hāritas. (58)
Hari gave necklaces to the king, to the queen, and also to the princes;
then, having received the benediction of the subjects, he ascended his magnificent chariot. (59)
The other classes of people ascended their respective seats; and the subjects offered counsel for the king's true welfare.
In ancient times, the camel performed austerities; Prajāpati approached him, and he then chose as his boon that his necks should be one yojana in length.
Brahmā said, "So be it," and the camel remained forever in the forest;
being exceedingly lazy, he would sit in one spot and eat the trees.
Surrounded for a league on all sides, he slept happily at night;
meanwhile, a jackal arrived and clung firmly to his neck.
My camel has a long throat because its neck was split at the middle;
likewise, in this world, one whose thirst is excessive dies, struck by illusion.
Therefore, one should not indulge in craving; rather, one should practice devotion to Hari.
One should take refuge in Me; I shall deliver him, there is no doubt.
In a certain forest, there was a preeminent swan belonging to a lion;
a poor Brahmin named Sattvavṛtti went to that forest.
A swan met him on the road and asked, "Where are you going?
He replied, "I am indeed going to another land with my companions for the sake of acquiring wealth. (67)
The swan said: "O sinless one, you are a brahmin and worthy of my worship;
I shall give you here the jewels acquired from the lion and taken from the elephant."
"Having killed elephants and obtained pearls from their frontal globes," having said this, the swan indeed took that brahmin along with him into the forest.
He went to where that lion was, and the swan said to the lion:
"This guest, a Brāhmaṇa, has arrived; he is worthy of honor. (2.200.70)
"By giving this [to him], the great sin born of violence shall be destroyed.
Thus addressed, the excellent tiger then washed his feet. (71)
Having drunk the nectar from the brāhmaṇa’s feet, he honored him with gifts of jewels;
as the brāhmaṇa was departing for his home, the swan then spoke to that twice-born man.
"Come back; let no further suffering arise here for me without you.
Having spoken thus, the swan departed, and after some time, the twice-born [Brāhmaṇa] returned.
Having reached that forest again through greed while remembering Hari, the swan was no longer his minister at that time; indeed, the crow had become the minister.
Seeing the twice-born, the crow said to the lion, "Devour him!
The lion replied, "It cannot be so; this brahmin is eternally purifying. (75)
He then drank the water from [the sage's] feet and placed the dust upon his head;
the crow said, "Indeed, the water from one's feet is truly purifying. (76)
He is full and pure; he should be consumed in every way.
By him we shall be purified, and likewise, internal sin shall perish. (77)
Thus addressed, the lion-king devoured that brahmin;
therefore, one should not give way to greed, for death dwells within the house of greed. (78)
Having abandoned greed and remembering Hari, one should indeed live with contentment;
such a person shall be happy in this world and happy in my abode hereafter. (79)
For one who is contented and firmly devoted to the supreme abode, [there is no need for others];
once, the Ocean said to the rivers and the trees: 2.200.80.
"Rivers indeed come flooding with water, but reeds do not;
thus say both the rivers and these trees that always stand upon the banks. (81)
Moreover, they never bow even when we prosper;
having uprooted them, we shall lead them into the depths of the ocean. (82)
Reeds fallen into a flood indeed bend,
yet when the force of the flood has subsided, they slowly rise back up.
We do not indeed lead away those who bow down like reeds;
rather, it is those people who, at the proper time, bow before the Great One who possesses such speed.
Those who remain steadfast do not suffer the destruction of their roots;
likewise, those who bow down during the time of the force of Māyā pass through that time.
Just as embodied beings here attain a gradual rising and thus live, so too should people here conduct their livelihoods so as not to encounter suffering. (86)
Relying upon me, you must gradually abandon illusion and proceed indeed to my divine abode, that blissful residence which is the most steadfast refuge. (87)
One who desires happiness must act only after considering the place and time;
"I am Nārāyaṇa, the Lord, the Master who is to be worshipped always. (88)
"I shall deliver him who worships me and comes to my feet; of this there is no doubt.
A fool indeed became a boar on his back, solely for the purpose of seizing the jackal. (89)
Then, at that opportune moment, the jackal ran with great speed;
leaping into the well, he reached the opposite bank and stood there.
A boar, possessing a stout body, ran with great speed and fell into a well;
plunging into the midst of the water, he died, overcome by ignorance. ||91||
Therefore, people should never engage in any action with impetuous haste; rather, a human being should cross over saṃsāra gradually by taking refuge in me. 92.
A person in this world should not resort to greed, which is like a jackal, characterized by passion, essentially flawed, a great rogue, and one that causes one to fall into a pit. (93)
Having abandoned desire, anger, intoxication, greed, and pride, one shall become happy;
by taking refuge in me, the Lord, the virtuous man, and the virtuous woman, one shall become happy. (94)
Having spoken thus, Hari gave the mantra to the king and his family;
and Lomaśa, being commanded, gave the mantra to the subjects.
Maheśvara gave the mantra to his subjects who had been deprived [of it];
then, having drunk the water, the Blessed One appeared in the sky.
Worshipped by the elephant and others with offerings of flowers, the Supreme Lord,
having repeatedly bestowed his blessings, ascended his own celestial chariot.
Then all the others remained in their celestial chariots in the sky;
indeed, musical instruments were played with great intensity for the sake of honor.
In that place, shouts of victory, sounds of glory, and likewise the noises of mechanical instruments arose; indeed, Hari quickly [reached] the celestial chariot.
He sent [them] by way of the sky toward the land of Kenāṭaka;
indeed, having crossed the ocean, [he reached] the regions of Kenāṭaka.
At midday, the swift celestial chariots indeed arrived;
seeing the lands scattered upon the water, they reflected upon Hari.
First, one must go to the sacrificial ground where it is being held;
thereafter, indeed, another task must be performed by the great seer Lālāyana.
Then Lālāyana, having remembered the circle of celestial chariots, quickly caused the royal armies to raise cries of "Welcome! || 103 ||
Hari also crossed the Dviphena ocean and the island of Dviphena itself;
having passed over Haḍḍikāsana, he went to the Vinipāra lake.
Where musical instruments were played then for the sake of welcoming Hari, and where innumerable people awaited the Supreme Lord. (1.05)
O Rādhikā, shouts of joy then arose, reaching to the ends of the quarters;
people, including those with divine vision, beheld her in the sky at that time.
There were sounds of drums and harsh noises that caused the wind to tremble,
as well as the sounds of musical instruments and songs during the honoring of Hari.

Thus ends the two-hundredth chapter, titled "The Description of Hari’s Descent in the City of Aparānāvikā, His Wandering, Worship, Feeding, and Resting; His Travel by Air-Vehicle throughout the Region, His Morning Meal and Departure after Nightly Rest, and His Return to Lake Vinipara in the Kenāṭaka Provinces," in the section on the Majesty of King Arka within the Tretā lineage of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*. 200.
Śrī Rādhikā said:
O Beloved, O Beloved, O Ocean of Mercy, O Lord of Rādhā, O Lord of Ramā!
What did Mādhava do in the regions of the immortals?
Where, where, and to what place did he go? Where did he stay? By whom was he served? And what wonders were displayed there by the Supreme Soul, O Hari? || 2 ||
What was done by the subjects there when the Supreme Lord, the Master, had arrived? To which countries did this Blessed One, the Creator of all beings, travel? (3)
Tell me the deeds of the Blessed One in the regions of Vadāmarī—
whatever occurred there while he was being attended by Brahmapriya.
Having become satisfied by the excellent discourses of this Lord,
my thirst to hear his life stories arises once again.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Rādhikā, as I relate to you all the accounts:
the sacrifice, worship, hospitality, offering, and the command.
Wandering, the bestowing of mantras, divine visions, the liberation of embodied beings, and likewise the consecration of rivers as sacred fords (tīrtha). || 7 ||
I shall describe to you, in brief, the auspicious and wondrous accounts that purify both lakes and oceans.
The Blessed One performed a sacrifice on the shore of the Vinipāra lake,
upon a vast and auspicious stretch of ground adjoining a forest of leftover sacrificial wood.
The Vaiṣṇava [sacrifice] grants satisfaction to all the gods and to living beings here;
it reaches the bodies and so forth of those situated within the three worlds, both the insentient and the sentient.
Through the hands of Bālakṛṣṇa, they attained eternal satisfaction; who else could be the sovereign of the various regions and districts of Aṭaka? || 11 ||
King Pañcasaras, known by the name Rāyakinnara,
and the sage Divimānāyana both rendered assistance at the sacrifice.
Those two supreme Vaiṣṇavas became the best of devotees through the power of Tuṣita at the confluence of the Lālāyana.
At the command of the sage, King Lālāyana, desiring to perform a sacrifice, dispatched auspicious letters to his disciples.
Through the practice of the Lālāyana system, the regions of the Cāmarīs are inhabited by Vaiṣṇava subjects who are righteous. || 15 ||
In every region there are kings and you, the subjects;
that we have attained the state of being Vaiṣṇavas—oh, what great fortune is ours! 16.
He who is indeed Śrī Nārāyaṇa among the Nārāyaṇas, the Supreme Lord,
and whose devotees we are here— he is Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
"Having arrived in my kingdom, he will indeed perform an auspicious Vaiṣṇava sacrifice;
therefore, everyone must come to that sacrificial festival."
On the seventh day of the bright fortnight of Bhādrapada, the commencement of the sacrifice will take place;
on the fifth day, that Supreme Self will descend from his celestial chariot.
On this day, before dawn, all the kings of Khaṇḍaga must assemble here,
along with all the subjects and the Sāttvatas, for the purpose of welcoming Hari.
The worship of Hari should be performed together with the full splendor of the army;
on the eleventh day, the completion of this sacrifice shall take place.
By the command of Lālāyana, I, Rāya Kinnara, write this;
all women and men, whether mentioned or unmentioned, must come here. 22.
In this manner, that king of the Rāya-kiṃnaras dispatched excellent letters to the various regions of the Cāmarīs by means of messengers.
Having received the invitations, the people—men, women, and others—along with their families, hastened quickly, eager for the sight [of him]. (24)
They arrived bringing offerings with celestial chariots, vehicles, and carriages,
consisting of gold, silver, grain, and other goods, as well as jewels, diamonds, and fine essences.
Accompanied by suitable sacrificial materials and gifts to be given,
millions of men arrived at the banks of the Śeṣa-kāṣṭha forest river.
During the Vinipārasara yoga, even kings were present there,
and the multi-colored armies of the rulers arrived.
Well-dressed and accompanied by musical instruments, they arrived for the purpose of welcoming Hari,
adorned with banners, flags, and archways.
With weapons in their hands, riding upon elephants, horses,
and camels, they were stationed in a newly constructed city ten yojanas in extent.
Then there was a great crush on the banks of the remaining forests and rivers,
and on the shores of the lakes, by millions of women who had been lying in wait.
Then that new city of sacrifice shone like heaven;
Hari-Kṛṣṇa gazed upon that city repeatedly from the sky.
Having surveyed the ground for the purpose of the pavilion within the expanse of the lake,
he observed a level plot of land facing the directions as prescribed by the divine architects.
Having arranged the chariot-wheel, he caused the celestial vehicle to descend above everything;
there were the sounds of musical instruments and the songs of the gods,
as well as cries of victory from the people, while those who move through the sky were present.
The sounds of trumpets and the rattling of mechanical instruments arose as Hari was being honored.
Ten preeminent sovereigns, lords of the entire earth, were present there, having brought excellent offerings in golden vessels. ||35||
King Rāyakinnaranṛpati, King Rāyarokīśvara, King Rāyaraṇajit, and King Rāyavākakṣaka;
King Rāyamārīśa and King Rāyabāleśvara. ||36||
And Rāyalambārabhūpa, as well as Rāyanavārkabhūpati. || 37 ||
King Rāyahaṇḍeśa and King Rāyakūpeśa were both well-equipped with their armies at that time for the purpose of welcoming Hari.
Having arrived there by means of celestial chariots, they had already assembled beforehand with well-adorned bodies on elephants, horses, chariots, and other mounts; thus,
the army stood ready for the purpose of welcoming them.

Those who engage in debate, those who formulate policies, those who seek to kindle fire with collyrium, those who carry water-instruments, and those who make loud noises with dance and music; ||2.201.40||
Those who know the power of lutes and instruments, those who play the flute and the *vaṃśī*, those highly skilled in loud instruments, and those who produce the sound of the *paṭaha* drum; ||41||
Accompanied by physical gestures, bearing weapons, and seeking to bow down,
there were those in the guise of attendants holding canes, as well as Bhāllukas in the guise of tigers.
Clad in tawny garments, they were surrounded by an aura and possessed the appearance of ascetics;
some bore tridents and discs, while others likewise carried shields and swords.
Even though they were marked by tāṃsaka cymbals, hand-claps, and flutes,
as well as by conchs and thunderbolts, they likewise sought out the daughter of Sukanya.
Some wore matted locks and were exceedingly handsome in the guise of warriors; some were clad in white garments, while others wore red robes and were adorned with variegated ornaments.
Having honored him with triple umbrellas, fans, chowries, and flower clusters, they stood ready with mirrors for the sake of welcoming him. (46)
There, the immortal women were pale-complexioned and in the prime of youth;
these maidens had lips as red as the *raktaka* flower and were filled with an intense, surging passion.
Clad in blue, yellow, and green garments, adorned with golden ornaments, and beautifully embellished with robes such as garlands of networks of tinkling bells; ||48||
Holding plates for the purpose of worshipping Hari, they were provided with parched grain and unbroken rice,
as well as white water-lilies, lotuses, night-blooming lilies, kādamba flowers, and pārijātaka blossoms.
They were adorned with thousands of lotuses from ponds, land-lotuses with beautiful filaments, campaka flowers, kāmala blossoms, pearl necklaces, crests, and garlands.
Accompanied by saffron gardens and possessing sandalwood worthy of worship,
hundreds of thousands of divine women, who were like immortals, arrived there.
Thousands of royal ladies and countless women of the common folk were present;
at that time, all the regions were filled with auspicious invocations.
In the palace of the emperor Rāyakinnara,
for the sake of obtaining a vision of Bālakṛṣṇa-Hari as he approaches for the supreme sacrifice.
Humans, from children to the elderly, numbering in the millions, billions, and trillions,
arrived and stood before Hari to welcome him.
They arrived at the ground of the confluence of the Śeṣakāṣṭha forest river with the Vinipāra lake, which was exceedingly vast. ||55||
The city named Makhasevā, extending for many yojanas and worthy of being a dwelling for guests, shone like another heaven. (56)
Formerly, from the lake near the city of Maṇisevā, the Blessed One, the beloved of Kṛṣṇa, [proceeded] by the path shown by the king. (57)
He brought down from the sky a celestial chariot resembling the sun;
illuminating all directions, it shone with the color of gold.
Having attained stability upon the ground, he appeared like the moon;
other celestial chariots as well descended from the sky there.
The skilled ones grasped his work with instruments that capture its form;
but the kings, standing upon a single thread, paid him homage.
Accompanied by their armies, with drums and other musical instruments, and with dances and artistic performances,
all the kings together with the emperor went into his presence.
Both Īśāna and Lomaśa proceeded to the front of the celestial chariot,
while both Vṛkāyana and Nīlakaṇa followed behind.
The gatekeepers and attendants stood in the courtyard with staffs in hand;
having reached the ladder, the kings stood there as spectators.
Then Hari, as Bālakṛṣṇa, accompanied by his parents,
arrived first in a brilliantly shining celestial chariot at the city gate.
His body shines with the brilliance of ten million suns, moons, fires, and lightning bolts;
and beneath the archway stands his beloved, radiant like flickering lightning.
Having touched Śrī Kṛṣṇa— that Bālakṛṣṇa— with his hand for a moment, King Rāya Kiṃnara offered him a charming, gentle smile.
Having prostrated, she placed upon his neck a garland of jasmine flowers fragrant with scent and variegated in color, and then she gave him a necklace of jewels.
She placed a cluster of flowers in his hand, an arka tree with sandalwood paste upon his forehead,
and fragrant essences held in a vessel within her garment.
With the ritual of honoring, the king scattered unbroken grains of gold upon his feet, fine rice upon his head, and flowers over his body.
He offered water, milk, betel-leaf, and fruit in his presence;
then, with palms joined in reverence, he requested that the earth be inspected for the purpose of the sacrifice.
Hari slowly descended by means of golden steps;
then, having been offered a lion-throne, he sat upon it for a moment.
Rāyarokīśvara worshipped him with flower garlands and jewels,
and King Rāyaraṇajit worshipped him with gems and other offerings.
King Rāyavākakṣaka honored him with gold and other riches;
King Rāyamārīśa also honored him with jewels and other gifts. ||73||
King Rāyabāleśvara honored him with diamonds, and King Rāyalambāra honored him with wealth and other gifts. ||74||
King Rāyanavārka honored him with rubies, and King Rāyahaṇḍeśa honored him with pearls. ||75||
And King Rāyakūpeśa honored him with silver [gifts];
then all the chief ministers also worshipped him with ornaments and other offerings.
The merchants also honored their lord with wealth, food,
and various delicacies, as well as with offerings for the gods and ancestors (havya-kavya), sacrificial fuel, and many other articles.
The groups of subjects worshipped the Lord of Fortune, Puruṣottama;
then, at the conclusion of the worship and the welcome, Śrī Hari questioned them.

Having bowed down with great respect, the king and others spoke these words of happiness out of compassion: "May there be freedom from disease, great well-being, security, spiritual practice, and happiness. (79)
"Everything of every kind exists here today; indeed, there is great happiness on this day.
A golden sunrise has occurred today, because Your grace has descended upon us. (2.201.80)
Today an eternal gain has been attained, namely this sight of you here;
today the fourfold perfections and the four aims of human life have been accomplished.
Today, indeed, the fruit of the burden of sovereignty has been obtained through the acquisition of what was yet to be gained;
for today, all prosperity that bestows even the rank of Indra has truly entered our home.
