"O Lord, by the sight of you, imperishable merit has been attained this very day;
indeed, because of your arrival, our lands have become purified today. (83)
Today your riches have been employed purposefully;
all your various and abundant treasures have surely become fruitful through this noble deed. (84)
Indeed, by the sight of Mādhava, we humans—men, women, children, the young, and the old—have accomplished our purpose; we are truly most meritorious. (89)
Today, indeed, animals, trees, creepers, and the like possess great merit;
so too do birds, aquatic creatures, those that dwell on the earth, and even forest-dwellers. (86)
That this earth rejoices when it touches your feet—this ground, which possesses great fortune—is indeed like a divine abode. (87)
Today, having been born, she is especially enriched with horripilation due to the offering of perfumes;
indeed, on this very day, the trees, grasses, and clumps of reeds have become blessed and fortunate.
Those who are purified by the dust of your feet here—be they even ants and the like—are blessed, for they partake of your grace. (89)
Blessed indeed are these lands where the advent of Nārāyaṇa has occurred;
today, the manifestation of you, Hari, which bestows liberation, has begun.
Wealth, grain, sovereignty, prosperity, sons, cities, elephants and the like, and the abundance of vehicles and mounts—all this is indeed fruitful. (9.1)
O Blessed One, by your scripture, what indeed could possibly be lacking?
For us, everything is already complete; for the attainment of Hari is truly difficult to find.
Having performed the sacrifice, purify us and grant us eternal welfare;
we desire that you always dwell in this land as our followers.
Having spoken thus, King Kinnata offered his salutation;
the other kings also bowed down, and then the Blessed One himself [responded]. 94.
Having risen, he wandered all around to look for a suitable site on the ground,
in a place to the south of the confluence of the Śeṣa, the Kāṣṭhavana, and the river.
Having observed that the auspicious ground, extending for many yojanas, was fit for a pavilion, he commanded the king to prepare the site for the pavilion.
The messengers of Indra, the messengers of Viṣṇu, and others who were the messengers of Śiva—remembered there, they arrived swiftly, and Viśvakarman also arrived. (97)
Having commanded them to construct nine sacrificial pits and an excellent pavilion,
he ensured that everything was fully prepared by dawn.
Then, at midday, Hari went to his residence and took his meal and so forth; thereafter, he rested together with his caravan.
They all constructed a most beautiful pavilion during the night itself,
adorned with sacrificial pits, altars, and great platforms, along with houses for the ritual jars.
Having constructed a beautiful pavilion extending as far as the city of Maṇisevā, provided with spacious rooms and fire-chambers; || 10 1 ||
The attendants went out in all directions to fetch sacrificial fuel, as did the sages residing throughout Gaṅgādvāra and the disciples of Lomaśa. || 102 ||
The gods and goddesses, composed of that [consciousness], prepared the materials for the sacrifice.
On the sixth day, having performed his daily rites, Kṛṣṇa [entered] the new city of Mahīmāna.
Seated upon the back of an elephant and accompanied by kings, he set out to inspect the kitchens,
the laboratories for medicinal juices, and the vast bath-houses.
He beheld sleeping quarters, halls for peace, and sacrificial chambers; he saw dining halls filled with kings and great kitchens. 105.
Having observed that all preparations had been completed with perfect materials,
Hari remembered the Lord of the Gods in the morning, accompanied by the nectar.
Mahendra quickly arrived there accompanied by the nectar;
there was a lake of nectar there that provided inexhaustible satisfaction on all sides.
There, the Kalpalatās arrived, laden with fruits;
indeed, mountains of fruit were fashioned by them for the very purpose of the sacrifice.
The trees, crops, and forest trees known as *puṣpakaṇada* were designated as *kalpavṛkṣas*; indeed, they fashioned mountains out of flowers, grains, and other such things.
Those cows, who grant all desires when remembered, have indeed arrived from their own abode; along with them came streams of ghee, streams of curd, and streams of milk.
Gathered in the sacrificial halls, imperishable and filled with materials,
the goddess Śivā, being full of food, was then remembered as Lakṣmī.
They arrived and fashioned mountains of cooked food;
the Earth herself, having appeared in personified form, brought a mountain of sweet sugar.
At the command of Hari, she produced the waters; the water-deities produced the juices;
and all the medicinal herbs produced the spices and other seasonings. || 113 ||
Brahmā himself, the four-faced one, being remembered there, arrived; he then fashioned suitable dwellings as well as the necessary implements.
And Kubera deposited gold, silver, and other treasures for the sake of sacrificial fees;
likewise did the other guardians of the realm, the world-protectors, and the lords of subjects.
Being remembered, they arrived swiftly for the fulfillment of the offerings to gods and ancestors;
when the sixth lunar day had reached midday, everything became fully accomplished and powerful.
It was perfectly prepared and nothing was lacking;
the king provided millions of men with delicious foods like those of the Kinnaras.
Hari, together with his family and accompanied by the circles of great sages, gratified all those subjects in many ways.
Accompanied by his own caravan, he indeed took up his meals there;
then King Rāya-kiṃnara entreated Kṛṣṇa.
O Rādhikā, Kṛṣṇa immediately replied, "Let Him come to His own home, honored by the army,
and also wander through the city."

Thus ends the two hundred and first chapter, titled "The Description of the Dispatching of the Auspicious Letter for the Sacrifice by Keṇāṭa, the Welcome and Enquiries of Welfare by the Ten Kings and Others upon the Arrival of Hari, the Command to Construct the Pavilion and Other Structures, the Feasting, and the Collection of Sacrificial Implements," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Rādhikā, the king of the Kinnaras quickly prepared his army,
which was resplendent with elephants, horses, and chariots, and with sounding musical instruments and various mounts.
The white elephant has four tusks and is as high as a mountain peak;
accompanied by Ambālikā, it is exceedingly richly adorned and beautifully graced with a golden saddle-cloth.
Urged by the elephant-keeper at the king's command for the sake of Hari,
he arrived very quickly before him, and Hari mounted the elephant.
Likewise, six other elephants stood there facing upward;
his parents, his brothers, and even his sister, who was dear to her brothers, were also present.
Lomaśa, Tuṣita, and likewise Lālāyana mounted those elephants,
while Īśāna himself mounted the most excellent elephant.
Women dear to Brahmā also ascended human vehicles,
as did playful young women in covered carriages.
There were also young maidens, those of a fair complexion, as well as those of a tawny hue and greenish-yellow;
moreover, the sons of Gaṅgā and other great sages were upon the chariots.
Endowed with happiness, they sat down to wander through the city of Maṇipattana;
and likewise, when all the great men had taken their seats.
Then, indeed, the armies of the people of the world were led forward,
well-equipped with musical instruments and adorned with banners, flags, and the like.
The attendants were singing the great glory of Nārāyaṇa even as they went;
then a magnificent elephant belonging to Lord Īśāna proceeded forth.
Behind the householders go the elephants, then the great sages' elephants, and indeed the human-carriages of Brahmapriyā and the others proceed.
Chariots, rich in splendor and equipped with golden jars, draped in variegated cloths, auspicious, and drawn by white horses, proceed forth. (12)
Then the great elephant, adorned by Śrīpati Kṛṣṇa, proceeded,
where King Kinnāraka held the parasol over its back.
Holding chowries, two young princes stood at his sides;
then the splendid vehicles of the kings indeed set forth.
Behind them were the immortal maidens, known by the name Gītanārāyaṇas,
who had donned festive attire and were auspicious with the sentiments of love and beauty.
Seated upon thrones of pearls, holding water-pots filled with fruit and auspicious sprouts,
and adorned with all manner of beautiful garments and ornaments, they go along singing the praises of the Lord.
Among those in human vehicles, there was the chanting of the praises of the Lord of Kambarā, the Lord of Śrī, the Lord of Kamalā; and among them were Rādhā, Lakṣmī, Prabhā, and Satī.
Pārvatī, Māṇikī, Haṃsā, Mañjulā, Saguṇāmbikā, Santoṣā, Amṛtā, Muktidevī, Lalitā, and Jayā. || 18 ||
These and other women, adorned and radiant, proceed along the royal road, as do other horsemen and guards. || 19 ||
Moving along the great highway commanded by the king’s decree,
Śrī Hari, possessing the splendor of the sun, shone brightly, honored by the people.
Thus that army marched from Maṇipurī for Hari;
first, rich with royal splendor, it proceeded to the royal palace.
Descending from his horse, the king seated Hari upon the royal throne, which was made of exquisite gold and resplendent with jewels and gems.
There were shouts of victory and likewise a rain of flowers;
an excellent [celebration] was performed by Pradhāna and others, by Kumāra and others, and by the queens.
The chief queen, the virtuous goddess, worshipped the Supreme Lord with a tilaka mark made of saffron and sandalwood, as well as with unbroken grains of rice.
He placed his hand upon the forehead of Śrī Hari to dispel his suffering,
scattered flowers over the head of Kṛṣṇa, and performed a prostration.
Having washed his feet with milk, he brought the milk into a vessel;
that royal family quickly drank that which was so pleasing to behold.
Afterward, having washed his feet with water, he placed a wealth of materials— necklaces, ornaments, and so forth— worth ten million, in the presence of the Supreme Self.
"O Kṛṣṇa, that which was offered by me at the sacrifice by the king's command is yours.
Having said this, she approached his side and, with a steady gaze, beheld him.
Then King Rādhika bowed at the feet of Hari and offered his family, jewels, gems, and other riches for the sake of worship. ||29||
Then Bālakṛṣṇa gave them two most divine eyes,
which were capable of perceiving the forms of others, as well as his own transcendental form.
Kṛṣṇa granted him a vision that was most divine and exceedingly beautiful,
with limbs corresponding perfectly to his form, as lovely as ten million gods of love.
It is the supreme state, served by millions of liberated ones and millions of Śaktis;
it is the most excellent, frequented by infinite, infinite liberated souls, Īśvara, and others.

He was worshipped by Brahmā and the other gods, resplendent with divine garments and ornaments, attended by Rādhā, Ramā, and others, and possessing a beauty that surpassed even the most beloved of lovers. (33)
Beholding that [manifestation] of Mādhava, which was frequented by the Lord of Gods through his incarnations, manifestations, and spies, those born of royal lineage were struck with wonder.
Beholding that supreme wonder, they remained as if stunned for a moment;
then the king, impelled by a divine state of being, offered praise. (35)
Resplendent, abiding in the supreme abode which is the nature of a mass of great splendor, He who is pleased by the service and attendance of the great liberated ones is victorious.
The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the bearer of infinite qualities, the Supreme, the Lord of the Imperishable, whose state is attained through Śakti and the others, reigns in triumph. (36)
You alone abide in Your own divine abode, the supreme imperishable realm;
You alone abide there in Your emaciated form with two arms, the bestower of supreme bliss.
In the world of cows, You are worshipped with offerings by the hosts of gopīs in Your own home.
He alone remains in the abode of Vaikuṇṭha, which is attended by Lakṣmī.
O Viṣṇu, you alone abide in the station of the Lord, the Infinite, filled with nectar; you alone exist in the unmanifest realm as the one whose body consists of the manifested emanations.
You are the Virāj, you are Hiraṇyagarbha, and you are the Puruṣa; O Viṣṇu, you are the three gods who bring about the welfare of human beings.
The Suras, Daityas, and other ancestors here, O Brahmins, the hosts of sages,
kings, and those dwelling in the netherworld— all that which is designated as insentient and sentient is Your body; and Nara, Nārāyaṇa, and those sages here are the limbs of the body of Badrīśa.
Those who know the Self and desire liberation indeed worship Him who has assumed a dual form. ||39||
Likewise, in the white world, your people, whose bodies possess a brilliant luster, serve you—the one who rests upon the serpent, whose feet have been served by Lakṣmī.
You alone are in the moon; you are in the halo of the sun; you are within the fire in the heart; and you become Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the one who effects the destruction of darkness.
O Viṣṇu, by the power of even a fraction of Your supreme grace, I behold this divine form of Yours abiding within my dull consciousness through my own vision;
for You alone existed in the beginning as the creator of the principles (tattvas) and all else, along with their attendants.
Having entered [the body], you become the nourisher; even during withdrawal, you are the agent of dissolution.
You alone remain, even while assuming countless forms, acting out of compassion as the creator of supreme welfare for those submerged in the ocean of worldly existence;
it is You, O Blessed One, who have arrived here, having taken the form of the sacrifice.
As the enjoyer in this sacrifice, bring about happiness for your own people. ||42||
Surely the wealth given by me was for you to enjoy long ago; indeed, this entire kingdom and all else has been placed at your feet.
As for me, I remain in the kingdom merely as a constant guest.
"O Great King, you are indeed a householder and the ruler of your own realm. ||42||
Having thus praised Bālakṛṣṇa, O Rādhikā, that king then observed a vow of silence; thereafter, the Lord of divine vision appeared.
Then, as he was concealing himself, they beheld him upon a golden throne;
with tears in their eyes and hearts constricted by grief, they suddenly bowed and prostrated themselves.
Then all the queens, grasping the feet of the wielder of the Śārṅga bow,
affectionately licked both soles, recognizing him as the Supreme Lord Śrī.
And there, fifty-one excellent daughters of the king were present as spectators; they were enchanted by Puruṣottama.
Placing the garland of choice upon their hands, they placed it around the neck of Hari;
then Bālakṛṣṇa, commanded by the king, indeed accepted their hands.
Having attained Kṛṣṇa, their beloved Lord, they had accomplished their purpose;
then Śrī Hari, having bestowed blessings upon the king there, [departed].
Having assigned the sacrificial materials and the measurement of the day to the Ṛṣi,
the king rose from his seat and felt that he had accomplished his purpose.
Then the Blessed Lord wandered everywhere— in temples, in the king's palace,
and throughout the many-storied buildings consisting of a hundred floors and more.
Having first purified the royal garden with his feet, he then proceeded to the royal palace and thereafter to the chief minister’s residence.
Then, having placed his feet in the dwellings of the guild-leaders and in the houses of the city-dwellers, he accepted worship for the sake of the sacrifice.
Having received worship on the royal highway, in the marketplaces, at the crossroads, and in every place, Hari offered it all for the sake of the sacrifice. ||54||
Thus, as he wandered through the city in every direction preceded by great honor, he captivated the minds of the people.
Seeing the Lord wandering on the royal highway, mounted upon a great elephant,
all the women sang his praises as if they were goddesses.
Blessed are those princesses who chose the Lord, the Consort of Śrī;
for how else could they have obtained the fruit of the penance and worship performed in former lives? (57)
In this world, women may find a beloved husband, Nārāyaṇa, in their home—one whom Rādhā, Kamalā, Padmā, Lakṣmī, Prabhā, and Pārvatī [revere]. (58)
Māṇikya and others, having attained him through the weight of their good fortune, serve him—he whom the beloveds of Brahmā serve, and whom other maidens serve as well. (59)
Those who were Gaurikas have attained him through the weight of their fortune;
those who were Hāritas serve him, the refuge of countless virtues.
Let them behold his supreme face, resplendent as the orb of the moon;
there, upon his brow, the arrow of Kāmadeva remains fixed.
The bow resides upon his eyebrows; there is beauty in his body;
and in his smile is a great wonder that captivates and enchants.
In the corner of his eye, a beautiful and wondrous luster shines;
in the middle of his lips, there is an exquisite beauty that acts as a magnet.
And let the people behold his broad chest, his powerful and enchanting form, which is the support for the splendor of the Kaustubha gem. (64)
Let the women behold the palms of Hari’s hands, rich with a splendor exceeding that of red lac;
let them behold his thighs, which possess the beauty of plantain trunks. (65)
His form is pervaded by supreme splendor and rests upon the far-reaching vision; his form is pervaded by supreme splendor and rests upon the far-reaching vision.
This is not a human body; he is divine, the Supreme Lord.
No limbs joined by joints are visible in her form;
O friends, behold her beauty on the outside, within, and on all sides! (67)
Free from the construction and arrangement of bones, channels, and so forth, this single reality shines forth; he is certainly the venerable Puruṣottama.

The Supreme Lord, higher than the highest, whose nature is Truth, Consciousness, and Bliss, and who has been heard of in the declarations of the scriptures—he alone is now being contemplated here. (69)
Indeed, by the mere sight of him, infinite happiness is attained;
he is a mass of bliss, the very locus of all fragrances and flavors. (2.202.70)
This [Self] bestows the light of the Self and indeed carries away our inner mind;
it must be attained by all means at the end of death in the supreme Imperishable.
"We shall certainly receive his mantra at the sacrifice;
indeed, we shall obtain that supreme beloved, Bālakṛṣṇa Janārdana. (72)
From his body there issues forth a mass of splendor, such as is transcendent:
blissful, captivating the very moment it is seen, gentle, bestowing virtuous conduct and peace, and imperishable. (73)
Thus, O Rādhā, the women of the city of Maṇipura, being utterly infatuated, spoke thus to one another—those women of the Amaryā caste. (74)
On every path, at the front of every house, at every crossroads, and in the vicinity of every mansion,
they honored the Supreme Lord with parched grain, unbroken rice, and flowers.
Uttering cries of "Victory!", they delight the Lord of the virtuous;
yet, gazing at their beloved from the windows, they bow down to the Sovereign.
Bestowing both worldly enjoyment and liberation, the Lord of the lords of gods, who dwells in the cave of the heart—
thus did Hari wander through the city named Maṇipūra.
Then he went forth to behold the preeminent city of sacrifice;
men and women of great honor, having seen the Lord of the lords of gods, [proceeded].
They caused [him] to prosper with desired gifts and offerings; they honored him exceedingly and offered him a most excellent welcome.
They worshipped the Lord with wealth, commodities, juices, alkalis, veṣavāra, grains such as kaṇa, products of the cow, sacrificial offerings, śāli rice, unbroken grains (akṣata), and so forth.
With garments, auspicious seats, vessels, blankets, tunics, and jackets;
with armor, ornaments, crowns and the like, and earrings. ||81||
With sandalwood, most delicious foods, fruits, dried fruits and the like, scents for the fragrance of the mouth, and likewise with jewel necklaces and garlands; ||82||
With various kinds of sacrificial fees— gold, silver, copper, and other metals—
all the subjects indeed worshipped Bālakṛṣṇa.
Encouraged by his army, Kṛṣṇa, having thus granted this supreme vision and having joined the people with his blessings, received their offerings.
Accompanied by the assembly of kings and others, Hari returned to his own abode,
the royal palace, which was fit for the residence of Ruma and equal to heaven.
The king, out of joy, caused all the wealth, grain, and other goods that had arrived for the sacrifice to be given away as if for evening entertainment. ||869||
At night, he organized a great festival with enthusiasm for dancing,
and furthermore, he made a gift of wealth on the occasion of bestowing his daughter in marriage.
Having eaten himself and having fed his family members, dependents, all the honored sages, and the women dear to Brahmā, Hari [departed]. ||88||
After causing his subjects to prosper happily, he slept soundly in the bedchamber of his queen;
then the immortal women attended upon that new and beloved lord with excessive devotion.
At dawn, musical instruments were sounded to awaken the Lord;
women performed auspicious recitations and songs. (2.202.90)
At that time, the sounds of musical instruments were sweet even to the ear;
Hari-Kṛṣṇa woke up, performed his daily rites, and went to the assembly hall.
Having partaken of milk and other refreshments, he went to behold the pavilion, which had been exquisitely constructed by Viśvakarman and others during the night. (92)
It was ten *krośas* in extent, adorned with ten thousand thrones,
frequented by ten million deities, and endowed with variegated banners.
There he saw nine sacrificial pits and likewise one supreme, highest pit; he also beheld the altars, the vessels, the halls, and the fire-sanctuaries for the oblations.
Having gazed upon the sacrificial fuel for the *homa* and likewise having looked upon the *kavya* offerings, the Blessed One was gratified; he became serene and exceedingly joyful.
Likewise, there were hosts of yoginīs possessing both divine and non-divine siddhis, as well as circles of goddesses, mātṛkās, and virtuous women. ||96||
The mandalas of the Sāṃkhya-yoginīs, which bestow sovereign power, exist for the protection of the great kitchens and for the perfection of the cooking. (97)
Beholding that, the Blessed One, the beloved of Kṛṣṇa, became exceedingly pleased;
he summoned Goddess Dharaṇī and then appointed her as his official. 98.
Hari likewise gave Annapūrṇā and Lakṣmī as assistants to Dharaṇī, for the purpose of fulfilling the food and other needs of all the worlds. 99.
There, Hari appointed Varuṇa for the purpose of providing water, Kubera for the sake of sacrificial fees,
and the two sons of the Aśvins for the sake of health.
One should worship Dharmarāja for protection, Vighneśa for the pacification of obstacles,
Sūryadeva for the sake of inexhaustibility, and the wielder of the trident (Śiva) for the sake of authority.
He appointed Viṣṇu for the purpose of giving gifts, Brahmā for the purpose of establishing order,
and Mahendra for the purpose of honoring those who had arrived.
For the purpose of digestion he joined the god of fire, for the purpose of illumination the Pārvaṇa [fire],
and for the purpose of increasing sound and so forth, he joined the lightning.
Thus, O Rādhikā, on the sixth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada, at dawn, the illustrious Bālakṛṣṇa appointed his servants.

Thus ends the two hundred and second chapter, titled "The Description of Hari’s Pastimes, Worship, and Meals in Maṇisevāpurī and Yajñapattana, His Resting at Night, and the Mobilization of the Workmen on the Morning of the Sixth Day of the Bright Fortnight of Bhādrapada," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O Rādhikā, then in the morning, having performed his daily rites, taken his meal,
and served the elders, Bālakṛṣṇa went to the assembly hall.
The king arrived there quickly, eager to behold the worship;
having performed the worship with sandalwood and other offerings, he then spoke to Hari with humility.
O ocean of compassion, O Lord, command me today regarding the matter of what is to be done;
I shall accomplish everything for the sake of the sacrifice with all my power through service.
Hari said to her: "O Suvarṇī, today fashion a beautiful and auspicious golden image of Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa, adorned with jewels."
Have a golden image of Nārāyaṇa made, nine fingers high with four arms,
and also one of Lakṣmī, eight fingers high.
"Have a beautiful image of me made, ten fingers in height;
have a ruby and a golden form fashioned, reaching above my ears."
Lakṣmī reaches as far as my shoulders; Padmajā is above my ears;
Ramā is above my shoulders; and Rādhā rises to the height of my neck.
"O King, for the sake of the sacrifice, have a very beautiful golden image made of your eldest daughter Amarīśā, who is looking upward with her face turned toward me. (8)
Having had eight images fashioned, have Satī and Śiva made;
and have Gaṇanātha and [another] made of gold.
O King, likewise have Nandin and Kārttikeya fashioned correctly; and having likewise caused the five forms of the Sun (Bhāskara) to be made, [install them].
And fashion Viṣṇu out of gold, and fashion Brahmā out of gold;
likewise, fashion my mother Kambharā and my father Gopāla out of gold.
Then, have a beautiful golden vessel of five [measures] fashioned;
likewise, have a large golden image of the deity Vāstu made.
"And construct a golden assembly hall, a dwelling for all the gods. Thus Kṛṣṇa gave the command: "Have a temple built. (13)
Having received the command, the king quickly had the sculptors work;
then Bālakṛṣṇa remembered Nārada, the knower of the worlds.
To Sanatkumāra, the virtuous one; to Garuḍa, his own vehicle;
to the Sudarśana discus; and to the yogi who is existence, consciousness, and bliss.
These five divine beings quickly arrived before him;
having performed the appropriate prostration like a staff, they offered their service in accordance with his command.
Then Bālakṛṣṇa gave them food as a token of his favor, as well as drinks and necklaces; he placed his hands upon their heads and then commanded the task to be performed.
He gave them an invitation leaf indicating the purpose of the sacrifice:
"On the seventh day, a Vaiṣṇava sacrifice will commence here on this earth."
In the regions of the immortals, at a place named Aṭaka,
on a vast expanse of land in the vicinity of the city of Maṇisevā.
At the confluence of the Śeṣakāṣṭha forest and the river,
on the bank of this lake at Vinipāraga, those liberated ones dwelling in the abodes celebrated a festival with pearls and pearl-like offerings.
And with all the incarnations, as well as their attendants,
and with all the female incarnations and their female attendants, [he was honored] with devotion.
"You must all come to this sacrificial festival with your various arrays, with your retinues, with all the Nārāyaṇas, and with all the Nārāyaṇīs. (22)
[He was surrounded] by the Viṣṇus and the Vaiṣṇavīs, by the Īśvaras and the powers of Īśvara, by Vairāja and Vairājñī, by Satī, by the Gaṇas, and by Śiva.
One should come by means of Māyā, by the principles born of Māyā, and by the Puruṣa in every way; one should come with great enthusiasm as Brahman through the powers of Brahman.
And by celibate ascetics and recluses, as well as by sages and holy men;
and also by fathers and mothers, and even by gods and goddesses. (25)
The guardians of the quarters and the guardians of the worlds must come, accompanied by their beloveds;
likewise, the gods and goddesses residing in heaven and those dwelling in the earthly realm (Bhūrloka). 26.
[He was surrounded] on all sides by planets, constellations, and stars; by *grahas*, *pretas*, and *piśācas*; and by *bhūtas*, *kuṣmāṇḍakas*, *vināyakas*, and [divine] hosts. ||27||
Yakṣas, rākṣasas, daityas, and dānavas must come, as well as the offspring of Kaśyapa, vetālakas, and śaktis. ||28||
By men of passionate and ignorant natures along with their families, by ascetics and yogis, and even by trees, grasses, and creepers; |||29||
By means of pillars, grass, insects, and even those born of old castor-oil plants;
likewise by those born of sweat, those born of particles, those born of bulbs, and those born of water. ||2.203.30||
Mountains, rivers, and lakes must come;
holy fords, forests, and wildernesses, as well as oceans with their deep and shallow channels. ||3 1||
The guardians of the field, the household deities from all sides, the family deities, the shrines, the gandharvas, the cāraṇas, and others must come. || 3.2 ||
By bards, panegyrists, and heralds; by dancers and actors;
by wrestlers who assume many forms; and by Vidyādharas, Kinnaras, and others. ||33||
By hosts of attendants, groups of courtesans, and even by the destitute and mendicants;
by merchants, those dwelling in the nether regions, and those residing as far as the depths of Pātāla. ||34||
The powerful serpents must also assemble with reverence, as well as the scriptures, the Vedas, the sciences, and worldly affairs from all sides. (35)
"All beings, both insentient and sentient, must come to this great sacrifice;
I am the Lord of Brahmā, the Master of the beloved of Brahmā, the Supreme Sovereign. (36)
I, Bālakṛṣṇa, the incarnate one, invite [you] to the sacrifice along with the preceptors of the gods and daityas, who are masters of sovereignty. (37)
O learned brahmins and sages, you must come to my sacrifice on the seventh lunar day of the bright fortnight of Bhādrapada, beginning at dawn and continuing until the eleventh.
The performance of the sacrifice is considered the highest duty; therefore, all householders must come.
To those who do not come, I, Narayana, pronounce a curse. (39)
And may the purifiers— Nara, Nārāyaṇa, and others, as well as Śeṣanārāyaṇa and others— certainly sanctify the land of Āmarī.
May Śrī, Ramā, Rādhikā, Gaṅgā, Śāradā, Tulasī, and Prabhā—each accompanied by their respective consorts such as Muktā and others—come here, bestowing happiness. (41)
May all the Yoginīs, the Mothers, the Kula-devis, and the Caṇḍikās, who dwell in their respective abodes, come to this great sacrifice. 42.
"Let all the female celibates indeed come to my sacrifice—those with their husbands, those with their sons, those with their lineages, and those with their followers, all being equal. (43)
And let them come to this sacrifice, requested by Anādi-Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa;
for here a great assembly shall take place, graced by the Lord of the Universe. (44)
May Brahmā and the others, as well as Viṣṇus with hundreds of thousands of faces, and all those who are supreme, likewise arrive at this Śrī-Vaiṣṇava sacrifice. 45.
I, the infallible one, who am the Supreme Brahman transcending the imperishable, and the beloved Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa, summon you, address you, and cause you to appear. 46.
Thus, O Rādhikā, Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa indeed gave this excellent letter, intended for the purpose of inviting [the sages], to Nārada and the others. 47.
He bestowed upon those of infinite forms a most wonderful capacity for sustaining [the universe],
as well as sovereignty, the power of movement, and omniscience with great speed.
Accepting the command of Hari, they all departed, seeking an invitation;
and at midday, the Supreme Lord remembered Yamarāja.
By his command, he caused the realm of Yama to be emptied of all bonds;
he liberated all living beings who had fallen under the power of Yama.
Then, at the sacrifice, he appointed the messengers of Yama as his ritual assistants;
having thus completed his midday meal and other duties, the Blessed One [proceeded]. ||5 1 ||
Then he himself caused [the sacrifice] to be performed for all those seeking the fruit of the rite;
thereafter, he partook of food and obtained rest for a moment.
There, Hari gave instructions to Brahmā, Viṣṇu,
and Śaṅkara regarding all embodied beings who were about to arrive.
He likewise gave instructions for the welcome of men and women seeking to perform sacrifices,
as well as for Satī, Lakṣmī, and Sarasvatī.
And he gave instructions to Nara and Nārāyaṇa for Svāgata;
and he also gave instructions to Dharmadeva and Vāsudeva.
Indeed, for the sake of welcoming all those guests who had come seeking food,
he then spoke to the venerable Lomaśa and likewise to the sage Bhāradvāja.

"May you all welcome the sons of Gaṅgā, the followers of Yavakrīta, who have come from the celestial chariot to this earth; may you offer a welcome to all embodied beings with water, food, fruits, flowers, and dwellings for those who have arrived. (57)
With respectful offerings of dwellings and necessary articles,

he spoke [of] wish-fulfilling trees (*kalpavṛkṣa*), wish-fulfilling creepers (*kalpalatā*), wish-fulfilling gems (*kalpamaṇi*), and wish-fulfilling rivers (*kalpagā*) throughout all the residences surrounding the sacrificial city (*yajñapattana*). || 58–59 ||
Let them all attend everywhere, endowed with the intent to welcome [you], providing ever-new offerings according to their requirements and as they desire. (2.203.60)

Then Hari commanded that for the sake of those of great majesty, there should be a lake of Brahman, the Virajā river, a well of nectar, and likewise ambrosia; he said, "Let these remain at every spot. || 6.1 ||
May they indeed offer everything desired and all that is to be drunk. || 62 ||
He said to Pavana and the god Vahni: "Become the one who provides the fan;
and you too, O bearer of many forms, become the provider of heat here."
The Sky said: "May you indeed grant the power of hearing from afar here.
The Siddhis said: "May you perform the bringing [of things] and other such tasks here. (64)
Thus he then spoke these words to the ministers: "Let various auspicious proclamations be made at the site of the sacrifice for the honor of those who have arrived. (65)
Then Śāradā said: "Let them perform auspicious songs;
let them indeed play musical instruments for the sake of welcoming those who have arrived.
And Hari said to the kings: "Let them proceed with their armies to pay honor."
Welcome to all those from every world who have come seeking the sacrifice.
Let them show great honor with musical instruments and the sounding of machines;
then, having summoned Viśvakarman, Bālakṛṣṇa spoke to him.
Quickly fashion dwellings for the liberated ones in the sky;
likewise, fashion [dwellings] for the Lords of Incarnation in the sky.
Fashion [dwellings] for the gods, the best of sages, and the ancestors in the sky.
"O you who dwell within the cosmic egg, upon the surface of the earth at the city of sacrifice,
fashion the successive regions of the land in an instant;
indeed, I grant you a divine power whose essence is the fulfillment of every mental resolve."
"Accomplish quickly through that [mantra] this most excellent recitation of the ritual procedure (*kalpaklṛpti*).
Having spoken thus, the Blessed One ceased speaking and remained upon his own seat.
At that moment, King Rāyarokīśvara offered a prayer to Hari.
If you have the desire today,
purify my kingdom by coming to my city on the bank of the divine Mahākañjī river— a land of radiant women and forests— and [establish] the realm of Dvimānāyana.
"Purify me, O Hari-Kṛṣṇa; there is nothing inaccessible to you.
"So be it," Hari replied, and having drunk the cool water, he ascended the celestial chariot together with his mother and father.
Accompanied by Lālāyana and likewise accompanied by Māṇakya. ||76||
Accompanied by his attendants with divine bodies, by hundreds of male servants and female slaves,
and by his twelve principal chaste wives, he departed.
Then, in the city of Sphūrtinārīvana, the king and the sage, together with their attendants, immediately honored them from the sky for a brief moment.
Having descended into the garden near the royal palace, they both performed a formal welcome for Viṣṇu according to the prescribed rites, accompanied by their army.
Having washed their feet according to the prescribed rite, they drank the water as if it were nectar;
then, with great reverence, they honored him with sandalwood paste, flowers, and garlands.
The king and the sage also honored the others who were present with them;
then they led the Lord of Śrī from the palace to the royal residence.
The queen performed the *ārārtrika* rite for him ten times;
then the young princes and princesses performed the *nirājana* ceremony. ||82||
Hari revealed his own divine four-armed form to them;
and the twenty-one maidens were struck with wonder and amazement. (83)
The princess, being under her mother's influence and deluded by her mother's command,
then placed the garland of choice around the neck of Bālakṛṣṇa.
Having obtained Janārdana as their beloved, they felt their purpose was fulfilled;
the king indeed celebrated that beautiful festival in the royal palace.
The king placed wealth amounting to ten million at the feet of Hari,
and he also gave him a dowry consisting of golden necklaces and other such items.
He presented ornaments and garments and performed the lustration ceremony (nīrājana);
then, having bowed to Hari, he quickly begged forgiveness from the Lord.
I have been purified; having accepted the maiden, you have taken me by the hand and made me your own, O Blessed One. Always protect me from illusion. (88)
Then the queens, having bowed to Hari, placed the moonstone upon their foreheads;
they begged for forgiveness from Hari and entreated him, saying, "Please lift us up."
Hari said, "I shall uplift you and lead you at the end to the supreme state.
Thereupon, He concealed His own divine four-armed form.
After wandering throughout all the royal palaces,
Acyuta then proceeded to the houses of the chief ministers and purified them.
Having accepted the performed worship, the Lord, resplendent with his army,
proceeded along the royal highway in the city of Sphūrtinārīvanāpurī.
He was highly honored by spectators, worshippers, and the common people; his feet were saluted and revered, and offerings such as wealth and other gifts were presented to him. ||93||
He was made to hear songs of glory by the goddesses, delighted by their worship,
strengthened by their blessings, showered with flowers, and highly honored.
Praised with shouts of victory and the sounds of musical instruments, and drunk in by the lotus-eyes, the Supreme Lord, drawn by their inner feelings, departed.
Then all the leading merchants, the citizens, and the women, having accepted the honors, gave them offerings after wandering through the city. (96)
Having arrived at the royal palace, he drank the water of Mahākāñcī,
honoring the lordly sage named Mahākāñcana.
There the king gave wealth to him, but the sage took that money and,
having placed it upon the sacrificial chariot for the sake of the sacrifice, brought it to the place of worship.
Then Hari, together with his family, ascended a celestial chariot;
along with the king, the queen, and the maidens, he [departed] from the kingdom of Dvimāna.
Having wandered through the path of the sky and observed various regions and places,
he arrived at the shore of Lake Vinipāra in the evening.
Having descended into the royal palace, Hari went to rest;
those maidens, whose truth was Brahman, took up their residence with his beloveds.
Then both Rāyarokīśvara and the great sage Mahākāñcana indeed gave wealth to Kubera for the purpose of performing the sacrifice.
Then, from the sky, celestial chariots of the great-souled ones descended from the vast firmament;
they came also from Akṣara, from Goloka, from Vaikuṇṭha, and even from Amṛta.
From the indeterminate Īśa-loka, from Vairāja, and from the golden [Brahma-loka];
from Satya-svarga, from Janaloka, and from Meru and all the directions. || 104 ||
From the eightfold city and from the intermediate spaces between the worlds they arrived;
from the nether regions and from the three creations, celestial chariots arrived. (105)
For those who were invited, vehicles numbering in the hundreds of billions arrived;
indeed, the sky was completely covered by millions of celestial chariots.
Then there arose heaven after heaven, great heavens, and the heaven of Brahmā;
shining indeed like the sun, it became a second celestial realm.
O Rādhikā, the creation of living beings, the divine creation of the Lord, and the supreme creation of Brahmā—every kind of creation indeed came at your invitation. 10.8
There, at night, within a single hair-pore of Śrī Hari,
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara offered a welcome;
and the great deities descended from the sky to their appropriate places.

Thus ends the two hundred and third chapter, titled "The Description of the Instruction to King Rāya-Kinnara regarding the Commissioning of a Golden Image, the Dispatch of Nārada and Others to the Various Creations with Letters Inviting Them with Saffron Seals, Hari’s Journey to the Kingdom of King Rāyarokīśvara and His Worship, His Wandering through the City of Sphūrtinārī and the Country, His Return to the Sacrificial Ground, and the Arrival of the Great Honored Ones," in the second section, the Tretā-Santāna, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O Rādhikā, the liberated souls from the supreme imperishable abode (akṣaradhāman) arrived there,
as did other liberated women seated within divine celestial chariots.
Śrī Hari performed a most magnificent welcome for them;
the incarnations of Dhāmeśvara, adorned with their divine powers, arrived.
O Rādhā, accompanied by you and surrounded by hosts of cowherds and cowherdesses, I ascended a celestial chariot and went along with my divine wives. || 3 ||
Then Śrīpati Nārāyaṇa also came there from Vaikuṇṭha,
accompanied by all his attendants and joined by the goddesses of fortune (Ramās).
Vāsudeva and the other members of the Vyūha came to that sacrifice;
likewise, all the incarnations arrived, attended by their respective Śaktis.
The illustrious Bālakṛṣṇa himself personally offered them honor and a welcome;
so too did Mahāviṣṇu, Bhūmā, Virāṭ, and Hiraṇmaya.
The lords residing in the eight enclosures, though situated within Māyā,
as well as those who had reached the world of Śiva— parts of him— also arrived there.
Śrī Hari himself extended a welcome and honor to all those inhabitants of Brahmā’s creation who had been created by the Lord (Īśa). || 8 ||
The incarnation Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa, the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama), provided a dwelling in the city fashioned within the ether of consciousness-bliss.
The ṛṣis, the ancestors, and the siddhas residing in Brahmā’s world of truth (satyaloka), as well as those dwelling in other worlds, indeed arrived there at that sacrifice.
The gods, the lords of the gods, and the guardians of the quarters who protect the world—
those inhabitants of the atmospheric realm (bhuvarloka)— arrived at the sacrifice in their celestial chariots.
The planets and stars, the lunar mansions, the gods and others, the Vasus, and millions of Rudras also arrived from the sky at Mount Meru.
The Ādityas, the Aśvins, Dharmarāja, and other gods likewise arrived at the sacrifice,
accompanied by their own families as ornaments.
The hosts of Kailāsa, the Gaṇīs, the Yoginīs, as well as the Caṇḍikās,
the Bhairavas, and those with bodies of spirits— all these followers of Śaṅkara arrived there.
Hari gave suitable dwellings to these tens of millions of deities;
Brahmā, Īśvara, and Viṣṇu offered them a most cordial welcome and great honor.
Lomaśa and the other sages offered great honor to the Vālakhilya maharṣis and to the munis of perpetual celibacy.
They paid great honor to the virtuous, the righteous, and the female practitioners of Sāṃkhya and Yoga; Lakṣmī and the others provided them with abundant dwellings and comforts.
Charioteers, bards, panegyrists, and others; Vidyādharas, Kinnaras, and the like;
Kimpuṃsas, Gandharvas, Cāraṇas, and the various classes of professional singers.
Storytellers and entertainers arrived, as did wrestlers and actors; men who performed dances likewise came there.
People of all castes and inhabitants of all lands arrived there,
including the men of Saurāṣṭra and those dwelling in the Deccan.

The people dwelling in the land of the camels, as well as the people born in Brahmabhūmi, those residing in the kingdom of Śiva, and the inhabitants of the ancient kingdom—[all these were present]. ||21||
The inhabitants of Rāśīyāna, those dwelling in Ketumāla, the people of Abrikta, and likewise those residing in the Ārakta region. ||22||
Those who dwell in the Ārātri and Guhā regions, those who inhabit the Cāmara country, as well as the Hārita, the forest-dwellers, and the mountain-dwellers; ||23||
Those dwelling in the water, those dwelling on land, and those dwelling in the sky all arrived together;
and Hara and the other gods granted them dwellings and showed them honor.
Trees, creepers, grasses, shrubs, as well as bulbous roots, roots, and so forth—those born from seeds and those born from sprouts—all arrived there with divine bodies. (25)
Beasts and birds as well—those of the species of swans and Garuḍas—and other creatures too, possessing divine bodies, arrived there. (26)
Hara and the others granted them dwellings and bestowed honor upon them;
so too did all the progeny of Kaśyapa and all those who inhabit the netherworlds and below.
Serpents, nāgas, and lords of nāgas came as mounts;
fierce daityas, dānavas, and rākṣasas also arrived. ||28||
Śaṅkara, as well as Satī, bestowed honors upon those who resided on the southern shore of the lake, according to their merit. ||29||
Nara, Nārāyaṇa, and others, as well as Śeṣanārāyaṇa and other incarnations, likewise arrived there at that great sacrifice.
The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, being eager for them, offered them honor and welcome and granted them auspicious dwellings. ||3 1||
Then the rivers, streams, and oceans, as well as the principles of reality (tattvas), the foremost of brahmins, and the great sages with divine bodies, all approached you. ||32||
Clouds accompanied by flashes of lightning arrived there at that sacrifice;
then Brahmā offered them a welcome according to their merit.
Time—consisting of moments, instants, days, fortnights, years, yugas, and months—arrived; Śaṅkara offered them a welcome. (34)
Craftsmen residing in ten million worlds arrived there at that sacrifice;
Viśvakarman then bestowed great honor upon them and gave them dwellings.
Then Vāsudeva Nārāyaṇa indeed bestowed upon all those of great splendor various gifts and other honors as was appropriate for each. || 36 ||
O Rādhikā, in those dwellings everything is indeed complete—lamps, drinking vessels, and all kinds of foods to be chewed and eaten. (37)
There were sweet foods, drinks, and things to be licked;
there were also items to be sucked, seats and the like, and very soft, suitable beds. (38)
There were male and female servants with jars of milk, excellent rivers of nectar, beautiful gardens, and attendants—both male and female servants. (39)
By the resolve of Bālakṛṣṇa, millions of infinite servants were manifested in all dwellings as laborers who abide by his commands. (2.204.40)
There are instruments for hearing from afar and for seeing from afar, aerial vehicles, and the attainment of all powers such as the ability to touch anything at will. (41)
There, streams of ghee, streams of milk, and mountains of sugar were prepared on all sides for the satisfaction of the great lords. 42.
O Rādhikā, how can I describe them? Mountains of golden ornaments and likewise mountains of garments were fashioned by the Supreme Soul.
At that time, vats of fragrant lac were prepared there,
and there were also vast mountains of every kind of cosmetic article.
There were indeed long ponds, wells, lakes of juices,
and rivers of liquids for the enjoyment of those seeking to perform sacrifices.
Whatever kinds of opulences exist in Akṣara, Goloka, Vikuṇṭha, Kailāsa, and Śvetadvīpa, such opulences appeared there as well. 46.
All those dwelling in every creation forgot their pride upon attaining their respective and abundant prosperity at the sacrifice of Hari. 47.
And thus it continued until morning; indeed, in this very manner, there was a warm welcome, as well as food, service, drink, the offering of a bed, and clothing. (48)
At that time, the gift of male and female servants was entirely fulfilled;
the honored guests were delighted and cast off all fatigue. (49)
Having reached other abodes of bliss, they became exceedingly happy;
there, at every spot, were pleasure-pavilions for their delight during the night.
There were [performances] of dancers and the like, as well as stories, warriors, displays of form, comedians, and singers of songs. ||51||
And at night, there were entertainments of stories and dramas;
in the morning, however, the seventh day was likewise auspicious and pleasant. (52)
O Rādhikā, Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa, having been awakened, performed his bath, offered worship and salutations, and summoned the sage Lomaśa. (53)
And he commanded the sage, his guru, who had performed his salutation:
"Apply yourself to the sacrificial rites, you supreme seer of all. (54)
And Lomaśa said to Kṛṣṇa about that great sage, your disciple:
"He is a treasury of the Vedas and Śāstras, yet he transcends the sphere of ritual action. (55)
He was a knower of the three times, a master of mantras, endowed with the perfection of samādhi,
possessed of all sovereign powers, an incarnation of Kṛṣṇa, and a yogi of the Supreme Lord.
He is capable, the best among those who have reached the ultimate goal, possessing the power to manifest many forms; he is named Self-Luminous, the supreme witness of all.
Therefore, in this sacrifice, appoint that tranquil one, a storehouse of virtues and a worthy witness who possesses all-pervading movement. 58.
Then Viṣṇu, Brahmā, Hara, Bṛhaspati, Kumāra,
and Gaṇeśa indeed rejoiced in that which was fitting.
Bhāradvāja, Vasiṣṭha, Bhṛgu, Vaiśvānara,
as well as the Viśvedevas and the Maruts, likewise rejoiced in him.
The Lord is self-luminous and the great treasury of omniscience;
the word of the Guru and the word of Hari bestow the state of being an all-seeing witness. (6.1)
Then, being humble, that beloved of Śrī Kṛṣṇa accepted it;
he gave him a neck-garland and a helmet for his purpose.
He gave him a tunic enriched with golden stars, a silken garment,
and likewise a washed cloth that signified his status as an all-seeing witness.
Then he had a great and excellent seat prepared there in that pavilion,
and subsequently sent him into the sacrificial enclosure.
The Lord Mādhava himself gave the Gurvāsana to Lomaśa, who is the embodiment of existence, consciousness, and bliss, and who is the object of his affection. 65.
Then Bālakṛṣṇa indeed granted his own representative status;
at that time, the king who was the patron (yajamāna) was considered to be Rāyakinnaraka. ||66||
Accompanied by the great queen Satīdevī, he entered the pavilion;
at that auspicious moment, all kinds of musical instruments were sounded.
Those authorized for the sacrifice arrived from all directions;
the earthly gods, the celestial gods, and the gods of truth all assembled there. ||68||
The lords of gods, the gods of gods, and all the gods arrived;
likewise, the liberated ones, the incarnations, and the lords, accompanied by their wives, came together. (69)
The sages, the ancestors, the gods, and human beings accompanied by their wives—
the gurus of all the worlds, as well as the Vyāsas and those even more extensive than the Vyāsas— [all assembled].
The Vedas, the Ṛg-verses, and the Sāman-chants arrived, their very selves worthy of worship;
those advanced in age, advanced in knowledge, and proficient in ritual action also arrived. (71)
Those advanced in voice, advanced in prosperity, and advanced in virtue arrived;
those advanced in wealth, advanced in righteousness, and advanced in worldly experience arrived. (72)
Those advanced in yoga, advanced in austerity, and advanced in their station arrived;
those advanced in song, advanced in the Vedas, and the most venerable of the aged arrived. (73)
Those advanced in years arrived, and kings also came together;
likewise, reciters, ritual workers, performers of fire-offerings, and givers of gifts arrived as well.

The gatekeepers and those guarding the pavilion, both primary and secondary, arrived; those who carry the ritual materials, those who carry the oblations, and those who carry the fuel arrived as well. (75)
Those who had prepared the sacrificial pits during the night, those who filled the decorative patterns on the ground, and all those who carried the banners and flags arrived there. (76)
Those who take water, those who collect vessels, those who carry away goods, and those who carry away fruits and flowers arrived there. (77)
Carriers of juices, carriers of cow-products, and carriers of sweets arrived while the musical instruments roared loudly and the sky resounded with their noise. 78.
All of them, eager to behold the ground of the pavilion, arrived there—
those who move through the sky in the heavens and those inner yogis who dwell in the intermediate space.
Then the inhabitants of Bhuvarloka gathered and remained upon the wind,
while the dwellers of Svarloka stayed in their celestial chariots amidst the luminous realms.
Then they all arrived and stood facing the pavilion—
the virtuous, the chaste, the fair-complexioned, the beloveds of Brahmā, and those who had been won over.
The immortal maidens and all the goddesses also assembled;
the wives of the gods had dressed themselves and were adorned with variegated ornaments.
All of them, filled with full bliss, arrived at the sacrificial pavilion—both the wives of the lords, the liberated women, and those who were practitioners of Sāṃkhya and Yoga. (83)
The daughters of Manu and the mothers, as well as the Yoginīs, arrived; the female ascetics, the wives of Brahmā, and the Brāhmaṇī women also arrived. ||84||
The deities of the site, the deities of the sacrificial pits, and the deities of the branches arrived;
as did the deities of the doors, the gods of the arches and so forth, and the deities of the pavilion.
The deities of the pillars, the deities of the banners, and the deities of the sacrificial posts arrived;
as did the thirty-three subordinate deities and the deities of the five abodes.
Hearing the sounds of musical instruments, ten kings, accompanied by their wives and endowed with many jewels, went to the sacrificial pavilion. (87)
Having the nature of the sacrificer himself, they arrived at the sacrificial pavilion;
likewise, the elemental principles beginning with earth, as well as the objects of the senses such as sound and the rest.
The fires, assuming embodied forms, arrived at the sacrificial pavilion;
there were also various kinds of fire-pits and altars, including the principal altar.

The sacrificial altars and the offering vessels also arrived in embodied form; likewise, the ladles such as the *sruk* and *sruva*, the ritual vessels, the leaves, and the deities of the *kuśa* grass all came together.
Fuel-sticks, grains of parched rice, and sacrificial offerings also arrived there; even the sacred cooked oblations came there in embodied form. (91)
Purifying substances and products of the cow, as well as the seven types of earth, arrived; even the seats and ritual implements came there in embodied form.
Then the Jyotirpuruṣa, possessing a physical form and bearing a divine appearance,
approached while making all the quarters resound with the beating of a drum.
And the Golden Pillar Man arrived there in bodily form;
all the sacred fords, assuming embodied forms, also assembled there.
The auspicious ones, the personages of the *śrāddha*, and those who were satisfied arrived there for the sake of attaining the supreme and unprecedented, all of which were previously unknown. (95)
The Madhyāpūrva, the Trikāpūrva, and ten thousand others arrived there;
all the ritual procedures (*vidhi*) of the *Kāṇḍikās* and their sequential orders (*krama*) likewise assembled there. ||96||
All those who were to be offered as oblations arrived in embodied form—the subjects and the lords of subjects, including children, the elderly, and the youth. (97)
Men and women arrived at the site of the sacrifice with the sounds of musical instruments—a place consecrated, endowed with splendor, possessing celestial luster, and rendered imperishable. (98)
It was filled with pairs and singles, providing new life;
it shone with pavilions and was exceedingly proud of its sacrificial cities.
She is the most excellent earth, the abode of all creations;
she is the sovereign power of the Supreme Lord, equal to the divine light itself, and the source of all splendor.
O Rādhikā, when the most auspicious moment for the commencement of the rites arrived, the sounds of conch shells resounded. 10.1.
Then there arose sounds of trumpets accompanied by the roar of lightning and bamboo-pipes,
serving as omens for the commencement of the ritual section of the sacrifice.
The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the glorious Puruṣottama,
arrived swiftly at the pavilion, accompanied by the swelling sounds of victory.
He sat upon a divine throne in the pavilion near the sacrificial pit;
then the kings, having arrived, sat down in the vicinity of the pits.

Thus ends the two hundred and fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Welcome and Accommodation of All Guests, the Preparation of Necessities, the Ordinance for the Universal Witnessing by the Self-Luminous Incarnation of Hari at the Sacrifice, the Sounds of Auspicious Musical Instruments, and the Arrival of All the Goddesses and Gods at the Sacrificial Pavilion," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Rādhikā; in the morning, in the pavilion near the sacrificial pit, King Rāya-kiṃnara was [honored] by the sage Dvitrimāna.
Accompanied by his wife,
King Rāyarokīśvara, the patron of the sacrifice, arrived together with Mahākāñcanakarṣin.
Likewise, King Rāyarājajit, accompanied by his own wife and together with the sage Ālāya, arrived at the vicinity of the sacrificial pit.
Accompanied by his wife, King Rāyavākakṣaka likewise went to the pavilion near the sacrificial pit together with the beautiful Lāṣarṣi.
Accompanied by his wife, King Rāyamārīśa likewise went to the pavilion near the sacrificial pit at the sacrifice, joined by the donor of the rain.
Then King Rāyabāleśvara, accompanied by his wife and joined by the sage Mālāvana, went to the pavilion near the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
Then King Rāyalambāra, together with the queen and the sage Rūparṭu, went to the pavilion near the sacred pool.
Then, accompanied by his wife, King Rāyanavārka went to the vicinity of the sacrificial pit,
drawing his body toward Vāśṛṅga.
Accompanied by his wife, King Rāyahuṇḍeśa went to the sacrificial pavilion near the fire-pit,
together with the sage who was the father of Vīrāka.
And King Rāyakūpeśa, together with his wife and the sage Heyatāna, went to the pavilion near the sacrificial fire-pit.
Together with his wife, he went to the sacrificial pavilion near the fire-pits;
in this manner, the two kings purified ten fire-pits.
Then, each [of them] sat down in the vicinity of their respective fire-pits;
at that time, Śrī Hari, the lifelong celibate youth, was at the fire-pit of the preceptor.
Accompanied by Lomaśa and together with his wife, he sat down upon an excellent throne on the mountain of the Rāya-Kinnaras.
Accompanied by other sages and seers, the kings, who were devoted primarily to the Vedas and existed in the form of pairs as described by Lomaśa, settled down according to their respective stations.
Then, O Rādhikā, the celestial brahmins, the earthly brahmins, and the brahmins of Satyaloka began auspicious rites there with melodious voices. || 15 ||
The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa is seated upon an excellent throne within the Sarvatobhadra maṇḍala, facing the deity Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa.
Hari likewise established [the deity] and had all the forms installed,
including a golden Garuḍa, as well as the gatekeepers and the attendants.
Hari established those endowed with power in the presence of Viṣṇu;
the installation of Gaṇeśa was in the northeast, and the pedestal of Rudra was likewise placed there.
In the east is the Kṣetrapīṭha, and in the southeast is the Śaktiprapīṭhaka;
in the south is the Gaṇeśapīṭha, and in the southwest is the Vāstupīṭhaka. || 19 ||
In the northwest is the Yoginī-pīṭha, and likewise the Snāna-pīṭha in the north;
all the Graha-pīṭhas are located within the center of the intermediate corners.
And having placed those deities there, O Supreme Lord, he established them;
he then sprinkled the sacrificial pit, the pavilion, the altar, and the ritual substances within the pavilion.
And he set aside the principal grains, as well as the *kaṇa* seeds and fuel-sticks, along with barley, rice, *kuśa* grass, *dūrvā* grass, curds, sandalwood, and mustard seeds.
Also siddhārtha seeds, rocanā, fruits, and likewise sugar;
perfumes, flowers, betel nuts, as well as incense, lamps, and so forth. ||23||
There, the teacher Lomaśa performed an auspicious svastika ceremony,
as well as providing garments, wool, a seal-ring, a vessel, madhuparka, and other offerings.
[He offered] golden lamps, vessels for the ritual bath, conch shells, and so forth, as well as sandalwood, agallochum, musk, camphor, and saffron. ||25||
The vessel for clarified butter, the vessel for the sacrificial porridge, rice grains, and various utensils;
the sacred thread, seats, ritual hand gestures, ornaments, and beautiful flowers. ||26||
Then Hari placed the betel and other necessary items there;
thereafter, the patron, together with his wife, went to the bathing hall.
Having performed his ablutions in the pavilion, the king then went to Gaṇapati,
worshipped him, and also performed the Śrāddha rite for the Mothers.
Then, having performed the worship of his mother, he received the Vaiṣṇava initiation;
thereafter, he performed an expiation and then conducted a Vṛddhi-śrāddha ceremony.

Then the king performed the protection against planetary influences, the hoisting of banners, and the pitching of the camp; thereafter, he conducted the formal selection of the preceptor and the other officials.
Having announced the place and time, he then presented the honey-mixture (madhuparka);
he performed the selection of the officiating priests (ṛtvij) as well as the selection of the Brahman priest.
The selection of the preceptor, as well as the granting of seats, the ritual enclosures, offerings, and even the fee for the materials; || 32 ||
He performed the selection of reciters and readers in that same manner,
as well as the selection of thousands, tens of thousands, and millions of Brahmins.

The Brāhmaṇas, masters of the four Vedas, chanted the mantras appropriate for themselves; and the learned priests, conversant with the Āgamas, performed the rite of declaring the day auspicious (puṇyāhavācana).
Then the seven ṛṣis and all the great ṛṣis, numbering one hundred thousand, uttered words of auspiciousness and bestowed blessings. (35)
The king released the *vardhinī* pitcher filled with water from sacred fords;
he then placed gold, sprouts, and jewels therein. (36)
Then Śrī Lomaśa [beheld] there the primordial Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa,
accompanied by Rādhā, Lakṣmī, Prabhā, Śrī, Māṇikī, Bhū, and Pārvatī.
Śrīmad Bālakṛṣṇa himself established a golden image and worshipped it according to the prescribed rites; there he shone in person. || 38 ||
He installed a golden image of Śrī Kṛṣṇa accompanied by Rādhikā, and Nārāyaṇa accompanied by Śrī; and indeed, they appeared there in person.
At that time, he indeed established the incarnations endowed with power;
they all stood visibly there at the sacrifice, each upon his own seat.
At that time, he indeed established the military arrays (vyūhas) beginning with Vāsudeva;
those four became the primary divisions, while others stood as subordinate supports.
He established Bhūmā, Hiraṇyagarbha, Vairāja, and the Lords of the Āvṛtis;
they all remained present there in person.
Each endowed with their respective powers and accompanied by their respective retinues and others—Īśāna, Viśvasṛṭ, and Viṣṇu, each joined with their own power. (43)
Having been invoked, they assembled and shone forth: the objects of perception, Mahāmāyā, the Puruṣa, and also the principles (tattvas) along with their essential constituents (tāttvikas). 44.
The Śaktis also appeared, having been directly invoked;
all the beloved consorts of Brahmā, being summoned, arrived at the sacrifice. (45)
All [the gods] shone forth visibly upon their own seats in the pavilion;
Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, remained visibly present in his station as Brahmā.
Rudra, possessing eleven forms, remained in the station of Rudra,
accompanied by the Rudrāṇīs and by Gaṇeśa, Kārttikeya, and the other hosts.
The divine golden [deities] themselves sat upon their own seats, and likewise the invited ancestors and the great seers as well. 48.
The Maruts, Vasus, Sādhyas, Viśvedevas, and the lords of the gods appeared there in person at their respective seats during the sacrifice.
The lords of the quarters, the guardians of the world, and the deities of the spheres who had been invoked arrived together with their wives and sat upon their seats.
Then the supernatural powers, the treasures, the planets, the secondary planets and so forth,
the stars, and their movements, along with their consorts, were summoned.
All of them— the seven seers, the Vālakhilyas, the Kṛttikās, and the quarters— sat down directly upon their own seats, composed in meditation.
The Ādityas, Kāmadeva, the Manus, and likewise the Tithis,
having been invoked, appeared in person and stood present at the sacrifice.
The constellations, the digits, and the thirty-three gods;
the qualities, the circle of Yoginīs, the sacred fords, and likewise the rivers.
The oceans, long ponds, wells, lakes, mountains, and so forth, having been invoked, all arrived there in person with their beautiful forms. (55)
Yakṣas, rākṣasas, bhūtas, pretas, piśācas,
vināyakas, kūṣmāṇḍas, vetālas, and others were present at the great sacrifice.
Accompanied by their respective families, they came in person to that sacrifice;
having been invited, they then sat down fearlessly within the pavilion.
The bards, panegyrists, and minstrels, as well as the professional singers, wandering minstrels, kinnaras, vidyādharas, kiṃpuruṣas, gandharvas, and crores of siddhas; ||58||
They were directly invoked and arrived, standing in the pavilion—the four castes, ascetics, and holy men such as Sanaka and the others. ||59||
And all those lifelong celibates were invited and stood within the pavilion;
likewise Garuḍa, the swan, the elephant, the horse, and the lion.
The bull and the rat, having been invoked, arrived together;
seated upon the offered thrones, they shone visibly in that magnificent pavilion.
Hanumān and others, who are long-lived, were personally invoked in the pavilion; all of them, possessing the luster of Brahman, indeed arrived.

Likewise, the castes, the stages of life, and their duties, along with Dharmarāja followed by his attendants, together with Citragupta and others, and joined by Śrāvaṇa and the rest [were present]. ||63||
Time, the years and other divisions, and the Yugas, all endowed with physical forms and visible to all, stood invited within the pavilion.
Even creatures dwelling in water or on land, such as grasses and the like;
creepers and trees and so forth; and even those with bulbous roots, tubers, or roots—[all these were destroyed]. (65)
The deities of the pillars and so forth, as well as the household deities, the village deities, the forest deities, and those dwelling at the boundaries, arrived in person at the pavilion. (66)
Likewise, the forest-dwelling deities, the deities of the branches and the archways,
the deities of the pillars, the deities of the doors, and the deities of the sacrificial pits were present at that time.
Also the deities of the threshold, as well as the deities of the flower-pots, all the deities of the enclosure wall, and all the deities of the gate-towers. ||68||
Then, in that sacrifice, there were the deities of the courtyard, the deities of the corners, the deities of the beams,
the deities of the mats, the deities of the banners, and the deities of the jars.
The deities of the staffs and the deities of the seats, accompanied by their respective goddesses,
having been invoked, stood there visibly present in embodied form.
Then Dharmadeva, together with his wives, daughters, and sons, arrived there in embodied form; having been invoked, they came into that place.
The Dānavas and the hosts of Daityas, the progeny born of Kaśyapa and others, as well as birds, beasts, living beings, and reptiles—[all these were his offspring]. (72)
All the serpents, nāgas, and others who had been summoned arrived;
they entered the pavilion in embodied form and sat down upon the prepared seats. (73)
And those dwelling in all abodes, those inhabiting all worlds,
and those residing in all created realms were summoned there into that pavilion.

For those endowed with consciousness stood there in embodied form upon the seats offered to them, as did the insentient objects, the classes of the dull-witted, and all embodied beings who were wretched or protectorless. (75)
Having been granted the opportunity, they entered the pavilion offering words of praise,
bringing with them *kāśa* grass, *kuśa* grass, leaves, splinters, and sacrificial fuel.
There were also oblations for the gods and ancestors, such as fruits, flowers, grains, and so forth;
savory juices, various substances, sweet delicacies, sweet foods, and likewise tree barks.
Then, all the essences of fragrance, having taken form, arrived at that sacrificial altar and pavilion; they were invoked and stood there visibly present.
Herds of wish-fulfilling cows (kāmadhenu), embodied kalpa-vines,
kalpa-trees, and even wish-granting gems (cintāmaṇi) arrived there as well.
They are embodied treasuries of the Kalpas, millions of inexhaustible vessels;
they are the weapons such as the conch and the discus, as well as the sacrificial implements of the rites.
All the ritual implements, millions of vessels for the limbs of worship,
having been invoked, all remained present in the pavilion in embodied form.
The mantras, the Vedas, the injunctions, and the various forms of the ritual sections (karmakāṇḍa),
as well as the purifications, the apūrvas, and the deities in embodied form, were present in the pavilion.
Having been invoked, they arrived and took their seats as appointed;
likewise, the Svaras, the Vidyās such as Śāradā and others, as well as the Brahmavidyā and so forth.
The Gītis, the Sāman hymns, the Svāhā, Svadhā, and Vaṣaṭ families, and all types of fires were invoked within the pavilion. (84)
Then those preceptors of the gods and daityas—Vyāsas who were the very embodiments of exposition—sat down upon the seats that had been offered to them in bodily form. (85)
Austerities, methods of yoga, knowledge, detachment, as well as devotion and all supernatural powers, being summoned, arrived. (86)
Multitudes of women stood visibly before him in embodied form; those obstacles appeared in the guise of non-obstacles, and diseases took on the appearance of health. (87)
Then Duḥkhā, Adūḥkhā, Ākārī, Dharmavaṃśā, Adharma, and their wives also arrived. (88)
And those belonging to his lineage, having become gentle, also arrived at that sacrifice;
then Adharma, transforming his form, appeared in the guise of Dharma. (89)
Then Ānanda, happiness, peace, contentment, satisfaction, and the others were invoked and arrived in embodied forms within the pavilion.
The objects of the senses, beginning with sound, as well as the six sheaths and other bodily constituents—
all these embodied forms arrived in the pavilion when summoned.
O Rādhikā, this pavilion, endowed with all created things,
was as beautiful as the divine abode present at the beginningless appearance of Kṛṣṇa.
Since the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the beloved of Śrī Kṛṣṇa and the Lord of all, resides wherever he may be, what partiality can there be? 93.
Inert beings, conscious beings, and those that are a mixture of the inert and the conscious—all these lineages belong to Hari; He dwells equally within them all. (94)
Whether characterized by passion (rājasa), darkness (tāmasa), or goodness (sāttvika), all embodied beings—whether virtuous, divine, or full of bliss—are indeed yogis of the manifest form. ||95||
Having been invited, they arrived and sat down in the beautiful pavilion;
the giver and the priest were Kṛṣṇa himself, the eternal Supreme Lord.
In that state, there is indeed no deficiency, nor even any contraction;
poverty itself has then been transformed into magnanimity. (97)
Even the syllable *na* has gone there, transformed into the state of *hā*;
even doubt has gone there, transformed into the state of certainty. ||98||
Fear suddenly vanished, and he then attained fearlessness; deficiency was revealed, and he reached a state of excellence. (99)
Thus, O Rādhikā, the deities and others, having arrived there in person within that pavilion, sat down for their own installation.
Those very beings who were invisible in form were all present there in person by the will of Bālakṛṣṇa. || 10 1 ||
Thus, O Rādhā, in the pavilion with its ten sacrificial pits, the installation of all the gods took place upon the altars and other sites according to their respective requirements.
All the kings performed that very same sacrificial rite;
thereafter, worship was commenced as directed by those respective sages.

Thus ends the two hundred and fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Arrival of Kings and Sages at the Pavilion, the Installation of the Divine Seats, the Selection of the Ritviks and Ācāryas, and the Manifest Glory of the Visible Deities," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmīnārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Rādhikā, in the pavilion, Kṛṣṇa likewise stationed his golden parents, as well as Sūrya, Candra, Śaṅkara, Satī, and Gaṅgā. (1)
In accordance with the ritual prescribed by Lomaśa, Rāya Kinnararāja worshipped the supreme lord, the beginningless Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa.
There he also worshipped his mother and father;
then he offered them an invitation, a seat, water for the feet, and the respectful offering (arghya).
He gave water for sipping (ācamana) and water for purification;
then, for the sake of further cleansing, he offered milk, curd, ghee, and sugar.
Then he gave honey and water from sacred bathing places for the purpose of the consecration, as well as garments for cleansing and fragrant oil for massage. (59)
The offering of garments and ornaments, sandalwood paste, unbroken rice grains, and jasmine flowers; garlands of blossoms, collyrium and the like, incense, lamps, and saffron. || 6 ||
Tulasī, lotus garlands, food offerings, and a sacred thread; an umbrella, chowries, fans, food offerings, and excellent fruits—(7).
He offered water, betel-leaf, the waving of lights (ārātrika), and a sacrificial fee;
he performed praise, a request for forgiveness, prostrations, a full-body salutation like a staff, and an offering of handfuls of flowers.
Having worshipped Śrī Narāyaṇa with various modes of adoration,
he then honored his incarnations, the liberated ones, the lords, the gods, and the sages.
The king worshipped the ancestors, the goddesses, and the deities;
and thereafter, he performed the oblation of the *vyāhṛtis* as a constituent part of the expiation.
Then the king performed the Viṣṇu-śrāddha, beheld the face [of the deity],
and gave the gift of a vessel of clarified butter to the preceptor.
He heard recitations for peace that were well-composed and conducive to happiness;
having heard the auspicious benedictions, he indeed paid homage to his preceptor.
Then the sage Lomaśa performed the primary ritual act of the sacrifice;
he caused that king to make the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) and the resolve regarding the constituent parts (*aṅga-saṃkalpa*).
The king performed the worship of the Earth, Kūrma, and Ananta, established the lamps,
and, taking mustard seeds in his left hand, he performed the protection of the quarters.
Having scattered [the offerings] in every direction, the king struck the ground with his left hand and then performed the worship of the water-pot (kalaśa).
Having invoked the sacred fords (tīrthas) into the water, he performed the sprinkling upon his own body;
with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), he performed the sprinkling of the sacrificial materials.
He performed the worship of Gaṇeśa directly with dūrvā grass and other materials,
as well as the worship of the surrounding deities (āvaraṇa-pūjana) with the sixteen types of offerings (upacāras).
Then he performed the worship of the Mothers beginning with Gaurī;
having performed the worship of the Mothers beginning with Brāhmī, the king then proceeded.
He performed the Nāndī-śrāddha and the libation (tarpaṇa) for the ancestors, which bring about their satisfaction;
then he performed the offering of water (arghya) and salutation, and wound a thread around the ritual pitcher (kalaśa).
He cast forth medicinal herbs, flowers, the five sprouts, and jewels;
he also threw fruit, gold, earth, grain, and dūrvā grass.
Then he performed the selection of the preceptor, followed by the selection of the Brahmā and other officiants,
the selection of Gaṇeśa, and the selection of the gatekeepers.
He performed the selection of the officiating priests and offered them the madhuparka;
he then partook of the madhuparka himself and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana).
Then the king gave wealth for the purchase of the cow to the brāhmaṇa,
and he also requested his spiritual preceptor, the illustrious Bālakṛṣṇa Lomaśa.
Then the sage Lomaśa applied a tilaka mark upon the king's forehead,
and he tied a protective thread on the queen's left hand for her safeguarding.
Then he also performed the rite of proclaiming an auspicious day (puṇyāhavācana) and placed a water-filled jar together with a full vessel upon the grain.
He placed [the vessel], worshipped the jar, and performed the libation with its waters;
then Lomaśa conducted the consecration of the patron.
The king also performed the installation of the Vardhanī jar;
having circumambulated it, he placed it within the pavilion.
Lomaśa caused a water-procession to be performed, accompanied by jars, auspicious women, musical instruments, vehicles, and the chanting of hymns. (28)
Having worshipped Varuṇa, Gaṇeśa, and Jalamātṛ at the sacred ford (tīrtha),
he also worshipped the water, Jīvamātṛ, and Sthalamātṛ.
May the Mothers of Water— the Fish-woman, the Tortoise-woman, the Boar-woman, the Frog-woman, the Crocodile-woman, as well as the Leech-woman and the Spider-woman— be satisfied.
May these seven mothers of life— Kumārī, Dhanadā, Nandā, Vimalā, Maṅgalā, Calā, and Padmā— be fully satisfied.
May Urmī, Lakṣmī, Mahāmāyā, Pānadevī, Vāruṇī, Nirmalā, and likewise Godhā—the Mothers of the Land—be satisfied. 3.2.
Then he also worshipped the circle of the sixty-four Yoginīs;
he fully honored the Kṣetrapāla, the host of Tīrthas, and Varuṇa.
