He performed the installation of the water-pot (kalaśa) and the worship of the Kṣetrapāla; then, having arrived at the pavilion accompanied by the water-pot, [he proceeded]. (34)
And the king worshipped the deities presiding over the door-panels;
having adorned the threshold with a circular ornament and having bowed to the site (vāstu), he paid his respects.
Then the sage Lomaṣa performed the ritual for establishing the site;
having prepared the sacrificial altar of the site (vāstupīṭha), he worshipped Gaṇeśa.
Having invoked the sixty-four deities of the site and worshipped them thoroughly, the sage Lomaśa fully honored the water-pot.
The sage worshipped the Vāstu-mūrti in the pitcher with the sixteen-fold offerings and other rites;
then, having performed the external fire-oblation, he presented the sacrificial offering (bali) to it.
Then he performed the worship of the pavilion and the worship of its pillars;
he worshipped the deities of all the corner pillars as well as the central deities. ||39||
Then the king worshipped the deities of the gates and archways;
thereafter, he performed the worship of the Vedas, the worship of the emblems, and the worship of the branches.
He worshipped the deities of the tree in the water-pot according to the prescribed rite; he offered an oblation of mung beans to the spirits and other beings, and then withdrew.
He worshipped the beautiful Sarvatobhadraka maṇḍala, which was filled with deities;
there, in that maṇḍala, he honored the thirty-three deities.
In the center [he saw] that Anādikṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the incarnate one, together with all his consorts, Rādhākṛṣṇa, the glorious Narāyaṇa. ||43||
He worshipped the incarnations endowed with power, even though they were not [supreme] lords;
likewise, he worshipped all the goddesses of the lords and other female powers.
The liberated souls and their consorts likewise worshipped the imperishable abode, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who was joined by Rādhikā and accompanied by the hosts of cowherds and cowherdesses. 45.
Then he worshipped the Lord Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa, together with His beloved consort, His attendants, and Garuḍa. 46.
The king worshipped with female attendants and the retinues of the goddesses;
he performed the worship of Gaṇeśa and the propitiation of the Vāstu deity.
Then the king performed the worship of the lords—namely Brahmā, Soma, Īśāna, and Indra as well. (48)
He worshipped Agni Vaivasvata, Rakṣas, Varuṇa, Vāyu, Kubera, the Vasus, and also the eleven Rudras. ||49||
There he also worshipped the twelve Ādityas and the two Aśvins;
he honored the Pitṛs, the Viśvedevas, and the seven sacrifices.
He worshipped the serpents, the Gandharvas, the Apsarases, Skanda,
Nandīśvara, Mahākāla, the trident, and the group of seven beginning with Dakṣa.
Likewise, he worshipped Durgā and Viṣṇu, as well as Vaiṣṇavī;
he fully honored Svadhā, Svāhā, Mṛtyu, Rogas, and Gaṇeśa.
He worshipped Varuṇa, the lord of sacrifices, and the Maruts;
he also worshipped the Earth, the river Gaṅgā, and all other rivers. ||53||
The king worshipped the seven oceans and Mount Meru;
he worshipped all his weapons and all the sacred fords.
He worshipped the divine ornaments as if they were embodied beings, and he also worshipped the most eminent great sages, such as Bhāradvāja and others. ||55||
He likewise worshipped Arundhatī and other goddesses there;
the king also properly worshipped the wives of all the world-protectors.
She indeed worshipped all the lords, the ancestors, the sages, the gods, and the seers, as well as virtuous men and women, and all the female practitioners of Sāṃkhya and Yoga. ||57||
He also worshipped all the Kuṣmāṇḍakas, Vināyakas, Vetālas, Rākṣasas, and Pretas who dwell in the Bhuvarloka. ||58||
There, the king honored all the messengers of Yama—those born of the lineage of Dharma as well as those born of the lineage of Adharma—both women and men. (59)
He worshipped the mountains, forest trees, creepers, species of grass,
clusters of blossoms, bamboo varieties, and even the sources of fluids.
He worshipped root-tubers, fruit-bearing trees, as well as those born from a womb and those born from eggs;
he honored all creatures, both minute and large, including those dwelling in the waters.
He also paid great honor to all the Kāśyapī offspring born from sweat,
as well as those born from the earth, from the wind, from fire, and even those born from excavations.
He worshipped all embodied beings born of the earth and those born of water—
whether they were sattvic, rājasic, or embodied beings of the tamasic nature, even if they were impure.
Then he honored the poor, the helpless, and even the mendicants—
those who were without refuge, dependent on others, and living off the fortune of others.
He honored his groups of servants, his distant attendants, and his groups of slaves;
as well as those who knew the arts, those skilled in crafts, and those who performed drama and dance.
He honored the charioteers, bards, panegyrists, and other storytellers,
as well as the dull elements, the specific principles, the qualities, and the unprecedented musical notes.
The king honored all the mantras and the objects of the senses,
as well as the songs, the embodiments of the Vedas, the sacrificial vessels, and the excellent grains.
He honored all the crops, the sacrificial fuel, and even the offerings—
whatever things were there at that time in the sacrificial pavilion by Hari himself.
The spirits were summoned and arrived at the festival, even those of lowly names and those possessing lowly bodies. (69)
Then the Supreme Lord worshipped His entire creation, regarding it as His own offspring, in His own Vaiṣṇava sacrifice.
The hosts of Daityas and Dānavas residing in Pātāla, who had the forms of Nāgas,
as well as those dwelling in the world of Dhāma, had indeed assembled in the pavilion.
Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the bestower of happiness, honored everyone;
indeed, Hari himself honored even the insects, moths, and other such creatures.
Having offered the sacrificial oblation (bali) to all, he indeed gratified those in his own sacrifice—
namely Saṃkarṣaṇa and the others, as well as the yogis beginning with Sanaka.
[He worshipped] all the attendants beginning with Viṣvaksena, the deities of the yantras,
Śuka and others, the paths of knowledge and yoga, and the Keśavas beginning with Matsya.
Then the king worshipped all those beginning with Praṇava and Śāradā, as well as the incarnations beginning with Ṛṣabha and Viśvāmitra. ||75||
The powers beginning with Brāhmī, as well as the supernatural attainments (siddhis) such as aṇimā;
likewise the guardians of the directions, their weapons, the Vedas, and the Gaṅgā and other [sacred rivers]. ||76||
Then the king worshipped the deities of the mantras along with their families;
thereafter, he performed the rite of bringing fire (agnyuttāraṇa) and anointed the embodied forms with ghee.
Having performed the consecration with streams of water, he [should contemplate] the vital breaths together with their seed-syllables:
here the vital breaths are ĀṂ HRĪṂ KRAUṂ YAṂ RAṂ LAṂ VAṂ ŚAṂ ṢAṂ SAṂ HAṂ. (78)
With the mantra "saḥ so'ham" and others, he performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) using seed-syllables (bījas) for all the golden images there in the pavilion.
Hari also performed worship again for those who had been established there— namely,
for his own father, his mother, and likewise for his sister.
And likewise the auspicious [form] of the brothers, of Gaṇeśa, of Rādhā-Kṛṣṇa, as well as of Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa and of Padmā. ||81||
Likewise, [he gave] a golden [image] of Ramā, as well as one of Māṇikī;
and also golden [images] of Sūrya, Candra, and Īśāna.
And Satya worshipped a golden image for the purpose of consecration;
he worshipped all the images for the sake of the sixteen vital breaths (prāṇavāsa). ||83||
Then Kṛṣṇa recollected the creation of Brahmā, the creation of Īśa, and the creation of the individual soul (jīva); at that time, he brought to mind the forms of his incarnations.
All the divine deities, who consist of all the principles (tattvas), arrived and took their places within the pavilion upon the images and other objects. 85.
Having thus installed the images according to the prescribed rite and having endowed them with life, Bālakṛṣṇaka entered into those conscious forms. (86)
Then, with the approval of Kṛṣṇa, the king performed the worship of the sacred seat (pīṭha-pūjā), as well as the worship of the Supreme Deity and the worship of the Guru. ||87||
He worshipped Vedavyāsa, Garuḍa, Durgā, and Sarasvatī, as well as Yama, Vāyu, Śiva, Indra, Nirṛti, and Rudra.
He worshipped Śakti, Kūrma, Ananta, the Earth, and the Mountain;
he honored the Ocean of Milk, Śvetadvīpa, the Pavilion, and the Lotus. ||89||
Even the solar orb is the golden Nārāyaṇa;
even the lunar orb is the divine Viṣṇu, Nārāyaṇa.
In the fire-pit, she worshipped the god Agni, Nṛsiṃha, and Narāyaṇa; she worshipped Sattvaśrī, Rajobhūmi, and Tamodurgā.
He worshipped the Self, the Inner Self, and the Supreme Self;
he worshipped Jñānātman and the Pīṭha-śaktis beginning with Vimalā. ||92||
He worshipped Pradhānapuruṣa and Prakṛtipuruṣa, as well as the worship of the Kuṇḍa and the worship of Viśvakarman. || 93 ||
Mekhalā worshipped Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and Rudra;
she then performed the worship of the yoni, the worship of the throat, and the worship of the navel.
Then the king named Rāyakinnara worshipped the deities of the site, as well as Brahmā and the others, the Vedas, and the tortoise and other [mythical beings]. (95)
Having worshipped the deities beginning with Dharma, he then performed the installation of the fire in the mandala;
having drawn the fire into the *sampuṭa* vessel, he circled it three times.
He established the fire in the sacrificial pit, Svāhā on the right and Svadhā on the other side;
he worshipped them according to the prescribed rite, and thereafter performed the drawing forth of the Praṇītā water.
The strewing of grass, as well as the placing of the vessels, the purification, and likewise the sprinkling with water; ||98||
Turning [the vessel] face upwards, pointing it towards the quarters, sprinkling, washing, as well as pouring, placing on the fire, and likewise encircling with fire; ||99||
The divine Lomaśa performed the rite of installing the planetary deities;
he worshipped the nine planets and likewise worshipped their presiding deities.

Then, one should perform the worship of the respective presiding deities (pratyadhidevatās) and the worship of the world-protectors (lokapālas), as well as the installation of the guardian of the field (kṣetrapāla) and the installation of the guardians of the directions (dikpālas). || 101 ||
He performed the installation of Mahārudra and their worship;
thereafter, he also performed the worship of the sixty-four Yoginīs.
Then he performed the worship of the fifty guardians of the fields (kṣetrapālas),
as well as the Supreme Lord, his incarnations, the Īśvaras, and the deities.
The king then meditated and caused the tilaka mark of Hari to be applied;
he also gave him a garland of tulasī and then offered him a [sacred] wreath.
And the king, indeed, while worshipping, offered a conch, a discus, and so forth,
as well as the mark of a fish, a trident, a bow, and an arrow.
Then he worshipped the svastika, the banner, the wheel, and the thunderbolt;
he performed the worship of the bell and conducted the worship of the water-pots.
Lomaśa performed for him the purification of the earth (bhūśuddhi), as well as the salutation (namaḥ),
the seat (āsana), the binding of the crest-lock (śikhābandhana), and likewise the binding of the directions (digbandhana).
He likewise performed the clapping of hands three times and the striking of the ground three times;
he practiced the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) and worshipped Kuṇḍalinī.

Having worshipped the six chakras, the King then worshipped the individual soul (jīva) as Brahman; and having meditated upon the burning away of the personification of sin (pāpapuruṣa), he performed that [rite].
The king performed the immersion of his body and likewise the purification of himself;
he also performed the consecration of life-force (prāṇapratiṣṭhā) along with the renunciation (sanyāsa) accompanied by seed-syllables (bījākṣara).
Having performed the recitation together with the ritual empowerment (*śakti*), he should perform the worship,
as well as the installation of the vital breath (*prāṇasthāpana*) for the deities of the five enclosures (*pañcāvaraṇa*).
Then he performed the internal placement of the Mātṛkā (antarmātṛkā-nyāsa), the external placement of the Mātṛkā (bahirmātṛkā-nyāsa),
and likewise the eleven placements (nyāsas) of Śrī Hari.

He then performed the placing of the ritual vessels and the offering of lamps; likewise, having prepared the water for the worship of the digits of the moon and having especially offered the arghya water.

O Rādhikā, in the sacrificial pavilion, the king worshipped the vessels for water for the feet, the respectful offering, water for sipping, sprinkling, and the honey-mixture according to the prescribed ritual.

Thus ends the two hundred and sixth chapter, titled “The Description of the Worship of the Golden Image, the Worship of Gaṇeśa, the Installation of the Water-Pot, the Maṇḍala, the Establishment of Vāstu, the Worship of the Lord of All Lords and other Devas, the Worship of the Devas, Goddesses, Yoginīs, Kṣetrapālas, the Self, and others, as well as the Purification of the Body, the Worship of Brahmā, and the Establishment of the Sacred Fire,” in the second section (Tretā-santāna) of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O Rādhikā, they worshipped the Lord of Śrī, King Ādikṛṣṇa Narāyaṇa,
along with His family, using the most magnificent and grand offerings.
Meditation, the formal invocation, the proper seat, water for the feet, the respectful offering (arghya), water for sipping (ācamana), the honey-mixture (madhuparka), milk, curd, ghee, and honey. (2)
She gave him sugar, an ointment, and pure water;
she provided a fragrant consecration bath and the cleansing of his garments.
He gave a garment, a sacred thread, ornaments, and a garland;
he gave sandalwood paste, saffron, collyrium, and unbroken grains of rice.
He also took up clusters of flowers and *tulasī* leaves;
he performed the worship of the limbs (*aṅgapūjā*) as well as the worship of the enclosures (*āvaraṇas*).
The worship of Śrī Hari, of His female attendants, and of His divine manifestations;
and the worship of His personal associates and the forms of His incarnations. || 6 ||
Likewise, there is the worship of the [goddesses] who have descended, the worship of the attendants (pārṣadas),
and the thorough worship of the weapons and their sovereign manifestations.
Likewise, there is the honoring of vehicles, as well as servants and slaves;
and the honoring of female slaves, sons, grandsons, and family members.
He indeed performed the honoring of the household guardians and the honoring of the gatekeepers;
[he offered] white powder, red powder, vermilion, and turmeric.
He offered incense, a lamp, lac-dye, food offerings, water, fruit, the apōśana rite, hand-paste, betel-leaf, and a priestly fee.
He gave him an umbrella, chowries, a fan, and a mirror;
he then offered the sandals, all manner of ornaments, and the lustration ceremony (nīrājana).
He performed the waving of garments, the waving of water, prostrations, circumambulation, and a full-length prostration; he offered praise and presented a handful of flowers.
Then the king himself performed the fire-oblation;
first, while the sacrificial porridge was being placed upon the heated vessel, he carried out the heating of the *sruva* ladle.
The wiping, the sprinkling, the heating, and the placing [of the vessel];
likewise, the lifting out of the clarified butter and the lifting out of the sacrificial porridge.
Then, with the two strainers (*pavitra*), one performs the purification of the clarified butter (*ājya*), its inspection,
the removal of any foreign substances, and likewise the purification of the sprinkling water (*prokṣiṇī*).
Having performed the sprinkling and the placement [of the fire], the king offered the oblation;
then, during the sacrifice, Brahmā performed the two Āghāra libations and the two Ājyabhāga portions.
He presented sacrificial materials such as *samic*, *caru*, parched grain, clarified butter, and so forth,
to the Supreme Lord, the Great Lord, and likewise to the Lord of Creatures.
To the guardians of the directions, likewise to the lords, and also to the world-protectors; to the nine planets, to the gods, and to the multitude of presiding deities. (18)
Then the king offered the oblation to the deities presiding over the higher realms,
and after that, he offered the oblation to the deities of the Vāstu-maṇḍala.

Then he offered *samit* grass, sesame seeds, milk-rice, and other offerings, as well as excellent fuel-sticks of *udumbara*, *aśvattha*, and other trees, along with clarified butter, honey, and milk. (2.207.20)
In that manner, the king performed the fire-oblation for the deities of the maṇḍala as was appropriate;
he offered the oblation with various distinct fruits and diverse ritual substances.
He offered oblations with clarified butter and other substances to the deities beginning with Brahmā,
and he also offered oblations with clarified butter and other substances to the deities of the sacred seats (pīṭha).
Then, with fuel-sticks, sesame seeds, clarified butter, sacrificial porridge, and milk-rice,
he indeed performed the primary oblation ten thousand times.
Then the king offered oblations to the obstructing demons;
he performed the *vyāhṛti* sacrifice with grapes, sugarcane, betel nuts, oranges, sesame seeds, and clarified butter.
And he gave citron, pomegranate, and likewise a khārikā measure [of grain],
coconut, pomegranate, guggulu resin, mustard seeds, and so forth.
Then the king himself offered milk, sugar, plantains, and ghee to Lakṣmī, as well as fruits, dūrvā grass, and unbroken grains, and performed the fire-oblation (homa).
Then he offered perfume, flowers, incense, lamps, and food offerings;
thereafter Brahmā performed the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation and the nine *āhuti*s.
And to all the gods, as was appropriate, he offered oblations;
to the guardians of the quarters, he gave an offering of milk-rice (pāyasa) accompanied by lamps.
The king offered the sacrificial oblation (bali) to Gaṇeśa, to the Mothers, to the Vāstu-deities, to the Lord of the Site (Vāstupuruṣa), and likewise to the Ādityas and the other gods.
The king offered bali-offerings to the yoginīs and the kṣetrapālas;
he also offered bali-offerings to the deities of the principal maṇḍala.
He offered oblations along with worship to the fifty-six deities,
and he also offered oblations to Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa and Rādhā-Kṛṣṇa.
And to Nara-Nārāyaṇa-Vāsudeva-Nārāyaṇa,
and to Anādi-Śrī-Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, he offered his own oblation.
The king offered oblations to all the powers of Hari,
and thereafter the king offered oblations to all the beloved wives of Brahmā.

He also offered the bali-offering to the guardians of the quarters (dhāmapāla), likewise the bali-offering to the guardians of the wives (dārapāla), the bali-offering to the guardians of creation (sṛṣṭipāla), and the bali-offering to the guardian of the field (kṣetrapāla).
Then the king offered the sacrificial oblation to those dwelling in cities, villages, fields, and so forth; he likewise offered the oblation to those residing in houses, forests, and woods. (35)

And he offered oblations to those dwelling in the netherworlds (pātāla) and so forth, as well as to those residing on earth and in heaven, and to those situated in the atmospheric world (bhuvarloka) up to the world of truth (satyaloka).
And from those dwelling in the Āvaraṇa [worlds], he received [offerings] from the inhabitants of Vairāja and Loka; and from those dwelling in the golden, unmanifest Goloka, he received them.

He offered oblations to those residing in Vaikuṇṭha and the imperishable abode, to those situated within Māyā, and likewise to sentient beings, insentient things, and to both embodied and disembodied entities.
Then the king offered oblations to the principles (tattvas) as was appropriate;
he gave oblations to the superior and the inferior beings as was fitting.
Then, to all those who had been invited and were standing in the pavilion,
including both men and women, the king gave auspicious offerings.
Those who were invited and arrived at the sacrifice, as well as those who did not arrive, along with their families, servants, attendants, and followers. ||41||
Together with their wives and lineages, and endowed with the qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas—
those who are born from the three guṇas are the Sādhyas, whose forms consist of both the means and the ends.

Those whose essence is sacrifice, whose bodies are sacrifice, who are the limbs of sacrifice, and who depend upon the ritual—all of them were there, and the king offered them their appropriate sacrificial fees (bali). ||43||
In all the sacrificial pits, these kings, impelled by their respective gurus and ṛṣis, offered the bali-oblation and likewise performed every ritual act accordingly.
The gods who are recipients and enjoyers, as well as those who consume the oblations—whether they be asuras or embodied beings—took their own offerings by the hand. (45)
It was directly perceived by you that they had eaten; it was directly perceived in their own moment that all those embodied beings there attained satisfaction while eating.
Whatever food belonged to whichever beings, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, having mentally resolved it, gave that very thing to each of them as was appropriate. 47.
All those inhabitants of the three worlds were satisfied to their very throats;
likewise, the principles of Māyā, those born of Māyā, and the embodied beings consisting of Māyā. 48.
The self and the principles arise from the self; likewise, embodied beings belong to the self.
The Lord and the principles arise from the Lord; likewise, embodied beings belong to the Lord. ||49||
The liberated principles arise from the Liberated One, and likewise embodied beings belong to the Liberated One;
the Brahman-principles arise from Brahman, and likewise embodied beings belong to Brahman.
The powers, the principles, those arisen from power, as well as the embodied beings, and whatever else there may be—such as qualities, sovereignty, weapons, ornaments, and so forth. 51.
Having offered oblations there to all [the deities], Śrī Hari, the Lord and Sovereign of All, indeed granted them eternal satisfaction, which is His own. 52.
In that sacrifice of the Supreme Lord, all the people attained such great satisfaction that they vomited their food and likewise ate until it reached their throats. ||53||
Those born from a womb, those born from an egg, those born from a sprout, and likewise those born from sweat;
those composed of the elements, those born from a sheath, those arisen from mud, and those arisen from sap. (54)
Everyone there attained satisfaction at the sacrificial fire of Bālakṛṣṇa;
then Lomaśa offered the final oblation into that sacrificial pit.
He performed a homa with many oblations, including ten thousand *vasordhārā* offerings;
thereafter, he provided relief for the gods and prepared their bed.
In this way, O Rādhikā, the offerings and other rites are indeed performed constantly until midday;
thereafter, Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa and the others [are worshipped].
Likewise, the high-ranking officials and others provided meals;
indeed, all the subjects provided meals constantly.
On the seventh, eighth, ninth, and tenth days,
as well as on the eleventh, the sacrificial rites are likewise performed constantly.
And there, various foods were always available;
countless embodied beings ate there day and night. (2.207.60)
"Give! Give! and "Eat!
Eat!"—such was the constant proclamation regarding the gift of food.
Aṇṇapūrṇā, Lakṣmī, and their many attendant powers serve you with gifts of food and other necessities as required by each individual according to their station.
Kalpalatās, kalpadrumas, and kalpagāvas were present without interval;
likewise, kalpakanyās, cintāmaṇis, and kalpacullikās.
The wish-fulfilling lakes, the wish-fulfilling vessels, the wish-fulfilling rivers and so forth,
as well as the wish-fulfilling chests, fill the desires of supplicants with whatever food they long for.
At the conclusion of the meal, all the people rested especially;
meanwhile, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa was entreated by the king.
Following the invitation, she proceeds to the royal palace;
then again in the evening, she returns here to the pavilion by means of a celestial chariot.
In this manner, Hari wandered through the kingdom for five days;
by the sequence of his movements, all the lands were purified.
The Blessed One bestows crores of sacrificial fees at the sacrifice,
and outside of the sacrifice as well, he grants whatever is desired even to a petitioner.
"Deyaṃ deyaṃ ca dātavyam"—this word indeed possesses such meaning that, when uttered before Hari, it truly bestows the fruit of all sacrifices. (69)
It is given constantly as desired; even kings give, and the subjects also give wealth when they find the opportunity.
The subjects performed various acts of giving, such as the donation of houses and the giving away of daughters in marriage; they also bestowed gifts of learning, ornaments, and garments. (71)
Where the Lord, the Supreme Brahman, the Consort of Śrī, the Beloved of Kṛṣṇa, is the agent, the giver, and the enjoyer, there indeed no inauspiciousness exists anywhere. 72.
Where the Lord of Light resides, there is no obstacle and no prohibition;
there is no time, no Yama, and no bondage in the Supreme Lord. (73)
Neither birth-impurity, nor grief, nor even ill omens exist there, nor is there an inauspicious moment, wherever the illustrious Pārvatīśvara resides. (74)
Everything indeed becomes auspicious where the Lord, the husband of Lakṣmī, resides;
everything indeed becomes nourished where the husband of Śrīmāṇikī resides. (75)
Everything becomes favorable and dear, and everything bestows prosperity, wherever the Supreme Lord, the Divine, resides. ||76||
Indeed, every auspicious thing arises where Mādhava is present; since all opposing forces are under his control, what contradiction could possibly exist in his presence? (77)
O Rādhikā, Śrī Hari thus performed the auspicious festival of the sacrifice;
then, O King, after midday on the seventh day and following his meal—
Then King Rāyarāṇajit entreated the Supreme Lord, saying, "Please come so as to purify my own kingdom. (79)
Hari said, "So be it," and then he quickly became ready,
as did the king Raṇajit and the great sage-king Ālāya.
Having quickly received the command of Hari, [he departed] by means of a celestial chariot for his own abode,
the city of Kṛṣṇa-pattana, situated in the region of Ālakṣā-kapa, where the sun is like a fish.
Then, having gone before him who was situated on the bank of the river Yūkāsana, he quickly [approached] together with his army and attendants, intent upon the circle of musical instruments. ||82||
The people, crowding together, adorned the king as was fitting;
and the royal attendants brought gifts for the sake of welcoming him. (83)
They arrived very quickly at the king’s vast garden;
then musical instruments were played and banners were hoisted in the sky. (84)
The sounds of musical instruments resounded for the welcome of Śrī Hari;
indeed, everything was prepared and adorned by the king within a single hour.
Meanwhile, the Blessed Lord, beloved of Śrī, was [attended] by his two parents, by Śaṅkara,
by Lomaśa, by the Īśas, and by the incarnations and the lords of the gods.
Together with those who were present, such as Rādhā, Lakṣmī, and others, he quickly ascended his own celestial chariot, illuminating the ten directions.
He went to the city of Mīnārka-kṛṣṇa on the bank of the Yūkāsanā river,
where he beheld the glorious aerial chariot of the Supreme Lord, which was like the sun.
King Rājaranajit and the excellent sage Ālāya both indicated a spot on the ground for the purpose of the descent of the celestial chariot.
Having circled through the very sky, that celestial chariot descended;
at that time, musical instruments and drums were sounded again and again.
Auspicious shouts of "Victory! and cries of joy arose from the people; they rushed with great speed to his side in order to behold him.
The subjects increase [his prosperity] with parched grain, unbroken rice, and fragrant substances,
as well as with flowers, offerings made with joined palms, and the casting of their glances.
They honored the Imperishable One with gifts of devotion, welcoming words, and other offerings.
O Rādhikā, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa was brought down from his celestial chariot by the king. 93.
Taking one hand by another, he was brought outside with great affection;
the king indeed placed a garland of flowers around the neck of Bālakṛṣṇa.
The sage worshipped the Supreme Lord with an offering of sandalwood;
the princes and others likewise honored him with garlands and other gifts. (95)
Having remained for a moment at the front of the celestial chariot and having granted his own vision,
Hari descended and accepted the worship offered by the people.
All the subjects attained happiness through his worship and his very sight;
thereafter, he entered the interior of the royal palace and sat upon an auspicious throne.
Hari sat down, and others sat upon appropriate seats—the king, the queen, the princesses, the princes, and the householders. (98)
They worshipped the Lord of Śrī, the beloved of Kṛṣṇa, with supreme affection; and out of intense devotion, the king gave ten lakhs of gold.
The king gave diamonds worth ten million to Kṛṣṇa;
twenty maidens indeed placed garlands upon Kṛṣṇa’s neck.
Then the queen gave those twenty daughters to the glorious Bālakṛṣṇa,
having obtained Bālakṛṣṇa as her husband and lord.
Having accomplished their purpose, they then drank the milk;
thereafter, at the city named Mīnārkakṛṣṇa by means of a white elephant.
Honored by great armies, he dwelt from house to house;
all the leading merchants honored him at every place.
Having wandered through the beautiful city, Śrī Hari arrived at the royal palace; O Rādhikā, assuming a state of tranquility, he gave instruction.
Thus, it brings forth progeny and likewise the supreme, ultimate king;
it bestows great bliss in both respects and accomplishes the goals of human existence.

Thus ends the two hundred and seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Worship of Śrī Hari with the Sixteen Services, the Offering of Oblations into the Fire, the Offering of Oblations to the Embodied Beings of the Three Worlds, the Offering of Oblations to All, the Departure, the Meal, the Return to the Kingdom of Rāyaraṇajit, the Wandering through the City, the Worship, and the Entrusting of the Maidens," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. || 207 ||
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Rādhikā; with many reasons, the glorious Bālakṛṣṇa gave instruction to them. I shall tell it to you; understand it from me. || 1 ||
Hari said: "The entire world created by me is indeed transitory;
no reality is born that remains stable, for it perishes even after a long time. (2)
The Great Self is imperishable, characterized by existence, consciousness, and bliss;
it is composed of innate bliss within the body, yet it partakes of the fruits that follow from karma.
As long as the karma remains stable, they go from there to another house;
for what is done here, one indeed experiences its result in the other world.
Having abandoned everything, one must certainly depart for another world;
therefore, one should indeed perform that spiritual practice by which happiness is attained once gone there.
Indeed, all the other worlds, such as Svarga and others, along with their pleasures,
are attained through abundant merit, through giving, and through deeds of service to others.
It is also obtained by serving the elders and the virtuous;
through their blessings and one's own merit, the supreme heaven is attained.
Beyond even that, there is the highest heaven, or Vaikuṇṭha which is beyond that;
or Goloka, the imperishable abode, and even my own supreme abode.
In Vaikuṇṭha, my auspicious families indeed exist,
as well as the circles of male attendants and female attendants.
There, divine couples indeed exist, and I too am a couple;
there, I am served by millions of maidservants, headed by Lakṣmī.
Likewise, even in Goloka, I am Śrī Kṛṣṇa, joined with Rādhā and served by millions of crores of pairs of gopas and gopīs.
I abide here as the king of kings, a great ocean of eternal bliss;
there exists the great, perpetual happiness of the divine couple.
Everything divine arises from my yoga; it is a state of liberation that does not pass away, eternally increasing, devoid of diminution, and the supreme bliss.
In the same way, that bliss always abides on Kailāsa, in the world of Śaṅkara which is resorted to by eternal yogis and is situated directly below Goloka.
I, Śaṅkara, dwell right there on the auspicious Kailāsa, being served by hosts of male and female divine yoginīs.
I have indeed assumed that form which demonstrates the practice of the householder's life;
though I am essentially Śaṅkara, I abide as a yogi within the state of a householder.
That bliss is eternal and certain for virtuous couples;
as the Lord and Master of the Yoginīs, I accept the service of the Satīs.
Then he dwells in the most excellent happiness, superior to the three worlds,
in my imperishable and eternal abode, according to his desire, belonging to the Supreme Lord.
Consisting of all sovereignty, the essence of all yoga, the highest happiness; assuming any form at will, it is the object of enjoyment in manifold forms, a bliss upon bliss.
Indeed, the supreme capacity to assume all forms exists there,
as does the divine sovereignty of those who are eternally liberated and endowed with all powers.
There is no end to happiness anywhere at any time; there is never any decrease.
The doubts regarding happiness always increase, while the oceans of bliss ever expand. 21.
Indeed, sounds, touches, tastes, smells, and visible objects pertaining to the various sense-faculties become divine and are designated as imperishable.
The selfs named Ānanda, who are mountains of bliss, always enjoy there in the imperishable realm a happiness even greater than that of ten million lotus-like Golokas. (23)
Likewise, all kinds of happiness exceeding that of Koṭi, Abja, Vaikuṇṭha, and Kailāsa, as well as whatever is desired by the mind, exists for the liberated ones. 24.
Even greater than that is my happiness in the abode beyond;
through my yoga, the happiness of my devotees is the most supreme of all.
It is infinite, attainable through my own form, and within the easy reach of all the senses;
it is beyond measure, unsurpassed, and eternal.
It may be obtained according to one's desire, either as a single form or as a pair;
it may be obtained through a state of oneness, or it may be acquired through all states of being.
"O Rādhā, after this description, that which is most desired among all things desired according to one's wish—thus did Hari describe His own bliss born of His own form. (28)
Then she said: "O Rādhikā, it is auspicious to dwell here for the sake of happiness;
those who bend and rise by the force of the wind and water [shall find joy]. (29)
Herbs, trees, and shrubs do not suffer defeat;
likewise, one who remains conscious can withstand even what has come from another.
Victory is always attained by one who swallows adversity;
merit is obtained in every way by that patient person.
By bowing down at all times, even while offering one's own body, senses, and so forth to the Self in any circumstance, that evil deed is destroyed.
Affliction and even passion must be endured with wisdom by those of sound intellect—whether by people of the world, by one's own kin, by spirits, or by the most excellent of realized beings. (3.3)
That embodied being who endures great suffering while giving is the one who attains victory and rejoices even in the highest heaven.
Whether directly or indirectly, whoever here reviles others—living by the habit of reviling—is like a dog in this world, equal to the dead, like a corpse. (35)
One should avoid such a person of sinful mind, who is like one dead, as he is a reviler, a dancer, and a "peacock with a naked tail. (36)
One should avoid at all times a wolf, an elephant, one who observes the vow of an enemy, and one who follows a wrong path when they are angry; thus one will find happiness even among people.
He whose entire circle of servants is skilled in theoretical and practical knowledge, who seeks his welfare, is devoted to his word, and is affectionate—he becomes happy. (38)
He whose ministers provide beneficial advice, grant wisdom, and bestow honor, and who discerns what is yet to come, always becomes happy. (39)
He whose companions share equally in his suffering and happiness, who act for his benefit, who are intent on his welfare, and who are truthful—he is always born happy. (2.208.40)
He whose circle of dependents is never distressed, who approaches him with sincerity, and who is skillful and devoted to the duty of service, always becomes happy. (41)
A king who acts for the welfare of others and his servant as well must always cultivate [virtue];
even one who possesses sovereign power, both of them find only happiness.
Since great sovereignty has been obtained through one's offspring and dependents, it must never be forgotten by him or by her under any circumstances. (43)
Furthermore, in the case of ingratitude, destruction will surely occur; there is no doubt.
He who pursues contrary goals encounters only suffering. (44)
In a great forest there lived in the woods a sage devoted to liberation, Kṛpāyana, the best of the twice-born, a most exalted devotee of the Lord, and pure. ||45||
Constantly worshipping Hari, self-restrained and established in austerity, he subsisted on fruits and roots; being the very foundation of sovereignty, he was truly happy.
Dwelling in the state of a being, he became a provider of many refuges;
him, who was thus endowed with goodness, non-violent, and possessed of equal vision—||47||
Having recognized the forest-dwellers, even those living nearby—mice, mongooses, cats, and dogs—[fled]. (48)
Leopards, bears, tigers, elephants, and great elephants;
lions, as well as other rhinoceroses, gaṇḍakas, and deer. ||49||
Having abandoned all enmity, they remain there during the daytime in the forest;
at night, however, they return to that very place for the sake of obtaining food.
Once, the mouse went out alone for the sake of his own food;
at that time, he encountered a cat far from that hermitage.
And when the mouse, falling due to hunger, was forcibly caught on his back, he fell with great speed onto the shoulder of the sage out of fear. (52)
"O Sage, a fear of this cat arises within me;
O best of Brahmins, grant me freedom from fear so that I may dwell here in comfort. (53)
The sage said, "Become a cat here yourself and be happy.
He was born as a cat, and a dog arrived to seize him. (54)
Furthermore, the compassionate sage made this prayer and said, "Become a dog!
and he immediately became a dog, remaining fearless at all times.
Then one day, a wolf arrived and pounced upon him to seize him;
the dog went to the sage and said, "Make me fearless."
The sage said, "Become a wolf here; thus you shall be free from fear.
Then, when he had become a wolf, a tiger, distressed by hunger, appeared in the forest.
A wolf, filled with fear, approached the sage seeking to kill him;
the sage, requesting a state free from fear, granted that wolf the form of a tiger.
Having become a tiger, he lived fearlessly and happily in the hermitage of the sages;
however, on one occasion, he was attacked by a rutting elephant with massive tusks.
And having been seen by him who arrived swiftly with great speed to strike him, he went to the sage and spoke thus: "This elephant will kill me."
The sage said: "In this very place, there was a powerful elephant of great body;
a tiger quickly attained the state of an elephant, becoming exceedingly strong and well-nourished. (6.1)
At that time, a certain lion once saw an elephant;
just as the lion approached to seize it, the elephant turned toward the sage.
Having approached, he spoke of his fear and begged for fearlessness;
the compassionate sage quickly granted him the state of being a lion.
Then, by chance, a śarabha arrived there at that time; out of fear, the lion fled from the lion, and the lion [fled] to the sage to take him as his prey.
Seeking a state free from fear, the compassionate sage spoke:
"O son, become a śarabha; let there be no fear at any time."
Then that śarabha was born, the destroyer of the life-force of lions;
for seven days he remained fearless within the forest. (66)
There was excessive rain, and the śarabha could not find food;
then he thought, "I shall indeed devour this ṛṣi."
By the power of his meditative yoga, the great seer, having understood that the mouse possessed such an intention, said: "Indeed, by the strength of my sovereign power, I shall [deal with] you."
And he granted him the state of a Śarabha, which is the most excellent and fearless;
likewise, he is the Lord who, out of compassion, is the protector and bestower of sovereignty. ||69||
"Since you desire to harm one who is sinless and a giver of life,
therefore, O you born of a sinful womb, go back once more to the state of a mouse!"
Thus cursed, he attained the state of a mouse; having reached the condition of a śarabha, he subsequently fell into a state of wretchedness and was finally cast out by the ṛṣi.

Having understood this, one should give alms-bowls and other items that are either characterized by purity (sāttvika) or devoid of such quality; likewise, one should never bestow excessive lordship or power upon them.
Trust in such people is not conducive to one's welfare;
this must indeed be understood by a master, a merchant, or a king who desires happiness. (73)
Never indeed should anything be given to an unworthy recipient without first examining them; one who has fallen into the snare of an unworthy recipient shall never attain happiness.
In this world, even one of noble birth who is common, or even one who has encountered suffering at some time,
does not set his mind upon evil if he is sattvic, even when being torn apart.
A man of noble birth who is divided [from his kin] and devoid of intelligence is a most foolish king;
even if he attains what is difficult to obtain, he will fall into enmity with those very things.
One who is of noble birth, educated, wise, and has reached the further shore of knowledge and discernment;
who is grateful, patient, contented, and has conquered the senses. ||77||
One who seeks the welfare of others, serves the virtuous, honors his father,
is devoted to the service of Brahman, and is endowed with the virtue of offering all actions to his chosen deity.
One who is of proper conduct, devoted to auspicious thoughts, knowledgeable in discipline, skilled in interpreting gestures, endowed with statesmanship, proficient, and rich in virtues; (79)
The wise husband who takes as his wife one who knows how to serve, understands gain and loss, is endowed with goodness, and possesses rare sovereignty—[attains great merit]. (2.208.80)
Whether he be a master, a king, or someone else, he always becomes happy;
having thus recognized the disciple, O King, I bestow this [knowledge] upon you here. (8.1)
O Raṇajit, always behold within my own essential nature that state established in the sovereignty of yoga, which is my eternal and divine being. 82.
"By this, that supreme perfection which bestows liberation shall come into your hands.
Having said this, Hari bestowed a divine state upon Raṇajit. (83)
To his father-in-law, the high-souled husband of the twenty maidens,
he too became possessed by that state, and his divine eyes became truly celestial.
He beheld the divine and prosperous great city of Kuṅkumavāpī;
he likewise beheld divine Vaikuṇṭha and the imperishable Goloka.
[He saw] Akṣareśa, Kāṃbhareya, Bālakṛṣṇa, and the husband of his daughter;
then Hari granted his own divine vision to the subjects.
At the end of a moment, having attained human form, he gave them his own mantra;
then those thousands of subjects became Vaiṣṇavas. (87)
Then the son of Gopāla went to the Yukāsanā river to bathe;
having bathed and quickly performed the meditation and worship offered by the king, he departed. 88.
Having accepted the worship and partaken of the milk and other offerings, he reached Kṛtaka by celestial chariot through the sky and departed from there after receiving honors.
Accompanied by Ālāya and Sarṣi, as well as by Bhūbhṛt;
Hari was joined by twenty maidens and attended by his ancestors.
He went to the sacrificial ground and, for the sake of charity, presented a hundred thousand crores of gold coins to the treasury-keeper at the sacrifice.
And at night, he partook of food and likewise held a most excellent great festival;
having fed all the people, the Supreme Lord went to sleep.
Then, in the seventh [kalpa], the people will be both native to that land and from other lands;
there will be seers, sages, and other people devoted to the narration of dharma.
In that most splendid sacrifice, they sang the narratives of the *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā* with great enthusiasm. (94)
On the banks of the Śeṣakāṣṭha forest river, where the virtuous dwell, there are indeed glorifications consisting of wondrous divine sports. (95)
Furthermore, all the Apsarases take delight in the form of donkeys;
indeed, the denizens of hell perform dances at night in the manner of a theatrical performance.
Then, O Rādhā, twenty maidens served Hari at night—the Lord of Śrī, the Master of Īśā, their beloved, enchanting with his beauty. 97.
Having served their new lord, who blazes with the power of yogic sovereignty, they attained eternal bliss and became fulfilled in all their aims. 98.
At dawn, Hari abandoned his sleep due to the hearing of auspicious sounds—
the meditations arising from auspicious musical instruments and the voices of bards and panegyrists.
And by means of songs from the beloved wives of Brahmā and by the hymns and devotional worship of the virtuous, Janārdana was awakened.

Thus ends the two hundred and eighth chapter, titled "The Description of how Hari instructed the people beginning with Rāyaraṇajit in the city of Mīnārkakṛṣṇapattana during the second Tretā cycle of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā; how He arrived at the sacrificial ground, slept at night, and woke up in the morning. || 208 ||
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Listen, O Rādhikā; having performed the ritual of bathing at dawn, the Lord sat upon a splendid golden throne to perform worship.
There he worshipped Yajñanārāyaṇa with excellent materials such as the sixteen [upacāras], and at that very moment, [the Lord] arrived there.
The sage Lomaśa worshipped the Supreme Lord for the sake of adoration;
likewise, kings who were dear to Brahmā arrived and paid their respects. || 3 ||
During that great festival of sacrificial rites, musical instruments were played;
and the kings, the subjects, and likewise the great seers gathered for the purpose of departing.
All the lords, beginning with Brahmā, quickly went to the sacrificial ground;
even the kings gathered together all the desired materials for the sacrifice.
Milk, sacrificial fuel such as wood, grains, fruits, and rice—
all these were instantly provided there by the gods and others.
The preceptor, all the deities, the officiating priests, as well as the reciters, the performers of the rites, the sacrificers, and their assistants, stood nearby.
There, the Brahmins uttered auspicious benedictions that bestow welfare,
and there was the proclamation of a holy day as well as the resonance of the Vedas.
While all the sacrificial priests remain in their respective places,
there shall be purification of the body, the tenfold bath, and prostration at the feet of the Guru.
The ritual resolve, the protection of the directions, the worship of the water-pot,
as well as the worship of Gaṇeśa and likewise the worship of the Mātṛkās.
Then there was the Nāndī-śrāddha, as well as the offering of water (arghya) and the honey-mixture (madhuparka);
followed by the consecration, the worship of the Vardhinī, and the propitiation of the site (vāstu).
Then there is the worship of the pavilion, the worship of the Sarvatobhadra diagram,
the worship of the deities, and likewise the honoring of the deities of the yantra.
Then follows the removal of the fire, the worship of the deities of the pedestal,
the worship of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), the worship of the deity, and thereafter the auspicious worship of the fire.
The worship of the planets and the Yoginīs, the honoring of the Kṣetrapālas, and the thorough worship of the liberated ones, the incarnations, and the lords. || 14 ||
The worship of the wives of Brahmins by those who are masters, the honoring of celibate students by yoginīs of the Sāṃkhya school, and the honoring of virtuous women by the righteous. (15)
The worship of the ancestors, the sages, and the guardians of the directions;
as well as the honoring of the world-protectors and the worship of those residing in heaven. || 16 ||
Likewise, there was the worship of the thirty-three gods and the five deities worthy of honor,
as well as the veneration of the Rākṣasas who dwell in the Bhuvarloka.
The honoring of spirits, ghosts, and demons, as well as of human beings; the worship of living beings residing in the four oceans, and of the classes of servants. (18)
The worship of shrines, both inanimate and animate, as well as the propitiation of all stationary objects that provide nourishment. (19)
There is also the worship of living beings and of the principles (tattvas) dwelling in the nether regions and below; likewise, there is the worship of Śrī Mahāviṣṇu and of Viṣṇu.
The sounding of conchs and bells, the offering of worship with one's own life-breaths,
the presentation of oblations, and likewise the performance of fire-sacrifices with many kinds of desirable foods, clarified butter, ghee, and so forth.

The lustration rite (nīrājana), the offering of oblations (balidāna), as well as the handful of flowers (puṣpāñjali), the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), prostration (namaskāra), praise (stuti), and the bestowing of blessings (āśīḥpradāna). ||22||
In that great sacrifice, all the foods were provided in succession;
indeed, millions and hundreds of thousands of gods attained satisfaction at the grand rite.
On that very eighth day, at midday, having performed all the prescribed rites in that manner,
the illustrious Bālakṛṣṇa ate together with his family.
He took betel-leaf and rested for a moment;
meanwhile, the king arrived there, eager to make his request. ||25||
King Rāyavākakṣaka, accompanied by Cārulāṣarṣi,
[ruled] his own kingdom, which was situated in the water like an island in the midst of a great ocean.
Then Hari requested that he might also sanctify the city of Tūryapadā; [the Lord] said, "So be it," and he then quickly made himself ready.
May the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the son of Śrī Kambharā, as well as his parents, brothers, and sister, be satisfied. (28)
Amṛtā, Bhrātṛjāyā, and the virtuous Brahmapriyā;
likewise Śaṅkara, Lomaśa, and the Ṛṣi Cāru. || 29 ||
Then King Rāyavākakṣaka quickly ascended the two celestial chariots; all followed with a measured pace.
Having crossed the salt-water ocean, they reached an island known as Viṣaturīya; the king went ahead of them.
In the city of Turyapada, he offered a welcome for the sake of Hari;
accompanied by the queen and the army, the king paid him due honor.
Having alighted from the celestial chariot in the garden circle near the royal palace,
Śrī Hari emerged from that vimāna.
The king performed worship with flowers and other offerings for Śrī Mādhava; likewise, the noble ones honored the Supreme Lord with saffron and other substances.
Then, cries of "Victory! and the sounds of musical instruments arose on all sides;
they celebrated the Lord of Lords with flowers, parched grain, unbroken rice, and other offerings.
And the subjects caused the Supreme Lord to increase [in glory] with shouts of joy;
then the king had Hari ascend his small palanquin.
And he likewise caused his family to ascend the celestial chariots;
having approached every house in the city with those chariots, [he honored them].
He indeed made the houses of the people pure,
and offered worship with great ritual services, wealth, goods, and excellent jewels.
Having reached and performed purificatory rites in his own homes,
he wandered once more through the divine city and granted his own vision [to all].
Then Hari came to the royal residence, a divine palace;
he rested for a moment, drank milk, and then everyone drank.
The king, the queen, the princes, and the three maidens likewise worshipped Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the beloved of Śrī Kṛṣṇa. ||41||
Then, with various offerings such as sandalwood, unbroken grains of rice, saffron,
other necklaces, and great jewels, they performed the lustration ceremony (nīrājana).
The three maidens, being enchanted by Hari, placed the bridegroom’s garland around his neck;
and Hari, indeed with the consent of the queen, took hold of their hands.
The maidens were fulfilled, having obtained a handsome husband; the king rejoiced in many ways, and the queen likewise rejoiced greatly. (44)
Seated upon the great lion-throne in the royal palace during the festival, Hari gave them a complete instruction that bestows happiness.
Devotion to Hari, the Imperishable Lord, must always be practiced by me;
the service of the virtuous must always be performed, for it is auspicious, bestowing merit and liberation. 46.
One should daily protect all living beings with compassion;
whatever is beneficial for a particular purpose should be adopted, and never anything else. (47)

Self-restraint through the intellect, acting with the understanding that all is to be grasped [as the Self], and liberation through supreme discernment—these are what must be attained by the embodied being in this world. 48.
One should apply oneself to those duties consisting of the knowledge of Dharma, which are taught in the scriptures and spoken by the gurus. (49)
One should act agreeably toward all without contradicting the principles of dharma;
indeed, the virtuous person should protect dharma alone and thereby accomplish his own true purpose.
The study of the scriptures is the duty of the Brāhmaṇa; the staff is indeed the duty of the Kṣatriya;
agriculture is the duty of the Vaiśya, and service is the duty of the servant. (51)
Truth is indeed the dharma for all; those rich in dharma are remembered as deities.
Such men are equal to gods; they are the very form of the life-force of all beings.
The scripture is that which effects instruction, characterized by the authority of its master;
it was created in ancient times by Brahmā at my command for the sake of protecting the world. (513)
And for the sake of the ease of worldly affairs, punishment—characterized by reliance on a protector and consisting of the auspicious nature of the Kṣatriya dharma—has also been ordained. (54)
Furthermore, another form of activity, consisting of industry, has been created;
it sustains all people by means of various coins obtained through economic policy. (55)
That third person, whose nature is the production of income and who is characterized by the support of his master, is also a created being intended as a means for happiness. (56)
Furthermore, another person was created, consisting of commands and instructions, characterized as the object of trust for all the low-caste people. (57)
Established in their command, they obtain the means of sustenance for all the worlds indeed, including the gods, asuras, and rakshasas. (58)
For those possessing humans and serpents, as well as for the stationary beings,
this fourfold legal procedure is characterized by reliance upon the master.
For the sake of a continuous flow of happiness and prosperity, I have previously performed [this] for him who is endowed with dharma, possessed of devotion to me, and solely intent upon me.
Having become that, one should always abide therein; indeed, I am the sustainer of those who are diligent in meritorious actions and their inherent natures.
I am the sustainer of all efforts, and I am the supporter even of those who support others;
I am the teacher and the restrainer, and I am also the one who maintains the course of the world.
Knowing this, people should indeed take refuge in me; they shall cross over [the ocean of existence].
Wealth always has its root in dharma, and likewise, pleasure is the fruit of wealth. (63)
In this world, all [pursuits of] dharma, artha, and kāma arise from the root of the mind;
all these, such as dharma and the rest, take the form of active engagement and are joined with phenomenal existence. (64)
Liberation is said to be the cessation from those [desires] along with their roots;
and the connection of the body with dharma is the bodily purpose that acts as an aid. (65)
Desire is the fruit, and it is a great bondage; all these, moreover, are characterized by passion (rajas).
Having abandoned them and their specific variations, one who is free from passion is truly devoted to me.
One whose self is disciplined through yoga proceeds toward becoming one with Brahman;
for if dharma does not grant me attainment, nor does wealth do so likewise.
If desire does not exist for me, those things which grant attainment are considered useless;
one should either employ those objects—which are in essence non-objects—for my sake, or else abandon them.
Otherwise, the intellect of one who wanders will surely go toward sense objects;
thus, the intellect that was withdrawn for the sake of liberation will indeed meet its destruction.
The destruction of the intellect is a great delusion, and even that which belongs to darkness increases; from that arises atheism, and from that, misconduct ensues. (2.209.70)
Indeed, through misconduct, progeny becomes ruined and mixed-caste;
virtuous people certainly do not go to the home of one who has fallen into misconduct.
But for him, evils increase and he encounters suffering in life;
for even while living, this is hell, since his existence is one of unhappiness. (72)
Therefore, for the sake of destroying those defects, for the sake of happiness, and out of a disposition toward all beings,
one should serve those people devoted to Hari who are firmly established in Brahman and endowed with devotion.
One should always recite my name and dedicate everything here unto me;
for that [practice] leads indeed to virtue, wealth, pleasure, and liberation.
One should always please the virtuous through action, mind, and speech;
one should constantly say, "I am yours," bow down, and practice service.
Through the benedictions of the virtuous, through their grace, through service,
through meeting them, and through yoga, a person becomes purified.
This association with the virtuous is sinless and cuts away all defects;
it pacifies even grievous sins—of this there is no doubt. (77)
In this world, spiritual teachers and holy beings are the most excellent for me, as they bestow liberation;
gold is supreme in every respect, and likewise, holy beings are so in every aspect. (78)
Those purifying forms of Kṛṣṇa, extending from my feet to the ends of my hair, will grant me union with Him whenever they are obtained by any means whatsoever. (79)
They shall offer devotion to me and they shall dwell in my abode;
therefore, virtuous persons endowed with my mantra and devotion are indeed to be served.
Those gurus shall proclaim to you my supreme dharma, that of the great devotee; those who practice it shall go to the Supreme Imperishable.
Indeed, through the grace of the gurus, they shall attain the supreme good;
for morality is the highest of all dharmas, and the virtuous are those whose nature is morality.
For by means of ethical discipline, the three worlds can indeed be conquered; of this there is no doubt.
Indeed, there is nothing whatsoever in the world that cannot be accomplished by those possessed of ethical discipline. (83)
On this earth, this morality is the nectar, the most supreme of all things;
such is the highest good that exists for one who is established in it. (84)
The cultivation of the company of the virtuous, the incarnations, and chaste women, as well as service, is declared to be the supreme conduct; it is the highest vow, the conduct of Brahman. (85)
Indeed, there is nothing equal to proper conduct toward one's guru;
for in a former kalpa, there was a king named Prahlāda who was always possessed of virtuous character.
At that time, his excellent vow was simply the practice of virtuous conduct.
Then, in the past, Bṛhaspati approached that auspicious one.
He bestowed upon Prahlāda eternal knowledge in the form of devotion;
then, as the Guru was departing, the King spoke regarding the sacrificial fee.
Bṛhaspati indeed requested the sacrificial fee in the form of good character;
Prahlāda then gave that character from his very body for as long as it took.
Divine virtue emerged, and Prosperity also went forth with it;
Prahlāda, however, remained there devoid of luster and abandoned by Dharma.
Deprived of both virtue and prosperity, he questioned that man:
"Who are you, and why are you traveling thus? Tell me the truth as it is. (9.1)
"I declare myself to be moral conduct and religious observance; when I am given away in charity, I depart.
And when I have gone, this Dharma and the person likewise depart. (92)
"Behold, O King, these others who follow the lineage of Dharma are departing;
when I have gone, Dharma’s consort Bhakti and likewise Ramā will depart. (93)
"Lakṣmī, Śrī, Bhū, and all those beloved of Hari surely depart [from one] due to the abandonment of good conduct. Having heard that, Prahlāda was seized with fear.
Where there is no service to the virtuous, no moral conduct, no restraint of the senses, and no harmlessness toward all beings, there is neither Nārāyaṇa nor [his presence]. //95//
Where Nārāyaṇa is not present, and where my Ramā is not, there indeed liberation does not exist; therefore, let people be virtuous. (96)
"Let them always perform service for me and for those worthy of honor;
for, in brief, that conduct consists of showing favor toward all living beings. (97)
Those who possess ethical discipline enjoy prosperity eternally through my grace;
if they lack ethical discipline, even if they obtain it, they do not enjoy it for long. (98)
Let her, though devoid of merit, be given for the purpose of performing sacrifices, charity, and other such rites;
indeed, let the people of this land live by the practice of sacrifice. 99.
"Happy, generous, and likewise endowed with the excellence of virtuous conduct"—
having said this, O Rādhikā, the Blessed One then became silent.
Honored by the subjects and respectfully received by the king and queen, Kṛṣṇa gave counsel to the people and partook of the milk-drink.
Having placed his two feet upon the royal palace and thereby sanctifying it,
Hari was honored with a welcome at evening through the sounding of musical instruments and other festivities.
Having ascended his own celestial chariot, accompanied by his entire caravan,
he [ruled over] Dvinaska, Pārśvarājya, and the island of Milvila.
Having traveled by means of a celestial chariot to Vilāsadvīpa and also to Bulandadvīpa, he then sported in the sky.
Having observed this, Śrī Hari quickly descended from the sky during the night on the eighth lunar day and swiftly returned to his auspicious abode at the site of the sacrifice.
Hari performed his bath, the twilight rites, and took his meal;
likewise, others took their meals, and Hari provided the materials for the sacrifice.
Served by the three maidens, Kṛṣṇa rested happily during the night; under the influence of yogic sleep, he awoke at dawn to auspicious sounds.
Awakened by songs, the resonant chanting of the Vedas, the sounds of musical instruments, hymns of praise, and the recitations of sūtas, māgadhas, bards, and others, the Supreme Lord arose.
O Rādhikā, for a moment He meditated upon His own supreme form, which is higher than the highest,
whose nature transcends the imperishable (akṣara), and which consists of the perfect Brahman, the Supreme Self.

Thus ends the two hundred and ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Performance of All Rites up to the Final Oblation at the Sacrifice on the Eighth Day of the Bright Half of Bhādrapada in the Second Tretā Cycle of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā," wherein it is related how, after the meal, Hari—being requested by King Rāyavākakṣaka—went to his kingdom, to the island of Viṣaturīya, and to Dvinaska and Milvilā; having purified them and instructed them, he returned to the sacrificial ground at night and rested. || 209 ||
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Rādhikā; having bathed in the morning and performed his daily worship, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa went to the sacrificial ground.
The sages headed by Lomaśa, kings who were performers of sacrifices, subjects,
gods, lords of the gods, and those devoted to ritual action all attended upon him.
There, new sacrificial offerings were brought from all sides;
there, the juices were provided by the wish-fulfilling trees and other such sources. || 3 ||
There were also utterances of "Svasti" and proclamations of an auspicious day;
there were sounds of musical instruments as well as the resonance of the Vedas.
And those kings who were performing the sacrifice, having arrived at their respective places early in the morning on the ninth day, became intent upon the ritual portion of the ceremony.
They became attentive, and the rites were performed in due order;
sprinklings, worship, and offerings of food and oblations were presented.
The offerings of oblations into the fire became sacrificial libations (āhutis);

the gratification of the deities was accomplished, and the gods and others attained satisfaction. At that sacrifice, the embodied beings residing within the creation of Brahmā, the creation of Īśvara, and the creation of the individual soul (jīva), visibly attained satisfaction through the sacrificial oblations.
In that sacrifice, Hari offered the final oblation and a handful of flowers;
then the Lord provided a dismissal and gave various foods.
He offered unwholesome food, food from delusive vessels, water with mung beans,
*laḍḍukas*, sweet *cūrṇalaḍḍūs*, pearls, and likewise *śaṣkulīs*.
Cloths, ghee-filled cakes, and hundred-holed sweetmeats; balls of flour, *barphikās*, sweet-filled *polīs*, and *pūrikās*. || 1 1 ||
Sweets, milk-rice, milk, saṃyāva, and birañjaka;
kaṃsāra, bundikā-laḍḍūs, and sugar-and-ghee laḍḍūs. || 12 ||
Sandalwood paste, black mustard, boiled vegetables, and soup;
rice, many kinds of greens, and leaf-plates for serving food. (13)
Chickpeas and beans, both boiled and roasted, as well as balls,
flower-shaped cakes, pancakes, and nectars.
The food of the liberated ones is divine; the food of the lords is that of living beings;
the food of the gods is nectar; and the food of the ancestors is the *cāma* offering.
The juices are the food of the elements, the intoxicants are the food of the Rākṣasas;
likewise, there are foods appropriate for all embodied beings according to their respective natures.
At that time, there appeared various kinds of bright buttermilk— sour, desirable, fragrant, and bestowing satisfaction— which were manifestations of the grace of the sacrifice.
There were cooks providing food that was both soothing and free from impurities, as well as various kinds of honey and honey-mixtures (madhuparka). || 18 ||
At that time, there were powders of bitter, sour, and pungent flavors, as well as *caṭanyas*,
delightful fermented gruels (*āranāla*), and various kinds of fruits.
Hari caused divine betel-leaves to be given to the guests;
having thus fed everyone, the Lord then partook of the meal himself.
Accompanied by his family, the Lord of Śrī rested there for a moment;
then at midday, King Rāyamārīśa prayed to Acyuta.
The Lord Hari prepared himself to return to his own island,
as did the others who were constantly engaged in yoga according to their respective needs.
Having taken his father and others, the Lord Śambhu, Satī, his own family,
and the sages headed by Lomaśa, he ascended the celestial chariot.
Then the king, the queen,
and the sage among the Dānavas went ahead in a celestial chariot to the island named Mālīsmara.
Then the city of Ṛddhīśā was beautifully adorned with decorations,
and a military force quickly assembled to offer a formal welcome.
Meanwhile, Kṛṣṇa’s aerial chariot, having crossed over Khāḍikā and passed beyond the high and low islands,
reached a most beautiful kingdom.
Hari reached the celestial chariot Ālīsmara and brought it down to the earth, into the great garden of Ṛddhīśā near the king’s palace. ||27||
Then musical instruments were played, shouts of victory arose, women sang songs, and the subjects raised cries of triumph. (28)
With warm welcomes, banners and other flags, victory standards, parched grain and unbroken rice, archways, flower garlands and the like, and with gestures such as the añjali salutation; || 29 ||
Through prostrations and offerings of flowers, there was great honor for Śrī Hari;
then, Śrī Hari quickly emerged from the celestial chariot.
Queen Kuśalakuṇḍalā, the wife of King Rāyamārīśa,
quickly washed his feet with the waters of sacred pilgrimage sites.
The kings and others drank the water that had arisen from Hari’s feet;
having colored their feet with saffron, they took up the sacred marks (mudrās). ||32||
Likewise, those women— Smārikās who remove suffering— offered garlands of flowers, scented water, and sandalwood paste with their joined palms, all directed toward Kṛṣṇa alone.
The maidens, filled with emotion, worshipped him with great devotion;
then the king seated Kṛṣṇa for a moment upon a magnificent palace.
Having led him to his own lion-throne, he gave him ten million pieces of gold,
as well as garments and other items made of gold, and all manner of household goods.
Then she gave him three auspicious maidens worth three hundred thousand jewels,
and her husband offered a triple garland around Kṛṣṇa’s neck.
Having understood this and received his mother’s word, the king obtained the three maidens as wives for his excellent beloved Kṛṣṇa, and he was deeply gratified.
The queen was born having accomplished her purpose; then the Lord drank the milk, and the others also quickly drank the milk while Kṛṣṇa remained in the celestial chariot.
Having resided for a short time in the city of Ṛddhīśā, where his army had increased,
and having been entreated by the subjects, he visited all their homes throughout the city.
Then, having performed purificatory rites and bestowed His auspicious vision upon them,
He received the worship offered by the subjects with various kinds of gifts.
Having taken [them], the Lord Hari, the Sovereign, went to the royal palace;
and sitting upon the throne of sovereignty, he gave instruction to the subjects and others.
Through great merits, my yoga has arisen here in this great ocean;
drawn by your meditative devotion, I have arrived from afar. (42)
Everything given for my sake indeed becomes eternal;
through union with me, it indeed becomes devoid of qualities and bestows liberation.
Having abandoned hope for all other illusory objects,
he delights in the yoga of the Self and finds the path to liberation.
Hope is a house of suffering, eternally as unshakable as the Himalayas;
it is as unfathomable as the great ocean and is fraught with defects. ||45||
The Raurava hell, as vast as the sky and without end, stands ready for the living;
even a king established in his kingdom goes forth for the sake of hunting out of desire.
In the forest, one experiences suffering just like a base hunter;
even though satisfied in all his senses, he remains held fast by the destruction of his desires.
Through the enjoyment of desires by improper means, one incurs great suffering;
yet desire is likewise present in the intermediate space—of these two, which indeed is the greater? (48)

To this question, [the answer is]: "The intermediate space (antarīkṣa) is indeed greater; for desire does not exist anywhere. Indeed, practitioners of yoga never reach the further shore of the intermediate space. (49)
Those who follow after hope never find its end;
in ancient times, a devotee of mine named Ṛṣabha [sought] the sacred Badarī forest.
He approached my divine hermitage of Nara and Nārāyaṇa,
where my lovely Badarī tree stands and the stainless celestial lake is located.
Wherever the most purifying Gaṅgā flows, the sage Aśvaśiras would come there to his delightful hermitage, to the pavilion in my presence. 52.

Having bowed and seen the excellent hut of the sage in the hermitage, he went toward a leaf-hut for the sake of dwelling there once more, with the desire to practice long breath-retention (dīrghavāsa).
On that path, he saw a sage named Tanu, whose wealth was his asceticism;
his body was eightfold taller than usual, yet in its leanness it was like a blade of grass.
His vision was indeed as wondrous as that of the little finger;
having bowed to him, Ṛṣabha stood by, and once a seat was offered, he sat down.
When questioned, he spoke only of his well-being as a consolation, and said:
"I indeed wish to build a leaf-hut here."
I desire to perform such austerity by which I may attain peace;
I wish to do all that—teach me everything, O Sage. (57)
The body replied: "I did not build this hut of leaves here at all;
since everything is indeed perishable, for whose sake was this hut made of leaves? (58)
As long as you remain intent on the construction of a leaf-hut according to your desire, so long shall there be no peace for you, for you are indeed enclosed within a hut of craving.
For one who is free from thirst, free from effort, and free from desire, there is great happiness;
for even through austerity, there is no happiness at all if desire remains awake therein.
For one dwelling in a hut of leaves, there may be no entry into Brahman;
but for one who has abandoned the hut of worldly desires, there shall be entry into Brahman. //61//
For one whose world has been entered by Brahman, peace is eternally joined;
therefore, having abandoned hope even for a pond from the sky.
"Find rest in the imperishable sky of consciousness, within the leaf-hut;
thus, by means of the eye of knowledge, that Ṛṣabha was liberated while still in his body. (63)
Abandoning his leaf-hut, he worshipped me, the Supreme Lord;
being a portion of me and my very own form, he thereafter attained liberation.
Therefore, having abandoned all hope, one should surrender the mind to Me;
by surrendering everything to Me alone, one shall attain eternal bliss. ||65||
He by whom hope has been made thin is, in my view, one whose self is nourished;
he for whom hope becomes nourished would undoubtedly be emaciated. (66)
That [compassion] which exists toward all beings—even toward those who are ungrateful, lazy, cruel, harmful, and malevolent—is [true compassion]. (67)

Toward sons, wives, wealth, and mansions; toward the body, the senses, and enjoyments; toward one's own kingdom for those childless in old age; and toward their realms for kings who have lost their sons—[these are the objects of attachment]. (68)
She was as certain as a mother is toward her children who long for gifts, who delight in playful pastimes,
and who are greedy for their favorite objects.
He by whom a vow has been made, even if he is emaciated, attains peace;
Gautama practiced austerities for sixty thousand years.
The King of Dharma approached that sage of fierce asceticism;
Gautama, having paid homage to the King of Dharma, offered him a seat. (7.1)
Then Dharmarāja inquired after his welfare and offered him a welcome; he questioned Gautama regarding his ascetic penance, O Sage.
"What is your purpose, and how do you perform such difficult penance? Gautama replied, "I practice this arduous austerity for the sake of peace."
"By which [path] shall I go to the worlds of the merit-makers, filled with happiness and the like? Yama has declared that your deliberation is proceeding along a wrong path. (74)
In the worlds of both those who have performed meritorious deeds and those who have not, the great suffering born of craving afflicts even the virtuous. (75)
Apart from the imperishable Abode, no other longing or suffering is found;
therefore, having abandoned all hope, remain motionless in Brahman. (76)
Through the yoga of Brahman, you shall attain all imperishable peace;
for there is no happiness for one possessed by desire, even though they practice austerity.
As long as there is hope and craving, and likewise here a greed for one's own interests, as long as there is desire, longing, and passion, how can there be happiness for an embodied being? (77)
For one for whom every movement and every cessation has entirely ceased,
the ocean of eternal bliss, filled with joy, stands ever-present.
Therefore, those in whose will Nārāyaṇa himself is established—even though they are virtuous knowers of Brahman—they alone enjoy peace. || 2.210.80 ||
Having heard this, Gautama abandoned his asceticism and became established in devotion;
free from desire and with a peaceful heart, he then attained supreme peace.
Therefore, I am to be worshipped with great sacrifices by kings, subjects, men, and women alike, and to be propitiated through service.
I alone am to be worshipped directly through the surrender of one's will;
having thus attained Me, one should achieve one's own liberation through services. 83.
And all you people, as well as the subjects, the king, and others, [should direct] your actions, thoughts, and speech toward me, Nārāyaṇa-Kṛṣṇa. (84)
"O Kṛṣṇa, having surrendered everything, let them worship me without indolence;
I shall grant them my supreme, great peace, which abides in the imperishable Supreme. (883)
Having spoken thus, Śrī Hari spoke the mantra to Rādhā and the progenitors;
thereafter, the Great Lord bestowed his own devotion and became silent. (86)
The king, the queen, and the subjects also fed Acyuta;
they fed the caravans, and the king and others provided food for them.
Then, having accepted the worship, he caused them all to ascend the celestial chariot; he himself also ascended it in order to go to the sacrificial ground.
The subjects, the armies, and the women paid him manifold honors;
and then Kṛṣṇa proceeded along with the king and the sage.
From one island to another, he indeed went to Kāśima in the evening;
thereafter he went to Dvivāma and arrived at Mīlavīla.
Then, during the final watch of the night, he arrived at the sacrificial ground;
having bathed there, he performed his twilight devotions and took his meal in his own dwelling.
And the three daughters of Rāyamārī fell asleep; they attended upon their beloved, the Blessed One, their new husband. (92)
At dawn, Hari was awakened by the chanting of the Vedas, by auspicious musical instruments,
by songs, by the sounds of musical instruments, and by hymns of praise.
Then the Blessed One, the king of kings, having performed the ritual of bathing,
worshipped his parents and granted an audience to his devotees.
Having performed his daily rites and being well-attired, he then arrived at the sacrificial ground along with the Dānava Ṛṣi,
Rāya, and King Ārīśa.
