He said this: "This ten-million-fold wealth that has come for my worship—let all of it be offered in the sacrifice for you both and for the subjects."
Having spoken thus, he summoned Kubera, the lord of the treasury, and gave that [wealth] to him;
the king of wealth then employed all of it for the expenses of the sacrifice.
Thus, O Rādhikā, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa himself, having purified the people, the lands, the men, and likewise the women, [departed]. 98.
Having gathered them into his refuge, he makes all embodied beings—children, the elderly, those of middle age, and the young—worthy of liberation through his grace. 99.
Having purified them, the Supreme Lord makes those worthy of liberation;
even the innocent daughters of kings were personally surrendered by Him.
Even though he is divine and the refuge of all people, he, whose nature is an ocean of compassion, assumes his own yoga according to the prescribed rule and bestows it [upon others]. 101.
O beloved, the compassion of Hari, that ocean of bliss, is such that he grants liberation even after assuming human bodies that are not divine. 102.
For the Lord of Time and Māyā, who is untainted, there is no stain anywhere;
indeed, his entire body, as well as all objects of enjoyment, are under his control.
Having specifically embraced that which arises from devotion, he indeed purifies it;
for one who is eternally satisfied, there is no satisfaction whatsoever that is dependent on another.
May he, the bestower of all bliss, be ever victorious everywhere;
for by devotion alone to Rādhā, even the Lord becomes subject to his devotees. 105.
In whatever manner one approaches Him, the Lord treats them in that same way;
in whatever manner a person serves Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa serves her in that same way.

Thus ends the two hundred and tenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Departure for Ṛddhīśāpurī in the Kingdom of King Rāyamārīśa on Ālīsmaradvīpa Following the Sacrificial Rites, the Wandering, Worship, and Teaching; and after Purifying Kāśima, Dvivāma, Mīla, and Vīladvīpas, the Return to the Sacrificial Ground and Resting at Night," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O Rādhikā, this Bālakṛṣṇa went to the sacrifice early in the morning on the tenth day;
he was then seated upon his own golden throne.
There were also the sounds of musical instruments, the songs of beautiful women,
the chanting of the Vedas by great sages, and the melodies of celestial musicians.
The sounds of the mantras and likewise of the sacrificial fires were heard;
the gods were ready, having performed their daily rites, and the fire-priests were intent on their duties.
The sacrificers, offering oblations, stood within the pavilion;
likewise, there was the recitation of benedictions, the sprinkling of the ritual materials, and their presentation.
The Brahmins' pronouncements of "Auspicious Day," the hymns of praise to the gods, as well as wakefulness, their direct presence, and worship [are required]. (5)

Gradually, the worship of the living beings belonging to the world of the living— who reside within the creation of the Lord established in the abode of the syllables— came to take place in due order.
Worship is performed by means of the offerings of the sixteen subsidiary articles, such as food and the like,
through the presentation of bali-offerings, oblations, and gifts of flavorful substances.

By the offering of fruits, food, and the like covered with nectar, by the giving of milk-rice (pāyasa) and other such items, by the offerings of sacrificial porridge (caru), and by the appropriate giving of barley, black gram (māṣa), and so forth.
By the giving of foods to be chewed and eaten, and by the giving of foods to be licked and sucked;
by the giving of foods to be tasted and drunk, and by the giving of foods that satisfy and are visible. || 9 ||

And by means of bestowals that are to be cultivated and those accessible [to them], by means of bestowals consisting of conceptualizations and those free from conceptualization, by means of bestowals that are gross and subtle, and by means of bestowals that are existent and non-existent. || 2.211.10 ||
The gods and others dwelling in all the created worlds become satisfied;
the fires consume much unctuous food of many varieties.
And there, in the sacrificial fires, there were countless and most excellent oblations of offerings, presented with many hands and with devotion.
Having performed the final oblation and having given abundant sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇās),
primarily consisting of gold, Hari granted a royal exemption (parihāra).
Kings and sacrificers gave gifts by the tens of millions;
thus, when the sacrifice had proceeded, at midday, the meals were served.
They all indeed prepared various kinds of pleasing food for the sacrifice;
likewise, the male and female incarnations dear to Hari were released.
The male attendants and female attendants, as well as the Sāṃkhya-yoginīs;
likewise the Satyas, the Sādhvīs, the Īśvarāṇīs, and the Īśvaras, who are the deities. || 16 ||
The sages, the ancestors, the gods, the guardians of the quarters, the protectors of the worlds, humans, Daityas, Yakṣas, Dānavas, and beasts and birds; || 17 ||
Even insects, moths, and the like, as well as trees, shrubs, and creepers—all these insentient principles are entirely sentient in every respect. (18)
Everything whatsoever created by Hari, consisting of name and form,
attained serenity and reached satisfaction at the sacrifice.
Hari, together with his family, accompanied by his followers and servants,
and joined by the beloved wives of Brahmā, partook of the sacrificial food (caru).
And Bālakṛṣṇa partook of sweet foods and vegetables that were flavorful and succulent, as well as all the divine delicacies.
Immediately after the meal, right there in his presence,
King Dvaipāyanadvīpa, the lord of that island, was together with his queens.
Named Rāyabāleśvara, accompanied by the sage Mālāvana, he prayed to the Supreme Lord toward the city of Vāyuphenā. ||23||
To bring Śrī Kṛṣṇa back to his own kingdom, she made him forget his wife;
Hari replied, "So be it," and immediately became ready.
Accompanied by his family, including Lomaśa and Śaṅkara,
the Lord mounted a divine celestial chariot and in an instant was in the sky.
The sage-king, together with his family, was in his celestial chariot;
he quickly went to his own city in order to offer a welcome. (26)
He quickly made the army ready for the purpose of honoring [him];
likewise, the subjects became prepared, carrying materials such as flowers.
Then they went to the vicinity of the city of Vāyuphenā, where, situated in a garden, stood a royal palace with a vast and spacious courtyard. 28.
At that moment, Hari’s celestial chariot,
exceedingly radiant and possessing the splendor of the sun, was seen in the sky, accompanied by various musical instruments.
Then sounds accompanied by cries of victory were sounded,
and the subjects were then eager to behold him with one-pointed vision.
And at that very moment, a celestial chariot swiftly arrived in the sky;
following the path shown by the king, it descended near the palace.
First, the sage Mālāvana increased the celestial chariot with garlands;
thereafter, the subjects increased it on all sides with parched grain, unbroken rice, and other offerings.
The king offered a garland and a golden necklace upon the neck of Hari;
having washed His feet, Hari drank [the water] and came outside. ||33||
The subjects quickly honored him with garlands and other offerings, as well as words of welcome;
the king, having led Hari to his palace, worshipped him with abundant wealth.
Then the king, having seated the Supreme Lord upon a golden vehicle,
led his family, Lomaśa, and Śambhu into the city.
Accompanied by his army, Śrī Hari was honored on the road by the subjects;
he was worshipped, saluted, and gazed upon with eyes full of devotion. ||36||
Entrusted with wealth consisting of many jewels and the like, as well as gold and silver, and having been honored by the most eminent [persons], he then wandered through the city. (37)
He arrived at that royal palace and sat upon the king’s throne;
then he delivered words for the welfare of his subjects.
Kṛṣṇa is desired by many, yet he is not obtained without merit;
he is obtained through great merit, yet he is not served without a state of detachment. (39)
It is served by many dispositions, yet one does not become attached without faith;
and when one becomes attached through all forms of surrender, that is the cause of grace therein.
Though I am myself the Lord, I have become powerless through [your] grace;
your country has been beheld by me, who am endowed with grace. (41)
Service performed with love is indeed devoid of [worldly] qualities and bestows liberation;
my yoga always grants liberation to every embodied being. (42)
And whatever [path] embodied beings follow here after reaching me according to their knowledge, for them I am the giver of results in that very way and the bestower of grace accordingly. 43.
Being pleased, I indeed grant happiness and protect from obstacles; I provide for the acquisition and preservation of well-being for this devotee, my servant. (44)
For a devotee rich in the power of service, all that is auspicious is present;
indeed, one should desire to exist within the power of service, for everything is under the control of the powerful.
The power of service, when established within oneself, protects one from great fear;
among all things, the power of Dharma is the Dharma that brings about all happiness. (46)
Dharma is established upon the power of service; I always abide in Dharma.
As long as I abide, Śrī remains—the means for achieving all happiness. (47)
Dharma follows the service of others just as smoke follows the wind;
the dharma of serving those who are powerful proceeds through all calamities.
For those servants who possess a state of serene devotion, there is nothing here that cannot be accomplished;
indeed, as recipients of my grace, they shall quickly become highly esteemed. (49)
In this world, one indeed receives honor, and in the next world, great fruit;
thereafter, one shall enjoy manifold happiness that is eternal. ||2.211.50||
Service to the gods, the ancestors, and ascetics must be performed with truthfulness;
likewise, so too for guests, the virtuous, the helpless, and women. (5.1)
One must certainly not practice non-service; for non-service is indeed malice.
Malice leads to causing distress, and because of that, they become enraged.
The fortune of those with whom their teachers and elders are angry is dissolved;
for them, there shall be no protector whatsoever in the three worlds. (53)
Whoever would revile them or even desire their destruction will himself go to destruction, just as darkness vanishes at the rising of the sun. (54)
One who perceives the future and possesses wisdom regarding the present prospers in happiness through service; those devoid of these perish. //55//
Service performed when the time has arrived is considered to be the service that bestows liberation;
for when the time has passed, the Lord has departed, and with Him, the source of prosperity has likewise gone. (56)
That gain which is sought for the sake of favor is not gain at all;
one should serve those who know Brahman, those advanced in knowledge, and ascetics.
One should serve virtuous people who are rich in learning, conduct, and character for the sake of one's own prosperity;
through such service, divine fame arises, whereas through lack of affection, there is the destruction of all that is auspicious.
That wise man, having performed service for the virtuous, should bring them joy;
for when the virtuous or even Hari are pleased, they protect him who has come for refuge. (59)
In the forest, a cruel and pitiless Śabara hunter, who was greedy for meat, was honored by a pigeon seeking refuge through the offering of its own flesh.
Formerly abandoned by his own kinsmen due to his sinful conduct,
Jana then went to the forest, and at that time there occurred a rain that surpassed all others.
Indeed, everything became water, as if consisting entirely of a great flood;
no living beings could be found there, neither birds nor even beasts.
Then, in the evening, that hunter found a female pigeon in the forest;
having placed her in a cage, he took refuge under a tree. (63)
Then, at night, the hunter, thinking the tree was a deity, joined his palms in reverence, prostrated himself, and spoke these words to the lord of the forest: (64)
I go for refuge to those deities who reside in this tree;
may they protect me, who am without support and have come here seeking your protection. (65)
Hungry, he fell asleep placing his head at the root [of the tree],
while a bird named Citrakapotaka remained perched on a branch.
His wife had gone out to seek food but did not return;
that pigeon, afflicted by the rain, grieved greatly during the night. (67)
"I think my wife has surely died today from the winds and rains;
is all well with that beloved of mine in the forest? (68)
Indeed, my house today appears empty because it is bereft of its wife, even though it is filled with sons, grandsons, daughters-in-law, servants, slaves, and the like. (69)
They do not say that a house is a house; rather, it is the wife who is the house itself.
Without a wife, a house remains like another wilderness, utterly empty. (2.211.70)
Without her, my life is indeed seen to be utterly purposeless;
she, firm in her vows, does not eat when I have not eaten, nor does she bathe when I have not bathed.
She does not stand when I am standing, but stands close by; she lies down only when I have lain down.
She is joyful when I am joyful, and she is sorrowful when I am sorrowful. (72)
When her husband is away, she is dejected of face; when he is angry, she speaks kindly.
Devoted to her husband, she takes refuge in her husband and delights in what is pleasing and beneficial to him. 73.
Blessed is that man who always has such a wife;
for she, a woman of ascetic virtue, knows me to be afflicted by hunger and seeks to pacify it. (74)
Devoted, steadfast, faithful, affectionate, and illustrious—by her, even a tree becomes a noble home, radiant and bringing happiness. (75)
Deprived of her, even a magnificent mansion truly appears like a wilderness;
for in matters of dharma, artha, and kāma, a wife is a man’s companion. (76)
Even when traveling abroad, she is indeed a vessel of trust;
for a wife is truly the supreme wealth of a man at all times. (77)
In this world, for one who is without a companion, a wife stands as his helper;
indeed, she is the supreme medicine for one overcome by the hardships of illness. (78)
There is no kinsman equal to a wife as a companion for the accumulation of dharma, for diversion, and in the journey to the next world; she is indeed a true friend. (79)
He who has a virtuous, chaste wife who is beautiful and speaks kindly does not need to go from his home to the forest. (2.211.80)
"Or must I die?"—thus he lamented profusely during the night;
while he was thus lamenting, a female dove, which had been caught in the forest, fell asleep. (8.1)
Remaining in her cage, she listened intently and spoke these words with affection:
"Oh, how exceedingly fortunate I am, whose beloved husband [is such as this]! (82)
He thus speaks of the virtues of one who does not carry out his commands; indeed, that woman is not to be esteemed in whom her husband finds no pleasure. (83)
"When a husband is pleased, all the deities are pleased with women;
that woman for whom her husband is not pleased is reduced to ashes.
Having reflected thus, the female dove spoke these words to her husband: (84)
O Lord, I shall speak that which brings happiness; you ought to act accordingly.
Be entirely devoted to the service of those who have come for refuge. 85.
This hunter, a seeker of birds, has come to your dwelling;
for one afflicted by hunger, serving him with the gift of food shall be a source of merit. ||86||
The merit of serving one who has come for refuge is considered to bestow heaven;
therefore, O dear one, serve this enemy by offering him your body. (87)
"Offer worship to him; do not harbor any longing for his body.
Having heard these affectionate words, the pigeon went down.
Having raised him up, he said: "Blessings upon you! Welcome; let me do service for you.
You are staying here as if in your own home; what is it that you desire? What may I do for you? (89)
"You have come here into the midst of this forest as one who has sought refuge with me;
for even toward an enemy, hospitality is the proper duty when he has arrived at one's home."
"The fruit for that householder who provides hospitality is equal to that of a sacrifice.
Having heard this, the Kirāta said, "I am indeed cold and hungry today."
If there is an effort to be made for the sake of removing that which afflicts you, let it be undertaken;
meanwhile, the pigeon has quickly flown up and gone to the blacksmith's house. (92)
Taking up a flaming arrow with his beak, he flew toward the tree;
the hunter then set fire to the dry leaves and scorched him.
When the cold had passed, he said, "O dear one, give me food.
The pigeon replied, "I have no store, for I am a forest-dweller. (94)
I live by the practice of constant alms-gathering; how could I destroy my hunger?
Yet, would you truly consider that I might satisfy you by the surrender of my own self? 95.
One should perform worship of the sages, the deities, the ancestors, the high-souled ones, the virtuous women, and the righteous, even by means of self-surrender.
Having spoken thus, the bird circumambulated the fire three times and entered it, repeatedly bowing to his guest while uttering the words, "Eat me! (bhakṣaya).
Then the hunter, seeing the pigeon roasted by the fire,
was moved by compassion and spoke of the sin born from the killing of a friend.
"What indeed might be the expiation for me, a cruel man, now that [this thought] has arisen?
Oh, by the offering of my body, hospitality has been shown! (99)
Thus, dwelling in the forest, I too shall practice that which pertains to the world beyond;
I shall perform righteous deeds, for devotion to Dharma is the supreme goal.
Having spoken thus, he quickly released the female pigeon from that cage and,
full of devotion, muttered "Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa" according to the prescribed manner.
Seeing her husband, the pigeon, consumed by fire, she too,
thereafter taking recourse in the dharma of a virtuous wife, entered the fire in her grief.
Then she beheld her husband wearing variegated armlets,
seated upon a celestial chariot, honored by goddesses and high-souled beings.
Having attained divine and celestial forms, they became dwellers of a celestial chariot (*vimāna*).
The hunter beheld those two gods situated in the sky within that chariot.
Having seen the fruit of the duty of service, even the Kirāta performed ascetic penance and practiced the honoring of guests dwelling in the forest.
The tending of cattle, birds, and other creatures, and the protection of those who have come for refuge—when the forest was consumed by a wildfire, he then became reduced to ashes. (106)
With his impurities destroyed by chanting the name of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa,
he indeed attained the divine state through service to those who serve Brahman.
"Thus perform service and go to the supreme state of liberation.
Having spoken thus to Rādhikā, Kṛṣṇa then became silent for a moment.

Thus ends the two hundred and eleventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Meal Following the Worship and Homa-offerings to the Deities of the Sacrifice in the Second Tretā Cycle of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā; and the Subsequent Journey to the Kingdom of Rāyabāleśvara and the Island of Dvaipāyana, as well as the Wandering, Worship, and Instruction in the City of Vāyuphenā," etc. || 211 ||
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Rādhikā, thereafter the glorious Lord Bālakṛṣṇa himself drank milk and took his meal together with His family.
Then the Great Queen arrived, accompanied by ten thousand maidens, to perform worship;
at that time, three maidens placed the bridegroom’s garland around the neck of Hari.
Having accomplished their purpose, those queens considered themselves most fortunate;
then the king bestowed ten million gold pieces upon Hari.
Then the subjects celebrated a great festival and performed the worship of Hari;
having received the worship, Kṛṣṇa quickly ascended the celestial chariot.
Then the king himself ascended [the chariot] along with his entire army;
meanwhile, he had the honor being proclaimed by musicians. || 5 ||

Then, having himself ascended a celestial chariot, Hari, accompanied by the king, appeared in the sky along with the sages; and having observed the regions well-ordered within the kingdom, he remained there.
Then, having sighted Sādhudvīpa and reached the Haṭṭāsana ocean,
they quickly crossed it and reached the land of Ādha at the onset of night.
He prepared a sweet meal and rested comfortably;
then the three maidens attended to Hari as he lay upon his bed.
The Great Lord was awakened by the sounds of trumpets at dawn, as well as by auspicious hymns and the songs of the wives of the Brahmins.
Having quickly performed his bath and other rites, and having worshipped his parents and elders,
Hari arrived swiftly at that sacrificial ground together with his kinsmen.
On the morning of the eleventh day, O Brahmins, sages, great seers,
virtuous men, ritualists, and others arrived at the sacrificial pavilion.
The gods and others, the enjoyers of their respective stations, all returned to their own abodes; the fires, having become personified, sat within the sacrificial pits as was appropriate.
There, benedictions were uttered and declarations for an auspicious day were made;
sprinklings, awakenings, and worship took place in due order.
The fire-offerings and libations took place exactly as was customary,
and likewise, the final performance of the oblation and the ritual dismissal were carried out.
The gods became the very food of the sacrificial offerings for the nourishment of that vow;
they received non-food sustenance from the hand of Śrī Hari.
There they were satisfied, having attained great satisfaction born from the grace of Hari;
then, there were great gifts of wealth consisting of gold and jewels.
Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, together with the kings, caused millions, billions, trillions, quadrillions, and even beyond that— parārdhas— the highest of numbers, to be given to the Brahmins.
Then all the kings, together with their queens,
performed oblations in their respective sacrificial pits, consisting indeed of the final offering (pūrṇāhuti).
The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa also offered oblations of the nature of nectar into the fire in the primary sacrificial pit for the sake of the deities.
Then the Blessed One performed the supreme Mahāpūrṇāhuti;
at that time, the incarnations, the lords, and likewise the sages were liberated.
The sages, all the deities, and the goddesses, as well as humans and others;
all the offspring of Kaśyapa, men and women endowed with physical forms—[all these were present]. (21)
For the sake of obtaining the grace of the sacrificial pap (caru) and for the attainment of the great fullness (mahāpūrṇāhuti),
all beings, both stationary and moving, indeed gathered in the pavilion.
By thousands of streams of clarified butter today, the deities and others are satisfied;
and by tens of thousands of streams of wealth, those of infinite creation are satisfied.
Immediately after the formal resolve (saṃkalpa) for the great final oblation (mahāpūrṇāhuti),
one should pay homage to the fire as Mṛḍa, place the clarified butter (ājya) upon it, and set out the large and small sacrificial ladles (sruk and sruva).

Having heated [the vessel] with darbha grass, wiped it, poured out the clarified butter (ājya), and inspected it, he consecrated the ājya, took some, and placed a bilva fruit (śrīphala) into the sacrificial ladle (sruk). || 25 ||
Having placed betel, fruits, areca nuts, unbroken grains, and so forth upon it, and having adorned the sacrificial fuel-sticks with flowers and sandalwood paste. ||26||

Having worshipped with "Salutation to the Full Oblation" (pūrṇāhuti) and having likewise held the sacrificial offering (havya) with both hands, the Lord and the sacrificers, headed by the King, [proceeded].
Thousands of streams of ghee, situated at the openings of conduits, flowed incessantly and repeatedly into the center of the sacrificial pit at that time. (28)
The Vedic mantras were uttered, and the deities of the fire [appeared];
then they performed meditation upon the fire, which stood visibly before the sacrificer. (29)
It has four horns, is bound in three ways, possesses two heads, and is brilliantly radiant;
it has two nostrils, six eyes, four ears, and three feet.
He is seven cubits tall, with four hands on the right and three on the left;
in his right hands he holds the *sruva* ladle, the *sruk* ladle, a spear, and a rosary.
Holding a thunderbolt and a fan, as well as a vessel of ghee, in his left hands; possessing seven tongues and three tongues in his northern forest [face]. (32)
Four-faced, possessing fifty-two kalās on the right side, known as the twelve crores of forms, and seated upon a red lotus throne. ||33||
Marked by the utterances of Svāhā, Svadhā, and Vaṣaṭ, the fire-god carries away the blood; he has tawny eyes, a red neck, and a black path.
We bow indeed to you, the fire Vaiśvānara, who consists of flames, who possesses seven rays, who is the bearer of oblations, and who is the domain of the gods. 35.
Having meditated thus and bowed accordingly, the twice-born recited Vedic mantras;
streams of clarified butter fell there into the fire by the thousands.
Oṃ! From the ocean a wave, rich in sweetness, has arisen; it attained immortality together with the Upāṃśu cup.
That which is the secret name of clarified butter is the tongue of the gods and the navel of immortality. 37.
Let us proclaim his name; at this sacrifice, we sustain him with our homages.
May the Brahman hear the hymn being recited; thus has the four-horned bull bellowed. 38.
He has four horns, three feet, two heads, and seven hands.
Bound in three ways, the bull bellows loudly; the great god has entered into mortals. 3.9.
The gods discovered the clarified butter (ghṛta) hidden by the Paṇis in three ways within the cow;
Indra produced one part, Sūrya produced one, and from Vena they fashioned one by their own inherent power.
These flow from the ocean within the heart, with a hundred paths, so that the enemy may not perceive them.
I behold the streams of clarified butter; in their midst stands the golden reed. 41.
The streams flow forth perfectly, purified within the heart by the sinless mind;
these waves of clarified butter rush forward like deer fleeing from a hunter's arrow.
Like swift birds on the path of the ocean, the mighty streams fly forth, driven by the wind;
the torrents of clarified butter flow like a ruddy steed, cleaving the barriers and swelling with their waves. 43.
Like beautiful women smiling as they go toward a gathering, the streams of clarified butter flow continuously like fuel; finding them pleasing, Jātavedas eagerly accepts them. 44.
Like maidens going to meet their bridegroom, I gaze upon them as they anoint themselves;
where the Soma is pressed and where the sacrifice is, there the streams of clarified butter flow and purify themselves. 45.
Flow toward our excellent praise in the contest for cattle; bestow upon us auspicious riches.
Lead this sacrifice of ours to the gods; the streams of clarified butter flow sweetly. 46.
Upon your abode the entire world is supported: within the ocean, within the heart, and within life.
Brought together in the assembly of the waters, may we attain that honeyed wave of yours. 47.

Oṃ! The gods generated Agni Vaiśvānara—the head of heaven, the steward of earth, born of the Eternal Order (ṛta)—as a seer, a sovereign, and a guest of men; they produced him as a vessel for their mouths. 48.
Oṃ, I offer consciousness with mind and clarified butter, so that the gods, who increase the Truth and are well-disposed toward the sacrifice, may come here.
For the Lord of all existence, for Viśvakarman, I offer every day an inviolable oblation. 49.
Seven are your fuel-sticks, O Agni, seven your tongues, seven the seers, and seven your beloved abodes.
The seven officiating priests worship you in seven ways; fill the seven wombs with clarified butter, Svāhā! 2.212.50.
Śukra, Jyotis, Citrajyotis, and Satyajyotis; Jyotiṣmat, Śukra, Ṛtapā, and Atyaṃhas. ||51||
Such as you are, and other than you, and similar, and exactly alike; measured and well-measured, and sharing the burden. ||52||
Ṛta and Satya, Dhruva and Dharuṇa, Dhartṛ and Vidhartṛ, and Vidhārayas;
Ṛtajit and Satyajit, Senajit and Suṣeṇa, Antimitra and Dūre-amitra, and Guṇa. (53)
Such as you are, of such a kind, like this, and resembling one another—come hither! O Maruts, being measured, well-proportioned, and bringing gifts together, be present at our sacrifice today.
Svatavān, Praghāsī, Sāntapana, Gṛhamedhī, Krīḍī, Śākī, and Ujjeṣī;
Ugra, Bhīma, Dhvānta, Dhuni, Sāsahvān, Abhiyugvan, and Vikṣipa—svāhā!
May the Ādityas, the Rudras, and the Vasus kindle you again; may the Brahmans, O leader of wealth, [kindle you] again with sacrifices.
Waxing strong with clarified butter, may the desires of the sacrificer come true. (56)
Thou art the purifier of wealth, with a hundred streams; thou art the purifier of wealth, with a thousand streams.
May the god Savitṛ purify thee with the purifier of wealth, with a hundred streams; O well-purified one, thou hast milked out the wish-granting cow.
O full ladle, fly away; well-filled, fly back again. Like two merchants bargaining for goods, let us exchange food and strength, O Śatakratu! Svāhā!
This [offering] is for Agni Vaiśvānara, for the Vasus, Rudras, and Ādityas, for Śatakratu, and for the Waters. Homage! 58.

This salutation is to those dwelling in heaven, to those dwelling on earth, to those dwelling in the great realm (mahaḥ), to those dwelling in the world of generation (jana), and to those dwelling in the world of austerity (tapaḥ);
and this is to the Lords dwelling in truth and dwelling beyond the veil (āvṛti).
Salutation to Virāja and Mahāvirāja. ||59||
This salutation to the Viṣṇus, the Mahāviṣṇus, and the Hiraṇyagarbhas;
this salutation to the Bhūs, the Mahāpuruṣas, the Mahākālas, and the Caturvyūhas. ||2.212.60||
And this salutation to the Imperishable One, to the six imperishable incarnations, and to the Incarnator;
this salutation to the beloveds of Brahman, to the sovereign mistresses, to the radiant ones, and to the virtuous ones. 6.1.
This is for the male attendants, the female attendants, the male hosts, and the female hosts; this is for the yogins, the yoginīs, all the guardians, and the lords of the fields—namas! ||62||
I bow to these [offerings] for the great seers and for the ancestors belonging to the wind and the water;
I bow to these for the Yakṣas and Rākṣasas belonging to Yama and to Kaśyapa. ||63||
This is for men and women, and for beasts and female beasts;
this is for female birds and male birds, and for male reptiles and female reptiles—salutations! ||64||
This salutation is for the male slaves and female slaves, and for the trees and creepers;
this salutation is for the grasses, the thickets, the shrubs, and the roots. ||65||
This salutation is to the sacred fords, to the rivers, to the oceans, and to the lakes;
and this salutation is to the shrines, to the insentient, to the principles, and to the sentient. (66)
This [offering] is for the Daityas, the Bhūtas, the Piśācas, the Bhūtīs, the Nādis, and so forth;
this is for those below, above, within, and those situated at the sides. ||67||
This salutation is to the Sādhyas, to the ascetics, and to the female practitioners of Sāṃkhya and Yoga;
this salutation is to the Aṃśas, to the Kalās, to the Āveśas, and to the Vibhūtis. ||68||
This salutation is to the forms of the Lord as the objects of worship and as the inner controller;
this salutation is to His manifestations, His reflected forms, and those who have descended [into the world]. (69)
This salutation is to those who renounce, to ascetics, to those of virtuous conduct, and to those most devoted to Brahman;
this salutation is to virtues, to ritual actions, to aesthetic flavors, and to beloved ones. 2.212.70.
This salutation is for those in the womb, for children, for the young, and for the elderly;
this salutation is for the deceased, for those bound by their vows, and for the times. (71)
This salutation is to the treasuries, to the senses, to the powers, and to the deities;
this is to the māyās, to the Īśānas, and to the Īśānīs.
And salutations to the Vaiṣṇavīs. ||72||
This salutation is to the Brāhmīs, the Brahmāṇīs, the Vairājīs, and the Bhūmnīs;
this is to the Dhāmas and the Vikuṇṭhas.
Salutations to those who are greenish-yellow and white. ||173||
This is for the tawny ones, the red ones,
the fair-skinned ones, and those who have been remembered;
this is for Lakṣmī, Rādhikā, and Sarasvatī.
Salutation to Durgā and Gaṅgā. ||74||
This [is offered] to Virajā, Padmāvatī, Ramā,
Māṇikī, and Mañjulā— salutations!
This [is offered] to Kamalā, Haṃsā, and Amṛtā.
Salutations to Sadguṇā and Sudevī. ||75||
This salutation is to Duḥkhahā, to Lakṣmī, to the contented ones, to Camarīs, to Kambharā, and to Śrī;
this is also for Dharma, for Vṛṣa, and for Gopāla.
And salutations to the Blessed One and to his beloved. ||76||
Salutations to this Śuka, to the self-luminous one, to the Great Vyāsa, and to the one whose authority is divine.
Salutations to this creation of Brahmā, to the creation of Īśa, and to the creation of the individual soul.
Salutations to the creator of all and to the non-creator. ||77||
This is offered as obeisance to the distinguished Supreme Lord, the beginningless Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the Master;
this is offered as obeisance to the sacrifice, to the oblation, to the recipients, to the ritual implements, and to Śrī-Kṛṣṇa-vallabha. ||78||
This [offering] is for the sacrificial pit, for the Vedas, for the pavilion, and for the musical notes;
this is for the great ones, for the wretched, for the helpless, and for the insects—salutation to them! ||79||
This is not for monks, nor for trustees, nor for servants, nor for those with expectations, nor for disciples;
it is for those who wait and for those who do not wait.
And salutations to the principles that are both embodied and unembodied. ||2.212.80||
This salutation is for those who are dissolved and those who are not dissolved, for those who have arrived and those who have not yet arrived.
This salutation is for those who possess light and those who do not possess light, for those who possess bodies and those who do not possess bodies, and for those who are limited. ||8.1||
This is for those who are mindful and those who are mindless, for the fierce and the gentle, and for those who are undiscriminating;
this is for those of the nature of goodness (*sāttvika*), those of passion (*rājasa*), and those of darkness (*tāmasa*), and for those touched by the three times—salutations to them! 82.
I bow to this [world] from those possessing sense-faculties and from those without sense-faculties, from the *kalala* stages and from seeds, and from the subtle;
I bow to this from as many as there are, from as few as there are, from the most minute atoms and from the non-atomic, and from the sprouts. (82)
I offer salutation to these [deities] from the desires, the pleasures, the sovereignties, the rains, and the wombs;
I offer salutation to these from the devotions, the others, the autumnal ones, the earths, and the lingas. ||84||
This salutation is to the *līlās*, to the *tulasīs*, and to the sacrificial fuel-sticks;
this salutation is to the acts of worship, to the offerings of honor, and to the welcoming gestures. (85)
This salutation is to the kings, to the subjects, and to those who possess faith; this salutation is to the lineages, to the collateral branches, and to the successive descendants. ||86||
This is for the virtuous women, for those pregnant, and for those who have recently given birth;
this is for those with venomous fangs, for those with tusks, and for those with horns. ||87||
This I offer to the ministers, both those with impurity and those free from impurity;
this I offer to the weapons, the garments, and the machines. ||88||
This salutation is to the celestial chariots that travel through the air, to the palatial mansions, and to the various vehicles;
this salutation is to the cosmic aeons, to the wish-fulfilling trees, and to the wish-granting creepers. (89)
This salutation is to the cows that grant all desires and to the wish-fulfilling gems;
this salutation is to the lake of Brahmā, to the pool of Brahmā, to the stream of nectar, and to the vessel of inexhaustibility.
And this salutation is to Him, the Great Black One, the Child-Kṛṣṇa who dwells within this [universe];
and this salutation is to Brahmā, the Supreme Brahman, Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Self. || 9.1 ||
Thus, O Rādhikā, oblations are offered with infinite names into the fire within the sacrificial pit, directly for the sake of the God of gods. || 92 ||
Coming again and again, they all take [the offerings] from the forest fire;
then, satisfied, joyful, with belches and blessings, they depart.
When the oblation was thus performed with coconuts and other offerings,
Bālakṛṣṇa appeared in the auspicious fire like a great final full-offering (mahāpūrṇāhuti).
He became visible in a divine form to all embodied beings;
indeed, Viśvambhara himself partook of various sacrificial offerings.
Having included each of those [offerings], one who is satisfied indeed bestows satisfaction:
namely, sugar, honey-mixtures, sacrificial porridges, and fruits. (96)
Clarified butters, divine grains of rice, sweet foods,
nectars, ambrosias, and various kinds of drinks as well— 97.
Grains such as those of Kaṇabhuj, seeds, sacrificial fuel, and other essences of milk are offered into the fire for Hari. 98.
Whatever edible things exist in the world for any beings, those very same things are offered into the fire of Hari. (99)
Whatever brings satisfaction to whomsoever, even the omniscient Bālakṛṣṇaka,
having offered that very thing or that person into the fire, he indeed satisfies them.
Thus the *pūrṇāhuti* was produced, and likewise the *mahāpūrṇāhuti*;
the entire world became satisfied, and indeed the circle of creation itself was satisfied.
The entire Brahma-maṇḍala was indeed satisfied and beyond further creation;
then the gods and others said, "Now we are not being cooked in his stomach."
"May the Supreme Lord provide the oblations"—
when such was the proclamation of millions of gods, Hari himself [acted].

Satisfied and serene, having produced an eructation, he performed the concluding oblation at the end of the *homa*. When the great *pūrṇāhuti* had been offered, the Nārāyaṇas then indeed offered fruits called "Amṛta," which were born of their own abode, into the fire.
Then the liberated ones offered fruits consisting of the very essence of the aeons;
then the lords offered the fruits of the nectar of sovereignty.
The sages and the deities offered fruits of ambrosia; likewise, human beings offered coconuts and sugar. (106)
Then the mountains offered sandalwood and other woods, the cows offered milk-rice, and the trees offered the finest juices and gundra-roots; they all sacrificed everything at that time.
There, the crops offered auspicious grains of rice and the like;
the creepers offered sweet flowers, and the goddesses offered sweet foods.
Just as they had attained prosperity, so indeed did they offer fruits and other oblations there into the fire of the sacrificial pit for the Supreme Lord, who is higher than the highest.
Those possessing leaves offered leaves, those possessing fragrance offered fragrant substances,
and those possessing excellent bark offered that bark there into the fire.
A smoky-smoke, fragrant and providing sweet satisfaction, pervaded the three worlds;
for when Hari was satisfied, O Rādhikā, the three creations were then satisfied.
Thus the great sacrifice was completed at midday;
there followed the distribution of sacrificial fees, the worship of the gods, and their dismissal.
The Blessed One personally performed the giving of sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) as well;
indeed, he caused all the mendicants to be provided with food and other necessities.
The preceptors and others, as was appropriate, accepted those ritual materials, including the sacrificial fees and other offerings; thereafter, the [period of] renunciation began.

Thus ends the two hundred and twelfth chapter, titled "The Description of the Offering of the Great Final Oblation on the Eleventh Day, the Satiety of All, and the Cessation of Sacrifice," in the second section, the Tretā-saṃtāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmīnārāyaṇīya-saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O Rādhikā, on the sacrificial ground, the great fire in the pit kissed the sky and, being delighted, then bestowed blessings.
May this earth always possess peaceful conduct and be filled with supreme prosperity;
and may the subjects here always be abundant in the happiness of righteous policy. (2)
May they be immortal, fortunate in happiness, and always prosperous here;
may kings indeed abide on the path of justice and possess great wealth. (3)
May the maidens be happy, and the youths be endowed with prosperity;
may the subjects be long-lived and free from disease. (4)
May there always be abundance of crops and great wealth in gold, silver, and other treasures;
may people be wise, and may women be endowed with good fortune. (5)
May the cattle yield abundant milk, may the trees be filled with sap,
may the earth be rich in flavorful juices, and may householders be equal to the gods.
May there be an empire of supreme authority, prosperous with wealth and other resources;
may this land become divine, and may its regions be full of abundance. (7)
May men become worthy vessels who worship the gods, sages, and gurus;
may sacrifices flourish in this world, and may gold be abundant.
Thus, at that sacrifice, the blessings bestowed by Vahni were heard by all the people with hearts full of joy.
Having thus bestowed these words of blessing, the Fire-god vanished;
and then the embodied beings took the grace of the sacrificial ashes.
When the sacrifice was concluded, the command for food then arose;
indeed, all kinds of sweet delicacies were then being served.
Then, during the sacrifice, the embodied beings— including the Lord, the gods, humans, and those of other species— partook of the sweet food, seated in rows.
"Give, give! "Eat, eat!
"Take, take!"—thus do the servers cry out. (13)
Then, food beyond counting and an incalculable amount of wealth were given;
indeed, garments and various kinds of vessels were also given in countless numbers.
Various kinds of food are also given there at that sacrifice;
on the eleventh day, great gifts are bestowed everywhere.
O Rādhikā, both kings and subjects offer all manner of honors, primarily consisting of gold.
And the recipients, having indeed accepted [the offerings], give them to other supplicants;
there, millions of embodied beings partake of the supreme sacrificial oblation (havya). || 17 ||
When the festival had thus commenced, the Lord addressed the people, the sages, and the subjects for the sake of the concluding ritual (avabhṛtha) at the confluence of the rivers and the lake: 18.
"Today we must certainly go to bathe; let everyone quickly prepare themselves!
Let the great drum be struck there for the purpose of making the proclamation. (19)
And let them come for the sake of the final purificatory bath (avabhṛtha), for the Blessed One is indeed proceeding there;
whatever sins there may be, arising from injury to living beings—[may they all be cleansed].
Whatever defects have arisen in the ritual section (karmakāṇḍa), as well as whatever misfortunes occurred during the oblation of rice grains, fuel-sticks, and clarified butter; || 21 ||
For the sake of their destruction, the *avabhṛtha* bath is always praised; it was performed by the incarnations of Īśvara, by the gods, and by men. (22)
One should bathe after having worshipped Varuṇa, whether or not one has also worshipped the water itself,
using either *āmalaka* fruits, ashes, or clarified butter.
"Then one should bathe with water using clay from a sacred ford (tīrtha) and sesame seeds";
thus were humans and others awakened by the drum.
The Īśvaras and the deities, the Nārāyaṇas and the lords of men, the goddesses, the Satīs, the Bhagavatīs, and also the Sāṃkhya-yoginīs. (25)
With the sounds of musical instruments and songs,
they indeed proceeded to the final ablution at the Vinipāra lake in the Śeṣakāṣṭhavana forest.
Then, at the sacred confluence, the sacrificers bathed according to the prescribed rites;
wherever they were on the banks, there they remained.
Having worshipped Varuṇa, as well as the sacred fords and the waters,
the blessed Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa and the women who are dear to Brahmā bathed.
The gods and goddesses bathed there, for the water had indeed become a supreme sacred ford;
so too did the incarnations of Nārāyaṇa, as well as Rādhā, Ramā, and the others.
There they bathed in the sacred fords and other purifying waters for the sake of purification; and when the concluding ablution was thus completed, they indeed returned to their own homes.
Then there was a great assembly for the purpose of distributing rewards; to all the employees, gifts fashioned of gold were presented. (3.1)
Indeed, Madhava bestows ornaments, jewels,
necklaces made of gold, and excellent garments.
There were golden moons adorned with jewels, indicating future undertakings;
there were lines revealing his virtues, and he was endowed with the marks of sacrifice.
Silver moons, as well as woolen blankets, garments, and shawls; looms, earrings, and also waist-bands, finger-rings, and seals. || 34 ||
There were finger-rings and bracelets, as well as auspicious garlands of pearls; beautiful golden vessels, platters, and likewise water-jars. (35)
Parasols, yak-tail whisks, fans, celestial chariots, beautiful lion-thrones, and four-legged couches with cushions. (36)
The beloved of Śrī Kṛṣṇa gave great necklaces of gold and gems, as well as garlands made of diamonds, in the form of rewards.
He gave weapons to the Kṣatriyas, sacrificial fees to the Brāhmaṇas, and indeed bestowed appropriate rewards upon others as well. || 38 ||
The noble Svāmī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa gave golden images, well-endowed with life-breaths, for the purpose of worship. (39)
Relying on the instructions of his preceptor, he performed all these rites there at the sacrifice from the mountains;
having thus completed everything, he indeed took a moment's rest.
Just then, King Rāyalambāra and the great Ṛṣi Rūparṭu arrived there and quickly made their request. 41.
O Great King, sanctify today on the Ekādaśī day those regions we have visited and likewise that beautiful city. (42)
Then Hari said, "So be it," and prepared his celestial chariot;
he was accompanied by his family, as well as by Hara and Lomaśa.
The king went quickly ahead by celestial chariot to welcome him;
Hari also went swiftly in the evening to the auspicious city of Ugrā.
Following the path shown by the king, he brought down the celestial chariot;
the king then offered a welcome in his own palace garden.
Then, many delightful musical instruments were played everywhere; the people who had gathered to see [the festival] offered praises to Acyuta.
From the celestial chariot, Śrī Hari emerged outside that garden and [honored] the Supreme Lord with parched grain,
unbroken rice, flowers, sandalwood, and other offerings.
The subjects, including men and women, honored him exceedingly;
the king, having bowed to Hari in his palace, worshipped him with many jewels. 48.
Then the queen performed the worship, and the six daughters of the king chose that Blessed One as their husband by offering the bridegroom’s garlands.
They had accomplished their purpose, and the king rejoiced exceedingly;
the queen also rejoiced in many ways and presented various offerings.
The queen gave him a dowry and then performed the lustration ceremony (nīrājana);
she then fed the wielder of the Śārṅga bow with milk-rice and other foods.
Then the king caused the preceptor, who was beloved by Kṛṣṇa, to be paraded through the city along the royal highway, accompanied by his army.
The leading merchants and others increased the prosperity of the Lord; likewise, all the subjects and the Vakriṇī maidens offered him worship. (53)
Then Hari honored everyone with necklaces, fruits, wealth, blankets, garments, and other ornaments; indeed, he bestowed all his riches upon them.
He gave the dowry to the sage Rūpārta and took it with him;
having arrived at the royal palace, he found rest there during the night. (55)
Having accepted the service of the six maidens, Hari indeed woke up at dawn;
having performed his morning rites and drunk milk, he became ready to depart. (56)
At sunrise, honored by the army, he arrived quickly;
having received worship on the sacrificial ground, he descended indeed to his own abode.
Having done this indeed, O Rādhikā, he then beheld the auspicious and purifying city of Uvakra, the site of a sacrifice on the morning of the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī). ||58||
In the assembly hall, he caused the universal monarchs to be honored;
likewise, the liberated ones, the abodes, the incarnations, the Nārāyaṇas, and the Īśvaras;
as well as the sages, the ancestors, the gods, the Daityas, and human beings.
Birds, aquatic creatures, and all those dwelling in the netherworld assembled together.
The immobile and the mobile, the insentient and the sentient—slaves, servants, masters, and mistresses alike—went to the assembly hall. (61)
The Īśvarīs, as well as the Nārāyaṇīs, the Satyas, and those dear to the gods; the Apsarases, who are beloved by all, and likewise the Mātṛkās, arrived there.
The female ascetics from the Brahma-lake, those who practice celibacy, as well as the female practitioners of Sāṃkhya and Yoga, and the various emanations, also arrived at the assembly.
Lord Hari, the Blessed One, being pleased, [bestows] the wish-fulfilling trees, the celestial cows, and the creepers; likewise, the wish-fulfilling gems, male attendants, and female attendants.
Then they caused that assembly hall to appear,
with divine thrones shining like the sun.
When they had all sat down, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa,
Mādhava, spoke to all the incarnations who had arrived.
I feel honored and blessed by you here, since you have come for the sake of the sacrifice even after leaving your own abodes. (67)
I offer my salutations and blessings to these lords and goddesses, who have arrived from afar for the sake of this sacrifice. (68)
I offer honor and thanks to the sages, the ascetics, the ancestors, and likewise to the women, who have come to this sacrifice. (69)
I offer honor and thanks to the gods, to the descendants of Kaśyapa, and to all human beings, since you have come to this sacrifice;
as well as to the trees and the like, the grasses and the like, the creepers, and the shrubs.
I offer honor and thanks because you have come to this sacrifice.
I offer honor and thanks to the sacred fords, to the deities, and even to the insentient beings, because they too have come to this sacrifice.
Of those dwelling in the depths of Pātāla, of those inhabiting water and land, of those dwelling in fire and wind, as well as of sacred fords and mountains; ||73||
And [he saw] the guardians of the worlds and the directions, the servants, the hosts, the lords of the hosts, and the yogis. ||74||
I offer honor and thanks to you all who have come to this sacrifice, as well as to the servants on every side who have exerted themselves for the sake of the rite. (75)
Of all the female attendants and field-protectors on every side, and of the groups of male servants and guardians on every side. ||76||

[This applies] to those who have attained all authority, as well as those who prepare medicinal juices and probes, the guardians of the storehouse of materials, and those who enjoy the objects provided by their resolve. ||77||
Of donors, of kings, of princes, and of the wives of Brahmins; of Brahmins, of Vedic mantras, of sacrificial offerings, and of those who hold the vessels for the sacrifice. ||78||
I offer honor and thanks to the principles, the knots of inertia, the shrines, and the architects of the universe, who have come to this sacrifice. (79)

Having granted a parting gift, with palms joined in reverence, and having bestowed His own grace and auspicious blessings, He gave me an image of Himself made of gold, silver, and other materials, as well as nectar and ambrosia.
He bestowed crowns, bracelets, and beautiful earrings;
he gave ornaments, garments, vessels, and even fine cloths. (8.1)
He bestowed parasols, celestial vehicles, garments and the like;
he bestowed beautiful helmets and silken cloths. (82)
He bestowed elephants, horses, chariots, and jewels, as well as diamonds;
he also gave various ornaments and garments such as bodices. ||83||
I gave you inexhaustible vessels, as well as wish-fulfilling trees and the like;
I also gave you wish-granting creepers, wish-granting cows, and wish-granting gems.
I grant you divine knowledge, great sovereignty, and divine splendor;
I grant you eternal divine power, peace, devotion, and service. ||85||
"I grant you divine perfections, great gain, and my own nectar," said the Blessed One, Kṛṣṇavallabhācārya, the fulfiller of desires. (86)
He then gave divine crowns and earrings made of gold with celestial letters to the primordial incarnations, who are supreme lords.
Then, [offerings] should likewise be made to the guardians of the world (lokapālas) and to the kings;
in this manner, they should be given to all others as well, according to what is appropriate and required.
He indeed bestowed rewards upon the men and women assembled there;
thereafter, Hari performed the act of giving in this manner every morning. (89)
The Lord bestowed wealth upon the bodies of his servants, slaves, and others;
he gave them suitable necklaces of gold and necklaces of jewels again and again.
He gave gold ornaments suitable for women to the female attendants,
and he also gave food in abundance to all those who had vessels for eating.
The Lord Nārāyaṇa gave garments of all kinds even from his own clothes and vessels; he bestowed gifts of houses upon many.
And from the royal gate, he caused dwellings to be bestowed upon the twice-born;
thus the lord himself brought all these acts of giving to completion.
Then he caused a universal feast to be prepared;
for the breaking of his fast, he fed [the guests] with auspicious and sweet milk-rice (pāyasa).
He fed them savory foods, honey-mixture foods, and sweet foods;
he fed them foods like nectar, foods like ambrosia, and foods like the essence of milk.
He caused them to eat food of merit, food of meditation, and also food of fruit;
he also caused them to eat food of grain, food of sages, and food of leaves.
He caused them to eat food from vessels, food from sprouts, and also food from grain;
he caused them to eat food from water, purifying food, and food from fire.
He caused them to eat the food of light, the food of the abode, and the food of the sattvic nature; he awakened them to the food of pure being and the food of the glory of divine play.
He caused them to eat seasonal food and non-seasonal food, as well as food born of the body;
he also caused them to eat the food of the cosmic cycles, the food of the perfected ones, and the food of the Siddhas.
He fed them all with the food of meditation, the food of contentment, and the food of satisfaction;
he fed them all with the food of bliss and the food of great happiness.
He fed him buttermilk, sugar, milk, soup, as well as rice and other foods, along with *pūrikās*, *polikās*, and various side dishes.
He fed him with sweet foods, boiled dishes, fried cakes, *parpaṭa* and other such items, as well as *sevika*, *apūpa*, and *saṃyāva*.
He served chickpeas and fried flower-shaped cakes, as well as auspicious and pleasant *meśubha* sweets; he also served *mohasthālā* dishes. (103)
He fed the Cakrapāras, the Sthirakas, and even the Granthakas;
he also fed those who subsist on black mustard and those who live on fermented gruel.
He fed him curd, clarified butter, fresh butter, molasses, and honey;
he gave him sour drinks and the juices of mangoes to drink in autumn;
and he fed him fruits, both fresh and dried, as well as seeds.
He provided mouth-fresheners, aromatic grains, and betel leaves for them to eat.
The Lord caused the water from the heart-lake of Brahmā to be drunk by all;
having thus fed them, Hari himself then ate.
Accompanied by his family and joined by Brahmapriyā, he was also accompanied by Rādhā, Ramā, Satī, Lakṣmī, Prabhā,
Pāravatī, Māṇikī, Duḥkhahā, Lakṣmī, Mañjulā, and Amṛtikā.
Accompanied by Guṇā, Āśā, Durgā, Sarasvatī, and Haṃsā. || 109 ||
The parents and the supreme gurus, headed by Lomaśa, partook of the meal;
indeed, all the embodied beings present at the festival also ate.
The descendants of Gaṅgā, the descendants of Amarya, the great sages, the maidens, the rivers, the streams, and the sacred fords all enjoyed [the offerings] with great longing. (111)
At midday, Śrī Hari fed the kings there; at the time following midday, he fed the dignitaries of the sacrifice. || 11 ||re||
He commanded them all to go to their respective worlds and their own abodes,
with the exception of all the beloveds of Brahmā and those beginning with Lomaśa.
Except for his own family— namely Īśāna, Satī, and Gaṇeśvara—
and except for the Cāmarikarṣins as well as Tuṣita.
Except for Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who is existence-consciousness-bliss, and you, Rādhikā;
except for Nārāyaṇa and Lakṣmī; and except for the people of Aśva-saras—1.15.
Thus, O Rādhikā, having repeatedly received permission in every way, they departed on their own celestial chariots; by evening, [the place] had become as if empty.
At night, those ever-active ones performed the dismantling of the pavilions built by Viśvakarman; by morning, the site had become a bare clearing.

Thus ends the two hundred and thirteenth chapter, titled "The Description of Vahni’s Benediction, Feasts, the Concluding Bath (Avabhṛtha), Rewards, Hari’s Evening Departure for King Rāyalambāra’s Kingdom, His Wandering, Worship, and Feasting in Kimuvakrāpuri, Resting at Night, Returning to the Sacrificial Ground in the Morning, the Performance of the Mahīmāna Ceremony, the Bestowal of Honors, Salutations, Gifts, and Rewards, Feasts, and the Parting Gift," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. || 213 ||
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Listen, O Rādhikā! On the thirteenth day, having performed his morning rites at dawn, Hari took his seat and became established in worship.
Just then, King Rājanavārkabhu arrived there and requested the Blessed One to return to his own kingdom.
Hari said, "So be it," and made everyone ready;
then, having summoned Rāya-kinnara-samrāj, he spoke to him regarding that procedure.
Then the king, having honored Kṛṣṇa, gave him leave to depart; Hari quickly descended from his celestial chariot and remained in the sky.
Then musical instruments were sounded during the *vidāya* rite dedicated to the Supreme Lord (*pārameśvara*):
Rokīśvara, Raṇajit, Mārīśa, and Vāyukakṣaka. || 5 ||
Then, O King, Bāleśvara, Lambāra,
and the others gave leave and dowry to their daughters, bestowing them upon Hari.
Honored by his armies and celebrated with musical instruments and songs,
he traveled swiftly in a celestial chariot accompanied by his entire caravan.
The kingdom of King Rājanavārkabhu, named Miśrasura,
was situated near the Supārīya lake at the confluence of the Miśrasura river.
In a garden on the outskirts of the city of Ciñcāgopurikā,
there was indeed a sage named Vāyuśṛṅgatanu who was with Kṛṣṇa.
The king went there in his celestial chariot, having already departed thither; he quickly and properly prepared his army for the purpose of welcoming Hari.
Then musical instruments were played by the subjects born of joy,
and the sounds of those instruments spread to the very ends of the quarters.
Maidens and young women also sang auspicious, beautiful songs; endowed with festive melodies, they approached the presence of Kṛṣṇa.
The celestial chariot descended to earth by the path leading to the awakening of the King;
at that moment, there was indeed a rain of unbroken grains, parched rice, and flowers.
Shouts of "Victory! and cries of "Live on! issued from all his mouths;
and Kṛṣṇa stood forth outside the stationary celestial chariot.
Then, honored by the people, the kings, and the maidens and others,
the king washed his feet, drank the water, and placed it on his head.
Then she gave milk for them all to drink;
and accompanied by his army, Kṛṣṇa was joyfully paraded through the city.
The subjects, as well as the leading merchants, men and women, both mortals and immortals, and the wives of the mixed-caste gods, worshipped him with love alone. (17)
They worshipped him with substances, flowers, garments, fruits, jewels, diamonds, various crowns, and ornaments.
They honored him with folded palms, with the disposition of offering their very hearts,
with prostrations, and also with offerings of gifts according to their ability.
Having thus wandered through the city and granted his supreme vision,
Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa, accompanied by his followers, arrived at the royal palace.
The king honored him with jewels and other precious items, with golden necklaces,
with divine garments, excellent wealth, and celestial offerings with great respect.
He performed the nightly lamp-offering and worshipped him with sandalwood paste and other offerings;
then, declaring "I am fulfilled," he fell at his feet.
His four queens and the seven daughters of the king, whose faces were like the moon, then worshipped the Supreme Lord.
They were bewildered before their beloved Lord Śrīpati, yet they grasped their husband with their minds;
and filled with great joy, they placed the garland of choice around Kṛṣṇa’s neck.
Both the king and the queens indeed became fulfilled;
they were satisfied and considered their good fortune to be supreme.
At midday, he celebrated a royal festival filled with joy.
Then the king fed them all with most delicious food;
having given them betel and other refreshments, he bestowed upon them dowries and gifts.
Hari took all of that and gave it to the sage Tanvartu;
he also placed [the sage] upon a celestial chariot (vimāna) according to what was appropriate and suitable for him.
After resting for a moment in the city of Svarlatikā, the king spoke to Hari, saying, "I wish to go to my own city"; in an instant, Hari became ready.
The king went there first to that city and offered him honor with the sounds of musical instruments, the joyful shouts of the subjects, and offerings of flowers and other gifts. (29)
Then, having descended from his celestial chariot in the great garden,
the Blessed One wandered through the city according to the king’s instructions, bestowing his vision upon all.
The Supreme Lord was worshipped and saluted by the worlds, offered with material gifts, beheld, and firmly held within his own heart. (3.1)
The Supreme Lord, pleased by the many kinds of offerings made by the people, bestowed his grace upon Vāyuśṛṅga, who had come for worship. ||32||
He rested in the king’s divine, golden palace;
there arrived Rāyahāṇḍeśvara, the ruler of the Mākṣika kingdom.
Then, in order to request Hari for his own kingdom, he made his request;
Hari quickly became ready in the evening, accompanied by his caravan.
King Rājanavārka gave him a parting gift as a dowry;
then Hari quickly departed through the sky by means of a celestial chariot toward the kingdom of Mākṣika.
And at the onset of night, he arrived at the city of Mākṣika,
a great metropolis shining on all sides with the light of lightning.
And King Rāyahaṇḍeśa went forth to meet him, offering a welcome with his army, the sounding of musical instruments, banners, flags, and other such regalia. (37)
Then the king offered a welcome to Śrī Hari with flower garlands, shouts of "Victory!", auspicious songs, sandalwood paste, and other offerings.
When the celestial chariot descended to the earth, Hari came outside;
it was illuminated by the lightning-like rays of its infinite branches, appearing like the sky by day.
Indeed, at the front of the celestial chariot, the Blessed One shone like the moon in the sky;
and beholding Him, the Supreme Brahman, the women and the people were struck with wonder.
They greatly honored Hari with sandalwood flowers,
unbroken grains of rice, parched grain, and delightful essences of fragrance.
At night, the king indeed caused Mādhava to be paraded through the city;
the subjects, filled with eager devotion, worshipped Kṛṣṇa who was accompanied by his army. ||42||
At the city gates, in the courtyards, in the center, at the crossroads, on the royal highways, at the fronts of the market stalls, and in the palaces, they joyfully celebrated with great eagerness.
With materials such as gold coins, fruits, saffron, sandalwood, garments, coconuts, and fragrant essences; ||44||
With flower garlands, jewel necklaces, and priceless articles,
the Blessed One, having thus wandered through the city, [arrived at] the royal palace.
He arrived at the assembly hall and, during the night,
he instructed them all regarding the purpose they desired for their own livelihood.
Both happiness and the absence of suffering are indeed the two purposes [of dharma];
dharma is sought for the sake of happiness, for from dharma happiness is born. (47)
One should indeed strive so that future suffering does not arrive;
for unrighteousness is said to be the giver of suffering, and unrighteousness indeed bears the name of demerit.
Violence, such as causing pain to others and so forth, malice, and sin are indeed unrighteousness;
likewise, theft, the telling of falsehoods, and deception are sinful. (49)
Furthermore, acting unjustly, deeds that cause the destruction of others, the ruin of another's livelihood, and the destruction of another's property; ||2.214.50||
The loss of one's own liberation and so forth, as well as the avoidance [of it] through knowledge, foolishness, and the failure to serve one's own parents—these indeed are sins. (51)
Bringing other substances and the like, as well as protecting those who have taken refuge; forgetting the God of gods, and showing disrespect to those worthy of worship. (52)
The oppression of women, the useless oppression of children, the destruction of trees, creepers, and the like, and the setting of fire in a great forest; 53.
Whatever causes living beings to be scorched is all a great sin;
likewise, a person must not inflict such suffering upon themselves.
A human being surely accomplishes every purpose for himself, whether it be happiness arising from the body, born of the senses, or produced by the self. ||55||
But impermanent happiness will surely meet with destruction; of this there is no doubt.
Having reflected thus, that [impermanent happiness] is not to be sought; rather, eternal happiness is indeed what should be sought.
Sacrifice, charity, compassion, the gods, truth, service, austerity, and virtuous conduct—these are considered the duties of a yogi that bestow happiness. (57)
These eight are indeed purifying, bestowing excellence and grace;
visiting sacred pilgrimage sites grants happiness and is eternally beneficial. (58)
Visiting sacred places is purifying and bestows prosperity;
if a mortal lives there, he shall be enriched with food, wealth, clothing, and other such things. (5.9)
Then, having performed sacrifices and other rites, one may acquire eternal happiness;
for there are indeed holy pilgrimage sites, and the virtuous who work for the welfare of the worlds. ||2.214.60||
Holy places indeed exist, and there are images of Hari in temples;
by going there, one attains liberation, for through that, eternal happiness is found.
The destruction of sin arises through the dread of penance;
if one does not commit it again, one is liberated from future sin. || 6.2 ||
If one should cultivate the company of the virtuous, one is liberated from evil association;
having bathed in the sacred ford of the righteous, one is released from the affliction of Yama.
One who frequents holy places becomes virtuous; one who frequents the green [sacred] sites becomes Hara (Śiva);
one who uses fragrant substances becomes fragrant, and thereafter one becomes scented with the fragrance of Kṛṣṇa.
Having performed an action, the conscious being should not think "I am [the doer]";
thus, one is never stained by the action, just as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water.
He who covers even the open flaws of the virtuous,
though he be a sinner or an evildoer, attains auspiciousness.
Just as the sun is the destroyer of darkness, so too is the person who performs virtuous deeds;
he is the remover of all sins and the annihilator of every evil.
A person devoted to service constantly receives blessings;
through such service, one then attains long life, food, wealth, and happiness.
Through service to the virtuous, one attains eternal happiness by union with Kṛṣṇa;
therefore, a man endowed with far-sighted vision should become a pilgrim to the virtuous.
O Keśava, they dwell eternally in that eternal treasury of bliss;
for those who take refuge in it, that eternal treasury remains ever-present.
I am the eternal treasury, overflowing with great bliss;
the virtuous, endowed with my joy, cause others to be joyful. (71)
Liberation, which is indeed the primary goal and eternal bliss, is found only among the virtuous; therefore, one should constantly serve the holy ones.
Having spoken thus, O Rādhikā, the Blessed One then ceased;
thereafter, in the midst of the assembly, the king performed worship with millions of articles.
With vessels of gold and silver, garments, and ornaments,
he placed a crown upon the head of Bālakṛṣṇa.
Śrī Hari gave necklaces set with jewels and made of gold;
he also presented those adorned in soft woolen garments with golden ornaments.
He gave him two excellent chowries with golden handles and a cane staff, as well as beautiful garlands adorned with diamonds and pearls. (76)
He gave rings, water-pots, and various types of covers,
and he worshipped him with fragrant essences, flowers, and unbroken grains of rice.
Queen Hīravatī performed the worship of Kṛṣṇa and the ritual waving of lamps;
she applied a saffron tilaka on her forehead and fashioned a crescent moon with unbroken grains of rice. ||78||
She performed the highest worship upon his head with unbroken grains, flowers, and other offerings;
then she placed morsels of sweet food into Kṛṣṇa’s mouth.
The Queen of Men spoke to the nine maidens standing at her side:
"O maidens, this Lord of Śrī, the Master of Rādhā, truly shines forth."
"Even to obtain the sight of him requires merit accumulated over many lifetimes;
yet now, by his grace, he has appeared in person within one's own home. (8.1)
May they dwell within their hearts and never abandon Him;
may they worship Hari with love and serve Janārdana. 8.2
"May they always practice devotion like Śrī, Ramā, and Kamalā.
Upon hearing this, the maidens were utterly infatuated with Kṛṣṇa, the Child-Kṛṣṇa.
Having attained nourishment through their mother’s words, they, with joyful faces blooming like flowers, chose that beloved and infallible one by offering him garlands.
Those nine maidens placed garlands of choice upon the neck of Kṛṣṇa;
thereafter, the Blessed One took their hands according to the prescribed rite.
Having fulfilled his purpose, the king indeed celebrated a festival at night;
then the monarch bestowed food upon all the merchants.
The subjects also performed worship of Hari there with great devotion;
then Rādhā and the others took their meal, and thereafter Kṛṣṇa [did so] within the night.
Served by young maidens, he took a brief sleep, but was quickly awakened at dawn by auspicious sounds and the resonance of musical instruments. (88)
On the thirteenth day, having performed his ablutions and worship, he drank milk;
others also drank milk and other such things in the palace of King Huṇḍeśa.
In the morning, the sage Vīrākaja worshipped the Lord Śrī Hari with various offerings and Vedic mantras.
Having performed a great worship, he chose eternal liberation;
Hari said, "O sage, remain in meditative absorption and attain liberation. (9.1)
Thus addressed, that sage immediately became steady in meditation;
in an instant, he beheld within his heart the auspicious, divine form of Hari.
Then they beheld a celestial chariot named Akṣara, consisting of divine splendor, adorned with divine pearls and other jewels, and enveloped in radiance.
O Rādhikā, the Blessed One, taking him by the hand,
led him to his own imperishable abode and caused him to reach it at that very moment.
The king and others, however, threw the sage’s body into the middle of a pit;
O Rādhā, I shall tell you of the wonder that occurred within that body. (95)
There, heroes endowed with weapons emerged from his body;
possessing massive frames and great strength, they stood before Hari after bowing down to him. (96)
Those sons of the Vīraka people requested a dwelling from the Lord; Hari granted them a residence forever among the attendants of Śambhu. 97.
Those heroes and those people, having received permission from the Lord and from Satī, all departed for the eternal abode of Kailāsa. 98.
Having obtained the *anava* [empowerment] from Śambhu, those Vaiṣṇavas were indeed always characterized by *tamas*;
yet they became devotees of Hara, renowned as "Vīrajanas. 99.
Then the king prostrated himself like a staff before the glorious Lord Bālakṛṣṇa, the son of Kambharā, the Great Lord, and indeed performed the ritual service of massaging His feet.
Having performed service, the king then performed the lustration ceremony (nīrājana);
he drank the divine water used for washing the feet and stood nearby. || 101 ||
Just then, King Rāyakūpeśa arrived there to lead Hari to his own highly illustrious city named Havāna.
Hari said, "So be it," and Huṇḍeśa quickly became ready;
he offered his dowry and begged for Hari’s forgiveness.
Having bestowed the gift of fearlessness, Hari ascended his celestial chariot;
and by the command of Keśava, the members of the caravan also took their places within the chariot.
And King Rāyakūpeśa went there for the sake of honoring him;
having first gone and led his own army, he remained stationed in the garden. (105)
Then King Rāyahuṇḍeśa granted him leave and honor, accompanied by shouts of "Victory!", the sounds of musical instruments, and songs. || 106 ||
When Hari’s vehicle arrived near Hāstina-purī,
musical instruments were sounded and shouts of victory were raised by the people.
O Rādhikā, the practitioners of mantra and the subjects, their hearts filled with joy, then became eager to see Kṛṣṇa in the great garden.

Thus, in the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, in the second section, the *Tretā-santāna*, on the morning of the thirteenth day: the departure for the kingdom of King Rāyanavārka; wandering through the city of Ciñcāgopurikā, where worship was performed; then the journey toward the city of Svarlatikā, where wandering, worship, and instruction were conducted; then in the evening, the arrival at the kingdom of King Rāyahaṇḍeśvara; wandering through the city of Mākṣikā, where worship and instruction were given; and resting for the night on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada.
The two hundred and fourteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Liberation of the Vīrāka People and Sages, and the Journey to the City of Rāyakūpa, the King, and the Kingdom. || 214 ||
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Listen, O Rādhikā! On an island situated in the ocean, there was a king named Kūpeśa;
he rendered great honor to Śrī Hari in the highly magnificent city called Kyūba.
Then, by means of water-machines, vehicles, and boats,
the subjects went to a garden in the vicinity of the city of Hāvanā.
Then the celestial chariot descended upon the auspicious ground near the shore of the ocean,
and from there the king went into the presence of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
She bowed at his feet and placed garlands of flowers around his neck;
the queen worshipped the Lord of Gods with flowers, parched grain, unbroken rice, and other offerings.
The royal sage Heyatāyana worshipped the Supreme Lord;
the king caused Śrī Hari to be carried through the city on vehicles. || 5 ||
Having seated Śrī Hari within a golden carriage, which was adorned with umbrellas and chowries, the people worshipped him with great reverence.
With substances such as fruits, garments, and the like; with jewels, sandalwood, and saffron; with betel nuts and the like, coconuts, sugar, and so forth.
Then the king himself, having placed Kṛṣṇa upon a boat,
sported upon the ocean near the island.
Then, at the time of midday meal, the Blessed One partook of his food together with the caravan; at that moment, the queen arrived.
For the purpose of worshiping Hari there, she gave her daughter to Hari;
indeed, she placed betel and a beautiful garland upon the neck of Hari.
Having obtained Kṛṣṇa as her husband, that maiden became one who had fulfilled her purpose;
her mother also became exceedingly joyful and celebrated a royal festival.
Then, having attained rest in that most excellent abode, the Blessed One was visited by the king,
his maternal uncle, who came for the purpose of seeing his daughter.
The lord of the kingdom of Kulambāyana, the master of the city of Vigoṣṭha,
known by the name Kālīmaṇḍalīna, also worshipped Mādhava.
He indeed requested Śrī Hari to go to his own kingdom;
Hari said, "So be it," and immediately became ready.
And Kūpeśa gave a farewell gift to Śrī Hari as a dowry;
then, preceded by the sages of the Pūrṇā assembly, he entered the circle of Kālī.
The Blessed One, situated in his own celestial chariot, traveled through the sky to the assembly;
having crossed the ocean, he reached that city in the evening.
The king, accompanied by his army, paid him manifold honors;
the Blessed One descended upon the ground near the vicinity of the cowherd settlement.
The subjects greatly increased his prosperity with unbroken grains and other offerings;
and the Blessed One, descending from his own celestial chariot, alighted upon the golden ground.
The king sat upon a divine seat, bowed at his feet,
placed a garland of flowers around his neck, and likewise offered him sandalwood paste.
He also gave betel leaves and water to the traveling merchants;
accompanied by his army, the king caused them to be paraded about on vehicles.
With elephants, horses, carts, and likewise with human vehicles,
the people in the city called Vigoṣṭha indeed worshipped Acyuta.
[He saw] Kṛṣṇa seated upon an elephant-vehicle, as well as his two parents, his family,
Īśāna, Lomaśa, Satī, Lakṣmī, and the others.
And other excellent sages who were servants, seated on horse-drawn carriages, as well as all the women, beginning with Brahmapriyā, seated in palanquins. ||23||
The subjects—foremost among them the Brahmins and others, as well as the merchants and the wealthy, the poor men, and all the women—worshipped him according to their means. (24)
By prostrations and hymns of praise, with hearts, eyes, and hands; by meditations, flowers, garlands, and the like, as well as fruits, sugar, and other offerings. || 25 ||
