They worshipped the Supreme Lord, who had arrived as an ocean of divine qualities.
Having thus wandered through that entire city, the Blessed Lord, the Sovereign, [proceeded].
Hari came to the dwelling of the sage and prepared a beautiful assembly hall;
there, he gave instruction that was appropriate and most fitting.
For those who have faith in God, the Creator of the universe bears fruit;
but for those who have no faith, no fruit arises. (28)
And because of your great trust, my arrival here has become a source of happiness, brought about by the mountain Kālīmaṇḍalī, who acts as the gateway. (29)
And I am indeed the Supreme Lord, the Master who assumes all incarnations; I am the Supreme Brahman residing in the heart, the inner controller, and the bestower of fruits. ||2.215.30||
In worship, service, sight, salutation, offering, massaging the feet, and giving, I am the bestower of fruit; of this there is no doubt.
In the past, Mahādeva, my devotee, restored a child to life even at the word of a jackal who was full of distrust; thus it truly happened.
The gods are worthy of universal worship, and kings abide by universal trust;
for those who have sought refuge, trust is the foremost foundation. (33)
Then the act of choosing [the Lord] is proclaimed, and after that, the act of offering oneself;
then also service like a wretched person, and after that, the state of steadfastness. ||34||
In whatever manner Hari may be pleased, one should follow that very way;
however, one should avoid any manner in which He might not be pleased. (35)
Such actions and means for liberation exist here within the human state; such is the condition everywhere. (36)
Therefore, O gods, I alone am to be served here for liberation and prosperity;
I, the Supreme Lord, am to be served for the attainment of eternal bliss. (37)
Served with faith and gladdened by trust, I bestow the entirety of my auspiciousness; I grant you my own Lakṣmī.
I grant life, wealth, prosperity, health, the expansion of one's lineage, enjoyments, objects of enjoyment, and the power to enjoy them; of this there is no doubt. (39)
Even those who previously committed evil but later devoted themselves to merit—though they have died, they are indeed considered as if alive; such is the certainty.
Even those who previously performed meritorious deeds but later devoted themselves to evil are considered to have already died long before, even though they still live. ||41||
Therefore, he who grants life to those whose hope for living has perished—that giver of life should be understood as the Guru, the Supreme Lord. ||42||
Even while living, he does not know Hari, the Lord who is within his range;
though breathing, he is considered as good as dead, like a bellows. 43.
Even such a person, through association with the virtuous, approaches the Blessed One; by worshipping him, even if he remains inactive, he truly lives as one who is immortal.
Life that is truly life-sustaining is indeed sweet through service to Śrī Hari;
however, life that is parched and devoted to sense objects and the like must be abandoned. 45.
Even when death is near, he who remembers me goes to my abode;
indeed, one should remember me with such an understanding and with trust, for I appear before him.
In ancient times, at the sacred ford of Aśvapaṭṭasara, in the field of Akṣara,
there was a single son for the brahmin Vṛddhadeva during his old age.
The son went into the water to bathe, and he fell indeed into the midst of the water;
though dead, he became as if dead, yet by drinking the water, he returned to life. (48)
The vital breath was located in his head, yet it did not enter his eyes; the channels did not expand at all, nor was there even any warmth. (49)
Whether dead or appearing as if dead, he was seen lying upon the ground smeared with cow dung; and the people, perceiving him to be dead, [departed]. (2.215.50)
Together with their father, they went to the cemetery where the portion of the earth had been dug;
there was an old vulture there as well, and he beheld the dead child. (51)
And then, weeping and unable to let go, Janaka held him in his lap;
for a father cannot truly bear to abandon his child.
Others also were unable to depart, having abandoned the child;
then a vulture approached and said, "Go indeed to your home. (53)
In this world, women and men indeed always come in numbers exceeding thousands;
yet, having abandoned those who have died, they always depart for their own homes. (54)
For no one who has died returns again to a body,
since the entire world exists as such, being so ordained.
Since it is pervaded by pleasure, pain, and so forth, what cause for lamentation is there?
Those who have died have gone; those carrying the dead will die in another moment. (56)
Knowing this, those who take refuge in Hari shall be long-lived;
for not a single living being has ever emerged from the mouth of Mahākāla.
There is equality toward both the beloved and the unloved; such is the course of time.
Indeed, every embodied being born here must inevitably pass away. (58)
When one's livelihood has passed away through the end of one's karma, life cannot be recovered again;
therefore, let them depart, abandoning their homes, and let them go toward the corpse that is death for the sake of peace. (59)
Having thus obtained this knowledge and casting it upon the earth,
the men went crying out to the bathing pool, for they realized that he was indeed dead.
There, an old jackal arrived and said to those people:
"All these men are merciless, cruel, and devoid of affection."
How is it that your hearts are resolved upon departing after having abandoned us?
The day and its moments pass away, assuming many forms. (62)
Sometimes even one who is dead departs from the cremation ground while still appearing to live;
how is it that you, being devoid of compassion and merciless, go away having abandoned him? (63)
His eyes, ears, nose, and entire body are present;
why do you have no affection for him, even though he is not even equal to a beast or a bird? (64)
But for fools who have increased their own self-interest, there is no similarity even among quadrupeds, birds, or insects, even when they have been nurtured. (65)
There was no arrival of fruit, nor was there any quality whatsoever;
nevertheless, they continued to see those dead children upon the ground.
As long as these [children] do not abandon you, and as long as such affection does not exist in you,
so let them not depart, having cast aside this excellent son who upholds the lineage.
Behold that son for a long time while the body remains intact;
for relatives stay only where others do not remain. (68)
Having heard the words of the jackal, those men, though already bathed,
overcome by affection for their son, returned to the cremation ground.
Then the vulture, having observed them, spoke to the people who were overcome with grief:
"Alas! Having been born as humans, why have you come here so utterly deluded? (2.215.70)
This corpse, composed of the elements, has been abandoned by the vital breaths and the senses;
it is withered and has reached the state of dry wood—how can you, who possess knowledge, grieve for it? (71)
Why do you not grieve for yourselves, who are subject to passing away? Why indeed do you grieve?
By austerity, sin is destroyed; by devotion, [the sins of] other births and so forth. (72)
What indeed can lamentation avail for a child who has passed away?
Bearing their debts, embodied beings on this earth depart after having given or taken. (73)
In the same way, this fool has departed after giving away his home, gold, cows, offspring, jewels, and all his wealth, causing endless grief. (74)
All austerity is indeed to be acquired; likewise, it is held that all is obtainable through devotion.
Everything is indeed obtainable through merit; therefore, purify that merit which is beneficial. (75)
Through the dharma of one's own evil deeds, one becomes happy or miserable;
whether father, son, or kinsman, one is happy or miserable by virtue of one's own actions. (76)
Therefore, O best of beings, go to your own homes and practice dharma;
abide in devotion to Hari, toward the virtuous, the gods, and the ancestors.
Abandon sorrow and turn away from delusion, leaving it behind;
whether one is wise or ignorant, a king or a pauper, or wealthy or poor. (78)
Everyone who has fallen under the power of time never returns again—not the young, not the children, not the elderly, nor even fetuses, women, or men. (79)
"Death enters all; it leads them away indeed from which there is no returning.
Having been told this, those men then departed, leaving the corpse behind.
Then the jackal said: "By whom was your affection destroyed?
How can those devoid of affection be made so by the words of one who is himself devoid of affection? (8.1)
Fate, human effort, faith, and trust—
these can indeed sometimes drive even destiny far away.
One must indeed remain free from despondency; for what fruit is there in despondency?
Everything is obtained through effort; let not the merciless ones prevail. (83)
This means for the sake of your paternal lineage arises from your own flesh;
having abandoned the corpse while the sun still stands there, where will you go, devoid of compassion? (84)
For when [the sun] has set, one must either depart or remain right here;
moreover, even the compassionate gods, when propitiated, grant life. (85)
Having been addressed thus, they considered it to be the truth and approached the corpse.
Then the vulture said to them, "It appears to me that you are fools. (86)
Indeed, many years have passed for me since being born here; yet, having died, I have never seen life again as a woman, a man, or a neuter. (87)
Embryos, infants, youths, and even the elderly, once dead, do not live again, even though they were loved by their kinsmen. (88)
But the kinsmen, relatives, and others, filled with grief, go home, saying:
"Let even this body, my son, be abandoned—it is empty and like a piece of wood. (89)
Having abandoned [this world] and gone elsewhere, how is it that you do not go to your own home?
Having abandoned the senses and the vital breaths right here, why do you not depart?
"O best of beings, indeed exert yourselves for the sake of happiness in the next world.
Having heard this, they desisted; then the jackal said to them: (9.1)
"Alas! These pitiless ones are indeed departing, abandoning a son who is like gold;
for even Rākṣasas do not depart after abandoning their own son. (92)
What is the use of instructions for those who possess no wisdom of their own?
Indeed, the son of Śvetarāja, though dead, was restored to life again.
Satyavān was restored to life by his wife Sāvitrī,
and even Hariścandra’s son, though dead, was brought back to life once more.
The son of Rukmāṅgada, having died, was restored to life again;
the son of Naciketas, having died, was also restored to life again. (95)
Even the gods named Maruts were killed in the womb and yet restored to life;
likewise, by good fortune, someone might obtain life once again after having died.
"The Lord will show compassion to the wretched; he grants life.
Having been told this, those affectionate ones returned once more, their hope restored. (97)
The vulture, having returned once more, spoke to those who were slain by hope:
"Even those who are sustained by austerity, who possess sovereignty, and who are of great intelligence," 98.
Once they have gone to death, they do not return again from the city of the departed;
enough with this bond of hope for the living of one who is dead in this world. (99)
Not even a hundred jackals will bring the deceased back to life;
nor can Īśāna, Hari, Brahmā, Yamarāja, or the other lords.
If they were to restore him to life, then he would live, but not otherwise;
for in this matter, there is no living through dwelling here, nor even by weeping.
"Let us gather together, united in righteousness, and perform the worship of the Lord even at the cost of shedding tears, gasping for breath, or being crushed."
"If there were life [in him], we would certainly perform it until dawn";
having heard this, they became despondent, abandoned the corpse, and departed.
Then the jackal, having approached, spoke again with words of peace:
"Let them not depart indeed in despair; fie upon the vulture who is devoid of affection! (104)
Suffering follows immediately after happiness, and happiness follows immediately after suffering;
since this inevitably occurs, do not depart from here by casting us aside.
"I see him alive even now; there is no doubt within a moment.
Thus, with their hopes fixed upon this, they all remained once more in expectation.
The vulture named Śmaśāna said: "This region called the cremation ground is indeed dreadful;
casting aside all hope and abandoning this corpse, perform the funeral rites."
When the sun has set, the fierce pretas, yakṣas, bhūtas, and rākṣasas who feed on flesh will assault you. (108)
"Believing the words of the jackal, you will all quickly perish.
Having been told this, they were about to depart when the jackal said: (109)
Do not fear; do not go, deluded by the words of the flesh-eaters.
Once you have been driven away, the vulture, seeking his own interest, will surely devour the corpse.
The vulture said: "I am certainly not seeking my own interest; rather, it is the jackal who seeks his own interest, for he desires his own prey, the corpse, through deception in the darkness. (11.1)
Having been addressed thus, they understood those two to be seekers of their own interests—
those who had girded themselves for the sake of their own ends, were possessed by hunger, and were full of chatter.
Having resolved that the corpse must not be given to the two deceivers,
they, overwhelmed with affection for their son, remembered Śambhu in the evening.
Just then, urged by the Goddess, the illustrious Śambhu arrived there;
they bowed to Śambhu and then reported their suffering to Hara.
He granted him a lifespan of ten thousand years;
though both were intent on their own interests and had been deceived, the son obtained life.
Having propitiated Hara, they obtained a son and became happy;
having returned home with full confidence, they indeed attained the fruit of their life.
But that which was obtained by the two deceivers has been brought to fruition through their own actions;
therefore, placing your trust in me, Hari, the Supreme Person.
Worship me with undivided devotion; I shall protect you, of this there is no doubt, and I shall grant you a life within my abode, filled with eternal bliss.
Having spoken thus, the Blessed One himself bestowed the mantras upon his subjects;
Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa made those who had taken refuge in him his own Vaiṣṇavas. 119.
O Rādhikā, having heard the words of Śrī Hari, the subjects then took refuge [in Him]; and after worshipping Hari, they returned to their own homes. || 2.215.1 || 20 ||
The four daughters of the king placed the garland of choice around the neck of Kṛṣṇa, their beloved and great lord, and made him their own husband and master.
He held a royal festival at night, had food and other refreshments served,
and while the maidens performed their service, Kṛṣṇa indeed fell asleep.

Thus ends the two hundred and fifteenth chapter, titled "The Description of Lord Hari’s Journey to the Kingdom of King Rāyakūpeśa in the Second Tretā Cycle of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā; His Wandering, Worship, and Teaching in the City of Havānā; and His Subsequent Journey to the Kingdom of King Kālīmaṇḍalī, His Wandering, Worship, and Instruction in the City of Vigoṣṭhikā, as well as His Meal and Resting at Night. || 215 ||
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O Rādhikā, on the fifteenth day at dawn, Bālakṛṣṇa was awakened with auspicious songs, musical instruments, and hymns of praise.
Having performed his ablutions, completed his worship, and drunk milk and other refreshments,
he sat upon the lion-throne after having paid homage to his parents.
Just then the king arrived before Hari for the purpose of worship;
he indeed placed a crown upon his head, as well as earrings and bracelets.
He also gave golden rings, chains, strings of pearls, necklaces of gems and diamonds, and wealth exceeding one hundred thousand.
He offered himself in surrender and likewise presented flower garlands;
having washed his feet, the king, together with his kinsmen, drank [the water].
Then she performed the lustration ceremony (nīrājana), bowed down, and sang, "Protect me!
The queen offered worship and a dowry, and chose as her boon that he always grant her protection.
This being the case, his brother—the elder brother of Kālīmaṇḍalin, the former ruler of the kingdom, and the lord of Vanajaleśa—[acted]. || 7 ||
Then the lord of Oṣṭrīpura, the ruler of the region of the forest fire,
arrived in his own celestial chariot together with his younger brother to bring Hari back.
Having arrived, he prostrated like a staff, placed a garland of flowers around [his] neck,
and offered a hundred golden rings in a golden vessel.
And Hari prayed to the Supreme Lord to sanctify his own regions; "So be it," the Lord replied, and in a moment He became ready.
The king, a follower of the Kālī-maṇḍala, bowed with his face beaming with joy;
he performed a great worship with sandalwood, unbroken rice grains, and saffron.
Then he performed the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) with various kinds of substances, gems, necklaces, crest-jewels, earrings, wedding gifts, and offerings.
Having performed the worship of the caravan of Hari with his army and musical instruments,
and likewise with shouts of victory, he bestowed honor and a gift upon Śrī Hari.
Then Śrī Hari, situated in his celestial chariot there in the sky, became visible;
the subjects beheld him and, filled with longing, bowed and offered hymns of praise.
"You must come; we are to be protected," they said again and again.
Then Hari, by the path he had shown, caused the celestial chariot to travel through the sky.
The great sage Rākāsaṇa and the royal preceptor came in their celestial chariot together with Kṛṣṇa; the king had already gone ahead to the city.
Indeed, the army was thus prepared there for the sake of honoring Hari;
likewise, all the subjects were present, carrying sacrificial rice and adorned with flower garlands.
For the sake of welcoming him, we stood before the great garden near the she-camel with our younger brother,
waiting for the direction from which Hari would come.
The sage Pūrṇāsanaka, a teacher belonging to the circle of Kālī,
arrived together with Hari, as did the sage Rākāsana.
Beholding the celestial chariot in the sky, the subjects were indeed filled with great joy;
the king, accompanied by his army, offered a welcome with the sounds of musical instruments.
And Dhvaja honored him with shouts of victory, with banners and small flags, with prostrations, offerings of flowers, songs, and auspicious rites. ||21||
The celestial chariot attained stability upon the surface of the earth, and Hari went outside;
the king placed auspicious flower garlands around the neck of Bālakṛṣṇa.
He performed an ablution with water at his feet; he drank that nectar together with his family and prostrated himself like a staff.
The queen worshipped her [the goddess] Nemi-Kambharā Mahālakṣmī;
thereafter, the king worshipped his father, Gopāla-Kṛṣṇa.
The householders honored their families and the beloved wives of Brahmā;
the king seated Hari upon a golden elephant-chariot.
Likewise, he seated others upon horse-drawn carriages, palanquins, and the like;
and accompanied by his army, he honored them with necklaces, crest-jewels, flower clusters, and other offerings. (26)
With the sounds of musical instruments and hymns of praise, the king led Hari into the city;
at the city gate, the princes each separately performed worship.
And at the crossroads, on a great site, the leading merchants also performed worship of Hari there along the main street, as did the subjects. ||28||

The young women worshipped with necklaces, flowers, and the like, with sandalwood paste, unbroken grains, and excellent fruits, with saffron, and with their hearts through meditative visualizations and other means. (29)
With garments, ornaments, and articles of gold,
and by touching her feet and placing them upon his head— even though these were causes for increasing his own suffering— [he honored her].
Having beheld the beloved Bālakṛṣṇa, who was most resplendent with form upon form, they worshipped him with joined palms, with their eyes, and with meditative contemplations.
Some beloved women indeed gazed upon Kṛṣṇa in their hearts with eternal, unforgetting love;
others, standing at a distance, beheld Acyuta.
Consisting of divine splendor, peaceful, as beautiful as ten million gods of love,
Kṛṣṇa is accompanied by Rādhā and others, and is worshipped by hosts of cowherds and cowherdesses.
Likewise, others beheld that four-armed Nārāyaṇa, worshipped by Ramā, as the Lord of the universe; while others saw him as the Lord of Badarī.
Some [saw] Śrī Hari Kṛṣṇa as an ascetic, while others saw the Lord Hari, who reclines upon Śeṣa, as golden and situated within the sun.
Likewise, other young women beheld the divine Lord, the noble person, standing in the midst of the fire—handsome and bestowing the bliss of fulfilled desires. (36)
The devotees beheld that god dwelling in the Great Imperishable;
likewise, the subjects—both men and women—beheld him in the form of Viṣṇu.
It was intensely served by Rādhā, Ramā, Satī, Vṛndā, Tulasī, and Śrī;
it was honored by the beautiful and excellent qualities of the smiles of Ramā, Padmāvatī, and Hāsā. 38.
There they beheld Hari in many forms, seated upon his elephant-vehicle, who removes the suffering of Māṇikī, who is Lakṣmī, Durgikā, and Kamalā, and who is worshipped by them.
The Lord was also worshipped by the Brahmapriyās and others, honored by the Piśaṅginīs, and adored by Gaurīs, Cāmarīs, and maidens.
And those women indeed beheld the divine Śrī Hari himself;
thus Hari then granted his own vision in many ways. 41.
Accompanied by his younger brother, he wandered repeatedly among the subjects in the city of Uṣṭrinagarī;
having thus roamed through the city, he arrived at the royal palace.
The queen shone resplendent upon the lion-throne and performed worship;
moreover, her five daughters offered her water for drinking.
They worshipped the Lord of Śrī, who is beloved, beautiful, and desired by the mind;
they placed a garland of Pārijāta flowers upon the neck of Kṛṣṇa. || 44 ||
They chose him who was truly difficult to obtain, yet easily attained as he had come to their own homes; and having obtained Hari as their beloved, they became fulfilled in all their desires.
The king, the queen, and the princes considered their own good fortune;
he held a royal festival and provided a midday meal.
Having eaten, the caravans attained complete rest after three watches of the night had passed;
meanwhile, the king bestowed both a dowry and a parting gift upon the wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
Then men and women came to that abode for the sake of a vision; to them Hari gave awakening and the auspicious Vaiṣṇava mantra. 48.
The power of Hari must always be protected, for it bestows all happiness upon men in times of calamity, at the time of death, at the time of Yama, and during the course of an evil destiny. (49)
"Movement alone is my strength, which wards off bows and other weapons;
even the silk-cotton tree, though devoid of strength, was victorious in the past by taking refuge in Brahmā."
Indeed, after Vāyudeva had brought about his defeat, there was a great tree named Śālmali on the Himācala mountain. ||51||
Possessing branches, a trunk, and leaves, he provides refuge for beasts and birds;
through flowers, fruits, and the like, he satisfies even his dependents when they are hungry. (52)
While traveling toward Viśālā, Nārada asked that Viśālin tree: "O tree, how is it that you remain fearless and happy? (53)
Since I do not see even a single branch of yours broken by the wind, what indeed is this wind to you—a friend who protects you? (54)
For the wind is of great power and could even destroy mountains; it is that wind which, having left you, remains here, and from that it will become the cause.
Elephants, gayals, and other wild animals stand below you;
indeed, you shine forth as one who is worthy of service by others and a benefactor in every way. (56)
I conjecture that the Wind is your kinsman, or perhaps your friend or well-wisher;
or else, you must surely have sought refuge with the Wind.
Having heard this, Śālmali said: "Vāyu is neither my friend nor my well-wisher;
he is neither my kinsman nor my refuge by whom I might have been protected. (58)
My splendor and strength are superior, exceeding that of Vāyu by eighteenfold;
by that [strength], Vāyu was obstructed and thus defeated by me.
"Therefore, I am afraid of the wind, not because it is angry with you, but because of its great velocity.
Nārada then said, "This which I have heard is truly a great marvel."
Varuṇa, Yama the King, and Kubera are not equal to the Maruts;
yet you have indeed conquered Vāyu, who is the performer of all activities.
Or rather, since you speak falsely, O lord of Drupada, out of a deficiency of intellect,
I shall indeed go to Anila and report your evil speech.
Neither by mountains nor by oceans, nor even by planets or celestial trees,
has the wind ever been cast down, just as you have described.
"They all pay homage to him; you, out of delusion, boast fruitlessly.
Having said this, Nārada went to where Vāyu was staying.
Having heard those words of the Śālmali tree, which were filled with provocation, Pavana went to the place where the Śālmali was located.
Enraged, he said: "O tree, because you have spoken words of reproach to Nārada, I shall show my power to you; stand firm! (66)
Since the Grandfather rested upon you during the creation of beings,
I always abandon you with speed, touch you, and seize you.
Having abandoned those virtues of yours, you now display strength before me;
today I shall lead you away, root and branch, stripped of the expansion of your lineage.
Thus addressed, Śālmali said: "I have no fear at all;
come against me with all your might, O wrathful one, and let your anger toward me be abandoned. (69)
"I have no fear of you, O Vāyu; my strength is even more powerful than yours.
For those who are strong in wisdom are always truly the strong."
"Those who possess strength only through their physical bodies are not truly strong in reality.
Having been addressed thus, Pavana became enraged and turned into a violent storm.
Upon merely beholding that śālmali tree, he indeed stripped away its own leaves,
branches, flowers, and fruits from its small twigs.
Becoming as motionless as a staff, he remained there, wondering, "What will the wind do?
Meanwhile, the exceedingly swift wind saw that the tree was devoid of branches.
Seeing the lord of the forest with its leaves and bark withered, he said with a laugh:
"Behold my power and sovereignty, through fear of which you have been reduced to this state."
Thus, by taking refuge in Brahmā and through a mere fragment of my compassion, you have become happy;
yet, having abandoned the refuge of the great, you now hold the great in contempt.
Therefore, you have become sorrowful and deprived of the expansion of your lineage;
I am capable of consuming you, so do not harbor pride at all.
"I am capable of uprooting it; do not carry this fruitless pride.
Having spoken thus, he blew with force through his own current with extreme speed.
The tree trunk became bent and intent upon breaking it;
and by the force of the wind, there was a trembling as if the earth itself were being uprooted. ||78||
Then the Śālmali tree, bowing down, remembered Brahmā in his heart;
it also bowed to Vāyu, and Brahmā quickly approached.
Vāyu granted them fearlessness and became indeed free from agitation;
those two best of gods, having been honored, departed for their own abode.
Thus, even though he is devoid of strength and as inert as a tree, if the embodied soul takes refuge in me, the abode of Brahman, within the forest; ||81||
Even though he consists of illusion, I protect him from illusory winds,
and I also shield him from time, from karma, and from the messengers of Yama.
If a person abandons my strength and the strength of the virtuous,
then Time, Karma, and Māyā, appearing in the form of the wind, shall surely destroy him.
Even having renounced leaves, flowers, fruits, branches, grandsons, wealth, happiness, and sons, one should take refuge in the virtuous; for such a person, no fear exists.
If, even when everything has been relinquished, there is no refuge for me, then fear will surely arise from the wind of time; therefore, one should obtain a refuge for oneself. ||85||
Thus instructed, the king and others—the people, both men and women—performed [the rites] centered upon the glorious Bālakṛṣṇa and received the mantra. (86)
They took up a tulasī necklace and an image of Hari;
they worshipped Śrī Hari with love, as well as Īśāna and the other deities.
He drank water and rested for as long as it took, when the king named Pārāvārapiba arrived by means of a celestial chariot (vimāna). ||88||
Accompanied by Ambikā’s son, he came to invite Kṛṣṇa to his own kingdom;
having entreated the Lord in many ways, Kṛṣṇa said "So be it" and brought him along.
Then the king quickly made the departure ready;
and King Vanajvāleśa gave him a dowry and marks of honor.
Then the venerable Lord, honored by the subjects and the king, quickly ascended his celestial chariot and traveled through the path of the sky. ||9 1||
Honored by him, he went to the kingdom, which was purified and freed from sin;
formerly, the king had gone to that kingdom, free from sin, for the sake of honoring him.
Then, in the vicinity of the city of Kānyākhyā, on the shore of the ocean, in a vast region of land within a great garden called Mahālaya. ||93||
Accompanied by his army, the king offered him honor and a welcome;
and the celestial chariot, arriving swiftly, descended onto the beautiful ground. (94)
The subjects, the king, and others likewise sang shouts of victory;
the armies circumambulated Kṛṣṇa, and the people raised cries of exultation.
The sounds of auspicious musical instruments resounded repeatedly as all the people—both men and women—from every direction came to behold Kṛṣṇa. (96)
Filled with joy, they arrived there at the pleasure-giving great garden, adorned with flower garlands and the like, and beautified by parched grain, unbroken rice, and other offerings. || 97 ||
Filled with great joy at the sound of "Go! Go!", the women also arrived swiftly, full of haste, accompanied by the sounds of "halahalā" out of love and the calls of their children from their laps.
At that time, the earth became like the heavens, filled with radiant beings;
Hari quickly emerged from his celestial chariot and came forward outside. 99.
The king bowed at his feet and placed a garland of flowers around his neck;
the queen honored him with flowers and other offerings, and gave him water like nectar.
They also honored the principal rim with garlands of flowers;
Hari accepted the salutations and honors from them all.
She accepted the welcome and the auspicious offerings such as the honey-mixture (madhuparka),
as well as the fruit, water, and milk that the subjects indeed presented to her.
O Rādhikā, upon beholding the charming Lord, the beloved of Kamalā,
the mental functions of the women there indeed attained a state of immobility.

Thus ends the two hundred and sixteen chapter, titled "The Description of Hari’s Awakening at Dawn, the Performance of Daily Rites, Worship, the Journey to the Kingdom of Vanajvālā with His Brothers, the Wandering through the City of Uṣṭrī, Worship, the Divine Vision, Instruction, the Taking of Food, and the Welcome in the Kingdom of Gatainasa," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*. 216.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Rādhikā, the king endeavored to lead Śrī Hari away from Kānyakubja;
he entreated Him as He sat upon His elephant.
Hari sat down upon a four-tusked elephant accompanied by his golden bride, and thereafter he caused the others to sit upon elephants and other mounts.
Rādhikā seated the beloveds of Hari upon palanquins,
while Gaurī, the beloved of Brahmā, and others likewise carried the chowries.
Then the glorious Kṛṣṇa shone resplendent amidst the military musical instruments;
Ambikarṣi, holding a chowrie, sat behind him.
In this manner, the king himself paraded Kṛṣṇa through the city of Kānyakubja, through its squares and other public areas, as well as through the palaces and the marketplaces.
At every place, the people worshipped that Bālakṛṣṇa—
the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa— with sandalwood paste and gold.
And with fruits, pearl necklaces, gems and the like, unbroken grains and so forth, garments, ornaments and the like, as well as sugar and desired objects. || 7 ||
Thus the illustrious Blessed One, having wandered through the city, returned to his residence;
he drank water in the royal assembly hall and indeed gave instruction at night.
When the night was full, the Lord, the Blessed One, said to the people of the land:
"Merit must indeed be acquired by everyone through whatever action possible."
Indeed, evil must be avoided, for it is that which obstructs one's welfare;
in the creation of evil, there exists a basis of influence, namely allurement.
Greed alone is the great evil; from greed proceeds sin.
Greed is the root of destruction, by which people go to their ruin. (11)
From greed, there arises in some cases anger, lust, and craving; as well as pride, deceit, delusion, arrogance, and even malice. (12)
Intolerance, the destruction of modesty, the loss of prosperity, fortune, and dharma, ill-repute, wretchedness, and a state of subjection—all these proceed from greed. (13)
Non-giving, failure to renounce, thirst, engagement in improper actions, intoxication, malice, contempt, lack of trust, and likewise crookedness; || 14 ||
Seizing the property and so forth of others, censure, impetuosity, lack of self-restraint, envy, contempt, boasting, stinginess, and wicked conduct; || 15 ||
Violence, deception, and theft—all these proceed from greed;
it is that which cannot be satisfied even throughout ten thousand lifetimes.
As he ages, his steadfastness matures; greed does not abandon his constancy. He always attains profundity and remains unimpaired when engaged in worldly affairs. (17)
When applied to an object of enjoyment, it always generates passion;
through greed, a human being incurs intense attachment and craving. (18)
That greed, together with delusion, must be conquered by one desiring the highest good;
for hatred and anger, which destroy the conduct of the virtuous, have their foundation in greed.
Cruel within and like hidden wells, they bring about the destruction of the worlds;
people who rely on greed deceive others here by means of various pretexts.
They plunder and destroy the paths of the virtuous and their own innate virtues;
they fall into terrible suffering and cause others to fall as well. 21.

For the sake of accomplishing their own ends, greedy people such as those driven by avarice and the like will overstep even their fathers and kinsmen; they treat the disciplined as undisciplined and the undisciplined as disciplined.
By that, there would be a loss of merit; likewise, such a person perishes.
Therefore, one should take refuge in virtuous people who are pure in their vows and free from craving.
Indeed, for those who are free from greed and delusion, there shall then be supreme welfare;
they are established in truth, bulls among the righteous, and endowed with the conduct of the cultured.
One should also serve those who have attained association with Kṛṣṇa and are full of compassion,
as well as those who honor the ancestors, the gods, and guests, and who are benefactors to all.
One should worship all the gods who possess the nature of existence in all phenomena and who delight in the welfare of all beings; by taking refuge in them, one will attain the highest good. (26)
Those whose conduct, established of old by the virtuous, is not broken;
who are neither fearful, nor fickle, nor cruel, but remain steadfast on the path of truth. (27)
One should serve those virtuous people who are non-violent, devoted to Me,
free from all faults, devoid of possessiveness, and free from egoism.

For the sake of one's well-being, one should attend upon those who are firm in their vows and steadfast in their boundaries—those for whom dharma is never sacrificed for the sake of wealth or fame. (29)
Those devoted to the activities of the body think, "This must certainly be done";
yet in them there is no fear, no anger, no restlessness, and no worldly grief. (2.217.30)
Those who are devoted to truth and uprightness, as well as those devoted to my form, do not fall away even when encountering pleasure, nor are they elated by gains. || 3.1 ||
Those who have taken refuge in the path of beings do not waver in the face of losses;
they maintain an even disposition, possess a nature of compassion, and are intent on benefiting others.
One should devotedly serve those whose minds are equanimous toward gain and loss, pleasure and pain, the pleasant and the unpleasant, and birth and death. 3.3.3.
One should take refuge in those of great power, the divine, and the virtuous; for the sake of one's welfare, one should also resort to divine gurus who remove ignorance.
Ignorance is rooted in greed and is also the producer of sin;
furthermore, due to ignorance, a person does not perceive the destruction of his own self. ||35||
Both of these—ignorance and excessive greed—are equal in their results, equal in their faults, and most significant; they are considered the destroyers of stability. (36)
Ignorance, which originates from greed, increases as greed grows;
when greed is diminished, it comes to an end, otherwise one follows the course of the lotus-born [Brahmā]. (37)
Through the subduing of the senses, greed may indeed be diminished;
through the destruction of latent impressions (vāsanā), the very root of greed perishes. ||38||
Self-restraint bestows welfare; self-restraint should be understood as the most excellent of dharmas.
Success indeed arises from self-restraint; self-restraint excels even generosity. (39)
Through self-restraint one's splendor increases, and one becomes a person possessed of splendor; the self-controlled person finds supreme happiness both in this world and in the next. ||2.217.40||
The self-controlled man sleeps in peace and wakes in peace;
he moves through the worlds in peace, and his mind remains serene. ||41||
For an undisciplined person repeatedly encounters suffering;
moreover, an undisciplined person produces many other misfortunes. (42)
The fruit of worshiping the guru has been declared for one who is self-controlled, virtuous, and righteous;
yet [these vices remain]: desire, anger, pride, greed, wrath, envy, and contempt. (43)
Vices such as envy and the like do not reside at all in one who is self-controlled;
the self-controlled person is like the ocean, by whom the fish of the senses have been destroyed. (44)
By whom both village and forest activities have indeed been destroyed—he who is of good conduct, endowed with virtue, serene in soul, a knower of the Self, and wise. (45)
Having received honor in this world, the self-controlled person attains a happy rebirth in the next;
for the conduct practiced by the virtuous is the way of life of the self-controlled. ||46||

The auspicious path that bestows well-being flourishes for the self-controlled among the virtuous; the self-controlled one, established in the Self and devoted to the service of the holy, shakes off all impurities. (47)
The devotee who delights in the midday [meditation] is fit for becoming Brahman;
for he has no fear of living beings, and living beings have no fear of him. (48)
Whether in the body or outside the body, he has no fear from any quarter;
having attained a state of friendship with all, he performs service for me. (49)
For one who has entered the path of the virtuous, my state is always similar;
having abandoned greed born of ignorance and becoming self-controlled, one should worship me.
Or rather, for him who has offered his actions to me and indeed offered his austerity to me, there are eternal worlds consisting of splendor as his liberation.
Having surrendered his discernment to me, with a serene soul and taking refuge in me,
he attains the enjoyments existing in heaven and certainly finds my own celestial realm.
Or else, it is the station of the Grandfather (Brahmā), or the Vairāja realm beyond that;
or the abode consisting of the mass of Brahman, the unmanifest, or the immortal state.
Through devotion and self-restraint, one attains Goloka and Vaikuṇṭha—[the state] of the devotee who delights in knowledge and does not oppose any embodied being. (54)
In this state there is no fear, nor is there any fear of the next world; the peace that belongs to one who is self-controlled is not attained by one who merely exerts effort. (55)
There may be one worldly proverb that must be endured by the virtuous:
that people consider him who is endowed with forgiveness to be weak. (56)
Through forbearance, even when one is powerless, his supreme quality is surely born;
by means of forbearance, those vast worlds which are otherwise difficult to attain become easily won. (57)
Forbearance is the duty of the virtuous; it is difficult for others of evil nature to attain.
Of what use is a forest to one who is self-controlled? Wherever he dwells is the forest. ||58||
Self-control is declared to be the supreme austerity; that which brings about the great destruction of desire is the subduing of the impetuous senses, which is itself the great battle. (59)
Indeed, that accumulated austerity grants all desires;
those perfected by austerity and endowed with self-restraint behold the three worlds. Whatever may be difficult to attain, all of that one may obtain through austerity.
Indeed, all forms of sovereignty have their root in asceticism.

Indeed, all sins are burned away when heated by austerity. For one whose group of senses has been withdrawn, austerity known as fasting increases in strength and becomes supreme, augmenting divine splendor.
There is no austerity more difficult than giving, and no penance higher than fasting. 63.
There is no skill equal to the attainment of one's own liberation; there is no happiness greater than contentment.
Through austerity, one is able to attain the state of being liberated by the Lord of Gods and other such states.
Speech is austerity, and truth alone exists; truth is firmly established among the virtuous.

Truth, dharma, austerity, yoga, sacrifice, and the eternal Brahman—65—all that is indeed of the nature of truth; austerity is offered unto Kṛṣṇa. Through union with Hari and by serving the virtuous, one becomes devoted to the vow of truth. 66.
One should perceive me in all things; this is called the vow of equanimity.
And through the destruction of desire comes the vow of self-restraint, and through the destruction of craving. 67.
Indeed, through the firmness of steadfastness in the Self, the vow of fearlessness is attained;
and through knowledge, stability, profundity, and fortitude are likewise acquired. (68)
Non-avarice is attained through the state of selflessness in every respect;
goodness is attained through patience, and ethical conduct is attained through the absence of volitional construction. (69)
Through wisdom, the highest good is attained, and prosperity through meritorious deeds;
modesty is acquired from righteousness, and likewise, patience is gained through fortitude.
Renunciation is the abandonment of affection as well as the abandonment of sense objects;

it is attained through detachment from passion and hatred, and by means of dispassion (vairāgya). Fortitude is the state of being free from emotional agitation even when confronted with that which bestows pleasure or pain.
And through the existence of the self, one also attains invincibility with respect to sense objects. 72.
In every way, one should be patient; one should be devoted to truth;
and one should be free from joy, fear, and anger for the sake of attaining what is auspicious. (73)
One who desires what is auspicious should always be free from malice and likewise full of compassion; one should be devoted to truth, righteousness, and virtuous conduct.
One should serve the virtuous and remain endowed with devotion to me.
One who desires the supreme good for others must indeed offer oneself in dedication.
"A Vaiṣṇava mantra must indeed be accepted, and likewise, Hari is my refuge;
by that, the highest good and what is most dear shall come to you.
Having spoken thus, the Blessed Lord Puruṣottama ceased.
The subjects worshipped him with love and received the mantra of Hari.
Then the king and the queen, as well as the princes, performed an act of worship;
likewise, the three queens and the three maidens performed an act of worship.
They performed the great *nīrājana* ceremony with camphor wicks and dressed the son of Gopāla in royal attire;
indeed, there were three suitable maidens, beautiful young women.
By their mother’s command, they all placed excellent golden garlands upon the neck of Hari with their own hands; likewise, they drank the water from his feet,
offered him the honey-mixture (madhuparka), and accepted the lovely gifts presented to them.
Having accomplished their purpose, those women, who possessed the luster of the petals of land-lotuses,
were present as the king, a drinker of the ocean's waters, celebrated the marriage festival.
After the exchange of greetings, they partook of a meal there;
then, having all stayed awake, the maidens attended upon Kṛṣṇa.
In the morning, the Great Lord was awakened by musical instruments and songs.
When Hari had completed his daily rites and performed worship, he became composed;
then the king arrived there to worship Kṛṣṇa and indeed offered him worship. At that time, the pure king named Koṭīśvara also arrived.
The ruler of the regions of Ekadvāra was possessed of excellent dharma.
Likewise, there came the pure king named Śrī Satīśa;
and the king of Pārūparaṣṭra was righteous and full of devotion.
Those two kings, joined by Mṛtyuharṣi and Koṣṭhakarṣin, were auspicious;
they requested the Lord of Śrī for permission to return to their own kingdom.
Hari said, "So be it," and he bestowed honors upon them. || 87-88 ||
Then the chief minister, Yājaneśvara—
known as Īśānapānaśiṣṭa, the counselor to the sovereign Brāhmileśitṛ— arrived;
having bowed along with his letter, he made this request to the Supreme Lord.

"O Kṛṣṇa, having come to our city of Goyājanī in the kingdom of Brāhmīla, please purify it with sacrifices and great festivals; may the Blessed One fulfill this request of the king, for it will bring about the welfare of the subjects. (2.217.90–91)
"And the fortunes of the immortals shall become auspicious through the sight of you, through your worship, and through your service.
Thus addressed, the Blessed One said, "Welcome to you and to the king."
"O best of ministers, I honor your words, which are appropriate and desired. || 93 ||
"But on the morning of the fifth day, having brought Lomaśa as well as the best of the great ṛṣis, and having brought Īśāna and Satī, I shall perform a festival of sacrifice there;
go now and inform the king."
Gather the collection of ritual materials and issue a proclamation.
Prepare an auspicious and suitable site on the riverbank for the sacrifice.
Let the commencement of the sacrifice take place at dawn on the fifth day, and its conclusion on the eleventh day.
"Let there be the final oblation for the sacrifice; let it be proclaimed everywhere!
Having received this command, the minister quickly departed for his own residence and reported everything exactly as it had been spoken regarding that fragment of Brahma's speech.
Lomaśa, Īśānadeva, Lālāyana, and Vṛkāyana. ||98||
Nīlakarṇa, Yavakrīta, and other sages departed;
the Lord Svayaṃprakāśa also went for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of the sacrifice. 99.
On the bank of the Āmrajanisarit river, frequented by peaceful forest-dwelling sages,
they established a sacrificial ground in the midst of an area measuring one *go-yojana*.
Then Kṛṣṇa, having drunk milk along with his family,
became ready to go to the kingdom of Ekadvāra as well as the kingdom of Pārūpara.
The king, who had drunk from both the near and far shores [of the ocean], gave him a parting gift as a dowry;
he gave all the wealth obtained through honors to Ambikarṣi.
Having received a welcome and honor, Hari ascended his celestial chariot;
at that time, Koṭīśvara went forth first to pay homage to Hari.
Then Śrī Satīśa and Hari also departed for their own kingdom,
accompanied by Mṛtyuharṣi and Suyukta, as well as Koṣṭhakarṣi.
He arrived swiftly through the sky toward the city of Peyi;
and then, O Rādhikā, seeing him, musical instruments were sounded.

Thus ends the two hundred and seventeenth chapter, titled "The Description of Hari’s Wandering through the City of Kāyanī, His Worship, His Instruction in the King’s Palace, His Meal, His Sleep, His Departure in the Morning, and the Journey on the First Day of the Dark Half of Āśvina to the Kingdom of King Koṭīśvara with One Gate," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmīnārāyaṇīya-saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O Rādhikā, on the morning of the first lunar day (pratipad) of the dark fortnight of the month of Āśvina,
indeed in the great garden in the presence of Peyisthā, there were millions [of devotees].
With his army, the king offered a formal welcome to Kṛṣṇa;
he beheld the aerial chariot of Bālakṛṣṇa, which possessed a splendor like that of the divine sun. || 2 ||
Seeing this, the people, filled with joy, raised shouts of victory;
and [the charioteer] brought down the celestial chariot by the path shown by the king.
In the garden of the city of Peyisthā, adorned with banners and other ornaments,
we caused a celestial chariot to appear and honored the subjects with unbroken grains and sandalwood paste.
With handfuls of flowers and songs, they offered a most cordial welcome;
then Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa descended from the celestial chariot.
Then, beholding the sun-like face, the men approached;
for a moment they were dazzled by his splendor, and thereafter he, the ocean of compassion, [revealed himself].
He quickly became moon-faced, raining down a shower of peaceful nectar;
and then all the people beheld that beloved of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
King Koṭīśvara placed a beautiful necklace around Kṛṣṇa’s neck and drank the nectar of His feet; thereafter, others also worshipped the Lord.
Having seated the Lord of All upon an elephant on the great highway leading to Peyisthā, [they proceeded].
Accompanied by a great army, that king marched forth with great honor,
together with his principal ministers, guild-leaders, and subjects,
carrying wealth, garments, diamonds, pearls, and necklaces of gems.
He was worshipped with fruits, flowers, sweet leaves, gold, and other offerings; he was honored with the waving of lights (nīrājana), saluted, and gazed upon by women.
Śrī Kāmbhareya Nārāyaṇa, whose form is captivating,
having thus granted his vision, arrived at the beautiful royal residence.
Having seated Janārdana upon a divine throne in his own palace and bowed at his feet, the king placed ten thousand gold pieces before him. || 13 ||
The queen, rich in devotion, worshipped with sandalwood, unbroken rice, and flowers;
and then, by her mother’s command, the two auspicious daughters placed [the garland] around Kṛṣṇa’s neck.
When their desire was fulfilled, they placed the choice garland upon him;
having obtained the Supreme Lord as their husband, they became immersed in bliss. || 1.5 ||
The king considered his own fortune to be the most excellent of all, and the queen likewise;
then Hari performed the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) and gave his instruction.
Anger, greed, indulgence in flavors, pride, theft, and backbiting— these,
when one is intoxicated by them, constantly afflict both man and woman.
From these proceeds suffering; from these proceeds evil.
From greed arises anger, and from pride it is born intensely. (18)
Likewise, anger arises from the faults of others as well as from the frustration of one's desires;
furthermore, anger arises from being insulted and from hearing harsh words.
Through forgiveness, anger is quickly turned away from the virtuous man;
sometimes the root of that anger is indeed desire, once it has been separated [from its object]. (2.218.20)
Volition is indeed the root of desire; it increases as its cause grows. When indulged in, it flourishes further; when abandoned, it perishes. (21)
Envy arises from pride, as well as from the destruction of one's reputation;
it also arises from poverty, from one's own inferiority, and from falling into a low state.
Delusion arises from ignorance and proceeds from the habitual practice of evil;
when struck down by the path of knowledge, delusion is eradicated from its very root.
The desire to perform action, when its fruit is offered to Me, does not cause bondage;
likewise, sorrow arises from affection through the separation from desired activities. (24)
When one realizes the worthlessness [of worldly things], all sorrow ceases—whether it arises from dependence on others, or from craving, greed, desire, or the pursuit of pleasure. (25)
That [passion] arises, but through detachment it is uprooted;
envy, however, constantly increases for one who relies on what is unreal. (26)
That [delusion] ceases through service to the virtuous and the awakening of truth;
it does not [cease] by means of status, excellence of qualities, noble lineage, fame, artistic skills, and so forth. (27)
From sovereignty and from knowledge as well, the arising of pride occurs;
having obtained their portion which bestows happiness, one should abandon other portions.
For one who conducts oneself in this way, mental anguish does not arise;
envy is spread by one who cannot endure the excellence and prosperity of others. (29)
One should indeed destroy [the mind] through equanimity, or through joy, or through investigation; otherwise, contempt arises from pride in one's own excellence regarding another object. (2.218.30)
One who understands the similarity between different states overcomes contempt, but not otherwise;
thus, those who are unable to do so toward a powerful and great-souled person [are overcome by it]. (3.1)
Envy arises in them and ceases through contentment with one's own fortune;
indeed, compassion arises in the world through discernment regarding the benefit [of others]. (32)
Likewise, among others who are miserly, greed arises wherever it is produced through the power of ignorance and by means of their own vices. (33)
In each case, one should contemplate its instability and its quality of producing suffering;
through such a nature of indifference, even greed ceases here.
One should always avoid cruelty, having understood it as it truly is;
likewise, one should avoid those who are covetous, arrogant, abusive, and deceitful. (35)

He is deceitful, mean-spirited, dishonest, and erratic; he is boastful, attached to his own company, disrespectful toward those worthy of honor, ungenerous in sharing, suspicious of everyone, and merciless. (36)
One who is miserly, full of hatred, given to violence, highly deceitful, greedy, a follower of heretical sects, and a slanderer—these indeed are the cruel ones. (37)

He who, for the sake of his own interests, regards one of virtuous character and endowed with good qualities as a sinner, and who strikes down those who are eminent, worthy of worship, righteous, and virtuous women; (38)
He does not trust anyone, acting according to his own measure of slander; he speaks of even a slight fault of the virtuous as if it were great. (39)
And he who considers a helpful friend to be a supreme deceiver will surely suffer in vain, even though that friend has repeatedly acted for his welfare. (2.218.40)
He who eats fine food only after first bringing it to those in the rows of spectators, and he who causes distress to his wife and distress to his parents; || 41 ||
These should be known as cruel men; one should not associate with them—those who, having given to the virtuous, eat [the food] together with their friends and kinsmen.
Having departed, they attain heaven; from heaven, they likewise attain higher and higher heavens.
Knowing this, one should avoid the cruel and take refuge in the virtuous, as well as in Hari.
One should know that excellent clothing must indeed be given to those who possess nothing;
likewise, one who is about to perform a sacrifice is a worthy recipient of gifts for all who possess knowledge.

One who performs the duties toward the teacher as toward a father, and one who lives on what is given for the sake of dharma—these indeed are declared to be the virtuous, devoted solely to the Supreme Lord. 45.
By taking refuge in them, there is liberation, the attainment of great heavens and the like,
the acquisition of all sovereignty, and the state of divinity through reliance upon them.
Those virtuous ones in whom my auspicious and excellent qualities reside are indeed of my own form; for that man named Nārāyaṇa possesses my qualities and is a portion of myself.
I declare those people who are to be abandoned, for association with whom brings fear:
the greedy, the cruel, the devoid of dharma, and those who are bereft of devotion to me. ||48||
One should avoid the deceitful, the rogue, the base, and the one of evil conduct; one should also avoid the lazy, the suspicious of everything, and the procrastinator. ||49||
One who is crooked, always abusive, a violator of the preceptor’s wife, addicted to vices, evil-minded, a slayer of his father, and shameless—[him one should avoid]. (2.218.50)
One should abandon a person who has evil eyes everywhere, an atheist, a slanderer, a rogue, one whose senses are unrestrained, one addicted to sensual desires, and one who is negligent. ||51||
One who follows an evil course of conduct, is hateful, unstable in his observance of commitments, treacherous, lacking in wisdom, envious, and sinful—[such a person should not be relied upon]. (52)
One who is immoral, of undisciplined mind, a gambler, cruel, treacherous toward friends, and possessed by a greedy longing for the wealth and property of others— (53)
One should abandon even a donor who is hateful, as well as one who is dissatisfied, lacking in fortitude, deficient in strength, and devoted to anger at inappropriate times. (54)
One should suddenly abandon what is improper, undiscriminating, and antagonistic;
one should avoid that which causes misfortune, is wicked, and is full of calamities. ||55||

One who is intent on doing harm, a fool who causes the destruction of merit, one who is an enemy with the face of a friend, and even a well-wisher who hates his friends—[these are to be avoided]. (56)
A man who looks askance, who seeks only his own self-interest, whose fame is fleeting, who praises one's face to one's face but slanders one behind one's back; ||57||

One should abandon those who are mild when it serves their own interest but stubborn when their own interest is at stake; one should abandon the drunkard, the hateful, the arrogant, the pitiless, and the harsh. ||58||
A wise person should avoid from afar one who causes distress to others, who is addicted to killing living beings, who is ungrateful, who is base, and who looks for faults. ||59||
Therefore, there is indeed no loss in this world, nor any distraction of the self anywhere;
there is neither destruction of the intellect, nor any obstacle to his spiritual progress.
Having examined them thus, the wise man should rely upon virtuous and beneficial friends who are of noble birth, endowed with knowledge, learned, and highly erudite;
who are possessed of good qualities, free from greed, self-controlled, and likewise victorious over fatigue.
[One should honor] good friends, those who are grateful, the omniscient, and those free from greed. ||62||
One should rely upon those who are endowed with the quality of sweetness, who are true to their word, who have conquered their senses,
who are habituated to physical exercise, who are faultless, and who follow virtuous conduct.

Nor those who are angry at the wrong time or for no reason, nor those who are dispassionate, nor those who are detached yet knowledgeable about wealth, but rather those devoted to the welfare of their friends. (64)
[He should appoint] guards who are trustworthy, free from malice, devoted to righteousness, regarding a clod of earth and gold as equal, friendly, and firm in intellect. (65)
Having reflected, one should take refuge in virtuous people who have surrendered all their possessions for the sake of their master;
that person who forms an alliance with such devotees of the Lord [attains success]. (66)
For them there shall always be prosperity, well-being, and likewise liberation;
they are constant in the scriptures, have conquered their defects, are contented, and are established in Hari.
Those supreme among men who are endowed with the virtues of moral conduct and tranquility should be associated with;
likewise, those who are cruel, wicked, and those described as even lower than that [should be avoided].
The ungrateful, those who betray their friends, and those devoid of dharma must be abandoned.
How can there be fame for the ungrateful? How a place? How happiness? (69)
For one who is untrustworthy is ungrateful, and for the ungrateful there is no atonement;
a man must especially never commit treachery against a friend.
One who betrays a friend goes to a terrible hell, experiencing suffering that brings about misfortune;
therefore, one should always be grateful and indeed desire the welfare of friends.
From a friend one obtains everything; from a friend one receives honor;
from a friend one attains enjoyments; and through a friend, misfortune is destroyed.
In this world, virtuous friends are the destroyers of the sins of living beings;
they are the washers away of latent impressions and likewise the bestowers of heaven and liberation.
They are the removers of existence and death, the protectors of those who have come for refuge; they are the dispellers of suffering in every way, compassionate and exceedingly virtuous. (74)
By men—whether young or old—and by women as well, the virtuous should always be served; they are adorned with good character and are free from all faults. (75)
Divine, endowed with divine qualities, and bestowing divinity upon those who take refuge in them, they are the constant attendants of mine, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. (76)
Even his grace is divine, and his vision is indeed divine;
even his touch is divine, and his service is likewise divine. (77)
Salutation, service, obedience to commands, and the nectar of their feet—all these are divine due to their divine yoga; therefore, they should be constantly served by people. (78)
There is no supreme merit such as this, nor is there any dharma like this; and my supreme devotion is toward the virtuous, for the virtuous are the saviors from worldly existence. (79)
Having thus instructed him, the Blessed One gave him the most excellent Vaiṣṇava mantras;
King Koṭīśvara then caused Hari to partake of food.
Then he gave all those honors, as well as betel leaves;
he also gave sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) such as gold coins and new garments. ||8 1||
Then, at the time following midday, Kuṣṭhakārṣi requested Hari,
who was named Pāru, to come to his own kingdom.
Formerly, King Śrī Satīśa had gone to welcome him;
Hari said, "So be it," and immediately became ready. 83.
King Koṭīśvara gave him a dowry and much wealth;
having received a parting gift of gold, jewels, and other items, Hari departed accompanied by his own kin. (84)
He ascended the celestial chariot and proceeded toward the eastern direction;
then, by the king's command, musical instruments were sounded with piercing blasts. (85)
Shouts of "Victory! were raised by the subjects, and Kṛṣṇa was bowed to by the people;
nourished by their devotions, he proceeded along the path of the sky.
He arrived from the neighboring kingdom toward the capital city;
the king, accompanied by his army, was in the royal palace within the great garden. ||87||
Having beheld the celestial chariot, which was like the sun, arriving swiftly for the sake of his welcome, he became composed; so too did the subjects and the troops on all sides. (88)
They uttered shouts of victory and displayed their prostrations;
eager, they also displayed their banners and small flags. ||89||
They displayed in the sky celestial paintings resembling the moon— both stationary and moving— accompanied by verses of praise and fame.
Then, along the path shown by the king, Śrī Hari slowly brought down the celestial chariot onto the ground in front of the temple in the garden.
Then that auspicious celestial chariot was increased in size by the subjects with flowers, leaves, and other offerings;
it was honored and bowed to by them with palms joined in reverence. (92)
Then the Supreme Lord Śrī Hari, out of compassion, quickly came forward in his celestial chariot to grant his vision to all the worlds. 93.
Hari is like the sun in his exceeding brilliance, yet his mind is as cool as the moon;
he has lotus-like eyes filled with love, and his face bears a gentle smile.
His form was completely enveloped by a halo of splendor, possessing the luster of gold;
the Lord was as beautiful as ten million Cupids and an ocean of parental affection.
He granted an audience to the people and accepted their prostrations and other marks of respect;
he then inwardly accepted the devotion offered by them with their hearts. 96.
Then the king placed flower-garlands and golden necklaces around his neck,
and he sprinkled upon his head and other parts [of his body] substances that were cool and fragrant.
He placed clusters of flowers in his hands, applied a saffron tilaka mark,
performed the washing of [the deity's] feet, and drank the nectar of grace.
The queen also worshipped the Lord of Śrī, the husband of Pārvatī;
she performed the *ārārtika* ceremony there in the palanquin with many wicks. || 99 ||
Then they performed worship and offered adoration with necklaces and other ornaments;
thereafter, Kṛṣṇa drank the cool, sweet water.
O Rādhikā, then the army set out toward the city;
for the king was eager to lead Hari astray. || 10.1 ||
The Blessed Lord Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa, having descended from the celestial chariot,
sat upon a golden throne on a white elephant adorned with ornaments.

Thus ends the two hundred and eighteenth chapter, titled "The Description of Wandering, Worship, Instruction, Feeding, and Departure in the City of Peyisthāna, and Subsequently the Arrival in the Kingdom of Pāru and Worship at Evening," in the second section (Tretā-santāna) of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Rādhikā, on the back of one elephant among many other elephants is Anādi-Kṛṣṇa;
then His parents are on another elephant, and His three brothers are on yet another.
Then, for Brahmapriya and the others, palanquins and such things appeared accordingly;
subsequently, they became immortal and likewise became fond of songs.
At the front, sharp-edged spears and the like, as well as kettledrums and other instruments, were prepared; the military drums were sounded, and shouts of victory arose. || 3 ||
The sounds of mechanical devices, the clamor of brahmins, and great roars arose from the moving gate-towers, the upper chambers, and the trees.
In the streets, on the royal highways, in houses and even in palaces,
upon joyful altars, in sacred shrines, and on the summits of forts.
In the mansions, on the main roads, and throughout the gardens,
men and women, seeking knowledge, came to behold Bālakṛṣṇa.
Then, having offered worship with their hands and other limbs, they stood nearby;
and the circle of ministers worshipped Kṛṣṇa at the city gate.
The wealthy dwell at the crossroads, the most eminent in the gardens;
these common folk are on the streets and in the marketplaces, while the people of noble birth reside at the crossroads.
They worshipped Hari with flowers, garments, ornaments, fruits, and the like;
likewise with necklaces of flowers, diamonds, and other gems, as well as with strings of jewels.
The immortal goddesses and maidens also honored him with unbroken grains and other offerings,
with garlands of land-lotuses and the like, with rings, and with sugar and other sweets.
Having wandered thus through the city, the Blessed One then quickly arrived at the palace of the king and partook of a drink of water. (11)
And at nightfall, the Blessed One taught the delightful true dharmas, which bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation, to the subjects, beginning with the king.
In place, time, and likewise in person, the intense succession of time arrives always, even if undesired, as that which generates detachment. (13)
This world is full of many faults, yet the virtuous here are indeed free from fault;
they are joined in yoga with the Blessed One and are liberated from the noose of time.
Having observed that everything is devoid of essence and filled with an abundance of suffering, those who seek their own liberation indeed become my followers through yoga. (15)
A wise person should indeed strive for the sake of their own liberation, for when wealth, wife, son, father, or master has perished, [nothing remains]. (16)
This world, deluded and dragged down by the sense of "mine-ness," goes toward suffering;
only the virtuous man, and no other, truly destroys that grief.
Just as two pieces of wood might come together in a great body of water and, having met, drift apart again—such is the meeting of embodied beings. (18)
In this way, grandsons as well as sons, wives, daughters, and kinsmen—even true husbands—are determined to be separated in the end. (19)
In this regard, one should not form an attachment, for separation from them is indeed certain;
having been unseen, they have come before, and once gone, there is no seeing them again.
Knowing thus that the entire world has the nature of a great illusion, wise people should conduct themselves in such a way that sorrow does not arise. (21)
Indeed, suffering arises from the moisture of craving; from suffering there is suffering again and again.
When what was attained has passed away, there is happiness, and when that too is gone, there is sorrow—suffering again and again. (22)
Indeed, pleasure and pain arise for people like a revolving wheel;
the body exists as the abode for these two as they alternate. (23)
That suffering shall not occur again; one must proceed upon that path.
The beginningless Śrī Hari is the path that brings about the destruction of all suffering.
I am that which is to be resorted to, for I am the medicine for the end of suffering;
yet those who do not resort to me, the virtuous ones, nor likewise to the Supreme Lord.
They experience their share of suffering and indeed become devoid of happiness; for they are bound by numerous snares of affection and by the longing for sense objects.
For those who have not achieved their purpose perish, deluded by the water of a mirage;
through attachment, everything is crushed like sesame seeds in a press during creation. (27)
Bound by attachment, he performs actions that result in a burden of sin; through that, he repeatedly encounters sufferings both in this world and in the next. || 28 ||
All embodied beings who are attached to sons, wives, and family are submerged in an ocean of grief; they truly do not attain happiness.
Just as a forest fire that has broken out upon the loss of what is desired, so too is a person who is consumed in vain,
reduced to ashes without any auspicious fruit;
for neither friends nor kinsmen are truly able to bestow happiness.
Neither one's own enemies nor others are capable of inflicting such suffering. (31)
Wealth is not capable of bestowing happiness, nor are its means;
poverty does not bestow suffering—only the wise man knows this, and no one else.
One who possesses discernment, is free from passion, and is indeed my devotee shall be happy;
I am the form of the cow, and those who milk me are happy.
Just as a cow daily provides milk that brings happiness to her calf, to the cowherd, to her owner, and even to the thief who drinks her milk—indeed, she is a source of joy to everyone. (34)
One who performs the drinking of my devotion shall become happy; of this there is no doubt—provided one relies upon the intellect, which is like a mother, discerning and nourishing. (35)
The wise person should acquire happiness so as not to be burdened by affliction in the interim;
for through solitude, peace, happiness, and even bliss are obtained. (36)
Those who have attained the bliss of solitude, who have transcended dualities, and who are free from worldly striving—
neither gains nor losses ever cause them distress at any time.
Those who are ignorant, lacking discrimination, deluded, and dragged down by their own nature, rejoice for as long as they suffer a hundredfold more. (38)
Peace born of discernment, prosperity accompanied by contentment, and abundant wealth along with glory— these dwell in the capable man, not in the indolent.
Grief enters in a thousand ways into a person who is deluded, whose memory is lost, who is possessed by craving, who is competitive, and likewise filled with envy.
Grief never touches one who has taken refuge in me—a devotee of the virtuous, discerning, highly intelligent, and free from malice and envy. (41)
Grief cannot touch one who is endowed with the existence of the Self, who is devoted to the practice of Brahman, and who cultivates the company of the virtuous. 42.
Whatever cause there may be for sorrow, distress, suffering, dejection, or lack of peace—one should abandon that from its very root; thus one will become happy. ||43||
Whatever has been imagined or striven for as one's own interest through the sense of "mine-ness" results immediately in torment within one's own self.
One who renounces desires here is always filled with happiness;
one who pursues desires and remains full of craving perishes along with those desires.
The destruction of craving is declared by the Yogins to be the great form of happiness;
[it is the state] of the world possessed by craving as it runs hither and thither in this [existence]. (46)
It is said that for one who maintains the doctrine that the body is the self, excessive grief would surely overcome them,
like one wishing to lick with the tongue nectar smeared upon the edge of a sword.
Non-attainment, separation, and suffering—thus threefold does misery arise for a person who is immersed in sensual pleasures and lost among beloved objects. (48)
In an instant suffering may arise; by renouncing desire, one becomes happy.
One should indeed loathe all desires, for desire born of the mind is death. 49.
Having withdrawn desires and intentions, and having abandoned fear, one becomes happy;
when there is neither longing nor aversion, then one has become absorbed in Brahman.

Happiness belongs to one who abandons that craving which is difficult for the foolish to relinquish, which does not grow old even as one grows old, and which is a disease that devours life itself. (5.1)
The world is struck down by death and is constantly enveloped by old age;
though seized by time, it does not understand how to accomplish its own ultimate welfare.
For an embodied being, day and night pass in vain without devotion;
knowing this, one should worship me, Hari, as Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa. (53)
As each day passes away, the lifespan of living beings is constantly diminished;
without devotion, the day goes by for embodied beings entirely in vain. (54)
Driven by excessive thirst, the seeker of happiness enters the dense thicket;
yet before his desire is attained, Death, the devourer, approaches him who is searching for pleasure, who is impassioned, and whose mind is distracted by things far away. (55)
Just as a snake seizes a female frog, death devours one and departs. || 56 ||
This very day one should perform what is beneficial; the wasting of time brings no profit.
Before one's tasks are completed, death will come and carry them away.
Therefore, one should today diligently and swiftly accomplish one’s own purpose.
Time does not perceive that "this work of his is incomplete. ||58||
No one knows when death will come to whom;
therefore, a wise person should first perform that which is for the sake of liberation.
From childhood indeed, the Lord of Śrī, Puruṣottama, must be worshipped;
when Kṛṣṇa is pleased, there shall be eternal happiness and stainless fame.
[One who is] possessed by delusion and deeply immersed in wealth, wife, sons, and fields—
Death will seize one who is asleep, even though endowed with fields, cattle, and other possessions. || 61 ||
Death seizes and carries away the one who is unsatiated, striving for the sake of sensual pleasures with great impetuosity, and running as he runs after them. || 62 ||
"I shall perform this task tomorrow, and that other one after that, and yet another after that"—
while he is thinking thus, Death will surely bring him near.
The fruit of undertakings is not attained, while one remains attached to other activities;
Yama seizes the one who experiences the suffering of what has been done and departs with him. (64)
Death takes away and departs with the king and the pauper, the wise man, the servant, and the helpless; it carries off even those who are protected in every way.
Death, old age, infirmity, dependence on others, and humiliation— [these all come]. || 65 ||
Perceiving disease and incapacity in this body, the wise person should worship Hari.
Birth is uncertain, as is childhood; likewise, death is uncertain.
It may indeed come suddenly; having reflected upon this, one should worship Hari.
For embodied beings, attachment to sense objects is indeed the place of death;
detachment, however, is like a great forest that bestows peace upon yogis.
The noose-like rope of the senses, rich with sense-objects, is the constant mode of existence for embodied beings;
having cut that asunder, the wise man should take refuge at the feet of Śrī Hari. 69.
No warrior conquers the approaching river of death;
but the warrior of truth conquers it, for immortality resides in Hari, who is Truth.

"Truth is indeed Brahman"—thus it has been proclaimed; one should become devoted to the Supreme Brahman. Established in the vow of truth and relying upon the yoga of truth, intent on the company of the virtuous, one shall conquer death through the yoga of the Real.
Only by conquering the death of delusion does one obtain immortality through the company of the virtuous. ||72||
One who seeks the goal of the virtuous, seeks the Supreme Lord, seeks service, and is established in the Self, crosses over death and attains the nectar of great bliss; he rejoices.
Established in the sacrifice of the virtuous, self-controlled, and having found delight in the sacrifice of Brahman,
one who is immersed in the offering to the Supreme Brahman indeed attains great liberation.
He with whom Kṛṣṇa is always pleased, and who is favored by the saintly ones who shower compassion like rain—such a person shall indeed attain everything. 75.
Knowledge is the eye, the divine vision; the vow of Brahman is the supreme austerity.
Service to the virtuous is the highest merit, and renunciation is eternal happiness. (76)
