For one who abides by himself, established in the Supreme Lord, free from passion and liberated—what need then for another savior? (77)
Wealth is divine, the virtuous are indeed divine jewels, and Hari himself is the jewel; for one whose active practice is devotion to Him, what need is there for any other means? (78)
Possessing nothing, one sleeps happily and awakens happily;
having attained Kṛṣṇa—who is blissful, wholesome, and auspicious—one rejoices as a happy person. (79)
He who possesses no wealth apart from Hari is indeed destitute;
yet that state of destitution is the supreme happiness, transcending even the three worlds.
Between poverty and sovereignty, there exists a great distinction:
one who possesses a kingdom is perpetually anxious, whereas one who is destitute is free from anxiety. (8.1)
He has no fear of fire or death, nor even from thieves or malevolent spirits;
neither does fear arise for him from an enemy or the force of time. (82)
Śiva and the other gods praise one who is renounced, a devotee of the Lord, whose body and home are a refuge for Hari, who is intent on serving the virtuous, and who is peaceful. (83)

Without renouncing, one does not attain happiness; without renouncing, one does not find Brahman; without renouncing, one does not abide free from fear; having attained renunciation, one becomes happy. ||84||
For one who is drawn by worldly striving and is miserable, negligence enters deeply;
for great calamities come upon one who is negligent and has abandoned the bounds of propriety. (82)
The best medicine for their destruction is the service of the virtuous;
through association with them, one gains wisdom and the dissolution of worldly desires occurs.
May there be a stream of affection for me, Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of Śrī, the Supreme Sovereign, who is full of eternal bliss; through union with me, may my devotee be happy. (87)
"O Rādhikā, men in this world should perform that action by which they may become full of eternal bliss"; having spoken thus, the Lord, the beginningless Śrīśa Nārāyaṇa, [remained silent]. 88.
"Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya pataye svāhā"—this mantra he gave to all the men and likewise to all the women. (89)
"May Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa be my refuge at all times"—
in this way, He granted refuge to everyone.
Out of fear of Time, Illusion, evil karma, enemies, Yama, and the treacherous,
he possesses the trident, fish, banner, bow, wheel, and the svastika.
Thus he then bestowed this protective mantra upon the people:
"I am Brahmā, an eternal devotee of Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. (92)
"Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, who is without beginning, is my Lord and my husband"—
it was with these very words that Hari indeed bestowed upon her the mantra of Brahman-realization.
Bālakṛṣṇa is the Supreme Brahman; he is indeed my eternal Lord. May he be my father, kinsman, well-wisher, friend, protector, and guardian. (94)
Lord Hari himself gave him the mantra for self-surrender:
"Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa; obeisance to the Master. (95)
Thus he caused [the mantra] of salutation and worship to be heard; then he declared:
"I am a devotee of Śrī Śrī Kṛṣṇa; Śrī Hari is my refuge. (96)
This Śrī Svāmī Śrīkṛṣṇavallabheśa is my refuge;
Śrī Hari, the Lord Śrīkṛṣṇavallabhasvāmī, is my refuge. ||97||
In this manner, the Blessed One himself bestowed his own mantras;
then the subjects, having bowed to Hari, worshipped him with devotion.
The queen of King Śrīsatīśa worshipped the Supreme Lord; likewise, the three daughters of King Śrīsatīśa, while still young women, worshipped Him. 99.
Having obtained Hari, her beloved and the object of her heart's desire, she placed a garland upon his neck;
in the form of a bridegroom’s wreath, she offered it and presented herself to him.
Hari took their hands and became their lord;
the queen and the king rejoiced, and the maidens felt they had accomplished their purpose.
The king held a festival for that occasion and gave many kinds of wedding gifts; then the king performed the ritual waving of lamps and provided a feast.
Then he indeed fed the great ones with various kinds of sweet foods;
the monkey rested during the night, and the three maidens attended upon him.
In the morning, King Harikṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa was awakened by auspicious musical instruments, songs, hymns of praise, and other such sounds.
When Hari had completed his daily rites and performed his worship, the king approached him;
the monarch then caused all of them to drink milk with ease.
He served him with desired gifts and the like, and received his blessings;
meanwhile, [the messengers] arrived there to lead away the illustrious Hari, the infallible one.
The royal sage Tretākarkaśa, accompanied by the ṛṣis Karṇa and Phāla,
went toward the city of Phānkalāśī as the lord of the kingdom whose wealth was his children.
He endeavored to lead Kṛṣṇa away and prostrated himself like a staff;
Hari said, "So be it," and the king offered a welcome to the lord of the earth.
Then, O Rādhikā, the Supreme Lord became ready;
the King granted him leave and bestowed honor upon his army.

Thus ends the two hundred and nineteenth chapter, titled "The Description of Hari’s Wandering, Worship, Teaching, Eating, Resting at Night, Departure on the Morning of the Second Day, and the Honors Received in Sañcalānagara," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Then, O Rādhikā, the great Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, having become ready and received the worshipful offerings, ascended into the sky in a celestial chariot.
The family and the celestial chariot became filled with great sages;
all those beginning with Brahmapriyā sat down within that chariot.
The sage Karṇaphāla sat in a celestial chariot together with Hari,
while the king, harsh in his adherence to the Tretā age, sat upon a small palanquin.
Having mounted his own [chariot], he quickly went forward to welcome him; meanwhile, upon Hari’s departure, musical instruments were sounded and the people raised a great clamor.
And shouts of victory arose, resounding to the ends of the quarters;
yet in an instant, the celestial chariot spread out and indeed came to a halt.
The kingdom, which had been deprived of its wealth by fools, shone like the sun in the sky;
then the king, harsh in his rule during the Tretā age, offered you a warm welcome.

With the sounds of musical instruments, songs and the like, with the joyful shouts of the people, with cries of "Victory!", with the drums of the army, with prostrations, flowers, and unbroken grains of rice; || 7 ||
Following the path shown by the sage, Hari quickly brought down the celestial chariot; he indeed emerged swiftly from the chariot and came forward.
The king sat down upon a golden seat and honored him with golden necklaces, garments, and other gifts, as well as sandalwood paste, unbroken grains of rice, and excellent fruits.
The queen, having sprinkled his feet with water, drank the nectar-like water;
the subjects worshipped the Lord of Lords, and then Hari drank the milk.
He caused all those of great honor to drink the excellent water;
and then the king caused the queens and the women to drink it as well.
Then that magnificent army was indeed adorned for the sake of Brahmā,
proceeding from the royal garden at the front of the city.
The great king, a sovereign as formidable as the Tretā age, seated Kṛṣṇa upon a magnificent golden chariot yoked with a hundred bulls.
With one hundred golden jars each, on a twenty-one-wheeled chariot of great width that could only be drawn along a royal highway; || 14 ||
The sages, the seers, and the attendants were with Hari,
as were the brothers, the king, and the king's sons.
But those beloved of Brahmā who traveled on other chariots then halted;
with the sounds of musical instruments, that army entered the city.
Then cries of "Victory! arose from the people on all sides;
there was a rain of flowers, a rain of fruits, and the scattering of drops of sandalwood.
The subjects offered gold coins, presented necklaces, showered flowers, bowed down, beheld him, gave gifts, and performed worship. (18)
The songs of the immortals resounded throughout the sky,
and women endowed with divine splendor offered praise to Acyuta.
The leading merchants and the common people also worshipped the Supreme Lord with all kinds of jewels and other offerings through their meditations at various places.
Having thus caused a commotion in the city of Phāṅkalāśī, he arrived at the royal palace;
there the king worshipped the Supreme Lord.
With joy, Karṇaphāla Ṛṣi seated the Lord, Kṛṣṇa, who is higher than the highest, upon a beautiful golden throne and honored him.
The queen applied a tilaka on Kṛṣṇa with saffron, unbroken grains of rice, and saffron filaments; she also placed a necklace of gold around his neck.
Then seven young maidens, beholding the enchanting Kṛṣṇa and resolving in their hearts that he was their beloved, made him their husband.
At their mother’s command, they joyfully placed the garlands of choice upon Kṛṣṇa’s neck; they performed the waving of lights and repeatedly exclaimed, "They have been offered! (25)
The queen and the king were pleased, and their daughters had accomplished their purpose; for here, O Rādhikā, Mādhava—who is to be attained through liberation—has been found.
On that day, the king celebrated a festival with dancing, singing, and other festivities;
and Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa gave instruction.
The fruit of attaining a human body is happiness from Hari;
following that, through devotion, comes great liberation—service to the virtuous is the greatest fruit.
He who is free from attachment and aversion, always delights in the stories of Kṛṣṇa, and possesses forbearance and discernment—that person shall be happy. (29)
Absence of passion brings the highest happiness; the absence of hatred bestows tranquility.
One who is free from aversion and endowed with forgiveness sleeps in peace, having become dispassionate. (2.220.30)
Between one who might obtain all desires and one who renounces all desires, it is the renouncer who finds great happiness, and not the one who possesses them all.
There is no end to sensual desires, neither one before nor one after;
one shall attain happiness by achieving the destruction of craving.
No one reaches the end of desire, even when it has been enjoyed;
no one reaches the end of wealth, even when it has been accumulated.
Having abandoned all undertakings, a person attains happiness; for one who possesses nothing, passion arises, but having acquired wealth, it increases even further. (34)
Upon the loss of what has been gained, there may be death or one grieves constantly;
since it will not be regained again, what indeed could be more painful than that? (35)
For there is no satisfaction with what has been gained; one seeks even more.
One who is insatiable here will indeed suffer again and again. (36)
The loss of wealth brings greater sorrow than anything else, along with universal contempt;
whatever fraction of happiness exists in wealth is the mother of a thousand sorrows. (37)
Robbers strike down those who possess wealth, and others carry it away;
therefore, having abandoned all hope, one should take refuge in Mādhava.
One should take recourse in world-weariness, renunciation, contentment, tranquility, forbearance, self-control, and also satisfaction; by doing so, one will indeed always be happy in this world. (39)
Having abandoned desire, greed, thirst, longing, and even miserliness, a person in this world may become happy, just like a person who is liberated.
In ancient times, the venerable Nārada questioned his own radiance:
"O Brahman, how do you abide in that bliss where there is no sorrow? (41)
Whenever I see you, at that very moment you are indeed in happiness;
you have never been seen by me in sorrow—tell me, what is the reason for this?
His own light said to him: "Listen, O wise one, to my thought:
I always see you happy; what indeed is this happiness of yours? (43)
"What indeed is his means of accomplishment, and how does he remain happy?
When the bull was pulling the cart, how was it that he was asked by me, 'How are you happy?'? (44)
And he said to me: "I have no concern at all for food, clothing, houses, and the like;
she was supported by a farmer who remained subject to my power. (45)
Thus, I contemplate the threefold purpose, but not in every respect;
therefore, I am always happy with food, clothing, dwellings, and so forth. (46)
I asked the eater of leftovers, "How do you live so happily? and he replied to me, "The wealthy man acquires wealth for the sake of fulfilling my needs with food. (47)
This other person constantly prepares food and gives it to me;
therefore, I have no concern whatsoever regarding wealth, food, or cooking. (48)
Having reflected on that, I shall not act in vain;
for I asked the parrot in the forest: "Why do you rejoice in the woods? (49)
And he said to me: "I have no bondage whatsoever; I wander wherever I please, whether in a nest or at the edge of a house, and I sleep according to my own will. (2.220.50)
Having gone to the forest of Uḍḍiyāna, I shall eat fruits and such;
I have no anxiety regarding accumulation, nor do I have any concern for protection.
I have no concern for a house or the like, nor do I have a family;
therefore, being free from anxiety, I always rejoice in happiness. (52)
Having reflected upon that, I too abandoned her and am now free from attachment.
Then the great lion was asked: "How is it that you appear so happy? (53)
And he said: "Having obtained food by the turn of fate after three days have passed, thinking 'no one shall kill me in the forest,' I sleep. (54)
Having reflected upon that, I have completely abandoned fear of time and other such things;
therefore, I move about happily and without fear, even as I sleep.
The sages who have taken refuge in the Supreme Brahman live in happiness, [observing] these states pertaining to living beings—decrease, increase, destruction, and birth. (56)
Thinking thus, they do not harm me; therefore, I always wander in happiness, [observing] that unions end in separation, and accumulations end in decay. (57)
Having realized that those endowed with patience have perished, I do not even grieve;
for my bed is overwhelmed by sleep and my weeping is stained by loss. (58)
Having abandoned the three types of joy born of acquisition, one is always happy.
Satī asked Śambhu: "How can one who is dependent on another be happy? (59)
She said to me, "O Lord, I have indeed made firm my obedience to your command;
for me there is no other duty, and he alone is favorable toward me. (2.220.60)
Therefore, great happiness is experienced by me in the Lord alone;
thus, O Supreme Lord, my favorability toward you must be considered by me.
Every kind of supreme rite for devotion to her husband has been performed by her;
she has offered herself to Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Lord. (62)
His will is indeed my fortune; my thoughts on fortune are offered to Hari.
And especially because of him, who is the very refuge of happiness, I am truly happy.
Having heard this, Nārada also adopted such a state;
wandering without support in the world, the sage was always happy.
The Lord who is his own light, as well as Sanatkumāra,
the sage Lomaśa, and Śambhu— these indeed are eternally blissful.
Those who indeed have their senses and their objects under control,
and those who indeed have the powers and the elements under control.
Those for whom wonders and supernatural powers are indeed under control, and for whom time, karma, inherent nature, and illusion are always subject to their will. (67)
Those who have their own selves under control and who are indeed under the control of the Supreme Self are always happy, both in this created world and in the imperishable abode.
Satī, Ramā, the beloveds of Brahmā, and likewise the liberated ones of that kind—
these are eternally happy, for they have dedicated their very selves to the sake of Hari.
Therefore, all should become subject to Hari and not follow others;
Hari, who possesses eternal bliss, makes his servants happy.
Having thus instructed him, the Blessed One then gave the mantras; thereafter, O Rādhikā, the king ceased his questioning and worshipped the Lord with devotion.
At that moment, the ruler of the Cilīrāṣṭra kingdom, the king known as Āṇḍajara, arrived there in his celestial chariot for the purpose of making a request.
Accompanied by Mantra, Agni, and Karṣi, we bow down with great devotion;
having received a welcome and due honor, the king approached Hari with a request.
"O Lord, O Master, purify my city which stood within [the womb] in the past.
"So be it," Hari said, and he quickly became ready.
And King Tretākarkaśa gave him a parting gift as a dowry, and with his army he paid honor to Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa. ||75||
Hari, together with his family, was in a celestial chariot in the sky,
accompanied by the mantra, the fire, and Karṣi, as well as joined by his caravan.
Then King Cāṇḍajarābha, wishing to offer a welcome, quickly departed for his kingdom and first mobilized his army. (77)
Just then, Hari arrived, traveling in a magnificent celestial chariot;
seeing him, the subjects cried out, "Victory to Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa! (78)
They raised shouts of joy, cries of victory, and the sound of trumpets;
and Mādhava, together with the sage, proceeded along the path shown by the king.
In the garden near the city where he had previously stayed,
hearing the sounds of his own welcome being proclaimed, he descended from the celestial chariot.
Then Śrī Hari quickly arrived outside at the front of the celestial chariot;
the women, with cries of joy, [welcomed] the Lord of Śrī, the beloved of Kṛṣṇa. 8.1.
With words such as "May you live long," with thoughts of "Protect us, protect us," and with hearts praying "Grant us happiness," they caused Acyuta to increase in glory.
At the outset, the king performed worship with sandalwood, unbroken rice grains, and flowers;
the queen also performed worship, and the subjects bowed down with devotion. ||83||
Then the king seated Bālakṛṣṇa upon a great elephant yoked with a golden female elephant, and likewise others upon chariots and other vehicles.
Then the king, together with his army, led them all— honored with clusters of necklaces—
to his own city, which was adorned and situated within the eastern region.
Then, on the royal highway, the leading merchants honored Kṛṣṇa with musical instruments, proclamations, and songs as they paraded him through the city gate.
Then, at the crossroads, there were the wealthy; likewise, in the marketplaces, the merchants;
and at the entrances to the streets, the women, their hearts overflowing with emotion. (87)
They worshipped the Supreme Self with necklaces, sandalwood, and saffron; with unbroken grains and other offerings, with coconuts and other fruits, and with sugar and other sweets. ||88||
Having seen that Mādhava had fulfilled his purpose, they honored him;
then the king led Kṛṣṇa to his own spacious palace.
Then he performed the *ārārtrika* rite and placed a crown upon his head;
at that time, the king also gave him necklaces of gold and jewels around his neck.
Having offered worship, she drank the nectar from his feet;
then, saying "I am fulfilled," the queen caused further honors to be performed.
He placed a golden plate upon the feet of Śrī Hari and worshipped the Supreme Lord with sandalwood paste, unbroken rice grains, flowers, and other offerings.
But taking into her heart all four of this woman's daughters— maidens and young women endowed with devotion— Mālikā did so by her mother’s command.
Joyfully placing their husband upon the neck of Hari according to the rite of offering,
they— impelled by good fortune and having accomplished their purpose— became fulfilled.
The king became exceedingly pleased and held a great festival; then Hari instructed the subjects, O Rādhā, during the night.

Thus ends the two hundred and twentieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Morning Departure from the City of Phānkalāśī on the Second Day of the Dark Half of Āśvina, the Wandering, Worship, Feasting, and Instruction; the Farewell; and the Journey after Midday to the City of Āṇḍajarānṛparaiṣṭra, as well as the Wandering and Worship in the Inner Eastern City," in the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, within the second section, the *Tretā-santāna*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O Rādhikā, Śrī Hari, established in his own nature and seated upon a golden throne, imparted instruction that brings great benefit to the subjects known as the Cillīs.
Wisdom is the foundation of living beings; wisdom is considered the bringer of liberation.
Having attained a human body, one may reach Hari through wisdom. || 2 ||
Wisdom is the highest good; pure wisdom bestows the happiness of heaven.
Through wisdom one attains one's goal, and the wise person is indeed always happy.
In this world, a human being endowed with hands and feet is considered meritorious;
having understood through his two hands and his wisdom, he should serve the Lord of the virtuous.
One should never have a mind attached to anything else, having abandoned the Supreme Lord;
for some become exceedingly happy, while others remain intensely miserable. (5)
In this world, absolute happiness never belongs to anyone anywhere;
having attained great wealth, people desire even a supreme kingdom.
From that [state], they desire divinity; from that, the status of being worshiped by Indra and others;
and the state of Brahmā and the nature of Īśvara—but they certainly never desire liberation.
Therefore, wisdom endowed with discernment is the giver of liberation;
through wisdom, liberation is attained and a firm station in the world of Brahmā is secured.
"Brahman is consciousness"—this [truth] is established even within the heart;
the supreme, eternal Brahman should be constantly worshipped. (9)
For one who is deeply attached to the essence of Brahman, no other desire arises, whether from touch, sight, or even hearing of Brahman. (2.221.10)
Through service and the practice of meditation, one becomes intent upon the essence of Brahman;
without that, there can be no satisfaction anywhere else, even upon obtaining other objects of affection.
Thirst is not quenched by water; rather, it flares up even more through enjoyments.
By wisdom alone, it is destroyed along with its very root; of this there is no doubt.
Having severed the impulse toward actions performed for desire and having fully restrained the senses, one should abide in the nature of the Self; thus, one's craving perishes.
Neither eating, nor touching, nor seeing;
likewise, neither tasting, nor hearing, nor smelling, nor feeling. (14)
Thus, this supreme restraint, established by wisdom, leads to the highest good;
for embodied beings, even those possessing hands, strength, and wealth, [are subject to death]. (15)
Having become slaves to craving, they suffer through slaughter and imprisonment;
they weep, yet they take delight, they rejoice, and they even laugh.
Thus, people of great strength who have acquired knowledge and captivated the minds of others resort to a loathsome, wretched, and base way of life. || 17 ||
They exert themselves, they grow strong, they fall, and they even weep;
yet neither the frog nor the boar nor the dog desires to abandon its own self.
Whether he be a Puṣkasa, a Cāṇḍāla, or even a bound insect within his body,
he remains highly content with his own womb through the power of Māyā.

Having seen those who are deformed, those with paralyzed wings, those with withered arms, and even those afflicted by leprosy, one who is healthy does not resort to Hari at all; he is struck down by my illusion.
Therefore, having investigated with the mind and reached a firm conclusion through wisdom, one should worship Me, the Supreme Self, abandoning attachment and delusion. (21)

One who desires to achieve the highest good should practice meditation, purification, recitation, worship, service to elders such as one's father, attendance upon the virtuous, and devotion to me. (22)

While one possesses a kingdom and the prosperity of a household, one should perform meritorious deeds under an auspicious constellation, at a holy time, on a favorable lunar day, and during a propitious moment. (23)
Those of virtuous character strive for merit through sacrifices, gifts, and other such acts;
their wisdom shines forth quickly through union with the Supreme Brahman. (24)
Through wisdom, one goes to my supreme abode, eternal bliss—even those who are ill-situated among the stars and asuras, or born under unfavorable moments (durmuhūrta). ||25||
Devoid of wisdom and hating sacred rites, they fall into a demonic womb;
they go to the burrows of jackals and dogs, for no higher good exists for them. 26.
Contented, vigilant, fond of sacrifice, charity, and austerity, devoted to serving the virtuous, and taking refuge in wisdom, he attains the supreme goal. (27)
Those servants who are devoted to the gods and guests, who are fond of the virtuous, and who have dedicated all their possessions for the sake of Hari, attain the supreme goal. ||28||
From festival to festival they go, from joy to joy again and again;
from heaven to the highest heaven they go—those who serve the virtuous man. (29)
The wicked, the deceitful, the rogues, and those who are deceivers and sinners, being possessed by their own self-interest, immerse themselves in sinful deeds.
Furthermore, having committed defilement, they come to exist in a world of suffering; from famine to famine, and from affliction to affliction, again and again. (3.1)
From fear they go to fear, and from agitation to agitation;
from death to death again go those who are poor and performers of evil deeds.
Just as chaff is among grains or gadflies among birds, so are those people devoid of righteous deeds; such are they among men. (33)
They are cooked like grains of grain in the fire of the womb, parched by time;
without wisdom, they never attain the supreme good by any means whatsoever. (34)
Agitated, they run forward, facing the forest of saṃsāra;
then karma, having become their follower, runs after them to seize them.
Whether he is asleep, in deep slumber, in a secluded place, or even while awake, it does not leave him;
clinging like a shadow, it never departs once it has attached itself.
Seeing that [the self] is drawn by karma, dependent on others, and enveloped by latent impressions (vāsanā), Mahākāla drags it into the ocean of suffering. (37)
Time bestows the fruits of one's own actions upon the doer,
just as time brings forth flowers and fruits upon the trees.
Beings are born and do not escape their previously performed karma;
through the remainder of what was done by themselves, they proceed to the bed of the womb. (39)
Whether a child, a youth, or an elder, one obtains that fruit;
for one purified by the fire of wisdom, there is long-lasting and infinite happiness.
For the virtuous who have shaken off evil through wisdom, whose passion and hatred have perished, and who are devoted to the Supreme Lord, imperishable happiness is attained. (41)
Whatever a person possessed of wisdom undertakes, all that leads not to bondage;
for one who is united with me through wisdom, no action exists.
Just as the track of fish in the water or of birds in the sky is not seen, so too no trace of action is found in me for the devotee who knows [the truth]. 43.
This is the goal of those who possess knowledge, having the abode of Brahman as its supreme refuge;
it is to be attained by men seeking liberation through virtuous wisdom.
I indeed dwell as the inner self, hidden within all beings;
I am to be attained only through supreme wisdom that perceives reality.
Taking food provided by my grace and attaining union with me through my blessings,
one who applies himself to me, the Lord of the self, becomes equal to Brahman.
And by means of the serenity of his mind, having offered his heart to me, he remains with a stainless self, a tranquil self, and a self surrendered to me. (47)
Abiding in me, Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme, one enjoys infinite happiness;
with steady resolve, one enjoys endless and boundless bliss. 48.
One should always conquer great craving, greed, and anger by every possible means;
then, indeed, the knowledge produced by wisdom attains purity.
Self-restraint alone is the soul of liberation, the most excellent bull;
by means of that self, one should always abide in the Self, in Me, Nārāyaṇa.
For one who conducts oneself in this manner, liberation is held in the palm of the hand;
indeed, I myself, residing within his heart, become the milker of his liberation.
Having thus instructed them, the Lord Kāṃbhareya, the Great Master,
gave the mantras to the subjects, and the subjects performed worship of Hari.
The subjects offered various articles, including garments and ornaments;
they gave gold and silver to Śrī Hari. (53)
Then, during the night, the king indeed fed Mādhava,
as well as his family, the great sages, and the maidens.
Then Keśava attained rest and fell asleep;
those maidens served their own beloved, the Supreme Lord. 55.
Then Hari was awakened by the sounds of morning musical instruments, by songs, auspicious chants, and by the Vedic recitations of the brahmins.
Having performed his daily rites, having completed his worship, and having consumed milk and fruit,
he was honored by the king during the night and seated upon a golden throne.
The king caused other merchants to drink milk;
meanwhile, the subjects arrived for the purpose of honoring him and beholding him. (58)
Then Kṛṣṇa bestowed wealth and other riches upon Mantrāgnikarṣi;
and the brother of King Aṇḍajarā arrived, bowing down to Hari.
Prostrating like a staff, King Bālyaraja spoke of his own most beautiful city,
named Mantriṇāṅgā, in order to purify it.
Hari, honored by the egg-born and the aged, said, "So be it," and the Lord, accompanied by the dowry and the wedding gift, departed.
Endowed with great majesty, he quickly ascended the celestial chariot;
then the younger brother of the king departed through the sky together with that chariot.
Piercing musical instruments were sounded again and again,
and at that time, a celestial chariot spread out in the sky before Hari.
Then the king’s aerial chariot indeed proceeded swiftly ahead toward the city of Maṅgalāvatī,
which lay along the path of the ocean.
An army had already been stationed there for the purpose of welcoming them;
and they beheld that celestial chariot, which was indeed as radiant as the sun and exceedingly brilliant.
The men welcomed him with banners, small flags, and other ornaments;
first the king descended, and then the celestial chariot of Hari.
She descended into the garden near the minister Aṅga;
standing before him there, the queen indeed paid him due honor.
Having bowed to Hari seated in the celestial chariot, she worshipped him with necklaces, flowers, unbroken grains, and sandalwood paste; having washed his feet, she drank the water from them.
Having led Hari to the royal palace, the sovereign lady caused him to dwell there.
Then a certain young maiden, being virtuous, performed the *ārārtrika* rite;
she then placed a beautiful garland around the neck of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, and the King celebrated a great festival.
Thereafter, he gave food to Bālakṛṣṇa and the others; then, having seated him upon a horse-chariot, he paraded him through the city. The subjects joyfully worshipped the beloved Lord Śrīkṛṣṇa.
At midday, Hari rested, and during that time the king himself performed the massaging of Bālakṛṣṇa’s feet; then,
in the evening, having ascended the celestial chariot, he wandered through the sky over the ocean.
Then, on the third day at evening,
Rāyasomanabhūpati, the lord of the kingdom of Pātragonaya,
arrived to take Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa to his own country in order to purify it. || 74 ||
After sporting about, Hari returned to his abode;
there the king bowed to him and prayed to the Supreme Lord for wealth and happiness.
"So be it," Hari replied, and having drunk water from his celestial chariot, he departed.
Accompanied by his entire caravan, he quickly ascended [the chariot] and then became ready to go to the city of Vāyumāna.
With joy, the king bestowed upon him leave-taking honors, worship, and wedding gifts.
Awakened by the sound of the chariot, Kṛṣṇa urged the celestial vehicle forward;
hearing the various musical instruments being played, the Blessed One himself arrived at the divine city, Vāyumānā, which was most beautiful.
Seeing the beautiful celestial chariot stationed on the riverbank, Kṛṣṇa,
following the path shown by the king, brought it down onto the river's edge.
Then musical instruments were played, and a great welcome was offered in many ways.
The subjects greatly honored him with flowers, unbroken grains of rice, and other offerings.
Then Hari descended from his celestial chariot and sat down upon a golden throne;
the king himself then worshipped him with a garland of flowers.
With sandalwood paste, unbroken rice grains, flowers, and the like, as well as with sprinklings of fragrant liquids,
the queen worshipped him with affection and performed the lustration ceremony (nīrājana).
Having seated the king upon an elephant, she caused him to be paraded through the city.
The leaders worshipped Śrī Hari there at the city gate;
the wealthy merchants likewise worshipped him on the main road;
the women worshipped him at the openings of the streets, and the local residents worshipped him in the vicinity of their homes.
The women worshipped the Lord of Śrī with songs and sang hymns of praise.
Having thus paraded Hari through his own city,
the king brought Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa to his palace for the night.
The queen also performed the nightly lamp-offering and worshipped with various articles. ||87||
Then the three maidens placed the bridegroom’s garland upon the neck of Hari;
having obtained him as their husband and lord of their lives, those auspicious women felt they had fulfilled their purpose.
O Rādhikā, the glorious Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa was present;
then, accompanied by Sārthaka, He partook of the meals during the night. 89.
On the night of the third day of the dark fortnight of Āśvina, he obtained rest; and three maidens served their own Lord with exceeding devotion. (2.221.90)
Hari indeed took up sleep, and at dawn he awoke to auspicious sounds:
the resonance of musical instruments, songs, Vedic mantras, and hymns of praise. 9.1.
Having performed his morning ablutions and daily rites, Kṛṣṇa paid homage to his own parents amidst the laudatory verses and poetic recitations of the bards, panegyrists, and minstrels.
On the fourth day, he performed the drinking of milk and other rites at the very dawn;
meanwhile, the subjects arrived at the very dawn for the purpose of worshipping Īśeśa.
The king first honored him, and the subjects praised the Imperishable One;
thereafter, Hari gave wealth and riches to that eminent brahmin boy.
King Rāyasoma and the young brahmin-sage likewise became supremely satisfied, and the subjects also became contented. (95)
Then Hari, the benefactor, instructed Rādhikā:
"The cause of my incarnation is the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. (96)

Thus, in the second section on the Tretā age of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, [the account includes] the instruction in the city of Āntaḥprāgsthāna, the meal, and resting at night; on the third day of the dark fortnight of the month of Āśvina, the departure in the morning for the kingdom of King Bālyarajas, the wandering through the city of Mantriṇāṅga, the worship, the meal, the farewell, and the dowry; and in the evening, the arrival in the kingdom of King Rāyasomana, the welcome in the city of Vāyumāna, the wandering, the worship, the meal, and resting at night.
The two hundred and twenty-first chapter, titled "The Definition of the Ceti and Other [Terms]."
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O Rādhikā, the Lord Bālakṛṣṇa,
the benefactor of all, instructed his subjects early in the morning in the vast royal palace.
King Rājasūdana heard it along with his family;
thousands of men and women, including the principal officials, also heard it. || 2 ||
Renunciation must always be practiced, as well as the relinquishing of active worldly duties;
for it is the renouncer who attains freedom from the qualities (nirguṇya), which is the means to liberation.
For one whose action is offered in renunciation, it shall not yield fruit;
having completely abandoned all insistence, he should always be free from passion.
May the sorrowless Supreme Brahman abide in me, by which great happiness is attained;
for the wise man, unattached amidst attachments, should conquer the unconquered mind.
Whatever is perceived by the senses should be abandoned, not grasped with attachment;
having restrained the mind, one should indeed sustain the vital breaths within the Supreme Self.
Thus, through this retention, there shall indeed be eternal bliss, the peace of Nirvana;
for bliss is attained by Brahma in every way through the offering unto Brahma.
Truth is always to be embraced as Brahman, while falsehood is indeed to be abandoned;
for falsehood is said to be darkness, which bestows blindness and leads one into a pit.
For one bound by the rope of latent impressions (vāsanā), falling into a pit is certain;
for one free from impressions and satisfied, it is said that light bestows the divine abode.
Relying upon light, one should strive for the destruction of suffering and the constant dispelling of darkness through association with the virtuous and other such means. (2.222.10)
He who is not agitated by physical or even mental sufferings,
who finds happiness through union with me— he alone is one who has entered my path.
Where there is suffering, that is hell; but happiness is the supreme state.
For one who has abandoned the undertaking of suffering, heaven is not difficult to attain.
Having burnt away all defects through the vow of Brahman, he shall conquer the supreme state;
he who practices the stage of liberation, possessing a liberated intellect, becomes beloved of Hari.
By offering everything to Hari, a person attains the world of Brahmā;
the virtuous who are devotees of Brahmā should be served, for by that, the attainment of Brahman arises.
Being devoted to right conduct and intent upon devotion to me, auspicious conduct must always be observed by householders as well for their own welfare. (15)
Purity must be maintained as an essential duty, as well as the worship of the gods, the libations for the ancestors, and likewise the honoring of the elderly. (16)
One should always worship the sun at the time of twilight and remember Hari;
being pure, one should take food and should not revile human beings or others.
One should always perform circumambulation around a temple, a guru, a virtuous man, a virtuous woman, a bull, a crossroads, a righteous person, and a divine being.
If one is capable, one should provide for guests and dependents with food and other necessities,
and should offer assistance to those who are helpless.
Eating either twice or once, but not in between,
one who eats in this manner is declared to be observing a fast and shall always be happy.
He is a giver during the performance of a sacrifice and a donor at the proper time, but not otherwise;
thus self-controlled and observant of celibacy, he is always auspicious. (21)

Indeed, that which is consumed by the gods is nectar; likewise, nectar is considered wholesome. He who accepts what is fivefold (the five products of the cow) is a man who, like a god, possesses happiness.
The virtuous worship the grace of the gods, which bestows long life;
indeed, the virtuous are worthy of worship by one who desires their favor.
Service to the guru must be performed, and salutation must be offered;
for by honoring the gurus, one is endowed with long life, fame, and prosperity.
The teachers of sacred fords are the sacred ford; the teachers of the pure are the pure.
That which is performed by the learned is praiseworthy; it is like the cow's tail, ever purifying. (25)
One should constantly serve a virtuous guru through both sight and touch;
for the head, hair, and body hairs of a virtuous person are indeed purifying. ||26||
The dust from the feet of the virtuous bestows liberation and destroys sin;
the touch of holy men is meritorious, and their eyes are always considered auspicious. (27)

For the ears of the virtuous are indeed meritorious, their nose is meritorious with its fragrance; the forehead of the good is truly meritorious, and their cheeks and jaws are indeed meritorious. (28)
The cheeks are entirely meritorious; the smile is meritorious and captivating;
likewise, the teeth, tongue, and lips grant merit and are purifying for the virtuous. (29)
The throat is meritorious, as is the sound; speech is meritorious, being Sarasvatī herself.
The discourse of the virtuous is indeed meritorious, and association with the holy bestows merit. (2.222.30)
The shoulders are meritorious; the arms and hands are meritorious;
the fingers and nails of the hands are meritorious; the lines [on the palms] are meritorious, and likewise the forearm is the bestower of merit. (3.1)
Likewise, the elbow and the palm are always auspicious for the virtuous;
the surface of the hand always bestows merit, and the chest is a producer of merit. (32)
The breasts are always meritorious; the navel is meritorious and purifying; the belly is also merit-bestowing; and for the virtuous, the hips are most meritorious. (33)
The hidden region is very purifying, and the pubic area is always purifying;
the hips are purifying, and likewise the thighs are purifying. (34)
The sense organs are always purifying, as are the two knees;
the shanks bring about purification, and likewise the two ankles are purifying. (35)
The soles of the feet, the feet themselves, the toes, and the nails are purifying;
likewise, the skin, flesh, blood, and the divine skeletal frame are divine. (36)
Marrow, fat, and even the vital essence (rasa) are purifying elements for the virtuous;
indeed, everything belonging to the holy ones is purifying, just like Śrī Hari.
The sons of the Blessed One are of three kinds, purifying like the Blessed One himself:
the virtuous sons of the Blessed One, those who have been initiated, and those living in the householder stage of life. || 38 ||
Likewise, those three sons born of the lineage are the most excellent purifiers;
and the fourth among them is also a purifier, being endowed with devotion to the Blessed One.
Endowed with initiation, ritual action, devotion, and knowledge, those virtuous ones are equal to Śrī Hari; they are considered the purifiers of the worlds.
His grace removes sin; that water is superior even to the Ganges.
All service to him destroys sin; offering to him is the offering to Brahman.
But whatever trees or other objects the virtuous touch, even those trees become divine in this world, bestowing liberation and destroying sin. (42)
Whatever garment is worn by the virtuous— whether made of cotton, wool, silk, or the bark of trees—
that divine cloth is always purifying.
Whether it be an animal, a bird, or any other person who is touched by a holy man, he indeed quickly becomes divine; though still a mere physical body, he becomes transcendent.
That which is impure becomes pure through contact with the virtuous;
even sin, or even greater evil, is purified by the touch of the righteous. (45)
Whatever is worn on the body by a virtuous person is pure; of this there is no doubt.
Water becomes a sacred ford (tīrtha) as soon as it is used for service by a virtuous person. ||46||
The earth, when served by the virtuous, becomes exceedingly sacred;
even a leaf, a flower, a fruit, water, or whatever else may be offered, should be accepted as food.
Whatever association with the virtuous one has attained is indeed considered pure;
one who serves the virtuous is always pure, for the virtuous woman is a divine body of Hari. 48.
One's vehicle and seat should be described as pure and frequented by the virtuous;
honoring the virtuous both morning and evening bestows heaven and liberation. 49.
Service to the virtuous is the highest dharma; service to the virtuous is the supreme wealth;
service to the virtuous is the highest desire; and even liberation comes from serving the virtuous.
The heart of those of virtuous conduct attains goodness in every way; the accumulated substance of goodness provides assistance at the station of the abode. 51.
Goodness toward all beings bestows peace and brings about security;
therefore, one should cultivate goodness as a companion on the path to the divine abode. 52.
The source of goodness for the gods, sages, and ancestors is devotion to Brahman; the source of goodness for the liberated is that same devotion. A wise person should always cultivate it.
Death is certain; that which was done and enjoyed has already passed away.
No new merit has been acquired; what will you eat in the future? (54)
Having reflected thus, one should indeed constantly serve the virtuous who bestow merit, as well as the ancestors and the deities. (55)
The great fruit of service will certainly stand before him in heaven;
the fruit of pleasing the guru will certainly stand before him. (56)
Having thus resolved, one should constantly serve pure holy men (sādhus);
for holy men are well-established embodiments of the Blessed One.
From whom this creation was born, from whom millions of incarnations arise, and from whom, having attained sovereignty, the lords and others are produced. ||58||
The sages, the ancestors, and the gods constantly worship him,
from whom even the sun and other luminaries arise as embodiments of splendor.
From which all beings are born and into which they are likewise withdrawn;
from which the senses, the mind, and the intellect are produced and exist. (2.222.60)
There, the conscious Lord stands as a witness, intent upon the performance of action;
yet that Supreme Person, the Master, remains within, restraining him.
By relying upon that Lord of Gods, by whom all this is pervaded, and who both exists and moves, one attains supreme peace. (62)
Having indeed abandoned the natural state and attained the divine state,
that devotee who finds delight in the Self shall go to the supreme goal.
Just as a water-dwelling bird is not smeared by water,
so too one of perfected wisdom, though remaining in the world, is not defiled.
The man who possesses contentment and satisfaction obtained through the grace of his chosen deity remains like a spider in its web, neither grieving nor exulting.
Having severed the firm knot called latent impression (vāsanā) situated in the heart of one's own self, he should abide in bliss and attain that supreme abode. ||66||
Just as one who is dirty becomes pure by taking water and bathing,
so too does one defiled by illusion attain purity through association with the virtuous.
One who knows the far shore of the great forest is indeed not deluded therein;
likewise, one who has realized the end of illusion is indeed not deluded regarding the principles of reality.
For one who has understood the three aims of life, and having perceived and enjoyed them, is released from attachment—
being unbound and free from desire— the path of Brahman shines forth.
For the wise there is no fear, yet for those ignorant of You there is indeed no freedom from fear;
however, when both are united with Hari, there is absolutely no fear whatsoever.
Whatever action arises in the world that is not preceded by intentional desire— that, whether pleasant or unpleasant, does not lead to bondage, being regarded as equal.

Having observed that the world is afflicted while the virtuous are likewise free from affliction, he who worships me by adopting the conduct of the virtuous shall indeed cross over [the ocean of existence]. (72)
One who grieves will certainly not see that by which grief is destroyed;
one who does not grieve will always see that by which the happiness of the virtuous is attained.
Those people in this world who proceed according to the path of the virtuous attain the state of the virtuous and go to the supreme station. ||74||
Wherein I, the great Hari, am eternally present and resplendent,
served and meditated upon by infinite millions of liberated souls.
Having spoken thus, O Rādhikā, the Lord Anādi-Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa ceased speaking and then personally bestowed the Vaiṣṇava mantras upon her.
The king and the subjects again worshipped Kṛṣṇa with many offerings;
then Hari desired to depart, and the king gave him a gift.
Hari gave him excellent wedding gifts and became ready;
at that moment, King Rājārāyapati arrived there.
Accompanied by King Giri and the sages, he went to request the Lord Hari to lead him and his kingdom, whose inhabitants were of sage-like nature, to his own abode.
Vyena then requested the Blessed One to reside permanently on the banks of the river Parībhāsā in the city of Ujjayinī.
Hari, moved by compassion, declared to him, "So be it";
however, he added, "The time for that is not yet; you must go quickly to the lower realm."
Tomorrow, on the fifth day, the commencement of the sacrifice shall take place in the kingdom of Brāhmīla.
Therefore, O King, having completed the sacrifice, [you must depart] at dawn on the thirteenth day. ||82||
"I shall arrive in your kingdom this very evening; of this there is no doubt. According to your wishes, I will remain in your abode for a long time. (83)
"You, however, must come to that sacrifice on the morning of the fifth day;
the conclusion will take place at midday on the eleventh day. (84)
Thus addressed by Hari, the king accepted the words of Hari;
having worshipped him, he quickly departed for his own kingdom, traveling by means of a celestial chariot.
Then a second king also arrived before Śrī Hari:
King Urugavākṣa, the lord of the city of Rāyagrāmā. ||86||
Urogamana, the lord of the kingdom, prayed to the Supreme Lord;
and Mānatriveda, the king of sages, also prayed to Mādhava.
"O Keśava, come and purify my kingdom and its subjects as well!
"So be it," Hari replied, and becoming ready, he ascended his celestial chariot.
At that time, the people living in celestial palaces became endowed with wealth;
and having bid farewell to the king and others, the people indeed ceased their cries of lamentation. (89)
Many musical instruments were played, and a celestial chariot appeared in the sky;
it was bowed to by the people and honored with flowers, unbroken rice, and other offerings while suspended in the air.
Then it spread forward, its course directed toward the chest;
"He is coming quickly indeed!"—thus the king descended before him.
The lord of the city of Rājagṛha performed a grand welcome and honored him;
the city was adorned and the palace became resplendent. (92)
With banners and the like, with leaves, plantain pillars, arches, and svastikas;
with water-pots, colored creepers, and likewise with sprinklings of water.
And in the vicinity of such a city, near the ocean,
he brought his own celestial chariot of Śrī Hari to the earth by means of a prearranged signal.
Then musical instruments were played and shouts of victory arose;
kettledrums and other drums resounded, and the songs of women became auspicious. ||95||
The sounds of musical instruments, roars of joy, and the auspicious voices of the people arose as a welcome, truly causing the celestial chariot to swell with splendor.
With flowers, unbroken grains of rice, and other offerings, the subjects went before Hari;
he was saluted and worshiped by the king, the queen, and the subjects as well. (97)
Then the Blessed Lord sat upon a beautiful golden throne;
O King, Rādhikā placed clusters of flowers and garlands around the neck of Hari.

Thus ends the two hundred and twenty-second chapter, titled "The Instruction and Farewell to the Subjects of the Kingdom of Pātragonaya, the Acceptance of the Request to Depart for the Kingdom of Ārṣajatānu from King Rājārāyapati, and the Journey to and Reception by the Kingdom of Urogamana," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O Rādhikā, in order to lead Śrī Hari to his own city, the king brought the army ready for action to the city of Rāyagrāma.
He seated Hari there upon a beautiful chariot drawn by white horses;
likewise, he placed the family members and the maiden, the beloved of Brahmā, upon other chariots.
Accompanied by the sounds of musical instruments and songs, the king joyfully paraded Kṛṣṇa through the city; meanwhile, the chief officers were at the city gate.
The most excellent merchants worshipped the Supreme Soul at the crossroads; the women did so at the entrances of the streets, and the subjects indeed on the roads and in the marketplaces.
With gold and silver coins, sandalwood, unbroken grains of rice, saffron, garments, flower garlands, coconuts, fruits, and so forth; || 5 ||
Having thus wandered through the city, Hari went to the royal palace;
King Urugavākṣa worshipped the Supreme Lord.
He performed the consecration of the feet of the Supreme Self with milk,
and thereafter indeed with sweet water and pure water.
The royal family and others drank the nectar from the feet of Śrī Hari;
then the queen performed worship and also offered the lustration ceremony (nīrājana).
Then the two maidens placed upon the neck of Kṛṣṇa, who was firm in his auspicious vow, a long garland of flowers in the form of a bridegroom’s wreath.
When you had accomplished your purpose by obtaining the beloved husband of Śrī,
the king and the queen then felt in their hearts that they too had fulfilled their life's mission.
Then the king caused that beautiful festival to be celebrated;
he fed Kṛṣṇa and the great men from all sides.
Hari gave all his wealth to the sage Mānatriveda,
and thereafter Mādhava bestowed instruction upon the subjects there.
When the mental fluctuations have dissolved, Kṛṣṇa always shines within the heart;
Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Lord, becomes truly accessible through meditation. 13.
In ancient times, sages attained supreme perfection through the yoga of meditation;
likewise, other yogis have attained it, and others will do so in the future.

People who are greatly satisfied by the knowledge of meditative absorption and whose hearts are set on nirvāṇa do not return to saṃsāra, for they are liberated from the mire of worldly existence. (15)
Those who have completely abandoned passion and hatred, who are established in their true self-nature,
and who abide eternally in purity, being liberated, do not return again anywhere.
The devotee who performs those pacifying rites that have been prescribed, which are free from contentious speech and deceit, attains me. (17)
Having risen early in the morning and restrained the mind,
one should indeed fix it upon my image in my presence and meditate upon my form.
One should not grasp at sound, touch, form, taste, or smell as they present themselves; rather, one should practice self-restraint and not contemplate other objects.
He who, having consolidated the senses and the mind, performs the restraint of them within Me, for him there shall be the manifestation of My form within his heart. (2.223.20)
If the mind, being indeed fickle in meditation, becomes like a fish [in water], one should forcibly turn it back and again concentrate it upon the image. 2.1.
One should first perform meditation upon me as being richly adorned with ornaments and fine garments;
thereafter, having dissolved that attire, one should contemplate me as mere form alone. (22)
Then one should contemplate me as divine, laughing and speaking;
thereafter, one should contemplate [me] as the bestower of bliss, of a single form. ||23||
In this way, the senses, mind, ego, and intellect dissolve gradually into the form through love; then one attains liberation. ||24||
This is the progress of yogins, characterized by the renunciation of karma;
the external functions of the senses, which are directed toward objects and are manifold, [are thus restrained].
Actions performed by practitioners are to be offered and rendered subservient through total surrender;
one who is pure and perfected becomes my devotee through this total surrender. ||26||
Even when the collection of sense-faculties becomes forcefully attached to something, one should recognize that object and mentally construct its form. (27)
In each instance, the mind should be made steady gradually;
by providing it with desired objects, it will attain stability once it is satisfied. (28)
Then, having dissolved that object into my image in its form, the devotee should contemplate it gradually; in this way, he becomes pure after a long time.
When my mind has become serene through yoga, the supreme arising of the sattva quality occurs;
by that comes my affection, by that my devotion, and by that liberation shall follow.
One should offer to Me all meditation, austerity, self-restraint, patience, activity, reflection and the like, as well as speech, movement, and every form of worldly engagement. (31)
Thus, having surrendered the impelling sacrifice to Me, one should become happy;
or else, having cast all duties behind one's back, one should remain inactive.
Having become [thus], one should indeed contemplate me with the mind and always mutter my name;
one should pay homage to the sense objects and not dwell upon worldly activity.
Having visualized my form within his heart, he should then become absorbed therein;
thus, having attained union with me, he goes at the end to the supreme state.
And for the yogi who is thus free from desire and has performed every renunciation, there is the attainment of the Brahmic body; he becomes equal to Me in the Imperishable.
One should constantly remember my form, chant my supreme name, and perform everything for my sake; such a person shall attain my world. ||36||
And having become untainted through abiding in Brahman, ascending above the realm of Māyā, he attains the nectar, the state of immortality, the Supreme Self. ||37||
The supreme attainment among all attainments is constant devotion to the Supreme Lord;
for the virtuous, attainment is the attainment of Hari, and the attainment of His abode, and nothing else.
All worlds created by the ego go to hell;
all worlds created by Brahman, however, go to the Imperishable. ||39||
A person who commits suicide goes to the hells guarded by Yama;
however, one who has attained union with Brahman is neither a suicide nor does he go to those abodes.
Wherever there may be longing for existence, even in the state of a preta, the living soul enters into rebirth; therefore, one should practice the contemplation of Brahman.
One who is intent on meditation for the sake of sovereign power attains only sattvic illusion, which grants rebirth;
therefore, one should be intent on meditation upon Brahman. 42.
He who is completely overwhelmed by powers, presided over by intoxication and pride, and conducts himself through illusion—he indeed experiences hell for that very reason. (43)
He for whom the Yakṣiṇī of craving and the Rākṣasī of seeking remain, and he who possesses the Piśācī of anxiety—these three are of the nature of hell. (44)
He who has passion as his rakshasa, he who has delusion as his yaksha, and he who has hatred as his pishacha—these three are of the nature of the Raurava hell. ||45||
Wherever these three exist for him, there he is reborn;
through them and by means of those [three], the one of evil intellect undergoes the turning of delusion.
Indeed, one of unrefined wisdom goes to the Raurava hell because of that;
through faulty wisdom, many hells indeed come to be here.
The flames here burn embodied beings moment by moment;
for one who is not satisfied, true happiness free from suffering never arises. (48)
That pleasure which is mixed with suffering is considered here to be what is called hell;
for illusion exists only in hell, and it is never free from suffering. (49)
For one possessing an illusory body, happiness is certainly neither absolute nor eternal; therefore, apart from the immutable state, happiness is essentially of the nature of hell. 2.223.50.
I shall indeed describe the various hells— those that are illusory,
those belonging to material nature, and those subject to dissolution— which become fruitless within the state of Brahman.
The enjoyments of human beings are indeed the domain of hell;
whereas for the gods and the sages, there are established abodes and dwellings.
Such indeed are the hells situated within the bodies of embodied beings—those of the world-protectors, the guardians of the directions, the planets, and likewise the winds. (53)
And the dwellings of the Sādhyas, the Viśvedevas, and the Gandharvas;
and those of the Rudras, Ādityas, Vasus, the Siddhas, and Parameṣṭhin. ||54||
Divine celestial chariots that move at will, assembly halls,
gardens, lotus ponds, and houses made of gold.
The nectars and enjoyments, the splendors and garments that exist, the prosperities of the gods and others, and the bodies of those who feed on nectar—[all these arise from it]. (56)
Celestial women, divine beds, and celestial perfumes, flavors, and so forth—these are considered hells resulting from the ripening of illusion when compared to the supreme abode of Brahman. (57)

The enjoyments of the lords, the sovereigns, and the primal person (pradhānapuruṣa), as well as those belonging to the abodes of Māyā, which consist of goodness (sattva) and are yet illusory (māyika). ||58||
All of them, born from the Mahat-tattva and known as the hells, are considered to be situated in front of the abode of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. (59)
Likewise, those worlds consisting of illusion that exist in the vicinity of the abodes of Goloka and Vaikuṇṭha are considered hells, even though they appear as enjoyments.
There is no other divine and eternal abode equal to the world of Brahmā;
for both Goloka and Vaikuṇṭha are indeed of the nature of the abode of Brahman.
Indeed, that which is empty of illusion is truly free from illusion and bestows liberation;
I am Śrī Kṛṣṇa in person, served by Rādhā and the others.
In Goloka, I am served by the cowherds and cowherd-maidens who possess my own form;
there I exist in a divine and eternal form where illusion does not prevail.
I am Nārāyaṇa, established in the supreme Vaikuṇṭha,
well-served by divine powers such as Lakṣmī and Ramā.
Served by attendants of divine form, I am divine and eternal;
I am of a divine and eternal nature where no illusion exists.
I am the very nature of Vāsudeva in that supreme, unmanifest state where Māyā does not exist at all; such am I, possessing a divine form.
Thus, that place where I have established my station is indeed divine for me;
through my yoga it has attained divinity, and there is no hell there.
Palaces separated from me, places, and likewise riches—all these masters and inhabitants have become like hells, destroyed by Māyā. (68)
Having thus observed this very thing through the wisdom bestowed by me, one should practice my yoga in every way; then the state of hell dissolves away.
And even divine status is attained, having entered into union with my purpose;
yet therein there is no connection of mine consisting of surrender.
In that regard, time is subject to me; it has no power over me.
I am the ruler of time; it does not operate within me.
Wherever I am, there my devotee goes and indeed does not grieve;
such is this supreme abode for the virtuous who are connected to Brahman.
But all those distinct from that are indeed hells, each according to its nature;
having reflected upon this, a wise person should practice what pertains to me.
Whether it be insentient or sentient, whatever is made connected to Me—that alone is declared to be "divine," due to its excellent union with the Divine. (74)
Having known this and having offered themselves to me, my devotees have attained divinity;
they are not born again in creation, nor do they pass away when time consumes all.
Having attained a state that is neither suffering nor pleasure, they abide in eternal bliss;
in my supreme joy, the ultimate abode, they enjoy all desires.
Those who perform my recitation and are devoted to my form become immortal;
having attained immortality, they become one with Brahman.
My yogis go to that station of Brahman, which is non-returning, known as the single syllable, free from suffering, undecaying, and peaceful. (78)
One who is possessed of passion perceives all worlds as being like hell;
but one joined with me, liberated from everything, rejoices happily in the Imperishable.
He delights in my form in many ways and is always with me;
filled with my bliss, he is liberated and does not exist as anything inferior to me.
Having thus instructed them, Hari then bestowed the mantras upon the subjects, the king's family, and the king himself.
Then King Kṛṣṇa again set his mind on departing;
he gave him various kinds of wealth, dowry, and farewell gifts. (82)
Through the sounds of musical instruments, he offered manifold honors by way of the subjects;
at that moment, the king named Parāṅvraja arrived there. (83)
Then Ālaṃtraṣi, accompanied by Āśanāpurīśvara and Pārāvātarāṣṭrapati, prayed to the Supreme Lord.
"O Abode of Compassion, come to my country and purify us!
Having heard this, Hari said, "So be it," and became ready along with his family. ||85||
Having quickly accepted the worship, he then ascended his celestial chariot;
so too did the daughters beginning with Brahmapriyā and all the sages at that time.
They were situated in celestial chariots, and their chariot expanded;
then, O King, Pārāvātarāṣṭra arrived with great speed.
For he had previously descended from the sky with his face turned away;
however, he offered a welcome to Śrī Hari along with his own army. 88.
Then musical instruments were played and shouts of victory arose;
the subjects, standing firm with their hands joined in reverence, offered a hearty welcome.
Following the path shown by the king, the celestial chariot descended into a beautiful garden near the city of Āśāsanā.
Upon seeing Hari, the subjects, the king, the queen, as well as the leading officials and all others who had arrived, offered a welcome and prostrated themselves. ||9 1 ||
The king worshipped him with flowers and other offerings, with golden necklaces and fine pearls;
the queen performed the lustration ceremony (nīrājana), and then she seated Hari upon his throne.
On an elephant accompanied by the golden Ambālikā, and on other chariots and vehicles,
he caused Mādhava to be paraded through the city at his command.
All the people worshipped me in the evening with jewels, garments, and other articles, as well as with gold coins, flowers, unbroken grains, garlands, and so forth. ||94||
Having led Keśava around the royal palace, the king brought him back inside;
he honored him and again fed him.
Then, by the command of the king’s mother, the two maidens worshipped the Supreme Lord Hari and chose him as their husband with an excellent garland.
Then, having placed the garland around his neck, the two maidens were themselves offered to Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of All, the Supreme Lord. (97)
The king rejoiced in his heart and the queen attained great joy; when the two daughters were born, the king held a grand festival. 98.
Indeed, Hari caused it to be performed at night; O Rādhikā, he taught in the royal palace the means of liberation for all. 99.

Thus ends the two hundred and twenty-third chapter, titled "The Description of Lord Hari’s wandering through the city of Rāyagrāma, His teaching, worship, and taking leave; then His journey to the kingdom of King Parāvāta, His welcome in the city of Āśāsanā, and His evening stroll on the fourth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Āśvina," in the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, within the second section, the *Tretā-santāna*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O Rādhikā, the Blessed Lord has told all the subjects, beginning with the king,
that tomorrow there will be a great and most excellent sacrifice in the auspicious kingdom of Brāhmīlā.
That place where a sacrifice takes place shall indeed be a bestower of merit;
for the sacrifice is Nārāyaṇa himself, and he is I, the Supreme Person. || 2 ||
I am indeed constantly pleased and attain satisfaction through sacrifice;
for all ritual actions offered unto Me are, without doubt, sacrifice itself. (2)
Indeed, no purpose whatsoever can be accomplished by a lack of means;
through this sacrificial rite, I shall achieve success in this sacrifice—of this there is no doubt.
Just as deer are captured by deer, birds by birds,
and elephants by elephants, so too is a sacrifice seized by means of a sacrifice.
Just as the moon is indeed not seen on the new-moon day because it lacks a visible form,
so too am I not seen at all when the heart is defiled.
Just as the moon shines forth upon reaching the full lunar day,
so do I, the Supreme Lord, shine resplendently upon attaining a mind filled with devotion.
Even when seized by Rāhu, the moon becomes clearly radiant;
likewise, even when seized by Māyā, the individual soul (jīvātman) becomes clearly manifest.
One who lacks understanding and has not cultivated wisdom is drawn outward;
dwelling upon sense objects, he is never satisfied. (9)
For one who is not content, there is no peace; for one who is not at peace, there is no happiness;
for one who lacks happiness, there is no liberation, but rather a descent into hell.
Sense objects are the first hell, the sense organs are the second, the mind is the third hell, and mental impressions (vāsanā) are the fourth. || 11 ||
The fifth is karma, and the sixth is hell, which consists of evil qualities;
the seventh is suffering in the home, and the eighth is poverty.
The ninth is the hell of disease, and the tenth is subjection to others.
The eleventh is ill-repute, and the twelfth is deficiency of intellect. || 1.3 ||
The thirteenth is being a householder and so forth; the fourteenth is servitude;
the fifteenth is physical deformity; and the sixteenth is even enmity with an enemy.
The seventeenth is indeed the manifest body known as hell;
these eighteen transformations born of the body are the hells.
Thus, these hells are attached here in the world to embodied beings;
yet, by means of sacrifice reaching the sacrifice, one becomes one who has gone beyond all hell.
As long as impurity remains, thirst is not cut off; that thirst does not cease until the end of impurity has been reached. (17)
Through association with sense objects, thirst always increases;
through detachment from sense objects, thirst diminishes and grows by means of knowledge. 18.
Through the mirror of knowledge, the observer beholds his own pure self;
by the restraint of the senses, a human being becomes happy. 19.
One should restrain the self from the senses and their objects by means of the self; one should abandon the worldly realms and, established in Me, partakes of the immortal.
Having experienced the sublime path through his actions, or having renounced it for my sake,
he shall attain heaven, eternal heaven, or my supreme abode.
When the self, freed from qualities that are to be abandoned, abides within me,
then it attains my own refuge, the abode of the world of Brahman.
When the supreme Brahman shines forth within the Self in the form of Brahman, all forms— including the functions of the mind and the intellect— become dissolved.
When an object of the senses has arrived, one should contemplate it as suffering, for it does not turn back;
the medicine for this is the non-contemplation of such things. //24//
Life, wealth, association with loved ones, home, and so forth are impermanent and devoured by time; having reflected on this, the knower of the Self should not covet them.
In that case, suffering would have been abandoned, as would the pleasure arising from sense objects;
for even that [pleasure] is mixed with suffering and is thus abounding in suffering. ||26||
Having deliberated upon both, one should indeed abandon them, for he approaches me when there is devotion within oneself toward the state of Brahman, which transcends all illusion.
Then Brahman is discerned and attained through meditative absorption;
having reached the touchstone of the state of Brahman, one attains dhyāna. ||28||
When I am meditated upon by this meditator, I indeed ascend into that interval;
I manifest within his own self when all his gates are restrained.
The dissolution of his qualities occurs without effort;
he becomes devoid of qualities yet possessed of divine qualities, taking on my own form.
All embodied beings endowed with qualities proceed from Prakṛti; all those who are fit for heaven possess qualities, but those who are worthy of me are devoid of qualities.
As long as this possession by a spirit, which causes extreme suffering, persists for him,
so long does his mind remain fixed upon the objects of this miserable saṃsāra.
When his separation from the elements occurs thoroughly,
and even from subtle causes, then he attains Brahman.
Through dharma, devotion, and detachment, one is elevated to the highest good by means of the self;
enriched by that supreme good, one attains Hari, the treasure-house of all supreme blessings.
Just as the earth, whose essence is equanimity, follows the various essences of the seeds sown within it,
so too the Self, whose essence is equanimity, dwells within bodies born of diverse karmas.
Just as gold mixed with base metal becomes purified by fire, so too the embodied soul is purified by my devotion and wisdom. ||36||
The ancient wisdom bestowed by me shines forth for one who has been purified;
having taken hold of the path of wisdom, the devotee takes refuge in me. (37)
The fruit of wisdom and devotion is my divine vision;
those who lack wisdom and are devoid of devotion do not see me at all.
Those characterized by goodness (sāttvika) are superior to those engaged in ritual action; even more so are those born of pure goodness (śuddhasattva).
Superior to them is Time, my own power, the all-devouring and mighty one.
But beyond time is my abode, the divine, imperishable dwelling; of that abode, neither beginning, nor middle, nor end is found.
That supreme state of Brahman, that highest abode, that ultimate station, wherein there exists no suffering born of birth, death, and old age. ||41||
Placing their feet upon the head of Kāla, my devotees go to that state, which is the auspicious dharma characterized by cessation and consisting of self-surrender to me. 42.
Relying upon that, they indeed proceed to the infinite, supreme, imperishable Brahman;
yet that Brahman is not to be attained through effort alone, and is thus considered equal to the Śabdabrahman (the Brahman of Sound). 43.
For that Brahman is to be accomplished through compassion, leading to the supreme Brahman;
[it is not attained] due to sin, the lack of means, attachment, and the bondage of karma. (44)
Mortals do not perceive their own stainless, innate nature, because they rest in sense objects and harbor the conceit of "I" and "mine. (45)
The Self does not readily attain Brahman due to the forceful flow of craving;
rather, it is attained through serving the virtuous, through meditation, and through the cultivation of devotion to my form.
Through the practice of Brahman, through supreme dispassion, and through affection, Brahman is revealed;
those who are struck by the thirst for sweetness perceive only the desired qualities. 47.
Yet they do not desire even the supreme, immortal, and infallible state; endowed with inferior qualities, they do not perceive those who have reached the further shore. 48.
Failing to reach the further shore, many are repeatedly tossed about here amidst heaps of eggs;
yet in the past, many have reached the further shore through the yoga of the virtuous.
The peaceful ones always move ahead of those who tread the path to the highest good;
if they indeed take refuge [in them], they will quickly reach the further shore.
If they take refuge through blessings, the power of merit, the fruit of service, or virtuous deeds,
then they quickly attain the auspicious body of Brahmā.
Those who meditate, those who serve, those who are devoted with affection, and those who abide in Brahman—
they attain that eternal, immortal goal which exists.
Having thus instructed him, Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Lord, ceased speaking;
having partaken of water and other refreshments, the Blessed Lord, the Master, went to sleep. (53)
Then, in the early morning, the glorious Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, attended by maidens,
was awakened with auspicious instrumental music and songs.
Having performed his daily rites and completed his worship, he desired to depart quickly;
the king granted him leave and likewise bestowed upon him a dowry.
Accompanied by his own purpose, Śrī Hari became ready at the moment known as Brāhma; he then ascended the celestial chariot.
Then musical instruments were sounded and the subjects offered their respects;
Śrī Hari was honored, and he gave wealth and ornaments to the sage.
Hearing his own fame echoing in the sky,
he caused his celestial chariot to move swiftly toward the sacrificial ground on the morning of the fifth day of the dark fortnight of Āśvina.
In the auspicious land of Brāhmīla, near the city of Goyāja, he quickly arrived on the bank of the river Āmrajānika. (59)
Then that celestial chariot (vimāna) indeed appeared, possessing the brilliance of a thousand suns;
the sages, the king, and the subjects waited expectantly for it.
Seeing the celestial chariot arrive, they ran to the place of welcome on the vast ground along the riverbank, which was frequented by countless people.
The people became steady and composed, and the celestial chariot descended;
indeed, the shouts of victory from the subjects then spread throughout the sky.
The sound of "tūpa" and the sounds of the *yantrīs* were most pleasing;
the echoes born of those sounds resounded on all sides. (63)
The songs of women, filled with joy, were heard,
and at that time there also arose various sounds of musical instruments.
As Hari approached, there arose the sounds of conchs on all sides, the blaring of trumpets, and the auspicious chants of the Brahmins.
The celestial chariot was enlarged and honored by the kṣatriyas,
and handfuls of flowers were offered to it by the gods and the hosts of deities.
It was sprinkled with sandalwood, marked with tilaka, and adorned with saffron;
it was saluted, worshipped, and honored with meditative contemplations.
Then Śrī Hari indeed stepped outside from the celestial chariot for just a moment;
at that time, the great sages likewise placed necklaces upon Hari’s neck.
Lomaśa applied the *tilaka*, Śambhu gave him a garland of flowers,
and King Īśānapānaśiṣṭa gave him a golden garland.
The sage Śāntārāma placed a garland of *vṛndā* flowers around Kṛṣṇa’s neck;
then the king honored the feet of his parents.
The king’s wives performed worship for those dear to Brahmā,
and likewise the princesses performed worship for all the women.
The great sage Lālāyana, Tuṣita the best of gods, and the Lord Svīyaprakāśa—these spoke of the Supreme Lord. ||72||

O Lord, quickly inspect the pavilion for the sacrifice, the sacrificial pit, the fuel, the *kuśa* grass, and other offerings, as well as the dwellings for the people and the various kinds of food and edibles. (73)
In accordance with your command, everything is provided;
there is nothing lacking. Purify all things everywhere with your glance.
Thus entreated, the Blessed Lord, traveling in his celestial chariot, went swiftly to the human dwellings located twenty yojanas from the earth to observe them well.
Through the invitation and the sacrificial leaf that signaled the auspiciousness of the rite,
he beheld the imperishable Brahman within the great liberated souls who had assembled there.
