He beheld the liberated wives of Brahmā who had come to the sacrifice,
as well as all the sovereign powers and all the virtues embodied in beautiful forms.
The Blessed One beheld all his ornaments, all his weapons in their embodied forms, and even his own incarnation as Kṛṣṇa.
He saw Nārāyaṇa accompanied by Rādhā and her companions, together with cowherds, cowherdesses, and cows, and playfully joined by Ramā, Śrī, and Kamalā.
The Lord beheld him accompanied by Bhū, Lakṣmī, Tūlasi, Vṛndā, Padmā, and others, together with male and female attendants.
He likewise beheld the manifestations beginning with Vāsudeva, those beginning with Pradhāna and Puruṣa, the conventions beginning with Mahākāla, and the Infinite One.
And he beheld Mahāviṣṇu, Vairāja, and the triad of deities beginning with Brahmā, together with their Śaktis, as well as Māyā joined with the Tattvas. ||82||
And all the Siddhas and Yogins, the great seers, the ancestors and deities, the gods and lords of the gods, the guardians of the worlds and the guardians of the directions; ||83||
The Lord beheld those who are of the nature of sattva, rajas, and tamas;
likewise the Rudras, Vasus, Ādityas, the two Aśvins, and the Maruts. (84)
He beheld the Vidyādharas, the divine Gandharvas, those dwelling in the quarters and the intermediate spaces, the oceans, the rivers, the trees, the creepers, and the grasses.
The sacred fords, the wish-fulfilling cow and others, the vowels, the Vedas, the qualities and so forth, the mines, the mountains, the Manus, the kings, women, men, and all creatures. ||86||

They likewise beheld the planets, the lunar mansions, and the stars; as well as those that are stationary, those born from eggs, those born from a womb, those born from sweat, and those born from sprouts.
The hosts of yakṣas, rākṣasas, bhūtas, and so forth, as well as the lords of the hosts, all the sacrificial deities, the mātṛkās, and the goddesses; ||88||
[He saw] the Yoginīs and even the Apsarases from the lake of Brahmā in every way, as well as the Ṛṣis’ daughters, the Vidyādharīs, the Śaktis, and the Sāṃkhya-yoginīs. ||89||
He likewise [conquered] all kinds of fires, the offspring of Kaśyapa,
those dwelling in the netherworld (talaloka), as well as the yakṣas, rākṣasas, and dānavas.
He [saw] the Daityas, those who had fasted and renounced food, ascetics, as well as officiating priests, the human participants of the sacrifice, singers, and the sacrificers. ||9-1||
He beheld the Hotṛ priests and the reciters, as well as the great sacrificers;
likewise, he saw streams of clarified butter, channels of curd, and cascades of buttermilk.
He beheld lakes of nectar-like milk, as well as rivers; he saw heaps of desirable foods such as rice and mountains of gathered fruits. (93)
He saw coconuts and other fruits, both dry and fresh;
he saw the laboratories for processing juices and the quarters for the wives.
He beheld the sacrificial post hall, the hall for oblations, and the hall for the gods;
and having observed that everything was indeed complete and ready, he stood there.
He praised Lomaśa, Viśvakarmā, Lālāyana, Śaṅkara, Svīyaprakāśa, and other great sages. ||96||
He beheld the assembled rulers of the earth who had come for the sacrificial rites—
those from the regions of the immortals and likewise those from the lands of Rāśīyāna.
[He conquered] the kings of the Ketumāla regions, as well as those of the eastern lands of Uṣṇabhū, of Prāgjyotiṣa, and of the region of Ajanābha. 98.
The Lord beheld the kings of the islands, sub-islands, and worlds, whose origins were from regions both white and red within the interior lands. 99.
He especially observed those kings of the regions of Dakṣa and Amarī who were engaged in performing sacrifices, yet had failed to obtain the fruits of their gains.
The king Kālīmaṇḍalīna, the lord of Vanajaleśa, the king Pārāvārapiba, and likewise the king Koṭīśvara. || 101 ||
And he saw King Śrī Satīśa, the king fierce in the Tretā age, as well as King Parāṅvrata and King Rājārāyapati.
And Rāyasomanarāja, as well as Aṇḍajarabhūpati, Bālyarajonṛpa, Corugavākṣa, and likewise Bhūbhata. || 103 ||
And he saw Īśāna, who remained after the departure [of the others], together with his wife;
he saw all of them, including their wives and others, born in the region of Dakṣāmarī.
Mahākṛṣṇa said to the kings, "May you be the sacrificers. They accepted the auspicious word of the Supreme Lord, saying, "Om."
Having thus honored those of great dignity who had come for the sacrifice,
and having caused whatever was deficient to be supplied, he quickly departed for his own abode.
Meanwhile, musical instruments were played for a moment to determine the auspicious time for the sacrifice;
and having prepared themselves, the people quickly assembled in the pavilion.

Likewise, the liberated ones, the incarnations and others, the lords, the most excellent of the perfected (siddhas), the seers, the ancestors, the gods, the lords of gods, and those who have mastery over the gods.
The goddesses and those under the power of the goddesses, humans, Daityas, and Dānavas, all the offspring of Kaśyapa, as well as all things stationary and moving. || 109 ||
The purpose of the sacrifice, the performers of the sacrifice, the ritualists, the means of accomplishment,
the mantras, the offerings to the gods and ancestors— all these were present at the sacrifice.
O Rādhikā, while auspicious and excellent rites were being performed for Kṣāmā,
Śrī Hari arrived at the pavilion, honored by all those present.

Thus ends the two hundred and twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Instruction, Worship, Feeding, Nightly Rest, and Departure from the Subjects and Kingdoms of Pārāvāta, as well as the Journey toward the Sacrificial Ground in the Kingdom of Brāhmīla on the Fifth Day of the Dark Half of Āśvina and the Reception of the Great Honors," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O Rādhikā, at the auspicious and most excellent moment at dawn,
the sages and the deities arrived at the sacrificial pavilion.
Chanting the name of Śrī Hari, reciting the sections of the Vedas,
and muttering the Veda-born mantra, they joyfully entered the pavilion.
The gods, the Lord of Gods himself, Brahmā and the other lords of lords, the sovereigns, the primary ones, their consorts, the goddesses, and the attendants and so forth—[all these were present]. (3)
Indeed, in that pavilion at the sacrifice, they arrived in person, filled with joy; and all the sacrificial requisites and oblations appeared there auspiciously, as if possessing physical forms.
The seats, the ritual implements, and the sacrificial fuel arrived;
the banner appeared in person, the water-pot appeared in person, and likewise the pavilion appeared in person. || 5 ||
Makha himself was present, the sacrificial altars were manifest, and the sovereign sacrificial post was visibly there;
the sacrificial pit was manifest, and Vāstupuruṣa himself had indeed arrived.
The Vedas themselves, the injunctions themselves, and the mantras themselves arrived;
the ritual applications themselves, as well as the kuśa and darbha grasses, arrived. || 7 ||
Then the sacrificial vessels, the cooked offerings, and the fires appeared in person;
all the necessary implements likewise arrived at the pavilion.
Auspiciousness, the proper time, the place, and the day of merit arrived;
likewise, the terrestrial sacred fords and the five nectars arrived.

In his sacrifice, all the wish-fulfilling cows (kāmadhenus) were present; the desire-granting creepers (kalpalatas), the wish-granting trees (kalpavṛkṣas), and the thought-fulfilling gems (cintāmaṇis) arrived.
All inexhaustible vessels, caskets that fulfill all desires, and imperishable treasuries of nectar arrived there. || 11 ||
The flavors, varieties of fruits, leaves, flowers, unbroken grains, and so forth—
all these arrived there at the sacrifice in personified forms, O Rādhikā.
According to their respective applications, all forms of prosperity, all branches of knowledge, and all true accomplishments are indeed applied. 1.3.
Likewise, the wondrous perfected ones (siddhas) arrived at that sacrifice;
there were all kinds of honey-mixtures (madhuparka) and mountains of cooked food.
All the solid substances for the sacrificial offerings arrived manifest and fragrant; likewise, gold and silver coins, as well as products of the cow, appeared in person. (15)
Thus, while all those who were present in the pavilion were indeed directly before them,
auspicious rites for the Brāhmaṇas and songs by the women took place.
There, the brahmins recited all-auspicious benedictions; the sage Lomaśa performed the formal declaration of the place, time, and other details of the rite.
In the pavilion, the sacrificer, remaining under the protection of Īśāna,
and the king in the form of the couple, were the primary figures there for the auspicious rite.
Urged by the sage, he likewise established another circle of kings;
in the pavilion near the sacrificial pit, he performed the ritual according to the secondary procedure.
Lomaśa performed the primary rite of formal resolve (saṃkalpa) and conducted the protection of the quarters as well as the worship of the water-pot (kalaśa).
He also had the installation and worship of Gaṇeśa performed;
he likewise conducted the recitation of auspicious blessings and the declaration of the meritorious day.
Lomaśa performed the consecration of the sacrificer and others, and he also oversaw the installation and worship of the Mātṛkās. ||22||
He likewise performed the *nāndī-śrāddha*, the formal selection (*varaṇa*) of the preceptor and others, as well as the offering of the *arghya* water, prostrations, and the *madhuparka*.
He also caused the installation of the *vardhanī* jar, as well as the entry into the pavilion and the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) of the pavilion and so forth. (24)
The consecration of the site, the worship of Vāsudeva, and the adoration of the pavilion there within the Sarvatobhadra mandala; 25.
Lomaśa indeed caused the installation and worship of the deities,
as well as the installation of the deity in the yantra and the worship of the gods.

The worship of the pedestal, the worship of the altar, the worship of the sacrificial pit, as well as the honoring of the deity of the pit and likewise the installation of the fire within the pit. ||27||
He caused the installation and worship of the planets, the installation and worship of the Yoginīs, and likewise the installation and worship of the Kṣetrapālas. ||28||
In the sacrificial pit, there is the worship of the girdle and other components, as well as the worship of the deity, the worship of the fire, and likewise the worship of the planets. (29)
Lomaśa caused the sage Ṛṣi to perform the formal resolve (saṃkalpa) for the preparatory rite (anvādhāna);
then Lomaśa performed the Āghāra and Ājyabhāga oblations.
He performed the oblation for the deities of the Vāstu-maṇḍala, as well as the oblation for the Yoginīs;
there he also performed the principal oblation and the Vyāhṛti-homa.
The sage Lomaśa indeed offered the animal sacrifice and the excellent oblation;
then followed the installation of the sacrificial post and the ritual consecration with water.

He also caused the worship of the Water-Mothers and the Water, the worship of the conch, the bell, and other implements, as well as the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) and the consecration of the vital breaths (prāṇapratiṣṭhā).
He performed the worship of a golden image of Bālakṛṣṇa,
offering the sixteen-fold service (ṣoḍaśopacāra) and presenting the sacrificial cooked rice (caru) as an oblation.
He also performed all the fire-offerings consisting of a thousand oblations, saying:
"I offer this food to those who are liberated. (35)
I offer this food as an oblation to Brahmā;
I offer this food as an oblation to the liberated souls (muktātmans). ||36||
I offer this food with salutations to the incarnations; I give this food with salutations to the female incarnations. (37)
This food is offered as salutation to the qualities, sovereign powers, and manifestations; this food is offered as salutation to the ornaments, weapons, and special powers. || 38 ||
I offer this food to the male lords and the female goddesses;
I offer this food to the divine manifestations and the attendants and their followers. (39)
To the Brāhmīs and to the Satīs, this food I offer;
to all those who are beloved by Brahmā, this food I offer. ||2.225.40||
This food is offered as *namama* to the Śaktis such as Rādhā and Lakṣmī; this food is offered as *namama* to the virtuous women such as Māṇikī. ||41||
This food is offered as an oblation to Gaṅgā, Sarasvatī, and Śrī;
this food is offered as an oblation to [the goddesses] together with their male and female servants. ||42||
Salutation to Mahāviṣṇu, Hiraṇyagarbha, and Virāj;
and salutation to Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa—this food is offered to them. 43.
Salutations to Sāvitrī, Kamalā, Durgā, and the others; this food is offered as an oblation. To Kaṃbharā, the Great Lakṣmī, this food is offered as an oblation. ||44||
To Santuṣṭā and Amṛtā, this food is offered;
to Padmāvatī and Ramā, this food is offered. ||45||
Salutations to Mañjulā, Sadguṇā, Hāsā, Ambā, and Bhojanā; likewise, salutations to Bālakṛṣṇā, Aṅganā, Duḥkhahā, Lakṣmī, and the others. 46.
This food is for all the wives; this is for the perfected sages—namas!
This food is for the ancestors and for those who belong to the ancestors—namas! 47.
This food is for the Ṛṣis; salutations, this food is for the gods, and this food is for the divine goddesses and the deities. (48)
To the guardians of the quarters, to the protectors of the world, this food is offered;
and to the Ādityas and the Rudras, this and that food is offered. (49)
To the Vasus and to the Aśvins, this and this food;
and also to the Directions and to the Principles, this and this food. ||2.225.50||
From the treasures and from the houses, this and that food;
from the supernatural powers and from the great seers, this and that food. ||5 1 ||
To the Kṛttikās and to the Manus, this and this food;
to the Maruts and to the Kalās, this and this food. ||52||
And this food is for the Tīrthas and the Vālakhilyas;
and this food is indeed for the Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, Bhūtas, and Pretas. (53)
To the Kūṣmāṇḍas and the Piśācas, this and this food; to the Vināyakas and the Gaṇas, this and this food. ||54||
This food is for the vetālas, the cāraṇas, and the sūtas;
this food is for the māgadhas, the bandins, and the servants.
Food for the ḍākinīs, the śākinīs, and the tāmasīs;
food for the vidyādharas, the gandharvas, and the kinnaras. ||56||
"Let this food be for the Viśvedevas, the male spirits;
and let this food be for the Daityas, the Dānavas, and the Nāgas. (57)
Food for serpents, hooded snakes, and reptiles;
food for trees, creepers, and grasses and the like. ||58||
This food [is offered] from sacred fords, from mountains, and from oceans;
this food is likewise from rivers, from lakes, and from shrines.
And from the wish-fulfilling creepers and trees, as well as from the cows of plenty,
from the thought-gems, and also from the inexhaustible vessels.

This food is for the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) and for the deities residing in the sacrificial pits; this food is indeed for the pavilions (maṇḍapas) and for the deities situated within the pavilions.
To the deities of the doors, to the deities of the door-posts, and also to the deities of the lintels;
to the deities of the banners and also to the deities of the sacrificial posts. (62)
To the implements such as the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, this food is offered with salutation;
to the pillars and the deities of the pillars, this food is offered with salutation. ||63||
"Also, this [is for] the Mothers, the virtuous, and the chaste;
and this food is for the female practitioners of Sāṃkhya and Yoga—salutations again and again! (64)
This food is an offering to the goddesses devoted to their husbands;
and this food is an offering to Kāmadeva and the seven ṛṣis. ||65||
Food for Īśāna, Varuṇa, and Mahendra;
and food for Agni, Kuvera, and Nairṛta. ||66||
This food is for Vāyu and for Yama; this food is indeed for the messengers.
This food is for the aquatic creatures dwelling in the wind; obeisance to them. (67)
This food is offered as an oblation to those dwelling on the earth and those residing in the snow mountains;
this food is offered as an oblation to those born from a womb and those born from an egg.
This food is offered as an oblation to those born from sweat and those born from sprouts;
this food is offered as an oblation to the minute beings, such as insects and moths.
To the sentient and the insentient, to those who offer oblations, I bow with this food;
to the clouds and the thundering ones, I bow with this food.
To all the gods, asuras, and others, this food is offered;
and to those created and sustained by Brahmā, this food is offered. (71)
To those created and sustained by Īśa, this food is offered as *namaḥ*; to those created and sustained by Jīva, this food is offered as *namaḥ*. ||72||
To those born from the eighty-four sources, this food is offered;
and to those remembered and those unremembered, this food is likewise offered. (73)
To the distinguished and the learned, to all of them collectively and individually, I offer this food. ||74||
And to as many Pratyekabuddhas as there may be, this food is offered;
to the active Brahmins, this food is offered. (75)
This is my offering to the Fire, the soul of all beings; Svāhā!
And this oblation, with its thousand streams, is for the Fire; Svāhā! (76)
In this manner, indeed, oblations, clarified butter, fuel-sticks, fruits,
sweet foods, juices, and even liquids were offered to the Fire-god.
Then the sage Lomaśa performed a sacrifice with many oblations;
thereafter, the sage caused a sacrifice of great oblations of clarified butter to be performed.
Then the gods and others, though already satiated, repeatedly accepted the excellent oblation offered together with the fire. (79)
Then the venerable sage Lomaśa performed the lustration ceremony (nīrājana),
and the sounds of musical instruments resounded on all sides at that time.
The sounds of the Vedas arose along with the songs of women;
then the king offered handfuls of flowers to the gods as well. ||81||
The Brahmins performed the purifying consecration for the sacrificer;
they bestowed blessings, and the king gave the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā). ||82||
Then the Brahmins, filled with an abundance of joy, sang words of blessing;
having bowed to the fire and offered salutations to the gods, they requested forgiveness.
Having performed the rite, Lomaśa indeed caused the dismissal;
at that time, the sky became filled with lotus-like celestial chariots.
On the fifth day of the month of Rādhika, following the conclusion of the sacrificial rites, Hari gathered together with all those who dwell throughout the three worlds.
Having fed the honored guests, the great sages, the twice-born, and all the visitors dwelling in various abodes, such as Dhāmadhāma and others; ||86||
Having fed those who were worthy according to their merit, he then took his own meal;
the Blessed One himself ate together with the kings who were the patrons of the sacrifice.
Thus, O Rādhikā, the sacrifice was commenced on the bank of the river, and the satiation of the ancestors through the offering of funeral cakes and other rites took place. (88)
Then the Blessed One performed his evening bath together with all human beings and embodied gods, after having fully worshipped Varuṇa.
Having worshipped the water, the Blessed One bathed together with everyone;
then he returned to his own abode and indeed bestowed gifts at that time.
He gave sandals to the liberated souls, crowns to all the incarnations, and golden garments to the liberated women and their female incarnations. ||91||
The Lord gave crowns to the Īśas and gave necklaces to them;
he likewise gave chains and girdles to the Īśānīs.
To the sages he gave golden jars, to the female sages golden bracelets;
to the Siddhas he gave golden garlands, and to the female Siddhas golden bodices.
For the ancestors, he gave vessels of nectar; for the female ancestors, inexhaustible jars;
for the gods, golden umbrellas; and for the goddesses, neck-garlands.
The Lord also gave bracelets to the lords of the gods and staffs to the spirits, ghosts, and piśācas; he bestowed tunics upon them.
He gave gold coins to the humans and jewels to the Daityas;
at that time, he also gave golden necklaces to the Sūtas, Māgadhas, and Bandīs.
There, the Blessed Lord gave goods and garments to the helpless, the young, and the old— whatever was required by each of them.
Whatever was required by those who were insentient and those who were sentient, the Supreme Self, the treasury of compassion, resolved and bestowed it all. (98)
He caused all the great gifts and those that are intermediate gifts—such as the giving of fields, daughters, and so forth—to be bestowed even upon his teachers. (99)
And the kings gave all their wealth, food, and houses;
they offered many gifts of maidens, as well as gifts of cows, horses, and elephants.
In this manner, the Lord bestowed gifts until the end of the night;
then, O Rādhikā, the *ārārtrika* ceremony for Bālakṛṣṇa took place.
Afterwards, meals were prepared by the kings;
then, during the night, the Blessed One imparted instruction to the people.

Thus ends the two hundred and twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Arrival of the Great Beings to the Sacrificial Ground with Hari on the Morning of the Fifth Day of the Dark Half of Āśvina in the Tretā Cycle of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā, and the Presence of All in the Pavilion, the Performance of Rites Beginning with the Recitation of Auspicious Verses up to the Offering of Many Oblations of Ghee in the Homa, and Their Subsequent Withdrawal."
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Rādhikā, to the instruction that Śrīmat Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa Hari gave, which brings about the welfare of one's own self. || 1 ||
I shall declare that to you: the Lord bestowed it upon his progeny by means of the imperishable Brahman, which was indeed applied by the Supreme Brahman.
The Puruṣa, situated in the Abode, is impelled toward the performance of creation;
he was joined with his own power, Māyā, and by that [power], the illusory beings were produced.
Those who are non-dualists absorbed in Māyā, being impelled by their own karmas, become either lords (Īśvaras) or embodied individual souls (jīvas). || 4 ||
Considering this aggregate— consisting of the body, the senses, the internal organ, the subtle elements, and the gross elements— to be one's own, one becomes bound therein by karmas.
Living beings repeatedly grasp at entities composed of aggregates;
they undergo separation once more and revolve like a wheel.
They encounter states that are peaceful, terrible, or delusive everywhere;
indeed, the states consisting of hair, blood, and flesh are born from the mother.
The elements of marrow, bone, and sinew are derived from the father;
they are always filled with pleasure, pain, and delusion, and characterized by cold, heat, and burning.
Even after encountering those various states of being, he who is not conditioned by them— reflecting "I am that, I am that"— shall become free from the bondage of objective phenomena.
Pervading this beautiful city with its nine gates, which is endowed with various states of being, the conscious self lies within; he is called Puruṣa.
I am superior to those infinite beings designated as "persons," for I am the inner self within the Virāj, just as I am in the world of Brahmā.
I alone am the Supreme Person, the teacher of all;
for I indeed dwell within all sentient beings.
Likewise, even though I am entirely insentient in this body, I am the knower of reality;
having realized Me, My devotee becomes bodiless (liberated) before long.
He is undecaying and immortal, subtle, and endowed with my virility;
one who offers everything to my form and to my devotee is liberated. 1.4
Fire always resides within wood, yet it is separated when the wood is destroyed;
likewise, the self departs to the supreme reality upon the destruction of the body.
Even sinners, by taking refuge in me, the supreme Supreme Self,
surely become meritorious, just as charcoal becomes [glowing] through contact with fire.
Through association with me, through the excellence of my sovereignty,
and by attaining a portion of my qualities, my devotee shall attain equality with me.
Just as one indeed leaves behind the objects seen in a dream upon waking,
so too does one leave behind illusion and the like, and merge into the Seer of all.
Just as water, having left the earth, flows through the mouth of a river into the great ocean, even so the Self, having abandoned this body, enters me, the Supreme Person. 1.9
Just as laborers return when their work is finished,
so too do embodied souls return once they have experienced their enjoyments.
Just as an arrow devoid of momentum falls motionless to the ground,
so this individual soul, when its momentum of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) has ceased, goes to my imperishable state.
Just as one becomes free from hope when desisting from action,
so too he who has turned away from the world, having abandoned all desires, indeed approaches me.
Since it is devoid of all states of being, one goes from there to my abode;
through practice of me, being attached to me, one does not return to primordial nature again.
Just as seeds scorched by fire do not sprout in any way whatsoever,
so too all the seeds of this [person] truly do not sprout again.
One who is attached to the taste of the nectar does not cling to other tastes;
one who is intent on my taste does not cling to the taste of the gunas. (25)
Indeed, those who know me are truly rare to find in this world;
everywhere, living beings who nourish their bodies, senses, and objects are easily found. ||26||
Just as currents of water flow swiftly toward low ground,
so too do people for the most part move with great speed toward the lowlands of the village.
Those who know Brahman, being of the nature of fire, go upwards; likewise, my devotees, through association with the virtuous, go upwards to my imperishable state.
Having reflected thus, one should constantly worship the Supreme Lord;
through the company of the virtuous, my devotion—which bestows the divine abode—should be practiced. (29)
For those who offer everything unto me, Kṛṣṇa, Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Lord,
Māyā shall indeed not be an obstacle.
That affection which is for children, wealth, and the like; that affection which is for women and so forth;
and that affection which is for one's own body and the rest—one should quickly transfer that affection to Me. (3.1)
That thirst for sensual pleasure, that thirst for the means of enjoyment,
and that thirst for honor and fame— let that [thirst] be directed toward me, Mādhava.

Whatever impulse there is for the attainment of one's own goals, whatever impulse there is in the conquest of enemies and the like, and whatever impulse resides in egoism— that should be directed toward me, Keśava.

The satisfaction that arises from obtaining what is desired, the satisfaction that comes with the departure of enjoyments, and the satisfaction found in great contentment—all of these should be directed toward me in every way. (34)

Whatever happiness exists in a state of sattva, whatever happiness exists in freedom from the pairs of opposites, and whatever happiness arises through discernment—that must be performed by me in every way. (35)

Whatever nourishment comes from prosperity, whatever nourishment comes from the accumulation of strength, and whatever nourishment comes from the subjects of the scriptures—that nourishment should always be bestowed upon me. (36)
That state which I always take as my refuge, that state which I have in my companions, and that state which is within my own heart—that must be accomplished by me in every way. (37)
That identity which exists in the body and so forth, that identity which exists in weight, and that identity which exists in one's own happiness—that effect resides in me, the true Lord. (38)
That hope which you have for your own son, that hope for future happiness, and that hope centered on gain—let all of that always be directed toward me. (39)

The sense of "mine" regarding what has been acquired, the sense of identity, and the sense of "mine" regarding what is desired—these should be directed toward me for the sake of liberation. (2.226.40)

Whatever effort is made for the sake of sense objects, whatever exertion is made for the sake of wealth, and whatever effort is made for the sake of life—that should be directed toward me, Mādhava. (41)
One who possesses a body takes up all forms of possession out of delusion;
by that indeed bondage arises, and he goes to hell.
Therefore, one who desires the state of Brahman should not practice what is impure;
a person of sound intellect should not desire the fruit of actions that take the form of obstacles. 43.
And whoever, out of greed, delusion, pride, or envy, performs actions that deviate from the path to liberation, perishes along with his followers.
Therefore, a discerning person should never become possessed by passion;
nor should one ever become childish, deluded, or dull-witted. (451)
Just as a house made of clay is plastered with clay, so too this body, which consists of food, must be nourished with food. (46)
This physical body indeed thrives through nourishment provided by earthly beings;
yet, one should not become attached to this body merely because of such ownership. (47)
Sweet, bitter, ghee, oil, unctuous grains, fruits, and the like, as well as soft preparations and soft earth—these indeed are necessary for the body. (48)
One should employ exactly that many [medicines], free from binding and other such defects;
having thus brought one's journey to completion, one indeed goes to the further shore of existence.
Just as a yogi who has gone to the forest takes food from a town at some point, yet is not bound by passion even for that, so it is here. (2.226.50)
Dwelling in the forest of saṃsāra like a weary traveler, one should take food for the sake of the journey so that it does not lead to bondage. (5.1)
Having examined even the objects of the senses with the senses, the mind, and the intellect, one who desires peace should not be greedy; then he shall be free from bondage.
Overcome by latent impressions and deluded by my māyā, the worlds revolve like a wheel in the cycle of birth, death, and existence. (53)
Therefore, having abandoned the defects born of ignorance as well as all bonds, one who possesses discernment shall attain liberation by resorting to my path. 54.
From an improper person, everything revolves within the ego;
one enjoys the fruit produced by that ego and again enters into māyā. ||55||
The state consisting of heaven, born of rajas, is indeed the supreme bondage; the state consisting of the realm of Rākṣasas and the like, born of tamas, is indeed the supreme bondage. ||56||
Therefore, one who possesses self-mastery should avoid both rajas and tamas;
for when sattva is freed from rajas and tamas, it attains purity.
When there is purity, one becomes rightly conscious and possessed of serene faith;
through the form of serenity, one attains the grace of the Supreme Lord. ||58||
Having attained a state of constant serenity, one achieves liberation;
the self is said to be the man, while latent desire is considered the woman. (59)
For this is a terrible sorcery that leads those possessed by desire into a pit;
it is a form composed of passion and darkness, bestowing strength upon the senses.
The wicked *vāsanā-ḍākinī* casts a man into the ocean;
she causes delusion within the body of a man or the body of a woman. (6.1)
He surely causes one to fall into the Saṃghāta hell, into the impure and filthy abode, upon the unadorned great path smeared with passion for form. (62)
Out of delusion, a man sows illusory seeds;
from those seeds are born creatures known by the names "son" and "daughter. (63)
In this case, there is a distinction regarding similarity even when there is equality with offspring born from sweat;
those born from sweat are called "crawlers" (kramayaḥ), while those born from the bodily constituents (dhātu) are designated as "offspring" (suta). ||64||
But one who seeks liberation, possessing a sense of equanimity toward his own born sons, should renounce them through dispassion and discernment and take refuge in me alone. (65)
In childhood, there is suffering due to helplessness;
even in youth, there is suffering from the desires for sense-objects and dependence upon the senses. (66)
In old age and in dependence on others, there is further suffering thereafter;
man is beset by physical and mental sufferings that have suffering at their beginning, middle, and end. (67)
Having recognized this palace of suffering, one should disregard it and take refuge in me—due to grasping, due to causes, and also due to cooperation. (68)
Likewise, all suffering indeed resides within the body due to its filling;
disregarding such [suffering], one should resort to cessation through renunciation.
For me, a discerning devotee who has attained restraint and is free from thirst, liberation through yoga is certain; there is no doubt.

For one who partakes of the nectar of the knowledge of reality, who drinks the essence of devotional love, and who is anointed with the ambrosia of affection for me, my imperishable state is considered attainable. 7.1
Celibacy is the form of Brahman; it is considered the conduct that is the sky of consciousness. Having fully taken hold of the space of consciousness, one should approach my own space.
The adept, having united the space of the body and the space of the senses— which provide internal expansion—
with the space of Brahman, should offer them into the space of Hari.
Thus one becomes truly liberated, having attained my yoga;
having performed such constant practice in this way, nothing further remains to be done.
Having spoken thus, the Blessed One, the beloved of Kṛṣṇa, ceased;
O Rādhikā, he then bestowed upon his devotees the mantras they had requested.
Then, during the night, he entered into supreme peace consisting of yogic sleep;
at dawn, [he was awakened] by auspicious sounds such as musical instruments, by hymns of praise, and by the hearing of his own glories.
The Lord himself remained awake; he brought auspiciousness to the three worlds. Having performed his daily rites, offered worship, and completed the formal ceremonies, the Master arose. (77)
Having honored all his devotees and guests, he proceeded to the pavilion;
then musical instruments were sounded to inspire enthusiasm for the sacrifice. (78)
There were auspicious songs from the women who were wives of Brahmins, and the sounds of the Vedas arose on all sides from those learned in the Veda. (79)
And those engaged in sacrifice, the performers of ritual acts, as well as incarnations, liberated souls, lords, gods, and great sages, quickly arrived at the site of the sacrifice.
The Pitṛs, humans, Daityas, Yakṣas, Suras, and Dānavas; all the progeny of Kaśyapa, and the goddesses who are the wives of Brahmā. ||81||
Then, on the morning of the sixth day, as before, the sages performed the sacrificial rites, while the Nāgas, Sarpas, and those born from the earth— both insentient and sentient— approached.
Having first performed the recitation of auspicious verses as was appropriate, the worship of the gods was carried out, as well as the offering of the bali-oblation. (83)
Likewise, there is the offering of oblations into the fire, the presentation of sacrificial portions,
the libation for the ancestors, the handful of flowers, and the ritual fees.
The nightly lamp-offering, the dismissal of all that had occurred as was appropriate, the feeding of the Brahmins, and the feeding of those honored at the great festival—all this took place. (85)
After the auspicious feasts for the worlds of the sacrificers and others had taken place,
Hari, having rested well, went to his splendid assembly hall in the evening.
There, the Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇavallabha himself performed the rites;
the venerable and eminent preceptor bestowed the mantras upon the people. (87)
And then, O Rādhikā, the beginningless Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of Śrī, the infant cowherd, indeed instructed him in that which bestows liberation and brings about welfare.
Śrī Kṛṣṇavallabhācārya is saluted by ten million liberated souls;
he is the Lord of the Abode of Abodes, the cause of all incarnations. 89.
The Supreme Lord, who was propitiated by the service of countless Brāhmaṇīs,
who was satiated at the sacrifice and honored by the gods and others, is the Lord who bestows liberation.
The compassionate Hari, the son of Kambharā and Lord of infinite power, was gazed upon by all with single-minded attention at the moment of his instruction. 91.

Thus ends the two hundred and twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Instruction Given to the Subjects on the Fifth Night, Resting at Night, and the Completion of All Sacrificial Duties Following the Daily Rites and the Taking of Food on the Sixth Morning," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O Rādhikā, Śrī Harikṛṣṇa has taught the vow of Brahman;
listen to that auspicious state of Brahman, which is the most excellent among all vows. (1)
That which is known as *brahmacarya*, the very pinnacle of all things—one who is devoted should indeed resolve upon this stainless *brahmacarya*. (2)
One who observes the vow of Brahman, practices celibacy, serves Brahman, and is virtuous—
having conquered time, illusion, and karma— shall attain my abode.
For that is indeed easy for the yogi, as well as for those who have attained perfection;
it is easy for virtuous women as well, but difficult for those who crave sense objects.
One who is vigilant should especially restrain the collection of the senses when it is intensely inflamed and powerful; such a person indeed conquers the giver of death.
One should not contemplate the nature of desire, nor its objects;
one should not look upon the signs of desire and should avoid the portions of passion.
One who possesses a body should avoid in this world those objects that nourish the *rajas* quality,
and likewise, one should completely renounce those enjoyments that nourish the bodily constituents (*dhātu*).
With a mind endowed with knowledge and accompanied by dispassion,
one who possesses self-nature should indeed act after having destroyed the state of passion.
One should certainly not place trust in this body, which is joined with corpses and impurities, which is the locus of desire,
and which will cause one to be cast into hell.
It is a house of wind, bile, and phlegm; a vessel of blood, skin, and flesh; rich with marrow, sinews, bones, and channels; and filled with impurities, urine, and the like.
Knowing that desire is based on the base and is inferior, one should abandon passion;
for the vessels carrying impurities spread out in every direction. (11)
Just as rivers nourish the ocean with their external waters, so do [the channels] nourish the body with external [substances].
Among them, however, there is one channel in the heart called the *manovāhā*.
It resides with its support in the realm of desire and emits semen born of conceptualization;
semen is said to be of many kinds, and that which is fiery in nature is located in the eyes. (1.3)
And that which is in the form of a fluid in the ears is indeed the grasper of sound;
likewise, it reaches the abodes of the other senses and bestows their respective powers.
Likewise, oil resides in water and ghee in milk;
that very essence, in the form of semen, is extracted through intense churning.
Even in a dream, that portion of passion born of the mind and produced by mental construction arises as semen; though it is weak, it enters [the womb] with great force.
There are three seeds of semen: food, its essence, and the mind-carrying [channel].
Having understood these three, one should repeatedly relax the triad.
And from that, by the non-arising of semen, one fully cultivates the vow of celibacy (*brahmavrata*).
For the mind is the subtlest part of food; therefore, it is the most nourished by it. (18)
Having indeed rendered it free from latent impressions, one should conquer that mind through dispassion; then the mind, luminous and stainless, attains the state of the nature of the Self. 19.
Having undergone a transformation from the nature of rajas, it arises as the nature of sattva;
and when permeated by the state of sattva, it attains the condition of being-existence-bliss (saccidānanda).

To whatever extent that [state] which has been recently attained appears as characterized by passion (rājasa), to that same extent one should practice the yoga of meditation for the sake of its dissolution. || 21 ||
One should practice one-pointed concentration; by that, youth dissolves. Having reached a state of ripeness, it becomes devoid of strength. || 22 ||
Then, relying upon that self and endowed with the power of the living self,
one does not go anywhere toward sense objects after having relinquished the [ordinary] self.
Nor does it approach the senses, nor the wonders of Īśvara and the like;
neither the supernatural powers (siddhis), nor speed and such, nor illusion (māyā), nor its qualities. || 24 ||
When one's own mind has thus become devoid of impetuosity, then it may follow the path of the kingdom of virtue, which is otherwise very difficult to traverse.
Having transcended the supreme path, he attains his own kingdom;
and having leaped over the path up to the boundary, he enjoys immortality in the Imperishable.
For one who conducts oneself in this manner, the world of Brahmā is held in the palm of the hand;
indeed, for one devoted to celibacy, the world of Brahmā exists right here.
Embodied beings who are attached to the objects of the senses perish;
those who are unattached and whose nature is Brahman go to my supreme abode.

Having seen that creation is continuous and pervaded by birth, death, old age, and so forth, as well as by mental anxieties, physical ailments, afflictions, and sufferings, one should strive for liberation.
Having united his body, sense-faculties, aggregates, and even his internal organ with the Lord of Śrī, the devotee should wander happily, free from all expectations.
One who desires liberation should not form an attachment even out of compassion;
for one should practice equanimity toward attachment, knowing that the world is the fruit of such attachment.
Having abandoned the fruit of attachment, even while performing action,
the liberated soul is not bound at all, just as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water.
He who possesses forgiveness, straightforwardness, and likewise freedom from malice shall be happy;
having known the way out of suffering, he who departs from it shall be happy. (33)
One should not harbor ill-will, nor should one covet, nor should one contemplate what is improper or evil;
rather, one should meditate upon the Supreme Brahman and listen to the nectar of my discourse.
One should speak words free from impurity, follow the dharma of Kṛṣṇa,
utter the name of Śrī Hari, and contemplate the supreme goal.
One should avoid that which brings about misfortune and leads to the hells;
having understood it to be contrary [to liberation], one should avoid that which pertains to saṃsāra. || 36 ||
Thus, being free from worldly effort and constantly liberated from all possessions, he wanders in solitude, observing his vows, with his sins burnt away by the fire of knowledge.
Having become possessed of self and steadfastness, one should seek the light within the heart;
where the gods shine, there Brahman shines forth. || 38 ||
Having thus attained this state of stability, one is born for the realization of Brahman;
or else, one should practice the great function of yoga very gradually.
Having established a regulation for food and likewise a regulation for thought, and having attained an increase in meditation, one should acquire the light of one's own self. (2.227.40)
The light of the Self, joined with the light of knowledge and nourished by it, shines forth like the sun when well-mixed with the light of devotion. || 41 ||
First possessing the light of the gods, then becoming self-illuminating, thereafter he shall become self-luminous; he indeed shall be the beloved of Kṛṣṇa. ||42||
Thus, having traversed the higher heavens by means of the path of light, he becomes eternally the light of consciousness, for he possesses the light of Brahman. ||43||
When the swan, endowed with qualities, beautiful, capable of reaching the further shore, and self-luminous,
becomes free from passion and knows liberation, it indeed approaches me, the Lord.
Transcending the qualities (guṇas) and having conquered old age and death along with the city composed of illusion (māyā),
one attains that which is the imperishable nectar— the eternal Brahman.
All this is eternally attainable through celibacy;
sleep, which destroys one's vows, must be abandoned by one who desires to practice celibacy. 46.
The mind, joined with sleep and distracted, is overcome by rajas;
when the state of rajas weakens, that distraction comes to an end. ||47||
Peace arises when the activity of the *sattva* quality predominates and there is a resting in gravity;
through that, there is a resting in sleep, and one sleeps by means of the activity of knowledge (*jñāna*).
When the functioning of saṃsāra dissolves, the dream state becomes exceedingly distant;
therefore, becoming intent upon Brahman, one shall attain the supreme Brahman. ||49||
Whatever the mind conceives with a serene disposition, that very thing becomes permeated by latent impressions (saṃskāra) and is remembered again and again.
Even among those of sattvic nature, one should contemplate me as the Lord of gods, the Supreme Lord, abiding as the Self within all beings; by that, one shall attain me in the highest state.
The devotee, desiring with his mind my yoga which brings happiness, as well as self-clarification, gentleness, and the vision of the gods within his heart, [should practice]. (52)
Through constant practice in this manner, one then perceives those impressions (saṃskāras) as the gods situated within the heart; thereafter, Brahman shines forth.
They say that celibacy (brahmacarya) is precisely that which consists in abiding in Brahman,
as well as that which consists in abiding among the virtuous gods who are united with Brahman.
That Brahman is supreme knowledge and the realization of the immortal, imperishable;
having known their own self in this way, they go to the highest goal. ||55||
One should know Māyā in order to abandon it, and one should know the Imperishable for the sake of liberation.
Having completely renounced worldly activity and become the Imperishable, one shall go to the Imperishable.
Activity leads to rebirth, while cessation is the supreme goal.
Dharma characterized by cessation bestows Brahman and is the eternal liberation.
One who desires to attain divine splendor should remember me, the Lord of Śrī, within the heart;
with one's whole being, one should perform penance through union with me for the sake of attaining me. 58.
Celibacy and non-violence are considered bodily austerity;
mindfulness of Me and restraint of the mind are indeed mental austerity. (59)
By my grace, food is indeed the highest austerity, as is penance that destroys sin;
even the crushing of latent desires is considered the supreme austerity of the intellect.
Steadfastness in the Self is said to be the supreme austerity of a conscious being;
and constant effort for the sake of union with Me is the highest austerity. (61)
He whose intellect remains unimpeded by others who are dull-witted and conscious of themselves,
having indeed attained a state of equality with Brahman, shall follow after me.
The capacity for illusory creation that exists in one birth does not persist in another;
rather, one rejoices through divine states such as the qualities of self-knowledge and the like. (63)
At the end of their lives here, some men worship the existent (Sat), while others worship the Self as being of the nature of the Imperishable (Akṣara). ||64||
Others indeed worship me as the supreme deity at the time of departure;
all these who possess the nature of the Supreme proceed to the highest goal.
Those who are endowed with my wisdom and intent upon my propitiation attain the Brahmic body, which is liberated and free from grasping. (66)
Having obtained my supreme refuge, they go to the highest goal;
having attained the supreme knowledge and become one with Brahman, they go to the highest goal.
Worshipping according to the true nature of things, all go to the supreme goal—those who are free from passions, peaceful, and devoted solely to me as their refuge. 68.
They are liberated from both virtues and afflictions and proceed to the supreme goal—
the Lord Viṣṇu, the unborn, divine Nārāyaṇa.
Having realized that Hari and I abide within themselves, those endowed with pure love and satisfied by my presence go unto me; they do not return, for they are imperishable.
Those who take refuge in me, or in my holy devotees who are my own portions,
having attained my supreme abode, rejoice in the imperishable and immutable.
The entire world, bound by craving, revolves like a wheel;
for one whose thread of craving has been burnt away, there is the seeking of my abode. //72//
Just as a weaver passes thread through cloth with a needle, so too is the thread of cyclic existence extended by the needle of craving. (73)
Therefore, the person liberated through devotion to me goes even to me;
out of affection, I lead him by means of a celestial vehicle to my own abode.
Having thus instructed them, the Blessed One paused for a moment;
then Śrī Hari himself bestowed the mantra upon Rādhikā and the newcomers. (75)
He brought the assembly to a close and performed the twilight prayers (sandhyāvandana);
and all those who had gathered for the sacrifice took their meal at night.
During the night, amidst all the festivities, there was great delight everywhere;
Śrī Hari, served by Brahmā, his beloved consort, and others, went to his bedchamber. ||77||
In the camps of those who were great in sacrifice and wealth, actors and others performed a preeminent dance at night, which made manifest his previous incarnations.
The wrestlers engaged in a wrestling match employing many maneuvers,
while the singing of singers took place in the Gāndharva pavilion.
In some places, however, there were indeed discourses and narrations by the learned,
as well as by the Sūtas, Māgadhas, Bandīs, Cāraṇas, and Śāstrins.
In the pavilion during the night, there were poetic recitations and historical narratives;
in some places, there were dances accompanied by songs performed by courtesans.
At that time, during the night, they were present in assemblies of various groups of kṣatriyas,
as well as among the gods, goddesses, and celestial women.
The songs and dances of the Apsarases from the lake of Brahmā took place;
for in some places, there were indeed great festivals of the creations of the Lord.
In some places, there are various diversions for the delight of the Dānavas and Daityas; there, various sports take place that signal the onset of festivals. (84)
Thus there were manifestations for the worlds, as well as for beasts, birds, women, men, and all embodied beings. (85)
In some places, there were displays of forest creepers, trees, grasses, leaves, fruits, and palanquins. ||86||
In some places, there were works of craftsmanship made from wood, stone,
and clay, as well as cotton, diamonds, silk, bark, and wool.
Likewise, there were visions of elephants, horses, cattle,
lions, as well as śarabhas, garuḍas, and camels.
And there were sightings of ruddy geese, swans, and parrots;
and sightings of armies, female buffalo, and deer. ||89||
Such novel objects as these, originating from many lands, and whatever other things have arisen among the multitude of people— || 2.227.90 ||
O auspicious lady, at that time all things consisting of the *kalās*, those characterized by primary causes, and others consisting of mechanical devices, came into being there.
Indeed, these were displayed by the guardians on the ground extending for eight yojanas;
thus the entire sixth night was filled with great enthusiasm.
Then, when half the night had passed, the people were happily absorbed in sleep;
then, at early dawn on the seventh day, various kinds of musical instruments were sounded.
There were auspicious recitations, songs, and likewise the praises of the panegyrists, along with the sounds produced by musical instruments. (94)
There were the sounds of the Vedas from the Brahmins, the virtuous acts of the holy ones, and the songs of women filled with the glory of Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa. (95)
Then there arose divine songs and narrations of stories concerning the deities for the goddesses, and songs of remaining conversations for the sovereign ladies. (96)
Even though they were sleepless during the night, having embraced great joy, they attained silence, peace, and cessation in that which is called the end of the night. 97.
And in the morning, having become composed through various auspicious recitations and the like,
they then performed their ablutions and completed their daily religious rites.
O Rādhikā, Śrī Hari, having bathed, performed his daily rites, and completed his worship,
Kṛṣṇa prostrated at the feet of his own parents.
Then the king and others, their tasks accomplished, arrived at the great palace, the auspicious abode of Śrīnivāsa, to worship Hari.
They worshiped Śrī Hari with love and drank the water from His feet;
having gathered in the house, the kṣatriyas performed the ārārtrika ceremony.
Having offered a handful of flowers and bowed down, the queens— possessing great fortune— bestowed words of blessing upon him and likewise worshipped him in that same manner.
The Blessed One also arrived at the sacrificial pavilion;
likewise, the sages, the experts in ritual action, and the deities came there.
O Rādhikā, all the sacrificial offerings, the fuel-sticks, the deities of the mantras,
and indeed all the fires arrived there in that pavilion.
Then, indeed, the sacrificial rites began from the very start,
performed with vigilance at the sacrifice according to their traditional sequence as before.

Thus ends the two hundred and twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Instruction and Dinner on the Evening of the Sixth Day at the Sacrificial Ground, and the Arrival at the Sacrificial Pavilion on the Morning of the Seventh Day," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O Rādhikā, on the morning of the seventh day, during the most excellent muhūrta,
the sacrificial rites were performed by Lomaśa and the others, just as they had been on the previous day.

The sprinkling with water, the recitation of auspicious blessings and so forth, as well as the proclamation of a "meritorious day" (puṇyāha), the awakening of the deities, and their worship according to the prescribed rules; || 2 ||
The nightly lamp-offering, the gift to Balarāma, the great food offerings, as well as the offering of water, the offering of betel-leaf, and the libation to the ancestors. ||3||

Furthermore, the oblations in the fire constitute the means of obtaining sacrificial offerings for all; likewise, the waving of lamps before the deities and the giving of priestly fees and so forth to the Brahmins [constitute the means of their sustenance]. (4)
Then, the offering of handfuls of flowers (puṣpāñjali) and the ritual dismissal (parihāra) occurred in succession;
thus was the task completed by the kings acting as patrons.
Then, by the command of Śrī Hari, all those foremost among the great-souled ones partook of the sacrificial offerings and sweet foods.
Tens of thousands of people belonging to the lowly classes enjoyed themselves there;
then, having found rest, the assembly gathered there in the evening.
The beginningless and illustrious Śrī Bālakṛṣṇasvāmī, the sovereign Lord Nārāyaṇa,
intent on compassion, issued these words for the benefit of his subjects.
I am the sacrifice and the Supreme Brahman; I consider the fire to be my mouth. Through that mouth, I swallow and consume all the oblations.
In the aperture of Brahmā within my form, the imperishable abode shines;
all liberated souls are in my hair, and those yet to be liberated are upon my brow.
All the incarnations dwell in the mouth, the eyes, the cheeks, the temples, the ears, and even in the beard; they all reside in the head.
Descending from the chin to the bridge of the nose, they dwell within me;
and in the throat, the lords Vāsudeva and the others abide in their array.
That which is proclaimed as Mahāmāyā, Prakṛti, Pradhāna, Puruṣa, Kāla, Bhūman, and Puruṣa resides upon the shoulders and back. || 13 ||
Mahāviṣṇu, as well as Rudra, Sadāśiva, and even Virāṭ—
all these abide within my sides, taking refuge in my belly.
The sovereign goddesses, the great goddesses, and the great Lakṣmīs—all those women, who are my Śaktis, dwell within the region of my chest. (15)
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśa, and others, as well as millions of Siddhas and Īśvaras,
dwell within my navel region and in my belly together with their wives.
The sages, the ancestors, and the gods dwell in my anus;
the yakṣas, rākṣasas, daityas, and dānavas dwell in the secret hairs.
In the Guptā [cave], the gods beginning with Kāma and kings of a passionate nature (rājasa) dwell;
on the slope [nitamba] are the Bhūtas, Kūṣmāṇḍas, and tens of millions of Pretas and Piśācas. || 18 ||
The Mānavas and others dwell in my two thighs, while the Cāraṇas and others reside in my two knees; indeed, the Daityas and others who wear sandals live upon my two shanks.
Serpents and nāgas dwell upon his two hoods, as do reptiles;
trees, creepers, and the like, as well as all forest trees, dwell within his body hairs.
Insects, moths, locusts, birds, and likewise beasts—these always dwell all around me, residing within the cavities of my body. (21)
Thus, all creations—both insentient and sentient—dwell within me;
when I am satisfied, all those who consist of my own self are satisfied.
Whoever, having worshipped me, the Supreme Lord, in the great sacrifice of Viṣṇu,
feeds my devotees, obtains the fruit born of a horse-sacrifice.
He who, having worshipped me as Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa at a sacrifice, feeds the twice-born,
shall obtain here the fruit of the Vājapeya rite.
Whoever worships me at the sacrifice through Bālakṛṣṇa, the son of Kambharā,
and feeds the virtuous, shall obtain the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice.
One should worship me here at this sacrifice as Gopālabāla Govinda, and one should feed virtuous and chaste women; the fruit of that is equal to that born of the Atirātra rite.
Likewise, he who worships me here at this sacrifice under the name Puruṣottama and feeds children shall obtain the fruit of a Pauṇḍarīka sacrifice.
Whoever worships me, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, in a sacrifice,
and likewise feeds those who are helpless, shall obtain the fruit born of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
Whoever worships me, the beloved husband of Brahmā, here at this sacrifice,
and likewise feeds maidens, shall obtain the fruit of a Gavām Ayana.
Whoever worships me, who am fond of the color piśaṅga, with devotion at this sacrifice,
and feeds Brahmins and ascetics, shall obtain the fruit of the Soma sacrifice.
One should worship Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of Śrī Rādhāmāṇikī;
by feeding the cowherds and cowherd-maidens, one attains the fruit of the Viśvajit sacrifice. ||3 1 ||
Likewise, one should worship me, the Lord of Prabhāpāravatī, in the sacrifice;
and by feeding the honored guests, one shall obtain the fruit of the Sautrāmaṇī rite. ||32||
Whoever worships me, the Lord of Gaurī, with devotion in this sacrifice shall attain the fruit of a Rudra-sacrifice, provided he feeds those who are proficient in ritual action.
Whoever indeed worships me, the Lord of Amarī, here in this sacrifice, and feeds the Amarīs, shall obtain the fruit of the Brahma-sacrifice. || 34 ||
Likewise, one should worship me, the Lord of Brāhmī, with devotion here at this sacrifice;
by feeding virtuous women of the Brāhma lineage, one shall obtain the fruit of the Mahārudra rite. (35)
Likewise, one should worship Lākṣmaṇīsvāmin and me here at this sacrifice;
by feeding the Sāṃkhya-yoginīs, one shall obtain the fruit of Nārāyaṇa. (36)
One should likewise worship the Lord Ābrikta and me here at this sacrifice;
by feeding those who carry water, one obtains the fruit of a rain-cloud of water.
He who likewise worships me and Uṣṇālīsvāmin here at this sacrifice,
and feeds those who cook, shall obtain the fruit of the Annakratu rite.
Likewise, he who worships me, the Lord of Īśvarī, in this sacrifice, and feeds the servants of the sacrifice, shall obtain the fruit born of the sacrifice. (39)
[He worshipped] the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the source of all incarnations,
the Lord of the liberated, the destroyer of suffering, and the beloved of Lakṣmī, during the sacrifice.
One should worship and feed them all; one shall obtain the fruit of the Sarvamedha sacrifice by pleasing me here at this sacrifice in my embodied form. 41.
Whatever my devotee may desire, all that shall he obtain;
I am the giver and the Lord of all, and I bestow everything upon my servant.
In this sacrifice, gifts should be given according to one's ability to the performer of righteous deeds;
whatever merit is gained here through these gifts shall certainly become inexhaustible. (43)
The householder who performs sacrifices, having ascended a celestial chariot adorned with networks of tinkling bells and possessing the brilliance of the sun, goes to my abode.
The gift of grains and fruits, as well as of sacrificial fuel, herbs, garments, and leaves—these too are indeed gifts. (45)
One who gives becomes long-lived, a partaker of heaven, and thereafter a partaker of liberation;
he who makes a gift of a manuscript of the Saṃhitā goes [to the highest state]. 46.
Heaven, truth, dispassion, liberation, and my imperishable state—whatever is most desired in the world, and whatever is dear in the home; ||47||
One who desires that very gift to be inexhaustible should indeed bestow each respective object for its own intended purpose;
one should not give a gift for the sake of fame, nor out of fear, nor out of greed.

For the sake of benefit in the next world and for the sake of liberation, one should give to a worthy recipient who possesses learning, who is without protector, who is a petitioner, and who is endowed with moral discipline. (49)
That which is given to a virtuous person becomes inexhaustible and yields great fruit.
My devotees are all-enduring, free from desire, and have conquered their minds.
That which is given to those who exist for the welfare of all beings yields great fruit;
for when the virtuous are satisfied, they deliver the donors along with ten thousand generations of their lineage.
One should cause temples, dharma-halls, and excellent monasteries to be built solidly;
however many bricks are piled there in those temples and other structures, [so many merits shall be gained]. (52)
For as many thousands of years as there are bricks, the virtuous builder rejoices in the heavens;
the builder of my temple goes to my abode.

Through the installation [of the deity], one attains the state of Brahmā; through the temple, the station of Īśvara; and through the practice of worship, one reaches the world of Brahmā—of this there is no doubt. ||54||
Having smeared [the image] with lime and other substances, one should carry out its restoration;
one should sweep it, smear it, and serve my image.
One may even cause wells, step-wells, and tanks to be constructed for my sake;
thus do cows and virtuous men drink the water. (56)
And all sentient beings, afflicted by thirst, drink [the water];
at that sacred bathing place, indeed, immeasurable merit arises. //57//
Indeed, leafy trees should be planted all around the palace, and gardens should also be constructed for the rest of embodied beings. (58)
Likewise, there are trees useful for their fruit, those useful for their flowers, those useful for their fuel-wood and leaves, and those that provide enjoyment for the ancestors and the gods. (59)
This merit is indeed infinite and shall bestow all prosperity;
performed with devotion, it shall lead one to my abode.
The site of the sacred ford must always be made livable through great festivals, especially by householders, the wealthy, and kings. (6.1)
The sacrificial ground is always meritorious, and the river on the bank of the Kratu is meritorious;
that land extending for a *goyojana* is considered to always grant liberation. 62.
Even while residing here, the people of Yama do not see them;
for one by whom Manu has been upheld, who is a Vaiṣṇava, there is liberation.
Even for one by whom my worship has been performed, there shall be liberation;
likewise for him by whom leaves, flowers, fruit, water, or food have been offered in the sacrifice.
"I shall effect his liberation and lead him to my imperishable state.
Thus even a wise man becomes a grasper of virtues, thinking, "Oh, what a sacrifice! (65)
O Keśava, I shall set ablaze that very ocean of his sins,
as well as the garment, the vessel, and even the milk-rice offered during the sacrifice.
"Whoever shall bestow this with devotion, I will lead him to my imperishable state;
he shall perform the gift of a cow, the gift of the earth, and the gift of a house."
The gift of a daughter, the gift of a son, and likewise the gift of a young man;
the gift of gold, the gift of silver, and the gift of vehicles and mounts. ||68||
Whoever shall perform the gift of a garden or grove, the gift of an umbrella, or the offering of an elephant at this sacrifice, I shall lead him to the imperishable state.

In this sacrifice, indeed, whatever there may be— whether the offering of oneself, the offering to Brahman, the offering to the Guru, or the offering to the virtuous— should be performed according to one's ability.
"To whoever shall perform this with a devoted heart, I shall grant the imperishable state.
Having spoken thus, O Rādhā, the beginningless Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa then [departed].
There, Hari bestowed Vaiṣṇava mantras upon the human guests; then he performed the twilight rites and offered the evening oblation to the gods.
Īśāna, Pāna, Śiṣṭa, and the others, as well as Rāja and the rest,
performed the *ārārtika* ceremony for Lord Hari and offered handfuls of flowers in worship.
And the subjects fed all those who had assembled—the great lords, the gods engaged in sacrificial rites, and all embodied beings as well. (74)
People and others provided meals for the guests who had come out of curiosity to see [the spectacle], whether they were present or had already departed. (75)
And they caused the families of Hari to be provided with an abundance of various kinds of sweet foods and other items suitable for their respective creations.
Then the lords fed all the inhabitants of the creation;
they gave them sweet drinks and betel leaves.
Consequently, there were indeed recitations of stories and public displays at night;
thus, all embodied beings became devoted to sleep during the night. (78)
Having rested as was appropriate, they quickly awoke at dawn amidst auspicious sounds of musical instruments and the songs of celestial women.
On the morning of the eighth day of the month of Rādhika, Hari himself was awakened from all sides by the songs of glory sung by bards, panegyrists, and minstrels.
Having performed his daily rites and completed his worship, he indeed honored his own parents;
and all those beginning with Brahmapriyā worshipped Hari, the Supreme Lord.
Then Śrī Hari, having bowed to Lomaśa, accepted his words of blessing;
and the kings, the royal servants, and the queens [bowed] to Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Lord.
They worshipped with sandalwood paste and other offerings, and they drank the nectar of his feet;
then, when the auspicious moment arrived, they heard the sound of musical instruments.
Hari went to the pavilion at the site of the sacrifice accompanied by his devotees;
likewise, Hari, having performed the purificatory rites, as well as the kings, the ritual experts, millions of other gods, and millions of incarnations of Īśvara [arrived]. (84)
Mānavas, sages, gods, ancestors, as well as the stationary and the moving, and men and women, quickly arrived at the pavilion. ||85||
The ritual ingredients in the form of oblations, the fires that carry the oblations, and the sacrificers who offer the oblations all assembled there at that sacrifice. ||86||
The Brahmins who perform the rituals, the Vedas, the musical notes, and the melodies,
as well as all the descendants of Kaśyapa, arrived at that pavilion.
The sprinkling with water, the recitation of benedictions, the declarations of an auspicious day, and the ritual awakening of the deities accompanied by mantras took place. ||88||
One should perform the ritual bath and worship with leaves, flowers, unbroken grains (akṣata), and other such substances,
as well as with all the auspicious services (upacāra) such as incense, lamps, and so forth.
Then there was the nightly lamp-offering, the presentation of food offerings, as well as the offering of drinking water,
the giving of betel-leaf and other items, and the offering of great oblations.
Then the offering of oblations into the fire became even greater than before;
there was the offering of sacrificial porridge (caru), the giving of milk-rice (pāyasa) and other foods, and the presentation of fruits.
In this manner, offerings were presented as far as the Pradehis;
thereafter, there was abundant gratification for the ancestors and extensive libations.
Likewise, there was the libation for the goddesses, the Mātṛkās, and the Īśvarīs;
and indeed, there was the Śrāddha and libation for the Śaktis and the Vāminīs. (93)
Then Śrī Hari performed the expiation for the three worlds that had been scorched by the sacrifice; thereafter, various foods came into being at that time.
At the time following midday, all the people partook of various kinds of sweet foods, which were like nectar and ambrosia.
[He partook of] divine flavors as well as auspicious divine nectars,
the essences of Brahman, the essences of the abodes, and the most excellent perfected essences.
The gods dwelling in the three worlds drank and partook of food; having obtained the meal, they were satisfied, and thereafter they drank water. 97.
They partook of buttermilk and fruit thereafter;
having taken betel, they rested in their quarters. (98)
Then, in the evening, Bālakṛṣṇa arrived at the assembly hall;
O Rādhikā, Hari gave his own instruction to the subjects. 99.

Thus ends the two hundred and twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Morning Sacrificial Rites on the Seventh Day in the Second Tretā Cycle of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā; the Instruction by Śrī Hari on His Being the Soul of All and Other Attributes, His Meal, the Night Festival, and Then the Completion of the Sacrificial Rites and Meal on the Morning of the Eighth Day."
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Listen, O Rādhikā; Mādhava has instructed the worlds that renunciation alone is considered the bestower of great happiness for all.
Abandoning is indeed renunciation; it is also the act of distancing oneself.
Furthermore, non-appropriation is also indeed renunciation in its essential meaning.

In the renunciation of craving there is great peace; in the renunciation of desire there is cessation. In the renunciation of material things there is the stilling of karma; in the renunciation of enjoyments there arises the vow.
Through the renunciation of pleasure, austerity is attained; through the renunciation of everything, there is liberation.
Indeed, the path of renunciation arises for the complete abandonment of sufferings.
Whatever causes suffering by whatever means, one should abandon that and become happy;
having abandoned illusion and transcended the qualities (guṇas), one should become filled with the bliss of Brahman. || 5 ||
When there is association with the qualities (guṇas), there arise the states of the qualities: pleasure, pain, and delusion.
Upon the abandonment of the qualities, the destruction of the states of the qualities occurs for the Self.
Sattva, rajas, and tamas are the means for [experiencing] cold, heat, and charcoal [fire].
Exultation, affection, bliss, happiness, and tranquility of mind [are the effects of sattva].
These arise from the quality of sattva through detachment and the attainment of what is desired;
[the qualities of rajas are] discontent, distress, grief, greed, and likewise intolerance. (8)
These arise from the quality of passion (rajas), whether through attachment, or from the acquisition of what is disliked;
likewise, lack of discernment, delusion, negligence, sleep, and lassitude [arise from it].

These [states] arise from the quality of tamas, either through dullness or from a delusion of the intellect; when one abandons what is desired, the dissolution of those characterized by sattva occurs. (2.229.10)
Upon the abandonment of aversion, there occurs the dissolution of those characterized by passion (rājasa);
upon the abandonment of delusion, there occurs the dissolution of those characterized by darkness (tāmasa). || 11 ||
Thus, upon the abandonment of the three qualities (guṇas), there arises the state of transcending the qualities;
the conscious being spontaneously discovers its own nature, which consists of existence, consciousness, and bliss.
This being so, at that time he indeed possesses no form, name, or shape;
nor does there exist in him an "I-ness" born of form, name, and shape, nor even a sense of "mine."
Upon the renunciation of those two, the state of liberation arises for the conscious being;
it is never smeared by karmas, nor is it bound, but is liberated.
When the firm fetters arising from his body and senses have passed away, and those born of the internal organ have also passed away, then he becomes liberated and goes before [the Supreme].
Possessing direct realization, he has transcended the fear of time and death;
devoid of the provisions of merit and demerit, he is free from the fruits [of action]. || 16 ||
Having attained the Self which is the ether of consciousness, one rejoices in the space of consciousness;
for like a spider, once released from its own web, one is truly liberated.
Just as a stone fallen from a mountain is indeed devoid of any binding, so too the ancient peak of Mount Ruru was abandoned; it was not for the sake of bondage.
Just as the cast-off, withered skin of a snake does not lead to bondage, so too the discarded plumage of a peacock does not lead to bondage. || 19 ||
Just as a tree falling into a river is abandoned by the birds,
so too, having abandoned the abode of the body, the liberated one indeed becomes possessed of great bliss.

Even while remaining in the body, he who conducts himself by relying on this wisdom is indeed liberated like one already liberated; unattached to the qualities (guṇas), he is possessed of great bliss.

Moreover, even while remaining in the world, one conducts oneself through the application of the qualities; for such a person, self-restraint alone is indeed the means for achieving an abundance of happiness.
Action, austerity, happiness, truth—all these are established in self-restraint (dama). Self-restraint increases one's splendor; it cuts away fear and evil. (23)
The self-controlled person sleeps in peace and wakes in peace;
he moves through the world in peace, and his heart is serene. (24)
Through self-restraint, one's inner strength increases and good fortune arises; the entire fruit of virtuous deeds is established in the self-controlled person who possesses restraint. (25)
These qualities are eternal for the embodied being disciplined by self-restraint:
freedom from meanness, absence of agitation, contentment, and faith. (26)
Absence of anger, straightforwardness, gentleness, absence of excessive speech, absence of backbiting, absence of pride, absence of envy, compassion, and reverence for the guru. (27)
He avoids idle gossip, falsehood, praise, and blame; desiring what is virtuous, he is free from craving, devoid of enmity, and possesses excellent conduct. (28)

Firm in his vows, possessed of virtue, free from idle chatter, and with a most serene heart; clear-minded, self-possessed, having conquered his defects, he is established in a state of self-abidance. || 29 ||
He was devoted to the welfare of all beings and bore no hatred toward anyone;
he was as unshakeable as a great lake, satisfied in wisdom, and full of serenity.
One who is self-possessed and self-controlled should wander through the worlds awaiting his time, as if free from all danger,
possessing such qualities as these, regarding both heaven and liberation as equal.
Worthy of homage by all beings, he rejoices happily like Brahmā;
renunciation is declared to be the highest austerity, and self-control is the supreme austerity. (32)
Sincerity is the best of austerities; silence is the supreme austerity;
eating only nectar is another austerity, as is the service of the virtuous. (33)

For one who has perfected wisdom, who is self-controlled, free from thirst for desires, devoid of expectations, and habituated to meditating upon Śrī Hari—his steadfastness is the supreme austerity. (34)
Through sincerity, vigilance, serenity, service, reverence for elders, and tranquility, the highest austerity is produced. (35)
But by the attainment of wisdom, a person indeed pierces through all evil;
the one free from deceit attains peace, and abiding in tranquility, he becomes serene. (36)
One obtains only what is to be obtained; one goes only where it is to be gone; one experiences only those sufferings and pleasures that are to be experienced. (37)
Having understood this in its entirety, that embodied being who does not become deluded remains forever well; he indeed is considered to possess all wealth. (38)

Therefore, having acquired virtues, one should indeed serve the virtuous and avoid the wicked; through association with the virtuous, there arises an increase in those qualities that lead to Brahman. (39)
"By this offering of everything to Mādhava, the attainment of Brahman shall be yours," having thus spoken to the subjects, the Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa [departed].
He caused those Vaiṣṇavas to hear it correctly and had them perform it;
then, on the night of the eighth lunar day, he gave the instruction.
The Blessed One fed all those who were honored on earth;
he likewise fed his subjects as well as his own family. ||42||
Having eaten himself, he obtained rest in the sleep of profound yoga on the ninth day, amidst auspicious sounds and the songs of bards and panegyrists.
The Great Lord was awakened by the multitude of songs of praise from the prisoners;
having performed his morning rites, his worship, and his honoring of the elders, [he arose]. (44)
At an auspicious moment, he arrived at the beautiful pavilion of the sacrifice;
the king and other sacrificers likewise assembled within the pavilion.
The entire sacrificial rite proceeded as before;
and at midday, having offered the oblation, the Blessed Lord Bālakṛṣṇaka [performed his duties].
The Lord caused them all to eat and ate himself;
then, at evening, he ascended his celestial chariot and traveled through the sky above the ocean.
