Then the Blessed One went with the kings for the purpose of recreation;
having returned to his own place, Keśava performed the twilight rites.
Having fed the people and eaten himself, he took rest at night;
and on the tenth day as well, in the morning, that Supreme Lord performed his daily rites.
Having arrived at the sacrificial pavilion together with the sacrificers and the great sages, he caused the rites of the sacrifice to be performed as well as the oblations.
Having given [the gifts], he fed the Brahmins at the time of midday;
then, after honoring all his guests, he himself partook of food.
There, the Lord, the Master, bestowed sacred mantras upon his devotees in the evening;
he caused the brāhmaṇas to perform śrāddha rites and abundant libations.
Having partaken of food at night and obtained rest, Mādhava,
the lord of the gods, quickly arose early on the morning of the eleventh day.
The primordial Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Blessed Lord Hari, having performed his daily rites and completed his worship, quickly entered the pavilion. (54)

Having caused the sprinkling of the ritual objects, the recitation of the *svasti* benediction, the proclamation of the auspicious day (*puṇyāha*), and the awakening and worship of the deities and others; ||55||
Then the Blessed One offered the animal sacrifice, the great oblation of food, the handful of flowers, as well as the fire sacrifice with various special offerings.
He gratified the deities with thousands of streams of clarified butter;
then those gods and others, appearing in their visible forms, partook of the meal.
All beings, both stationary and moving, have attained satisfaction through these excellent oblations; and this offering is for the Lord of the Imperishable Abode—namas! (58)
We offer these oblations even to those who are already liberated;
we offer these oblations to all their incarnations. (59)
These are the oblations for the lords; salutations again and again to them!
These are the oblations for all the sages; we pay homage to them.
These are the offerings for the ancestors; to them, salutations again and again! These are the offerings for the gods; to them, salutations again and again! ||61||
We offer these oblations to those who dwell upon the earth, and we praise them; we offer these oblations to those born of the human race, and we praise them. ||62||
We offer these oblations to those who dwell upon the seven [mountains], and we praise them;
likewise, we offer these to all the trees, as well as to the creepers and the grasses.
We praise those for whom there are oblations ranging from bulbous roots and tubers up to [the finest delicacies];
we praise those for whom these oblations are even insects, moths, and the like. (64)

We offer salutations to these [goddesses] who surpass all women dwelling within the three worlds; we also offer salutations to these [goddesses] who transcend both insentient and sentient principles. (65)
"May these oblations offered by you bring satisfaction indeed to all embodied beings.
Thus [he speaks], while [offering] excellent clarified butter, bilva fruits, and sacrificial fuel sticks into the ladle.
Having placed leaves, flowers, fruits, and all kinds of sweets,
I bow to and offer salutations to the Great Full Oblation (Mahāpūrṇāhuti), while performing this meditation.
Agni is Nārāyaṇa himself; I offer salutations to him.
This [offering] is for Agni Vaiśvānara, the Supreme Self. 68.
Having spoken thus, Hari offered coconuts and other items into the fire;
the kings also then presented offerings such as bilva fruits.
Salutations to you, O Gārhapatya fire; salutations to you, O Dakṣiṇāgni fire;
and salutations to the Āhavanīya fire and to that which resides upon the great altar.
To Brahmā as the Gārhapatya fire, to Viṣṇu as the Dakṣiṇāgni fire, and to Śiva as the Āhavanīya fire stationed upon the sacrificial altar; ||71||
Salutations to you in the form of the assembly member; salutations to you in the form of the domestic fire;
salutations to you in the form of the five fires; salutations to you, the Supreme Self.
Salutations to you in the form of the Agnihotra sacrifice; salutations to you whose form is the Parva-iṣṭi;
salutations to you whose nature is the Cāturmāsya sacrifices; salutations to you in the form of the Paśu-iṣṭi. ||73||
Salutations to you who are the Sautrāmaṇi sacrifice; salutations to you who are the Agniṣṭoma;
salutations to you in the form of the Atyagniṣṭoma, and salutations to you whose form is the Uktha.
Salutations to you who possess sixteen forms; salutations to you, the Vājapeya sacrifice;
salutations to the one whose nature is the Atirātra, the self of the Sarvamedha.
You are the mouth of all living beings; with what is taken by you, one should satisfy the gods.
That which is considered the creation of individual souls, the creation of the Lord, and the creation of Brahmā—[all these are contained within you]. (76)
You are indeed the provider of satisfaction to them; O consumer of oblations, bring the offerings!
May the oblations reach all [the ancestors] through the utterance of "svadhā" and "svāhā."
Kālī, Karālī, Dhūmrā, Manobhavā, Sphulliṅginī, Piṅgā, and Raktā—these are your tongues; with them, swallow the oblation repeatedly. (78)
They offered betel nuts and whatever other fruits there were into the fire, saying, "May the Supreme Lord be satisfied. (79)
Having spoken thus, Śrī Harikṛṣṇa, the great lord Bālakṛṣṇa,
then offered the final great oblation (mahāpūrṇāhuti) to the Lord of Śrī.
Having thus performed the fire sacrifice, Śrī Hari offered the vessel to Brahmā and performed the consecration of Brahmā as the patron of the sacrifice.
Having performed the consecration with nectar (amṛtābhiṣeka), Hari then bestowed the gift of spiritual welfare;
he also performed the offering of the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) within the pavilion.
The Lord caused gifts of gold, cows, land, sesame seeds, and other such things to be bestowed;
at that time, the kings gave gifts suitable for royalty. (83)
Then the sages, headed by Lomaśa, performed the consecration;
indeed, the sages sang purifying hymns and blessings at that time.
Having bestowed abundant blessings, they likewise said:
"May divine prosperities be yours, inexhaustible and granting eternal happiness. (85)
May your family lineages expand, free from disease;
may your male and female servants abound with the splendor of royal power. (86)
May there be long life, divine glory, and at the end, heaven and liberation;
may all objects of enjoyment be yours here forever. (87)
May all beings be happy; may all be free from disease.
Having enjoyed heaven and the supreme long life, may they in the end attain the imperishable state. (88)
Having spoken thus, Lomaśa and the others offered a handful of flowers to the sacrificial deities; thereafter, the ritual dismissal took place.
In that sacrifice, everyone partook of the sacrificial remains as the oblation;
indeed, each person received exactly those offerings which were intended for them.
To each of them, Hari-Kṛṣṇa gave all kinds of foods—both sacrificial offerings and nectarine delicacies—by means of his own potencies. 9.1.
He bestowed various kinds of nectar and millions of vessels for drinking the ambrosia upon those who were worthy, satisfying as many as there were.
Then he gave even more food to the traveling mendicant,
and he also gave food to the female mendicants and the destitute women.
On the eleventh day, after midday, he gave all kinds of food to everyone; thereafter, he performed the ancestral śrāddha ceremony for his forefathers. ||94||
He bestowed many fruits and other such things, as well as water and the like;
in the evening, the Blessed One sat down upon an auspicious seat in the assembly hall.
He bestowed mantras upon the people and established them as the best of Vaiṣṇavas;
he granted his own divine vision and went to the imperishable abode.
The supreme realm of the Lord was frequented by those liberated through their devotion to Brahman;
there, he again manifested in the form of Bālakṛṣṇa.
And she proclaimed the greatness of Yajñatīrtha to the people;
O Rādhikā, at that time, the three worlds indeed heard it with joy. 98.

Thus ends the two hundred and twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Performance of Sacrificial Rites and Other Duties on the Ninth, Tenth, and Eleventh Days of the Dark Fortnight of Āśvina, the Offering of the Great Final Oblation (Mahāpūrṇāhuti), the Exoneration, and the Feasting," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Rādhikā, those holy places which resided upon the sacrificial ground, Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa spoke of them on the bank of the river Āmrajānī.
That land where I, Nārāyaṇa, the supreme lord and performer of sacrifice, am present,
is equal to the imperishable (akṣara), divine, and bestows a divine destination.
The divine river Āmrajāninī is the celestial Gaṅgā born from Badarī;
she is the divine Apsaras Āmrajānī, brought forth by Nara through his own power.
In ancient times, she was produced by the *āmramañjarikās* through their crushing [of seeds], for the purpose of creating an obstacle to his ascetic practice; long ago, Mahendra arrived there.
Accompanied by many apsarases at Badarī in the presence of Śrī Hari,
all those dancing women were directed by Nārāyaṇa, as if commanded by Indra.
Then, indeed, they were observed by me for the purpose of shattering their pride;
and at Badarī, through Naradavara, Urvaśī was manifested.
In her presence, they all then became as if dark-complexioned;
casting aside pride in their beauty, they begged for forgiveness there.
Then, by means of a Vaiṣṇava mantra, I indeed transformed them all;
Mahendra then requested Āmrajānī, who was beautiful in form.
That one of singular form was indeed offered by me to Mahendra;
my second daughter, remaining in celibacy, stays here in my presence.
She indeed dwells in Badarī; she has come here in the form of water for the purpose of bestowing the fruits of their ascetic practices drawn forth by the Pārā.
There, indeed, a royal sage named Pārāka performed supreme austerity for a thousand years for the sake of the liberation of his ancestors.
For the sake of satisfying his ancestors and for the sake of water, he also prepared [an offering];
meditating upon me for the purpose of obtaining water, he requested a most excellent sacred ford (tīrtha).
Absorbed in meditation, he praised my form with great devotion;
and by me, being well-pleased in heart, my daughter who takes refuge in me was remembered.
Then, by my command, this daughter of mine, who was of the nature of water,
became the sevenfold stream and appeared upon the surface of the earth as Brāhmī.
Wherever the ancestors had gone by the force of the current, there they were liberated; and they went to the imperishable state.
This divine river Āmrajānī exists as a bestower of liberation;
here it has seven forms, among which Āmrajānī is the most excellent. (16)
Rākāntikāsanā is proclaimed as the second;
Gonikaṣā is the third, and Goyājñī is the fourth. || 17 ||
The fifth is Mādvārikā, and the sixth is considered Sāpuruṣā;
the seventh is Mānāsanā—all of these indeed bestow liberation.
This city is a garden of peace, and the port of Pāreśvara is here;
the confluence of the Āmrajānī and the ocean is always a bestower of liberation.
Indeed, this assembly is the cleanser of great and even greater sins;
for here on this earth are the sacrifices, the sacred fords, and likewise the mountains.
Furthermore, I have already resolved that Merv and other mountains, as well as lakes and rivers, shall find their dwelling here; therefore, let the sacred fords (tīrthas) indeed reside in this place.
Let the liberated incarnations of the Lord and the gods also dwell here at the confluences of the six other rivers originating from the Āmrā river.
"May the goddesses, the Śaktis, the oceans, and likewise the rivers, all dwell here as the abode of every sacred ford (tīrtha)—such was the command. (23)
The site of Bālakṛṣṇa lies between Śāntārāma and Pāreśvara;
it is indeed the abode of all holy places (tīrthas) and is like the imperishable syllable Om. 24.
Within the window-like opening of Goyājanyā, the entire earth extending for three hundred krośas is auspicious and bestows liberation. ||25||
By bathing here in the step-well, the well, or the pond, one shall attain liberation;
by drinking the water of the rivers, a person shall go to my abode.
By the act of giving even a small amount of food, one shall obtain the fruit born of sacrifice;
by the gift of a cow and the gift of gold, one shall attain heaven—of this there is no doubt.
He will perform the gift of a daughter in marriage, the gift of land, the gift of clothing, the offering of cows,
the gift of ornaments, the gift of food, and the gift of worthy recipients.
On this ground, he shall obtain the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice;
[this includes] the gift of medicinal herbs, the gift of knowledge, and the offering of water. (29)
The gift of juices, the gift of an umbrella, the gift of requisites, the gift of a house, the gift of vehicles, and the gift of knowledge. ||2.230.30||
Whoever shall perform here the planting of trees, the gift of fruit, the construction of a dharma-hall, and an altar, for him there shall be the fruit of all sacrifices. || 31 ||
Whosoever shall cause a house, a palatial mansion, or a riverside landing-place to be built, for him heaven shall be certain, and in the end, even liberation shall be attained. (32)
What is given at an auspicious time and to a worthy recipient becomes inexhaustible here;
likewise, the gift of a bed, the gift of a grass mat, and the gift of woolen cloth. (33)
He who gives this [gift] here shall attain heaven, as well as various prosperities in this world, royal enjoyments, and the wealth of an expanding lineage. (34)
Those people who, at this sacred site or wherever there are the seven rivers,
shall perform drinking of the water and bathing, will go to heaven.
Having spoken thus to Rādhikā, Śrī Hari ceased there;
and Īśvara and the others, who were the very embodiment of the sacred ford (tīrtha), returned to their own abodes.
At that very moment, seven rivers arrived there as young maidens and [bathed] their father,
Bālakṛṣṇa, the Supreme Lord, with sandalwood paste and other offerings.
Having bowed at his feet, they worshipped him and said, "May you always dwell here.
The Lord himself, in the form of an image, replied, "So be it. (38)
From that time forward, Śrī Hari Acyuta always resided in those very temples and bestowed golden images upon the kings.
Those maidens, who were like personified holy places, returned to their own abodes;
the kings, for their part, then constructed palaces upon the riverbank.
The kings installed golden images of them according to the prescribed rites.
Thus indeed, O Rādhikā, is the glorious Bālakṛṣṇa, the Supreme Lord. ||41||
Then, having instructed him, he bestowed upon him large golden bowls and water-pots made of gold as rewards.
Various golden necklaces, as well as golden crowns,
golden garlands, earrings, chains, and bracelets.
Gold and gems, ornaments, golden threads and garments, vessels made of gold, diamonds, and excellent jewels, as well as water-pots; ||44||
He gave garments, shawls, and bodices made of silk, along with golden ornaments,
vehicles, mounts, male servants, female servants, and likewise finger-rings.
He bestowed such gifts as these as rewards for their services;
then, at the sacrifice, he offered words of praise to the dignitaries.
There too, he joined those who had assisted in the sacrifice with blessings;
and there, during that night, were meals consisting of milk-rice and fruits.
Indeed, the Blessed One caused all those festivities to take place there;
and at the conclusion of the celebration of dance and song, the Supreme Lord rested. 48.
The Blessed One took sleep and awoke at dawn with auspicious sounds; having performed his morning rites and offered worship, he attended upon his mother and father.
Then he sat down upon the seat, and the kings and others arrived there;
they performed the worship of Śrī Hari and placed their offerings before him.
Then, on the twelfth day, the Lord himself fed them all various kinds of sweet foods, savory juices, and whatever drinks there were.
He caused many kinds of foods, both solid and soft, to be served everywhere;
then Kṛṣṇa himself ate well and subsequently prepared the assembly hall.
They all set out with the Blessed One for the sake of the ritual bath (avabhṛtha).
There, they heard the auspicious songs of the goddesses and women. (53)
Then, amidst the sounds of musical instruments and the chanting of the Vedas by the lords of the earth,
there was a great festival at the confluence of the Āmrajā and the Goṇikā.
They performed the principal great ablution as well as the worship of Varuṇa and the other deities; and whoever was present there also bathed in that very place.
There arose the sounds of trumpets, the sounds of mechanical engines, and the thundering of *śataghnī* weapons, like the roar of rivers meeting the ocean at their confluence. ||56||
Having traveled by means of celestial chariots and divine vehicles, the subjects bathed;
and even the lords, the gods, and other embodied beings likewise bathed.
Then, at the time following midday, Śrī Hari and the others arrived at their dwellings by means of celestial chariots and performed the ancestral śrāddha rites.
All the ancestors also arrived there in embodied form;
having attained satisfaction, they departed for heaven by the thousands in celestial chariots.
Then Mādhava served a meal of sweet foods;
everyone partook of the sweet food, and once again a gathering took place there.
There, Śrī Hari bestowed appropriate farewell gifts upon the ritualists,
the performers of the rites, and the circle of his assistants.
He bestowed auspicious [gifts] upon the liberated ones, the lords, and the incarnations,
as well as upon the female lords and the liberated women.
He also offered [his homage] to the goddesses, the deities, and the ṛṣis; likewise to the sages, to the women of Manu’s lineage, to human beings, and even to the great seers.
Hari indeed bestowed appropriate gifts upon all, both the insentient and the sentient,
and likewise fashioned provisions for the women as well.
To the male and female servants who were the performers of his work,
he also gave gold necklaces and appropriate golden coins.
"Furthermore, whenever I remember you during a sacrifice, you must come"—
thus spoke the illustrious Hari, having then obtained a messenger.
Afterwards, he dismissed the assembly; those who were honored by the earth then departed for their own worlds, regions, and villages at evening from all sides.
On the twelfth day, the assemblies likewise returned to their own homes;
at night, the Blessed Lord remained in comfort, served by the kings.
Accompanied by his family, including Brahmapriyā and the others,
he attained sleep in the form of rest and woke up in the morning.
On the thirteenth day, after performing his morning ablutions and daily rites, Kṛṣṇa sat upon an excellent seat amidst auspicious musical instruments and songs.
Then, at dawn, King Īśāna, his queen, and their daughters, remaining after their meal, came there to worship Hari.
The forty-one Brāhmaṇa maidens of the king performed the lustration ceremony (nīrājanā) and worshipped him with sandalwood paste and other offerings.
They placed a beautiful garland around the neck of Hari and made Hari their beloved;
the king became exceedingly pleased and gave them a supreme dowry.
The queen also, having accomplished her purpose, rejoiced there;
she gave gold, silver, wealth, and other gifts as a dowry to Hari.
The king held a great festival on account of the giving away of his daughter, providing a spacious palace, as well as more than a hundred male and female servants. (75)
At midday, the king, out of great devotion, gave excellent food;
he also gave food to all the other kings.
Thereafter, the great king bestowed farewell gifts upon the monarchs;
the kings, seated in their celestial chariots, departed for their own lands. ||77||
There, on the thirteenth day, the illustrious King Rāyapati,
accompanied by the sage Rāyagi, prayed to Keśava.
Then Hari said to Viśvakarman and the others, "So be it," in order for them to return to their own country and sanctify their own city.
Indeed, for the very purpose of setting aside all materials required for the sacrifice,
he quickly commanded Tūrṇaka to prepare the pavilion and other divine structures.
In an instant, Viśvakarman caused that very thing to vanish;
then Kṛṣṇa became ready, accompanied by his family and others. 8.1.
Then, having been honored by Śaṅkara and his attendants as well as by all the great sages, the king, accompanied by his army, took his leave of Hari.
Then Hari repeatedly played delightful musical instruments, while receiving auspicious flower garlands as marks of honor.
Hari, having been honored and worshipped with *brāhmī* leaves, parched grain, and other offerings,
and being made to hear shouts of "Victory!", ascended his own celestial chariot.
Then Kṛṣṇa, together with his family and the great sages such as Śaṅkara,
ascended a celestial chariot and advanced through the sky at the head of the procession.
And by the king's command, the sounds of the Vidāya-machines arose;
and King Rāyapati went swiftly ahead in his celestial chariot.
To welcome Hari, he quickly stationed his army there on the bank of the river Parīṇasā within his own kingdom,
assuming a form born of the ṛṣis.
In the city of Vyenojarāśā, King Samālika, accompanied by his army, stayed in a vast and magnificent garden for the purpose of honoring [him]. (88)
Then, from the path of the sky, that beautiful celestial chariot arrived swiftly like the sun, illuminating the cardinal and intermediate directions. (89)
Then musical instruments were sounded and shouts of victory arose;
people ran about from all sides with eagerness to catch a glimpse [of him].
Following the path shown by the king, Śrī Hari slowly descended the aerial chariot onto the ground in the middle of the garden. Hari quickly emerged from the front part of the chariot. ||9 1||
A rain of flowers indeed fell upon the celestial chariot from the people,
and the Supreme Lord was honored with offerings of unbroken rice and other gifts by the subjects.
The king placed a golden garland around Kṛṣṇa’s neck and bowed down; then the queen joyfully placed a flower garland around Kṛṣṇa’s neck. 93.
The young men and maidens performed an act of worship with sandalwood paste and other offerings;
thereafter, Hari sat upon the throne for a moment.
Having granted him his audience, the king rose from his lion-throne and joyfully went to the courtyard toward that magnificent elephant, which was beautifully adorned.
He also settled the family of Śrī Hari upon elephants and other mounts,
as well as upon carts and draft animals, and the women were placed according to what was appropriate.
He seated him upon palanquins as well as divine chariots;
then, he was greatly honored by the sounds of musical instruments and songs.
In the city of Vyenojarāśā, Śrī Hari was completely overwhelmed on all sides by shouts of joy, cries of victory, as well as songs and hymns of praise. 98.

The Lord was honored at the top of the gate-towers by the royalty, in the city by the leading citizens, in the courtyards by the subjects, and at the front of the market-stalls by the wealthy merchants. (99)
And the beloved of Kṛṣṇa was honored at the front of the street by women with gifts of gold coins and the like, as well as coconuts and other fruits.
Adorned with garments, alms-bowls, and ornaments, and sprinkled with sandalwood paste, unbroken rice, and water, he was honored on all sides as he paraded through the city accompanied by his army.
Then Hari, the protector of dharma, arrived at the royal palace, that auspicious abode;
having partaken of water, he took his rest.
Having taken his meal, Keśava, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, who is served by Brahmā, Pārvatī, and others, fell asleep at night. || 103 ||

Thus ends the two hundred and thirtieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Residence and Greatness of the Divine Tīrthas in the Seven Rivers beginning with Āmrajānī, the Avabhṛtha Rite, the Reward, the Passing of the Night, the Morning Departure, the Removal of the Mahīmāna Pavilion and other structures, and thereafter the King’s journey to the kingdom of Rāyapati, his wandering through the city of Vyenojarāśā, his meal, and his sleeping at night," in the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, within the second section, the *Tretā-santāna*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O Rādhā, at dawn on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Āśvina,
He was awakened by auspicious sounds of musical instruments and songs.
Having performed his ablutions and worship, Bālakṛṣṇa took his seat;
Rājārāyapati then approached to worship Kṛṣṇa. || 2 ||
Then, with devotion, he bowed at his feet and performed an ablution with water; thereafter, he drank the nectar of his grace from those very feet.
Together with his family, he applied a sandalwood tilaka to that Lord of Śrī, and likewise placed beautiful collyrium with a moon-design upon His two eyes. || 4 ||
He placed a crown upon his head and earrings upon his ears;
he gave him necklaces rich with gold and jewels, and a long chain for his neck.
On the arms, bracelets; on the fingers, rings;
on the waist, a girdle; and on the feet and forearms, anklets.
The king honored the Blessed Lord, the husband of Ramā;
he then anointed his limbs with fragrant sandalwood paste and other unguents.
And he offered fragrant flower garlands as was appropriate;
the king then donned a beautiful royal attire.
Hari joyfully performed this for the sake of increasing the king's affection;
then the king, accompanied by his queens, performed the lustration ceremony (nīrājana).
And thirty-three maidens performed a great lustration ceremony for him;
the charming girls placed a bridegroom’s garland upon the chest of Bālakṛṣṇa.
Having obtained the Lord as their husband, they then felt their purpose was fulfilled;
the king [installed] him upon a beautiful golden throne honored by kings.
Having seated him, he placed the crown of King Śrī Hari upon his head and said,
"O Kṛṣṇa, this kingdom and these maidens are bestowed upon you for the sake of your liberation."
From this moment on, we offer our kingdom to you; we are your male and female servants.
O Blessed One, ocean of compassion, supreme beyond the supreme, remain right here! 1.3
You are the Self, you are the inner self, and you are considered the Supreme Self, the Lord;
O Viṣṇu, Lord of all living beings, protect me from the ocean of saṃsāra.
The kingdom bestowed by you has been governed by me until the completion of the sacrifice;
now, O Lord, the Blessed One has arrived—bear the burden.
I shall carry out your command like a servant; remain as the protector of the kingdom.
By our good fortune, the Blessed One has been obtained through his grace without effort.
You, whom even yogis perform oblations for their own lives in order to obtain, yet you are not attained even through austerities accomplished with great hardship.
Even the Siddhas, though constantly engaged in meditative absorption, worship you;
yet, even so, you do not become visible to their eyes.
O Lord, this very person has come here to my house without performing penance, solely by Your grace,
for the sake of my own liberation and that of my family members.
Having entrusted everything into your hands, I shall have fulfilled my purpose;
therefore, O Blessed One, accept this kingdom given by me and grant me liberation.
I have recognized you as one of divine form yet acting like a human; you are the Supreme Lord, the source of incarnations who has taken descent, as declared in the Vedas.
O Lord of the beloved of Brahmā, O Lord of the female practitioners of Sāṃkhya and Yoga, O Beloved of Lakṣmaṇā, O Kṛṣṇa, protect me like the Lord of those who are devoted.
O beloved Kṛṣṇa, you who are the lord of the ruddy ones, O Master, lord of the tawny ones,
lord of the reddish-brown ones, and lord of the greenish-yellow ones— protect me, O Kṛṣṇa!
O Beloved of the fair-complexioned ones, O Blessed One, O Lord of the immortals, O All-pervading One, O Lord of those merged in Brahman and of the perfected ones—O Lord of Rādhā, protect me! 24.
O Lord of Lakṣmī, ocean of compassion, Master of Ramā, Lord of the virtuous, Sovereign of kings, and Lord of the gods and others—protect me, O Lord of Īśa! 25.
O Keśava, those two feet of Yours which even Lakṣmī serves—those feet have been obtained by my daughters through the accumulation of great merit. (26)
Those two divine ones, whom Lakṣmī, Jayā, and Mañjulā serve, and who are endowed with the virtues of Nārāyaṇa—they have both met with me. 27.
Māṇikya serves those two who grant liberation, as does her friend Muktā;
the virtuous Padmāvatī and Hāsā also serve those two givers of final release. (28)
Indeed, one hundred and forty million others, dwelling in the three worlds, shall become your female servants. (29)
If they are flooded with His grace, even lords, incarnations, liberated beings, gods, and great sages serve His two feet.
O Kṛṣṇa, those two purifying feet of yours have been well-attained by me in my home,
where former kings offered their very selves.
O Lord, those two have indeed been attained by me;
therefore, deliver me from the fear of Mahākāla, the fear of Māyā, and the bondage of karma.
Nothing else is capable of leading me away from that; therefore, worship Me alone.
O Janārdana, you are the refuge and the protector of those who have come for shelter. 33.
O Maheśvara, lift me up who have fallen into the stream of worldly existence;
by means of your yoga, may my kingdom, home, wealth, and so forth become divine.
A great sacred ford has arisen on earth, a divine abode equal to the Imperishable;
oh, what fortune, what fortune for Rājārāja upon this world! (35)
In whose house the beloved of the maiden, the illustrious Puruṣottama himself, resides—oh, what fortune! Oh, what fortune, even surpassing that of the river Pārīṇasā! ||36||
Where all sacred fords come together by your power, the great fortune of the kingdom of Ārṣaja-tantru flourishes. ||37||
O Lord, the city of Ayodhyā, where Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Lord himself, resides, has come into your presence. 38.
But from your dwelling, there has arisen that which is meaningful from the very beginning, which destroys all evil, and which is free from death, old age, and the like. (39)
"O Hari, stay here forever; I shall perform service unto you.
Having spoken thus, she prostrated herself like a staff before Śrī Hari.
Then Queen Rādhikā prostrated herself like a staff before Hari;
thereafter, she celebrated a most magnificent festival on the fourteenth day.
Then the subjects, both women and men, being preeminent, arrived from very distant lands on all sides indeed for the purpose of seeing him. ||42||
To them Hari gave the mantras as well as the bliss born of his vision,
by completely drawing the mental faculties toward his own form.
He also caused the eternal meditation upon the Blessed One to be performed;
and the Supreme Lord accepted the excellent worship offered by him. ||44||
Having given them his gracious countenance, Keśava delighted them and bestowed upon them his divine vision, which belongs to the Supreme Lord.

Likewise, the omnipresent Lord [reveals] His own form as residing in the Imperishable (akṣara), as residing in Goloka, as residing in Vaikuṇṭha, as residing in the Unmanifest (avyākṛta), and as residing in the Immortal (amṛta). ||46||
Likewise, he is golden, situated within the circle of fire;
furthermore, he resides in Viśālā, has attained the white abode, and dwells in the Ocean of Milk.
Likewise, he showed the Supreme Lord in his own form as Bālakṛṣṇa residing at Kuṅkumavāpī; thus, indeed, he revealed the Supreme Lord through many forms. 48.
By that means, those men and women indeed became ones who had accomplished their purpose;
to them, the illustrious Svāmī Śrīkṛṣṇavallabha gave the mantras. 49.
Then the king, having worshipped the Lord of Gods, fed him;
thereafter, all the queens, their purpose fulfilled, attended upon that husband.
Hari said to the king: "O King, this kingdom is mine without a doubt;
it was given to me by you and obtained by me, yet I give it back to you."
"By my command, rule this great kingdom as is fitting;
and cause a firm palace with seven peaks to be constructed."
"There, establish me indeed in a golden form together with Śrī; I shall always abide within that golden image and accept whatever is performed by you. (53)
"O King, perform worship at all times and observe my command.
"So be it," the king replied immediately, O Rādhikā. (54)
Right there, in that very presence, he had a golden image fashioned;
Kṛṣṇa himself entered into it together with Śrī, becoming perceptible to the senses.
The king guarded him within his home; then, in due course, he established Hari in his palace and served him with the utmost devotion.
On the fourteenth day, at midday, the king fed [the guests];
at the time of sunset, he performed the ancestral rites (pitṛpūjā) on the bank of the Pūrṇā river.
The Blessed One himself performed various *śrāddha* rites;
Keśava brought satisfaction to the ancestors with water, funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*), and other offerings.
Then he performed his twilight devotions and subsequently went to his palace;
at night, all those maidens attended upon their own husband.
In the morning, Hari was awakened by auspicious songs and the sounding of musical instruments as well as hymns of praise; thereafter, he bathed in the waters of the river.
On the day of the new moon, he indeed performed the offering of water to the ancestors;
at the foot of a Plakṣa tree, he offered water to all created beings.
The ancestors arrived there from the hand of Hari for the sake of satisfaction, as did those known as the Akṣaras and the cowherds residing in Goloka. ||6 2||
The attendants (pārṣadas) are residents of Vaikuṇṭha, residents of the Unmanifest (avyākṛta),
residents of the Immortal (amṛtastha), as well as liberated souls (muktas) who reside in other Vaikuṇṭhas.
Those established in truth, those designated as Brahman, the Siddhas, the great seers, as well as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśa, and others— the sages, the deities, and so forth— [all abide there].
Aryaman and the other ancestors, the Mātṛkās, and the wives of the ancestors,
as well as others residing in the realm of Yama and those situated everywhere throughout the three worlds.
Desiring to satisfy him and longing for the waters of Nārāyaṇa, they approached that place;
there, with his own hands, Śrī Hari offered water to them in cupped palms.

All the ancestors drank [the water] and attained liberation; those who were destined for the abodes of the liberated attained satisfaction and departed for their own respective heavens and other realms.
Then all those who were situated in the state of the ancestors attained satisfaction;
thereafter, the Blessed Lord returned to his own abode, the celestial palace.
Thereafter, he performed various kinds of ancestral śrāddha rites with the offering of rice-balls (piṇḍas),
milk-porridge (pāyasa), and meals of milk-rice and other foods.
He gratified them with offerings of fruits, flowers, and grains, with sugar and other sweet, delicious juices, with nectar-like delicacies, and even with the simple food of sages.
Having performed the ancestral rites (śrāddha) according to the prescribed rules, he then provided an exemption;
he fed the brahmins with delicious foods worthy of praise.
The wretched, the helpless, and the miserable; virtuous women, the righteous, and the ascetics; those who have sought refuge, as well as maidens, youths, and laborers. ||72||
The Lord indeed caused all his devotees and servants to be fed, as well as the king, the royal retinue, and the Vaiśyas devoted to service. ||73||
The Blessed One caused him to be fed, and by the command of Hari, the king also ate that food of his grace immediately after midday.
Hari indeed constructed a very great assembly hall and gave this instruction:
"The mother and likewise the father must always be served by householders. (75)
Furthermore, the guru is to be served, and one should abide by his command as is appropriate, through mind, speech, body, and wealth. (76)
A single teacher is said to be equal to ten students;
in this world, a father is considered great, being equal to ten teachers. (77)
The mother, who protects her son, is ten times more excellent than the father;
for he was indeed held by the mother in the womb and likewise nurtured by her in childhood.
Since he was united with a wife during his youth, the mother is more venerable;
however, the teacher who imparts knowledge is considered ten times more venerable than the mother. (79)

The Guru, who destroys the bonds of latent impressions (vāsanā) that cause birth, death, and old age; who effects the destruction of sin; who is worthy of worship; and who grants liberation to the individual soul (jīva). || 2.231.80 ||
Mother, father, and the guru are to be honored and worshipped by those who desire their own welfare;
for one by whom these three are worshipped, prosperity shall never fail.
These three are indeed of divine form, and they are considered to be the three fires;
by whomsoever their service is performed, the auspicious fruit of birth is attained.
They are not to be reviled by your sons, nor indeed are they ever to be struck;
nor are they to be caused distress here, for all three of them are to be nourished.
Whoever indeed performs a circumambulation and likewise offers salutations to his mother, by that act the entire earth has been circumambulated; of this there is no doubt. (84)
By him by whom the father is fully honored, Viṣṇu is honored;
and by him by whom the guru is honored, the gods and others have been worshipped. (85)
To them, one should give wealth, food, and clothing according to one's ability;
whatever is appropriate and required, that indeed should be given in every way. (86)
Those in whose home the three sacred fords reside labor in vain at other holy sites;
by serving these three, the merit of all sacrificial rites is surely attained. (87)
By receiving the blessing of the Three, the obstacles of Yama depart far away;
all kinds of fortunes come to his house from every direction. (88)
These three ancestors are declared to be alive for the purpose of being served;
by him who serves them here, the world beyond becomes auspicious. (89)
He by whom these are made to suffer shall himself suffer in the next world;
and those sons and others who serve them until they reach satisfaction pass away unto death.
Your ancestors shall indeed become liberated, destined for heaven and other higher realms;
they shall certainly not remain in the state of a preta, nor shall they fall into any lowly rebirth.
Birth does not cause suffering for those who have passed away with serene minds; however, it does cause suffering for those people who have passed away with unserene and distressed minds. (92)
For those cruel beings residing in the ancestral regions (vaṃśya) indeed drink the blood [of the deceased];
therefore, sons and others should offer a śrāddha for the sake of their attainment of a good rebirth. 93.
May obstacles in the lineage perish, and may there likewise be prosperity for the lineage;
today, this Śrāddha—consisting of food, water, and fruit—has been performed and offered.
One goes to heaven wherever one's ancestors indeed reside;
there the ancestors, having received [the offerings], are always satisfied and happy. 95.
Therefore, one should perform the śrāddha for the sake of achieving liberation for the ancestors;
food, water, clothing, fruit, and even milk-rice should be offered under their names. (96)
Beds, vessels, grains, and especially juices should be given;
indeed, foods should be offered for the sake of the satisfaction of the ancestors. 97.
When worthy recipients are present at sacred sites, one should give according to one's capacity and as is appropriate;
gold, silver, copper, and wealth, in particular, should be given. (98)
Whatever vehicle or conveyance was indeed dear to him, that very thing should be given to a worthy recipient; for such merit shall be infinite.
Having spoken thus, he then ceased; the subjects then performed worship with wealth, food, garments, vessels, and the like, as well as sandalwood, unbroken rice grains, and flowers.
Then Kṛṣṇa bestowed as a gift upon the royal sage Girikarṣi that wealth which had arrived in abundance and was intended for worship.
At night, the son of the cowherds attained sleep and rest;
the Supreme Lord was served by Rādhikā and all his beloveds.
Awakened by auspicious morning instruments and the songs of women,
Harikṛṣṇa performed meditation within his own heart.
Having performed his ablutions and other rites, having completed his daily devotions, and having offered praise to his guru, the king sat upon a divine seat; at that very moment, [the sage] arrived.
He performed a great worship of Śrī Hari with sandalwood paste and other offerings,
and he caused all the honored guests to drink milk-rice (pāyasa).
The queen performed worship, and then the subjects also worshipped;
the king, moreover, endeavored to lead Acyuta into the interior of the city.
Hari said, "So be it," and immediately became ready;
O Rādhikā, he took his place in his own celestial chariot together with his family.

Thus ends the two hundred and thirty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Worship of Hari, the Instruction on [His] Worship, the Performance of Śrāddha for the Ancestors, the Offering of Water, and so forth on the New Moon Day, followed by Resting at Night and the Morning Worship on the First Day of the Bright Fortnight of Āśvina," in the second section, the Tretā-saṃtāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O Rādhikā, on the morning of the first day of the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvina,
at the request of King Rājārāya, Śrī Hari became ready.
In the kingdom consisting of Khaṇḍarāṣṭra, he went to the city of Lāpalātrī,
located near the ocean, a city situated on the seashore.
He descended into a palace resembling a continent within a great garden;
the king honored him with gold and various kinds of wedding gifts.
With diamonds, the finest gems, pearls, and likewise with jewels,
and amidst the sounds of musical instruments in the city, he was honored with great respect.
King Rājārāya caused Kṛṣṇa to whirl about in every direction;
there in that great garden, Hari performed service and exerted himself.
Kṛtārāma spoke for the sake of pacification for two days:
"On the third day of the month of Āśvina, the Daitya Navajīvana will indeed [arise]. (6)
Illusory and possessing great speed, his body was like a massive mountain;
he drew in many clouds with the hair growing from his head.
Striking the force of the lightning bolts with his mace made of many living beings, roaring at the sky with his laughter, and agitating the ocean with his claws; || 8 ||
Covering his body with the thickness of his form, he entered at night;
and having recognized it as a divine celestial chariot, he lifted it up with a single hand.
Rudra, recognizing that Daitya, let out a roar:
"Who is this that touches my celestial chariot? Go far away, or you shall be dead!"
Having heard this, he quickly let out a loud, boisterous laugh;
thundering in the sky with his mace, he spoke, causing terror.
"Who are you? Are you the lord of this celestial chariot, or whose is it? Speak!
I shall take the chariot away, so be resolute for battle. (12)
Śaṅkara said: "Do not desire battle; go far away!
In battle there is no welfare for you; abandon your celestial chariot immediately. (13)
The Daitya said: "In this world, victory cannot be achieved without battle.
I shall take away the celestial chariot and carry off all these women from here. (14)
Having spoken thus, he struck Rudra on the head with great force using his mace;
Śaṅkara, being swift and impetuous, quickly pierced it with his trident.
When the Daitya’s mace was indeed shattered and fell into the ocean, at that moment the tides of the sea became flooded with water. 16.
Then indeed, being deprived of his mace, the Daitya fell into agitation;
he thought, "Having done what, or having taken what, shall I flee? (17)
In the great garden of the royal palace belonging to King Rājārāya,
there was a younger sister who was sleeping together with her mother.
Having lifted her up and placed her upon his shoulder, he ascended into the sky;
Vidyunmaṇi wept bitterly as the maiden was carried away by the Daitya.
A great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose from the men who were crying out, "Save us! Save us! Indeed, their shouts were filled with terror at that time.
Upon hearing this, the lord of kings and queens awakened in an instant;
Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa also arose. ||2 1 ||
The subjects also woke up, filled with clamor;
and the women of the earth became wide awake on all sides.
Having heard the account told by Śaṅkara, the king of the Daityas, taking the maiden,
indeed rushed swiftly through the sky under the name Navajīvana.
O Kṛṣṇa, he is not very far away; he is moving through the western sky. Having received your command, he must by all means be slain by me. (24)
"So be it," said Hari, the king, the lord of kings.
Then the mother also spoke thus: "Indeed, this maiden has been given to you. (25)
"Protect, protect, O Great Kṛṣṇa! Protect! Quickly ward [the danger] off!
Kṛṣṇa said to the king as he was entering his prepared celestial chariot:
"I am departing for the sake of protection; you [must remain] here in this auspicious chariot of mine."
Or else, follow me here in this celestial chariot along with your mother.
Having spoken thus, Hari quickly followed after the Daitya toward the western quarter,
swiftly accompanied by his family.
The king also, followed by his servants, subsequently caused his own celestial chariot to be drawn with speed through the sky; he became a follower equal to the sun.
Upon seeing the celestial chariot of Hari as well as that of the king,
the Daitya fled through the sky in fear, even though he was accompanied by the maiden.
Light as he was, he was lifted up by the force of the wind;
he rushed over the ocean at night for a thousand yojanas.
After the celestial chariot of Śrī Hari,
the chariot of the king also pursued with great speed, in order to seize that foremost of the Daityas.
The Daitya also fled with great speed even before dawn;
meanwhile, a vast island situated within the ocean arrived.
Bestowing new life, he descended to that earth,
which was a hundred yojanas in extent and divided in two by the waters within.

The city, consisting of the dwellings of the Daityas, was adorned with the splendor of walls and gate-towers that inspired fear through the Daityas' meanness, and was richly beautified by royal palaces and other structures.
Entering swiftly, the Daitya indeed roared aloud to awaken the others and struck the kettledrum that announces the commencement of battle.
Hearing that great roar of Jarā, the Daityas, filled with eagerness, roared;
grasping their weapons for the sake of battle, they went forth like mountains.
Navajīva also, having quickly cast that maiden into a cave,
arrived for the sake of battle accompanied by the Daitya army.
Śrī Hari, assuming youthfulness and beauty, took his Sudarśana discus and went to that cave; he brought the maiden away in his own celestial chariot.
The Lord, having fashioned another girl out of clay exactly like her— an illusionary maiden capable of deluding all the Daityas— deposited her in a deep cavern.
She quickly and truly handed her sister over to the king;
meanwhile, the Daityas, unaware of this, rushed forward by force to do battle.
And she was presented for offering to Kṛṣṇa by her mother and her brother;
placing her hand upon the neck of Hari, she chose him as her husband while seated in a celestial chariot.
Having taken the garland of flowers and the excellent garland, she became the beloved of Kṛṣṇa;
then the glorious Bālakṛṣṇa, the Supreme Lord, appeared. 43.
Then Śaṅkara gave the command to Īśāna to slay the Daityas in battle; instantly, out of anger, he loosened his matted locks and dispatched the leaders of the Gaṇas.
He then created ten lakhs of terrifying forms of Rudra,
and gave them the command to fight with weapons born of his mere resolve.
Leaping up again and again, they struck those Daityas with tridents;
indeed, until midday, there was a great battle that brought about the destruction of the Daityas.
All twenty lakh Daityas were destroyed;
there was a great cry of "Alas! Alas! and the weeping of the women.
The compassionate Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa, for the sake of their happiness,
gave orders to his attendants to reside in that region in the householder's stage of life.
The Gaṇas performed the marriage rites for all the wives of the Daityas;
they were all sons of Śaṅkara, yet they were Vaiṣṇavas, impelled by Kṛṣṇa. ||49||
Taking each of their respective wives, all those attendants went to the houses in their various regions to see the king, Kāmanāyaka.
Mādhava established the group named Kāmanāyaka,
and having consecrated them in the great kingdom, he likewise granted ten million attendants.
Having performed a grand and auspicious festival, the Lord Śrī Hari wandered through the entire city of Vallīliṅga and rendered it holy.
Then, having ascended his celestial chariot and crossed over Khāḍikā,
he went to the city of Dinediṣṭhā and wandered among the lords of the Gaṇas.
Having caused him to dwell there and having received the excellent worship performed by him, the Supreme Lord, the Lord of Māyā,
gave the king permission to take his meal.
Having gathered together in his own celestial chariot, Hari gave food to all the inhabitants of the vimānas; having bestowed safety and wealth upon them in the evening, he departed.
On the fifth day of the bright fortnight of Āśvina, having abandoned sleep at dawn, he spent the night in the royal palace in Dvinediṣṭhapura.
Śrī Hari, having surveyed the island on all sides from his own celestial chariot,
[prepared] for the king, his mother, and the army to depart.
Then, having issued commands for his own kingdom, Hari, accompanied by his family and endowed with great mental composure, ascended the celestial chariot.
Having swiftly crossed the ocean by way of the path of the sky, he arrived at the city of Hambārtana on the island of Trāsamāna. ||59||
For the celestial beings of the aerial chariots indeed took their meals at midday;
thereafter, the great sages, who were devoted and dwelt in warm regions, [partook of theirs].
Previously protected by him, they arrived in celestial chariots for the purpose of seeing him;
Hari joyfully offered them a welcome.
Having received the worship and bestowed his blessings, Hari swiftly crossed the ocean by means of his celestial chariot and went to the city of Allālī.
Having stayed for one night in the region of Bhūśiras within the Uṣṇālaya, the abode of the Vandārukas,
they took their morning meal at dawn.
In the morning, Narayana, having performed his worship and drawn forth the multitude [of devotees],
arose and departed by celestial chariot, accompanied by his family.
In the northern direction, at a distance of fifty yojanas,
he reached the island named Siṃhala, situated in the midst of the ocean.
Having taken his meal at midday, Hari, traveling in his celestial chariot, flew through the air;
reaching Lake Pampā in the evening, he spent the night upon its shore.
Then, on the morning of the seventh day, the Lord ascended his celestial chariot and went to his own sacred site in Saurāṣṭra for the purpose of concealment.
Having performed worship and a meal for the Lord of the Gopas at midday on the seventh day of the bright fortnight of Āśvina, the Lord [arrived] slowly in the evening.
Traveling by way of the sky, he arrived at the sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpikā;
there, the people of Kuṅkumavāpī, afflicted by the pain of separation, waited for his arrival.
Those men, women, boys, and girls who, having become emaciated, always performed service for their master, Śrī Hari, attained His vision. ||2.232.70||
Seeing a mass of light in the sky and inferring the arrival of his beloved,
he was filled with extreme joy near the Aśvapaṭṭa lake.
Eager for a sight of him, they ran toward the great garden;
at that very moment, a celestial chariot also arrived nearby.
Then, shouts of victory, the sounds of trumpets, the blares of conchs,
and the songs of women arose on all sides.
The guardians of the fields, the sacred fords, and the deities residing there;
likewise the liberated ones, the lords, the incarnations, the attendants, and so forth. ||74||
Great seers, royal sages, Brahmins, the truthful, the virtuous, yogis, perfected beings, and likewise holy men established in their vows. ||75||
The maidens and boys dwelling in Akṣarabhūmi, as well as the fortunate women, were all endowed with auspiciousness. ||76||
Those dwelling in Lomaśa’s hermitage as well as those residing in the mango grove set out quickly toward the lake to welcome Kṛṣṇa.
The ascetics set forth, delighted at the news that Kṛṣṇa had arrived;
they brought sandalwood, flower garlands, perfumes, unbroken grains, and fruits.
Even after taking the heartwood of the sandalwood trees, those who work in the house abandon their tasks;
likewise, farmers and others, having released their work at the boundary, leave it behind in the forest.
Abandoning their forest duties and commercial activities,
all the merchants quickly went toward Aśvapaṭṭasara, the lake of Lord Hari.
Leaving their own homes, they went quickly for the sake of welcome and worship; indeed, Hari’s celestial chariot descended there upon the earth. 8.1.
Honored with sandalwood paste and other unguents, as well as flowers, unbroken grains of rice, and saffron,
the Blessed Lord Śrī Hari quickly took his place at the front of the celestial chariot.
He granted his audience to all people from every direction;
filled with affection, he inquired after the welfare of them all. (83)
All of them, filled with longing, inquired after the health of the Lord of Life;
then, shedding tears of love, they embraced Hari again and again. (84)
They placed flower garlands upon the neck of Hari, and then they performed his worship with sandalwood and saffron,
with unbroken grains (akṣata) and other fragrant substances.
The group of men prostrated at the feet of the illustrious Gopāla, while the group of women repeatedly prostrated at the feet of Kaṃbhārā. 86.
Then the assembly of the Gaṇas prostrated at the feet of Īśāna,
and they also bowed to the virtuous Goddess, the foremost of the circle of Yoginīs.
Indeed, all the women paid homage to the beloved wives of Brahmā—namely, Gaurī, Hārītakī, Cāmarī, and Brāhmilī. (88)
Indeed, all the women there were like new brides of Kṛṣṇa;
moreover, in the temple of Hari, they were filled with musical instruments, songs, and auspicious rites.
The son of Ṛṣya joyfully caused Hari to enter along with his family;
and all the sages and seers prostrated themselves like a staff and performed worship.
The subjects, distressed by his absence, came and inquired after his welfare;
Hari, having likewise inquired after their well-being, bestowed auspicious honors upon them. (9.1)
Having informed his devotees at the onset of night that his tasks were accomplished,
the Lord then arose and departed to perform his bath and twilight prayers.
Having first performed the rites of hospitality, he subsequently caused meals to be served;
and having duly honored Lomaśa, as well as Śaṅkara and his parents.
Mādhava fed the great sages, Yavakrīta and the others;
likewise, Kṛṣṇa fed the maidens who were dear to Brahmā. 94.
Having fed all those beloved women in the auspicious hermitage of Lomaśa,
he then sent them all to the assembly of the Brahmin women.
And Bālakṛṣṇa gave them all divine requisites;
assuming many forms, Kṛṣṇa bestowed happiness upon them during the night.
Thus indeed, O Rādhikā, having purified all devotees everywhere in every land upon the earth, He shines resplendent, dwelling in the imperishable realm. 97.
Blessed is Kuṅkumavāpikā, blessed are those maidens as well, and blessed are those lands that are directly connected with Nārāyaṇa. (98)
Those humans on earth who shall hear this divine life-story, and those people who, filled with devotion, shall read and proclaim it; (99)
For them there shall be the destruction of sin, and indeed the most excellent enjoyment;
and at the end, liberation in the imperishable world shall surely occur—of this there is no doubt.
And some men will proclaim the divine accounts of sacrifices, as well as those of the sages and the kings, and the stories of the devotees. (101)
They shall obtain the fruit of sacrifice and prosperity shall dwell in their homes;
by hearing the life-story of those dear to Brahmā, they shall attain the supreme heaven.

O beautiful lady, by listening to this, one obtains the fruit of the sacrifice of recitation (japayajña), the fruit of visiting sacred fords (tīrtha), the fruit of religious observances (vrata), and likewise the fruit of all forms of worship. 103.
This divine conduct of the Supreme Lord was indeed the first to appear on earth as a universal sovereign; others will likewise come to be.

O Rādhikā, through the incarnations of those born of the Lord’s lineage, such as myself and others, and also through the devotees who are followers of the Bhāgavata, these [deeds] bestow auspiciousness.

Thus, in the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, in the second section, the *Tretā-santāna*, on the first day of the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvina, Hari went to the city of Lāpalātrī. There, a Daitya from the ocean arrived and abducted the king’s sister, named Vidyunmaṇi. Both the King and Hari pursued him in their two celestial chariots; having reached Navajīvadvīpa, they fought with the Daitya. Twenty thousand Gaṇas sent forth by Śaṅkara destroyed twenty thousand Daityas. Hari then bestowed the kingdom upon the Gaṇa leader Kāmanāyaka.

The maiden named Vidyunmaṇi chose Hari as her husband. Having purified Dvinediṣṭhapura, she arrived at Trāsamānadvīpa by celestial chariot on the fifth lunar day; from there she went to Vṛndāruka, then to Siṃhaladvīpa, and reaching Pampāsaras, she arrived at Kuṅkumavāpikā on the evening of the seventh day of the bright fortnight of Āśvina. [This concludes] the two hundred and thirty-second chapter, titled "The Description of Welcome, Welfare, Food, Bedding, and so forth."
Śrī Rādhikā said:
O Lord of the gopīs, O Hari, O Kṛṣṇa! You have narrated this most wonderful and auspicious account of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. || 1 ||
Having heard again and again this purifying, divine, and primordial [account], ever new at the beginning of creation, my faith arises to hear it yet once more. (2)
Indeed, I am not satiated by the speech emerging from your lovely mouth, especially so;
O Lord, please cause me to hear again about the great master Bālakṛṣṇa.
What did he do thereafter in the sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpikā? Whatever divine or worldly deed was performed that bestows liberation—[tell me that]. || 4 ||
Whether it be a domestic tale, one concerning holy places, or one filled with wonders—
be it small or great— one should cause it to be heard without any laziness.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Listen, O beloved Rādhā, my dear one, to the excellent stories of Puruṣottama,
which bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation, are divine, and shower the highest bliss upon devotees.
Even as I speak, no satiety arises for me regarding these noble stories concerning my own root, who am known as Puruṣottama.
Moreover, O Rādhikā, you are Puruṣottamī, my very own half;
yet I, having separated myself from you, have remained apart in Goloka.
From my original form, which is the nature of the Supreme Brahman, I have assumed the form of Kṛṣṇa; for your sake, I have manifested in this way to fulfill your desires.
O Rādhikā, you and I, as well as Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa—
though appearing as separate entities, we are not distinct at the root.
Persons like you and like me exist by the millions at the root of the Supreme Brahman;
what then need be said of me alone? || 11 ||
Of that Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa, the son of Śrī Kambharā,
the delight of Gopāla Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of Brahmapriyā, who is Hari himself.
O supreme mind, listen to me as I relate those deeds of the Lord of all, the Supreme Ruler, which bestow bliss. 1.3.
They grant liberation in every way to both listeners and speakers here, and they are auspicious, bringing about the destruction of the latent impressions (vāsanās) of those who remember them. 14.
Those that are sattvic are for the sake of the sattvic; those that are rajasic are for the sake of the rajasic;
those that are tamasic are for the sake of the tamasic; and those that are beyond the gunas are for the sake of the liberated.
Although Hari is devoid of qualities, he joins with Māyā and remains among those possessed of qualities as if he himself were endowed with them, for the sake of securing their happiness.
People who possess women and children imagine him to be like themselves;
for those whose vision is fixed on qualities, he is not divine when he is bound by women, sons, and lineage. (17)
O Rādhā, I am devoid of qualities; what talk can there be of Me, the Supreme Self? O Rādhā, You too are devoid of qualities; what talk can there be of the consorts of Brahman? (18)
Even my cowherds and cowherdesses are divine, as are the cows dwelling in Goloka;
and the divine residents of Vaikuṇṭha—what then can be said of the Supreme Soul?
His divine wonders and his divine, unconditioned activities, as well as the divine yoga of that Hari and his dalliance consisting of tasting and so forth—[all these belong to him]. (2.233.20)
His conjugal union is entirely divine, his lineage is divine,
all his qualities are divine, and even the illusion (māyā) therein is of that same nature.
Everything divine bestows liberation and grants eternal bliss;
even worldly activities, when directed toward Kṛṣṇa, become divine and grant the happiness of liberation.
Even as I describe his greatness, my heart melts;
indeed, I am not able to provide a full description of my own attendants.
Then, O beloved Rādhikā, who indeed could be capable of describing the infinite Lord, the Sovereign who descends in all forms? 24.
I find no satisfaction in describing your virtues for your sake alone; where a worthy recipient may be found, there true fulfillment arises. (25)
Unsatiated, I shall recount the most sweet qualities of Hari;
on the full moon day of Āśvina, after the rising of the moon.
At midnight, he indeed celebrated the Rāsa festival with his beloveds on the exceedingly white shore of a lake, in a most charming mango grove.
Vidyunmaṇipriyā spoke to the most beautiful Bālakṛṣṇa:
"O Kṛṣṇa, the rising of the moon has occurred; whiteness is spreading far and wide. (28)
The night of milk has arisen; my mind desires to take delight.
The minds of all my other sisters as well [are likewise inclined]. (29)
O Lord, Rāsa-delight, even though you are hurrying to enjoy yourself in this autumnal, cool, and peaceful season, please perform that Rāsa-sport for us and grant us auspiciousness. ||2.233.30||
Thus addressed, the illustrious Lord Bālakṛṣṇa,
who is exceedingly affectionate, [acted] in order to fulfill the desires of all his own women.
He assumed a divine form upon reaching his own imperishable abode;
he took up the flute and donned the attire appropriate for the rāsa dance.
And upon his head he wore a crown of peacock feathers;
he applied a tilaka of saffron and collyrium to his eyes. (33)
She wore earrings on her ears and a crescent moon-mark on her cheeks;
she applied decorative dots on her temples and a leaf-pattern on her forehead.
She wore hair spread across her shoulders that resembled the hair of a woman;
she wore bracelets on her wrists and jewels on her forearms.
He placed the Kaustubha gem and strings of pearls upon his neck, along with flower garlands; he wore an auspicious red-colored tunic enriched with gold and stars. ||36||
She wore a firm, blood-red girdle that was comfortable to the touch;
it was made of gold and resounded with a network of tiny bells.
She put on beautiful anklets adorned with clusters of tiny bells,
and rings enriched with diamonds released a fragrant scent.
It nourished a rain of moisture, yet it also released the state of bodilessness; it manifested the condition of youth, yet it revealed the state of being a young woman.
He manifested the state of the innocent girl, the state of the adolescent, and the states of the mature woman and others among all his beloveds.
Then, O Rādhikā, all her other beloveds, having themselves donned attire adorned with erotic grace, prepared themselves to urge Kṛṣṇa forward. (41)
Having approached their beloved, they indeed entreated him:
"O Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa, Mahākṛṣṇa, Bālakṛṣṇa, Lord of the Night! (42)
"Make this night fruitful by fulfilling our hearts' desire, for you are our lover.
Having heard these words of the group of beloved women, which were overflowing with intense passion, he— ||43||
O Rādhikā, Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa quickly rose from His bedchamber,
went outside to the lake, and arrived at the auspicious southern bank.
He caused his heart-pleasing flute to resound with sweet notes;
by the sweetness of those melodious sounds, the hearts of the women were truly captivated. 41.
Having attained coolness, pleasure, and trembling, and indeed having become liquefied,
they experienced a delight called *kampa* and approached Kṛṣṇa.
Then all those maidens, their own wives, having bowed to the sage at the hermitage of Lomaśa and taken leave of him, returned to their own beloved husbands. ||47||
The maidens, filled with all-encompassing bliss and adorned with every ornament, seeing their beloved approaching before them, ran forward swiftly. 48.
Seeing his own beloveds, numbering in the millions and billions, Kṛṣṇa fashioned a vast, divine ground for the Rāsa dance.
In that divine, radiant, and imperishable realm, neither lake, nor mango grove, nor hermitage, nor city, nor even the earth itself is seen.
A great divine garden has arisen, filled with trees bearing every kind of fruit;
it is a hundred yojanas in extent and likewise a hundred stories in height.
The compassionate one arranged for the Rāsa dances of five hundred thousand celestial maidens as well as his own wives. 52.
Having assumed that very form for as long as the beloveds were counted,
the entire divine garden was indeed adorned with divine couples.
Abounding in the splendor of the circular dance (rāsa), he was born with fresh activities;
his principal consorts were Māṇikī, Rādhā, Lakṣmī, Padmāvatī, and Ramā. (54)
Sadguṇā, Mañjulā, Hāsā, Muktā, Lalitā, Jayā, Hemnī, Dayā, Campā, Śānti, Manu, and Maṅgalā. (55)
Then the Śris and Saurāṣṭris came in the number of one hundred and forty; fourteen thousand Meghanādis then arrived; and those Devikas from Ājanābha, mixed together, then came as well. (56)
Sixty million mental lamps arrived, and from that [lamp], ten million wish-fulfilling cows and celestial maidens arrived. (57)
A hundred *ārjanīs*, one *krodhanikā*, ten million *gahvaras*, a hundred thousand *sūcīs*, a hundred thousand *vanadevīs*, and a hundred thousand *rākṣasīs* arrived. (58)
Six thousand Kaṅkatālīs likewise arrived,
and one hundred thousand daughters of the Pitṛs came, eager for the Rāsa dance.
There were five thousand Rāsātalyas and sixteen Vāsantyas;
five hundred Sālamālyas and twenty Nāga maidens.
Ten thousand nāginīs, one thousand śāvadīnīs, one thousand masters of illusion (aindrajālika), and seventy-five sciences (vidyā). ||6 1||
Two thousand Lakṣmaṇyas also came there for the sake of the Rāsa dance,
and at that time, seventy-two thousand Vaidhasyas arrived as well.
The Vaiśvāvasvīs numbered three hundred; the Jummāsemlyas, one thousand;
the Sāntapanyīs, five hundred; and likewise the Sauratyās, one hundred.
Bāleśvarī went to Tila, while Cailavīlā went to Ekalāya;
[the other two] went to the hundred lords of the daughters of Dakṣa and the thousand daughters of Prajāpati.
Twenty thousand female attendants belonging to the ancestors, as well as ten million daughters of subjects beginning with Prācīnabarhis, arrived there. (65)
Sāntāraṇya and the two maidens, Śaibya brought one hundred,
Thārkūṭasthya fifty, and Vīrajārya likewise a hundred.
Sixty Śāktyakṣikas and a hundred Picāśinīs arrived;
two hundred Kāliyāśmas and thirty born from Uralaketu.
Five Krāthakyas and twenty Pārtharājyas arrived;
ten Auṣṭrālyas, five Hāṃkāryas, and five Kāṣṭhalīs.
There were six Tīrās, five Aśvālvinīs, seven Vardhikās, one Anāthā, two thousand Prakīrṇikās, and other maidens. (69)
Seven were named Alpaketu, one was Jayakṛṣṇavakanyā,
twenty-one were Pārīśānyas, and two were the daughters of Indurāyu.
There were fifteen Maudrāṇḍyas, nine Gaṇḍanṛpātmajas,
four Līnorṇyas, and eleven Bṛhaccharas.
Forty female attendants, five lion-like women, five Rāyagāmalikas, and three others arrived. (72)
Ekalā, Stokahomī, and likewise Kāṣṭhayānī;
Ekalā and two Kolakīs—these six, honored by the day, arrived together. (73)
And fifty-one rāyakinnarikās arrived there, and twenty-one daughters of the rāyarokīśvarīs also arrived. ||74||
The Rāṇajityas are twenty, as well as three Vākakṣikas;
likewise there are three Mārīśyas and three Bāleśvaryas. ||75||
There are six Lāmbāryas, seven Navārkīs, and nine Huṇḍaśās;
there is one Kūpeśikā and four Kālīmaṇḍalīnikās. ||76||
Jeleśya, Pārāvārya, and Samāyayu—these five and three [respectively] arrived; as did two daughters of Koṭīśvarī, and likewise three Sātīśikās.
There were also seven *karkaśikās*, four *aṇḍajārikās*, one *bālyarājasī*, and likewise three *saumanikās*. (78)
Two Gavākṣīs turned their faces away, and two arrived at the Rāsa dance; forty-one from the northeast also arrived at the Rāsa dance. ||79||
Thirty-four thousand and forty thousand auspicious maidens from Rājapātya,
as well as twenty thousand maidens from Ājanābha, arrived;
all these together amounted to four crores, that is, four hundred thousand maidens.
Fifty-five thousand and six hundred [verses]. ||81||
Those twenty maidens arrived as offerings to become the wives of Kṛṣṇa;
their companions were the daughters of Kubera, Indra, and Yama.
The Vāyavya, Vaiśvakarmya, Vārkṣya, Raudra, and Vahnija; the Śrāvaṇya, Khānijya, Sāṃvatsarya, and Gopikā [offerings]. 83.
The Prācīnyas, Piśaṅginyas,
Rāśiyānyas, Raumāyaṇyas, Pāraśvas, Dhaivryas, and hosts of Kinnarīs also arrived.
Likewise, there are the immortal ones, the Gaurīs, the Paryas, the Hāritikas,
the Ābriktyas, the Pātālyas, and the celestial Apsarases.
Ten million young Gandharva maidens arrived from the lake of Brahmā,
adorned with amorous grace and illuminated by the radiant circles of light of pure consciousness and bliss.
Indeed, they were gazed upon by their Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the beloved husband, who possesses infinite forms and whose fist strikes with great force against the shattered wheels. (87)
Having become two years older, Rāma took delight with the throngs of Ramās through the rhythmic clapping of palms,
the graceful movements of their feet,
the offering of their sides, the presentation of joined palms, and through songs. (88)
By touching their cheeks, by embracing their shoulders with their hands, and by repeatedly pressing against their chests; ||| 8-9 ||
With various kinds of whirling movements, both backward and forward,
with stepping and tossing, with glances from the eyes, the breasts, and the surrendering of the mind,
and with gestures (*hāva*), expressions (*bhāva*), the reddening of the cheeks, and likewise with embraces, he took his delight.
In this manner, there were millions of mandalas everywhere upon the layers of light.
Indeed, the Rāsinīs were present in the rāsa dance on all sides with their beloveds;
this Supreme Lord Nārāyaṇa is the performer of universal attraction. 9. Re.
By his own sovereign power, the Inner Self bestowed the supreme great bliss—
the divine, impetuous, and eternal bliss of all the senses;
yet he granted that bliss which is never subject to disruption even at the moment of its attainment.
In seeing, touching, hearing, and even smelling [it]. || 94 ||
In tasting and in grasping, in placing the feet and in proclaiming, in embracing and in being at the back, in front, on the sides, and in close proximity; || 95 ||
The Lord placed a great surge of bliss from all his senses into every sense of his young wives;
and when they were drawn by that bliss, they all became absorbed in him.
Having attained satisfaction, they did not desire the bliss of sexual union as something separate at all. || 97 ||
The streams of bliss from beloveds, having merged with the streams of self-bliss, and those streams arising from one's own will, dissolved away.
Indeed, within the stream of Brahman-bliss, what measure can the bliss of desire possess? || 98 ||
In the imperishable bestower of happiness to millions upon millions of lords,
born from union with the limbs of Bālakṛṣṇa— what indeed is this wretched Kāma?
For the Lord himself is the one who casts away the nature of desire within desire during the rāsa dance.
For he, the bestower of all desires and pleasures, delights with his beloveds; O Rādhā, at the sight of his form, the women’s heads bowed low,
and abandoning the circular dance of the rāsa, they lay down beside him.
Having placed their beloved upon their own breasts, they attained great bliss;
having obtained happiness as long as an age, the women reached a state of complete rest.
Then, regaining consciousness, they raised their own beloveds up onto their laps.
They wandered about once more until the moon reached the ocean;
meanwhile, Bālakṛṣṇa sounded his own flute again and again.
Hearing that morning-awakening sound, which was like the cry of a cock, [he rose].
And all the wives, having prepared their attire and ornaments in a uniform manner, [set out].
Having quickly embraced their beloveds and received their permission, they immediately set out in haste to perform their morning rites. (106)
That entire divine, radiant maṇḍala dissolved away,
and there the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake was seen once more as a copper-colored forest.
This earth is the site, that hermitage belongs to Lomaśa;
this is the Rāsa, the marks of the Rāsa-dance, and the places of dalliance.
O Rādhikā, by the will of that Supreme Lord, they all vanished;
then, having bathed in the lake, they performed their daily rites.
They went to their own dwellings, and Bālakṛṣṇa went home;
O Rādhikā, I then arrived there indeed to see Rādhā. (2.233.110)
In what manner did Rādhā take her delight, and how did I become invisible at that time?
You have propitiated the beloved, the enchanting Bālakṛṣṇa. (11.1)
Behold how much indolence has arisen in Rāmaṇa;
see your own beloved sporting within your heart exactly as he is situated there. (11.2)
Behold the Supreme Lord as He vibrates with life; O Gopī, you have not forgotten Him.
O Rādhikā, through the attainment of His supreme bliss, your every desire is fulfilled.

Thus ends the two hundred and thirty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Playful Sport of Rāsa-Bliss with All His Own Wives by Bāla-Kṛṣṇa on the Night of the Full Moon in the Autumn Month of Āśvina," in the second section, the Tretā-Santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Rādhikā, from that time forward— beginning from the dawn of the autumn night—
not even a single moment passes for them in the desire for happiness without Bāla Kṛṣṇa.
Whether on a bed, while eating, traveling, in the forest, bathing, or likewise sitting;
whether in conversation, in dalliance, in singing, or in playful jesting with her friends.
For this Bālakṛṣṇa flashes before their eyes and even within their hearts;
remembering supreme bliss again and again, those whose very being is Kṛṣṇa wander about.
"When will he come again, and when shall we celebrate the autumn festival in this way, O beloved, which bestows such joy upon my heart?"—thus did the lover reflect. (4)
Constantly remembering the bliss of Brahman, the maidens could not find sleep;
Kṛṣṇa indeed fulfilled their desires with his divine forms. || 5 ||
Always together, they all prayed to Acyuta to protect them in their own home, and not indeed in the hermitage of Lomaśa.
Bālakṛṣṇa, however, said to them, "In the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, according to the prescribed rites, I shall lead you to my own temple"; hearing this, they regained their composure.
Then, on the eighth lunar day of the dark fortnight of the month of Urja, which is the birth-tithi of Hari,
Gopālakṛṣṇa arrived and celebrated a festival there.
Fourteen years have passed for Bālakṛṣṇa on this earth;
today, the fifteenth year—the anniversary of his birth—is underway, and it falls on the eighth lunar day (Aṣṭamī).
There, in accordance with his fame, the father of Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa celebrated a supreme festival that surpassed all previous ones.
He remembered Viśvakarman to construct an auspicious pavilion;
and Viśvakarman arrived quickly and bowed at his feet.
For I am indeed a servant of Kṛṣṇa, standing here at his command;
give me an order, and I shall quickly perform it as you desire, however excellent it may be.
Having heard this, the father said to his son, "The fifteenth day has arrived as the auspicious birth anniversary of Bālakṛṣṇa; [prepare] the pavilion."
"Have a vast, new, and divine assembly hall constructed with exceptional care, using divine materials,
located to the north of the assembly of the Lord of Gods."
Saying "So be it," he then bowed to the Lord, the beloved of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, and went to his side to worship him; having worshipped him, he attained his favor. || 15 ||
Having quickly received the command, he envisioned a divine pavilion that was heart-pleasing;
for the order had been given to construct an unprecedented pavilion, and so it shall be.
I shall construct a divine pavilion upon the four great works,
so that the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake may be situated beneath it.
Having thus mentally envisioned the image within the pavilion in his heart,
he then remembered that [image] extending for four dhanus and one yojana in length.
The bow of Indra, the bow of Śaṅkara, and the bow of Viṣṇu;
and also the firm, auspicious bow of Manobhava, which is capable of bearing a great burden.
In the eastern direction of Aśvapaṭṭasaraḥ,
he established the very temple of Indra, extending long from south to north and consisting of masonry;
and likewise, he established the bow of Īśa in the northern direction.
In the west he established the Vaiṣṇava [liṅga], and it remained exactly so; and in the south he established the Kāma [liṅga], and it remained exactly so.
On a stretch of ground one *yojana* in length, he caused eight boundary markers to be placed;
thus he fashioned a square enclosure in the form of a fourfold path.
There he caused rays of the sun, which are repositories of splendor,
to be placed by means of sun-stones, moon-stones, crystals, and gems.
Having fashioned that square enclosure as the very form of a wall,
he created a golden rampart, rich with gate-towers and provided with mechanical devices.
He quickly caused a beautiful assembly hall to be constructed in the center,
with a canopy made of plaster-like material produced from the rays of the moon.
It was endowed with pillars possessing the rich splendor of creepers born from nectar,
and its middle portion was circular, shining with a golden seat on its sides.
