It was adorned with the light of the planets, lunar mansions, stars, and so forth, which served as its lamps,
and it was endowed with the shadow of a canopy formed by the mass of Kaustubha gems clinging to it.
As long as she wore a garland possessing a splendor corresponding to the very nature of Lakṣmī herself,
and as long as she moved with a natural grace worthy of the dances, offerings, and songs of the Apsarases.
She who possesses the four assemblies— the Sudharmā, the Brahmābhūmi, the Īśī, and the Sabhā—
and is accompanied by the Kāmadhenu cow, the Kalpalatā creeper, and the Cintāmaṇi jewel.

It was adorned with wish-fulfilling creepers, the celestial wish-granting tree, and inexhaustible vessels, and was endowed with fragrances from all quarters, the taste of all flavors, and a breeze pleasant to the touch.
The auspicious [goddess], who is the locus of all powers such as hearing from afar and seeing from afar, in whom Hari is seen in embodied form within whatever objects exist. (3.1)
The self-luminous Lord, the sovereign of the devotees of Bālakṛṣṇa,
commanded that Tvaṣṭṛ should fashion the forms exactly as he had directed.
The Lord Tvaṣṭṛ fashioned all liberated forms as the very nature of the Imperishable, and likewise the individual forms of those who are liberated.
Within them, the auspicious Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa is seen as the inner self, as well as all kinds of incarnations and the consorts of those incarnations. (34)
In those [assemblies], the auspicious Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa is seen as the inner self within the military arrays, the commanders of the arrays, and likewise the lords and their consorts.
The Siddhas, the Sāṃkhya-yoginīs, the Satyas, the Sādhyas, the Sādhus, the Ṛṣis, the Pitṛs, the Devas, and the Devīs are their husbands. (36)
The human beings, the guardians of the quarters and other world-protectors together with their wives,
all the offspring of Kaśyapa, and all the divine principles in their entirety.
The Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, Gaṇeśas, and other mountain lords, as well as renowned earthly kings, were appointed by Viśvakarman. || 38 ||
Within all of them, the divine Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa was visible.
Having thus prepared this entirely new assembly hall, complete with pavilions,
he announced it to his father on the seventh lunar day when half the night had passed.
Seeing the steps on all sides, his father became pleased.
He saw the paths for vehicles, the spaces between the celestial palaces,
the tracks for elephants, and the routes for chariots and foot-soldiers.
Seeing the roads with their resting places for repose, and the gardens laid out on all sides, filled with fruits and flowers, the father indeed rejoiced.
Beholding those things variegated with many colors, the father indeed rejoiced;
everywhere there, he beheld his own son dwelling within his heart.
Everything exists as being of the nature of reality, and this is a distinguished illustration of that;
it was fashioned on earth by Tvaṣṭṛ at the command and through the inspiration of Hari.
A divine lake is seen below the summit of the earthly mountain,
rich with the beauty of ten million lotuses and graced by the serpent Śeṣa in the form of a tortoise.
Thus, having beheld that divine pavilion, rich with the splendor visible even from the netherworld (Pātāla) and fashioned like a mantle of light, [he saw] the throne of Hari.
He beheld that supreme, great, and divine throne, elevated above all others,
fashioned from gold produced by divine beings, and supported by elephant pedestals.
Within the parts of the lion-throne, all divine, auspicious, and celestial lion-thrones, together with their presiding deities, were indeed fashioned. 48.
The Kārṣṇa, the Nārāyaṇa, the Vāsudevīya, the Bhauma, the Acyuta, the Sādāśaiva, the Hairaṇyagārbha, and likewise the Vairājaka. ||49||
The realm of Brahmā, that of Indra, that of Varuṇa, and likewise that of Yama; the realm of Kubera, that of Agni, that of Anila, that of Īśāna, and likewise that of Nairṛta.
The remaining throne of Saura, as well as all other thrones, were contained within the interior of Kṛṣṇāsana.
Tvaṣṭṛ indeed fashioned such a divine elephant-throne,
upon that elephant-throne [adorned] with clusters of divine pearls and rows of bells.
In that most beautiful, great, divine, and fragrant pavilion, which was adorned by those standing with handfuls of flowers and hands bearing unbroken grains and sandalwood paste.
Within that [palace], which was radiant on all sides with syllables and luminous substances,
the great Lord Kṛṣṇa shone forth, manifesting in infinite forms.
The illustrious Gopālakṛṣṇa, beholding that supreme and most divine throne for his son, rejoiced; indeed, the entire family rejoiced as well.
Brahmapriyā and the other wives rejoiced with extreme intensity,
seeing the universal sovereignty of their own husband upon his throne.
Then, having made such an arrangement, Tvaṣṭṛ became filled with joy;
seeing his own unprecedented creation, he indeed attributed it to the grace of Hari.
He considered that great throne, which had arisen from his own intellect though it was unworthy of him, to be the internal abode of its Lord and its creator.
Then Gopālakṛṣṇa also, beholding the pavilion pervaded by splendor and that sacred field made imperishable by the radiance of the pavilion, [proceeded].
Seeing him shining like the sun, he quickly became bewildered at dawn;
he then awakened Gaṇeśa, Īśāna, Satī, and Lomaśa.
He is indeed Sat-Cit-Ānanda, as well as Tuṣita and Sadāśiva;
he is Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇī, as well as Sanatkumāra and Ṛbhu.
He quickly commanded:
"Let them go forth in every direction at once, intent upon bestowing blessings on the occasion of Kṛṣṇa’s Janmāṣṭamī."
May those created by Brahmā, those created by Īśvara, and those created by the individual soul, who reside upon this earth,
come together in Saurāṣṭra to the temple of Gopālakṛṣṇa.
"May all who have gathered increase [our merit] on this festival of the eighth day!"—having formed this hope, they quickly departed for another world. (64)
The liberated ones went to their respective abodes, Gaṇeśa went to the station of Śaṅkara,
Īśāna went to Satyaloka, and [Gaṇeśa] went to the dwellings of the virtuous Satī.
Lomaśa, however, quickly went to the great sages, the Tuṣitas, the circle of the Pitṛs, and to Sadāśiva among the worlds of the Īśvaras.
Liberated into the state of being, consciousness, and bliss (saccidānanda), he indeed went to the abodes of Viṣṇu;
and Lakṣmī, the bestower of all things among the goddesses, then departed for the worlds.
Then Nārāyaṇī went to Badarī, Kṣīra, and Śveta;
and the blessed Sanatkumāra traversed all the worlds in an instant.
Assuming various forms, they departed swiftly in every direction;
having reached those respective places, they were honored by the presiding deities.
Having offered their invitations, they arrived at the field of syllables;
and all of them, being thus invited, were accompanied by their families and retinues.

With hearts blossoming with joy, quickly endowed with the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) and other aesthetic moods, and accompanied by divine offerings, celestial chariots, and vehicles, [they departed]. (71)
They arrived at the sacred precinct of Kuṅkumavāpī, at the divine pavilion;
even at dawn, Hari had bathed and performed his worship and salutations.
Having served the elders and being adorned in every way,
he likewise bowed with great joy to all those beloved of Brahmā.
Endowed with blessings from his mother and having performed the auspicious marriage-thread ceremony,
he assumed a divine form and was attended by hosts of great sages.
He went to that pavilion, seated upon an elephant-throne amidst the resonant sounds of musical instruments,
accompanied by the songs of women and the recitation of Vedic mantras.
Having arrived, Kṛṣṇa sat down, and then shouts of victory arose;
Lomaśa honored him with Vedic mantras and sandalwood paste.
All the great sages also worshipped the Imperishable One;
they magnified him with blessings, honored him with unbroken grains, and performed acts of adoration.
His mother applied the *tilaka* to him, his father gave him a crown, the wives of Brahmā offered garlands of flowers, and Śrī then fashioned the crescent moon upon him.
All those who had gathered at the pavilion performed the *ārārtrika* rite;
then, beholding him of such divine form, the inhabitants of Saurāṣṭra [were struck with wonder]. (79)
There they became absorbed, having attained supreme meditative concentration;
the sounds of the Vedas arose from the Brahmins there on all sides.
The elder brother, the Lord Śuka, and Vallabha as well followed;
they all gave great gifts and donations there in their entirety. ||81||
Then those who had been liberated arrived from the imperishable world (akṣara-loka);
having honored Bālakṛṣṇa, they then performed the ārātrika ceremony for him.
Then they entered the beautiful seats shown by their attendants;
thereafter, the incarnations arrived along with their wives and their retinues.
O Rādhikā, I then came there together with you;
Nārāyaṇa also arrived there, filled with joy, accompanied by Lakṣmī. (84)
All the other Nārāyaṇas, each endowed with their own respective powers, arrived, offered worship, and sat down upon the seats that had been shown to them. (85)
Likewise, the Vyūhas and Īśvara and others, along with the Īśvarīs, arrived there;
they worshipped him with offerings and sat down upon the seats that were shown to them.
Brahmā and the other lords of the three worlds, indeed innumerable, arrived;
they honored him with offerings and sat down upon the seats that were shown to them.
The sages, their fathers, the gods, the goddesses, and the guardians of the quarters came there with their families. (88)
The Ādityas, Vasus, and Rudras, together with their Śaktis, arrived;
they worshipped him with offerings and entered once he had indicated a seat for them.
Virtuous men and virtuous women, as well as truthful ones, arrived;
those dwelling in the netherworld, those dwelling in the forests, and those dwelling on the mountains all came together.
Siddhas, Cāraṇas, Gandharvas, Vidyādharas, Uragas, Rākṣasas,
Kinnaras, and Kiṃpuruṣas arrived and worshipped the Imperishable One.
Sacred fords, oceans, rivers, lakes, and groups of shrines; trees, divine creepers, cows, and likewise birds—[all these were present]. (92)
Exquisitely divine vehicles, male servants, and female servants likewise arrived;
they honored him with offerings and magnified him with blessings.
And the forms of the gods and others who dwell in the various worlds sat upon thrones and other seats within the pavilion endowed with divine splendor. (94)
Having observed their own forms upon the elephant-thrones everywhere within the pavilion, they were indeed struck with great wonder.
For this is not the work of the gods, nor of the divine Tvaṣṭṛ;
we have no access to his craftsmanship regarding the creation of the very nature of the syllables and so forth. (9.6)
Therefore, its creator must indeed be one established in the eight syllables; it is inferred that this [world] was fashioned by dwelling in the abode of Brahman.
Thus all those seated within the decorated pavilion remained filled with doubt;
for they gazed intently at Bālakṛṣṇa amidst those very principles (tattvas).
Seeing Kṛṣṇa indeed entered into the womb, they all became bewildered;
thus, until midday, there was worship and the offering of blessings for his growth.
There, the dancing of Hari ceased, as did that of the Apsarases;
instead, there arose divine singing and the recitation of the Saṃhitās.
There were also narrative accounts and songs of praise for Hari,
performed by Vetradhāra, Hemanta, and Vasantaka.
The sounding of the great drum, rich in victory, was proclaimed;
and there, Satyāmbikā stood with palms joined in reverence to dispel his sorrow.
His mother placed the *sucandraka* mark, accompanied by unbroken rice-grains (*akṣata*), upon his forehead.
Thus blessings were bestowed, and likewise betel-leaf was offered.
In the assembly hall, sugar and other refreshments, as well as khārikā and other grains, were distributed; likewise, suitable drinks, betel leaves, and other items were prepared.
Then, for all those who had arrived, the Lord of Masters offered a warm welcome and blessings, expressing his deep affection with sweet words.
The offering of nectars, ambrosias, and sweet foods;
the providing of drinks, fragrant substances, and betel leaves. 106.
He bestowed garlands, flower wreaths, and clusters of blossoms;
indeed, he rendered manifold honors to those who had come for the sake of the pavilion.
The entire three worlds were present there at that festival;
then, in the morning, according to the ritual rules, Rādhikā’s turn for the removal of her veil arrived.
The dignified ones went to where their dwellings had been assigned;
they found rest in divine palaces for half the day.

Thus ends the two hundred and thirty-fourth chapter, titled "Description of the Splendor of the Divine Pavilion, the Arrival of the Invited Guests, the Worship of Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Bālakṛṣṇasvāmī, and the Honoring of the Great Assembly," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, on the occasion of the fifteenth birth-anniversary festival of Hari.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Rādhikā; all the people and others who arrived there obtained the grace of Hari and were filled with joy.
At midday, the brahmins performed the rite of benediction for Bālakṛṣṇa;
the women sang songs, and then the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) took place.
Then Bālakṛṣṇa indeed revealed his own form,
which resides in the abode beyond the Imperishable (Akṣara), divine, and the most excellent among the excellent.
In the pavilion and upon the comfortable seat, whatever deities are stationed within, as well as the worlds, the world-protectors, and the powers that are incarnations of Īśvara; || 4 ||
As Bālakṛṣṇa remained in his totality,
all those inhabitants of every creation were seen to be liberated from the cycle of rebirth.
There the entire universe is seen, consisting of its fourteen realms;
the surface of the earth is seen, and likewise the land of Saurāṣṭra is seen.
The saffron pond is seen, and likewise the assembly hall is seen;
the pavilion is seen, and Kṛṣṇa’s beloved is seen.
Thus, everything regarding Śrī Hari became visible to the eyes of all his attendants;
thereafter, they beheld Bālakṛṣṇa within their own hearts.
The divine one, the abode of divine qualities, the son of Kambharā, the Great Lord,
the cowherd boy, the master and lord of Brahmā’s beloved and the others.
Then, having displayed his divine form, Hari thereafter assumed his own form as a child; indeed, the dismissal from the assembly took place.
The illustrious Gopālakṛṣṇa gave food to everyone—various kinds of sweetmeats and various kinds of drinks. (11)
Then, having bestowed leave-taking accompanied by gifts and honors,
those residing in the other world departed for various regions in every way.
There, an assembly of the people from the Saurāṣṭra region became firmly established;
likewise, a wrestling match took place at night before Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa.
Then, various dramatic performances took place before Śrī Kṛṣṇa;
there were diverse songs and musical concerts as well.
And there, during the night, foods and drinks were provided repeatedly;
likewise, dances by courtesans took place throughout the night. (15)
Indeed, rewards were given to the laborers;
having completed everything, at midnight the people fell into sleep from exhaustion. (16)
Having risen early in the morning, having performed auspicious rites with musical instruments and other ceremonies,
and having bowed to Hari and received his leave, they departed for their homes.
And having received the command, Viśvakarman caused that excellent pavilion to vanish even as he was there, in a mere moment at dawn.
To him, Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa gave an excellent reward: a golden crown and an unsurpassed necklace for the neck.
The Lord, out of compassion, bestowed upon him divine intellect and granted him the power of vision everywhere throughout the three worlds.
When the pavilion was suddenly removed, Lake Aśvapaṭṭasara became visible;
all the people, observing the duty of the morning twilight prayer, bathed there at dawn.
In this manner, O Rādhikā,
the fifteenth birthday of Śrī Hari passed away, bringing his fifteenth year to completion.
Indeed, many people come for the sake of seeing Śrī Hari;
consequently, a great throng of men occurs there day and night. (23)
From the lowly down to the outcaste Cāṇḍālas, they all come and go,
having obtained the compassion of the King of Kings, which takes the form of his grace.
Having obtained food and other things, they became happy;
O Rādhā, at that time on the Jayantī day, a certain Cāṇḍāla arrived there.
There was one named Tāmasākṣi, accompanied by his wife and sons; he was a devotee of Hari, and therefore he never committed theft in any way whatsoever.
He did not speak untruth, nor did he practice deceit;
dwelling constantly in Calālaya, he performed the work of cleaning the village.
With the food he obtains, he indeed constantly maintains his body alone;
however, the food acquired through sweeping is never sufficient. (28)
There is no other outcaste in the village who is so esteemed as to be permitted to perform this task; for he never commits violence, nor does he ever act unjustly.
Likewise, he does not even wander about for the sake of acquiring food like a beggar;
yet people, regarding him as a *caṇḍāla* and an unworthy recipient, do not give to him either. (2.235.30)
Then, having encountered hardship and being excessively emaciated by the pain of hunger, he, together with his family and accompanied by his five sons, [remained there]. ||3 1 ||
Likewise, accompanied by two maidens and even by children who lack effort,
he came in person on the Jayantī day as the ninth [incarnation], joined by his wife.
Taking refuge in the shade of a banyan tree on the bank of the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake,
he beheld Bālakṛṣṇa ever anew.
Even with his family, he performed the spinning of garlands;
on that festive day, he obtained a full measure of alms-food both by day and by night.
On the ninth day he obtained it, and on the tenth day he indeed obtained it;
however, on the eleventh day, no food was obtained at all because of his observance of the vow.
Indeed, being hungry along with his family, he remained in a state of fasting day and night;
at night, accompanied by his wife and children, he was overcome by a state of darkness.
With his heart broken by hunger and other afflictions, and desiring to die, he fell with great force into the lake; his wife fell after him in order to hold him back.
And the sons and daughters, weeping, cried out to their parents;
then, due to the depth of the water, they reached the bottom.
At the time after midnight, no one knew this;
having drunk that water of yours, they then became as if dead. (3.9)
Remembering Bālakṛṣṇa within their own hearts, these people felt as if they were dead;
then the Lord Bālakṛṣṇa also quickly awakened.
Having left his bed during the night of darkness, O Rādhikā,
Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa, in the form of Vāsudeva, went to the lake within the waters.
Then the four-armed Lord, the true Master, entered while taking hold of his devotee, the dog-cooker (Śvapākin),
and brought his wife from the bank outside.
Again, Hari went into the water and drew out the two daughters as well as the son from the water;
having placed them on the bank, he returned once more to the water.
Having quickly entered, Hari likewise brought forth his four sons and protected them for a moment on the bank.
Then the Blessed One drew forth the children, the wife, and the husband;
likewise Vāsudeva, Aniruddha, Pradyumna, and Saṅkarṣaṇa. ||45||
Having assumed the fourfold posture and holding them separately by their feet,
he lifted them up and kept them face-down for exactly one ghaṭikā.
In that very manner, he held back the exit of the swallowed water from their mouths, having caused them to regain consciousness in every respect. (47)

Having placed [the vessel] below with its opening downward, one should arrange small sticks (*kāṇḍikā*) around it on all sides, together with *vaṭa* leaves and other materials, in order to eliminate the cold. 48.
Having gathered [the materials] there quickly, the Lord kindled the fire;
having placed pieces of wood therein, he performed the heating.
Śrī Hari himself gradually scorched them all,
bringing their life-breaths from the crown of the head into the cavity of the heart.
Having attained the power of wakefulness and beholding the fourfold form beginning with Vāsudeva, they quickly bowed at the feet of the Lord.
There, at the end of the night on the eleventh day, they praised Hari:
"O Lord of the wretched, the helpless, and the poor! O Sustainer and Protector! (52)
We, though outcastes, bow with reverence at your feet;
you are the creator, you are the giver of food, you are the sustainer, and indeed you are the nourisher.
"You alone are the giver of breath, for you have indeed restored our lives from the water;
we, who were always suffering from the lack of food, are now suffering from the lack of life. (54)
Indeed, out of a state of detachment from sufferings, they offered their lives into the water even at the cost of their own deaths;
for it was by obtaining that memory [of the teaching] within the waters that they performed the casting away of their bodies.
There, you, our lord of life, arrived and performed our deliverance;
just as the protection of our bodies was provided, so too was the protection of our lives ensured. (56)
O Lord, protect us by granting us our lives and providing for our livelihood;
or else, lead us, your devoted servants, to the world of Brahmā.
Protection was afforded by you within the womb even during the union with the embryo;
protection was afforded on the path of birth, and you were protected even in the state of infancy.
Even now, indeed, you have sustained the trees, the creepers, the beasts, the insects, and likewise the birds with food and other provisions. (59)
O Protector, though you are already protected by [others], protect us here; protect us!
You are the one who raises up the lowly and the remover of the suffering of those who suffer. (2.235.60)
To those who are without refuge, you are considered the father who provides a support;
you are the resort for the young, and you are the life of all living beings. (6.1)
You are the refuge for those fallen into calamity and the savior of those sinking [in the ocean];
you are the remover of the suffering of the afflicted. O Lord of Lakṣmī, take away my distress! (62)
O Lord of the Earth, be the provider of food and clothing to those deprived of food and clothing;
be the ordainer of good fortune for the unfortunate. (63)
"O Blessed One, I was submerged in a lake due to the suffering caused by lack of food;
together with my family, I was rescued by you, the compassionate one, during the night. (64)
Therefore, O Acyuta, having shown full compassion, destroy the suffering caused by hunger and cold for me, your devotee, who has fallen for refuge in you.
Having spoken thus, she joyfully placed her head upon the ground with palms joined in reverence and bowed repeatedly while gazing at the glorious Bālakṛṣṇa.
The Blessed One manifested the forms of Vāsudeva and others;
then, assuming the form of Bālakṛṣṇa, he spoke to Tāmasākṣika.
Dwell here in this city with your family at all times;
perform the cleaning and other duties here upon the streets and the royal highways. (68)
Your livelihood shall be maintained through the nature of your clothing and other such items;
tomorrow morning, I will give you a beautiful house suitable for your residence.
Do not be distressed, O devotee; do not act thus ever again.
This sin is equal to self-destruction and is a great obstacle to liberation.
Nothing else exists beyond that; therefore, do not commit suicide.
There is no greater merit equal to the gift of one's own life. 71.
There is no other means for attaining liberation than this; therefore, one should indeed protect one's life.
Accept this food as well—sweetmeats and even the fruit of meritorious works (pūrta). ||72||
Having spoken thus, Vāsudeva gave him the sweet food he had brought;
full of compassion, he also gave garments to his family.
"Come to the front of my gate in the morning; I shall give you a house.
I am going to my mansion; resort to me and remain asleep. (74)
Having spoken thus, O Rādhikā, the glorious Bālakṛṣṇa vanished;
and the Cāṇḍāla became filled with grace and performed worship of Hari. (75)
With the clapping of their hands, they all performed the glorification of Kṛṣṇa;
having bathed in the morning, all those deeply devoted ones went to the gateway of Hari. (76)
Indeed, Bālakṛṣṇa himself, for the sake of protecting his devotee,
rose from his elephant-throne and then proceeded toward the city gate.
He envisioned a most beautiful house within the mango grove—
a lovely, new dwelling resplendent with trees, creepers, and grass.
It was spacious, equipped with a broom, a hearth, a mortar, and other such items; it was provided with a water-pot and a grinding stone, as well as a bed and other furnishings.
It was filled with grain in granaries, well-stocked with all kinds of food and soups,
abundant with vegetable gardens and leafy plots, and graced by the water of wells.
Accompanied by a milch cow, beautiful, circular with four enclosures and so forth—thus Kṛṣṇa made that excellent abode endowed with his own wonderful [decoration]. (81)
He gave everything endowed with splendor to that dog-cooker;
having reached his house, the devotee became pleased and rejoiced. (82)
At that time, he indeed received the Vaiṣṇava mantra from Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa:
"Obeisance to Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa; I am Your servant; deliver me, O Lord! (83)
Thus the Blessed One, the son of Kaṃbhārā, gave him this mantra:
"In the village, at the Kumakuma pond, and in the city, perform cleaning and other such duties. (84)
He indeed appointed that devoted follower, who was untainted by tamas, to perform [the task];
and he too, having obtained this auspicious gain, practiced devotion day and night.
His family constantly served Śrī Hari in embodied form;
and his only daughter, the goddess Dugdhikā, remained a celibate student (brahmacāriṇī).
Through devotion to Kṛṣṇa, she became established in samādhi and possessed a divine body;
she was the goddess Dugdhikā, the family deity of the Cāṇḍālas. (87)
But there was always in the world one named Mantrikā, who devoted herself to Bālakṛṣṇa and was another maiden well-versed in the performance of many mantras. (88)
Through the practice of devotion to Hari, she indeed became possessed of self-mastery;
whatever Mantra he would compose, she would speak it truly and even teach it to others. (89)
That very mantra becomes powerful and likewise fruitful;
thus she became a master of mantras, capable of manifesting the power of the mantra.
Consequently, that [mantra] became the ṛṣi for the mantras of the Cāṇḍāla caste;
all five sons were truly devoted, virtuous, and endowed with devotion. || 91 ||
In his own hermitage, they were born as leaders of the community;
for those virtuous ones became the gurus of the Cāṇḍālas through their devotion.
After a long time had passed, their parents, filled with devotion and possessing divine hearts, became their attendants and then cast off their bodies. (93)
Yayāti and Yātudhāna attained the imperishable abode of Śrī Hari upon liberation;
O Rādhā, in the course of time, they became sons and two virtuous daughters through their devotion.
Having cast off their bodies, they went to the eternal abode of Bālakṛṣṇa.
Thus, the Blessed Lord indeed protected his devotees for Rādhā. 95.
The Great Lord also provided for their nourishment and gave them a livelihood; furthermore, at the end, he granted liberation even to the outcastes (śvapacas). 96.
Those who are helpless, poor, wretched, or bereft of fortune—even they, having gone to the land of Hari at the site of Kuṅkumavāpikā, [attain their goal]. (97)
Those who will perform service and offer their respective bodies, lives, hearts, wealth, and families; (98)
Bālakṛṣṇa will certainly provide protection for them in every way;
having granted them worldly enjoyment in this world, he will then indeed bestow liberation. 99.
From reading this, from hearing it, from chanting it, and even from teaching it, there shall indeed be both enjoyment and liberation, O Rādhikā; there is no doubt in this matter.

Thus ends the two hundred and thirty-fifth chapter, titled "The Avoidance of the Pavilion, the Distribution of Gifts at the Mahīmāna Festival, and the Protection, Nourishment, and Liberation of the Cāṇḍāla Devotee named Tāmasākṣi along with his Family who were Submerged in Water," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Rādhikā, on the thirteenth day of the month of Dhanus, Bālakṛṣṇa performed the worship of Dhanalakṣmī according to the prescribed rites.
He had his own beloved Lakṣmī fashioned as a golden image, a beautiful form intended for distribution as a gift, according to the prescribed rites.
He worshipped him with the sixteen primary services and offerings such as sandalwood paste,
and he fed him in many ways with cooked foods made from the nine kinds of grains.
Then, having seated his own wife Lakṣmī, the goddess Śrī, who was visibly present before him upon a golden throne, he worshipped her with sandalwood paste and other offerings.
Kṛṣṇa himself indeed fashioned the hair-dress and other ornaments for the two women; having arranged their braided locks, he himself tied the knots of their tresses.
And there she strung together flower garlands and ornaments,
using excellent jewels for decoration, diamonds, collyrium, and other such items.
He performed the adornment of those two with saffron, sandalwood paste and the like, with filaments, with water-jars and other vessels, with flower garlands, and with drops of unguents and so forth.
He performed the Aratritra rite before the two maidens who were visibly present; for both of them were well-pleased and offered their blessings.
They both said, "O Lord of Śrī, O Lord of Lakṣmī, perform the marriage!
And Śrīpati replied, "O Lord of Lakṣmī, come together with the auspicious moment."
Become the Lord of Rādhā, the Lord of Ramā, and the Lord of Padmāvatī; become the Lord of Māṇikī and also the Lord of Brahmapriyā.
"O Destroyer of Suffering, Lord of Lakṣmī, become my husband through the rite of marriage; become my husband by means of this union, for you are the lord of countless wives already brought here."
"O Kṛṣṇa, this time for your marriage has arrived;
O Lord, you are now a fit youth, possessing the sprouts of manhood. (12)
O Śrīkṛṣṇa, at this auspicious moment, become Lakṣmīkṛṣṇa quickly;
we all, being maidens, await our marriage.
May you be possessed of fortune, wealth, excellence, prosperity, and a noble lineage;
even now, you are praised as a celibate student and a great yogi. 14.
Moreover, by the power of our yoga, you shall become the fulfiller of our desires;
it remains forever unimpaired. For what indeed is impossible for a yogi? (15)
"Nevertheless, perform the wedding festival for Kṛṣṇa according to the prescribed rites.
Thus addressed, the Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa replied, "So be it."
"In the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, I shall perform the marriage ceremony for me and all these women;
therefore, both of you and the others must maintain your composure."
Having spoken thus and offered the priestly fee (*dakṣiṇā*), he performed the ritual dismissal (*visarjana*).
He also gave various kinds of sacrificial fees to the venerable sage Lomaśa.
He also gave two golden images to the venerable sage Lomaśa;
he gave sacrificial fees to the Brahmins, as well as golden vessels and wealth.
Having thus celebrated a great festival, Hari went to the lake,
to the Vāsudevīya Tīrtha, where the Cāṇḍāla had been uplifted.
Having bathed there at Vyūhatīrtha, Hari went to the banyan tree;
there, all the beloveds of Brahmā had arrived to sport.
Having given them wealth indeed brought by Kubera, he remained there.
Having honored all the wives with gifts such as maidens and sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā), he... || 22 ||
Having propitiated all the necessary materials and made his offering, he approached the edge of the bank under the pretext of cleaning his teeth in order to sport at the barburaka tree.
Then Bālakṛṣṇa indeed went to touch Rādhikā;
meanwhile, all those women, beginning with Brahmapriyā, were gazing upon Mādhava.
As he was walking, having gone to the top of a barbuṭa tree and touching it,
he then [reached] a terminal branch suitable for cleaning the teeth.
And the women beheld him grasping and pulling [the tree],
when suddenly that babūra tree sprang up together with its very roots.
He prostrated himself upon the ground, and from that [place] there suddenly appeared another great divine being, resembling Mahendra. || 27 ||
Having seen Hari, he paid obeisance and fell upon the earth at his feet;
he quickly performed prostration like a staff and praised the Supreme Lord. || 28 ||
O Supreme Lord, ocean of mercy, having remembered you, I have been delivered by you;
you are the supreme lord, the savior of living beings and the bestower of liberation.
You abide here as the granter of grace in order to uplift all people.
One with a physical eye does not recognize you as the Supreme Person.
I have attained You, the Supreme Lord, the deliverer from the womb of the tree;
today, indeed, by Your command, I shall go to the divine heaven.
Having spoken thus, she bowed down and, having offered flowers at the feet of Mādhava, desired to depart.
Just then, all those beloved wives of Brahmā arrived there, filled with supreme wonder, and questioned their beloved.
"Who is this that has emerged from the tree, and how was the tree felled?
We have a great curiosity regarding this; O Lord, tell us the cause of it. (34)
Having heard this, Bālakṛṣṇa also commanded that man to describe his entire account and his own story before him.
The king, having prostrated before them all, related this wonderful account:
"In former times, I was indeed a sovereign emperor on the banks of the Sābhra in Gaurjara."
There was indeed a king named Barbura, devoted to righteous deeds, skilled in protecting his subjects, and a worshiper of the gods and the virtuous. || 37 ||
Constantly devoted to vows and charity, always serving the elderly, intent upon the stories of Kṛṣṇa, such a Vaiṣṇava is a punisher of the wicked. (38)
Once,
however, accompanied by only a few servants, I went deep into the forest on the banks of the Sābhramatī in the vast wilderness to survey the woods.
While traveling on foot through a distant forest, he beheld a divine horse,
possessing seven forms, with a coat of hair as radiant as gold.
He is white in the face, red at the hooves and the lips,
dark brown on the tail, the back, and the belly, while the neck is indeed blue.
It is yellow in the ear and on the lateral parts, tawny in the shanks,
green in the channels of the veins, and variegated at all the joints of the limbs.
Having beheld such a form—variegated, firm, well-nourished, endowed with strength, and beautiful—I set my mind upon seizing it. (43)
Having slowly approached his side so that he might feel secure,
he then seized him by the ear with his hand and by the neck with his rein.
Having taken hold of it, I made him sit upon its back;
and he, being urged by me, proceeded exactly as directed.
I do not know from where this man’s simplicity has come, nor his straightforwardness;
for however I try to move him, he simply goes forward. (46)
Having thus recognized him as a divine steed, he led him to my city;
considering it his own good fortune, he became repeatedly filled with joy.
"I shall certainly not leave that divine horse even for a moment at a distance.
Thereupon, he became enraged and, speaking with fury, cursed me. (48)
Since you do not release me at all, nor do you recognize me as such, you find no satisfaction at all in seeing me bound in fetters. (49)
Having understood my true nature, you do not grant me what is sweet out of sincere affection;
instead, perceiving me as a beast in this bondage, you have made me your own and hold me captive.
Therefore, O King, by my curse, become a thorny barbara tree in that forest; endure suffering there day and night. (5.1)
Having been addressed thus, I then quickly recognized that sage as the most worshipful one;
for the sake of swift liberation, I fell at his feet. (52)
Whether you are that god, or a sage, or anyone else whom I have sought out—you are unknown to me and yet worthy of my worship; please grant forgiveness to this fool.
Act in such a way that the suffering of this curse may be swiftly removed;
O Lord, reveal your own form to me, for I bow before you. (54)
"O Lord, this offense was committed by me through ignorance and not otherwise;
therefore, having granted supreme forgiveness, reveal your own true form. (55)
Thus repeatedly entreated, that great Ṛṣi, the horse,
vanished and became known by the name Āśvalāyana himself, the preceptor of the royal lineage.
Realizing that he was my family preceptor, I wept profusely;
becoming most humble, I begged for forgiveness so that the curse might be withdrawn.
A son may commit an offense, but a father reconciles him; a father forgives day and night.
For even teachers desire the defeat of their own disciples. ||58||
"O venerable one, out of ignorance, greed for horses, and my royal status, I have committed an offense against you;
please forgive me and grant me peace.
Thus entreated, the blessed sage Aśvalāyana—
Having granted me forgiveness there, he said: "O King, what shall I say to you? (2.236.60)
"Indeed, merit is entirely destroyed by insulting great beings, by overstepping their seats, and by the omission of honoring those worthy of honor.
Your entire merit has indeed perished because you mounted my back."
There is no longer any devotion to the king, and even you have been consumed by a curse.
"After you have experienced the effects of the curse, heaven will quickly be yours.
O King, from union with another's wife, from insulting one's gurus, and from causing pain to others, the destruction of one's lifespan indeed occurs. (65)
And because of grasping at false positions, and because of reviling gods and virtuous men. || 64 ||
Indeed, by committing acts of malice toward the virtuous, the destruction of one's lifespan occurs;
likewise, from causing suffering to one's parents and even from the oppression of one's wives.
Indeed, from the act of violence, the destruction of one's lifespan occurs;
likewise, from the faults of intoxicants, meat, sexual indulgence, and so forth, there arises the oppression of dharma.
Furthermore, the destruction of one's lifespan arises from defects such as possession by malevolent spirits;
you have committed a great offense, yet I did not speak of it out of shame. (67)
"Since I am her preceptor and have been in the form of a horse in the forest, this king has seen me; he might not recognize me as his preceptor. (68)
Thus, I did not turn back your form in your presence;
for after this moment, the king will depart far away.
Having reflected thus, the horse assumed my form;
meanwhile, I turned back and came into your presence.
Having arrived, I was taken and escorted toward home;
nevertheless, I thought that I must not show myself to him at all.
When he releases me from the stable or from his house, whether in a secluded place or in the darkness, he will assume his own form here within the home. (72)
"O King, I thought thus: 'I shall indeed go to the forest; because of that, he will have no grief for this great offense against his guru. (73)
But by you, out of a greedy disposition, I was not indeed abandoned in that desolate place; rather, I have been cast into bondage like a thief, as if firmly established in a prison cell. (74)
Then, overcome with anger, I indeed cast a curse upon you;
by that, your merit was destroyed. Tell me, how much compassion do I have for you? (75)
Therefore, your kingship has been consumed this very day due to the cause of your fault;
your body shall become like that of the varbuḍa tree. (76)
I shall bestow my grace upon you here for the swift destruction of the curse,
in the field of Kuṅkumavāpikā, on the imperishable ground near the lake.
O Indra among kings, may you become hairy and enjoy the pleasures of drinking water;
[for] Śrī Parameśvara is the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. ||78||
The Blessed One will be residing there; you shall go to him for that purpose.
He will take a branch from you for the sake of obtaining a tooth-stick. (79)
When you have truly attained a divine state and a divine body through his direct touch with your own hand, you shall indeed become a deity.
You shall quickly go to that heaven where Indra always dwells;
having enjoyed the bliss of heaven there for a kalpa, you will proceed to the imperishable state.
Abandon anxiety for the kingdom, for your son, and even for your beloveds;
for kings have gone before you, and others shall go as well.
"Those who have attained [liberation] through union with Hari have truly reached their goal, and no others," thus he spoke to me, and then the sage departed for another forest. (83)
Having seen me depart after I had said to him, "May it be well with you," even though I was dead, I became a barberry tree on the shore of Lake Aśvapaṭṭasara. (84)
"Ten years have passed for me here on this excellent barbur tree;
O Kṛṣṇa, you have rescued me, and the sin of the curse has been destroyed. (85)
I have become meritorious through your touch, O Giver of Liberation;
I am your servant, and you are my refuge—grant me the Vaiṣṇava mantra.
"Act in such a way that my liberation may occur at the end;
I am a king, so show me your own royal form. (87)
"O Rādhā, having meditated upon that true nature of yours at all times, may I attain liberation from heaven"— thus was Hari, who had assumed a royal form, entreated at that time.
He indeed became King Pṛthu in personified form to fulfill the desires of his devotee;
and he gave him the Vaiṣṇava mantra consisting of sixteen syllables.
"Oṃ, salutations to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Master; Svāhā!
Having taken this mantra, he ascended an excellent celestial chariot.
Having thus honored Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Person, with flowers and other offerings,
as well as all the beloved wives of Brahmā, he, worshipped by the gods, departed for heaven.
Then the beloveds of Brahmā beheld their own husband, Bālakṛṣṇa, who possessed a vast form and was the sovereign lord of the three worlds. 9.2.
Then those wives, having fallen into a state of delusion, took pleasure with Pṛthu, who was Viṣṇu himself, bearing the bow and discus, firm, youthful, and infallible.
After worshipping the ocean of compassion for a long time in the mango grove,
they later departed and bathed together with their husband on the shore of a lake.
That sacred ford (tīrtha) was named Varbu, and from that it became known as Pṛthutīrtha;
by residing there, one attains heaven, the destruction of curses, and liberation.
The beginningless Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa, having bathed and put on his garments,
then delighted the beloveds of Brahmā and sent them back to their hermitage.
Then, returning to his own home at night, the Blessed One again performed the worship of Lakṣmī;
indeed, he lit lamps of ghee during the night.
Then, while requesting the nightly lamp-offering and the food offering for the sake of prosperity, Lakṣmī became pleased; she became abundant in every single house. 98.
Having thus celebrated a festival for Rādhikā, he fell asleep;
by reading or hearing this, one becomes possessed of fortune and attains liberation. 99.
For those who have been cursed, there shall be liberation from the curse and the destruction of their transgressions;
for the meritless, there shall be the attainment of merit—of this there is no doubt. (2.236.10)

Thus ends the two hundred and thirty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Worship of Dhanalakṣmī and Brahmapriyā by Hari on the Thirteenth Day of the Fortunate Month, the Liberation of King Barbura—who had been cursed by the sage Āśvalāyana and turned into a *barbura* tree—and the Establishment of Pṛthutīrtha and the Dispatching of Barbura to Heaven," in the second section, the *Tretā-santāna*, of the glorious *Śrī-Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Rādhikā, then on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, the venerable Supreme Lord indeed performed the worship of Śambhu, the protector of his own sacred field.
Having bathed in the morning and worshipped his parents,
he then summoned the god Īśāna as well as the Rudras.
Having summoned the god Śaṅkara, the protector of the field, together with Satī,
he seated the Lord Śambhu upon a golden throne.
Bālakṛṣṇa worshipped that yogi, the lord of the lotus-born [Brahmā];
he offered him water for his feet, the respectful offering (arghya), sandalwood paste, sacred ash, and unbroken grains of rice.
And he placed a garland of *dhattūra* flowers around the neck of Hara;
on his forehead, he applied a lunar tilaka, as well as the *tripuṇḍra* and the *ūrdhvapuṇḍraka*.
The illustrious Blessed One caused laughter for that Maheśvara,
and he also placed earrings and lotus-bud ornaments upon his ears.
He also gave a rosary of rudrākṣa beads to that Hara;
and the Blessed Lord himself gave him a tiger skin and an elephant skin.
Hari gave hemp preparations, he gave sweet foods and sweet drinks;
he also gave flower garlands and likewise bestowed ornaments.
He gave her fragrant essences, he presented golden garments,
he gave her golden necklaces, and likewise he gave Satī ornaments.
He gave new garments and ornaments;
he gave all desired articles of personal use in their entirety.
Then he performed the nightly lamp-offering and gave pearls and diamonds;
thus having worshipped the Lord Bhūtanātha together with Satī, the Blessed One— || 11 ||
Then, on that day, Hari celebrated a festival;
at night, he fed and honored Śambhu, Satī, and the Lord of the Gaṇas.
Having worshipped Kārttikeya, Nandin, and the circle of Yoginīs, as well as the nine Durgās, one should also worship Gaṅgā, the consort of Śaṅkara.
Vīrabhadra, as well as Jālandhara, the Asura Tāraka,
Tārakākṣa, Gaja, Mahiṣaka, Caṇḍa, and Pracaṇḍaka.
Śṛṅgin, Bhṛṅgin, Rīṭin, and Kirīṭin;
likewise Agni, Candramas, Maṅgala, and Viṣa. || 15 ||
He gave him a skull-cup, divine beings, as well as a garland of skulls,
a lion, rudrākṣa beads, and Vāsukī, the progeny of Śaṅkara.
He likewise honored Hanumān and Niṣādin, and he worshipped Bhairava, Kāla, and Mahākāla. || 17 ||
He worshipped the bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, and even the kūṣmāṇḍas;
he worshipped the followers of Vināyaka, the vetālas, the gaṇas, and the diseases.
She worshipped Death, the nooses of death, Caṇḍī and the other goddesses,
as well as the Mothers, the planetary spirits, and likewise the Pretas.
And he worshipped the female deities of disease, such as Mahāmārī and others;
he also worshipped the Kṛtyās and the Kālikā-Brahmacāriṇīs.
Śītalā and the others worshipped all the residents of Kailāsa;
they also worshipped the Gaṇas, the wives of the Gaṇas, and the Rākṣasīs. ||21||
Then he gratified them with cooked foods such as flour-cakes made of black gram;
he likewise honored the yakṣas, the rākṣasas, the wives of the bhūtas, the ḍākinīs,
the śākinīs, the yoginīs, and the vetālas.
Likewise, all the subjects honored Kālarātri and Rātri. || 23 ||

Having thus performed the worship and offered the sacrificial oblation (bali), the Lord Hari then performed a fire-sacrifice (homa) according to the prescribed rite with clarified butter and other offerings for the sake of satisfaction.
And with mustard seeds and the like, mung beans and the like, black sesame and fruits and the like,
as well as black flowers and the like, he gratified the deities.
Having performed worship in this manner, as well as the offering of oblations (bali) and the invocation (hava),
the Lord, the Blessed One, offered lamps everywhere.
Thus, on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika at midnight,
having worshipped Kālī-caturdaśī as well, Hari himself—
Having worshipped Mahālakṣmī, he performed the ritual dismissal;
then, on the day of the Dīpotsava festival, he fell asleep at night and woke up in the morning.
Then, awakened by the sounds of beautiful musical instruments and by hymns of praise, the Lord performed his morning rites and worship; having done so, he then performed the worship of the ancestors.
And Lakṣmī and others, beloved of Brahmā, having performed the auspicious marriage rites, came before Śrī Hari for the purpose of worshipping their own beloved.
They all worshipped Rādhikā with every kind of offering; and having received her blessings and fed their own husband, [they departed]. (3.1)
Having accepted the favor bestowed by him, they went to the hermitage;
at evening, Keśava celebrated the festival of lights together with all of them.
The entire Aśvapaṭṭasara lake was filled with lamps upon its waters;
indeed, the city, being of such a nature, shone like heaven itself. (33)
At night, the Blessed Lord likewise performed the worship of Śāradā,
as well as of Śrī, Śāradā, Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, and Satī in person.
Having summoned the five supreme goddesses, Kṛṣṇa honored them with betel leaves, areca nuts, and offerings of sweet foods. (35)
The Blessed One was gratified by fragrant essences, ornaments, fine garments, excellent unguents, and other such things, through the offering of whatever objects were desired.
He performed the nightly lamp-offering (ārārtrika) and delighted [the deity] with jests;
having given gold and other sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā), he fed [him] milk-rice (pāyasa).
Then he offered an explanation and thereafter slept peacefully;
the maidens, having gone to the hermitage, fell asleep full of longing. (38)
At dawn, Hari quickly awoke and went to the lake;
having performed his ablutions in the waters of the lake, he remembered his own former life. (39)
On the bank of the lake where that great holy place exists by virtue of his own yoga, he remains in his eternal true form, the protector of all.
O Rādhikā, Śrī Hari meditated upon Himself within Himself there;
at that moment, the army of King Saṃparka arrived at that place. 41.
On the shore, [he saw them] afflicted by the suffering of a great pestilence, crying out "Alas!
Alas!", emaciated, overcome by hunger and thirst, exhausted, and on the verge of death. (42)
Śrī Rādhikā said: How indeed did he come there accompanied by his army?
Of which country was he the king, and how did the disease come upon his troops? (43)
"O beloved, tell me in brief the entire auspicious story of Hari: what indeed did Bālakṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa, do for him at that time?"
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Listen, O Rādhā, that king was Saṃparka, born in the land of Kaccha;
for the purpose of a pilgrimage, he had indeed gone to Somanātha. (49)
While ruling his kingdom without any thorns in his side, he constantly worshipped his preceptor Dattātreya, who was a portion of himself from a previous kalpa, at Kaccha.
He was devoted to the morning bath, intent upon the worship of the gods, dedicated to the duty of charity, and a worshiper of guests at food-distributions. ||47||
He was constantly devoted to meditation, a provider of food to the poor and the helpless, intent on serving the virtuous, and followed the instructions of his elders. ||48||
He was devoted to serving cows and Brahmins, a worshiper of virtuous and faithful women, non-violent, and truthful in his conduct; thus he was honored by his subjects. (49)
Upon seeing or hearing of the virtuous, he rises and approaches them like a servant;
likewise, he serves them with gifts of clothing, food, and other such offerings.
And in whose kingdom there exist circles of virtuous men everywhere, solely devoted to devotion for the Divine and intent upon the stories of Kṛṣṇa. (51)
In the kingdom, on the banks of the Nārāyaṇa lake, there occurs every year an excellent Vaiṣṇava sacrifice accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees.
This very King Rādhika, indeed, accompanied by a complete array of troops, was resplendent with elephants, horses, camels, bulls, carts, and vehicles. ||53||
For the purpose of a pilgrimage to Somanātha in Saurāṣṭra, he set out in the month of Āśvina accompanied by a multitude of thousands of people, including brahmins and virtuous men. (54)
Having performed the libations for the ancestors at the holy ford at the confluence of the Hiraṇyā, and having also offered baths, gifts, and so forth, and worshipped Someśvara; ||55||
Having visited the Mūladvārikikā tīrtha and worshipped Gopati,
he went to the Prācīsarasvatī and performed the Nārāyaṇabali sacrifice.
Then, having seen the Vāmana region and the Svarṇarekhā river, and having performed his ablutions at Cakratīrtha, he went to Indreśvara.
Then, having visited the holy site of Tūrikā in the Sītāphala forest,
one should proceed to the Mango Grove to bathe in the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake.
Then, due to the particular exhaustion from the journey, the lack of regular meals, and the influence of the heat, the army became afflicted with disease. (59)
Afflicted by a great pestilence and a major disease, and suffering under the power of illness, he came to the vicinity of the lake for the sake of obtaining the benefits of the sacred ford.
Having observed his servants and others, as well as the animals shedding blood,
and even seeing himself wounded, the king remembered his own preceptor.
"O Lord Dattātreya, on this earth of Bālakṛṣṇa, protect my afflicted human beings here in this sacred region. (62)
O True Guru, come quickly and grant us the gift of life; this disease destroys our strength and takes away the vitality of our group of servants. (63)
Even the slaughterer of animals brings about a most dreadful outpouring of blood;
protect me, protect me, O ocean of compassion, Dattātreya, teacher of the world! 64.
"May Lord Bālakṛṣṇa also protect me, who have come to him for refuge"—having thus entreated him in the vicinity of the lake, O King, [he remained there]. (65)
Accompanied by his army, he took up residence among the kadamba trees;
having reached the shore of the lake, he drank water on the bank at dawn.
Together with his caravan, the king performed the chanting and worship of Hari,
accompanied by rhythmic beats and clapping, consisting of descriptions of His names according to their qualities.
O Bālakṛṣṇa, O Hare-Kṛṣṇa, O Nārāyaṇa, O remover of distress, O Hari! O Dattātreya, O Guru, protect us; O Supreme Lord, save us! 68.
Thus the king performed worship together with a thousand men;
and this roar of his reached to the very ends of the quarters.
The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, having heard this, remained steadfast;
yet he proceeded toward the city to observe their worship and other devotional acts.
A great throng gathered all around the lake, like that of the inhabitants of the banks,
as spectators assembled on the shore of the lake where the saffron fields were situated.
O Rādhikā, absorbed in worship, they do not see at their sides;
nor indeed before them, nor behind them, for they do not even open their eyes.
For they made single-minded devotion their vessel for the pacification of disease, and they bound Hari within their own hearts with the rope of constant practice. (73)
Having seen and heard this, Hari himself, the Lord Bālakṛṣṇa, quickly appeared there in the form of Dattātreya. ||74||
Carrying a small water-strainer at his waist, a water-pot in his hand, as well as matted hair, a loincloth, a rosary for recitation, and auspicious sandals; ||75||
Chanting "Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa," he approached the presence of the king;
and upon seeing him, the king quickly prostrated himself on the ground like a staff.
The soldiers also prostrated themselves like staffs on all sides;
then the gracious-faced Lord Dattātreya spoke to them.
"How have you remembered [this]? Tell us the reason quickly!
The king said, "There is the calamity of a great pestilence; therefore, protect us! (78)
For the blessed Dattātreya, having opened his belly at that time,
gave him a small amount of ash which was contained within a hollow in his abdomen.
"Throw it into your mouth," he said; and the king threw it into his mouth.
The Great Plague (Mahāmārī), having taken form with a distorted face, went outside.
Terrified, she bowed down to that god Śaṅkara and fled toward him;
and at that moment, the army also became free from disease in an instant. ||81||
Just then, Dattātreya, the son of Atri, arrived there;
he who was born of Kambharā quickly became Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa.
Then the king, accompanied by his army, beheld Hari there, the Lord of Ramā, in that form as a great protector, and was struck with great wonder. ||82||
Dattātreya worshipped the great lord Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa;
and being pleased, Śrī Hari spoke to him for the purpose of granting a boon.
Then Dattātreya said: "Protect me here in your presence;
I am a portion of you and wish to dwell forever in your field. (85)
Hari said, "So be it; dwell in the waters of Lake Aśvasaras. This great holy ford (tīrtha) shall be known by your name as Dattātreyamahātīrtha. (86)
Then you shall take up residence on the peak of Mount Revata;
the mountain known as Raivata, called Mahendra, shall also come there. (87)
And in Saurāṣṭra, Kumuda and others will dwell all around him;
then, O Dattātreya, your residence shall be upon that peak. (88)
That great sacred site shall always be the mountain ridge of Dattātreya;
here, in my place, the sacred water in the form of a tirtha shall remain forever. (89)
"Therefore, that sacred ford shall remain forever in the sky upon Mount Raivata.
Having been addressed thus, the Blessed One Dattātreya dwelt within those waters.
Indeed, that great holy ford of Dattātreya arose within that lake;
through its contact, it became a sacred bathing place that truly provides protection. ||91||
On the southern bank of that lake, the king had a beautiful temple constructed, graced by Dattātreya. ||92||
Having worshipped Bālakṛṣṇa, Niru indeed departed for his own country.
O Rādhikā, Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa thus protects those who are suffering;
protecting His devotees is the very nature of His incarnation.
Having become manifest, the Blessed One, the one higher than the highest, performs his descent.
All incarnations are his alone; everything proceeds from him.
He is the Lord of all; he provides protection for all when he is merely remembered. (95)
Whether in a forest, on a mountain, by a river, in the ocean, or even in a wood;
in a treacherous and fearsome place, my Lord protects me when remembered. (96)
In the midst of enemies, at the mouth of Death, in fire, when the wind is turbulent, during an earthquake, and in a great battle—the All-pervading One, when remembered, protects [one]. (97)
In cases of the three humors, during massage, in a well, in illness, in a year of famine, in fetters, and in the snares of others—the All-Seeing One is remembered as the protector. (98)

Indeed, when one is facing poison, facing violence, at the falling of weapons, in a thunderbolt, in a fall from the sky, or in a precipice, that which resides within oneself is remembered as providing protection. (99)
In fear of kings, in fear of one's home, and even in fear of being driven away;
in fear for one's life, and in every kind of fear—the Possessor of Power, when remembered, protects.
O Rādhikā, for those who have become His own, Kṛṣṇa becomes their very own;
for the sake of protecting them, He indeed maintains great anxiety day and night.
From reciting and hearing this, the fruit of visiting sacred fords shall be obtained;
there is no doubt that protection and the destruction of suffering will surely occur. (102)

Thus ends the two hundred and thirty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Worship of Śāradā during the Great Autumn Festival on the Fourteenth Day of Kālī in the Dīpāvalī, Following the Worship of Śaṅkara, His Gaṇas, Servants, and Male and Female Slaves, as well as the Offering of Lamps by Śrī Hari; and the Destruction of Disease for Kings and Others Afflicted by the Mahāmārī Plague through the Granting of an Audience in the Form of Dattātreya on the First Day, and the Establishment of the Dattātreya Tīrtha," in the second section, the *Tretā-santāna*, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Rādhikā, in the new year, the Lord, the husband of Brahmā’s beloved,
celebrated the festival of the mountain of food (annakūṭa) in the sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpī.
He fed all the people of Kuṅkumavāpikā—
men, women, children, youths, and the elderly— from every side.
Hari indeed fed all the domestic animals, as well as those that were visitors, the birds, the aquatic creatures, and all sentient beings that dwell upon the earth.
On the first day of the lunar fortnight, the illustrious Bālakṛṣṇa spoke to Lakṣmī and Annapūrṇā in his own abode, desiring food.
"Today I have a desire for food for everyone;
if it is possible at the time after midday, please do so. (5)
Having received the command, Annapūrṇā spoke to the illustrious Supreme Lord:
"O Blessed One, for the sake of bringing [the food] to its cooked state, there is indeed a period of five ghaṭikās."
The time is awaited and such a moment is now present;
we shall provide a complete supply of cooked food—of this there is no doubt.
Having spoken thus, Annapūrṇā called to mind her friend Bhūmi;
she quickly called to mind Śrī, and Vārkṣī also called to mind [her companions] there.
He quickly remembered the nectar of grains and the goddess Lakṣmī;
he likewise remembered all his companions, the hearths, and the sacrificial fuel.
He remembered the leaves of the śāka tree, all kinds of seasoned meat preparations, the Gaṅgā and other rivers, and the wish-fulfilling cows.
Pākalakṣmī remembered the fires,
and there she also remembered the vessels known as Akṣaya, as well as the excellent flavors.
Annapūrṇikā remembered all those dear to Brahmā;
she remembered the cooks and remembered the servers.
Then she remembered all her female friends who prepare sour gruel and the like, as well as those who provide buttermilk drinks; and they arrived.
And she commanded the earth, "Quickly prepare a kitchen!
Within half a *krośa* and in a circular space, she quickly made it so in an instant.
He spoke to the rivers for the sake of water, and they brought that water;
he spoke to the hearths, and they remained situated in their proper places.
He spoke to the fires for the purpose of providing a dwelling, saying, "The fires are situated within the hearths."
He spoke to the frying pans that were situated upon the tops of the stoves.
The ladles and other implements were immediately employed for their respective tasks;
he then placed the grains, cereals, juices, and so forth into the vessel.
And likewise, clarified butter and other offerings stood within the cooking pots;
then, the female cooks stood all around in front, possessing beauty on every side.
At that time, all those dear to Brahmā became his benefactors;
and by the will of all the Lakṣmīs, clarified butter and other substances were provided. || 19 ||
And in cauldrons and vessels they come and they heat;
and therein, according to their requirements, grains and the like, as well as flour and other such things, [are processed].
Having gathered for the sake of cooked food, they enter from all sides;
likewise, there are sweets such as sugar-candy, and prepared dishes such as *veśavāra*.
Desiring food, they quickly assemble and enter;
indeed, the eight supernatural powers (siddhis) attend them there, stationed on all sides.
At the end of two ghaṭīs, the attendants (pārṣadas) and guardians of the field (kṣetrapas) of Śambhu presented many prepared cooked foods and invitations. ||23||
For the sake of food for all those dwelling in the imperishable fields, mountains of cooked foods indeed appeared in the kitchen. (24)
From that, numerous preparations such as sugar-candies and the like were produced;
and from that, also, foods of countless varieties came into being. (25)
Edible foods were also quickly prepared there in countless varieties, and likewise, many kinds of lickable delicacies were made.
Then, all kinds of chewables were prepared in great abundance, and all kinds of drinks were quickly concocted. (27)
There were also sour gruel and other such drinks, as well as various kinds of cakes; likewise, there were boiled salts, chickpeas, black gram, and similar items. (28)
There were various kinds of vegetables, as well as diverse preparations of them,
along with many savory curries rich in the essence of sweet and sour juices.
Curd, ghee, fresh butter, milk-rice, milk, and buttermilk—
all these were prepared, both cooked and uncooked, according to requirement.
Having performed everything while being protected by all the wives of Brahmā, by the Lakṣmīs, by the maidens and others, and also by the virtuous Siddhis.
Within five ghaṭikās, everything beneficial had been accomplished; then the goddesses prayed to the Lord, Śrīpati, the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama). ||32||
Everything here proceeds as already accomplished, though appearing in various forms;
perform the Vaiśvadeva rite and cause the sound of the bell to resound.
O Rādhikā, let there indeed be rows of people everywhere for the purpose of eating at midday, for the Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa is present here. (34)
Having bathed, performed the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice, and offered libations to the fire and the ancestors,
and having gratified all the deities, he caused the sound of bells to be made.
"Let the illustrious ones come in rows for the sake of a meal. Then, according to their rank, all the worthy recipients took their places in those rows.
Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and other men also arrived there quickly from all sides for the sake of food. || 37 ||
The groups of Brahmins, performing the service of serving food, fed the men and women in great abundance from all sides. (38)
Bālakṛṣṇa indeed gave them as sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) rings,
as well as *laḍḍukas*, *śaṣkulis*, and *khājikas* with a hundred holes.
[He offered] auspicious items, sweetmeat bowls, pieces of *parpikā*, excellent balls, small sweets, knots, and likewise *modaka* cakes.
He also offered *kalikāla-ḍaḍukas*, *mudgala-ḍaḍus*, *maṇḍakas*, *sohilakas*, *saṃyāvas*, *kaṃsāras*, and *ghṛtapūrakas*. ||41||
Sevikās, polikās, sweet pūrikās, as well as pāyasa,
delightful virañja, pheṇī, gundrapāka, and apūpakas.
Cakes and *ghurghura* sweets, as well as *vaṭaka* balls and sesame flour cakes;
*śāṭaka* pastries and *sthiraka* sweets, as well as plantains and mangoes. ||43||
Vegetables such as bhiṇḍaka, svarṇadugdha, kośātakī, as well as rājakośātakī, gavāhārā, and mārgarī; ||44||
Karkoṭikā, śimbikā, karkaṭī, and likewise cirbhaṭa;
red yam (raktālu), rājamāṣa and other pulses, as well as the fruits of śimbī and bimbī. ||45||
Also sugar-cane, watermelon, bitter gourd, pumpkin, taro, and the seeds of the muni plant, as well as patola. (46)
Also karkaṭī, methikā, pāravalla, and mūlaka; likewise śatapuṣpā, amblaloṇī, jīvantī, and syandikā. ||47||
Also fried eggplants, those coated with black mustard seeds, grapes mixed with *khārika* sugar, and *vaṭīvaṭa* cakes mixed with curd. (48)
And there were flower-stalls, various foods, and fragrant rice;
as well as soups, broths, buttermilk, and curd-mixtures. (49)
Fried harimantha beans, flat beans, parched grains, and likewise parpaṭas; fresh butter, fermented rice-gruel, and snacks made from coriander and other spices.
Milk boiled until sweet, curds, ghee with saffron, very bitter black peppers, as well as cardamom and long pepper; ||91||
He also offered bhūphalī, sugar-cane seeds, and valla beans; vaṭāṇaka, flower-buds, sweet polīs, ghārikās, and sweet jambukas.
Roṭakas, mūśalīpākas, vāsudevī, mallikā, śrīkhaṇḍa, taralā, māṣalaḍḍukas, and kalāvaka—[these were prepared]. (53)
There, the Brahmins and others, having eaten one hundred and one items of food and attained supreme satisfaction, then indeed departed for their homes.
The kṣatriyas, the classes of vaiśyas, and the śūdras enjoyed themselves with joy;
so too did the poor, the classes of the helpless, the mendicants, and those without support. ||55||
Then all the groups of male servants and female servants enjoyed [the festival];
all those residing in the field of Kuṅkumavāpikā enjoyed it. 56.
In each and every case, among those objects, no deficiency ever arises;
rather, it increases when the substance is served into an inexhaustible vessel.
Everything given away becomes inexhaustible and imperishable;
thus did the great seers, the virtuous, and the noble women enjoy it.
At that time, everyone from children to the elderly, including cowherds, all partook [of the food];
and all the guardians of the fields, deities, and others likewise partook.
By the will of the Lord of Śrī, she enjoyed the entire family of Hari;
she fed all the beloved wives of Brahmā and others in order to please her dear husband.
Then, full of enthusiasm, they came before Bālakṛṣṇasvāmin with vessels set upon golden plates for the sake of Hari.
They placed vessels filled with cooked food before Hari;
the Lord Hari sat properly upon a golden throne, while [the others] sat upon woolen seats.
Having sipped water for purification, she began to eat, preceded by the recitation of the *vyāhṛtis*;
they then worshipped Śrī Hari with sandalwood, saffron, and filaments of flowers. (63)
They fed him exceedingly with great affection and intense devotion;
Lakṣmī placed a vast golden platter before him.
O Rādhā, small pavilions were established by you on all sides;
Māṇikī placed a water-filled drinking vessel upon a pinnacle.
And Ramā, holding a fan, indeed performed the gift of air;
Padmāvatī, holding a silken cloth, stood by his side. (66)
Then all those beloved of Brahmā, hailing from every land,
performed the serving of all the various dishes.
The goddesses, beginning with Annapūrṇā, said to the illustrious Supreme Lord:
"Eat, O Lord, O beloved of compassion; we, being purified, desire to behold you here. (68)
Then Kṛṣṇa, taking a morsel in his hand, ate it with joy, saying:
"Oh, how sweet! Oh, what a delicious food! By whom has this auspicious meal been prepared? (69)
Having asked the names of its makers, he praised them repeatedly;
and having commended it as being exceedingly well-prepared, he ate of it once more.
Brahmapriyā and all the other women beheld Hari as he was eating; gazing upon their husband, the lord of their lives, those women were struck with wonder.
When Hari, having eaten very little, desired to rise up, Śāradā, making him stay, sang this hymn of praise: "Eat! (72)
Accompanied by musical instruments, Sarasvatī sang songs of praise before Śrī Hari for His pleasure, especially in order to feed Him. (73)
"O Lord, provide food; O Yogin, grant your grace; O Beloved, Master of my heart, O Yogin!
Accept this mouthful, O Kṛṣṇa, most delicious indeed."
Taste this heap of food of exquisite fragrance. ||74||
O Blessed One, giver of the goals of human life, enjoy this at your pleasure; O Lord, master of yoga, this entire [offering] is ready—
prepare your meal, O Lord, master of yoga!
O beloved, O lord of my heart, O yogi, grant me your grace.
O Lord, O Yogin who is my very life, partake of this meal: a dish of mangoes and milk-porridge, excellent *śaṣkulī* cakes and *pheṇī*, along with sandalwood and sweet *polī* pastries.
O Yogi, O life of my beloved, grant me your grace! //76//
O Lord, O Yogin who sustains life, partake of this meal: *suparpikā*, rich in flavor, *modakas*, *virañja*, the beloved *sugandhapāka*, and the *suśāṭaka* sweets with their crackling sound.
O beloved, O companion of my life, grant me your grace! ||77||

O Lord, O Yogin who sustains life, partake of the delicious and sweet chickpeas, the excellent king-beans and fritters, along with the vegetable gardens of various greens, side dishes, and other foods; please take your meal.
O beloved, O lord of my heart, O yogi, grant me your grace.
Parpaṭas, fried cakes, auspicious rice-puddings, soured gruel, milk, and all kinds of food—
O Lord, O Yogi, provide this sustenance for my life!
Grant your grace, O beloved, O lord of my heart, O yogi!
O Lord, O Yogin, provide for our livelihood food that is fragrant, sweet, and as desired— such as soup with rice, blossoming fried cakes, and other well-cooked delicacies like *ghurghurā*.
Grant your grace, O beloved, O lord of my heart, O yogi!
O Lord, Beloved, Master, partake now of this betel leaf mixed with cardamom and cloves and smeared with lime, eating until it fills your throat; give what remains to others,
and take your meal.
O beloved, O lord of desire, O enjoyer, grant me your grace! 8.1.
In this manner, O Rādhikā, she fed her virtuous husband; thereafter, the Blessed One ate his full meal, and then all the women did likewise.
Taking morsels of food in their hands for their own husband, Viśvambhara, they exerted themselves with great effort to force-feed him. (83)
To fulfill their mental desires in such a manner, Hari, the Lord of Yoga,
assumed an infinite number of forms, equal in count to all his wives.
He ate morsels from the hands of all the wives of Brahmā at the same time, pleasing them with his affection. (85)
There, Hari drank water and betel leaf from each woman's hand; he accepted them there, and they were then fulfilled in their desires.
Then the Blessed One, with his own hand, repeatedly fed cooked foods and gracious gifts to all his companions.
And having fed them betel-juice and betel-leaves, he caused all those millions, billions, and trillions of maidens to drink it as well. ||88||
And those beloved wives of Brahmā, as well as others—the women who were servers and cooks—became fulfilled in their purpose. (89)
Women are those who assist in cooking, those who take away material goods, those who bring forth material objects, and likewise, they are the givers of aesthetic flavor (rasa). || 2.238.90 ||
Whatever [merits] were performed there by Annapūrṇā and others, all of them indeed resulted in the rare grace of the illustrious Bālakṛṣṇa. ||91||
Having obtained what was easily accessible, they enjoyed it and attained satisfaction;
having thus eaten their fill of the mountain of food, they began to clear away the remains.
He also granted this supreme favor to aquatic creatures, as well as to birds, beasts, insects, and all others on every side. (93)
There the Blessed One bestowed his unimpeded grace upon the trees, the forest creepers, and the clusters of blossoms on all sides. (94)
Hari indeed gave delicious, soft, and pleasing food to the Mūlas;
likewise, the gods and great sages came for the sake of receiving his grace.
The ancestors, having been liberated and possessing divine bodies, also arrived;
wherever that grace was seen, they appeared there in such a manner.
Having become manifest, they all accepted his favor;
and having thus received this grace, they indeed departed for their respective worlds.
Having enjoyed all those supernatural powers and having obtained the supreme command of the Lord,
they then brought about the disappearance of the kitchen area.
Everything indeed became still, and the city attained a state of contentment;
filled with great joy, it sang the cry of victory for the beloved of Kṛṣṇa. 99.
Then, having gone to their own abode, they indeed attained rest;
thus did Rādhikā’s beloved celebrate the great festival.
By reciting or hearing this, one obtains the fruit of a mountain-peak of food;
moreover, through the propitiation of Bālakṛṣṇa, one attains both worldly enjoyment and liberation.

Thus ends the two hundred and thirty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Festival of the Mountain of Food (*annakūṭa*) ordained by Śrī Hari and the Feeding of All Creatures," in the second section, the *Tretā-santāna*, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Rādhikā, now hear of another miracle of the Lord Hari,
which the Master performed at the end of the night on the eleventh day of the month of Kārtika.
There was a king named Puṇḍarīka, a great Vaiṣṇava of Gaurjara;
endowed with all virtues, he protected his kingdom on the edge of the earth.
Every morning he performs the worship of Viṣṇu and Lakṣmī with excellent offerings;
having honored the virtuous and the elderly, he always takes his meal.
Guests constantly come to and depart from his house;
having performed the worship of Hari’s names, they eat your food. || 4 ||
He also performed vows for the sake of the festivals of Hari's birthday;
by that king, a auspicious drum was sounded throughout his own kingdom.
All subjects, with the exception of the elderly, children, and the sick, must observe as many Ekādaśī fasts as possible, abstaining from food.
Then all his subjects, remaining steadfast in their virtuous vows, indeed obeyed his command;
and being devotees of Viṣṇu, they worshipped Hari according to their vow.
That king went to Aśvapaṭṭasara for the purpose of a pilgrimage;
by him, the Ekādaśī of the month of Kārttika was observed in that sacred field known as Akṣara.
And having gone to Kuṅkumavāpikā on the tenth day,
he fed the virtuous ones, the brāhmaṇas, and Bālakṛṣṇa.
With devotion alone, he worshipped Lomaśa and the circle of sages;
he performed an immersion in the sacred ford and beheld the gods and other celestial beings.
He gazed upon the divine city of Kuṅkumavāpikā and performed a circumambulation of the lake on all sides.
The king worshipped all the deities residing on the banks with various offerings; at night, however, he performed the *ārātrika* ceremony for the lake.
He found rest in the hall; then, rising quickly in the morning, he performed his daily rites, bathed, and worshipped the Brahmins.
Having performed the rites at the sacred bathing place (tīrtha), he then went for the sake of beholding Kṛṣṇa;
he worshipped the Lord Bāleśa, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa.
The king bestowed infinite gifts of gold, silver, and garments;
he gave wealth to the Brahmins and to those who had come from sacred pilgrimage sites.
The king indeed gave garments and vessels to the virtuous, and necessary items to the destitute; he also bestowed gifts of cows and gifts of food.
He also performed the concluding rite (udyāpana) of the vow to obtain its excellent fruit,
consisting of the gift of golden jars and other items, as well as the offering of a golden image.
The king gave gifts of wealth, grain, clothing, and vessels,
as well as listened to the recitation of the Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā.
Having gone to the hermitage of Lomaśa, the king spent the day there;
he paid homage to the sages and likewise to the virtuous women.
The king performed a salutation to his devotees, conducted their evening worship,
performed the lustration ceremony (ārārtrika), and kept a vigil throughout the night.
Without water and without food, accompanied by his entire caravan,
he performed worship at night preceded by the playing of cymbals.
O Hare Kṛṣṇa, O Bāla Kṛṣṇa, Supreme Lord, Transcendental Master, Son of Kambharī, Supreme Soul, Glorious Joy of the Gopīs! 22.
O Lord of the husband of Brahmapriyā, O Lord of Lakṣmī, O Lord of Rādhā, O Master, O Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, O Lord, O All-pervading One! ||23||
Thus he performed worship, chanting, and glorification;
then, within his own heart, he meditated upon the beloved of Śrī Kṛṣṇa as if directly perceived before him.
Having performed his morning devotions, he became absorbed in meditation;
and all his followers went to the lake for the purpose of bathing.
