At the hour of Brahmā (brāhma-muhūrta), the king meditated upon Śrī Narāyaṇa within his own heart and chanted: "So'ham, so'ham, so'ham, so'ham.
He also chanted "Haṃsa, haṃsa" and "Haṃsa-haṃsa."
The Blessed Lord Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa, having heard the recitation, remained present within his heart.
Having quickly remembered his ancient form as a swan, he became gracious;
Hari himself swiftly assumed the form of a swan right there.
White in color, with white luster, possessing the form of a white swan, with both divine and human faces, he was a swan-bodied being endowed with splendor. || 29 ||

His limbs were proportioned to his form; he was as beautiful as ten million gods of love; he was a treasure-trove of all sciences, as well as a treasure-trove of the Vedas and other branches of knowledge.
And he approached the presence of the king, walking very slowly on foot;
the king beheld within his own heart a region on the bank of a lake.
Even as the swan was approaching, he beheld Lakṣmī by his side;
his heart was filled with wonder and his body was suffused with love.
Having risen, he became filled with haste to approach the Blessed One; at that very moment, he attained the state of being awake. ||33||
O Rādhā, as soon as he opened his eyes and looked into her presence,
he beheld a mass of great splendor in every direction.
In an instant, his own two eyes were produced as fit for that splendor;
then, within that womb of light, he beheld the Lord of the worlds.
Seeing one of white complexion, in the form of a swan, laughing and endowed with splendor,
the king suddenly rose and then prostrated himself like a staff.
Having declared, "I have achieved my purpose," he placed the dust of [the king's] feet upon his own face;
he rolled repeatedly on the ground in the vicinity of those feet as well. (37)
The king shed tears of great joy;
Lakṣmī, moreover, consecrated the king’s head with water from her water-pot. 38.
Having obtained grace, the king, filled with joy, drank that water;
having attained his purpose through the sight [of the deity], he spoke. (39)
Oh, what great fortune! Oh, what great fortune for me, this body of a king, that I have beheld the Supreme Lord, the Perfect Brahman, who is supreme bliss! 2.239.40.
In the form of a swan, endowed with splendor, you have come here in person out of compassion;
I am purified, I am liberated, and I have been rescued from the ocean.
Having spoken thus and grasped the feet of the swan, he observed a vow of silence.
The swan said, "O King, choose a boon, whatever you desire."
The king said: "O Hari, grant me liberation here and lead me to your state; I have no desire for a kingdom, nor does the craving for worldly existence exist within me. (43)
All other desires remain unfulfilled, O bringer of liberation;
for that gain which belongs to yogis does not exist even when the age has passed away. (44)
"Indeed, that gain has been attained by me today through the vow of Ekādaśī;
therefore, O ocean of mercy, grant me liberation from this in every way. (46)
O Rādhikā, having accepted the king’s words, the Supreme Lord, smiling, said, "So be it," at which point the king, his followers, and the others [responded]. (47)
Beholding those splendors, they gazed upon that Hari;
indeed, they felt their purpose fulfilled upon seeing him in the form of a swan.
Just then, a celestial chariot as radiant as the sun arrived there;
the king, having cast off his body, attained a liberated form.
In an instant, he became four-armed and equal to Viṣṇu, seated upon a celestial chariot;
then his queen quickly [took hold] of that chariot with her own hand.
Even though she had attained touch, she was still able to go along with him;
having cast off her own physical body, she became possessed of a divine form.
Then, that celestial chariot immediately appeared there in the sky;
and Haṃsa Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa also became the four-armed Viṣṇu.
By means of that celestial chariot, he led the king directly to Vaikuṇṭha;
then, in the form of Bālakṛṣṇa, he remained on the bank of the lake.
The light vanished, and the caravan was struck with wonder;
all the members of the caravan and the king’s followers performed the funeral rites for the body.
Then they went to their own country; the kings told their son this entire account, and having heard it again, he rejoiced.
O Rādhikā, in the waters of the Tattvaśvapaṭṭa lake, there is the auspicious Haṃsatīrtha located in the southeastern corner, which bestows liberation. 55.
Through bathing, giving gifts, immersion, drinking the water, and frequenting [the site], there shall be enjoyment, heaven, and liberation; of this there is no doubt. (56)
There, self-knowledge arises from bathing and drinking the water;
furthermore, the merit of a sacrifice is obtained at Haṃsatīrtha through the gift of food.
Indeed, by feeding a single virtuous person on the twelfth lunar day, one obtains the highest merit;
there is no doubt that this merit is equal to that of feeding a hundred virtuous persons.
By the gift of fruit on the eleventh day, one obtains a reward equal to the gift of gold;
and here, from the gift of gold, there arises a reward equal to the Rājasūya sacrifice. (59)
Listen, O Rādhikā, to another marvel of the Great Lord:
the king of Utkala, named Rolā, [set out] for the sake of pilgrimage to Somanātha.
Having visited the great pilgrimage site of Somanātha and the Prācīsarasvatī river, he arrived at it with his own army after many months, proceeding very slowly.
Having visited the Mūladvārikikā tīrtha and Vāmanasthalī, and having visited the great Bhadrāvatī tīrtha and Kuṅkumavāpikā; ||62||
He arrived at the shore of Aśvapaṭṭasara on the full moon day;
having arrived in the evening, he performed the ritual ablution according to the rules and drank the water of the sacred site.
His army, having satisfied its thirst by drinking water, received its meal at night;
and he heard the sounds of the lamps being lit for the gods and well-recited hymns of praise.
Having found rest during the night, he then fell under the power of sleep;
the army, having slept, arose at dawn on the bank of the lake. (65)
There was a garden of fruits and flowers belonging to Aśvaśuṇḍin;
the king’s cattle went there to graze upon the grass. (66)
The garden trees were devoured and even destroyed by the beasts;
then the king, having risen at sunrise, went to the Horse-Lake (Aśvasaras) free from sleep.
Having performed his bath, charity, and ritual duties, the king returned to his own residence;
meanwhile, he continued his daily worship of her.
That image of Śrī Nṛsiṃha became visible there;
the king grieved in his mind, thinking, "Indeed, an offense has been committed by me here."
"Otherwise, there would undoubtedly be a desecration of the image";
thus he praised Nṛhari with a grieving heart.
O Lord, O shoreless ocean of compassion, why indeed are you angry with me today?
I do not know what offense I have committed here that you have departed. (71)
I shall die, having abandoned food; I will not take water or fruit.
May I indeed be a transgressor; this is my penance. (72)
When he had spoken thus, a voice from the sky indeed arose:
"O King, here in the eastern direction there is certainly a garden of fruits and flowers. (73)
The beloved of Kṛṣṇa belongs to Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Self;
behold without delay how its destruction is indeed brought about by your cattle and other such beings. (74)
"Restrain them quickly and have a great garden constructed;
however, you have committed this offense, so hear now of another thing you have done."
In this matter, you have not performed the worship of the glorious Bālakṛṣṇa;
he of whom I am an incarnation is the cause of my own incarnation. (76)
If my worship were to take place without first worshipping him, it would be an offense against you;
therefore, having first worshipped him, I have attained dissolution—you must worship him first.
Therefore, worship me here; by that I shall be pleased with you.
Install my image here on the bank of the Aśvapaṭṭa lake. (78)
I shall dwell there in that beautiful temple in the presence of Kṛṣṇa, for the purpose of guarding the garden and also for the protection of the forest. (79)
"Then, O Rādhikā, I shall indeed come along with you; it shall not be otherwise. Having been addressed thus, the king, after honoring the celestial voice, [proceeded].
Having gone quickly to the vicinity of the army, he restrained those beasts;
seeing the garden destroyed, he fell into great sorrow. ||81||
Having quickly reported this account to the army commanders,
he then issued orders for the protection of the garden and for the construction of a new one.
Having issued the command for the swift construction of the palace,
he, equipped with the materials for worship, went to the abode of Bālakṛṣṇa.
Seeing Rola approaching, the Lord of the Satyas smiled and said:
"O King Rola, tell me, when did you arrive at this sacred field? (84)
Is all well with your army?
Furthermore, are your beasts of burden and your human travelers happy? (85)
"O Lord of Men, accept food in my house today.
Thus addressed, Rolarāja shed tears and spoke to him.
O Nārāyaṇa, ocean of mercy, I have indeed committed an offense against you here;
the garden was destroyed by my troops as if by beasts—therefore, grant me forgiveness. (87)
I shall cause a garden to be built, and I shall cause a temple to be built;
here, the installation of your form as Nṛsiṃha shall take place forever. (88)
"I shall go to my own kingdom to protect the fields and gardens;
O Kṛṣṇa, without your worship, Nṛsiṃha has vanished from me. (89)
"O Supreme Person, forgive this offense of mine," having said this, Rādhikā worshipped the glorious Bālakṛṣṇa. (2.239.90)
Then, with royal attire, garments, ornaments, perfumes, garlands, unbroken grains, and other such items,
he prostrated himself like a staff and offered food offerings and funeral cakes.
He offered betel-leaf and accepted the favor of Hari;
then, having been told by Hari, "You are forgiven," he went to his own home.
Then the Blessed Lord Nṛsiṃha, manifesting in bodily form upon his own throne, accepted the king's worship with heartfelt devotion.
The king also had a new, very firm temple constructed;
he installed Nṛsiṃha in the temple and provided for his maintenance.
Having planted a garden and appointed a guardian there,
O Rādhikā, that devotee of Kṛṣṇa then departed for the land of Utkala.
Thus, that Nṛsiṃha-tīrtha came to exist within the waters of the lake, as did that beautiful Roḷa-tīrtha and the temple of Nṛhari. (96)
Through the majesty of Bālakṛṣṇa, everything there became composed of sacred fords;
those who perform their ablutions therein attain worldly enjoyment, liberation, and an auspicious state.
For indeed, those who plant trees that bear fruit will surely go [to heaven], as will those who plant clusters of flowers and those who lay out great gardens. (98)
For all those men—even those who merely perform the watering of the roots of trees—shall go to the eternal and immutable abode of Brahman. 99.
Having reached heaven and enjoyed its pleasures for a long time, they shall go to my imperishable state;
by reading and hearing this, one obtains the fruit of planting a garden.
Those who plant trees and creepers anywhere on earth within the sacred field of Aśvapaṭṭasara, or along its banks, shall attain the supreme goal. 10.1.
Through the protection of the earth, those without lineage will obtain a lineage, the poor will likewise become wealthy,
and the sapless will become full of essence.
Those who plant trees near horse-roads and lakes will become prosperous with wealth and grain, and shall enjoy desirable food and fruit. (103)
O Rādhikā, those who fell these trees are dear to me;
I dwell among the throngs of cowherd women in the forests, within the fruits and flowers. 104.
I dwell, endowed with prosperity, in the houses of those people who protect the trees;
of this there is no doubt. Indeed, upon their destruction, I depart.

Thus ends the two hundred and thirty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Liberation of King Puṇḍarīka who attained Lord Hari in the form of a swan through the Kārttika Ekādaśī vow; the Haṃsa-tīrtha at the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake; and the establishment of Nṛsiṃha on the bank of the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake by the Cola king through the yoga of Nṛsiṃha, as well as the Nṛsiṃha-tīrtha," in the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*, within the second section, the Tretā-santāna.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Listen, O Rādhikā, to another miracle concerning the Lord of Śrī that occurred at the sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpikā regarding Yogeśvara.
Vītihotra, the great yogi and lord of yoga, came to dwell in the forest;
on Mount Himavat at Badarī, he performed most rigorous penance.
He attained all the arts of yoga and became just like Śambhu;
by the power of that yoga, he indeed beheld with his divine eye.
Sacrifices were performed in Ketumāla, and sacrifices were also performed in Kenāṭa; that which was done by Hari, however, was in the regions of the immortals.

The great festival for the birth [of Kṛṣṇa] on the eighth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Ūrja which was performed, as well as the worship of Śāradā and other rites, and the grand festival of the mountain of food (annakūṭa). || 5 ||
Having understood all this through his divine vision, he approached the Supreme Lord Kāmbhareya Bālakṛṣṇa to behold him in person.
Assuming a thousand forms, that self-possessed Vītihotra came to the sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpī to see Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
On the third day of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, having reached the shore of the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake and taking recourse at the Setu,
he established his own seat beneath a banyan tree.
Assuming a thousand forms by his own resolve, he sat down;
and the Lord of Ramā, having come, would embrace my own essential form.
Then that Lord shall again embrace her with a thousand forms,
provided she causes others to behold the true Guru, Ṛṣabha.
Therefore, I shall dwell here forever as a constant follower in the presence of Śrī Hari;
I shall attain liberation right here, so there is no need for Badarī.
For the guru alone is the giver of liberation, and not any other;
he through whom one's own self attains nourishment and by whom one crosses the ocean.
Because it is the great peace of the self, people should take refuge in that Guru;
because it is the destruction of sin, and because it is the destruction of ignorance. (13)
One should take refuge in that Guru from whom comes the cessation of mental fluctuations, the destruction of latent impressions, and the self-manifestation of the Self. (14)
Since one may obtain training, as well as sovereignty, wonder, and abide in a divine state through him, people should take refuge in that Guru. (15)
There are many gurus, both worldly and unworldly;
indeed, those who dwell in the world must be treated as gurus according to worldly custom.
Unworldly gurus were supported by unworldly disciples;
likewise, I too must support this extraordinary Lord as my guru. (17)
For everything that ought to be done is indeed completed in Hari;
for the mother is the giver of birth, and the father is the giver of the seed. || 18 ||
For there are others who act as protectors of the body, namely one's gurus;
and others, such as kinsmen and women, who provide speech and knowledge. (1.9)
Likewise, there were others who provided instruction, as well as those who bestowed knowledge; there were also teachers who gave instruction in the arts and crafts. (2.240.20)
Indeed, these indeed become one's gurus during the journey of this body;
however, he who bestows the knowledge of the Self and he who bestows the mantra of Viṣṇu [are the true gurus]. || 21 ||
That teacher who bestows the practice of Dharma is indeed considered the most excellent;
he who bestows the state of Brahman and he who bestows the perfection of Yoga. || 22 ||
He who bestows fearlessness upon the intellect is indeed a most excellent Guru;
having rendered the latent impressions stainless, he reveals the Supreme Lord. (23)
He who leads one by oneself to the Supreme Self, who bestows divine liberation, and who sends one to the world of Brahmā—he indeed is the most excellent Guru. (24)
The letter *ga* is blind ignorance, while the letter *ra* is radiant knowledge;
the Guru is considered venerable because he destroys ignorance and bestows knowledge.
By means of the syllable *ga*, he leads [the disciple] to the abode of light, which is full of delight (*rama*).
This very Guru is the giver of liberation; there is no other teacher superior to him.
The Guru is a yogi, a celibate, a follower of dharma, a man of knowledge, and one free from passion;
the Guru is also of virtuous character, and Nārāyaṇa is the supreme Guru. || 27 ||
Hari, the Guru, is the giver of enjoyment, the giver of liberation, and the giver of all one's possessions;
since he is the one who brings about the direct realization of the Guru, he is therefore the Guru of the Guru. (28)
He alone is this glorious Hari, the supreme teacher of the liberated;
he is the teacher of all incarnations, and the teacher of virtuous women and the righteous. (29)
Likewise, [he saw] the abodes of the lords, the creative consciousnesses of the yogins,
and those former great seers who were creators of the world and dwellers of heaven.
He is the supreme teacher of the lords of creatures, of those devoted to ritual action, and of devotees;
he is the foremost among all gurus and the teacher of Nārāyaṇa-guru.
The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the beloved of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇavallabha, the son of Kambharā, who is higher than the highest. || 3.2 ||
"This glorious young cowherd boy is indeed the Lord of all embodied beings;
having been obtained by me, he will surely fulfill my heart's desire. (33)
"I shall dwell at his feet and attain the imperishable abode," thus reflecting, Vītihotra became absorbed in meditation in a thousand ways.
Having seen him born with a thousand forms on the bank, the men who were bathing went away, struck with great wonder, saying, "Whose are these [forms] indeed? (35)
Indeed, thousands of yogins have arrived here;
they are identical in dress, identical in body, and identical in limb, being all alike. || 36 ||
Having identical hair, identical complexions, and identical proportions,
these either become brothers or they become liberated from their abode.
"Are they inhabitants of Badarī who have come here, or white-clad liberated souls;
or perhaps the attendants of Śaṅkara, or gods in the form of ascetics? (38)
Are these perhaps the deities to be propitiated, or ascetics dwelling on Mount Meru?
For who indeed could they be, with faces like the moon and radiance like the sun? (39)
Thousands of yogis, masters of yoga, through the practice of meditation,
neither speak nor see, nor do they even move their vital breaths.
"Who are these lords, remaining silent and steady-minded?"—
thus indeed did the people of Kuṅkumavāpikā reflect.
Indeed, they come in groups, filled with curiosity; some bow as soon as they see him, while others praise and speak [of him]. ||42||
This glory belongs to Bālakṛṣṇakṛpānātha;
yogins come constantly for the sake of obtaining a vision of him. 43.
All these who were previously invisible have now become visible—thousands of Rudras and thousands of Viṣṇus as well. (44)
Even thousands of Brahmas come to see him, which is truly excellent;
likewise, the great seers, the ancestors, and the deities always do so.
The Viśvedevas and the Maruts, who are to be propitiated, come constantly to behold [it];
even the sacred fords and the world-protectors who guard creation arrive there as well. ||46||
Or else, the divine attendants residing in Goloka and other realms arrive,
and the eternal attendants of Vaikuṇṭha also come constantly.
Planets, lunar mansions, and stars, as well as thousands of suns and moons, and those traveling in celestial chariots, arrive with great respect from other worlds. 48.
Are these the Vālakhilyas arriving, or perhaps Brahmin sages from the assembly of Brahmā? Or could they be Gandharvas, Yakṣas, or even the attendants of Kubera? (49)
Whether they be wandering minstrels dwelling in the mountains or sages residing in the forest,
it is their supreme resemblance alone that conveys their unprecedented nature.
The Vaiṣṇava mark on the forehead, the matted locks on the head like those of an ascetic,
and the eye-gesture nourished by yoga— all these proclaim him to be a portion of Acyuta.
Whoever they may be, those whom we—meritorious and fortunate ones through the power of destiny—have here directly perceived. (52)
"Without doubt, their realization will occur in this very moment"—
thus did those people speak, gathered together in groups.
Then, thousands of yogis beheld him on the shore of the lake;
he was the illustrious Bālakṛṣṇa, the preceptor of Nārāyaṇa-guru.
Then, on the shore of the lake in the presence of the yogis, he arrived;
perceiving that very moment the one who knows the heart, he quickly beheld him in his primordial form.
Having lifted him up and called him by name, "O Vītihotraka,
arise!", he took hold of the hand of that yogi and placed him upon his chest.
As he embraced her quickly with laughter, he himself became a thousandfold;
Acyuta was embraced by thousands of forms that had arisen from him.
Then Hari quickly became one in form,
and Vītihotra also suddenly manifested as a single form.
The people, struck with wonder, uttered cries of "Victory!
at that moment, while the illustrious Bālakṛṣṇa became the preeminent teacher.
An aged ascetic, possessed of white matted locks, naked and grey with dust, appearing as if senseless or insane, yet having conquered all his senses. ||2.240.60||
Pervaded by the splendor of his own nature and devoted to the supreme state of Brahman, that person remains as if non-material,
appearing as though dispirited among embodied beings.
And Vītihotra, seeing his guru Ṛṣabha, prostrated himself like a staff and,
in many ways, offered praise there to the Supreme Lord.
You are the Guru, you are the inner self, and you are the bull among sages, the sovereign of yogis;
you alone are the Lord of Yoga, you are the Lord, and you are the Supreme Lord.
You are liberated, you are the Great Liberated One, and you are indeed the Lord of the Liberated;
you are the Imperishable, you are Brahman, and you are also the Supreme Brahman.
You alone are the Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa, and you are Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa;
you are the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Supreme Lord. (65)
O Lord of Śrī, O All-pervading One, the incarnations such as Ṛṣabha and others are yours alone;
you alone are the husband of Rādhā, and you alone are the husband of Lakṣmī. (66)
You are the husband of Vāsudevī and likewise the husband of Nārāyaṇī;
you alone are the husband of Muktā, the husband of Brahman, and the husband of Dhāma.
You are the cause of Mahākāla and the cause of Mahāviṣṇu;
you are the cause of Sadāśiva and the cause of Vairāja.
You are the Abundant One (Bhūman), known as Puruṣa, and also as Puruṣottama.
You are the creator of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśa, and the Rudras;
you are the creator of the gods, the world-protectors, and the ancestors;
you are the creator of the great sages, the ascetics, and the virtuous ones.
You are indeed the lord and protector of the virtuous ones, such as Kamalā and others,
as well as of the gods, humans, animals, and birds.
Among the creepers and the trees, you are the Sarjaka that bestows sap;
you are the creator of the wish-fulfilling cow, the desire-creeper, the thought-gem, and all such things.
Among the yakṣas, rākṣasas, and piśācas who move through the air, you are the creator;
you are the progenitor of those born from water, those dwelling in the forest, and those dwelling within the earth.
O Janārdana, you are the creator of the Daityas and Dānavas;
you are the protector and the nourisher of the wretched, the helpless, and the poor. (74)
He is the giver of food to those who depend on him, the refuge for embodied beings in distress,
the granter of desires to those who long for them, and the fulfiller of the wishes of those possessed by desire.
You are woman and you are man; you are the embryo and you are the young child. You are the seed, you are the form of the harvest, and you are the flower as well as the fruit.
You are Indra, you are the sense organ, you are sleep, and you are wakefulness.
You are deep sleep, you are great bliss; you are affection and likewise delight.
You are Manmatha, born of the mind, and you also abide within the mind;
you alone are knowledge, the knower, and the object of knowledge, O Supreme Lord.
You are the season, you are the day and the night, you are exertion and cessation.
You are trust and refuge; you are mother, father, and teacher.
You alone are wealth and grain; you alone are power and strength.
You indeed are policy, devotion, virtue, passion, and renunciation.
You are the vital breath and you are life; you exist as manifold and yet as one.
You are illumination, you are activity, and you are cessation; you are composed of the qualities (guṇas).
You alone are beyond the qualities (guṇātīta), the locus of all perfections and qualities;
you are the wonder, you are the marvel, you are sovereignty and lordship. 82.
You are earth and water; you are fire, wind, and likewise fire (light);
you are space, you are the subtle elements, and you are the intellect and the threefold desire.
You are discernment, you are forbearance; you are hunger and the desire for liberation.
You are affection, you are the state of meditative absorption, and you are the Samādhi that is higher than the highest.
You are the worshiper and you are the object of worship; you are dullness and likewise you are minuteness;
you are equality and you are inequality—you alone are indeed everything.
I am you, Vītihotra; you are the Guru and likewise Ṛṣabha.
Whatever is seen, whatever is experienced, and even that which dissolves—all this is born from the manifestation of the portions, parts, and manifestations of your very own power. || 86 ||
For you alone are that which, where, by what means, and for what purpose [exists]. || 87 ||
To that Kṛṣṇa, the Protector, the Brahman, the Supreme Brahman—to Him I perpetually offer myself, who am named Vītihotra. 88.
I offer myself to you as a gift alone—not as a deposit, nor likewise as a loan—fit for disposal according to your will. (89)
Having thus offered praise, Rādhikā fell at the feet of Hari;
then Kṛṣṇa, like the sacrificial fire, raised her up.
When Hari embraced him again, placed his hands upon his head, and directed Vītihotra toward the attainment of boons, [he spoke]. 91.
Then Vītihotra said: "I shall remain here at your feet;
O Lord, at the end, you will attain liberation and reach your imperishable abode."
"Always dwell here," Hari indeed said;
"O Rādhikā, that great holy site (tīrtha) called Ṛṣabha is in the lake,
as well as the holy site named Vītihotra and the holy site of the thousand yogis."

Thus, by that name, it became renowned as the auspicious bestower of liberation. Hari suddenly assumed the form of Bālakṛṣṇa and, remaining on the bank of the Vītihotra, departed for his own abode. || 94-95 ||
Embracing the banyan tree, the ascetic Janadarśana [resides] there;
those who have performed their ablutions at that sacred ford shall attain the supreme goal.
O Rādhikā, they shall attain perfection in yoga even without the practice of yoga;
by bathing there, their sins will go to destruction.
Whether it be fresh or dry, great or small, and whatever causes suffering to others—
all that sin is swiftly destroyed even by drinking that water.
In that regard, from the gift of food there shall arise a fruit equal to the horse-sacrifice (vājimedha);
for one who builds a temple for me, the Bull, he shall attain my imperishable abode.
Thus indeed the Blessed One spoke regarding the majesty of Rādhikā-tīrtha;
by reading or hearing this, the fruit born of that sacred place shall be attained.

Thus ends the two hundred and fortieth chapter, titled "The Description of Hari’s Appearance to Vītihotra Yogeśvara in the Forms of Ṛṣabha and Sahasrarūpa, the Consecration of Ṛṣabha-tīrtha, and the Hymn of Praise," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O Rādhikā, listen now to another marvel of the Lord which occurred on the fifth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa.
Of that Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Lord of the Imperishable,
there exists an incarnation named Vāsudeva, who is designated as a vyūha.
A portion of Him is Saṃkarṣaṇa, whose activity consists of creation and dissolution;
he who is described in the scriptures as Saṃkarṣaṇa is born. (3)
He exists repeatedly in the form of Rudra and likewise repeatedly in the form of Śambhu;
he alone remains as the soul of dissolution, and he is known by the name Śeṣa.
Where Hari indeed reclines as Śeṣanārāyaṇa, he himself is born as the great yogin Patañjali. (5)
The sage Patañjali, who is indeed a portion of Hari and the instructor of yoga, dwells here on earth with a divine body; that Lord always resides in Kāśī.
And he, for the purpose of beholding Hari through the vision of yoga every morning,
comes to the site of the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake for the sake of worship.
Having worshipped the Supreme Self, the beginningless Śrī Nārāyaṇa,
and having performed the lustration ceremony (ārārtika), he then indeed obtained His grace.
In a mere moment, he departs from Kāśī for his own abode through meditative absorption;
thus the great sage Patañjali comes here constantly.
O Rādhikā, while moving through the sky, the king of yogis named Camasa beheld the Lord Hari there, honoring that sage.
He indeed descended to the earth and questioned that Patañjali: "O Blessed One, is the illustrious Puruṣottama worshipped here by you? (11)
Bālakṛṣṇaka is the manifest sovereign of all incarnations;
how can he go again to Kāśī, having abandoned the Great Lord?
"Tell me the reason, O learned one; I have come for the sake of a sacred ford (tīrtha).
Having performed the rites at the ford, I shall then depart along with the Revā. (13)
"I shall worship the Lord and then indeed depart with you";
having spoken thus, he prostrated like a staff and worshipped Bālakṛṣṇa.
Having performed worship and received permission from both, they went to the bank of Lake Aśva and took refuge under a Dhātrī tree on the eastern embankment.
The sage Patañjali declared the reason for his residence in Kāśī:
"O Camasa, listen to the cause why I am going to Varāṇasī."
She who is the embodiment of the great sovereignty of the Supreme Soul, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, and who assumes a form that is half of His own.
She who is the foremost among all powers, the supreme sovereign of them all, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇī, the primordial mother, and the half-body of Hari. (18)
She is the mother of the worlds and of the Brahma-worlds, the one who descends through yoga;
she is the remover of suffering and the creator of happiness for those who are liberated, bestowing power upon them. || 19 ||
She is the embodiment of all the powers of all the Nārāyaṇas,
and she who rests upon the chest of all those who are dear to Brahmā is the foremost among them.
It shines forth as belonging to the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa alone;
for a moment it does not go far away, nor is she ever born again once liberated.
She whose nature is both visible and invisible, who is joined with inseparable existence, is the Supreme Goddess to be served by Rādhā, Ramā, and the other goddesses. 22.
That maiden, the beloved of Śrī Hari, remains today with her body sustained;
the young girl Satī, the daughter of Narāyaṇa, stays in the house of Śivasvāmin.
By name she is Dhanalakṣmī, the destroyer of all suffering;
that divine lady exists as a goddess arisen from the earth. 24.
The auspicious Kṛṣṇā, along with her younger brother, was also waiting for the garden of Hari, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, on behalf of Vijaya and Śaśin. 25.
Indeed, I go into servitude to perform worship and service for her;
I go indeed by the command of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. (26)
O Camasa, you understand through yoga that Hari, who is to be attained,
is indeed this very Supreme Self (Paramātman) who shines upon the ground smeared with saffron.
Indeed, his constant vision is non-conceptual meditative absorption (samādhi), and direct service to him is the supreme fruit of that absorption. (28)
In my view, the observance of the restraints (yamas) is indeed the practice [of yoga];
non-violence is to be adopted as the glory of Hari, and serenity consists of being absorbed in Him.
Truth is the constant refuge for one whose nature is truth, and non-stealing is conduct before Śrī Hari with the disposition of servitude. (2.241.30)
Celibacy (brahmacarya) is considered to be attachment to the form of Hari with love;
non-possession (aparigraha) likewise consists solely in not obtaining anything other than Him. //3.1//
Even my religious observances consist of service to Kṛṣṇa;
my purity comes from touching him and holding him within my heart. (32)
Contentment is the constant presence in the heart of Śrī Hari through His grace; austerity is indeed the effort to restrain the mental faculties (vṛttis) therein. 33.

Self-study consists of reciting His words, praising Him, and performing worship and so forth; furthermore, it is the mental application toward His form and the complete surrender of the mind to Him. (34)
Thus, in this way, the auspicious restraints (yamas) and observances (niyamas) reside in Śrī Harikṛṣṇa;
likewise, the postures (āsanas) reside in His command, and the stations (saṃsthānas) reside in His presence. 35.
Prāṇāyāma is the offering of the vital breaths to the Lord of Breath;
Pratyāhāra is the withdrawal of the senses, whose food is the Supreme Lord. (36)
Dhāraṇā is when the Lord, who is eternally dark, is held within one's own self; and dhyāna is the constant, single-pointed concentration of my conviction upon Hari. (37)

Meditation on form is meditation on the form of Hari; meditation on taste is meditation on Hari in taste; meditation on fragrance is meditation on Hari in fragrance; and meditation on touch is meditation on Hari in touch. ||38||

Meditation on the word is focused on the speech of Hari; meditation on the hand is focused on the deeds of Hari; meditation on the foot is focused on the purpose of Hari; and meditation on the voice is focused on the qualities of Hari. (39)

The meditation on delight during union with Hari, the destruction of obstacles, the dismissal [of the deity], the contemplation of Him in the heart, and the reflection upon Hari in the mind. (2.241.40)
There is constant awakening to Śrī Hari and perpetual ego-identification with Hari;
one's mental state remains fixed upon Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa through latent impressions and contemplation. (41)
From that supreme lord Nārāyaṇa comes great bliss;
from union with him comes the abandonment of the qualities (guṇas) and the divinity of those very qualities. 42.
Service to Śrī Hari, whether performed with or without qualities, as well as the realization of the Supreme Person and the eternal vision of Hari— this is the state beyond the three modes.

Even the thirst for the qualities [of Hari], as well as attachment to the qualities of Hari, the proficiency of the intellect, and that which is the constant mindfulness of Hari—[these are the means]. (44)
That very cessation of mental fluctuations exists everywhere as the manifestation of Hari;
it is indeed savikalpa-samādhi, for it is the practice mixed with its own object. 45.
Worship with gross objects is accompanied by discursive thought (savitarka), while mental worship is indeed free from discursive thought (nirvitarka).
Devotion through hymns is accompanied by subtle reflection (savicāra), while the contemplation of the limbs [of yoga] is free from subtle reflection (nirvicāra). ||46||
With joy is the taking of the flavor; without joy is the offering of the flavor.
With the sense of "I-am-ness" (sāsmitā) is the appearance of the distinction between master and servant in Hari. (47)
There is no longer the egoism of being a servant toward the eternal Kṛṣṇa;
when I am absorbed in Kṛṣṇa, there is oneness, and no longer any sense of separation from Him. 48.
The fruit [of devotion] is the attainment of the nature of Kṛṣṇa, as well as sālokya, sārṣṭi, sāmīpya, and avinābhāva, which is constant absorption therein. (49)
"Because the attainment of all sovereign powers, wonders, and so forth is not distinct from that [state], Camasa, everything consisting of yoga has thus been attained by me. (2.241.50)
In me and in you, nothing other than Śrī Hari truly appears;
therefore, with that disposition, worship Him and dwell here at Lake Aśvasaras.
Thus instructed by the practitioner Patañjali, Camasaru always made his dwelling on the shore of Lake Aśvapaṭṭasara. (52)
Patañjali went to Kāśī, and Camasa followed Patañjali to the shore of the lake for the sake of rest and for the purpose of a scholarly assembly.
He constructed an excellent hut made of wood and leaves for Patañjali;
consequently, that sacred site became renowned in the world as Pātañjala-tīrtha. ||54||
Where indeed Camasa constantly held a yoga-discourse, staying together with the illustrious Patañjali, the knower of yoga. (55)
Then King Manu, the son of Vivasvat, arrived there for the sake of visiting sacred fords;
he beheld the purifying site of Camasa and Patañjali.
Then he caused a firm temple made of stone to be built;
indeed, in that extensive grove of trees, [he installed] Śeṣa and Patañjali.
By means of the ritual for consecration, King Manu installed the sage Śeṣanārāyaṇa, who was adorned by a multitude of a thousand hoods. 58.
Upon each and every hood there is the mark of a svastika;
it is made of gold, silver, green, or white. (59)
With a red face and eyes like pearls, served by the Śeṣikās,
it was beautiful, soft, delightful, and arranged in the form of a coiled ring.
In this manner, he likewise established the remaining divine sage Patañjali, the Guru, the great ṛṣi and yogin, in that very temple. ||61||
At his side, he established his beloved Kuṇḍalinī as the presiding deity of Siddhi;
likewise, that Manu indeed established his son named Yoga.
Likewise, he installed the god Saṃkarṣaṇa, resplendent with a mace, a lotus, and other emblems,
together with his beloved Saṃkarṣaṇī, in a temple.
He installed Rudra, accompanied by Rudrāṇikā, and also the three-eyed one;
he likewise installed Īśāna, joined with Īśinī, in the temple.
For the sake of their livelihood, he also granted large fields and groves to those Brahmins;
furthermore, he appointed them with wages and other provisions for the purpose of worshipping them.
At that Pratiṣṭhā, Manu caused the auspicious Mahārudra sacrifice to be performed according to the rules, and he had the Rudriya hymns recited.
He had sacrificial pits and auspicious pavilions constructed,
and he invited the lords of yogins, sages, and the most excellent great seers.
The Brahmins, the foremost of the Kṣatriyas, the Suras, the Devas, the Prajāpatis, and all the Gaṇas and attendants who are the disciples of Rudra. ||68||
[He saw] all those residing on Kailāsa and all those residing in the Ocean of Milk,
as well as the Nāgas of the Śeṣa lineage and the best of yogins who are devotees of Śambhu.
And also the Yoginīs and Devikās, all of them virtuous and chaste; and likewise the Avadhūtānikās and the Mātṛkās in their entirety.
In the sacrifice, Manu summoned Vīrabhadra and the others, as well as Nandin and all the rest— the Gaṇeśas and the Kārtikeyas.
And there was the great preceptor Pulastya as the leader;
he was indeed a beholder of the Mahārudra and an expert in all branches of medicine.
There, the diligent sages, having thoroughly prepared all the necessary materials, uttered words of benediction and made auspicious sounds. (73)
Then there occurred the purification of the body, the ritual resolve (saṃkalpa), the worship of the water-pot (kalaśa), the adoration of Gaṇeśa, and the worship of the Mothers (mātṛkā). ||74||
Then there occurred the Nāndī-śrāddha, the offering of Madhuparka, the recitation of the Puṇyāha, the placement of the Vardhinī jar, and the water-procession.

Then followed the laying out of the site (vāstunyāsa), the worship of the pavilion (maṇḍapārcā), the worship of the deities of the mandala, the worship of the pedestal (pīṭhapūjā), the worship of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍapūjā), and the ritual placement of the fire (vahninyāsa). ||76||

The placement of the house, the installation of the Yoginīs, the installation of the Kṣetrapāla, the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi), the consecration of the vital breaths (prāṇapratiṣṭhā), and the placement of the Mātṛkās. ||77||

The recitation of the Śatarudrīya, as well as the lustration rite (nīrājana) for Rudra, the sequential fire-oblation (kramahoma), the oblation to all the gods, and the worship of the upward-facing [liṅga] took place. (78)
Or with goat’s milk or deer’s milk upon the brick,
one should likewise perform the oblation with a *arka* leaf in the northwestern corner.
And the Adhvaryu, reciting the Śatarudrīya,
offered oblations to Śambhu with a stream of clarified butter and a stream of the milk of the Arka plant.
He offered an oblation to the assembled gods, beginning with Rudra;
thereafter, the handful of flowers became a great full-oblation (mahāpūrṇāhuti), which was the homa. ||81||
Then there was the beholding of the deities in the temple and the presentation of offerings, followed by the bestowing of great sacrificial fees.
There were also foods for all those present at the sacrifice; then followed the honoring of the guests, the welcoming reception, and the final purificatory bath.
Thus, O Rādhikā, Vaivasvata Manu [praised] Śaṅkara, as well as Śeṣa, Patañjali, Saṃkarṣaṇa, and Īśāna. ||84||
He installed [the deity] in a new temple with great festivities on that purifying ground in the eastern direction of the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake. (85)
Then Arkāyanī became the great divine Śeṣasthalī;
likewise, at Aśvapaṭṭasara, there is the supreme Pātañjala Tīrtha.
Cāmatīrtha, as well as Śeṣatīrtha which is likewise great, the supreme Sāṃkarṣaṇa-tīrtha, and the Śatarudrīya-tīrtha. ||87||
The Avabhṛtha, the great Tīrtha, the Śambhu-tīrtha which bestows happiness,
the Vaivasvata-tīrtha, and others such as these.
And the holy fords (tīrthas) became forever bestowers of worldly enjoyment and liberation;
they became well-renowned at the Aśvapaṭṭa lake. (89)
Wherever the Gaṇas bathed, those places became Gaṇatīrthas;
likewise, there was the Gaṇeśa-tīrtha and the Skanda-tīrtha.
Likewise, Nāgatīrtha and Pārṣadatīrtha were there, as well as Satītīrtha and Devikāsutīrtha, which was indeed purifying. ||9 1 ||
Thus, O Rādhikā, in the eastern quarter there arose this auspicious circle of holy fords (tīrthamaṇḍala), which bestows all perfections through its residual power. 92.
Where, by bathing, drinking the water, sipping it, or even by touching it, that sacred ford became a bestower of the fruit of yoga and indeed a means for attaining the Self. (93)
In that place, through giving, one indeed attains the state of eternal Kailāsa;
and by receiving initiation there, one reaches residence in Vaikuṇṭha.

There, by performing sacrifices according to the prescribed rites, one shall indeed attain the eternal heaven; there, by the consecration of the image, one shall attain the abode of Sāṃkarṣaṇa. ||95||
Because one dwells there eternally, there is indeed no fear of Mahākāla;
and by performing vows and other rites there, the fruit shall be infinite. ||96||
By providing a means of livelihood specifically for ascetics, female practitioners, and especially for Vaiṣṇavas, there shall arise eternal liberation that leads to Brahman. 97.
O Rādhikā, by bathing in its dust, there is the destruction of sins;
and it is held that even animals who die in that region attain birth as gods. 98.
O Patañjali, O Śambhu, O Rudra, O Lord Saṃkarṣaṇa, O Manas, O Śeṣa, and O Camasa, may you all bring about my auspiciousness! 99.
Having spoken thus, one should sleep at night; no evil dream shall arise.
He who conducts his affairs while recollecting them will gain profit at every step.
Having reflected upon those very goods for purchase and sale at dawn, one should place one's hand upon the merchandise and conduct the trade; thus, there will be profit for him moment by moment.
May the goddess Annapūrṇā, Satī, Pārvatī, Śeṣiṇī, Śivā, Sāṃkarṣaṇī, and Yoginī grant me auspiciousness. (102)
Having spoken thus, a woman—whether a maiden, a young girl, a married woman, or a widow—should engage in this practice; her gain shall be moment by moment. (103)
Through even a fraction of His grace, there arises the destruction of suffering and poverty, the fulfillment of all desires, and the increase of happiness, prosperity, and lineage. (104)
O Rādhikā, by reading this, hearing it, causing others to hear it, or even reflecting upon it, there shall be the destruction of all sins, as well as worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Through the grace of Saṃkarṣaṇa, the attainment of one’s mental desires, the swift destruction of illusion, and the realization of the Self shall arise. (106)

Thus ends the two hundred and forty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Temples of Saṃkarṣaṇa, Patañjali, Śeṣa, and Others Built by Vaivasvata on the Eastern Bank of the Aśvapaṭṭasara Lake during the Union of Patañjali and Camasa, as well as the Collection of Tīrthas such as Saṃkarṣaṇa and Śeṣa in the Water," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Listen, O Rādhā, to another story, purifying and most wonderful,
which took place in the supreme imperishable field (Akṣara-kṣetra) and is exceedingly ancient.
There was a Brahmanical sage named Paṅkila who possessed a lifespan of five kalpas;
his mother was a virtuous woman, a maidservant who attended upon the great sage. || 2 ||
A maiden whose father had died wandered through the circle of sages;
from her childhood she had been without a protector, without kin, and her mother was dead.
She was a Brāhmaṇī who knew the Veda, having attained awakening from the great seers;
she was devoted to self-realization, a mistress of yoga, and possessed the wealth of meditative absorption.
She took refuge in Sāṃkhya and Yoga, was a treasury of discrimination between the self and the insentient,
remained equanimous in pain and pleasure, served the elderly, and was devoted to dharma.
Virtuous in thought, word, and deed, as well as in her qualities,
she was devoted to the service of the sages through diligence and the giving of gifts.
She was one whose heart had been burnt by the fire of great wisdom;
she remained ever undisturbed by dualities and was a constant meditator upon the glorious Nārāyaṇa.
In this manner, that young woman was born,
free from the state of passion (rajas) and devoid of desires or volitions.
Devoted to the holy life, virtuous, subsisting on the alms of sages, and auspicious—
her garment always dries in the air by the wind.
Her alms-bag hung in the sky like the wind;
indeed, it became such a manifestation of wondrous supernatural power.
She heard that divine discourse in the assembly of the great sages;
she listened to the truthful words of Gaṇeśa regarding the awakening of his son.
The sons born from the mind of Brahmā, Sanaka and the others,
heard that story, as well as the divine and purifying account of Añjanī’s son.
Then, having heard those stories of women who had sons, she reflected:
"May I too have one son in my mind who is an abode of virtues."
That I am an object of honor in the midst of the assembly of mothers of sons—this indeed is the fruit of my own son, the very support for women. (14)
"I must obtain a son who is a devotee of the Lord," she thought;
this was in the fourth previous kalpa, during the Tretā age, from Vāmadeva.
By the mere touch of the sage, she obtained a mind-born son;
though born without a womb, that boy was immediately a youth of exceeding beauty.
Endowed with both knowledge and discernment, devoted to the contemplation of Brahman,
he constantly travels through the path of the sky, performing the act of leaping across the four oceans.
Furthermore, by means of the procedure for the great pilgrimage site of Caturdhāma,
he became capable like a mother and likewise attained perfection like a father.
The possessor of divine power was the founder of the Vāmadeva lineage;
he [honored] his mother, Queen Dākṣī, and his father, Vāmadeva.
Having constantly worshipped [the deity] both within his heart and externally,
he would then go eagerly to the forest every day for the sake of wild fruits and other provisions.
Having gathered sacrificial wood and flowers, he places his seat upon the mud in the waters of the Ganges and enters into meditative absorption during the night.
He was celebrated by that name, Paṅkila, by the goddess Dākṣī;
thus the famous brahmin-sage named Paṅkila was born.
Once, even during the day, he established his seat in the midst of mud and,
having entered into meditative absorption, remained motionless by restraining his vital breaths.
There, by chance, five virtuous women arrived at the riverbank;
they were devoted to Brahman, possessed of good character and vows, and were equal to Nārāyaṇī herself.
The female masters of yoga were the disciples of Vāmadeva and were the refuge of supernatural powers:
Āpastambī, Drumastambī, Marutstambī, and the third.
Phenastambī was the fourth, and Dhūmrastambī was the fifth;
having bathed in the waters of the Gaṅgā, they stood for a moment upon its bank.
At midday, they saw the boy in the mud;
he was radiant, established in Brahman, and possessed a halo like that of the sun.
Those sisters quickly approached the side of the yogi, the son of Vāmadeva, who was absorbed in meditation and possessed a divine form, and they bowed down to that sage.
The sage, having seen them near his own seat while he was in meditative absorption,
quickly came outside, offered them a seat, and bowed down.
"I repeatedly salute my elder sisters, who are knowers of Brahman and established in the highest state.
Having spoken thus, she placed her eyes upon their feet and her head [at their feet].
That sage placed the dust from his feet upon the heads of his sisters;
he quickly prepared seats for the purpose of welcoming them.
Just then, other non-skin seats arrived there;
he then remembered water held in a water-pot for the purpose of washing the feet,
and when that was presented, he then remembered the honey-mixture (madhuparka).
Sweet things, desired items, honey, various fruits, sugar, and so forth—33.
Then, as soon as they were remembered, the honey-mixture (madhuparka) and all the materials for worship arrived, and he presented them to the two of them.
Paṅkila honored his sisters with all kinds of articles;
he provided them with delightful food consisting of various cooked delicacies.
Then he gave her nectar-like, delicious water for drinking,
as well as very beautiful bark garments for the purpose of making a lower garment and an upper robe.
Likewise, he gave the female ascetics very suitable bracelets;
he also requested their blessings and their favor.
Having been offered hospitality, they were pleased and bestowed auspicious blessings upon their brother.
Then one said, "O brother, may you live for a kalpa and be happy."
The second also spoke likewise: "Live for an eon and be happy.
The third, the fourth, and the fifth also spoke in the same way.
With hearts full of joy, they said, "Live for five kalpas and be happy! Through the auspicious blessings of his sisters, he lived for five kalpas.
O Rādhikā, Paṅkila Ṛṣi became so through the honoring of his sister;
thus he lived for five kalpas, possessed of dharma, knowledge, and detachment.
Devoted to the worship of Brahman in this world, the sage lives as he pleases;
at times he goes to Satyaloka, Vaikuṇṭha, and likewise to Badarī.
He likewise goes to Śvetadvīpa, to heaven, and to the realm of Yama;
he goes to the realm of Indra, to the realm of the Sun, and to the realm of the ancestors.
In some places toward Mount Meru, in others toward the mountain known as Lokāloka,
in some places toward the world of the Seven Sages, and in others toward the world of Dhruva.
He goes to the lunar world, the realm of coolness, or even to Pātāla; this king of yogis wanders at will through the mire of existence. 45.
In some instances he remains in meditative absorption for ten thousand years;
at other times he dwells upon the earth, and at others in the water, bearing a body as indestructible as a diamond.
In some places he is in fire, in some in wind, and in others he abides in space;
like Brahmā, his goal is Brahman, through the service of his own sister and mother. 47.
Through the power of his ancestors and the power of yoga, his movement indeed became unimpeded;
he could assume many forms and bodies, and he could also cause his body to become invisible.
Like the sun, he shines sometimes in the sky and sometimes on the earth;
sometimes he has the form of a god, and sometimes he possesses the form of a human.
In one place he has the form of a parrot, in another the form of a bull;
in one place he has the form of a deer, and in another the form of a swan.
In some places he is equal to a mountain, and in others he has the nature of a tiny particle;
thus, though established in Brahman, he who possesses independent power appears as if defiled by mud.
He dwells as the equal of Vāmadeva, a treasury of all sovereign powers;
and he, indeed, in this fifth kalpa of his, at the very break of dawn— ||52||
Wandering along the path of the sky, he beheld Lake Aśvasaras—
vast, with pure water, its surface tranquil and exceedingly brilliant.
Shining like the moon and beautifully adorned with many lotuses,
it resounded with the sweet calls of royal swans, royal parrots, and cranes.
It possesses the four-fold beauty of Bhavya’s bridge, with waters as deep as the netherworld;
it is the sacred ford of the Kṣīrasarasvatī, consisting of the water from the feet of Brahmā.
It was resplendent on all sides with great gardens of fruits and flowers,
where the God of gods had made his abode and which was frequented by hosts of great sages.
It is constantly purified by the bathing and immersion of those dear to Brahmā,
and it is provided with divine flights of stairs for descending into the water for ritual ablution.
The great bank was shaded by the dwellings of ascetics and by banyan trees and others,
and it shone brilliantly on all sides with women carrying water.
To the west of the city of Kuṅkumavāpikā is a place resembling the Imperishable (Akṣara);
to the south, it is exceedingly purifying due to the hermitages of the great sages.
It is adorned in the north with divine palaces that serve as dwellings for the Kṣetrapālas of the Śiva-tattvas, and in the east it is inhabited by holy men and virtuous women.
He beheld the Aśvasaras lake as being constantly filled with yogis, ascetics, those free from passion, renunciants, and likewise those who have surrendered themselves.
He beheld great mansions with golden pitchers,
and on all sides he saw temples richly adorned with gold.
He heard the sounds of musical instruments, the blasts of conch shells,
hymns of praise, and the songs of the Apsarases as well as the magnificent eulogies of the virtuous.
Having heard and observed everything both collectively and individually, he then descended from the sky with all his might into the Paṅkila Aśvasarovara lake.
Having drunk water and likewise bathed, he attained supreme peace,
remembering Nārāyaṇa, the glorious Bālakṛṣṇa, the Supreme Lord.
O Rādhikā, this very person, though muddy, chose to dwell in the water out of fear of the crowds of people everywhere outside. (66)
By day he remains on the surface of the water, and by night he even resorts to the bridge;
he also wanders at will among the dwellings of ascetics. ||67||
Sometimes he wanders in the evening through the regions of the great sages' hermitages;
every morning, however, he goes to the temple and worships Bālakṛṣṇa.
In one place he goes to the most purifying Somanātha with his mind;
in another place he suddenly goes to Mūladvārikā with his physical body.
In some places, having become a maiden herself, she remains among the beloved wives of Brahmā;
in other places, having become a young boy, he stays with the cowherd children.
Thus, O Rādhā, that king of sages took up his eternal residence at the auspicious Aśvapaṭṭasara lake, which is the refuge of Bālakṛṣṇa.
Then one day, the illustrious sage Lomaśa beheld him,
who had assumed the form of a maiden and had arrived at his own hermitage.
He said, "Who are you, and from where have you come here? Speak, O maiden!
And she replied, "I am Paṅkilā, for I am the daughter of Dakṣa and Devī."
"I have come to your hermitage for the sake of seeing young maidens;
I am indeed Vāmadevī now, but at other times I am Paṅkilā. (74)
Having spoken thus, he abandoned his maiden form and became Paṅkila;
Lomaśa, for his part, recognized him as one he had previously known.
Having closed his eyes in his heart, he then offered great honor;
having received the mantra of Hari from the sage Lomaśa, that sinful man [was purified].
He muttered the mantra, "Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya," and having bowed, he entered his dwelling within the water and remained there in the midst of the waters.
Then, on the second day, when he had arrived,
the sage Paṅkila spoke to him there regarding the leaf-hut.
My life is indeed at its end; this fifth kalpa of mine is passing away along with the day of Brahmā—what need have I for a hut of leaves? (79)
Therefore, I shall dwell here in the water, in this carefree abode within the mud; for as long as I remain here, I shall not go anywhere else in this world.
A leaf-hut must not be built at all, nor even completed;
for if I were to construct a leaf-hut while only a short time remains,
those sages who have lived for many kalpas would laugh at me.
Having spoken thus, he chose to dwell eternally in the water.
Fixing his mind on Śrī Hari, he attained meditative absorption (samādhi) within the water.
While he remained in that absorption, the duration of an entire Yuga passed by.
Then, in the world, the powerful King Bali was indeed requested for land during his sacrifice in Saurāṣṭra by Vāmana, who had manifested himself.
Bali gave the earth to Vāmana, who was carrying an umbrella;
yet Vāmana, a deceptive Kṛṣṇa, increased his own stature.
And his big toes and fingers fell into the water of that lake which was filled with cranes;
by his splendor, the ground of the lake was filled.
Then the waters quickly receded from all sides onto the ground at his flanks;
indeed, Varuṇa brought about the subsiding of those waters.
Having emerged from the mud when the lake was drained of water, he became as small as a nit clinging to the big toe of Vāmana. || 88 ||
Having emerged, he too praised [the Lord] for a moment with his thumb placed upon his heart;
meanwhile, Vāmana, assuming the form of a child, conquered the three worlds.
Upon seeing him, he became muddy yet thrilled with love;
he desired once more to bathe in the lake abundant with water as much as he wished.
Then the illustrious Vāmana said: "Build for me an auspicious temple, and on the Setu, install me as Vāmana and dwell there."
"By my command, become my servant and dwell in my palace.
Having thus commanded him, the Lord Śrī Vāmana departed for Vastrāpatha.
By the power of his yoga, Paṅkila constructed a temple at night;
there he installed the beautiful Lord Śrī Vāmana. ||93||
Paṅkila indeed established himself in the service of Vāmana;
for the sake of service, Paṅkila appointed Jālakīlaka as his disciple.
There, the sage remained forever invisible in the abode of Vāmana;
as Cirañjīva, he offered himself at Jālakīlā when the time had come. (95)
Indeed, even Jālakīla, that king of yogis and a brahmin, became the lord of the net (Jāleśvara), possessing various yogic perfections and a lifespan equal to a kalpa of Brahmā. 96.
He also always made his dwelling on the shore of Aśvapaṭṭasara;
thus, O Rādhikā, is that sacred ford Jāleśvara, which is full of mud.
There is also the Vāmana Tīrtha, as well as the Aṅguṣṭha Tīrtha,
and the Kanyaka Tīrtha within the waters of the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake.
It bestows liberation, destroys sins, grants happiness, and likewise bestows the perfection of yoga, prosperity, and heaven. ||99||
By bathing there, as well as by giving gifts and by worshipping Vāmana,
a person may obtain the kingdom of heaven, the supreme state of Brahmā, or the sovereignty of the earth.
Remembering Kāṃbhareya Bālakṛṣṇa, the beginningless Nārāyaṇa,
whoever bathes in the Vāmana Tīrtha shall go to the abode of Brahmā.
Having remembered Vāmana Paṅkila, one should perform bathing, giving gifts, and other rites;
likewise, having remembered the goddess Dākṣī, one should perform the giving away of a daughter in marriage and other such acts.
One should give food to young maidens, food to the virtuous, and food to chaste women; thus one shall obtain the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice.

Thus ends the two hundred and forty-second chapter, titled "The Description of Paṅkila— the Mind-born Son of Goddess Dākṣī and Vāmadeva— Receiving Blessings for Longevity of Five Kalpas through the Honors of His Five Elder Sisters, Remaining in Samādhi at Lake Aśvapaṭṭa until the End of the Yuga, Awakening upon the Touch of the Toe of Vāmana’s Foot, and Building the Temple of Vāmana by His Command, as well as the Vāmanādi Tīrtha," in the second section, the *Tretā-santāna*, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Rādhā, listen; having learned that the five daughters of Vāmadeva were residing with their brother at the Aśvapaṭṭa lake.
Having questioned their mother, Divyamuktānī, who was always residing in Satyaloka, they all returned to the Aśvapaṭṭa lake.
To behold, to choose, and to attain the state of having fulfilled one's purpose, [one seeks] the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the beloved of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Possessing divine bodies like the Kaumudika stars or the daughters of Candra,
they had performed every kind of adornment for the pleasure of Nārāyaṇa.
Even those devoid of a portion of Māyā, yet deluded by a portion of the Supreme Brahman, arrived suddenly through the path of the sky along with Cirañjīva. || 5 ||
On the sixth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, at Akṣarakṣita,
they arrived and bowed down to their own brother, the Lord Vāmana;
they worshipped him with supreme devotion, and the brother offered them a welcome.
They spoke the same words of instruction regarding the proper measure even to their younger sister,
for their brother had attained great joy because his sisters were so dear to Hari.
Having heard that their state as Nārāyaṇīs had indeed been brought about by whose grace, she rejoiced exceedingly, for they were destined to live until the end of five kalpas.
On the morning of the seventh day, having adorned themselves with beautiful ornaments,
they went at dawn to the magnificent abode of Bālakṛṣṇa together with their mother.
With materials for worship in their hands and likewise adorned with excellent garlands,
they possessed a disposition of offering all that they were in the presence of the beloved of Kṛṣṇa.
There, they first worshipped their mother Śrī Kambharā with supreme devotion and offered her their own introduction.
Having bowed down to his father, his sisters, and his two elder brothers,
as well as his brother’s wife Amṛtā, he then repeatedly [bowed] to Nārāyaṇa.
Having bowed down again and again, they performed worship with many articles;
presented by their brother, they arrived having offered their very selves.
Upon seeing their devotion, Hari accepted it, saying "So be it," as the hands of those women were taken by Hari from the hand of his brother, the sage Paṅkila.
Then, with love, he indeed took hold of the hands of those who had been offered to Śrī Hari;
Āpastambī was the first, and Drumastambī was the second.
Marutstambī was the third, Phenastambī the fourth, and Dhūmrastambī the fifth; these were the beloved wives of Hari.
Having worshipped their own beloved, they placed the garlands of choice around his neck; then Hari, having seated those women by his side, [honored] the garlands of choice.
Then he bestowed a favor upon them and placed it around their necks;
having eaten there, they went with their brother to the hermitage of Lomaśa.
O Rādhā, by the command of Hari, they dwelt among the beloveds of Brahmā;
thus, having obtained the Lord of Rādhā, they became like Rādhā herself forever.
Now, O beloved, listen to another delightful and purifying narrative concerning one born of the lineage of King Svarṇāṅgada of Saurāṣṭra.
And there was a king named Haimakalgi, who possessed the armor of dharma;
he was indeed a Sāttvata, a devotee of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. ||21||
He constantly worships the Lord of Śrī even during his daily activities day and night;
he does not keep the rosary far away, nor does he ever abandon His remembrance.
During eating and lying down, she keeps Kṛṣṇa ever-present in her heart, repeatedly crying out, "Bālakṛṣṇa! Kṛṣṇa! Hari-Kṛṣṇa! (23).
Day and night he would say, "Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa," and at the end of every sentence, he would always call out, "Bāla Kṛṣṇa" and "Kāṃbhareya. (24)
He utters the cry "pravakti" (he speaks) regarding the Supreme Self, whether at the time of His worship in any house or in the forest. (25)
Whether on the shore of a lake, in a garden, in a pavilion, or in a temple;
in a solitary place, amidst a crowd, in a throng, or in private—the bond of love [prevails]. (26)
For Bālakṛṣṇa himself indeed goes and stands before one;
he accepts all the materials offered during worship.
Having eaten all the food offerings— fruits, edibles, milk-rice, and fried cakes— Bālakṛṣṇa gives the remainder to the king.
Then the King indeed vanishes, and he takes his meal;
in this way, through devotion to Hemakalpa, the Lord Śrīpati [is pleased]. 29.
Rādhikā remained under his control, being well-pleased with him;
likewise, his queen, named Kumudākṣī, behaved in the same manner.
She too, rising quickly and bathing, cooked excellent,
sweet food with great devotion for the pleasure of Bālakṛṣṇa.
Milk-rice, cow’s milk with sugar and boiled rice, fried cakes cooked in ghee, and other items appropriate for the season. (3.2)
Having prepared even food cooked with *guṇḍrā* and sweetmeats made from ground black gram (*māṣa*),
she offers them to the King in the morning during the presentation of worship.
She provides betel leaf, water, sweets, honey, cold and warm [beverages], as well as whatever substances are required for massage, all at the appropriate time. (34)
She constantly sings the praises of His glorious fame in her palace amidst her companions;
her friends sing along with her, keeping time with the clapping of their hands. (35)

Victorious is Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa, the son of Śrī Kambharī, who brings happiness to the people, removes the sins of the world, is the sovereign of kings, and is the cowherd boy Murāri who upholds my fortune! 36.
He who sports with Rādhā, who removes the fear of worldly existence, who wanders among the gopīs, and who provides for my nourishment;
he who spreads affection, who delivers his own devotees, and whose manner is to dispel the suffering of women. 37.
He who illuminates the eyes, who shines within the heart, who dwells in consciousness, and who resides in many abodes;
who casts off illusion, who is a slave to his own devotees, and whose radiance extends toward those who long for service. (38)

She who blossoms through devotion, who dwells in her own true form, and who says "I am your servant" to the world—she, the ever-residing one, must be protected; therefore, O dweller within my heart, become my home. 39.
Thus, O Rādhikā, the queen, accompanied by her friends, constantly sings and extols the virtues of that very possessor of virtues.
Having heard that, Bālakṛṣṇa too became delighted in his mind;
and as time passed in this manner, Kṛṣṇa gave him armor that dispels all fear.
Having worn this, the king always remains fearless together with his queen;
even Mahākāla, upon seeing that armor, flees to a great distance.
It is a continuous composition on the perfection of yoga, adorned in its center by the Kaustubha gem,
and surrounded on all sides at the margins by the eight sovereign powers.
On whose head the Sudarśana shines as armor, and on whose shoulder the mace and on whose side the noose resplendently gleam; ||44||
Such is gold—the most excellent of metals—luminous, soft, yet firm in protection; gentle in appearance and light when worn. (45)
The armor, which was indeed in the form of a garment, was bestowed by Bālakṛṣṇa;
the king wore that armor as a continuous bodice.
For old age surely advances far, as does the staff of Yama;
and the destruction of Saṃkarṣaṇa also proceeds far beyond one's armor.
The noose of the god Varuṇa brings fear even to his armor; at the sight of Śaṅkara’s coat of mail, even his attendants tremble as they walk along the path.
If Death enters the path of the armor, he goes to the state of death;
for such indeed is that armor, endowed with the power of a child. ||49||
O Rādhikā, having taken up the role of a king on earth, he rejoices like one who has been liberated;
since Kṛṣṇa Himself stays by his side, tell me, O Rādhikā, what fear can he have? (2.243.50)
"O beautiful lady, tell me, what fear can he have by whose side Nārāyaṇa stands?
Like Rādhikā or like Ramā herself, this king is fearless in the forest. (5.1)
He continued to dwell in the forest, devoted to Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa;
then the king went to the tiger-infested forest with the desire to sport there. ||52||
Then, traveling by aerial chariot through the sky, he went to Siṃhāraṇya;
from there he proceeded to Daṇḍakāraṇya, and then he went to Dharmāraṇya.
Having also visited the Naimiṣa forest and the Māhendra forest,
he traveled to Saurāṣṭra together with the queen.
But beholding that great celestial chariot, which bore the splendor of the Kṣatriyas,
Paraśurāma, the slayer of Kṣatriyas, trembled, impelled by Time.
Having quickly taken up his own axe from Mount Mahendra,
and having grasped his bow and arrows as well as his sword, he became filled with extreme rage.
He, possessing great splendor and moving swiftly, descended quickly through the sky onto the back of the celestial chariot as it approached from behind.
The king, traveling fearlessly in his celestial chariot, did not perceive this;
yet within the hearts of the subjects there was a turmoil like that of wind in the atmosphere. (58)
Then the circle of planets became agitated, foreboding future terror;
and the earth, unable to endure the two-fold radiance, trembled as well.
"At the moment of their collision, the dissolution of these two imperishable luminaries will occur.
Thus did the gods and the yogis, endowed with divine vision, tremble at that time.
Then the great sages were deeply distressed out of fear for what was to come;
the guardians of the quarters, the guardians of the fields, and others perceived the impending destruction of the world.
Then the Siddhas praised the Lord Viṣṇu Nārāyaṇa:
"May there not be the destruction of the worlds upon the encounter of the axe and the armor!"
Then the king’s aerial chariot, swift as thought, descended in an instant and arrived at the shore of Lake Aśvapaṭṭasara.
The king drank water while joyfully remembering Bālakṛṣṇa;
the queen also drank, having first made her lord drink.
Then, like the sun through the path of the sky, that cruel sphere, composed of light and red in color, descended with great speed. (65)
Then the earth trembled and the waters of the lake were agitated;
the dwellers of the sacred fords perceived fear and thought that a calamity had arrived.
Seeing the iron ball in the path of the sky, they conjectured: "Is this a planet that has become agitated, or has it fallen from its own place? (67)
Or does a portion of the sun arrive accompanied by flames of fire?
Or does the Fire himself abide here, perhaps filled with wrath? (68)
Or has the god Saṃkarṣaṇa, or the wrathful Śeṣa, arrived? Or has the Brahmā-weapon been discharged by someone and remained unwarded off? (6.9)
Or rather, has he come here so that the worlds shall not be reborn? Or perhaps it is the Vāḍava fire that has risen up once more from the ocean?
"Who is this one of cruel appearance who comes here to burn the worlds?"—thus did I reflect upon the thoughts of embodied beings. (71)
Then, he was clearly seen approaching with a manifest form:
having a terrifying face, holding an axe in his hand, and wearing matted hair.
Bearing a quiver and equipped with weapons, he was invested with the sacred thread;
his eyes were wide, his fangs and lips protruding, and his body was fully expanded.
Who is this that dwells in a warrior clan, living among those who wield the battle-axe?
Disguised here, he appears for the sake of destruction, though he possesses a celestial chariot.
Speaking thus, he quickly descended to the shore of the lake;
at that moment, he was recognized by the people as the twice-born Paraśurāma, the bringer of destruction.
Terrified men, as well as beasts and birds, fled away;
then Parśudhra appeared at the front of the golden vimāna.
On the delightful bank of the Āśvapaṭṭa river,
in the sacred field named Akṣara belonging to Bālakṛṣṇa— the wielder of the Śārṅga bow who humbles pride— there lived a Brahmin who possessed only a loincloth.
Just as the wielder of the battle-axe set his own foot upon the ground,
the nail of his big toe was pierced by a thorn.
Although that inauspicious birth had occurred for the Brahmin who was desirous of victory,
nevertheless, out of a sense of pride, he went forth to slay the golden [mountain].
"Who are you, O scion of the Kṣatriyas? You shall be devoured by my sword.
Speak quickly! Fight, and go to the realm of Yama! (2.243.80)
Thus addressed, King Haima, with the swift splendor of a kṣatriya,
spoke to him so that no offense might be committed against the brahmin.
O son of Jamadagni, Brahmins are to be honored; do not be overcome by the power of the Kshatriya.
You too are worthy of honor; do not employ your axe or your strength against one who is not a fit object for them.
For one who has been highly esteemed, defeat in an unworthy place is death itself.
O Brahmin, I am a Kshatriya; I do not wish to commit an offense against a Brahmin. (83)
Do not give way to anger, O best of Brahmins; do not wash away your merit, O twice-born one!
You are worthy of worship, you are indeed unslayable, and you are a protector of the earth, O Brahmin. (84)
"Therefore, you accept this worship and please forgive this impropriety.
Having spoken thus, King Haima indeed stood before the brahmin to honor him.
As Rādha proceeded, that twice-born man bearing an axe became intent on killing him, driven by rage and adopting a martial stance. (86)
Remembering the glorious Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, who is like molten gold,
he bound Parśudhra with the rays of the Sudarśana discus.
The divine Sudarśana discus, which had been bestowed by Śrī Hari,
formed a net with its own fire-like rays and bound him.
In that moment, Parśurāma— though full of wrath, armed, and accompanied by his forces—
had his power neutralized by the discus’s splendor as its edge blazed with fire.
Becoming as if senseless in an instant, he fell to the surface of the earth;
the King said, "Forgive me here, O illustrious one, for I am an offender. (2.243.90)
"O Brahmin, release your anger toward one who has insulted you; depart quickly!
Parśudhra replied, "Release it! I have no power to proceed. (91)
O King, I am pleased with you; I grant you a boon:
I worship and go to Cakradeva, [carrying] nooses and nets. ||9.2||
"Release me quickly, for I am being scorched by the rays of the discus!
The king said, "May you not indeed seek to kill my devotee."
The kṣatriya power has arisen from the brāhmaṇa; therefore, a brāhmaṇa must not kill one who is devoted.
Rather, protect this one boon, and dwell right here with the other.
"Stay in the field of Aśvapaṭṭasara, assuming a physical form.
Thus addressed, Paraśurāma then granted him two boons. 95.
Then Parśurāma was installed by the king in the palace;
he was bathed in the waters of the horse and honored with ritual offerings.
O Rādhikā, thereafter, to the east of that place, there was the Paraśurāma-tīrtha and the Haimakalpi-tīrtha. 97.
Having worshipped Hari, Paraśurāma indeed went to Mandara;
there, in the form of an image, he dwells eternally at Aśvapaṭṭasāgara. (18)
Then the king went to the glorious Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa;
having worshipped Hari, bowed down, and related the news, he departed. (99)
Having established a sacred bathing place (tīrtha), he went to his own capital, Himāvatī.
By bathing, giving gifts, and sipping water at this tīrtha, one shall attain victory. (2.243.10)
By reading or hearing this, the defects of the heart are indeed destroyed;
one shall obtain food, liberation, health, wealth, and sons. (101)

Thus ends the two hundred and forty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Acquisition of Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa as Consort by the Five Daughters of Vāmadeva in the Second Tretā Cycle of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā; King Haimakalgi’s Eternal Vision of Hari through Devotion; and the Defeat of Paraśurāma by the King, as well as the Description of Paraśurāma-tīrtha and Haimakalgi-tīrtha at Aśvapaṭṭasara. || 243 ||
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Listen, O Rādhikā, to what happened thereafter at Lake Āśvasara; on the eighth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, the commencement of the sacrifice took place.
Indeed, the king named Aśvapāṭala, a devotee of Viṣṇu,
came from Mount Arbuda along with his followers to Lomaśa for the purpose of performing a sacrifice.
He who possesses a hundred elephants in his house, vast fields, and a wide kingdom produced in the region of Arbuda; || 3 ||
Accompanied by a thousand young men and likewise by a thousand bulls,
he set out for the sake of the sacrifice, bringing with him many ritual materials.
On the shore of Lake Aśvapaṭṭasara, in the auspicious and purifying northeastern region,
he established his military camps in the Pālāśaka forest.
Having summoned Lomaśa and having obtained the vision of Hari,
he also invited the great seers and performed an excellent sacrifice.
O Rādhikā, he performed that Soma sacrifice for five days;
having gathered living Soma plants, he placed them in water-pots (kuṇḍikās).
They were nourished and also fed by the king on the bank of the Aśvasaras;
then, on that very bank, a five-day Soma sacrifice known as the Ahīna was performed.
In a very spacious pavilion, the king, together with his wife, having appointed a *somapravāka*, had an excellent sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) constructed.
He dispatched a learned Brahmin as the *somapravāka* to invite the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*);
that Brahmin, having gone there, brought the gods on earth (the invited priests).
Having offered the madhuparka, the king performed the formal selection (varaṇa) of the Adhvaryu,
the Pratiprasthātṛ, and also the Neṣṭṛ.
Then he also chose the Unnetṛ, and he chose the Brahman;
he chose the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin, the Āgnīdhra, and the Potṛ. || 12 ||
He chose the Hotṛ and likewise the Maitrāvaruṇa;
he chose the Acchāvāka, the Grāvastut, and the Udgātṛ. || 1.3 ||
The king there chose the Prastotṛ, the Pratihartṛ, and the Subrahmaṇya;
he also chose the Sadasyas and the officiating priests (ṛtvij). || 14 ||
Having worshipped the deities and placed the fire upon the two kindling woods (araṇis),
