he went to the sacrificial ground of Soma-kratu and then churned the fire from the araṇis.
Then the Adhvaryu priest, having led forth the Āhavanīya fire, established that very fire which had arisen in the Gārhapatya hearth.
Having offered twenty-four oblations and dismissed the fire,
and having brought it from the Gārhapatya fire, he should again offer seven oblations.
Having prepared that fire and cast it away, he performed the initiation sacrifice (dīkṣaṇīyeṣṭi) and caused a sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) on eleven potsherds to be prepared.
Thereafter, the sacrificer, having constructed a sacrificial hall with its ridgepole facing east, offered oblations to Agni and Viṣṇu as well.
And having had his head shaved in the northern outlying region, he bathed at a sacred ford; then, when the Adhvaryu priest presented him with two auspicious silk garments, he put them on.
In that manner, the queen put on her nail-clippers and other grooming tools;
having bathed, she put on two beautiful silk garments.
Then the husband and wife indeed ate food in the pavilion,
and there they anointed their own limbs with fresh butter.
Then, after his own eyes have been anointed with collyrium,
the Adhvaryu priest offers six initiation oblations (dīkṣāhuti) into the fire there.
Then he gave two black antelope skins to the sacrificer;
the sacrificer, having accepted them, went near the Āhavanīya fire.
Then, having spread [the seat] and sat down, and having tied a girdle around his waist,
he likewise took up a deer-horn and a staff of udumbara wood.
Likewise, the wife held the bundle of *iṣīkā* grass and the *muñja*-grass cord;
the sacrificer made the fist-grasp, and the Adhvaryu spoke.
"This sacrificer is initiated; these Brāhmaṇas are initiated.
The sacrificer has restrained his speech, and indeed, there is no rising of the stars. (27)
Then she drank the milk offered by the Adhvaryu priest;
subsequently, the wife also drank it, and thereafter the husband and wife both released their speech.
There, the couple partook of their meal as they desired: curd, parched grains, flour-cakes made from udumbara fruit, and boiled rice. || 29 ||
Then, seeking to obtain materials for sacrifice, Brahmins and gods went out to beg; meanwhile, the husband and wife remained awake during the night.
They also observed their vow, thinking, "One should not speak a falsehood.
Likewise, they did not eat meat or drink liquor, nor did they approach women.
He did not even sleep on a bedstead or similar furniture, but wore a black antelope skin and other such items;
thus the king performed the ritual duties of the Soma sacrifice on the eighth day.
Then, during the night in the assembly hall, Lomaśa gave an instruction for the sake of his own self-attainment, which was richly endowed with both theoretical knowledge and realized wisdom.
Sacrificial rites (*adhvara*) should always be performed by the wealthy for the sake of happiness;
embodied beings should always perform sacrifices that bring about their own liberation. (34)
Those people who perform the sacrifice of liberation, who have conquered their senses, and who take away the merit [of others],
attain the supreme abode of Hari, which is eternal and beyond primordial nature (prakṛti).
They do not rejoice when being praised, nor do they become angry even when reviled;
having attained this wisdom, they reach the abode of Hari.

Those people who have matured their knowledge, conquered their defects, are free from envy, do not cause harm, and do not burn with jealousy at the prosperity of others—such people do not commit offenses. (37)
They do not engage in blame or praise, nor are they affected by them;
being perfectly tranquil, they delight in the welfare of all beings.
They neither become angry nor do they rejoice, nor do they deceive others;
having untied the knot of the heart, they go to the abode of Hari.
Those who have no kinsmen whatsoever, nor are they the kinsmen of others; those who have no enemies, nor do they become the enemies of anyone. (2.244.40)
Those who adhere to the Dharma live happily and without anger;
yogis should find satisfaction in being treated with contempt, as if it were nectar.
The wise tremble at honor as if it were poison;
yet when they are disregarded, they sleep happily, free from fear from any quarter.
Those who are freed from all defects go to the imperishable state;
having undertaken these vows, the virtuous prosper in happiness.
Having performed all sacrifices and having made the mind exceedingly pure, they attain that goal.
They attain the supreme abode of Hari, which is eternal and beyond primordial nature.
Neither the gods, nor the gandharvas, nor the sages, nor even the ancestors, can follow the path of those who have attained the supreme state. || 45 ||
Those who possess no egoism arising from their qualities or conduct, and whose speech and heart are not at variance, are honored both here and in the next world. (46)

Those who know the reality of the internal discipline, who are patient, capable, and have conquered their senses, who are upright and truthful in speech, are honored both in this world and the next. (47)
Those endowed with splendor, fame, intelligence, knowledge, humility, noble birth, and austerity are honored both in this world and in the next. 48.
Those who are well-behaved, who sleep in peace, who possess pleasant voices, who are free from envy, and who are full of affection— such people are honored both in this world and in the next.
They perform what is beneficial for others, where no evil is found; they do not take pleasure in the sufferings of others, and thus they are honored both here and in the hereafter. (2.244.50)

Those who are patient, impartial in conduct, and likewise enduring both the pleasant and the unpleasant; who speak for the sake of what is beneficial, who are tranquil—they are honored both in this world and in the next.
Those who are undepressed, free from anger, devoid of greed, and intent on helping others—who do not quarrel even over wealth or desire—are honored both in this world and the next. (52)
Those whose faults have been utterly eradicated, who possess firm devotion to Hari,
and who are free from delusion and pride, are honored both in this world and in the next.
Those who are unattached to all worldly ties, whose doubts have been destroyed,
and who do not devote themselves to self-praise, are honored both in this world and in the next.
They do not harbor malice toward anyone and proceed along the path of justice; making their time fruitful and remaining gentle, they are honored both in this world and the next.
Those who have exerted effort and perfected their wisdom are never satiated with the chanting of Hari’s praises;
being ever-devoted and vigilant, they are honored both in this world and the next.
Those who are free from shame, who do not obstruct the welfare of others, who are generous, and who do not divulge the secrets of others, are honored both in this world and in the next. (57)
Thus, even the gods honor those who are endowed with all virtues, who are skillful, who seek their own welfare, who know the proper time, and who recognize what is pleasing. 58.
Those people who have that as their goal and offer everything to it surely attain the eternal, divine Supreme Brahman, which is without beginning or end and unborn. (59)
Austerity is his supreme good; its roots are tranquility and self-restraint.
By means of these, he attains everything that may be most desired.
Through austerity, the embodied soul is born as the master in sustaining all beings;
by that same austerity, the lords and the great seers were likewise born.
Those devoted to the Brahman of Sound (Śabdabrahman) attain the upward-leading Brahman;
the Kṣatriyas are considered protectors of the sacrifice, and the Vaiśyas are considered performers of the Havis-sacrifice.

In the Tretā age, Śūdras performed service as their sacrifice, while the Brahmins performed sacrifices through austerity; these auspicious sacrifices were unified and granted the attainment of Brahman.
By means of austerity, knowledge, sacrifice, or even charity, people attain unblemished fame and establish that fame upon the earth. (64)
Those who go to the supreme heaven enjoy infinite happiness;
it is the donors at the sacrifice who establish here a foundation for their glory.
As long as his fame shall endure, so long shall he enjoy unbroken heaven for the sake of the gods,
sages, ancestors, and teachers, and for the sake of the elderly, the sick, and guests.
For the sake of the helpless, the distressed, and the noble, and for the sake of virtuous, chaste, and good women—those who have nothing that should not be given have attained heaven. (67)
Gautama, having always served the Brahmins with food and other offerings during times of drought,
subsequently attained the celestial heaven and reached the abode of Nārāyaṇa.
Having given water that bestows happiness to Vasiṣṭha, Rantideva,
indeed through that blessing, enjoyed heaven and attained the abode of Hari.
Having offered infinite wealth in the sacrifice, Indradyumna went to the divine heaven through devotion, having attained the state of Nārāyaṇa.
Śibi, having given his son for the sake of a brahmin, went to the supreme heaven;
Pratardana, the lord of Kāśī, gave his eyes to a twice-born man.
Having enjoyed heaven through devotion, he went to the abode of Nārāyaṇa;
having offered his head, Dharmāṅgada went to the imperishable state, while Svarṇāṅgada went to the eternal realm.
Having given a golden umbrella to a Brahmin, King Devāvṛdha,
together with his kingdom, departed for the supreme abode of the Supreme Lord.
And Sāṃkṛtika, having instructed his disciples, departed for the divine, supreme station of Hari, which abides within. ||74||
And Ambarīṣa, having given a multitude of cattle to the Brahmins—
even by the hundreds of millions— enjoyed heaven and went to the imperishable state.
Vṛṣādarbhi, having bestowed all his jewels upon a brahmin, departed for the imperishable realm;
Yuvanāśva [renounced] his beloved women and charming dwellings.
Having bestowed gifts upon the Brahmins, Nimi then went from heaven to the imperishable state; likewise, Janaka, the King of Videha, became known as Janaka after giving away his kingdom.
The son of Jamadagni also, having given away the earth, became Nārāyaṇa;
and Gaya, having given it to a twice-born, went to heaven and attained the station of Īśa.
The royal sage named Marutta, having offered his daughter to Aṅgiras,
departed for heaven and from there went to the divine, imperishable state.
Brahmadatta, the king of Pañcāla, having given the treasure Śaṅkha to a twice-born man,
enjoyed heaven for a long time and then went to the supreme state of the Lord.
And the royal sage Mitrasaha, having bestowed his own beloved wife Madayantī upon Vasiṣṭha, departed for the imperishable realm together with his [other] wife. ||81||
Likewise, the pure King Sahasrajit gave up his dear life for the sake of a brahmin; he went to heaven and, having enjoyed its rewards, attained the state of liberation.
King Śatadyumna, having given his own golden palace along with its furnishings to Mudgala, enjoyed heaven and went to the imperishable state.
Having bestowed his kingdom upon Ṛcīka, King Dyutimat enjoyed heaven for a long time through devotion and thereafter went to the imperishable abode. ||84||
Having given Śāntā, the daughter of Lomapāda, to the yogi Ṛṣyaśṛṅga,
he enjoyed the divine heaven and then departed for the imperishable abode.
And the royal sage Madirāśva, having given his most beautiful daughter to Hiraṇyaka,
went from there to the imperishable heaven.
Prasenajit, having given a hundred thousand cows as a gift to the twice-born, enjoyed heaven and thereafter went to the imperishable abode of Śrī Hari known as Akṣara. ||87||
The fourteen levels of dwellings, the ancestors, the great sages,
the gods, kings, subjects, and their own daughters were given by him to the wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
In previous kalpas they have gone to the supreme Goloka; and by giving even now for the sake of Hari alone, they shall go there again.
Or even by giving away their entire possessions or some small thing with devotion, they shall go to that state;
indeed, many have gone to heaven through gifts, austerities, and devotion.
Their fame is indeed firmly established forever in the world of Brahmā,
and likewise their renown remains upon the earth as long as the sun and other celestial bodies endure.
Those refined ones who have acquired wisdom from the virtuous and are dedicated to Nārāyaṇa,
having surrendered all their possessions for the sake of Hari, abide in the eternal, imperishable state.
People who possess fortitude, who are vigilant, self-controlled, and knowers of the Dharma—
having cast off joy, pride, and anger— never indeed come to grief.
Through charity, study, sacrifice, austerity, modesty, self-control, and uprightness, one increases one's own splendor, and all evil is destroyed. (94)
Those who have shaken off evil, who are endowed with devotion, who have conquered their senses through withdrawal,
and who are not overcome by desire and anger, go to the eternal Brahman.

One should always bow to Agni—the wise, the true, the divine, and the ancient—and one should avoid harsh speech; thereby, one attains Brahman. Established in wisdom and established in the Self, one is not tainted even while acting.
And one should strive to cross the river whose body is the latent impressions of saṃsāra. || 97 ||
It has the waters of all the sense-faculties as its current, with greed and delusion as its banks;
it has anger as its mud, is long-lasting through time, and has affection for one's family as its crocodiles. (98)

By means of the raft of service or through devotion as a boat, with the assistance of the virtuous, the peaceful and steadfast followers of the Sātvata path cross over, their vision fixed upon the further shore. 99.
Those who are without devotion and lacking in wisdom do not cross over this river;
therefore, one who possesses the virtue of charity should strive for the sake of emerging [from the cycle].
Taking refuge in the Eternal One, one should cross over that [ocean of worldly existence] through sacrifice, devotion, and renunciation;
one should abide by the dharma of the virtuous and perform the actions of the virtuous.

Those virtuous ones who possess special knowledge of devotion to the Dharma cross over the river that is difficult to traverse; through their devotion to Śrī Hari, they act as rafts to carry the ignorant across.
Thus, O Rādhikā, the illustrious teacher Lomaśa himself, having instructed her in this manner, ceased speaking; thereafter, the resolution was reached.
The foods there indeed provided satisfaction according to their desire,
and thus, O Rādhikā, all the people attained complete rest.

Thus ends the two hundred and forty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of King Aśvapāṭala Commencing the Soma Sacrifice on the Bank of the Aśvapaṭṭa Lake on the Eighth Day of the Dark Fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa, the Observances of the First Day, and the Instruction Given by Lomaśa," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Listen, O Rādhikā; on the second day, the sage Lomaśa performed whatever duties were required for the Soma sacrifice.

Having first performed the necessary preliminary rites and virtuous deeds, Lomaśa then indeed performed the Prāyaṇīyeṣṭi sacrifice early in the morning. He established and worshipped the five deities beginning with Pathyā;
Pathyā Svasti was the first, and Agni Sura was the second.
Soma is the third, Savitṛ the fourth, and Aditi the fifth;
the sacrificial material for Aditi is boiled rice, while for the other four it is clarified butter alone.
Having cooked the rice, he then offered it as an oblation into the Āhavanīya fire;
there, the king purchased Soma for ten articles.
And with a one-year-old cow, gold, a goat,
as well as a milch-cow with her calf and a bull, the lord of the earth [performed the sacrifice].
He purchased Soma indeed with a bullock that draws a cart, and also with a young bull, a heifer, and a garment.
Having purchased the Soma and seized the two thieves by the right hand,
the sacrificer placed it upon the sacrificial cart (havirdhāna-śakaṭa) and proceeded to the sacrifice.
Standing before the Prāgvaṃśa hall, he performed the Ātithyeṣṭi sacrifice,
offering a cake made of grain on nine potsherds as the sacrificial substance for Viṣṇu.
Then he gave that Soma and had it placed upon the royal throne;
the officiating priests and the sacrificer made an oath for the sake of non-enmity.
Then the Pravargya rite commenced with all its implements:
three vessels known as Mahāvīras, and two milking bowls. || 1.1 ||
The vessel for clarified butter, as well as two horses, and two earthen potsherds;
and likewise the wooden implements made of Udumbara wood, as follows: || 1-2 ||
The imperial throne-seat, two *sruva*-ladles, and also two *sruc*-ladles set in a pit;
two *śapha*-hooves, two *dhṛṣṭi*-stirring-sticks, a central pillar, and three *śaṅku*-stakes. || 13 ||
There are three fans, two golden ornaments, as well as one named after its description; there are cords for the branches, and likewise muñja grass. || 14 ||
Thus the Adhvaryu brought the materials for the Pravargya rite, and then,
authorized by the Brahman priest, he performed the Pravargya ceremony.
He prepared the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) named Rauhiṇa according to the prescribed rite;
furthermore, having driven four stakes near the door, he likewise prepared a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila).
Having kindled the fire and placed the mahāvīra vessel right there,
one should fill its mouth with clarified butter and cover it with gold.
Having repeatedly performed this in the same manner, the Adhvaryu priest thereafter tied a cow, a calf, and a goat to the stakes and milked them.
When the great hero has offered the milk, heat arises;
when the clarified butter has been satisfied, the pouring of milk is called *pravṛñjana*.
And the Adhvaryu alone performed this Pravargya rite;
thereafter, the Pratiprasthātṛ [prepared] the Rauhiṇa sacrificial cake.
They used to offer oblations into the Āhavanīya fire with a ladle that had no handle;
and so too did the Adhvaryu perform the call for attention and the response. || 21 ||
Having prepared it, he offered into the fire clarified butter mixed with milk for the sake of the hero;
the milk thus poured while the Great Hero was present is celebrated as the *gharma*.
The Aśvins and Mahendra are proclaimed as its two deities;
with what remained, he performed the Sviṣṭakṛt oblation.
Having filled the mahāvīra vessel with curd, he performed that oblation;
then the pratiprasthātṛ placed the remainder upon the altar.
He performed the oblation of the Rauhiṇa sacrificial cake to some extent;
then the Adhvaryu indeed performed the six-fold oblations.
Having performed the Agnihotra and the Homa sacrifice, he partook of the remnants together with the Hotṛ, Brahmā, Āgnīdhra, and the sacrificer.
In this way, the Pravargya rite was indeed performed in the morning at that time;
likewise, the evening Pravargya will also take place in the same manner. || 27 ||
For the purpose of rejoining the severed head of the sacrifice, the Pravargya rite was performed;
in ancient times, O Rādhā, Viṣṇu, being the sacrifice itself, engaged in a sacrificial session with the gods.
Yashoravi alone attained [victory], for those gods were not superior to him;
they fought together with Vishnu, while Vishnu [struck] the gods with his bow.
Having conquered Dhanuṣkoṭi and placed it below his chin,
he then stood upon the ground while the ants remained upon the bowstring.
By the force of the bow, it flew up from the edge of the earth;
having been torn from Viṣṇu’s neck, his head went into the sky.
When Viṣṇu, whose form is sacrifice, had his head severed, the gods became unsuccessful in their worship; they then petitioned the two Aśvins.
Then, in order to rejoin that head, the two of them said to the gods: "From this day forward, let there be a share of the sacrificial oblation for us both in the Soma sacrifice. (33)
The gods granted him a portion, and they two joined it to the head;
that indeed was the Pravargya, the joining of the head of the sacrifice.
O Rādhikā, Mahāvīra was the form of the head of the sacrifice, and Bodhya was likewise;
from that, in the morning, the upasat and the iṣṭi were also produced.
Agni, Soma, and Viṣṇu—these three are the principal deities;
he offered clarified butter as the sacrificial substance in the oblation to those very gods.
Having performed the invocation of the Subrahmaṇyā priest, he then paused;
likewise, in the evening, he performed the Pravargya and Upasad rites.
Then he performed the invocation of Subrahmaṇyā, and from that there was a cessation;
thus indeed was the rite of Soma completed on the ninth day.
Then they all partook of meals consisting indeed of sweet foods;
and at night, the venerable Lomaśa instructed them in the means for liberation.
Therefore, for one devoid of worship, there shall be the severing of the head;
thus, the Blessed Lord, the Supreme Sovereign, the Lord of Śrī, is to be worshipped.
When one maintains [the practice] toward Śrī Hari by drawing sustenance from others, then single-minded devotion toward the Supreme Lord arises. 41.
Through the withdrawal of the senses and the cessation of food, and by abandoning mental nourishment, knowledge of the Self arises through the dissolution of the ego by means of the intellect. 42.
One should restrain the self by means of knowledge; thereby one shall attain peace, for one becomes steady as a witness even to the internal senses. 43.
One who sees the Self by means of the self crosses over the difficult-to-cross hardship, whether one is by nature a tiger, a dog, or even a pig. (44)
Whether it be a lion, a śarabha, an elephant, a cat, or even a monkey; a jackal, a crow, or even a serpent, or even a scorpion. ||45||
Whether it be a dog or even a donkey, one who is of such a nature; whether a sinner or a doer of merit, or one afflicted by suffering or situated amidst affliction—(46)
Whether free from affliction or active, whether poor or even a deceiver—even one who was inferior in his former state—if he resorts to the Sāṃkhya dharma, [he attains success]. ||47||
One who possesses yoga, associates with the virtuous, and is devoted to the dharma of Kṛṣṇa,
surely crosses over the difficult terrain of the inner disposition— the vast ocean of latent tendencies.

The sacrificial seat has modesty as its fender, dharma and dispassion as its pole-axle, the vital breaths as its yoke, discernment as its axle-pin, wisdom as its path, and the heart as its interior. (49)
It has conduct for its rim, the sense-faculties for its vehicle, knowledge for its hub, tranquility for its whip, merit for its charioteer, and is mounted by the horses [of the senses]. ||2.245.50||
One should cause the chariot of the living soul, well-yoked, to cross over the long path;
one should establish it in the garden of the Imperishable and protect it in the supreme abode.
Established in the knowledge of Brahman, devoted to all sacrifices, endowed with infinite sovereignty, and whose inner heart was won over by devotion. 52.
Kṛṣṇa shines within the heart and manifests both internally and externally;
in such a supreme devotee, indeed, the entire universe is contained. (53)
Thus, there is nothing whatsoever equal to the nature of his majesty;
having conquered the earth, and likewise having conquered water, fire, wind, and space. (54)

Having conquered those subtle elements (tanmātras) and then the sense of ego (ahaṃbuddhi), one who also conquers the state of being a lord (īśabhāva) shall proceed to the station of the Supreme Lord (parameśapada). ||55||
Having conquered human effort, destiny, time, and the planets, and having overcome inherent nature, latent impressions, and illusion, one shall go to the imperishable state. ||56||
Those devoted to the dharma of austerity are said to belong to the Satya Yuga; those devoted to the dharma of sacrifice are said to belong to the Tretā Yuga. 57.
People devoted to the duty of giving are said to belong to the Dvāpara age,
while those devoted to the destruction of righteousness are said to belong to the Tiṣya age.
Those who are devoted to the Brahman and the Dharma are said to be indeed yogis seeking liberation; if they are devoted to the Supreme Brahman, they become established in the Imperishable. ||59||
A human being does not find liberation without knowledge and austerity, without the restraint of the senses, and without the renunciation of everything. || 2.245.60 ||
In the past, at the very moment of creation, having brought forth all the principles (tattvas),
he bestowed them upon the individual soul (jīvātman) for the sake of worldly enjoyment, heaven, and liberation.
Earth is placed in the body, water in the belly, fire in the mind and the eyes, wind in the vital breath, and space in the internal cavities and so forth. (62)
Indeed, all the subtle elements (tanmātras) are held within the physical spheres;
likewise, the objects of the senses and the sense-objects are deposited within their respective things.
Viṣṇu was placed in the feet, Śukra in the strength, Indra in the hands;
Agni in the stomach, the quarters of space in the ears, and Sarasvatī on the tongue. (64)

Candra is placed in the mind, Brahmā in the intellect, and likewise Hari in the heart; all the gods are thus situated there, while Keśava, the inner controller, resides within the individual soul (jīva).
Thus, all these are placed within the Imperishable (akṣara) at the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra);
however, the supreme radiance is established within the Suṣumṇā at the heart.
"Everything indeed exists here; it is only the seeker who is difficult to find.
Having thoroughly sought the supreme deity through meditative absorption, one reaches the path of Brahman. (67)
Having mounted the chariot of devotion, the virtuous one shall go to the imperishable abode;
by the light of his own lamp, he shall behold the Supreme Self.
One who perceives thus is indeed fit for becoming Brahman after death;
for the Supreme Lord, the Sovereign, dwells within all moving and stationary beings. (69)
Having seen that Self as the Supreme, one attains the Brahman that is beyond;
to whatever extent the Self is known through self-surrender, to that same extent is the Supreme known through surrender.
One who constantly places their trust in Kṛṣṇa is fit for immortality;
Time ripens all beings, yet it is Time by which Time itself is ripened.
Having attained that supreme state of digestion, no further "grasping" arises;
having become the Imperishable Brahman, one indeed proceeds toward the Supreme Brahman.
He is subtle, He is immensely gross; He is within and He is without as the Lord.
Abiding as the permanent amidst the impermanent, He does not shine through external appearance.
And Kṛṣṇa is seen within as an inner radiance, sought by the luminous Self; through the power of grace, he converses within by means of devotion.
Even while abiding here in the state of the divine, immortal, and imperishable word,
he remains within his own self, which is equal to that [divine state], the refuge of the Lord, and free from all impurity.
He who is tranquil and self-controlled, whose garment is the internal discipline of virtue, who delights in the Self and has awakened to the Truth—he goes to that supreme state. (76)
One should conquer desire, anger, fear, greed, pride, sleep, and mental obsession through lack of volitional construction, through tranquility, and through vigilance—these three. || 77 ||
One should conquer the three [organs] through nobility, reflection, and courage; likewise, one should control the genitals and the stomach with fortitude, and the hands and feet with the eyes. (78)

One should conquer the eyes and ears through the mind, speech through the mind, and action through the performance of deeds; and one should conquer all actions by offering them entirely to Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa. (79)
One should perceive all things as consisting of the splendor of Brahman and as Hari, whose essence is rasa;
for spiritual luster increases through meditation, and meditation increases through devotion.

Devotion increases from affection; affection arises from the realization of His greatness; and that realization comes from the company of the virtuous, who themselves exist through a fraction of the grace of Hari. (8.1)
Compassion consists in protecting [beings] from taking refuge [in wrong paths], as well as from the pursuit of worldly ends;
the purpose is happiness in this life, for the sake of which one exerts oneself. (82)

If there is activity, it arises from desire; desire arises from knowledge; and knowledge, born of the scriptures, arises from the greatness of hearing the sacred discourse. Thus, divine contemplation is produced. (8.3)
Therefore, a wise person should always listen to this divine narrative; for what more need be said of one who has obtained the wish-fulfilling gem that consists of this very story? (84)
By these, one's splendor, sovereignty, and the ultimate truth increase;
all goals are accomplished, and the splendor of Brahman shines forth. (85)
Having conquered primordial nature through spiritual splendor, one should proceed to the eternal Brahman;
for the senses are indeed like holes that cause wisdom to leak away.
One should restrain those [senses] by fixing the mind upon one's own self, which is the supreme self;
thereby the inner reality becomes serene, and through that, Brahman is revealed.
In the divine Brahman, indeed within their own eternal self which is Brahman itself,
they beheld one another like two liberated practitioners.
Thus, having practiced in secret, one should attain identity with the Imperishable;
disregarding the supernatural powers, lordships, and obstacles, one should proceed toward the Imperishable.
Having risen early in the morning, one should contemplate Hari on that very seat,
having performed the sacrifice of Vedic study, the sacrifice of meditation, and the sacrifice of worship.
Thereafter, one should perform the sacrifice of material substances and restrain the speed of the mind;
one should not, even in thought, become attached to objects situated nearby.
One should not contemplate insults or honors, nor the stirrings of joy or fear;
one should meditate upon the Lord of Gods, the Supreme Lord, who resides within the self and is supported by the sacrifice.
Thus, for the virtuous one whose self is absorbed in meditation and who is devoted to equanimity,
the stainless Supreme Brahman quickly shines forth within his own inner cavern.
By this very path, whether a woman or even a person of neutral gender,
having propitiated the supreme Brahman, shall attain the highest goal.
Having become liberated, one should behold the liberated Hari, who is without beginning;
having become Brahman, one should behold the imperishable Brahman, the abode of bliss. || 95 ||
The liberated king perceives the Supreme Brahman through the eye of Brahman;
indeed, a living being is bound by action that has not been offered to Hara.
A living being is liberated by that knowledge when it is offered to Hara;
therefore, both types of yoga pertaining to Hari should indeed be practiced here by an ascetic. 97.
Those two divine beings, who receive everything as an offering, lead him to the abode they have taken refuge in,
where having gone, there is no death, no sorrow, and no rebirth.
One should know oneself as a portion of that Supreme Self;
therefore, one should offer sacrifice, action, oblation, and state of being unto Hari. (99)
Having spoken thus to Rādhikā, the glorious Lomaśa became silent;
then there was a dismissal from the assembly, and the meals were served.
The people, chanting the name of Śrī Hari and meditating upon Hari, became truly providers of satisfaction and brought rest to the night. || 10.1 ||

Thus ends the two hundred and forty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Duties on the Second Day of the Soma Sacrifice in the Tretā Age within the *Śrī-Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*, including the Instruction by Lomaśa regarding the Subrahmaṇya, Upasada, Pravargya, and other rites, as well as the avoidance of the oblation."
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Rādhikā, then on the third day of the sacrifice,
on the tenth lunar day, the performance of the Soma ritual commenced once again.
Lomaśa arrived, and King Kṛtapuṇyaka also arrived;
in the morning, the Guru performed the Pravargya and Upasada rites.
The Guru then constructed the great altar at a distance of six paces from the pavilion in front, according to the prescribed rules.
It is considered to be seventy-two paces long from east to west,
and sixty paces wide from south to north.
Extending forty-eight [units] across both the hip region and the shoulder region,
one should then construct such a complete altar (vedī) as this.
The sacrificer indeed maintained his vow consisting of drinking milk;
he also performed the oblations and all other duties that were to be observed.
Even at evening, after performing the evening Pravargya and Upasad rites of the afternoon session,
one should perform the milk-vow and then invoke the deity Subrahmaṇyā.
Having invoked the one whose essence is Indra, he then undertook a vow;
thereafter followed the cessation [of the rite], the relinquishment, and finally the meal of grace.
When Miṣṭānna had become as full as a wooden vessel through sweet foods such as milk-rice (pāyasa) and other delicacies, the venerable sage Lomaśa then [spoke].
But at night, in the assembly hall, the one who effects liberation taught as follows:
"By means of celibacy, indeed, the supreme seers conquer the worlds. (2.246.10)
And thereafter, subsisting on roots and fruits in the forest and performing extensive austerities, they attain the eternal and supreme good beyond that.
Dwelling in temples of the gods and intent on the welfare of all beings,
those who are absorbed in the assembly of the virtuous are ordained for the state of becoming Brahman.
Virtuous ones who follow the conduct of celibate students, householders, or forest-dwellers,
remaining intent on Hari and following the conduct prescribed for themselves, attain the supreme goal.
For those who perform their daily duties with their fruits burnt away by knowledge, being free from the defects of desire and aversion, they are established in the supreme Imperishable.
For this four-stepped ladder is the means for ascending to Brahman;
having ascended it and reached Hari, one indeed goes to the world of Brahman.
A celibate student (brahmacārī), remaining steadfast in the vow of Brahman, shall indeed attain everything;
for the Guru is Brahman, the vow is Brahman, the Veda is Brahman, and likewise Hari is Brahman. || 16 ||
One should serve them constantly; one shall thereby go to the world of Brahmā.
Indeed, by performing service to the guru, one obtains fruit equal to that of a sacrifice. || 17 ||
Whatever must be done by a disciple or a servant, that he should perform;
he should be a doer of all tasks, free from pride, and exceedingly devoted.
When summoned, he should abandon everything and approach his guru;
he should speak what is pleasing and indeed gaze upon the guru with eyes full of love.
Having fed his teachers, he should then eat and likewise drink;
he should perform a foot-massage for them and touch their feet gently.
"Command me, O Blessed One; I shall do it"—thus he should serve.
For the sake of serving the Guru alone, he should remain nearby and dwell there. (21)
Even a householder should indeed revere his teacher, the deity, and his virtuous wife; he should practice righteousness and irreproachable conduct, performing his duties with unwearied devotion.
One should give cooked food to a deity, to a teacher, and to a traveler;
one should also give it to a trustee, but one should never cook for one's own sake alone.
No guest who has come to his house should remain unhonored;
[he should give] even to those worthy of worship, to the poor, to children, and to the helpless and the guests. (24)
One may indeed offer oblations to the gods (havya) and to the ancestors (kavya) to those who are virtuous, chaste, and righteous;
for such people, being practitioners of austerity, are always worthy of worship. ||25||
Likewise, one who dwells in a house should give to those who do not cook for themselves;
he should eat only the remains of the meal (vighasa) and thus become a consumer of nectar (amṛta). ||26||
One should eat the remains of offerings (vighasa), the remnants of what has been given to servants, and likewise the remnants of what has been offered to the gods as nectar;
one should not engage in disputes with kinsmen, family members, or relatives.
The teacher is the lord of the world of Brahmā; one should not engage in debate with him. The father is the lord of the realm of Prajāpati; one should not engage in debate with him. ||28||
The guest is indeed the lord of the world of Indra; one should not engage in dispute with him.
The officiating priest is the lord of the world of the gods; one should not engage in dispute with him. (29)
One should not quarrel with one's kinswoman, for she is the mistress of the world of the Apsarases;
nor should one cause a rift with one's paternal relative, for she is the sovereign of the world of the Viśvedevas.
One should not create enmity with kinsmen, relatives, or the lords of the directions;
nor should one cause a rift between the earth and the groups of maternal uncles and their kin.
One should not cause separation from the sky for the elderly, children, the sick, or the emaciated;
for a brother is like a father, a wife is a son, and a daughter is one's own body.
One's shadow, one's circle of servants, and dependent, wretched people belong to oneself;
therefore, when reviled by these, one should endure it and not revile them in return. (3.3)
Even while performing all the duties prescribed for the householder's life,
if one should act while pervaded by desire, greed, and fear, and devoid of the mind [of yoga], [he falls].
If one who is free from dualities and devoid of pride conducts himself like a virtuous person,
and having found refuge in Hari, he is liberated and not bound.
He indeed attains the supreme goal in this world marked by the discus.
And he attains the auspicious destiny that is characteristic of those who have conquered their senses. ||36||
For householders, heaven consists of the essence of fruits, flowers, and juices;
and for householders, there is also a second, supreme, eternal heaven. (37)
That householder, seeing his own body overcome by wrinkles, grey hair, and infirmity,
should indeed worship the Supreme Lord like one dwelling in the forest.

One should eat little, subsisting on pure food, eating roots and fruits; and one should protect the Dharma contained in the Upaniṣads, which is cherished by Brahman. Having made one’s dwelling like a great seer—whether in a forest, a wilderness, or a house— [one should live thus].
Being absorbed in the supreme Brahman, one shall attain liberation.
Having performed a sacrifice, a fire-oblation, and likewise provided all ritual fees—whether he be a virtuous man or even a son of Brahmā who is non-human. ||41||
One should perform the *jīvacchrāddha* (the funeral rite for the living), for one becomes established in the Self within the self;
having projected [all duties] upon one's own self, the observer of vows should practice the ritual section (*karmakāṇḍa*).
Constant devotion, worship, meditation upon Nārāyaṇa, sacrifice, recitation, remembrance of Kṛṣṇa, and contemplation on Brahman. ||43||
For that purpose, one should perform all actions while remaining established like one who is liberated;
having attained fearlessness and steadfastness within oneself, one should give [the teaching] to those who are proud of others.
One who possesses the virtuous Dharma should take up the life of renunciation for the sake of the next world;
for him, the worlds will be full of splendor, with ever-increasing great happiness. (45)
Even while remaining in this world, he shall possess inexhaustible satisfaction;
and having cast off the body through union with Hari, he attains imperishable infinity.
Possessed of a body, he always exists here as the fullness itself, like space;
he should neither become angry nor rejoice, remaining pure and behaving like Brahman. 47.
One should neither rejoice in death nor in life as it arises by nature;
one should await Brahman alone, just as a servant awaits his master. 48.
One should always have an unassailable mind, liberated from evil, and should also grant fearlessness to all beings, as well as that which has been done for them. (49)
For one who is liberated from delusion and for whom no fear exists, immortality dwells eternally; he is the refuge of all embodied beings. (2.246.50)
Satiated by wisdom, free from worldly striving, liberated from attachment, and having transcended death—he whose life is for the sake of Dharma, and whose Dharma is solely for the sake of Hari. (51)
Released from all bonds, this knower of Brahman, becoming a true Brāhmaṇa,
offers the substance of his own arising states into the Supreme Self.
Through the satisfaction born of the *homa* sacrifice, Hari attains a state of graciousness;
and by accumulating that merit, one indeed reaches the eternal Brahman. (53)
The gods nourish that very [state] and long for the supreme goal;
having attained that longing made fruitful, he beholds the Supreme Self.
Having observed that both the primary elements and their modifications have passed away, he who has attained the immortal state,
with his fever of passion stilled and his mind equanimous, surely reaches the immortal goal.
Having utterly subdued all volitional thoughts, one should direct the mind toward sentient beings;
by conquering time through the assistance of the Supreme Lord, one shall attain the deathless state.
Upon attaining clarity of mind, both the auspicious and the inauspicious cease.
Having taken refuge in the divine Self alone, one enjoys infinite happiness. ||57||
He whose sleep is attained with ease finds serenity within himself;
and Hari, being pleased with him, bestows upon him a treasure-trove of bliss.
For one for whom there is worthlessness even in being appointed to a position or in being invited, his favor remains constant, like the imperishable. (59)
When one restrains the rays of the senses with the mind,
and the mind is restrained by the intellect, then the Self is fully revealed.
Being liberated from both internal and external virtues and defects, one is not stained by them;
for one who is unstained, delight arises in that Supreme Self. 61.
With the functions of the qualities (guṇas) destroyed and no longer engaged in the activities of the qualities,
and being free from the knot of the heart, he attains the knot of Brahman.
One who is intent upon the Supreme Brahman attains peace as well as spiritual power;
self-knowledge and tranquility are the supreme means for the state of becoming Brahman. (63)
The state of Brahman here is the attainment of the Supreme Brahman; of this there is no doubt.
Indeed, there is no attainment higher than this, for it is the supreme attainment of Hari.
That which one performs without prior intention is devoid of qualities (nirguṇa); but that performed with the intention of [pleasing] Hari is divine and indeed bestows liberation. || 65 ||
For there is no dharma higher than this dharma here in this world except for Hari;
the dharma of Brahman is the supreme dharma, the veil that covers all other dharmas.
The cessation of all activities is the supreme dharma and the highest austerity;
being satisfied with the Self through austerity, one enjoys the bliss of the fruit.
Having attained the internal path, he resorts to the supreme Lord residing within the palace—the self of all, his own self, now revealed. (68)
Then the inner self indeed bestows everything upon him—
the yogi who possesses the light of knowledge and has attained his own true nature.
He has crossed this ocean of saṃsāra, which is composed of illusion;
he has entered that which is composed of Brahman, and here itself, Brahman shines forth.
The Self is neither female nor male, nor even neuter;
it is neither inert matter nor inherent nature, but is the eternal form of Brahman.
He is protected by the Supreme Brahman, awakened by the Supreme Brahman, nourished by the Supreme Brahman, and likewise fed by the Supreme Brahman. ||72||
He is the essence of the Supreme Brahman, rejoicing in the Supreme Brahman, possessing the body of the Supreme Brahman, and immersed in the bliss of the Supreme Brahman. ||73||

He is a friend of the Supreme Brahman, a traveler on the path to the Supreme Brahman, one whose purpose is the expansion of the Supreme Brahman, and one who exerts himself in taking refuge in the Supreme Brahman. ||74||
Having made his abode in the Supreme Brahman, he indeed goes into the Supreme Brahman;
possessing the Supreme Brahman as his entire wealth, he attains liberation which consists of that very essence.
When one indeed does not form a separate mental state toward any living beings, nor [feels] suffering or even evil, then one attains Brahman. (76)
Indeed, latent impression (vāsanā) is the one and only supreme bond;
liberated from the bond of latent impressions, one is fit for becoming Brahman.
The secret essence of knowledge is tranquility; the secret essence of tranquility is happiness;
the secret essence of happiness is contentment; and the secret essence of contentment is renunciation. ||78||
One who renounces, whose mind is serene, and who is established in Hari, attains infinite bliss, being steadfast in the Supreme Brahman. (79)
He enjoys imperishable bliss—unborn, indestructible, eternally established, unmixed, and perceivable through the attainment of the Supreme Brahman. (2.246.80)
For one whose mind is devoid of impulse and whose firm foundation is in the Supreme Lord, there is satisfaction in the Supreme Deity, and for such a person, indeed, there is eternal contentment. 8.1
The wise man should choose that Hari by whom one who has not eaten is satisfied, by whom one who possesses no wealth is satisfied, and by whom one who lacks affection is endowed with strength.
Having restrained his own senses, he should open the door to the Imperishable;
with that provision for the journey consisting of delight in the Self, he attains the imperishable state of Acyuta.
When one is perfectly rested in the Supreme Lord Kṛṣṇa,
who is the source of all desires, one attains happiness from every side from that inexhaustible ocean of bliss.
Neither old age nor death find him who has destroyed illusion, who has destroyed the impurities of his own self, and whose meditation on Hari remains unimpeded.
Thus, indeed, being liberated in every respect, one shines as the unliberated Brahman; and for such a person, O noble lady, the supreme Brahman itself becomes unliberated.
Having thus transcended the three qualities and attained the imperishable abode here,
he does not return again, for he has reached the supreme state.

That tree which has ignorance as its root is said to be like a desire-tree (kalpavṛkṣa); the attainment of sense-objects is its cluster of blossoms, and the sense-objects themselves are considered its branches. (88)
Its enjoyment is the stalk, its tastes are indeed the leaves of that tree;
its joy is the flowers, and its happiness is truly the fruits.
Therein lies the mixture of suffering: the foul mire of putrid moisture, delusion, thirst for sensual flavors, and the matrix of ignorance and illusion. (2.246.90)
Having reached Hari, the practitioner of yoga should indeed dispel that māyā;
by that means, everything indeed attains dissolution for the practitioner of yoga. 91.
While remaining in his own home, Kṛṣṇa shines as the jewel of heaven;
having obtained that cooling light which bestows the imperishable, one shall go [to the supreme state]. ||92||
That bliss, known as the Imperishable (akṣara), is concentrated upon the Supreme Brahman;
and that vessel in which it is placed is the very form of Brahman, one's own self. 93.
It is flawless, very firm, bound together by the plaster of devotional service, fully ripened in the essence of divine love, and filled with the nectar of affection. (94)
It is inhabited by the divine form known as one-pointed concentration on Hari,
and it does not perish because it is protected by those who have attained the state of liberation.
That is imperishable, immortal, and filled with eternal bliss;
it is one's own innate happiness, fulfilled by the fulfillment of Śrī Hari.
Whether this [state] has been attained through compassion or even through spiritual practices,
there is no longer any outflow from his treasury, by virtue of the grace of the Supreme Self.
Indeed, this alone is to be attained through sacrifices, gifts, and oblations;
once this is attained, nothing else remains for the self to be attained.
Thus, O Rādhikā, the venerable Lomaśa himself, the true guru, having thus instructed her, ceased speaking; at night, she partook of milk. 99.
The king caused all of them to drink milk;
then those performers of the sacrifice took rest for the night.
Remembering Nārāyaṇa, the supreme Kṛṣṇa, within their own hearts,
the great kings and other great sages fell asleep.

Thus ends the two hundred and forty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Instruction on Eating and Other Duties Following the Performance of the Soma Sacrifice on the Tenth Day of the Third Day," in the second section, the *Tretā-santāna*, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O Rādhikā, having risen at dawn, the sacrificer Aśvapāṭala, King Lomaśa, and other great sages performed their daily religious rites.

Having performed their daily rites, they arrived at the sacrificial ground with concentrated minds on the fourth day, the eleventh lunar day (Ekādaśī), provided with all necessary materials and preparations.
They performed the recitation of auspicious verses, the sprinkling of water and other rites, the purification of their own limbs,
and all other daily duties exactly as they had been prescribed.
I shall explain this in detail; listen to it briefly:
after having performed the Pravargya and Upasad rites in the morning, thereafter—
Having concluded the Pravargya rite and cast the vessels into the northern fire,
the Guru commenced the ritual procedure for the Agniṣoma sacrifice involving fruit and animal offerings.
Having placed the sacrificial fuel-wood upon the Āhavanīya fire so that it was no longer visible,
he took up the blazing fire together with Sīmā.
He caused the fire to be placed upon the altar situated within the Mahāvedi;
that fire was both the Gārhapatya and the one known as the Prājahita.
And he established the Soma upon the very cart of the oblation-holder;
having taken the dust from the Cātvāla pit, he scattered it over the Dhiṣṇya hearths with that dust.
Having performed the offering of the omentum (vapā), the Adhvaryu priest then proceeded with the invocation of the Subrahmaṇyā for the sake of pressing the Soma and increasing its essence.
Then, at midday, they drew the *vasatīvarī* water from the pond into a jar and established the *śālāmukhīya* fire.
He indeed performed the animal-cake sacrifice (paśupuroḍāśa-yāga) in the forenoon,
and even in the evening, he carried out the worship of the heart and other limb-offerings.
Having performed the ritual limbs up to the conclusion of the Patnīsaṃyāja offerings, he did not complete them;
then everyone partook of their meals as was appropriate and according to their vows.
At night, the Adhvaryu priest himself took the pitcher containing the Vasatīvarī waters upon his shoulder and, moving around the sacrificial altar, set it down.
Thereupon, the Pratiprasthātṛ performed the ritual processing of the curds for the sake of the āmikṣā required on the following day, beginning with the driving away of the calves.
He prepared thick curd for the sake of the *dadhighraha* libation,
and he procured sacrificial grass (*barhis*) for the purpose of the *savanīya* oblations.
Then, the conclusion of the sacrificial rites occurred;
accompanied by his wife, the sacrificer performed a vigil during the night.
Preceded by a grand festival for the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa,
he performed the worship of Lord Hari with sixteen and other ritual articles.
The king likewise performed the concluding ceremony of his vow at night;
the sages and the people also engaged in the chanting of Hari’s praises.
In the early morning, Hari himself appeared as the flute-bearer;
he is the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, united with Rādhā and Ramā.
Assuming a divine form, adorned with a circle of divine splendor,
Hari appeared visibly before them all, wearing ornaments and smiling.
Kambharā was on his right and Gopālakṛṣṇaka on his left;
Māṇikya and others, including Brahma and Satya, were situated all around him.
"I am pleased today by your vow, and especially by this sacrifice;
I shall be the bestower of the fruit you desire, whether it be liberation or heaven."
Then the king and others worshipped Kṛṣṇa with the articles they had obtained;
for the Lord Hari had become invisible, accompanied by his own caravan.
Then Lomaśa instructed them all in that purifying [teaching]:
"Dharma is manifold, existing both among the worlds and among men. (24)
The dharma of sacrifice is itself the essence of Nārāyaṇa and bestows the world of Brahmā;
the dharma of service is great and, through the medium of blessings, grants heaven. (25)
The dharma of non-malice toward all beings indeed bestows supreme happiness;
and benevolence toward others is truly the giver of the great prosperity of bliss. (16)
The satisfaction of the gods as well as that of the great seers is of such a kind;
moreover, the satisfaction of guests is an aid for the next world. (27)
Formerly, a great sage named Jaṭilāyana, dwelling in the forest,
practiced various forms of austerity with a firm body, always remaining as motionless as a mountain.
A pregnant sparrow made her nest in his matted locks;
then the compassionate great seer indeed watched over her.
In a nest made of grass, fibers, and other materials within his matted locks, that female sparrow laid her eggs;
however, the sage was unaware of them. || 2.247.30 ||
Even though he understood this, his mind remained fixed on righteousness, and thus he did not move from it.
Righteousness consists in providing shelter to all beings and protecting those who seek refuge.
Then, from the fully developed eggs, little birds were born.
They grew up right there, and once their wings had grown,
they would fly up again and again at evening and return at night;
having rested, they would depart again in the morning, desiring grains of rice.
Then, when time had passed and those birds had set out on their journey,
as they did not return, the Ṛṣi departed.
And he thought: "This dharma has been perfected by me, who am devoted to austerity;
it indeed provides a refuge once a hermitage filled with trees has been established. (34)
He indeed honors all guests with great respect;
Nārāyaṇa himself has come there to test him. (35)
Assuming the form of a hunter, he arrived carrying a dead deer upon his shoulder;
he also brought a wooden seat, a hearth, a vessel, and sacrificial fuel.
"I am a Cāṇḍāla, a dog-eater; give it to me if it pleases you.
Having reflected thus, Jaṭāyana gave him the hearth as well as the fuel.
He gave him a vessel and fire, and likewise provided a leaf-hut; thus, there would be no deficiency in serving the people who had come for shelter. (38)
Having then made a vow regarding this dharma called Itivratā,
the dog-eater cooked everything and ate it with complete satisfaction.
He threw all the remaining meat onto the floor of the hall;
having thus rendered everything impure, he sat down on the ground outside.
He gave that great seer the command,
"Clean it," and the great seer, being well-pleased, had that hall made clean.
When the dog-eater said, "If you have anything you desire, I shall give it to you," the dog-eater replied, "My feet require a massage. (42)
The sage devotedly massaged his feet,
and furthermore, with sincere devotion, he offered him fruit, leaves, and water to drink.
"May the Lord, the Master dwelling within this shelter, be pleased here.
Having said this, he offered water and immediately vanished.
With his body pervaded by splendor, he became possessed of a divine form;
the glorious Lord Hari, served by Lakṣmī and Śrī, appeared with four arms. ||45||
Jaṭilāyana himself bowed at the feet of the Lord;
O Hari, you have shown mercy here, and he has been made one who has fulfilled his purpose by you.
"O Lord, grant me your imperishable abode immediately after your manifestation.
"So be it," Hari replied; and the sage, having cast off his body, [departed]. (47)
He went to that imperishable abode by means of the practice of service in every way;
therefore, [he attained it] through sacrifices, gifts, houses, and likewise through material objects.
Guests are to be served there, for Nārāyaṇa meets with them;
indeed, the protection of those who have come for refuge is the service of Nārāyaṇa. 49.
The Lord who dwells within that [body] certainly becomes pleased;
perceiving Him and aiming for that embodied soul, people should serve Him.
And that sacrifice remains great, auspicious, and bestowing the attainment of the sacrifice;
indeed, without Hari, those great sacrifices truly become non-sacrifices.
Furthermore, others also maintain that buying, selling, and liberating [beings]—
all of which is performed for the sake of benefiting the world— is devoid of spiritual merit.
Indeed, the Supreme Lord dwells within all embodied beings;
Nārāyaṇa himself is the buyer or the seller, and no one else.
Upon obtaining a gain, the supreme Lord, who takes it away, experiences joy;
likewise, upon receiving wealth, the supreme Lord, who gives it, experiences joy. (54)
In former times, there was indeed a certain merchant named Śākavikraya who,
having resorted to the path of truth, conducted his buying and selling.
Having first worshipped his parents in the morning and fed them, that merchant,
having received their instructions, goes to the marketplace.
Then he weighed out the vegetables for the purchaser, whether that purchaser was a child, an old man, a youth, or anyone else. (57)
Whether it be a woman, a maiden, or anyone else of unripe intellect who has approached,
having said "Salutations to you, Viṣṇu," they indeed give whatever was requested.
There, on the scale, it does not fall short even in the slightest;
indeed, by virtue of his state as a lord, he bestows the fruit [of the gift] even upon a mendicant. //59//
He gives to all indeed in due order, not by skipping over them;
considering Narayana to be present therein, He gives exactly as is appropriate.
And he, constantly performing the act of selling, indeed imparts knowledge; you who are buyers should, in every way, worship the Supreme Lord. 6.1.
He who is eternally the friend of all, who delights in the welfare of all through action, mind, and speech— worship that Inner Self with devotion.
Abandon hatred and desire, and remember the glorious Supreme Lord;
do not become attached to anyone, and do not enter into conflict with anyone.
Knowing Nārāyaṇa to be equal [to all] therein, worship that Hari;
become possessed of divine dispositions, regarding a clod of earth, a stone, and gold as the same.
Just as the blind do not see and the deaf do not hear, so too should one always regard sense objects as if one were blind and deaf. 65.
In the Supreme Lord, there is neither blindness nor deafness regarding the hearing of discourse;
yet in other matters, there is muteness, whereas in the Supreme Lord, there is eloquence.
In this manner, everything—whether sentient or insentient—should be ordained within Nārāyaṇa;
for men in this world, that which is insentient is to be attained through the objects of the senses.
Just as the elderly, the sick, and the emaciated are naturally devoid of desire,
so too should people here in this world remain free from longing for sense objects.
When one has no fear of oneself and no fear from oneself, for one who is void of passion, hatred, and the like, the attainment of Brahman is certain. (69)
For one who is free from the state of evil, there is the supreme attainment of Brahman;
where there is fearlessness, that great Dharma attains the state of fearlessness.
He from whom others have fear incurs great fear himself;
for the virtuous in this world, who practice non-violence, never cause fear to anyone at all.
Likewise, adopt a livelihood and proceed toward the eternal Brahman; maintain a disposition free from malice, refrain from theft, be steadfast in purpose, and avoid deception.
For one in whom these qualities have taken root, Brahman shines forth;
through the gift of both [knowledge and action], others such as sacrifices become equal to it. (73)
He who in this world bestows the gift of fearlessness upon all embodied beings,
having performed all sacrifices, attains the gift of fearlessness.
Nārāyaṇa, who has indeed become the self of all beings, is the witness;
he bestows upon the giver of fearlessness the imperishable state free from fear.

For those whose conduct is that of agriculture, who possess a violent disposition, who perform tasks such as cutting grass, and who have the state of driving oxen and other beasts, they indeed bring suffering and are filled with fear. (76)
Beasts carry people about, bind them, and subdue them;
likewise, humans enjoy other humans as their slaves. ||77||
Having made horses and other such animals their vehicles, they lead them through lands of much mud;
indeed, those who cause fear and are violent in this world attain that very fruit of fear.
"Aghnyā" is the name for cows; who is worthy to kill them?
"Agniṣoma" is the dear name for calves, while "vṛkṣaphala" refers to tree fruit. (79)
The removal of the calf is indeed the heart of it, for it is the ripening of the essence;
even the limbs are for the sake of the fruit alone—by this, Kṛṣṇa is thoroughly pleased.
I do not kill even a blade of grass or a fruit with my hand,
nor with a weapon, nor by any other means, because I maintain the vow of granting safety to all beings.
Once suitable items such as leaves of the *śāka* tree have been cooked and separated from the tree, I indeed perform their purchase and then their sale. (82)
Pleasure and pain are equal to me; indeed, neither the pleasant nor the unpleasant exists for me.
O people, protect the Dharma in this way by granting the gift of fearlessness. (8.3)
By that, you who abide in the path of fearlessness shall attain liberation;
for the Blessed One Nārāyaṇa is always pleased by it.
Salutations to the sacrifice of the Brahmins, and salutations to the ritual of procreation;
salutations to those people who are experts in service, and repeated salutations to them. (85)
The gods are always gratified by well-performed deeds, by excellent oblations, by prostration, by offerings, by hymns of praise, and by the heart. (86)
For the Ādityas, being well-satisfied by the oblations of sacrifice, cause rain to fall;
from that come the juices of the crops and food, which lead to the increase of progeny. (87)
People perform sacrifices and therein the Brahman is pleased;
those devotees who cause the Brahman to be pleased also satisfy others. 88.
Therefore, let them all offer devotion to whatever has Brahman as its deity;
when Brahman is satisfied, the entire world is indeed satisfied—of this there is no doubt. ||89||
For one whose libation of the Veda satisfies all the gods in sacrifice,
there is eternal satisfaction arising from happiness for that person who is satisfied by wisdom.
Those who are the support of the Dharma, the source of the Dharma, and devoted to the meditation on Brahman;
those endowed with devotion and wisdom, desiring to cross to the further shore—having seen, attained, and reflected upon the Supreme Brahman abiding in all things. ||9 1 ||
From merit, they attain the most meritorious place, the imperishable state.
Having gone where there is no sorrow, no decay, and no pain of death—for such as these, there is neither sacrifice for the sake of heaven nor the pursuit of fame. (93)
That sacrifice consists of the conduct practiced by the virtuous, is free from malice,
is intent on the satisfaction of Brahman, and is performed with sacrificial fuel, medicinal herbs, fruits, and roots.
For the sake of heaven there is merit alone, while freedom from qualities (nirguṇya) leads to liberation; having placed that in my heart, I indeed practice this state of being beyond qualities.
Others, having made a firm resolve, perform sacrifices in rituals for the sake of prosperity;
by that means, they go again to heaven by the path of the gods.
They fall into obscuration, for those devoid of virtue do not return;
having themselves taken up sacrificial posts, they perform sacrifices with abundant fees.
Again to heaven, again to earth—the whirlpool of transmigration does not cease.
Therefore, let them indeed be performers of the sacrifice to Brahman, and not sacrificers to other [deities]. 98.
Having made Brahman their deity, let them attain liberation through sacrifice;
let them perform the pure sacrifice at the sacred ford of the Self with divine contemplations.
Having received such instruction, the merchant who sold vegetables remained constantly devoted to the service of all and worshiped Puruṣottama.
Once, Śrī Hari came to his presence as a purchaser and said to him, "Give me some eternal vegetables. He replied to him, "I have only salt."
The merchant, having understood [the situation], gave a leafy vegetable to the wielder of the Śārṅga bow;
[he offered it] with the words: "Salutation to Kṛṣṇa, who is Pāravāla, the one who strides, and the seeker of wealth."
"Salutations to you, who indeed carry us across the ocean of saṃsāra.
Having spoken thus, he possessing divine vision prostrated himself like a staff before the Wielder of the Discus.
Then Hari, having become four-armed,
touched him with a hand marked by the signs of the fish, the banner, the bow, the trident, the svastika, and the discus.
Having established them in a celestial chariot and led them to the divine, imperishable state—
thus do those who always worship Hari by way of the sacrifice.
Those steadfast ones go to the abode of Hari along with Hari;
therefore, people should constantly worship Nārāyaṇa, who dwells within. 106.
To the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the son of Gopāla, the child of Kambharā, the Lord of Śrī, the Master beloved by Śrī Kṛṣṇa. (1.07)
Having thus addressed the Lord, the Supreme beyond the supreme, the beloved of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, Lomaśa departed for the lake during the Brāhma-muhūrta.
Then Rādhikā and all the others went to the lake for the sake of bathing,
after having performed the vigil and the daily worship.
On the fifth day, the great sages, the sacrificer, and other performers of sacrifices arrived at the pavilion for the sake of the Soma ritual.
O Rādhikā, having established what is eternally attained and practicing the specific [discipline], I shall declare to you that which is auspicious and bestows all merit.

Thus ends the two hundred and forty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Vigil, the Concluding Rite, and the Instruction on the Duties of the Eleventh Day of the Soma Sacrifice on the Fourth Day within the Second Section, the Tretā Cycle, of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā. || 247 ||
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Rādhā, on the fifth day at dawn, following the moon,
I shall explain the entire procedure which Lomaśa performed.
On the twelfth day, at the commencement of the Brahma-hour, all the officiating priests,
having awakened and bathed, began the rites for the pressing of Soma.
The Adhvaryu priest then placed those vessels upon their respective stands;
thereafter, the Hotṛ priest began the recitation known as the Śastra-anuvāka.
And he performed the pouring out of the *savanīya* oblations with five [portions]:
namely, with parched grains (*dhānā*), with flour-mash (*karambha*), and likewise with the *parivāpa*.
The Pratiprasthātṛ [should offer] with the *puroḍāśa* and likewise with the *āmikṣā*;
the *dhānās* are to be understood as parched barley, and the *karambha* as barley flour.
The *parivāpa* consists of parched grains (*lāja*), while the *payasyā* is considered to be curd-mixture (*āmikṣā*).
Their deities are five; Indra is the first among them, being the one characterized by greenness (*haritvan*).
Indra accompanied by Pūṣan is the second; Sarasvatī is the third;
Indra is the fourth; and Mitra and Varuṇa are the fifth deity.
Having worshipped those [deities], he then performed the distribution of the curd-offerings (dadhighraha), as follows: having taken excellent curd in a vessel made of udumbara wood...
He offered an oblation to Prajāpati with a vessel made of udumbara wood;
then he prepared the Adābhya cup for Soma, in this manner.
Having filled the vessel with either curd or milk and likewise bound it up, and having taken three fibers from the stalks of the Soma plant, [he should proceed].
Having placed that draught into the vessel for the Grahas, he indeed shook that vessel five times or seven times and offered it as an oblation.
Then, having taken the cup for the Aṃśu draught, which contains only one portion of Soma,
he cast it into the stone vessel and sprinkled it with the Vasatīvarī water.
Having pressed [the soma] with the stones and placed it in the Adābhya vessel, he then offered it as an oblation to Prajāpati as the deity. || 1.3 ||
Having taken that vessel and entered the assembly hall,
he then indeed consumed the Soma juice contained within the vessel.
Then he placed the vessel on the donkey and prepared the Upāṃśu cup;
having purchased it there, he likewise placed it in a cloth and tied it up.
Having untied the Soma and taken it all up, he specifically divided it into two parts for the sake of the morning pressing (prātaḥsavana). || 16 ||
Having indeed set aside a very small portion from the Soma for the purpose of the midday pressing,
he likewise took it from the Soma used for the morning hymn solely for the sake of a single draught.
Having taken up the Soma and placed it in the Hotṛ’s cup, he then sprinkled it with the Vasatīvarī waters and ground it with the pressing-stones. || 18 ||
Having squeezed it and obtained the juice, the Adhvaryu himself poured it three times into the Upāṃśu vessel with his joined palms and offered it as an oblation.
This very act of drawing the stream was indeed for the sake of the deity and the vital breath; having offered it to her, they then drew the streams ending at the *dhruva* vessel.
This very person is the Soma-presser, and he is considered the Great Presser;
then, having sat down at the place of pressing, the Adhvaryu priests likewise [sit] there.
The Adhvaryu sat down facing west in front of the pressing-stones, and the Pratiprasthātṛ sat down facing north on the south side. || 22 ||
In the west, the Hotṛ priest sat facing east, and in the north, the Unnetṛ sat facing south,
having placed the Soma upon a stone slab.
Having sprinkled [the grains] with the *vasatīvarī* waters and ground them, they should press [the juice];
Dakṣa, having performed it in this very manner three times, [proceeded].
Having placed crushed pieces of Soma plants into the *ādhāvanīya* vessel and a clay bowl, and having squeezed them to extract the juice, [he takes] that juice. ||25||
Having taken them in another vessel, he scattered the husks to one side;
then [he took] a navel made of goat's hair, fashioned to the measure of a span.
Then, having supported her upon a piece of purifying cloth in a wooden vessel, they spread it out and held it up; and after that, the Udgātṛ priests [performed their duties].
The Unnetṛ, having taken the Soma juice from the Ādhavanīya vessel by means of a dipping-spoon,
poured it into the Hotṛ’s cup.
One should hold it so that the liquid falls onto the portion of the purifying cloth;
then, from that flowing stream, [it should be poured] into the vessel called the Antaryāmin.
Having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the Antaryāma cup, the Adhvaryu offered the remnant;
and having poured the residue from the Āgrayaṇa vessel back into it, he completed the libation while leaving a remainder.
Then, after pouring the remainder of the oblation into the fire, the Guru himself offered that sacrifice to the deity named Indra.
Then they took up the cups beginning with that for Indra and Vāyu;
thereafter, the Guru, having drawn the cup for Indra and Vāyu from the stream, [proceeded].
Having wiped them externally with the fringe of the purifier (*pavitra*), he placed them upon the mound (*khara*);
likewise [he placed] the cup for Mitra-Varuṇa, the *śukra* cup, and the *manthin* juice. (33)
He then placed, in due order upon the sacrificial mound (khara) in the domestic ritual, the Āgrayaṇa cup, as well as those for Agni, Indra, and Sūrya together with the Ukthya,
and finally the Dhruva cup.
After the seizing of the *dhruva* vessel, the stream [of soma] ceased;
and from the *havirdhāna* shed, the five officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) went outside. (35)
They proceeded together for the sake of the *bahiṣpavamāna* chant;
first the *adhvaryu* moved forward, and then the *prastotṛ*, holding onto his girdle, followed.
Having grasped the hem [of the garment], the Pratihartṛ then followed the Udgātṛ;
thereafter, the Brahmā and the Sacrificer followed with their hems.
Having gone to the site of the *cātvāla* pit and sat down, these three—the *udgātṛ*, the *prastotṛ*, and the *pratihartṛ*—let go of their girdles. (38)
At that time, they purified them with the Bahiṣpavamāna hymn;
by that means, the two Aśvin cups were rendered fit for the sacrifice.
Having performed the rite for the Aśvins once the fires had been kindled upon the hearths by the Āgnīdhra,
the Adhvaryu, having set down the cup, placed it from the wooden trough onto the mound.
Then, having performed the rites beginning with the presentation of the sacrificial portions for the *savanīya* animal,
he proceeded thereafter toward the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*), ending with the offering of the omentum (*vapā*).
The Adhvaryu, Brahman, Yajamāna, and Sadasya,
having entered the sacrificial hall (sadas), likewise [prepared] the vessels such as the grahas and camasa cups.
Then, having held the ritual substances, Brahmā, acting as the patron,
should thereafter perform the ritual attendance upon all the vessels with their respective mantras.
Having gone to the north of the *havirdhāna* and likewise through the eastern door,
they entered the *sadas* and sat down in their respective places.
Then they performed the ritual procedure for the *savanīya* oblations, and likewise carried out the drawing of the *dhārā-graha* cups in the prescribed manner. (45)
Having performed the rites ending with the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering,
the Adhvaryu priest proceeded to draw the three portions for Indra-Vāyu, Mitra-Varuṇa, and the Aśvins.
After the Adhvaryu has drawn the portion for Indra and Vāyu,
the Pratiprasthātṛ then indeed draws from the wooden trough (droṇakalaśa) into the Āditya vessel.
Having held the *aindravāyava* cup as a *nigrāhya*, he offered it together with the *āditya* vessel, following the mutual pouring of their juices.
And the Guru gave the vessel containing the *sampāta* residue to the *hotṛ*;
in this manner, the performance and the pouring out of the subsequent two cups were carried out. (49)
The Unnetṛ priest, as well as the Ācchāvāka’s cup,
he set aside; there, he filled nine cups, excluding those of the Hotṛ,
the Brahman, the Udgātṛ, and likewise the Yajamāna.
Likewise, for the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin and the Maitrāvaruṇa as well. ||51||
Likewise, nine cups belonging to the Potṛ and the Agnīdhra were filled by pouring the Soma juice from the *kalaśa* vessel using the *pariplavā* ladle.
Having taken Soma from the *pūtabhṛt* jar, he then fills the cups;
having placed [the remainder] in the *droṇakalaśa*, he then places it into the cups.
The first pouring is considered to be the act of spreading [the ghee] (upastaraṇa);
the second pouring is considered to be the place for the subsequent sprinkling (abhighāraṇa). ||24||
In this manner, the entire drawing out [of the Soma] must indeed be performed for the purpose of filling [the vessels].
Then the Adhvaryu, having taken the Śukra vessel containing the Soma—
The Pratiprasthātṛ, having taken the Manthin vessel together with its Soma,
stands facing each other at the eastern door of the Havirdhāna shed.
Standing in their own house, having joined their elbows with one another,
and having followed in front of the *āhavanīya* fire which was established by the mantra-maker.
The two five-faced [offerings] became ready for the purpose of the planetary oblation;
at that time, the nine *camasādhvaryu* priests were indeed accompanied by their respective *camasa* vessels. //58//
Then, having gone to the site of the Āhavanīya fire, facing eastward,
they prepared for the oblation and likewise performed the ritual of listening to the sacred words.
They performed the ritual responses and so forth; then the Guru gave the *praiṣa* (direction).
When the *vaṣaṭkāra* had been made by the Hotṛ and the *anuvaṣaṭkāra* had been performed, [the rite proceeded].
After the second offering had been made, the Hotṛ and the others, having been prompted by the Adhvaryu, brought the cups to the Sadas for the purpose of partaking [the soma]. ||61||
Having filled the cups for the Adhvaryu, beginning with those for Mitra-Varuṇa, and having brought them quickly toward the Āhavanīya fire for the purpose of offering, [they stood ready]. 62.
The Adhvaryu and the Pratiprasthātṛ performed the oblation:
"Svāhā to Indra as the deity; Svāhā to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt. (63)
The Pratiprasthātṛ performed the offering of the remnants upon the embers with the formula, "Svāhā to Rudra"; then the Adhvaryu, having finished the cup, [proceeded].
He offered oblations to Mitra and Varuṇa with the cry "Svāhā! in due order;
likewise, all the Adhvaryu priests each offered their own respective goblet.
"To Indra, to the Maruts, to Tvaṣṭṛ, and to Agni, Svāhā! Homage!
Then they indeed consumed the remnants of the sacrificial cups.
Then the Acchāvāka also indeed consumed the cup;
thereafter, the two of them performed the ritual procedure for the Ṛtu-grahas.
The Adhvaryu and the Pratiprasthātṛ offered auspicious oblations:
"Svāhā to Indra Mādhava, and to the Maruts Mādhava! (68)
Svāhā to Tvaṣṭṛ and Śukra; svāhā to Agni and Śuci; svāhā to Indra and Nabhas; svāhā to Mitra, Varuṇa, and Nabhasya. ||6 9||
Hail to Draviṇodas for food; hail to Draviṇodas for strength;
hail to Draviṇodas for power; hail to Draviṇodas for the victorious. ||2.248.7||
"O Aśvins, to Tapa, Svāhā! To Gṛhapati Tapasya, Svāhā!
Then the consumption of the cups took place according to the prescribed rule. (7.1)
Then follows the recitation of the *śastra* and the recitation of the *pratigara*:
"O Adhvaryu, *śoṃsāvaḥ*, *im*; *śoṃsāmoda*, *iva*. (72)
Oṃ mothāmoda iva, othāmoda iva;
performing the recitation beginning with "oṃ othāmoda iva" and so forth. ||73||
Then the Adhvaryu himself offered the Nārāśaṃsa oblation:
"To Indra and Agni, svāhā! To the ancestors, svāhā! Homage! (74)
Having thus performed the *nārāśaṃsa* rite, he recited the *prauga-śastra* and offered the oblation with the words, "Svāhā to the Viśvedevas! (75)
Then they drank from the cups until nothing remained;
