they performed the ritual procedure for the Ukthya-vessel, the oblation, and the consumption of the entire contents.
One should perform everything, including the washing and placing [the vessel] upon the donkey, with the mantras:
"Svāhā to Mitra and Varuṇa" and likewise "Svāhā to Indra and Agni. (77)
Having thus appointed the officiating priests and performed the ritual up to the point of the *sādana*,
they then completed the morning libation (*prātaḥsavana*) and went out from the pavilion.
And at midday, they performed the Mādhyandina pressing;
having performed everything just as in the morning, they carried out the pouring of the streams.
"Śukra, Manthin, and Āgrayaṇa—svāhā! Homage!
Then they sang the Pavamāna hymns and performed the Dadhi sacrifice.
They performed the consumption of the offerings at the sacrificial ground and various other rites;
the sacrificer also indeed gave the sacrificial fees.
Cows, horses, mules, donkeys, goats, and sheep, as well as sesame, beans, rice, barley, elephants, garments, and gold. (8.2)

At that time, during the festival of the sacrifice, the king bestowed his entire possession— including the kingdom and so forth, as well as maidens' quarters and gardens— as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
Then indeed followed the performance of the Marutvatīya cup-offering;
subsequently, the Adhvaryu performed the Vaiśvadeva offerings and the five oblations.

Having offered the oblation, the Adhvaryu and the Pratiprasthātṛ performed the consumption [of the remnant]; they performed the fire-oblation and the shaking, saying: "Svāhā to Indra accompanied by the Maruts! ||85||
Svāhā to the Pitṛs of the thighs; homage and svāhā to Mahendra;
svāhā to Agni and to Indra; svāhā and obeisance to Rakta. ||86||
Having performed the ritual of the Ukthya-vigraha, the recitation of the five stotras,
and the concluding oblation (samāpti-homa) of the Savana, they then went outside.
They also performed the third pressing (savana), as well as the oblation and the consumption [of the soma], saying:
"Svāhā to the Ādityas! Homage! This milk, curd, and soma! (88)
Then they proceeded to the crawling-rite for the Ārbhava-pavamāna;
having performed everything up to the consumption of the iḍā, they kindled the sacrificial hearths (dhiṣṇyas).
Having performed the offerings of the *savanīya* oblations, the Adhvaryu alone then performed the single *sakṛddhoma*, and after that he performed the subsequent *homa*.
The Camasins, intending their respective ancestors, caused them to take their seats;
thereafter, he performed the oblation for Savitṛ and for the Viśvedevas. || 91 ||
Then, after the consumption [of the sacrificial food], the sacrifice of the gentle *caru* indeed proceeded;
it was a *caru* consisting of boiled rice-grains that had not been drained.
And he offered an oblation to Agni Patnīvat with the cry "Svāhā!"—so says the Guru—and they sang the twenty-one-fold hymn of praise for Prakhya. || 93 ||
They also offered the *camasa* vessels into the Vaiśvānara fire with the mantra "Svāhā!
To the Maruts, Svāhā! and thereafter performed the consumption of the remnants.
Then they prepared the *hāriyojana* vessel for the movement of the self-grasping [deity], and the *unnetṛ* priest [prepared] the soma juice mixed with parched barley and other ingredients. (95)
He offered oblations with the *patnīsaṃyāja* mantras and likewise performed the *juhū-homa* and other rites,
as well as the expiatory *prāyaścitta-homas*.
Then, for the sacrificer, the Viṣṇukramaṇa and other rites are performed;
having thus completed the third pressing and the meals, || 97 ||
All the great lords, the people, and those dwelling at the sacred fords, as well as the residents [of the city], performed [their rites];
thereafter, the avabhṛtha sacrifice took place.
The sacrificer, accompanied by his wife, as well as the other officiating priests and people,
took up the Soma vessels upon the royal throne and grasped the *jīṣaka*.
Singing the melodies of the Sāmaveda, they went to the vicinity of the water;
then, in the water, they offered the two portions of clarified butter (ājyabhāga) to Agni and Varuṇa.
They performed four fore-offerings (prayāja) and likewise two after-offerings (anūyāja);
they offered a sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) to Varuṇa, saying, "Salutation indeed to the waters."
Having cast the *ṛjīṣa* and other remains into the water, the king and his wives bathed;
others also did likewise, and they all bowed to the sun.
Having assembled at the entrance of the hall, they performed the *udayanīya* sacrifice;
thereafter followed the *ānubandhya-paśu-yāga* and the *āmikṣā-yajña*. (103)
Having offered the appropriate *bali* oblation with the words "Svāhā to Mitra and Varuṇa," the sacrificer then has his hair, beard,
nails, and body hair shaved; having bathed according to the ritual procedure, he performs the five [sacrificial acts].
Dhātṛ, Anumati, Rākā, Sinīvālī, and Kuhū—
having worshipped these deities with clarified butter,
he likewise performed the Udavasānīya sacrifice, which has an eight-pot-sherd cake as its ritual substance. || 105–106 ||
Having offered the Agnihotra at night with the mantra "Svāhā to Viṣṇu," the sages then performed the ritual circumambulation of the Soma sacrifice.
Then the king, together with his wife, performed the drinking of the soma;
and all the performers of the sacrifice indeed partook of the meals at the ritual.
Thus, O Rādhikā, on the twelfth day, the Soma sacrifice was completed.
And at night, Yajñanārāyaṇa himself became complete.
He granted his vision to the king and likewise bestowed a boon upon him:
"May it be well with you always, O King; at the end, may you attain the state of liberation."
"And establish me here in this palace in the form of an image of Nārāyaṇa.
O Rādhikā, that king quickly had a temple constructed.
There, Yajñanārāyaṇa, accompanied by his sacrificial wife, was installed according to the prescribed rites; therefore, that very sacred site is named Yajña.
Likewise, Somatīrtha became a bestower of the fruit of sacrifice through bathing;
it is indeed purifying, located in the northeast corner of Aśvapaṭṭasara.
King Aśvapāṭala received a Vaiṣṇava necklace from the hand of the illustrious Bālakṛṣṇa and received the mantra from Lomaśa.
Oṃ, salutation to Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Lord; svāhā!
Then, having fully worshipped the Lord of Gods and having bestowed gifts in every way, || 1 15 ||
King Rādhika returned happily to his own kingdom, while the other sages, deities, and others departed for their respective regions. (116)
There, through giving, drinking water, immersion, eating, and even through worship, one may attain heaven; in the end, one shall go to the imperishable state.

Thus ends the two hundred and forty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Morning Savana, the Midday Savana, the Afternoon Savana, the Pūrṇāhuti, the Avabhṛtha-offering, the Parihāra, and so forth, on the twelfth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa during the fifth day of the Soma-sacrifice in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā."
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Rādhikā, thereafter they all indeed took to sleep;
having performed their ablutions and worship on the thirteenth day, they attained the dawn.
In the assembly, the sage Lomaśa indeed instructed those embodied beings:
"Those who perform sacrifices with faith are possessed of fruit, while those without faith are devoid of fruit."
In this world, sacrifices become fruitful through clarified butter, milk, curd, Soma,
and fruit, as well as by the final full oblation and by faith.
And those who are incapable of performing a sacrifice indeed cross over by means of the sprinkling of the tail,
or by the consecration, or even by the dust of the feet.
Having established Faith as his wife through a vow of perfect truth, the sacrificer worships the Lord and certainly crosses over; of this there is no doubt. || 5 ||
Having made one's chosen deity the object of worship, one should sacrifice repeatedly with faith;
by means of such devotion and the rite of offering, that performer of sacrifice surely crosses over.
The sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) is always pure and brings satisfaction to the gods;
all rivers are Sarasvatīs, and all mountains are meritorious.
For an embodied being established in Brahman, the entire earth is the abode of Hari;
however, that faith which is nourished by a person nourishes that person in turn.
He who destroys faith in the Dharma is himself destroyed; that destroyed faith destroys that person, even as the virtuous and the faithful perform the extensive expansion of sacrifice.
For she is the progenitor from whom every fruit is produced;
one who is mature in knowledge and mature in mind is protected by faith in the Divine.
Hari Nārāyaṇa never abandons one whose faith has increased;
one who lacks faith is not worthy of offering oblations to the gods. 11.
One must never, under any circumstances, eat the food of one who does not offer oblations;
lack of faith is the supreme sin, and that which is permeated by it should certainly not be accepted.

Faith is indeed the purifier, the most excellent, the bestower of cessation [from worldly existence], the giver of happiness, the granter of peace, the form of the Supreme Brahman, and the sanctifying one. (13)
Faith bestows Brahman; likewise, non-violence is the giver of Brahman.
Non-violence is considered superior to all dharmas for all living beings. (14)
Indeed, in all sacrifices, Viṣṇu partakes of the oblation, which is milk-rice (pāyasa);
[he is offered] with milk-rice, flowers, fruits, gundra-roots, and juices as the sacrificial offering.
Purifying and satisfying, it produces a state of pure devotion toward Viṣṇu;
indeed, all that is pure, such as medicinal herbs and the like, is worthy of the gods.
One should sustain the body with medicinal herbs so that it does not waste away,
and one should always satisfy the sacrifice with bulbs, roots, fruits, and the like.
Faith is indeed the mother, the means for attaining all fruits;
non-violence is her sister—for these two are the revealers of the gods. (18)
A mother who always benefits her children must never be killed;
non-violence is the supreme dharma, and the protection of one's mother is one's own specific duty.
Who indeed could ever be happy after killing faith and their mother?
She is the cause of the body; with her as one's protector, there is always security.
Even if devoid of wealth, a virtuous person returns to his home;
and even a child, accompanied by sons and grandsons, seeks his mother.
Or, if the mother protects [the child] for too long, then old age arrives, accompanied by the defects of suffering. || 2.2 ||
Then the world is empty for him when he is separated from the mother;
indeed, there is no support equal to the mother anywhere upon this earth. (23)
There is no protector equal to a mother; she is the beloved vessel for one's life.
Because she carries one in her womb, she is called *dhātrī*; because she gives birth, she is indeed the *jananī*. 24.

By nourishing the limbs, she is the mother; by bestowing honor upon the child, she is the nurse; as faith, she is the mother within the womb of heaven; and among the divine beings, she is the progenitor. (5)
And because she bestows the syllables "Amba," she is the Mother; since she grants liberation, it is held that one who desires heaven should perform sacrifice with faith. (26)
The herbs are the fuel-sticks, the trees are the plants, and the clarified butter, milk, and curd are the oblation; the earth, the directions, faith, time, the *ṛc*s, and the *yajus* verses;
the *sāman* chants, the sacrificer, and the fire—thus the sacrifice consists of seventeen components.
With clarified butter, milk, curd, whey, and fruits. ||28||
Through the ritual flavors and through faith, Viṣṇu indeed becomes pleased at the sacrifice;
for sacrifice originates from the Brāhmaṇas and is dedicated to the offering unto Brahman.
The entire world follows the sacrifice, and the sacrifice follows the world;
"Om" is the name of Brahman—namas, svāhā, svadhā, vaṣaṭ.
For one in whom these are employed, no fear exists;
the glorious Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa is the bestower of fearlessness upon him. Hari, the son of Kaṃbhari, is manifest as the Supreme beyond the Imperishable (Akṣara). 31.
"He whom you beheld at the sacrifice in the field of Kuṃkumavāpikā—
he alone is the Lord who knows the fruit of all sacrifices;
and when approved by his mother, he surely bestows that fruit in its entirety."
Therefore, one should perform sacrifices and cause others to sacrifice to Yaśas, who is dear to Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
For one who worships according to the prescribed rite, there is eternal heaven, which is beyond the imperishable.
For those who do not sacrifice, neither this world nor the next exists, as is certain;
nor does there exist here on earth any dharma that leads to a higher rebirth for those who do not sacrifice. (35)
Aśvapāṭala said: How is this world superior, and how is the other world attained? And how does dharma become the means for reaching the higher realms on earth? Tell me that here.
Śrī Lomaśa said: For one of virtuous conduct, self-controlled, impartial toward all embodied beings, and performing every act of hospitality, this superior world is intended.
For the devotee who perceives Brahman everywhere, who delights in the worship of Brahman,
and who is established in Brahman, the next world shines forth.
[This is true] for one who is worthy of universal favor and who is endowed with the desire to help all.

Indeed, for one whose dharma consists of non-violence and truth, that dharma shall surely become the means to liberation. For one who is free from the state of illusion, who has attained the state of the Imperishable, and who is truly established in the Supreme Brahman, those three are indeed held within the palm of his hand.
This very Upanishadic knowledge is indeed the means of union with Hari;
by it, the supreme Brahman and the eternal, imperishable abode are attained.
Brahman is attained through knowledge, and knowledge is considered to be the Upanishad;
Brahman is attained through devotion, and devotion is considered to be the Upanishad. Through the Bhāgavata dharma, Kṛṣṇa is attained—he alone is that [Upanishad].
And if, through detachment and by means of suffering, one has gone toward Hari; || 43 ||
That by which dwelling is produced is considered an *upaniṣad*;
it is that by which, as a cause, dwelling in the temple of the God is brought about. (44)
A virtuous intention is indeed considered the cause and the secret doctrine for attaining Brahman; even if a child goes to the temple out of a desire for favor, [it serves as such a cause]. (45)
Indeed, in the presence of Hari, his Upaniṣad (the secret doctrine) is that which brings grace,
whether through ritual action, or even by an enemy, or by desire, or even by effort.
That by which proximity to Hari is attained—whether through sacrifice, service, or even by means of wealth for one's own sake—is considered to possess the nature of the Upaniṣads. (47)
Whether by means of charity or even through craving, proximity to the gods is attained; indeed, this is the secret doctrine (upaniṣad) recognized on earth for that purpose. 48.
That association with the virtuous which, when practiced excessively, truly leads to the attainment of Brahman—
that is declared to be the Upaniṣad, for it bestows Hari upon those who associate with the good.
In this matter, for women, merely listening to the discourse bestows the yoga of Brahman;
and that should be understood as the Upaniṣad by which one may meet Nārāyaṇa.
If affection, tranquility, cultivation, conduct, and even passion lead to the attainment of Brahman, then all of these are indeed considered the doctrine of the Upaniṣads.
The Gopīs attained Him through desire; likewise, the Brahmins through sacrifice;
the cowherds through friendship; and even the Daityas through hatred. (52)
Through Sudāman’s greed for the sake of gaining a livelihood, through Dhruva’s ascetic penance, and through Prahlāda’s firm resolve, [the elephant was obtained]. (53)
Due to Pūtanā’s state of enmity and due to Nārada’s glorification, Hari is attained by anyone through whatever cause whatsoever. (54)

That is the cause, and that is the secret means (upaniṣad); it is considered the bringer of the attainment of Brahman—whether it be knowledge, devotion, ritual action, contemplation, or surrender. ||55||
And all that is declared in the Upaniṣads is that by which Brahman is indeed attained;
[He is] Anādikṛṣṇanārāyaṇa through the Aśvapaṭṭala sacrifice. //56//
Indeed, you have attained here this divine form, beloved of Śrī Kṛṣṇa;
right here, your Soma sacrifice is established as eternally approved by the Upaniṣads. 57.
The Lord’s union with living beings is considered to occur in some cases through grace;
in some cases through effort, and in others, union may even occur by birth. (58)
She is considered by those yogins to be the cause, the pure secret doctrine (upaniṣad), just as all actions reach their completion in their fruit. (59)
The fruit [of action] lies in tranquility, and that [tranquility] is fulfilled in enjoyment; yet that [enjoyment] is fully realized only in Brahman.
The state of being Brahman is fulfilled in the Supreme God, the Parameśvara. (2.249.60)
Those who know Him, see Him, and go toward Him are free from dualities, free from bonds, liberated, pure, and stainless. (6.1)
Those who have reached perfection in liberation, who are most devoted to Brahman, who dwell in Brahman,
who are free from delusion, and who have become one with Brahman— their goal is eternal.
Free from worldly undertakings, steadfast, pure, and identified with Brahman, those who seek the truth satisfy the Supreme Lord, the God, with sacrifices. (63)
For one who has become the self of all beings and perceives both himself and others,
his devoted follower proceeds along the path, having been granted the eyes by him.
Having secured the protection of the nine gates and opened the heart,
for one who has traveled by way of Brahman, there is abiding in the abode of the Supreme Brahman.
The Agnihotra, the Pūrṇamāsa, the Darśa, as well as the Prayājas, the Sviṣṭakṛt, the Anuyājas, the Pitṛyajña, and the Aṅgayāga; || 66 ||
The Cāturmāsya, the Vaiśvadeva, the Sākamedha, the Vāruṇa, the Somayāga, the Savana, and also the Āgrayaṇeṣṭi. ||67||
The Avabhṛtheṣṭi sacrifice, the Uktha, the Ṣoḍaśī, and the Atirātra;
likewise the Atyagniṣṭoma, the Vājapeya, and the Viṣṭuti. ||68||
The Vāyavya, the Śatarudrīya, the Vāsava, the Rājasūyaka, the Sautrāmaṇi, the Aśvamedha, the Puṃmedha, and the Sarvamedhaka. || 69 ||

The Gomedha and the Brahmamedha, as well as other sacrifices devoted to ritual action— those rites devoted to knowledge, those devoted to austerity, and those sacrifices devoted to material offerings.
The offerings made for the sake of welcome, as well as those given as gifts for charity—
all these, when offered to Kṛṣṇa, bestow liberation and lead one upon the path of Brahman.
Whether [the ritual] has been performed or not, nothing remains to be taught to him;
Hari is satisfied, and by that, everything has indeed been attained.
Even when sacrifices have been performed and the gods have been gratified with libations,
if it is devoid of the light of Kṛṣṇa, that does not bestow liberation.
Therefore, within those sacrificial rites, Kṛṣṇa is the eternal Dharma; the virtuous are those who practice yoga through Brahman and block the external gates [of the senses]. (74)
Seeking immortality, they gratify that Kṛṣṇa in all sacrifices;
having closed every other door, one should open wide the door of Brahman. 75.
Aśvapāṭala said: O Lomaśa, tell me how the gates are to be closed;
furthermore, tell me what should be done after they are closed, or what the fruit thereof shall be. (76)
Śrī Lomaśa said: "The supreme nectar exists within the treasury of Brahman, protected by the Self;
yet, because its door is covered, it goes elsewhere and becomes difficult to attain. (77)
Playing with dice with the hands, running elsewhere with the feet, whatever low desire there may be, and sitting in another courtyard—[these are forbidden]. (78)
Description concerns another object; representation is mixed with the world;
tasting is clarity; and smelling is the moisture of the body. (79)
Touching is the result of subtle illusion; hearing is the fruit of movement; reflection is the mark of the sense of "mine"; and awakening is that it may become manifold for me. ||2.249.80||
"I have two chowries and the title 'I'; there is no one like me"—thinking thus, one regards everything as nectar, both in the waking state and even in a dream. (81)
Everything indeed flows out incessantly; the vessel will become empty.
Therefore, a wise person should provide a lid by means of discernment. 82.
One should not gamble with dice, nor should one run through muddy ground;
one should not desire low land, nor should one sit at the crossroads of delusion.
One should not praise other [deities], nor should one fashion their images; one should not taste other offerings, nor indeed should one smell anything pertaining to the body. (84)
One should not touch a soft bed, nor listen to, nor speak of anything else; one should perform meditation upon the Lord of Māyā, and my realization shall become Brahman. 85.
"May my thought be nectar, and may I dwell within that"—
in this way, one should indeed perform the protection of the door, which has the form of Śrī Hari.
Just as terrestrial water indeed increases from rainwater,
so too does one's own nectar of immortality increase through the protection of Brahman.
Just as terrestrial water, dried up by the heat of summer, dissolves away,
so too one's own nectar reaches dissolution when the door is closed.
One should indeed not go about in vain in this world, nor should one ever accept gifts in vain;
one should not indulge in desire in vain, nor should one sit down anywhere in vain.
One should never utter speech that is vain, devoid of truth, and bereft of Kṛṣṇa;
nor should one ever look upon a form that is vain, devoid of Kṛṣṇa, and purposeless.
One should not accept pleasant tastes that exceed what is necessary for the maintenance of the body;
one should not take scents in vain, but should practice filling oneself with breath.
One should never engage in touch that is in vain, except for the touch of Hari; one should never apply the ears to that which is in vain, except for the hearing of the Supreme Lord.
One should perform the honoring of Śrīhari, the Lord of Śrī, the Lord of Kamalā;
one should perform the awakening of the Lord of Śrī, and always maintain the contemplation of Śrīhari. 92.
"I belong to him alone and never to anyone else;
thus, for the sake of the Lord of Lakṣmī, I am everything and consist of his very self. (94)
"May my abode in all the senses be in Narayana, the Supreme Lord"—thus indeed is the protection of the gateway, seeking the nectar of awakening. (95)
For one whose gates are all closed, or for whom they are devoid of movement, there shall be attainment of Hari; he drinks from the ocean of nectar.
One who has a secret door should partake of the nectar of the eternal devotee;
all sacrifices are completed for one who seeks the nectar of the eternal.
What is the use of his austerities, hardships, sacrifices, or other such afflictions, if the nectar of Nārāyaṇa has indeed been acquired and held within his heart? 98.
O Aśvapāṭala, knowing that your own nectar is contained within the treasury,
you must not let it flow out through an improper path, nor should you allow it to go to waste.
Just as one requires clothing, just as one requires a seat of grass, and just as one requires a pillow, so too should one take food only for the sake of sustenance. (2.249.1)
Having abandoned delight in dualities, one should always resort to the inner delight;
having abandoned the external caravan, one should take refuge in the internal caravan. 101.
"By this, the one who has gone to the further shore of the long path shall become a Sugata.
Thus, O Rādhikā, Lomaśa spoke these nectar-like words to the king. || 10.2 ||

Thus ends the two hundred and forty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Knowledge Bestowed by Lomaśa upon King Aśvapāṭala, Consisting of the Secret of Faith, the Upaniṣads, and Nectar," in the *Lomaśagītā* within the second section, the *Tretā-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Rādhikā, having heard Śrī Lomaśa again, Aśvapāṭala then inquired about the path of renunciation and likewise that which bestows manifest fruit.
Aśvapāṭala said:
O Great Sage, tell me here what is directly perceived as the fruit that arises through the path of renunciation; and what is the direct perception, and what is the fruit?
What is it here that you worship as most directly perceptible?
Indeed, among all things, equality is observed in what is directly perceptible. (3)
You too, in this world, experience both sorrow and joy;
for your sense objects are the same as those of all embodied beings.
For among all those who are equal, what is directly perceived as being free from affliction?
What indeed is your superiority, other than that you are a householder? (5)
Śrī Lomaśa said: Regarding Hari, the path of renunciation is itself the path of surrender; what else is there to be abandoned?
This renunciation, consisting of the offering of one's very self, is the most excellent form of renunciation toward Hari.
Therefore, indeed, the direct perception of the Self occurs through the vision granted by Him;
and the fruit, which is the bliss of the Self, also arises from the grace of the Supreme Lord. (7)
I worship the manifest Bālakṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa,
the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the son of Śrī Kaṃbharā.
He who is indeed the most directly perceptible here through both the eyes and the mind,
that very Supreme Brahman, the Lord of Śrī, abides within the self alone.
Lord of Lakṣmī, Master of the virtuous, Lord of the liberated, Supreme Sovereign,
lover of the sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpikā, beloved of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Hari is the beloved husband of Brahmā, the Lord of the Self, the Lord of Knowledge, the Sovereign,
the Lord of Liberation, the Master of the Imperishable, and the Overlord of the Abode.
O King, he is most manifest to me in this matter; look upon him!
O King, I experience joy and sorrow like the costumes of a drama.

The sense organs themselves are indeed the same within the body, and there is also equality in their functioning; likewise, the activity of perception and so forth is likewise the same. Nevertheless, [there is a distinction]. (1.3)
Like one possessed by a spirit, I always move through the Supreme Self;
He is the enjoyer, He is the controller, and He alone possesses the power of perception and so forth.
Whatever joy or sorrow I experience while possessed by the presiding spirit of all beings, that alone knows it within this body; this embodied self does not know it.
Nevertheless, I shall show everything like a dramatic performance, just as I know it;
for the great sage Mārkaṇḍeya knows it exactly as I do.
Sanatkumāra knows it, as does Nārada or Nārāyaṇa;
or Śambhu, who is self-luminous, knows it—none other dwelling on earth knows it.
Kapila and the others exist in the water like lotuses, untainted;
we, however, though smeared by Kṛṣṇa, are defiled. (18)
Kings and others, though smeared with their own self-interest, are visibly seen to experience both happiness and suffering;
whereas we are the virtuous ones, eternally devoted to Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
They have surrendered all their possessions for that purpose, they are absorbed in it, and they are distinguished by it;
for among us virtuous ones, there exists no disease of anxiety.
Whatever disease belongs here to those who live as proponents of the body, the senses, or the self—that disease has departed from us;
therefore, we are free from ailment.
Latent impressions (vāsanā) are the root of disease, and they have been entrusted to Nārāyaṇa;
they have been placed entirely within the hands of Dhanvantari, the great physician, like a surgical probe.
"O King, we here are free from all affliction; may you likewise become so.
Through the knowledge bestowed by Hari, we dwell here within our bodies. (23)
Impelled by that, we perform every purposeful action free from affliction;
and every practice performed by him remains entirely free from affliction.
And the wisdom bestowed by Him eradicates sorrow from its very root;
without that, the knowledge arising from the pursuit of self-interest destroys living beings.
Therefore, O King, we are indeed possessed of wisdom and free from affliction.
He attained the stainless state of oneness with Brahman, Nārāyaṇa. || 26 ||
Many who have not realized the truth, having fallen under the sway of egoism, do not understand such a state of freedom from affliction, despite their strength in debate. ||27||
Then they become thieves of Brahman, fallen under the sway of delusion;
for those submerged in the cultivation of darkness, darkness becomes their ultimate destination.
Those who abide even above the realm of Brahmā, being worldly-minded, inevitably fall back into their own nature, which consists of defects such as hypocrisy, falsehood, and pride. (29)
Thus, through internal awakening, those virtuous ones who delight in Nārāyaṇa abandon both the auspicious and the inauspicious, beholding the supreme goal.
Charity, study, sacrifice, progeny, and straightforwardness—without Hari, even if these are performed according to the rules, there is no liberation. (3.1)
This is indeed a ground for reproach: all exertion regarding kingdoms, women, the worlds, and the enjoyment of the objects of the body and senses is utterly useless. (32)
Even while living in the present, he who is dedicated to Kṛṣṇa is free from affliction; though without clothing, without companions, without a bowl, and without possessions, he is truly liberated.
Even one who endures everything is indeed subject to decay and disease unless there is dedication to Kṛṣṇa;
therefore, O King, become free from disease through your sons and your wives as well. 34.
Through dry knowledge or through ritual action, how could freedom from affliction arise?
Only through devotion to Kṛṣṇa and through the devotion of self-surrender will one certainly become free from affliction. || 35 ||
The chanting of the Name should be understood as the stainless Śabdabrahman;
having attained proficiency therein, one shall reach the realization of the Supreme Brahman. || 36 ||
In this way, a Brahmin becomes one whose conduct is pure, who practices renunciation toward all things, and who is free from worldly possessions. || 37 ||
He whose resolve is perfected through the mind, whose certainty is pure awakening, and for whom birth, action, and knowledge are considered pure in relation to Hari; || 38 ||

Having realized Brahman through direct perception, full of faith in the higher and the lower, he is one who has attained the company of the virtuous, whose self is purified, and who is devoted to moral conduct, contentment, and holy vows. ||39||
He who practices the Bhāgavata Dharma here even in times of great hardship—
he is indeed like a son of Brahmā, one who reclines upon the lap of Brahman.
Indeed, there exists an eternal state free from affliction and devoid of calamity;
for him, nothing whatsoever remains to be accomplished regarding the celestial realm.
There is no atonement for him, because he has offered all his actions to Hari.
Thus, O Brahmins, there are many kinds of people devoted to the performance of sacrifice.
Pure and observant of vows, they offered three portions of oblations while remaining steadfast in their golden hue;
performing sacrifices day after day, they were entirely free from the bonds of worldly desire.
They were straightforward, self-controlled through tranquility, and devoted to the duties of sacred knowledge;
for them, the supreme dharma was the Veda, and the Veda was always their highest purpose.
Desire is Brahman, and liberation among these is the eternal Brahman;
whether in deficiency or in excellence, their very mode of being is the perpetual Brahman.
For those whose supreme Brahman is the highest, whether their path be transgressive or sequential,
there is eternal [bliss] for those best of Brahmins whose very self is Kṛṣṇa.
They go to that supreme state—Heaven, the best of heavens, eternal, free from ailment, great bliss, and filled with everlasting joy. 47.
Whether in the home, in the forest, or in renunciation, those who abide in Brahman, O King, go to the Supreme Brahman, the Supreme Lord—those Sātvatas. 48.
Those gods are seen in heaven with their desires fulfilled, consisting of light; and the hosts of lunar mansions and stars possess many enjoyments in their celestial abodes. ||49||
Those who are without desire are not seen at all, having gone far away to the further shore;
but those who possess desire, once they have become perfected beings, shall go to that state.
For those who are free from thirst for even the self of Brahmā, there is that painless, eternal,
imperishable abode— the supreme station of the highest Brahman, which is entirely free from affliction.
For the sake of the conventional world, dharma is known as "benefiting others";
it bestows merit upon one of virtuous character and likewise grants birth in a noble home. (52)
Through the merit of his birth, he attains his purpose, and the gain of merit arises for him;
moreover, desire devoid of passion is produced in this self-realized person.
There shall be the perfection of renunciation and contentment, and wisdom shall become confident;
there shall also be the mind intent on liberation, and one shall be devoted to the dharma of Brahman. ||54||
Seeking the station of Brahman, he proceeds toward the world of Brahman;
yet, though seeking security as he goes, the weak man perishes here.
If he eats, gives, or performs sacrifices with objects that have been acquired [by others], even his virtuous possession is not equal to the happiness of renunciation. (56)
The ripening of karma is indeed the body; the ripening of knowledge is dispassion.
The ripening of devotion is the state of Brahman, and the ripening of Brahman is the supreme state.
Compassion, forbearance, contentment, truthfulness, tranquility, non-violence, straightforwardness, modesty, endurance, and the abandonment of pride and arrogance. ||58||
Association with the virtuous, a spirit of devotion, service to the good, and worship of the gods—these are the paths to Brahman; by means of these, one attains the supreme state.
The state to which the virtuous go is called the supreme goal;
worldly existence is a mass of latent impressions, while contentment is liberation.
O King, even though the group of senses is equal, some are subject to illness while others are free from it;
these [factors] have been pointed out here as bringing about freedom from disease.
Aśvapāṭala said:
"In this world, embodied beings constantly pursue virtue, wealth, and pleasure;
some desire liberation. Therefore, those three are indeed powerful. (62)
In that regard, O Lomaśa, show me by whose support a gain is truly distinguished for an embodied being, what its fruit is, and of what nature it is. (63)
Lomaśa said: O King, formerly, in a previous kalpa, I went into the midst of a forest known as Puṣkarāraṇya; there lived a brahmin named Viśālika.
And by that ascetic—who was weak, destitute, yet full of passion—I was honored with fruits, water, and other offerings. (65)
Then I asked him about his welfare, and he said to me:
"O Lomaśa, poverty brings suffering in this world; please dispel it for me. (66)
Then, taking him with me, I went toward the northern direction through the sky to the divine city of Kubera, desiring to obtain wealth.
Kubera welcomed him and gave him wealth as much as he desired;
Viśālika became pleased and took the treasure-trove of riches.
Moreover, by Dhanarāja, you two were protected at night in his own auspicious city; you remained sleeping in a beautiful palace. (69)
I know all that was seen by the Brahmin during his sleep—that great marvel, indeed full of impurity; listen to it.
He saw some people rich in dharma and pure in mind, while others were overcome by desire and devoted to dancing and singing. ||71||
Some, laden with gold, jewels, gems, wealth, and ornaments,
were departing toward their own city after taking riches from Kubera.
At that moment, an earthquake occurred repeatedly, causing the destruction of living beings;
those who were situated in pits in the earth indeed died, crushed by the soil.
The messengers of Yama arrived there to lead away many who had died;
they led off those full of desire, having bound them with firm fetters. (74)
Even the wealthy led them away without even a binding;
then he beheld Desire, Anger, Greed, Fear, and Pride.
[He struck] those who stood there, shrouding them in sleep, lethargy, great indolence, and sin—
those obstructors of the gates to heaven, who bring fear and bestow the sufferings of Yama.
The Brahmin saw those very same men, who were previously standing all around him called "the hells," now dissolved within his own substance.
And having observed those faults in a dream, the brahmin indeed fell into fear;
at that moment, the gods arrived, intending to lead away the righteous ones.
Having honored those deceased ascetics— who were righteous, equal to gods, and enriched with celestial palaces of auspicious splendor— they led them away.
Beholding those righteous ones, joyful and having attained the divine realm,
that brahmin reflected upon the supreme happiness that is the fruit of ascetic penance.
Wealth is fraught with faults, and desire is filled with impurity;
both wealth and desire are causes of hells and grant no peace.
Furthermore, desire is essentially unwholesome and possesses the nature of suffering;
asceticism and dharma lead only to heaven, therefore I practice dharma.
Then, by the power of Lomaśa’s compassion, I shall practice the Dharma;
having obtained his grace, I will surely attain the happiness born of the Bull. (83)
Even having obtained the earth filled with jewels or a vast heap of gems,
I shall never again go through the gateway to the world of Yama.
Having spoken thus, the twice-born man abandoned his wealth right there in that temple at dawn, and after bowing to Kubera, he departed indeed for the sake of ascetic penance.
Together with Lomaśa, he performed supreme and divine asceticism;
he was constantly devoted to the worship of the gods and always honored his guests.
Having taken refuge with Lomaśa, he subsisted on a diet of leaves.
Thereafter, he subsisted on water and then became one who feeds only on air. || 87 ||
With his divine vision, the twice-born man also saw the kings who had gone to the city of Yama,
as well as thousands of kings submerged in a pit in that hell at that time.
And by means of his ascetic power, he beheld the denizens of hell, who were utterly deluded by desire;
then, in an instant, that dream vanished right there for him.
Viśālika quickly left his bed and bowed down to the venerable sage Lomaśa; he also spoke, saying that everything unfavorable had been seen.
"O Guru, desire and wealth are always seen by me in the city of Yama as givers of suffering in the world of Yama; dharma, however, is considered the bestower of heaven. (9.1)
From righteousness comes the highest state seen, and through austerity, heaven is attained;
even the gods with their celestial chariots honor the righteous here on earth.
They do not honor those who are wealthy in riches, nor even those who are lustful here;
for a mere fraction of happiness resides in dharma, so I shall practice the beneficial bull-like path.
"This wealth must not be accepted by me, for it is attended by the faults of suffering;
O Teacher, I have seen that all faults reside in wealth. (94)
"Today, indeed, I saw in a dream the trembling of the earth;
for this vision here at the commencement of my wealth is surely a burden of great sorrow. (95)
"May that very thing today become an inauspicious omen for me; I have no desire for that wealth.
Having said this and given the wealth to the giver of riches (Kubera), the Brahmin [departed]. (96)
Accompanied by me and Lomaśa, she went to Kuṅkumavāpikā;
there, having accumulated merit through her austerities, she worshipped Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Brahman.
He attained supreme devotion to Nārāyaṇa through that very devotion;
for, O King, that sacred site formerly became known as Vaiśālika there.

Therefore, Dharma bestows great heaven and liberation, and grants happiness and peace; it is faultless, the remover of misfortune, established by Śrī Hara, and characterized by desirelessness and sattva. || 99 ||
The conduct of the Sātvatas consists of austerity, meditation, the performance of sacrifices,
and the constant worship, service, and taking refuge in the God of gods.

Being absorbed in that, being intent on that, having that as one's purpose, and having that as one's very self—all this is nothing but divine conduct, which is like a constant relationship with Him. (101)

Bathing, twilight prayers, and so forth are bodily [devotions]; worship through the Smṛtis is internal; worship, adoration, and the like are conventional; while association with the virtuous and so forth arises from the True Purpose.
Indeed, everything that is purifying, meritorious, known as dharma, and beneficial to the self, also destroys sin and obstructs the messengers of Yama. (103)
"O Rādhikā, it bestows the abode of Viṣṇu, leads to heaven, and grants eternal bliss. Having spoken thus, the glorious Lomaśa became silent.
Having fixed his mind upon dharma, the king once again questioned his guru,
Lomaśa— the divine-souled bestower of knowledge who was devoted to Brahman.

Thus ends the two hundred and fiftieth chapter, titled "The Description of Aśvapāṭala’s Inquiry Regarding the Direct Fruits of the Path of Renunciation, the Inquiry of Nirāmaya, the Inquiry as to Which is Best Among the Three Purposes of Life (Trivarga), and Lomaśa’s Response," in the *Lomaśagītā* within the second section, the *Tretā-santāna*, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Rādhikā, thereafter King Aśvapāṭalaka questioned his preceptor Lomaśa: "Tell me, what kind of sacrifice for dharma is this?"
Lomaśa said: O King, whatever causes harm to living beings must be abandoned by all means; that alone is a sacrifice of dharma. || 2 ||
The gods do not find satisfaction by causing living beings to suffer;
rather, let all beings be happy, just as the gods are in that state.
They exist solely for the purpose of bestowing grace; therefore, sacrifice is non-malice.
Non-violence is indeed the sacrifice of dharma, while violence is considered the abode of Yama.
Non-injury toward all living beings is the sacrifice born of the very nature of the virtuous;
indeed, service rendered with affection is the sacrifice of dharma on this earth.
Aśvapāṭala said:
If the self is pure, by what means does it become a sinful soul?
How does the self become a bearer of dharma, and how does it cast off passion?
How does one indeed attain liberation, and where does one dwell? What is the mode of conduct there, by virtue of which one does not return again?
Śrī Lomaśa said: This Self is of the nature of existence, consciousness, and bliss, and is devoid of Māyā;
it is free from the notions of "I" and "mine," yet through association, it appears to possess them.
Attachment, indulgence in illusion, and constant proximity within [the heart]—
by these, the sinful soul, filled with faults, becomes truly drawn away.
In the absence of knowledge, the ascetic indeed incurs attachment to illusion;
however, for the discerning one, the defects of attachment are destroyed by means of knowledge.
But when desire for objects arises after one has repeatedly cognized them,
then activity or cessation occurs for the sake of attaining them.
In that regard, passion (rāga) is the motivator, which arises from the cognition of something as desirable;
aversion (dveṣa), on the other hand, is the deterrent, which comes about from the awareness of something as undesirable. || 12 ||
For whatever purpose one strives, for that end one undertakes action born of the body;
and by means of that, the embodied being performs practice pertaining to the senses.
Because of that, attachment and other defects become very firm and cause suffering;
greed and delusion are produced, which destroy the stability of dharma.
Dharma arises through pretense; one practices righteousness with pretense. Like a bull, he shines forth for wealth through pretense alone, and by means of riches. 15.
The ignorant embodied being commits sin, causing suffering to others and himself;
from that cause, his creation of unrighteousness increases through such contemplation. (16)
Those of a single character, when united, increase evil;
with the increase of evil comes lack of peace, agitation, and the appearance of obstacles. (17)
Quarrels, the onset of disease, loss of wealth, poverty, the death of kinsmen, humiliation, infamy, and being disregarded by people. (18)
Theft, false speech, deceit, and a habit of trickery—
all these prevail extensively among those of sinful nature, who act without fear.
They find no happiness here, much less in the next world; moreover, they undergo the wretched destinies of the hells and the animal realm again and again. (2.251.20)
Now, O King, hear of the path of those who uphold the Dharma, which bestows happiness:
by means of merit accumulated in successive previous lives, or through association with a caravan of fellow travelers. (21)
Through constant association with the virtuous, the embodied soul always desires everything auspicious;
he performs only what is wholesome, speaks the truth, and never speaks falsehood.
He reflects upon truth alone and accomplishes the means to truth;
he conducts himself always with truth and finds neither passion nor hatred. ||23||
Through the functioning of discernment, he brings about the welfare of both himself and others;
indeed, having abandoned greed and delusion, he engages solely in what is auspicious.
And he maintains his bodily existence solely through wholesome qualities:
by means of giving, service, chanting, and devotional worship. (25)
Through sacrifice, garlands, worship of the gods, as well as austerity, and by constant increase in the company of the virtuous, one attains the supreme dharma. || 26 ||
Through service to the elderly and through service to the world, the virtuous man prospers;
and having recognized all faults, he indeed abandons them from afar.
Having recognized virtues, one embraces them and always delights in virtues;
having encountered the company of the virtuous, one surely increases the excellence of good conduct. (28)
He constantly serves the virtuous and practices the virtues of the virtuous;
through the power of practicing the conduct of the virtuous, his merits always increase. (29)
His wisdom is firm as a bull and delights nowhere else;
the embodied being, devoted to the practice of Dharma, strives even for the sake of wealth. (2.251.30)
Having acquired the wealth of Dharma, one spends it upon Dharma;
for those who possess Dharma naturally come to have virtuous friends by their very nature. //3.1//
One whose soul is devoted to Dharma, whose character is righteous, and who is adorned by association with the virtuous,
attains the happiness born of Dharma both in this world and in the next.
Likewise, he attains sovereignty in heaven, in the world devoted to heaven, as well as sovereignty over sound, touch, taste, form, smell, and enjoyment. (33)
Having thus obtained the fruit of the Dharma, he rejoices like one free from desire;
and through the vision of knowledge, he indeed nourishes world-weariness within his mind. (34)
Even when enjoyments are present, the wise man does not become attached to them;
for his mind, lacking any contemplation of them, possesses the force of dispassion.
He never pursues sensual desires,
nor does he ever abandon righteousness, even in the midst of dire calamity or violent destruction.
Having seen that the world is subject to decay and having attained freedom from passion even toward the Dharma, he, being diligent, indeed seeks the path of liberation for himself. //37//
And exerting himself daily in the practice for liberation by resorting to the proper means, he then gradually attains the step-by-step ladder of liberation. (38)
This person indeed commits every kind of evil;
he certainly never abandons the sin that has come upon him, yet he attains purification. (39)
Pure in soul, contented, and devoted to taking refuge in the Divine,
being free from idle talk and the like, he indeed attains supreme liberation.
Whether in Vaikuṇṭha, Goloka, the imperishable abode, or even the supreme realm,
one surely reaches the station of liberation that is higher than the highest, according to one's mode of worship.
Having bathed there in the Brahma-lake, one becomes like Hari in the body of Brahmā;
one attains such a form, beautiful and divine. ||42||
Eating, playing, and sporting, he dwells enjoying every desired object;
he becomes indeed one-fold or many-fold, according to his wish. ||43||

He is born as the essence of all tastes, the fragrance of all scents, and the joy of all; he is the source of all happiness, the embodiment of all forms, and the locus of all the qualities of spiritual accomplishment. ||44||
Having the nature of the Supreme Brahman and endowed with its power, one who is devoted to its service becomes liberated and exceedingly joyful. (45)
That king of the liberated, having attained great bliss through the streams of the Brahman-form, indeed perceives all creations upon the tip of his hand. ||46||
Omniscience arises for him, and lordship is fully attained;
neither here nor in any other world does his return ever occur.
Wherever he indeed proceeds, there the imperishable abode shines before him;
for one with divine vision, nothing else whatsoever appears at all. 48.
Even his worldly activity becomes divine, and even when he is associated with illusion, it quickly becomes truly divine; what then need be said of the principles (tattvas) and so forth? 49.
Whether in the world of men, in the world of the gods, in the realm of the ancestors, or even among the sages,
or in the divine descent of the Lord— this very one is indeed liberated.
Wherever one may dwell, or wherever one may wander, it makes everything divine indeed and bestows liberation upon the embodied soul. 51.
By merely seeing this [image], people are liberated; by touching it, they too become emancipated.
Through association and service, women, men, and others are born free.
Just as it is in his abode, so it is in creation, in the body, or in the state of liberation;
for him, everything is equal, and there is no difference in his conduct.
Thus, being liberated, he always experiences that attained state which is eternal, blissful, joyful, virtuous, delightful, and dear.
O King, by indeed following the path of dharma of the virtuous, you shall attain the destination that has been proclaimed; what is the use of anything else that is perishable?
Making consciousness the charioteer, making devotion your companion, and making Dharma your guide, go to the eternal Brahman. (56)
Aśvapāṭala said:
"O Great Sage, explain how the destruction of faults may occur so that there may be progress toward dharma; for tell me that by which embodied beings attain the highest good. (57)
Śrī Lomaśa said: One should conquer anger through forgiveness alone, by means of repeated reflection;
one should indeed conquer desire through non-attachment, by abandoning intention and worldly involvement.
One should conquer sleep through austerity, fasting, and the cultivation of the quality of goodness (sattva);
one should conquer fear by abandoning its causes and through discernment (viveka).
By practicing self-discipline, one should always abandon the fear of death;
through fortitude, one should likewise conquer desire, longing, hatred, and strife.
One should turn back delusion, confusion, and the sense of "mine" through the knowledge of differentiation;
by attaining the knowledge of reality as it is, one should abandon error and the like. (6.1)
One should conquer all complications through skillful application according to the prescribed rules;
one should conquer diseases by overcoming their causes and by consuming wholesome, digested, and moderate food.
One may conquer greed and thirst either through solitude or through contentment;
one may also conquer sense-objects either through the realization that they are like poison or through the vision of reality.
One should conquer unrighteousness through compassion for oneself by perceiving it as harmful;
and one should conquer [worldly] righteousness with the intent to protect [the self], practicing that which bestows liberation.
One should conquer hope by not rising [to pursue it] and by making future gains insignificant;
one should conquer wealth by regarding it as a misfortune and by abandoning attachment.
One should conquer attachment through the vision of impermanence and through detachment from bondage and the like;
one should conquer hunger through sustenance and through yoga and the necessary observances.
One should conquer pride through non-returning, compassion, and discernment;
and one should likewise conquer greed through contentment and the knowledge born of discernment.
One should conquer drowsiness through a state of composure and by rising up with effort;
one should always conquer doubt through the words of the scriptures and through definitive resolution.
One should always conquer the defects of speech through the state of a sage, the defects of the mind through knowledge, and even the impurity born of darkness through purity.
Through the vision of knowledge, the ascetic should also conquer darkness known as ignorance;
and through self-awakening, he should conquer mental knowledge.
One should conquer oneself by surrendering to the Supreme Lord;
indeed, through that surrender, all remaining defects are swiftly destroyed. (71)
Then his splendor increases, illuminating the world of Brahmā;
his supernatural powers arise, and his higher knowledge flourishes.
Having attained the conduct of the virtuous and abiding in the refuge of the virtuous,
he may, by his own will alone, desire to lead himself to the supreme state, the imperishable Brahman.
O King, this path to liberation is indeed always a source of auspiciousness,
wherein no obstacles arise due to taking refuge in Hari, who is himself free from all impediments.
With divine sensory activity and divine food, abiding in divine and virtuous conduct, and established in the divine darkness (kṛṣṇa), he goes to the eternal Brahman. //75//
Furthermore, when the aggregate has dissolved, one who is liberated does not suffer at all;
for it is the bound person who suffers, because their attachments bring about pain. (76)
No self belongs to anyone, nor does anyone belong to this [self]. How can this [self] take upon itself suffering produced by another within its own being? (77)
The self is neither born nor does it perish anywhere;
having cast off the body and attained Kṛṣṇa, it goes to the supreme goal. (78)
The body, composed of merit and demerit, perishes through the exhaustion of karma; thereafter, being fully liberated, the embodied soul attains the state of Brahman. ||79||
Indeed, the dedication of actions to Kṛṣṇa is prescribed for the purpose of exhausting both merit and demerit;
likewise, having attained freedom from the qualities (nirguṇya), one goes to the supreme state of Brahman.
Since even riches, though laden with prosperity, are indeed burdens of suffering, they delude the undiscerning man who is wrapped in the longing for their taste. (8.1)
The divine pleasure of all the senses is a defilement for one free from craving;
yet it is fashioned by one possessed of craving through the sense of "mine" as the fulfillment of self-interest. (82)
That very same thing results in even greater torment upon its destruction;
therefore, recognizing that it causes suffering beforehand, one should not acquire it. (83)
Always considering himself as one who has accomplished his task, even while living thus, he should not be distressed;
having abandoned both the desirable and the undesirable, he should offer everything to the Supreme Lord.
One should abandon that supreme disease consisting of craving which ends only with life;
for one enters the bottomless abyss of the underworld, which is likewise composed of craving. (85)
Having performed service with virtue, contentment, peace, devotion, forgiveness, wisdom, and total surrender, one shall enter the abode of Brahman. ||86||

Perceiving death as dwelling in the crest-lock, and Time as dwelling within the vital breath, and seeing action as dwelling in one's own self-performed deeds, one should cultivate the abode of Brahman.
The days and nights pass away, and one's journey is broken;
as each night elapses, one's lifespan becomes shorter. (88)
Like a flower, death carries away the embodied being whose desires remain unfulfilled;
therefore, one should first accomplish one's spiritual purpose, and thereafter attend to bodily matters.
Subsequently, one should act so as not to be deceived by that which arises from attachment to the body;
for death arrives and departs, taking everything away, even before one's tasks have been accomplished. (2.251.90)
No one knows when death will occur;
whether one is asleep, awake, or healthy, death comes and carries one away. (9.1)
While one is forming many plans for the prosperity of sons, cattle, and property, Death seizes him and departs, even as his heart is distracted by other things. (92)
No one, however powerful, is able to turn back the army of death;
only one whose strength is Brahman and whose strength is devotion is capable of driving death far away. 93.

Richly illuminated by the knowledge of Brahman, with the company of the virtuous as his vehicle, and having obtained Śrī Kṛṣṇa as his charioteer, he crosses over death and goes to the Imperishable. ||94||
O Indra among kings, do not fall into delusion regarding that which has been performed as merit; for even heaven is known to be transitory, so remain steadfastly devoted to Keśava.
Keśava is the end-maker of Time, the death of death, the Supreme Lord;
he is the foremost enjoyer of the fruits of all actions—surrender your task unto him. (96)
Be fearless, O Indra among kings, for fear is indeed the sheath of karmas;
release [your anger] toward the divine Nārāyaṇa and be unsheathed, O King.
Taking refuge in the fearless feet of Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, and abiding in the state of Kāṃbhareya, may you partake in eternal bliss. 98.
Having spoken thus to Rādhikā there, Lomaśa became silent;
King Aśvapāṭala attained peace through the supreme sovereign Śānti. 99.
Regarding the nectar brought by the venerable Lomaśa as abundant,
the king of devotees, though already satiated, did not attain further satisfaction.

Thus ends the two hundred and fifty-first chapter, titled "The Exposition of Śrī Lomaśa’s Responses to the Questions Regarding the Nature of Sin, the Nature of Merit, the State of Liberation, and the Destruction of Faults as Perpetrated by Aśvapāṭala," within the *Lomaśagītā* of the second section, the *Tretā-santāna*, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Then, O Goddess Rādhikā, King Aśvapāṭala,
his mind still unsatiated, again inquired about the duties of the Bhāgavatas.
Aśvapāṭala said: What vow does he observe, what is his conduct, what is his realization, and what is his refuge,
by which one goes to the abode of Hari called the Imperishable, which is beyond the supreme?

Śrī Lomaśa said: One who is devoted to his vows, of virtuous conduct, possessing self-knowledge of Brahman, pure, and taking refuge in the Supreme Brahman, goes to the imperishable abode, higher than the highest.
Dwelling in every house, peaceful, having abandoned both self-interest and what is harmful,
neither rising nor sitting here, and free from expectations, he shall go to the Imperishable.
One should not disclose a fault, whether directly or indirectly, nor should one even imagine it within oneself;
thus, being free from fault, one shall proceed as an immortal.
By practicing non-malice toward all beings, one becomes a giver of bliss;
and by living thus, O Ajātaśatru, one shall go to that Imperishable.
One should not engage in disputatious reasoning nor increase one's pride;
one should act in a way that is pleasing and beneficial, for such a person shall go to the imperishable abode.
Having only what is necessary for the maintenance of life, he should not acquire anything extra;
when honored, he should not rejoice, nor indeed should he be affectionate toward those who are affectionate.
One should not criticize food, nor should one revile another man or woman;
remembering Hari, one should dwell at the foot of a tree, in the forest, or in a cave.
He should wander in a state of unrecognized conduct and not conform to worldly beings;
always content and satisfied, with a serene mind and countenance.
O Japan, Kṛṣṇa is free from passion, devoid of desire, possessed of equal vision, whose self is bliss through the Supreme Self, and who has stilled all worldly impulses. || 11 ||
Standing as if indifferent, behaving like one who is neutral toward all,
and having established friendship with the Supreme Brahman, he goes to the imperishable abode.
Aśvapāṭala said:
When, having resorted to renunciation, should one go to the state of Brahman? Or when, indeed, should one depart from the duties of a householder for that state of Brahman? (13)
Śrī Lomaśa said:
Having observed his sons, grandsons, and others, and having perceived the cessation [of worldly life], and having practiced and relied upon a nature that is unimpeded and goodness; || 14 ||
Having performed devotion here, one should abandon this body and go to the imperishable state;
for even though liberation is difficult to attain, it comes to those who are diligent in its presence.
[This applies] in Kārttika, Mārgaśīrṣa, Māgha, Caitra, or Āṣāḍha.
In the month of Śrāvaṇa, one should formally undertake renunciation endowed with goodness.
When one turns away from the world, then one should renounce that place;
having dispelled all darkness through wisdom by the power of Śrī Hari.
Having attained the light of Brahman, one should go to the abode of the syllable Kṛṣṇa;
it is easily accomplished for the liberated, but for others, it lies within the sphere of effort.
Through effort one attains heaven as well as the supreme state of Brahmā;
yet that very attainment, achieved through effortful action, is also considered to be subject to destruction.
Through austerity one obtains even more; through austerity one enjoys heaven;
and by means of austerity practiced with the self, even the imperishable abode is attained.
By the very sattvata dharma alone, the Lord Hari Nārāyaṇa—the infinite Puruṣa, Anādi Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa—is attained. ||21||
Viṣṇu, Kṛṣṇa, the one with golden hair, the one with golden beard, the infallible Acyuta;
he whose abode is Vaikuṇṭha and Goloka, who is dear to Brahmā and his beloved, the all-pervading Lord. 22.
In that [Brahman] resides the entire world, both the inert and the conscious, the moving and the unmoving;
everything subtle, when attended by Brahman, comes into being upon attaining grossness. (23)
From that, he attains nourishment and then enters into him entirely;
this very Blessed One is to be attained through devotion and self-restraint.
Purified by that state of being, the wise one, stainless and established in Brahman, having mastered the state of Brahman, enjoys infinite bliss. (25)

Just as gold, when repeatedly heated and joined with the thousand-fold radiance of fire, becomes pure, so too does the self become purified when joined with knowledge, devotion, and other such virtues. (26)
Whether through a hundred future births or even within a single birth,
the self, though defiled, becomes purified through great effort.
The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, Hari, the Lord of Śrī, through His grace, bestows His presence upon this person in the yoga of devotion. ||28||
Just as [the Lord] comes to dwell and take delight in the imperishable or the perishable worlds, so too does he come to your home and sport there himself, impelled by his own grace. (29)
The world of Brahmā is his head, the worlds of the Īśvaras are his heart and other organs, and the worlds of living beings are his feet; thus the threefold creation is established.
Nārāyaṇa himself is the fruit of karmas, of austerities, of various kinds of knowledge, of services, and even of non-actions.
He whose every hair-pore contains more than the supreme Brahma-eggs,
and whose tongue is the Vedas and Sarasvatī throughout all creations.
Dharma is devotion directed toward Brahman; Brahman is that which resides within the heart.
And the divine Lord who dwells therein is the Supreme Ishvara. (3.3)
The mantras are the impellers, and the deities as well as the vessels are of that same nature;
so too are Brahmā, the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin, the Potṛ, and the Āgnīdhra, who consist of that very essence. (34)
The Hotṛ, Acchāvāka, and the pressing-stones are indeed of the nature of *stuti* (praise);
the Adhvaryu, Pratiprasthātṛ, Neṣṭṛ, and Unnetṛ are of the nature of *mada* (intoxication). ||35||

The Udgātṛ, Prastotṛ, Pratihartṛ, and Subrahmaṇya—whatever the nature of these [priests], that is the nature of the sacrifice; and whatever the nature of the sacrifice, that is the nature of the Supreme Lord. (36)
The world of the liberated syllables (Akṣaraloka), Goloka, Vaikuṇṭha, Amṛta, the Unmanifest (Avyākṛta), and the forest of Badarī—all these have that as their essence. ||37||
The abode of milk is the white ground; that which is of its nature is Mādhava.
Likewise, Rādhā-Kṛṣṇa and Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa are the white couple.
He is indeed Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the beloved of Ramā and the Lord of the Lotus-born;
for Vāsudeva and the others are his manifestations (vyūhas) and millions of incarnations (avatāras). ||39||
The lords such as Bhūman, those born of Pradhāna such as the Vairājas, and even Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśa, and the Rudras—he indeed is their very self. (2.252.40)
The sages, the ancestors, the Vasus, the Siddhas, the virtuous ones, the Ādityas, the two Aśvins, Sūrya, and the rest—He indeed is their very self. (41)
The guardians of the directions, the guardians of the worlds, the gods, humans, and so forth—O King, all that consists of Him; it is both distinct from Him and not distinct from Him.
Beholding through great knowledge, one becomes possessed of the radiance of Brahman;
radiant with the splendor of Brahman, one indeed perceives the Supreme Lord. ||43||
Empowered by the majesty of the Supreme Lord, he directly perceives and realizes all heavens through the power of those respective visions. (44)
Aśvapāṭala said:
"O Guru, tell me here which of those creations he, being one whose self is liberated, perceives— those that are impermanent or those that are eternal."
Śrī Lomaśa said: In the creation of Brahmā, there are indeed five forms of Brahman:
the Supreme Brahman (Parabrahma), the Beloved of Brahman (Brahmapriyā), and the Imperishable Brahman (Akṣarabrahma). ||46||
"Released ones are indeed different from those not released"—thus he has five forms;
likewise, in the creation of the Lord, he exists as tenfold, including the virtuous. (47)
The incarnations and female incarnations, the manifestations, the primary principle, the infinite beings, the Great Viṣṇus, and tens of millions of Vairājas. ||48||
Sādāśiva, Gava and the others, the female attendants (Pārṣadāṇīs) and the male attendants (Pārṣadas), the cowherds (Gopas) and the cowherdesses (Gopīs)—these twelve forms he also assumes. 49.
In the creation of individual souls, there is a tenfold creation composed of sentient beings:
the three classes of gods, the Siddhas, the Puruṣas, the Ṛṣis, the Pitṛs, and the Suras.
The Āsuras, Mānavas, animals, species of insects, and immobile beings—these are the primary categories, while within them there are further sub-divisions. ||51||
Innumerable beings are born according to the will of the three gods;
this twenty-seventh kalpa alone is primary, while the secondary ones are infinite.
And for immobile beings, insects, and animals, it occurs through auspicious conjunctions, by dwelling in a sacred field, or again, through contact with a holy place (tīrtha). ||53||
Through union with the virtuous lords of the gods, she attained human birth; through union with the Asuras and through the yoga of Kṛṣṇa, she likewise attained human birth. (54)
In that regard, through the attainment of dharma and so forth, a divine destiny indeed arises;
or, through devotion to the six [classes of ancestors] and through merits, a paternal destiny is produced. (55)
Then, by the great merit of the gift of śrāddha, there is the state of the Ṛṣis;
superior to that is the auspicious state of the Siddhas, attained through the power of the practice of yoga. (56)
For them, there arises through the practice attainable by the water of yoga either the state of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, or Śambhu, born from the attainment of the excellence of pure being (sattva). 57.
Their destination is that of the Vairājikas due to the excellence of their worship;
or else, they attain the state of the Mahāvaiṣṇavas or another [higher] destination.
And then there is the path of Sādāśiva, and from that, by the power of ritual worship (aupāsana),
there is the path of Bhūmnikā, and thereafter the path of Pradhāna and Puruṣa.
Furthermore, through superior worship, there is the attainment of the nature of the divine manifestations (vyūha),
as well as the state consisting of cowherds and cowherdesses, and likewise that consisting of the personal attendants (pārṣada) and so forth.
She is the one who descends and likewise the state of liberation;
she is the very nature of the incarnations and the very nature of Muktānikā.
Through the power of worshiping Hari, one attains the state of Brahmī, a form dear to Brahmā, as well as the state of the Imperishable (Ākṣarī). ||62||
Everything up to Brahmā is born; the Supreme Brahman is not born.
He alone is the one Supreme Self, the Lord who dwells within all as the inner controller.
He is the incarnation of the Supreme Brahman, known as the Supreme Lord;
he is the highest among the highest Nārāyaṇas, surpassing millions of Nārāyaṇas.
O horse-keeper, when an embodied being here resorts to unrighteousness,
it then goes to the womb of an animal or insect, or even to the state of an immobile being.
He enters a lowly birth, whether among the Asuras or the Mānavas;
then, having reached the realm of Yama, he proceeds according to what remains of his [karmic] residue.
Whether birth is impure or pure, it is the result of dharma performed over a long period;
however, one who follows the path of adharma is never liberated from a base womb.
But by means of a pure heart, seeking Kṛṣṇa while contemplating Brahman,
one attains that which is pure, eternal, imperishable Brahman, and the Supreme.
The entire creation proceeds from the world of Hari and enters back into Him alone; therefore, worship Him who dwells within, the manifest beloved of Kṛṣṇa. (69)
Weave a thread for as long as you have need, like a spider spinning its web;
swallow it back again when your task is finished, and remain intent upon the snare.
When you have cast off the web of delusion, reveal once again that which is new;
having abandoned even the dharma-bound, manifest that other [state] which bestows happiness. (7.1)
O Lord of the Earth, having abandoned both the net and the repository of the net, become happy;
enjoy infinite bliss in the eternal Brahman.
The knots of the heart here exist based upon latent impressions;
once destroyed by the realization of Brahman, they do not arise anew.
And being free from the bondage of the knots [of the heart], one attains the eternal Brahman;
indeed, the wise who have taken refuge in Hari never suffer.
The worlds, possessed by delusion, hope, and the like, continue to languish amidst the waves—
even those who know the past, the future, and that which is yet to be.
Their commencement, dissolution, and the arising of results—whether equal or unequal—neither arises as suffering nor as agitation for one who understands them. (76)
The destinies of karmas are diverse: some are wealthy, others are destitute;
some possess very firm bodies, while others are afflicted by disease or deprived of food.
Whether they be poor men with many sons, or virtuous women with wicked husbands, or childless kings, or gods afflicted by Daityas and other demons; ||78||
The learned who are devoid of honor, servants who are lazy, those who are handsome yet malicious, and those famous for their thieving deeds; ||79||
Behold the downward slope of saṃsāra, where those with thirst for royal enjoyments live—both those who possess thousands and those who possess only hundreds. (2.252.80)
The poor become lords of ten million while living on mere food;
all pass away into death, whether they are beset by exertion or free from effort.
Having reflected upon this, O Great King, do not resort to imprisonment;
for neither kinsmen, nor gold and such wealth, nor noble lineage, nor prowess, nor even the power of Manu [the law] can avail against it. (82)
They are able to protect one from suffering; therefore, one should take refuge in Nārāyaṇa.
One should always abandon that which is pleasant, for it generates excitement and bestows pride. (83)
One should always worship that which is dear [to the Lord], for it bestows Brahman, liberation, and peace;
whereas wealth and desire are great fetters that turn one away from dharma and liberation. (84)
These two alone, when applied during the month of Mādhava, are considered to bring about both dharma and liberation;
and for one who conducts himself in this way, neither death nor even Time itself can cause affliction.
Aśvapāṭala said:
"For one who is devoid of the knowledge of reality, possessed of many doubts, and has not attained certainty in this world—tell me here that by which his welfare may be secured. (86)
Śrī Lomaśa said: "The constant service of the virtuous, the gurus, and the elders;
likewise, the worship of the gods and the listening to the scriptures. (87)
One must always serve one's mother and father with sincerity; serve one's husband, serve virtuous women, and receive the blessings of those worthy of worship. ||88||
Indeed, even the mere act of worshiping Hari bestows auspiciousness;
however, supreme liberation arises through devotion to the Supreme Lord. (89)
Even secondary benefits arise through auspicious means;
for the virtuous, blessings of well-being are constant, being naturally imbued with the merit of giving.
Dwelling in a temple of the deity is auspicious and bestows supreme liberation;
it consists of the state of Brahman everywhere and the practice of serving all beings. 9.1.

Worship of the gods, ancestors, guests, and dependents is likewise conducive to spiritual welfare; so too is freedom from the delusion of illusion, and contentment, which is the cessation of all seeking. (92)
Dwelling within the inner self, meditation on the Self—which bestows the highest good—and likewise the undertaking of vows that are means for liberation [are the path]. (93)
The wealth of knowledge and steadfastness in the Self are the highest good that bestows liberation;
one who desires the welfare of all should indeed practice for universal excellence. (94)
One should speak of the virtuous qualities and so forth of others with extreme praise; one should bestow honor and encouragement upon them and perform acts of worship for them. ||951||
One who is devoted to self-worship, yet considers the worship of others, and is intent on attaining wisdom, always finds the highest good. (96)
One should desire to dwell among the virtuous, cultivate straightforwardness toward the wise, and maintain friendship with those of meritorious character, which bestows the highest good. 97.
One should not find pleasure in dwelling anywhere where people lack spiritual excellence; rather, one should indeed dwell where the utterances of *svāhā*, *svadhā*, and *vaṣaṭ* prevail. //98//
Where there is happiness, there indeed one should dwell for the sake of liberation—that happiness which is liberation itself;
there, liberated people, free from bonds, move about in bliss. (99)
O King, even insects and the like exert effort in amassing stores;
those who are unattached are happy, while those who are attached are afflicted by the ocean of suffering. (2.252.10)
A wise person who seeks their own welfare and possesses discernment should certainly not worry about how their kinsmen will live without them. (101)
All abide under the power of karma and meet their end through karma;
both union and separation likewise occur according to karma.
Death is true in every respect; for the sake of the highest good, death is auspicious.
Having performed many kinds of meritorious deeds, that death leads to death [in the higher realms].

He who has constructed a fortress for the sake of others, yet resorts to a trench for his own sake, shall find no prosperity in this world; how then could there be supreme, ultimate liberation for him?
Therefore, O King, having indeed abandoned negligence, devote yourself to that which leads to the highest good;
worship Kṛṣṇa day after day and Hari night after night.
Behold your own self as the state of Brahman; be liberated here from rebirth, O foremost one, for you have no desire to remain in this world.
With a need for sustenance and medicine like a traveler, and likewise indifferent toward enjoyments as if they were objects for one whose mind is distracted— he is certainly liberated in this world.
For one for whom food, clothing, dwellings, and the like are like sloughed-off skin, and for whom even contact with the prosperity of others results in the piercing of one's vital organs; || 108 ||
Even when the senses are in perfect condition, he possesses a state of being beyond the senses;
even amidst the abundance of objects of enjoyment and wealth, his discernment is like that of one facing calamity.
O King, he is thus liberated here and also in the hereafter;
indeed, through union with him, even other people may attain liberation.
Having enjoyed the earth as sages, kings, and great emperors, they have gone to their death;
seeing this, one becomes liberated, freed from the hope for worldly bondage. (119)
In this world, sufferings are easily obtained while happinesses are difficult to find; even those gained through great effort perish. How, then, could one not revere liberation? 1.12
When wealth exists, everyone on all sides exclaims "Aho! in praise;
they honor him by speaking auspicious words, saying, "O brother! O father! 12.
Intent only on their own self-interest, they are indeed hostile once the wealth has departed;
in times of poverty, they do not know where the brother is or where the father is.

Having understood this, how could a wise person not become dispassionate toward those intent on their own self-interest, and toward human existence which is like a pithless core, and life itself which is likewise fruitless? 1.15
Therefore, the Dharma of the Blessed One is superior both in this world and the next;
for the righteous, both the Dharma and devotion always bestow the highest good.
Thus, O Rādhikā, the glorious Lomaśa instructed Aśvapāṭala in many ways; the king questioned him again.
