Thus ends the two hundred and fifty-second chapter, titled "The Description of Aśvapāṭala’s Inquiry Concerning the Means of Attaining the Course of the Imperishable, the Inquiry Concerning the Goal from either Renunciation or Householder Life, the Inquiry Concerning the Creation of the Threefold Emanation, and the Inquiry Concerning the Highest Good, along with the Answers Given by Lomaśa," in the *Lomaśagītā* within the second section, the *Tretā-santāna*, of the glorious *Śrī-Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O Rādhikā, having heard the supreme means for ultimate liberation, Aśvapāṭala questioned Lomaśa once again regarding his own deliverance.
Aśvapaṭṭala said:
Speak to me again in this matter concerning that which is beneficial and brings happiness both here and in the hereafter,
which is to be accomplished through duty, and which results in ever-increasing prosperity.
Śrī Lomaśa said:
A cart carrying a heavy load travels for those who are travelers;
so too does the body travel upon this earth for one intent on the journey of life, devoid of contentment.
Hunger and thirst are the two bulls; sorrow and delusion are the two wheels;
pleasure and pain are at the front and the back, while latent impressions (vāsanā) are situated in the middle. (4)
The charioteer himself, having taken the cart, goes for his own greater profit;
greedy for more than the mere fare, he gains six [coins] here in this world.
For this very reason, the driver, though constantly afflicted, does not perceive sleep, as he repeatedly transports countless goods by means of the cart. (6)
And in the forest of the senses, one is plundered helplessly;
the thieves carry away entirely the wealth consisting of happiness and peace. (7)
Therefore, the two bulls need not be guarded, nor likewise the cart;
by abandoning them, there is indeed happiness and peace in the maintenance of the body, like that of a yogi.
For this chariot-warrior who employs the vehicle merely for travel, there arises [the attainment of] clothing, food, water, and a dwelling; he should not desire anything more than that.
One should perform meritorious deeds and those rites dedicated to the gods; one should carry out acts of service to others according to one's own capacity.
This human life is difficult to obtain; one should not waste it in a pit of misery, but should strive for liberation in order to achieve excellence and spiritual advancement. (11)
Through meritorious action, as well as through vows, effort, practice, good fortune, and the blessings of the virtuous, there arises both excellence and worldly prosperity.
One should not imitate the deeds of the gods, the sages, the virtuous, or the great; for there is no fault in the actions of those who possess such splendor.
One should never disparage the seemingly impossible deeds of the great;
with a tranquil mind, one should perform auspicious acts, for such a person beholds only what is favorable.
One should not acquire cruel deeds, wealth, honor, or authority,
because all of that will surely result in suffering in the world of Yama.
One should perform everything that is praised, renowned, and conducive to prosperity—whether it pertains to the gods, the ancestors, guests, humans, or animals. (16)
The virtuous great seers attain perfection through action that does not involve expenditure;
kings do so through action involving expenditure; and yogis through worship. (17)
Śūdras [attain it] through service to women, as do male and female slaves through their servitude;
the learned through the path of knowledge, and artisans through the science of their craft. (18)
Cows and the like [attain merit] by the giving of milk; trees and the like by the giving of fruit;
shrubs by the giving of leaves; and creepers by the giving of flowers. (19)
And when human beings assist one another through mutual service,
they indeed attain supreme perfection and proceed to the perfection of liberation.
Even sages of firm vows, having performed oblations in the fire,
attain supreme perfection by directing their aim toward Śrī Nārāyaṇa.
The wife, oneself, the mother, the father who begot one, the son, the teacher, and the daughter—these are the deities to be served by one who desires the fruit of happiness. 22.
All those are declared to be fires; that is the act of offering, and that indeed is the office of the Hotṛ priest. Upon their satisfaction, Hari, who dwells within, becomes satisfied.
The fruit of that satisfaction is happiness in this world and eternal bliss in the next, whether attained through devotion, service, giving, or sacrifice. (24)
By means of austerity known as *kṛcchra*, even those unworthy attained worthiness;
Uśanas, Viśvāmitra, and Vālmīki reached the state of the virtuous.
Through ascetic penance, Uśanas attained the state of Śukra from Śambhu; thereafter, he was always born in heaven as Śukrācārya, the preceptor of the Daityas.
The Kṣatriya Viśvāmitra indeed attained the status of a Brahmarṣi, and Vālmīki, though a Śabara, became forever liberated. ||27||
Through service, Śūdra women attain a supreme and auspicious state;
association with the virtuous always bestows the dawning of good fortune and grants great merit. (28)
Through association with the virtuous, a person indeed becomes good;
even a single cowrie-coin earned through honest labor brings happiness. (29)
Gold acquired through unjust means bestows suffering and brings about shackles;
food acquired through unjust means leads to disease and vomiting. || 2.253.30 ||
A field acquired through unjust means leads to fire and to hell;
a woman acquired through unjust means leads to death and to infamy.
Wealth acquired through unjust means leads to the destruction of one's roots;
in ancient times, Brahmā indeed created the son Dharma for the happiness of all creatures.
All castes established in their own duties indeed abide in heaven and are happy;
for the sake of their liberation, Dharma then emanated from his own body.
Just as people attain devotion and the eternal heaven of Hari,
through those two they shall meet with heaven for a long time and also eternally thereafter.
One should exert effort in this way so that victory over the two heavens may be achieved, when action arises free from mental impressions and devoid of attachment. (35)
Taking refuge in the Inner Controller dwelling within the heart, one who is pure shall acquire auspiciousness;
for generally, O King, this is the case for the virtuous, the renouncers, and those free from passion. (36)
Through the power of wisdom or through devotion, bondage shall not become firm;
moreover, looseness is attained through knowledge, discernment, and the study of the scriptures. (37)
For householders or for the dull-witted, bondage becomes firm by relying upon houses, cattle, fields, and wealth. (38)
Through wives, sons, and servants, bondage becomes firm;
passion and hatred always increase through the delusions of sensory enjoyment and the like. (39)
Through those [objects], pleasure indeed arises; he finds delight in vulgar pleasures and the like.
For he does not know, for the sake of the Self, the discernment that even liberation is [a goal]. (2.253.40)
But one who strives [for enjoyment] thinking "I shall be an enjoyer" perishes once again;
therefore, one should remain unattached to home, wife, wealth, and the like. 41.
In this world, the fruits of austerity and material riches bind people;
so too do the Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, Maruts, and Manus. (42)
The Viśvedevas, the Aśvins, the Siddhas, the Sādhyas, the great ṛṣis, the Kiṃpuruṣas, the Gandharvas, Vahni, Indra, Sūrya, and Candra;
the Pitṛs, the Lokapālas, the Rākṣasas, Yakṣas, and Kinnaras. ||43||
The Gaṇas and the Pārṣadas, as well as the Grahas, Devas, and Dānavas;
kings, the elders, teachers, Siddhas, and virtuous women—
all these, having attained perfection through austerity, enjoy the fruit of their austerities.
Those born into great families, who are wealthy and rejoice as lords, possess garments of fine silk, as well as ornaments of gold and diamonds. (86)
Vehicles, seats, and foods; drinks, women, male and female servants;
excellent and soft beds; and garments upon the floors of palaces. (47)
All desired things— all that fruit of ascetic practices—
is born for the sake of enjoyment, and all action leads to hell.
Discontent leads to great suffering and likewise destroys wisdom;
it causes one to wander and is exhausted by running in vain. (49)
For the heat-pleasure born of desire, lasting no longer than the flight of an arrow through contact, leads entirely to suffering and to hell;
therefore, having understood it to be momentary and full of misery, [one should abandon it].
And even one who follows the duties of a householder, if he is wise, should strive for the sake of liberation.
Even humans who do not aspire for liberation, being engrossed in the pleasures of desire and the like, seem to destroy their merits just as swine destroy [clean things]. (52)
They employ a worthy recipient who is equal to the wish-fulfilling creeper when it has been obtained;
for the unfortunate ones indeed crush, wither, and destroy it.
Men and women waste away this body, which is like a wish-fulfilling gem obtained and yet shrouded by the illusion of a queen, having rendered liberation fruitless.
Although the world of the king, by its very nature, possesses desire and other such impulses,
it is not constantly restrained against its will, for it indeed proceeds toward actions.
Although there were many objects that bestowed physical delight,
nevertheless, by the word of his guru, he [directed] himself toward those other duties.
One should perform even more actions known as devotion by which one is liberated;
for those who, though immersed [in worldly existence], desire to uplift themselves, they do so by abiding in the conduct of the virtuous.
Having attained merit, happiness, and tranquility, they shall reach the supreme heaven, even if they were attached to sense-objects, provided they were free from malice. (58)
Performing actions for the sake of Hari, the cowherd women seem to uplift themselves by ascending the path of action leading to liberation, which is the chariot of Hari.
The caravans of the virtuous— those devoted to devotion and intent on total surrender—
go to the undecaying, imperishable station, the heaven that is the upward path.
Devotees are victorious everywhere, whether they possess attributes or are devoid of them;
sons, disciples, and even women who are full of devotion are truly victorious.
Father, friend, teacher, wife, king, mother, husband, and deity—even these do not please those who lack devotion, nor do the virtuous ancestors. ||62||
For devotion is the supreme means for pleasing [the Lord], while service is auspicious;
likewise, in this world, waiting upon and servitude are the best ways for attaining Him.
Therefore, the Supreme Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa must be quickly propitiated through devotion and other means by one who is conscious of this very body. 64.
No king can protect one who has fallen into the snare of death;
nor can anyone drag away one's remaining merit or demerit. (55)
O King, there exists no enemy here equal to ignorance;
under its power, a person constantly commits terrible violence. (66)
Therefore, they undergo sufferings, new births, and new deaths;
for one who seeks to overcome these here, it is indeed by attending upon the virtuous elders that this is achieved. ||67||
Having attained wisdom, one should banish that enemy along with its caravan;
then, having cast the wish-fulfilling gem into a pit, one will surely not fall from liberation.
Even in the state of a *caṇḍāla*, human birth is auspicious for the sake of devotion;
indeed, the human womb is supreme as it is the means for the protection of the self. (69)
This body must not be wasted on useless enjoyments;
as long as it has not perished here, we shall perform the highest good.
Having obtained such a human form, which is the seed for [attaining] liberation, he who hates his own liberation is considered to be perpetually deceived. (7.1)
One should indeed perform service for the sake of the world through acts of giving;
one should provide assistance for the sake of one's family with wealth and material goods.
One should undertake appropriate exertion for the sake of sons and other worldly goals;
however, for one's own ultimate benefit, one should practice the supreme means that grants liberation. (73)

For the sake of spiritual welfare, one should always perform sacrifices, acts of charity, worship, meritorious deeds, rites for the ancestors, and rituals for the gods, as well as devotion and service. 174.
Aśvapāṭala said: "O Guru, tell me: what is the root of all that is auspicious? What, once performed, never perishes? Where, having gone, does one not return? Tell me this. (75)
Śrī Lomaśa said:

Conduct characterized by goodness, freedom from attachment, service to the virtuous, and association with them, as well as receiving the blessings of the elders, constitute the inexhaustible root of all that is auspicious. (76)
Austerity, devotion, the gift of fearlessness, taking refuge in Nārāyaṇa, and the offering of oneself—all this never perishes. (77)
Among all bodily austerities and penances, this alone is the supreme austerity:
the cessation of mental activity directed toward Hari. Indeed, it bestows direct perception [of Him].
And once this direct experience has been attained, it never ceases.
And the gift of fearlessness surpasses all other gifts. || 7.9 ||
For one who bestows fearlessness upon all, there is imperishable fearlessness both here and in the hereafter;
though dwelling in the midst of sense-objects, the wise man does not truly dwell therein at all.
The ignorant person dwells excessively even amidst non-existent objects; however, objects do not overpower a wise person who possesses inner luster. 8.1
Even very slight [afflictions] indeed surge powerfully against one who lacks wisdom;
they never leave the perpetrator of evil deeds.
Those who have disciplined their selves are not divided by sense objects, even by tens of millions of karmic actions.
In this world, fear never leaves one whose self is undisciplined. ||83||
Indeed, for one who is free from passion, liberation alone is seen because birth no longer occurs;
there is no stain upon him while he lives, owing to the action performed.
Even for one who has died, there is indeed no experience of [the fruits of] his karmas;
for one who has set out upon the path of devotion, it is held that he attains the supreme abode.

Elaborate pursuits are joined with afflictions, while concise ones grant happiness; elaborate pursuits are for the sake of others and lead to suffering, so one should resort to renunciation, which is for one's own benefit. (86)
In this world consisting of day and night, the embodied soul stands in the jaws of death;
he is swallowed constantly and is born incessantly with his lifespan cut short. (87)
Bitten by many worldly snares of attachment and by the venomous scorpions of delusion, one becomes agitated by their poisonous fangs and finds no happiness anywhere. 88.
Having severed the bonds, abandoned the home and possessions, and having offered salutations, he who proceeds upon the path of Hari shall indeed reach the further shore. ||89||
This world is like a pale horse: when one is healthy, it steals away the sense of well-being;
when one is ill, it remains far off, intent solely on its own self-interest. (2.253.90)
The benefit of others is always considered superior to one's own self-interest;
moreover, one who is devoted to the welfare of others and is patient is truly distinguished.
Even one who is patient, the wise man is superior; and even among the wise, the one endowed with devotion is superior.
He indeed is the one who, through abundance of devotion, always brings about liberation by awakening the protected Brahman. 92.
It is the supreme treasury of immortality, the highest gateway to liberation,
the most excellent vehicle to heaven, and likewise the storehouse of dharma.
Indeed, a devotee in the world of mortals remains liberated like one who is already liberated;
through association with the devotee, those who are devoted indeed become goers to Brahman. ||94||
Whatever kind of person a living being serves, such he himself becomes;
if one serves a virtuous person here, he too is born as a good man.
The gods are satisfied by the virtuous, as are the ancestors and the millions of Siddhas;
the liberated ones are satisfied by the holy men. Therefore, one should resort to the state of being a virtuous man.
The gods abandon from afar those people who are intent solely upon their own self-interest;
the gods, the liberated, and the virtuous dwell together with the virtuous.
Thus, by means of this excellent yoga, he proceeds to the world of Brahmā;
established in the Supreme Brahman, liberated, he enjoys infinite bliss. || 98 ||
O Rādhikā, having thus instructed [her] regarding the horse and the *pāṭala* tree, the venerable Lomaśa ceased; the king then questioned him once again.

Thus ends the two hundred and fifty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the King’s Inquiry Regarding Prosperity, the Inquiry Concerning the Root of Welfare and Other Matters, and the Answers Given by Lomaśa," within the *Lomaśagītā* of the second section, the *Tretā-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O Rādhikā, Aśvapāṭala asked about the propitiation of the deity by which one’s own pleasure may also arise without obstacle.
Aśvapāṭala said:
"O Great Sage, residence in the worlds of the gods indeed belongs to those who sacrifice with wine;
and residence in the world of Brahmā arises for those who sacrifice to Brahmā. (2)
Moreover, by worshipping those who sacrifice to various lords—even among the lords in this world—and by worshipping the abodes and incarnations, one shall attain residence [there]. (3)
"By what means can the satisfaction of the gods be brought about?
Having shown compassion toward me, tell me this, as well as regarding other abodes. (4)
Śrī Lomaśa said:
The gods are pleased by sacrifice, by worship, and by ritual service; likewise, they are gratified by food offerings, oblations, the propitiation of mantras, and their respective vows.
Through truth, non-violence, purity, and through virtue (vṛṣa), as well as through self-surrender, humility, taking refuge, and so forth. || 6 ||
O King, the gods are pleased by ritual performance, even with difficulty, by giving gifts, by remembrance, by festivals, by chanting their praises, and so forth.
When the gods are satisfied through self-purification, discernment, meritorious deeds, and devotion, they surely bestow their own happiness, both of this world and of heaven.

The ancestors are the lords [to be propitiated] through Śrāddha rites, grand concluding ceremonies (udyāpana), the recitation of the Vedas (pārāyaṇa), the study of Vedic knowledge, and the worship of images.
Through the consecration of temples according to ritual injunctions, through worship and other rites,
through great festivals, and through the Vedic dharma, millions of Lords are pleased.

The manifestations (avatāras) of Hari are attained through devotion, worship, ritual service, the veneration of his forms, and so forth, as well as by visiting sacred fords, observing his vows, and cultivating the corresponding spiritual dispositions.
Through the manner of surrendering by His command, through hearing His stories and so forth,
through seeking no other refuge, through the state of being fixed in oneness with Him,
through constant attendance, through remembrance, through meditation, and through service—
And by means of a pure livelihood, constantly endowed with stainlessness. || 13 ||
By means of service to His powers, His attendants, and so forth; by taking refuge in the state of offering;
through various amorous gestures, gifts, and the like; and by mental worship and other such acts. || 14 ||
Through service and the offering of food to those men and women who are devoted to Him, the incarnations become well-pleased and bestow their respective sovereign powers. (15)
When gratified by devotion, they become bestowers of various abodes;
however, O King, it is the Supreme Soul, the primordial Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, [who grants the highest state]. (16)
In this matter, the Lord of Śrī is pleased solely by devotion consisting of total self-surrender, through trust, devotion, the act of entrustment (nyāsa), servitude, and steadfast service. (17)
And by following his will, by choosing him as one's own, by honoring him, by selfless service, by worship, and by virtue; || 18 ||
He is pleased by meditation, by worship, and indeed by self-surrender;
yet meditative cultivation is the great cause, for affection is what truly satisfies Him.
Whether it be very small or even great, worship accompanied by devotion certainly pleases Govinda, who is the sole creator of all modes of existence.
By whatever means possible, through constant remembrance, and by means of a continuous flow of consciousness absorbed in that [object], consisting of the rope of love; || 21 ||
And by viewing all beings as one's own inner self, by performing acts that bring satisfaction to all, by offering a warm welcome to those belonging to Him, and by serving virtuous people; ||22||
By pleasing the Sātvatas, by helping the distressed, by nourishing the helpless, and by showing no malice toward any living beings; ||23||
By means of all the duties of the devotees of the Lord, by the knowledge of reality, by self-realizations, by the recounting of His stories, and also by the descriptions of His qualities; ||24||
And also by reciting its names, by applying the logical arrangements of its meanings, by a mental state whose form consists of that [reality], and by protecting the dharma of its creation. || 25 ||

The Supreme Brahman is fully satisfied by the offering of one’s entire wealth of affection toward Him, just as He is pleased by bestowing upon the classes of sentient and insentient beings exactly what each requires. (26)

By means of the practice of giving, vows for the sake of sentient beings, non-malice, non-deception, and so forth, and by means of the duties of the virtuous and the acts that satisfy devotees and female devotees; || 27 ||
Hari, the beloved of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, abides within all;
indeed, all things, both insentient and sentient, are but the images of this very Kṛṣṇa. (28)
Men, women, and all other embodied beings existing within the entire creation—
everywhere, even within the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*— [should perceive] by means of that [divine] intellect.
I shall indeed serve that very form; may my Lord, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the son of Śrī Kambharā, be pleased with me.
The delighter of the cowherds, the most beloved and dear friend of Kṛṣṇa, the Lord;
the husband of Lakṣmī, Rādhā, Ramā, Māṇikī, and Padmajā. ||3 1 ||
The beloved husband of Brahmā’s consort, the Lord of the Liberated, the glorious Puruṣottama, the Lord of the virtuous, the Lord of the Self, the Lord of all—he is my Lord. 32.
Thinking thus, one should indeed worship that Inner Controller within embodied beings, through the vision of Him, the contemplation of Him, and acts such as the offering of all to Him. ||33||
One should be free from desire for rewards in all such worship;
for Kṛṣṇa is indeed pleased by that, as he is honored within all embodied beings.
"I am yours; protect me, save me!"—thus one should always pray:
"O Lord Hari! O Hare Kṛṣṇa! O Bāla Kṛṣṇa! I am yours. (35)
Just as you conduct me, so do I conduct myself by your command;
all this belongs to you alone, for there is nothing here other than you.

"Everything within my field of vision belongs to you alone, and you yourself are that very same thing"—for an embodied being who has been thus permeated by the vision of the Blessed One, [there is no sense of "mine"]. (37)

Whether it be out of desire, anger, or delusion; for the sake of one's own interest, or even out of devotion and refuge—[this applies] to one who has fallen into [the Buddha's] protection and whose mind is fixed thereon. (38)
The compassionate Blessed One, who is affectionate toward his devotees, is quickly pleased;
in this matter, there is no other means required, nor any ritual substances, oblations, or the like. (39)
He who depends on someone else for the sake of their gratification is indeed gratified by that person;
"this is mine, not another's"—such is the nature of Hari’s grace, for it is born from that very dependence.
By grace Kṛṣṇa is attained; by grace one is led to the Imperishable;
and by grace the Lord of the virtuous bestows His own abode as well. (41)
By means of inferior cultivation, the gods and others certainly do not come into being;
they are satisfied with all phenomena through action that is excluded [from the higher path]. //42//
Indeed, together with their devotees, the gods and other lords, along with their servants, attendants, and even their restrainers, those sovereigns rejoice in contentment. (43)
For those beings shrouded by ignorance, stained by the ink of envy and other vices, and dragged down by defects such as greed, neither heaven nor liberation provides satisfaction. (44)
The wise devotee attains the Imperishable and rejoices with those who are blissful;
having obtained the power of his own chosen deity, he experiences peace.
The divine nature of embodied beings is indeed that action performed for the sake of Kṛṣṇa;
devotion to Kṛṣṇa is godliness, and self-study is purity as well. 46.
Vows, moral conduct, and the conquest of the senses are esteemed by the virtuous; whereas quarreling, reviling, deceit, roguery, and the like [are not]. (47)
One should understand that these are unwholesome; death dwells together with them.
Having examined where death resides, the wise man should abandon those [unwholesome things]. (48)
By taking refuge in Hari here, one may banish death far away;
and free from the fear of death, one should practice the means to attain the Imperishable.
"O King, one should practice that by which the attainment of the abode of the Supreme Brahman may occur;
for one who conducts oneself in this way, there is no turning back. (2.254.50)
The attainment of that imperishable world shall indeed be eternal;
for by devotion, one attains that abode wherein residence is without end. (51)
Aśvapāṭala said: "O Guru, what kind of liberation indeed results from the discrimination between the Self and the non-Self? And what kind of liberation might arise through the worship of Hari? (52)
Tell me here: what kind of liberation would there be through the practice of yoga?
And what kind of liberation is considered possible even by relying on mere dharma alone? (53)
"O Guru, tell me: by the mere taking of refuge in you, will liberation surely occur or not? By what means is the attainment of liberation certain? (54)
Śrī Lomaśa said:

The body is indeed considered to be a composite of the five gross elements, as well as the internal sense organs, the instruments of action, the vital breaths, the three qualities (guṇas), and the subtle elements (tanmātras). ||55||
The Self is distinct from them, eternal, conscious, and unconditioned;
it is eternally liberated, eternally pure, eternally awakened, and always abiding [in itself]. //56//

Because of the destruction of ignorance through the knowledge of the insentient, the sentient, and consciousness, and because of the illumination [arising] from the practice of reality—that "I am not," "nothing is mine," and "there is no 'I'"—[the self is realized]. ||57||

Indeed, through the exhaustion of karma, one is liberated from the body; being liberated, one is truly devoid of qualities (nirguṇa), consisting of existence, consciousness, and bliss (saccidānanda), and free from produced illumination. ||58||
The self of liberation, which exists for an eon as its own essential nature, attains [this state];
it is indeed neither happy nor formless, but remains forever the locus of insentience. ||59||
If one worships Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Lord who removes dullness, one becomes established in the supreme abode of Brahman as the very nature of the Supreme Lord. (2.254.60)
As is Hari, so is the devotee; he attains residence in the same world (sālokya), equality of power (sārṣṭi), proximity (sāmīpya), and similarity of form (sārūpya), and enjoys all delights. ||6 1 ||
Having bathed in the Brahma-lake and indeed attained a Brahmanic body,
he becomes liberated into the state of Brahman, endowed with divine qualities, by the will of Hari.
For in that state, this body is not a composite formed of material causes;
rather, it is the Self alone, the single reality, which has assumed a corporeal form through its own power. (63)
Through the yoga of worshiping Hari, one who has become capable and whose form is that of the Divine Image becomes liberated;
indeed, upon liberation, Māyā no longer exists there.
He is the savor of all desirable tastes, the locus of the bliss of all fragrances;
endowed with all sovereignty, he is the treasure-trove of eternal joy and fragrance. ||65||
Immersed in imperishable bliss, he rejoices together with Brahman;
possessing the nature of Brahman, he enjoys all desires established within the Self.
And having attained union with the Supreme Brahman, he becomes the possessor of all bliss;
for there, indeed, nothing is lacking for the liberated devotee of Śrī Hari.
And thus, through the yoga of worship, supreme liberation shall become the highest attainment for the yogi who remains steadfast in yogic effort if he worships Kṛṣṇa. (68)
Then he attains the supreme liberation described therein; of this there is no doubt, provided that he does not worship others such as Īśvara or Vairāja.
Just as lords attain worlds created by a Lord,
that liberation consisting of natural sovereignty brings about exhaustion in the Great Abode (Mahālaya).

Having attained supernatural powers (siddhis) and secured their stability, they finally reach either dissolution into their own remainder, or else they attain the state of another Lord, or the status of a deity. || 71 ||
They enjoy sovereignties equal to those beginning with the thousandfold manifestation;
that [other] liberation is inferior and leads to downfall, whereas this is superior to the high ground.
Or else, through the yoga of meditation upon the form of Hari,
their liberation consists in becoming absorbed into His very self-nature by means of the samādhis beginning with "non-differentiation" (abhinnādi).
Devoid of the relationship of master and servant and so forth, she arises;
she is always of the nature of concealment within the Supreme Lord and is certainly not separate from him. //74//
O King, by the power of meditation, they indeed become absorbed in that and identified with it;
as supreme lords in the Supreme Lord, they attain once more the state of non-becoming.
This supreme liberation is that state which belongs to the Supreme Lord;
herein, service in the form of a servant is by no means taught. (76)
Liberation through mere dharma, however, is inseparable from enjoyment;
it is indeed residence with a physical body in worlds such as heaven and the realm of truth. //77//
Having enjoyed the Dharma, there is again birth upon the earth and the acquisition of merit;
then again to heaven, then again to the earth—thus it is a continuous cycle. (78)
Even when such a person is born, if that nature consists of devotion to the Lord, or takes the form of a connection with Brahman, or is designated as being beyond the qualities (nirguṇya); ||79||
If it consists of service to Hari, or takes the form of sacrificial fees in a ritual,
or consists of gifts for the pleasure of Hari, then indeed there is eternal liberation.
Indeed, dharma performed for one's own sake alone does not lead to liberation;
when practiced with the intention of benefiting others, it gives rise to spiritual welfare. ||81||
If performed with the intention of offering to the Supreme Lord, it bestows liberation in the Imperishable;
O King, all actions are thus, whether they be auspicious or inauspicious. (82)
Born from a state of non-attachment and rendered tranquil through the spirit of dedication to Kṛṣṇa, all these [actions] are indeed accomplished by the remembrance of Kṛṣṇa and bestow liberation. 83.
Moreover, the master of a field, having prepared the field, uproots [weeds] and plows it;
he sows the seeds and ears of grain, and he also reaps and eats them. (84)
Having offered everything as an oblation to Brahman, one acts like the King of the Kurus, or like Janaka, or like the brahmin-sage Kūrmi. ||85||
All that becomes faultless and free from impurity;
the goldsmith produces the ornament through his honest livelihood. ||86||
If it is offered to Kṛṣṇa, even that craftsmanship becomes a bestower of liberation;
whatever is done for the sake of Hari is considered to be beyond the guṇas and a giver of liberation. (87)
Everything performed without Hari is fruitless or even a source of suffering;
yet the twice-born practice the Vedas while devoid of the constant remembrance of Hari. (88)
If that were so, then even a cowherd boy would experience the effects of practice and the devouring by dogs, even without the greatness of the jewel, upon the neck of a buffalo. (89)
One binds oneself with a mere trifle, considering it to have value while its true fruit remains unperceived—
even though one considers the Śālagrāma stone to be the eternal Viṣṇu.
The virtuous Vaiṣṇavas indeed protect and serve [Him] day and night;
for Viṣṇu, perceiving their service as fully realized, becomes manifest in that very form.
Having manifested, he appears as four-armed and within the range of vision;
yet if his state of being changes, he immediately vanishes from there. (92)
If that very Supreme Lord is bound by the noose of affection for his worshipper, then the Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa is indeed an incarnation of the Supreme Brahman. ||93||

Having descended and caused [the disciple] to descend, that which is without beginning, without end, and likewise without interior shines forth in the heart and before one; thereafter, it leads one to the Imperishable.

Therefore, O King, the applications of ritual action performed by means of the body, senses, and so forth, lead to bondage when done for one's own sake; however, when performed for the sake of Hari, they indeed grant liberation. 95.
The peaceful ones, through their connection with Kṛṣṇa, become divine, having Kṛṣṇa as the essence of their hearts;
sustained by Kṛṣṇa’s sovereignty, they become bestowers of liberation and givers of happiness. 9.6.
They bestow the divine world, they bestow divine bliss, and they bestow the Imperishable;
they grant the yoga of the Lord’s image and they are givers of knowledge. ||97||
They are destroyers of obstacles, eliminators of worldly cycles, warders off of delusion, preventers of suffering and faults, and bestowers of the world of Brahmā. || 98 ||
One should perform all services toward them, free from doubt, with the firm conviction that they are indeed specific manifestations of the Blessed One. 99.
Just as affection exists for one's wife, son, parents, and one's own kinsmen, it is directed toward self-interest and motivated by the sense of "I" and "mine. (2.254.100)
Likewise, one should always cultivate affection for the true guru, for that indeed bestows liberation;
whether it be dharma, the sacrifice of dharma, merit, charity, or any auspicious action [is likewise attained]. 101.
One should offer everything unto the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa;
then there is liberation—the great liberation consisting of union with Brahman.
She possesses the same power and form as Brahmā, she bestows the world of Brahmā,
she creates a form equal to the Supreme Brahman, and she is the most excellent of the excellent.
By means of this very powerful human body, union with the Lord is attained; nothing further remains to be achieved. 104.
The gopīs have attained supreme yoga; indeed, the beloveds of Brahman have likewise attained liberation through supreme yoga, and not by the desire for any other yoga.
Thus, O lord of the earth, apply yourself here to yoga directly before my eyes;
having assumed a supreme, divine, and eternal body, apply yourself to yoga.
O Rādhikā, having thus given this interval of instruction to the king, Lomaśa ceased his teaching, and the monarch rejoiced greatly.

Thus ends the two hundred and fifty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the King’s Inquiry into the Cause for Satisfying the Devas and Others, the Inquiry as to What Kind of Liberation is Attained through Discrimination, Devotion, Yoga, and the Duties toward Gurus, and the Answers Given by Lomaśa," in the *Lomaśagītā* within the second section, the *Tretā-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Rādhikā, thereafter Aśvapaṭṭala asked the sage Lomaśa about the nature of the power and the lack of power of yoga. || 1 ||
Aśvapāṭala said:
O Sage, what is the nature of the power of yoga? I wish to know its strength, by which one might be liberated, or by which a weak person might be held fast. (2)
Śrī Lomaśa said:
Purity, austerity, compassion, truthfulness, non-violence, abstention from theft, restraint of the breath, restraint of the senses, and meditation are indeed equal for yogins. (3)
For one whose practice is powerful, yoga becomes perfected;
for the weak, however, practice is itself weak, and by that, bondage [persists].
Though one may cut through desire, greed, delusion, affection, anger,
and passion by means of yoga, if one is weak, one becomes attached to those very things once again.
Just as fish with large bodies, having broken through the net,
enter the water again even if they are weak, so too do these six indeed enter once more.
And just as powerful wild animals, having burst through their snares,
go to another distant forest, even so do the best of yogis proceed to the Supreme.
Those who are devoted to the Supreme Self, being most powerful, surely cross over the ocean of illusion;
whereas those devoid of strength, such as the hares and other small creatures, indeed remain bound.
Having reached it, even yogins are likewise unable to depart;
indeed, the weak are not at all able to escape from the net to the outside.
And fish that are weak do not indeed escape by cutting through the net;
likewise, weak yogis do not escape by cutting through māyā. || 2.255.10 ||
Powerful birds, having torn through the net, go to the ends of the earth;
indeed, powerful yogis, having torn through illusion (māyā), proceed to the sky.
Just as a powerful fire consumes everything that comes before it,
so too do the most powerful yogis burn away illusion by their own splendor.
Just as a weak fire is extinguished even by pieces of wood, so too a strong person,
if lacking strength, surely meets with defeat when faced with the sixfold group.
Just as a weak current of a river, having dragged [something] along, carries it away in the water,
so too does the group of six, being powerless, drag one along and lead one into the realm of illusion.
Just as a powerful elephant both obstructs the current and moves through it, so too the most mighty yogi proceeds after having restrained the six [senses]. || 15 ||
Those who possess strength are liberated, while those who are weak fall into bondage;
just as the great sun rising at the time of universal dissolution dries up the world.
In the same way, the yogi who has arisen through the power of liberation dries up the defects;
by the power of yoga, the yogis enter the abode of the Lord.
Whether it be the abodes of the gods or the dwellings of Prajāpati, the power of yoga increases for one who is constantly habituated to practice. (18)
Then, having again pierced through illusion itself, they proceed to the Imperishable,
just as a skilled archer who has practiced well hits the target.
Just as one attains victory by piercing a target, so too does he attain the Imperishable;
having placed a vessel of oil upon his head, he becomes perfected through practice.
Just as an actor moves along a rope without stumbling and attains victory, so indeed does the yogi, through the power of the perfection of practice, proceed to the Imperishable.
Just as a helmsman reaches the far shore by means of his practice, so too does one who is disciplined reach the further shore of the world through the power of yoga. (22)
Just as a strong charioteer, having restrained the horses, proceeds with certainty, so too the best of yogis, being thus disciplined, goes to the imperishable and eternal state. 23.
The knower of yoga who indeed perceives the Supreme Lord within his own self truly cuts through the net of illusion and attains the supreme state. || 24 ||
Having moved through the wheels situated within the body and having repeatedly burned away the impurities, one indeed proceeds along the path of Brahman and departs by force.
And whenever he so desires to go to the Imperishable,
then, having abandoned his physical body, he goes to that abode independently.
Through the worship of one’s chosen deity, who is most powerful, one may obtain strength by means of practice,
self-yoga, self-restraint, and virility.
Through austerity, the yoga of meditation, and concentration, one may attain strength;
however, O King, only a few indeed reach the further shore in the great forest.
Since those who conquer the most powerful dwell indeed in the forest, they are unable to reach the further shore—the state that is full of doubt—without Nārāyaṇa. (29)
Indeed, even the most powerful are carried away by enemies who are even more powerful,
who dwell in the abode of divine sovereignty, wonder, and supernatural powers.
When the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa appears before him,
he proceeds forward and leads [the devotee] away, having conquered even the most powerful beings.
O King, considering the qualities within the body, never become bound; [realize] your own supreme state, which is divine, eternal, and the highest liberation.
The body, the abode of variegated impurities, must be scrutinized with discernment.
Understand from me the ten states of the *sattva* within it; I shall describe them. (33)
Joy, delight, exhilaration, radiance, the performance of meritorious deeds, contentment, straightforwardness, faith, renunciation, and sovereignty as well. (34)
Likewise, learn from me the ninefold nature of passion (rajas); I shall describe them:
faith in the scriptures, lack of miserliness, and likewise the pursuit of dualities. (35)
Lust, hatred, intoxication, pride, dispute, and harshness, as well as shadow and darkness—understand these to be my absence; I shall declare them to you.
Tamas-ness, delusion, a smoky state, loss of intellect, sleep, negligence, laziness, and destruction—such are its characteristics. (37)
Understand from me that the principle of intellect (buddhitattva) possesses seven states; I shall declare them to you:
egoism (ahantā), possessiveness (mamatā), pride (māna), long-standing desire (dairghya), hope (āśā), and self-worship (svapūjyatā). ||38||
I shall tell you of those six states of the mind, beginning with "lordship":
restlessness, impetuosity, doubt, and independence; (3.9)
Furthermore, you have always considered even affection to be untrustworthy in your mind;
understand now my fivefold nature, which I shall describe to you.
Non-satisfaction, attachment, indifference, observation, and movement—understand these four states of the element of earth; I shall describe them to you. (41)
The basis, bondage, destruction, and production—these three states, along with the reality of the sheath, constitute the six sheaths that reside within the body. ||42||
Your hair, blood, flesh, marrow, bones, and sinews—
these states consist of moisture, impurity, and likewise, the quality of being an object of enjoyment.
Prāṇa indeed possesses a dual nature; understand from me those two states:
life and wandering. Thus have the principles been explained to you. (44)
O King, through the discernment of reality, those states of being which take the form of defects are indeed obstacles on the path to the liberation of the self, if they are such for you. (45)
Having discerned those [states] as being of one essence—the state of bliss that is his own self—one should offer them with devotion to the Supreme Lord; for him, liberation stands certain. 46.
Or else, having observed all entities, one should cause the cessation of the desire to see them—namely, all human objects as well as the objects of the piśācas. (47)
He also [saw] the realms of the yakṣas and likewise the realms of the nāgas,
the realms of the gandharvas and likewise the realms of the ancestors.
He likewise beheld the realms of the animals, the realms of the Maruts,
the realms of the birds, and the realms of the royal sages.
He likewise beheld the realms of the Brahman-sages, as well as the realms of the Asuras,
the realms of the Viśvedevas, and the realms of the Yogins.

Having fully understood the objects of the senses—those pertaining to Prajāpati, those pertaining to Īśvara, those pertaining to Brahmā, and those born from millions of Īśvaras—and having experienced pleasure and pain, [one attains liberation]. ||51||
Having observed the virtues and faults and thereby attained peace, one should thereafter establish oneself in liberation through the self and through discernment.
Endowed with both knowledge and discernment, and himself cultivated by skillful means, he attains divine liberation, the state that is eternal bliss and imperishable. ||53||
O King, one should contract the vital breath along with the six sheaths within the elements;
likewise, the elements joined with their constituent parts, the sense organs, and the mind.

One possessed of discrimination should dissolve that which is joined with egoism and the like within the intellect (buddhi), and then offer the intellect into one's own true nature, known as the Self (ātman). //55//
One should unite the self, which is of the nature of Brahman, with Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa within the heart; by that means, one shall go to that imperishable abode (akṣaradhāma) which is liberation. ||56||
Having known that the gods, the lords of creatures, the seers, the seven seers, and even the royal and celestial seers are always swallowed by the jaws of Time; (57)
Having recognized that the Brahman-sages and Lord-sages are subject to the end brought about by time,
one who walks the path leading to liberation should certainly not practice meditation there.
Having understood the destiny of sinners enveloped in the world of Yama,
and having observed their births in various wombs and their states as hungry ghosts (pretas), [he spoke].
Having truly understood the miseries of the womb and the loathsome conditions of living beings,
as well as the most terrible calamities and the falling of stars and constellations.
And seeing the miserable and sudden separation of couples, as well as the pitiless devouring of living beings by one another; 61.
Having understood the wickedness of sense objects, that there is no life for those whose vitality has departed, and that the destinies of sinners are likewise dreadful and full of suffering; ||62||
Having observed the suffering of animals and their day-by-day depletion of life-span, having seen the decay of embodied beings, and having beheld the misery of death; ||63||
Having thoroughly understood the defects of the body as well as its nature as a prison of hell,
one should cast off the body through the aperture of Brahma and proceed to the supreme state.
One should take refuge in the deity of breath (prāṇadeva), and after that, the deity of wind (vāyudeva);
then also the deity of space (vyomadeva), and after that, the ray of the sun (sūryaraśmi). ||65||
Then also Cāndraraśmi, and after that Puṇyaraśmi;
then also Satyaraśmi, and after that Sattvaraśmi. ||66||
Then one should likewise cultivate the light of Īśvara, thereafter the light of Brahmā, and then the light of Mukta; after that, one should realize the Supreme Brahman.
Having attained the Supreme Self, he becomes stainless, with that as his abode;
having reached the supreme immortality, he does not return again.
O King, that is the supreme goal for the virtuous, for yogis as well, and for the Sāttvata devotees who perform all actions for the sake of Hari. (69)
In that state, there is indeed knowledge and omniscience, gathered from the multitude of sovereign powers;
there is satisfaction that transcends all else, and even the measure of bliss is overflowing.
For omniscience is considered to belong to one who is unattached and forever free from dualities;
therefore, those who are eternally contented are endowed with the state of omniscience. (7.1)
They are eternally blissful, eternally peaceful, eternally satisfied, and free from desire;
though they are indeed all-seeing, they do not perceive the cycle of worldly existence.
Even those who perceive saṃsāra are devoid of various states of being;
they are empty of the transformations of existence and have attained the perfections of sensory withdrawal and the other [aṅgas]. ||73||

Capable of perceiving both the graspable and the ungraspable, they are free from the defects of creation; they do not at all bind themselves to the states produced by inferior creation within their own knowledge. //74//
Aśvapāṭala said:
O learned one, what is that imperishable abode from which one does not return again?
And what is the perishable, distinct from that, from which one returns again? (75)
Śrī Lomaśa said:
O King, that is the imperishable, auspicious abode of the Supreme Lord, of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, who descends in supreme incarnations. (76)
This belongs to the Supreme Brahman himself, to that Lord Nārāyaṇa, who is designated as Puruṣottama and who transcends the Imperishable (akṣara), eternal. ||77||
It is auspicious, secure, brought forth by longing, endowed with all perfections, the station of the Lord of all lords, the abode of liberation, and higher than the highest. (78)
That which does not perish at any time in the past,
nor is ever seized by the future— that is the imperishable abode of Brahman.
And even above Goloka and Vaikuṇṭha is the infinite and infallible realm,
where indeed there are endless abodes created by the incarnations.
Indeed, there exist manifestations of Nārāyaṇa created by Nārāyaṇa himself, wherein millions of incarnations dwell within their abodes. ||8 1 ||
Wherein those shine forth, that is the imperishable, all-pervading abode;
it is the world of Brahman, the space of consciousness, the treasury of the realms of unbroken light. ||82||
Wherein the Lord shines as the imperishable Brahman in embodied form—that is the supreme abode of the Imperishable, dearer even than Hari himself. ||83||
There indeed exists the supreme abode where the throne of the Supreme Brahman is eternally situated;
it is the most excellent of all, a beautiful seat upon which an elephant is seated.
Indeed, all those who are dear to Brahmā serve there as maidservants of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the givers of liberation. ||85||
Indeed, other than Mukta, there dwell the infinite powers and infinite perfections of Hari’s form, as well as the Siddhas of infinite number and the Sādhya deities. (86)
Those who are beginningless and liberated dwell in that supreme abode;
however, those who are eternally liberated (ādimukta) dwell forever in the imperishable abode.

This is known as the Imperishable (Akṣara); it is that abode which is beyond Māyā, transcending the qualities (guṇas), consisting of great bliss, and filled with eternal bliss and other such attributes. ||88||
By the mere pleasure of a single hair-pore,
all other abodes indeed become filled with the bliss of the nectar of bliss.
And other worlds called the realms of Īśvara, filled with their respective pleasures,
as well as all types of creations, were then gladdened by that bliss.
Creations consisting of illusion are indeed subject to decay;
likewise, the three qualities, darkness (tamas), illusion (māyā), and the unmanifest (avyakta) are established within the Puruṣa.
The principle of Mahat indeed becomes manifest as the ego (ahaṃkāra), as well as knowledge and ignorance, merit and demerit, and likewise the two others: injunction and prohibition. (92)
Dharma, knowledge, dispassion, and sovereignty are established in the Manifest;
likewise, all that is contrary to them is also established in the Manifest. (93)
Sound, touch, taste, form, and smell are indeed the subtle elements (bhūtasūkṣma);
and the mind, as well as the senses for the purpose of perception—namely, the ear, skin, eye, and tongue.
The nose, and likewise the others—speech, hands, feet, the anus, and the generative organ—as well as space, air, and fire, exist for the purpose of action. (95)
Beyond that, others are water-bodied, and further still, others possess bodies composed of the six sheaths;
all of this dissolves day and night, and therefore it is called "the perishable" (kṣara). ||96||
In all embodied beings, there are indeed twenty-four levels;
however, they may be deficient, for the *kṣarikās* are missing, and therefore it is called *kṣara*.
Whatever possesses form is entirely subject to the nature of decay,
whether it be in water, on earth, in space, in air, in fire, or in that which is beyond them.

Whether on a field of merit, in a supreme place of accomplishment, or even among a multitude of sentient beings, this entire substratum of the flux flows away, characterized by manifest perception. (99)

The imperishable (akṣara) always abides within the perishable (kṣara), and the Self (ātman) is also called imperishable; he who has his station in that imperishable Self is the Supreme Lord (Parameśvara).
That very Hari dwells within the heart in all forms;
O King, worship that Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, who is accompanied by Ramā. 101.

[He praised] the Lord of the creation of white, red, and black, the Lord born from the lotus, the one who has gone to the further shore, the one dwelling within, the son of Kambharā, the beloved Master.
O King, [worship] the Lord beloved of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of Kuṅkumavāpikā,
the child Gopāla, the favorite of Lomaśa, and the Lord of Patiśvara.
[He worshipped] the Sun-god of the Aśvapaṭṭasara field, the beloved husband of Brahmāṇī,
Bālakṛṣṇa, the Lord of the Imperishable, the Sovereign who dwells within all as the inner controller.
At the beginning of creation, he beheld this earth, Surāṣṭrikā,
who was devoted to him— the son of Mahāviṣṇu and the sole child of the illustrious Mahālakṣmī.
Then he saw Him who possesses manifold forms and assumes many incarnations;
then that Kṛṣṇa, the son of Dharma, the son of Bhakti, and Hari.
Nara and Nārāyaṇa as well, who were devoted to the conduct of Brahman;
likewise, the Master, the Renouncer, the Omniscient One, and the Teacher.
The teacher, the true guru, the lord of the celestial sphere, the sovereign of the noble mandala,
who observes the vow of celibacy, who lives with his own innate nature, the all-seeing, and the infallible one.
"O King, resort to the Supreme; go to liberation through a mere drop of my grace.
Thus did the sage speak to King Aśvapāṭala, O Rādhikā.
Having thus instructed him, he ceased, remembering the beloved of Śrī Kṛṣṇa;
the king too, from the mass of his bliss, was filled with internal joy.
Having attained an exceeding relish for the nectar of the discourse on the Supreme Brahman,
he, like one thirsty and longing for more, questioned Lomaśa once again.

Thus ends the two hundred and fifty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the King’s Inquiry Regarding the Strength and Weakness of Yoga, the Question Concerning the Worlds of the Perishable and the Imperishable, and the Answers Given by Lomaśa," in the *Lomaśagītā* within the second section, the *Tretā-santāna*, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Rādhikā, I shall now relate in brief that which the king then asked of Lomaśa; understand it from my heart. (1)
Aśvapāṭala said:
This cycle of existence is indeed perishable, while the conscious self therein is imperishable.
Why does he not abandon this perishable [existence] and go to that which is imperishable? || 2 ||
Lomaśa said:
In the womb, one who is asleep is cooked by the power of karma like a ripe grain;
as if having attained identity with the impressions of the elements, he is roasted.
Having encountered perishable phenomena and being overwhelmed by a state of ignorance,
the perishable self falls into the delusion that "this is I," and from that it is born again.
I am a foolish man or woman, expanded by external sounds; I am drowsy with the delusion of perceiving objects as white, red, or black.

Having fallen into confused conceptualization, he has been rendered dull by association with worldly crowds; though emaciated or stout, miserable or happy, he is awakened to the notions of "mine" and "I."
Bound by the ropes of the noose of karma and the life-span, and rendered powerless; knotted within the seam of the chest-casket of the vital breaths, it remains indestructible.
Sprinkled with the water of the heat of illusion and made firm,
he was smeared with the juices of the six sheaths and took his seat right there.
And once smeared with the great ointment, one is unable to go out;
there itself, one remains in a state that is either tāmasa, rājasa, or sāttvika.
Having reached the flow, the ripened essence, and the practiced taste, it then attains nourishment through those various excellent essences brought by the senses. (2.256.10)
He nourishes himself with pleasures and joys, runs about for their sake, and strives again and again to know and to obtain them. (11)
Driven by the latent impressions of that momentum, the deluded one—perishable and consisting of perishable nature—is intent on consuming, abandoning, renewing, and accumulating again and again. (12)
Indistinguishable and not separate, he exists as one who has been dragged by his hair;
being devoted to the attributes of the body, he is delighted by the pleasure of the body. || 13 ||
Furthermore, he indeed performs merit for the sake of attaining a divine body and so forth;
thus, by means of this cycle, one goes from body to action, and from that, to a new form.
Again there is action, again a body; thus, in this pit of transience, the ignorant self falls repeatedly and repeatedly desires delight. (15)
For one who acts in this manner, liberation from transmigration will never occur;
on the contrary, delusion increases, as do bondage and the cycle of worldly existence.
Following from delusion to further delusion, and seeing ever-new [objects] again and again, one strives to obtain and enjoy them, thereby binding karma consisting of that very [delusion]. (17)
Through its actions, it undergoes thousands of bodies—from among animals, the classes of gods, humans, and birds. (18)
He is born again and again among the Daityas, Dānavas, and Rākṣasas;
though free from dualities, he encounters pairs of opposites within those very same wombs.
It churns everything in every way in order to obtain the enjoyments of the gods, the enjoyments of the Sādhyas, the unsurpassed enjoyments of the Siddhas, and likewise the enjoyments of the lords.
In sickness, in enjoyment, in movement, in agitation, in decay, in emaciation, and in injury, the embodied self—though distinct from delusion—yet conceives the notion "this is mine. (21)
Indeed, while his body is being torn apart, he lies down— his kingdom divided—
upon a bed, a ball, in some hole, in a state of duality, or in the mud.
In a brick, in the sky, in a pit, in a cave, on the earth; in a thorn, in ashes, in a dried-up place, in water, in fruit, in wind, and in fire. (23)
He gave beautiful garments, woolen blankets, mats made of grass, silken cloths, those made of kārḍamaya fibers, and skins. || 24 ||
Whatever womb one may be born from, one shall take possession of that very thing—whether it be various foods, fragrances, or even things devoid of fragrance. (25)
Due to delusion, he considers his own excrement and phlegm to be food;
for the sake of spiritual perfection, he undergoes various difficult vows and ascetic practices. (26)
And it also brings about those desired things which the person pursues in the morning:
various gains that are pleasing to the heart, consisting of one's own form and qualities. (27)
And it runs after the objects of enjoyment, thinking "these are to be enjoyed by me," and being constantly enveloped by the sense of "mine-ness," it revolves right there. (28)
Throughout thousands of millions of creations, in the three worlds, one experiences the fruit of that [action] according to one's karma within bodies that end in death. (29)
Even one devoid of food becomes possessed of food;
even one without sense organs perceives himself as having sense organs and being afflicted with wounds. (2.256.30)

The signless one regards the possessor of signs; the deathless one regards that which is subject to death and beset by the fear of death; the sorrowless one regards the sorrowful; and the imperishable one regards the perishable.
Thus, through the conceit of being perishable, he does not at all emerge from the perishable.
O King, for this state of ignorance, no end exists anywhere.
Apart from the secret instructions of the guru, the study of the scriptures, association with the virtuous, the attainment of holy discourse, and service to the saintly devotees of Hari; ||33||
It is the favor of Hari residing in the heart, the following of the liberated ones, the propitiation of Hari, and the meditation upon that Supreme Self. (34)
For these very means are divine and bestow divinity;
by them the self is joined with the self, and therein the supreme self is joined. ||35||
Then he goes to the further shore, reaching the Lord who abides beyond the Imperishable;
yet this occurs only so long as he does not take refuge in Hari and does not practice the company of the virtuous.
One should not perform ritual worship nor carry out formal meditation; rather, one should practice devotion through service to the manifest Lord Hari, to the guru, and likewise to the virtuous.
As long as he does not do so, his cycle of existence will certainly not dissolve;
he passes through thousands of millions of creations that end in a fall.
By means of his own splendor, he traverses thousands of abodes that end in death;
through the service of illusion and its products, he becomes one characterized by the three qualities and full of conceit. ||39||
Through the application of the connection with Māyā, one becomes composed of the qualities of Māyā;
this occurs because of the mutual attachment for the sake of pleasure and through the reliance upon each other's qualities. (2.256.40)
During the fertile season, he repeatedly assumes a illusory form through his dependence on the womb;
for one who is thus born, how could there be the dharma of liberation? (41)

Therefore, having cut and pierced the knot known as latent impressions (vāsanā), one should proceed after bringing about the destruction of craving through austerity alone or else through knowledge. 42.
Having distinguished [the Self] through discernment and realized the Self as free from illusion, one should proceed by the path of the light of knowledge and upon the way of truth. 43.
Then the qualities (guṇas) are indeed separated from the qualityless conscious self (cidātman).
From the very moment of conception, through merit, one perceives that which is distinct from the qualities. ||44||
Just like Prahlāda, as well as Madālasā and Bālā,
or else by the grace of Śrī Hari, divine vision is manifested.

Through the discrimination between the self and the non-self, and by the abandonment of the qualities (guṇas), the disciplined soul perceives its own true nature, as well as the Supreme Hari, who is higher than the highest. 46.
One-pointedness is the power therein, and the power of meditative concentration (dhyāna) is the cause;
liberated from all attachments, one remains steadfast during the Brahma-muhūrta. ||47||
One should hold the mind upon Kṛṣṇa within the heart during the final watch of the night, having made the function of the intellect steady, remaining unshakable and motionless. (48)
When he perceives Hari dwelling within, then he becomes one who is disciplined (yukta);
for one who is disciplined, there is a constant manifestation centered upon the Supreme Lord. 49.
It hears nothing else, nor smells, nor tastes, nor sees; it does not touch, grasp, move, speak, or urinate. (2.256.50)
He does not perceive, nor does he form mental constructs; he does not think, nor does he understand; at that time, the self rejoices within the supreme Self. 51.
The sun shines in the sky like a lamp in a windless place;
that [Self] the sages perceive, who are masters born of Brahman. 52.
Then one should behold that Supreme, the Supreme Self, with the vision of the Self;
the vision of the Self is considered true knowledge (vidyā), while mental vision is ignorance (avidyā). ||53||
Ignorance (avidyā) is characterized by creation and destruction, whereas knowledge (vidyā) is indeed eternal liberation;
ignorance produces the unmanifest, while knowledge attains the Self.
Through ignorance one goes to death; through knowledge one attains immortality.
Upon the attainment of knowledge, indeed, there arises in the self a discernment that has many branches.
"O King, listen as I tell you how one who has perfected the self is born;
what indeed have I accomplished in all this time through my illusory power? (56)
Just as a net is followed here by an ignorant fish, the fish, whose life is dependent upon water, knows nothing other than water. (57)
Likewise, obscured by delusion, I did not recognize anyone else;
fie, fie upon my following after delusion, and upon this confusion regarding my own conduct! (58)
Having followed after delusion, I did not know the Supreme Lord;
covered by Māyā and deceived, I remained ignorant of the Paramātman. (59)
"Controlled by illusion, I did not realize this for so long;
I have been deceived by it, for I did not attain the path to liberation. (2.256.60)
This is not her fault, nor is it my fault,
that I dwelt here attached, greedy, and possessed by the latent tendencies of sense-objects.
Though I am formless and incorporeal, I became possessed of form and body through her;
thus, I was overcome and deceived by that worldly sense of "mine-ness."
Devoid of the sense of "mine" yet possessed of the notion of "mine," what have I done by casting myself into hell that I have obtained liberation? (63)
"I have no further need for this courtesan, who, having multiplied herself in many forms, seeks to unite with me through deception. (64)
Now I am awakened by the grace of the true Guru, Hari; having departed from this [state], I today take refuge in the Supreme Lord, the Guru, the Master. (65)
"I shall attain equality with the Lord, not through this deceitful woman;
I shall attain safety through Kṛṣṇa and go to the supreme state. (66)
Having thus reached this conclusion regarding solitude by means of his own self,
one who follows the dharma of association with Hari attains equality with Hari through that very association.
O King, this is called the Supreme Brahman from which one does not return again; it is that by which supreme knowledge, which bestows final liberation, is attained. 68.
By whom the perishable and the imperishable are known, for him no fear exists;
and for one who performs what is beneficial here, there is indeed no fear whatsoever.
For him, fear never arises in the next world;
indeed, for a man who takes refuge in the Dharma that is beneficial to the virtuous, there is truly no fear.
For those who desire delicious tastes and sensual pleasures, freedom from craving is always fearless;
for one who cultivates familiarity with knowledge and the Dharma, there is no fear anywhere. (7.1)
For one who constantly gives much, who always serves the virtuous,
and who is habituated to honoring the good, there shall never be any fear whatsoever.
For one who bestows justice upon the worthy, whose heart is pure, who possesses true knowledge, who is dispassionate and free from attachment, fear shall never arise at any time.
For one who has completely eradicated all faults, who serves all living beings,
and whose nature is to assist others, there shall be no fear whatsoever.
Fear never comes to an embodied being who is patient, enduring, free from anger, upright, and a doer of good. (75)

For one who possesses a virtuous basis, who is a giver, who practices self-restraint, who is endowed with compassion, and who maintains a sense of honor in all circumstances, fear shall never arise at any time. //76//
For one who is self-controlled, tranquil, wise, acting with devotion,
ascetic, and a servant, fear indeed never arises.
For one who is liberated from merit and demerit, who has destroyed all doubts, and who is freed from birth and death, the supreme good is indeed certain. //78//
For one who is liberated from merit and sin, who is a yogi graced by Brahman,
and who transcends the three bodies, the supreme good is indeed certain.
He who is bound within the principle of primordial nature (*mūlaprakṛti*), within the sixteen transformations (*vikāra*), and even within both nature and its modifications, is liberated. (2.256.80)
He who knows the other body as distinct from his own self is not defiled;
he should know the gnat as one thing and the udumbara fruit as another. (8.1)
By means of the application of fresh udumbara fruit, a mosquito becomes smeared there;
one should know the fish to be one thing, and likewise the water to be another.
And a fish is not defiled there by contact with water;
fire is one thing and the hearth another, for the fire is not defiled by the hearth. || 83 ||
The water is one thing and the lotus another; the lotus is not defiled by the waters.
Although they dwell together, their abode is indeed distinct from one another.
Thus, he who perceives this state of separateness truly sees.
Thus, for one who sees in this way, there is no bondage when the substratum is destroyed.
If, through the flood of various lives, a further life should meet him, then, having attained that life, he rejoices there in happiness. || 85–86 ||

The Supreme Self is indeed life, bestowing the nectar of all bliss; having attained that refuge, there is neither fear nor death nor destruction. It is the supreme good, the Supreme Brahman, supreme liberation, and the highest state.
And here, one who is disciplined and liberated eternally experiences a world free from old age and death, an ocean of imperishable bliss and happiness within one's own self;
ever-gracious, with a satisfied soul, and tranquil like one in a pleasant sleep. (88–89)
Just as a rock does not move at all because of clouds, so too is he of such a nature;
he would not tremble even at the making of sounds, roars, songs, and instrumental music. Like an actor, he proceeds while holding a vessel of oil in his hand by means of a rope.
Indeed, with his self restrained even while using a cooking pot, he is fearless and free from trembling;
not even a single drop of oil leaks from his vessel, and when joined with that [skill], he reaches the northern limit and attains victory. || 91-92 ||
"Such a one, united with Brahman, beholds Brahman here;
having attained the Supreme Brahman, being liberated, he shall obtain final liberation.
O Rādhikā, having thus instructed the king, Lomaśa—
The king attained peace and again asked about the path of that [liberation]:
how those great-souled ones, seeking the supreme good, become liberated and depart by means of which upward-ascents; these he asked Lomī.

Thus ends the two hundred and fifty-sixth chapter, titled "The Question of How the Self’s Release from the Perishable and Its Journey to the Imperishable Occur, and the Description of That Release and That Journey," in the *Lomaśagītā* within the second section, the *Tretā-santāna*, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
When the pure self, having become distinct from the body, indeed departs...
"O Rādha, how does he thus depart? the king asked Lomaśa.
Aśvapāṭala said: "O Sage, what is the nature of his departure, how does it occur, and why does he go forth?"
O Lord, tell me how the self departs from the body. || 2 ||
Śrī Lomaśa said: In whatever manner one departs from this place— whether by the power of yoga and austerity, or by the power of devotion, or even by the power of merit— (3)
Just as by the power of evil, and also by the power of karma,
and likewise by the power of illusion, and even by the power of latent predispositions (vāsanā).
He goes to the worlds of the various deities residing in those respective places; for instance, if he departs by way of his feet, he indeed goes to the abode of Viṣṇu.
If he departs by means of his two calves, he goes to the abode of the Vasus;
if he departs by means of his two thighs, he goes to Prajāpati;
and if he departs by means of his anus, he attains the station of Mitra.
Departing through the linga and the yoni, he reaches Satyaloka;
departing by way of the jaghana, he attains the abode of Meru.
If it indeed departs from the navel, one attains the heaven of the gods;
if it goes out through the two sides, one reaches the worlds of the Maruts.
If he departs by means of his two arms, he shall attain the world of Indra;
if he proceeds by means of his chest, he shall attain the world of Rudra. || 9 ||
If he goes with his neck, he would attain the world of men;
if he goes with his mouth, he would attain the Viśvedevas. || 2.257.10 ||
If he departs through the ear, he shall become a guardian of the quarters;
if he goes out through the nose, he shall attain the world of Vāyu. || 11 ||
By departing through the two eyes, he goes to the world of the Sun or the abode of the Moon;
and by departing through the two cheeks, he proceeds to the world of Fire.
By departing through his eyebrows, one attains the world of the Aśvins;
but by departing through the forehead, one's destination becomes the world of the ancestors.
If [the breath] exits through the crown of the head, one goes to the eternal world of Brahmā;
if it departs from the [other] wheels, it likewise proceeds by taking recourse to the path of the Suṣumṇā. || 14 ||
Then, O lord of men, he indeed proceeds to the worlds of those respective deities;
this departure has been described according to the power of their stations. 15.
Moreover, by the power of worship, the departure [from the body] is indeed distinguished;
and by the power of sin and merit, the journey is indeed differentiated. || 16 ||
Through the worship of Śambhu, one goes to Kailāsa, which is adorned by his attendants;
through the worship of Viṣṇu, one goes to Śvetadvīpa, the ocean of milk.
Through devotion to Nara-Nārāyaṇa, one goes to the Lord of Badarī;
through devotion to the Sūrya-Gāyatrī, one goes to the solar orb.
Through the practice of worshiping sacrifices and the like, one who possesses the merit of such rites goes to heaven;
indeed, by the worship of the ancestors, a human being goes to the world of the ancestors.
Through celibacy one reaches the world of the Siddhas, and through the practice of austerity, the world of Truth (Satyaloka);
but by means of the Puruṣa-sūkta, one goes to the abode of Vairāja.
By the worship of Mahāviṣṇu, a human being goes to Vaikuṇṭha;
by the worship of Nārāyaṇa, one attains Mahāvaikuṇṭha.
"Indeed, by the worship of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa, one attains Goloka; and by the worship of Māyā, one attains the worlds of Māyā, such as Āvaraṇa and the rest."
Through the meditation on the Bhūman, a human being attains the unmanifest;
and through the meditation on Vāsudeva, one goes to the immortal abode. ||23||
By worshiping the incarnations beginning with Kapila, one goes to their respective abodes;
by the worship of the Imperishable (Akṣara), one attains the eternal, imperishable realm.
Through the worship of the Supreme Brahman, one attains the supreme abode;
through non-worship and by means of ritual acts, one becomes subject to birth within various wombs.
Through actions characterized by tamas, one becomes a Daitya, a Dānava, or a Rākṣasa;
such a person enters the womb of an animal or even takes birth among immobile beings.

Through royal deeds one goes to a kingdom, and even to the status of a merchant prince; through [deeds of] the Vasus, one reaches the worlds of the Gandharvas, and through those of the world-protectors, the celestial abodes. (27)
Through sattvic qualities, O Brahmin, one is born as a virtuous man, a holy deity, or a saint;
through sinful acts, one is born as a bird, an animal, an insect, or even a beast.
Through meritorious deeds, one is born as a king, a god, a teacher, a chaste woman, or one devoted to vows.
But those who owe debts are reborn as draft animals, such as stallions and the like. || 29 ||
And donors are born [again], adorned with seats of honor;
thus indeed they proceed with broken carts to a broken mansion.
And even while remaining in the householder stage of life, those endowed with the fire of knowledge burn away all karmas and illuminate the Self within the self.
Just as stainless renunciants attain the supreme Brahman, so too those who have not formally renounced are truly renunciants when they have taken refuge in the renunciation of knowledge. ||3.2||
Aśvapāṭala said:
"O Teacher, how is it that those who have not renounced are called 'renouncers'? And how do those established in the householder stage attain that supreme goal? (3.3)
Śrī Lomaśa said:
O King, listen here to this most wonderful story concerning the queen Kuśalā and the king of Ānarta, which took place in ancient times.
In Saurāṣṭra, there was indeed a king of Ānarta who was a devotee of Kṛṣṇa;
by him this land of Surāṣṭra was settled after he had brought people from the presence of Kṛṣṇa.
This king was a devotee of Viṣṇu, faithful to his wife and a follower of the twice-born;
indeed, he attained authentic knowledge from the brāhmaṇa Patnīvrata.
And he, devoted to knowledge, dwelt in the assembly of the virtuous, having severed the bond of "I" and "mine" by means of the science of wisdom. (37)
He constantly abides in yoga, in meditative absorption upon the Supreme Lord;
and for the virtuous and the great seers, there arise discourses on knowledge.
O King, because he was always present in the assembly at Camatkārapura in the evening,
the fame of that yogi of Ānarta spread to the ends of the quarters.
Having heard that, the virtuous and skillful Yoginī, endowed with spiritual powers,
the supreme goddess residing in the sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpikā, [spoke].
Until she is perfected in the entire collection of yogic arts, she enters the bodies of others;
assuming desired forms, she is a wise one, a treasure-trove of the meaning of the knowledge of reality. ||41||

The aged Vaiṣṇavī ascetic, having discarded the attributes of the body, was profound and composed of the attributes of the Self; she was a virtuous woman, invincible by the attributes of the elements. 42.
Existing in the state of Brahman with unperceivable marks, she is Nārāyaṇī;
having attained the supreme state in Kṛṣṇa, she abides in the renunciation of all things.
Under whose control the entire world stands, such as Lakṣmī is;
she who is the Goddess appearing in various incarnations, Satī, and the Śiva-Śakti herself. || 44 ||
That virtuous woman, known as Kuśalā, having assumed a beautiful form of exquisite youth, went to Camatkārapura;
she arrived before King Ānarta, who was seated in his assembly hall surrounded by virtuous men.
