By yogins, by renunciants, and also by great seers who are knowers of the Vedas. || 46 ||
Seeing her supreme delicacy and her fresh youth, everyone was filled with wonder, thinking, "Who is she? To whom does she belong? And from where has she come here?
The king also offered a welcome and gave her a seat in the assembly.
And being honored with marks of respect, she was a yoginī who was virtuous. ||48||
Desiring to question the king, she bound him with yogic bonds;
for this king is renowned in the *Mokṣadharma* and is celebrated everywhere. (49)
"Let me see how this liberated King Sāttvata abides.
She immediately entered the *buddhisattva* of Ānarta by means of her own intellect. (2.257.50)
Restraining the rays from his two eyes with [his own] rays, he entered the fluctuations of the intellect through the arrows of knowledge in order to conquer them. ||5.1||
A dispute arises in the heart of two practitioners of yoga within their own intellects;
when one of them is truly a yogi, the other suffers defeat. (52)
"An unyoked man does not attain victory, nor is he even like a king.
Having reflected thus, she brought that king under her control through her perfected intellect. (53)
The king, perceiving her intention, thought, "I shall make this yoginī mute," and with this thought,
the virtuous woman seized his mind through the powerful means of yoga.
Having honored her who had entered the king's body— she whose form was intellect—
and having established her within his subtle body (liṅgadeha), the king remained together with her.
At that time, those two yogis, unattached to their gross bodies, remained within their subtle bodies (liṅgadeha) and engaged in a mutual debate for the sake of self-conquest.
Ānarta said: "O you whose truth is yoga, where was this practice performed, and where will you go?
Whose are you, from where do you come, who are you, and how indeed have you arrived? (57)
I, the king, am also freed from those marks and have established myself in yoga;
therefore, O yoginī worthy of honor, I desire to know you quickly. (58)
Listen to me: from my preceptor, who was known as Patnīvrata, I specifically obtained extensive knowledge of yoga and liberation. ||59||
Having attained stability in these three— knowledge of reality, the supernatural powers of yoga, and the method of sovereignty— which bestow liberation, I move about free from passion.

The absence of passion is the cause of liberation, and it is brought about by knowledge; through knowledge and the resulting state of passionlessness, the accomplishment of liberation has been achieved by me. (6.1)
Free from duality and unattached, I abide with an unwavering intellect;
like a parched field devoid of water, yet containing seeds that have sprouted.
The cause does not exist at all; thus have I become parched.
I do not take delight in sweets, nor do I feel distress at cruel things.
One might worship with sandalwood on the right, or pierce with a weapon on the left.
"O virtuous lady, someone there has told me that my equality with him exists in truth."
I am happy, having accomplished all my goals; to me, iron and gold are equal.
Though I dwell in the state of kingship, I remain unattached through association with the virtuous.
Furthermore, the threefold cause for liberation exists: knowledge born of discernment, as well as [the other two].
Furthermore, there is either the renunciation of actions or devotion to the Supreme Self. ||66||
I have received from my guru the Trika system, which, when integrated, leads to liberation;
and with discernment, I perform every action imbued with devotion.
Just as renunciants are supreme because they have indeed resorted to actionlessness (naiṣkarmya),
so too [are those who are free] from restraint, observance, desire, hatred, and possessiveness.
I attained freedom from action (naiṣkarmya) while engaged in pride, hypocrisy, passion, and affection;
if those [others] were destined for liberation, why am I not likewise on that path? (6.9)
If liberation were to arise in every way for those dwelling in a leaf-hut,
then how could liberation not be within my grasp while I dwell in this magnificent palace?
Whatever object a person has need of, that very thing they grasp:
one takes a staff and a garland, another an umbrella and a fly-whisk. (7.1)
Having perceived the defects in the householder's life and having gone to the stage of renunciation,
the ascetic abandons the primary duties of the former state and adopts the subsequent ones as they are appropriate.
Having attained union through the cessation of attachment, he would be liberated, for he is no longer bound;
indeed, their sovereignty over my kingdom is equal to that in the forest.
If indeed the mendicant may be liberated, tell me, how can I not be liberated?
For food, clothing, drink, sleep, and the accumulation of desired things [are common to both]. (74)
If my sovereignty is indeed equal to that of a monk in any respect, then if they are partakers of liberation, mine too must surely be liberation. (75)
If you truly possess a share in bondage, then you are equal to householders;
if liberation comes through knowledge alone, then the wearing of saffron robes is in vain. (76)
The abandonment of clothing is in vain; the wearing of matted hair is in vain;
the renunciation of gold and garments is in vain; and the wearing of fire as a garment is in vain. ||77||
The abandonment of a mouthful of cooked food is useless, and therefore begging is useless as well;
for if knowledge—which is indeed the cause of liberation—exists only when the tongue-tips are present. (78)
My knowledge, rich with the signs appropriate for the stage of life, is the cause of liberation;
or rather, having observed sufferings and evils, my mind is set upon the stage of renunciation.
Then, having observed that pleasures and merits are equal within the householder's stage of life,
one's engagement— whether impelled by attachment or aversion— is equally conducive to bondage.
Without the state of "nothingness" (ākiñcanya), knowledge is not found anywhere, even in a hermitage;
the state of "somethingness" (kaiñcanya) is a bond equal in all hermitages, both for me and for you. (81)
Therefore, know me to be unattached in every way to virtue, wealth, pleasure, and liberation, even though I remain within the very abodes of bondage. 82.
O virtuous lady, sovereignty and power are a firm snare, a bond consisting of affection, karma, and other attachments;
these have been severed by me with the sword of knowledge, which flows like a stream of liberation.
Through knowledge, I move about in renunciation and do not incur attachment at all;
even in a kingdom, I do not fall like a king, nor am I bound as if by fetters.
Since the knots of latent impressions have been burnt away by me with the fire of knowledge, I move about within the kingdom of the body accompanied by my household, the senses and so forth. (85)
I wander with persistence, established in the assembly of the virtuous; I am intent on liberation, not on bondage, nor even on sovereignty in the forest.
Thus, being eternally liberated and having conceived devotion toward you, O virtuous one who assumes contradictory forms, I ask you: how is it that you are liberated? (87)
Your beauty is enriched with a golden luster, your body possesses fresh delicacy, and your youth is preeminent; endowed with such form and wealth in every way, how can you be a virtuous wife? (88)
If she were virtuous but not passionate, she would not be a truly passionate woman; nor would she be virtuous if she lacked passion.
Seeing that both qualities are incompatible in you, even your yogic power is incongruous.
The assembly was filled with doubt, wondering whether she was liberated or not;
it was enriched by the splendor of King Bhoga’s court and endowed with the full expansion of erotic sentiment.
How can you proclaim yourself to be one perfected in yoga and a virtuous woman, when you have fallen from my yoga and are enveloped by the defects of touch? 9.111.
How indeed can this yoginī be a teacher who restrains my heart, she whom that person introduced into my kingdom and assembly? (92)
Having fallen under his influence, you are seen to have strayed from your virtuous conduct;
having encountered me, a Kṣatriya, do not cause a confusion of castes once again. (93)

"You are a virtuous woman devoted to the dharma of liberation, while I am a householder devoted to the dharma of kingship; yet, if there were oneness of heart between us two, that would be a second confusion of dharmas. (94)
Therefore, if you proceed by resorting to independence as a practitioner, then the dharma and other teachings heard by you, a yoginī, will now fall into ruin. (95)
The desire to conquer through passion is a hope for victory bound by fetters;
you are already bound like me, and there can be no grasping of your hand.
Or else, if you are so arrogant as to show that you have conquered all those on my side, thinking them already defeated, then you are truly deluded. (97)
Filled with indignation and deluded by ignorance, you desire to conquer that which is called Yoga, which is like poison yet is nectar residing within you. (98)
For one who desires it, yoga is supreme; for one who does not desire it, however, it is like poison.
Do not display your own excellence; whether you are liberated or not, this man is indeed no ordinary king.
The strength of kings is great sovereignty; the strength of women is beauty and youth;
but the strength of the liberated is indeed Brahman—do not display your strength before me.
The powerful should be approached with straightforwardness, for they grant happiness;
however, through dishonesty, the powerful destroy even one who has realized the truth (tathāgata). 10.1.
Therefore, casting aside all audacity, tell me truly of your birth, family, learning, austerity, conduct, disposition, status, desire, and purpose.
Lomaśa said:
Though thus disregarded by Ānarta with many improper and inconsistent words, Kuśalā did not indeed succumb to fear.
Then that virtuous Aśvapāṭalā, who was exceedingly beautiful to behold and possessed of lovely wisdom, proceeded even further to offer a reply.

Thus ends the two hundred and fifty-seventh chapter, titled "The Demonstration of the Cause for the Soul’s Departure from the Body in the Lomaśa-Gītā, within the Second Section on the Tretā Age of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā," concerning the inquiry into renunciation and non-renunciation, and the dialogue between King Ānarta and the Yoginī Kuśalā.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O Rādhikā, Lomaśa, Aśva, and Pāṭala— after them,
he spoke the reply of Kuśalā according to their respective origins.
Śrī Lomaśa said: Listen to what Aśvapāṭalā—the virtuous woman who had reached the further shore of yoga and whose impurities were burnt away by the fire of the knowledge of reality—said.
Kuśala said: Listen, O King of Ānarta; you abide established upon two scales:
you protect the state of a householder through your words, yet you also extend the practice of a yogi. (3)
O King, you awaken unskillfulness toward what is wholesome through your corruptions; if such is your defilement, how can you remain liberated? 4.

The word of a trustworthy person is indeed a valid means of knowledge when it is endowed with appropriateness and other such qualities, augmented by power, and honored by its conformity to universal categories and similarity.

It is free from defects such as verbal fabrication, has not arisen from the field of delusion, and is clearly endowed with the manifestation of characteristics and so forth, being filled with manifest meaning. (6)
Listen with an undivided mind to my words, which are authoritative for you:
just as flour is to stone, so is a cloud to a circle of smoke.
Thus they danced closely joined together; closely joined were those who sustain life:
sound, touch, taste, smell, form, space, water, earth, and fire.
O King, they become as closely joined as flour and water, or like stones within one's own body;
they dissolve like clouds and scatter like smoke.
They do not recognize their own nature; how then could they perceive that of another?
At that time, the mind is conjoined with them and follows after external objects.
Furthermore, even there, there is the state of arising, magnitude, and connection with the external.
Furthermore, the state of being a yogi regarding oneself also serves as causes for what is to be grasped. || 11 ||
Thus, in all cases of perceiving external objects, these are indeed the causes:
the mind first forms a conceptualization of my nature, and from that, the intellect arrives at a definitive conclusion.
Out of conceit, he indeed performs actions and forms an opinion within himself;
he then projects that self [onto objects] and thinks, "This is mine. (13)
From those [impressions] seen and released, a latent impression (vāsanā) arises which bestows memory;
and ignorance (avidyā), or darkness (tamas), is the subsequent state of non-cognition during deep sleep.
And therein, a memory consisting of delusion arises repeatedly;
from that, there arise pleasure and pain, gain and loss, as well as the agreeable and the disagreeable.
In that regard, time would be the cause and primordial nature (prakṛti) the fulfiller;
whatever the unseen force (adṛṣṭa) may be, from that a corresponding fruit is produced.
The aggregate of twenty-four is indeed the cause of sensation;
it does not perceive the unmanifest, but perceives that which has a manifest form. || 17 ||
He who perceives only the gross is said to be one who is mixed with "mine" and "I";
however, he who discerns the unmanifest beholds the Self.
This very one, contemplating the inner self, shall go to the further shore;
all of us—men and women alike—are but the manifest manifestations of primordial nature (prakṛti).
Seated upon the seat of the embryo (bindugarbha), they are first a mass of semen and blood;
after ten nights, it becomes the *kalala*, then the *budbuda*, and from that, the *peśī*.
Thereafter, the limbs, including the nails and the ends of the hair, are produced;
and in the ninth month, the child is born as either a boy, a girl, or something else. || 21 ||
Names depend upon the physical characteristics (liṅga); from that [characteristic] come states such as childhood and so forth. The name "Kumāra" is applied to those whose limbs are delicate.
Indeed, that very same foolishness of the fool is like that of one who is unawakened;
he is considered "young" (yuvan) because he joins with desire through his youthful state. || 23 ||
Remaining and remaining, the hero indeed departs, becoming aged;
thus, through the transformation of other moments and parts at every instant.
O King, this subtle differentiation of name-and-form and so forth is not perceived;
neither their passing away nor their arising is observed.
For this entire world, which is always rushing about like the flame of a lamp, who is it, what is it, from where does it come, for what purpose, to whom does it belong, or by what means? (26)
"From where, or how, to whom, by what, or not—what is it, and who?
Indeed, these are the relations [that exist] even among living beings with their own limbs. (27)
In this way, those characterized by transience cannot be known through their mutual power, just as rays [are not known] from the sun, or fires from fuel-sticks. || 28 ||
Those who are indeed momentary cannot be determined at all;
likewise, all ordinary beings are composed of aggregated selves.
Aggregated forms are born and die moment by moment;
the self, however, is eternal and permanent, established in its own nature, and not an aggregate. If it has attained yoga, being discerning, it remains as one who is liberated.
And you perceive the aggregate as transitory, yet as your own eternal self.
If you perceive your own self by means of the self within the self itself, or if you perceive it as non-self, as a separate entity, and as momentary. (31–32)

In this very way, if through the attainment of disciplined yoga you perceive the eternal Self within yourself, as well as the Self in others and that which pervades all, [then you have attained success]. 33.
If you thus determine the equality between yourself and another, then who are you, to whom do you belong, and for what purpose do you ask me? 34.

"O King, for you who are liberated from the dualities of 'this should be mine' and 'this should not be mine,' what is your identity, from whence do you come, or for what purpose are you here? What need have you for such words? (35)

Nevertheless, since you do not intend for [the self] to have a separate existence from that which is subject to change, but rather maintain its identity with the body, what liberation can there be for you? 36.

Whether in sovereignty, toward an enemy, a friend, or one who is neutral; whether in defeat or victory; and while you, a kṣatriya, still possess the sense of "mine" and "I"—what indeed can be called liberation in such a state? (37)
Attached to the pursuit of dharma, artha, and kāma, following after attachment to fruits, and most arrogant with the nature of a king—what liberation indeed can there be in you? (38)
Whether in a man or a woman, whether beautiful or ugly, you perceive distinctions;
since you are entirely pervaded by the sense of embodiment, what indeed can be called liberation in you? (39)
Placing the attributes of the body foremost and speaking of the faults of attachment, what kind of liberation can there be for you who have fallen into a vulgar state? (2.258.40)
Even while you abide in yoga, you are mocked by non-yoga;
having fallen into ordinary sensory contact, what liberation can there truly be in you?
You are indeed a treasury of knowledge, yet you speak to me as if I were a mere artificial woman.
O Indra among kings, having reflected and observed this, what freedom indeed can there be for you?
In the material world there is a material nature, and in the conscious there is indeed a conscious nature;
for you, who possess no equal vision, what liberation can there be? (43)
This wholesome consciousness exists within the transformed aggregate;
O King, know me to be a divine consciousness, free from attachment. (44)
"Who belongs to whom, from where, by what means, and for what purpose is this union with a body? I am distinct from that; behold myself as situated within a human being. (45)
If you cannot see [the self] in this way because you are obscured by the composite aggregate,
then your desire for liberation is fruitless, O King, since you are not fit for it.
She must be restrained by the virtuous, for she is like unwholesome food for you;
having known this, there is no progress in conduct, nor is there any speed in knowledge.
In common worldly practice, it certainly does not exist; so what is the fruit born of yoga?
It is merely a vain exertion, a vain pride, and likewise a vain verbal abuse. (48)
If you perceive the body as the self, then your effort to associate with the virtuous is in vain;
for the self is neither woman, nor man, nor neuter, and yet it does not exist [as such]. (49)
If you are indeed such as this, O King, why do you not perceive others?
Having observed common things and distinguished them from the reality of the self. (2.258.50)
One should perceive the Self everywhere; what other characteristic of liberation could there be?
One should view all objects of attachment within the Supreme Lord, the Sovereign.
Playing with the self and delighting in the self is indeed the characteristic of one who is liberated;
now hear from me also about the places rich in attachments for one established in liberation. || 5.2 ||
For the kingdom is a bond compared to the realm, and the capital city is indeed a bond compared to that; even more than that is the royal palace, for it is a common bond. || 53 ||
Even more than that, one's own home is a bondage; indeed, one's own bed therein is a bondage.
Even that [bed] is half-bondage when shared with a woman; without a woman, it is no longer a bondage.
Even the mere performance of desire is bondage, and nothing beyond that;
yet even there, if there should be latent impression (vāsanā), it is bondage rooted in attachment.
The cause for the acquisition of the elements is food, medicine, and so forth;
then there is indeed bondage, such as that of a king, and the bondage of servants and others. || 56 ||
In this way, one becomes bound here even by the fruit of attachment to women and the like, as well as by food, clothing, garments, and ornaments. (57)
Furthermore, for a king, both punishment and favor consist in imprisonment;
moreover, due to his pride, the king is always dependent on others even in matters of minor business. (58)
He must be entirely subject to his servants in matters of war and peace, as well as in the company of women, in sports and diversions, and in the deliberations of the circle of ministers. (59)
How can there be independence for a king who follows the words of others? He remains under the control of his ministers, and he would not act against their will even if it were undesirable.
Busy with people seeking their own interests, he finds no sleep at the proper time;
even while sleeping on his bed, he is awakened somewhere by the messengers of his enemies.
And in some places, she is constantly brought under control by female slaves through commands such as:
"Arise! Bathe! Take hold! Drink! Eat! Speak! (6.2).
"Listen! Come! Look! Desist!
Delight!"—thus is this king always dependent, under the sway of attachment.
Supplicants arrive, yet he does not even venture to give;
there is anxiety regarding the depletion of the treasury when giving, and enmity arises from not giving. ||64||
Constantly anxious regarding protection, the king is always obsessed with worry;
indeed, driven by the fear of death, the king suspects everyone.
The king’s subjects become fearful of one another;
everyone is a king in his own house, and everyone is a householder in his own home.
In every house, all possess the power to both punish and favor:
sons, wives, home, self, treasury, friends, and accumulated wealth. (6.7)
To all of them, those associations are indeed equal states of bondage;
my country is ruined, my village is burnt, and my horse is killed.
His wealth was lost, his crops were scorched by the fire of frost, his field was devoured by birds, and his cows were carried off by thieves. (69)
My food has been ruined by diseases; my independence has been destroyed by enemies;
I have been assailed by the arrows of their words and driven from the royal throne.
Thus, indeed, one is tormented by states of attachment and by false cognitions, as well as by mental sufferings produced by a controller, by birth, and by passion and anger. (7.1)
And he is tormented by the sufferings born of disease and contempt;
not being free from attachment, he constantly and forcibly experiences suffering. (72)
Who that knows yoga would take up a kingdom, which offers little pleasure, is exceedingly full of suffering, is devoid of essence, and is like a seat of glowing coals? (73)
"You consider this city, kingdom, and supreme wealth to be yours;
tell me, O knower of the self—who are you, and to whom do this wealth, kingdom, and city belong? (74)
This body of yours, composed of the five elements, shall enter the fire;
and mine likewise shall do so there, for there is equality and no distinction between us.

For one who desires the destruction of the natural state of being a substratum and a superstratum, there can be no non-attachment whatsoever toward the body, which is by nature subject to attachment. (76)
But for the conscious one who is unattached, there is no attachment whatsoever;
for he is devoid of the relationship of container and contained, non-material, and eternally existent. (77)
Speak, O King! I am capable of explaining this in a thousand ways through my knowledge.
I have no attachment to a woman's body; how then could there be any such attachment to you as my husband? (78)
Considering her to be a woman, you ought not to speak so plainly of the nature of attachment;
for surely you have heard from Pativratā about liberation in its entirety.
You are both unattached and free from bonds; how then can you be attached to kingship?
All that you have heard has become fruitless for you, as you dwell in the state of identifying with the body.
Either what you have heard has merely passed through your ears, or you conduct yourself with sheer deceit; for you have neither retained it nor digested it within yourself. 8.1
By which you now remain attached to worldly and bodily things—you appear bound, O Self, like an ordinary beggar. (82)
I have entered into you, my own self, the Lord;
tell me, what harm have I done there, I who am eternally liberated? (8.3)
"O King, it is a constant rule for the virtuous to dwell in solitude;
having entered a deserted place, what fault have I committed against you here? (84)
I do not touch you with my arms, nor with my thighs, nor in any way with my limbs;
let there be no speaking of good or evil between you and me in this assembly.
Whatever has been done between a man and a woman, whether good or bad, is known as their union;
these virtuous ones are gurus, and you, O King, are the supreme guru. (86)
One should never speak disparagingly of yogis among yogis;
just as water resting on a lotus leaf remains unattached. (87)
In that manner, I shall dwell within you with a mind free from attachment;
I shall live by the way of the yogi for the sake of attaining the supreme perfection of self-realization.
Where indeed those virtuous and steadfast ascetics who have reached the further shore of yoga dwell, having ascended to the station of the Supreme Lord and being truly embodied in His form. (89)
Who would not desire to dwell there by means of the practice of yoga? O King, if you perceive the touch of my dwelling within yourself, [then you shall know it].
All the knowledge you have cultivated is indeed devoid of seed and is merely an ornament for speech;
having fallen away from the life of a householder, you truly do not find the state of liberation.
Standing here in the interval between both, you are a mere pretender;
for there is no meeting between one who is liberated and another who is liberated, nor between one who is wise and another who is wise.
For the conjunction of two things possessing the same quality gives rise to a confusion of natures;
thus, the union of purity with purity is the union of the self with the Self.
For a yogi, there is indeed no confusion of yoga with another yogi;
likewise, O King, you are a knower of Brahman, and I, Savarṇikā, am a knower of Brahman.
In our union, no confusion of castes (varṇasaṃkara) is considered to occur;
for Brahmā himself resides within the body of the Daughter of Brahmā at Somanātha. 95.
Formerly, when summoned by Śaśin for the purpose of the consecration of Somanātha,
the mental skill of Kriyā arose at that sacrifice.
I am indeed Satī by form, called Kriyā and named Kuśalā; I am the wife of Kratu, the Sacrifice, appearing in such a manner through the state of embodied existence.
"I am virtuous by nature and have reached the further shore of yoga;
therefore, O King, I exist here as my own self and am not fashioned as a woman. (98)
Furthermore, there is no confusion here when the state of equanimity is attained;
for you have cultivated an intellect directed toward liberation and seeking what is wholesome upon hearing [this teaching]. (99)
O virtuous one, I have come here for the sake of desiring liberation from you,
in this imperishable field of Saurāṣṭra, at the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake.
Having established my dwelling on the bank of the pool named Kuṅkuma, I shall reside there;
after staying within your body for one night, I will depart for my own abode.
O King, I, a practitioner of Brahman-yoga, do not remain long with one who is greedy; yet I have been honored by you through hospitality, your personal nature, and the food of wisdom. (102)
"Without having attained one who stands in equal yoga, tomorrow I shall go to my own abode, where Lomaśa, the best among those who know yoga, dwells with a gait equal to mine. (103)
The Lord is my own light and the supreme knower of the Self; having become one with Him therein, I, being skilled, indeed carry forth the bliss of Brahman.
"O King, I assumed this form merely to behold the assembly hall and its yogic power; for there, the foremost of those who perceive physical forms was seen by me. (105)
"These sages are indeed arrogant, for they are practitioners of yoga who perceive only the body.
What shall I say to you? Do not be arrogant, O King. (106)
O King, the strength of the self does not increase in this way for those who perceive only the body;
nor can there be the attainment of the Self for those who associate with their equals.

Liberation does not arise from the state of a householder as long as one has not realized the nature of the Self; for as long as one remains attached to worldly existence, one truly possesses attachments despite claiming to be liberated.
O Ānarta, do not harbor anger; eat and digest [this] truth.
For the sake of attaining the perfection of mastery over yoga, go to the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake.
Worship Lomaśa, the lord of yogīs and great spiritual teacher, who is his own self-effulgent light, as well as the Goddess Yoginī, who is ever-contented; thus become one who never falls away.
Śrī Lomaśa said: While she was speaking thus, King Ānarta then,
with a composed mind, did not grant her a heart worthy of dwelling there.
There, both of them indeed engaged in conversation with each other until dawn;
then the sages, having understood their intent, departed for their respective abodes.
Aśvapāṭala and Ānarta, having recognized their own inherent inferiority, attained the highest perfection through the company of a spiritual friend. || 113 ||
Then he set out with her for the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake,
where he had indeed attained full power of yoga from the sage Lomaśa.
Having attained her own supreme awakening through the light of her own self, and having become satisfied, she was further instructed by the Yoginī in the state of Brahman.
Ānarta departed for his own city of Camatkārapura;
therefore, O King, householders require renunciation. 1.16
Or rather, through the yoga of those who practice renunciation, liberation comes into the palm of one's hand;
by association with the virtuous, Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa will certainly be met.
Even for one who is incomplete, fullness is attained through every effort;
indeed, householders who have not renounced become renunciants through the yoga of the Guru. (1.18)
Just as a dancer is born through skillful application, so too do householders attain the supreme goal through association with such virtuous people. 11.9
"They will surely depart, there is no doubt—even those who are deceptive—this is certain.
Having spoken thus to Rādhikā, the glorious Lomaśa maintained silence. (2.258.120)
King Aśvapāṭala also attained satisfaction upon hearing that this sacred ford was known as Kuśalatīrtha and also as Ānartatīrtha.
And the Yogitīrtha exists within the waters of Aśvapaṭṭasara;
by bathing there or by drinking its water, one attains the vision of the Self.

Thus ends the two hundred and fifty-eighth chapter, titled "The Discussion between the King of Ānarta and the Brahmin’s Daughter Kuśalā-Sādhvī, and the Exposition that Liberation Comes Either from Renunciation Even While in the Householder State or from Association with the Holy," in the *Lomaśagītā* within the second section, the *Tretā-saṃtāna*, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Listen, O Rādhā; thereafter, the king of horses again questioned Lomaśa, and I shall relate that which is for the benefit of the virtuous. (1)
Aśvapāṭala said:
O Teacher, how did the weariness with one's own manifestation arise as the eternal refuge, and how did the certainty regarding the reality of the formless Hari come about? (2)
Śrī Lomaśa said: To the ascetic Brahmin named Brahmakallola, a devotee of the previous kalpa,
there was born a son, a lord named Trivikrama.
That incarnation of Śrī Hari was Hari again in another kalpa;
he became Trivikrama, who then seized the kingdom from Prabalī.
On the bank of the golden river, he suddenly beheld a superhuman man on the ground of the Nārāyaṇa lake, absorbed in yoga within his heart.
He is endowed with the conch, discus, mace, lotus, bow, trident, and arrow;
he possesses right hands marked with the banner, svastika, thunderbolt, and other such signs.
Laughing, pervaded by splendor, serene, with long eyes,
with arms reaching down to his knees, exceedingly radiant, and endowed with beauty.
The Lord, his own self-luminous light, beheld within himself his own form as Brahmā, as Vāmana, as Trivikrama, and as the powerful preceptor of Bṛhaspati.
Then, upon seeing his own form within the glorious Nārāyaṇa, he suddenly fainted for a moment and thought, "Who is this separate being? (9)
Then, through his divine vision, he recognized his own original form;
he offered praise to Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa, his Master and Supreme Lord.
O Inner Self, You are the Supreme Self, the sustainer of all incarnations;
You are the cause of all manifestations, abiding in the heart of all. || 11 ||
Everything—whether consisting of Brahman or not Brahman—resides within your heart;
you are my distinct abode, yet I am also your non-distinct abode.
You alone are the supreme reality; by your grace, you have become the object of my vision.
And your form has become the object of my perception, enriched by direct experience.
Having attained the vision of the self, and having attained the vision of the supreme self—
having attained both visions, I have today become one who has fulfilled his purpose.
Give your command, O ocean of mercy, O friend of the world, O Janārdana!
Having attained you, the Supreme Self, nothing remains to be attained.
"Once you have performed your yoga, nothing will remain for you to do in the garden.
Thus was the Lord, the illustrious Śrīśa, the beginningless Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, praised.
Then, within his own form of light, he showed him that entire wheel of worldly existence, even greater than his own abode, as one with himself.
The lords, the persons of Brahmā, the liberated ones, the many abodes,
the gods, the sages, the hosts of ancestors, the lords of the gods, and human beings— || 18 ||
[He saw] serpents, Rākṣasas, Daityas, Dānavas, and even Asuras;
as well as beasts, birds, and even stationary beings, both insentient and sentient.
He showed all the great elements, the stable primordial nature, the modifications, and the embodied beings, along with their dissolution into that [nature].
Having thus demonstrated this, he indeed vanished;
for this very knowledge, which is direct and eternal, resides within the Self.
Having revealed it to him, he established it firmly within his heart;
he granted him this boon: "May you always possess a nature consisting of light."
And let this knowledge, known as self-luminous, not be concealed;
from that moment on, this Lord Trivikrama is self-effulgent. (23)
He became renowned among yogis as one possessed of self-luminosity; and having beheld the sacred field known as Akṣara, he made this request. (24)
In that heart-pleasing place, he beheld a divine form of such a kind, rich with garments of yellow silk and adorned with a horse-patterned sash, intended for his own residence.
At that moment, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa said, "So be it," and there Nārāyaṇa appeared with a divine body and four arms.
The mental son of Śrī Hari, who is the refuge of eternal knowledge,
was indeed [established] there in the Nārāyaṇa lake by Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa.
Having bathed together, she then quickly reached the site of Kuṅkumavāpikā by means of yoga, speed, power, and the grace of Hari.

In this way, having attained another birth, another body, and likewise another mode of existence—even though he was beyond the need for a physical form—he assumed the state of being a son through the notion of "sonship. (29)
Always in the form of an incarnation and in the form of Viṣṇu,
[he beheld] the mental-born form of Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
Having attained a divine state as soon as he was born, Nārāyaṇa was endowed with righteousness and dispassion, devoted [to the Lord], and sixteen years of age. || 31 ||
In the field of Kuṅkuma, the Lord became one whose complexion was like saffron;
he indeed became a natural treasury of all branches of knowledge.
He is the very locus of omniscience, endowed with all sovereign powers, the creator of all that is auspicious, and one who is devoted to the dharma of the yogis. ||33||
Performing deeds that surpassed all others and possessing a description that excelled all others, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa moved about within the imperishable field (akṣara-kṣetra). 34.
He instructed him in all the dharmas for the sake of establishing the lineage beginning with his guru:
those pertaining to the world, those pertaining to the Vedas, and those mental ones that follow them.
Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa said: "O son, practice the Sāttvata duties which bring about welfare;
conquer your vital breath, endure hunger and thirst, as well as cold and heat. (26)
Having conquered the senses through austerity, protect truth and self-restraint;
protect freedom from malice, lack of envy, uprightness, and virtuous conduct. ||37||
O traveler, partake of Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Lord, who is the remnant of the food offered to the gods, ancestors, guests, and dependents; do not sleep in the realm of darkness. 38.
O son, do not place your trust in this transient body, which is as unstable as a bubble on the water, accidental, and dependent upon consciousness; do not act like one who is ignorant.
For enemies who are heedless, sleepless, and ever-exerting find a vulnerability in this body; do not be overcome by them.
The days pass away in succession, truly cutting short the lifespan of people;
life is constantly wasting away—take refuge in the Guru. 41.
The ignorant desire the increase of flesh and blood through the body and its like;
yet at the end, all that is transitory, while they remain asleep regarding the means to liberation.
O son, do not proceed with that alone as an ordinary person does, merely by means of the limited suffering at the end, which carries one toward the non-existence of rebirth. ||43||

By means of which [qualities], the righteous path—leading to liberation and culminating in the Imperishable—is attained by the virtuous, those established in the bull-like state, and the great-souled yogins. 44.
Therefore, attend upon him properly, inquire, and retain his words;
restrain the churning of the mind and bring about steadfastness toward the Lord of the Good. (45)
Having grasped the ladder of Dharma and ascended the stage of devotion, go to the eternal abode by means of the impulse of self-abidance. 46.
O best of Brahmins, cast aside atheists and those devoid of devotion to your left;
O son, abandon hope, craving, anger, and delusion far away from you. (47)
Relying upon the boat of yoga, cross over the ocean of saṃsāra;
this world is being led away by death and is being crushed on all sides by old age. (48)
One indeed carries one across the Vaitaraṇī; cross it by means of the boat of knowledge—whether he is standing, walking, drinking, or lying down on his bed. (49)
Death watches over the mortal; do not become one who falls into its power—namely, one who is gathering objects for the sake of pleasure, who is insatiable, greedy, and arrogant. (2.259.50)

Death, moving with sudden speed, seizes the sleeping man and departs—taking him while his obstacles are yet unremoved, while he is being crushed, while he is most arrogant, and while he is treading upon a wrong path. (5.1)
The interior of the cosmic egg is a chamber filled with darkness;
hold fast to the lamp of knowledge in order to emerge from it. (52)
While wandering through many bodily cycles in vain, you have indeed attained Brahminhood through divine merit; carry this state which is composed of Brahman. 53.
The great body of a Brahmin is most excellent; it is not suited for trivial desires, but is considered fit for liberation, the attainment of dharma, austerity, and the highest good. (54)
Such a priceless jewel, which grants the fruits of one's desired objects,
must not be treated with contempt as something worthless, like a small copper coin.
Filled with desire within, she hides her face from above;
she displays her modesty to this enjoyer in the presence of other people.
Pervaded by internal poison and nectar, and intent on binding [others], she strives for her own gain; having consumed [them], she makes them suffer. (57)
Even as one abandons it, this [desire] does not leave; it goes along with him to another place.
Though treated with contempt, it remains attached, for its bond is rooted in latent impressions (*vāsanā*). (58)
Behold the play of illusion: she who is called Hell makes a guest dwell for a long time within her own palaces, once he has become intoxicated by the drinking of wine. 59.
Who indeed could be bound or impassioned there by that divine eye? Never let the flow of pride attach itself to the body as if it were a worthy vessel. (2.259.60)
The body is bound by karma and, in turn, produces further karma;
it has desire as its limit and anger as its boundary—perceive that as your own nature. (2.1)
Wherever there is fear of kings and likewise fear of thieves,
leave that behind and acquire divine wealth as your provisions for the journey.
"O son, acquire that imperishable wealth by which one lives in the next world and is never separated from anything."
For neither mother, father, friend, nor kinsman follow one into the state of transmigration;
indeed, only one's karma goes with one. Therefore, practice the state of actionlessness (naiṣkarmya).

Accumulations of gold, kingdoms, male servants, female servants, and beloved offspring—all these cease to exist upon the dissolution of the body; therefore, worship the Lord who is your true companion.
Always worship the Supreme Lord, the witness dwelling within, the bestower of Brahman-bliss, the master, the deliverer, and the treasure-house of joy. 66.
Those who follow the dharma of householders go to the worlds of Prajāpati, Bṛhaspati,
and Śatakratu, only to perish at their end.
O son of Brahmā, do not fix your livelihood upon the householder's state;
instead, uphold the vow of Brahman, which is a treasure-store that is fearless and eternal.
Free from attachment and possessing divine vision, you should remain in the presence of Brahman,
having surrendered all your actions to me, Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme.
Enjoying the supreme state beyond the qualities (nirguṇya), you shall become liberated in the Imperishable as if already free;
indeed, dwelling in a village is bondage—cut it off and enter the forest.
What use have you for wealth, friends, kinsmen, and even a son? Having become self-luminous, enjoy your own innate light. (7.1)
Having observed those standing in the world who are dying and those who are equal [to them],
and having reflected upon those who will die, one should seek the Self that has entered the cave of the heart.
One should perform auspicious deeds quickly; what is to be done tomorrow should indeed be done swiftly today.
I know not what death will seize and depart in another moment. (73)

In this cycle of existence, which is like the crest of death and the devouring of Mahākāla, you who possess discernment should seek refuge in the Guru and strive with all your soul for liberation. (74)
Death is the liberation of the self; strive for that alone with diligence.
The wise man is intent on attaining liberation, while one devoid of it belongs to the class of the ignorant.
Human birth is a staircase to heaven and is indeed difficult to obtain in this world;
by means of it, accomplish this liberation, which is infinite and eternal bliss.
He whose mind does not run toward anything other than the path to liberation is indeed a person of meritorious deeds and is beyond the grief of all human beings. //77//
For one whose mind is pure and firm for the sake of liberation, who has commenced the practice thereof, and who is devoid of other dispositions, there is no fear of time. (78)
For one who is bound by merit and demerit, greedy, whose soul is intent on sense objects, and submerged in the ties of affection, there exists danger from time. (79)
Thousands of mothers and fathers, and tens of thousands of sons and wives, have passed away in the course of time; to whom do they belong, and to whom does this [present person] belong? (2.259.80)
I alone am known as the Self, and you yourself are the Self alone;
others have gone elsewhere, for these do not indeed see one another.
They have no business with you, nor do you have any business with them here;
they have gone by their own actions, and you shall go by your own deeds. (82)
This world is preoccupied with its own self-interest, affectionate toward its own interests, and intent on its own pursuits;
having quickly accomplished its own ends, it suddenly abandons a person who is devoid of merit. (83)
For the wealthy and prosperous, even a solitary place acts like one's own kin;
for the poor and destitute, even one's own kin acts like a stranger.
Having encountered the union with a wife, a person accumulates inauspicious karma;
from that arises a birth fraught with afflictions, followed by suffering again and birth once more. (85)
Thus, for one who is submerged in the whirlpool and impelled by latent tendencies,
reaching the shore from the middle of the ocean does not occur.
Therefore, my son, having attained the Dharma accompanied by dispassion, and with the eye of wisdom as your lamp, proceed to the supreme state through devotion. (87)
Time cooks all beings in the cauldron known as delusion,
using the sun as fire and the days, months, seasons, and years as the stirring ladle.
I see no protector here; you do not see one, nor does anyone else.
I do not see him for whom I exist, nor do I see him who belongs to me.
Therefore, always worship the Supreme Lord, the Lord of Śrī,
the Illustrious Supreme Sovereign here on this land of action, so that you may go to the imperishable abode.
Of what use is birth, or the body, or knowledge, or virtue, or austerity, or dwelling in the forest, if through them liberation does not come to pass? (9.1)
He is called Aśvapāṭala; indeed, he is self-luminous.
And having attentively considered what was spoken by the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, [he remained so]. 92.
Dwelling constantly in celibacy, he always set his mind upon liberation;
indeed, he lived upon the earth sometimes visible and sometimes invisible.
In the sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpikā, he possesses a divine body that is exceedingly radiant;
he is long-lived, a great liberated soul, and his conduct transcends that of ordinary men. ||94||
Free from all attachments and having attained union with Brahman,
he became twofold and then, with one body, went to the supreme imperishable state.
Another always dwells here in this field known as Akṣara, being devoted with his whole being to Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. || 96 ||
Out of devotion, the teacher is the refuge of all sciences, a treasure-house of knowledge, and the Lord;
he may have four arms or two, being a storehouse of bliss according to his will. (97)
O King, having quickly attained knowledge of that reality through my yoga, worship this Supreme Self and become one with a divine body here. 98.
O King, that sacred ford known as Svataḥprakāśa indeed exists within the waters of Aśvasaras; it bestows divinity through bathing, drinking, and other such acts. 99.
Having attained this knowledge, liberation will surely occur; there is no doubt.
It shall be the illumination of all sciences and the illumination of the Self.

She shall be illumined by the gods and illumined by the consciousness of the Intellect (cic-caitanya); O son, that which cannot be attained through knowledge, nor through dharma, nor even through austerity.
"O Rādhikā, that is indeed attained and obtained through even a small fraction of the Guru's grace. Having spoken thus, the glorious Lomaśa became silent. (102)
Then the king, exceedingly gratified and drawn by the delicious taste, while remembering Hari within his own heart, questioned him regarding the fruits of the deeds he had performed.

Thus ends the two hundred and fifty-ninth chapter, titled "The Purifying Study Arising from the Instruction of the Beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa and the State of Liberation for the Son of Brahmakallola," in the Lomaśagītā, within the second section on the Tretā Age of the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Listen, O illustrious Rādhikā, to how King Aśvapāṭala once again questioned Lomaśa regarding the means for attaining happiness.
Aśvapāṭala said: "O Guru, whether it be gifts, sacrifices, penance, or service to the teacher—even when performed by a yogi—is that fruitless or does it yield fruit with respect to liberation? (2)
Śrī Lomaśa said:
O King, that which has been performed never becomes fruitless here;
having experienced its fruit, even for yogins it suddenly comes to an end.
In all creations, there is the enjoyment of the fruits of all karmas;
however, when a gift is given, there is certainly no enjoyment of it for the giver in that [creation].
All actions, whether merit or even sin, should be offered and entrusted to the True Lord; once offered, they are no longer experienced.
This very state of being free from the qualities (nairguṇya) becomes one that is offered to Hari;
the fruit of such offering therein is the grace of Hari. || 6 ||
For the devotee who offers [this] with devotion, the attainment is the state of having one's self centered in Hari;
residence in the abode of Hari shall be the result, and the bliss of liberation is considered the fruit.
If ordinary action yields extraordinary fruit when offered to Kṛṣṇa, yet this same [action] is experienced among the lords and others when it is not offered to Kṛṣṇa; (8)
Among gods, humans, and other various high and low wombs,
the doer is led into affliction and suffering when the time has arrived.
From poverty to poverty, from disease to disease, from fear to fear, and from famine to famine indeed do the sinful go again and again. (2.260.10)
From prosperity to prosperity, from joy to joy, from heaven to heaven,
and from happiness to happiness, those who perform meritorious deeds proceed indeed to great festivals.
Non-givers, those deprived of hands, and predatory beasts such as serpents and the like are born; these are the bodies of those characterized by tamas, which result from a lack of faith.
They indeed become donors, deities, those to be propitiated, residents of sacred sites, lords, and those who are dear to gods, guests, Brahmins, and the virtuous. (13)
In this world, people who do not give are like shriveled grain among crops, or like jackfruit eaten by an elephant, or like rotten eggs among birds. (14)
Those who possess neither righteousness, nor faith, nor charity, nor even benevolence—they are merely bellies; they shall certainly not attain a new, higher rebirth.
In this world, people who merely fill their own bellies consume only sin;
they will not give what was not given, nor will they do so in other future births.
The king named Śveta did not obtain food or water in heaven,
because he had given nothing here [in this world], considering that gift to be indeed insignificant.
Gold, diamonds, and the like were given, as well as vehicles and mounts;
all that was indeed obtained by him in heaven, but neither food nor water. (18)
Then, having come from heaven while hungry, he made an effort for the sake of satisfaction by licking the ashes produced from his own corpse.
Having seen that, Nārada also caused his sons to perform an excellent śrāddha for him, as well as many other rites such as the offering of food and water.
Then indeed that king named Śveta attained satisfaction;
therefore, O King, everything given on the land of action (karmabhūmi) is fully obtained. 21.
Nowhere is what has not been given ever obtained; therefore, one should give according to the prescribed rule.
The white or black karma that has been performed runs after one as one flees.
Each respective experience is consumed like a shadow belonging to the self;
it is enveloped by karma, accompanied by mental distraction, and seeks the prospect of happiness. (23)
Time draws away the various multitudes of beings that cover it,
just as it withers the natural flowers and fruits of a tree.
Likewise, embodied beings remain for a time with their performed actions;
and their fruit—happiness and suffering, gain and loss, decay and prosperity—endures. (25)
Honor and dishonor, poverty and prosperity, joy and sorrow—these continue until death; they do not cease even when struck.
Then, one experiences in successive order all the suffering previously acquired by oneself, such as dwelling in the womb and so forth, which has been created again and again. (27)
Just as a calf seeks out its own mother even among thousands of cows, so too does karma reach its own doer. (28)
Just as the staining of a cloth is dissolved by alkaline water,
so too is internal impurity destroyed by austerity and dissolved through righteous conduct.
O ascetic lady, just as the footprint of a fish is not seen in water,
so too the footprint of karma does not appear in one who is a treasure-house of knowledge.
Enough with unattainable practices; enough with harsh disciplines.
By the mere service of the Guru, all perfection rests in one's hand.
Whatever kind of perfection one attains through austerity and the restraint of the senses—
Then, through yoga, a human being attains a reward a thousand times greater than that. || 32 ||
Then, through the grace of the Guru, one obtains ten thousand times that merit—
the fruit of a thousand horse-sacrifices and the like— which resembles a fraction of the power of Yoga.
O King, without yoga, without knowledge, and even without higher realization (vijñāna), as well as without service to the guru, liberation is indeed difficult to attain. (34)
Having acquired knowledge from the guru and having served the supreme teacher, and having offered devotion to Hari, one shall swiftly attain the highest liberation. || 35 ||
Having become one whose self is purified by knowledge and discernment, a vessel for the guru’s blessings,
and possessing the nature of Brahman, she shall swiftly attain liberation. Indeed, in the first stage of life, by the grace of the guru, she quickly becomes virtuous.
One certainly attains liberation; what is the use of other efforts belonging to the [other] stages of life? || 37 ||
Having abandoned states of being characterized by passion and darkness while established in the hermitage of the Brahma-vow,
and having firmly set out upon the path of purity, one should perceive the Self by means of the self.
Having perceived the Self as the essence of all, the Supreme Lord abiding within the self, and Him as existing in all things, one should cast off the bondage of karma. (39)
Just as clouds, having abandoned the ocean, go toward the dry land,
so too do the liberated ones, having left the earth, go toward the realm of Brahman.
The light, united within the Self, shines in all bodies;
it can be seen through austerity, devotion, and also through grace. ||4.1||
For one who is free from hatred and attachment, there is no fear of others arising from oneself, nor is there any fear of oneself arising from others; the Supreme Brahman shines forth. (42)
For one who is devoid of the nature of evil, endowed with the nature of Brahman,
and established in self-abidance, the Supreme Brahman indeed shines forth.
Having united the self with Śrī Hari and abandoned the deluding Māyā, the Supreme Brahman shines forth for one who is immersed in the lake of Brahman. 44.
When one has attained equanimity toward both the external and the internal, and remains even-minded even amidst the uneven, then one attains Brahman. ||45||
Praise and blame, iron and gold, pleasure and pain, the liked and the disliked, gain and loss, cold and heat, as well as life and death—[these he regards with equanimity]. (46)
When one perceives one’s own self, another person, an insentient object, a shrine, and even that which is external or internal with equanimity, then one attains Brahman. 47.
Just as one might see a cave pervaded by darkness by means of one's own light, so too can Brahman be beheld by means of the lamp of self-knowledge. 48.
There is no eye equal to knowledge; there is no home equal to Brahman.
There is no suffering equal to craving; there is no happiness equal to contentment. ||49||
The cessation of latent impressions, constant conduct in accordance with Brahman, virtuous behavior, and service to the good— this is the highest good that bestows liberation.
If someone, having become attached, should think "I am happy," he should not be considered happy; for attachment is indeed filled with suffering. (51)
The intellect of one who is attached wavers and spreads the net of delusion;
for one ensnared by that net, indeed, the sources of suffering gather from all sides. 52.
For both desire and anger destroy the welfare of the embodied being;
consisting of attachment and aversion, these two defects are considered to lead to hell. (53)
One who is focused and auspicious should always protect oneself from those two;
for a virtuous man deprived of those two is always [deficient], and a faithful wife likewise when deprived of them.
He who renounces those two achieves the great renunciation and becomes a renouncer of everything; he who does not become attached to them attains the imperishable state. ||55||
Deprived of those two, he is deprived of [the power of] beings; abandoned by the drawing together of the assembly, he, being liberated, soon attains the supreme good. ||56||
Freedom from possessiveness, perfect contentment, desirelessness, and steadiness—this is declared to be the highest good; by means of it, one attains the supreme state. (57)
There would be sorrow in possession; how could there be grieving for that which is empty?
Noble men, citizens, and those born in the realm do not resort to one who is devoid of virtue. (58)
Even a beloved wife becomes despondent upon realizing that he is devoid of qualities and tranquil;
even Māyā, having abandoned her attachment, dissolves away when he is devoid of qualities and tranquil. ||59||
Those who are worldly and full of passion do not leap about in the sky;
they do not speak to one who is indifferent, nor indeed do they cause him to speak.
Satiated by wisdom, satisfied by knowledge, and overflowing with the bliss of Brahman, people abandon the worlds of delusion, infatuation, and pleasure as if they were devoid of consciousness.
There is no end to thirst; contentment is indeed the supreme happiness.
Having attained the contentment of wisdom, one becomes immersed in the bliss of Brahman. (62)
By establishing residence and social interaction with yogis skilled in the inner self,
and by cultivating loving-kindness toward those most eminent among the knowers of Brahman, one shall attain the bliss of Brahman.
In every respect, people are seen to be dominated by passion (rājasa), or by darkness (tāmasa), or only half-purified by goodness (sāttvika);
devoid of the guru’s blessing, they are fit for hell. 64.
Dwelling in deceit and having set their minds on violence, they disregard their teacher and the Dharma; by such means, they are led to hell. (65)
Prosperity attends those groups who are entirely composed of sattva;
where Nārāyaṇa dwells, there is accomplishment and liberation.
Everyone desires to go higher and higher in the world; yet, striving by divergent paths, one does not reach one's desired goal. (67)
Therefore, O King, having fully embraced the path of yoga— the path of Hari, which is higher than the highest—
a yogi should set forth, equipped with the provisions of compassion.
But without yoga, it is not possible to attain the eternal Brahman;
and without yoga, even the bondage of karma cannot be cast off. (69)
O King, dwelling of the mind in Kṛṣṇa is the yoga that bestows supreme liberation;
O King, dwelling of the self in Kṛṣṇa is considered that eternal liberation.
Nara, Nārāyaṇa, Hari, and Kṛṣṇa, born of Dharma,
were brothers who, by meditating upon the Supreme Brahman, attained absorption in it.
Kapila, Ṛṣabha, Datta, Sanaka and the others, as well as Nārada; Pṛthu, Vāmana, Paraśurāma, Rāma, and the rest. (72)
Śvetavyāsa and others, as well as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara,
having accomplished the yoga of the Supreme Brahman, attained identity with it.
The cessation of all phenomena is considered the supreme Nirvāṇa;
for that very activity is indeed offered unto the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. (74)
Śrī, Lakṣmī, Kamalā, Rādhā, Bhū, Līlā, Pārvatī, Satī, Ramā, Kṛṣṇā, Māṇikī, Gaṅgā, Durgā, and Sarasvatī. ||75||
Ramā, Jayā, Virajā, and those others such as Brahmapriyā, having accomplished the yoga of the Supreme Brahman, attained identity with it. ||76||
Sacrifice, which is of the nature of worldly engagement (pravṛtti), is offered unto the Supreme God;
but this [sacrifice] fashioned by you, O King, is indeed of the nature of renunciation (nivṛtti).
Therefore, you have indeed obtained the supreme fruit of all sacrifices, since the Lord Anādi Śrī Nārāyaṇa has come here. (78)
At dawn, the Supreme Lord granted you his vision;
O King, when Hari was satisfied, all the gods were satisfied at your sacrifice.
Today you have accomplished your purpose regarding the four aims of human life;
may there always be well-being for you and for all people who follow the dharma of service.
Aśvapāṭala said:
How did the Blessed One become the one who receives no portion in sacrifices?
And how were the deities made by Hari entitled to shares in the sacrifice?
Śrī Lomaśa said: Listen indeed to what occurred at the beginning of the Kalpa, at the commencement of creation;
the deities together with Brahmā and the sages whose wealth is austerity.
Desiring an increase in their splendor, they went to the northern shore of the Ocean of Milk;
standing on one leg with their arms raised and their gaze fixed upward, they performed austerities.
At the end of a thousand years, they heard a voice from the sky:
"O gods, including Brahmā, and you sages whose wealth is penance! (84)
You must perform the work of active engagement that increases your own strength;
you shall enjoy the supreme fruit of my propitiatory austerities.
All of you, worship me; conceive of me as my own portion;
and partake of me in the sacrifice, for service to me bestows strength.
O King, having come to this auspicious land of Kṛṣṇamaṇi known as Surāṣṭra, they performed sacrifices here, where [the sacrifice] was performed by you.
O King, at that time I was present here among this assembly of great seers;
it was then that this first divine sacrifice was performed by the gods and others. (88)
According to the ritual prescribed in the Vedas for the Sarvamedha sacrifice,
Brahmā himself assigned the portion for Hari in that sacrificial session.
The gods and the celestial sages also assigned portions to Hari;
they all offered their respective shares to the Supreme Soul for the sake of the sacrifice.
Those divine portions, characterized by the dharma of the Kṛta age,
then became entirely offered to Śrī Hari and took on the form of Brahman.
Those liberated beings praised the Supreme Lord, the Puruṣottama, who is effulgent like the sun and beyond all darkness. || 92 ||
Then, for the sake of granting boons to the gods, that boon-bestowing Hari,
remaining bodiless in the sky, spoke from near the lake of Aśvasaras.
Whatever portion was assigned by each of you has all come to me;
being pleased, I grant you here a boon that bestows strength.
All of you, performing sacrifices yourselves with excellent sacrificial fees,
shall in every age be partakers of the fruits of worldly activity.
Those other people who, following your ritual manual, shall perform sacrifices after assigning portions for you, will attain the supreme fruit. (96)
And you shall receive those portions being given to you;
in age after age, you shall be partakers of the fruits of worldly activity (pravṛtti).
Activity and cessation, having been offered unto me, shall exist just as those portions were conceived by you here. (98)
Portions have been assigned by me for you, the givers of portions, in the sacrifice;
do you, who bestow the fruits of the sacrificial shares, cause the worlds to flourish.
"O gods, having obtained your share of the fruit from this sacrifice,
you shall repeatedly have your strength replenished and shall indeed sustain the worlds."
"You indeed have been consecrated by sacrifices performed by men in all sacrifices; you shall likewise consecrate me. This is my thought regarding your consecration."
That very nature of the injunction has indeed been established by me within the Vedic texts;
having performed sacrifices and partaken in the feast, you should contemplate the welfare of all beings.
The sages such as Vasiṣṭha and others, the great seers such as Sanaka and others, the lords such as Brahmā and others, and the deities such as the Ādityas and others; || 103 ||
Other humans and others as well are entitled to the path of sacrifice; go forth and perform your respective duties, conducting great sacrifices.
Let the ritual sacrifices proceed, and let the ordinances likewise be prescribed;
this age called Kṛtayuga, the most excellent of times, now begins.
"The entire four-footed divine Dharma proceeds herein.
Having said this to Brahmā, Kṛṣṇa revealed his own true form.
Having indeed caused the auspicious Vedas to revolve, he who is the very form of Hayagrīva embraced him and said, "O Brahman, I cast this burden upon you."
"Whenever the work of the gods becomes unbearable, I shall manifest myself again and again to you, who possess the gift of knowledge"; having said this, he vanished.
The great holy site of Hayagrīva was born within that lake;
by bathing there and drinking its water, one becomes possessed of Vedic knowledge. 10.9.
Brahmā went to his own world, and the gods went to heaven and the other realms.
Thus, O King, Hari became the foremost recipient of the sacrifice.
At that time, Kṛṣṇa himself indeed established the portions for the gods, as well as the path of action and its cessation, and the state of actionlessness which bestows strength.
This very one is the Supreme Brahman, the primordial Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa;
he, the son of Kambharā, who grants liberation to the worlds, has been described to you by me.
O King, let my words be done: let the young Kṛṣṇa be served;
let Kṛṣṇa be constantly sung of, and let him who dwells within be worshipped. (113)
"Go to the imperishable abode and enjoy eternal bliss," having thus instructed Rādhā, Lomaśa became silent.

Thus ends the two hundred and sixtieth chapter, titled "The Description of How Even a Yogin Attains the Fruit of Serving His Desired Guru and Others, and the Emergence of the Shares for Hari and the Deities in Sacrifice," in the *Lomaśagītā* within the second section, the *Tretā-santāna*, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Listen, O Rādhikā; later, the King of Āśvapaṭṭala asked the sage about the realization of Śrī Hari as manifest before his eyes.
Aśvapāṭala said:
O Sage, this Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, who is without beginning, the manifest Blessed One, is present here; O Master, cause me to realize Him.
I perform my worship daily under that name, seeking its true meaning;
instruct me, who am endowed with all goals, in the supreme realization of the Lord. (3)
Śrī Lomaśa said:
O King, the devoted ones who are exclusively dedicated, the wise, and those who have mastered the Vedas—
only they know the etymologies of Hari’s names, and no other people do.

For those who are single-mindedly devoted are indeed the best— those who have no other deity, whose very selves are that, who are intent on that, whose conduct is that, and whose actions are performed in conjunction with that.
They know when, where, how, and by whom it was born;
thereafter, the devotees proclaim it, as it was previously revealed by them.
The beginning is both birth and origination, as well as the conjunction of the body, senses, and so forth;
it is the primordial emission within the fivefold creation, which does not exist at all in the [Supreme] Form.
Time is the imperishable which, being at the beginning, is never dissolved anywhere;
it is the very first and the supreme Lord of all things other than itself.
Since there was nothing else prior to him, he is indeed beginningless;
and he, whose eternal glory is supreme among the most excellent divine splendors, is the one whom she relies upon.
Divine attire, artistic arrangement, speech, prosperity, majesty, all lordly powers, and virtues— all these qualities of the state of Śrī reside therein.

Therefore, because he is identical with Śrī, that Blessed One (Bhagavān), the Supreme Lord, is indeed called "the Possessor of Śrī" (Śrīmān), as he is the refuge of Ramā, Lakṣmī, and the others. || 11 ||
He who is indeed the ancient refuge of men and of souls;
all divine forms and powers (nārāḥ) have their abode in Him. 12.
Where there is no fear, illusion, or poverty for those who have attained liberation—Nārāyaṇa is indeed considered that very abode where liberated men reside. (13)
He draws forth the entire world, and at times he leads all created bodies toward dissolution; therefore, Kṛṣṇa is so celebrated.
Agriculture, the destruction of impurity, and liberation are said to be [the goals];
such is Śrī Kṛṣṇa himself, the beginningless Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa. || 15 ||
Who is that eternal bliss, or who is that supreme Lord Brahmā,
whom she bears within her own womb— or indeed, in her heart— she being Kaṃbharā?
And here, the son of Kambharā is indeed Kāmbhareya Hari, he who himself protects the cows—the rays—of Kṛṣṇa. (17)
He protects the cows, the milch-cows, the earth, speech, and the divine goal;
his father is Nanda, the cowherd who delights in tending cattle.
Ancient cities, bodies, sentient beings, and insentient things—all these indeed approach Śrī Hari, the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama). || 19 ||
Because of his greatness, his all-pervasiveness, and his transcendence, he who is the Supreme is Brahman; Hari is indeed the Supreme Brahman, and he alone is the Blessed Lord himself.
Supreme and complete sovereignties exist therein, and he alone is the Supreme Lord;
thus he is renowned as the Supreme Lord (Parameśvara). || 21 ||
Everything that is perishable consists of *māyā*, while that supreme abode is the imperishable (*akṣara*).
Hari transcends even that; he is thus called "transcending the imperishable" (*akṣarātīta*).
All the incarnations of Hari manifest from Him alone;
the Incarnator Himself, Śrī Hari, is said to be their source.
Indeed, this Hari carries away the minds of his devotees;
he also carries away their sorrows, and thus he is celebrated as Hari.
From him is born Hara and Saṃkarṣaṇa, the Lord who performs his duties;
for that reason, the Blessed Lord Hari is also called by that name, as he possesses sovereign power.
He dwells within all things and shines forth while remaining internal;
he is indeed called Vāsudeva, the eternal Supreme Lord.
He whose nature is desire and whose power is indeed the Śāla tree—
Mādhava alone is the husband of that Māyā, who is his very nature.
The Lord is also declared to be Time itself, possessing the power to create all things;
he is indeed Viṣṇu, into whom all creations enter and from whom they arise.
He pervades and encompasses all; thus he is called the all-pervading Viṣṇu.
By means of self-restraint, people ascend to my supreme abode. (29)
Therefore, Kṛṣṇa is called Dāmodara because he delights (ramati) in giving (dāna) and in joy (moda).
His hairs (keśāḥ) are said to be his rays; indeed, Kṛṣṇa possesses them, and thus he is Keśava.
Agni and Soma are my two forms, as are both my mouth and my essence;
therefore, the sacrifice named Agniṣṭoma is Nārāyaṇa himself.
Agni is the Kṣatriya and Soma is the twice-born; the unity of these two is Hara and Hari.
Agni is the woman and Soma is the man; Agniṣṭoma is Nārāyaṇa. || 32 ||
In ancient times, he recovered the lost cow and the earth;
therefore, he became renowned as Govinda, the "Cow-finder," and as Gopāla, from his protection of the cows.
He rules over the senses (hṛṣīka), which are the organs;
therefore, that Hari became Hṛṣīkeśa, the Lord of the Senses, in the place of austerities.
Because he perceives everything below and everything beyond, he is called Adhokṣaja;
dharma is his bull, and his abode is the monkey (Kapi), who is this one in the form of a boar (Vārāha). 35.
Yogins delight therein; the Lord Rāma is the one who possesses that delight.
Through the application of qualities and actions, its names are infinite. (36)
Worship the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Brahman;
Kṛṣṇa himself exists in the form of a child in the imperishable realm of Kuṅkumavāpikā. (37)
Worship always that Bālakṛṣṇa who shines resplendent in the sacred field;
because Vāmā attains dissolution (laya) here in Kṛṣṇa, he is therefore called Bālakṛṣṇaka.
Having directed people who are children, completely enveloped by ignorance, toward the true path, He draws them to the ground of the imperishable abode and bestows supreme bliss. 3.9.
Bālakṛṣṇa, Harikṛṣṇa, Śrīkṛṣṇa, Puruṣottama, Anādi-Śrīkṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of Brahmapriyā. || 2.261.40 ||
O King, let Janārdana—the Lord of the virtuous, the Lord of the liberated, the Lord of all, the Lord of devotees, and the Lord of His own—be served and attained. 41.
Aśvapāṭala said:
Oh, what knowledge! Oh, what awakening! Oh, what nectarine elixir!
This divine [truth], which grants divine liberation, has been constantly made to drink by my heart. 42.
O treasury of austerity, the nectar of the story of Nārāyaṇa has been told to me by you;
such a Lord as this has been shown and awakened within my heart. (43)
The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa has been directly beheld;
this very Lord, whose nature consists of both fire and moon, has been gratified by me. 44.
Thus, having been propitiated, he was directly attained;
there is nothing superior to him, nor is there anyone else equal to him. (45)
Indeed, there exists no other narrative equal to that story even within the three worlds;
it is the supreme purifier of all sacred fords and the bestower of fruits. 46.
And yet, my own merit has not increased by much here, whereas yours has increased greatly,
since, having reached the land of Kuṅkuma, I have beheld Hari.
O Rādhikā, having thus considered himself to have fulfilled his purpose,
the king prostrated like a staff on the ground before his own guru, Lomaśa.
Then Lomaśa said to him, his body bristling with horripilation and his eyes filled with tears of joy:
"Blessed are you! You have been graced, since you have beheld Hari. (49)
In that matter of seeing the invisible, compassion alone is indeed the cause;
for the Blessed One, the Supreme Person, is difficult to behold even when he has descended [into the world].
There is no one in the world dearer to him than his devotee;
therefore, O best of kings, he has himself revealed his own self.
From that, O King, arises forbearance which indeed resides upon the earth;
from that arises the essence by which the waters are filled with flavor.
From that arises form, by which the sun and other luminaries possess beautiful forms;
from that arises touch, by which the vital breaths of the true yogis [are sustained]. ||53||
From that arises sound, by which people speak;
from that arises the mind, which sustains the quality of luminosity. ||54||
Therefore, O King, let the intellect that effects the determination of reality arise; having known through that intellect Kṛṣṇa, the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) of the Sātvatas. 55.
With concentrated minds, they enter the Supreme Self dwelling within the heart;
O King, worship that Supreme Lord, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
He who is the supreme deity, the sacrifice, the eternal Supreme Self, and the Lord of the universe—he is eternally worshipped in all sacrifices. 57.
Those who worship the gods, the ancestors, teachers, holy men, as well as guests, cows, Brahmins, the poor, the earth, and their virtuous mother; |||58||
Serving the sages, servants, wives, husbands, and children;
honoring those worthy of worship, the helpless, the destitute, as well as animals and birds;
and even toward pillars, trees, and winged creatures—they worship Viṣṇu alone. (59)
That Blessed One is present within; he is established in every morsel of food. He accepts what is given with faith and brings about the satisfaction of all living beings.
He is this very Anādi-Śrī-Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, as heard in the Śruti.
O King, worship that Supreme Self who is within the range of direct perception—He who is our guru here, the joy of Kambharā.
Who else could possibly go everywhere across this entire circle of the earth without him? (62)
He would perform the great sacrifices and would deliver and liberate people.
How else could thousands and millions of princesses choose that Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who enchants the entire world? (63-64)
How could the gods, the sages, the lords, and the lords of lords come and perform worship at his sacrifices without Hari?
How [could it be] with Rādhā, Ramā, Lakṣmī, Kamalā, and others by the millions?

And the wives of Kṛṣṇa would perform service to him alone, excluding Nārāyaṇa. Furthermore, how could all the marks that transcend the three worlds truly exist upon his form alone, without Nārāyaṇa? (66–67)
Kṛṣṇa is indeed the treasury of the Vedas and the very treasury of austerities;
he is the treasury of yoga and knowledge, and he alone is the belly of all.
The Vedas have the Supreme Brahman as their ultimate goal, and the sacrifices have the Supreme Brahman as their ultimate goal.
Liberation has the Supreme Brahman as its highest goal; austerity has the Supreme Brahman as its highest goal.

Truth has the Supreme Brahman as its highest goal; the immortal has the Supreme Brahman as its highest goal. Merit has the Supreme Brahman as its highest goal; the ultimate destination has the Supreme Brahman as its highest goal. (2.261.70)
The dharma of engagement and withdrawal culminates in the Supreme Brahman;

O King, the fragrance within the earth, which is of the nature of the Supreme Brahman, is the most excellent. And the auspicious qualities of the waters, consisting of taste, are likewise devoted to the Supreme Brahman.
The supreme form of the Parabrāhmaṇa is likewise the form of all luminous bodies. Touch, whose essence is the Parabrāhmaṇa, is pervasive and follows all that is tangible.
Sound, whose essence is the Parabrāhmaṇa, encompasses all that is audible. (72–73)
The mind is the supreme Brahman; the intellect, ego, and the sovereign goddess are the supreme Brahman.
The subtle elements consist of the supreme Brahman; the qualities consist of the supreme Brahman.
Time consists of the supreme Brahman; form is devoted to the supreme Brahman.
Kīrti, Śrī, Devatā, Lakṣmī, and Bhū, who is devoted to the Supreme Brahman;
Bhūti, Līlā, Sarasvatī, and Satī, who are devoted to the Supreme Brahman;
all the Ṛgvedic verses, as well as those dear to Brahman, are likewise devoted to the Supreme Brahman. || 75-76 ||
Supreme knowledge, yoga, renunciation, and auspicious actions—
all these causes are directed toward the Supreme Brahman;
for those desiring to know the Truth, the Supreme Lord is the Highest Reality.
That supreme Lord knows the intentions of all.
Hari himself is the divine rite, the ancestral rite, austerity, charity, and the refuge of all;
