he is the dwelling place for all beings and has his abode at Kuṅkumavāpikā.
He who dwells in the imperishable Brahman is indeed that very Bālakṛṣṇa;
he is the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of Nārāyaṇa.
Indeed, the Blessed Lord Hari delights all those who are single-mindedly devoted;
the Blessed Lord himself accepts the excellent worship performed according to the prescribed rites.
For those people who are single-mindedly devoted reach the abode of Śrī Hari, which is the entirety of the religion of exclusive devotion and is dedicated to the Supreme Brahman. (82)
In the primordial Kṛta Yuga, it was established in accordance with the Sāmaveda;
indeed, it is upheld by Bālakṛṣṇa, the Lord Nārāyaṇa. 83.
In ancient times, Nārāyaṇa performed the sacrificial rites for the gods and the ancestors on the bank of the river Svarṇarekhā at the Nārāyaṇahrada lake. 84.
In a former kalpa, the sages, the deities and others, as well as Soma and human beings, all taking refuge in Hari, established the dharma of sacrifice.
In the Kṛta Yuga, Rudra indeed protected the dharma of Nārāyaṇa;
likewise, in the primordial Kṛta Yuga, Hara instructed the brahmins.
And the great sage named Suparṇa, having received the sacrificial dharma from Śrī Puruṣottama, established that virtuous practice upon the earth. (87)
Then, O King, Samudra set forth the sacrificial rites;
after that, the sage named Āraṇyaka also set them forth.
Then the virtuous Manu set the sacrificial duties in motion;
the blessed Sanatkumāra set those devoted to them in motion.
Vīraṇa, Suvrata, Barhiṣad, Dakṣaka,
and Vivasvān established this eternal dharma.
The Sāttvata dharma, which consists of total self-surrender, is difficult for people to practice;
yet it is upheld by Anādikṛṣṇa and established once again upon the earth. 9.1
O King, by the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, who has assumed the form of the sacrifice, Dharma— consisting of the total surrender of all things— has been established upon the earth.
That very Blessed One, having established the imperishable Dharma in the world, thereafter sports and indeed governs all creatures according to his will. ||93||
Thus, O best of kings, the doctrine of single-minded devotion has been declared to you.
O King, those people on earth who are single-mindedly devoted are difficult to find.
If this world were filled with exclusive devotees of Viṣṇu toward one another, it would become the city of Brahmā here, and the Kṛta Yuga, free from all defects, would prevail. (95)
And where there exist those who are single-mindedly devoted to the Supreme Brahman—men and women, as well as beasts, birds, deities, and so forth. (96)
All castes there are indeed Vaiṣṇavas, and that place is considered the imperishable state (akṣarapada);
there is no unrighteousness there at all, nor even those born of an unrighteous lineage.
All human interactions would become millions of liberated beings, whether in Vaikuṇṭha, Goloka, Śveta-dvīpa, or the Badarī forest. 98.
If all people on this earth were exclusively devoted to the Sātvatas and possessed of devotion, they would certainly attain liberation. (99)
For having attained their heart's desire, they would constantly worship the Supreme Person,
being single-minded devotees ever devoted to the Supreme Brahman.
For those who have Hari as their youngest brother, Hari is the provider of yoga and kṣema;
Hari looks upon that person whom He makes His own as soon as they are born.
He shall become a follower of the Sāttvata path here, possessing exclusive devotion to Dharma; through that, he attains the supreme goal in liberation, which is of the nature of the Supreme Brahman.
He who is seen by Nārāyaṇa indeed becomes awakened;
O King, one does not become awakened anywhere by one's own will alone.
Hari himself does not perceive him as being endowed with the characteristics of phenomenal activity;
rather, Mahāmāyā, Brahmā, the gods, and human beings behold him thus.
Then all those deformed beings indeed become bound by illusion;
however, if they perform service to the Sātvatas with true devotion, [they are liberated]. || 105 ||
Then, after some time, having attained freedom from the qualities (nirguṇya), they go to the Imperishable;
or else, being beheld with compassion by the Sāttvata, they enter the assembly of the Sāttvatas.
And when they come to be regarded with exclusive compassion for what is wholesome,
then indeed there will be a swift transformation of their hearts.
There is no doubt that [liberation] will occur, either through meals offered with grace by Hari,
or by partaking of morsels of water and food from the devotees of Hari.
Pure intellect, directed toward the state beyond the qualities (nirguṇa), gradually arises;
then it becomes stainless and serene within the circle of the Sāttvatas. 109.
By dwelling [there], they will gradually attain the state of the Sātvatas and reach liberation;
of this there is no doubt, for that state is indeed accomplished through grace.
Having spoken thus, the great sage Lomaśa then became silent;
O Rādhikā, Aśvapaṭṭala then worshipped the sage Lomaśa.
And having fulfilled his purpose through many collections of ritual materials, he proceeded with a desire to visit the sacred fords on the northern shore of the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake.
Then, having requested Lomaśa, he went together with Lomaśa to the lakes and sacred fords, accompanied by his entire caravan.

Thus ends the two hundred and sixty-first chapter, titled "The Description of Lomaśa’s Revelation of the Primordial Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa as the Manifest Supreme Lord to Aśva and Pāṭalā, and the Revelation of the Dharma Devoted to the Supreme Brahman," in the *Lomaśagītā* within the second section, the *Tretā-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmīnārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Listen, O Rādhikā; that king named Aśvapātala first went to Somatīrtha together with Lomaśa.
Having bathed there according to the prescribed rites and having given various gifts many times,
he paid homage to Yūpasthalī and then proceeded to Rāmatīrtha.
Aśvapāṭala said:
O Great Sage, how did this sacred ford (tīrtha) named after Rāma come to be?
Please relate this ancient story in brief. (3)
Śrī Lomaśa said: In ancient times, there was a king named Bhāṇavīrya of the Siṃha lineage;
he ruled the beautiful kingdom of Gopanāthādikaṇḍa.
The king Dharmadhara rules over the regions of Śatruñjaya,
constantly uttering "Rāma, Rāma," "Rāma, Rāma," and "Rāmāditya."
"Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa! Kṛṣṇa! O Kṛṣṇa, the Sun!"—thus indeed does the Vaiṣṇava chant together with his own family.
The subjects of that king were established in happiness, dwelling in bliss, and abiding in joy;
they always worshipped Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, Govinda, and Acyuta.
He constantly performs his duty with the vigor of recitation even toward guests;
he practices charity, fire-offerings, and circumambulation toward the virtuous and in rites for the gods.
While he was living in this manner, once indeed a painful physical affliction arose;
there was a king named Kṣamābhṛt, whose forehead [was marked].
For the sake of victory, he set out with his own army toward the ocean; having crossed the Sābhramatī river, he passed through the regions known as Dhavala.
Having conquered the kingdom of Bhāṇuvīrya,
he advanced to defeat the army of that king as well, which was arrogant in its villages and cities.
Having made Siṃharāyikā his own territory, he wandered about;
indeed, in order to conquer the capital city, he quickly drew near.
Having encircled the city of Siṃharājya with a wheel of troops on all sides,
he besieged the capital and dispatched a messenger to the king.
The messenger also spoke the king’s words: "Accept subjection, or else give battle here, or else [give] the entire kingdom. (14)
Bhāṇavīrya also spoke to the messenger of the king:
"In his kingdom, no injustice exists, nor does any unrighteousness exist likewise. (15)
The Lord Rāma and Kṛṣṇa are always worshipped by me;
all virtuous people are protected, and guests are always honored.
The kingdom has been entrusted by me for refuge to Rāma;
it is perceived that no one else here possesses authority, nor is there any war with men.
The gift of the kingdom was made to Rāma; how can it be enjoyed by another?
For I am his chief minister, and the Blessed One himself will fight.
Speak; I shall not grant the kingdom, nor even submission, for the Blessed One himself will perform the battle for his own sake.
"Be armored, O Indra among kings, and do not harbor pride," he said;
"speak to the lord of the earth, or else go back to your own abode. (2.262.20)
"Or rather, I shall welcome you in the guise of a friend;
tell me again what you desire here," he said, looking about.
Then the messenger went and reported this exactly as it had been spoken.
And he dispatched a messenger to the king, saying, "Be prepared."
"Having fought, I shall seize the kingdom; do not give way to pride.
For Nārāyaṇa will certainly not protect his devotee in battle. (23)
Having thus dispatched the messenger who signaled for battle,
he caused the sounds of kettledrums, cymbals, and conchs to be raised all at once.
He caused various kinds of mechanical devices to be constructed near the fortress,
as well as fortress-guards stationed at the gate-towers and door-keepers for the gates.
Having bound them and brought the kings under his own control, the monarch,
accompanied by his army, entered the city of Siṃharājya.
Trembling with fear, the subjects remembered the infallible Rāma—the Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the protector and Supreme Controller. ||27||
Having proceeded directly to the royal palace, he, accompanied by his forces,
requested from the king either a wrestling match or a contest of national strength.
Then Bhāṇavīrya, who was greatly devoted and possessed equal vision toward the king, greeted him with a welcoming look and spoke as follows: ||29||
O King, in battle there will surely be the destruction and injury of men;
whether victory or defeat shall belong to me or to you.
While we both remain established in our own respective realms, we shall undoubtedly stand victorious;
for there will be no end to the severing of the threads known as craving.
Worship Kṛṣṇa, Hari, and Rāma, and do not bear useless suffering;
neither my kingdom, nor your kingdom, nor the earth shall go with you.
Neither army, nor kinsmen, nor servants, nor wealth, nor kingdom, nor subjects will accompany one at death; when death occurs, there is no moment’s delay.
The kingdom has been surrendered by me to Kṛṣṇa; my own kingdom does not excel it.
O King, do not entertain a vain longing for Rāma’s kingdom.
O Earth, hand-to-hand combat is not your strength, nor is it mine in any way;
for that is indeed the strength of the army and of the enemy in a battle with weapons.
Strength must be acquired from Rāma; whatever strength is his companion, without that, all other strength is fruitless and indeed powerless. (36)
The King said: "O virtuous one, having become a king, you speak words of praise like one who is weak.
This is not the conduct of a royal family, O holy man, nor is it anywhere conducive to fame. || 37 ||
Neither Rāma nor Kṛṣṇa is here; Hari is not the protector in battle.
A kingdom may be conquered by force, for the dharma of war is eternal. (38)
"Either give up the kingdom through battle, or seek refuge;
otherwise, having bound you in fetters, I shall lead you to the house of darkness."
Bhāṇavīrya said: "O King, these fetters were fashioned by the illustrious Rāma, not by you;
for such fetters are intended for the wicked, as I am indeed such a person. (2.262.40)
"I shall undergo imprisonment; do not indeed worry about that.
Since there is no imprisonment for one who is innocent, act as you see fit. (41)

The earth, water, and fires were created by the Supreme Lord; so too the wind, the vital breaths, the ether, as well as sound and the other objects of the senses, and the sense organs themselves. (42)
The body was fashioned by Him; the kingdom was created by Him alone;
and the status of royalty was bestowed by that very Supreme Self. (43)
"O King, since you have granted me this entire world as your kingdom, I shall indeed exercise that sovereignty; being thus granted [the realm], may you be happy. (44)
Do not covet the food of another that rests in the hand of the Supreme Lord;
for a person who is excessively greedy may perish along with his very roots and all his possessions. 45.
In all matters, O King, one should always give to the Supreme Self rather than to another;
in this world, offering is indeed worship—therefore, you must cultivate such devotion.
O King, by taking what was not given, you have committed a most terrible sin;
may it not indeed obstruct your attainment of liberation on this earth, O descendant of Manu.
Behold, O King, if the cultivators in the kingdom [pay] taxes and the like once every year, or every two years, or even every three years. (48)
If they do not give at all to the king, they shall share in the fault;
they shall be subject to royal punishment and likewise be expelled from their homes.
Deprived of their fields and enclosures, they shall be punished by the king;
they are innocent by the non-payment of taxes, but guilty by the payment of taxes.
Whatever belongs to a farmer—the domestic compound, fields, gardens, and so forth—becomes the property of the king alone for the purpose of collecting taxes. (5.1)
There, the cultivator indeed lives by means of agriculture and other such works while paying taxes;
the king must never be forgotten by the cultivator. (52)
If the king should be forgotten, the cultivator would become subject to punishment;
but by paying the tax and remembering the king, he indeed lives free from affliction. (53)
In this very way, O King, the world is the kingdom of the Supreme Self;
by Him the earth was created, as well as water, fire, air, and light. (54)
By him the body was fashioned, as well as material wealth, food, flavors and the like, men and women, sons, cattle, trees, creepers, houses, and so forth. (55)
Day and night, sun and moon, happiness and tranquility, family, prosperity, food, and drink—all this belongs to him alone as his kingdom. (56)
Indeed, that [tribute] must be surrendered to that king, for he is the very essence of sacrifice;
yet it must not be offered or surrendered as a tax to Nārāyaṇa.
If we all, though being farmers, were to eat what has not been offered, then we would undoubtedly become liable to punishment. (58)
Therefore, O King, neither the earth belongs to you nor to me at any time;
rather, it is protected by us who stand upon the earth through our role as cultivators.
"He is indeed the sovereign emperor; do not wage war against me, O King!
You may enjoy what has been offered to you by him, whether with me or with him."
Therefore, whatever exists here in this world, all that belongs to him;
you should enjoy what he has given, and do not covet what truly belongs to another.
Abandoning your own [nature] and offering it to Hari, bring about liberation;
understand from me that you shall attain the supreme kingdom, the kingdom of liberation. 62.
The King said: "The path of worldly sovereignty, the path of liberation, and the path of knowledge—these three are distinct.
For kings, there is indeed the path of battle; in that regard, [the path of] knowledge is not applicable. (63)
Everything belongs to Nārāyaṇa alone; he who is powerful obtains it.
If he enjoys a prosperous kingdom, it is indeed the duty of a king to fight.
"O King, having placed you in shackles, I shall carry off the kingdom!
Having said this, he suddenly bound the king's attendant.
O Rāma, O Kṛṣṇa, O Hari, O Hari! Carry away the treasury and the royal palace, along with the family, the ministers, and the entire army! 66.
"Bālakṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa, Lakṣmīnātha, Hare, Hare!"—
even while bound in chains, he performed his worship thus, free from fear.
The household performed worship with fearlessness through the power of the Blessed One;
and the king rejoiced, having obtained a kingdom free from thorns.
For the Blessed Lord is fond of his devotees; the Lord is the helper of his devotees.
Residing in Vaikuṇṭha, the glorious Lord is the husband of Śītā and the Supreme Sovereign.
She heard his worship and the supreme power of his voice;
there Sītā said to Hari, "What is this great chanting? (2.262.70)
"O beloved, it is heard that this intense agitation has been stirred up by someone;
Rāmāditya then said, 'Look, Lakṣmī, at your own devotee. (71)
Indeed, Bhāṇavīrya, who was held in fetters in Surāṣṭra under King Siṃha, was released by the king in his own city. ||72||
Not seeing her husband, who was bound in shackles, Sītā rose up suddenly;
and Rāma, along with his attendants, likewise rose up.
In an instant, he arrived on earth near the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake,
[to see] the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa as well as the beloveds of Brahmā.
Having taken Sītā along with him, he then arrayed Rāma’s fourfold army for battle; it was capable of moving through the sky and possessed great speed.
Indeed, for the sake of protecting his devotee, he sounded the war-trumpets all around the walls of the city of Siṃharājī. ||76||
Having formed a wheel-array for his army, he alerted the king, the supporter of the earth,
who was also accompanied by his troops, for the purpose of battle.
He came swiftly for the sake of battle, and a most fierce conflict ensued;
ten thousand warriors of that king were broken.
The mountain was held by great warriors with arrows, shafts, lances, thunderbolts, discs, swords,
and nooses, while its life-force was sustained.
Indeed, Sītā herself displayed great perseverance and exerted her strength;
Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa Rāma granted him his own vision.
The beloved of Brahmā also granted an audience to the king’s wife;
Lomaśa bestowed his blessings upon the family and the subjects.
O King, I am indeed Lomaśa; I gave him this Vaiṣṇava mantra, having bound the mountain-king and bestowed the kingdom upon his devotee. (82)
Having abandoned that region for the sake of the Kuṅkuma field, he [established] Bhāṇavīrya along with his lineage, and Rāmāditya together with his retinue. (83)
The Blessed Lord Bālakṛṣṇa caused Ānāyya, Aśvasara, and Vāra to bathe for the sake of purification, and he granted liberation to those who had been slain.
Then Rāmāditya, together with his circle of attendants, dwelt there;
being honored and treated with hospitality, he performed his ablutions in the lake. (85)
O King, that sacred ford (tīrtha) thus became known as Rāmatīrtha;
furthermore, this lake is called Sitātīrtha and Muktitīrtha. ||86||
Indeed, through the power of his recitation, a beautiful temple was constructed here;
for Rāmāditya shines here together with Sitā. (87)
Accompanied by his attendants and wielding a bow and weapons,
the Supreme Lord thus indeed provided protection for his devotee.
Likewise, the famous Bhāṇatīrtha and Vaikuṇṭhatīrtha are situated to the west of Īśāna, from the Somatīrtha. (89)
Bathe here, drink the water, and with devotion offer libations to the ancestors;
give gifts to the virtuous Brahmins and likewise to the virtuous women.
And here you shall obtain the fruit of all forms of giving from even a small gift; and here you shall obtain the fruit of the gift of the earth from the gift of a mere morsel of food. ||9.1||
And here, the fruit of bestowing the gift of heaven comes from the giving of cows;
and here, the fruit of bestowing the gift of prosperity comes from the giving of daughters. ||92||
And here, the fruit of the gift of liberation comes from the bestowing of the gift of fearlessness;
thus was King Bhāṇavīrya, who possessed great strength, addressed, O Rādhikā. (93)
The king of devotees performed the rites of bathing, giving, and worship according to the prescribed rules;
for a moment, he meditated upon Rāmāditya, the Supreme Soul. (94)
The vision of Rāma appeared within the heart amidst that splendor;
the king rejoiced, and Lomaśa too, through his meditative absorption,
beheld him with divine vision, being reminded by the beloved of Kṛṣṇa.
Then, having been seen face to face, Rāma indeed vanished from sight.
Thus, O Rādhikā, this supreme sacred ford named Rāmāditya is conscious;
even by remembering it, one brings about the vision of Rāma. (97)
It removes the torment of sin, destroys the perils of enemies and other such dangers, grants residence in Vaikuṇṭha, and is the beautiful, auspicious abode of Viṣṇu. 98.
Where even dead animals go to the supreme Vaikuṇṭha, and where men and women who have bathed go to the supreme Vaikuṇṭha. (99)
Having bathed there in the Rāmahrada, those who possess desires proceed truly to the world of the gods, while those free from desire go to the imperishable state.
O Rādhikā, they depart after being honored by the most excellent attendants;
one shall obtain all that fruit simply by hearing or reciting this. || 101 ||

Thus ends the two hundred and sixty-second chapter, titled "The Description of Aśvapāṭala Reaching Rāmāditya Tīrtha, Hearing the Story of the Devotee Bhāṇavīrya, Performing Ritual Bathing, Giving, and Other Duties According to Prescribed Rules, and the Mutual Dialogue between the Two Kings," in the *Lomaśagītā* within the second section, the *Tretā-santāna*, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Listen, O Rādhikā, to another sacred site proclaimed by Lomaśa,
belonging to Sūryanārāyaṇa himself, which destroys all forms of leprosy.
Having made Rāmatīrtha his highest goal, Aśvapāṭala proceeded further to a beautiful holy site on the shore of a lake, its pure waters radiant with the sun.
Where even the mother-of-pearl shells appear as radiant as the sun, emitting rays of light even when situated within the lattice-work. (3)
Beholding that water shining so intensely, Aśvapāṭṭala,
overwhelmed by great wonder, then questioned the divine Lomaśa.
Aśvapāṭala said:
O Guru, this sacred ford is the source of illumination for all sacred fords;
how, why, and when indeed did it come to have such a solar orb?
Even the waters shine as if they were filled with the sun;
O Lord, tell me, what indeed is its name, what are its qualities, and what is its fruit?
Śrī Lomaśa said:
Listen, O King, to a great marvel that occurred there in ancient times.
Formerly, in Stambhapura, there lived a scribe who performed the work of writing. (7)
He served his master constantly and became a royal official; indeed, being highly intelligent, he became a scribe and an assistant in matters of justice.
Shrouded by the defect of poverty and excessively restless with thirst for fortune,
he sought to acquire wealth and such through whatever means possible.

In the composition of strings of words, through a disruption of the sequence of what precedes and follows, even the intended meaning may become meaningless, resulting in the loss of profit. (2.263.10)
Likewise, having concealed the words within a document,
he who gives wealth to that creditor in such a written paper [is one who acts] in the form of a swindler.
Having written down the letter of profit, he indeed grants that which bestows victory—
a letter possessing a double meaning, intended for a combination of meanings, and yielding nine meanings through the division of words.
Thus, due to greed, because he had scrutinized the legal and illegal matters of many people,
he was born with this wasting leprosy on both hands as a result of the burden of his sins.
For that scribe, named Ūrjavrata, suffered from a disease of the hands;
consequently, he abandoned his work as a writer and went to Gopanātha for the sake of visiting holy places.
Then he went to the holy ford consisting of Kṛṣṇa’s pastimes; having bathed there, he bestowed the sacred field of Guptaprayāga, which wards off sin.
Having bathed there, he then proceeded to Mūladvārikā;
from there he went to Somanātha, and from there he went to Prācīplakṣa.
Having performed his ablutions in the Sarasvatī and taken refuge at the foot of a Plakṣa tree, he mentally recited the mantra: "Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa, O Supreme Mādhava! (17)
O Nārāyaṇa, Hari, Rāma, Janārdana, protector of people! O merciful one, ocean of compassion, O Lord, protect me from disease. (18)
In this world, the fruit of actions performed with intense application arises immediately;
for those performed with weak momentum, it arises after a lapse of time. (19)
Or else, everything must be experienced in another birth or in the abode of Yama;
for wherever a living being may go, the karma they have committed does not leave them.
In my writings, I have indeed elevated the untrue over the true;
by representing the true in the form of the untrue, I have committed an unwholesome act. (21)
O Blessed One, by that sin, leprosy flowed from my two hands;
it was born upon my fingers as a holy site that destroys evil. (22)
"Even though this has been done, O Blessed One, this disease does not subside.
Therefore, O Lord of Gods, O ocean of compassion, please deliver me out of mercy. (23)
"I shall never again commit such a fault in this world. Homage to you, the remover of sins; homage, homage to you, the remover of diseases. (24)
Salutations to you, the protector of this sacred ford who bestows happiness upon devotees;
salutations to you, whose ears are all-pervading, and salutations to you, whose eyes are all-seeing. ||25||
Salutations to you who know all; salutations to you who abide in the hearts of all. Salutations to the one whose form resides in the body; salutations to the conqueror who joins the aggregates.
"Salutations to you of invisible form, the protector of those who have sought refuge"—thus did the scribe pray, as if despondent. (27)
He sat down beneath a Plakṣa tree, despondent and contemplating death;
at that moment, a certain brahmin wearing matted locks arrived there. (28)
Go here and propitiate the Field of the Sun (Ārkakṣetra) which is situated nearby;
taking refuge under a *arka* tree, constantly recite the mantras of the Sun. (29)
The divine Sūryanārāyaṇa will destroy your leprosy;
having bathed in the river Sarasvatī and drunk its purifying water.
"Salutations to you, O Brahma-Savitṛ, the remover of leprosy; salutations again and again.
Reciting this very mantra, one should go to the auspicious Sūryakṣetra. (3.1)
Thus addressed, O King, that scribe then went to Arkatīrtha,
where in ancient times the Sun-god, fashioned by Viśvakarman, was ground upon a whetstone.
Having asked that matted-haired one and bowed down to him, he went to the place where Khaṇḍa had fallen and where the Sun had attained the state of the Arka tree. ||33||
Upon seeing the forest of *arka* trees, he, whose vow was vigor, was indeed delighted;
for there were white *arkas*, those with the hue of the sky, and those with large blossoms.
Seeing many trees that yielded abundant milk, appearing in the form of stalks and creepers, and rich with fruits, flowers, and leaves, he was indeed filled with joy.

He searched in many ways for a sacred site (tīrthasthala), wondering, "Where indeed might it be? and thought, "Seated in the presence of the most excellent Sun-god, I shall perform my recitation (japa). ||36||
Then, at the foot of that very arka tree— covered with many branches and leaves,
and serving as the abode of many flowers— he beheld the wheel of the crest-lock (śikhācakra).
There, his mind was fixed upon the Sun’s excellent house, which resembled a hut;
he took up residence in its shadow at the foot [of the tree], chanting the mantra.
"Obeisance to you, O Brahmā-Savitṛ, the remover of leprosy; obeisance, obeisance!"—thus he muttered there, even though he was distressed by hunger and thirst. (39)
He passed the night without obtaining even a moment's sleep;
rising in the morning, he fashioned a garland of flowers from blades of grass.
With devotion, he offered [the stone] to the Sun-god Śilācakra;
he poured water upon the stone and offered the fruit of the sītā plant.
He offered even a leaf of Tulasī to the one in the form of a stone;
he then performed praise and prostration, and indeed gave him the fruit of the Sītā plant.
Afterwards, he enjoyed the prasāda and indeed constantly recited prayers;
thus, O King, when a month had passed while he was devoted to subsisting on fruits, ||43||
A certain person, white in color and endowed with many rays, arose from the wheel; he was beautiful in form, though his nature was ignorance. ||44||
With golden earrings on his ears, wearing a crown and bracelets, with a jeweled necklace upon his chest, he was golden-hued and radiant.
With bracelets and armlets upon his arms, he laughed, overwhelmed with affection;
his head was encircled by a halo of luster, shining with golden garments. (46)
Approaching slowly from a distance of the discus, he spoke to Ūrjavrata, who stood there:
"Speak, my son; what do you desire? Do not delay. (47)
Then Urvajravata said: "O God of gods, O Teacher of the World!
I desire the pacification of my leprosy; please show me compassion. (48)
"Who are you, O Blessed One, who sits here endowed with all splendor?
I think you are the Sun himself, or perhaps the wondrous Nārāyaṇa out of his grace toward me. (49)
Having appeared here, He bestows grace upon His devotees;
salutations to the one of a thousand forms, salutations to the one of a thousand rays.
Salutation to the one who shows compassion to his devotees; salutation to the thousand-eyed one;
salutation to the illuminator of the world, the all-seeing eye of all beings. ||51||
Salutations again and again to the one whose nature is the Supreme Brahman, the bestower of liberation;
salutations to the destroyer of [worldly] splendor and the healer of disease, salutations again and again. ||52||
Having spoken thus, that Ūrjavrata fell at his feet;
the Sun quickly vanished, and a divine voice spoke.
"O you who observe the *ūrja* vow, may it be well with you; your disease shall be destroyed.
Since you have not yet performed the expiation, you truly ought not to touch me here. (54)
"By reciting my mantra one hundred thousand times, your expiation shall be accomplished;
therefore, perform that and go to the Aśvapaṭṭa lake. (55)
The sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpikā, which takes refuge in the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa known as Akṣara, is presided over by Puruṣottama. (56)
And staying on the northern shore of that very lake, in the sanctuary of Śaṅkara, beneath a *arka* tree, he recited my supreme mantra. (57)
"The destruction of your leprosy will indeed occur there very quickly.
Having heard these divine words of Śāradā, he did not even turn toward that direction. (58)
Pleased and observing the *ūrjavrata* vow, he went to Śrī Balikhātaka;
from there he went to the site of Vāmana, and thence to Vastrāpatha.
Having bathed in the Suvarṇarakṣā water, in the Nārāyaṇa lake, at Indreśvara, at the Mahālakṣmī Tīrtha, and at the Cakraka Tīrtha; ||2.263.60||
Having bowed to Śaṅkhalādevikā and having prostrated before Turādevī,
he then bowed to the goddess Vyāghrī and prostrated before the virtuous Śrīkharkharī.
Then, having bowed to Rāṇikā, he went to Kuṅkumavāpikā,
and after prostrating before Mahālakṣmī who was situated on the bank of the pond, [he departed].
Having bowed to the golden-hued city and the abode of Nārāyaṇa,
and having bowed to and beheld Aśvasaras, he went to the northern bank.
Having bowed to Śāṅkara and Kṣetrapaiśa and then drunk the water,
he searched for the Arka tree and saw it nearby.
Having begged for alms consisting of fruits, roots, and leaves and having eaten them,
he stood for a moment at the foot of an Arka tree, meditating upon the Lord Sun.
At the root of the Arka tree, he heard an invisible voice saying:
"May it be well with you, O Kāyastha; stay here, recite your prayers, and remember the Sun. (66)
Worship eternally in the morning the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa;
worship Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of the Sun and the Master of the virtuous. (67)
I worship Him, the Lord of the lords of the gods;
from Him I have obtained all splendor and sovereignty as well.
"I am Sūrya; I shall bring you prosperity. Worship Hari!
After performing one hundred thousand recitations, O Sārasa, merely by bathing with [the water from] my hands," (69)
"By the power of the Sun, you two shall become full-bodied and free from disease.
Having heard these words, Corjavrata performed his vow beneath a tree sacred to the Sun.
He dwells in the root region, clothes himself in bark garments and the like, and sustains his life through a livelihood that is unasked for and free from excess. ||71||
Subsisting on fruits, roots, and leaves, and likewise subsisting on water at times;
salutations to you, O Brahmā-Savitṛ, the remover of leprosy; salutations, salutations!
With his mind fixed on the Sun, that king of devotees constantly recited this great mantra;
he performed five thousand recitations every day.
On the twenty-first day, when the hundred thousand recitations were completed,
Corjavratika, full of enthusiasm, remained mindful of Sūryanārāyaṇa.
In the morning, he went quickly to bathe on the shore of the Aśvapaṭṭa lake;
O King, having plunged into the water there, he bathed repeatedly on that bank. (75)
Diving in and emerging again and again, the scribe looks at his hands;
yet he does not see them as healthy, so he bathes repeatedly.
Again he looked for his two hands, but he did not see them at all;
thus, having bathed and undergone exhaustion, he became despondent. (77)
The scribe reflected upon his own failure regarding his recitation and vows;
then, overcome by grief, he remembered Sūryanārāyaṇa.
A voice from the sky said to him: "O devotee, your vow here has indeed been fulfilled in every respect; nothing remains to be done there. (79)
Having meditated upon the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa at the hour of midday, you shall bathe quickly; then your hands will heal.
Those fingers and both hands that have been destroyed by galat-kuṣṭha, as well as the entire palm—that everything shall cause to grow anew. (81)
Having been addressed thus, the scribe Corjavrataka went to Arkasthalī;
and at midday, he bathed according to the rules prescribed by the Smṛtis.
Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa and Sūryanarāyaṇa, both having become boys of equal age and identical form, [appeared]. ||83||
Beautiful, with faces graced by gentle smiles, wearing divine earrings, their limbs were proportionate to their form, and they were worshipped by the gods of gods and others. ||84||
Having arrived, he took by both hands the two arms of Kāyasthabhaktaka, who was bathing while standing in the middle of the water, and having lifted him up, he brought him out.
The two of them placed the moon, with its full orb, upon the shore of the lake;
however, when held by the Sun, his left hand became "most full" (pūrṇatama).
The hand of Dakṣa, held by Hari, became most perfect;
though his body was dark-complexioned, it likewise became so through splendor and ascetic power.
Through merits resulting from the touch of Nārāyaṇa, he then became white in form;
like the sun, like Kṛṣṇa, he then became equal to them.
The people there, devoted to a great wonder, beheld three men of identical form, endowed with a splendor like that of gods. ||89||
Then that devotee, his desires fulfilled, fell again and again at the feet of both the glorious Nārāyaṇas.
I have been delivered from leprosy and delivered from the disease of worldly existence;
O Hari-Kṛṣṇa, if I were to attain satisfaction upon obtaining [you] in my hands! 9.1.
Since we two have met, our reunion is no longer certain;
therefore, O Lords, do not abandon me once you have purified me by meeting me.
Having firmly resolved upon the *ūrjavrata* vow, he indeed spoke to their feet: "I must no longer remain in this world of mortals, which is an ocean of suffering. (93)
"O you two Nārāyaṇas, Kṛṣṇas, grant me deliverance!
Thus spoke the Sūrya, remaining here in my palace as a *kāyastha*. (94)
"Perform a small auspicious rite for me; establish my consecration so that, following the bathing of those afflicted by leprosy, [they may attain health] merely by the sight of me. (95)
Likewise, by worshipping the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Lord of Diseases is likewise appeased, and one's pilgrimage becomes complete in this world. (96)
Having done this, you shall indeed proceed from there to the solar orb (ravimaṇḍala),
and from there to the world of truth (satyaloka), and then to the circle of the Siddhas.
"From there you will go to Vaikuṇṭha itself, and from there to the Imperishable (Akṣara).
Having spoken thus, the two deities—the Sun and Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa—vanished.
Stationed as a scribe and possessing a divine body, he caused a temple to be built and duly installed Sūryanārāyaṇa therein. 99.
O King, at that time, the splendors of the two Nārāyaṇas became completely pervaded throughout the waters on all sides.
Then the fish, the oysters, the gems, and the waters, as well as the particles of dust pervaded by that light, became like suns. || 10.1 ||
Such were those primordial elements; even today they exist within the waters, and from them indeed are born the lustrous mother-of-pearl shells.
Jewels, pebbles, dust, and lotuses—
along with their stalks— are always completely pervaded by its rays.
And here, Sūryanārāyaṇa exists, endowed with splendor, even in water, in mother-of-pearl, and in gems; though his form is invisible within the temple, he dwells there.
O King, that splendor always spreads everywhere;
from that, Sūryatīrtha was born, manifest with the orb of the sun.
Then, after some time, one who observed the *ūrja* vow went to the chariot of the Sun;
through the power of Nārāyaṇa’s grace, he attained liberation by means of his devotion.
This holy site, which destroys leprosy, offers the direct vision of the Sun;
its waters, oyster shells, and other objects are resplendent, pervaded by the brilliance of the Sun.
Likewise, there is Arkatīrtha and this auspicious Urjavratatīrtha,
as well as Kāyasthatīrtha, which destroys all diseases.
Thus addressed by Rādhikā, the king performed the pilgrimage according to the prescribed rites;
having bathed, he gave gifts and worshipped the Sun-god Narāyaṇa.
Then the king, together with Lomaśa, proceeded further to another sacred site;
by reciting or hearing this, a person shall attain health and liberation.

Thus ends the two hundred and sixty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Sun-worship by the clerk suffering from leprosy who performed the *ūrja-vrata*, his recovery from disease and liberation, the Sūryatīrtha, and so forth," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmīnārāyaṇīya-saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Then, O Rādhikā, Aśvapaṭṭala, accompanied by Lomaśa,
went ahead to the supremely purifying Śārṅgadhra-tīrtha.
Aśvapāṭala said:
O gentle one, what is the nature of this beautiful and delightful Kavi-tīrtha,
wherein my knowledge that awakens the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas flashes forth?
Śrī Lomaśa said: O King, this supreme tīrtha, filled with great wonders,
indeed exists here due to the power of the high-souled sage Śārṅgadhara.
The high-souled Śārṅgadhara was a Brahmin devoid of intelligence;
he was the son of Śṛṅgadhara and resided in Dharmāraṇya. || 4 ||
From his childhood, however, he did not know how to speak at all, like one who is dull-witted;
moreover, due to the defect known as "shortness of the tongue" (jihvāhrasva), he behaved like a mute. || 5 ||
Aśvapāṭala said:
How did his tongue become short? Tell me also about his stupidity; and how is it that he remains like one mute, even though childhood is the abode of fickleness? (6)
Śrī Lomaśa said: In a previous birth, he was a Śūdra who dwelt in the Daṇḍaka forest;
he was devoted to violence and likewise intent on reviling the scriptures and the gods.
He indeed tormented the Brahmins who performed sacrifices with harsh words;
moreover, being an atheist, he did not acknowledge the incarnations of Nārāyaṇa at all.
Wherever a discourse takes place, she speaks it falsely;
devoted solely to her own interests, she says everything merely for the sake of nourishing her belly. (9)
Thus, once while wandering along the banks of the Gautamī intent on disparagement,
he went there for the sake of hunting and beheld a horned deer.
Just as he was fixing an arrow to his bow to kill the deer,
the deer, out of fear, quickly fled toward the Gautamī river.
Thereafter, having vanished into the thicket of trees,
Śūdraka also fled toward the bank in pursuit of him.
He saw that deer again on the banks of the Godāvarī;
and an arrow released by the Śūdra entered the back of the deer.
The deer, having leaped, fell into the current of the river;
deprived of consciousness, he sank into the bottomless water of the swift-flowing stream.
Drawn by the force of the water, he went to the bottom with his arrow;
having died in the midst of the water, he was indeed devoured by a crocodile. || 15 ||
Constantly remembering, "Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa, O Hari-Kṛṣṇa, Nārāyaṇa," even that deer, by virtue of the greatness of the holy place and through the remembrance of the Supreme Lord, [attained liberation].
Born in Dharmāraṇya from death at a meritorious tīrtha,
that brāhmaṇa was indeed a child of Parṇadhara, marked with the sign of a horn.
In the house of the brāhmaṇa, a group of brāhmaṇas devoted to Kṛṣṇa became rememberers of their past lives, and they indeed continued to worship Mādhava.
Remembering the Gaṅgā, Godāvarī, Sindhu, Yamunā, and Sarasvatī, he bathes; O Hari-Kṛṣṇa, he indeed praises you day and night.
Although he was but a child, he grew up; his father made him wear horns, and the powerful youth, wearing the sacred thread, studied the scriptures.
He was devoted to righteous deeds and had indeed married;
then, that Śūdra died in the forest on the bank of the Godāvarī.
His kinsmen performed the cremation of his body on the Godāvarī;
by the power of that merit, his sins were consumed by fire.
At the time of death, he too remembered that deer upon which the arrow had been fixed;
by the power of that [act], that Śūdra became the son of Śṛṅgadhara.
In the Forest of Dharma there was a brahmin who, though born of a śūdra mother, was as dull-witted as one following the conduct of a śūdra.
His father, possessing the nature of one who remembers his past lives, knew everything;
this son, however, did not know at all: "Who was I in my previous body?"
That child, deprived of speech, was born as if mute. ||25||
Since his tongue is short, he does not even know how to speak properly from childhood;
he pronounces syllables that are clipped and broken, saying "mamma" and "caccā. (26)
Mute and unable to speak, he was given the name Śārṅgadhara;
though bound by his father’s debt, he was invested with the sacred thread.
Indeed, he experiences muteness as the fruit of the censure committed in a previous birth;
likewise, he experiences foolishness and lack of mental clarity as the fruit of atheism.
The fruit of his killing a deer was indeed his birth as her son;
for the purpose of repaying a debt, he was born in your abode on Śṛṅgadhara.
The fruit of his death at a sacred ford is considered to be rebirth in the house of a Brahmin;
yet, due to his folly, his muteness, and his dullness, he is devoid of human qualities.
Like one who is dull-witted, he set his mind on performing penance in Dharmāraṇya;
indeed, having stood there, he began [his practice] while remaining upon the crest of an anthill.
Subsisting on fruits, roots, and leaves, he performed severe penance;
bathing daily at the three periods of the day, he engaged in mental recitation.
People came together to see him, thinking, "The mute one is indeed established in austerity," yet he did not look at anyone; he then remained with his eyes closed.
Performing his recitation with a rosary, he did not consider that a wonder;
he remembered that Blessed One who bestows Sarasvatī upon the tongue. (34)
To Kṛṣṇa, the treasure-trove of the Vedas, Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Lord, the refuge of all sciences, the omniscient one, the beloved of Śrī Kṛṣṇa. ||35||
Thus he muttered prayers for ten years and performed corresponding austerities;
during the rainy seasons he lived in an anthill, while in other times he resided at the foot of a Plakṣa tree.
Deprived of his leaf-hut, likewise lacking a canopy, deprived of seats and the like, and destitute of coverings; ||37||
Wearing matted hair, a beard, and ashes, he was an ascetic of extreme austerity;
possessing only bark garments and a loincloth, he was always a bowl-in-hand mendicant.
Ten years later, in the month of Kārttika, on the Prabodhinī lunar day, a voice from the sky sang to him at night, entering between his ears: (39)
O Brahmin, you have attained perfection through austerity; much of your impurity has been removed, for you have brought an end to the offenses committed in your previous births.
Then, through ascetic penance and devotional worship,
you must go with great vigilance on foot to the foremost sacred site, the Aśvapaṭṭa-sarovara lake.
In the vicinity of the western ocean, on the island known as Ānarta, in the region of Saurāṣṭra, there exists the field of the Imperishable (Akṣarakṣetra). ||41||
By name it is the city called Kuṅkumavāpī, the refuge of Acyuta;
for it is the eternal abode of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. (43)
"Oṃ, salutation to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord; svāhā!
Recite this mantra constantly and go to that supreme land. 44.

Through the power of place, the power of location, the power of the hermitage, as well as the power of the deity and the power of effort, even that which is impossible to accomplish becomes accomplished. 45.
Having spoken thus, that voice ceased;
then the Brahmin, having bowed to his father and mother, and having prostrated at the site of his ascetic penance, [departed].
Having bowed to Valmīka and Plakṣa as well, the pilgrim proceeded to Gayā,
Kāśī, Prayāga, Indraprastha, and the forest of Yamunā.

And having visited Puṣkara and the river Sarasvatī, which is frequented by the Siddhas, as well as Bahucarā and Satī, and having performed his ablutions at those sacred fords (tīrthas), [he departed].
He entered Saurāṣṭra and reached Mount Catuṣṭila;
having gone there, he arrived at the field named Akṣara, known as Kuṅkumavāpī.

Having seen that most magnificent and delightful lake, which resembled the ocean, which was the refuge of all sacred fords (tīrthas), and the eternal abode of the God of gods, the Goddess, and the virtuous women; || 1.264.50 ||
It was beautified by the meditative rites and other practices performed by great sages during the twilight hours,
and it was augmented by the people dwelling at the holy ford through their bathing, giving of gifts, and other such acts.
It was filled with flocks of birds such as swans, garuḍas, and peacocks,
and was surrounded on all sides by groves of mango trees and trees bearing the fruit of immortality.
It was always protected by hosts such as Īśāna and Vaśyadeva,
and it resounded with the chanting of the Vedas from the sacrificial grounds, pavilions, and other sites.
It was adorned with wish-fulfilling cows, desire-granting creepers, and wish-fulfilling gems, and it held a Vaiṣṇava sacrifice performed by devotees intent on chanting his praises.
It was adorned by celestial maidens, princesses, and the beloved consorts of Brahmā, and it was endowed with the city of Kuṅkumānagara, which possessed a splendor surpassing that of Vaikuṇṭha. 55.
He was endowed with a crown that pervaded the halo of light, and he possessed Rādhā, Ramā, Satī, Lakṣmī, Kamalā, and Mandirā. 56.
At the summit of the temple of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa,
it was filled with the spreading radiance of a thousand golden jars.
It was filled with great abundance due to temples, the abodes of the virtuous, and celestial palaces;
it resounded with the noise of the celestial chariots traveling back and forth along the paths of the sky.
It is praised by its own supplicants for destroying the suffering of the afflicted;
its water is as cool as the moon, sweet as honey, and possesses the fragrance of musk.
Beholding that lake— which purifies even sinners, bestows liberation, and grants Brahman—
a Brahmin suddenly attained a divine state.
Having forgotten all other sacred fords, he attained supreme peace;
and having gone to the northern bank, he partook of a drink of water.
Having bathed according to the proper rite and partaken of bulbs and roots,
he then performed the rites for the gods and the ancestors, and thereafter offered circumambulations.
O King, standing on this northern spot, he chanted the mantra,
bathing daily at the three periods of the day and constantly worshipping the great sages.
Pure and devoted to the worship, hymns, and offerings due to the gods, he was constantly joyful,
as if he had already attained Vaikuṇṭha or Goloka.
Thus, with joy, the mute Brahmin realized that he had accomplished his purpose;
then, having learned [the way], he went to Lomaśa’s hermitage filled with delight.
Having bowed, he rejoiced in many ways and fell at the feet of the sage;
filled with devotion, he performed a massage of the sage's feet.
Then, holding the tip of his tongue with the tips of his hands, he showed it [to him] and also made a request through gesture: "O Lord, let there be speech for me. (67)
The sage replied, "So be it," for his tongue abandoned its shortness;
O King, it became capable of grasping phonemes while in my hermitage.
Then he received from me the mantra of Nārāyaṇa:
"May that Lord Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa be my master."
Having thus received the mantra, the brahmin bathed again on this bank and, during the night, recited the two mantras according to the prescribed rite.
Then, indeed, during the Brāhma-muhūrta on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Kārtika,
the Blessed One manifested himself, becoming visible to his sight.
Aśvaśiras, the upholder of the Vedas, the refuge of the Vedas, the great Lord;
horse-faced with a human body, he is resplendent with all branches of knowledge. ||72||
Then Kṛṣṇa, accompanied by Śāradā, spoke to the brāhmaṇa:
"Speak, O brāhmaṇa; I am pleased. What is in your heart? (7.3)
Having thus seen and heard the ancient Lord, the brahmin rose up suddenly and performed a prostration like a staff according to the prescribed rite.
Having worshipped him with the flowers of his inner disposition, he paid homage with auspicious words:
"O embodiment of Dharma, O son of Dharma, O awakener in the Forest of Dharma! (75)
O Lord, seeing you who are righteous and performing austerities, you became filled with compassion and rescued me as I was submerged in the ocean of saṃsāra. ||76||
Without compassion there is indeed no other cause here;
this is the reason I have obtained the cleansing of my former sins in this world. (77)
O divine one of divine form, O ocean of compassion, you have indeed obtained here the vision of that divine place through the words of the venerable Lomaśa. (78)
By your blessing and by seeing you now, I have become one who remembers my past lives; here I remember your reproach. (79)
Whatever sin was committed by me in a previous birth while belonging to the Śūdra caste in the Daṇḍaka forest— all that has gone to destruction because of the deer that was killed by me.
And my father Śṛṅgadhara dwells there with his wife Śṛṅgikā; however, to repay his debt, I, Mūkaputra, am staying at his house.
I was born through my connection with the Gomatī-tīrtha and attained the status of a Brahmin;
yet, if a Brahmin is devoid of knowledge, he is a sinner who merely bears the name. (82)
"Therefore, bestow upon me here that knowledge which liberates one from the debts to the ancestors.
Having said this, he prostrated himself, saying: "Oṃ, salutations to the Supreme Self! (83)
Then the Blessed Lord said: "O Brahmin, by my desire and by a mere drop of my grace, you have become a true follower of the Vedas, O wielder of the Śārṅga bow. (84)
Be one who understands all medicinal herbs, who knows the true nature of tastes, and who likewise recognizes their qualities; indeed, be possessed of divine strength in every way. (85)
Having spoken thus, O King, the Blessed One quickly vanished there;
likewise did the goddess Śāradā and that medicinal luster disappear before the brahmin.
The brahmin, possessing the long-life-bestowing Veda, entered [the body] which was yellowish-green in color;
at that very moment, he obtained the knowledge in his hand.
Thereupon, he quickly composed the compendium named Śārṅgadhara in the field of Kuṅkumavāpikā, in the presence of Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa.
Having gone there and received their blessings, he honored Lomaśa and caused the brahmins to be instructed. || 89 ||
Thus, O King, Śārṅgadhara also obtained a vision here of the horse-headed form of Hari; that very place is the sacred ford known as Śārṅgadhara.
It is known as Āśvaśirasa and also as Śāradātīrtha; it is indeed supreme, for it is there that penance and other such practices are performed.
The knowledge of the Vedas, which destroys censure, sin, and other evils, is thereby obtained;
bathe and give auspicious sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to the Brahmins and to the destitute.
Then, after some time, that brahmin went to Dharmavana;
having reached his father, he rejoiced and attained eternal fame. (93)
That which cannot be attained through austerity, material wealth, effort, or even prosperity,
is indeed achieved through meditation, blessings, and devotion.
O King, through the power of instruction, the power of the basis, and service such as this, that which is difficult to obtain becomes easy to obtain. (95)
Thus addressed, the king there, having honored Śārṅgadhara as well as the twice-born, performed his ablutions in the waters of the lake. (96)
O Rādhikā, knowing thus the power of that very holy place, he then gave gifts many times according to the prescribed rites. (97)
He gave gifts of jewels, gifts of cows, and gifts of knowledge;
he gave gifts of umbrellas, gifts of garments, and gifts of ornaments. ||98||
Then Aśvapāṭala,
having bowed to the sacred ford and the gods, together with Lomaśa, performed the gift of food and the gift of gold.
Filled with a sense of its greatness, he went forward to another auspicious holy site;
by reciting or hearing this, one indeed becomes possessed of knowledge.

Thus ends the two hundred and sixty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Birth of the Mute Brāhmaṇa in Dharmāraṇya through Death in the Godāvarī by a Censuring Śūdra and Deer-Slayer; the Knowledge of the Science of Herbs at Kuṅkumavāpī for One Whose Sins are Exhausted by Austerity; the Removal of Dumbness and the Authorship of the Śārṅgadharasaṃhitā; and the Description of Śārṅgadharatīrtha, Aśvaśiras-tīrtha, and Others," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā. || 264 ||
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Rādhikā, listen further to that holy place which destroys all decay.
Having gone there, King Aśvapāṭala questioned Lomaśa. (1)
Aśvapāṭala said:
"O Guru, tell me the majesty of this sacred site along with its names;
tell me what kind of fruit it yields, when it originated, and for whom."
Śrī Lomaśa said:
O King, in ancient times there was an auspicious Śūdra named Pārṣṇirada,
a protector of goats who lived on the banks of the Bhadrā river.
In the forest, that merciless one indeed casts groups of men, women, and even children into a thicket of small jujube trees.
For this world is intent upon its own self-interest; without its own interest, it does not protect others.
Even the daughters of goats become givers of milk only after two years have passed.
But his many sons who are childless, fruitless, and useless—
he considers them a mere burden to be protected in vain, and thus abandons them in a desolate place.
Indeed, at the time of giving birth to a goat, he gazes upon the young female and the young male;
being merciless, he casts men into nets and the like, or upon thorns and the like.
But the girls always protected the goats out of hope;
thus indeed were the children abandoned in the net by those who roam the forest.
And at night, they are devoured by cruel creatures such as jackals;
thus, those children meet their death with great suffering.
And there the children curse those tormentors who cause them suffering, saying:
"Just as we were cast into the forest, slain, and devoured. (2.265.10)
"Likewise, your children shall be devoured by forest-dwelling creatures;
thus do animals curse, for those who protect them are like their own sons. (11)
Thus, fools who repeatedly inflict suffering upon others surely perish;
they are born without progeny, for by them have been slain those in the form of sons.

Sons are indeed said to be of many kinds; he who is born of one's own wife is the aurasa (legitimate son). He who is begotten on a woman without a husband is an adopted son (dāyāda), having been placed in the lap by another.
The son of one's family, as well as the servant who is like a son,
the disciple who is indeed a son, and the son who has come for refuge— || 14 ||
O King, those who have been protected and those who have been instructed are also called "sons";
these are declared to be the sons and daughters of Manu.
By constantly saying "Father," one becomes a son who is truly like him;
likewise, there are cattle, goats, camels, horses, deer, and sheep. (16)

Thus ends the two hundred and sixty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Curing of Tuberculosis through Bathing and Other Rites at Aśvapaṭṭasara Lake by the Śūdra Cowherd named Pārṣṇirada, and the Nārada Tīrtha," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Śrī-Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O beloved Queen of the Rāsa, afterwards the king went to that foremost of holy places;
there he inquired of Lomaśa regarding its greatness and even its name.
Aśvapāṭala said:
O Guru, tell me briefly when this holy place (tīrtha) attained fame here, what its power is, and by whom it was established— explain all of that in summary.
Śrī Lomaśa said: O King, in ancient times, at the commencement of creation, Vyāsa himself, who is Hari,
came here in the form of Śvetavyāsa with a desire to visit the sacred fords (tīrthas).
Having established a supreme sacred site (tīrtha) here, having bathed and worshipped Mādhava, and thereafter having bowed down to the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa; || 4 ||
He went to Vastrāpatha, Somanātha, and Mūladvārāvatī;
likewise, he visited Gopanātha, Stambhatīrtha, and Puṣkara.
He went to Kurukṣetra, where indeed his own residence was located;
at that time, he had many disciples on earth who were knowers of the Vedas and other scriptures.
In ancient times, there were those who performed acts such as the giving of knowledge for the sake of the liberation of the world;
here, indeed, at a distance of one yojana from Arkapura, [he] came to be.
The brahmin Dharmasumantuka was indeed a disciple of Śvetavyāsa;
that great ṛṣi, who was equal to Vyāsa, always resided on the bank of the lake.
Having made his own abode in the banyan tree, he [taught] many people the path of spiritual welfare, which consists of knowledge, devotion, and is endowed with righteousness.
He gave instructions constantly and was attended by Brahmins;
the people of the neighboring villages were eager there to hear his discourse.
They always arrive in the evening and depart once again;
without Hari there is no auspiciousness, and without devotion there is no liberation.
Without knowledge, there is no dissolution of darkness in this illusory house;
indeed, without a saintly person, there is no direct attainment of the Blessed Lord.
The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa indeed dwells within us; worship that Hari-Kṛṣṇa who exists in the form of Śveta Vyāsa. 1.3.
Thus he gives instruction and even causes [others] to recite the Saṃhitā;
and he goes daily to Aśvapaṭṭasara for his morning bath.
Having performed the rites for the sacred ford and bowed to Śrī Puruṣottama,
and having paid homage to the sages and worshipped the gods, he proceeds to his own abode.
While the Brahmin, a knower of the Vedas who was thus engaged in performing rites at sacred fords,
was traveling on a path in a desolate place, he was bitten by a snake.
Quickly becoming intent on yoga and sitting in meditative absorption (samādhi),
he restrained his breath and [beheld] a serpent moving along the bank of the path.
That brahmin challenged him and forcibly brought him under his control;
even the powerful serpent, having fallen into terror, then [departed] from that spot.
Though he strove to flee, he was unable to run away;
having fallen under the power of the brahmins, he repeatedly ran back into their presence.
Having arrived, he fell down crying out, "Protect me! Protect me!
and said, "O twice-born one, I have indeed committed an offense against you here by biting you."
"Do not kill me, O best of Brahmins; my life-breaths are as dear to you as they are to me.
I beg your forgiveness, for I am of a tamasic nature and my disposition is such. (21)
"O twice-born one, you are of a sattvic nature; your disposition is the dharma of compassion.
When will my liberation come about as I wander through the wombs of animals? (22)
"By your yoga, my liberation shall come even though I am an offender here;
O Brahmin, act in such a way that my liberation may indeed be achieved. (23)
Or rather, bestow upon me knowledge alone and make me pure;
I pray that you do not kill me with the thought that I am an enemy. (24)
Having heard the serpent’s words, Dharmasumantu then became filled with compassion and questioned him regarding the cause of his birth.
"Who are you, and by what karma have you come to this serpent birth?
You know how to speak of everything, yet you do not act for your own welfare. (26)
What is the reason for this, O serpent? Being one who knows, why do you wander about? Knowing me, you have bitten me; what benefit do you consider yourself to have gained from this? (27)
The serpent said:
"Listen, O Brahmin, I shall tell you everything afterwards exactly as it happened;
I am about to relate news of my gain, for this question is not appropriate. (28)
The Creator fashioned creation in three ways, consisting of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*.
Those characterized by *sattva* desire tranquility, while those characterized by *rajas* likewise desire passion. (29)
Those of a tamasic nature desire suffering; this is their inherent nature, difficult to overcome.
Fire indeed blazes forth; what gain is there truly in its burning?
Water always wards off thirst for living beings;
rain pours down—tell me, what is the benefit of water here? ||3 1||
The wind blows in some places harshly, in others cruelly, and in others gently with great force;
what gain could there be in that, since such is its very nature? (32)
The person of sattvic nature attains peace; water carries coldness, the moon is cool, and the stone is cold—what benefit is there in that for their sake? (33)
The ocean is salty by nature, yet its water is sweet; the neem tree is bitter, while ginger is pungent—what indeed is gained for him therein? (34)
The flower of the Japā is red, saffron is red, and the classes of deities are characterized by passion (rājasa); what indeed is the gain in being passionate? ||35||
The fall of lightning, the fall of thunderbolts, death at the time of universal destruction, as well as death and darkness—these are indeed tamasic by their very nature. (36)
Bhangā, gañjā, and dhattūra are tamasic by their very nature;
tell me here, O learned one, what benefit indeed arises from them that is born of tamas? (37)
In the vow of darkness (tamas), the attainment of one's own true nature is indeed not seen;
beings proceed according to their qualities, like water flowing downward. //38//
Activity proceeds according to its own nature, like the chewing of teeth; however, action that is innate would be like the killing caused by the falling of a weapon. (39)
I have done this for that reason; you ought not to be angry with me.
You have no news of profit either, like a bull among Brahmins who has finished his ritual bath.
Sleep occurs at night and likewise wakefulness during the day;

In childhood the mind is intent on play, in youth on desire, and likewise in old age on delusion;

Some are virtuous, some are engaged in deeds such as theft, some possess divine power, and some are seekers of gain; tell me, what is the significance of this? (43)
I am indeed a serpent of the nature of darkness (tāmasa), and my fangs are considered to be of that same nature;

Poison indeed has the nature of fire; it flows in the form of saliva.

Just as water and other fluids flow through the network of channels, so too does blood;

For an embodied being, both gain and liberation depend upon this transient body;

The attainment of liberation is the supreme gain for you, as it is for me and for all embodied beings.
Do not harbor anger, O best of Brahmins; indeed, wrath leads to hell.
"O Brahmin, it was through my own anger that I attained this womb, so fierce with poison and known as hell; therefore, do not direct your wrath toward me. (52)
Dharmasumantu said:

Gain is indeed acquisition and conjunction; what indeed is the use of that for the insentient?

O serpent, you are a sharer in the sin of Brahmin-slaughter; you are the bearer of this fault here.

If I were to kill you, no gain would be found for me either;

"Non-gain is equal for both of us; tell me, who are you, a man of such discernment?

The serpent said: "O Brahmin, by nature you are gentle and devoted to compassion;

That time has passed and will never return once gone;
yet at that time, I dwelt here within this human being who possessed the body of a Kṣatriya.
In Arkagrāma, your prosperous village endowed with every abundance,

One who is an atheist, a reviler, one who treats Brahmins with contempt, devoid of righteous deeds, and always devoted to rationalistic sophistry; ||72||

"This tiger cursed me, saying, 'Let the reviler meet his death';

Snakes and scorpions, poisonous dogs and anti-poisonous herbs;
bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, and the like, as well as the messengers of Yama and the planetary spirits (grahas). ||88||
Fire, water, fever, and even enemies are merely instrumental causes;

"Indeed, not knowing this truth, they hate the scorpions and other such creatures;
therefore, O Brahmin, death is certain for you here, and my own death is also certain."
"You are capable of bringing about liberation for both me and yourself;
for the human body is the field of action, and by means of it, everything is attained. (91)
"Even at the cost of one's life, a superior person surely protects the doer;
death is indeed certain, so perform our deliverance. (92)
O Brahmin, the gift of fearlessness to living beings indeed yields a fruit greater than that of all sacrifices; therefore, grant me liberation. 93.
