He indeed abandoned his body right there in that desolate wilderness on the road;
meanwhile, his soul reached Lake Aśvapaṭṭa.
There, at the feet of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, he remained until the end according to his understanding. Then, the Brahmin was seen dead by the local farmers. 98.
The farmer went to the village and related that event to the brahmins; the twice-born ones then took the corpse to the Aśvapaṭṭa lake in order to cremate it. (99)
All the kinsmen arrived and wept on the bank of the lake;
having laid down the corpse, they all indeed sang the praises of the twice-born man’s virtues.
Equal to Śvetavyāsa, devoted to the performance of dharma, and a bestower of liberation upon the worlds—such a brāhmaṇa is indeed rare to find. (101)
This disciple of Śvetavyāsa, who had reached the further shore of the state of meditative absorption (samādhi), died due to the bite of a snake; that indeed is a marvel.
Life that has reached the state of being severed is not joined together by anyone, except by the Supreme Self and the yogi who is the Guru. (103)
Speaking thus, they called to mind Śvetavyāsa;
they also called to mind Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the glorious Puruṣottama.
Then, O King, his wife Viprāṇī, afflicted with intense grief, approached the vicinity of the funeral pyre out of her desire to remain chaste. 105.
She remembered Śvetavyāsa as well as Kṛṣṇa-Narāyaṇa;
having worshipped the corpse according to the prescribed rites, she committed it to the funeral pyre.
Having kindled the fire, as he strove to burn [the world] from the tips of his feet, at that moment the Blessed One, beloved of Kṛṣṇa, appeared there by the power of devotion.
The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, possessing a white form and manifest as Śveta Vyāsa, arrived there together with Dharma Sumantu.
Going together to the side of the funeral pyre, he said to Satī:
"This husband of yours is indeed here; take him, do not follow me into the flames."
At that moment, the Brahmin arose, breathing and laughing as if alive; Satī became submerged once more, and the Brahmins also became pleased.
Having performed their ablutions at that sacred ford, they all then proceeded toward Arkapura; O King, that place is the sacred ford known as Śvetavyāsa, as well as Satītīrtha.
"This is Jīvatīrtha; bathe here and perform the ritual of the sacred ford.
Thus was King Aśvapāṭala instructed there, O Rādhikā. (112)
He performed worship to Śvetavyāsa, undertook ritual ablutions,
gave many gifts, and then departed for another place.
Together with Lomaśa, he remained steady on another sacred ford (tīrtha) on the bank;
he remembered Śrī Hari, yet he did not pay homage to that tīrtha or the temple.

Thus ends the two hundred and sixty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Serpent’s State for King Arkapurī due to the Curse of the Sages Dharma and Sumantu, the Brahmin’s Bite by the Serpent, the Liberation from the Serpent, the Revival of the Brahmin through the Prayer of his Wife Satī by Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa at Aśvapaṭṭa-sarovara, and the Description of Śvetavyāsa-tīrtha and Satī-tīrtha," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Then, O Rādhā, having gone to that holy place which increases the dharma of women,
King Aśvapāṭala questioned the sage Lomaśa.
Aśvapāṭala said:
O Guru, what is this auspicious holy place that grants liberation from the female state?
Tell me when it came into being—this bestower of dharma and great power. (2)
Śrī Lomaśa said: Listen, O King, to the account of Satītīrtha, which is purifying and most wonderful.
It was there that the wife of the king of Surāṣṭra, who resided in Vastrāpatha, [performed her penance]. || 3 ||
And there was a great virtuous woman named Rāṇikā, devoted to her husband,
who protected King Rakṣāṅgāraka, who resembled Lord Śiva.
In that most excellent city named Svarṇapattana, the virtuous woman, eager to serve him in every way, attended upon her beloved. || 5 ||
In the capital city of Sadurgā, situated near Mount Kṛtasmara on the banks of the river Svarṇalekhā,
there was a golden royal palace.
A woman who never looked upon the sun, being endowed with the dharma of a virtuous wife,
constantly worshipped Hari, namely Dāmodara Vāmana.
That virtuous Rāṇikā, the mother of the king, indeed observes a vow of chastity;
she must never touch any other man anywhere except her own husband.
One should not touch the garment of another man, except for a new one;
nor should one ever look upon the face of another man, except for one's own husband.
She should not go anywhere outside the house without her husband;
she always performs service for her husband with her own hands.
The diligent Raṇikā herself provided everything— food, drink, betel, and body massage.
He constantly worships Dāmodara, Kṛṣṇa, and Vāmana,
having offered leaves, flowers, fruits, water, and food to Viṣṇu.
Having first given [food] to a great and virtuous guest, as well as to a cow, to her husband,
and to the circle of her dependents, that virtuous woman then eats.
Thus she remained devoted to the Dharma, dedicated to her vows and observances;
in whose house Śrīdevī, the sovereign of existence, always dwells.
Mahālakṣmī, in the form of a female companion, accepts the worship performed by her;
thus it was for that lady of delicate limbs as the night drew to a close.
Indeed, during a dream within his sleep, there was a vision of Mlecchas;
an army had arrived from all sides to seize his kingdom. (16)
Then King Rakṣāṅgāraka also set out for battle;
however, the husband died in the fight, and indeed, an undesirable sight appeared.
Quickly rising from her bed, Satī said to her husband:
"O Lord, today I have seen an inauspicious, evil dream that portends destruction. (18)
Then I worship Śrī Mahālakṣmī, the sovereign lady of existence;
I worship Vyāghreśvarī and I bow down to Vighnarāja.
Having thus gathered his hopes, he quickly bathed and worshipped them;
and having paid homage to the deities, he prayed for their protection.
For the sake of destroying inauspiciousness, Queen Rāṇikā repeatedly prayed to Vighnarāja and likewise bestowed gifts.
Then he had the propitiation of the planets performed by the twice-born and others;
thereafter, Mahālakṣmī, the sovereign lady of existence, appeared visibly and was well-pleased.
He said to her: "An obstacle to the kingdom will arise from the Mleccha tribes;
moreover, a battle will take place here between both of our armies. (23)
"O King, let not Rakṣāṅgāraka go forth to battle; let him certainly not go outside the fortress, and then you shall indeed have victory. (24)
And the enemies shall perish on all sides outside the fortress;
you have victory within the fortress, but defeat outside the fortress. (25)
Thus addressed, that virtuous woman related all of that to the king;
the king, too, remained attentive within his own abode.
Then, from the five directions, Mlecchas arrived accompanied by their armies;
numbering in the tens of thousands, they were armed and mounted upon elephants. ||27||
The cavalry and those stationed on chariots, having blocked the gates of the fortress on all sides and secured the closure of the entrances, remained steadfast.
Indeed, the arrogant royal officers, along with their armies, blocked the gates within the city and stood there armed. (29)
And from all sides, many enemies hurled destructive mechanical balls at the fortress to conquer the city. (2.267.30)
Even after many days, they were not at all able to enter;
then those foremost of Mlecchas employed a stratagem to create a breach.
Having given wealth in gold and silver, he also bribed the inhabitants of the market towns; having learned from an informant the secret path for entering the city...
Having broken through the fortress and entered through its gate, the Mleccha tribes fought, plundered, and proceeded to the royal palace.
Then the royal armies fought on, staking their very lives;
indeed, many were slain according to their will, and many royal soldiers were killed. (34)
The commanders of the armies were indeed slain by the blows of weapons,
when the army consisting of Mleccha people reached their own abode.
Then the king descended into the fray to fight for his own protection;
thereafter, the subjects also, together with their forces, slew many of the Mlecchas.
The great army of the Kṣatriyas, joined with the protective power of embers, fought against the great Mlecchas and slew them while they were still alive. ||37||
Others fled even through the middle of the city;
abandoning the fortress, the Mlecchas ran out in all directions.
The king, indeed, being intoxicated by battle, forgot the words of his own virtuous wife and went out from the fortress to fight and slay the fleeing Mlecchas.
Turning back, they then fought by giving up their lives;
with blows from their weapons, they struck Rakṣa Aṅgāraka on all sides.
The king died, casting off his life-breaths as he fell upon the ground;
meanwhile, Rāṇikā was indeed performing worship of the gods in her own palace. ||41||
For the sake of protecting her own beloved, she first observed two marks on his feet—
red and uninjured— which were indeed like two lines upon the earth.
Seeing her own saffron-marked feet upon the ground, Satī was seized with fear;
crying out "Alas, my Lord!", she beheld the truth of Satī's devotion.
In another moment, Satī became established in the state of truth;
having then seen her beloved’s subtle body with her divine vision. (44)
Having seized her as she arrived at her own home, he quickly emerged from his dwelling, having been provoked by the defeat [she had inflicted]. ||45||
Indeed, that virtuous Satī departed from that place in male attire;
having gone outside and reached a great camel by the power of her fortune, she [proceeded]. (46)
Having gone by a secret path through the trees, she emerged from that land of fear;
abandoning the kingdom, the sufferer of misery went toward the Aśvasaras lake.
In just a single day, she reached the northern bank of the lake;
having disembarked on the shore of the lake, she bathed and wept within.
There she offered a handful of water to her beloved who had departed with her, and then to the Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa in his subtle form. 49.
Having remembered, bowed, and made her request, she stood firm in her resolve upon the bank here in the presence of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
"Having kindled the fire of my body, I shall indeed depart for the auspicious heaven.
Having thus resolved in the evening, she remained devoted to her virtuous vows.
Then he praised Satī, the Truth, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa:
"I bow down to Nārāyaṇa, the truth of truths, the eternally true. (52)
Oṃ, salutations to Brahmā-Savitṛ; salutations to you, the protector of truth.
Salutations to you, whose very nature is devotion to one’s husband, and who are the fire of the five sacred fires. ||53||
Salutations to you who are the three sacrificial fires and the very nature of the seed;
salutations to you who are the form of the embryo, to childhood, and to youth. ||54||
Salutations to you who are both the beloved and the lover, together with your entire lineage;
salutations to you who are the couple, the elder, and the threefold self.
Homage to the Blessed One Kṛṣṇa and homage to you, O Blessed Lady! Homage to you, the Dharma whose nature is virtue, and to the attainment of the Dharma! ||56||
Salutations to you whose nature is consciousness, salutations to you who are the very form of the Lord;
salutations to you who are the caravan for the traveler, salutations to you who are the guide across the path. ||57||
Salutations to the Sun, to the Cloud, to the Lightning, and salutations to the Moon;
salutations to you whose nature is day and whose nature is night.
Salutations to the one who manifests as the two solstices, the initiator of the ages;
salutations to the divine, the Truth; salutations to the dweller of Vaikuṇṭha. ||59||
Obeisance to Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of virtuous women, the Sovereign of the world of the Satīs;
obeisance to the Beloved of Goloka, obeisance to the Dweller in the Imperishable.
Homage to the one worthy of worship by the liberated, and homage to the Lord of the virtuous!
Homage to you, the Lord of the Lords of the Liberated, the beloved Lord of Brahmā! 6.1
Salutations to the Lord of Māṇikya and Muktā, salutations to the Lord of Ramā;
salutations to the Lord of Padmāvatī, Satī, Lakṣmī, Rādhā, and Śrī. || 62 ||
Salutations to the All-Knowing One, the Supreme Lord, to the Illustrious Supreme Self;
salutations to the Lord of Lakṣmī, to You, the Illustrious Puruṣottama. || 63 ||
Salutations to the Lord, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa; repeated salutations to You, the inner controller, who are united with all. ||64||
O Lord, salutations to you, the joy of the cowherds;
salutations to you, the moon of Aśvapaṭṭa and the illusory sun. ||65||
Salutations to you, the bestower of prosperity, the one who brings about dispassion, and the destroyer of all [bondage].
I am this so-called "house," and you, O Truth, are my home. (66)
"O Rakṣā, you whose name is Aṅgāraka, and whatever women are devoted to you—having obtained you as my supreme helper, I offer this [sacrifice]; accept me! (67)
Whether knowing or not knowing, they offer everything ultimately;
by both methods, O Lord, I indeed perform the oblation within you.
You are the sacrifice; you exist in the sacrificial pit in the form of the Āhavanīya fire;
you are the Gārhapatya fire by nature, and you possess the nature of the Āvasathya fire.
"You are indeed the fire of the sacrificial pit and the fire of all pits;
lead me by the path of truth and righteousness to the world of Satīs, and have mercy."
Indeed, the virtue of faithful wives (*satī-dharma*) is that which brings about the upliftment of the world;
in ancient times, Satī, the daughter of Dakṣa, was born, yet she burned her body with fire.
Reṇukā was born as a virtuous woman, and Śabarī likewise in ancient times; women who have resorted to performed dharma attain the state of being a *satī*.
"O King, thus did that Rāṇikā, whose limbs were so delicate, say: 'O Śrī Hari Kṛṣṇa, I shall indeed attain the state of a virtuous wife.'"
Just as he was about to ascend the funeral pyre and kindle the fire,
Śrī Lomaśa, the god Īśāna, and the other deities appeared.
The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa and Lakṣmī became perceptible in their presence there; Satī bowed to them from all sides.
Being virtuous, may you attain victory; you shall go to the world of the virtuous. Together with your husband, enjoy happiness for as long as heaven endures.
Having spoken thus, they bestowed blessings, flowers, and sandalwood paste;
then, having bowed to Viṣṇu, she again remembered her husband. ||77||
Then Nandin, having gone [to the sky], quickly brought the corpse of Aṅgāra, which was a gaṇa of Śaṅkara consisting of a gross body, from the sky.
He gave her to Satī upon the funeral pyre; she too, delighted, embraced that body which had united with him according to the prescribed rite, even as the gods looked on.
While the people were looking on, she produced fire from her foot;
she sang out, "Kṛṣṇa! Kṛṣṇa! Kṛṣṇa! Rādhā-Kṛṣṇa! (2.267.80).
"O Gopīnātha, O beloved of Satī, O Lord of Ramā, look upon me!
Having spoken thus, Lambikā lay down upon the funeral pyre with the corpse. (8.1)
The fire did not touch her; it shone only at her feet. At that moment, Hari Kṛṣṇa became Rādhākṛṣṇa there. ||82||
The Lord remains there together with Muralī, granting his vision;
with his own hand, he offers water, clarified butter, flowers, and sesame seeds. (83)
There, the Blessed One himself offered sandalwood upon the funeral pyre;
the two selves, beloved by Satī, became possessed of divine forms. (84)
They departed from the place of the corpse and stood for a moment in the sky;
then a divine celestial chariot, radiant as the sun, arrived from heaven.
And as they were forbidding it there, they saw the cremation of corpses;
the fire burned two bodies, but those two did not bow to the supreme lords.
They both went to the world of Satī, where they shall remain for the duration of a kalpa;
thereafter, they will go to the imperishable abode of the Supreme Self by means of their higher nature.
And there the gods, having established the Satī-tīrtha and gone to the abode of Nārāyaṇa, worshipped the glorious, beginningless Śrī Narāyaṇa.
They departed for their own divine realm, and Kṛṣṇa vanished;
meanwhile, Śambhu’s attendants indeed cast the ashes of the funeral pyre into the water.
Even the Rāṇikā-tīrtha became known as the Rakṣāṅgāraka-tīrtha; it is further renowned as a place that awakens the virtue of chastity in women.
O King, it protects the dharma of virtuous women and destroys the torment of sin;
here, through bathing, giving gifts, and especially by drinking the water [of this place], [these benefits are attained]. 91.
And by performing the worship of Satī, one shall attain the fruit of the world of Satī; likewise, whatever woman here who is a widow bathes while remembering her husband [shall do so]. (92)
By that merit, she shall indeed lead her beloved to the world of the virtuous (Satyaloka);
for whatever maiden shall perform drinking of water or bathing here [at this place]. (93)
Having indeed attained the state of a faithful wife and obtained a husband who bestows happiness,
and having lived out her full lifespan here, she shall go to the worlds of virtuous women.

A woman endowed with good fortune, having obtained the fruit of her devotion to her husband through bathing, giving gifts, and other such acts in this world, shall go to the worlds of the virtuous (satī). ||95||
Even an old woman, by the mere act of bathing there, grants liberation to a hundred families;
and even a man, by the mere act of bathing, becomes devoted to truth and righteousness. ||96||
Having reached this Satītīrtha, even one who has gone to her death will attain the heavenly realm;
such indeed is this purifying site for women. (97)
And here, let the queen and others perform their ablutions, give gifts, and offer handfuls of water, just as at the most excellent Satī-tīrtha on the celestial Gaṅgā. (98)
Just as there is the Reṇukātīrtha on the river Revā, so too here is the Rāṇikātīrtha, the most excellent purifier in the three worlds. 99.
"O King, when the Kṛta Yuga had begun, he was born as the ancient [being]; thus was Aśvapāṭala addressed, along with his wives and even his female servants. (2.267.10)
O Rādhikā, the two wives of Sarasas bathed in the waters at Satīsthala;
thereafter, they performed the libations after having indeed bestowed gifts.
The king and the others, accompanied by Lomaśa and knowing the greatness of the sacred site, proceeded ahead to that most purifying tīrtha.

Thus ends the two hundred and sixty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Satī-bhavana and Satī-tīrtha on the Banks of the Aśvapaṭṭa Lake, after King Rakṣāṅgāraka was slain by the Mlecchas in Svarṇapattana in Saurāṣṭra, and Queen Rāṇikā-satī arrived at the Kuṅkumavāpī," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Rādhā, listen then; having gone to that holy place (tīrtha) frequented by the virtuous, King Aśvapāṭala questioned Lomaśa.
Aśvapāṭala said:
"What is this supremely purifying holy site (tīrtha) pervaded by the virtuous? O Guru, tell me of these two types of holy sites: the immobile and the mobile. (2)
Śrī Lomaśa said:
King Amohākṣa lived in the vicinity of the Himālaya mountains;
having approached a teacher named Prabodha, he gratified him with his service.
The Guru granted him a vision of Śrī Hari in His own form—
four-armed and resplendent with the conch, discus, mace, lotus, and other [emblems].
Then, in another moment, he again became the Guru himself;
named Amoha and filled with wonder, he lay meditating upon the Lord of Śrī.
"This teacher is a human being, yet he appears four-armed;
I consider him to be Nārāyaṇa himself, encountered through my good fortune."
Therefore, I shall indeed honor him and serve him in every way;
having meditated upon and worshipped him with devotion, I shall attain the supreme good.
Having thus made this awakening resolve in his heart,
the king served his guru Janārdana with supreme devotion.
The queen, the sons, the subjects, and the daughters served their guru, Hari,
by providing food and water, massaging his feet, and other such services.
By the preservation of sacred words, by the washing of garments and similar acts, by the offering of beds and seats, and by the presentation of leaves, fruits, and petals; || 2.268.10 ||
With sandalwood, unbroken rice, and oils, with fragrant garlands and ornaments, and with all the enjoyments fit for a king, the entire royal family was indeed constantly provided for. (11)
Considering the Lord to be his guru, he served Hari without sloth;
he worshipped him by means of awakening him and by the chanting of His names.
The Guru reflected: "Bondage has arrived;
indeed, royal enjoyments become fetters leading to hell. (13)
Therefore, enjoyments that obstruct liberation must be avoided from afar;
one ought not to indulge in illusory awakening.
Having thus made this firm resolve, Prabodha gradually,
through instructions and observances, indeed renounced all enjoyments.
And for the sake of dispelling delusion, he spoke these auspicious words concerning the Dharma:
"O King, the duty of kings is one thing, while the duty of ascetics is another. (16)
I am a virtuous man of awakening; worldly enjoyment is not fitting for me. Indeed, the ornaments of householders are truly the blemishes of the virtuous.
What are faults for householders are indeed ornaments for the virtuous; forgiveness is declared to be the duty of the virtuous, while punishment is the duty of kings. (18)
The dharma of the virtuous consists in the three daily ablutions, while the dharma of kings consists in the final purificatory bath.
The dharma of the virtuous is the protection of moral conduct, whereas the dharma of householders is the pursuit of women. 1.9
The dharma of the saint is indeed contempt, while the dharma of the householder is honor; the saint lives on alms, whereas the householder eats food earned by his own labor. (2.268.20)
A virtuous man may wear tattered clothes, while another possesses garments of gold; a virtuous man may be inclined toward wandering, while another dwells in a magnificent mansion. (21)
A virtuous person is devoid of attachment, whereas a householder dwells in the desire for family;
a virtuous person is always intent on the Self, while a householder is likewise intent on his household.

The virtuous householder is homeless, while the householder who dwells in kinship has a home; the virtuous householder always eats moderately, whereas the householder always eats for the sake of physical nourishment. (23)

The virtuous householder is always free from dualities, whereas the householder is possessed of dualities; the virtuous householder is always free from desire, whereas the householder is enveloped by desires. ||24||
"The dharma of the ascetic bestows liberation, while the dharma of the householder indeed grants heaven;
thus, there exists a distinction between us regarding the paths of dharma. (25)
Furthermore, O King, listen now to the distinction between us two regarding knowledge: "He is my son," "She is my wife," "This wealth, elephants, and so forth, are mine. (26)
"Indeed, my field, my kingdom, and my home appear splendid to me as a householder;
yet I have no son, no wife, and no wealth such as elephants and the like. (27)
I have no field, nor indeed any kingdom; yet the world of the virtuous shines before me.
These householders are my kinsmen, and likewise, they are mine. (28)
"My servants and my subjects shine for me as a householder;
yet neither are they my kinsmen, nor likewise are they my family members. (29)
I have no servants, much less subjects; indeed, I shine before the world of the virtuous.
My body, my form, my command, and my strength are all mine alone. (2.268.30)
To me, a householder, all beings appear as "mine" and everything appears as "mine";
yet neither my body nor my form belongs to me, nor is ignorance mine, nor is strength mine. (3.1)
"Beings do not exist for me; indeed, everything appears as the world of the virtuous.
My nourishment is mine, my disease is mine, my sweet is mine, and my coolness is mine. (32)
"My suffering, my pride—thus does the householder appear.
'Not mine is nourishment, not mine is disease, not mine is sweetness, not mine is coolness. (33)
I have no suffering, nor do I have pride; indeed, I am not perceived by the world of the virtuous. [They do not say: "I am maimed," "I am stout," "I am a leper," or "I am lame. (34)
"I am a Buddha and I am dull-witted; such is the appearance of me as a householder.
I am neither maimed, nor corpulent, nor leprous, nor lame. (35)
The Buddha is certainly not dull-witted, nor does he appear so to the world of the virtuous; for [the Buddha] does not think, "My birth, my death, or my heaven shall be mine. (36)
For the householder, my worship and my fame indeed shine forth;
for me there is neither birth nor death, neither heaven nor bondage. (37)
Neither my worship nor my fame among the virtuous shines forth;
yours is the village, yours the grove, yours the garden, and yours the land. (38)
"This is yours and this is mine"—such a distinction indeed shines for the householder;
yet for you, there is no village, no garden, no grove, and no land. (39)

"This belongs to you, not to me, nor indeed does it belong to the world of the virtuous"—even when such knowledge exists, there remains a sense of separation; hear now, O King, about dispassion (*vairāgya*). (2.268.40)
My wife is desirable, my home is desirable, and my body is desirable; for indeed, the householder’s state is one of passion. (41)
I have no wife, no home, and no body; how then could there be any loveliness?
On the contrary, these things are foul, impure, and loathsome, being mixed with moisture.
Thus, by their very nature, virtuous people are free from passion;
oh, what wealth! Oh, what enjoyments! Oh, what means for attaining them! (43)
"Alas! What wonder is this for a householder on my account?
What indeed is the wealth, what the enjoyments, and what the means? (44)
For the virtuous man, there is no egoism, no sense of "mine," and no wonder;
[to him] today is a festival, today is a wedding, and today is dancing and singing.
Today there is a theater, and today there is a drama; yet for the householder, it is a delusion.
The festival of the self is the carrier to liberation, and dancing and singing are always directed toward Hari. (46)
In the drama of life, the virtuous person’s dedication to Kṛṣṇa for the sake of the Supreme Lord is like this:
"This is the stake, this is the prize won, this is what was conquered, and this is what was seized and made one's own. (47)
For a householder, both giving and receiving are characterized by passion;
yet he has won his own self, attained Brahman, conquered his mind, and made it steadfast. (48)
Not taking what is not given, being free from passion toward the virtuous, always resting in happiness, and never falling under the thread of craving—[these are his qualities]. (49)
The state of following greed is passion for the householder; constant self-attachment is the wearing of the sacred thread. ||2.268.50||
The virtuous person always follows the state of goodness and remains ever detached;
likewise, observe the distinct nature of dispassion even within devotion. (51)
For the householder, devotion is toward the home; for the saint, however, devotion is toward Mādhava.
For the householder, devotion lies in sexual pleasure; for the saint, indeed, it lies in renunciation.

The devotion of a householder is for his own sake, while the devotion of a saint is for the sake of others; the devotion of a householder is directed toward this world, whereas that of a saint is directed toward the supreme goal. (53)
For the householder, devotion is directed toward his own station; for the ascetic, devotion is directed toward the station of another.
For the householder, devotion is directed toward aesthetic flavor (*rasa*); for the ascetic, it is directed toward that which is the self of all flavors.
The devotion of a householder is toward delusion; the devotion of a saint is beyond delusion.
The devotion of a householder is toward the ritual season; the devotion of a saint is toward Hari alone, apart from the seasons.
Devotion leads the virtuous man to the non-returning state, whereas for the householder it leads to the cycle of rebirth;
devotion places the householder within the womb [of worldly existence], but the devotion of the virtuous man resides in the golden realm.
The virtuous householders who eat at home are worshippers of the planets;
indeed, the virtuous householders who eat only at night are devotees of devotees.
Householders are eaters of many meals, while holy men (sādhus) take but one meal;
householders indeed eat with their families, whereas holy men are always free from such attachments.
All householders are indeed devotees, while the virtuous (sādhus) are truly non-devotees;
thus, O King, there is a distinction between householders and the saintly on the path of devotion.
Even regarding their destination, there is indeed no concomitance whatsoever;
the destination of a householder is downward, while the destination of a virtuous person is always upward. (2.268.60)
A householder who has attained the state of Rāma is always a virtuous one whose course is that of Rāma;
though a householder, he possesses the path of passion yet is always a virtuous one whose course is pure.
The householder moves within the realm of dualities, yet the virtuous one likewise transcends the movement of dualities;
the householder dwells in the home, while the virtuous one always dwells in the state of the planets.
The course of action for a virtuous householder is likewise the course of Brahman;
the course of the self for a virtuous householder is the self, which is the true goal of the self.
The goal of the perfected one is in the *bhagavatī*; the goal of the householder is in the *bhaga*.
Thus, O King, there is a distinction in the goals even among virtuous householders. (64)
Tell me, how could there be a simultaneous conjunction of these with you?
For passion and dispassion do not coexist, nor indeed do light and darkness.
Bondage and liberation do not exist together; they never exist at the same time.
Therefore, I have resolved to dwell in the forest, a course approved by the virtuous.

Behold, O King, how the body indeed arises from the embryo (kalala), born from the embryo; through the region of the downward wind (apāna) and the gateway of the constituent elements (dhātu), it is produced.
In the womb, in the place of the downward breath (apāna), it is always cooked by the embryonic tissues;
it attains nourishment and emerges outward through milk and boiled foods.
Everything is pervaded by the embryo; indeed, the embryo is the treasure-store of the embryo.
Within it, there exists both the embryonic matter and water.
Even that which consists of the physical body, including the foul-smelling skin down to the nails, is seen to be composed of impurity and is merely a repository for filth. (2.268.70)
Richly fragrant when first consumed and swallowed, it quickly becomes foul-smelling once it has descended below the throat; having become waste, it remains there, protecting itself.
The fragrance and the essence of scent that fills the nostrils becomes foul-smelling within the stomach and then exits through the exterior.
Indeed, from all nine gates of everyone, foul-smelling impurities flow forth, as if from a hellish pit. (73)
Behold the loathsomeness of your own body; do not associate with others, for it is fit only for the acceptance of water and food once it has been transformed by the moisture of the embryo.
And in the discharge of excrement and urine, what pure impression could there be?
Perceiving the impure as pure, one takes delight in it, just as one might take pleasure in fetters.
Indeed, from the saliva-like water that is a transformation of what has been consumed,
and which is mixed with earth, fire, and air, the embryo (kalala) arises.

Therefore, from that [consciousness] arise the body, therein the sense organs such as the physical seats, the subtle elements (tanmātras) and so forth, and likewise their powers of movement and action. (77)
And from that very [source] indeed arise the states of the grasped and the grasper;
in that case, what conscious person, being subject to necessity, could find delight therein? (78)
Indeed, different forms are seen from moment to moment, quite unexpectedly;
at what moment will this composite body meet its destruction? (79)
Having understood that the covering of the body is like a cloud, like smoke, or like a mass of dust, the wise man should not place his trust in it.
But when the vital breath departs, this [body] becomes empty in an instant;
for suffering is directly perceived, since that is indeed its own characteristic. (81)
If his body is such as this, what need is there to speak of his kinsmen?
Therefore, O King, I shall dwell within myself, which is known as the forest.
"Beyond this, I shall dwell in Anaraṇya, the supreme lord;
if what I have said is pleasing to you, then prepare that excellent path. (83)
O wise one, grant me this boon: I shall depart from this separation; do not grieve, for as long as the body remains as described toward the guru, it shall indeed always remain so.
Even in the forest, he remains exactly the same; association with him is terrifying.
If you dwell even in the forest in his company, it will happen [to you]. (85)
Since you perceive all things with equal vision, my forest and my home are the same to you;
therefore, O Lord, please take up your residence here permanently and do not depart.
Prabuddha said:
"O King, what you have spoken is indeed true, and what I have said is likewise so.
Having gone to Avighna-bhavana, I shall attain liberation, which is difficult to obtain. (87)
"O King, your palace is seen to be full of many obstacles, whereas the forest indeed has few obstacles; therefore, I shall strive according to my strength. (88)
Having attained self-knowledge, O Knower of Brahman, I shall indeed enter into the knowledge of Brahman;
through that knowledge of Brahman, I shall realize the eternal Supreme Brahman. ||89||
Amohākṣa said:
"O Guru, how may I obtain the vision of the nature of the perfect Brahman? Grant me here the revelation of the perfect Brahman. (2.268.90)
Prabuddha said: "O King, through the burning away of the impurities of karma, Brahman shines forth;
I am not yet so endowed, being still enveloped by the web of karma. (9.1)
Amohākṣa said:
"There is no trust in this body; it perishes at the end of a moment.
From the presence of the Guru, there is no gain that does not fall within the sphere of the Supreme Brahman. (92)
Then the disciple said: "When and where indeed will that attainment be obtained?
O Guru, grant me the direct knowledge of the Supreme Self. (93)
Prabuddha said:
"I am not capable in that way; such capability rests upon devotion.
However, thousands of incarnations like me have been born as Buddhas. (94)
O King, by means of devotion and the worship of that very Supreme Brahman, you shall undoubtedly cross over [samsara] through that practice; of this there is no doubt. (95)
"O King, if you desire it, I shall go to the forest immediately to behold Brahman right here, even without the accumulation of ritual means. (96)
Out of compassion, I shall speak of the land known as Surāṣṭra,
specifically the field of Aśvapaṭṭasara— a field of imperishable merit that brings about auspiciousness.
At the holy site of Kuṅkumavāpikā, the Lord himself is manifest—Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the glorious Puruṣottama. (98)
The Supreme Brahman, having assumed a human form, shines resplendent;
go quickly to that place, and you shall meet the Supreme Brahman. (99)
Having established me, your guru, there in that palace, you shall thereafter go to the world of Brahmā; indeed, go quickly and do not delay.
"I shall go; may you have well-being at all times, O King!
Having spoken thus, O Lord of Men, the Buddha departed for the forest expanse. (10.1)
Amohākṣa, having quickly prepared himself, arrived;
and having reached this sacred field, he beheld Anādikṛṣṇanārāyaṇa directly before his eyes and likewise resided here at this holy site (tīrtha).
Having established the awakened one here, he went to the liberation that is higher than the highest.
Having ascended the divine celestial chariot to the imperishable, eternal abode—
this indeed is the ford of Buddhahood, as well as the ford that dispels delusion.
O King, which always destroys delusion and brings about the attainment of the perfect Brahman, perform your ablutions while meditating upon the Guru, and bestow gifts as well. 105.
Thus addressed by Rādhikā, King Aśvapāṭalaka then performed auspicious bathing and charity according to the directions spoken by Lomaśa.
Then he went suddenly to yet another sacred ford;
by reciting or hearing this, one attains the state of the Supreme Brahman.
Discrimination arises, and likewise one becomes established in Brahman;
there shall be both enjoyment and liberation, and eternal heaven shall be attained. || 108 ||
In this place, through giving, austerity, devotion, and by means of a raft,
as well as by drinking the water, one shall obtain the fruit of the horse sacrifice (Aśvamedha).
Even if a sinful person comes here and gives up their life, having become awakened here, they shall proceed to the state of liberation. || 2.268.110 ||

Thus ends the two hundred and sixty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of King Amohākṣa’s Arrival at the Sacred Field of Kuṅkumavāpī through the Instruction of Guru Prabuddha, His Attainment of the Supreme Brahman in Person, the Buddha Tīrtha, and Liberation," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Rādhikā, listen; having gone to that holy place, Aśvapāṭala again questioned Lomaśa regarding the name and other details of the tīrtha. || 1 ||
Aśvapāṭala said:
"O Guru, by what name is this famous sacred site (tīrtha) known, and when did it come into being?
Tell me all that in brief, as well as what its fruit is. (2)
Śrī Lomaśa said:
Listen, O King, I shall describe a most purifying sacred site;
it is Lakṣmītīrtha as well as this Nārāyaṇatīrtha, O monarch. (3)
In former times, there was indeed a king named Abhayākṣa, the lord of the Pañcālas;
he was devoted to the practice of righteous deeds and endowed with charity and devotion toward Hari.
In whose house virtuous guests and wretched embodied beings constantly eat by the hundreds and attain eternal satisfaction; || 5 ||
There Nārāyaṇa himself shines in the form of a virtuous man,
the Lord who is unknowable to all the worlds and is served by the brahmins.
Lakṣmī and Rādhā likewise shine forth in the form of virtuous women;
the gods and goddesses know this, but human beings do not. ||7||
Only those sages who possess divine vision know this, and no others;
the king constantly serves the illustrious Lord Śrī Puruṣottama.
He worships Nārāyaṇa, the four-armed Lord of Śrī,
and he constantly listens to the sacred stories from virtuous Brahmins.
Accompanied by his family, the king became devoted to self-knowledge,
intent on serving the virtuous, and dedicated to the protection of his subjects.
Among his subjects there was neither unrighteousness, nor theft, nor violence;
the people maintained purity and protected one another, being content with their own possessions. (11)
Indeed, the brahmins who were his ascetics partook of his meals;
they were constantly devoted to the chanting of the Vedas and dedicated to the six traditional duties and other such practices.
Even those worlds devoted to sacrifices and offerings, and those solely intent upon Nārāyaṇa,
as well as those devoted to the conduct of Brahman, do not highly esteem desire.
For they acquire only the wealth that is required and nothing more than that;
indeed, they devote all their remaining time to the pursuit of liberation.
In his kingdom there was no widow, nor any woman without a son, nor any childless person;
there was no householder without a wife, and the subjects were endowed with wealth and grain.
In the morning, everywhere in the city, auspicious and melodious sounds of "Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa" arise; auspicious songs are heard and recitations are performed. || 16 ||
There is no one who exists without having bathed, nor likewise anyone who exists without worship;
on the foreheads of men there should be a sectarian mark (tilaka) accompanied by a crescent moon. 17.
And the auspicious sandalwood mark of Lord Hari is seen upon their foreheads as a reminder;
indeed, garlands of *tulasī* are seen around the necks of all the subjects. (18)
Even in the hand, the rosary of *tulasī* awakens the task of recitation;
even on the tongue, the name of Śrī Hari [is present]; and indeed, even in a mere salutation, there is Hari.
In acts of charity and in helping others, Śrī Hari is remembered by people;
so too by maidens, by youths, and by those who are devoted to the study of knowledge.
Having first performed the glorification of Śrī Hari in the hall, the preceptors who take refuge in Hari then practice and teach [the scriptures]. (21)
Even in the court of law, at the very end, he is constantly heard saying before [the judge]:
"O Hari, O Rāma, O Kṛṣṇa, O Nārāyaṇa, let there be salutation unto You! (22)
On riverbanks, in houses, in fields, in gardens, and even in forests—there were farmers, artisans, wood-gatherers, and those who collect grass and other such materials. (23)
All are devoted to Kṛṣṇa; indeed, remembering Kṛṣṇa, they perform their labor.
The cooks, who are devotees of Hari, having placed what has been cooked in a vessel, [serve it]. (24)
Having offered all kinds of food, as well as fruits, roots, water, and so forth,
to Hari, they afterwards feed their householders.
Even while standing at their shops, the excellent merchants eat and drink only after first making an offering to the gods; they likewise perform the worship of Gaṇeśa. (26)
Having lit a lamp of ghee, they then perform the worship of Śrī Kṛṣṇa;
they occupy themselves during the day and worship Mādhava at night.
Having bowed to Hari and worshipped the cow, the cowherds then beheld the temple of Śrī Kṛṣṇa and subsequently obtained a vision of Kṛṣṇa. ||28||
Devoted solely to the remembrance of Hari, wood-gatherers go to the forest regions; chanting "Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa," they indeed proceed along the path while worshipping Him. (29)
Indeed, while washing bundles of clothes, the washermen chant the name of Rāma;
saying "Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa," they wash them in the reservoir of water.
O Śrī Narāyaṇa, even birds such as parrots and others will utter [the name],
and even the animals, being Vaiṣṇavas, will indeed low the sound of Oṃkāra.
Performers of the triple arts play musical instruments with songs in praise of Kṛṣṇa;
poets, bards, and others compose compositions concerning Kṛṣṇa. (32)
Having himself revealed his own name as Abhayākṣa,
the king proclaimed that secondary name of Hari, Adhokṣaja, as his own.
He also gave the subjects names endowed with the meaning of the Supreme Lord;
thus, having caused this kingdom to be so established, it truly became a Vaiṣṇava realm.
A devotee of the Fearless One, having reflected thus, [sees] that the home is perishable, and that wealth, kingdom, prosperity, and even his own body are transitory. (35)
Overcome by a surge of dispassion, he went to Aśvapaṭṭasara;
the subjects, the brahmins, and the elders likewise followed after that king. (36)
Seeing them approaching on the road solely out of devotion to kīrtana, the people who had come from the villages along the way were filled with curiosity. (37)
Together they returned with eager anticipation to the Aśvasaras tīrtha;
on the northern bank of the lake, they took up residence in a dwelling among the trees.
Having visited all the sacred fords (tīrthas), they went to the hermitage of Lomaśa;
from there, they proceeded to the temple of Anādikṛṣṇanārāyaṇa.
Having bowed to their mother and father and beheld the Kuṅkumavāpikā, they worshipped the glorious Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa with supreme love.
Having drunk the water of Kuṅkumavāpikā and likewise performed the worship of Śrī,
they gave gifts and went once again to the shore of the lake.
That King Adhokṣaja indeed desired to perform a sacrifice here on this spot in order to propitiate Nārāyaṇa with a great offering.
That Adhokṣaja also requested Lomaśa for the sake of the sacrifice;
he indeed performed a Vaiṣṇava sacrifice with hundreds of thousands of golden coins.
He gratified the gods with oblations, the ancestors with śrāddha rites, the virtuous with food,
the common people with gifts, and the holy ones and lords of the gods with acts of self-surrender.
At the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti), Kṛṣṇa himself, the four-armed Nārāyaṇa, bearing the conch, discus, mace, and lotus, became visible within the fire. 45.
The Lord, endowed with splendor, partakes of all sacrificial offerings, served by Ramānanda, Sunanda, and others, and accompanied by Garuḍa. ||46||
With a serene countenance, dark-complexioned, and youthful, he shone like ten million suns;
and all the other people, including the brahmins, were filled with wonder. ||47||
Oh, how great is the king’s devotion and Nārāyaṇa’s affection!
Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa himself partakes of the sacrificial offering presented by the monarch. 48.
The Blessed One said to the king: "Have a temple built here;
I shall dwell together with Lakṣmī. O King, install me. (49)
"Having indeed taken the initiation of a saintly person, perform my worship;
O King, I shall remain under your control. O saintly one, O Adhokṣaja, accept me."
Having thus spoken and having consumed the sacrificial offerings, the Blessed Lord then vanished from the sight of the king, the gods on earth, and the others. 51.
Having bestowed sacrificial fees and fed everyone, he personally received the initiation of renunciation from the sage Svataḥprakāśa. ||52||
He observed a fast and purified his body;
he had his head shaved, and having bathed, he performed an oblation in the fire.
He worshipped Nārāyaṇa within the Sarvatobhadra maṇḍala,
and he bestowed gifts of cows, gifts of land, gifts of gold, and so forth.
For the sake of the temple of Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa as well,
he gave a gift of one hundred thousand gold coins to his preceptor.
Oṃ, salutations to Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Lord; Svāhā!
May Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa be my refuge at all times. (56)
Out of fear of Time, Illusion, evil karma, enemies, Yama, and treacherous friends,
one should wear the trident, fish, banner, bow, wheel, and svastika.
I am Brahmā, an eternal devotee of Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa;
the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa is my Lord and my husband. (58)
Bālakṛṣṇa is the Supreme Brahman; he is indeed my eternal Lord. May he be my father, kinsman, well-wisher, friend, protector, and guardian. (59)
The venerable Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇavallabha is my refuge;
I am a devotee of Śrī Kṛṣṇavallabha, and Śrī Hari is my refuge. (2.269.60)
"Śrī Kṛṣṇavallabhasvāmī, Śrī Hari, is my refuge"—
with these words, he received the mantras directly from his self-manifested true guru.
Thereupon, observing virtuous vows, he donned saffron robes;

he placed a sacred thread around his neck, a tulasī garland on his hand, anointed himself with sandalwood paste as a tilaka, applied the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra), and wore the marks of the discus and other emblems.
For the purpose of worship, he also took up a golden image of Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa accompanied by Ramā,
and he performed worship of his guru.
Having duly completed the two-fold initiation as a limb of the ritual on the bank of the lake, he indeed preserved his own name, "Adhokṣajaprakāśa."
He made his permanent residence there in a leaf-hut on this sacrificial ground;
with supreme devotion, he chanted the names of Śrīśa Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa. (65)
He caused a beautiful temple for Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa to be built,
and he installed Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa within that shrine.
O King, this very temple shines, being the abode of Śrī Hari;
therefore, indeed, behold there both Śrī and Hari.
Bestow gifts, O Indra among kings, and perform your ablutions here;
this sacred ford is a great tīrtha that bestows the fruit of all sacrifices. (68)
Yajñatīrtha, Sādhutīrtha, and Lakṣmītīrtha are likewise considered [sacred], as well as the tīrtha named Adhokṣaja and the tīrtha named Nārāyaṇa. ||69||
Likewise, this very place is renowned as Dīkṣātīrtha, for it is indeed purifying;
having worshipped Keśava here according to the prescribed rite during the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, [one attains purification].
In the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, one obtains the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice through bathing and giving gifts;
and in Pauṣa, through bathing and giving gifts, one attains Nārāyaṇa endowed with Śrī.
By bathing and giving gifts in the month of Māgha, and by fully worshipping Mādhava, one obtains the merit arising from the Vājapeya sacrifice. ||72||
And here, by bathing and giving gifts in the month of Phālguna and by fully worshipping Govinda, a performer of sacrifices obtains the supreme fruit of the Rājasūya.
Indeed, by bathing and giving gifts here in the month of Caitra, and by worshipping Viṣṇu, one who performs the pilgrimage shall obtain the fruit arising from the sacrifice known as the Atirātra.
By bathing and giving gifts in Vaiśākha and worshipping Madhusūdana, the founder of the holy ford attains the purifying fruit of the white lotus.
O King, by bathing and giving gifts there in the month of Jyeṣṭha, and by worshipping Trivikrama, that pilgrim obtains the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
By bathing and giving gifts here in the month of Āṣāḍha, and by fully worshipping Vāmana, one obtains the fruit of the Gavāyana sacrifice.
By bathing and giving gifts here in the month of Śrāvaṇa, and by fully worshipping Śrīdhara, one indeed obtains the fruit produced by the Soma sacrifice. ||78||
By bathing and giving gifts here in the month of Bhādrapada, and by worshipping Hṛṣīkeśa, one obtains the fruit born of the Viśvajit sacrifice, as does a Tīrthakṛt.
By bathing and giving gifts in the month of Āśvina, and by worshipping Padmanābha, one obtains here the fruit of the Sautrāmaṇi sacrifice, as does a Tīrthakṛt.

By bathing and giving gifts during the month of Kārttika, and by worshipping Dāmodara, one attains various merits arising from the conjunction with the moon, like those of a founder of a sacred ford (tīrthakṛt). ||81||

By bathing and giving gifts during the intercalary month (adhimāsa), and having worshipped Puruṣottama, one who sleeps here at the sacred ford (tīrtha) obtains the fruit arising from a sacrifice to Viṣṇu.
By bathing, giving gifts, reciting prayers, and other such acts performed on any day whatsoever here, one obtains the supreme fruit of all *medha* sacrifices, just as a Tīrthakṛt does.
O King, a Tīrthakṛt indeed obtains the fruits of all sacrifices;
by bathing and giving gifts on Śivarātri, the fruit of the Mahārudra rite shall be attained.
This is that purifying field proclaimed by Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa;
perform your bath and likewise the worship of Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa.
"Having meditated upon all the Blessed Ones, may you attain all merits.
Having been addressed thus, O Rādhikā, the king indeed became as pale as a horse.
Together with his family, he bathed in the water and worshipped Hari in the temple,
accompanied by Śrī, with the sixteen types of service (ṣoḍaśopacāra), including the waving of lights (nīrājana) and other rites.
Then, indeed, upon the image of Śrī Hari, fourteen Blessed Lords beginning with Keśava appeared to him exactly as described. (88)
Having granted a moment of his own vision to Anādi Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa,
all those incarnations merged into him, and he too vanished from sight.
King Aśvapāṭala was filled with great wonder;
he then considered himself to have accomplished his life's purpose through that holy place dedicated to Adhokṣaja.
Aśvapāṭala said:
"O Lomaśa, here I have obtained a vision born of Keśava and the other deities;
I am truly one who has accomplished his purpose—what need have I for other holy places or extensive acts of charity? (9.1)
Śrī Lomaśa said:
O King, understand that all this has arisen through the power of sacred fords (tīrtha).
One who lacks a tīrtha possesses neither strength, nor merit, nor purity.
There is no state of purity, nor is there favor from the Dark Lord;
there is no devotion for the sacred ford, nor is there liberation or even heaven.
Whether moving or stationary, a sacred ford (tīrtha) is the destroyer of impurities;
once the destruction of impurities has occurred, the pilgrim attains fitness for the state of a true seeker of the ford.
When fitness is truly present, Brahman indeed shines forth in the heart;
in that state, love for the one whose form is Brahman arises in the devotee. (95)
A natural proximity to the Supreme Brahman arises for him; consequently, the vision of Hari, which is otherwise difficult to attain, becomes easily accessible. 96.
Thus, for the sake of gathering the world, sacred sites (tīrthas) have always been ordained as duties for one who has attained right vision. 97.
Therefore, one who possesses compassion should perform pilgrimages and acts of charity;
for whether he be liberated or perfected, a god, or one possessing a divine form of Brahman— (98)
Whatever one performs that bestows liberation or bestows heaven, another person, being a doer of merit, follows by adopting that very same conduct. 99.
By that, liberation shall indeed be attained, and it shall also become a gift of fearlessness;
one should practice the pilgrimage through action, mind, speech, and inner disposition.
Having spoken thus to King Aśvapāṭala,
Lomaśa led him before another sacred site, the supreme temple of Viṣṇu.
O Rādhikā, there indeed shines the eternal white form of Viṣṇu,
joined by Kamalā and graced by Garuḍa.

Thus ends the two hundred and sixty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of King Abhayākṣa’s Devotion, Renunciation, and Sacrifice on the Shore of Aśvapaṭṭasara Lake; His Taking of the Vow of Renunciation, the Vision of Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa and Others, the Construction of the Temple, and the Lakṣmītīrtha and Nārāyaṇatīrtha," in the second section (Tretā-santāna) of the glorious *Lakṣmīnārāyaṇīya-saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O Rādhikā, listen; later, King Aśvapāṭala asked Lomaśa about the origin of the holy sites at the foremost of tīrthas.
Aśvapāṭala said:
O Lord, what is the name of this sacred ford (tīrtha), when was it created, and by whom?
O Guru, tell me what the fruit is and what ritual should be performed here.
Śrī Lomaśa said:
O King, listen to the majesty of this sacred place; I shall tell it to you.
There was a Vaiśya named Devānīka, a cultivator who was exceedingly devoted.
This guard resides day and night in a garden within the radiant village; indeed, during the rainy season, he stays having made his own dwelling there.
He constantly worships Śrī Hari; having bathed in the morning, he also performs His worship.
At midday, having offered all his food to Hari, he eats.
During the rainy season, there indeed arise various crops, leaves, petals, vegetables, bulbous roots, and fruits.
Having first offered those fresh [fruits] from the fields and the garden to Hari, that householder then partakes of them himself.
Sugarcane stalks, ears of grain, seeds, bhājikā and similar items,
the food of sages, sacrificial offerings, fuel-sticks, and likewise juices— (8).

Then Lakṣmī herself, four-armed, manifested from the jar;
having displayed her form for a moment, she vanished right there on the spot. (65)
Then, a temple for Lakṣmī was caused to be built here by me;
and Lakṣmī herself dwells here, worshipped as Dhanyeśvarī. (66)
Likewise, Lakṣmītīrtha, Dhanyeśvarītīrtha, and Ghaṭasthalī became renowned; this [place] is the remover of the sin of theft.
It is a means of removing the mass of sins and likewise bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
furthermore, bathing, giving gifts, and other such acts performed here result in the destruction of all impurities.
By worshipping Lakṣmī here, one becomes possessed of fortune and wealth;
one attains the world of Lakṣmī and becomes devoted to the service of Lakṣmī. ||69||
"Bathe, give, and cause her to be honored with splendor, O King!
Thus addressed, Aśvapaṭala bathed, gave gifts, and worshipped her.
O Rādhikā, he then went ahead with Lomaśa to the great holy site of Śālagrāma, which was resplendent with temples. 71.
Aśvapāṭala said:
"O Guru, this holy place where Śālagrāma has established its presence is most excellent. When and how did it come into being? Teach me its ritual procedure and its fruit. (72)
Śrī Lomaśa said: There was a brahmin named Caityabrahman who followed a degraded way of life;
he made his dwelling among the low-born and subsisted on the food of the low-born. (73)
Having encountered a sinner, he always became devoted to sin;
he drank liquor and, through association, he committed theft.
Likewise, he committed adultery; thus, though a Brahmin, he became like a Caṇḍāla, fallen from his caste, family, and so forth. (75)
Then once, at night, a holy man arrived at his house;
the brahmin treated that guest with contempt, as one would treat a base person.
Having recognized his wicked conduct, Sādhu summoned a messenger of Yama;
then, O King, that messenger of Yama quickly arrived at his house.
Then he killed him in many ways like the slaughter of an animal; but when that virtuous man, devoted to compassion, begged for forgiveness, [he relented]. (78)
Then he liberated that wicked man from the fear of Yama’s messengers;
the virtuous one went his way, while the wicked brahmin approached Lomaśa.
Desiring his own liberation, he then went to my hermitage and earnestly entreated me, his guru,
in many ways for a likeness of himself for the sake of his deliverance.
"I am Lomaśa, and I have indeed granted you an expiation lasting for a year;
he then performed that vow of twelve Cāndrāyaṇas. (8.1)
He gave a Śālagrāma stone to that pure brāhmaṇa;
and that brāhmaṇa worshipped it appropriately for the sake of worship. ||82||
Then, out of devotion to Viṣṇu, I gave him this mantra:
"Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya svāmine svāhā. (83)
He performs the recitation of mantras and the worship of the Śālagrāma;
he also practices meditation and devotion to Hari day and night. (84)
In the early morning, during the Brahma-muhūrta, he indeed arrived there at the riverbank with a Śālagrāma stone and performed worship until sunrise.
He always performed this at the Setu in the presence of the Tulasī tree;
and when much time had passed in this manner, [the Lord], beholding his devotion, [acted].
Śālagrāma became gracious and indeed became the divine Viṣṇu;
at that time, O twice-born one, the Śālagrāma stone attained dissolution there.
"Protect, protect, O ocean of compassion! O Lord, grant me deliverance!
Having spoken thus, he then fell at the feet of Viṣṇu. ||88||
From that very tulasī tree, the goddess Lakṣmī was born;
Śrī then spoke to the brāhmaṇa regarding this abode of tulasī.
Furthermore, cause a residence for the Śālagrāmas to be built on the shore of the lake;
by that means, you will attain both worldly enjoyment and liberation, without a doubt.
Having spoken thus, she vanished and became a tree;
Viṣṇu also vanished and became a Śālagrāma stone.
O King, this temple was caused to be built by that brahmin;
in its center shines the divine Tulasī in the form of a tree.
At its base resides the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu, whose very nature is the Śāla stone;
by bathing here, as well as by giving gifts and worshipping the Lord of Tulasī, [one attains liberation].
By taking hold of Tulasī, one attains both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
all sins are destroyed, and one reaches heaven and even beyond. (94)
The auspicious Śālagrāma, the Tīrtha of Tulasī, and the holy site known as Caityabrahma—this indeed exists as a purifying place. (95)
O King, bathe and offer what is fitting to Tulasī and Kṛṣṇa, who reside within the temple; thus attain the favor of Kṛṣṇa. 96.
Thus addressed by Rādhikā, the king bathed, gave gifts, and performed worship;
he likewise received the nectar of the water and the nectar of the divine grace.
Having performed a circumambulation and prostrated like a staff before another holy ford,
he indeed departed with his hair standing on end, his mind exceedingly delighted.
"Aha! All sacred fords are indeed permeated by the Blessed Lord; they have been visited by me, a fortunate one who has become a vessel for Hari’s grace. (99)
Thus, the king, filled with wonder, attained great peace within his heart;
for a moment, he meditated in his own heart upon his guru Lomaśa, the bestower of knowledge.
And the king, situated in the northwestern corner, remembered the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama), and bowed to Lake Nema.

Thus ends the two hundred and seventy-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Kuṅkumeśvara Tīrtha established by the Brahmin Kuṅkuma, the Durgāsatī Tīrtha established by Satī Śācāraṇī, the Lakṣmī Tīrtha established by Dhanyeshvarī the merchant’s wife, and the Śālagrāma Tīrtha established by Caitya Brahmadvija," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Rādhā; thereafter, having gone to the holy ford named Nara-Nārāyaṇa, the king questioned the best of sages, Lomaśa.
Aśvapāṭala said:
How and why is this sacred ford (tīrtha) named after Nara and Nārāyaṇa? What is the ritual procedure here, and what is the fruit thereof? Tell me, O Lord Lomaśa. (2)
Śrī Lomaśa said:
Listen, O King, I shall describe a sacred ford (tīrtha), the most excellent among the best;
for here indeed were Gopāla and Kṛṣṇa, and the cowherd master who was the father of Hari.
First, indeed, for the sake of a son, he performed severe penance;
and that deity who dwells on the Himalayas as Nara-Nārāyaṇa— || 4 ||
A protector of the dharma of ascetics and devoted to celibacy,
he practiced penance after meditating upon the supreme excellence among all practitioners of austerity.
First he gave up food, and thereafter he became devoted to eating roots; then he subsisted on leaves, and after that, he ate only dried leaves.
Thereafter he subsisted on water, and from that he developed the practice of subsisting on air;
he indeed constantly chanted the name of Śrī Nara-Nārāyaṇa within his heart.
Thus, at the end of a hundred years, four Blessed Lords— Nara, Nārāyaṇa, Kṛṣṇa, and Hari— arrived there together.
Having approached him, they spoke directly to that cowherd Kṛṣṇa:
"O Mahāviṣṇu, O Nārāyaṇa, why indeed do you perform penance?"
"O Vāsudeva, sustainer of the world, what is the reason for your penance?
We, the four Nārāyaṇas, are indeed pleased."
"Speak as you wish; we shall grant you here a boon according to your desire.
Having heard this, Gopāla-Kṛṣṇa spoke for the sake of auspiciousness: ||| 1 || 1 ||
And likewise for the worlds, the gods, the ancestors, and women;
for birds, animals, creepers, and trees as well. || 12 ||
"May you become my sons from the stumps and the grasses. "So be it," they said, and then they entered into those bodies.
Those four supreme lords— Nārāyaṇa, Nara,
Kṛṣṇa, and Hari— were his mind-born sons.
The portions of Kaṃbharā and Bālaka were for the sake of the world's welfare;
Nārāyaṇa became the eldest, known by the name Śrī Bhagavān.
From him was born a man named Śukadeva, the second;
[and] Kṛṣṇa, the beginningless Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the beloved of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
This Akṣarādhipati was the third incarnation;
then the fourth Hari appeared, known by the name Śrīvallabha.
And they were equal, possessing equal sovereignty, endowed with equal bodily radiance;
indeed, O King, those boys there became supreme lords.
This ground where Gopālaka-Kṛṣṇa performed most severe penance is purifying; this very place is his temple. (19)
There, Gopālakṛṣṇa installed images named Nārāyaṇa, Nara, Kṛṣṇa, and Hari within the temple.
This is that supreme among all holy places, the abode above all sacred sites;
having attained rest here, seize the fourfold powers in meditation.
From remembering, seeing, bathing here, drinking [the water], worshipping,
giving gifts, and also from serving, liberation alone is the great fruit.
Indeed, there is no fruit equal to this among sacrifices or vows;
nor is there any fruit equal to this among sacrificial fees or initiations.
O King, that vast region known as Brahmaloka which existed here was what is seen today as the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake. (24)
Aśvapāṭala said: O sage, when did this beautiful lake, which embodies all holy fords and is the refuge of all Nārāyaṇas, truly come into existence here upon the surface of the earth?
Śrī Lomaśa said: Formerly, I was in the abode of Vaikuṇṭha,
and there once I heard [of] the Lord of the Imperishable, Anādi Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
In the universe of the four-faced Brahmā, within the abode of Gopāla-Kṛṣṇa, one becomes a human being for the sake of the welfare of the world. 27.
Then all the Nārāyaṇas, all the liberated ones, as well as the Īśvaras, the sages, and the ancestors, assembled here upon the earth. ||28||
The goddesses, the wives of the lords, the liberated ones, and likewise the cowherd girls;
the daughters of Nārāyaṇa, the daughters of Brahmā, the celestial nymphs, and the wives of the gods. ||29||
All the beloveds of Brahmā, the beloveds of Hari, and all the powers (śaktis) belonging to Viṣṇu also arrived there. ||2.272.30||
For the sake of welcome, for the sake of worship, for the sake of dwelling together,
and likewise for the sake of service, they worshipped those supreme goddesses as the Supreme Lord.
They and they all were then awaiting his very manifestation;
and then I beheld this entire festival.
Then, in that supreme, imperishable abode, Māṇikya realized:
"My Lord is the Blessed One, the Lord of the lords of all lords. (33)
The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa proceeds to the surface of the earth;
she had previously come from her abode to the Vyāghra forest on this earth. (34)
Desiring to become the vehicle for this vow of celibacy, Satī wished to take the form of Aśvinī, the maiden who was her equal by choice. (35)
Having become a mare and remaining unrecognized, she wandered over the land;
here at this auspicious tīrtha called Akṣara, she remained seeking Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. || 36 ||
Beheld by Īśvara and the other gods, that beloved of Hari possessed a divine form;
and wherever she appeared, that ground became a horse-strap (aśvapaṭṭikā).
It became a sacred ford for us, and a definitive conclusion was reached:
the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa shall dwell here.
At that moment, Brahmahrada arrived there from the imperishable state (akṣara-pada),
taking the form of water, possessing a divine luster, and consisting of the Aśvapaṭṭasaras lake.
On this earth, that essence of water became a divine lake;
O King, remember that divine lake which is the Brahma-lake.
He alone was King Aśvapāṭala, the performer of the Soma sacrifice;
you yourself, having assumed a human form, shine resplendently upon the earth. ||41||
Thus addressed, O Rādhikā, that king indeed beheld his own [true nature]:
the lake of Brahman, released from Brahmā, which is the descent of the waters of the lotus-born. 42.

He considered that supreme knowledge to be a miracle, for everything had indeed become still for a moment; then he perceived that all of his own material nature had once again returned to dissolution. ||43||
Then the venerable Lomaśa said: "O King, this supreme sacred ford is the purifying Māṇikītīrtha, and it is also known as Āśvinītīrtha."
I have seen all this—the great holy ford of Brahmahrada and the Aśvapāṭala-tīrtha—directly with my own eyes; and after that, [furthermore].
I have always made my residence here in this auspicious hermitage;
likewise, the incarnations, the liberated ones, the lords, the deities, and so forth [have dwelt here]. (46)
After the manifestation of Hari, all the goddesses and gods resided in the imperishable ocean of horses and cloths within the field of Hari. 47.
With supreme love, they worshipped the primordial Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa—Rādhā, Lakṣmī, Pārvatī, Padmā, Ramā, Jayā, and Rati. ||48||
Lalitā, Padminī, Rambhā, Māṇikī, Śrī, Sarasvatī, Gaṅgā, Durgā, Sāvitrī, Saṃjñā, Yamunā, and Rohiṇī. ||49||
Mañjulā, Sadguṇā, Hāsā, Haimī, Śānti, Supuṣpikā, Manu, Kastūrikā, Devī, Campāmbujasvatī, and Vṛjā. (2.272.50)
All the goddesses, the wives of Brahmā, numbering in the hundreds of billions and trillions,
arrived and dwelt right here in this very lake, at the abode of Hari.
The Gaṇḍakī, the Svarṇarekhā, the Narmadā, the Tuṅgabhadrā, the Godāvarī, the Brahmaputrā, the Kāverī, and the Phalgu-īśvarī. ||52||
The Kṛṣṇā, the Śoṇā, the Gomatī, the Sindhu, and likewise the Coralikā;
the Śoṇabhadra, the Cerāvatī, the Sālvīnā, the Menakāṅgikā, the one named after me (Mannāmnī), the Aṅgaśikṣāṅgī, and likewise the Kāñcanagaṅgikā. ||53||
Tryaṅgahā, Cāmūrakā, Vīṇā, Yānāsanā,
Ombā, Trivalī, Cāmū, Vālagā, Nīparā,
Devikā, Dīnyubā, Utkrośī, and Nāilī. ||54||
Prapattikā, Sevikā, Nāstijarā, Kaṅgukī, Kyubagaṅgā, Rañjikā, Viṣatūrā, and Jampikā. ||55||
Śvetā, Nārāyaṇī, Matkuñjā, Yūkanāyikā,
Niraśāṇā, Miśrajalā, Āmajanā, Parānikā,
Śvānā, Grāsakāyānā, Viṣatūryā, and Kaliṅginī. ||56||
Likewise, other rivers such as the Mūrā and all others arrived at that lake in the form of sacred fords (tīrtha), indeed for the purpose of residing there forever. (57)
Mānasa, Indradyumna, Nārāyaṇa, and Puṣkara;
Pampā, which has the form of Indraprastha, Sudarśana, and Revata. ||58||
Likewise, there is Śivasaras, Citkṛtsaras, Kaularaka-saras, Śivaśīla, Mīnakaṅgu-saras, and Sābharaka-saras. ||59||
Also Bālakṛṣṇa Lake, Dvikala Lake, Saṭālapha Lake, and Viṣatūra Lake. ||2.272.60||
Also Urala and Sara, as well as Triguṇorasa;
likewise Pherumaṇḍa, Lūrāsara, and the lake named Maśaka. ||61||
Also the Rukma, the Trināsika, the Ebāla, and likewise the Sara;
the Saṭālpaka, the Alparūkṣa, the Ārdravārta, and likewise the Sara.
Furthermore, there is Tryaṅgānaka, Mayūrasa, Saras, Bangapāla, Nyūnajāmī, Śirāvāsa, and likewise Saras. (63)
Aitasa, Cauniyāgara, Lenduga, Pāyuga, likewise Yoniga, Aurasa, Tūronasa, Gaura, and Saras; ||64||
Gogrāsa, Bālarīśa, Ubarāsa, and likewise Saras;
Jayaśāna, Grātavāra, and likewise Grātaslāva and Saras. ||65||
Kṛtasthāna, Ceṣṭavāsa, Pīlipārśva, and likewise the lake;
Supārayāra, Kālīya, and likewise the lake Itarīśa. ||66||
These lakes also remained here, having come from that place:
Vṛndāvana, Mahākālavana, and likewise Tapovana.
The forest of Indraprastha, Dharmāraṇya, the Pauṣkaraka forest, Siṃhāraṇya, the Badaryāraṇyaka, and the Sundaraka forest. ||68||
Prāgjyotiṣāraṇyaka, Kāśamāraṇya, Irāraṇya, Śikṣāraṇya, and likewise Rāśavana. ||69||
Also the Uralāraṇyaka, as well as the Khāsīnāraṇyaka, the Bālāyana-mahāraṇya, and likewise the Sahārāraṇya. ||2.272.70||
Vālajīvāraṇyaka, Śādayānavana, Amarīvana, and likewise Abriktāraṇyaka. ||71||
Likewise, they arrived here at Siṃhāraṇya and the divine forests;
having offered a welcome and worship, they established their residence there with Hari.
They indeed performed them always at the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake;
thus, O King, this Aśvapaṭṭasara is a supreme sacred site (tīrtha).
It is the purifier of all sacred fords (tīrthas), auspicious and consisting of the Brahma-lake;
it is so on earth, in the heavenly world, and likewise elsewhere as well. (74)
There exist here holy fords such as Viraja and others;
and oceans of divine waters dwell here perpetually within these waters. (75)
Where Anādikṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the beloved of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, resides, there all the incarnations, the liberated souls, and whatever abodes there may be are also present.
Male and female lords, gods and goddesses dwell there; all sovereign powers reside there, and supernatural accomplishments abide there. (77)
That indeed is the supreme Anādi-Śrī-Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa-tīrtha;
here the Blessed Lord Puruṣottama took up his residence. (78)
Then, all his beautiful and auspicious beloveds stood together with him in bodily form on the left side of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. (79)
One hundred and twenty-five noble women arrived at the beautiful western lake, which was divided by a causeway.
They entered [the water] in the form of sacred fords (tīrtha); that is called the Hundred Tīrthas.
On the day of the manifestation of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, [they appeared]. ||8 1||
Accompanied by the cowherds and cowherd women, Śrī Kṛṣṇa arrived there at Gopītīrtha, Gopatīrtha, and Golokatīrtha. (82)
And that Kṛṣṇatīrtha was born there, which bestows supreme liberation and Goloka;
it was when Śrī Kṛṣṇa arrived here that he spoke to Rādhikā. (83)
"O Rādhikā, you must understand this," he said to his beloved Rādhikā;
"thousands of universes have indeed been created by Vairāja. (84)
In various places, he prayed to Hari, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, to enter and establish himself there. (85)
Hare Kṛṣṇa, Hare Kṛṣṇa, O Nārāyaṇa, Lord of lords!
In all the universes created by me, you are the sovereign. (86)
O Mādhava, until he arrives, who will establish the legal proceedings for living beings engaged in religious duties? (87)
Who will provide instruction to the Daityas and those of a tamasic nature?
Who, other than you, will effect the destruction of the sins of the sinful? (88)
Who else but you will perform the rites for Vedic initiation and the like, as well as the divine and ancestral ceremonies such as sacrifices and offerings that bestow merit? (89)
And who, indeed, other than you, will establish the boundaries for embodied beings, as well as bestow self-knowledge upon the virtuous and protect the dharma? (2.272.90)
And who will perform the marriage rites for virtuous women—those embodied beings who are submerged in passion and hatred and wandering in delusion? (9.1)
Without you and without association with you, who indeed will bring about liberation, as well as the dharma of worship, the dharma of protection, and the dharma of what has arisen? (92)
Without you, who would explain to human beings the duty of service, the duty of moral conduct, the duty of householders, the duty of forest-dwellers, and the ritual actions of ascetics? (93)
Who other than you will carry out the duty of renunciation, self-surrender, ancient policy, and even the conduct prescribed for the social orders? (94)
Even without your manifestation, those very cosmic eggs are all cremation grounds, giving birth to and delivering the cycles of birth and death. (95)
Without you, the perfected ones (sādhus) who have attained liberation will not depart from the imperishable state;
likewise, the attendants and the goddesses of fortune will not go to the millions of cosmic eggs.
Without you, there will be no auspiciousness among the gods and others;
without you, there will truly be no protection whatsoever. (97)
"O Blessed One, without you, our entire home will become empty; even the dwellings of the yogins will no longer exist in any way. (98)
Likewise, even those incarnations will pass away;
among them, who could go first, except for the sovereign of all creation? (99)
O Lord, even the sattvic gods and others will certainly not understand the knowledge of the path to liberation and so forth, nor their proper worship and other such practices, in every respect.
Having reached the veil of Māyā, embodied beings, enveloped by it,
will cast off their own divine nature and fall into the realm of darkness.
Therefore, O Blessed One, may You manifest in all the cosmic eggs;
go forth, O Lord, ocean of mercy, primordial Śrī Puruṣottama! 102.
Thus entreated, the beginningless Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, residing in the imperishable supreme abode, heard Virājaka through a divine voice.
The Blessed One, the Supreme Lord of the highest abode, spoke thus: "So be it; I shall go through millions of cosmic eggs. Having said this, he departed.
Desiring to become many for the sake of all that is auspicious,
that Supreme Lord became a distinct form in every egg and in every manifestation.
In all the many cosmic eggs, he is present everywhere with his qualities, lordly powers, and manifestations,
together with his attendants, liberated divine beings, consorts, and Śaktis.
Accompanied by devotees, religious enjoyments, and acts of worshipful devotion,
that very Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa indeed manifested Himself, O Rādhā.
Where Brahmā the Self-born, Śaṅkara Somanāthaka,
and Viṣṇu Nara-Nārāyaṇa reside, there dwells Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
In the western Naranārāyaṇakhaṇḍa, in Surāṣṭra upon the surface of the earth, in the field of Akṣara, to the east of Bhāviraivata.
At the holy site of Kukumavāpikā and on the banks of the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake,
in the city of Kuṅkumā, that glorious Lord Hari manifested Himself.
This very one is the supreme Kṛṣṇa, from whom infinite dark forms manifest; O Rādhā, you should indeed understand his greatness. 11.111.
Thus indeed did Kṛṣṇa himself speak then to his beloved Śrī Rādhikā;
that was heard by me directly, O lord of men.
This very one, the son of Śrī Kambharā, the illustrious Lord, the delight of Gopāla—this youth Bālakṛṣṇa, the beloved of Kṛṣṇa—is performing the sacrifice. (11.3)
All incarnations, abodes, liberated souls, as well as Īśvara and the others,
gods, sacred fords, and virtuous beings— truth indeed dwells here.
Liberation and emancipation shine here upon this earth in embodied form;
therefore, O King, whatever small amount you may have, offer it at this sacred ford.
Thus addressed by Lomaśa, the king, having abandoned delusion, his kingdom, and his home, undertook the Vaiṣṇava initiation according to the prescribed rite.
Having obtained the Vaiṣṇava initiation from her, that king became perfected;
thereafter, the sage was known by the name Citprakāśa, O Rādhikā.

Thus ends the two hundred and seventy-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Naranārāyaṇa-tīrtha, Harikṛṣṇa-tīrtha, and Māṇikī-tīrtha; the Previous Account of Aśvapaṭala; the Arrival of All Tīrthas at the Place Named Aśvapaṭṭa; the Arrival of the Supreme Brahman through the Praise of Vairāja; and the Initiation of Aśvapaṭala as a Saint," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmīnārāyaṇīya-saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O Rādhikā, at Kuṅkumavāpī, five hundred other sages who have taken refuge in Hari were impelled by the initiation of the light of consciousness (citprakāśa). || 1 ||
Having bowed down to the true guru Lomaśa, they quickly spoke for the sake of initiation;
Lomaśa also bestowed upon them the auspicious Vaiṣṇava initiation at that very spot.
Clad in saffron robes and endowed with all mantras, she was esteemed by the virtuous;
they all had observed fasts and performed purification of their bodies. (3)
Having performed the fire-offerings, those clad in saffron robes took up the mantras:
"May Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa be my refuge forever. (4)
Thus, with firm minds, they firmly took up this refuge-mantra:
"Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord; svāhā! (5)
Thereafter, they received that mantra known as *samarpaṇa* out of fear of Time,
Illusion, evil karma, the enemy, Yama, and the wicked-hearted.
Then, thereafter, they received this protective mantra: "Possessing a trident, a fish, a banner, a bow, a discus, a svastika, and a conch."
I am Brahmā, an eternal devotee of Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa;
the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa is my Lord and my husband.
Finally, they received this mantra known as Brahmabhāva:
"Bālakṛṣṇa is the Supreme Brahman; he is indeed my eternal Lord."
