for it is for the sake of Lakṣmī that the marriage horoscope is written, which is unlike any other.
For the sake of prosperity, Bṛhaspati is unrivaled by anyone else whom one approaches;
yet today, for the sake of prosperity, even your fame is sung, which is peerless among others. (45)
In former times, nothing else was so capable of producing joy for the sake of Lakṣmī;
the heart of Bālakṛṣṇa for the sake of Lakṣmī is peerless. (46)
Today, both worldly speech and divine speech are perceived for the sake of *lakṣmī*;
the world’s fickleness is seen as bringing about auspiciousness for the sake of *lakṣmī*. (47)
Oh, how the world-ness of the world attains its true reality today through the glance of Lakṣmī and Kṛṣṇa—that which indeed consists of divine vision! 48.
"Oh, how great is my fortune! That higher state has truly become meaningful for me, for my Guru has always remained elevated by being sent forth upon the leaves of the Lakṣmī tree. (49)
Thus, O Rādhikā, that brāhmaṇa Bṛhaspati, who was filled with wonder at seeing all that, became even more devoted to Bāla-Kṛṣṇa.
The great devotee, a true bhakta who had offered himself,
attained his own true nature by surrendering everything he possessed to Hari.
Then Bṛhaspati, intending to depart, said to Gopāla-Kṛṣṇaka: "Inform me that today I wish to go to Kāśikā. (52)
"On that new moon day, the Lord Śiva will indeed wait for me there.
"So be it," Gopāla replied, and he spoke further to Bṛhaspati.
"Go quickly, O Guru, and inform Śiveśvara of Kāśī;
let your desire be fulfilled, for I shall honor your word. (54)
Having worshipped the horoscope document, I accepted it with devotion;
for that which is certain for gods such as yourselves will surely bring happiness. (55)
If things were reversed, it would lead to a contrary outcome and bring great suffering.
"The girl is suitable and the boy is also suitable; let it be so," he said, and having given his verbal consent, he then provided a written agreement. (56)
Śrī Rādhikā said:
What is that letter of union like, and what is the reply-letter like?
I desire to hear about that, as well as the notification and its response. (57)
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Listen, O Rādhā, I shall tell you about both these auspicious letters;
they were written according to the facts and adorned with excellent qualities such as profundity.
In the auspicious dust of the venerable Lord Śrīśvara, within the sacred field of the imperishable Brahman,
shines the glorious Lord of Lakṣmī in the excellent place known as Śrīmat-Kuṅkumavāpikā;
there, in his abode, sports the Supreme Lord Hari, the illustrious Bālakṛṣṇa.
Adored by ten million lords of the lotuses, the Lord Gopālakṛṣṇa reigns supreme. || 59 ||
He who, being the father of Vairāja, shines forth as Mahāviṣṇu himself;
he who, at the command of Hari, exists in the first creation assuming the conduct of a human;
whose fame is sought by the three worlds for his creation, and who is celebrated here as the abode of auspicious qualities.
I bow perpetually to that very Lord, the husband of Śrī Kaṃbharā.
For those whose treasure-trove of a well-heaped mass of merit manifests here in this world; for whom the abundant blessings of virtuous people bear fruit in the long term;
and for whom the fruit of sacrifices and austerities, as well as the fruit of serving the elders, truly arises—
But for them, a relationship with a Viṣṇu such as you would be difficult to attain.
The virtuous offer their merits and even their blessings at the feet of their sons;
the lords of the abodes offer the crowns resting upon their heads in worship;
and the gods offer divine prosperity, supreme jewels, gems, and the like to the deities.
Kings [attain] unsurpassed sovereignty, mountain lords [attain] gold and other riches, and merchants [attain] preeminence. ||6 2||
To that Lord Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa, the dweller in the Imperishable, the Lord of all lords, the worthy one who is the abode of supreme qualities— to Him indeed [I bow].
For Śiveśvara resides in Kāśī, while the Lord of the gods resides on Kailāsa.
"O Śrī Pārvatīśa, I grant you this gift of my sinless daughter every day. (6.3)
That Lakṣmī who formerly came here from the abode of Hari by the power of Nārāyaṇa’s will, and manifested herself in my auspicious home as one devoted to Him—
she is now present here, worthy of being chosen as a bride and fit for the giving and receiving of gifts.
The procedure for giving it away takes place on the fourth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa. || 6.4 ||
While this most auspicious and meritorious moment, the best of hours for the festival of that act of giving,
was being determined by us as the most excellent and propitious,
our virtuous kinsmen and friends arrived at my residence with hearts full of joy.
O illustrious ones, let the Self be fully realized by your son through the practice of holding the hand and other such means.
I am a devotee of Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa on this earth, and here Hara is also a Sāttvata;
with the grace of Gaṇanāyaka, may I complete this sacrifice without obstacle, performing your excellent service according to the rules and to the best of my ability every day.
Having seen me, they shall be well-pleased; therefore, let them accept this request of mine. || 65 ||
Indeed, this beautiful letter of mine, which awakens my mind and is intended for bestowal, sprinkled with auspicious drops of sacred saffron,
accompanied by witnesses for two years, was placed in the hand of Bṛhaspati and sent by me.
May she, who has come into your hands, and may my daughter likewise, bring auspiciousness to you and to your sons. ||67||
Having quickly dispatched me with due respect to this Teacher of the Gods (Bṛhaspati),
and having entrusted me with the festive bond for my elevation,
may the residents of glorious Kāśī indeed grant us what is most fitting.
[Protect] us, your devotees who are intent on Brahman, who uphold the Vedas, and who are your Sāttvata servants, O Hari. ||48||
Or whatever other day is graced by virtuous deeds and the like, or whatever auspicious day belongs to the illustrious—
let that be announced most swiftly as fit for giving along with a true guru.
Furthermore, whatever else has come into my own possession according to family custom, and whatever is worthy of me—
"Let all that be reported," saying this, Śambhu attains peace—Om. (69)
Thus, O Rādhikā, this letter of donation sent by Śaṅkara has indeed been spoken by me to you out of consideration for you; now hear the subsequent reply-letter.
Listen to that [work] which the illustrious Gopālakṛṣṇa wrote to Śaṅkara—a source of auspiciousness for all that is auspicious, and filled with manifold meanings. 7.1.
Oṃ! Formerly, in the auspicious land of Goloka, which is the abode of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, he manifested from Śrī Kṛṣṇa with half his body as his own consort;
then, in his own realm, he shines as Śiva, known by the name Sadāśiva, a true Vaiṣṇava on Mount Kailāsa.
In Vaikuṇṭha, in the presence of Hari, he performed an excellent dance accompanied by songs. ||72||
For Śrī Lakṣmī knew that Hari’s departure at an improper time would be an obstacle to her amorous play;
she cursed him, decreeing his birth as a human accompanied by his wife.
Upon hearing this, Śrī Hari himself became a follower of his devotee, even though he had to leave Śrī behind.
That Lakṣmī, following her desire for the attainment of Hari, remains as your daughter. ||73||
Thus may Lord Kṛṣṇa always grant auspiciousness here to Śiva, who possesses the form of Śivā, as well as to the Fortune of the true Lord of Pārvatī;
and may your son Gaṇādhipa, together with his consort, bestow welfare and auspiciousness—so prays Gopālakṛṣṇa, whose residence is in the glorious Kuṅkumavāpikā. 74.
Indeed, my good fortune has been greatly increased by you, having given your daughter to Śārṅgin—
my son Narāyaṇa, who is Hari himself, the illustrious Bālakṛṣṇa.
Even though you have associated with Bṛhaspati, the preceptor of the gods, my home has been rendered most pure.
And by him, too, the deed of gift was offered here, and it was indeed accepted by me with affection. ||75||
Having reached the city of Kāśī, where the most auspicious opportunity has been ordained, may you behold the supreme vision of Śambhu today for the sake of attaining peace and tranquility; thus,
having performed all the various rites at the sacred site, even though they were difficult to accomplish.
Indeed, I shall behold the eternal happiness ordained by fate for this couple.
O Lord of Umā, on the third day of the bright fortnight, immediately after midday, I shall come there quickly by means of celestial chariots, accompanied by my family and my lotus-like attendants.

Furthermore, those other kings on earth who have performed sacrifices and are devoted to Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa— ten million of them, along with their vehicles and hundreds of billions of men, shall also arrive here.
Countless lords who are Nārāyaṇas, though they dwell in the abode of light;
likewise the perfected ones (siddhas), the hosts of seers, the ancestors, the gods, and human beings;
even the divine groups of conscious beings endowed with bodies, the elements, and the sacred fords—indeed, all these.
Even the goddesses, though situated beyond creation, shall proceed even further, beyond a parārdha.
Even though millions of maidens and women dear to Brahmā are already present here, they will also come to your temple, eager for the yoga of the beginningless Brahman.
O omniscient one, whose form is Śiva, what secret could there be between me and you?
O Hari, who abides on the Vaiśālī ground, what need is there to speak of your welfare to you, who are so perfectly disciplined in yoga? (79)
Having thus bowed down and likewise petitioned the Lord of Kāśī,
I now respectfully present this letter to my Guru along with ten thousand jewels.
Whether there be deficiency or excess, whether the reply be unpleasant, sweet, weighty, or pungent— [I offer it].
My conduct must be forgiven in every way by Śambhu, whose soul is disciplined.
Thus did Śrīmad Gopālakṛṣṇa, encouraged by Nārada, give this reply to Hara regarding Rādhikā.
He performed a great worship of Bṛhaspati with tens of millions of jewels,
as well as with fine garments, sandalwood, pearls, and offerings of necklaces.
He delighted the true guru with foods and honors of drink, and presented him with a beautiful celestial chariot adorned with jewels. (83)
The true guru ascended the beautiful Kalpalatā tree and,
on the morning of the first day of the lunar fortnight, traveled through the air to Kāśī.
He gave the letter containing the reply to Śambhu, and Hara rejoiced;
he read the auspicious letter and rejoiced yet again.
One should also perform salutations and other such acts of discipline, as well as cultivate affection toward the illustrious Gopālakṛṣṇa and likewise toward Bālakṛṣṇa. (86)
The true guru spoke thus to Lomaśa and the others:
"A great arrival of an army, known throughout the world, is imminent here. (87)
"When both [types of] fame exist, the three worlds will surely come under one's power through generosity"; thus did the Guru speak at that time. ||88||
Śambhu, with a gracious heart, spoke to the Guru according to his strength:
"Indeed, the three worlds shall come into the courtyard of this worthy recipient of merit. (89)
We shall perform appropriate, auspicious, and supramundane service;
and my hosts, numbering in the millions, billions, trillions, and quadrillions, dwell in the world.
Tens of millions, billions, and trillions of goddesses become my consorts;
likewise, Saṃkarṣaṇa, Mahākāla, Mahārudra, and Rudraka [become my attendants]. ||9.1||
I am Hara; my forms exist even by the millions.
Kṛṣṇa is my father manifest, and Goloka is mine in every respect.
Mahāmāyā is my creation; Hanumān is indeed my son;
and Gaṇeśa, along with crores, hundreds of millions, and billions of attendants, are mine.
Everything is auspicious for me, and you are likewise my preceptor among the gods; what is lacking for me today? Everything is fully accomplished for me. (94)
Having spoken thus and honored Bṛhaspati as he sat upon his seat,
Śaṅkara fed him and caused a pavilion to be constructed.
He caused the sounds of musical instruments to resound in all directions and dispatched messengers throughout the three worlds for the purpose of issuing invitations.
O Rādhikā, Śaṅkara, the benefactor of the world, was accompanied by Kuṃkumapatrikā; and all auspicious things came to pass in the abode of Hara. || 97 ||

Thus ends the two hundred and seventy-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Auspicious Songs of the Women of the Three Worlds in Every House, the Great Festivals in the Abode of Gopāla-Kṛṣṇa on the New Moon Day during the Tretā Cycle in the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā; the Honoring of Bṛhaspati, the Description of the Deed of Charity, the Return of the Honored Bṛhaspati to Kāśī after Accepting the Gift, and the Invitation Sent by Śambhu to the Three Worlds. || 277 ||
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O Rādhikā, on the first day of the lunar fortnight, women indeed sang auspicious hymns of Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa in the morning.
All musical instruments were played everywhere; in every house and courtyard, festive decorations were filled out by the people.
Exceedingly beautiful archways, adorned with fresh sprouts,
were placed on all sides at the doors of the houses by the young women.
Ghee lamps were also prepared, and banners and small flags were held aloft;
festoons, beautified with colorful designs, were fastened across the expanse of the sky.
The entire splendor of Kuṃkumavāpikā was like that of the celestial abodes, created by the delighted subjects through various artistic arrangements. || 1 ||
The carriage-roads, the royal highways, the side streets,
and the alleys were swept clean, sprinkled with water, and decorated with colorful paintings.
The marketplaces were already adorned with arches and colored festoons,
and rendered auspicious with curd, sprouts, and betel leaves.
Dwellings, temples, palaces, rows of mansions, vast halls, and beautiful gardens were adorned by the people. (8)
The Aśvapaṭṭasara lake was also adorned with colorful pigments,
while the crossroads were purified with water-filters and auspicious lamps.
The railings and altars, as well as the door-frames, were very difficult to scale;
and the gate-towers were beautiful, adorned with seven-tiered finials.
Indeed, they were adorned with leaves, sprouts, threads, and fruits;
there, the beautiful abode of Bālakṛṣṇa was made of moonstones and other precious materials. || 11 ||
At that time, it was adorned on all sides with groves of wish-fulfilling creepers (*kalpalatā*), fruit-bearing trees and the like, as well as sun-stone (*sūryakānta*) and other precious gems.
That temple of Śrī Hari, which possessed a thousand single-pitchered domes,
was then adorned on all sides with new articles of beauty and other ornaments.
Is it Vaikuṇṭha, or something else? Is it Goloka, or even another place? Is it the abode of Brahmā, or perhaps some other immortal realm? Or is it something different altogether?
Was heaven or some other entire realm imagined by the people? For in such a city, both women and men were indeed dressed in new garments. (15)
At that time, there were new ornaments, new colors, and beauties with ninefold charms; there was new enthusiasm, new strength, and new prosperities.
They partook of new food and drink, they sang new hymns of praise, they were noble in their new resolutions, and they were endowed with nine excellent qualities. (17)
The cattle became dull, and the birds lost their zest;
the cows yielded no milk, and the buffaloes were devoid of vigor. (18)
On the first day of the lunar fortnight, bulls possessed new vigor, elephants and other animals exhibited ninefold curiosity, and horses and others displayed ninefold joy.
The trees were laden with new fruit, and the creepers were covered in fresh blossoms;
the branches possessed every new flavor, as did the crops and the ears of grain.
Then, fresh honey was found everywhere;
the Brahmins were filled with new joy, and the virtuous were possessed of new devotion. || 21 ||
The wise ones possessed a new mindset, and the principles were indeed renewed; they truly became radiant, endowed with ninefold splendor.
In particular, the inner hearts of people indeed became stainless;
through the intensity of their devotion, they truly became bestowers of eternal bliss.
Thus, O Rādhikā, Kuṅkumavāpī was like a maiden newly endowed with youth, adorned with every kind of ornament. (24)
Thinking that a new, divine Lakṣmī would arrive, she became "Nūtanā" (the New One),
for the sake of attaining fresh joy from her new co-wife.
For the sake of the welfare arising from the affection of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, a divine pavilion from the abode of Akṣara arrived there. 26.
Some bowed to the illustrious Blessed One, and some to Gopālakṛṣṇa;
having prostrated before their mother, that pavilion was filled with those whose true nature was liberated.
By the mere will of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa,
he manifested his divine form as a liberated soul within a moment.
Having come to propitiate the Supreme Self,
I pray that by His command I may become a beautiful pavilion leading to the abode of the Imperishable.
Hari said, "So be it; you have indeed been remembered for that purpose.
Build a beautiful pavilion so that it shines according to the sacred syllable."
Having received the command "Om," O Rādhikā, the pavilion itself,
being liberated through the Great [mantra], assumed the form of the pavilion as its very essence.
Having assumed two forms, one small and one large, the small form became firmly established in front of the temple of Bālakṛṣṇa. ||32||
It was enriched with a hundred single pitchers and beautifully adorned with a hundred pillars;
it had seven stories and was like the path of the sky both around its perimeter and in its center,
shining above with a priceless central pitcher.
Just as the moonlight of the moon appears upon the earth on the full-moon day,
so too did his white luster, resembling water, spread in every direction;
it pervaded that land of Akshara like the world of the moon.
In its center, where a natural sun-gem shines, it is illuminated by a thousand gentle and soft rays. (36)
Then, lightning-stalks on their sides, possessing the luster of lamps and white as milk, flash forth on all sides.
There were gems and woven cloths—white, red, and variegated;
blue, yellow, green, and tawny, possessing diverse splendors. (38)
Tied to every corner, those stars indeed shine forth;
likewise, there are various leafy creepers at their sides. (39)
Herbs shine like leaf-lamps here and there;
the stalks serve as the bases for the sacrificial pits, and the pits are adorned with cloth strips.
The water-carrying conduits, the secret channels for conveying fire, and the secret flows of fire shine forth according to their respective locations. (41)
The bamboo poles, pillars, figurines, and rafters, as well as the arches, branches, and sub-branches—all these parts of the bamboo framework and so forth—are made visible by the rafters. (42)
There is no deficiency in their splendor; they shine just as they do in the Imperishable (Akṣara), for he alone is indeed liberated, being the very self of the pavilion.
Rays of light become cool, and likewise they become hot;
they manifest as both cold and hot, and also as neither hot nor cold.
They possess a touch like that of sweet nectar, bestow the bliss of Brahman, and also grant joy to all the sense organs. ||45||
Thus, in this pavilion endowed with lamps and possessed of great splendor,
there were pillars in the form of plantain trees joined with unbroken leaves.
Even among hundreds of seven-storied mansions situated in separate divisions,
there were indeed divine seven-colored cloths draped like garments.
Within that stream, the abode of splendors, all creations are perceived, just as the dwellings of the gods are seen within Mount Meru at its center. ||48||
In some pillars there are indeed sages, and in others there are perfected beings (siddhas);
in some places there stand liberated souls, infinite in number, in the form of Hari.
In some places the incarnations reside; in some places the attendants reside;
in some places indeed are the groups of liberated women, virtuous and beloved of Brahmā.
In one place there is Goloka of Kṛṣṇa, and in another Vaikuṇṭha;
in some places the unmanifest abode, and in others the immortal realm shines forth.
In some places the golden abode shines forth; in some places the realm of Vairāja;
and in some places the abodes of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra manifest themselves.
In one pillar is Satyaloka, in another the abode of the ancestors;
in one are the gods and the guardians of the quarters, and in another the lords of the universe.
In some pillars shine the planets, such as the sun and the moon; in others dwell the Vasus, Indras, and great sages.
In some places there were human beings, and in others Daityas and Dānavas;
in some places there were oceans, rivers, and wildernesses and forests.
And some mountains were fixed upon a pillar, while others dwelt in the netherworld;
some lay in the water upon the pillar, and others even lay upon dry land.
In some caves there, elephants and other such creatures are seen,
as well as Garuḍas, parrots, sāras, peacocks, and mayūrakas.
Bhāsas, swans, and cātakas are seen there, as well as beings of divine origin;
and sometimes the Apsarases of the Brahma-lake appear as dancers. (58)
Within the pillars and the painted rows, as well as in the pavilion composed of imperishable syllables, the threefold creation is indeed seen to be contained. (59)
Upon the surface of the earth, on that land of gold, indeed, divine grounds shine forth;
in some places water, in some places fire, and in some places the earth itself resplendent.
In some places there are oceans, and in others there are forests;
in some places there are mountains, as well as lakes and rivers.
In some places, most delightful gardens and even cities are seen within the interior of the earth, upon its level surface above.
In this manner, the Ocean of Milk and the Lord Nārāyaṇa likewise appear;
there, Hari is seen within the pavilion in the interior of the earth.

The deities of the site (vāstudevatā) are seen everywhere at the bases of the pillars; they are also observed in their respective places within the pavilion (maṇḍapa) and the central chamber (kṣitigarbhaka). 64.
The deities of the branches are seen, and there are also the deities of the door;
likewise, the female friends of the archway are goddesses adorned with garlands.
Paintings are seen with beautiful young women as their subjects;
they are well-attired, adorned with garments and ornaments, and illuminated by a divine light. (66)
In the center, circular lamps hang suspended,
and in the gateway, the goddesses, imbued with the sentiment of laughter, shine forth together.
All the women born of delight, diverse as if they were sentient beings, shine forth, situated upon the support of vision at the tip of the circle. 68.
There were also Gandharva singers existing as couples;
they shone with banners upon the floors within the pavilions. (69)
In every corner there were seven golden jars each, arranged along a single thread; shining like the sun, they were most beautiful to behold.
Fruit-laden branches hung down, supported by pillars and posts; and there, ropes were fastened with garlands of gems and pearls.
And here, in this pavilion, a variety is seen in the display on all sides:
on one side there is the fortune of ten million, and on the other side, indeed, more than ten million.
On one side were the Sarasvatīs, and on the other side were the Koṭidurgikās;
all of them were seen bearing weapons and adorned with every kind of ornament.
Upon the floors above the gateways were all the enchanting creations;
and above those were the attendants and the cowherds in their own forms.
All the Gandharvas as well as the hosts of Śaṅkara, and whatever divine weapons exist even throughout the three worlds; ||75||
All of those indeed exist situated above that;
and above that are the portions of Dhruva, accompanied by twelve suns.
And the circular pavilions, enriched with splendor and canopies, shine forth;
likewise, the delightful quadrangular halls and the brilliantly radiant upper chambers gleam.
All the stairs were covered with cloths of gold and silver;
the walls were draped with fine fabrics, and there were jewels and golden-winged arrows.
All the canopies made of silk shone brilliantly, just as the divine Vaikuṇṭha and other realms appear upon the higher planes. 79.
In the great garden, it was in full bloom and graced by the delight of the rāsa dance;
there were vehicles such as elephants, lions, and Garuḍas for the inhabitants of heaven.
Whatever things there are that are most excellent, delightful, and auspicious,
all of those have been placed, as it were, in due order upon the higher levels.

It is auspicious, endowed with wish-fulfilling creepers, wish-fulfilling trees, and wish-fulfilling lamps; it is distinguished by the splendor of a kalpa and likewise bestows the fruits of the earth of a kalpa.
For that pavilion was adorned with garlands of wish-fulfilling pearls;
it possessed the pleasant touch of the *kalpa* wind and was resplendent with the fragrance of the *kalpa* tree. ||83||
He is the giver of garments of the Kalpa-tree, accompanied by the betel-vines of the Kalpa-tree;
he is the bestower of drinks from the Kalpa-tree, and possesses a celestial chariot as small as a Kalpa-atom.

He provides couches and coverlets of divine quality, adorned with celestial pillows; he bestows celestial footstools and cushions, and is the means for accomplishing all that is desired. He is endowed with celestial grass mats, soft seats of divine quality, and lion thrones.
It is as beautiful as the assembly hall of Kalpapīṭha and is adorned with a Kalpa-paṭṭika. || 86 ||
It was joined with crooked door-bolts of refined gold and unbroken cloth-fringes;
it possessed arches made of glass and portals adorned with jewels and gems.
Its walls were adorned with chests and door-panels set with precious gems;
its side grounds shone, graced by swings, hammocks, and other such delights.
It was equipped with lightning-displaying machines and lightning-sound-producing mechanisms.
Possessing lightning-conducting instruments and excellent machines for lunar touch, he was equipped with well-crafted devices. || 89 ||
He who has perfected the ritual procedures at the piercing of the kalpas, who effects the transformation of secondary rituals,
who is enriched by the machinery of temporal designations, and who sets in motion omniscience;
he who possesses the yoga-rituals within the microcosm, the macrocosm, and the supreme wheels.
He manifested the sounds of musical instruments, his own voice, and songs through the mechanism of his imagination. || 91 ||
Adorned with the yantra that reveals the entire essence of both the individual body and the cosmic egg,
he bestows the satisfaction of desire through his touch and grants the supreme wonder of sublime experience.
Merely upon being remembered, he bestows his grace in an instant;
endowed with the wonder of primordial creation, he is the consciousness of existence, awareness, and bliss.
He is the bestower of eternal bliss, possessing the bell, the conch, and the drum;
he is joined with a lake of all kinds of enjoyments and is perfectly filled by the ocean of nectar.
Whatever excellent women exist throughout the entire creation, and of whatever kind they may be—
all those, assuming various distinct forms, were caused to be established there.
In the corner is a pillar named Māṇikya, made of gold, resplendent with red colors, possessing four corners and a beautiful capital. || 96 ||
He was worshipped with vermilion, flowers, unbroken grains (akṣata), lotuses, and other offerings,
as well as upon a sandalwood plank and within a circle of unbroken grains.
A golden water-pot filled with water and accompanied by a *pūjikā* [offering vessel], adorned with a necklace, a sacred thread, and fine garments, should be filled with water in the center. || 98 ||
It was made beautiful, provided with mango, *aśoka*, excellent *campaka*, and *nāgavallī* leaves, along with *śrīphala* fruits, precious gems, and mineral ores.
By Gaṇeśa, who was worshipped with gold, who was well-conquered by the gods,
who was accompanied by Siddhi and Buddhi, and who was endowed with the attainment of auspiciousness—
thus indeed did that pavilion there become described as divine.
Whatever splendors exist in the world through diversity, those were created by him himself. || 101 ||
O Rādhikā, it is impossible to describe him;
he holds a vessel of auspicious unbroken rice grains and saffron, which is the sprout of all blessings.
Endowed with the perfection of all articles for worship and honor, Bālakṛṣṇa, standing at the forefront, shone most brilliantly. || 103 ||

Thus ends the two hundred and seventy-eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Morning Auspicious Rites on the First Day of the Bright Fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa, the Splendor of the Kuṅkumavāpī Lake and the Saras, and the Beauty of the Divine Courtyard and Pavilion," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.
Śrī Rādhikā said: How is it that a ruby pillar is placed here in this pavilion?
And for what purpose indeed is the installation of the water-pot (kalaśa) performed there? (1)
O Kṛṣṇa, how is the installation of Gaṇeśa performed, as well as the installation of the Mothers (Mātṛkā),
the installation of Vāstu, the installation of Viṣṇu,
and the installation of the family deity (Kuladeva)?
What fruit is declared for establishing [the image], and what is the unpleasant consequence for not establishing it? || 3 ||
O Kṛṣṇa, tell me all of that which is the cause of happiness for those in the cycle of existence,
knowing which people in the higher worlds will perform it according to the prescribed rules.
O Lord, why is it that the sages who are devotees of the Blessed One establish the Sarvatobhadra maṇḍala together with the deity? What is the reason for this?
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Listen, O Rādhā, I shall describe the happiness that brings benefit to both husband and wife,
especially for the householder, and particularly for the husband.
He who brings about the abundance of jewels, gold, and other riches always resides in the house of the householder;
he is worshipped as having Indra as his deity and also as having Agni as his deity. (7)
Even the ruby pillar is said to have the Cow as its presiding deity;
installed here in the pavilion, it has Indra, Agni, and the Cow as its deities.
A householder should always make his prosperity equal to that of Indra,
and his family should be perpetually as radiant as fire.
May the cow always yield flavorful milk, and may the home indeed be full of flavor. May the prosperities of Indra always abide in the house of the householder.
May there always be prosperity of the sacred fires in the house of the householder; may there always be prosperity of cows in the house of the householder. (11)
Thus, the deities stationed there bestow their blessings;
otherwise, a threefold poverty arises for him:
indeed, his home shall be lacking in prosperity, lacking in cooking, and lacking in flavor.
Indeed, everything here would consist of suffering due to the failure to worship the ruby (māṇikya). 13.
Wherever there is indeed the dwelling of Māṇikya, there is always the dwelling of Hari;
and wherever there is the residence of Hari, there is the residence of Lakṣmī.
Wherever Lakṣmī dwells, there the abode of prosperity is found;
therefore, those who know the ancient lore worship the Māṇikya pillar.
Many earthly defects—such as sleepiness, lethargy, heaviness, dullness, and dryness—are dissolved by the worship of that [deity]. 16.
Destruction, widowhood, separation from one's husband, illness,
and even childlessness— these all dissolve through the worship of him.

Through the worship of that [image], one attains the state of being a wanderer, homelessness, the emptiness of the house, and the emptiness of fruit-bearing trees and the like; they all dissolve away. (18)
The lack of love between husband and wife, the lack of mental focus in one's own home, and the lack of good fortune for the wife—all these dissolve through the worship of that [deity]. (19)
The bride’s lack of fortune on the earth, her lack of fortune in the house, and likewise her lack of fortune in the family—all these surely perish through the worship of this [deity]. (2.279.20)
By the worship of the Māṇikya gem, one is released from the debt to the Rākṣasas, the debt to the goddess Kumārī, and the debt to one's father and other ancestors. (21)
The testimony of Indra, Agni, and the Cow indeed establishes the world beyond and other matters;
from that, every domestic rite and all actions become fruitful.
Thus, O Rādhikā, should the fruit of worshipping with rubies be understood.
Now hear from me the auspicious fruit of worshipping with a water-pot as well. (23)
Indeed, Varuṇa shines resplendent within the water in the pitcher;
all sacred fords as well as the oceans and rivers come there.
The lakes, the deities, and the lords of the jars also brought that which was required for the wedding rite, which bestows peace and happiness. (25)
He is the giver of water and food, and the bestower of all flavors;
even the bodily acts of desire become purifying through his worship. ||26||
It bestows all prosperity of sons and makes the home eternally pure;
it also removes the natural impurity found in the bodies of both women and men.
By sprinkling with the waters of Varuṇa, all of that [impurity] is removed;
therefore, the husband becomes a sacred ford (tīrtha), bestowing the fruits of a sacred ford. ||28||
"A wife is the embodiment of a sacred ford (tīrtha), bestowing the fruit of all holy places;
indeed, the deity Varuṇa has declared that the couple alone constitutes a sacred ford. (29)
Wherever indeed is the station of Varuṇa, there no debt arises;
all juices and all fragrances there belong to Varuṇa.
The abode of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa shall be in that house where there is a place for the water-pot,
and where his water-pot is filled with milk.
He shall dwell always nourished by milk, ghee, fresh butter, curd, buttermilk, Soma, and nectar. ||32||
Likewise, elements of the nature of jars reside within him;
for he is worthy of the offering of golden, silver, and jeweled jars containing precious gems.
His house shall be graced by daughters, auspicious jars, and daughters-in-law; it shall be endowed with the prosperity of his lineage and adorned with golden pitchers. (34)
Thus, O Rādhikā, I have declared the fruit of being worthy of the water-pot;
yet, if the pot is not installed, all that which was declared does not come to pass.
Everything would become the opposite, increasing suffering and poverty;
I declare that there is no fruit for one unworthy of Gaṇeśa, for I, Kṛṣṇa, am indeed the Lord of the Gaṇas. (36)
The Blessed One is the bestower of prosperity, the fulfiller of all desires, the granter of every success, and likewise the giver of supernatural powers and accomplishments. || 37 ||
I am the bestower of auspicious gains, the destroyer of all obstacles, and my protection is ever-present through my worship. || 38 ||
May sweet foods such as *laḍḍukas* and other delicacies be provided for one who performs my worship;
for that worshiper of mine, houses made of gold and silver shall arise. (39)
His house shall abound in elephants, horses, and chariots, and be richly furnished with vehicles; his attire shall always be resplendent with yellow garments and other fine ornaments. (2.279.40)
The face of Gaṇeśa, endowed with a trunk, bestows cattle and wealth;
his belly, like that of a woman, bestows food and grants sons and other blessings. (41)
Through the worship of Gaṇeśa, the region below the waist—the seat of all desires—becomes the fulfiller of every wish, and even adverse *prārabdha* karma is destroyed. (42)
"No calamity shall befall him from the wicked yogis of the hosts.
Thus, O Rādhikā, has this been declared to you here regarding the worship of Gaṇeśa. 43.
I am Gaṇeśa in the form of Kṛṣṇa, abiding in the home as the most excellent fruit;
there, in every respect, the householder obtains both worldly enjoyment and liberation. 44.
O Rādhikā, listen also to the excellent fruit of establishing the Mātṛkās;
for Śaṅkara’s Yoginīs are sixty-four in number. (45)
The Mātṛkās and likewise other Ṛṣi-wives who are Mātṛkās, as well as other water-deities and others such as Caṇḍī and the rest. ||46||
The Mothers such as Koṭarā and others, who take the form of child-seizing spirits (bālagraha), as well as the Rākṣasīs beginning with the goddess Ṣaṣṭhī, are also Mothers (mātṛkā). ||47||
Thus, in many ways, they exist as those who, when worshipped, always bestow happiness;
yet when unworshipped and provoked to anger, they devour the house, the child, and the fetus.
In some houses, they even become enraged and devour the bride or the groom; therefore, these women must be honored, for when satisfied, they bestow prosperity as well. (49)
Just as they ward off the danger that has arrived from water and even from fire,
so too should these family goddesses (kuladevīs) always be worshipped.
The family goddesses (kuladevikās) are worshipped for the sake of increasing the lineage, for the sake of increasing prosperity, and for the sake of averting destruction. (51)
One should always worship Vāstupuruṣa for the constant satisfaction of the Earth,
whether in the construction of a house, a pavilion, a sacrificial altar, or a ritual pit.

The worship of the site (vāstupūjana) destroys the sins arising from the destruction of living beings; it likewise destroys the defects of the directions, the defects of the earth, and the defects of the spirits on all sides. (53)
O Rādhā, when the Vāstu deity is indeed worshipped, all [obstacles] are destroyed in every way;
he certainly becomes the provider of a dwelling for the couple for a long time. (54)
If the star Dhruva is on the ground, there will be fortune for both the bride and the groom;
when the Vāstu rite is performed for the deity, all actions offered therein shall become auspicious. (55)
Thus has been described to you here the worship of the site (vāstupūjana), which destroys disease;
as well as the installation of Viṣṇu, which bestows prosperity and grants auspiciousness.
Where Viṣṇu dwells, there resides prosperity that bestows all happiness;
when worshipped and saluted, Viṣṇu shall make one's home like Vaikuṇṭha.
The eternal Viṣṇu shall bestow devotion upon his family, as well as the welfare of the husband and wife; he shall grant them fame, glory, and a virtuous nature.
Being duly worshipped, he should provide protection with the Sudarśana discus;
likewise, he should bestow Dharma and impart knowledge endowed with discernment.
When well-honored, he bestows even the internal, divine eye;
and when propitiated through the offering of everything, he grants nirvāṇa.
Thus, O Rādhā, has the fruit of worshipping the gods and others been described;
now hear, O Rādhā, the auspicious fruit of the pavilion as well. (66) 1.
The pavilion is said to be the support; the pavilion is the abode of the deities.
And the pavilion is celebrated as the dwelling place of all creation. (62)
It may be called a cloth pavilion (paṭamaṇḍapa), or even a relic pavilion (dhātumaṇḍapa);
it may also be called a merit pavilion (puṇyamaṇḍapa) or a wooden pavilion (kāṣṭhamaṇḍapa). ||6 3 ||
There was a jeweled pavilion, as well as a house pavilion;
there was indeed a tree pavilion, and likewise a garden pavilion. (64)
The Kāṇḍamaṇḍapa, the Pārthivamaṇḍapa,
and the Kalpamaṇḍapa— these indeed are the pavilions.
In all those places, whatever beings there may be, beginning with the gods,
who abide within the three qualities, all come together for the great festival.
Therefore, the worship of the pavilion indeed bestows the fruit of all worship;
for by the honoring of the pavilion, all beings, beginning with the gods, become truly satisfied. (67)
Through the worship of the pavilion (maṇḍapa), the temple shall become auspicious, heaven shall meet with auspiciousness, and all prosperity shall also be attained. (68)
In the case of a welcome and respectful reception, a pavilion is considered auspicious in front;
it brings peace to the mind and bestows tranquility upon him.
The auspicious one always gives whey, buttermilk, and even nectar;
he gives curd-whey and also causes the fire-oblation to be performed.
The pavilion always brings about supreme prosperity rooted in that;
it is considered to provide satisfaction and happiness for all the gods through the oblation. (71)
O Rādhā, for a householder, this oblation always destroys sin;
it is said to bestow all enjoyments and increase all longevity. (72)
Bestowing all health and considered to be the liberator from all debts, the auspicious Sarvatobhadra diagram is likewise installed in the pavilion. (73)
Its fruit is the destruction of afflictions caused by the planets and the destruction of sins;
it likewise bestows gold, silver, and utensils, as well as a house.
It bestows supreme prosperity and merit, grants beds and furnishings,
as well as vessels and ornaments, and provides parasols and chowries.
This great and auspicious circle of omens (Bhadramaṇḍala) bestows royal power, sovereignty, and authority, as well as prosperity; it is likewise a source of good fortune for all portents.
The Bhadramaṇḍala is the supreme among meritorious gifts and the performer of the highest merit;
the Bhadramaṇḍala is indeed the supreme among heavens and the bestower of heaven.
And for liberation as well as devotion, for dharma and for sacrifice, for all meritorious works such as digging wells and planting trees—indeed, for all these. (78)
The Auspicious Maṇḍala indeed bestows the merit of all dharmas, as well as the giving of a daughter and the giving of a son. (79)
The auspicious Maṇḍala bestows merit upon yogis, likewise bestows merit upon those who serve, and bestows merit upon those who perform deeds of altruism.

Through the worship of the Maṇḍala of Auspiciousness, may the maiden always behold what is auspicious, may the husband always behold what is auspicious, and may the family also behold what is auspicious. (81)
By worshipping Bhadra, a maiden obtains good fortune, a man attains the status of a householder, and a virtuous woman becomes possessed of a husband and sons. (82)
Through the worship of Bhadra, there shall be no separation between husband and wife;
this indeed wards off obstacles and fulfills all prosperity. (83)
Wherever Kṛṣṇa is worshipped, there the deities, the sages, the attendants, the incarnations, the planets, and so forth, are also worshipped. (84)
Wherein the guardians of the quarters (dikpālas) are worshipped, as well as other guardians of the house;
and the lords (īśvaras) and goddesses (īśvarīs), such as Śāradā and others, are worshipped. ||85||
The Ekādaśīs and the excellent Śaktis beginning with Rādhā are worshipped;
the divine lineages are worshipped, as well as the auspicious Bhadramaṇḍala which bestows prosperity.
Therefore, O Rādhikā, in that pavilion, the auspicious mandala must be worshipped according to the prescribed ritual, and likewise, Hari is to be worshipped.

In whatever connection with ritual action there may be—whether at a great festival, a joyful celebration, a wedding, the procession for a bridegroom, the giving away of a daughter, or at a site sacred to a virtuous woman (satī)—[one should perform the rite]. 88.
During the gift of the Veda, the gift of mantras, the initiation, and in rites such as vows;
during the great gifts and on one's birthday, Hari should always be worshipped. (89)
The worship of the Supreme Lord indeed bestows the fruit of all worship;
it grants the fulfillment of all intentions and completely fulfills every desire.
It bestows the fruit of all sacrifices, fulfills all duties, and is rich with the fruits of every undertaking, always at the beginning of the worship of Śrī Hari. ||9 1||
Likewise, the worship of Lakṣmī at the beginning of any undertaking bestows happiness;
it grants prosperity as well as peace and good fortune. (92)
It destroys misfortune and also destroys suffering and poverty;
indeed, through the worship of Lakṣmī, the destruction of miserliness occurs. (93)
The jewel of a daughter, the jewel of a bridegroom, and whatever jewels of wealth there may be—these shall become free from obstacles through the initial worship of Lakṣmī. (94)
Thus, O Rādhikā, since you have asked about the fruit [of this], it shall surely result in the attainment of happiness and prosperity from worshipping [it] anywhere at all. (95)
Generally, people are indeed possessed by the latent impressions of bodily pleasure;
for them, the abundance of happiness increases through the aforementioned forms of worship. (96)
By reading or even by hearing this chapter on the fruits [of merit], that same fruit which arises from worship as well as from giving is obtained. (97)
In the three worlds, there exists no gift equal to the giving away of a daughter; for she is the support of all dharma and the means by which the lineage is expanded. (98)
That which is the support of the entire world, upon which all creation depends, without which dissolution is proclaimed, and without which emptiness is conceived. (99)
Just as there is no state of Indrahood without the self, so too there is no kingdom for the self without a woman;
yet the self has been made a king by her.
Therefore, O Rādhā, a woman is indeed taken by a man through marriage;
at that time, the bridegroom attains his established status through the woman. || 10.1 ||
Even without a kingdom, Vararāja shall indeed have a beloved wife;
when that Vararāja has ascended to this position, the kingdom shall be established in the prince.
The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the glorious Puruṣottama,
will become the great king who both bestows and receives gifts for two days.
"He shall become the husband of my son and of Śambhu’s daughter;
upon hearing this, joy arises for you, and it arises for me as well. (104)
Thus, O Rādhikā, the supreme Lord, the glorious Bālakṛṣṇa, made his own abode beautiful with a small pavilion.

Thus ends the two hundred and seventy-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Fruits of Worship," concerning the worship of the ruby pillar, the pinnacle-vase, Gaṇeśa, the Mothers, Vāstu, Viṣṇu, the family deity, and the Sarvatobhadra diagram, within the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmīnārāyaṇīya-saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Rādhikā, listen to another auspicious and great pavilion;
it is called Maṇḍapa, endowed with greatness, and assumes its own essential form. 1.
It is ten yojanas wide and ten yojanas long;
it is one yojana high and consists of fifty-six stories.
There, ten thousand golden jars, adorned with banners and flags, shone like a thousand suns.
In their midst, hundreds of water-jars shine one above the other;
or rather, do the planets and stars themselves gleam like these jars? (4)
And there shines a divine golden canopy,
like the garment of the space of consciousness merged with the great ether.
Ten thousand peaks shine in the highest sky;
pure clouds enter the pavilion and pass through its waist.
On each level, they remain equal in number to a thousand moons—
full, white, white-shining, lunar, and consisting of the imperishable.
And within the inner chambers of those pavilions, the moonlight flows;
all the golden walls are entirely suffused with the radiance of Brahmā.
Flowing with the nectar of Brahman and raining down great bliss,
it is a circular canopy consisting of ten thousand Vaikuṇṭhas.
Indeed, in the upper part of the pavilion, within the inner sanctum, auspiciousness is beheld;
in the center are pillars made of jewels, possessing the brilliance of the moon.
Indeed, all around the peak mansions shine forth wish-fulfilling creepers (kalpavallīs), wish-fulfilling trees (kalpavṛkṣas), and likewise wish-fulfilling gems (saṃkalpamaṇis).
Upon the tops of the pillars shine those which fulfill all desires;
and upon the pillars, streams of ghee and streams of curd flow on every side.
Streams of honey, streams of water, and streams of drink flow forth;
and channels for autumnal drinking and streams of nectar pour down.
Channels of nectar, channels of fresh butter, pools of ambrosia,
and streams of nectar dwell within the interior of the pillar and flow forth.
Rivers carrying the juices of food and drink for those dwelling in each respective abode stand there on all sides at the archways.
There, desire-yielding creepers were fashioned that grant all desires, providing male and female slaves, as well as all objects of sensual enjoyment. || 16 ||
All the archways, resplendent with various colors,
were fashioned there in that pavilion by the yogi known as Maṇḍapa.
The reservoirs, the bathing halls, and even the bathing requisites shone like Indra’s halls, being endowed with fragrant substances. || 18 ||
The halls are also provided with unguents, collyrium, musk, sandalwood, and the like, as well as fragrant essences and juices. (19)
And dining halls for the inhabitants of those respective abodes were constructed,
adorned with wish-fulfilling creepers and jewels belonging to each of those dwellings.
For them, there arise dining halls that yield fruits according to their intentions, providing whatever they desire as gifts, and enriched with various enjoyments and pleasures.
Equipped with various vessels, implements, seats, and ritual requisites,
they provided beds, gardens, assembly halls, and rest-houses.
They were furnished with divine couches and possessed divine pillows; they were adorned with divine coverlets and provided with divine curtains. ||23||
They are suited for divine attire, they wear celestial garments, they are substances of divine grace, and they produce a divine state of being. ||24||
In that pavilion, there are garments of divine fragrance, which grant celestial pleasure and indeed bestow divine bliss. (25)
Whatever is remembered regarding food, drink, sleep, or even sexual union—all that appears for couples as purely divine. (26)
Variegated gambling halls and auspicious performance halls,
complete with all necessary implements, shone forth within the pavilion.
There were various theaters for dramatic performance, as well as separate wrestling arenas, dance halls, costume rooms, and dressing areas. ||28||
Indeed, there were infinite halls for viewing, workshops for the machines to be heard, pleasant houses for news, and also fragrant chambers. (29)
Delightful pleasure-houses, various kinds of palaces for enjoyment, and beautiful singing halls exist there in that pavilion.
The five elements, the principles (tattvas), and the objects—both gross and subtle—as well as the principles that are effects and causes, are [to be contemplated] in the pavilion. 3.1.
There, the Brahma-lakes were created, as well as those beginning with Virajā;
and rivers of nectar and sacred pools were fashioned at every spot.
There were various gardens filled with fruits and flowers,
and within that pavilion were groves of sugarcane stalks and juice.
Delicious sweet and sour juices, betel nuts, areca nuts,
and cloves, along with portions of cardamom, cinnamon, and other edibles, indeed shone brightly within the pavilion.
In that pavilion there are dwellings for each of those entrances,
and there are also temples for each of those weapons.
Indeed, the childhood toys of those various maidens,
which serve as the objects of play for children, shine brilliantly within the pavilion.
Royal highways, as well as carriage roads, crossroads, and pavilions, along with great courtyards and pleasure gardens, shine resplendent within the pavilion. (37)
There were private chambers and moon-lit attics with windows on all sides;
there were both small and large doorways as well. (38)
The gentle canopies, arranged like groves and featuring upper chambers in the form of doorways, shine there within that pavilion. (39)
Parrots and cranes, as well as peacocks and pheasants;
swans and kāraṇḍava ducks, and also garuḍas and vultures.
Hawks, pigeons, celestial birds, ruddy geese, partridges, peacocks, cātaka birds, and likewise divine pigeons; ||41||
Likewise, other birds, fresh and beautiful to behold, filled with happiness, shine forth upon the archways on every side. (42)
Cuckoos warble and others coo as well;
they dwell upon the tops of pillars and in the sights [of the surroundings]. (43)
Elephants, śarabhas, lions, and maned tigers;
cows, islands, tigers, two-tusked elephants, bears, and likewise gayals. ||44||
There were also gaṇḍaka deer, rhinoceroses, and variegated śṛṅgasābharas; there were reṇḍakas, rabbits, and even white horses of various breeds. ||45||
Bulls, camels, crocodiles, and tortoises, as well as timiṃgila fish and large sea-monsters, were flashing on all sides. ||46||
Then, in the sky, the central sections of every temple shone, adorned with jewels such as gems, diamonds, and pearls.
Garlands and clusters of flowers, as well as divine garlands of exceeding fragrance,
and radiant kaustubha gems, shine brilliantly here and there.
The divine goddesses, the sovereigns, the celestial ones, and the most excellent maidens—virtuous and true—are sporting, stationed at the entrances and gateways. 49.
Then, the moon-chambers and celestial palaces capable of moving at will shone in their hundreds of thousands within the pavilion, reaching toward the sky.
The creepers of the garden groves even become pillars of flowers, and the dwellings of lotuses perfume the pavilion. (51)
Filling the pavilions and every house with cool breezes that are fragrant and pleasant to touch, they come from the forest paths.
There was no lack of objects of enjoyment—clothing, ornaments, garments, and the like—and heaps of sweet foods were present here in every house within this pavilion. (53)
Indeed, for those dwelling in each respective abode, there exist appropriate objects of enjoyment;
these consist of portions of mirrors and reflecting surfaces, as well as liquid reflections. (54)
The supernatural powers, such as atomization (aṇimā) and the rest, indeed shine forth in the pavilion;
there are also infinite male and female servants, and even crores of maidens. (55)
At that time, those who bestow the bliss of immortality were present in the pavilion;
indeed, O Rādhikā, listen to the wonderful novelty that occurred there. (56)
In every house, however, a single jewel was placed upon the threshold; wherever it was looked upon, the entire pavilion appeared clearly reflected within it. (57)
All parts of the pavilion, as well as all those who preside over the pavilion,
and all the great honors [of the ceremony] take place during the day, and certainly not at night.

O Rādhikā, what need have I to speak? There are women there equal to you in number to the arbudas; besides those who are liberated, there are other female attendants and maidservants present there. ||59||
Even though I am situated in Goloka, upon remembering and seeing you, I have fallen into a state of delusion;
your playful charm appears as if it were empty even in your presence.
In various places, Goloka and Vaikuṇṭha also exist;
there, a higher realm has been established for the inhabitants of the imperishable abode (Akṣaradhāma).
Below that is the auspicious and glorious Vāsudeva-sthala, situated beneath all the abodes and all the inhabitants of Goloka.
Below that, the supremely auspicious and beautiful Vaikuṇṭha was fashioned;
and below that, the divine, unmanifest, and auspicious region was created.
Then the netherworld (Amṛta) was created below, and from that, the terrestrial land (Bhauma) was made;
then the realm of Hiraṇyagarbha and the realm of Vairāja were indeed established beneath it.
He likewise established Mahāmāyāsthala as Sādāśaiva,
and he also established Vaiṣṇava as the second Vaikuṇṭha.
The realm of Brahmā, that of Rudra, and likewise that of Śiva, and below that the station of the Siddhas; and below even that are the dwellings of the Īśvaras and the Ṛṣis.
And those of the ancestors (pitṛs) are below that,
and even lower than those are the thirty-three abodes of the gods.
Then [he saw] the devotees born of Diti who dwell below even that— namely, the humans residing in the Bhuvarloka and those residing in Atala and the other netherworlds.
And likewise for the Danujas, the Nāgas, the aquatic creatures, and those dwelling on the earth,
as well as for all wild beings who assume forms at will.
The abodes of the wish-fulfilling cows, the multitudes of stationary beings, as well as of oneself,
of sacred fords, mountains, and so forth, were also beneath the pavilion.
These were performed by the one known as Maṇḍapa, who was liberated within his own pavilion, at the will of the eternal Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, in this new [age]. (71)
Sacrificial halls, temples, and halls for silent recitation were likewise constructed;
furthermore, schools for the Vedas, medical schools, and schools for piercing [the body] were established. ||72||
Rows of marketplaces and cooking halls were likewise constructed,
and many pleasure-grove pavilions were built down upon the earth.
There were various stairways made of all kinds of jewels, as well as multicolored ladders that moved at will according to one's intention.
There were houses with ascending and descending staircases provided with chains for securing them,
as well as attendants stationed at various spots who could perceive one's mental intentions.
Carriers were appointed for the weary to relieve their fatigue;
for both the king and the pauper, there was equal prosperity in the pavilion of Brahmā.
And auspicious dwellings were constructed for holy men, ascetics, and celibate students,
as well as for virtuous women, faithful wives, and those who have attained liberation.
In the pavilion, forest-dwellers who had made their abodes in the wilderness were gathered,
and likewise, garlands for the sūtas, māgadhas, and bards were prepared.
Likewise, temples were constructed for those who play musical instruments, for panegyrists, and for Vedic scholars;
and likewise, abodes were made for all branches of knowledge and for the fulfillment of all desires.
And dwellings were made for his servants, the elephants of the quarters, and the serpents;
likewise, dwellings were provided for the tortoises and the remaining [serpents] who are without food.
Dwellings were established for the great seers, ascetics, devotees, and those engaged in Brahman-yoga, as well as for renunciants and avadhūtas. ||8 1||
For the subjects of various castes, residing in different lands, and possessed of diverse natures, dwellings were established in the pavilion. (82)

Just as dwellings for protection against cold, heat, and so forth have been constructed according to need, so too have abodes for those of gross and subtle natures been created according to need. ||83||
Just as abodes were made for those of divine and non-divine forms according to their requirements, so too were abodes made for bodies, both illusory and non-illusory. ||84||
Great highways for the celestial chariots were constructed in the pavilion and in the sky; following the pattern of staircases, pathways for the feet were also fashioned. (85)
There, the names of the worlds and the designations of the inhabitants were established for every house,
consisting of innate syllables.
Just as in the Veda, so here in this pavilion were names assigned:
woolen coverings and the like, as well as soft silken ones.
Indeed, beautiful footstools made of gold and silver, as well as thrones, were fashioned within the pavilion. (88)
And there, upon those garments made of silk and composed of living beings, all the syllables were inscribed at every spot. (89)
Whatever foods there may be—whether chewed, eaten, licked, or sucked; all those that are to be drunk or tasted, and whatever has been cooked by fire. || 2.280.90 ||
All forest-grown fruits, as well as those that have been roasted, uncooked flour-dusts, and whatever betel-leaves there may be— 9.1.
All intoxicating substances, all types of cooked preparations in every respect, all those prepared with juices, and those prepared with leaves— (6)
Delicious foods cooked in alkaline solutions, those cooked in ghee, all varieties of milk-rice (pāyasa), and likewise those prepared with sugar-candy; ||93||
All kinds of sugarcane products prepared by confectioners, as well as fried cakes and soups, were placed in the kitchen. (94)
All kinds of desired honeyed foods and various preparations of molasses were placed in the dining hall.
O Rādhikā, what more need be said? That which was displayed in the pavilion is superior even to that which exists in the world of Brahmā, and is most excellent even in the world of the Lord.
That which is most excellent in the true heaven, that which is most excellent in the world of men, and that which is most excellent in the netherworld and the celestial realms, is named Ratna. (97)
All that was deposited there within the pavilion in the form of the pavilion itself;
there, long ponds and beautiful lakes were also deposited.
The pathways of light were established, filled with existence, consciousness, and bliss;
and there were sections for the discourses of the learned, as well as halls for exposition. 99.
Those assembly halls throughout the creations that are renowned and considered the dwellings of the inhabitants—
all of them have been displayed here within this pavilion in the form of a pavilion.
O Rādhā, an even greater wonder was seen by me than that:
a beautiful gem placed at the threshold of every single house. (101)
Where the entire pavilion was seen to be transparent,
even within that pavilion, another auspicious jewel was seen by me.
There, I beheld the threefold creation consisting of the insentient and the sentient;
all abodes were seen, which are the domains of the Lord of All. (103)
I have seen all the worlds of living beings in their entirety; whatever was to be seen by me has been seen, and nothing remains.
Indeed, there is a jewel at the threshold, and there is a pavilion made of jewels;
everything is contained therein, for such indeed is this very variety.
That great wonder—indeed, the vision of everything—is not found in Goloka, nor in Vaikuṇṭha, nor in any other abodes; it truly exists within one's own home.
Therefore, those who are liberated from the syllable (akṣara) indeed become omniscient;
they all perceive directly, like one seeing a gem within a gem.
"O Rādhā, why do you not remember now what was shown to you by me? Thus, O Rādhā, has been described the inspection of the pavilion.
Even upon hearing this, one may attain divinity, the desire for knowledge, the desire for liberation, liberation itself, the state of Brahman, and even fitness for residence in Brahman. (109)
This true nature of the pavilion, auspicious and consisting of all abodes, should not be retained by one of small intellect, nor by another who lacks self-mastery. (2.280.110)

Thus ends the two hundred and eightieth chapter, titled "Description of the Divine Nature of the Great Pavilion Constructed by Mahāmukta," in the second section, the Tretā-saṃtāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmīnārāyaṇīya-saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Then, when the pavilion had thus been established, resplendent with all the worlds,
the solar rays turned away from the sky and the heavens of Saurāṣṭra.
The splendors of the pavilion itself brought about day in Saurāṣṭra;
at that time, night, deprived of its luster, departed for another land. || 2 ||
But for the people dwelling in the imperishable realm, it was night;
and by the splendors streaming forth from the pavilions, it was known through inference.
When that universal perception which occurs within the jewel for those situated inside the pavilion does not arise at all, then there is no inference of night.
When indeed the creations shine within the jewel and within the inner jewel,
then the appearance of day arises for those dwelling in the light.
When such a pavilion has been produced, what wonder is there in the house of Hari?
For everything is possible for him; this pavilion is indeed quite small.
Thus, during the construction of the pavilion, various divine musical instruments as well as worldly musical instruments were sounded there.
People came from all sides to see that pavilion;
indeed, the gods, in the form of swans, arrived through the sky and then departed again.
Then the father of the Blessed One summoned the great sage Nārada and Lomaśa, and he drew the figure of Kuṅkumapattrī.
At that very moment— half a ghaṭī and a half after sunrise— he questioned the self-luminous Lord.
Observing every moment of the day, those three said:
"Today the time that brings all victory and is auspicious is at hand."
"Let the auspicious agreement proceed; let him write the document.
Having said this, those excellent brahmins [recited] the mantras of well-being and auspiciousness. (12)
[He recited] the hymns contained in the Ṛgveda, which are beautiful and auspicious in every way;
as well as the leaf, the pen, the vessel for liquid, and the tablet. (13)
Then all of them, full of eagerness, worshipped the flowing blood;
they performed the worship of Gaṇeśa with incense, lamps, unbroken grains (akṣata), and other offerings. || 14 ||
They performed the worship of Śrī Viṣṇu, as well as the worship of Gopāla,
and at that time they indeed performed the worship of Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa.
Bālakṛṣṇa, together with his father, honored them as well;
the sages, the brahmins, and others were also given seats and shown respect.
Those groups of venerable persons sat down, while the women sang songs;
they recited a saffron leaf-inscription intended as an invitation and awakening to yoga.
The illustrious Mahāviṣṇu, Gopālakṛṣṇaka, his father, wrote this after bowing to the gods, sages, and elders, and having remembered Śrī Puruṣottama. (18)
For the Lord is indeed the sovereign of the glorious city of Brahmapura, the master of all incarnations;
he is Śrī Kṛṣṇa, Nārāyaṇa, Hari, Śrī Vāsudeva, Śiva,
Śrī Viṣṇu, the elder brother of Nara, and Nārāyaṇa residing in Dhavaladvīpa.
May Hari, who remains as the Residue (Śeṣa), and Gaṇeśvara grant us auspiciousness.
May the Goddess, who is identical in form to the glorious Brahman, the sovereign of all incarnations—Śrī Rādhā, Nārāyaṇī, Hariṇī, Śrī Vāsudevī, and Śivā—grant us auspiciousness. || 19 ||
May Śrī, Lakṣmī, Kamalā, Ramā, and Nārāyaṇī who dwells on the White Island (Dhavaladvīpa), as well as Sāvitrī and Sarasvatī, and those who reside in heaven, bestow auspiciousness upon us. 2.281.20.
Śrīkānta, Puruṣottama, the Vibhavas, the Vyūhas, and the Lords of the Abodes;
the Lakṣmīśas, as well as the Īśvaras, the Pitṛs, the Ṛṣis, the Suras, and their wives;
the Ādityas, the Vasus, the two Aśvins, the Lords of the Quarters, the Rudras, and the Lords of the Three Devas.
May these [verses], composed for the domestic duties of a married couple, extend auspiciousness and well-being. ||21||
May there be supreme auspiciousness for Lakṣmī, the daughter of Śrīnidhi Śaṅkara— who is the Lord of the illustrious city of Kāśī and is worshipped by the wise—
and indeed, through my son, the illustrious Bālakṛṣṇa, may it come to pass in Śrīkāśī.
On the night of the fourth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Mārga, from the field of the letter *U* (the end of the vowels),
[it appeared] in the Egg of Brahmā (*brahmāṇḍa*) within the lotus-throne of the four-faced Creator (*vidhi*),
and also on the earthly realm (*bhūloka*) in the region to the south of Meru, upon the navel of the Unborn (*ajā*).
Let those who are with me, Gopāla-Kṛṣṇa, dwelling in Surāṣṭra, come quickly together with their own people to the famous city known as Kuṅkumavāpikā. 23.
On this very first day, it is the time for the pavilion and for the chewing of betel;
tomorrow shall occur the massaging of the body of the illustrious son with fine flour-paste.
On the third day, however, there will be the worship of the gods and the procession toward Kāśī.
For in the fourth [case], there will indeed be the grasping of the hand; therefore, I pray that you may illuminate that.
Those indeed who belong to the creation of Brahmā, born from the syllables and dwelling in the primary abodes;
those who belong to the creation of Īśvara, including the insentient beings and the eight classes of obstructive spirits;
and those who belong to the creation of Jīva—the various worlds and the lords of the worlds.
Let the kings, their own subjects, friends, and kinsmen come. ||25|||

Endowed with their respective sovereignties, accompanied by their own servants, joined by all their followers, and together with those who have taken refuge in their respective divine [abodes]; accompanied by their wives, sons, and daughters;
joined by their respective friends, together with their kinsmen, and including both children and the elderly.
O Sumaṅgalā, let those who bring splendor come here from all sides for the sake of my son. ||26||
The most excellent Śrī Bhagavān, his elder brother Bhrāja, and the other Śuka,
as well as the attendant named Śrīmad Vallabha— these are your kinsmen in every respect;
likewise, we who are members of another family also offer our desired prayers to you all.
O sinless one, we shall act so that your sight may surely be ours here.

May the liberated ones who have attained the state of Brahman and reached the divine abodes; those attendants of the Lord of Śrī who have gone to the realms of Īśa, Īśāna, and others, as well as those who possess great sovereignty and are liberated;

those perfected beings (siddhapuruṣas) esteemed by Brahmā and the rest, and those who are virtuous saints—may they bestow auspiciousness, supreme auspiciousness, and eternal peace upon the couple. (28)
Thus, O Rādhikā, Gopāla-Kṛṣṇa wrote there and sent forth a letter smeared with saffron throughout all of creation.
He sent the sages, such as Nārada and others, to the spheres of the cosmic egg, to the abodes of the liberated, and to the worlds of the Lord, after bestowing [these gifts] upon them. (2.281.30)
It should be worshipped with saffron, unbroken rice grains (akṣata), flowers, and the like;
it should be enclosed within a leaf-cup and wrapped with a cord.
Taking with them a representation of [the deity] equal to ten million times a hundred million in size, joined with *tulasī* leaves,
they all departed at the speed of thought, having been thus commanded.
Having received saffron leaves, they offered them and received honors;
then, O Rādhā, the cowherd Kṛṣṇa gave [them] here in this pavilion.
During the festival, milk, sweet food,
and betel leaf were offered to the assembled kings, devotees, Brahmins, and the common people.
He also [honored] merchants, the helpless, and even those who were very poor;
as well as those worthy of respect, worship, and salutation—namely, Vaiśyas, male slaves, and female slaves.
Servants, as well as those who perform tasks, residents, pilgrims, guests, and honored persons who have arrived there by chance. ||36||
Gopāla-Kṛṣṇa gave him drinks, betel nuts, milk, milk-rice, sweet food, fruit, water, and even leaves.
There, various musical instruments and drums were played,
and songs were also produced by all the women in the pavilion.
They come and they go, having arrived and received betel leaves and other offerings;
indeed, they do so throughout the entire region of Saurāṣṭra and the whole city.
O Rādhā, at that festival of the Samāya, during the festival of betel, the gift of betel is constantly offered there, O beloved. (2.281.40)
Even at midday, rows formed for the purpose of eating;
moreover, thousands of people came there to behold the pavilion. (41)
All of them—the residents of the city and those who had come from various countries—also took their meals at the house of Śrī Hari during the festival. ||42||
Having honored Bālakṛṣṇa and received a most cordial welcome from him, they partook of meals and attained supreme rest. ||43||
Brahmins and others, as well as servants of various castes belonging to their masters, the wretched, the helpless, and mendicants all partook of the food. (44)
They ate sweet foods, milk-rice, milks, and various edibles, as well as savory and delicious salts, until they were completely satiated. ||45||
Having thus obtained betel leaves and areca nuts, the guests partook of their meals and departed for their own homes. (46)

Those who are honored today and invited for the ancestral rite—whether they reside in this country or in foreign lands, whether they belong to different worlds or inhabit different realms of creation. (47)
Yogis, swift as thought, arrive there at that festival;
in the pavilion, they partake of the offerings of honey-mixture with devotion.
Having likewise received betel-leaf and beheld the pavilion,
and having offered blessings to Bālakṛṣṇa and taken up the foods, [they departed].
And having gathered together, they then proceed to the offered seat;
meanwhile, the unsurpassed sounds of musical instruments arise, unimpeded.
And songs of young maidens resounded everywhere:
"Give! Give! and "Eat! Eat! (6.1).
The sounds "Let hospitality be accepted! did not cease;
from the path of the earth they went to the path of the wind, and from the sky the hosts of men returned to the earth. (52)
The servants of Gopāla-Kṛṣṇa brought them into the center of the great pavilion by means of celestial chariots and other vehicles that were as swift as thought.
And they indeed cause him to dwell in houses prepared according to his desire;
and the attendants stand constantly before him for the sake of welcoming him. (54)
Then maidens, male servants, and female servants serve those virtuous ones;
thus indeed, O Rādhikā, the offering of drink continues until evening. (55)
The offering of betel leaves and other items, as well as the meal, proceeded;
thereafter followed the twilight worship (sandhyā-vandana) and other rites, as well as the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) for Hari.
Then, during the night, a great festival was held;
singers accompanied by instrumentalists sang in accordance with rhythmic measure and tempo. (57)
Then the female musicians sang songs, and the female singers sang melodies; the dancers, well-attired and dear to the gods, performed their dances.
The Apsarases sing songs at the Brahma-lake,
and likewise the Nṛ-sarasas sing while engaged in dance around the Parya-lake.
The maidens, their fatigue dispelled by various postures,
revealed their slender bodies as they displayed their mastery of the arts of sitting.
Thus, O Rādhikā, when she was born, they then came for the sake of the rāsa dance;
those maidens performed the rāsa in the middle of the performance pavilion.
All of them were identical in dress, identical in beauty and attire;
with identical ornaments and identical dispositions, they indeed performed the rāsa dance in the pavilion.
The instrumentalists were indeed playing their instruments, and likewise the singers were singing;
meanwhile, two dancing women in the midst of them were dancing at that time.
Others sing and whirl about by means of the circular movement of the cakra, while performing hand-claps, rhythmic foot-steps, and heroic strides.
In the maṇḍala, they take delight with those who have backs for feet, crooked feet, and crooked bodies,
as well as those with crooked necks and crooked eyes.
When the rāsa dance had thus been performed, afterwards the wrestlers arrived there;
they were powerful, like mountain peaks, well-nourished, and roaring with loud cries.
Naturally fickle and causing laughter by leaping upon each other's backs,
they then approached in pairs within the circular arena.
In battle, they also engaged in pulling apart and dragging down,
as well as tossing each other face-upward and throwing each other face-down upon the ground.
Also by throwing their own faces [into the mud], by pulling at their masters' [limbs] and so forth, by striking the backs, and likewise by striking the thighs. (69)
In the sky, they fought with forward thrusts, with projectiles,
as well as with whirling movements, discharges, and the maneuvers of feet and arms.
There were also those who fought with their chests, devoted solely to victory or defeat; others carried heavy burdens, while some transported loads upon their tusks.
There are those who break stones with their chests, those who ride upon the backs of elephants, those who obstruct carts with their hands, and those who carry ten people on their shoulders. (72)
In this manner, the wrestlers display many such variations;
thereafter, the auspicious performers of the dance, wearing their stage costumes, enter. (73)
The boys and the girls also performed the auspicious preparations and enacted the drama of the incarnation of Bālakṛṣṇa exactly as it occurred.
They created something exceedingly beautiful, enchanting, and captivating,
just like the arrival of Nārāyaṇa and Lakṣmī from Vaikuṇṭha.
Also, the beautiful dance of Śambhu, as well as his descent upon the surface of the earth;
likewise, the penance of Lakṣmī and the vision of the glorious Bālakṛṣṇa. (76)
Thus indeed did they perform that drama based on the ancient events of Hari;
when the performance on the stage was concluded, the learned ones arrived there.
Charioteers, panegyrists, bards, and poets likewise recited entirely new poetic compositions within the assembly. (78)
He also [described] the qualities of Nārāyaṇa and his ancient deeds,
as well as the qualities of Lakṣmī, who destroys suffering, and those of Satyā and Śiva.
Then there arose delightful discourses concerning Śrīmad Gopālakṛṣṇa and Kaṃbharā, as well as Hari, which are established within the Saṃhitās.
Then, at midnight, the worship of Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa took place with offerings of drinks and the like, as well as garments and ornaments. (81)
Then Gopālakṛṣṇa indeed gave betel leaves, foods, and sweet drinks to all the cowherds.
Whether he be a child, intoxicated, or distressed, none shall be left out;
everyone shall receive food, betel-leaf, and a sacrificial fee. (83)
And the Lord’s father gave excellent rewards to the performers and to the singers who held the vessels for the distribution of gifts. 84.
Gold, silver, and gems; jewels, pearls, and diamonds; priceless necklaces and ornaments, as well as divine garments. ||85||
The father of Hari gave him necklaces, golden bracelets for the forearms, rings, and other articles of adornment. (86)
The spectators were satisfied with them, as were those who enhanced the beauty of the stage;
even the laborers were satisfied, for they were endowed with skill in their arts. (87)
Displaying their respective branches of learning and arts, they were pleased with wealth;
exclaiming, "Blessed! Blessed! they bowed to Kṛṣṇa and the cowherd Nanda.
The women skilled in the arts, such as dancers and singers, as well as their garments, ornaments, and raiment, bowed down to your father. (89)
Having received rewards consisting of garlands of gems and pearls,
diamonds, silken garments, and bodices woven with gold thread.
Having obtained the requisites for amorous enjoyment, they indeed went away with satisfaction;
then, having drunk, eaten, and offered salutations, they departed for their respective abodes.
The dignitaries went to their residences within the great pavilion,
while the great sages of the city went to their own huts.
