O Rādhikā, those women who remember that Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa and His sixteen-year-old pastimes—which bestow liberation and peace from Hari—[attain their goal]. (98)
The fruit of complete liberation arises imperishably from hearing these;
the fruit of worshipping Brahman arises imperishably from hearing these. || 99 ||
This is the Yoga of the Supreme Person, the highest among all yogas;
this is the Yoga of all incarnations, the highest among all forms of knowledge.
This bestows all prosperity and likewise grants all liberation;
it bestows all good fortune—having heard this, Ramā was filled with joy. (101)
Desiring for himself the eternal liberation that is most highly coveted, he liberated him; likewise, the Blessed Lord went to his imperishable abode after performing this rite for him.
Then the relatives, their minds fixed upon Hari, said:
"O Rādhikā, this union of Śrī Hari with you bestows liberation upon all."
It bestows all prosperity and is named Tretāsantāna;
it is the essence of all vows, sacrifices, gifts, and meritorious deeds.
He is the bestower of the fruits of all austerities, of the applications of initiation, of the duties of renunciation, of the duties of world-renunciation, and of all forms of devotion. || 105 ||
Because it contains the essence of the duties of all stages of life, this [text] is considered to yield fruit upon being heard;
indeed, this is the very heart of the Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā. (106)
He is the life-force of all living beings, whose essence is Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa;
he bestows the fruit of all foundations and grants the merit of all sacred pilgrimage sites.
He bestows the fruit of all service and grants the fruit of all knowledge;
he bestows the fruit of the dharma of virtuous women and grants the fruit of devotion to one’s husband. || 108 ||
It bestows all enjoyments and grants all prosperity certainly upon hearing it;
it brings about divine nature and causes the destruction of all latent impressions. || 109 ||
In this regard, it is the kindler of all sins and the bestower of great merit;
indeed, the constant hearing of this is action performed without desire for fruit.
Likewise, its worship and the giving of gifts to it yield great fruit;
its preservation within the home brings about the destruction of death, time, and other such evils.
By the power of this section, Śrī Hari himself—endowed with Lakṣmī and the other divine powers of Brahmā—shall grant his own divine vision upon hearing it. (112)
The narrative of this [text] should be performed, as well as the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa).
For those who have no other recourse, there shall be liberation; for spirits and the like, there is complete release.
There shall always be the destruction of suffering and poverty, as well as prosperity, lineage, and family;
wherever this [mantra] exists, there one shall obtain a dwelling at all times. 1.14
Wherever this fragment is honored or even recited, there shall be the increase of the lineage and the attainment of sons, wealth, wives, and lordly prosperity.
Wherever there is a discourse on Rādhikā, there is Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa,
all the beloveds of Brahmā, and even the entire circle of liberated souls.
I am Kṛṣṇa, as well as Nārāyaṇa, whose entire circle is his own;
together with all the lords of the gods, we both dwell there to hear that story.
And the worship of the reciter must be performed according to the prescribed rite,
including ornaments for men and women, garments, and even wealth.
Those who desire to hear [the scripture] should, according to their ability, bestow houses, fields, villages, gardens, elephants, horses, diamonds, and so forth upon the reciter.
Indeed, for the sake of granting liberation to one who seeks the supreme goal, everything that one possesses must be given away;
likewise, the concluding rite (udyāpana) should be performed along with an auspicious and great festival.
Upon hearing it but once, illusion (māyā) is indeed destroyed; of this there is no doubt.
This is considered to be the wish-fulfilling creeper, the wish-granting tree, and the cow of plenty. 121.
O Rādhikā, I am indeed Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the wish-fulfilling gem, the wish-fulfilling vessel, and the fragment of the Tretā age; I speak here because of my service to the lineage of the Tretā age.
I shall grant the station of Rādhā to a woman and the station of Viṣṇu to a man.
Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Self.

Thus, in the *Śrī-Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*, within the second section, the *Tretā-Santāna*, [is described] the departure for their own country of the beloved wives who had resided for a long time at the hermitage of Lomaśa along with their fathers and others; the abandonment of the pavilions and other structures; the manner in which Lakṣmī and the women of Kāśī performed service; the arrival of all people on the eighth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Kārttika during the sixteenth birthday festival; the great festival; the liberation of Śiveśvara and others through the instruction on liberation; the giving of gifts during the northern solstice (*uttarāyaṇa*) in the sixteenth year; and [the conclusion of] the *Saṃhitā* and the *Tretā-Santāna*.
Thus ends the two hundred and ninety-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of Majesty."
Śrī Rādhikā said: O beloved of Kṛṣṇa, tell me all the stories in brief;
for a great peace arises in my hearing regarding the Tretā-khaṇḍa. || 1 ||
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O Rādhikā, when the Blessed Lord Śrī Mallakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa was united with Lakṣmī, He became the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
Those who are devoid of the vision of the heart do not know this Supreme Self, the eternal Supreme Brahman, according to its true nature. (3)
Thus, out of compassion, he has appeared upon the earth for the sake of deliverance, and to fulfill the desires of the hearts of both men and women who are devoted to him. || 4 ||
Blessed are those bodies here by which Hari himself has been attained;
blessed indeed are those senses that have entered into union with Hari.
Blessed are those supernatural powers, blessed are those lands as well,
and blessed are those householders who are yogis united with the Supreme Person.
Wherever the Saṃhitā of Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa is recited, that land is indeed blessed; and so too is the place where Puruṣottama resides.
In the second section of the Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā, within the lineage of the Tretā age, this first [chapter] named "The Auspicious" has been proclaimed. (8)
The universal sovereignty and majesty of the Supreme Brahman have been proclaimed;
from that [Brahman] arose the sheath and the inner lining of the golden egg.
Then the two demons named Hiraṇyakūrca and Hiraṇyāṇḍa fought with Saṃkarṣaṇa using their maces.
Those portions of Meru that were separated became the planets;
then Kṛṣṇa, being entreated by all the gods, manifested himself from his abode.
One should perform service on the earth and also in the house of Śrī Kambharā;
furthermore, offerings, hymns of praise, and so forth should be performed during the festival of Prādurbhāva-jayantī. || 1-2 ||
On the tenth day, while the gods, goddesses, humans, trees, creepers, and other beings were on the earth, an injury was committed against the Lord by the Daityas.

The forest of Bālakṛṣṇa was established by the remnants of the birth-impurity of the sixth [child] and others; herein is the origin of that birth-impurity and the granting of boons to the son of Sūtā. (14)
During the festival of the naming ceremony, the demons Sāṇa and Vyāghra were slain;
on the eleventh day, the ritual of mounting the swing was performed by those who are the very embodiment of Ananta.
The demoness Talājā was liberated from her delusion and attained true devotion for Hari;
by the power of his grace, she became the auspicious Lājā, the performer of sacred rites. (16)
On the day of drinking milk, he consumed the milk of cows in many forms;
he drank the living breast-milk of those who were Rākṣasīs in the form of cows.
During the ritual known as Hari’s seating upon the ground, Siṃhikā’s cave and other places also served the Lord Kṛṣṇa, the Master.
During his purificatory rite of ear-piercing, even the deities beginning with Sūcī performed service and took refuge in Kṛṣṇa, their lord who assumes many forms.
During the *annaprāśana* sacrament, she gave abundant foods;
having fed him, the herbs then sought refuge with her beloved Kṛṣṇa.
Indeed, to understand the modes of conduct, he simultaneously grasped thirty-two subjects with as many hands; his divine nature is thus proclaimed.
Then the widowed wives of the Daityas came to engage in battle;
a tumultuous conflict broke out between the Rākṣasīs and the maidens.
When the maidens were victorious, the Rākṣasīs sought refuge.
Divinity and the nature of a maiden’s form were bestowed upon her by Śrī Hari.
Then Śrī Lomaśa spoke to them concerning service and the bulls of liberation;
thereupon, all the maidens of the hermitage undertook the vow during the rainy season.
The Śatrughnas, who dwelt on Mount Adrisaṃvāsa, were killed in battle by Kaṅkatāla;
and the Kaṅkatālī Rākṣasīs became divine beloveds of the monkeys in the fight.
They then stayed at the hermitage of Lomaśa, where they realized their own true nature.
The daughters of the Pitṛs performed worship to Hari and brought about the liberation of the deceased.
The worship performed by the zodiac signs, the description of Kṛṣṇa’s palace, the splendor of the great pavilion, and the description of Hari’s adornment. ||27||
The battle of Prahlāda with Nārāyaṇa, his victory through devotion, the liberation of the Dānavas, and the choosing of Hari by the maidens. (28)
During the caulam (tonsure) sacrament of Śrī Hari, the hairs are said to be of the nature of Nārāyaṇa;
however, it is proclaimed that for living beings, the hairs are of the nature of sins. (29)
The destruction of the Sālamālā asuras and the capture of their women by Hari;
at the festival of the sacrificial thread (yajñasūtra), the daityas of the Sālamālā and other tribes [were subdued]. (2.300.30)
Likewise, the destruction of the dharma of liberation as described by Lomaśa;
the narrative of Sukeśin; and the Aśūnyaśayana vow. ||3 1||
Then there was the worship of Devasvāpa on various different lunar days,
and subsequently the destruction of Kāraṇḍava, the lord of Pātāla.
The maiden was protected at the abode of Lomaśa by Svastika for the sake of the daughter of the humble son of the king of Ārakta-deśa.
The worship of the goddess Śāvadīnā was performed with offerings of children;
then the destruction of kings and others by the goddess took place at Badarīvana.
Kuru-kṣetra is for Hari, while the arrival at Kuṅkuma-vāpī is for his ancestors; the offering of the child to his fathers is said to bring liberation to the mothers. (35)
In ancient times, the boundary of unrighteousness was demonstrated by Śvetaketu;
likewise, Aśmaka, the son of Vasiṣṭha, was born from the wife of Saudāsa, as was Vṛṣa.
Bṛhaspati forcibly took possession of Utathya’s wife;
Dīrghatamas begot many sons upon the wife of Bali.
All the child-seizing spirits have been described according to their respective natures;
now, indeed, the destruction of the tigers and demons was accomplished by Hari.
On the fifth-year festival, there were songs performed by celestial musicians (gandharvas), and lions were brought to life from the skins of lions, tigers, and other beasts. (39)
Then Hara, joined by his dancing wife, performed various dances;
and by the pleased Hara, they were made to dwell forever in that sacred field.

The attainment of all branches of knowledge by Śrī Hari, the burning away of his cowrie-shells through penance, the destruction of the army of cowries, and likewise the account of the staff and other matters were thus narrated. (41)
O twice-born ones, it is said that Hari brought about the destruction of the barbarians of the quarters when Śaṅkara was naked and had gone to the hermitage of a sage.
Due to Satī’s curse, they indeed struck the Lord;
thereafter, their demonic nature was destroyed by Śrī Hari.
On the occasion of the festival marking the commencement of her sixth year, Kṛṣṇa and others performed a worship;
thereby, the outcaste status of the brahmin Devāyana and his wife was destroyed.
In the narrative of the Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā, there is a marvelous account;
the hymn of praise and the pilgrimage site performed by the sage Ūrjavrata have been proclaimed. (45)
The conduct of Kanthādharas is wonder, their transcendence of death is marvelous; they possess mastery over the subtle body (hṛḍḍakāyanikā), and their atheism is derived from the Kuru lineage. ||46||
The son of the Brahmin who had died was restored to life by one named Vṛṣaparva;
however, because of his atheism, he died and was reborn as a Mleccha, while the [other] son [attained liberation]. ||47||
Having become a Vaiṣṇava through the initiation performed by the sage Lomaśa,
he became the mount for the Yakṣa maiden for the sake of the sacrifice to be performed at Raṇaṅgama.
The seventh excellent birth-festival of Śrī Hari was celebrated when he had gone to the battlefield with the desire to behold the Southern Pole Star (Dakṣiṇadhruva).
The King of Antārkīdeśa, Lakṣmaṇārya, offered his hospitality to him,
[who had been delivered] from the Rākṣasa who committed offenses against his wife, his mother, and his own mother.
The protection of his wife by Śrī Hari from her mother, as well as the victory of Raṇaṅgama himself in battle, and those [gifts] offered by Lakṣmaṇa have been described. (51)
Indeed, there is the instruction of Lomaśa to two thousand maidens, as well as a description of sons, daughters, husbands, wives, disciples, grand-disciples, and so forth. ||52||
The daughters of Vedhas— Suṣumṇā, Iḍā, and Piṅgalā— traveling by celestial chariot, beheld Hari and departed for various regions out of a sense of devotion to their Lord to observe the world.
Having heard from them about Hari, seventy-two maidens set out in the vehicle of Brahmā to behold Him clearly, and they went to Satyaloka.
The aerial chariot was blocked in the sky by the armies of Abhiketu;
there, the discourse of the messengers and others, as well as the description of the punishments inflicted by Śukra, Aṅgāraka, and the rest, [is recounted]. (55)
Then follows the description of Viśvakarman, Citrāṅgada, and the Asura chariots;
thereafter, in the battle, millions and even hundreds of thousands of Mlecchas were destroyed.
Discernment and lack of discernment were described, as well as taking refuge;
furthermore, in the battle of guile, thousands of Mlecchas were slain. (57)
Even hundreds of thousands of Mleccha women fought and were bewildered by Hari;
then, destroyed by the Kṛtyās, they beheld the vision of King Śrī Hari.
In this context, his merits from previous births and so forth were indeed mentioned;
Hari granted him an empire over a land free of enemies through his two devotees. (59)
Having conquered the kingdoms of Ārabīja and Pradeśa in battle,
Dharmarāja bestowed them upon the gods and the Maruts who were born from the wombs of Daityas.
There, the story of the previous births of the gods and the Maruts was recounted,
as well as the narrative of the Daityas beginning with Raktabīja, Arabīja, and Dhundhu.
It has been described how Hari provided protection for the boat caught in a river flood and for King Udayākhyana, as well as for his subjects.
Indeed, the demon-nature of Krūrasimha was liberated by Hari;
in his eighth year, health was bestowed upon those who were diseased, deformed, and so forth.
Then, the Jalamagna Vasumedhaśreṣṭhirakṣodita was described, followed by the great holy site of Gopanātha in Saurāṣṭra. ||64||
The great festival of Bālakṛṣṇa’s sacred thread ceremony is described;
therein, the instruction of the supreme knowledge (parā-vidyā) spoken by Nārada is described. ||65||
The bestowal of rewards and the presentation of gifts,
as well as the fruit of serving, honoring, and worshipping the Lord, have been fully described.
Indeed, through six births, [he suffered] from dullness due to giving gifts with improper examples;
the diversity of his former natures has been thoroughly described in detail. (67)
The yoga of actionlessness has been fully described, as well as spiritual knowledge;
through devotion that offers oneself to the King and Queen, there is liberation for both. 68.
The protection of the one named Sudhana, who dwelt in the city of Āmoda, from thieves was indeed performed by Hari in a divine form. (69)

Through the yoga of Kauśika-ambarṣi, there was the liberation of a low-caste man who had committed three sets of eight sins, even though he was accompanied by his wife; likewise, there was the destruction of leprosy and dropsy.
Hari destroyed the Rākṣasas who were the destroyers of six hundred Brahmin children in battle,
and he restored the boys to life once again.
Hari declared that the fruit of the lunar days, the astrological divisions, and the rivers was destroyed by the terrible acceptance of gifts from brahmins who were motivated by greed. (72)
The testing of King Bāleśvara was also performed by Śrī Hari through the cooking of his son and the taking of his daughter as a wife; so it was told. (73)
The vision of Śrī Hari at the sacrifice of Jayadhvaja has been described;
and at the concluding bath (avabhṛtha) of the mountains beginning with Droṇa, there is the destruction of sins. 74.
Kolāra, Cilā, Śambhala, Nārāyaṇa, and Sarāsya also attained divinity and liberation; this story has been beautifully narrated. (75)
The religious duties of the four ages have indeed been declared and demonstrated by Pulastya;
the majesty of Akṣarakṣetra and that of Kauṅkumavāpika have been proclaimed.
The residence of the subjects of the Harivaṃśa on Mount Sahya has been described;
[therein is found] the unrighteousness, the life as an asura, and the atheism of the sons of Khara toward Hari.
Having shown the path to the unreal, he subsequently granted a boon for the sake of their departure;
then, at Kumbha and Prayāga, there arrived ten million holy places and the like.
Following the words of Sanatkumāra, they went to Kuṅkumavāpikā;
then there was an affliction caused by the Rākṣasīs dwelling in Siṃhala.
When Hari had gone to Badarī, those who had previously died were destroyed by the great pestilence and other calamities; but having returned, they were restored to life by Hari.
Now, knowledge that is non-dual in its particularity is considered the bestower of liberation;
therefore, the manifestations (vibhūtis) of Hari, which grant liberation, have been described.
The self-luminous nature of even the fourfold array has been described in the *Kuṅkumavāpī*, where it is consecrated as a sacred site (*tīrtha*). (82)
Then, during a great storm at Mahākhaṇḍa, the abode of camels, protection was provided by Śrī Hari; those who were then dead were restored to life. (83)
Urvashi’s state as a female ruddy goose and likewise her state as a female cat were prevented by the mutual curse of the sage named Sanatsujata. (84)
Likewise, water was made to be drunk by female ruddy geese on the peak of the mountain,
and protection from fire was provided for the kittens of the female cats in the frying pan.
And indeed, the liberation from the curse was accomplished by Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa;
thereafter, the greatness of the Mother was also proclaimed in the abode of Vaikuṇṭha.
Indeed, while Nārāyaṇa was reclining on his bed of Lakṣmī,
the cowherds and others arrived for the purpose of beholding him.
When the time for the dance and other festivities had passed, Lakṣmī cursed them in anger;
consequently, Śiva and the others took human birth upon the earth. (88)
Leaving Lakṣmī behind, the Blessed One went to where Śiva and the others were;
Lakṣmī and her companions, having indeed felt great sorrow, took up births. (89)
Lakṣmī and Urvaśī went to Śrī Hanumān’s grove for the purpose of performing penance;
Nārāyaṇa, being pleased, arrived there to grant them the fruit of their practice.
The drinking of water by the female cakravāka birds on the peak offered by Hari, as well as the arrival of Śivavarma, his family, and others in Kāśī. ||9 1||
Having obtained a residence and other honors while being honored [by the king], Hari returned to his own abode,
which is described as the sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpī.
In the great region of Uṣṭrālaya, at the house of Hemaśālāyana,
King Dakṣaja Vaṅgara indeed performed a sacrifice to Viṣṇu.
Having bestowed a hundred royal maidens and a thousand subjects' daughters upon Kṛṣṇa, the king and the others went to Kuṅkumavāpikā.
Having performed their ablutions at the sacred ford, they returned to the abode of the camels by means of celestial chariots;
then, at that time, the daughters of the Pitṛs also arrived for the purpose of seeing them.
The Rākṣasas blocked their celestial chariot; they were slain by Hari.
Hari arrived in the regions of Prāgjyotiṣa by means of his celestial chariot. (96)
At the conclusion of the sacrifice, a great battle took place there, in which tens of millions of Asuras were destroyed; thereafter, kings devoted to Viṣṇu were established in the kingdom.
Having performed the sacrifice, Hari then showed his own city within his own body to the maidens and made them his own captives.
[This was] proclaimed by the greatness of the consecration of the image of the river Lāṣāhās.
The forms of devotion are ninefold, as are the destructions of obstacles and the fruits [of practice]. ||99||
It is declared that for the virtuous, their own self-nature is the highest state in every respect;
it is the abode of all beings, free from desire, and characterized by the sovereignty of the dark-complexioned goddess and others.
The kingdom of Brahmā was determined, and thereafter the arrival at the field of Akṣara occurred;
he performed the festival of the flower-swing and celebrated the birth festival.
When King Samīraṇa had gone out for the sake of hunting in the forest,
he indeed acquired the skin of a Śarabha due to the curse of Pārṣṇigraha.
This Aśvapaṭṭasara, known as the Sūtīrtha of Dattātreya, was visited on Mount Raivata upon beholding Dattātreya. 103.
The Vārāha-tīrtha has also been described along with its narrative;
and the tīrtha named Pavamāna arose at Aśvasarovara.
In the form of a tortoise, he rescued from drowning in the water the Brāhmaṇas led by Santāraṇa; therefore, that place became known as the Kacchapa Tīrtha.
It is proclaimed that by one devoted to the temples of the gods, the subjects of the world-protectors (dikpālas) are created;
however, those who have been liberated by the names of Śrī Hari through the month of Śrāvaṇa are truly released. 106.
In regions such as Rāśiyāna and others, the liberation of the twelve zodiac signs was indeed proclaimed at Bālakṛṣṇa-sarovara. 107.
The great sacrifice was described, as well as the divine dance;
at the conclusion of the sacrifice, Śibi indeed gave a hundred maidens to the wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
Furthermore, the merits of virtuous yogis have been described;
the sacred fords have been mentioned, and likewise, the liberation of the ancestors has been accomplished at the lake.
Śrī Hari went to the lake-ground known as Dvikalā for the sake of a sacrifice;
there, he gave instructions on dharma and likewise brought about the liberation of the deceased spirits. || 2.300.11 ||

The instruction in political ethics for the king, the arrival at the third sacrifice, and [the account] of the dwellers of the solar world and the celestial beings such as Vīrajaras at that sacrifice. 111.

Liberation has been declared, as well as the giving of daughters in marriage and instruction; the true meaning of the final purificatory bath (avabhṛtha) and its fruits and so forth have been told. || 11 2 ||
In the fourth sacrifice, his own form and so forth were subsequently taught;
in the fifth sacrifice, indeed all the Piśācinīs were delivered.
The causes for becoming a Piśāca have been declared as initiation into mantras and various forms of worship; therein, his own divine and excellent form was revealed. 1.14.
Then, at the conclusion of the sacrifice, the saint named Lālāsana arrived;
he then received from Hari the Vaiṣṇava initiation of a true practitioner.
Five thousand others attained the auspicious initiation; Lālāyana departed for the Northern Kurus out of a desire for Kṛṣṇa.
Śrī Hari, together with his own family, arrived at the realm of Akṣara by means of a celestial chariot; there, indeed, he assumed the form of the temple of Devāyana.
Hari has shown the nature of the temple along with its ancillaries;
everything from the excavation of the temple site up to the hoisting of the flagstaff has been described.
The essential nature and the inseparable divisions have been clearly elucidated;
likewise, the lion-thrones, the deities and others, and the palaces which are not distinct from them [have been explained]. (1.19)
Palaces of the Meru-type have been described in their entirety,
as well as the embodied forms of the Vedas and the deities.
Furthermore, the weapons and other implements have been described;
thereafter, the banners and so forth were mentioned, as well as the sacrificial pits according to the number of oblations.
The configuration of the Vāstupuruṣa is declared to be rich in divine rites; it includes the selection of the preceptor and the worship of Śrī Gaṇeśa and the other deities. || 122 ||

The installation of the deities, the performance of the Nāndī-śrāddha and other rites, their full worship, the installation of the deities situated upon the Vāstu-pīṭha, and the recitation of the Svasti-vācana. || 1.23 ||
The worship of the Yoginīs, the worship of the Kṣetrapālas and others, the adoration of the deities of the pillars, and the worship of the respective deities of the branches and so forth. || 124 ||
The worship of the installation of the fire, the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), the limbs, the womb (yoni), and the enclosure;
the worship of the fifty-six deities, and the adoration of the presiding deities (pratyadhidevatās). || 1.25 ||
The worship consisting of the invocation of the world-protectors (lokapālas) and the planetary deities (grahas), and so forth, has been described;
likewise, there is the offering of oblations to the various deities such as the Yoginīs and the Kṣetrapālas.

The group of six beginning with Rādhā, the one hundred and forty-two [deities] beginning with Parāvidyā, and the incarnations of the Supreme Lord and so forth were worshipped with the offering of bali. || 127 ||
The application of collyrium to the eyes, ornaments, and other such items, as well as the various nyāsas and so forth, have been described;
likewise, the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti), the bathing with horn-water (śṛṅgasnāna), the cooking of the sacrificial porridge (caru), and the rest.

Mounting the chariot, wandering through the village, the yoking of the vital breaths, the waving of lights (ārātrika), the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti), the pronouncement of blessings, and the final purificatory bath (avabhṛtha). || 1.29 ||

The ascent to the water-pot (kalaśa), the ascent to the pillar of pride (mānastaṃbha) and the flagstaff, the consecration of mobile images and so forth, and the restoration of ruined temples are thus proclaimed.
By the grace of Turī Lakṣmī, Śrī Hari granted liberation to the fisherman Dhanameghadhīvara at the holy site of Kuṅkumavāpikā.
The attainment of knowledge by those carrying the palanquin was declared to result from austerity;
the protection of the cattle-wealth by the lion provided rest for those traveling through the sky.
And then Hari spoke thus: "Vṛkāyana and the others have gone there to Ketumāla; there is the meeting of sixty Gāṅgeyas. (13.3)
In Ketumāla, a great sacrifice was performed by Hari as described;
all the mountains arrived there, and in those regions, Hari’s presence is found.
And for all the people of the creation, there were also entertainments at night, as well as morning meals and the complete distribution of mantras. 1.35.
Therein, Hari performed the worship of all the gods and others according to the rules, as well as oblations in the sacrifice; and he assumed forms such as Koṭirudra and Abja.
The birth of Avabhṛthakumāra and Tṛptikumārikā occurred;
for this Kumāra, the giving [of her] was performed following their marriage.
Then, in the royal capital of Orala-ketu, there was a grand welcome for Hari;
Śrī Hari performed the liberation of the ancestors of the king.
The realization of one's own true nature and the establishment of the tradition have been explained; now follows the departure of Krathaka from the capital city of Hari.

In matters such as the construction of temples and the like, the times and other factors— namely the lunar mansions, yogas, karaṇas, the zodiacal signs, the moon, the lunar days, and the stars— are declared to be auspicious.
Auspicious and inauspicious moments have been well explained and declared;
in the capital city of Jarasthālī, there was a welcome reception and worship of Hari.
The account of the previous births of the twenty-six kings has been told; now the Lord, together with his family, went to the kingdom of Uṣṭrāla.
Having received honors, he then went to the capital city of Tīrāṇā;
there, the householder duties and other practices, which grant liberation, were taught by Indra to the yogis. (143)
Then Hari, having received worship, went from Ayodhyā to the kingdom of men;
having gone to the city of Arthaśrī, he attained liberation through the Tuṣita-rākṣasa.
Having given [the gift], he then went to the capital city of Jinavarddhi;
after wandering through Rāmapurī, [he encountered] the rākṣasa named Janahārī.
For the sake of destruction, the Supreme Lord went to Mount Naya with his bow;
through Rudra, he slew the Rākṣasas by means of the wheel-fire of the mountain.

The making of weapons from iron, the taking of brides in marriage, the protection of subjects, and the placing of those who have committed crimes in fetters—these are declared to be the duties of the Kṣatriya. (147)
The gift of life from the bones of the dead; the journey to the city of Jīvanī; the theft of what was written by Śaṅkhavāṭī; and the amputation of the hands. 148.
By bathing in the Bāhudā, there was again the healing of his hands;
then followed the sight of the city of Varaṇā by King Jayakṛṣṇa.
Having established [the kingdom], Hari went to the realm of Parīśāna;
from there he wandered, and after purifying [the land], he went to the kingdom of Parījara for the worship of the bow.
There, Hari performed his bath in the waters of the Indirā, which are like a city for the winds, and he brought about the liberation of the Vetālas. || 151 ||
Thereafter, the four-armed Lord was granted a vision to the king;
then followed the arrival of Mudrāṇḍarāṣṭra and the beholding of Madrirāpuri.
Having received worship and then given instruction, and having visited the city of Śaivāla,
he reached Līśavana, the city of the lord of Gaṇḍaka.
Having received worship and given instruction, he then departed for Līnorṇarāṣṭraka;
after wandering through Vāruṇīpurya, he went to Dhīvarāpurikā.
Having wandered through the city of Milinda and the city of Vālinī,
he received great honor in the kingdom of King Balalīna.
Then followed the instruction on vows, the journey to Śīlāpurī,
the instruction on worship, and the wandering through the kingdoms of Rāya and Āmalaka.
Then there was the journey to that city of Rīmāna and a great welcome; the arrival of King Phenatantu and his kingdom, along with worship and other honors. || 157 ||
The wandering through the city of Trinayā, the instruction, and the worship;
here the illustration of the crow is told, as well as the destination of the ground of the small oblation. 158.
The wandering through Umāpuri by means of a wooden vehicle for the sake of the kingdom, and having wandered about, the giving of instruction in the city of Tuṇṇavāya. 159.
Then there was Hari’s arrival in the kingdom of King Kolaka;
in the city of Muramāṣā, he received a grand welcome, worship, and other honors.
Hari’s bathing took place in many forms within the Ganges, the Kanyakā, and other waters;
thereafter, in the lands conquered by Hari, specifically in the city of Aparānta.
The Lord, the Master Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, traveled by celestial chariot upon the surface of the earth to honor the greatness of the royal sage Dinamāna. 162.
In the city of Aparāntikā, there was a welcome reception by the people of the land; in the regions of Kenāṭaka, there was the cessation of the course of various diseases. (163)
In the sacrificial city, the sending of invitation cards for the purpose of the sacrifice was carried out;
those who performed the duties at the sacrifice are said to be the images of Kṛṣṇa’s wives.
Then, by the will of Rāyarokīśvara, there was a wandering through the city of Sphūrtinārī, as well as the performance of a sacrifice and the subsequent return to the sacred site. 165.
In that sacrifice, the gods themselves shone visibly as the witnesses of the self-luminous Brahmin, who was the seer of all; for the worship of the gods took place in the fire.

Then follows the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti), the victory over enemies, the attainment of the kingdom and the worlds, the worship of twenty maidens, the offering of flower garlands, the seizing [of the disciple], and so forth. (167)
In the kingdom of King Rāyavākakṣaka, his movement was restricted to three continents;
however, during the reigns of Kings Rāya and Mārīśa, he traveled throughout all four continents.
In the kingdom of Rāyabāleśvara, at the city named Vāyuphena, he was welcomed;
thereafter, the great final oblation (mahāpūrṇāhuti) of the sacrifice was performed.
Blessings, sacrificial fees, and the like, as well as the purificatory bath that bestows knowledge—even in the kingdom of Rāyalambara—is there not a path leading to the city of Uvakra? (2.300.170)
The journey was to the city of Svarlatikā, belonging to King Rāyanavārka;
the journey was to the city of Makṣikā, within the kingdom of Rāyahaṇḍeśvara. || 171 ||
In the kingdom of Rāyakūpeśvara, the destination is the city of Havānāyā;
in the kingdom of Kālīmaṇḍalīna, the destination is the city of Vigoṣṭhikā. || 172 ||
In Vanajvālārāṣṭra, his destination is the city of Uṣṭrī with his younger brothers;
from there, in Gatainasarāṣṭra, his destination is the city of Kāyanī. || 173 ||
In the kingdom of Koṭīśvara-kṣmeśa, at the city of Peyisthā, there was the movement of Hari;
in the kingdom of Pārūpa, at the city of Sañjālā, there was the reception and other honors. || 174 ||
Hari went to the kingdom of Bālāvittaka, to the city of Phāṅkalāśī,
to the kingdom of King Āṇḍajara, and to the city of Antaḥprāgastha.
Then there was a welcome for King Bālyarajas in the city called Aṅgānagarī, belonging to his ministers; and thereafter, again, a welcome and so forth.
In Vāyumānāpura as well, that instruction was given by King Rāyasoman to the subjects of the Pātra, Goṇaya, and Naya districts. || 177 ||
Then the illustrious Blessed One proceeded from there to Rājārāyapatirājya, Ārṣajatanurāṣṭraka, and Urogamanarāṣṭra.
Welcome to the city of Rājagṛha and to the city of Āśāsanapura;
likewise, welcome to the wandering [of the Buddha] in the kingdom of King Parāṅvṛta. (179)
Then there was the instruction in the kingdom named Brāhmīlā at the site of the sacrifice;
the arrival of the gods, their installation, worship, and so forth.
The mantras for offering oblations, the instructions for rituals, and so forth were proclaimed;
likewise, the greatness of celibacy was proclaimed there at that sacrifice. (181)
The state of being the self of all belongs to oneself as well, and likewise, there is the great full oblation;
it is the remedy even for the sacrifice, and the seven rivers possess the status of sacred bathing places.
The destruction of the ocean-dwelling Daityas by Lāpalātrīpurīyāna;
the seizing of the lightning-gem with his hand; and the journey to the city of Dvinediṣṭha. (183)
Having arrived at Trāsamānadvīpa, Vṛndārukādvīpa, Siṃhala,
and at Lake Pampā, he proceeded to Kuṅkumavāpikā.
Then, on the eighth day of the birth-festival of the fourteen incarnations, a celebration was held for Hari by his own wives, who were as playful as the full moon of autumn.
The description of the wonder of the divine assembly, the conclusion of the festival, and the liberation of the outcaste Tāmasa, along with his family, from the eyes [of the Lord]. 186.
By the grace of the sage Aśvalāyana, who had assumed the form of a horse,
King Barbura was liberated from his state as a barbura-tree.
On the night of the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, there is the worship of Śaṅkara and others;
on the festival of Dīpāvalī, the celebration of Śāradā was performed by Hari.
The destruction of the disease of King Samparka was accomplished by Śrī Hari;
having assumed the form of Dattātreya, he also established an auspicious sacred ford (tīrtha).
Then the festival of the mountain of grain was proclaimed by him in the form of a swan;
thereafter, the liberation of King Puṇḍarīka was brought about by him in the form of Nṛhari.
Liberation was also attained by Colarāja; that is indeed the pair of sacred sites [attained] by the yogi Vītihotra, who assumed a thousand forms.
Hari granted him a vision of himself in a thousand forms and also in the form of a bull, and he offered praise as well.
On the shore of the lake, at the Śeṣamandira built by Vaivasvata,
there was an installation of Śeṣa, Saṃkarṣaṇa, Patañjali, and others.
That particular holy site was likewise declared to be the Vāmanāṅguṣṭha-tīrtha;
it arose and was fully described in connection with the sage Paṅkila.
The defeat of Parśurāma by King Haimakalgi was proclaimed, and the performance of a Soma sacrifice by King Aśvapāraratna was described. 1.95.
The Pravargya and Upasad rites, the invocation of the Subrahmaṇyā, the pressings of Soma, the great Pūrṇāhuti oblation, and the Avabhṛtha bath and so forth have been described.
The knowledge of the Upaniṣad of Faith, which provides a vast demonstration, is declared as the dialogue between the sage Lomaśa and Aśvapāṭala. 1.97.
This is that very song sung by Lomaśa, which demonstrates the liberation of all;
herein [is told] the story of the King of Ānarta and the yoginī woman Kuśalā.
Furthermore, the consensus has been shown for one who possesses self-luminosity;
the previous account has been told, as well as the instruction of the Guru. (199)
The discourse on the meal of Bhāṇavīrya, arising from the occasion concerning Rāmāditya, describes the destruction of leprosy for a scribe who observed the *ūrja* vow. 2.300.200.
This *Saṃhitā* named after Śārṅgadhara is the work of a Śūdra who was a silent Brahmin;
it is composed with narratives and belongs to one whose soul was purified by austerity. (20.1)
Then, due to the curse of the brahmin Arkapurīśitṛ, the wasting disease of this Śūdra Pārṣṇira was halted by the spreading [power] of the serpent.
The Brahmin was bitten by a snake and died, but he returned to life because of Kṛṣṇa; the protection of King Aṅgāraka and the story of Rāṇikā have thus been told. (203)
The liberation of King Amohākṣa through the words of the awakened Guru, and also the description of the initiation of the renunciant for King Abhayākṣa. (204)
Then, after being awakened by the friction of the host of gods submerged in the waters of the lake, there occurred the vision of Puruṣottama for the Brahmin named Brahmastamba. 205.
Being pleased, Mahāviṣṇu married the immortal maiden;
he also provided protection for the elephant and for one who was carrying wood from a forbidden tree.
The account of Kuṅkuma, Satīśā, Dhanyā, and Īśvarī, as well as the wonders of Caityabrahman and the twice-born, have been proclaimed. ||207||
Likewise, Harikṛṣṇa-naranārāyaṇatīrtha is proclaimed, as well as Māṇikītīrtha and that which is certainly named Aśvapaṭṭa. 208.
Then, the initiation of the one known as Aśvapāṭala was proclaimed;
from Kāśī, he received a letter called "Yoga" sent by Śiva-Śambhu.
Having led him there, both Bṛhaspati and Nārada approached Hari;
then Nārada spoke of the maiden’s sovereignty, virtues, and divine characteristics.
The yogic leaf and the counter-leaf, both filled with virtues, have been shown;
the divine pavilion has been described, as well as the worship of the ruby pillars. || 211 ||
The worship of the water-pot (kalaśa), Gaṇeśa, and the Mothers;
the worship of Vāstu, Viṣṇu, the family deity, and the Sarvatobhadra diagram. ||212||
The description of the great pavilion, endowed with the assignment of its fruits, has been proclaimed;
as well as the dispatching of saffron-leafed messages and the festival of betel-leaves. (213)

At night, there were singing, dancing, instrumental music, wrestling, poetry recitals, feasting, and festivals; the kneading of flour-paste, amorous dalliance, and the arrival of people for Lord Hari. ||214||
While she was preparing for the pilgrimage to Kāśī, she became intent upon countless maidens;
yet, as a carrier of yoga, she reached Kāśī and remained in the city of Śiva. ||2186||
Pārvatīpura is also described here as Śivapattana; there is mutual honor, inquiries after one's welfare, and the descent of Kailāsa. (21.6)
Then, in Śivapurī, there was the worship of the family deity (kuladevī), as well as Hari;
and the testing [of the devotees] took place in the forms of Kṛṣṇa and Rādhā.
He resolved that the girl must not be given to Bālakṛṣṇa under any circumstances,
both in the presence of Śiva-Śambhu and also in the presence of Girijā.
Even in the presence of Lakṣmī, Hari spoke and tested his firm resolve;
he described the sending of garments, ornaments, and other gifts for the sake of the maiden.
The description of Yogavāhinī was shown to Pārvatī by means of a Ṛk verse;
the women who witnessed it were enchanted as they gazed upon him within the limbs of Kṛṣṇa.
In the pavilion of rest for Kṛṣṇa, there was the offering of madhuparka;
in the pavilion of Hari, there was the arrival of the beautifully adorned maidens. ||221||
Hari took the maidens in forms numbering ten million, a hundred billion, and a trillion;
and every rite was performed, as was the proclamation of the bridegroom's intent. (222)
The dissolution of all forms and so forth, the completion of the rite of marriage, and resting and sporting together with all [the goddesses] in manifold forms. (223)
In the morning, there was the procession of the Phullaka and the untying of the knots of yoga;
then, for all the classes, the distribution of rewards and other gifts upon the Gaṅgā. ||224||
On the bank of the five Gaṅgās, there is the excellent holy site named Bālakṛṣṇa; there, he gave alms to Śambhu and arrived at Śivapura. ||225||
There was also honor and worship, a parting gift, and a request for forbearance;
this was the arrival at the Kuṅkumavāpikā field for those traveling on the path of yoga. 226.
Entering the home of beloved women, recreation, diversion, receiving the teacher’s mantra, and surveying the forests. ||227||
Seeing the pastimes of Hari— who assumes ten billion lotus-forms— enjoying himself with his beloveds, Dyaus, in the form of a maiden, was utterly infatuated.
Then Hari induced a state of meditative absorption (samādhi) in all the maidens;
Hari revealed to them the abode of the syllables of the three worlds and other such things.
And this Mahimāna, having learned of it, mutually requested forgiveness and other virtues;
all the daughters were entreated by their mothers and bestowed by Śrī Hari.
The avoidance of the ceremonial pavilion and other such rites, the service of Lakṣmī, and the expression of joy; the return of their own virtuous wives at the sixteenth birthday festival. ||23 1||

The fruit of hearing the *tretāsantāna* [scripture] is liberation through Śiva, Śambhu, and the others; this is the topical outline concerning the *tretāsantāna* and the conclusion of the section. (232)
The greatness of the Tretā age has been declared, and these subjects have been briefly stated;
O Rādhā, those described in the lineage of the Tretā are indeed bestowers of liberation.
Furthermore, there are thousands of divine narratives here concerning kings who were devoted, as well as sacrifices, women, and sacred pilgrimage sites.
In this *Santānaka*, there are thirty-two thousand verses and exactly three hundred chapters, which are devoted to the Supreme Brahman.
Indeed, by reading, hearing, remembering, or even reciting [this], or by protecting it in one's home, people become endowed with both worldly enjoyment and liberation. (236)
The Saṃhitās consist of five hundred and ninety chapters;
indeed, with the Tretādhyāyas added, they become eight hundred and ninety.
There are eighty-seven thousand verses in the Saṃhitā;
next, the third is called the Dvāpara-santānaka. (238)
O Rādhā, there will be a section concerning Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, which describes the nature of Kṛṣṇa in his sixteen-year-old form. (239)
Women become dark-complexioned consorts and men become servants of Kṛṣṇa through the connection with this narrative; I, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, truly declare this.
May the Supreme Brahman, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, grant you well-being; may he bestow blessings upon you.
May mother, father, husband, wife, and kinsmen bring you prosperity. (241)
For the sake of liberation, all one's possessions should be given with faith and divine understanding to Vyāsa, the speaker of this; salutations to the listeners for their prosperity. (242)
Gold, jewels, beds and the like, diamonds, pearls, elephants, horses, cattle and so forth, celestial chariots, and vehicles; 243.
A vehicle, a mansion, a garden, or similar gifts should be given to Vyāsa Śārṅgin,
because Vyāsa himself is indeed the beloved Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa in his own essential form.
All forms of good fortune should be granted to this listener; for by listening, one indeed obtains wealth, prosperity, sons, a wife, and sovereignty. (245)

May this scripture, which brings about the attainment of Brahman, which is the source of all sciences, which constitutes the lineage of the Tretā age, and whose essence is Kṛṣṇa, be most victorious! 246.
Through hearing it, as well as through giving, there is the destruction of all suffering for him, the attainment of total peace, and the production of all accomplishments. ||247||
The Veda bestows the fruits of knowledge, land, maidens, and gold;
it grants the fruit of liberation and yields the lordship of Kṛṣṇa.
Victorious day and night is the Lord, the protector of the noble, the child Kambharā, the master of all, the lord of the virtuous, whose form is truth, the Supreme Self. 249.
May this second lineage, offered unto that very Supreme Brahman, extend here eternally for you, O fortunate one; may it be well.
In this [section] on the sons of Tretā, there are thirty-two thousand, two hundred and fifty-four verses. (251)

Thus ends the three hundredth chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa, a Concise Indication of the Subjects Contained in the Tretā-Santāna Section, the Introduction to the Dvāpara-Santāna, and the Benedictions," in the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*, within the second section, the Tretā-Santāna.
Thus ends the second section, the Sāntāna-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā.
Oṃ! May this be offered to Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
Śrī Nārāyaṇī Śrī said:
Oṃ, salutations to the glorious Supreme Brahman, who transcends the imperishable, the wielder of the discus;
to the Supreme Lord, whose emblems are the banner, the trident, and the bow, the bearer of the Śārṅga bow. || 1 ||
Salutations to the Beloved of all, the Beloved One;
salutations to the Inner Controller of all, who has released himself from bonds, who is dear to the heart, and who descends in every incarnation. || 2 ||
Salutation to You, the Beloved, from whom all this has arisen, by whom it attains growth, and in whom it shall finally abide.
Salutations to You, the Beloved, from whom all incarnations such as Śrī Kṛṣṇa and others arise, and of whom Time and Māyā are but partial manifestations.
Obeisance again and again to you, Nārāyaṇī Śrī, who, having become the beloved daughter of Viśveśvara, became the Lakṣmī who bestows happiness upon you. || 5 ||
Infinite maidens have been born, beloved of Hari and known as Nārāyaṇīs;
salutations again and again to that beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa!
Salutations to You, the beloved of Lakṣmī; salutations to You, the beloved of Rādhā;
salutations again and again to You, the Lord of Ramā, who brings forth rubies.
Salutations again and again to the one who lies with Śrī, the lord of Padmāvatī; salutations again and again to you, the lord of those beginning with Brahmā, Priyā, and Aśana.
Salutation to the goddess who is the sixth, who is with the mind, and who is for that oblation; salutation to the Lord of the rows of lamps, to the Lord of the earth. || 9 ||
Salutations to the Lord of the Arjantīs, who protects the Kāmadhenu;
and salutations to the Lord of the Dharāputrīs, the Master of Krodhana. 3.1.10.
Salutations to you, the beloved of Sūcīkā and the lord of the forest goddesses;
salutations to you, the lord of Dāmanī and the lord of Kaṅkatālikā. || 11 ||

Salutations to you, Bālakṛṣṇa, who are beloved by the daughters of the ancestors, who are the lord of the progenitor of the people and their sons, and who are also the master of the maidservants of the ancestors.
Obeisance to you, the beloved of the women dwelling in the netherworld;
and obeisance to you, the lord of the women who hide within the rows of *sāla* trees. || 13 ||
Salutations again and again to you, the lord of the Svastikī Nāga maidens;
salutations to you, the supreme lord, the husband of the Nāginīs. || 14 ||
Salutations to You, the Supreme Lord who has begun the destruction of Śāva;
salutations again and again to You, the Lord of those who are beloved to magicians. || 15 ||
Salutations to you, the Lord of Knowledge and the Master of Sarasvatī;
salutations to you, the Divine Lord of Lakṣmaṇā and the Master of the Nāḍīs. || 16 ||
Salutations to you, Jummasemlīśa, the lord of the Gāndharvīs;
salutations also to the lord of the Sauratīs, the supreme ruler of the Sāntapanīs. || 17 ||
Salutations to you, the Lord of Mahābāleśvara; salutations to you, the Lord of Cailabīla.
Salutations to you, the Lord of Dākṣajāvaṅga; and salutations to you, O Auṣṇīśa. || 18 ||
Salutation to you, the lord of the Prācīnas; salutation to the lord of the Piśaṅgas; O Lord of the Sāntāṇaris, O Kṛṣṇa, salutation to the lord of the Śaibīs. || 19 ||
Obeisance to you, the Lord of the Śrīpramada region, the Sovereign of Vīrajārī;
obeisance to you, the Lord of the Śāktyakṣī women, the Sovereign of the Piśācīs. ||3.1.20||
Obeisance to you, Kālimāśīśvara, Kṛṣṇa, Friend of the Wretched; obeisance to the Lord of Auralakaithavī and to the Lord of Krāthakī. ||21||
Salutations to you, the lord of Pṛthuputrī and the master of the row of camels;
salutations to you, the lord of Hāṃkārī and the sovereign born of Jayakāṣṭha. ||22||
O Lord of the lords of the Tīrāṇīs, O Protector, O Lord of Cālvīnārī, salutations to you! Salutations to you, the son of Jīnavardhi, the Lord of Īśā, and the protector of the protectorless. ||23||
Salutations to you, the Supreme Lord, whose domain is the scattered regions of the goddesses;
salutations to you, the Lord of Pārīśānī, who possesses a lovely consort with a slight artifice. ||24||
Salutation to Indu, the lord of Āyāsuta, and to Mudrāṇḍīpati; salutation to Gaṇḍabhūpa, the lord of Suta, and to Līnorṇāpati. ||25||
Obeisance to you, the Lord of Bārhacchārī; obeisance to you, the Lord of Bālalīnī.
Obeisance to you, the Lord of Vārasiṃhī; obeisance to you, the Lord of Rāyagāmī. ||26||
Obeisance to you, the Lord of the Sthokahomas, who are beloved by Phainatāntavī;
obeisance to you, the master of Kāṣṭhayānī and the lord of Kolakī. || 27 ||
Salutations to you, my master who bestows daily honor; salutations to you, my beloved;
salutations to the Supreme Lord; salutations to the husband of Rāyakiṇṇaṭī. ||28||
Salutations to you, the Supreme Self, the Lord of the Mistress of millions of riches;
salutations to you, the Lord of the daughter of Rāyaraṇajit; salutations to Hari. || 29 ||
To the one whose hair is Rāyavākakṣikā, to the one whose hair is Rāyamārīśakā; to the one whose lord is Rāyabālāśvarī, to the one whose hair is Rāyalambārikā. ||3.1.30||
Salutations to you, O Lord of Rāyanavāri, the glorious Supreme Self;
to the Lord of Rāyahūṇḍeśika, and to the Lord of Rāyakūpeśika.
Salutations to you, the Lord of Kālīmaṇḍī; to you, the Lord of Vanajaleśika; to the Lord who drinks the two oceans; salutations to you, the Lord of Koṭiśa. ||3.2||
Salutations to the divine Lord Satīśa, who possesses hair as coarse as the Tretā age,
who is the master of those born from eggs, and who possesses the splendor of youth during the Rājasa state.
Salutations again and again to you, the Lord of all, the master of Rāyasoma;
salutations to the lord of the wide-eyed one, and to the one whose hair is turned away from the face.
O Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, O Consort of Rāyāsvarī, obeisance to You!
O Beloved of Aiśānapānī, O Lord of Rājārāyī, obeisance to You! ||35||
Salutations to the Lord of Ajanābha, who is preceded by auspiciousness;
salutations to the Lord of Kauberī, salutations to the Lord of Māhendrī. (36)
Obeisance to you, Kṛṣṇa, the lord of the Yamīs and the master of the Vāyavīs;
obeisance to you, the lord of the Vaiśvakarmīs and the protector of the Vārkṣīs. || 37 ||
Salutations to the Lord of the Raudrīs, to the Lord of the daughters of Vahni;
salutations to You, the Lord of the Śrāvaṇīs and the Master of the Khānijās. ||38||
Salutations to you, the lord of the Sāṃvatsarīs; salutations to you, the lord of the Gopīs;
salutations to you, the lord of the Prācīnīs; salutations to you, the lord of the Piśaṅgīs. || 39 ||
Salutations to you, the Lord of Rāśiyāna and the Lord of Romāyana;
salutations to Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of Pāraśī and the Lord of Dhīvarī.
Salutations to the lord of the Kinnarīs, salutations to the lord of the dark goddesses;
salutations again and again to you, the lord of the fair-complexioned ones and the lord of the enemies. ||41||
Homage again and again to you, Hāritīśa, the lord of the Ābhīrīs; homage again and again to you, the lord of Pātāla and the lord of Svarga. ||42||
Salutations to you, the lord of the Apsarases, the sun among them, the sovereign of the Brahma-lake; salutations to you, the husband of the Gandharva women, the master of all auspiciousness. ||43||
Salutations to you, the Lord of the Vidyanmanis; salutations to you, the Lord of the Bhauminis.
Salutations to you, the Lord of the Danavinis; salutations to you, the Lord of the Shaktis. ||44||
O Lord of the maidens of Kāśī, O Lord of Dhenupālī, salutations to you! O Lord of the beloved of Kāntā, O Lord of all, O Lord of my life-breaths, salutations to you! ||45||
Salutations to the son of Śrī Kaṃbharā; salutations to you, whose younger brother is contented.
This entire world is pervaded by you; salutations to the inner controller of all. (46)
Salutations to Śrī Kṛṣṇa, Viṣṇu, my Lord and Master;
you alone are the Lord of Lakṣmī, you are the best of sages, and you are the most excellent of kings. ||47||
You are the sacrifice, you are the digestive fire that grants satisfaction, O Supreme Lord;
having attained You, Aruṇā and other women have indeed attained liberation here. 48.
Men who have been liberated and attained liberation become those who reach the highest state;
by worshipping you, they go to heaven and they go to the realm of truth. 49.
By worshipping you, they go to Vaikuṇṭha and the earth of Vairāja;
by worshipping you, they indeed go to the world of immortality and Goloka;
for by worshipping you, they reach the imperishable, supreme abode.
O Blessed One, you have indeed shown us everything within meditative concentration;
from that time forth, a desire to know has arisen in me regarding the scope of time. (51)
You shine forth within the liberated maṇḍalas during the ultimate dissolution;
yet when the ordinary creation is again commenced, impelled by time. (52)
When Pradhānapuruṣa was born, and likewise when Mahāviṣṇu arose, and then when Vairāja was born, and likewise when Vedhas was born; ||53||
Tell me now, O Hari, how much time has passed up to this present limit; and if there is anything further that ought to be known, tell it to me.
If I am a vessel for knowledge, O protector of my life, tell me:
how much time remains for me now upon this earth? Tell me this. (55)
O Nārāyaṇa, you alone are the Supreme Person, the omniscient one who perceives all directly;
indeed, no one other than you is capable of speaking [thus]. 56.
Śrī Puruṣottama said: Listen with respect, O Śrī Nārāyaṇī, to the enumeration of time,
which cannot be described by anyone else and is likewise impossible for others to know.
When Mahāmāyā, who consists of the three qualities and takes the form of creation, did not exist,
she remained dissolved in the imperishable state in the form of my own will.
When Mahākāla did not exist as a person for that purpose,
he was dissolved, having been liberated in the Imperishable while possessing the form of intoxicated sovereignty.
That syllable was my own supreme abode and nothing else;
that was solely the creation of Brahmā, not of Īśvara—how then could it be life-giving? (3.1.60)
O Nārāyaṇī, you must understand that this very event is the great dissolution;
for I, endowed with Māyā, performed the contemplation: "I am one, yet may I become many."
Then that Māyā, whose nature is will, came into manifestation;
she is my divine power, Muktānikā, who consists of the qualities (guṇas). 62.
Furthermore, the Puruṣa known as Kāla was revealed by me;
he, whose nature is my own sovereignty, having been liberated, entered into union with her.
That pair was indeed Prakṛti and Puruṣa, my two children;
by them, an order was given to me for the sake of creation itself.
And by those two, as soon as they were born, the commencement of creation was made at dawn;
one excellent pair was created, consisting of Pradhāna and Puruṣa. (65)
By him was created a manifestation consisting of millions and billions of Great Viṣṇus; he is this very Pradhāna-Puruṣa, and from that, he divided himself into Sāya and Vyaśana.
And at the end of the night, at dawn, by the power of time and nature, another pair consisting of Pradhāna and Puruṣa is indeed created anew. (67)
Having performed creation in the evening, that which was destroyed is brought forth once again;
this day is proclaimed as the Mahākāla-kalpa within the Imperishable (Akṣara).
A thousand Mahākāla kalpas constitute one year;
and the time of Prakṛti exists there in every respect. (69)
Fifty such years have indeed passed;
for the primordial person (prakṛtipuruṣa), this constitutes exactly fifty-one years.
From this very day until today, so many creations have passed;
fifty thousand Pradhāna-puruṣas have died.
There is indeed a primary person (puruṣa) consisting of fifty-one thousand [years] and more;
listen further to the duration of the creation of Nārāyaṇīśrī.
This primary person (pradhānapuruṣa) produces, right at dawn, ever-new Mahāviṣṇu, the creator of the Vairāja creation.
That Mahāviṣṇu indeed perishes at the end of the day;
thus, the year consisting of a thousand days is fashioned by Pradhāna. ||74||
Fifty years have indeed passed for this Pradhānapuruṣa;
fifty thousand such Mahāviṣṇus of yours have died.
In the fifty-first year, on the very first day,
the Great Viṣṇu, beginning with fifty-one thousand [years], reigns.
Listen further to the time of the creation of Nārāyaṇī-Śrī;
here, at the very dawn, Mahāviṣṇu [creates her] ever anew.
He indeed generates the Vairāja, who is the cause of the creation by Brahmā;
and that Vairāja perishes at the end of the day in the evening.
In this manner, a year consisting of one thousand days belongs indeed to me,
my father Mahāviṣṇu Gopālakṛṣṇaka.
Fifty years indeed passed there for this Mahāviṣṇu;
fifty thousand Vairājas, his sons, died.
In the fifty-first year, on the very first day, the Vairāja [mantra], beginning with fifty-one thousand, shines forth. (8.1)
Listen further, O Śrī Nārāyaṇī, to the time of creation;
here, at the very dawn, the Vairāja egg becomes ever new again and again.
He indeed produces Brahmā together with Viṣṇu and Rudra;
yet that Brahmā also always perishes at the end of the day in the evening. (83)
In this manner, a year consisting of one thousand days was constituted by Virāṭ; and fifty such years have indeed passed for this Vairāja Puruṣa. (84)
Those fifty thousand Brahmās, his sons, died in the fifty-first year, on the very first day. (85)
He who shines as the Creator, consisting of fifty-one thousand [years] and more—listen further, O Śrī Nārāyaṇī, regarding the duration of time for creation. (86)
And here, at this very dawn, the Creator likewise brings forth anew, again and again, everything from the gods, seers, and humans up to the very limits of heaven. (87)
Indeed, that which exists up to the end of heaven constantly perishes in that same manner;
thus, a year according to Brahmā consists of a thousand such days.
One thousand such kalpas are proclaimed to be a single year of Brahmā; fifty such years of this Creator have also passed. (89)
Fifty thousand triple-worlds have indeed perished;
this occurred in the fifty-first year, on the very first day.
The first kalpa, known as Vārāha, consists of fifty-one thousand [years];
this is the current day, comprising the first four yugas.
This four-faced Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, remains here;
a day of Brahmā has been designated by me by the name "Kalpa. (92)
The day of Vairāja has been designated by me as a Mahākalpa;
the day of Mahāviṣṇu, however, is the Kalpa known as Mahāmahā. ||93||
The day of Pradhāna and Puruṣa is called the Prākṛta-kalpa; the day of Māyā and Kāla is known as the Mahākāla-kalpa. ||94||
Upon the destruction of that [egg], it is said that the Great Dissolution (mahāpralaya) indeed occurs;
Brahmā remains for a hundred years, and Virāj likewise remains for his own duration.
The Lord Mahāviṣṇu lives for his own hundred years,
and Pradhānapuruṣa likewise lives for his own hundred years.
Furthermore, the period of one hundred years for Prakṛti and Puruṣa is likewise [one day];
such a century of years constitutes the Great Dissolution (mahāpralaya), which is essentially a night.
Again there is creation, and again the great dissolution; in this very manner, O Śrī Nārāyaṇī, I have composed this eternal Tantra.
Furthermore, the great creation itself is the cause of the great dissolution;
and in a single day of Brahmā, there are fourteen Manus. (99)
They arise and they dissolve; what reckoning can there be of them, O beloved?
One thousand kalpas, however, is considered to be one year of Brahmā.
Eight thousand such years are recorded as one *yuga* of Brahmā;
a thousand such *yugas*, however, are considered to be one *savana* of Brahmā.
Upon one hundred thousand occurrences of the destruction of the three worlds, Brahmā perishes;
and upon one hundred thousand occurrences of the destruction of the Unborn (Aja), Virāṭ perishes.
Upon the destruction of a hundred thousand Vairājas, Mahāviṣṇu perishes;
upon the destruction of a hundred thousand Mahāviṣṇus, there occurs the destruction of Pradhāna and Puruṣa.
Upon the destruction of the characteristics of both Pradhāna and Puruṣa, there is the dissolution of Prakṛti and Puruṣa; in this manner, O Nārāyaṇī, you should understand the calculation of time.
And in all those various creations, I am with you—
the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the glorious Puruṣottama.
I, the Supreme Lord, the Consort of Śrī, manifest as an incarnation;
indeed, my incarnations arise there in countless numbers.
I know them, and no one else; I am omniscient, and not another.
Nor do the incarnations know them, for they are aware only of previous creations.
Do not entertain doubt in this matter; my length is difficult to endure. Ask further whatever you wish to know, and I shall explain it to you in brief.

Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Description of the Praise of Puruṣottama by Śrī Nārāyaṇī and the Calculation of the Time of Creation," in the third section, the Dvāpara-santāna, of the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā.
Śrī Nārāyaṇī Śrī said:
O Creator, O Hari, O Kṛṣṇa, O Puruṣottama, my Lord!
I desire to know the names of these fifty-two years.
From that, desire is born; therefore, O Śrī Puruṣottama, tell me even the mere names of the fourteen Manus. (2)
O Blessed One, I desire to know, within this Vārāhaka Kalpa, those kalpas that have reached their end during the fifty-first year. (3)
I also wish to know those [powers] of yours that are joined with manifestation;
tell me briefly, O Beloved, if it is not a burden. (4)
Śrī Puruṣottama said: The first year of this Brahmā is the Padma-year;
the second is the Nāla-krama, and the third is the Nālordhva-ga.
The fourth is Stāvanavarṣa, the fifth is Vyomavāṇa,
the sixth is Tapovapsara, and the seventh is Yamavatsara.
The eighth is *niyama*, the ninth is *varṣa*, the tenth is *āsana*,
the tenth [variant] is called *prāṇarodha*, and the eleventh is *pratihṛti*.
The twelfth is the year of retention (dhāraṇa), the thirteenth is the year of meditation (dhyāna), the fourteenth is reflection (manana), and the fifteenth is absorption (samādhi). || 8 ||
The sixteenth is proclaimed as the age of Brahmā known as Prajñāta;
the seventeenth is Aprajñāta, and the eighteenth is Līnatā.
Then follows the nineteenth year, called Sākṣātkāra;
and then the twentieth year, called Sṛṣṭibhāna.
The twenty-first is indeed known as Vedavatsara,
and the twenty-second year thereafter is by the name Rudravatsara.
Sanātana is the twenty-third, and likewise the twenty-fourth is Ārṣaka;
the twenty-fifth is Dharmavarṣa, and the twenty-sixth is Anaṅgavatsara.
The twenty-seventh is known as Adharma; the twenty-eighth is the year of Anala;
the twenty-ninth is the year of the Pitṛs; and the thirtieth is the year of the Devas. || 13 ||
The thirty-first is called Mānava, the thirty-second is Kalpapādapa,
the thirty-third is named Sasya, and the thirty-fourth is Pāśava.
The thirty-fifth is called the Yakṣa-year, the twenty-sixth is named the Rākṣasa,
the thirty-seventh is known as the Cāṇḍaja, and the thirty-eighth is the Gharmaja.
The thirty-ninth is the year of the Nāgas, the fortieth is that of the Yādases;
and thereafter, the forty-first year is indeed called Adhvara.
Then follows the Hiraṇyavatsara and the forty-second;
after that, the Rājata is the forty-third, and following that is the Kāpālaka.
Then there was the forty-fifth year of the Apsarases;
after that came the year of Brahmā, and then the year of the Svardhūnī.
The forty-eighth year was called Arcirmārgābhi; then followed the year Abdhimantha, and the year named Nārada. (19)
Then the fifty-first year will be Somanātha,
and the fifty-second year will be known as Vaiṣṇava.
The fifty-third year, named Gāyatrī, will proceed;
this Kalpa named Vārāha occurs in the fifty-first [year].
In the form of a boar, the earth was lifted by me from the waters;
here indeed, fourteen Manus shall become kings.
First was Svāyambhuva Manu, then Svārociṣa Manu;
then Uttama, Tāmasa, Raivata, and Cākṣuṣa.
Vaivasvata and Sāvarṇi are the [seventh and] eighth Manu respectively; the ninth is Dakṣasāvarṇi, and after him is Brahmasāvarṇika.
Then Dharmasāvarṇi, then Rudrasāvarṇika;
then Devasāvarṇi, and then Indrasāvarṇika. ||25||
These fourteen Manus and fourteen Indras are born together during the day; their dissolution is considered to be of equal duration at night. (26)
In age after age, I indeed become the Supreme Person upon the earth;
fifty thousand such kalpas of Brahmā have passed away.
O Nārāyaṇī, indeed, I have appeared on earth as many incarnations as there were;
I am the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the glorious Puruṣottama. 28.
In age after age, my incarnations occur according to what must be done;
there is no end to their number, for I alone know them and no others.
In that regard, there are infinite names according to [my] qualities and actions;
however, in every kalpa, I appear but once as Puruṣottama.
I am the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, known as Bālakṛṣṇa; the incarnate one, the Lord of millions of devotees, and the Sovereign of Lords.
In whichever eon and at whatever commencement my descent occurs,
that very eon is made manifest by me through that name as well.
Therefore, these designations of the eons were indeed created by my own cognition;
it is not possible to state them in their full detail according to their sequence.
For because time is beginningless and because the creators are innumerable, this period until the dissolution of all beings is traditionally known as a day and night of Brahmā. ||34||
Whatever beings exist in the three worlds, whether mobile or immobile, they dissolve as far back as the primary elements;
therefore, it is called the dissolution of the primary elements (ābhūtasamplava). ||35||
When a thousand cycles of the four yugas have passed at the end of a day of Brahmā,
the Creator of the Universe then makes his own night for the purpose of sleep.
Then he dwells for a night in the waters of the single ocean of darkness;
at dawn, impelled by the desire to create, he acts as before.
Whatever principal rite Brahmā performs on the first day of a year, that year indeed comes to be known by the name of that very rite. (38)
In the fiftieth year of that Kalpa of the Creator,
I have been born many times together with you, O Nārāyaṇī.
In the Brahma-kalpa, the Padma-kalpa, and likewise in the Vairāja-kalpa;
in the Śveta-kalpa, the Lohita-kalpa, and similarly in the Kṛṣṇa-kalpa, I existed.
I existed likewise in the Sanat-kalpa, the Bhava-kalpa, and the Bhuvaḥ-kalpa;
similarly in the Tapaḥ-kalpa, the Bhāva-kalpa, the Raṃbha-kalpa, and in the Ṛtu-kalpa.
In the Ṛtukalpa, the Vahnikalpa, and also in the Havyavāhanaka,
I was then that Anādi-Śrī-Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
In the Sāvitrakalpa, the Bhuvaḥkalpa, and the Ūśikakalpaka;
also in the Kuśika, the Gāndhāra, the Ṛṣabha, and the Ṣaḍjakalpaka. (43)
They were likewise born as Mārjālīya, Madhyama, Vairāja, Kalpaka, Niṣāda, Prāṇaka, and Meghavāhya.
In the Cintaka, Ākūtika, Vijñāta, and Mānasa [Samhitās], as well as in the Bhāva, Rathantara, Śvetalohita, and Raktavāsas [Tantras]. ||45||
O Nārāyaṇī, they likewise became yellow, white, and multiformed in the Pīta and Sitakalpas,
and in other kalpas according to their respective functions.
My incarnations have been both non-existent and existent, numbering beyond count;
in every eon, you, O Śrī, are born in manifold ways.
Just as my wife is to be wed today, so are you born as my son;
your names are infinite and your incarnations are countless.
I know all that entirely, O Śrī Nārāyaṇī;
indeed, O Nārāyaṇī, all this is pervaded by my own splendor alone. 49.
By my fortune, by my sovereignty, by my virtues, by my manifestations,
by my portions, by my powers, and by the abundance of my prosperity.
My fire is also in the moth and in the lamp;
it is in lightning, in the planets, the lunar mansions, and the stars, as well as in the moon and the sun. (51)
For my splendor is indeed everywhere; by me, O radiant ones, have you been empowered—in jewels, in medicinal herbs, in the celestial path, in heaven, among people, and even in ascetic power.
Indeed, my splendor resides in Maharloka, Satyaloka, and on Mount Meru;
it is also in Lokāloka, in Śaṅkara, in Viṣṇu, and in the unborn Virāj.
In Mahāviṣṇu, the Lord of Pradhāna, the Lord of Prakṛti, and in the Imperishable One; likewise in all liberated souls and in all incarnations in every way. ||54||
Indeed, those very qualities of sovereignty, virtue, and splendor belong to me alone;
they attain nourishment and satisfaction through the rays of my form.
The manifold variety of the rays from the form of Puruṣottama nourishes the multitude of liberated beings by bestowing diverse forms of satisfaction.
Always sixteen years of age and alone in the supreme imperishable state,
I nourish the liberated souls by bestowing upon them great bliss and other gifts.
All my splendors are indeed considered to be great bliss;
they are filled with the nectar of peace, coolness, and contentment. (58)
Those liberated beings who enjoy that, as well as others who are liberated along with you, indeed become eternally satisfied, filled with perpetual bliss. (59)
From the form of his body, rays indeed emerge, bearing the essence of rasa;
with those essences, the medicinal herbs of the three worlds perpetually nourish it.
Released and nourished by those essences, they are always of a single measure;
indeed, their sun-like splendors issue forth from their two eyes.
By its radiance, the embodied beings of the three worlds behold [all things];
from the rays of its right eye, suns arise in every direction.
From the rays of his left eye, moons emerge on all sides;
and from the circumference of his head, thunderclaps arise.
Indeed, streams of lightning from the three worlds arise,
and the sweetness and splendor of Hari’s face radiate forth in every direction.
And by the honey of its sweetness, millions of liberated souls are satisfied;
for by its rays, which bestow contentment, the embodied beings of the three worlds are nourished.
From the two cheeks of my form, enchanting splendors emerge;
by them, Īśa and the other [deities] are released and indeed become infatuated within that form.
Indeed, rays of light emerge from his two lips, bearing nectar;
by drinking that essence of nectar, those who dwell in the three worlds are satisfied.
From the corners of the eyes, rays of light charged with love emanate;
drawn by them, portions of love residing within the three worlds are brought forth.
Indeed, rays filled with nectar are produced from his teeth;
by drinking that nectar, all created beings are forever satisfied.
Indeed, rays of nectar emerge from the center of his forehead;
and those who abide in the triple world become satisfied by drinking that nectar.
From their two ears, streams of light consisting of the essence of high-pitched sounds are produced;
by means of these, all those with divine ears hear.
On all sides of the body, pleasant touches that bring happiness arise;
touched by the tactile rays, they enjoy unshakable bliss.
Indeed, from the tongue, rays proceed toward desired tastes;
by means of them, all created beings experience relish and consume that flavor. ||73||
From the nose, fragrant rays indeed go forth;
by means of those fragrances, all beings dwelling in creation smell that sweet scent.
Indeed, from my heart, O Śrī Hari, rays of bliss that are full of eternal joy truly stream forth in every direction. (75)
Immersed in great bliss, they abide within the threefold creation,
emerging from the aperture known as Brahman, which is the nature of the space of consciousness at my crown.
Great bliss arises, as does the supreme, sweet speech;
indeed, from those [two], the words of all beings dwelling in the three worlds are uttered. (77)
By my word, all [beings] become eloquent and pursue the goals I have set;
and by my two hands, rays of light proceed forth, becoming active in their functions.
And by those [rays], beings dwelling in the three worlds become diligent in their efforts;
likewise, rays issue forth from my belly in all directions.
And by those [rays] which bestow life, all beings dwelling in the three worlds live;
indeed, from my procreative power, they proceed as rays rich in bliss.
The embodied beings dwelling within the three worlds possess only a fraction of that bliss;
indeed, they proceed toward the playful rays [emanating] from the feet of my form.
By means of those [rays], the embodied beings of the three worlds possess their respective destinations;
indeed, rays issue forth from the region of my form’s waist.
Indeed, by means of them all become powerful;
from the backbone, rays proceed, supported by their foundation. 83.
By him, the pillars that support millions of cosmic eggs are always sustained;
indeed, the light emitted from my anus proceeds throughout millions of creations.
By those rays, emissions and births come into being;
and from my two hips, rays also proceed forth. (85)
Bound by the power of this mouth, all the worlds come into being through them;
the radiances that have entered within me proceed throughout all creations.
By those rays, embodied beings attain mental reflection, awakening, honoring, as well as contemplation, ascertainment, and direct higher knowledge. 87.
By the rays of my Kaustubha gem, lamps come into being;
and by the rays of my own beauty, these beautiful women are created.
By the rays of my Lakṣmī, the household goddesses in all creations become the graces of the home,
adorned with every auspicious fortune.
For all creations are indeed bound by affection through the rays of my parental love; and all creations are indeed endowed with generosity through the splendors of my magnanimity.
By my rays called Abhirūpa, everything is always endowed with beauty;
by my rays called Kalpa, [beings attain] powers such as Kāmāvasāyitā (the power of subjugating desires).
The supernatural powers proceed like creepers on a wish-fulfilling tree; and by the rays issuing from my Dharma-treasure, the three worlds are satisfied.
Through those [rays] of mine, the creations undergo ripening and transformation;
and through my fierce rays, they even pass into concealment.
And by means of rays consisting of the power of stability, the entire mandala, which comprises the threefold creation, proceeds toward stability within its own respective sequence. (94)
For by my filling rays, all creations are filled;
and by my purifying rays, even the lords and others are purified. (95)
By the rays of my consciousness, embodied beings attain omniscience;
and by the splendors of my compassion, embodied beings indeed rise up. 96.
By my splendors and radiances, the leaders of creation are made beautiful;
by my secret and hidden glories, they become masters of concealed sovereignty.
Through constant meditation upon my form, the virtuous always become identical with me; for "Sat" is my name, and those who truly possess that [reality] are indeed called Sādhus.
"Those virtuous ones who are my eternal companions and my beloved forms shall become you in the field of Kāśī after performing the circumambulation of the sacred fire. 99.
Having attained union with me, those beloved ones are truly my own forms;
having worshipped me, they have entered into my yoga—they are my very forms.
The liberated lords, the gods, the Brahmins, the virtuous, the cows, and the maidens; the youths of Vedic character and truth—these are my very forms. (10.1)
And by the rays of my form, which possess substantiality throughout the three worlds, kings are born; through my yoga, they are indeed my own forms.
Indra, Brahmā Svāyambhuva, his father Vairāja,
and even the father of that one— all these are my forms.
Śacī, who possesses a hundred forms, Sāvitrī, Vairājikā,
Mahālakṣmī, and Pradhānā— these are my primary manifestations as Prakṛti.
The Vyūhas such as Vāsudeva and others, the forms such as Śrī Kṛṣṇa and others, as well as the Nārāyaṇas and virtuous beings—these are my forms. (1.05)
Agni, Viṣṇu, gold, the heart, consciousness, the Guru, the pair [of Kṛṣṇa and Rukmiṇī], and Tulasī—these are truly my forms at all times. (106)
The Veda, the sun, resolve, punishment, affection, the guest, happiness, the child, the dependent, the helpless, and the seeker of knowledge—these are my forms. (1.07)
The royal preceptor, the chief minister, the instructor, Vyāsa who removes suffering, the protector, the guardian, and the sovereign—these are my forms as objects of refuge. (1.08)
