Devoted to her vows, the lawful wife, desiring a son, made this wish during the worship:
"May I have an only son who shall live a long life. (71)
Thus she always made this request with a handful of flowers as an act of devotion;
and I said, "So be it," and that he shall become long-lived.
"Your eleventh [son] has been heard of, and I am the twelfth, Hari";
having said this, I ceased speaking, and she spoke to her own husband.
The couple became joyful; then, at the end of that year, my elder brother Saṃkarṣaṇa was born there, O Janārdana.
Two years later, I became the glorious Kṛṣṇanarāyaṇa there, and a rain of flowers fell upon the gods. ||75||
Your parents have become joyful, serene, and partakers of happiness;
likewise, O Lakṣmī, your own incarnation has been desired by you as well. (76)
Having fully accepted my command, [you must honor] your mother Devīvrata and your father Devavrata, a brahmin devoted to righteousness.
I shall give [this] purifier of all the Vedas, the knower of Brahman, the one who knows the Supreme Brahman, and who is ever engaged in the service of Hari. (78)
He was worshipping me, Yajñanārāyaṇa, the witness of the self of all,
established in samādhi, a yogi from a previous birth, and one of pure and virtuous vows.
There you yourself were born as Lakṣmī, enriched with all auspicious marks;
at that time, a rain of flowers and other things fell from the sky on every side.
The celestial drums resounded and the gods worshipped you;
indeed, you were adorned with all the purificatory rites, such as the investiture of the sacred thread. 8.1.
For you were indeed fit for marriage; at that time, you performed my vow—the beautiful and auspicious vow of a devoted wife, which bestows all good fortune. ||82||
In a dream, I appeared to your mother and father along with another bridegroom, and having granted my vision, I said: "Give me your daughter. (83)
Considering that your parents were awake and that the dream was true, they summoned you and gave you to me according to the prescribed rite, with fire as witness. (84)
Then I, the beginningless Śrīvara Nārāyaṇa, married Jayālakṣmī, the daughter of Devavrata, by name. 85.
Then there was a great assembly of gods and great seers;
at that time, a grand festival took place everywhere upon the earth and in the heavens. (86)
My brother Saṃkarṣaṇa married Sarojinī, the eldest daughter born there,
who was the daughter of Devavrata.
When that marriage had been completed, your two excellent parents gave you a most excellent dowry of priceless jewels and diamonds. (88)
Elephants, horses, bulls, cattle, a field, an excellent mansion, a garden, male and female servants, wealth, and gold. (89)
Having taken many golden vessels as well as ornaments and garments,
I then went to my home, which was a place of great comfort.
The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the glorious Puruṣottama, the Supreme Brahman beyond the Imperishable, the eternal Supreme Lord. || 91 ||
At that time, I remained there with you until the end of the kalpa;
my brother Saṃkarṣaṇa was also there, endowed with the splendor known as Vijaya.
He remained upon the earth until the end of the kalpa as a protector of the Dharma;
remember, Lakṣmī, that your birth and my own birth were indeed at that time.
I alone know this, and no others, for they have been worn down by the decline of time;
likewise, my other incarnations number in the thousands, tens of thousands, and millions.
In that year, [omens] were born for me that grant liberation, bestow happiness, and are auspicious;
thus everything regarding my manifestation at that time has been told.
Indeed, that which bestows liberation through mere remembrance, hearing, or even reflection—by it a sonless man obtains a son, and one who is destitute becomes wealthy. || 96 ||
The suffering of those who suffer shall be destroyed; the reciter shall attain success; his lineage shall become devoted, and a wife shall find her husband. 97.
The reciter surely attains sovereignty, heaven, and prosperity;
for those who practice devotion to me, no taint of illusion arises. (98)
Nor indeed is there any fall, O Lakṣmī; there shall always be prosperity.
There shall be both enjoyment and liberation, and one shall surely attain eternal bliss. (99)
One shall obtain the fruit of all sacrifices and the fruit of all sacred fords;
one shall also obtain the fruit of serving the virtuous and the fruit of devotion to one's husband.
Furthermore, by hearing this, one obtains the fruit of all worship, the fruits of all vows, and the fruit of all giving. (101)

Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Manifestation of the Beginningless Śrī Varanārāyaṇa along with His Elder Brother, Following the Liberation of One Hundred and Ten Sons in the House of the Brāhmaṇa Dharmavrata during the Fifteenth Year of the Creator [Brahmā] in the Third Age, the Dvāpara Cycle," in the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Puruṣottama said: Listen, O Lakṣmī, and then hear further: in the sixteenth year known as Prajñāta of the Creator (Brahmā), and likewise in the eleventh Kalpa.
And during that ninth Manu-period, just as my manifestation occurred upon the earth, so too did the dharma of the Brahmacārin-yogi appear at that time.
And there was a son of Brahmā known as Brahmakumāra;
from his very childhood he remained a celibate student (brahmacārī) in Satyaloka in ancient times. || 3 ||
His lifelong disciples then came to dwell in Satyaloka;
devoted to his instructions, they wandered through heaven and upon the earth.
And the disciple known as Ārṣakumāra taught on this earth to human beings the dharma of virtuous conduct and lifelong celibacy.
Those embodied beings, whether men or women, who are meritorious,
or even those who are sinful, remain established in celibacy if they are lifelong students (naiṣṭhika).
They indeed become liberated, freed from the snares of illusion;
for celibacy is the burning away of desire and the conquest of desire by embodied beings.
Through virtuous conduct and religious observances, one should perform the supreme means for attaining liberation;
likewise, a woman must remain chaste, and a man must remain free from transgression.
Thus, one who observes the vows of moral conduct should always cultivate this way of life throughout their existence;
for celibacy is the very form of Brahman and the cause for attaining the Supreme Brahman.
When the Supreme Brahman has been attained, neither debt nor sin exists;
there is no impurity whatsoever in that state, nor in a virtuous woman, nor in a steadfast ascetic.
Celibacy is the great initiation; celibacy is the supreme strength;
celibacy is the path to liberation; celibacy is the highest state. || 11 ||
Even though many births may occur in this world for those who perform sacrifices and give gifts, liberation comes through the vow of Brahman. || 12 ||
For one who observes the vow of Brahman, liberation shall occur in a single birth alone;
for the Supreme Lord is always well-pleased with the one who maintains the vow of Brahman.
The fires, the deities, and others approach the celibate student;
for the celibate student, there is unimpeded progress toward liberation, as well as in other matters. 1.4.145.
The celibate student (brahmacārī) purifies great sins at that very moment;
even the ancestors drink the water used for the bathing of the celibate student.
The celibate student is himself a god, and the wife of the celibate student is a goddess.
The portions of Hari are indeed incarnations, people devoted to the practice of celibacy.
Through association with those who practice the holy life (brahmacārin), they indeed become one with Brahman;
for even seeing, touching, saluting, serving, and so forth [with them leads to this]. (1.7)
The water for washing the feet, honor, a welcome, food, and so forth—whatever is offered to a celibate student at that very moment surely purifies [the giver]. (18)
In this world, there are many gurus who bestow knowledge yet strive in vain;
those gurus who are endowed with virtuous conduct are the true ones, the supreme saviors. (19)

A woman who is truly virtuous and observant of her vows is to be recognized as the manifest Nārāyaṇī; a man who is truly virtuous and observant of his vows is to be recognized as the manifest Lord Nārāyaṇa. (3.13.20)
Thus, at that time, the ultimate tradition of the celibate student was indeed established upon the earth by Ārṣakumāra. || 21 ||
Indeed, millions of men and women became devoted to the practice of celibacy; they lived as lifelong celibates, dwelling in separate hermitages.
The virtuous women dwell separately in the hermitages of women alone;
the men dwell separately in the hermitages of men.
Neither women nor men ever enter one another's hermitages.
Virtuous men and women do not touch one another. || 24 ||

Listen, O Śivarājñīśrī; indeed, even the gods and the ancestors come to behold those who are thus radiant with their virtuous conduct. Those chaste women, possessing the character of Brahmā, shine like the moon.

Then they shine with splendors born of their virtuous conduct, like the sun. Thus, seeing those bodies composed of light, gods and men alike [behold them] from afar, whether from the hermitage, from the sky, or even from the forest.
Many, being devoid of fortitude, fall into delusion regarding virtuous women—whether they be Daityas, Dānavas, Rākṣasas, gods, or men. (28)
There were men, groups of kings, and even virtuous men,
as well as groups of chaste women who were absorbed in Brahman and possessed the character of Brahman, found here and there.
Seeing those dwelling at sacred fords in the woods, the forests, and on the banks of rivers,
the deluded women fell into a state of extreme infatuation and, in some instances, committed acts of violation.
Arrogant, they break their vows and enter the hermitages; they assault women of virtuous character or even carry them away from the hermitage. (3.1)
For the asuras, human piśācas, kings, royal servants, thieves, and likewise warriors, cause one to fall from the vow of Brahman. (32)
Violently entering the hermitages, they cause virtuous women to fall from their vows;
thus, indeed, when many such [sons] had been born, once there was an asura named Śukraka.
Then he arrived together with the Daityas on the bank of the Mandākinī,
at that well-guarded hermitage of celibate women.
He suddenly descended through the path of the sky before the assembly of yoginīs;
there were also women dwelling in the hermitage who were devoted to the practice of celibacy.
Seeing the Daityas with semen, they then fled out of fear;
overcome by terror, they ran hither and thither among the trees of the hermitage.
There, the virtuous women, being assaulted and their vows violated, were overcome with terror;
however, among them there was one virtuous woman, a faithful wife named Sudarśinī.
With unimpaired and inviolable senses, supreme in celibacy, radiant as the moon, perfected in speech, and possessing a divine form, the Yoginī is like a wish-fulfilling creeper. //38//
Her speech is intent on wonder and brings about the reduction of all things to ashes;
she is radiant as the sun, well-nourished, youthful, and a celibate practitioner.
Agni, Sūrya, and likewise Vāyu— whatever fear arises upon their touch—
he beheld her beneath the tree, absorbed in meditation, established in union with Brahman.
Having seen her, Śukraka quickly approached to violate her;
just as he touched her by force, the virtuous woman looked at him. ||41||
"He who obstructs my vow shall be reduced to ashes this very instant!
Thus he cursed Śukra; and though he was the one worshipped by the Daityas, he was turned to ashes at that very moment.
Then other female celibates reported a breach of her vow;
thereupon, the virtuous Sudarśanā became enraged and cursed them once again.
From this day forward, those who commit acts of assault against virtuous women—
whether they dwell on the earth, in heaven, or elsewhere— [shall be punished].
"Let them be reduced to ashes right there this very day, in an instant!
Having said this, that virtuous woman released the water held in her hand. (45)
Meanwhile, all those who had been destroyers of the Brahma-vow were burnt away in whichever worlds they might have been. ||46||
Then the virtuous Sudarśanā, having become incensed, reflected there upon how to pacify the obstacles caused by men. (47)
Men from the worlds such as heaven who have descended to the earth, those who desire to violate them, even if they merely seek to assault virtuous women, [are punished]. ||48||
"Let those who dwell upon the earth—whether they be men, kings, or others—be women here forever and never men again;
for even those who forcibly violate virtuous and faithful wives shall always [become women] on this earth. (49)
"Let them always be women and never men again;
let this human race on earth, which breaks its vows, cease to exist.
Let all of them indeed become women and let there be no men at all. (3.13.50–51)
Whether they be children, the elderly, or young men, may all people— indeed, even women— be free from the fear of the vow of chastity (satīvrata).
Having spoken thus, Sudarśinī released the water from her hand; at that moment,
by the power of Satyā, this entire world on earth quickly became such that all men turned into women, and only women remained.
Not even a single group of men remained in human form;
boys became girls, the elderly became old women,
and likewise, young men and young women appeared in every house at that time.
In every city and in every district, the ocean completely surrounded them;
even the women who were aboard ships became like exiles at that time. There was a great cry of lamentation, and it was a most extraordinary sight.
In the fourteen worlds, and especially upon the earth, all men indeed perceive their own secret marks;
at that time, there is a manifestation of the limbs of the body consisting of the marks of women. || 57-58 ||
They were seized with extreme shame and did not show their faces;
they were beardless, yet possessed hair, and likewise had drooping breasts and private parts.
All the men on earth became female in form;
and all of them, remembering their former births, then experienced supreme suffering. (3.13.60)

In other worlds, the Daityas and others within their respective circles of kinsmen felt supreme shame, and they then became objects of ridicule. The gods as well were likewise rendered ineffective; they were merely creators of obstacles.
They even took on female forms and became objects of ridicule among the gods;
in the presence of their own wives, they were then subjected to contempt and even met with cries of "shame," for they had violated the bounds of proper conduct.
A great wonder has arisen in the three worlds regarding men and women:
indeed, there are no men on the face of the earth who are vessels of anger. (64)
Indeed, the entire surface of the earth became a kingdom of women;
at that time, the whole world was composed entirely of female offspring.
Then indeed, the son of the Creator, Kāmadeva,
was born as a man and also in the form of a woman— he who had been residing within the body of the virtuous lady.
And he, having abandoned his wife Rati and Prīti, assumed the form of a woman and went quickly to Satyaloka, even while beholding her like counterpart in heaven.
On that path, he indeed heard of the divine state consisting of the absence of sin even while in truth, as well as the burning away of Śukra's [impurity].
In all creations, the cause of Sudarśanī’s wrath was the violation of chaste women;
that is the root of the destruction of men. (69)
In every place and throughout the entire world, this report spread:
"On account of Sudarśinī’s great wrath, men and women have become [non-existent] upon the earth. (3.13.70)
Kāmadeva, having gone to the assembly of Brahmā,
indeed reported everything exactly as it was to Brahmā and also to the sons of Brahmā.
Beholding both the female form and the bodiless god of love, they all then laughed, struck with wonder, exclaiming, "Aha! How true indeed is the power of Bala!"
The power of celibacy is the most excellent, the strongest among all powers;
there is no other power found equal to or superior to celibacy. (73)
All spiritual practices, all austerities, and even all religious vows are contained within celibacy. (74)
This celibacy is distinguished as the means for liberation, the supreme means for protection, and the most excellent means for attaining sovereignty. (75)
Then, O Śrī Nārāyaṇī, listen: afterwards, all those women on earth who were without husbands performed my worship. (76)
All the women were distressed—even those who were pregnant or had young children—and they could not bear the sight of the boys; consequently, they were even more deeply afflicted by grief.
"The seeds of the lineage have perished; how shall the flow of the family continue?
Thus they all became rememberers of their past lives, as did those men. (78)
They propitiated me, Śrī Hari, the Supreme Person;
for such a curse as this, there is no other who could have prevented it.
Even Surā spoke likewise, saying that [there was no one] except for me, Puruṣottama;
thereafter, Brahmā and Hara also spoke in the very same way.
Except for Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Brahman, the Illustrious Supreme Lord, there is no other master who can bring about the pacification of this curse. ||81||
The curse of the devoted, celibate Satī is inexorable; yet the Supreme Person, whose soul is eternally fixed in the dharma of perpetual studenthood, is capable of dealing with this. 82.
Having thus resolved, the throngs of women in all the worlds worshipped me, Hari, the Supreme Person, with devotion. 83.
The kingdom on earth is exclusively female; its subjects are women, and likewise, whoever comes to that land indeed becomes a woman. (84)
They all indeed performed my worship with devotion for a hundred years on earth; it was solely the creation of women. 85.
Or rather, that ancient creation was not yet born;
for at that time, the fourteen abodes existed out of fear of the female state. (86)
On this earth, not even any deities come for the sake of worship;
neither does Gaṇeśa arrive, nor do the sages come either. (87)
Furthermore, due to fear, the gods do not come to the worship or the vow-garden;
this curse is exceedingly terrible, for even Viṣṇu himself is afraid of it.
Out of fear of women’s abodes, Brahmā indeed does not come there;
nor does the youth of Brahmā (Brahmakumāra) come to the earth at that time. ||89||
Indeed, some gods do not come at all for the sake of averting Satī’s curse;
and those who do come are born on the surface of the earth as women. (3.13.90)
Thus a great obstruction has arisen, consisting of women that is unbearable;
for even those who arrive unaware become women. (91)
Even those attendants of Viṣṇu or messengers of Yama who had come to the earth to lead away the deceased women became women themselves. (92)
Thus those attendants, having gone before Hari in the form of women, became a source of wonder; the curse was true and difficult to overcome.
The messengers of Yama, having become women and assuming a state of laughter, have thus blocked the arrival of those who lead [souls] even to the next world. (94)
Even female messengers become like that when consumed;
what then can be said of others? Death does not come there out of fear of them.
At that time, death did not occur even when their lifespan was exhausted;
the earth became immortal, and the woman was like Vaikuṇṭha itself.
"Oh, how great indeed is the power of the strength of the celibate student here!
Otherwise, there would have been the inability to act, just as occurred for Nārāyaṇa at that time. (97)
At that time, Kāla did not indeed come to the earth for fear of becoming a woman;
nor did the male class come to the world out of fear of Satī’s curse.
Then Śrī Hari, having been propitiated by the women, did not wish to come to the earth at that time due to fear of their female form. ||99||
However, without reflecting on it, she thought, "A warding off of the curse must be performed by my power," and thus, having become a woman through that very power, she arrived.
The divine ones, those of divine form, and the divine attendants—all having assumed the forms of women—descended to the earth. || 101 ||
"Indeed, we are all laughing, well-united with Lakṣmī and the others;
we are all mutually delighted in your company."
They arrived at the beautiful surface of the earth where the virtuous Sudarśanī resided,
as did the gods, the sages, and others who were liberated.
Then all those women, filled with curiosity, arrived there to see; and all the gods likewise came, having become women.
This festival of the female Brahmāṇḍaka pervaded the three worlds in every way,
spreading everywhere from ear to ear.
In former times, women saw women and men saw men;
they all remembered their past lives and rejoiced and laughed. 106.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa also arrived from Goloka together with Rādhā;
she too became a friend of Rādhā, indeed becoming a second Rādhikā.
Nārāyaṇa also arrived from Vaikuṇṭha together with Lakṣmī;
she too became Nārāyaṇī, a radiant companion to Lakṣmī.
Then Nara and Nārāyaṇa became Nārī and Nārāyaṇī on earth; those two women were then beautiful female ascetics.
Śaṅkara’s daughter Śāṅkarī was born and seen there by Satyā;
likewise, others who had arrived there out of curiosity were also present.
All became women, for he had indeed become Mahākhela; they looked at one another and touched one another like the nature of women.
They laugh and rejoice, for the world is indeed made by women; she made Nārāyaṇa her husband, and Sudarśanī became Nārāyaṇī.

Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Description of how Śukra and others who attempted to violate her were turned into women by a curse upon the people of the world and others, due to the fault of the female ascetic Sudarśanā—a pupil of the Ṛṣikumāra—in the sixteenth year of the Creator, within the third section, the Dvāpara-santāna, of the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā. || 13 ||
Śrī Puruṣottama said: O Śrī Nārāyaṇī, having thus beheld the Supreme Lord, who was like her own self, having become a woman, the women were then filled with wonder.
Having seen the pair of Nārāyaṇīs and the equal pair of Rādhās—who are worthy of service and even touchable—the virtuous women served them. || 2 ||
All those women, being celibate practitioners (*brahmacāriṇī*), served Hari there at the festival with all their being and through various modes of appropriate service.
All the women, preceded by their husbands, arrived from all sides;
indeed, an innumerable assembly gathered on the banks of the Mandākinī.
In the assembly of women, I appeared there in the form of a woman;
and I was entreated by those women regarding the liberation from the female state.
"We women were previously men, O Sudarśanī; by virtue of a curse, we have been born here as such, though without fault, due to the transgression of wicked Daityas and others. (6)
Due to the faults of wicked kings and the sins of those who violate chaste women,
even men dwelling on earth who were faultless have attained womanhood.
Because your punishment was transgressed due to our devotion to Sudarśana,
O Kṛṣṇa, show us mercy and grant us back our male bodies.
Even the women, whose desires were naturally established, made this request:
"O Blessed One, grant us husbands; make us young and youthful in spirit. (9)
"Command men here—men who dwell in the world of mortals;
both Hari and I shall do so. Having heard that, he spoke in the assembly of women.
"I am dependent on my devotees; I do not transgress what has been spoken by a devotee. We women have gathered here, requesting the sight of the Divine Mother. (11)
Having thus instructed him, I rose from the assembly;
and then, in that gathering, I spoke to Sudarśanā, who had been summoned there.
O virtuous lady, for one devoted to Brahman and endowed with great sovereignty,
it is proper to punish the wicked and to protect one's own vow.
Indeed, it is improper to inflict punishment upon innocent beings—whether children, the elderly, the young, or even those who are righteous. (14)
Therefore, I myself, the beginningless Supreme Person, beg you:
by my word, turn back this woman-form that has been assumed at your request. 15.
O beautiful lady, bring about the warding off of the curse for all the worlds;
the entire world will not exist as consisting of women without men. (16)
"Having reflected, grant the withdrawal of the curse requested by me, your devotee.
Hearing this, the beautiful goddess reflected and quickly said to me: || 17 ||
O Kṛṣṇa, the cause of the curse was that the violation of chaste women was committed by gods, daityas, humans, and others,
even within hermitages.
Thinking, "Let it not be so," I have always made women [my subjects];
for if you are indeed the protector of us and the destroyer of the wicked, [then let them be safe]. (19)
"Then I shall remove the curse; dwell upon the earth until the end of the kalpa.
Having spoken thus, that virtuous and beautiful woman then [fell] at my feet.

Falling prostrate like a staff, she performed worship with flowers and other offerings; she placed a garland around the neck of the one who had assumed the form of a woman amidst the multitude of women.
For the sake of protecting his devotees, he said to her, "Oṃ, so be it.
Thereafter, Satī, who was beautiful to behold, placed water in her hand.
By means of a curse, the Supreme Lord was brought to the surface of the earth;
blessed indeed is this world where the Best of Men resides. (23)
And Hari shall make his own abode here until the end of the kalpa;
accompanied by Kusaṅgita, he will provide protection for those observing the vow of Brahman.
Thus, through this exchange, I withdraw my most terrible curse here in the presence of Śrī Hari, amidst the equality of the world.
Having said this, she released the Karatoya water upon the feet of Kṛṣṇa,
upon the ground, in the assembly, and elsewhere in the world on different spots.

Those women who had previously been men in Satyaloka, Svargaloka, Mānava-loka, Pātāla, and so forth, instantly became men at that time. Then this triple world was as it was before, consisting of couples.
Kṛṣṇa became Kṛṣṇa in his true form, Nārāyaṇa himself;
and Puruṣottama likewise assumed the form of Puruṣottama.
In that very manner, everything there was produced exactly as it had been before.
Then, in that assembly, Nārāyaṇa himself spoke again:
"The one who has committed an assault upon Satī must indeed be slain by me here with the Sudarśana."
At the end of her body, she will undoubtedly become a woman;
she will be among the Daityas, the Dānavas, kings, and even millions of gods. || 31 ||
Then, seeing Sudarśana— the scorcher of the wicked,
made of fire, difficult to withstand, and terrible— those who had committed the assault on Satī fled.
Then they begged for forgiveness there, and they were banished;
all of them, indeed, went far into the depths of the forest, filled with sorrow.
Furthermore, those of evil intent who were cut down by the discus [were likewise removed].
Those who were possessed of evil intent have been destroyed in the other world; likewise,
all those virtuous and truthful women who were devoted to celibacy— even those who suffered violation— have found their refuge in the presence of Hari.
Having approached, they drank the auspicious water from the feet of Hari;
it was purifying of all sins, and by means of it, they indeed attained purity.
One should serve the manifest Puruṣottama with ninefold devotion; for those who have been purified by Him have become liberated, seeking the meaning of the Imperishable (Akṣara).
O Lakṣmī, I am Śrīpati, the Supreme Person, together with you.
And I, whose primordial glory is without beginning, dwelling under the names of Strī, Puruṣa, and Nārāyaṇa—
unborn from a womb, independent, and having manifested myself—
attained renown through the names of my devotees, O Lakṣmī, just as you did, O beautiful one. || 38-39 ||
"Thus, O Śrī, you are renowned as the supreme sovereign, Sudarśanī;
you were born from the union with Sudarśana as the nourisher of virtuous conduct and vows.
In this way, O Śrīsukteśrī, my own manifestation indeed occurred in ancient times.
Remember all that which was told: this wonderful world is composed entirely of women. 41.
Furthermore, O Lakṣmī, there were indeed tens of millions of other incarnations of mine there as well;
I know them all, O Lakṣmī, exactly as they were performed by me according to the requirements of each task.
Listen further to another manifestation of mine as well, occurring in another year—
the seventeenth year of the Kalpa of Brahmā known as Aprajñāta,
during the tenth Manvantara. || 43 ||
The world was exceedingly oppressed by the race of great Daityas.
In ancient times, there was a great Daitya named Timiṅgila, who moved through the waters in the domain of Varuṇa as a Makara, assuming any form at will. || 45 ||
On the island of Śrīśīla, which was surrounded by water, there was his home;
others of that same lineage were likewise able to assume any form at will.
And crocodiles, numbering in the tens of thousands, were dwelling there;
men and women emerged from the water and came outside. 47.
They dwell on the great island and in houses adorned with the beauty of precious gems;
yet they go abroad into the lands as meat-eaters, devouring both men and beasts. 48.
Having carried them off, they devour them either in the midst of water or on an island;
and those who appear in human form on earth frequent cities and other such places. 49.
They carry off women, as well as boys and girls;
these sea-monsters travel through the sky and even upon the peaks of great mountains.
Indeed, they forcibly carry away ascetics dwelling in forests, on mountains, or in mountain caves, as well as sages, brahmins, beasts, and flocks of birds. ||51||
Having carried them to an island, those who are mines of man-eaters devour them;
likewise, they devour fish and other aquatic creatures in the midst of the ocean waters.
They also forcibly devoured men from the ships;
in this manner, humans and others were eaten for a hundred years. (53)
A great proclamation arose throughout all the regions of the worlds—in the mountains, in the caves, and among the ascetics everywhere. (54)
There was fear of sea-monsters, and embodied beings trembled; in the presence of the powerful, no one at all went for protection. (55)
Then the kings everywhere became agitated with fear;
at that time, the great king Cakravartin was Dharmavāhana.
He went through the sky to the edge of the ocean to fight in battle with the Makaras;
however, he was struck down by a rain of illusions from the sky by those who assumed many forms.
And that King Dharmavāhana died in the ocean;
consequently, others in the world fell into fear due to the battle with the makaras.
The strength of the sea-monsters has flourished following the destruction of the king;
they forcibly carry off the wealth and women of those dwelling on the shores of the ocean. (59)
Boys, girls, and even the cattle, adorned with ornaments and rich in garments, enjoyed themselves without fear, flourishing on all sides. (3.14.60)
Then those who were the regional kings were also gradually seized one by one by those crocodiles who feed on flesh.
The continents and those regions resembling continents were brought under their control; assuming various illusory forms, they enjoyed them as they pleased. (62)
At that time, great tyranny arose in every region;
the weak people wept, both men and women being oppressed. ||63||
At that time, many became childless due to the calamities caused by sea-monsters; their children, wives, and husbands alike were devoured.
Thus, at the end of a hundred years, those crocodiles indeed attained growth;
they were born by the millions, appearing everywhere like Rākṣasas.
Sometimes these, even when accompanied by their forces, dwell on the edge of the water; at a moment of weakness, they enter the ocean at that very instant.
In battles, men and kings do not obtain victory at all from these [enemies], who employ illusions and mantras, assume many forms, and are exceedingly terrible. (67)
Having conquered the kings, they divided the kingdoms into fragments under their control;
then the subjects were subjected to extreme tyranny by the Mākarakāsuras.
We could not endure what they had done; we were capable of destroying them all.
At that time, they destroyed sacrifices everywhere by means of the path of the sky.
Festivals and the abodes of the gods are destroyed on all sides;
even the gardens filled with fruits and flowers are being ruined. (3.14.70)
And the crops, rich with grains, are destroyed on all sides;
whatever in the world consists of jewels, all of that is carried away by them. (71)
Thus, when this calamity had arisen, the Mānavas repeatedly entreated me, the Supreme Lord, who am the Supreme Brahman beyond the imperishable.
With all the emotions arising from their hearts, they worshipped me within their hearts;
the wretched, the protectorless, the women, and others entreated me for the sake of protection. (73)
Then I heard from them, in that very syllable, how to propitiate those Makaras for the sake of their destruction and for the purpose of protecting the Dharma. (74)
Then, for the sake of protecting human beings, I too, equipped with my weapons, quickly descended to the earth in a celestial chariot along with you. (75)
He arrived swiftly from the sky, having reached the gateway of the island;
at that moment, I rendered my celestial chariot invisible there.
I assumed the form of a forest-dweller, and you likewise adopted the life of a forest-dweller; having taken on the appearance of an ascetic, I wandered through the forest.
Then those Makaras, having come from the island, carried me along with you to their own island; thereupon, I [addressed] the ascetic.
A landmass was seen, adorned with settlements, villages, and cities; then those sea-monsters (mākaras), as if in a festival, came forth to devour me. (79)
I hurled the Sudarśana discus, and at that very moment it indeed destroyed him and likewise consumed him with its flames of fire.
In the mere space of a ghaṭikā, the ocean was made devoid of makaras;
the makaras, mākaras, reptiles, and large fish fled away. (81)
And having become aquatic creatures, they entered the abode of sea-monsters;
meanwhile, I, an ascetic, dwelt with you in the middle of an island. (82)
At that time, the cities were indeed empty;
then the Daitya Mākareśa [emerged] from the midst of the waters for the sake of battle. 83.
Having become fully prepared for battle along with his army, he advanced;
indeed, those makaras were cut down by me with the Sudarśana alone.
Seeing his defeat, the Daitya, intent on saving his life,
suddenly fled and entered the deep depths of the ocean.
The Daitya, possessing a thousand arms, a thousand heads,
and endowed with a thousand feet, returned once more for the sake of battle.
Furthermore, my Sudarśana discus was dispatched by me,
and indeed, many of his arms were severed at that time.
Then he entered the ocean once more, and I too did so at that time,
having searched for those Makara-asuras who were stationed in various regions.
With the Sudarśana discus, I shall destroy them on all sides, wherever these Makara-dānavas may be upon the earth. (89)
At that opportune moment, I struck them all with the edge of my discus;
then indeed the Daitya Mākara appeared, endowed with ten thousand arms.
Ayutānana himself arrived with Ayutapād;
it appeared to me that his destruction must certainly be carried out. (91)
Then the affliction of the sea-monsters will come to an end.
Thereupon, I entered into a compact with that evil-minded sea-monster.
When his three thousand hands and three thousand faces were struck down,
the Lord of Makaras fled and went to the ocean.
O Lakṣmī, together with you I became a water-man, possessing a hundred thousand hands, a hundred thousand faces, a hundred thousand feet, and a hundred thousand weapons. (94)
Equipped with a net of a hundred thousand [loops], I entered the abode of the sea-monsters;
seeing me, he assumed a massive form and fled in all directions.
From one ocean to another, and from there to yet another ocean—seeing me thus traveling upon his back, he became intent on saving his own life. (96)
Agitated by fear, he entered the Ocean of Milk;
I dispatched the Sudarśana discus for his destruction.
Clinging to his back, it blazed up and consumed him on all sides;
the entire ocean was agitated and the earth trembled repeatedly. ||98||
Then, realizing his own impending death, he stood face-to-face for the sake of battle;
I gave that high-souled one a combat that was the very essence of justice.
In whatever manner I struck him, he was renewed;
even Mākara, assuming ten million forms through his illusory power, arose again.
At the end of that month, having given battle, that asura was slain by me with my Sudarśana discus; hundreds of thousands of those with dark necks were cut down.
Then, indeed, the kettledrums of the celestial dwellers resounded in the sky;
a rain of flowers fell, and the ocean honored me.
The attendants of all the abodes and the liberated lords arrived;
both gods and humans also worshipped me, the Supreme Person.
Know me as the Lord of Śrī, Puruṣottama, whose form consists of water,
possessing a hundred thousand faces, a hundred thousand hands, and endowed with a hundred thousand weapons.
I am indeed white in color, soft, and shining like the moon; my height is a hundred thousand feet, I dwell in the waters, and I am worshipped by the gods and the goddesses of the water.
The embodied beings, liberated from suffering, worshipped me, the Supreme Lord,
the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the glorious Puruṣottama.
Then, O beloved, you saw me, the Supreme Lord Śrī Parameśvara himself, in the form of a man within the water, known by the name Anādi-Śrī-Jalanārāyaṇa.
They indeed worshipped you as the primordial Jala-Nārāyaṇī;
then, having emerged from the water onto the surface of the earth at Śrīśīlika, [they continued their worship].
I made my dwelling on an island, in the city of sea-monsters;
then many of my attendants came there to me at that time.
Śrīdvīpa became my island, situated on the shore of the ocean; it was there, in that auspicious place, for the sake of asceticism by the liberated ones who were practitioners of penance.
O Lakṣmī, remember him in the seventeenth year of Brahmā;
just as Śvetadvīpa is the foremost, so too is the one named Śrīdvīpa.
It was on the auspicious Śīladvīpa itself that they became my dwelling places for the sake of providing me with shelter;
likewise, there was Jaladvīpa and that abode of Śvetanārāyaṇa as well.
At that time, the people and the scriptures spoke in many ways;
remember all of that, O Lakṣmī, which is more ancient than the ancient.
This divine place, consisting of the sound "cakatkāra," was acquired by me in the past;
through its recitation, hearing, and remembrance, one shall attain liberation.
Other incarnations of mine have likewise arisen by the thousands;
I indeed know them all, for I possess direct knowledge.
Then, by me, my attendants, yogis, seers, sages, and holy men were made into Vaiṣṇavas upon the earth.
From that, all creatures were born; they belong to Viṣṇu and have taken refuge in me.
The path to liberation was set forth, and sacrifices, offerings, and other rites came into being.
The subjects have become happy, and men are also free from fear;
indeed, Vaiṣṇavas devoted to my worship are seen upon the earth. || 1.18 ||
Men, women, and those who travel through the sky come indeed to behold me;
for from all directions, Śrīdvīpa has become the bestower of liberation.
Then, O beloved Śrī Suśīlikā, I dwelt there on that island until the end of the kalpa; thereafter, I returned to my own imperishable abode.

Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Manifestation of the Beginningless Nārāyaṇa as a Man-Woman for the Protection of the Female-Inhabited Beings of the Earth through Prayer, and the Manifestation of the Beginningless Śrī Jala-Nārāyaṇa in the Seventeenth Year of Brahmā for the Destruction of the Daityas beginning with Mākara," in the third section, the Dvāpara-Santāna, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Puruṣottama said: Listen, O Śrī, born of Śiva, regarding the Creator’s year; specifically, within the twelfth cycle of kalpas, during the eighteenth year known as Layabhāva.
In that eleventh Manvantara, indeed, due to the power of the decline of the Yuga, when the righteous dharmas have perished and the initiation of the virtuous has likewise come to an end; || 2 ||
When the path to liberation was obstructed and the rites for the gods and ancestors had fallen into neglect,
Hari himself, together with Revā, returned for the purpose of re-establishing them.
And I appeared in the excellent home of the Brahmin Vaṣaṭ, the elder brother;
that Brahmin, devoted to his vows, became known by the name Vaṣaṭkāra.
That ascetic, whose entire property had been seized by wicked atheists and who was oppressed by them,
left my village and went to the forest, for he was my devotee.
She always worshipped me, Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa Hari,
with fruits, roots, leaves, flowers, as well as with meditations and mental offerings.
Every day at dawn, he indeed worships me with offerings;
likewise, his wife is virtuous and devoted to the practice of recitation.
He constantly worships you, the eternal Śrī Satī Lakṣmī, the consort of Nārāyaṇa, according to the prescribed rites, and indeed feeds you with excellent fruit.
He respectfully offers water, flowers, and even leaves;
both he and you always perform kīrtana and bhajana unto Me. (9)
At midday and likewise in the evening, those two inhabitants of the forest, devoted to meditation on me, remained constantly thus, O Videha.
O beloved, he for whom worldly splendors and enjoyments are never intended for his own body, but whose riches are solely for the sake of Hari— he indeed becomes bodiless (videha).
Living thus, childless yet resting in happiness, they eventually reached old age while dwelling among the trees in the forest.
As they were living in this manner, a desire for sons and daughters arose between them;
in Vaṣaṭkāra’s mind, the desire for a son was born. (13)
In the mind of Svadhāvatī, the desire for a son arose;
however, as a mother, she truly desired a daughter who would be her companion in all affairs.
The father indeed questioned his son, who was a helper in all affairs;
they were both intent on the desire for sons and daughters, devoted to the duties of the household.
"O Lakṣmī, at the conclusion of their worship, both of them requested a boon from me;
indeed, in this world, people repeatedly give rise to the pursuit of the three aims of life. (16)
Indeed, there are the desire for worldly status, the desire for wealth, and the desire for offspring;
however, for the devotees of Nārāyaṇa, the desire for worldly status is extinguished. (17)
Since devotees will certainly attain the supreme abode through devotion,
even the desire for wealth among virtuous and contented people shall be stilled.

Since for the virtuous there is only the acquisition of water, food, and clothing, as well as the mere act of traveling, the desire for sons among those with sons—and for the wise, the desire for knowledge—is stilled. (1.9)
Creditors are born in the form of children for the purpose of recovering their wealth;
when such offspring do not exist, that indeed is happiness.
Indeed, there is suffering regarding offspring—whether in their conception, birth, protection, nourishment, marriage, or even in their expenditure and illness. (21)
Nevertheless, those who are touched by worldly talk—such as "this man is destitute," "he is sonless," "he is without lineage," or "he is all alone"—[are affected]. (22)
For those who lack tolerance for such words, and who are overcome by illusion, suffering arises from their craving. (23)
The value of a devotee devoid of knowledge is merely worldly;
but for my devotee who possesses knowledge, my entire inner self is consumed within him. (24)
For one by whom all that is illusory has indeed been burnt away, what indeed remains here—whether it be a son, worldly affairs, a kingdom, or power? (25)
For a son born of the elements, the desire for offspring leads to bondage; however, it is said that for the Brahmin Vaṣaṭkāra, the desire for a son resulted instead in liberation.
"But let her come within my range; let her become my daughter.
And let this Lakṣmī, the very embodiment of Svadhā, also become my young girl. (27)
Thus, may my yoga and resolve remain as their auspicious supports;
may those two resolves always be divine and free from the bondage of māyā. (28)
Therefore, let their two auspicious [sons] remain; I have performed meditation upon them.
Those two must be appointed as my parents for the sake of establishing the Dharma. (29)
And for the fulfillment of those two forms of devotion and those two resolutions,
I, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, together with you, [shall act].
Having reflected upon that forest, I went there and became a wandering ascetic;
I became your guest, you were my companion, and the female mendicant was my caravan-leader.
The two ascetics, with matted hair, clad in rags and bark, and of rugged appearance, went to the city where those two devoted ones were dwelling in the forest.
Two brahmins named Nārāyaṇa, adorned with garlands and following the dharma of holy men, arrived as mendicants at midday. (33)
Then, with joyful minds, the two of them offered a gracious welcome,
as well as water for the feet, the arghya offering, a seat, the honey-mixture, fruits, and other gifts.
Then those two indeed gave us auspicious words:
"Alms have been accepted by me, and they have been accepted by you as well. (35)
The two of them massaged his feet and offered him water for washing;
they thought, "Blessed are we, that today we have obtained the service of these two virtuous ones. (36)
Service to the virtuous destroys sin and bestows divine merit;
it grants worldly enjoyment and liberation, fulfilling all one's intentions. || 37 ||
For the virtuous, service is like a wish-fulfilling creeper, equal to the wish-granting tree in yielding fruit,
comparable to the thought-gem, and similar to the cow of plenty.
That house where saintly persons, who are dear to Lord Hari, come to dwell,
is always a sacred pilgrimage site— whether it be a forest or a city.
Other holy places purify people according to their capacity over time;
but the holy place of the virtuous purifies those who serve it immediately.
Where there is the arrival of the virtuous, there indeed is the certain arrival of Śrī Hari;
where there is the arrival of Hari, there is the certain arrival of the liberated souls. ||41||
Where there is the arrival of liberation, there is indeed likewise the arrival of devotion;
and where there is the arrival of liberation, there the arrival of devotion is certainly established. (42)
Where there is the arrival of devotion, there indeed the arrival of dharma is certain;
and where there is the arrival of knowledge and dispassion, the arrival of all prosperities is also certain.
Where Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa is present together with the virtuous, there reside Lakṣmī, Kamalā, Śrī, Siddhi, eternal and constant. 44.
Where Nārāyaṇa Kṛṣṇa is, there are the sacrifices and the vows;
all austerities and all the gods are also there. 45.
Where Nārāyaṇa partakes of fruits, water, and other offerings along with the virtuous, there indeed the gods and the ancestors partake of the three worlds. 46.
"Today, indeed, our forest dwelling has become fruitful because of the arrival of these two virtuous ones; it is even more joyous than our sovereignty. (47)
Today our childlessness has dissolved through service to the virtuous;
today our poverty, too, yields fruit for a great purpose. (48)
Today our life has become meaningful and truly well-lived; today our mental dispositions have been fulfilled and established here with certainty. (49)
We believe that even today time shall attain purity;
for auspicious omens alone arise from your arrival. (3.15.50)
Through your scripture, our limbs of auspicious awakening are throbbing;
therefore, O venerable ones, as we dwell here, we shall indeed serve you with devotion. (51)
Through the practice of serving the virtuous, embodied beings cross over worldly existence; and here, even in a lonely forest, dwelling with you is auspicious. (52)
"Daily we shall have the joy of the company of the virtuous;
here, indeed, beneath the Bakula tree, is the leaf-hut. (53)
"This beautiful hut, which wards off cold and heat, has been offered by you both;
however, we two shall construct another hut that will provide us with shelter. (54)
Having spoken thus, the pair of brahmins fell at our feet;
and I then said to them, "May there always be well-being for both of you. (55)
May there be freedom from disease, prosperity, and eternal happiness;
for we two are forest-dwellers here, not inhabitants of a single fixed place. (56)
Free from all attachments and dwelling in a secluded hut, they were present for the assembly of devoted Brahmins such as yourself. ||57||
By the will of fate, we remained there while the cows were being milked;
nevertheless, [this was the case] for those pure ascetics who were devotees of the Lord. (58)
Indeed, some partiality has arisen in us toward this house quite needlessly;
yet, out of affection, we have accepted the hospitality and likewise the welcome. (5.9)
"Having received your command, we shall go to another forest; may there be peace for you.
Then, shedding tears, they both spoke with joy: "May it be so for us as well. (3.15.60)
A hut where there is association with the virtuous is a true hut, not one made of leaves;
a dwelling where there is communion with the virtuous is a true dwelling, not merely that which rests upon the ground.
Life lived with the virtuous is true living, not merely eating;
one should always serve the good for the sake of happiness, and no other auspicious duty should be performed [to the contrary]. 62.
"Since we two are of virtuous nature, we shall go to the state of experiencing [the Absolute];
or else, let us dwell here, for we shall surely obtain alms. (63)
Upon your arrival, the trees rejoice with the forest birds;
upon your arrival, the creepers blossom with beautiful flowers. (64)
Upon your arrival, my limbs, enriched by my heart, experience in every way unprecedented pleasures and joys that bring delight. (65)
"And he remained right there, saying: 'You two shall be my servants here. When I spoke thus to them at that time, they asked: 'Why such extreme persistence? (66)
"What is being done here by you two? Speak truly from your hearts.
To that, both of them replied there in the forest, "We are always alone. (67)
We two shall make our dwelling here while you remain;
indeed, the company of the virtuous is rare, and thus our stay together will be meaningful. (68)
For a householder with his wife, dwelling alone in the forest is indeed a source of fear; therefore, he should remain there accompanied by a companion.
The dwelling of two householders in the midst of the forest is indeed beautiful; the dwelling of three or more is truly most excellent. (3.15.70)
Indeed, virtuous women who possess the dharma of faithful wives shall provide assistance in the observance of dharma;
for virtuous women are the refuge of happiness.
Therefore, we choose to grant you a dwelling here, for you two who are established in righteous conduct;
indeed, without your residence, there will be no peace.
Then I said, "So be it," and having assented with "Om," they quickly attained happiness and became filled with joy.
Having performed worship in their abode, we two remained there in comfort; we spent the evening with joy in conversation that awakened us to the true Dharma. (74)
Having performed their twilight prayers at night and having engaged in conversation concerning Hari, the four of them slept; and at the end of the night, both pairs likewise slept.
At that auspicious time, during the Brāhma-muhūrta,
we two indeed arrived in a dream before the Brahmin and his Brahmin wife.
Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa themselves have arrived in the form of ascetics;
though I was born as your son, you became a daughter in a dream.
And that twin pair, appearing in the form of children, was indeed obtained by the two brahmins;
having received them, the two brahmins were greatly delighted, and then the dream came to an end.
We two became invisible, but they remained awake at that time;
consequently, neither of them was able to see us within their own hut.
Having seen that most great wonder, we both then attained joy;
O Lakṣmī, we were there at that time when Vāyu was indeed within the womb.
Having summoned them, they gave the command regarding the womb and the vision of the embryo,
so that the woman might indeed become pregnant in the prescribed manner.
And Vāyu likewise acted even while dwelling constantly within the womb of her belly,
so that she displayed her abdomen as if she were pregnant with a child.
Remaining in that shrine in an invisible form, we two shall indeed become twins when the appointed time arrives. (83)
When Vāyu emerged from the opening of the womb, there appeared two identical twins bearing the conch,
discus, mace, and lotus.
And both the maiden and the prince appeared before him like two children born of no mother; though not born from a womb, they were then as if indeed born from a womb.
A rain of flowers fell from the sky, released by the gods; drums resounded, and a great festival took place in the forest. ||86||
The sages also gathered there for the purpose of seeing [the child];
at that time, many kinds of auspicious signs occurred there for the sake of the birth of us two. ||87||
Having undergone all the purificatory rites,
we two, being twins by nature, grew up there in that forest as celibate students.
Devoted to the dharma of the virtuous and endowed with the initiation of the virtuous,
we two were born right there of our own accord, even though we were already provided with the sacred thread.
Then we also taught the duties of the virtuous to those dwelling in the forest and those dwelling in villages, who were seekers of the stage of renunciation.
The renunciation of the god of love, the avoidance of tasting with the tongue, the abandonment of deluded views, and the avoidance of affectionate touch. ||91||
The abandonment of moving objects such as sound and the like, the avoidance of unpleasant odors, non-attachment to possessions, and the complete relinquishing of passion and hatred. || 92 ||
Taking only as much food and water as is necessary for sustenance, having no fixed abode, observing silence, renouncing ritual actions, and offering everything to Hari with one’s whole being. (93)

The dharma of austerity, self-restraint, the constant abandonment of latent impressions (vāsanās), the relinquishing of the notions of "mine" and "I," and the awakening to the non-difference between the body and the Self. (94)
Abstaining from all acts of malice, forgiveness, endurance, compassion, constant reflection on the supreme self, and the worship of the Supreme Lord. || 95 ||
Conducting oneself by abiding in Brahman, the avoidance of grief and delusion, contentment when what is unasked for is obtained, and likewise straightforwardness. (96)
Wearing saffron-colored robes, using the hands as a bowl, accepting whatever clothing is obtained by chance, and dwelling in the forest according to one's ease. || 97 ||
"Oṃ, salutations to the illustrious Śīlanārāyaṇa, the Supreme Self. Even this much alone—this recitation as well as devotion toward the Supreme Self—is sufficient. (98)
Thus indeed, this virtuous conduct of both men and women, which brings happiness to human beings, was taught by us to them at that time. 99.
By me, the Supreme Soul, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, and by you, the eternal dharmas of the saintly were then set forth.
By the Supreme Self, the beginningless Śrī Śīlanārāyaṇa, accompanied by you, the beginningless Mistress Nārāyaṇī. || 101 ||
Indeed, by me, your uterine brother who possesses the form of a virtuous man,
and by you, my uterine sister, a virtuous and excellent woman.
Tens of millions of virtuous men have been born, abiding in moral conduct;
and tens of millions of virtuous women have been born, devoted to their vows and observances.
From that, sacrifices were born, as well as various vows,
and also my worship, my adoration, and even my temples.
The observance of moral conduct, as well as rites for the gods and ancestors, service at sacred fords, and service to the virtuous—all these religious duties were set in motion. (105)
O Lakṣmī, by me, who am indeed Nārāyaṇa of beginningless glory and virtue, all that was known at that time; remember clearly what took place.
Furthermore, at that time, there were many other incarnations of mine there as well, undertaken for the sake of specific tasks; I know this, but no one else does.
Thus have I declared this manifestation to you for the sake of moral conduct;
through its recollection, hearing, and even by its recitation, it bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Until the end of the kalpa, that shall be our dwelling place for the sake of dharma, in the form of a virtuous man together with ten million holy men.
At that time, the branches of disciples and grand-disciples flourished upon the earth;
then, having granted liberation to their mother and father, they departed to their own imperishable state.

Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Manifestation of the Beginningless Śrī Śīlanārāyaṇa for the Purpose of Establishing the Dharma of the Holy Ones in the Eighteenth Year of the Creator [Brahmā] during the Third Age (Dvāpara)," in the glorious *Lakṣmīnārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, within the lineage of the Dvāpara age. || 15 ||
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Śrī Nārāyaṇī, then; in the year of Brahmā, during the thirteenth Manu, in the sixty-fourth kalpa named Sākṣātkṛt.
Rudra, whose abode is Kailāsa, indeed came to the earth for the sake of visiting sacred fords;
while wandering on Mount Cāṭula, he arrived at Viṣṇutīrtha.
On that very mountain, a delightful and excellent river named Śāradā, the daughter of Brahmā, flowed; on its bank was auspicious water where he rested.
Having drunk and sprinkled [himself with water], he sat down and became absorbed in meditation for a moment;
he meditated upon Viṣṇu, Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of All, the Supreme Ruler.
Just then, a boar possessing intoxicated speed arrived from the forest;
rushing toward Śambhu, Hara, he struck him with his head as if he were a termite mound.
Having looked up at Hara, who was indistinctly visible and covered in ashes,
Śaṅkara quickly rose from his meditation upon seeing Vārāha.
She suddenly became enraged, her brow knitting and turning red;
from her [mouth] emerged Vyāghrānala, filled with garlands of flames like the fire of a forest conflagration.
A great asura, born of darkness and resembling a mountain, was produced;
yet, impelled by Śambhu, he destroyed the boar in a mere moment.
Taking up a boar’s hide at the command of Hara,
Vyāghrānala requested food from Hara for the sake of pacifying his internal digestive fire.
Śambhu said to him, "I have indeed granted the family of aquatic creatures dwelling within the ocean as your food; go now to the edge of the waters."
The exceedingly powerful Gaṇa Vyāghrānala, who can assume any form at will,
fearlessly approached the shore of the ocean for the sake of allaying his hunger.
He devoured aquatic creatures—makaras, tortoises, and timi-fish;
and the more he made them his food, the more they increased for him.
The digestive fire blazed forth and increased as the cooker [of food], and likewise his body grew like a mountain. || 13 ||
Having become ten yojanas in width, he entered the ocean;
and day after day, he devoured many aquatic creatures.
At the end of a month, he became a hundred yojanas in width;
at the end of a year, he became a thousand yojanas in length.
Having entered the great ocean, he drinks the water with his breath;
millions of fish and other creatures enter his belly and are digested there.
All the water was consumed by fire, and it even came into existence again;
then, after time had passed, it expanded to ten thousand yojanas in extent.
Vyāghrānala became the ocean, drinking it day and night;
he dried up the ocean for a thousand yojanas, making it waterless.
In this manner, indeed, all the oceans were drunk by him in succession.
The entire great ocean, born of the waters surrounding the earth, was gradually drunk up.
Without water, clouds indeed do not arise from the circle of the ocean;
within the oceans there is fire, and from that fire of the tiger, this [conflagration] has spread forth.
The cavities of the oceans became composed of fire, and the earth likewise became parched and devoid of water; the waters within its womb were consumed by the blaze.
The entire surface of the earth became parched and a cessation of rain occurred; most embodied beings perished, but the yogis, having perceived that [state] in the three worlds, remained.
Indeed, the sages who were absorbed in meditative concentration ascended to heaven;
for an untimely dissolution has occurred upon the earth through the fire of the tiger.
Upon the loss of water, the tiger-like fire indeed devours the mud and other [substances] from the depths;
and due to the total depletion of water, the earth has reached a parched state.
The Vārdhaya demons, who were nearly dead, sought refuge in Śrī Hari, crying:
"Save us, save us, O Lord of Mercy! [From] the tiger and the most fierce fire! (25)
He devours the sea-monsters, the mud, and the waters;
an untimely dissolution has occurred, and because of that, we are as if dead.
This terrible [fire] now prevails, extending for ten thousand yojanas;
increasing in length, it will swallow the entire cosmic egg.
Therefore, you must put an end to this; we have come to you for refuge.
For the alkaline poison was drunk by you as your very essence, while all others were drunk only in fragments.
There is no other who can bring about the end of this asura while you are present;
everything is protected by you at all times, as if it were your own offspring.
We are all indeed oceans, the sons of Rādhā, whose very nature is water;
our father is Śrī Kṛṣṇa himself, the Blessed Lord, the husband of Rādhikā.
He who is indeed the beginningless incarnation of Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of Goloka, the Lord of the Gopīs, the Lord of Śrī, and the Supreme Sovereign. || 3.1 ||
"Therefore, we are your sons; protect us, O Supreme Person!"—thus was I entreated by the seven oceans at that time.
O Mahālakṣmī, together with you, I became the range of the oceans,
bearing the conch, discus, mace, lotus, svastika, banner, and trident.
Honored and saluted by them, and greeted with sweet water,
I was then born from Puṣkariṇī, the wife of Miṣṭoda.
"Though I was a mere child at birth, I have become a youth, the son of the Ocean;
you, O Śivasatyā, were then the daughter of Puṇḍarīka. (35)
And you became the queen of kings, distinguished by all sovereign power and beauty;
known by the name Śrī Puṇḍarīkaśrī, you were the bringer of all auspiciousness. (36)
Then I also remembered my water-going vehicle;
at that moment, a marvelous aquatic horse emerged from the sweet water.
He has a trunk and testicles, and he also possesses webbed feet; he can assume any form at will and masters the meditative absorption that restrains the breath. ||38||
In strength he was like the ocean, in speed like lightning, unassailable and mountain-like; such was the white-colored horse.
Moving through earth, water, and sky, possessing the powers of gross and subtle bodies and other such siddhis,
he is a speaker of all languages, possesses a divine body, and is indivisible.
Accompanied by Svambālikā, he was a treasury of skill in warfare;
he was endowed with the Cintāmaṇi jewel and adorned with gems and pearls.
The brilliance of a lamp within water is clearly visible even in darkness;
it is naturally endowed with a firm casing and possesses a quiver that produces weapons. 42.
Abounding in filaments dripping with nectar, adorned with a sword that struck down death,
robust and possessing copper-colored limbs in every part, he too bowed down to me.
With the sound of his joyful neighing, with his praises, with the spreading of his wings,
and with the high vibrations of his swift movements, he offered me a welcome.
I worshipped him in his form as a vehicle without any obstacle, and for the sake of victory, I placed my capable hand upon his back. ||45||
He was made to drink nectar, marked with a tilaka on his forehead,
instructed for the sake of his journey, and dispatched to the battlefield.
O Lakṣmī, the sound of his neighing indeed reached the houses of the guardians of the quarters;
the entire sky trembled, so what must have been the state of the earth? 47.
The mountains, the oceans, the water-deities, the Mothers, Varuṇa, the male rivers, and the female rivers have all assembled with me for the sake of battle. 48.
Summoned by me, they arrived, each joined with their own vehicle;
[and there was] the great white elephant born from the palm of Viṣṇu’s hand. 49.
And having mounted it, O Lakṣmī, the king of the gods arrived there [upon] the one named Pauṇḍraka, who was born from the power of Rudra and was black in complexion.
Then Dharmarāja arrived, having mounted a buffalo named Jaladhī, which was dark-complexioned and produced from the ear-wax of Brahmā. 51.
Varuṇa arrived there mounted upon a crocodile;
likewise, [Yama came] as a beautiful man with a body like a mountain, whose eyes were like the axles of a cart-wheel.
And Dhanada stood upon the vehicle born of Ambikā,
while the Gandharvas and the lords of the serpents likewise mounted white bulls.
The Rudras arrived there for the purpose of destroying the fierce Asuras;
and Candramas mounted a chariot adorned with five hundred swans.
And thus they arrived: the Ādityas with horses, camels, and chariots as their mounts;
the Vasus seated upon elephants; and the Yakṣas borne by men.
The Kinnaras mounted on serpents, the two Aśvins likewise mounted on horses, and the powerful Maruts seated upon deer also arrived. (56)
The Gandharvas are mounted on musical notes; Agni is upon the back of a ram;
the oceans are mounted on sea-monsters (makaras); and the gods travel in vehicles and celestial chariots.
Brahmā was mounted upon a swan, Viṣṇu had Garuḍa as his vehicle, the sages were seated upon their thrones, and the ancestors were on their meritorious vehicles.
The Earth is borne by Śeṣa, and Śeṣa has the tortoise as his vehicle;
the tortoises are borne by the clouds, and the clouds have the wind as their vehicle. ||59||
Mountains with wings, lightning borne upon clouds,
and rivers with their waves, all bearing weapons, arrived together.
Then musical instruments were sounded by the gods and the Tānūnarohis; and the roars of the Baladas, who dwell in heaven, were heard at that time.
Vyāghrānala heard those roars resounding to the ends of the quarters;
enraged and unable to endure them,
he repeatedly slapped his arms and let out loud bursts of laughter while striking his thighs with his palms.
And having flown upwards and looked down upon those standing ready for battle, [he said: 63.
Deluded by pride, he quickly seized his heavy mace and,
filling the sky with his body, rushed toward me and the gods.
Reaching up to the sky with his touch, ten thousand *yojanas* in length, and as broad as the ocean, Vyāghrānala came forth for the sake of battle. (65)
He waged war against Indra, the King of Dharma; he waged war against Varuṇa and the Giver of Wealth (Kubera). ||66||
He fought even against Candramas, as well as the Rudras and the Ādityas;
having fallen into a swoon, the powerful one engaged in battle again and again.
The powerful one fought with the yakṣas, the kinnaras, and the maruts;
he fought repeatedly with Agni, Brahmā, and Viṣṇu.
Assuming a thousand forms, he, most terrible, fought with mountains and lightning bolts, and he also fought together with the gods.
Racing along the path of the sky, drawing the circle of planets toward him,
and causing the stars to fall, he rushed forward and even fought.
Then even that firm sky appeared to be trembling;
the winds, shaken, utterly abandoned their steadiness and power. (71)
Then, by the trembling of the earth, they abandoned their established positions, and even the courses of the stars became obstructed. (72)
Vijaya also gained confidence, for the doubt between the two had vanished; and Pralaya rejoiced greatly upon seeing his own long-term prosperity.
Having entered all their weapons and the body of the asura,
they emerge from his pores as if traveling along a path to the further shore.
At that time, not even the touch of a weapon-wound could be felt upon his body where the fetus was located;
he remained as he was and fought with extreme vigor. (75)
Having staked his very life as the wager at the moment of destruction,
or having made a firm resolve regarding his own ruin, Vṛkānala fights on.
With maces, javelins, spears, nooses, and swords;
with scimitars, projectiles, mountains, stones, and the like.
And with spears, as well as with discs, clubs, and arrows;
and with blows from the chest, the arms, and even with elephants and other such [means]. (78)
In this manner, the asura Vṛkānala waged war at that time,
and even the powerful gods experienced great exhaustion.
Then, O Lakṣmī, having resolved that he was difficult to overcome,
I released at him the Sudarśana discus, which possessed a hundred thousand edges.
Fierce as the fire of universal dissolution, burning heaven and the netherworld,
that great and increasing form consumed him on all sides.
Then, indeed, from the bodies of Vyāghrānala, fragments were cut away by the millions; those who were thus separated also became Vyāghrānalas once again. 82.
In that battle, the Asuras indeed become equal to him;
yet, when commanded by me, the discus swiftly burns them as well. (83)
Then the entire intermediate space became like the sky of fire,
pervaded as if by the fire of universal dissolution, or indeed like the Brahmā-weapon.
Then you were commanded by me, assuming the form of Mahāmāyā; taking on the form of a seductress, you were to bring about the dullness of the Asura. 85.
Having encountered you in the sky nearby, the Asura fell into a state of delusion;
abandoning his countless forms in battle, he came to seize you. (86)
And for as long as he embraced you, the entire fire of the tiger was indeed drawn inward by the fire of your own body. (87)
Vyāghrānala, who was devoid of luster and lacked fiery brilliance,
became paralyzed as soon as he was pierced by Sudarśana.
It fell into the great ocean in a hundred and even a thousand pieces; fragments of that body became the sword-fish in the sea. (89)
And they became lifeless in the midst of the water like mountains;
thus, O Lakṣmī, when the fire of the tiger was extinguished, there arose the roarings of clouds.
Then, due to my exertion, streams of water issued from my body; the sky became filled with them there, and the oceans attained a state of moisture. (91)
Increasing, they filled the oceans;
from the sky there fell a rain consisting of victory-flowers and consecrated grains. 92.
The gods attained great joy and worshipped me, the Lord of Śrī;
I too honored the gods, who, their task accomplished, returned to their own abode. 93.
Then Lakṣmī departed, and you too entered a state of invisibility;
even my horse, your father’s mount, vanished along with you.
Having brought you home, I have come to Miṣṭoda;
having paid homage to the gods, I have come to Miṣṭoda. ||95||
Then, on earth, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Person (Śrī Puruṣottama), appeared under the name Anādi Śrī Vārdhi Nārāyaṇa. 96.
And it became well known to me that Puṇḍarīka was your father;
he gave his daughter to me, her worthy inner self, according to the prescribed rite.

Then, having married you—who possess the splendor of a lotus—according to the prescribed rites to the Supreme Self, the Lord of Lords, who is worshipped by the gods beginning with Śura, [he attained] that [state]. 98.
Having obtained the horse Uccaiḥśravas as my mount, I wandered through the three worlds and remained there until the end of the kalpa for the sake of protecting the Dharma.
I am that beginningless Śrī Hari, the eternal Supreme Brahman;
I know all this, and my manifestation is supreme.
For in this way, my incarnations have indeed arisen there in countless numbers;
[this occurs] through reading, hearing, chanting, or even remembering.
All of them bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation, being solely devoted to wonders;
O daughter of Śiva, remember the marvel of the glory of Nārāyaṇī. 102.

Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Manifestation of the Beginningless Śrī Vārdhinārāyaṇa for the Purpose of Destroying the Raudra Demon Vyāghrānala in the Nineteenth Year of Brahmā during the Dvāpara Cycle," in the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, within the third section concerning the lineage of Dvāpara.
Śrī Puruṣottama said: Listen, O Śrī Nārāyaṇī, to my manifestation,
which occurred during the first kalpa, in the year known as Sṛṣṭimāna of the Creator.
When the first Manu had come into being, Brahmā, having abandoned his sleep,
went at dawn to bathe in the celestial river while reflecting deeply.
Today, what kind of creation shall I bring forth that will beautify the three worlds?
I shall create one like myself, entirely devoid of the sense of duality.
Having thus resolved, he bathed, performed the twilight prayers (saṃdhyā), and went home;
having performed his daily worship, he entered the laboratory of creation.
He touched the machine of creation and inspected the womb-machine;
"May the entire four-faced creation be brought forth today. (5)
As he was thus forming this resolve, all those great sages,
the twice-born ones, immediately became four-faced and equal to himself.
All the gods likewise became four-faced and auspicious,
as did the humans, Gandharvas, Kinnaras, and Sādhyadevatās.
What are men, beasts, birds, and reptiles; what are those born from sweat, those born from eggs, and other embodied beings born from a womb? (8)
And there are aquatic creatures arising from the *kalala* stage of embryonic development,
those born from mud, those produced from leaves, those arising from grass, those emerging from crevices, and those originating from the netherworld (*pātāla*) and other such realms.
Indeed, all the Daityas, Dānavas, Rākṣasas, and likewise the Āsuras, were born from the creative resolve of the Four-faced One (Brahmā).
Yakṣas, piśācas, bhūtas, and all beings with four faces; by Brahmā, by the ancestors, by the gods, and by men who are foremost among devotees. || 1.1 ||
In every context of discourse, I am described as four-faced;
indeed, the Vedas themselves declare that all are four-faced.
"All the liberated ones have four faces, and all the lords have four faces"—thus did the storytellers conceive this notion, as if it were their own. (13)
Then the Brahman-sages, the Sādhyas, the virtuous, and the celibate students—
wherever they held discussions in the assembly halls, they did so on my account.
Some say that the Blessed One has a thousand heads;
others say that the Blessed One has innumerable heads. || 15 ||
Then others proclaim that he is everywhere and without end; yet others say that the glorious Lord exists with but a single head.
The four-faced one and the others spoke thus:
"As we are, so is he; as Hari is, so indeed is the Unborn. (17)
As is Brahmā, so are all the great seers and likewise the gods;
as are all human beings, so too are we, and as we are, so is Hari.
Thus, some there spoke; in this way, there was dispute. For the sake of reaching a decision on this matter, many debates took place. (19)
Then, having assembled on the surface of the earth at the northern bank of the Suvarṇagaṅgā, a council was convened by the Ṛṣis, the Mānavas, and the gods.
Thereupon, the foremost of the twice-born, the sage Śrautavṛṣa, asked: "Of what nature is that Blessed Lord, the Supreme Brahman, who is worshipped as the Sovereign? (21)
Then those who follow the authority of the Vedas said:
"The Puruṣa has a thousand heads, a thousand eyes, and a thousand feet. (22)
Then others spoke to Hari, the Lord of the lords of gods:
"He has hands and feet everywhere; he has eyes, heads, and faces on all sides. (23)
The Lord of Śrī, the soul of all, who possesses ears everywhere, abides there;
they call him Hari, the Supreme Lord, the eternal one. (24)
Others, however, then declared him to be four-faced and invisible to his own [creation], devoid of qualities, formless, inactive, and stripped of material form. (25)
Brahmā said: Hari resides in the imperishable abode, having a single head, two arms, two feet, two eyes, and two ears. ||26||
Then others spoke at that time: "Never indeed, never was it so;
he is the three-eyed Hari, the Supreme Lord, who exists eternally. (27)
When such deliberation had arisen, no conclusion was reached thereupon;
then Brahmā spoke regarding the propitiation of the wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
"What indeed is Hari like, so that he may become the object of our worship? We have worshipped that Janārdana for a long time. (29)
Then the divine Blessed One will likewise become visible;
then all of them, having gathered together on the bank of the golden river, [will behold him].
"O beloved, they commenced the primary worship of Me, which consists of the sacrifice of recitation (*japayajña*), augmented by great devotion, with the thought: 'May You become accessible to us.'"
They performed my propitiation with a thousand divine measures;
then they performed that oblation consisting of the concluding rite of completion.
They celebrated a truly grand festival consisting of congregational chanting (kīrtana),
as well as acts of charity and feasting, preceded by dance and song.
However, for the sake of fulfilling their meditative cultivation, for the purpose of determining my true form, and to bestow the fruit of devotion, I then became perceptible to them. (34)
The supreme light, whose nature is the space of consciousness and which consists of a mass of radiance, was first seen there as a dense [expanse] pervading everywhere. (35)
It is shoreless, invisible, impenetrable, and of a single form;
it outshines the splendor of infinite suns, moons, fires, and planets.
Then, from that single point, there issued forth multitudes of rays, as numerous as the countless [atoms], distinct and radiant, reaching into the highest numerical magnitude (parārtha).
It was visible on all sides—around, below, above, and at the flanks—and from that spot, it could be seen everywhere; it was stainless, cool, and pleasant.
Heart-pleasing and likewise irreproachable, consisting of a cloth of all splendors, the root was indeed seen as a surrounding border and a veil. 39.
In her midst was she who abounded in gentle smiles, a mine of affection and love, truly divine, surpassing the pride of beauty of countless goddesses of desire. (3.17.40)
The form, however, has one face, is endowed with two eyes and two ears, possesses one head, two hands, and two feet, and is exceedingly radiant. (41)
She appeared beautiful, full of bliss, and enchanting, her hair being curved, glossy, lustrous, and endowed with a brilliant radiance. 42.
