a great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose, portending the dissolution of heaven. ||27||
On earth, cities with abundant prosperity are consumed by fire;
even the forests where sages dwell are burnt by the fire of Vṛṣaṇa. ||28||
The halls, villages, and dwellings were consumed by those fires of the *vṛṣaṇas*;
then the living brāhmaṇas offered prayers to the gods.
May the gods protect us, who are surrounded by the jaws of death; we shall perform expiation for any transgressions and the like—protect us! 3.22.30.
We shall never act thus again; we shall surely abandon our delusion.
Protect us, protect us, O Mādhava, who have crossed to the further shore of the ocean of compassion! 3.1
Thus, as they were dying, they fell at the feet of Hari;
then the presiding deities of the sacrifice, directed by me, spoke to the twice-born.
Indeed, from the two testicles of Śālā, those villages emerged;
they are the divine Śālagrāmas of Hari, possessing divine wonders.
For the sake of protecting his devotees, Anādi-Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa himself, Lord Hari, has appeared before you in the form of a human beast to discipline you. (34)
Indeed, these Śālagrāmas are his two testicles;
O twice-born ones, they are the form of fire, the form of the thunderbolt, and the teachers of you all.
For you are performers of what should not be done, deluded by violence, and followers of a wrong path;
for us gods, neither an oblation nor meat has ever been desired. (36)
Milk-rice is most desirable; with it they should perform sacrifices, as well as with fruits, sugar, seeds, and lotuses. (37)
Grains, rice, barley, and also śāli rice and its husks;
sesame seeds, sweet food, honey, and excellent juices. ||38||
"Fuel-wood is always dear to the gods, but never meat;
you twice-born ones have indeed been deluded, so do not commit violence here. (39)
"O pure gods, do not employ us in impurity;
for the fruit of sin is indeed suffering, and that shall befall you. (3.22.40)
O twice-born ones, that which is performed in the sacrifice for the destruction of virility is being carried out by you yourselves in heaven, resulting in the destruction of your own virility. (41)
Even for you, the destruction of heaven arises through the fault of violence;
and we too are deprived of purity by the fault of meat-eating in the sacrifice. (42)
"O twice-born ones, we shall perform rites of atonement here;
for in heaven, one cannot go to one's own abode without performing the rite of atonement. (43)
Since they are unable to enter, let them instead commit violence against us, so that there may be peace here for the great fire of the Śālagrāma. (44)
Likewise, let us here ourselves—gods, sages, ancestors, and humans—propitiate Viṣṇu, Hari, Kṛṣṇa, Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Lord. (45)
Hari himself will perform the pacification of the fire there;
and this god Nārāyaṇa is himself Nara, who is without testicles.
"He has been prepared and consecrated here by you for the purpose of the fire-sacrifice;
let them take refuge in this very Supreme Self. (47)
"For he, indeed, having made the earth his protection, will act as its guardian.
Having been told this, O Lakṣmī, those lords of the gods then offered praise.
The ancestors, humans, and Brahmins worship me alone, the showerer of boons, the golden-hued Hari;
you are the Supreme Brahman, the Blessed Lord, the primordial Śrī Puruṣottama. ||49||
You alone are one without a second, the supreme Lord of all lords;
you alone are the imperishable cause even of the imperishable and the liberated.
You are the cause of the incarnations and non-incarnations of those endowed with powers;
you are the cause of all powers, and you are the cause of all lords.
You are the cause of sacrifices, and you are the cause of mantras;
you are the cause of rituals, of treasures, and of all ritual materials. (52)
You are the cause of all ritual sections and of the gods;
you are the agent, the instigator, the knower, and you alone are satisfaction itself.
The twice-born and the performers of ritual action, as well as you yourself as the sacrificer—
O Blessed One, you alone are all the materials and all the sacrificial offerings.
Who else besides you is capable of demonstrating the knowledge of meaning, the knowledge of ritual injunctions, the Vedic knowledge of mantras, and the knowledge of practical application? (55)
O Lord Hari, having granted forgiveness, protect, protect this world that is being consumed here; O ocean of mercy, forgive our offenses as well. (56)
O Lord, please forgive us out of compassion for this slaughter of a man that we have committed, being ignorant of the true nature of mantras.
Wise people forgive the offenses of the ignorant;
you are the father, the mother, the protector, the wise Maheśvara. (58)
You are the Lord, the creator of all, the teacher of all, and the bestower of happiness;
you are the one who reveals the truth as it is—govern us, O Supreme Person! (59)
"O Lakṣmī, having been thus entreated, 'These have come to you for refuge; protect us who have sought your shelter,' I, the Supreme Person, then spoke."
Out of compassion, he instructed them all in the meaning of the Vedas as spoken by me, and [granted] the status of the twice-born through the practice of what is beneficial and non-violence.
It arises through purity, through devotion, through freedom from passion and hatred,
as well as through lack of greed, lack of desire, absence of thirst, and likewise through austerity.

Through right conduct, through dharma, and through contentment, one is born; through truth, through the divine way of life, and through dedication to the Lord, one attains the state of a brahmin. (63)
It arises through non-violence, the granting of fearlessness, and the granting of liberation;
that state of Brahminhood is further illuminated by sacred knowledge and the Veda. (64)

Having committed such an act of hostility toward the twice-born, it is not righteousness at all; for in this matter, violence and malice are great obstacles that block the way to heaven and liberation.
The self, which causes suffering to others, also experiences such suffering;
while living under the dominion of that [self], boundless suffering arises therein. (66)
In this way, by inflicting suffering, dharma attains the state of adharma;
furthermore, O best of Brahmins, listen with great discernment to another point as well. (67)
Even the finest food—pure, delicious, and fragrant—becomes refuse once it has entered the mouth;
it turns into filth once it reaches the stomach. (68)
Its transformations, such as the fleshy mass and so forth, are of the nature of impurity; how then could they be [consumed] by gods and others who consist of pure sattva and eat nectar? (69)
O Brahmins, reflect upon such a reality:
for there, even the flies of darkness become truly agitated. (3.22.70)
For that which is impure, foul-smelling, characterized by darkness (tāmasa), and indeed soiled—how could the gods and the twice-born ever desire such food? (71)
Milk is fragrant, excellent, and indeed consists of the essence of flavors; it is combined with ghee, and those characterized by sattva desire this pure food, which is milk.
Just as flies desire fragrance, sweets, honey,
and various kinds of sweet flavors, so do the gods desire those same things.
Therefore, O best of the twice-born, do not perform a sacrifice characterized by violence;
likewise, avoid the binding, the slaughtering, and the dismembering of animals.
For the extraction of the sacrificial victim, the oblation, and so forth—all that is indeed of the nature of violence;
"violence is never to be committed"—such indeed is the Vedic revelation.
"The Vedic revelation is my teaching that everything must be offered to Hari:
a leaf, a flower, a fruit, water, clothing, a house, wealth, and even a son. (76)
"The daughter, the wife, the husband, the cow, the field, wealth, and even one's own self—these are to be given to Nārāyaṇa; such is the Vedic revelation. (77)
Having meditated upon it as being of the nature of Nārāyaṇa and having offered it to Nārāyaṇa, one should consume it as is appropriate; however, no act of killing is enjoined.
Having indeed offered each [portion] to its respective deity as assigned,
and having made everything pleasing, the Vaiṣṇava bull should be employed.
Having meditated thus, "Everything belongs to Nārāyaṇa," and thereafter [realizing] that it must be accepted as nothing else, one should offer everything that is one's own to Hari.
In the Vaiśyasava sacrifice, a four-year-old female animal is likewise offered;
she must be released for Hari, and she must never be eaten under any circumstances.
"She is indeed a goddess worthy of worship"—such is the Vedic revelation;
likewise, even in the Gosava sacrifice, cows are to be offered to the Supreme Lord.
Ten thousand cows, honored and worshipped, are considered the proper sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā);
they should be released, worshipped, and given for the sake of obtaining milk.
In the Marutstoma sacrifice as well, there are seventeen five-year-old male animals, as well as those that have not yet touched a womb and are three years old. (84)
Women and animals should be offered to the Supreme Lord, the Supreme Self; thus they become true practitioners, and likewise those women become virtuous ones who bestow the awakening of Brahman.
In the first, second, and third year, as well as in the fourth and fifth year, there were likewise an equal number of men and women. (86)
"They are to be given in the stage of renunciation (tyāgāśrama) and belong to the lineage of Acyuta;
they are to be made Vaiṣṇavas"—such is the Vedic revelation. ||87||
Even in the horse sacrifice,
that divine horse which has been offered to the deity as the path of the gods must certainly not be put to use.

The fruit known as *kuṣmāṇḍa* should be offered to the Fire-god, the enjoyer of the oblation; likewise, sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*) and boiled rice offerings (*caru*) should be presented as is appropriate. (89)
Thus it is; no doubt should be entertained here by the Brahmins.
For I am the speaker of the Vedas, and I alone am the very soul of sacrifice.
"I alone abide within the mantra; let the twice-born know this in their hearts. Let them make this solemn vow: 'No living being whatsoever shall be slain.'"
"Let them perform worship of my two testicles in the form of Śālagrāma stones;
by that, there will surely be peace for the fire. (92)
Otherwise, there would be no extinguishing of the fire, and the world would be reduced to ashes;
indeed, my testicles, which contained my virility, were cut off by me in the sacrificial halls. (93)
From those two, villages and communities were produced in numbers exceeding ten million and a hundred billion;
for all those Śālagrāmas are indeed my own form and consist of my very self.
"Let all the twice-born indeed worship those who reduce the world to ashes.
Thus addressed, all the lords of the earth honored them with many offerings. (95)
The Vaiṣṇavas worshipped them again and again with Sāman mantras and the Puṃsūkta hymns;
yet even then, those Śāla stones did not become pacified.
O Brahmins, listen with concentrated minds as I speak:
without a suitable seat, those stones will not attain peace. (97)
"Let them pray for Śrī, the Goddess of Fortune; she will provide what is appropriate.
Then, you were worshipped by the Brahmins with the Lakṣmīsūkta and other hymns. 98.
Having been worshipped, saluted, and offered for the sake of peace, you then became the very nature of the seat in the form of a *pippala* leaf. (99)
They became divine in nature, possessing a celestial golden form;
indeed, those very stones assumed the name "Lion Throne" (Siṃhāsana).
Then peace and stability were attained by the rocks, which became motionless;
they were free from all disturbances, and the fire was extinguished in every direction.
Then the Śālagrāmas were worshipped by all the gods, the ancestors, human beings, and sages with various offerings, including sandalwood paste.
Through services rendered with fragrant offerings, those monkeys became divine;
they were of the nature of Hari, portions of Hari, and always possessed the form of Hari’s worship.
Consisting of the limbs of Hari and identical with my own self, those stone images became endowed with splendor and were bestowers of liberation. || 104 ||
Then, when my two testicles were held by me in their proper place and became firmly attached to me,
at that moment I was endowed with virility.
I indeed became Pūrṇamūrti, for those devotees were protected by me when I appeared in manifest form during an ancient human sacrifice (naramedha).
Then I became the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the glorious Puruṣottama,
and the beginningless Śrī Śālapuṃstva Nārāyaṇa.
O Lakṣmī, I became the gentle Śālagrāma image upon a beautiful and auspicious pedestal; remember me as such, and likewise remember you. 1.08.
And the embodied Supreme Person, the Lord of Śrī, dwelt together with you;
O beloved, those other incarnations of mine also appeared there in that kalpa.
"I know all my incarnations according to their purpose, O beloved;
indeed, from reading or even hearing [this], enjoyment and liberation arise. (3.22.110)

Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "The Manifestation of the Beginningless Śrī-Puṃstvanārāyaṇa for the Protection of Devotees during the Human Sacrifice in the Twenty-Seventh Year called Avṛṣa of the Creator, along with His Knowledge of the Purpose of Sacrifices such as the Naramedha," in the Third Section (Dvāpara-Santāna) of the glorious *Śrī-Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Puruṣottama said: O Nārāyaṇī Śrī, listen to my most purifying story,
which concerns the divine manifestation of the Creator in the year of fire.
In the first Manvantara of the eighteenth cycle of one hundred and eight Kalpas,
there was a king named Sūryavarcas, who was enlightened by Brahmā.
Devoted to the path of the Vedas, he was the sovereign lord of all the stars,
seated in the assembly of the gods within a celestial chariot that moves through the sky.
Moving through the netherworlds as well as Mount Meru and among the planets, that youthful observer of vows was constantly intent on my worship and a servant of the Siddhas.
One day, that man of virtuous and noble qualities, who was diligent in inspiring devotion among my subjects, reflected thus while in his own home together with his queen.
"O beloved, this human body of mine was designated as 'nṛpa' (king) by the Lord;
O beloved, when will it truly function according to its etymological meaning—that which protects men (*nṝn pāti*)? (6)
The queen said: "This body of human beings is for the attainment of liberation;
yet, regarding the granting of liberation to men, the king acts for his own self-interest. (7)
Otherwise, the word "king" (nṛpa) would not be considered meaningful in the teaching;
human beings, driven by their karma, are dissolved after having come into being again and again. (8)
Even when the task of protecting them has been performed, they go to their destruction;
for the protection of the body is not true protection, and being the master of the body is not protection.
Food, water, fire, and wind protect by their very nature;
there is no need for kings in that which is protected by nature.
In the Kṛta Yuga, there is indeed no theft, no deceit, and no plundering;
thus the age proceeds, for it is not [otherwise] protected by kings there.
Since a king was useless during the Kṛta Yuga when truth was the established dharma,
the meaningfulness of kingship must be sought [in other ages] if it is to exist at all.
O Lord of Subjects, it appears clearly to my mind that you are truly making your name "Nṛpāli" (Protector of Men) meaningful by bestowing the gift of liberation; therefore, please do so.
Just as the king himself attains liberation through devotion,
so too shall the subjects surely attain liberation through supreme devotion.
The state of kingship has been made meaningful by him who understands the nature of birth;
O King, you too should exercise such sovereignty that it grants liberation. 15.
Having heard these words of the queen, the king rejoiced within himself,
considering his wife to be a virtuous woman equal to the Vedas and a companion in his quest for liberation.
Again he questioned his own beloved, named Mudgāyanī:
"By what method can liberation be brought about for human beings? Please instruct me. (17)
Then Mudgāyanī, having summoned the virtuous sages, perfected ones, and ascetics, as well as the saintly men and women from other worlds, spoke to them.
Having caused a temple to be built and having installed the image of the Supreme Goddess who bestows liberation, you should always perform great festivals. (19)
Subjects [perform] service, worship, beholding, as well as remembering, chanting, hearing, being a servant, servitude, salutation, and praise. (3.23.20)
They shall perform worship, dancing, and meditative surrender; they shall offer food, clothing, vessels, and sandalwood paste. (21)
The offering of erotic delights, as well as the offering of fragrances, the offering of the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), and also the offering of song and the offering of recitation. ||22||
They will offer themselves and go to the supreme state;
they will perform sweeping, smearing, the offering of lamps, and the offering of banners. (23)
The offering of musical instruments and their playing, likewise the offering of fruits and flowers, the offering of saffron, unbroken rice grains, and garlands, and the offering of incense. ||24||
The offering of food (naivedya), likewise the offering of the waving of lights (nīrājana), circumambulation, praise, prostration, as well as salutation with joined palms (añjali). ||25||
People will describe the gestures, the internal states, the glances, the reflections, the deliberations, and even the final conclusions of Hari. (26)
Wealth such as gold, silver, copper, or a staff;
divine ornaments, jewels, gems, and diamonds. ||27||
Mañjarīs, flower garlands, clusters, and most beautiful garments;
likewise, a crown, bracelets, a wreath, chains, and a girdle. ||28||
He also gave him a signet ring, weapons such as the conch and discus,
a cloak, a comfortable bed, sandals, and an excellent vehicle.
Vehicles, celestial chariots, wealth in cattle, juices and the like, most delicious foods such as sugar and other sweets, honey, clarified butter, long pepper, and so forth.
Men will indeed offer jars, beautiful pitchers, bowls, vessels for worship, wicks, and the various implements required for festivals. (31)
Having offered everything to Hari, they shall go to the supreme abode;
even those devoted to ritual action, having performed sacrificial sessions in the temple of Hari, [shall attain that same goal]. ||32||
And the mendicants, having eaten the food offered with faith, shall go to that state, even those who have committed offenses after seeking forgiveness in the presence of Hari. (33)
Even the wicked, having confessed their evil deeds, shall go to the supreme goal;
likewise, one who observes vows, having fulfilled those vows, shall go to the highest state.
Having worshipped the god Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Lord, those women will go to that beloved Sovereign of All and attain the supreme state. ||25||
Whether they be children or the elderly, wealthy or even destitute— in every way,
by having worshipped that Blessed One, they shall go to the supreme state.
Therefore, O King, in order to open the path of liberation for living beings and to make your kingship truly meaningful, [you must build] the temple of Śrī Hari. 37.
Have constructed an auspicious and excellent [temple], provided with one thousand jars, beautiful with a thousand peaks, and adorned with golden finials. (38)
In that very place, according to the prescribed rite, install the golden Lord Hari, the Blessed One, the Sovereign God, whose splendor reaches to the heavens.
The Supreme Lord, the creator of the universe, who possesses a beautiful and handsome form, is the deity manifested in the likeness of an image, awakened by the hosts of celestial sages.
Establish him there, endowed with his own power, served by his own sovereign attendants,
and joined with his own abode.
To the Lord who is visible to all, to be served by all, the destroyer of all sins, the bestower of all peace—the divine Śrīpati, the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama). ||42||
Having spoken thus to her husband, the queen remained silent for a moment;
the king then considered those words—which were both wholesome and truthful—to be a means of liberation.
He performed a month-long sacrifice of recitation accompanied by hymns of praise;
he invited the Siddhas, the Ṛṣis, the gods, and human beings.
He caused the monthly worship of the name "Akhaṇḍa" to be performed:
"Hare Kṛṣṇa, Hare Kṛṣṇa, O Lord of Śrī, Supreme Person! (45)
"O Inner Self, O Lord Viṣṇu, O Supreme Ruler, salutations be unto you!"—in this manner the king performed worship incessantly. (46)
He indeed gave various foods that were as delicious as nectar,
and he joyfully performed every kind of service for all those performing the sacrifice.
O beloved, gods and others constantly come from and depart to the worlds; there, worship occurs perpetually and without ceasing.
Thus, when the month of Śrāvaṇa had passed and on its final day, under the full moon,
the king posed a question in the midst of the assembly.
"May the path to liberation for human beings remain unbroken here; in such a way, may the gods and others reveal to me their auspicious manifestation. (3.23.50)
Then, when it was accomplished, they said, "Build a temple here";
thus spoke the sages, the gods, and the humans as well. (51)
"O Indra among kings, through this temple, supreme nourishment for liberation will arise here; therefore, cause it to be built and establish it there. (52)
To Śrīpati, the Supreme Self, the Supreme Brahman, the Supreme Lord, the God in the form of an image, the Master who bestows liberation from all [bondage]. ||53||
Having uttered "Oṃ" and thus completed the sacrifice of recitation (japayajña),
the king then had [the mountain] fashioned out of gold, endowed with a thousand peaks.
The first temple on earth, visible from the stars and beautiful to behold, was completed with all its primary and secondary parts in their entirety. ||55||
He pondered over the matter of his form, wondering from where and by what means it might come about;
at night, the king reflected thus and became despondent in his mind.
He remembered me, the Supreme Brahman, the Lord of Śrī, the Puruṣottama.
O Lotus-born One, having perceived that remembrance by my devotee, I [appeared] together with you.
He went to where that king had become visible to me;
then Sūryavarcas, seeing me within his range of vision before him, bowed down.
He prostrated, offered the honey-mixture (madhuparka), and performed the ritual salutation like a staff;
he then gave me a seat adorned with all ornaments.
To the inner self who blazes with all splendor, who is endowed with all sovereignty, and who causes the rain of universal grace; 3.23.60.
Filled with devotion, the king offered food, drink, and worship; he even made the offering of his very self and the surrender of all his possessions.
There, in that auspicious mansion he had constructed— which was indeed fit for permanent residence and surrounded by a great garden— he entreated me to dwell there.
O Blessed One, dwell here visibly; remain forever steadfast, accompanied by Lakṣmī and endowed with your attendants and all necessary implements. (63)
"For the sake of the liberation of the world, I have spoken thus: 'Let it be so. Then it was said: 'Go, O Indra among kings, to the śiṃśapā tree at the edge of the forest.'"
He saw a great and supreme tree standing in the midst of the hermitage of the sages,
and to its left, a most auspicious banyan tree situated nearby.
Just as my residence is here in this temple, so it is there as well;
O King, those two trees in your kingdom are our very forms in personified shape. (66)
By my own will alone, both of these eternal and divine forms of mine were fashioned and created by me and Lakṣmī; they are ancient, having existed for many years.
The illustrious Narayana and [His consort] abide as eternally nourished and worthy of worship by the gods;
O King, go to those two, who are like unto yourself, and worship and honor them. 68.
"Always worshipped by the sages, we two abide here in the form of trees;
then, indeed, in our true embodied forms, we were revealed here by those two."
"And we two shall remain here, O King, established by our own power according to the prescribed rite.
Having been thus addressed, the king went to the vicinity of a banyan tree in the great garden.
Beholding a bright banyan tree joined by śiṃśapā trees and endowed with divine sap, the king was struck with wonder. (71)
Having bowed down to the sages according to the prescribed rites, the king himself performed the worship of the two joined trees, which had been carried out by the assembly of great seers.
Having offered incense, lamps, water, food offerings, and a handful of flowers,
I then performed the threefold circumambulation at the Śiṃśapā tree.
In the Stamba [Tīrtha] resides Nārāyaṇa himself, the eternal Supreme Self, the illustrious Puruṣottama, who bears the conch, the discus, the mace, and the lotus. ||74||
I became dark-complexioned, of a dark hue, and possessed of a divine form before me;
I am indeed that very *śiṃśapā* trunk, and I am not distinct from the trunk. (75)
Then all my male attendants and indeed my female attendants appeared as branches;
for they were possessed of my body and were of my own nature.
Furthermore, O Beloved, you abide within the tree, the banyan, and the trunk;
you are non-different from the trunk, you are the interior of the trunk, and you take the form of the cause of the banyan tree.
Your branches, your friends, and other beautiful beloveds were seen as non-different from you—your yoginīs, whose very essence is you. (78)
Thus, seeing both me and you, King Sūryavarcas was filled with joy;
he quickly prostrated himself like a staff and consecrated us with Vedic mantras.
Indeed, with great honor, he caused you to ascend onto a golden chariot, adorned with a hundred jars and as beautiful as a celestial vehicle.
Then, accompanied by a great festival, he was brought according to the prescribed rites to the pavilion on the grounds of the temple, which could be carried by a hundred elephants.
Having established me, you, as well as your attendants and your consorts in the temple according to the prescribed rite, having performed the consecration with all ritual acts; ||82||
He established me, who had appeared visibly before him in my divine form;
indeed, until the end of the kalpa, I dwelt in my own abode together with you.
He possesses a divine form for those who possess divine vision and are devoted to him; he possesses a physical form for those who possess the eye of flesh and are subject to illusion.
I am the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Supreme Person;
I became the dark-complexioned Anādi Śrī Śiṃśapā Nārāyaṇa. (85)
You have attained the renown of Anādi-Śrī-Śyāma-Nārāyaṇa;
you, O most beautiful one, have attained the fame of Vaṭaśrī by my side. (86)
The humans there were indeed fair-complexioned, white, and golden-hued, possessing divine bodies and enchanting forms; so too were the gods and the great sages eternally.
O Lakṣmī, in that kalpa, both the Pitṛs and the Asuras, having served me and you, attained liberation; indeed, they became kings there along with their followers.
By that king, following the queen's instruction, the granting of liberation was performed;
indeed, the bestowing of safety upon all was accomplished by the king through his surrender to me. (89)
"I know this, O Lakṣmī: my form is dark-complexioned, while yours, O Lakṣmī, is fair; remember that as well as her abode. (3.23.90)
Remember also that attendant, the king, and the queen-consort;
remember the innumerable millions, billions, and trillions who were then born and liberated. 9.1.
Even then, O beloved, many other incarnations of mine occurred in accordance with specific tasks; indeed, I know them all. 92.
Thus, through this dark form, [He bestows] the supreme devotion of His devotees:
hearing, chanting, serving the feet, and likewise bowing down. (93)
Worship, as well as friendship and self-surrender, anointing, sweeping, massaging the feet, and feeding [the deity]. (94)
The offering of water for drinking, the gift of garments and ornaments, as well as the act of adornment, worship, prostration, riding together in a vehicle, and dancing; ||95||
Singing, dalliance, sporting in the grove, wandering about, and likewise laughing—
I, having become manifest before them, graciously accepted all of these.
She led even my own abode, the supreme state known as the Imperishable (Akṣara).
The entire earth became Vaiṣṇavī, and both men and women became Vaiṣṇavas. ||97||
Even beasts and birds attained liberation through my yoga;
Śyāmala and Śyāmala were Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Lord. ||98||
O Beloved, at that time in the kalpa, multitudes of living beings came to me singing;
even sinners, O Śyāma Hari, became virtuous as they offered salutations.
By reading, hearing, and remembering this, one shall attain liberation;
at the end, the king, along with his country, his lineage, and his subjects [shall do so].
Accompanied by his dependents, his servants, and his wives, he indeed attained liberation;
even the cows, horses, and other animals likewise reached the supreme state of liberation.
Therefore, the construction of a temple and the installation of my image constitute for me the supreme gift of fearlessness to the living beings on this earth. (102)

Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, titled "The Manifestation [of the Lord]," in the third section, the Dvāpara-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*, concerning the appearance of the primordial Śrī-Śiṃśapā (the Dark Nārāyaṇa) together with Vaṭa-Śrī in the palace through King Sūryavarcas during the twenty-eighth year of Brahmā’s life.
Śrī Puruṣottama said: Listen, O Śrī, Queen of Śiva; in the twenty-ninth kalpa consisting of ninety [cycles], during the seventh Manu, in the year of Brahmā’s father.
Listen, O Lotus-born one, to how my manifestation came about here in this world:
from the secret pores of Brahmā, an Asura of variegated form appeared. (2)
One named Mayūra was born, possessing wings, tail-feathers, and a beak; he had feet, could assume any form at will, and was as large as a mountain. || 3 ||
Flying through the sky, he draws along the circle of planets;
traveling upon the earth, he drags along the peaks of villages and mountains.
Having entered into the water, he agitates the oceans;
he causes the earth to tremble and strikes terror into the gods. || 5 ||
He even carries away thousands of humans, nāgas, and serpents;
at times he becomes a god, possessing his own form with a splendor like that of Mahendra.
In some places he assumes a human form resembling that of a sovereign,
and in others he is like a great seer, resplendent with a halo of brilliance.
He was indeed born with the power to assume any form at will and was full of delusive strength;
out of greed for the kingdom, he performed austerities for a thousand years.
Brahmā, being pleased, granted him a boon: "Death shall not come to you except through Hari.
Having thus received these words, he was satisfied and remained entirely free from fear.
Assuming the respective forms of beings in the world of truth, among men, in heaven, and in the regions of Manu such as Atala and others, he goes there, enjoys [them], and rejoices.
In some places he goes to temples and departs after consuming nectar;
or, having abducted a goddess or a human woman, he goes to another region. (11)
Having taken a yakṣiṇī or a rākṣasī, or having taken wealth, he departs;
or having taken a virtuous dānavī or a nāgī, he goes to the interior of the forest.
Having taken cows, heifers, horses, and elephants,
he proceeds to a forest-rich valley of Mount Meru extending for a hundred yojanas.
Having repeatedly abducted men, women, goddesses, and even rākṣasīs, she established a magnificent residence in the forest, splendid with excellent enjoyments.
Having performed all his own duties, he enjoys that which consists of worldly pleasures;
due to the granting of a boon by Brahmā, he does not meet death in battle.
And because he possesses the power to go everywhere, he always attains victory;
thus, by his own strength, he has indeed become like a universal monarch upon the earth. (16)
Having gradually conquered other kings, he then became a lord of kings;
and he declares, "My sovereignty over the earth extends everywhere. (17)
And he made this proclamation: "I alone am a universal monarch; being powerful, I go everywhere and conquer the entire circle of the earth. (18)
Having established kings over the realms of the asuras, he ruled the kingdom;
thus, in due course, Mayūraka became a universal monarch (cakravartin).
Then, in order to violate Indrāṇī, he went to the heavenly world;
and having lifted her up, he flew through the sky toward the earth.
Just as Indra was advancing, he struck him with his thunderbolt;
however, that thunderbolt, which resembled fire, was seized by him and held within his beak.
Then Indra, beholding the peacock army, was seized with terror;
he retreated to his own abode and reported [the matter] to the guardians of the quarters.
All the guardians of the quarters, fully prepared, assembled for the sake of battle:
Yama, Kubera, Īśāna, Varuṇa, Nirṛti, and Anila. (23)
Anala, Arka, and Rudra all arrived upon the earth;
accompanied by their armies and with weapons ready, they roared in the sky.
Having heard the sounds intended for battle as well as the roars of the gods,
Mayūra quickly went forth with his army for the sake of combat.
Accompanied by ten thousand generals and joined by his lotus-born soldiers,
he indeed fought a terrible battle against Mānava for a full year.
Indeed, he revived his own army, which had been slain in many ways, by means of the asuric lore;
thus he fought with the lords of the gods.
The extremely cruel Māyūrakas, who were indeed Asuras, fought on all sides together with all the hosts of gods, entirely devoid of fear. ||28||
The battle did not come to an end, nor did the peacock perish;
there was no cessation for the gods, and human beings fell into misery. (29)
The daughters of Manu, the daughters of the gods, the truthful daughters of the Nāgas, and even the daughters of the Daityas—being terrified, they did not indeed go outside. (3.24.30)
At that time, agitation and suffering were constantly present for him throughout the three worlds, among all people, and even among kings.
Then the gods became despondent, having undergone great exhaustion;
the sun grew lusterless, and Mahendra’s mind was broken.
Varuṇa’s power was exhausted, Yama fell into confusion,
and Nirṛti likewise had his army depleted in that battle.
Even Īśāna was deprived of his vigor, Kubera’s strength was exhausted,
Agni was bereft of his sharpness, and Marut began to weep.
The other gods became despondent, while the kings fell under their control;
thus, when this time had arrived, suffering became excessive on all sides.
Abandoning the battle, the gods went to the abode of Brahmā;
they entreated him most fervently and spoke of their own inferiority. (36)
And they fortified the strength of Āsura for the sake of protection;
but Brahmā, having heard them, said: "I shall strive on your behalf."
"Let all of you remain here and propitiate Hari, the Supreme;
for by my boon, there is indeed no one else capable of destroying him except Hari."
Thus addressed, the deities and others, filled with zeal,
worshipped me— the beginningless Śrīśa Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Person (Śrī Puruṣottama).
O Lakṣmī, mounted upon an elephant along with you, I quickly departed from Akṣara and then proceeded to Satyaloka, to the assembly hall of Brahmā.
Then Brahmā and the others offered me a welcome and worship;
thereafter, they spoke of their own suffering and resolved upon the destruction of the asuras.
Then, O Lotus-born One, I contemplated the destruction of the asuras and said to the gods, "Let them go back to their own regions. (42)
The gods quickly departed for their own lands, and I,
assuming a human form, came to the earth where the abode of the asura was indeed located.
Assuming the form of a warrior, equipped with a bow and an arrow,
I went to his city gate and caused him to perform the act of begging for alms.
Then Mayūra himself, having been informed by the messengers, came to his own gate in great eagerness for the sake of hospitality. (45)
Having bowed to me, he said, "Why indeed do you beg for alms?
[I replied,] "Give me the alms of battle here; I beg for nothing else. (46)
Being thus entreated, he then took water in his hand and gave alms;
having joined weapon with weapon, she was obtained by me as well through the bow.
Right there, at the front of the city gate in that excellent forest, a terrible and most fearsome battle took place with him alone until the end of the month.
It causes the hair to stand on end for the gods, humans, and ancestors who delight in virtuous conduct, as well as for kings and great heroes.
Having perceived the commencement of the battle, the gods traveled by way of the sky;
arriving right there, they then proclaimed victory to me.
"I alone shall indeed fight with the peacock, and no one else;
at the end of the month, with my arrows, weapons, missiles, clubs, and so forth. (5.1)
His feathers were quickly shattered and he became despondent;
then he deployed his own peacock warriors in the battle.
Those Arbuda Mayūrakas, acting as his helpers, surrounded me on all sides and fought with great speed.
They assume illusory forms and likewise bear illusory weapons;
they wear illusory disguises and likewise wage illusory battles. ||54||
Those who bore illusory bodies and manifested illusory armies were all slain by me there, one after another, with the Sudarśana discus.
Those peacocks were burnt and killed by the splendor of Sudarśana;
the city of Māyūrakī was burnt, while those devoted ones were well protected by me. ||56||
Śacī and the other beloved wives, as well as the Mānavīs and the Mānavas—men, women, and deities—were all protected by me right there. (57)
All those Asuras, who were followers of the lineage of Māyūra, have been slain;
indeed, they have all been rendered completely extinct by the Sudarśana.
Then Māyūraka, seeing his own total destruction,
became blind and, seizing a great sword in his hand, [rushed] through the air.
Having assumed a body consisting mostly of rock, he fell upon my head with the edge of a sword to kill me; at that moment, I [wielded] the Sudarśana.
Driven downward from above, it then consumed him in the sky;
having been entirely reduced to ashes, he became nothing but vapor in the firmament.
The divine drums resounded, and a rain of flowers fell upon me;
there was also a rain of sandalwood and unbroken rice grains, as well as shouts of victory. (62)
Then the women born of the lineage of Mayūra wept in vain;
they summoned the gods and descended there into that city. (63)
In the great Māyūraka forest, which was exquisitely adorned with every prosperity,
even upon seeing a prison, I liberated the people from that place.
I swiftly liberated the gods, and likewise I liberated the goddesses;
I liberated the deities headed by Śacī, as well as the human women.
In that kingdom, all the deities, as well as the gods and human beings,
[worship] me— the Kṣatra, the Supreme Self, Śrī Hari, the Puruṣottama.
Having consecrated him with the waters of sacred fords according to the prescribed rites,
they, filled with eagerness, installed him together with Śrī.
Then many maidens and women born of the lineage of Mayūra, being without a protector, joyfully chose me as their supreme lord. 68.
Purified by me at the sacrifice and taken by me according to the prescribed rite,
they were all then offered to me by Brahmā and the other gods, and became my wives.
In this way, the great asura named Mayūra was slain by me in the past;
for his destruction could not have been brought about by anyone other than me.
His splendor, having emerged, indeed found rest within me;
that asura attained liberation, as did the others who were slain.
All those who were slain by my Sudarśana have indeed attained liberation, and even the kings, having worshipped me as the Supreme Lord, have been liberated. (72)
They indeed returned to their own lands, and the gods went to the third heaven;
so too did the wives of the Nāgas, the daughters of Manu, and even the protectorless goddesses.
O beloved, when all of them remained after having married me,
you then became Śrī, the queen of all those royal consorts.
"Born not from a womb, possessing the form of a Kṣatriya, and standing by my side—you must now take the peacock's tail-feathers and use them as a broom. (75)
Indeed, my attendants also performed the sweeping of the ground;
they fashioned all the brooms to be both beautiful in form and splendid. (76)

Then, O beloved, by means of my own celestial chariot, I went everywhere on the surface of the earth in every direction; wherever the asuras were who had been made kings by Mayūra, there I went and struck them down at their very root.
He bestowed all the kingdoms upon the Kṣatriyas according to their respective rights;
thus, my entire empire on the surface of the earth was established by me in every direction.
And then that supreme Vaiṣṇava [liṅga] was established by the Supreme Self, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the wielder of the discus. ||79||
O beloved, remember Him who protects in the form of the beginningless Śrī Kṣatranārāyaṇa, together with the beginningless Śrī Rājarājñī. 3.24.80.
I have protected all the bulls among the Kṣatriyas upon the circle of the earth; I have performed all sacrifices and have also guarded my subjects. (8.1)
The deities were protected and the paths of Dharma were set in motion;
the fame of the sacrificial sessions was established and the ways of the Vedas were nourished. ||82||
The codes of conduct were established and the virtuous were protected at that time;
excellent monasteries were constructed, and temples for the gods and other deities were built. ||83||
The sacred fords were indeed protected, and the mendicants were also protected; furthermore, all the stories of Nārāyaṇa were constantly recited. (84)
They were truthful, virtuous, and protected; they were always guarded in accordance with dharma, and my devotion toward them was extended throughout the entire earth. (85)
And at that time, O Lakṣmī, the Vedic realization of the Self was proclaimed by me in my assembly, where ten thousand virtuous ones were present.
There were ten thousand Brahmins, ten thousand virtuous women,
ten thousand young students, and ten thousand Vedic scholars.
There were ten thousand guests, ten thousand monks, ten thousand who were without protectors, and ten thousand reciters. ||88||
There were ten thousand performers of the Aśvamedha sacrifice, ten thousand performers of the Sattras, ten thousand restraints of the senses, and ten thousand ascetics. ||89||
There were ten thousand observers of vows, ten thousand wise men, ten thousand male servants, and ten thousand female servants. ||3.24.90||
Knowing the yoga of ten thousand, wandering through ten thousand [worlds], those established in purity remain eternally devoted to the yoga of knowledge. ||91||
All of them were endowed with devotion to me, partaking in my sacrificial feast;
they bore my form and were intent upon the path of meditation. ||92||
They lived there, always offering themselves to me;
by me, the kingdom of the earth, encompassed by the seven oceans, was ruled. (93)

Indeed, for the sake of the liberation of human beings and for the gods to attain happiness, there are those who dwell in the netherworlds (pātāla) and so forth, as well as those who reside in the heavens (svarga) and other realms. 94.
All followed me and took refuge in me, the Lord of all;
and from then on, I dwelt incessantly upon the earth until the end of the kalpa.
At that time, the earth became free from all distress, equal to Vaikuṇṭha;
likewise, there were wish-fulfilling trees, celestial cows, and desire-granting creepers.
Through my yoga, wish-fulfilling gems were present everywhere at that time;
moreover, there was always the Kṛta Yuga, and time itself became uniform.
At that time, there were indeed creations consisting of mental, tactile, and visual beings, as well as those that dwelt together.
"O Queen of the King of Kings, remember all this royal sovereignty!
I alone know it all; others of dull intellect do not know it. (99)
Furthermore, my other incarnations were likewise appropriate for the time; appearing in the forms of gods and humans, they accomplished their respective tasks. (3.24.10)
Thus has this manifestation of mine been described to you here, O Lotus-born One;
by reading or even by hearing it, one obtains the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.

Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Manifestation of the Beginningless Śrī Rājanārāyaṇa, accompanied by the Queen Śrī, for the Purpose of Destroying the Asura Māyūraka in the Twenty-ninth Year of the Creator [Brahmā] during the Third Dvāpara Cycle," in the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Śrī Nārāyaṇī, to my manifestation;
it occurred during the thirtieth year of Brahmā, known as Deva.
O Lakṣmī, in the past, in the fourteenth Manvantara, during the thousandth Kalpa of the year, I shall indeed tell you of Camatkāra along with me.
Listen now to how our manifestation occurred in the world upon the surface of the earth:
at the end of the Kṛta age, there were five devotees of us two in Surāṣṭra—
Devasakha, Kīrti, Ciklīta, and Kardama.
And the wise ones, Jātavedas and his brothers, were endowed with the quality of goodness (sāttvika).
They were ascetics restrained by dharma, contented, and exponents of the Veda; they were devoted to purity, austerity, contentment, self-study, and worship.
They were practiced in non-violence, truthfulness, honesty, virtuous conduct, and non-possessiveness;
they were also devoted to tranquility and the restraint of the senses.

They were ever established in endurance and forgiveness, in gentleness and that which is most beneficial; they were always established in yoga born of discernment, in knowledge, and in the excellence of sattva.
They are established in meditation, burnt offerings, recitation, worship, and respectful service;
in the realization of the Self as Brahman, and in the complete surrender of the self.
Likewise, the eight supernatural powers (siddhis) and the nine treasures (nidhis) are always present for them;
the wish-fulfilling trees (kalpavṛkṣas), the celestial nymphs (apsarases), and the cows of plenty (kāmadhenus) remain in their service.
These [sages] sleep in the open air, are clothed in the directions, subsist on fruits,
drink water and nectar, have their own radiance as lamps, and are absorbed in meditative concentration.
They were self-restrained, honoring the sacred word of Brahman, assisted by their inner selves,
endowed with devotion, associated with the virtuous, and intent upon honoring chaste women.
All were worshippers of guests, free from worldly desire, and bodiless; they possessed unobstructed states of being and moved about without impediment.
Devoid of contact with the elements and the like, and free from bodily defects and the like, they possess divine bodies as firm as adamant and are devoted to divine bliss. || 13 ||
They possess the yoga for the enjoyment of all things obtained by mere thought;
they have mastery over speech, are destroyers of suffering, and are compassionate toward those who seek refuge.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśa, Arka, Candra, and other gods are renowned on earth, as well as in the worlds of Bhuvaḥ, Svar, Mahar, Jana, and Tapaḥ.
In the world of truth, as well as on Mount Meru and in the netherworlds (pātāla),
all those possessed of sovereignty were like other lords.
Like gods, they remove suffering; like yogis, they reveal the Self; like merchant-princes, they bestow wealth; and like husbands, they grant sons. || 17 ||
The protectors are like their own masters, and the givers are likewise like Viṣṇu;
in knowledge they are all like the assemblies of Brahmā, and in fulfilling desires they are like the wish-fulfilling trees.
Even in their physical bodies, they were radiant with celibacy; likewise, they possessed the splendor of the earth in their fortitude.
Among these thousands, these virtuous ones had their desires fulfilled and were like those already liberated.
Knowing that such renowned beings exist, suffering people come day and night for the sake of destroying their own afflictions. (3.25.20)
The sick, as well as those who enjoy pleasures, the wretched, those sharing in poverty, the miserly, those suffering from enemies, the distressed, and those without sons; || 21 ||
Those lacking food, clothing, and palaces; those possessed by desire; those seeking enjoyment; those seeking liberation; and those on the verge of death—these always come for refuge. (22)
Devoted to bestowing blessings, they destroy the afflictions of those [beings], for they are givers of all things—of happinesses and of wealth and prosperity. (23)
And men and women go forth with their desires fulfilled—delighted, their wishes accomplished, their hopes realized, and their minds complete. ||24||
To those seeking wealth, these two indeed grant riches born of spiritual accomplishment;
to those seeking sons, they grant desired offspring.
They bestow a husband, a wife, a home, a kingdom, a field, an elephant, and likewise cattle; they also grant health, the expansion of one’s lineage, and prosperity. (26)
Those seeking refuge bring about the absence of the threefold suffering and other afflictions;
thus, all who possess such wonders are equal to the Lord. || 27 ||
O Lakṣmī, they were entirely devoted to me on this earth;
then once, while they were at home, there was one among them who was possessed by Lakṣmī and intent upon desire.
An Asura named Prasaviṣṇu, possessed of great strength, approached;
he was this very ascetic who had assumed the form of a Brahmin, driven by the impulse of desire.
"May she who is the wife of Nārāyaṇa become my wife"—with this desire directed toward Lakṣmī, he came before his devotees. (3.25.30)
Then that Asura begged for his desired alms even from the five [Pāṇḍavas]:
"O givers, grant me Lakṣmī, the wife of Nārāyaṇa. (31)
Upon hearing that the alms were unfit for them, the devotees then thought so;
however, merely to avoid the touch of being counted among those who do not give, they said, "Om."
"Either Hari, who is indeed powerful, or Lakṣmī will destroy him.
Having reflected thus, the lords of the givers remembered my beloved Śrī.
And by me, acting in accordance with the devotee's desire, you were indeed swiftly commanded;
for you have appeared before the five [sages] from the Imperishable. (34)
The maiden was beautiful, twelve years of age, enriched by the splendor of all ornaments, with a body like a golden campaka flower. (35)
Beholding you, who were so beautiful and enchanting in form, that demon then considered his own purpose accomplished; equal to her in passion, he rejoiced in his heart.
Then Devasakhā and the others, having seen her,
worshipped the Goddess Nārāyaṇī, who is capable of all things, and also made a request for forgiveness.
O beloved, having then announced the task for the sake of the gift's form to Āsura, they took water in their hands and gave it to Āsura.
Having approached you, the procreative demon, assuming the form of a brahmin, went to his own home; there, you undertook a supreme vow.
Indeed, that lifelong vow known as *brahmacarya* must be strictly observed;
one who remains unbroken in his asceticism should never, under any circumstances, touch an Asura.
Then, when you reached that house, he desired to touch you;
however, you were enveloped in garlands of flames possessing the brilliance of the fire of universal destruction.
Upon seeing you, his mind filled with terror, he turns back from where he came;
yet, after deliberating for many days, he seeks another cause. (42)
In order to accomplish your touch, he indeed returned once more to those five devotees for the sake of a good harvest, as well as to Rati in her embodied form.
"May Kāma, Sumūrti, and the Bāṇas grant me the spring season," they said;
and when that was done, those five devotees remembered them there.
Then, as soon as they were summoned, Kāma and the others quickly arrived before him;
and he then bestowed them as gifts upon that great Asura.
Taking them with him, the Asura went toward his own abode;
he commanded Kāma and the others to enter the body of Kamalā.
"By whomsoever that Lakṣmī has been oppressed, she will come to me of her own accord";
thinking thus, that asura also waited expectantly.
Then Kāma discharged his arrows, beginning with the "Intoxication" shaft; and Vasanta, most enchanting, surrounded him on all sides with beautiful flowers.
Blossoming there with splendor, he even brings others to a state of full bloom;
then Rati herself, personified, gradually [unites] with Lakṣmī. 49.
As she was entering, Lakṣmī approached her accompanied by her laughter;
for Lakṣmī recognized that wicked woman, the wife of Kāma, who harbored evil intentions.
Then, O Supreme Goddess, you suddenly fell into a rage and yourself produced the fire of universal destruction from your two eyes.
She beheld Rati, Kāma, Vasanta, and the arrows,
as well as the Asura— all of them reduced to ashes in a mere instant.
O Goddess of gods, as soon as she had performed [this act], being devoted to her lifelong vow, a cry of "Alas! Alas! arose among both the gods and humans.

Due to the destruction of passion, the destruction of desire, and the disappearance of spring and other seasons, in the absence of the proper seasons, forests, jungles, gardens, and the like will be devoid of flowers. (54)
Then they became devoid of new sprouts and empty of prosperity;
indeed, even though prosperity existed, the world became truly destitute of fortune.
The delights of both women and men have gone to dissolution; their joys have met with destruction due to the slaughter of those capable of procreation. (56)
Thus, O Lakṣmī, Rati and the others were consumed by you with the fire of your eyes;
indeed, the entire world has become established in its final state through your vow.
The gods, humans, and great sages—all embodied beings—having deliberated together, [asked] what this was and how it came to be. || 58 ||
They went to Satya and told it to Vedhas, saying, "Alas, this is a state of impotence!
There is no pleasure, there is no desire, and indeed, there is no spring anywhere. (59)
"What is this, and how has it come to pass? Ward off this intense suffering!"—thus addressed, Brahmā then spoke after reflecting for a moment.
Those who were previously the five gods and the five Indras,
they thereafter became five devotees in this kalpa and worship the Supreme Lord.
Devasakhā and all the others are givers who fulfill the needs of supplicants;
those five lords are capable of bestowing every kind of prosperity.
And to them, that procreative great asura— who was born from the impurity of my linga, powerful, wicked, and a bearer of extreme faults— entrusted Lakṣmī.
Then those brahmins, having been summoned together, gave Lakṣmī to him;
the asura, taking her with him, went toward his own home.
Lakṣmī observed a vow and maintained the state of perpetual celibacy;
nevertheless, the Asura, driven by the force of passion, approached Lakṣmī to touch her.
Beholding her, who possessed the brilliance of the fire produced at the end of an aeon, the great asura was terrified;
he went back to the brahmins and begged for Rati once more.
O twice-born ones, having taken Kāma, Vasanta, and those Bāṇas who possessed physical forms—
giving them all their bodies— he, the Asura, went to his home.
He indeed incited them all to make Lakṣmī fickle;
Lakṣmī, becoming enraged, produced the fire of universal dissolution from her two eyes.
He reduced them all to ashes, and likewise the world by means of the arrows of desire, the spring season, and Rati, rendered it devoid of purpose.
This very reason has arisen for the absence of joy;
indeed, that which was stated there is the case, for there is no other means to prevent it.
Through the wrath of Lakṣmī, Kāma, Rati, Asuraka,
Prasava, Bāṇa, and Vasanta have always been dead.
If Lakṣmī, being propitiated, were to bring all of them back to life again,
they would even complete their lifelong vow (naiṣṭhika-vrata) in the presence of Hari.
If, by the command of the Supreme Lord, he should sustain all beings, then this defect of impotence will depart from the three worlds. (73)
Thinking that it cannot be otherwise, we strive toward Śrī Hari for that purpose;
here we perform worship, and Hari himself will be thoroughly pleased.
"He will arrive here quickly and will dispel our suffering.
Having been told this, they performed my propitiation in Satyaloka. (75)
Even though remembered by you, who were distressed by separation from Lakṣmī,
he arrived at Satyaloka and stood before Brahmā and the other gods.
And they indeed beheld me, the eternal one, possessing a divine form—
the Supreme Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, bearing the conch and the discus.
Richly adorned with all kinds of ornaments and possessing a serene face and eyes,
they honored him, welcomed him, and then offered their praises.
O beloved, having heard their prayer for the sake of pacifying all suffering, I, Hari, the Supreme Person, then spoke to them.
"I am not able to undo what has been done by Lakṣmī;
therefore, let us go to where the goddess Lakṣmī shines in the forest. (3.25.80)
Remaining indeed in celibacy within the forest of Prasaviṣṇu, that virtuous lady,
the great goddess, abides in the ascetic practice of perpetual religious observance.
Then we all came to that place where your hermitage was;
seeing me, you were filled with joy and fell at my feet. || 8.2 ||
She offered a most sincere welcome to the deities and informed them of the sorrow concerning the prince, Rati, and the others.
Praised by all the gods and others, and propitiated again and again, you said to all the gods and the rest: "The end of the day is now approaching. || 8.4 ||
Tomorrow morning, those sons of Brahmā born from his body— Kāma and the others,
as well as Rati and the rest— will indeed become capable of assuming physical forms.
Moreover, an asura named Prasrava, whose nature is to flow, will come into being;
indeed, at this time of twilight today, there is no purpose for them.
Adopting the lifelong vow (naiṣṭhika-vrata), let them worship the Supreme Lord, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the illustrious Puruṣottama. 87.
And here I shall worship the Supreme Being along with my husband;
let the Blessed One, my beloved, remain here as well, even if he is eternally established [in liberation]. (88)
"I have indeed undertaken this lifelong vow until the end of the dissolution;
let all remain firm in that vow, which bestows the highest welfare. (89)
Then those gods, humans, and sages whom you addressed all remained there in that lifelong vow until the end of another day.
O Lakṣmī, by your will I then dwelt upon the ground in the forest,
known by you as the beginningless Śrī-Brahmacārin Nārāyaṇa.

Together with you, O beloved Lakṣmī, you have undertaken vows and have always remained established in austerity; you are a virtuous wife, possessed of dharma, and the very embodiment of steadfast glory.
Then, at the end of that creation,
the subjects— both the dead and the aged— having gathered together from all sides, were gradually restrained by Manu.
Then, at the onset of night, the time of dissolution arrived;
everything was withdrawn by the Supreme Lord (Parameṣṭhin) in due order, as if it were a daily occurrence.
O Lakṣmī, having completed your own vow, you went with me toward the hermitage of the Friend of the Gods (Indra), and from there, taking them along, you went to heaven.
Having led those five devotees, who were like future great lords (Indras), to Maharloka, Janaloka, Satyaloka, and beyond that; || 96 ||
"Having led her to Brahmā and entrusted her to Vaikuṇṭha along with me, she then departed for my supreme, imperishable abode. Thus,
O beloved, has my manifestation and hers been told."
O Mistress of the Imperishable, remember that form of the ascetic, which is characterized by lifelong celibacy.
Other incarnations of mine have also occurred in that year, and they are indeed innumerable; I alone know them all, and no other gods do.
Then, in another kalpa, Rati and the others were born as the offspring of Aja;
indeed, by his word, they provided assistance to Aja while still possessing their bodies.
From reciting and hearing this definitive work, there shall arise the fruit;
both worldly enjoyment and liberation shall occur, and one shall likewise attain whatever is desired. (101)

Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Manifestation of the Beginningless Śrī-Brahmacārī Nārāyaṇa Together with His Eternal Śrī for the Purpose of Maintaining His Vow of Celibacy," following the reduction to ashes of the Asuras Prāsra-vaṇa, Rati, Kāma, Vasanta, Bāṇa, and others by Lakṣmī—who had attained her splendor through the devotion of Devasakha and others—during the thirtieth year of the Creator in the third Dvāpara cycle of the *Śrī-Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Puruṣottama said: Listen, O Śrī Nārāyaṇī, to my manifestation hereafter,
during the thirty-first year of the Manu known as Vedhas.
Formerly, in the thirteenth period of six hundred Manvantaras,
from the lower, depressed regions of Brahmā's back, the Asura Malimluca [arose].
There was also one named Hallaka, a terrifying eater of corpses;
he performed a most dreadful and fierce penance for half a kalpa.
Then Brahmā was pleased, and he became visible on the earth;
the Asura had turned into clay and was climbing over creepers and trees.
Where there was merely the existence of bone and clay, the Creator of the Universe went there,
sprinkled it with water, and cleared away the trees from its sides.
From a portion of the root of a clay tree, he brought forth a *hallaka* plant;
it had a body like a creeping vine, was green in color, and extremely weak.
The bearded son of the Creator rose up from the root-cluster;
seeing his own father restored to life, he bowed down with great devotion.
He also requested the most excellent boon, the cause of the destruction of time—
that which is either Time itself, or the one in the form of Time, the destroyer of embodied beings.
"I shall likewise bring about this withdrawal; grant me a boon, O Grandfather.
Brahmā said: "This boon of mine exceeds [all others] in power."
"I am not able to give it, for I am subject to time," he said;
then Hallaka replied, "If you will give that one, and no other."
"O Grandfather, I shall constantly perform penance for that purpose;
indeed, no one at all is capable of slaying Kāla except for Hari. (1.1)
There is no specific manifestation born of creation whatsoever;
therefore, O Hallaka, listen to what I say if it pleases you.
Indeed, there are many forms of Time within the creations;
you shall become the slayer of only one of those forms at once.
"If this pleases you, then accept my boon.
Thus addressed, Hallaka, falling under the power of delusion, then accepted the boon.
Abandoning that penance, he took it up and went toward a cave on Mount Meru;
by virtue of a boon from Brahmā, he remained forever exceedingly arrogant.
The Suras, Daityas, Rākṣasas, Dānavas, Kinnaras and others;
the Tāmasa and Rājasa gods, Yakṣas, Kiṃpuruṣas and others. || 1.6 ||
He does not even count the Gandharvas and Cāraṇas;
he indeed treats them with contempt and fights at every single place.
He reveals even the futility of Brahmā’s granting of the boon, and he proclaims himself to be none other than the Destroyer of Time. (18)
Having attained victory in heaven, he then went to the netherworlds;
having achieved victory there as well, he indeed proceeded to the Lokāloka mountain.
Having achieved victory everywhere, he then went to the realm of Yama;
Yama, recognizing him as the destroyer of Time (Kāla), paid him homage.
Then, having realized that his own supreme master was victorious,
Hallaka went to the world of Kailāsa to conquer Rudra, Śiva, and Hara.
The Gaṇas dwelling on Kailāsa, namely Jaṅgama-bhadra and others, indeed restrained him at the gateway; thereupon, that Hallaka became enraged.
He fought with the gatekeepers, having conquered those other hosts,
and thereafter with the lords of the hosts, Bhairava and others, who stand at the head of all beings.
The cruel, wicked, and impure-minded one went to the abode of Śambhu—
specifically to Kailāsa— in order to bring it under his own control as well as to subjugate Satī.
Seeing his riches, he desired to make [the gods] into hosts and servants;
he said to Śambhu, "O Śambhu, become my servant, otherwise yours shall be mine."
"I shall indeed bring about your destruction; give me back my virtuous wife.
Having given me the kingdom of Kailāsa, go to Mount Meru. (26)
"Furthermore, at another time I shall give [it] to you; I am satisfied with you as is fitting.
Śambhu then reflected: "How great might his strength be? ||27||
"I shall fight with this powerful one, who possesses the power of Brahmā’s boon;
I will destroy this asura, endowed with the granting of that boon, in an instant. (28)
Having reflected thus upon the terrible form of Time,
Śaṅkara took up his trident, which was composed of fiery energy and capable of bringing about the final dissolution.
Having assumed the formidable form of Sāṃkarṣaṇa, he quickly arrived for the sake of battle; meanwhile, Hallaka also drew near to him.
He assumed a mountain-like form, terrifying and destructive;
he held in his hand an iron weapon, a spear adorned with moon-shaped markings.
Just as Kālakāla appears, so does Hallaka appear here;
the drums of war resounded on Kailāsa, struck by the Gaṇas. ||32||
The gods, the lords of the deities, went there drawn by curiosity;
all the guardians of the quarters also arrived to assist Śambhu.
A battle that caused universal destruction broke out between Hallaka and Haraya;
the clouds were destroyed by their lightning-flashes, and the mountains were destroyed by their weapons.
The earth was shattered by the blows of his falling [limbs], the oceans were agitated by tremors, the stars fell with great force, and the quarters of the sky roared with thunderous sounds. (35)
There, the hosts and the lords of the hosts were struck with terror at the prospect of death;
some were broken at the waist, and others at the region of the shoulders.
Others, broken between the throat and the knees, went to their death;
[they beheld] the Bhūtas, Pretas, Piśācas, and others, as terrifying as Kālabhairava. (37)
Grasping them with one hand and placing them in his mouth, Hallaka eats Śūrabhadra, Vīrabhadra, Jaṅgabhadraka, and Subhadraka. (38)
Placing them simultaneously in his mouth with his left hand, he devoured them;
such is this great Asura, the Great Time who is the Time of Time. (39)
Śaṅkara fell into doubt regarding victory because of the slipping of his trident;
the trident repeatedly slipped from Śambhu’s hand.
Then both the bull and the lion were likewise cut down by Hallaka’s discus and met their death. ||41||
Satī, having fallen into doubt regarding the life of Śaṅkara, quickly vanished from the body of Śambhu. ||42||
Śambhu, perceiving that Kailāsa was shattered and split apart following the deceased,
abandoned all hope for life and fled toward the presence of Hallaka.
Having quickly returned, he hurled his own trident, which was like the fire of universal destruction, at the head of this Hallaka, striking him above the neck.
Having been violently severed from his hand, that trident of Hara, which resembled fire, entered the throat of Hallaka. ||45||
Having entered there in a liquefied state and become absorbed within it,
it became wholesome, like nectar in the belly of a peacock.
This most wonderful thing has occurred: indeed, the Kāla-śūla has been digested;
likewise, other śūlas, triśūlas, and weapons [have been consumed]. (47)
All of them, having attained the stature of the *hallaka* plant and reached the state of its sap, then became the painless Śaṅkara, as well as Viṣṇu and the Unborn (Aja). 48.
Śiva quickly remembered [Viṣṇu], and Viṣṇu indeed arrived there;
he gave his own discus to that Hara, and Hara likewise [gave it] back to him.
He released a discus at the throat of that Hallaka, and it indeed turned to liquid;
then he took up another discus, but that too, once released, turned into liquid. (3.26.50)
In this manner, all the wheels then moved with the speed of mercury;
meanwhile, Brahmā arrived there and beheld Śaṅkara.
Then, by Hallaka, who moved with great speed and was armed with a spear and a crescent-shaped blade, the head of Śaṅkara was indeed severed from his neck.
A great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose; even the fierce Rudra was indeed slain.
All the gods, humans, and great sages were overcome with grief. (53)
Moreover, all living beings became filled with grief;
even the power of Hallaka was overcome by the one whose weapons are the trident and the moon.
But all that [power] vanished at once due to the granting of a boon by Brahmā;
he became powerless, recognized as such by all the warriors. (55)
Then, having understood exactly what was spoken by Brahmā, the gods and the Gaṇas rushed forward indeed to slay the Asura.
At that moment, all those tridents and wheels indeed fell away; having emerged, they quickly returned.
All [the weapons] were directed toward Viṣṇu, while those of Śaṅkara were aimed at the corpse;
just as Viṣṇu was about to release his discus at him, that Hallaka [intervened].
"O Hari, Viṣṇu! O Hari, Kṛṣṇa! Save me, who have come to you for refuge!
Having spoken thus, the asura suddenly fell at the feet of the wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
"One must not kill; for Viṣṇu, the vow is the protection of those who have come for refuge.
Therefore, O Viṣṇu, O Viṣṇu, your discus did not strike that speaker."
And because of a boon granted by Brahmā, he was endowed with such auspicious signs;
he was the son born from Brahmā’s back, devoted to him, and an ascetic yogi.
Hari bound with nooses that offender of Śaṅkara, who was crying out, "O Hari!
O Viṣṇu! O Nārāyaṇa, protect me! (62)
To him who was crying out, remembering me with his mind and me with his heart—such a slayer of Hara—the sin of killing a god and the sin of drinking liquor [overwhelmed him]. (63)
That Hārā, of cruel form, with a hundred wheels in her hands, distorted and with a distorted face, leaped about,
possessing the power to swallow up living beings.
And seeing her leaping so fiercely and causing such misery,
Hallaka cried out there on the field of battle in many ways in the presence of the gods.
Struck by the gods and beaten by tens of millions of Gaṇas,
nearly dead as he lay dying, he chose the protection of Hari, the guardian.
O Mādhava, grant to me, who am in the form of a devotee seeking refuge,
the supreme station and great sovereignty, even though I am an enemy of Śaṅkara.
And by the granting of a boon from Brahmā, as well as from Mahākāla,
this single form of Śaṅkara was indeed destroyed by me without any gain.
"Having been slain, I am born again, impelled by pride through illusion;
O Lord, all my ascetic merit has been cast away into dark, demonic action. (69)
Therefore, O Viṣṇu, out of compassion grant me happiness and show mercy;
this slaughter of the gods is consuming me—ward it off, O Keśava!
Having spoken thus, she wept excessively and even reached the point of death;
Viṣṇu declared that the time of Manu was likewise a completed night.
"O Hallaka, eat the sin committed by the killing of a god in the Raurava hell for fifteen manvantaras, at the end of time, within the interval of a day. (72)
After having experienced various sufferings, being defiled and performing the deeds of barbarians,
you shall become a lord of the Mlecchas and a devotee of me, Brahmā.
"The great preceptor of many countless Asuras," having said this, the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu [addressed] Hallaka along with the messengers of Yama.
He sent that wicked Sahatya to the abode of Yama.
Then the gods, sages, ancestors, humans, and the twice-born—||75||
The attendants and the hosts, the devotees, the goddesses, the virtuous wives, the yoginīs, the mothers, and even the planets and other celestial dwellers; ||76||
All the devotees gathered on Kailāsa were remembered by Hari;
and Viṣṇu likewise [remembered] them for the sake of restoring Śambhu to life.
He spoke in order to perform the propitiation of me, the Lord who manifests in all incarnations, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, who truly exists. (78)
Then, full of eagerness, they worshipped me—the inner controller of all, the Lord of Śrī, the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama)—who am ever established in the abode of the Imperishable (Akṣara). ||79||
"Having heard of your propitiation, I have come here with you at once;
I am present on Kailāsa, visible to those with sight, possessing a divine and beautiful form."
Upon seeing me, they all became free from grief and then made this request;
for the sake of restoring Śambhu to life, I then entered his body.
By means of yoga, having bestowed the power of life upon both the headless trunk and the head of Śaṅkara, I restored him to life and joined them together.
Then, in Kabandha, he worshipped the head of Śambhu along with millions of gods, as well as by the ancestors, humans, and great sages. (83)
Śūrabhadra and the others who were chewed up and died then, as well as all those who died, O Lakṣmī, and those hosts who were slain; ||84||
Remembered by me, they became born of mind and endowed with life; having come before Śambhu, those newly created beings stood there. (81)
There, indeed, Vṛṣabha and the others who had died were restored to life by me;
likewise, all the crores of Gaṇas and the crores of gods [were revived]. (86)
Having restored them all to consciousness, I then revived them;
furthermore, a festival for the restoration of Śaṅkara’s life was celebrated on Kailāsa. (87)
Then Satī, having emerged from the very form of Śambhu and becoming perceptible, appeared visibly as the Great Goddess and became gracious. ||88||
Śambhu constantly requested me to remain on the surface of the earth at Kailāsa together with you and Lakṣmī, and he indeed made this very request. ||89||
Both gods and humans entreated me, the Supreme Person,
to remain in the sacred field of Kailāsa for the welfare of all embodied beings.
Therefore, O Śivarājīśrī, I, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the glorious Puruṣottama, have always dwelt together with you. (91)
O beloved, at that time you became Śivanārāyaṇī there, while Śiveśvara was known by the name Anādiśrīśivanārāyaṇa.
Then all the gods, humans, and ancestors departed for their respective worlds, as did the sages; I, however, remained there on Kailāsa. ||93||
O Queen Śivā, until the end of the kalpa I know [this], and no one else;
O beloved Kamalā, remember also that divine manifestation of mine.
On the auspicious, cool, and delightful mountain Kailāsa, which extends for ten thousand yojanas, I have always dwelt upon that terrestrial region. (95)
At that time, the entire earth became Vaiṣṇavī, created by me;
and all the gods were likewise Vaiṣṇavas, entirely devoted to me. 96.
O Lakṣmī, my fruit manifests even in a devotee who is rajasic or tamasic;
whether it be an asura or a sura, when the time has arrived, it sprouts forth.

Therefore, devotion is the most excellent of all, bestowing the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation; indeed, it is established by me in this dharma-endowed age, at this time, and on this day. 98.
Whether at the end of an eon or at its commencement, I shall always establish that which is beneficial;
through the recitation and hearing of this, both worldly enjoyment and liberation shall be attained. (99)
He shall possess abundant prosperity, be blessed with sons, and become a treasury of bliss;
endowed with great sovereignty, he shall also attain a form resembling that of the Supreme Lord.
There shall be the destruction of all obstacles and the enjoyment of all nectar;
there shall be eternal residence, and one shall attain union with Brahman. || 10.1 ||

Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Manifestation of the Beginningless Śrī Śiva-Nārāyaṇa for the Purpose of Reviving Śambhu’s Severed Head during Hallakāsura’s Campaign of Victory, Following Brahmā’s Bestowal of Boons upon Him," in the thirty-first year of the Creator (Brahmā) within the third section, the Dvāpara-Santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Nārāyaṇāśrī, to this supreme nectar of a narrative concerning how my manifestation and that of the Supreme Lord (Parameṣṭhin) occurred during the thirty-second [cycle]. || 1 ||
In the year of the Kalpadru tree, during the fifty-sixth aeon, in the eighth Manvantara,
there was once a Yakṣa named Suvarṇamālika belonging to Kubera.
He went to sport in heaven, and from there he went to the city of Viṣṇu;
then, having beheld Satyaloka as well as the abodes of the guardians of the quarters, he departed.
Having seen [the messenger], he set out for the city of Saṃyamanī to behold the abode of Yama;
meanwhile, the end of his lifespan arrived and he indeed met his death.
Yama, the King of Death, performed the final rites for the yakṣa;
and Kubera, having learned of the yakṣa’s death in the abode of Yama, [acted accordingly].
Thinking, "I have been killed by the messengers of Yama," he then went forth in person to the realm of Yama, blazing with fury and accompanied by his army.
He then fought with Yama in many ways;
having defeated Yama, he brought Svarṇamāla back to his own home.
Then King Yama quickly summoned Nirṛti along with his army of Rākṣasas; and Nirṛti likewise [summoned] those stationed on the ground.
And he summoned to his side those rakshasas dwelling in the netherworlds and elsewhere who were skilled in battle, numbering in the millions, billions, and trillions.
Then they set out to conquer Kubera and his kingdom; indeed, war-drums were sounded in the sky near Alakā.
Having learned this, Kubera set forth with ten million yakṣas;
then a sudden battle broke out there, causing total destruction.
Millions of Yakṣas were slain by the messengers of Yama, and likewise by the Rākṣasas;
even Kubera was then killed by Yama, who split him in two at the neck.
The entire kingdom of Kubera was brought under his control by Yama,
and likewise, by Nirṛti, the Rākṣasas were established in the kingdom.
Then some other yakṣas, being terrified, went to Indra, Varuṇa, and Vāyu— the lords of the northern and western quarters— and reported that matter to them.
They all went quickly toward the city of Kubera;
having seen Dharmarāja in such a state, as if utterly destroyed.
Īśāna, taking the side of his own disciple Kubera, indeed waged a terrible battle for the sake of avenging their enmity. || 16 ||
Mahendra, as well as Vahni, Vāyu, and Varuṇa,
taking the side of Kubera, waged war against Yama.
Then Sūrya took the side of his own son Yama, as did Svarbhānu, Śanaiścara, and other Rākṣasas as well. || 18 ||
Taking the side of Yama, they waged a most fierce battle;
there, crores of Gaṇas, as well as gods and Yakṣas, were slain once again.
