Having practiced the arts of war, the followers of Yama attained victory once more;
the Rākṣasas belonging to the side of Yama achieved triumph in the battle.
Cruel and performers of cruel deeds, with hands scarred by iron and the like, they are experts in clods of earth, fire, weapons, machines, and missiles; pitiless, they are like Yamas.
They struck Vāyu, Indra, Varuṇa, Īśāna, and Agni excessively;
broken and with their armies destroyed, they fled.
Then a great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose everywhere on earth;
the gods were terrified and fled to the truth, while others likewise went into mountain caves.
Then, on earth and in heaven, as well as everywhere in the regions of the world-protectors and among the inhabitants of the netherworld, that power increased.
O Lakṣmī, then the sky indeed trembled in all directions;
in the disputes of the guardians of the quarters, millions of their servants were slain and died.
King Yama became the sovereign over Alakā on all sides, and the very existence of Kubera was indeed expelled from every direction. (26)
All the Nirṛtis, Rākṣasas, Yamas, Ārka, Śani, Rāhu, and others as well, became strengthened by their own respective powers. ||27||
As if independent in the three worlds, those who harbor enmity strike down their adversaries and expel the gods and others from their own dwellings if they do not bow down. (28)
Thus, even in the heavenly world, there arose a state of instability among one another;
the power of the guardians of the quarters was destroyed in the presence of Yama’s staff.
O Indra, the other gods, such as the Sun, the Moon, and others, do not abide by your command;
yet even those who depend upon them have indeed attained the supreme heaven.
Then, having thus observed Kamalā, Īśāna, Indra, Agni, Vāyu,
Varuṇa, and the other gods went to the abode of Mahendra.
There, devoid of a plan for what ought to be done, they held a consultation;
the lords also remembered Brahmā and remembered Viṣṇu.
Those supreme lords also remembered the remainder and restored it;
they heard of the destruction of Kubera and his defeat by others.
At that moment, they caused grief for Dharmarāja Vijaya, thinking, "May no injustice ever occur there in the house of Dharmarāja. (34)
Having understood the entire cause of the Yakṣa's death, as well as Kubera’s unjustified resorting to combat based on what was improper, [he reflected]. || 35 ||
Shaking their heads, they did not believe in victory again;
for where there is injustice, victory can never possibly occur.
If Kubera were to partake in injustice, this death would surely come to him;
for Yama is the lord of embodied beings throughout the fourteen worlds. (37)
At the end of one's lifespan, [death] surely leads one away; what lamentation can there be for that?
[One departs from] Indra, Vāyu, Varuṇa, Īśāna, Agni, and those other lords. (38)
Yama, the Lord of Death, surely leads [the deceased]; what need is there to mention anyone else?
Therefore, the god Vijaya indeed triumphs here over the god Yama.
We must consider ourselves defeated in this undertaking if Kubera,
having become the guardian of a quarter, should act unjustly.
For all those who hold such views, suffering would indeed increase further;
therefore, in this matter, [the fault does not lie] with Viṣṇu, nor with Śeṣa, nor even with Brahmā.
O gods, others as well will surely attain victory through their cleverness;
therefore, you must not go to that place where Yama himself resides.
O gods, [this will lead] especially to the destruction of everything in Alakā;
however, Maheśvara is the lord of the gods who are the supreme deities. ||43||
The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the illustrious Puruṣottama, the Lord of Akṣara, the Lord of Śrī, Śrī Hari, the Supreme Lord. ||44||
In this debate, he will indeed provide the final decision;
let them perform a great sacrificial session (*mahāsatra*) consisting of progeny in the house of Indra. (45)
"O gods, the Supreme Lord himself will come," having been told this, Hara and the other gods then [gathered] in the abode of Indra. 46.
And all the lords of the gods performed a sacrifice of recitation (japa-sattra), chanting:
"Hare Kṛṣṇa, Hare Viṣṇu, O Supreme Lord, O Highest of the High! (47)
"O Anādi-Śrī-Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, O Supreme Lord, protect us! Thus they performed constant chanting for a full year. 48.
At the end of the year, Śrī Hari, the Lord who bears the conch, the discus, and other emblems, and who is the object of perception for all the gods, arrived along with me. (49)
O beloved, at that time, seeing me together with Lakṣmī, who was adorned with every ornament,
the gods, intent on their own purposes, departed very quickly.
Having risen, they bowed down in many ways and performed worship for me;
they offered the honey-mixture (madhuparka) and then provided further hospitality.
They gave me a great seat there, and I sat down together with you; then the guardians of the treasure reported the entire account to you.
It brings about the destruction of the yakṣas, the defeat of one's own [enemies], the victory over Yama, and likewise sovereignty in heaven. (53)
O Lotus-born One, I heard that there was no fixed order among the gods;
then, having meditated for a moment, I spoke this to the guardians of the quarters: [54]
"You must indeed go with me to where Yama resides;
for in the city of Kubera, every happiness shall be yours. (55)
"I shall bring an end to all dispute through conciliation, which brings happiness"—
having said this, I [went] together with you and all the hosts of gods.
I went to the land of Alakā in the presence of Yama and Nairṛta;
hearing of me, he indeed approached quickly with a terrified mind.
O Lakṣmī, even though I felt fear in my presence, he did not think of it;
he washed my feet and drank the nectar-like water from them. (58)
He offered a welcome and a seat, played musical instruments, and while all the gods looked on, he spoke to me like a servant. (59)
"O Kṛṣṇa, an offense has been committed by me; Kubera was slain by me.
This city has been brought under my control; forgive me, O Puruṣottama. (3.27.60)
"O Keśava, punishment inevitably falls upon those who follow an unjust path;
if I am such a person, then let punishment be meted out to me as well. (61)
Having spoken thus and sought refuge, he fell at my feet;
for indeed, punishment is not appropriate for one who is devoid of wrongdoing.
That this Kubera has been slain would not be fitting here;
the Lord of the Yakṣas must be restored to life, as must his attendants. (63)
O Yama, those such as Surādya who were slain in battle must be restored to life;
furthermore, the city of Kubera must be given back to him.
"You must proceed toward the city of Yama, the King of Death; always protect Saṃyamanī and conduct yourself without greed for the property of others. (65)
Thus addressed by me, Dharmarāja indeed begged for forgiveness;
then, relinquishing the region of Kubera, he set forth from there.
O Lakṣmī, I then performed the invocation of Kubera there once again;
consequently, the Lord of Wealth was born as my son from my mind.
The supreme Vaiṣṇava devotee and the Yakṣas were born again;
all the other gods who had died were born as my mind-born sons.
Those gods and others, my sons, indeed worshipped me with great joy;
furthermore, they offered to Kubera, the son of Manas, the place bestowed by me.
Thus requested by him at that time for the sake of a permanent residence, I,
possessing a golden complexion, indeed dwelt in the city of Svarṇavatī.
Having worshipped Śaṅkara and the others, they indeed departed for their own abodes; Yama went to the realm of Yama, and the others went to their respective dwellings.
Upon the new birth of Kubera, a great festival was celebrated by me in the Golden City; he was honored and likewise nourished.
You are the ever-golden Lakṣmī, resplendent along with me;
you are the Sovereign Lady together with the beginningless Śrī-Svarṇa-Nārāyaṇa. 73.
I, the Supreme Lord, Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, Śrī Puruṣottama, indeed dwelt in Svarṇavatī until the end of the kalpa. ||74||
The controller of all the world-protectors and guardians of the quarters, the performer of all protection, the Supreme Lord Śrīpati is manifest here. (75)
O Lakṣmī of golden hue, remember that at that time both you and I manifested in the form of the Queen of the Kings of Kings, overflowing with all bliss.
Then Sūrya and the other gods, as well as the followers of Yama,
having asked me for forgiveness, thereafter worshipped Svarṇanārāyaṇa.
The golden-hued Puruṣa with a golden beard, the subduer of Yama, the controller of the guardians of the quarters, and the discipliner of adversaries. (78)
May he who brings peace to the afflictions, the bestower of prosperity, the burner of heaps of sins, and the remover of misfortunes—may he protect me. (79)
For the gods and others worship the eternal Supreme Lord, the Supreme Brahman who transcends the imperishable, the Lord of Truth served by those who are liberated.
By reading this, by hearing it, or even by remembering it, one shall partake in liberation and also partake in enjoyment; one shall attain the splendor of gold—of this there is no doubt. (8.1)

Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Manifestation of the Beginningless Śrī-Svarṇanārāyaṇa together with Kānakī-Śrī for the Purpose of Reviving Kubera, Who was Killed by Yama in the Thirty-second Year of Brahmā, within the Third Section on the Lineage of Dvāpara," in the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, consort of Nārāyaṇa; hereafter I shall describe my manifestation in the thirty-third year of Brahmā, formerly known as Sasya.
In the thirty-first kalpa and likewise in the eleventh manvantara,
the mountain Aruṇācala appeared on the Śveta-khaṇḍa to the east of Meru.
This mountain is exactly one yojana in height and ten yojanas in width;
it always contains flames within its core and possesses caves rich with liquid fire.
There are no human beings on the flanks, nor even any forests or woods.
The rivers indeed have scorching currents, and the earth resembles glowing embers.
In one hundred years, or two hundred years, or after eight hundred years have passed,
Jvālāruṇācala becomes entirely composed of flames.
Fires and fluids flow even in regions and rivers;
by his majesty, O beloved, even distant lands are scorched.
Human beings, as well as beasts and birds that move through the sky,
indeed become senseless and lifeless due to the heat of the scorching sun.
The burning of crops and forests by means of pouring fire [upon them] certainly results in the destruction of fruits, flowers, and so forth, even for those situated at a distance. (8)
In whichever direction the currents of the winds flow,
those regions, extending for a hundred yojanas, become scorched by the fires.
The living beings, having been revived by the sprinkling of fire, indeed remained in a state of dissolution;
then, at one time, a great whirlwind arose in the sky.
And Aruṇācala, blazing with flames, also assumed the form of fire;
driven by the wind, he brought forth floods of the heat of fiery flames.
With extreme velocity, reaching a speed of a hundred yojanas toward the east, hundreds of thousands of embodied beings came to dwell upon the slopes of Mount Meru.
Their bodies burnt by the long-flowing heat,
millions of elephants, cattle, horses, and others, along with thousands of cities, perished.
There was a city there called Svāminagara, one yojana in length,
which was inhabited mostly by my devotees and holy people.
And auspicious monasteries were established for virtuous male and female ascetics,
for those observing the vow of celibacy, and for chaste women who are the wives of Dharma.
There were many hermitages belonging to those who performed the sacrifice of silent recitation (japa-yajña),
as well as great abodes for Vaiṣṇavas, yogins, and those devoted to ritual action (karmaṭhas).
There, for those who served them, the gods became the very objects of their devotion;
there, indeed, were the devotees of Videha who practiced austerities for my sake.
They have me as their sole goal, having renounced all enjoyments for my sake;
they take me alone as their support and are intent upon my propitiation. (18)
Devoted to the dharma of serving the circles of my devotees,
they offer up their own selves and all their wealth, and are absorbed in me as my very self.
In this city, everyone is intent on devotion to the goal, while those established in the means are few; thus, here, by the heat of the flame of fire, [all] quickly [attain their end]. (3.28.20)

But devotees devoid of the practice of yoga, though they may die anywhere, [are surpassed by] those virtuous practitioners who know yoga, who are truthful, and who have realized the state of Brahman. ||21||
There and there we remembered me, the beginningless Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Brahman beyond the imperishable, the beloved of Śrī, the Puruṣottama. 22.
The Rudras and Maruts, joined in single-minded devotion, praised him:
"Protect us, protect us, O Supreme Brahman, O Inner Self, O Puruṣottama! (23)
"O Lord of All, come! Protect my life from this blazing fire!"—thus was he entreated by those who were single-minded and possessed of intense devotion. (24)
Swiftly, together with you, Lakṣmī, for the sake of rescuing Jīva,
I indeed became visible in every house and among every person.
I cast a drop of nectar from my own Brahma-lake directly into the mountain of the flaming fire, traveling swiftly indeed by way of the sky. || 26 ||
The fire also reached dissolution, its flames carrying coldness;
the heat was transformed into coolness, thereby bringing about the cessation of the burning.
Then, by means of that cool nectar, the wind touched whatever embodied beings—both stationary and moving—who had died. ||28||
Having attained new life, the living beings became filled with joy;
and that Aruṇācala too [revived] through the connection with the nectar from the Brahma-lake.
In an instant, he became a mountain of cool nectar;
thus, until the end of the kalpa, that mountain remained as cool as nectar.
By all devotees and yogis, by ascetics established in the nature of Brahman, by holy men and virtuous women, and likewise by renunciants. ||3 1||
I was beheld right before their eyes by Vaiṣṇava men,
and there I was constantly entreated to remain as a protector among my devotees.
Honored and even worshipped by you, I indeed dwelt together with you in that city of the Lord, O Anādi-Svāmin-Nārāyaṇa. (33)
"Accompanied by you, the Mistress, and Lakṣmī, [he is] Puruṣottama.
In this way, the manifestation of yourself as the Mistress Śrī has been told to you. (34)
O Lakṣmī, my mistress, remember the protector of the city of your Lord, the beginningless Śrī Svāminārāyaṇa, the glorious Puruṣottama. (35)
Indeed, through recitation or even by hearing [this], there shall be protection from calamities, together with you, the protector, the primordial Sovereign Goddess Śrī.
Then, in another thirty-fourth year known as Pāśava,
long ago in the sixty-seventh kalpa after three hundred [years] of the Creator (Brahmā).
And in the twelfth Manu-period on earth, there was a pair of the twice-born caste in the city of Kauśeyaka, who were purifying and possessed of devotion and fortune. (38)
A Brahmin wife named Nirvāṇikā, who was childless and virtuous,
spoke to her own husband, a Brahmin named Kṣmācolaka, seeking happiness.
Poverty persists constantly, the hearth remains fixed in the practice of the Cāndrāyaṇa fast, and the teeth, free from disease, perform the vow of total abstinence from food. (3.28.40)
Just as one who has set out on a journey does not return home, the smoke-colored fire, becoming filled with shame, does not even grant its sight. ||41||
Living beings, such as ants and others, have already gone from their homes to the sacred bathing place;
even if the door were closed, there would be no purpose in doing so. ||42||
The door is forever open, like the auspicious gateway to heaven;
your halls are adorned with garlands, yet they are entirely free from passion. (43)
O Brahmin, liberation, though footless, has arrived at your house;
even I, whose nature is illusion (māyā), am now free from the snare.
O twice-born one, though your home is devoid of qualities, I have taken refuge in that very qualitylessness;
even while living, your state remains without support.
Having had an object of support, I have now become supportless and free from possessions.
Oh, how great is the power of fortune! That which possessed qualities has become as if devoid of qualities. (46)
Having come into being again and again, they dissolve when the vision of Nirvana is attained—crows, pigeons, sparrows, dogs, deer, and mice. (47)
O husband, cats and other such creatures never enter our house at any time;
when all good fortune has been cast out, who would dwell there with any attachment? (48)
There is no mortar or pestle, no broom, and no small bedstead;
by day it is illuminated by the light of the sun, and at night by the moon, planets, and so forth. (49)
O Brahmin, our home shines like the abode of Brahmā and gleams like heaven;
our matted hair is natural, yet it also radiates like the matted locks of a yoginī.
Oh, the malice of fate and the worthlessness of this worldly existence!
Though the prosperity of the household remains, the fortune of true destiny is not found. (51)
"O Brahmin, it is true that the house of one who is free from misfortune always becomes like the abode of Brahmā; such a stable home as this belongs to us both. (52)
Fortune, luck, the various enjoyments, and even food do not exist by mere speech;
therefore, O twice-born one, your home, which must necessarily be resorted to by yogis, truly shines.
There is no house worthy of being inhabited that is devoid of fortune and lacking in merit;
therefore, I constantly contemplate how fortune might reside within my own home. (54)
O Lord, I shall likewise perform the propitiation of Lakṣmī by means of vows and yogic practice, so that my home may become filled with prosperity. (55)
Thus requested, his own master said to him, "So be it";
she too performed the Lakṣmī-vow for a year, subsisting on a diet of milk.
Devoted to the practice of celibacy, she sleeps on the bare ground without a seat;
she remains awake until midnight, after which she rests in peace.
She sleeps while mentally reciting "Lakṣmī, Lakṣmī, Lakṣmī" in her heart;
every morning she always bathes in the river and returns home with her clothes still wet.
Having arrived, he daily performs the worship of Lakṣmī with one hundred and eight lotus flowers, as well as with incense, lamps, and other offerings.
He indeed performs the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) and offers fragrant incense;
he presents the food offering (naivedya), such as milk-preparations and fried cakes (polikā). ||3.28.60||
He performs one hundred and eight circumambulations while revolving prosperity;
having paid homage to the earthen image of Śrī, he indeed turns his rosaries.
O Lakṣmī, Śrī, Kamalā, Padmā, Ramā, Nārāyaṇī, Indirā; O Hiraṇmayī, Mahālakṣmī, Īśvarī, Parameśvarī! ||62||
O Kṛṣṇā, O Hariṇī, O she who is called Dravyā, O Vaiṣṇavī, O Puruṣottamī; O you whose form is prosperity, O Bhagavatī, O servant of Hari, O beloved of Hari! ||63||
Brāhmī, Vaikuṇṭhikā, Smṛddhā, Śālagrāmī, Trayodaśī, Cakriṇī, Padminī, Bindvī, Ābdhijā, and Svarṇarūpiṇī. ||64||
O dweller in cow-dung, O you who abide in the heart of Brahmā, O Mistress of Wealth!
O Ṛtambharā, O dweller in the Plakṣa tree, O Māyā, my Mother, O Sovereign! 65.
O Amāyā, O Meruputrī, you who are Dhṛti, Raudrī, Praśātanī, Kaumudī, Bhūyasī, Devavīthī, Anantā, and Kālī! 66.
O Ārṣī, Jyotsnā, Śivā, Śārdūlikā, Sarasvatī, Prabhadrikā, Sarvabhadrā, Svatantrā, Jayā, Sudarśanī, and Mātā! 67!
O Jalanārāyaṇī, O Svadhātmajā, O Mākṣikī, O Satī, O Puṇḍarīkī, O Ratnikā, O Kṛpāvatī, and O Bhaktijā! (68)
O you who possess half the splendor of Pippala, O you who are upon the half-and-half seat of the Vaṭa tree, O Acyutā;
O Queen of Kings, O Naiṣṭhikīśrī, O Śaivī, O Sovereign Kānakī! 69.
O Nirvāṇikī, O Brahma-śakti, O Ātmātmikā, O Antarātmikā; O you of shimmering form, O restless one, O radiance that brings forth the excellence of all beings! ||3.28.70||
Śrīvatse, Yantrikā, Aindrī, Jayantī, Maṇḍalātmikā, Sarvatobhadrī, Padmaśilā, Prajñā, and likewise Akṣarī. (71)
In the form of fortune that is present in the body, in the accomplished, the peaceful, and the descending;
in the supreme portion, the pervasive, the fragmentary, the object of worship, the abundant, and the abode of light.
O Mother, O Doer, O Delightful One, O Sovereign of the Goddesses, O Sovereign of Sovereigns!
O Muktānikā, O Consort of the Supreme Brahman, O Nourisher, O Action! 73.
For I am indeed the beginningless consort of Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the beginningless one; thus, I possess one hundred and eighteen names. (74)
Having shown compassion, come to my home, O Mistress of Sovereignty!
O you who are all fragrance, all flavor, all form, and of beautiful form! ||75||
O you who are all-touch, all-sound, come to my home;
O you who are all-bliss, all-happiness, and the constant increaser of prosperity! 76.
O you who possess the power to provide infinite upliftment, come to my home;
O destroyer of the suffering of poverty, O you who drive misfortune far away! (77)
O Lakṣmī, increaser of fame and splendor, bringer of happiness to those who enjoy their own sacrifices, O beautiful Śrī, come to the home of me, your devotee! 78.
Thus did that Nirvāṇikā, the beloved of the twice-born, entreat you;
and having heard her and observed her devotion, O dear one, you became gracious in thought. (79)
"Taking my command, go to his house to grant him even a mere glimpse; then proceed to the abode of Nirvāṇa. (3.28.80)
Standing before you in the form of Gocara, I then said:
"Without Nārāyaṇa, I shall not remain here in this house of yours."
"Worship him, O Mother; Mādhava will surely come.
Having said this, you vanished into her very body. ||82||
You were born as a beautiful daughter, a fair maiden;
by her I was propitiated from that tree known as Savana.
The Supreme Lord appeared as a youth of divine form—Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the glorious Puruṣottama. (84)
He holds the conch, discus, mace, and lotus, and possesses radiant splendor;
he is known by the names Anādi-Śrī-Sāvanadru-Nārāyaṇa. ||85||
She begged for alms, and her mother then gave you to me according to the marriage rite—you who are beautiful with every auspicious fortune. (86)
Then, O beloved, by the command of Kṣmācola, Nirvāṇikā protected both me and you at all times while serving us in her own home.
Then he established his residence on earth for an entire kalpa;
endowed with the glory of final liberation, he firmly established the Dharma upon the world.
From that, the house of Nirvāṇika was properly maintained;
indeed, many [gifts] were also offered there by the lords of the gods during the wedding ceremony. (89)
At that time, there were jewels, wish-fulfilling vessels, cows, wish-granting creepers, celestial chariots, mansions, and indeed ornaments.
Variegated garments, beds with coverlets,
as well as golden seats, couches, swings, hammocks, and the like.
Wealth consisting of gems, rubies, pearls, and auspicious things;
necklaces, fields, groves, and likewise great gardens. (92)
They also gave elephants, horses, and bulls, as well as hundreds of male and female slaves;
thus, through that gift, their house became prosperous and exceedingly magnificent. (93)
With golden jars, the royal peak was like Indra’s palace;
thus, indeed, did my manifestation occur for your sake at that time.
O Lakṣmī, remember all that was previously manifest of my blissful prosperity;
there were also countless other partial incarnations (aṃśāvatāras) and so forth of mine. 95.
O Śrī Nārāyaṇī, I know all [these things], but no other people do;
that house in which I dwell is like unto my own abode.
It becomes an abode of holy fords accessible even to Mukteśvara and others;
it is always a most purifying field for the virtuous. 97.
Even the forms of sacrifices and incarnations become my very self; and all abodes, too, dwell within my dwelling. 98.
Thus, by my dwelling here, enjoyment and liberation are held in the palm of one's hand;
this occurs for people through both reading and hearing [this work]. (99)
Through remembrance, all perfections arise; there is no doubt in this matter.
Whatever merit arises from all the various vows, it is surpassed by this. (3.28.100)

Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Manifestation of the Beginningless Śrī Svāminārāyaṇa along with His Consort Śrī for the Protection of the Subjects Residing in Svāminagara, Who Were Being Consumed by the Flames of the Aruṇācala Fire during the Thirty-third Year of the Creator [Brahmā] in the Dvāpara Age; and the Manifestation of the Beginningless Śrī Sāvana-Nārāyaṇa together with Lakṣmī—the Brahmin woman Nirvāṇikā—who had worshipped Him with one hundred and eighteen names during the Thirty-fourth Year," in the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, within the third section, the *Dvāpara-Santāna*.
Śrī Puruṣottama said: Listen, O Nārāyaṇī Śrī; in the Kalpa named Yakṣa, during the thirty-fifth year of the Creator's life, in the eightieth century.
And hear, O beloved, how my manifestation occurred during the third Manu;
at that time, there was a royal sage named Aṃśumat who was observant of vows in the southern region.
In a region adjacent to Meru, there was a ruler of subjects named Nalaveya; he was the governor of the entire land-portion of Nalava.
Other thousands of kings also became his tributaries;
he was a donor, a meditator, observant of vows, devoted, a servant of the virtuous, a listener to sacred texts, and a performer of sacrifices.
O Lakṣmī, King Aṃśukra was devoted to me, offering oblations, full of faith, and my worshiper; he performed the excellent rites of a great Vaiṣṇava.
Just as he was, so too were his wives initiated by Hari;
numbering one hundred, they were Vaiṣṇavas devoted solely to Hari.
They were givers, nurturers, and observers of vows; they were devoted, servers of the virtuous, listeners, performers of sacrifices, and even depositors of offerings to Hari. || 7 ||
All these female worshippers have surrendered themselves to me; they are full of trust, devoted to their husbands, and offer every mark of respect toward me.
Their minds are fixed upon my image; they possess the divine vision of my holy devotees;
and toward their husbands, Lord Hari, and the virtuous, they always maintain equal service and equal respect.
The king had three hundred sons and likewise two hundred daughters;
they were devoted to the service of the virtuous Hari, like unto fathers and mothers.
They served the family of the Blessed One with their minds, material objects, and bodies;
all were of divine nature, bodiless, and the foremost among the perfected ones (siddhas). || 1 1 ||
In their kingdom, there were never any policies that caused the calamity of suffering;
there was no drought, no excessive rain, no war, and no earthquake.
There was no overwhelming cold nor any affliction of heat anywhere;
no diseases occurred in the kingdom, and no people met with untimely death. (13)
The subjects were always delighted by food, clothing, and other such things; they adorned themselves and held great festivals, and they remained forever gracious and affectionate toward one another.
Always assisting one another and engaged in my worship, having offered yourselves to me, you who possess the power of flight and enjoyments, offer everything to me.
In their kingdom at that time, men and women were joyful and well-nourished, free from hatred, violence, and the like; there were no thieves and no misers.
The earth bestows all flavors, and the seasons grant fruits and flowers;
yet creepers and climbing plants are in vain, for they yield neither fruit nor blossoms without a supporting trunk.
Untruth did not exist among men, nor was there any deceit even among the subjects;
there was no craving for the pursuit of enjoyment, but contentment prevailed. (18)
Gods, great seers, holy men, perfected beings, virtuous women, ascetics, and those whose character is Brahmanical eat from this [vessel] by the thousands day and night.
In the kingdoms ruled by that monarch, food-donations were established,
where hundreds of thousands of students seeking knowledge and maidens seeking learning partake.
At every mound, at every village, and indeed at every town,
guests receive excellent food at his continuous feast of alms.
Every morning, as a constant practice, the worship of the gods and all the lords of prosperity in every village is carried out by the king himself through wealth and other means. (22)
Having performed the chanting of Hari's names for a period of one ghaṭikā,
the groups of guests, the destitute, and others eat at this assembly.
People resort to me in the evening and even chant my praises at night;
by day, however, people are intent on their own affairs and devoted to their own interests.
His subjects shall be of such a nature: devoted to the disregard of their bodies, intent on austerity, full of devotion, and dedicated to the service of the virtuous. (25)
For the Blessed One is always present here on earth in a virtuous form;
indeed, he shines as ten million forms, bringing about the welfare of all creatures.
The Blessed One is indeed virtuous; He is indeed the virtuous Savior. He is the virtuous bestower of the supreme goal, the Lord Himself whose very form is virtue. (27)
That it appears in a human form similar even to our own is indeed wonderful;
that form is divine, its actions are divine, and he is the Lord himself, the bestower of liberation.
Seeing, touching, massaging the feet, serving, eating together, and various forms of attendance—all these lead to the liberation of the virtuous one. (29)
Whatever service is rendered to the virtuous, whether once or many times, it destroys all sin and bestows the liberation of Brahman. (3.29.30)
Those sons who are initiated, who belong to the lineage of Hari himself, and who abandon birth and worldly prosperity—they alone are truly the very form of Hari. ||31||
In that performance [of the ritual], celibacy, the vow, charity, the sacrificial fee, austerity, righteousness, discernment, and devotion—all are established. (32)
The hands of the virtuous are the hands of Hari; the feet of the virtuous are the feet of Hari.
The face of the virtuous is the face of Kṛṣṇa; the skin of the virtuous is the skin of Śrī Hari. (33)
The two eyes are the two eyes of Śrī Hari; with the tongue, she is the tongue of Hari;
with the head, she is the head of Hari; with the nose, she is the nose of Hari. (34)
The ears of the virtuous are the ears of Śrī Hari; the teeth of the virtuous are the teeth of Hari;
the throat of the virtuous is the throat of Hari; and the chest of the virtuous is the chest of Hari.
The belly of the virtuous is the belly of Hari; the hips of the virtuous are the hips of Śrī Hari.
The vision of the virtuous is the vision of Hari; indeed, the touch of the virtuous is the touch of Hari. (36)
The clarity of mind found among the virtuous is indeed the grace of Hari;
the happiness of the virtuous arises from service [to Him], and that happiness of Hari is my own happiness. (37)
Delight, joy, bliss, and festivals—whatever is considered by the virtuous to be such, all those are indeed the bliss of Śrī Hari alone; they are certainly not separate from me.
Everything that brings satisfaction to the virtuous is indeed my own satisfaction;
for the aggregate of the senses of the virtuous is truly my own senses. (39)
The intellect of the virtuous is my intellect; I am always the virtuous ones on earth. I exist in the world as the virtuous ones, assuming many forms. (3.29.40)
Those who possess the quality of non-possessiveness are, for me, embodiments of Brahman;
those who embody the dharma, artha, and kāma of the virtuous are always considered by me to be all of these.
Thus, in this way, the king and the queens with pure hearts, as well as the princes, the princesses, the subjects, the servants, and others likewise [worshipped] in the lotus. (41)
All were associated with the virtuous, for they were my supreme refuge;

in that house, the supernatural powers (*siddhis*) were like wish-fulfilling creepers, the vessels of fortune were like the *kalpa*-trees, and even the *cintāmaṇi* gems and the cows of plenty always resided there. (43)
Hundreds of thousands of virtuous men and women, having performed acts of devotion, dwell in their respective stages of life;
free from desire and devoted solely to me, they worship me. (44)
Then, observing their devotion offered through self-surrender, I, out of compassion, desired to dwell for some time among that assembly of virtuous and saintly women. (45)
In my month named Mādhava, the king performed the monthly [sacrifice] unbroken for thirty days, consisting of a sacrificial rite. 46.
O Hare, Nārāyaṇa, Viṣṇu, Kṛṣṇa, Keśava, Mādhava!
O Supreme Brahman, Lord, Śrīśa, Puruṣottama, Lord of the virtuous! ||47||
Salutations to the Supreme Soul, the beginningless Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa;
salutations to the Inner Soul, whose nature is that of the saintly, the Soul of all. 48.
Salutation to the one whose nature is that of a virtuous wife, to the beloved of Śrī, the eternal Self;
salutation to the one who is won over by devotion, who is attained through service, the wielder of the discus. ||49||
You are independent and the Lord of the Imperishable, abiding among millions of liberated beings;
therefore, come here directly in your divine form, just as you truly are for us.
Thus did the king, the subjects, and the virtuous perform their worship;
with them I celebrate, I dance, and I laugh. (51)
I eat, I stand, I walk, I sit, and I speak;
I also drink, I smell, I taste, and I even sleep. (52)
In joy, I delight, I sport, and I bow;
I serve as one in the guise of a holy man among the virtuous during their festivals of sacrifice. (93)
But they do not recognize me, Mādhava, in my hidden form;
some in the assembly perceive me as merely some ordinary saint.
At that time, you were a virtuous and noble young woman, devoted to moral conduct;
though clothed in saffron robes, you were visibly manifest yet possessed of hidden, excellent qualities.
Concealed in form and with hidden signs, devoted to the service of virtuous women,
I moved about there within the circle of those virtuous women, conducting myself with impartiality.
Even those virtuous women do not recognize you, Lakṣmī, though you are within their range;
for my Māyā likewise remains there, consisting of independent concealment.
The sacrifice of food, the sacrifice of the ritual,
and likewise the sacrifice of chanting were fully completed at the end of the month of Mādhava, under the full moon.
On that evening, during the great festival, the virtuous and truthful people, as well as the king and his subjects, engaged in conversation that awakened them to my greatness.
Then they performed my worship at night with excellent materials upon the image;
thereafter they performed the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) and offered handfuls of flowers.
Then they offered foods accompanied by instrumental music and dancing,
along with kīrtana performed in beautiful voices using rhythmic measures, time-keeping, cymbals, and clapping.
Accompanied by the jingling sounds of small bells, they kept a vigil;
then, drawn by their hymn of praise, I appeared there as a dancer.
"You are a dancer and indeed a young girl; I am a boy of sixteen years.
You are fourteen years old and endowed with beautiful attire and ornaments. (63)
Wearing a crown of peacock feathers and adorned with divine earrings, she is richly arrayed in every costume suitable for dance; she is gracious and skilled in the art of drama.
And I too, appearing in such a form and assuming all the necessary roles, entered the midst of the assembly from an unobserved place. (65)
"Indeed, I have not been recognized by anyone, nor how could these two [be recognized]? Seeing us filled with apprehension, the king and the other members of the assembly sat [silent]. (66)
Indeed, our great splendor then radiated throughout the assembly hall,
and joy, delight, and happiness spread indeed among those gathered.
Then, through the union of us two, there arose for the people a sweet, desired, and cherished great happiness, accompanied by dancing, singing, and rhythmic clapping. (68)
Then they all became absorbed, extended solely by their conviction;
their speed was directed toward the visual alone, while their minds were drawn by hearing.
With unblinking eyes, they gazed upon me— you, the divine Śrī, the Lord of Fortune—
resembling infinite millions of suns and as beautiful as countless moons.
People beheld me and you as compassionate and filled with mercy;
the cause was chanting [our names], loving devotion, and the service of the virtuous. (71)
Divine nature always resides in the virtuous, for they are indeed the cause of our vision [of the Lord].
Then other devotees danced, their minds fixed on Kṛṣṇa. (72)
Immersed in supreme bliss and devoid of any perception of their own bodies, our auspicious vision was present there for all embodied beings. (73)
Then, for a moment, it became divine within the imperishable abode;
immediately thereafter, I caused that radiance to vanish.
Their mental dispositions were drawn forth and attained stability according to their respective faculties;
consequently, they beheld us two standing before them, appearing exactly like themselves.
Turning away quickly from dancing, singing, and even chanting, the people, overwhelmed by great wonder, prostrated themselves like staffs before you and me. (76)
The kings and others offered us the principal seat, a golden lion-throne;
and having seated us upon that throne, they worshipped us with great reverence.
With sandalwood, unbroken rice grains, flowers, and fragrant garlands;
and with kings and others [honoring him] with jewel-garlands, golden girdles, and so forth. (78)
With ornaments such as crowns, with incense, with food offerings and meals, with sweet drinks and betel, with the waving of lamps (nīrājana), and with hymns of praise; ||79||
And they all paid homage again and again by prostrating themselves like a staff,
with shouts of "Victory!", cries of joy, and the proclamations of those bearing canes.
Then they all propitiated you and me exceedingly; having recognized us as the Supreme Lord, they praised us with supreme affection. 8.1.
The virtuous ones said:
"Wherever our birth may occur hereafter by the power of our merit, O Blessed One, we have come for refuge to you; we are your sons. (82)
O Śrī Hari, he whose father is indeed Acyuta has offspring who are truly unswerving; we too have attained the state of being Acyuta—this is Your grace, O Lord. (83)
Out of compassion for these divine and excellent sons, you have arrived;
beholding those who are vessels of affection, you have become manifest as one devoted to mercy. ||84||
Therefore, one should always dwell among the virtuous just as one dwells in one's own body;
O Kṛṣṇa, dwell in the midst of the virtuous, for this is the ultimate compassion.
Just as he dwells in his own abode, may he always reside within the circles of the virtuous; may he, in the form of a holy being, bestow supreme grace. (86)
The virtuous women said: "O Mother Lakṣmī, O Great Lady, we have come to you for refuge;
desiring liberation, we virtuous Brahmin women are your daughters. (87)
O Mother, you grant us your vision by placing foremost that innate maternal affection which you feel toward your children to an extreme degree. (88)
Today fortune, endowed with strength, prevails for those who were weak;
having attained divinity through yoga, we shall indeed attain liberation.
Your compassion is likewise incomparable, in that you show favor even toward those who are wicked; and therein lies your supreme mercy, should you choose to grant them your dwelling.
Having accepted this prayer,
O Sovereign of the Imperishable, act as you desire here by the command of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
The queen said:
"I am blessed, as are my daughters and sons, the kingdom, the king, and likewise the subjects;
O Lakṣmī, I am blessed because of this vision of you here. (92)
Dwell here forever; everything shall be yours.
I am always your servant; dwell here, O Lakṣmī, and show me your grace.
In this cycle of existence, this alone is the gain obtained here: meeting with a virtuous woman.
To behold you in person is itself a gain that cannot be matched by anything else. 94.
The king said:
"O Kṛṣṇa, my family, kingdom, wealth, lineage—everything has been offered by me for your sake;
it has all been made yours and dedicated to your purpose. (95)
Through this meeting with the virtuous here, this very vision of yours has been directly attained;
everything that was to be obtained has today been reached, as well as the ultimate fruit.
"O Supreme Lord, having shown mercy, dwell forever in my home.
Having spoken thus, the king prostrated himself and fell at his feet. (97)
Having said to him, "So be it," O beloved, I, the beginningless Śrī Sādhu Nārāyaṇa, continued to dwell together with you in the circle of the virtuous. 98.
Then, O virtuous one, I shall dwell upon this earth with Nārāyaṇī until the end of the kalpa;
remember me, you, and all others, as well as our future incarnations. 99.
Through recitation, hearing, or even remembering it, one shall attain liberation.
Out of compassion, I have indeed revealed to you this [teaching] which bestows liberation.

Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Manifestation of the Primeval Holy Nārāyaṇa along with the virtuous Nārāyaṇī Lakṣmī through the devotion of King Aṃśukramatha in the thirty-fifth year of Brahmā," in the third section, the Dvāpara Cycle, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Puruṣottama said: Listen, Lakṣmī; thereafter, Hari, who was constantly served by the king, indeed granted Śvetadvīpa to the monarch as the fruit of his service to the virtuous.
Having enjoyed happiness together with his family, he then went to heaven;
there, having experienced all pleasures, he became one with the nature of the Vairāja deity.
Having become [thus] and experienced pleasures, he went again to Satyaloka;
then, having reached Vaikuṇṭha and enjoyed happiness there, he went again to heaven.
He has arrived solely by my will for the purpose of promoting devotion;
therefore, he shall become the lord of more than ten million worlds.
Having led those innumerable worlds who have taken refuge in him, together with their devoted followers, he, whose nature is that of Nārāyaṇa, shall go to my imperishable abode.
Moreover, this Aṃśukra was devoted to me just as no others in the world shall ever be devoted in such a manner. (6)
Sons, daughters, queens, kings, subjects, and followers—
all of them and all kingdoms [are for me] as my every possession.
Those Vaiṣṇavas, facing in all directions, were indeed engaged in their service.
Now I shall tell you something else; listen, O Mādhavī, to their manifestation.
Then again, O beloved, in the thirty-sixth year known as the Rākṣasa,
within the ninety-sixth Kalpa and during the seventh Manu, [it occurred] for the Creator.
Listen to me as I declare how my manifestation came to be—that of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa himself, who has taken descent. 3.30.10.
In the fifteenth Kṛta Yuga, a yogi named Haripratha became a potter on this earth, on the auspicious bank of the Viṣṇupadī river.
From his childhood, through the practice of virtuous yoga, he became a king among my devotees;
even his mother, Śreṇimatī, gave him excellent instruction.
In the lap, while nursing at the breast, on a swing, in a loincloth, in a hammock, likewise during sexual union, and even when children are tumbling about. (13)
"Speak, my son, the name of Hari: Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa, Nārāyaṇa!
Speak, my son, the name of Śrī: Lakṣmī, Lakṣmī, Nārāyaṇī! (14)
In this way, a mother indeed instructs her own son for the sake of liberation, for his welfare, for the destruction of sin, and as a means to make his birth meaningful. 15.
O Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, O Śrī Puruṣottama, O Supreme Brahman beyond the Imperishable, O Lord of Śrī, O Supreme Lord! || 16 ||
In this way, her mother herself also performs my glorification;
for she is always devoted in all her undertakings and possesses virtuous qualities. 17.
The potter named Virana is also always devoted to me;
even while being a servant of the virtuous, he remembers me in every undertaking. (18)
He constantly worships Hari alone, remembers Janārdana alone, and performs the act of offering to me alone; thereafter, he eats as is appropriate.
Every evening, with her mind fixed on me, she constantly recites my garland of names;
she also always performs auspicious service for the virtuous who are devoted to me.
Even when he performs household chores, duties regarding his alms-bowl, or service to the village, he likewise chants the name of Śrī Narāyaṇa.
The potter always wears a rosary on his hand and a garland around his neck;
chanting the name of Hari, he makes his time meaningful at all times.
Listen, Lakṣmī: for one who possesses true devotion, devotion is not difficult at all;
it is always easily attained by one who offers self-surrender in all undertakings. (23)
Rising early in the morning, Viraṇa, uttering the name "Nārāyaṇa," takes his water-jar and goes to the river; he bathes and chants the praises of me, Hari.
Having filled a vessel with water, he goes to the root of a Pippala tree;
there, remembering me, he sprinkles that water. (25)
Having bowed to the sun and having prostrated before me, who am made of clay, he cries out and eats the flatbread offered to me this morning. (26)
In that very same way, the potter’s wife ate, and his son also ate;
then the three of them went to fetch clay, chanting the praises of Hari.
Whenever they bring earth suitable for the back of a donkey, then three who recite the praises of Hari go toward the house. (28)
Even for a female donkey or a male donkey, they offer grass and the like, as well as water and the like,
after sprinkling them with the waters of Hari’s grace.
Then they moisten the clay with water and chant the name of Hari;
and as they knead the clay, they likewise chant my name.
Holding the wheel upon the pivot, they whirl it about and remember me;
placing the *piṇḍa* upon the wheel, they remember me, Janārdana.
They fashion jars, bowls, and vessels while remembering me;
having separated them with thread, they also lower them down. (32)
Remembering me, they brandish their vessels with the implements of branding;
remembering me, they place them in a fiery frying pan and cook them. (33)
They sell their bowls and yet remember me;
with the wealth they have obtained, they purchase food, vegetables, and other provisions from the market.
They cook the foods, remember me, and cry out to me;
having filled the vessel and offered it to me, they eat what has been presented to me. (35)
Thus, devoted to me, they maintain the livelihood of their families;
in the evening, they listen to discourses from the mouths of the virtuous in my abode.
At night they indeed remember and contemplate what was heard [during the day] for the sake of liberation;
yet there is no liberation without food, nor is there devotion without merit.
Merit does not exist without service, nor does service exist without grace; grace does not exist without servitude, and servitude indeed does not exist without faith. (38)
Faith does not exist without knowledge, nor does knowledge exist without hearing;
hearing does not exist without the company of the virtuous, nor does the company of the virtuous exist without the virtuous themselves. (39)
Existence does not occur without a being, nor does a being occur without existence;
moreover, the mental impression known as "cultivation" (bhāvanā) does not exist without what was previously acquired. (3.30.40)
That which was acquired previously is experienced right here in the form of its fruit;
that which is acquired today will be experienced elsewhere, in the state of the highest blessings.
All kinds of spiritual welfare are to be accomplished, but Narayana is the supreme welfare;
liberation resides at His feet and is to be attained through the thread of love. 42.
The form of Hari is the vessel of love, and consciousness is known as the saint;
those who desire their own welfare should propitiate the saints with services. 43.
Food, water, and clothing—these three are the means for sustenance;
a home, a beloved wife, and a cow—these three are considered the supports. (44)
Exertion, my son, health, and the Tretā age are the means for achieving fortitude;
income, a treasury, and kinsmen are the threefold means for achieving power.
Loving-kindness, pride, and fame are the threefold means for stability;
knowledge, conduct, and mastery are the threefold means for freedom from craving. (46)
Contentment, dispassion, and sovereignty are the threefold means for achieving tranquility;
virtue, forbearance, and endurance are the threefold means for achieving happiness. (47)
Virtue, Hari, and character—these three are the means for liberation.
Suffering, solitude, and humiliation—these three are the means for dispassion. (48)
Karma, craving, and latent impressions—these three are the causes of cyclic existence.
Malice, slander, and nihilism—these three are the means for reaching hell. (49)
Negligence, delusion, and worldly striving—these three are the invitations of death;
freedom from action, self-surrender, and devotion—these three are the means to liberation. 3.30.50
Therefore, having completely set aside all other things here, one should strive continuously for the sake of liberation alone, which is the cause of nirvāṇa in this world. (51)
Just as jars are indeed produced in various forms, so too here are beings, worlds, actions, and pleasures destroyed day after day. (52)
By the force of time, the wealth of the body and its worldly enjoyments perish;
what woman, what man, son, or daughter is there here that is not artificial? (53)
Just as names and designations arise from clay, so too are the names and designations of the sixfold aggregate and other such things artificial. //54//
Having obtained this artificial body and having understood the means to liberation, if liberation were not to be achieved, then human birth would indeed be in vain. //55//
Everywhere there are sense objects, hunger, thirst, and pleasure;
all this pertaining to this world is but a momentary bondage of the soul. (56)
New and new bondage is produced constantly and perpetually;
there is no end to these bondages, for in every new year, new jars [are made]. (57)
The potter goes to his death, while another takes his place there;
the stream of pots and of potters does not cease.
Living beings fallen into the stream are bound by the snares of "mine" and "I";
even when the jar is destroyed, they remain bound in its fragments, ensnared by delusion. (59)
In this world, the destruction of all things inevitably occurs in due time;
yet those who perceive this and strive for the sake of liberation are indeed not dead.
They will die again and again without the service of the Eternal;
therefore, Nārāyaṇa Viṣṇu is Śrīmat Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
The glorious Hari, the inner self within the supreme Brahman, is to be served at all times on this earth;
let people worship the Supreme Self and chant the name of Hari. 62.
And let them meditate upon Hari-Kṛṣṇa and attain the Supreme Lord;
thus, Viraṇa and the others always [practiced] their own welfare during the night.
They contemplated the meaning of truth and always worshipped me;
thus, after a short time had passed, those three potter-men—
They became entirely devoted to serving the virtuous and took refuge in the virtuous;
because of my service to the virtuous, that house became a temple for me. (65)
The virtuous always perform my narrations and other such acts here;
Viriṇa’s son, the potter Haripratha himself, [does so as well].
He received the excellent initiation from the preceptor Ānandabrahma;
having become a virtuous practitioner, he worships me, his Lord, constantly day and night. (67)
His perfection of speech was accomplished such that whatever he spoke came to pass;
then once, during my worship in the assembly of the virtuous there— (68)
While that mixture was being produced, Manu himself,
the seventh [Manu] known as Varṇiśāla, emerged from the sky in a celestial chariot.
After their worship, the virtuous men, such as the potters, and the virtuous women went to the banks of the Viṣṇupadī for bathing and other rites, accompanied by kīrtanas. (3.30.70)
Some bathe there, while others praise the Supreme Lord;
meanwhile, at the landing-place, that very mantra wanders far through the sky.
By chance, he descended to the bank of the Viṣṇupadī;
in the form of a king, accompanied by his servants, he came to the water’s edge.
In that vessel where the virtuous ones of old and others are immersed for the sake of bathing,
they remain worshipping me while chanting the glories of Hari.
There, the proud Maṇuśāla spoke to his servants regarding all these people here, both women and men: ||74||
"Let them drive them away and confine them far from the riverbank, so that I may not depart until I have finished my bath in the waters of the river. (75)
"Let the servants seize them by the hands and cast them far away!
Having spoken thus, those groups of servants advanced from all sides to meet them. (76)
They indeed drove them far away and even restrained them;
though they were virtuous, they turned back, impelled by the bliss of Brahman.
Haripratha, a virtuous devotee, said to the messengers: "How is it that this obstruction and prevention of my bathing is being carried out by you? (78)
The messengers said: "What is the purpose of this investigation?
Go far away; let everyone depart, for no possession shall occur here. (79)
Speaking thus, the messengers seized his very arm and cast him,
as well as the others, a great distance away.
Then Haripratha said, "Let the king indeed die for you!
When this was spoken, Manu died there at that very moment while he was still alive.
O lotus-born one, the lifeless corpse quickly fell to the earth with its hands and feet outstretched, and it cried out with a terrible force. ||82||
Then a cry of "Alas! Alas! arose, for an improper act had occurred;
the messengers went quickly to his side and attended to him with fanning.
Even with the massaging of his feet and the offering of water to drink,
Manu then departed for the abode of Dharma, casting off his life-breaths.
Then a cry of "Alas! Alas! arose among all the guardians of the people, among all the guardians of the quarters, and among the gods who dwell in truth.
Among the great sages, including Mahendra and others, Manu had indeed died as Śuka; then all the gods, beginning with Brahmā and Śambhu, arrived at the place where he had passed away.
Then, O daughter of Padma, for the sake of their livelihood, they all performed the worship of Hari, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, who is I myself. (87)
O Narayani, I, the glorious Puruṣottama, bearing the conch, discus, mace, and lotus, arrived there together with you. (88)
When they requested me for the sake of their livelihood, I then instructed them;
however, I am not capable of turning back what has been done for the sake of my devotee. (89)
"He is pleasing and devoted to me; he will surely bring about our welfare.
Then the gods bowed to Bhakta and made this very request.
They repeatedly entreated him for their lives and for his forgiveness;
they even honored the virtuous ones, while Hari then spread his fame.
Having recognized me as the Supreme Self, and having bowed to and worshipped me upon the corpse, he cast water [upon it]; at that very moment, Manu became endowed with life.
He rose up and praised me, Hari, and worshipped me;
having bowed to the holy ones and obtained their forgiveness, he returned once more to his own abode. ||93||
O Lakṣmī, requested by the virtuous, I always dwelt in the house of Hariprathas, in the home of the righteous along with you. (94)
Then you yourself became the Lord known by the name Anādi-Śrī-Bhakta-Nārāyaṇa, and you attained the renown as Śrī-Kuṃbhikā-Śrī. 95.
I know all of this, including the dissolution of the mind as the means to liberation;
remember everything—the banks of the Ganges and the like, as well as the virtuous women.
I dwelt for a full cycle of four yugas together with the virtuous;
from that time forth, other lineages of my tradition were also born.
Other incarnations have appeared for the sake of protecting the world;
through reading and hearing this, there shall be both worldly enjoyment and liberation. (98)

Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, titled "The Manifestation of the Beginningless Śrī Bhaktanārāyaṇa, together with Kuṃbhikā-Śrī, for the Purpose of Reviving Varṇiśālamanu—who had died by the curse of a devotee of Hari during the thirty-sixth year of Brahmā in the lineage of the Dvāpara age"—in the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*, within the third section concerning the continuity of the Dvāpara age.
Śrī Puruṣottama said: Listen, O Lakṣmī, to another story concerning the beauty of my manifestation,
which occurred long ago in the thirty-seventh year of Brahmā, known as Aṇḍaja.
In the ninety-first kalpa, during the sixth Manu-period,
there was a great ascetic named Jahārita who became a sage.
Though dwelling alone in the forest, he was a knower of the Vedas and a follower of the virtuous dharma;
he taught the Brahmins and others, and honored those who came to him.
He honors other guests and provides them with shelter;
he dwells in a leaf-hut within a grove of trees in his hermitage.
And he, for the sake of his livelihood, always nurtures trees rich in fruits, tubers, sprouts, leaves, and roots, after first taking water from them.
And he offers a welcome and other courtesies to the gods, the virtuous, and guests who have arrived, with offerings of ripe and sweet fruits, roots, and the like.
Then the king, the lord of Vidrava, accompanied by his army,
while proceeding on his expedition, arrived at the hermitage by that path.
At midday he found rest, yet he did not recognize that ṛṣi,
perceiving him merely as some forest-dweller capable of residing in a hermitage.
The king did not honor that virtuous brahmin of noble character;
on the contrary, he [honored] camels, elephants, and bulls upon his wooden pillars and other structures.
They released the horses, and they indeed devoured them;
they broke them down to the very roots and destroyed them as well.
Seeing the trees in flower and bearing fruit, the sage said to the king:
"O King, do not bring about the destruction of my trees from their very roots."
"Drive the animals far away to the side, to the forest filled with trees.
The king said, "The entire forest belongs to me; it also belongs to the king."
"Beasts overcome by hunger will surely devour the trees;
therefore, go far away from this place, for you are a forest-dweller. (13)
The sage quickly devised a punishment for King Garviṣṭha;
taking water in his hand, he cursed him, saying, "Become a horse! (14)
Immediately, a most magnificent horse appeared there;
the entire army fell into distress and entreated that sage. || 15 ||
For the sake of that king’s liberation, the queen also entreated him repeatedly;
then the sage said to her, "Your husband is this horse, O Uttara."
When your son has again performed the Aśvamedha sacrifice at the proper time,
King Nara, having bathed in the concluding purificatory rite (avabhṛtha) through union with Nārāyaṇa, [will attain his goal].
"There will be no doubt; now, indeed, let him go home.
Having spoken thus to her husband, she took the horse and went to her own home. (18)
Accompanied by her army, she went home and propitiated the Supreme Lord.
She had a son named Dharmadhara, born of the queen known as Yaśovārā. (39)
For the sake of his father’s liberation, he who was named Varmadhara began a sacrifice;
having been initiated, he gathered all the various materials required for the rite.
On pure ground, at the four corners of the sacrificial pavilion for the horse sacrifice,
while the ritual was being performed by his preceptor, who was conducting a divine session of sacrifice.
While the clarified butter was being offered into the fire for the attainment of everything, for universal victory, for the severance of all curses, and for the pacification of all sins; (22)
The gods—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara in person, along with other deities who were entitled to their respective shares—indeed arrived. ||23||
The priest of the gods, the preceptor Brāhmaṇa, worshipped that horse,
which was black in its forepart and white in its hind part.
On his forehead was a beautiful mark in the shape of a cart;
he was born under the constellation Aśvinī and had repeatedly drunk the essence of Soma in former lives.

Then the king, having caused the newborn to drink the essence of Soma and having raised him, performed the Sāṃgrahaṇī sacrifice on the full moon day of Caitra and the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice on the full moon day of Vaiśākha.
After that, he performed a sacrifice dedicated to Prajāpati,
as well as the new-moon sacrifice (Amāvāsyeṣṭi), and likewise had his hair shaved.
Wearing fresh garments, observing silence, and having performed the hospitable rites for the sacred fire,
he went to the pavilion on the following day and offered eleven oblations.
Having caused the sacrificial porridge to be served to the officiating priests and having properly honored them,
the sacrificer [prepared] the sacrificial horse and the four-eyed dog.
Having led them both along with the officiating priests to the water of a pond or similar body of water, he performed the ritual sprinkling;
then, having released the dog, the Adhvaryu priest likewise performed the sprinkling.
Then the king himself released the horse upon the earth for the purpose of its wandering,
accompanied by four hundred brave archers acting as its guardians.
The king, moreover, performed every single day the oblations known as the Viṣṇukramaṇas, both evening and morning, while the two lute-players sang the Vīṇā-pragāthas.
Having summoned the Brahmins and Kṣatriyas, he indeed causes glory to be sung;
he listens to the Pāriplava recitation and awaits the arrival of the horse.
Along the paths leading to the horse's hoofprints, he caused the appropriate oblations to be offered for the horse’s teeth, jaws, thighs, feet, and penis. (34)
Recalling [the horse's deeds], the king himself caused the oblation to be offered,
as well as acts of going, running, crying out, and even neighing.
Recalling the qualities of horses— their lying down, their sniffing, and their rolling— and treating them as deities, the king offered oblations to them.
Then, having achieved victory and brought back the purifying horse,
the king worshipped it, established it in its place, and caused the Sutyā ceremony to be performed.
On the second day of the three-day Soma-pressing, the king stationed the Udgātṛ priest at the horse-stable, accompanied by mares. (38)
The horse neighed, and that [sound] became the Udgītha;
then he caused twenty-one sacrificial posts to be fashioned from the horse.
In the center and well-positioned in the northern and southern corners,
he tied that horse to a post made of *rājjudāla* wood situated in front of the fire-altar.
On both sides of this central sacrificial post (yūpa) were two posts made of Devadāru wood;
on the sides of those, there were three posts each, fashioned from Bilva trees.

On its two sides were three by three sacrificial posts made of khadira wood, and on the two sides of those ponds were three by three sacrificial posts made of palāśa wood; he worshipped them all equally.
Having girthed the horse with a rope, the king bound thirteen other animals to that rope with cord-fastenings. || 43 ||
On the forehead of the horse, he bound the victim for Agni; in the fifth part, that for Pūṣan;
and above, the king bound the victim for Indra and Pūṣan.
The king bound to his two arms the two [goats] known as Ājñeyaka, black-necked;
to his two thighs the two belonging to Tvaṣṭṛ, white-backed; and to his two sides the two belonging to Bṛhaspati. || 45 ||
Then the king tied to the lower part [the goat] whose belly was white and whose deity is Dhātṛ; he also tied to the tail a white goat. 46.
He bound the black-colored goat of Sūrya on his right side,
and likewise, he bound the black goat of Yama on his left side.
He captured three hundred and forty-nine domestic animals, and he also captured three hundred and sixty wild ones. ||48||
Goats and other such domestic animals, as well as wild beasts and other forest-dwellers—
these he prepared for sacrifice, performing likewise the rite of circumambulation with fire.
Having paid homage to all the animals and designated them for the sake of the deities,
the king removed those divine and worshipful animals and released them.

Having prepared a fine kuṣmāṇḍa fruit under the name of a horse, he placed it upon a blanket smeared with ghee, and performed the ritual slaughter by laying it down with its head toward the east and its feet toward the north.
Thereafter, the queens and wives reviled him with vulgar words;
he then offered six oblations of the omentum containing fruit to Prajāpati.
He performed the Viṣṇukrama steps and other Kuṣmāṇḍa rites; having immolated the sacrificial animals, he caused all the oblations to be offered.
Having offered three oblations with clarified butter and other substances,
and having thereafter performed the rites concluding with the *patnīsaṃyāja*, the king desisted.
On the third day, the day of the Soma-pressing, having performed the rites pertaining to Soma,
[he should sacrifice] eleven Prājāpatya animals in the form of Kuṣmāṇḍas.
Having offered oblations and performed the ritual acts, he indeed undertook the final purificatory bath (avabhṛtha) upon the head of a man who had tawny eyes and white leprosy.
Having offered three oblations and bestowed a hundred gold pieces,
he performed the Traidhātavīya sacrifice for a full year.
Honoring the horse with the seasonal fruits of each respective season, the most righteous king worshipped it; the king regarded the divine horse as being like a god himself.
At the end of the year, he honored a hundred thousand virtuous men and ascetics,
as well as chaste and noble women, Brahmins, and children seeking knowledge.
The king indeed fed female students and female mendicants;
throughout the year, at the conclusion of his daily fire-offerings, he gave gifts with sincere devotion.
Reflecting on when his father, in the form of a horse, might attain human state,
the king fell asleep at night.
At the end of the year, during the suspension of sacrifices, he beheld at night Narayana,
the infallible one, in a divine form adorned with a crown.
Adorned with all ornaments, endowed with every beauty,
complete with all sovereign powers and other perfections, and slightly less than sixteen years of age.
At that time, you were resplendent with Lakṣmī until your fourteenth year, possessing a gracious countenance and the beauty of true auspiciousness.
While in sleep, he praised Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Person:
"You are the sacrifice; you are the horse, and you alone are the Aśvamedha. (65)

You are the king, you are the protector of the kingdom, and you are indeed the sovereign of kings; you are the world, you are the lord of the world, you are the god, and you are the lord of the gods. ||66||
You are Viṣṇu, you are Brahmā himself, you are Vairāja Maheśvara;
you are the Infinite (Bhūman), you are the Lord of Pradhāna, Vāsudeva, Janārdana. ||67||
You are Dhāmeśa, Mahākāla; you are Māyeśa, the Supreme Lord.
You are the Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the illustrious Puruṣottama, the Sovereign of all. 68.
You alone are the creator, the sustainer, the controller, the protector, and the destroyer, abiding within all; O Blessed One, you are everything, and everything is offered unto you.
O Lord, you are indeed the refuge; O Nārāyaṇa, O Keśava, quickly destroy this horse-form born of my father’s curse.
When the king had thus praised me, I then said to him:
"O King, you have abandoned me at this great sacrifice of the horse-sacrifice."
Indeed, other deities were worshipped without my remembrance;
and the horse-sacrifice was not offered to me, being devoid of dedication to me. (72)
O lord of men, today there is no one who can fulfill your desire;
therefore, perform the horse sacrifice once more and worship me again. (73)
Therefore, in all places and in all undertakings, that man Janaka will undoubtedly return once more to human state. ||74||
"Furthermore, my vision shall be such that everything will become suitable.
Having said this, O Śrī Narāyaṇī, I attained invisibility from you.
Dharmadhara, O King, having abandoned sleep,
rose up immediately and then understood the dream to be indeed true.
Having fashioned my golden image exactly as it was seen by you,
he performed the horse sacrifice once again according to the prescribed rites, worshipping me.
Furthermore, O Lakṣmī, having bathed in the purifying water together with you at that time, I attained a divine form once again during the final ablution.
While his father was on horseback, Nārāyaṇa himself indeed cast [the weapon];
that king, named Varmadhara, having shaken off his sin, [was liberated]. 79.
He immediately regained his former royal form;
with tears in his eyes and remembering his past lives, he praised me with many faltering words.
The queen named Yaśovarā performed a respectful reception for you;
her guru, Devasatrī, worshipped me, the Supreme Lord. (8.1)
He entreated him again with the sixteen auspicious objects and other offerings;
O Blessed One, you have arrived because of his words of persistence. (82)
"O Blessed One, dwell here always for the sake of this king's release from the curse.
"So be it," said the divine sacrificer, whose wealth is his asceticism, when thus addressed by me. (83)
I, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Supreme Person (Śrī Puruṣottama), became established under the name Anādi Śrī Medhanārāyaṇa. 84.
Together with you, Medhāvatī-lakṣmī, in the region of Vidrava, many horse-sacrifices (aśvamedhas) were indeed performed upon the earth. ||85||
The lords of men performed various sacrifices according to their capacity, repeatedly honoring the divine horse even without engaging in battle. (86)
While I was present on earth, honored during the horse sacrifice, some people, out of fear of me, did not tether the released horse. (87)
All the kings came to know that Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Lord, was visibly present at the horse sacrifice, in his winged palace, and at the ritual itself. ||88||
One must by no means create an obstacle to his sacrifice through battle;
it is certain that no one shall attain victory by means of war. (89)
Thus, in that kalpa, the sacrifices were indeed free from violence; those who partook of the offerings to the gods and the sacrificial animals were performers of what pleases me.
A Brahmin who had abandoned all deceit and was devoted to the dharma of the virtuous, having heard of me, quickly came to Śrīpati, the Supreme Person. 9.1.
Having met with King Rājagṛha, thereafter he appeared as a virtuous devotee of mine, shining in my service. 92.
Commanded by me, he bestowed upon the Manus the Vaiṣṇava doctrines for their welfare;
he awakened the subjects and caused those who take refuge in me to practice them.
Although he was a bearer of armor, through dispassion he received the true initiation and indeed taught to the worlds my direct method of worship.
The virtuous [king], who was ever devoted to the dharma of the righteous, sent me;
and Queen Yaśovarā also, having received initiation from me, [sent me]. (95)
Endowed with splendor and eternally devoted to the dharma of virtuous women, she bestowed upon the other women that excellent Vaiṣṇava initiation of mine. 96.
He caused the Vaiṣṇava women— who were virtuous, established in the nature of Brahman, and protectors of the stream of Brahmanic conduct— to perform the worship.
"And I shall remain with you until the end of the kalpa, O Nārāyaṇī;
remember, O illustrious Nārāyaṇī, your own entire wisdom. (98)
In this way, many other incarnations of mine have arisen from that [source] as well;
yet I know them all to be solely devoted to the work of the Dharma.
By reading, hearing, remembering, or even retaining this,
one attains the fruit of a horse sacrifice and shakes off all sins in every way.
If he possesses desire, then after enjoying many heavens for a long time,
he shall thereafter go to the supreme abode of Brahman, which is eternally dear to me through devotion.
But for the disinterested devotee, devotion to me arises quickly;
fully satisfied with all forms of happiness, he goes to my supreme abode.
By listening to this birth story, one shall obtain the fruit of all sacred fords (tīrthas), the fruit arising from all vows, and likewise the fruit of all forms of service.

Thus ends the thirty-first chapter, titled "The Manifestation of the Beginningless Śrī Medhanārāyaṇa, together with the Goddess Medhāvatī-Śrī, at the Horse Sacrifice performed by the son of King Varmadhara—who had been transformed into a horse due to the curse of Ajahārita—in order to grant him liberation," in the third section (the Dvāpara-santāna) of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*, during the thirty-seventh year of Brahmā.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Śrī Nārāyaṇī, to my manifestation thereafter;
it occurred in the thirty-eighth year of the Creator (Brahmā) during the sixth Kalpa and the eighth Manvantara.
Born from the essence of Brahmā, the Asura Ariṣṭa,
who was insatiable and possessed of exceeding splendor, grew as soon as he was born, being filled with hunger.
All other splendors dissolve into his body from every side;
he consumes all fires, for from birth he eats nothing else.
Water does not swallow the earth; it swallows only fire.
Wherever there are fires, there he is present.
Having gone again and again, he forcibly seized the fire and, holding it repeatedly, devoured it entirely;
he consumed even Mahāgni, the mind-born son of Brahmā.
There he devoured his three sons— Pāvaka, Pavamāna, and Śuci— as well as Saharakṣas, the son of Pāvaka.
He also devoured Pavamāna’s son Kavyavāhana;
and having seized Śuci’s son Havyavāha, the asura likewise devoured him.
She devoured Agni’s fourth son, Brahmaudana;
and she also devoured Bharata, the son of Brahmaudana.
Likewise, he devoured Bharata’s son Vaiśvānara;
then he devoured Agni’s fifth son, Atharvan.
The great Asura then consumed four [beings]: the son of Atharvan, Amṛta, Dadhyañc, and likewise Aṅgiras, having churned them out.
He likewise consumed the son of Nirmathya, Gārhapatya;
he likewise consumed Śaṃsya and Śuka, the two sons of Gārhapatya.
He [consumed] Āvasathya, Sabhya, and Āhavanīyaka, the sons of Śaṃsya.
An asura named Mahāriṣṭānalāda was devouring them. || 12 ||
Likewise, that great asura devoured other sons of Śaṃsyā who were born from rivers, as well as his sons known by the name Dhiṣṇis.
Ṛtu, Pravāhaṇa, Agnīdhra, Samrāj, Kṛśānuka, Pāriṣada, Pratalka, Nabhasa, and likewise Vasu; || 1.4 ||
He also devoured Ajaikapād, Ahirbudhnya, Gṛhapati, Hotrīya, and Śāntapracetas. || 15 ||
He likewise consumed the Viśvadeva cup, and he consumed the Acchāvāka cup;
he also consumed the Uśīra cup, the Kavi cup, and the Potṛ cup. || 16 ||
He also consumed the Bhāri, the Naiṣṭhīya, and even the Vyaratni; likewise, he swallowed the Mārjālīya, the Phūrja, the Abja, and the Jāṭhara.
He likewise devoured the wrathful son of Jaṭhara;
he also devoured Savartaka, Manyumān, and Vāḍava.
The great asura devoured Vāḍava, who was born from Uttha; Saharakṣa, who was born from Kṣāma; and Kravyāda, the son of Kṣāma.
He devoured the son of Śuci, Āraṇeya, and yet another;
and he also devoured Āyu, the son of Āraṇeya, as well as Āyuja and Mahimānaka.
He also devoured Mahimānasuta and Savana,
as well as the wonderful Savanottha and the various sons of Adbhuta.
The great asura likewise ate the son of Vivasvat (Yama),
as well as the sons of Arka— Vājasṛg and Anīkavat.
The great Asura then devoured Yaṣṭikṛta, Rakṣohan, Surabhi, Vasu, Annāda, and Rukmarāja as well.
In this manner, the great asura also devoured others situated in the cremation grounds;
thus indeed did he consume Nārāyaṇī, Śrī, and the world devoid of fire.
Burning with a fire devoid of fuel and parched by a heat devoid of moisture, the entire earth appeared like the Himalayas; seeing everything facing death, she was indeed overcome with grief.
She went there to the abode of Truth and sought refuge with Brahmā;
for the sake of protecting herself from the fire, she praised him with supreme devotion.
For the sake of not destroying the fire-altar, Brahmā indeed made repeated prayers;
he then remembered me, Puruṣottama, within his mind.
[He meditated upon] the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the glorious Puruṣottama, Hari, the Supreme Brahman who transcends the imperishable, the inner controller of all.
O Lakṣmī, having heard your prayer, I became manifest before Brahmā;
then, O Lotus-born one, Brahmā worshipped me along with you.
The Earth worshipped you for the sake of protection;
then, by my command, you acted for the purpose of destroying the Asura.
She became the daughter of Pṛthvī, the royal glory Pārthivīśrī, a virtuous maiden;
having taken you, she of pure intent quickly departed for the earthly realm.
Assuming the very form of fire, I became composed of flames;
seeing me, the asura Analāda rushed toward me on Mount Meru.
And for the purpose of devouring you, I rushed toward the earth,
where you, together with the earth, were waiting for my arrival.
I arrived there in a cave of that very mountain Bhānumat;
and while you were looking on, O Earth, the great asura was also there.
I entered within that great Asura, who was the Supreme Lord— a blazing fire of great flames— and I indeed consumed him.
Having reduced them to ashes, I restored those fires to life once more;
then all the fires were endowed with life, conscious, and auspicious.
Just as they had existed before, they praised me and also worshipped me—
the beginningless Śrī Vahni-Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama).
Commanded by me, those fires quickly proceeded to their respective places, engaged in their respective functions, endowed with power, and fully equipped. ||38||
Then the worlds, the realms, and the living beings, together with the fires, came back to life; the state of being like frost had passed for them, and they indeed became possessed of life once again.
Having learned of my manifestation there, all the gods and others arrived for the purpose of worship; thereafter, a rain from the sky occurred.
There was likewise the sound of "Victory! amidst sandalwood and flowers;
a great festival was celebrated there for me by all the gods and others. (41)
The earthly glory has been bestowed upon me by the Earth herself and wedded to me;
and I shall remain with you, O Nārāyaṇī, until the end of the kalpa.
O Lakṣmī, my manifestation has been described to you; remember that which bestows happiness.
At that time, many other incarnations of mine occurred during that year. 43.
I indeed know all these; no one else knows them at all.
By reciting or even by hearing them, enjoyment and liberation are produced.
There shall be no calamity from fire, nor shall diseases ever arise;
the reciter here shall eternally attain the bliss of Brahman. (45)
