Delicious new grains should be given to the seeker;
for the sacrifice of the first-fruits bestows long life in this world.
When there is new grain, all men, women, and even boys should worship the Supreme Lord with fire using pure food.
One should worship the Supreme Lord with curd, which possesses a sweet and sour-sweet taste, as well as with milk endowed with a sweet essence. || 4 ||
One should worship Mādhava with milk-rice, milk-preparations,
and milk, as well as with ghee, foods cooked in ghee, and auspicious offerings anointed with ghee.
One should worship the Supreme Self with auspicious fresh butter combined with sugar, presented in vessels filled with milk.
O Lakṣmī, one should worship me, Hari, with offerings of *pūrikās*, *polikās*, and secret *puṭaka* foods, by which I am satisfied.
One should worship me in every way with sugar, candied sugar and the like, honey, jaggery, saffron, various juices, and cold drinks.
One should worship with mangoes, sweet fruits, grapes, plantains,
ambrosial fruits, and coconuts and other such ripe fruits.
With cold-fruiting rāyaṇa trees, jambūs, and likewise panasa trees, as well as with fresh cirbhaṭas and karkaṭīs, my bride shall indeed worship me.
These two—honor and dishonor—are always to be understood as poison and nectar respectively;
having suffered the overwhelming impact of contact with them, the group of women falls into despair.
Therefore, womenfolk should conduct themselves with a spirit of service;
they should walk along a path purified by their sight and perform actions purified by their mind.
A daughter-in-law should perform service purified by her master and dwell in a home purified by righteousness;
she should always obey her master’s command and never act in violation of that command. (13)
For obedience is the duty of wives; therefore, she should desire the highest success.
A wife should avoid deceit, hypocrisy, dishonesty, and backbiting. (14)
Excessive laughter, haughtiness, playful gestures, and acting according to one's own whims—
the young wife should avoid these with every effort in the presence of her elders.
She should not speak words that are contrary to his speech or improper toward her teacher; indeed, the group of wives should never recall anything unpleasant.
One should not touch a woman in her menses, a woman who has recently given birth, or one who carries impurities; on the fourth day, a bride does not become capable of sexual union.
At that time, she will give birth to one who is short-lived and destitute of vows, knowledge, wealth, and other such qualities;
therefore, she shall indeed be afflicted by powerful planets.
One should associate with virtuous women, for she brings about the accomplishment of all goals;
one should abandon association with unvirtuous women, which is beneficial neither in this world nor in the next. 19.
One should avoid association with the base, as well as discord with one's own kin;
one should avoid devotion to enemies, attachment to others' wives, and evil company. (3.42.20)
For one who forms alliances with the noble, engages in virtuous discourse with the wise, and maintains friendship with those free from greed, does not come to ruin. (21)
A man and a woman should never engage in association with others, nor should they engage in jesting in an improper place, nor should they ever dwell in the house of another.
If another person acts for one's benefit, they are a kinsman; if not, they are otherwise.
A disease born of the body is harmful, whereas wild forest medicine is beneficial. (23)
She alone is a kinswoman who is well-wishing; he alone is a father who provides nourishment;
he is a friend in whom one has trust; and that is a country where one can live. (24)
He is a servant who serves according to the prescribed rule; that is seed which sprouts;
she is a wife who is devoted to her husband; he is a son who exists for the attainment of happiness. (25)
She lives who possesses virtues; she lives who possesses righteousness. For the life of one devoid of virtue and righteousness is fruitless. (26)
She is a true wife who is skillful in the household, attentive to her husband's needs, sweet-spoken, beneficial, devoted, compliant, and the increaser of all prosperity. (27)
He whose wife is devoid of affection, with eyes full of deceit, fond of quarreling, eager for dispute, attached to others, shameless, and arrogant; ||28||
That which is devoid of the service of a wretched wife is not old age; it is not true old age for one whose wife is of equal conduct, appreciative of virtues, and devoted. (29)

She who is content with her husband’s lot, who is affectionate and acts for his pleasure, who is devoted to her husband’s duty and inseparable from him—she is truly beloved; any other woman is not beloved. 3.42.30.
A wicked wife, a deceitful friend, a servant intent on his own interests, and where there is a snake—in such a place, residence indeed brings death. 3.1.
Where the husband is ignorant of virtues, the co-wife is angry and fault-finding, and everything is full of doubt—there, in such a dwelling, there can be no peace. (32)
May they abandon association with the wicked, cultivate the company of the virtuous, perform merit incessantly, and remember me, Hari, as their Lord. (33)
One should save wealth for times of misfortune; one should protect one's wife with wealth and other means;
and one should always protect one's husband, son, and virtuous wife with wealth and other means. (34)
One should abandon an individual for the sake of the family; one should abandon the family for the sake of dharma;
one should abandon dharma for the sake of Hari; and for the sake of liberation, one should renounce everything.
It is better to dwell in a forest region than ever in a wicked house;
a home of evil conduct and suffering are both manifest hells.
The wise woman moves with one foot while standing on the other;
she does not abandon her former dwelling without first examining the new location. (37)

One should abandon a person of wicked conduct; one should abandon a residence that is fraught with calamities; one should abandon a miserly master; and one should abandon a deceitful and wicked man. (38)
Those who are friends to one established in wealth are not truly so;
indeed, for one devoid of the path of wealth, friends are truly meaningful.
A friend who provides protection in times of calamity, a beloved wife during the loss of wealth, and a companion during famines and other hardships—these belong to the fortunate man. (3.42.40)
A tree whose fruit is exhausted, a dried-up lake, a master who has lost his wealth, shade, fish, and a lawful wife—these are never abandoned. (41)
Even birds and cranes abandon those courtesans; one should understand that they act out of self-interest and should not place trust in such people. 42.
One should win over a greedy woman by the gift of wealth, an excellent one by joining the palms in reverence,
a foolish one by compliance with her whims, and a wise woman by speaking the truth as it is.
A woman should win over virtuous young women by serving them with sweet words;
for both virtuous women and deities are pleased by pure intentions. (44)

An unfaithful woman is satisfied by food, drink, and the like, while a deceitful woman is pleased by deceit; whatever a woman’s disposition may be, the wife should enter into her with that very same nature. (45)
Rivers, clawed animals, horned creatures, those with weapons in hand, royal households, and beggars are by no means to be trusted in every respect. (46)
A daughter-in-law must certainly not disclose the loss of wealth, domestic distress, misconduct within the home, as well as insults or deception. (47)

Abandoning one's master, associating with the lowly, and destroying the character of one's wife—these three cause the loss of profit: being arrogant, being fault-finding, and being addicted to vice. (48)
Where there is neither honor, nor joy, nor knowledge, nor peace, nor friendship;
where there is no love for the husband in the wife—that house is indeed a dwelling of fire. 49.
Wealth free from fear is to be sought, as is friendship free from fear;
likewise, affection free from fear exists—indeed, that is heaven itself, free from fear. (3.42.50)
A woman should always be charitable and never stingy; she should be patient, virtuous, and likewise one who accumulates merit for the sake of happiness. (51)
Naked, emaciated, a mendicant, wretched, and intent on begging—such is the state resulting from not giving; therefore, a daughter-in-law should be a giver. (52)
If that which has been accumulated, requested, and obtained is not employed for a worthy purpose, it will surely be seized by thieves, the king, or the earth itself. (53)
The wealth of a miser goes to the earth, to thieves, or to kings; the punishment for a woman is a separate bed, and the punishment for a husband is indeed non-attendance.
Wicked people, servants, drums, and likewise animals, as well as a wicked woman and a man addicted to vice, become gentle when struck. (55)
Rivers, women, and those of even temperament who are impetuous and flow very lowly—these cause bank after bank to fall if they follow their own will. (56)
There is no satisfaction in desire, nor in a son, nor in wealth; there is no satisfaction even in pleasure or life itself. Having conquered these, one should devote oneself to Hari.
One should accomplish the eternal through future means such as worship of the deities;
however, having understood it to be impermanent, that which is bodily must be renounced.
She who abandons the certain liberation and pursues that which is uncertain will not go to that uncertainty together with her own self; therefore, one should pursue the certain.
One should accept an oblation even from a family that has fallen into ruin, and a well-spoken word even from a child;
one should take gold from an impure place, and likewise, liberation from a virtuous person.
Servants, ornaments, and even women should be employed only in their proper places;
for so too are a virtuous woman, a noble horse, and a person devoted to truth.
One who is indifferent does not tolerate harsh blows or falsehood;
likewise, even when deprived of wealth, a virtuous woman does not serve a base person.
One should never reunite with a friend who has once proved treacherous;
by seeking such a reconciliation, death may result, especially in the case of a wife.
The offspring of an enemy is like a vessel of poison;
it is never a vessel of trust, for when adverse times arrive, it brings about calamity. (64)
When destiny is favorable, everything else is useless;
if destiny is not favorable, then all that has been done is in vain.

A woman who casts aside shame in the pursuit of wealth, in expenditure, in the acquisition of knowledge, in eating, in sexual pleasure, and in accomplishing her own purposes, shall obtain happiness. (66)
Shame, protection, water, a king, a teacher, a temple, and one's own people—where these do not exist, staying there indeed brings only suffering. (67)
One should not dwell where there is no assembly of virtuous astrologers, wise men, and elders; nor where there is no affection, food, or a physician. (68)
A virtuous daughter-in-law should properly protect her own kinsmen with food, clothing, and other necessities;
she should constantly worship Viṣṇu, who bestows longevity, fame, and strength. (69)
In an instant wealth may perish; riches and such are not under one's own control.
Realizing that time is momentary, O virtuous lady, serve me and surely achieve liberation.
For both the tigress of old age and the enemy of disease approach by force;
knowing that life is like a broken water-jar, one should strive for liberation.
She who looks upon another man as her father, upon the wealth of others as mere fodder, and upon all living beings as herself— she alone is truly virtuous.
Friends belong to the wealthy, and kinsmen belong to the wealthy;
the wealthy woman is highly honored, for the wealthy woman is indeed wise.
One devoid of sacred learning is perpetually blind; therefore, one should possess such learning.
A woman who possesses the eye of sacred learning prospers in the happiness of sovereign bliss. (74)
By her, the Lord was satisfied; she returned the favor to her female servants;
and by her, the group of women in the household and the rest conquered the earth. (75)
A wife should not give way to mental anguish even in the face of great calamity;
possessing equal wisdom and rich in discernment, she should remain equanimous toward both happiness and suffering. (76)
One should not consider the house of another as one's own; the husband’s house is one's own home. Whatever belongs to the husband is all one's own; thus, one should rejoice with discernment.
One should restrain the gaze from fickleness, restrain false speech, restrain the mind from deceit, and restrain oneself from cyclic existence. ||78||
One should never emit the sound "huṃ" nor knit one's brows toward one's own people;
having looked upon the group of women, the daughter-in-law should please them and bow down to them. (79)
Diligence, discernment, fortitude, capability, good character, and enthusiasm—these six qualities in a woman always grant success and bestow happiness. (3.42.80)
Gentleness, the spirit of servitude, humility, forbearance, compassion, cheerfulness, and affection—these seven bestow happiness upon a wife. (81)
Endowed with noble birth, good conduct, and virtue, devoted to truth and the Dharma, beautiful and serene—such indeed should be the female superintendent. 82.

She who knows the relative strength and weakness of others shall indeed be the commander of the army; and Ramā, who understands gestures, facial expressions, and inner dispositions, shall be the female gatekeeper.
Intelligent, eloquent, devoted to truth, and having conquered her senses, she shall indeed be a teacher, skilled in many scriptures and other sciences. (84)
A woman who is intelligent, capable of discerning the minds of others, truthful in speech, of noble birth, and endowed with the power of authority is considered a suitable messenger. 85.
She who knows all the rules, whose power of reasoning is fully developed, and who possesses knowledge of place, time, and so forth—she indeed shall be the Superintendent of Dharma. (86)
Devoted to her mother and maternal grandmother, diligent in the labor of cooking, pure, well-versed in the methods of purification, and possessing a refined palate, she should be the cook. (87)
One who has practiced Ayurveda and possesses the wisdom of the system of diagnosis shall indeed become an excellent physician, bringing benefit to all. 88.

The preceptor should be one who knows the truth of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, is devoted to meditation, fire-offerings, and recitation, speaks words of beneficial blessing, and likewise serves as an instructor. (89)
One who knows proper conduct, knows the rules, understands place, time, and so forth, and is skillful and clever—such indeed should be the teacher who writes and recites. (3.42.90)
A woman who is double-tongued, a giver of affliction, as well as one who causes agitation, deceitful, cruel, and harsh—she is considered to be one who brings harm. (91)
A wicked woman must be avoided even if she is adorned with learning;
likewise, a malicious daughter-in-law should be abandoned in legal proceedings. 92.
One should employ in the affairs of state a woman who is equal in purpose and equal in capability, who knows the vital points [of counsel], who is resolute, heroic, and endowed with influence. //93//
Free from laziness, contented, providing happiness, and a source of awakening;
equanimous toward pleasure and pain and steadfast—such servants are rare to find everywhere. (94)
One who lacks patience and truthfulness, who is cruel, deceitful, and slanderous; who is hypocritical, greedy in disposition, and a snatcher of food—such a person should be abandoned. (95)
One should employ a virtuous beloved in the home, in the kingdom, or in an auspicious place;
however, one should employ a beloved who lacks virtue on the path of liberation or in service. 96.
A beautiful woman should always remain in the company of virtuous women; she should not sit with unvirtuous women, nor should she form friendships with them. 97.
One should remain even while imprisoned with wise women who are devoted to truth, but never with wicked women. (98)
The remaining tasks must be performed by the womenfolk;
if they are abandoned while incomplete, a loss occurs for themselves. (99)
A virtuous wife should extract the honey from her husband like a fly;
she should always make each day fruitful through service, devotion, and other such acts. (3.42.100)
One should abandon passion that is devoid of policy, cultivate affection accompanied by virtue, and practice knowledge free from indolence; she who does so shall conquer the three worlds. 10.1.
A house is not truly called a home by a husband alone; it is only through the mistress that it becomes a home.
Therefore, the house must always be protected by the mistress as if she were its presiding deity.
This must be done by women—by brides and by wise wives—who, considering everything as their own, should serve it and especially cause it to increase. (103)

Thus ends the forty-second chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Demonstration of Right Conduct and Other Matters," within the *Vadhūgītā* of the third section, the *Dvāpara-santāna*, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Puruṣottama said: Listen, O Śrī Nārāyaṇī, to that which the Supreme Lord has spoken regarding the supreme conduct of Śivarājñī-Śrī. || 1 ||
Good character is the ornament of virtuous women; a husband is the ornament of wives;
modesty is the ornament of all; and Lord Hari is the ornament of ornaments.
She who is not Lakṣmī herself, nor even equal to Lakṣmī,
yet whose fortune is fixed upon Hari— she indeed is known as Nārāyaṇī.
She whose mother is Lakṣmī herself and whose father is Janārdana possesses great fortune;
yet she who has no devotion to Hari is to be pitied, for she is bereft of the Lord of Monkeys.
Indeed, the embodied being experiences in due order everything that was previously performed;
for the bed of the womb was created by Brahmā for the sake of the ripening of karmas.
In whatever age, at whatever time, and in whatever manner something is fashioned from whatever cause, it proceeds exactly so, impelled by destiny; it never happens otherwise.
Gifts given, knowledge acquired, and desires fulfilled in the past—
all of these indeed come to embodied beings here in this world in due time for their enjoyment.
In this body obtained through karma, there are indeed many diseases;
moreover, the disease of the womb-cavity always resides within women.
Therefore, O beautiful lady, having reflected with an intellect pregnant with the sacred scriptures,
one should render oneself free from disease from that which is diseased.
She whose self is always purified by truth and purity is pure; she attains heaven, and from there, the state of the Supreme Lord.
With a heart captivated by worldly existence and joined with the leprosy of craving,
one is not purified even by thousands of ritual baths or acts performed at sacred fords.
She who feels no joy in being honored and no agitation in being insulted,
and whose character is always marked by forgiveness— she is considered a virtuous wife and a true daughter-in-law.
Just as a river flowing downward consists of a mass of millions of grains of sand, so too does a noble woman flow downward, consisting of a well-compacted mass of millions of karmas. || 13 ||
The aggregate of the consciousness of water becomes the river that flows along the bank; the aggregate of the consciousness of virtue becomes the noble person who has reached the further shore. 14.
For women of divided households who are attached to distant lands,
there is this supreme action consisting of devotion that unites them with me, Kṛṣṇa.
She who has once uttered the name "Hari" with devotion has attained the imperishable abode, which is characterized by eternal bliss.
If she desires eternal love for me, Mādhava, the Lord of Śrī, she should observe my service; this, I consider, is the supreme means for attaining me.
Trust in all beings, a disposition of goodness born of one's own nature, and constant service to Hari performed in secret—this is indeed considered the "bull" (virtue) by the virtuous woman. 18.
Even if she be wealthy, the Lord abandons a woman who is unclean, whose teeth are stained with grime, who eats excessively, who is harsh, and who sleeps at twilight.

Even a lord abandons a wife who writes on the ground, who cuts grass, whose teeth are unclean, who wears soiled garments, whose hair is coarse, and who sleeps naked—even if she possesses fortune. (3.43.20)
One must never pass between a married couple, between two women, between two animals, or between two swift machines; likewise, one must not go between two people who are angry or engaged in combat.
A verse with six ears is leaked; one with four ears is preserved;
but a report with only two ears never becomes public. (22)
For people attribute fault to a person endowed with forbearance;
they perceive it as incapacity, a lack of strength, worthlessness, and insignificance, like a withered flower offering.
For she is ungrateful, ignoble, long-suffering in her resentment, and crooked;
indeed, a Caṇḍālī is of four kinds, and the fifth is even worse than those. (24)
A young woman who is peaceful is always a peaceful wife;
however, when her physical constituents have declined, women become as many [types of] peaceful beings as there are [remaining]. (25)
For where there is dharma, the ascetic rises for the sake of the sacred ford;
truth exists as the means of his journey, while deceit remains at home. (26)
That house where poverty and strife exist like kinsmen,
and where violence takes the form of a wife— that house is the hollow of Yama.
There is no peace with a bad king, nor is there peace with a bad wife;
there is no fearlessness with a bad friend—one should not act without having reflected upon this.
Another's food, another's property, another's bed, another's wife, another's man, and another's mansion—these indeed cause the destruction of prosperity. (29)

Those with passion for afflictions are indeed base; those with passion for reconciliation are middling; and those with passion for pride are superior—yet they become fit for destruction when their integrity is shattered. (3.43.30)

Among embodied beings, wives are of three types: the lowest are those whose passion is for wealth; the middling are those who follow after the wealth of honor; and the best are those who abide in honor alone. (3.1)
Separation, humiliation, debt, service to the wicked, poverty, and quarrel—these six are burners even without fire. (32)
Life, wealth, youth, and likewise the mind are unstable;
even sons, wives, and husbands are so. Therefore, one should worship the eternal Hari.
Time, consisting of days and nights, carries away the multitude of embodied beings;
knowing Hari to be the Death of Time, one should take refuge in me, the Supreme Person. 34.
What is the life of that woman of pleasure in this world, who is not compassionate toward her own kin, nor toward her teacher, servant, husband, or the destitute—she who is like a crow? (35)
That house in which one passes even a moment devoid of devotion to the Dharma and so forth should be understood as a mere bellows-house, a dwelling for those who merely breathe and sit. (36)

Women fall [from virtue] through indulgence in tastes, negligence, and misplaced trust, as well as through pride and the pursuit of self-interest; therefore, one should always keep them far away from these things. (37)
One should indeed fear as long as the danger has not yet arrived;
but when intense danger has actually presented itself, one must remain truly fearless.
May the life of her who shows no compassion toward a wretched servant, a teacher, a woman, a friend, or a helpless husband be like that of a crow.
Those dependent on others are as if dead, while those who depend on themselves seek the means for life;
those who act for the benefit of others are truly alive even when they have died.
For in whatever measure women here become disciplined by the scriptures, in that same measure they shall be wise and even exponents of the Veda. ||41||
And to whatever extent they apply their own minds to what is wholesome, to that same extent women become truly worthy recipients of honor and deeply beloved. (42)
She who ruins one's affairs behind one's back but speaks pleasantly to one's face must be avoided with great effort, like the *indravāruṇī* creeper.
Even a virtuous woman is ruined through association with a wicked woman;
therefore, a wife must diligently avoid the company of a wicked woman. (44)
Where there is clarity of mind, there indeed are auspicious blessings;
where there is the favor of women, there indeed is the abode of prosperity. (45)
She is a true woman who does not give way to intoxication; she is a true wife who is dear to her husband;
she is truly happy who is free from craving; and she is a daughter-in-law who increases the lineage.
One should not excessively investigate the origins of the virtuous, of rivers, of chaste women, of brides, or of medicinal herbs. (47)
Royal fortune ends with the exhaustion of merit; virtuous conduct ends with sexual union;
family reputation ends with the character of its women; and the end of a lineage is brought about by its women as well. (48)

There is no excellent dwelling where there is no leader, nor even where there are many leaders; there is no excellent dwelling, nor even one that is secure, where the leader is a woman or a fool. (49)
In childhood she is dependent on her father; in youth, she is dependent on her husband;
in old age, she is dependent on her sons; and likewise, in the stage of religious life, she is dependent on truth.
A wife who is dependent on modesty in times of adversity, dependent on fate in prosperity, and dependent on giving in her role as a spouse—that bride is the bestower of happiness. (51)
Having carefully avoided a barren woman, one whose children have died, a mother who speaks unpleasantly,
or one who has no sons, he may marry another for the sake of obtaining a son.

For a woman who is destitute of wealth, even if she is full of fear, she is dependent on her lover; indeed, a woman who is full of wealth, even if she is fearless, is praised only when she is dependent on her lover. (53)
Dharma does not belong to one distressed by wealth, nor fear to one driven by desire; happiness does not belong to one distressed by anxiety. A wife should avoid these states. (54)
Where is there happiness for a servant, a pauper, or an unchaste woman?
Where is there happiness for one burdened by debt, one afflicted by disease, or one who is barren? (55)
For Padmā while established in her place, Varuṇa and Bhāskara are her friends;
for her when fallen from that place, those two cause the withering away of her afflictions.
Even women and even children are well-honored when they remain in their proper place;
but when fallen from their place, they are not honored—just as hair, teeth, nails, and kings [are not honored when out of place]. 57.
Sleep is pleasant for one who is free from debt; likewise, it is pleasant for one who is fearless.
Sleep is pleasant for one who is free from disease, and likewise, it is pleasant for one who has renounced worldly life.
For one who is unattached to men and yet united with the Wielder of the Śārṅga bow, there is a blissful sleep, free from craving—whether she be his own wife or the wife of another. (59)
Just as a lotus attains elevation through its connection with water, so too does a wife attain a high station through a powerful husband. (3.43.60)
In this world, the value of a family is known by its conduct, that of a region by its speech,
that of affection by the eye, and that of food by its appearance.
There is no value for rain upon the ocean, nor for food for one who is already satiated;
likewise, there is no value for a gift to the wealthy, nor for merit bestowed upon the base.
It is said that for one who has gone afar, there is a dwelling in the heart through affection;
for one who stays nearby, dwelling afar is spoken of through enmity. (63)
Miserliness, a dejected voice, extreme emaciation of the limbs,
wretchedness, and fear— these are the signs of those who seek through begging.
For even the great Lord Viṣṇu was born as a dwarf when he was begging;
what other woman, then, would not incur insignificance by seeking a suitor? (65)
The wealth of knowledge should always be acquired, for it is virtuous, bestows goodness, makes one beloved, grants dignity, and destroys suffering. (66)
Knowledge is the supreme deity, a treasure-trove of divine wisdom;
knowledge should be understood as a bride who accomplishes the prosperity of the household. (67)
All external objects are indeed filled with the fear of destruction;
but know that the substance of the Self is free from the fear of destruction.
A wife who possesses self-knowledge is undoubtedly like a sacred pilgrimage site; sons born of such a ground are purifiers and partakers of liberation. 69.
Even for a man who possesses the yoga of sacred pilgrimage sites, liberation may come through his wife;
likewise, the members of the household shall become partakers of the purifying substances of those sites. (3.43.70)
Purified by the merit of their wife as a sacred ford (*tīrtha*), they go to the state of liberation—those whose wife is a great virtuous woman, devoted to the vows of the righteous. (7.1)

Constantly devoted to the practice of dharma, the bride was dedicated to her husband; possessing limbs of great merit and blessed with excellent sons, she was worthy of auspiciousness and spoke the truth. (72)
Pure, acting for the pleasure [of her husband], devoted to pleasing vows, serving her husband, knowledgeable, virtuous, a listener to sacred stories, and possessing great asceticism. (73)
By the very nature of dharma, a virtuous wife is eternally a partner in meritorious deeds;
she follows the path of her husband and is endowed with sacrifices in which her husband is the deity.
A beloved wife who, through her virtuous nature, never leaves her husband, is like a shadow—devoted to the same vows and duties as he. (75)
That husband whose wife is ever established in the vow of devotion to her husband— a vow that grants liberation to women— is indeed one who is composed of Brahman.
She who, though being the wife of her own husband, regards his left foot as the imperishable abode and always considers his right foot to be of the nature of the Supreme Brahman; 77.
A beautiful woman who bathes in the water from his feet becomes equal to Brahmā;
indeed, she is considered to be equal to all sacred fords and to dwell in all sacred fords. 78.
Whatever merit arises from the performance of sacrifices, a much greater merit than that is produced by devotion to one's husband. (79)
There is no duty for a noble woman apart from service to her husband;
therefore, accompanied by her beloved, she is always the bestower of happiness. (3.43.80)
Meritorious, most meritorious, and virtuous, she is preeminent throughout the three worlds;
she should never be abandoned, neither in this world nor in the next. (81)
By him who has abandoned a wife who is well-conducted and a practitioner of dharma, even the tenfold dharma itself would be abandoned here. (82)
Whenever the husband goes to another village,
the virtuous wife indeed lies upon the ground and does not even apply cosmetics.
The virtuous woman does not consume ghee, oil, milk, or drinks; she does not eat curd or sweets;
indeed, she never eats betel leaf, honey, or sweet foods. 84.
Wearing a single braid of hair and clad in a single bodice, she,
unable to endure separation, awaits his arrival.
A union with a husband arises for women through the accumulation of merit;
indeed, the husband is always the sacred ford for women, and she likewise is for the husband. (86)
One should always mutually invoke [the deity] through speech, body, and actions;
one should always worship with a sincere heart and a spirit of truthfulness. (87)
The right limb and the left limb are indeed always two sacred fords (tīrtha);
they constantly enable one hundred members of the family to cross over.
Great happiness, the good fortune of having sons, and even the good fortune of wealth—as well as beauty, splendor, renown, and fame—all come to a husband through the grace of his wife. (89)
For women, youth and beauty are considered the wealth of their husband;
when the husband is satisfied, all the worlds in this cycle of existence are auspicious for the woman. (3.43.90)
Even if she is beautiful and endowed with all riches, how can there be happiness for her who is bereft of a husband? [What of] beauty, fame, renown, sons, and so forth? (91)
Wicked women, deprived of their husbands, experience misfortune and great suffering;
yet when the husband is satisfied, the gods, sages, humans, and celestial beings are all pleased. (92)
The ancestors, too, will be satisfied and bestow happiness upon both worlds;
for the husband is the lord, the master, the guru, and a deity along with all the gods.
For women, the husband is their sacred pilgrimage site, their merit, and the weight of their fortune;
he is their adornment, their beauty, their complexion, and even their fragrance. (94)
The husband is heaven, the husband is dharma, and the husband is indeed good fortune;
the husband is the lineage, the husband is splendor—for a woman, her very being depends upon the husband. (95)
Without dharma, without a wife, and without a virtuous master, even a home becomes like a forest and indeed like a cremation ground. (96)
Where the bride is devoted to her husband and the husband likewise observes his vows toward his wife;
where there is prosperity and affection, and indeed where there is devotion to Brahman.
Where there is constant worship of the gods, where there is honor for women, where there is the protection of maidens, and where there is service to mothers. ||98||
Where the fool rejoices, and where the woman delights;
where indeed the heart of the woman blooms and exults. (99)
In that regard, there is heaven for the lords, as well as prosperity and the state of the Brahma-world;
therefore, O Lakṣmī, let those devoted to virtuous conduct become dear to Brahmā.
They are always devoted to me, truthful, dedicated to virtuous conduct,
eternally intent upon the true Dharma, and devoted to the worship of the gods.
They were entirely devoted to their husbands and devoted to the vows of Hari, and they were always solely intent upon the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
"O all my dear daughters-in-law, may you receive this treasure-trove of bliss;
for through your happiness, all my own eternal happiness is secured. (103)
The duties of a wife are as sharp as the edge of a sword, yet they remain dear when performed for the sake of her beloved;
by remaining steadfast in guarding them, you shall become one with my very self.

Thus ends the forty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Conduct and Duties of the Bride," within the *Vadhūgītā* of the third section, the *Dvāpara-santāna*, of the glorious *Lakṣmīnārāyaṇīya-saṃhitā*.
Śrī Puruṣottama said: Listen, O Nārāyaṇī Śrī, to this auspicious tale of a former birth,
which the great seer Vedāyana related to his wife in the past.
I shall proclaim the most excellent and unsurpassed devotion to one's husband;
listen, O beautiful lady, to that which is expressed through speech, mind, and action. (2)
O Āgrayaṇa, listen with joy to the duties that bring prosperity to a bride:
she performs service to her husband every day with her own heartfelt devotion. (3)
Whether he is angry or even destitute, the devoted wife does not abandon him;
she does not perceive his fault and remains satisfied even when struck.
She who serves her beloved husband—whether he be afflicted with leprosy or even a mere beggar—always stands before him in all his tasks; she is a virtuous wife (satī).
By the grace of her husband, she surely goes to the auspicious world of her lord,
even if he be fallen, diseased, humpbacked, maimed, or afflicted by illness.
If a wife desires her own welfare, she should never abandon her husband—even if he is impotent, devoid of dharma, fallen into sin, or beset by calamities. (7)
If she should abandon her beloved husband and go elsewhere for the sake of some business, devoid of affection,
she would incur her husband’s curse and fall into the state of a wanton woman.
If, when her husband has departed, she indulges in amorous decoration and lewdness,
she shall, through the force of passion, fall away from her current state of existence.
That woman who, having abandoned her own husband, always dwells in her father’s house, is devoid of ritual and devoid of dharma; such a woman deserves punishment.
For she who, having abandoned the life of a housewife, wanders to another dwelling, is not complete; indeed, such a woman is unfortunate, for her husband is her god.
Having abandoned her husband, that pitiless sinner dwells in the great garden and other places, adorned with ornaments and attire fit for amorous dalliance.
She who has abandoned her own husband is called a *puṃścalī*;
a wife who sleeps on a separate bed is declared a *puṃścalī*, devoid of dharma. (13)
Deprived of sight and lacking the eye of Dharma, she was abandoned by her husband; for in every situation, a man who upholds the Dharma is the sole husband of his wife.
A maiden who remains long in her father's house goes to ruin;
a beloved wife who resides in her husband's house attains long life. (15)
Devoted to her husband, highly fortunate, and embodying all sacred fords,
that virtuous goddess is eternal, consisting of all things, and indeed composed of all dharma.
Furthermore, whoever gives even for a single day the merit arising from devotion to her husband to a woman who has fallen into an evil state, [attains great reward].
Through the Piśācinī rite, liberation shall occur and likewise the pacification of sins;
though the body inevitably perishes, one should cultivate the virtue of devotion to one's husband.
Two worms named Piṅgalā and Śṛṅgalī are located at the roots of the ears;
Capala and Pippala are these two that reside at the tips of the nostrils.
Bhṛṅgalī and Jaṅgalī reside within the eyes,
and likewise, ever-new worms exist throughout all the limbs.
And by those [fires], the body of one devoted to the duty toward her husband is consumed;
therefore, having reflected, a daughter-in-law must accomplish the dharma consisting of devotion to her husband.
Indeed, the incomparable power and majesty of virtuous women who regard their husband as their deity is such that neither the Creator,
nor the sun, nor even fire is capable of enduring it.
Worthy of honor and true, her virtuous nature is always revered;
she possesses patience, tranquility, celibacy, compassion, self-restraint, and friendliness. (23)
Wisdom, contentment, sovereignty, straightforwardness, and likewise purity—these perfections, like wish-fulfilling creepers, truly dwell within the body. 24.
The gurus and the ancestors, Viṣṇu accompanied by Lakṣmī, Hara together with Satī, and the Creator of the Universe along with Sāvitrī. (25)
The gods, led by Agni, come to the house of a virtuous woman,
even if she is a mere housewife, provided she stands upon the path to liberation.
Even when there are virtuous householders who abide in the nobility of wisdom and are devoted to the Dharma, the deities always dwell among them.
I, Mādhava, dwell in the house of even a devotee’s family;
and wherever there are capable holy men and virtuous women, there too I dwell.
Indeed, for me who am united with ten thousand beloveds of Brahmā, my home is truly the chamber of Satī;
I always dwell within that house, which is adorned with the virtues of devotion to one's husband and the like.
O Narayani, even all the lords and masters go for the sake of a sight to the home of a devoted wife where I dwell.
Physical beauty, charm, elegance, pleasure, and even prosperity—these shine as the constant and total possession of women when directed toward a beloved. (31)
A beloved wife, even if she is destitute, must never be abandoned by her husband;
he who abandons her incurs fault and becomes a violator of the dharma of virtuous women.
He who departs, abandoning his disciplined, pure, and meritorious bride, has rendered all his performed merit futile by causing the bride to lament. || 33 ||
He who departs, abandoning a virtuous wife who is devoted to righteous conduct, meritorious, chaste, and endowed with excellent qualities, does not obtain the fruit of dharma. || 34 ||
Devoted to all proper conduct, virtuous, and intent on accumulating a mass of merit; she was devoted to the service of her husband with supreme fidelity, wise, and a source of delight. (35)
In whose house there is a wife who possesses the qualities of wisdom, is auspiciously devoted, and is a great satī, O God, the deities always reside there. (36)
The ancestors desire such a son and daughter-in-law in every respect;
the daughter-in-law is meritorious, virtuous, and abides in truthfulness within the home. (37)
There, sacrifices, gods, and merit-bestowing sacred fords, as well as wish-fulfilling cows and desire-granting creepers, dwell forever. (38)
Therein reside all meritorious holy places, rivers, and streams; therein dwell the goddesses of fortune and prosperity as well. (39)
At the sacred ford of the wife, yogis abide, possessing the nature of all merit;
through the union with the wife, the feet of the husband take on the very form of a sacred ford.
By dwelling with a virtuous wife, the household life becomes truly auspicious and divinely blessed;
it indeed consists of all sacrifices and bestows the fruits of all vows.
The home of a householder is meritorious, and a wife devoted to her husband is meritorious;
it is there that all the eternal dharmas prevail.
The practices of giving and virtuous conduct prevail, as do festivals of great joy;
yet a forest devoid of a wife is infested with tigers and filled with suffering. (43)

There is no sacred ford equal to a wife, the supreme means for accomplishing dharma; whether in the forest, the village, or the wilderness, the sacred ford of a faithful wife indeed bestows liberation.
There is no merit equal to a wife; there is no happiness equal to a wife;
there is no wisdom equal to a wife for the sake of crossing over and for one's welfare. 41.
Having abandoned his virtuous lawful wife, he who sets his mind elsewhere—having forsaken the duties of the household, what fruit indeed shall there be for him? (46)
When auspicious śrāddha or charity is performed at a sacred site (tīrtha) without one's wife, everything becomes fruitless; therefore, one should not abandon one's spouse. ||47||
Just as the satisfaction of the ancestors arises through the offering of nectar, so too does their satisfaction arise through the funeral cake (piṇḍa) offered by the wife. ||48||
In the dharma of the householder, however, the wife is the mistress;
for without her, the śrāddha offered becomes merely lukewarm. (49)
And when the wife cooks food with her own hand that is like nectar, the ancestors eat that very food with delighted minds. (3.44.50)
By that alone they attain satisfaction and become content;
therefore, without a wife, the dharma of men is not accomplished.
A virtuous wife is a daughter-in-law who constantly and certainly accomplishes dharma;
sacrifices do not attain success in a home devoid of a housewife.
The sons of Dharma—beginning with Puṇya, Jñāna, and the others—are powerful and have truth and righteousness as their gateway;
they are indeed the companions of Dharma who protect Satī in every way. 13.
Satī remained devoted to protection, dedicated to self-restraint and tranquility;
neither Time nor Yama himself was indeed able to overcome her.
If any person should look upon a virtuous wife in the absence of her husband,
he too shall surely be reduced to ashes by the fire of that virtuous woman's eyes.
Wherever the highly fortunate Satī, the bride who is the embodiment of all auspiciousness, resides,
the gods, satisfied by her truthfulness, grant even boons.
Even the fires and the deities follow her as she goes;
the household deities follow her, and the forest goddesses follow her as well. (57)
When Satī goes to bathe in the water, the goddesses of the waters come to meet her;
and when Satī goes on a pilgrimage to sacred fords, the sacred fords themselves come to meet her.
When Satī was going to the temple of the gods, the deities rushed toward her;
and when Satī was going to the garden, the goddesses of the field rushed toward her. (59)
When Satī goes to the sacrificial ground, the goddesses of sacrifice follow her;
and when Satī departs for exile, the Earth follows after Satī.
The divine mothers of the ancestors, seeking water, attend upon the virtuous woman as she bathes;
they drink the water squeezed from her garment by means of her body.

The joy that a wife always experiences in her own home through devotion to her husband does not exist even in heaven; the happiness of a virtuous woman is attainable only through spiritual perfection.
The supernatural powers, such as atomization (aṇimā) and the rest, indeed serve the devoted wife;
her desires reach fulfillment exactly as they are conceived. ||63||
Viṣṇu, Brahmā, Hara, Indra, Sūrya, Candra, Yama,
and Guru bow to Satī and worship that virtuous woman.
All the gods desire their own wives to be virtuous in every way;
even the kings who protect the quarters of the world stand in awe of the power of a woman’s virtue.
Where truth is her vow, she is considered a *satī* in every respect;
where her husband’s vow is her own, she is indeed a *pativratā*.
She who observes the vow of Brahman is Satī Brāhmī, devoted to her husband;
and she who is exclusively mine is Satī Śrīpuruṣottamī.
I, the Lord Śrī Puruṣottama, am obtained through great merit;
my attainment occurs here from the treasury of virtuous conduct accumulated over a hundred births.
Merely by the power of her true resolve, diseases depart far away;
obstacles likewise flee afar, and even Gaṇeśa indeed stands in awe.
King Yama fears such a place, and Time keeps far away;
moreover, the mothers are gracious in that household where a devoted wife resides.
Having attained peace, Caṇḍī and the other goddesses protect the house of the chaste woman;
indeed, the seizing spirits of children do not enter the boundary of the house of the chaste woman.
Even plagues, diseases, and spells that cause delusion and confusion, as well as rites of eradication and the like, flee from the home of a virtuous woman upon reaching her. (72)
Even Hanumān, though possessing the character of Brahmā and being a virtuous commander-in-chief,
and even that personage known as Brahmacharya, bows from afar to a chaste woman.
Even portents such as lightning, rain, and oceans become terrifying;
even the virtuous abandon their own persistence at the word of a chaste woman.
Even the lords, when in the presence of a devoted wife, sometimes suffer defeat and yet honor her command of truth. (75)
By the anger of Satī, serpents and other venomous creatures were reduced to ashes;
mountains and the like dissolved away, and even the oceans dried up.
The planets, having abandoned their course, become motionless when struck by punishment;
likewise, the mental deities such as desire and the rest go to dissolution through the power of a virtuous woman.
By the true blessing of Bhavānī, latent impressions are utterly consumed;
and through the will of Satī, the dissolution of Mahāmāyā occurs.
Drought results from the anger of a virtuous woman; rain comes from her delight.
Even the prosperity of the world-lineage perishes through the curse of a virtuous woman.
By the will of Satī, the entire world is born anew;
wherever Satī, the bride, dwells, there I myself am present as the Lord.
In Virāja he is joined with Dhāman, and likewise with Muktā and the others;
in Virāja he is united with his attendants (pārṣadas), and in Virāja he is endowed with Dharma.
In Virāja, Śrīpati Puruṣottama is endowed with devotion;
in Virāja, I am present in person at the home of Satī, endowed with all prosperity.
She is indeed Satī, the virtuous one, devoted to Brahman, and a devotee of Nārāyaṇa; she is considered a faithful wife, a follower of the Sāttvata path, and a great Bhāgavatī. 8.3.
I, known as Saccidānanda, dwell in the house of Satī; moreover, by the will of Satī, I manifest my birth within her lineage. (84)
I am ever pleased in the home of the illustrious Satī; I am the Lord Himself, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, who is affectionate toward His devotees. (85)
And in that regard, I am most perfectly complete; no deficiency exists, nor does any lack occur, nor even any doubt. (86)
Truly, his birth is fruitful, his home is likewise fruitful,
and the expansion of his lineage is fruitful— he in whose house Hari and a virtuous wife reside.
For him in whose house Hari dwells as a virtuous wife, dharma is always fruitful, his actions are fruitful, and all his efforts are fruitful. (88)
And there is constant bliss, as well as welfare and health of every kind, where there are virtuous women, Hari, Dharma, ascetics, holy men, and gods. (89)
In that place where worldly and otherworldly success may arise, the virtuous remain for even a moment; there, Hari himself is present.
In a previous birth, he performed supreme and incomparable merit, by which he obtained a virtuous wife and Lord Hari, the Supreme Person. (91)
The principal gods and the virtuous come constantly to behold Satī;
this Aśvapaṭṭasara lake is my own abode, known by the name of Śiva.
Therefore, indeed, great merit prevails in this land, where my wives exist by the millions and tens of millions. || 93 ||
O Lakṣmī, you have been beheld by me; those who are like you are my very self, and I am Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, Hari, the most perfect one.
Together with my daughters-in-law, I reside in the divine land of Surāṣṭra, at the imperishable and excellent field of mine known as Kuṅkuma. || 95 ||
I, the lord of the abode of creation, have been brought under control by your devotion;
O Lakṣmī, I dwell before you and remain subject to your will in your palace.
"Oh, all these beloveds of Brahmā receive my essence from Hari;
out of compassion, they drink the mass of bliss and my nectar. (97)
May you, who are dear to Brahman, whose form is the Supreme Brahman, and who are identical with me, be devoted to my dharma; for women are indeed the bestowers of auspiciousness. 98.
Blessed is this Kuṅkumavāpī, blessed indeed is this Vyāghravana;
blessed is the Aśvasaras lake, and blessed is the land of Surāṣṭra.
Blessed is the land, and blessed too are its people, its trees, and its creepers;
blessed are the clumps of grass, the plants, the cattle, and the men and women. (3.44.100)
Blessed indeed is this time, and blessed too are these living beings,
for whom union with the glorious Hari occurs here moment after moment.
Wherein the eternal and blissful Dharma, enriched by the family, abides;
and wherein liberation, devotion, and love are indeed firmly established.
Thinking thus, those men and women who consider themselves blessed and remember the duties of a faithful wife (satīdharma), they too shall go to my abode.
From reciting, hearing, and reading this dharma of virtuous women,
as well as from its preservation, liberation and spiritual perfection shall certainly be attained.
Through this investigation, his lineage, prosperity, fame, honor, health, influence, abundance, and lordship shall flourish. (1.05)

Thus ends the forty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Power of Satī’s Truth," within the *Vadhūgītā* of the third section, the *Dvāpara-santāna*, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*. || 44 ||
The illustrious Śrī Nārāyaṇī said: O God of gods, ocean of mercy, Supreme Person, Mādhava!
Your yoga of devotion is beyond the material qualities; how can it be truly accomplished toward You?
For the benefit of all the worlds and for the sake of all women, I wish to hear what must indeed be performed by us, who are all beloved of Brahmā.
Likewise, whatever has been done by other women and even by men—just as it was done, I wish to hear that correctly; please tell me that.
All these sisters of mine, numbering in the hundreds of millions, billions, and trillions, desire to hear this; they have sent me here, O beloved one.
Therefore, I ask you: please tell us here about the yoga of devotion which is beyond all qualities.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
"Indeed, actions accompanied by the qualities (guṇas) are truly fruitful;
those very same actions, when their fruits are surrendered unto Me, are indeed devoid of qualities (nirguṇa)."
O beloved, action joined with desire for fruit becomes a cause of bondage;
action joined with no desire for fruit becomes the giver of liberation.
People who are characterized by *sattva*, having performed deeds of *sattva*, go to heaven; those characterized by *rajas*, having performed *rājasa* rites, remain in the world of men.
People who are characterized by darkness go to worlds of impurity, where they dissolve into that darkness;
but having attained Me, who am devoid of qualities, they indeed go to My imperishable state.
O beloved, those people who dwell in the forest practicing the five-fire austerity, who are free from blemish and partake of the fruits [of their penance], go to the world of the Seven Sages.
Those who dwell in the stage of renunciation (saṃnyāsa), carrying the staff and other emblems,
and whose dharma consists of having conquered their senses and minds, go to Satyaloka.
Endowed with the eightfold yoga, self-controlled, with vital energy drawn upward, and cleansed of all taints, they proceed to Maharloka and Janaloka. ||1||
The performers of sacrifice and the patrons go for long to the abode of Indra;
the givers go to the world of Soma, which rains down nectar.
Those who observe vows indeed go to the world of the Sun with great splendor;
and those who follow the paths of the sacred fords go to the radiant world of Fire by virtue of their merit.
Those who observe the vow of truth likewise go to the supreme world of Varuṇa;
those endowed with devotion to Viṣṇu go to Vaikuṇṭha, from which there is no return.
Those endowed with devotion to Śambhu go eternally to the upward-moving Kailāsa;
likewise, those who perform sacrifices for their ancestors do so out of a desire for the happiness, sovereignty, and other blessings for their sons.
By the southern path, they go to the world of the ancestors through Aryaman;
those who perform meritorious deeds and are devoted to the dharma of mindfulness go to heaven.
Those richly devoted to the worship of the five deities go to the celestial realm;
those who perform sacrifices to Prajāpati go to the world of the Prajāpatis, such as Dakṣa and others.
Those who perform sacrifices to the elements go to various kinds of beings,
and those who worship the principles beginning with *bhū* (earth) indeed proceed to the enclosures (*āvaraṇas*).
Those who sacrifice to the Yakṣas go to the worlds of the Yakṣas, such as that of Kubera;
and those who sacrifice to the Īśvaras attain the stations of the Īśvaras.
Ascetics go to Badarī, while the virtuous go to Śvetadvīpa; those who observe the vow of Brahman go to the worlds of the Vairājas for their disciplined conduct.
Virtuous women go to the worlds of chaste wives, possessing the splendor of the sun;
likewise, those women devoted to dharma go to the worlds of Lakṣmī and the worlds of Śrī.
Devoted wives go to the worlds of Hari and the worlds of their husbands;
even those who practice celibacy go to the worlds of those who practice celibacy.
Those who know their duties go to the world of the Gaṇas and to the worlds of the Gaṇas;
those devoted to Īśa go to the worlds of Īśa, and those devoted to Prāṇa go to the realm of the Maruts.
The Asuras go to the worlds of Nirṛti, while the sinners go to the world of Yama;
those who practice self-restraint and those devoted to austerity go to the worlds of the Ṛṣis and others.
Those who delight in the knowledge of the Vedas and are free from passion go to Satyaloka;
those who practice renunciation go to Vaikuṇṭha, situated above the region surrounded by water.

Those who perform sacrifices for the sake of power go to the worlds of the Siddhas and beautiful women; those who give wealth go to the world of the Vasus, and those who smear themselves with ashes go to the abode of Rudra.
People who practice the penance of the five fires go to the solar orb;
those possessed by desire go to the lunar world, as do those devoted to the giving of cooling gifts.
Those who perform cruel deeds go to the abodes of Rākṣasas;
even those possessed of strong latent tendencies (vāsanās) go into the wombs of Piśācas.
Those who perform acts such as offering lamps proceed to the realm of fire;
those who bestow prosperity go indeed to heaven, which is like a constellation and full of exquisite splendor.
Those who give gardens and fields attain the status of a sovereign on earth;
likewise, those possessed of learning attain the station of Sarasvatī.
Those who destroy the Dharma go to a terrible state belonging to the Dānavas; indeed, the Daityas become unrighteous and filled with agitation. 3.1.
And when enraged, those of cruel deeds become nāgas and serpents;
they go to births among aquatic creatures, causing the depletion of water.
All worlds are considered to end in truth, yet they are subject to return; the path of actions accompanied by their causal motives consists of coming and going. (33)
Joy and delight endure only as long as merit exists;
when merit is exhausted, one indeed descends to a lower world in the course of time. (34)
Therefore, O Lakṣmī, whatever action is performed should be offered to the Supreme Lord;
through the renunciation of the fruits of action, it becomes free from the qualities (nirguṇa) within me. 35.
Having become devotees without motive, endowed with knowledge and detachment, and possessed of loving devotion, they were dear to Kṛṣṇa and to the people who are devotees of Hari. ||36||
"O beloved, resort to my feet, which are served by swans and free from fear;
O beloved, always resort to me, in whom even Death is not powerful. (37)
O Lakṣmī, the yoga of devotion is twofold: with attributes (saguṇa) and without attributes (nirguṇa).
The saguṇa is indeed manifold, while the nirguṇa is considered to be of one kind. (38)
The disposition of women is indeed always differentiated according to their qualities;
from the threefold set of qualities, they arise as devotees, beautiful in their threefold divisions. (39)
Resorting to violence, hypocrisy, envy, deceit, and self-interest, she manifests a state of being that is full of anger; she is considered to be *tāmasī*. (3.45.40)
O Queen Śivā, that [worship] which one performs with effort, without aiming for fame, power, or sense objects, is proclaimed as the rājasī. 41.
She who, thinking "this must be done," performs service free from attachment for the sake of liberation, is known as a sāttvika devotee who serves Me. 42.
One who is suffering, one who seeks his own interest, one who is discerning, and a wise man—these indeed worship me;
women, however, worship me for some motive, as they do with any vessel of merit.
Out of affection, my devotees, ever happy, worship me;
others also worship and remember me, whether through virtues or faults.
The virtuous perform the path of devotion (bhaktiyoga) toward Me which is devoid of qualities;
and those virtuous women who are free from passion worship the excellent Hari. 45.
To the most perfect one, the cause of all causes, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the beloved Lord of Śrī; ||46||
The movement of love is uninterrupted, indivisible, causeless, and auspicious;
that devotion is beyond qualities, divine, and has as its fruit serenity toward me. 47.

That affection which is for the sake of destroying suffering, neither for one's own sake nor purposeless, and which is obtainable through the grace of Hari—she who possesses that is considered *nirguṇā* (devoid of [worldly] qualities). 48.
Just as devotion is beyond the material qualities (nirguṇa), so too is the maidservant beyond the qualities;
she is a natural stream of love directed toward that Supreme Person (Śrī Puruṣottama). ||49||
That form of love, though devoid of qualities, flows toward me when directed;
its fruit is the nature of bliss, and its result is eternal satisfaction.
Full blossoming is the fruit, enthusiasm is the fruit, and joy is the fruit;
oh, oh! that state which is wise, sweet as nectar, and most desirable.
And the fruit of the *nirguṇī* is considered to be the giver of the essence of nectar, which occurs immediately after the marriage of a young bride or a youthful woman. (52)
Just as a stream flows from the desire to unite with one's own beloved, so too do fresh bliss, joy, blossoming, and clarity arise. (53)
An abundance of oil, complete satisfaction, contentment, and likewise peace—indeed, everything that is sweet and excellent shines forth as it does for a bride. (54)
Likewise, for noble ones possessed of devotion, everything shines forth within me;
she is this Vidyā, the mother of the Vedas, devoid of attributes (nirguṇā), and identical with my own nature.
This [knowledge] is never produced anywhere apart from me;
it is this very eternal Vidyā of the Bhāgavatas, belonging to Puruṣottama. (56)
This very state of serenity is attainable through dwelling within me;
it is indeed not obtainable by any other means, for it is devoid of attributes and cannot exist without that which is devoid of attributes.
Indeed, for a servant there is no affection for the king without the king's grace;
likewise, this yoga does not arise at all apart from my grace. (58)

O Lotus-born One, hear from me the characteristics of my devotees who are free from the material qualities (nirguṇa), as well as the imperishable realm (akṣara), Goloka, Vaikuṇṭha, and the White Realm (śvetabhūtala). 59.
The abode of milk, Badrikā, or the station of Parameṣṭhin;
the unmanifest (avyākṛta), the immortal (amṛta), the world of Lakṣmī, Prakuṇṭhaka,
Vairāja, and the various stations of the Īśvaras.

The throne of Śakra, universal sovereignty, lordship over the [six] flavors, the status of a world-protector, the state of Yama, the supernatural power of yoga, and the supreme Vaiśvara [status]. ||61||
Those devotees who serve at my feet do not desire wonders, supernatural powers, or even great sovereignities.
O Lakṣmī, though I offer them even the supreme state of residing in the same world as me,
those who are filled with the bliss of my service never accept it.
Moreover, due to the pride of their love, they do not even desire proximity, for it is indeed a wound;
even separation is an obstacle to union, for that [proximity] is a great obstacle to touch.
But when love that exists for one who is near sometimes attains a state of distance, then, because it is equal to my own association, no proximity exists anywhere [for me]. (65)
Moreover, even when a likeness is being offered, gathered from my own mind, my devotees do not accept it at all, because of their pride in their own equality [with me]. (66)
Impartiality toward my servants is an obstacle, and indifference is likewise an obstacle;
therefore, those eager to serve me do not accept a form identical to mine.
Now, my people do not desire unity even when it is being offered;
for indeed, unity would only exist in a state of melting or dissolution. (68)
If that were so, how could there be happiness arising from the relationship between master and servant? Surely the happiness obtainable by a maidservant would not come from her beloved, Hari. (69)
If, however, the devotee were formless, unity would indeed be possible;
but this being so, how could the bliss born of yoga exist in one form within another form? (3.45.70)
Because they do not desire solitude, they do not obtain the happiness of service;
thus, they are independent, peaceful, and endowed with equal vision.
Women devoid of virtue seek after the pleasure of their beloveds;
those who have taken refuge in Hari possess detachment, which is the supreme happiness. (72)
Those with desires experience great happiness, but those free from desire do not;
indeed, the yoga of devotion without desire leads to the ultimate state. ||73||
Free from expectations, my beloved ones always worship me through various means:
by mindfulness, by chanting, by hearing, and by service. (74)
Through worship, through salutation, through servitude, through friendship,
and even through self-surrender, they indeed practice devotion with love.
Rare are those women who possess devotion for me, who are imbued with the contemplation of my nature, and who likewise show respect toward great beings as well as compassion. (76)
Those who practice loving-kindness toward the wretched and the equal, who drink the nectar from my lotus feet, and who long for union with me—[they are the ones]. (77)
May they remember me, their lord of life, as do women whose husbands are away from home;
for at the mere thought of me, their hair stands on end and perspiration breaks forth. (78)
With tears of joy falling and their complexions changed by the intensity of love,
they continued to chant the praises of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
Day and night they are attached to me; they are indeed the most excellent devotees of the Lord (bhāgavatottama).
Their minds are fixed on me, their hearts are mine, and they have surrendered their very bodies to me alone. (3.45.80)
And those most excellent great devotees, who experience bliss in me alone—whether on earth, in water, in fire, in air, in space, or among the stars—[attain liberation]. (81)
In forests and wildernesses, among moving beings, they behold me, the Supreme Lord, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, and are filled with great joy. (82)
Looking about, the amorous women weep and speak;
in some places they rejoice, run, laugh, and search.
They sing and call out to the fierce one; they dance and take delight;
they sport, chatter, and behold me within the midst of the trees.
In some instances, these [energies], whose nature is mine and whose essence is mine, become silent;
having accomplished their task and achieved their purpose, they are overflowing with all-encompassing bliss. (85)
Merely by the sight of them, others attain their purpose;
for those brides are divine, possessing celestial forms and divine activities. (86)
For those who are eternal, neither Time nor Yama, nor the Earth, nor Mahārudra is ever capable of inflicting punishment. (87)
In whose left hand is the Kaumodakī mace and in the right the Sudarśana disc;
at the front is the Śārṅga bow, and at the back the conch Pāñcajanya.
The great sword Nandaka and the hundred-mooned shield are likewise in front;
arrows are all around, and a parasol is positioned above. (89)
The staff, as well as the feet and the sides, are the millions of sovereign powers; and all the supernatural attainments (siddhis) are my beloved ones who protect me within my form. 3.45.90.
Above, the great lotus umbrella provides beautiful shade;
moreover, Garuḍa becomes the remover of fatigue with the winds from his wings. (9.1)
Wherever the virtuous go, there the Lord Hari is present;
I, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, wander everywhere.
I shall make the regions of the earth sacred through the dust of your glorious lotus feet;
for wherever you, O virtuous ones, have stayed for even a moment, there indeed lie holy shrines.
Even a sinner who dies there attains the supreme goal; and upon seeing her from afar, even mental anxieties and physical ailments vanish for those dear to Kṛṣṇa.
The spirits, ghosts, piśācas, and others, as well as seizing demons, obstacles, rākṣasas, asuras, and those who partake in faults, all flee out of fear of me. (95)
Rivers, streams, mountains, walls, moats, pits, abysses, oceans, and likewise fires— (96)
They grant the path to virtuous women who are indeed indifferent [to worldly things], for [the path belongs] to those women who are virtuous, established in knowledge, and dispassionate. 97.
For those who consist of me, there is indeed no obstruction anywhere;
they are purified by the penance of a hundred births and endowed with a multitude of merits. 98.
She attains their union, which is difficult to obtain for those whose merit has declined—that in my lineage a devotee is born indeed, possessing the characteristics of Brahmā. (99)
That family is stainless and worthy of awakening; though lowly, it shall ascend upward.
O Lakṣmī, you who are endowed with devotion shall be possessed of all sovereign powers.
He also delivers ten generations of ancestors born from his own family, as well as those on his husband’s side and those on his mother’s side, an equal number of each.
She is considered endowed with the power to uplift the entire universe, and indeed capable of casting those bound by sin into the hells. (102)
Those who possess bodies, as well as relatives—both male and female—and those such as servants, friends, and laborers, both male and female; || 103 ||
Birds, beasts, and other creatures such as mosquitoes; ants, moths, insects, flies, and the like. || 104 ||
For those male and female devotees of mine who reside in their homes, there is indeed liberation for them—of this there is no doubt—even without sacrifices, pilgrimages, or bulls. 105.
Through association with virtuous women, even they go to the abode of Hari;
indeed, my devotees purify even a defiled region.
Whosoever has their mind attached to me through any state of being,
even they attain my own nature through such practice of mine, in whatever way that may be.
Having become absorbed in my nature through affection, desire, fear, anger, unity, friendship, and delusion, that virtuous woman goes to my abode.
Out of affection, parents and villagers [follow]; out of desire, those dear to Brahmanas;
out of fear, Daityas and Dānavas; and out of anger, warriors on the field of battle. (109)
Through oneness, there are countless householders; through friendship, the stainless sages;
and through delusion, women by the millions—having all become meditations upon me.
Those whose minds were intensely attached to the state of my own form, qualities, and power have indeed attained me, the Lord Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. 111.
Therefore, by whatever means one may fix the mind upon Me, let there be constant remembrance of Me; through that, one attains My state of being. 11.2.

Thus ends the forty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Yoga of Attribute-less Devotion," within the *Vadhūgītā* of the third section, the *Dvāpara-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Nārāyaṇī Śrī, to the specific application of devotion;
neither fame, nor sacrifice, nor dharma, nor austerity restrains me.
Neither yoga nor even solitude, nor vows nor restraints; neither sacred fords nor Vedic meters, nor meritorious works nor observances [can save one]. (2)
Neither charity, nor sacrificial fee, nor the officiating priest can ever exist without devotion;
whatever is attained through fame and the like, all that is indeed attained [through devotion]. (3)
O Lakṣmī, by even a very slight degree of devotion one attains the state of devotion;
however, that state of devotion cannot be attained by those who are incapable and who merely occupy their seats.
For my devotion is indeed the purifier that removes all sins from the universe;
it is the deliverer from the ocean of worldly existence and the destroyer of karmas.
The Vasantapañcamī bestows honors, grants the highest blessings, and bestows the state of Hari; it grants delight to the hearts of devoted followers.
She is a wish-fulfilling creeper for those who are affectionate, a thought-gem for those who have desires,
a flash of lightning for those devoted to the blind, and a lamp for those who follow the scriptures.
The Festival of Lights is the preeminent celebration for those of virtuous deeds;
this Vijayā-daśamī is auspicious for those who are victorious through self-restraint.

She is a boat for those desiring to reach the further shore, a celestial chariot for those seeking the sky; she is a source of warmth for those immersed in cold, and a giver of life to those afflicted by hunger.

Initiation is the life-giver to those scorched by poison, the bringer of prosperity to those desiring the highest good, the ladder to the abode of the Imperishable, and the mother of those undertaking the sacred vows.
My devotion is beyond the gunas; she who holds the staff [of authority] for me always bestows yoga.
She grants the abode of Brahman, bestows the bliss of Brahman, and is never-receding.
Śrī, Pārvatī, Kamalajā, Tulasī, Padmā, Padmāvatī, the daughter of Bhṛgu, Padminī,
Rādhā, Ramā, Virajā, and Sarasvatī.
Durgā, Ramā, Badarī, Padmaratī, and Lakṣmī. || 12 ||
Revā, Rati, Lalitā, Jayā, Haṃsī, Bhakti, Mādhavasutā, then Māṇikī,
Nārāyaṇī, Suguṇā, and Mañjulā.
By means of this recitation, women cross over the ocean of existence. ||13||
Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of the Imperishable, the Supreme Person, Kṛṣṇa, Hari, the Supreme Sovereign, the Lord of Lords,
the Master, the Ruler, the Lord of the Supreme Abode, and the Highest Lord.
Here, Kṛṣṇa, who has assumed a human form, dwells within all.
Dark-hued and white, the Lord of all devotees, dwelling in the heart;
though transcending Brahman, he abides within the assembly of his own devotees.
By the recitation of my auspicious name, "Lord of the Beloved of Brahman," [may there be liberation].
But those men who possess devotion to me go to the further shore. || 15 ||
Through association with the virtuous, the sprout of devotion indeed becomes well-leafed;
and when watered by association with the chaste, it grows with extreme rapidity. (16)
Therefore, one should always perform the service of Satī through body, mind, speech, action, attendance, and even by the total surrender of everything. 17.
O Lakṣmī, I shall proclaim the method of service, by which a householder may likewise cross over;
through service, one may attain me, Hari, the Lord of Śrī, the Supreme Brahman. (18)
By taking refuge in a virtuous Guru who is solely devoted to the meditation upon the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, a human woman becomes a Siddha.
A human woman becomes virtuous by relying on a virtuous guru;
indeed, humans, having obtained a guru, cross over the ocean of worldly existence.
My preceptor, the most excellent of teachers, shall indeed be initiated by me;
as shall he who holds the authority for my service, or she who holds that authority.
One should indeed teach the method of service to me, my Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa;
one should cause a beautiful temple for me to be constructed facing north.
It is enriched with a thousand pitchers and further increased by a single pitcher;
therein is a lofty elephant-throne, complete with its pedestal and adorned with a water-pot (kumbha).
It is called Akṣara, consisting of the nature of existence, consciousness, and bliss; it is fashioned of gold, adorned with many stairs, and embellished with jewels and gems. ||24||
It was covered with precious gems, adorned with a cloth for the back,
possessed the finest cloths for its coverings, and was beautified by cotton cushions and other such items.
It was provided with soft side-cushions and pillows, adorned with gold,
furnished with bolsters, and shaded by canopies and the like.
The Sarvatobhadra maṇḍala was enriched with the beauty of variegated sacrificial pits;
it shone with lovely archways, lattice windows, and water-fountains,
and was illuminated by the light from the extensive networks of four-winged halls.
And the courtyard was beautifully adorned with an excellent assembly pavilion.
It was beautiful, adorned with tulasī plants, and graced by two elephants;
it was further embellished in front by auspicious lions, tigers, garuḍas, and other beings. ||29||
The Sudarśana discus, together with the names of my gatekeepers, should be placed above the archway at the entrance; my names should be written on all sides of the ornamental gateways.
The conch, the lotus, the mace, and the Śārṅga bow should be depicted on the walls;
arrows, archers, and quivers are considered appropriate on both sides in every respect. (3.1)
On the rear part of the temple, the hundred-mooned discus, the Nandaka sword,
the plough, and the pestle should also be depicted in an auspicious manner.
Indeed, upon the back of my elephant-throne, on its sides, are my queens;
and then there are the beloveds of Brahmā, the gopīs, the cows, and the maidservants.
The liberated ones, as well as virtuous women, truthful and pure men,
and the cowherd incarnations, were at the steps and on the door-panels.
At the threshold are wish-fulfilling trees, and likewise creepers upon the pillars;
on the walls are the Gomatī, the Gaṅgā, the Svarṇarekhā, and the Aśvapaṭṭaka.
The sacred field of Kuṃkumavāpikā, Bhadrā, Yamī, and Sarasvatī;
the depiction of the Rāsa-sport, the festival of His birth, the horse sacrifice, and so forth. (36)
The paintings of the ten incarnations, the hermitage of Nara and Nārāyaṇa, and sacred pilgrimage sites should be fashioned with colors in the middle of the hall. (37)
I am my own self, possessing the form of a youth with hands bearing the conch, discus, mace, and lotus, and measuring fifty-six and a quarter finger-breadths in height.

Having caused [the image] to be made with the luster of the color of a white campaka flower, one should worship it after it has been installed in the temple by the hand of the Guru according to the rite of consecration (pratiṣṭhā). 39.
With supreme devotion, the devotee should worship the Supreme Lord,
the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the husband of the beloved of Brahmā.
A devotee, even while being devoted, should always, day and night, remain intent on me;
by my grace, let his tongue taste [only] my nectar and his nose smell the petals of my lotus.
One should make the skin for my touch, the ears likewise for my hearing, the eyes for my seeing, and likewise the hands, feet, and so forth. 42.
One should grant her permission for the practice of service, and thus she shall become intent on service;
indeed, they call that devotee who is filled with love the most excellent of Bhāgavatas. (43)
Even ten thousand horse-sacrifices and ten thousand Rājasūya sacrifices do not equal even a fraction of a part of my service. ||44||
The manifestation of the worship of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa and service unto Him indeed bestows fruit; there is no doubt in this matter. ||45||
Ten million sins are destroyed by serving one's guru and teacher;
at the end of the body, I shall become liberated and divine, with the luster of a white campaka flower. (46)
Having led the elephant, they come to take her to my imperishable abode;
having placed her upon a celestial chariot, upon Garuḍa, or even upon the elephant, they lead her away.
Having risen during the Brāhma-muhūrta, the virtuous woman should remember my name;
then, having bowed to me, her guru, she should perform the washing of her face. 48.
Having quickly sat upon a seat and mastered one's breath, one should then place both hands in the lap and meditate upon me, the beloved of my devotees. 49.
