Thus ends the fifty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Narrative of Nahuṣa at Guru-tīrtha, the Narrative of the Kuñjala Parrot, the Narrative of Kāmodā, the Narrative of Cyavana, and Others," in the *Vadhū-gītā* within the third section, the *Dvāpara-santāna*, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Śrī, Queen of Śiva, to that by which the self becomes purified;
having attained complete purity, young women have gone to the supreme state. || 1 ||
One should indeed know the Guru to be the Supreme Lord Śrī Parameśvara, whose nature is Brahman;
and one should know the Guru’s wife to be Lakṣmī, whose nature is Śrī, and one should serve her as a daughter-in-law.
These two—honor and dishonor—should indeed be understood as poison and nectar respectively;
therein, dishonor is the nectar, while honor is truly poison. (3)
One should show honor to the guru, but one's own pride must be laid aside; for she who remains ever free from pride is then a wife who bestows honor.
She shall always receive honor and become worthy of respect among women;
through her service, even a lion and even a planet come under her control.
For the service of elders brings them under one's influence for the sake of a daughter-in-law;
and by means of a daughter, a daughter-in-law, a handmaid, a slave, or even a servant, [the same result is achieved].
Everything is accomplished through service that is undertaken with devotion, whether it be toward a queen, a teacher, a goddess, a cow, or even a demoness. (7)
Through service, Śrī—the virtuous Ramā—becomes subject to one's own will;
service to the guru is a great weapon that provides assistance in bringing others under one's influence.
Therefore, a daughter-in-law should indeed serve her mother-in-law with humility;
for service to the husband is service to the gods, and the fulfillment of the mother-in-law’s commands is likewise.
Service to the household, service to the children, freedom from anger, service to the teacher, purity, and attendance upon the elderly—these indeed are the five vows of a daughter-in-law. (3.53.10)
For the sake of her husband, all her possessions and the observances prescribed for a wife are considered necessary;
the wife’s duties consist of household tasks, performing sacrifices, honoring guests, and the worship of the gods. (11)

Devotion to the husband’s favor is her twilight ritual; pleasing her mother-in-law is her bath; and service to her husband is her self-restraint—all of which accomplish both dharma and worldly purpose.
Devoted to virtuous conduct, peaceful, and a protector of her own duty,
she, having conquered all worlds, proceeds to the world of Brahmā.
One should perform all acts of rising from one's seat, prostration, and salutation toward those who are elders, who possess the instructions of the guru, and who follow the traditional sequence.
A venerable woman who is steadfast in her vow of chastity should be saluted by prostrating with eight or five limbs at her feet, or by performing three circumambulations.
All elder sisters are to be saluted; moreover, an elderly woman should be saluted again and again.
One who desires his own spiritual success should never disobey their command.
One should avoid with every effort the forest-caves of wicked practices, the employment of base mantras, and [the influence of] poisons, planetary seizures, and demonic afflictions. (17)
A virtuous woman should avoid deceit, stinginess regarding wealth, and backbiting;
as well as excessive laughter, excessive pride, and frivolous behavior devoid of modesty. (18)
One should indeed avoid acting according to one's own whims in the presence of the guru; nor should one speak anything contrary to his words, nor anything that is improper. 1.9
One should never recall what is undesirable, nor should one ever recall a quarrel;
one should not utter abuse, nor should one practice dejection.
One should not touch with one's feet any vessels for liquids, vessels for cooking, vessels for food, or garments, nor should one move them away. ||21||
The sacrificial vessels, as well as the vessels for the materials of worship, the vessels suitable for purificatory rites, and whatever household articles there may be; ||22||
The broom, the hearth, the fire, the fruits and vegetables, all the drinking vessels, and the liquid ingredients for the cosmetic preparations. ||23||
Books and the like, darbha grass, flower vessels, collyrium, weapons, ornaments, garments, and whatever articles of adornment there may be; ||24||
Whatever foods there may be—those to be chewed, those to be swallowed, those to be licked, and those to be sipped—as well as vessels for seasoned meat and the like, and wooden seats and such; ||25||

The bride should not touch [the ground] with her foot, nor should she ever move it away; likewise, she must avoid offending the gods, offending her guru, or even offending her mother-in-law and others. (26)
One should never commit an act of hostility against a village or against the virtuous.
[One should bathe] with waters that have had their hot foam removed, which are purified by the "cloth-eye" (a cloth used as a filter).
One should perform everything with pure water and avoid turbid water—that which is corrupted by smell, color, or taste, or that which has remained in an impure place. (28)
One should avoid water from the ocean or from a pond that is defiled by mud or stones, or likewise tainted by moss or other such defects. (29)

Having poured water from a vessel for fetching water, such as a jar or a pitcher with a spout, one should never wash one's face or feet while holding the añjali (the hollowed palms) in the hands. || 3.53.30 ||
Having removed any excess water from above, one should likewise not leave any remnant;
a drinking vessel touched by the mouth should not be immersed in a water vessel. (31)
One should certainly not touch food items and the like without having washed one's hands;
nor should one perform tasks such as serving food with unwashed hands.
Wearing unclean clothes, she must never perform the work of cooking;
moreover, the bride must always ensure the purification of liquids by means of fire.
The bride should always effect the purification of objects such as grass and wood by means of inspection, by rubbing, and even by sprinkling with water. 34.
One should indeed purify even the pestle and mortar with water;
the purification of horns, bones, and wood is by means of scrubbing with cloth or similar materials.
For substances that are in a heap, purification is indeed by sprinkling;
however, for grains in an unopened heap, if only a single part has been defiled, [the rest are purified by sprinkling].
Having set aside just that much, one should indeed sprinkle it with water infused with *kuśa* grass;
for vegetables, roots, fruits, and the like, purification is achieved by washing.
For oily substances, purification is achieved by wiping; for dry substances, however, it is by means of water and the like.
Likewise, the purification of a house is achieved by sweeping or by scraping.
One should effect the purification of the earth by smearing it in some places, by sprinkling it with water, by fanning it with air, and by the dwelling of cows. (39)
Water situated on the ground is pure, stainless, and sweet-smelling;
a calf is pure at a spring, during milking, and even at birth.
When fruit falls, it is auspicious; during sexual union, the face of the wife is pure;
and merchandise spread out for sale is pure when cleansed by wind and sunlight.
O Brahmins, all that is produced in a mine is pure; so too is the mouth of a dog when it is in a deer-pen, as well as shadows, droplets, virtuous men, chaste women, and flies.
Earth, wind, fire, and water are pure when touched by a child;
likewise, they are pure during sexual intercourse and the discharge of waste, as well as upon touching something impure. (43)
It is declared that purification from touching those who are menstruating and the like occurs through bathing;
a physician, a butcher, and a servant are always considered pure.
The cattle of the house, children, and birds; the courtyard of the house, the fourfold crossroads, the sacrificial altar, trees, the door-panel, and even the umbrella. 45.
Having swept away the swing, the ball and such, the cart, the broom, as well as the grinding stone, the wooden board, the stairs, and even the peg; 46.
The chain, the tethering rope for cattle, the water-rope, the channels, the cooking pot, the ladle, the staff, the vessel for measuring envy, and the puppet; 47.
A pen, a manuscript, a lamp, an image, a fan, as well as an ornament box, a clothing chest, and a vessel for ghee, oil, and so forth. ||48||
A window, a turret, a storehouse for wealth, a king, a virtuous person, an ascetic, a celibate student, a teacher, pure things, and a cow are always [auspicious]. (49)
Indeed, by their very nature, they are purifiers through both wind and heat;
likewise, those initiated, storytellers, and those devoted to ritual action are always purifiers.
Grain on a threshing floor is always pure; likewise, men are pure in an assembly;
women are pure during a festival; and maidens are considered always pure. (51)
Of lifelong celibates, of kings, of queens, of the preceptors' wives, of courtesans who perform dance and song, and of female servants; ||52||
The purity of female attendants (sairandhrīs), courtesans, and women skilled in dance and instrumental music who provide protection for children must always be understood [as essential]. (53)
In the Satya Yuga, women were always pure and free from menstrual flow;
in the other Yugas, they are purified by menstruation at the end of each month.
Women are always purified by bathing and by religious observances; however, a woman in her menses must not, with great care, touch another woman who is in her menses.
Having bathed on the fourth day, one should indeed serve the Lord as one's husband;
for if one serves him at night on the fourth day, she will give birth to a short-lived child.
On the fifth lunar day, by serving [the deity], one gives birth to a daughter who is devoid of learning, poor, yet brings satisfaction to her father; on the sixth day, one gives birth to a son.
On the seventh day, by engaging in union, a girl is born; on the eighth, a son is born.
By engaging in union on the ninth, a girl is born; on the tenth, a wise son is born. (58)
On the eleventh day [one obtains] a daughter; on the twelfth, an auspicious son devoted to dharma;
on the thirteenth, a dull-witted girl; and on the fourteenth, an excellent son. (59)

On the fifteenth day she gives birth to a virtuous daughter, and on the sixteenth day she gives birth to one who has reached the further shore of knowledge; thereafter, having become pure, she should indeed serve her husband.
During her menstrual period, however, she always gives birth to a Cāṇḍāla who is defiled;
yet, through the power of the sacred ford of the husband, the offspring of the woman becomes pure.
As is the husband, so is the wife; as is the field, so is the seed that is sown therein.
If the field is corrupt, the offspring born will be corrupt. (62)
As is the purity of the mind, so is the offspring;
as is the purity of the reality, that indeed is the ultimate purity.
Purity itself exists in the form of purity within a pure vessel;
in an impure vessel, purity indeed abandons its state of being pure.
Indeed, even in an unworthy vessel, conditioned phenomena lose their nature as conditioned phenomena;
and even upon a physical body made of earth, the gods lose their divinity.
The virtue of a faithful wife surely dissolves in the house of a base man;
the divinity of a goddess certainly perishes in the house of those who follow the Asuras.
In the house of a commoner, the queenship of a queen does not endure;
in another's house, the chastity of a bride is not preserved. (67)
Chastity does not abide at all in the house of a courtesan;
likewise, devotion does not exist in an atheist, nor atheism in a devotee. (68)
She does not indeed remain anywhere else; therefore, one should be dear to her husband.
She who is devoted to her husband becomes dear to Brahmā and becomes dear to Hari.
A woman who is dear to Nārāyaṇa should always be a companion to the virtuous; she should be fond of the holy, for the sake of liberation, and never fond of the unholy. (3.53.70)
She should always be fond of righteousness and not fond of unrighteousness; that virtuous woman should be fond of her vows and not fond of improper conduct. ||71||
She should be dear to the gods, not dear to the asuras;
she should always be fond of virtue, never fond of vice. (72)
She should always be fond of purity and not take delight in impurity;
she should be fond of austerity and self-controlled, and not take delight in what is not austerity. ||73||
May she always be beloved by Hari, but never beloved by Hāri;
may she always be beloved by Brahmā, but never indeed beloved by Bhrama. (74)
She should always be dear to Kṛṣṇa, and likewise she should be dear to herself;
she should always be fond of liberation, but she should certainly not be fond of worldly enjoyment.
She should always be dear to the Lord, and never dear to anything else;
she should always be dear to the embodied soul, and never dear to the body.
She should always be dear to another, not dear to anyone else;
she should be the beloved of another man, never the beloved of anyone other than him. (77)
The Supreme Person is Hari, Kṛṣṇa, Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Lord;
may she become the beloved of that beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. (78)
Nārāyaṇa himself is her husband, and she shall always be dear to him;
indeed, she is dear to him as his very self, and never merely by means of her body or other such things.
This very state, O Lakṣmī, is the abode of Brahman, which manifests the beloved of Brahman;
this alone is the purity of Brahman, and having attained it, one rejoices in Me.
In the state of being a bride, she is to be attained by the bride as one who increases [virtue], bestows the service of yoga with Hari, and grants liberation. ||81||
This very body is indeed impure, and so too are the senses;
the objects of the senses are also impure, illusory, and consisting of nothing but delusion.
The mental modifications arising from that should likewise be understood as impure;
the enjoyments and their fruits are also indeed impure.
For even the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) are impure, as are craving and worldly desires of that same nature.
For indeed, the activities and effects become truly impure. ||84||
Likewise, the qualities (guṇas) are also eternally impure and lead to hell;
since all this is entirely impure, what purity can be found therein? (85)
The one pure Self is itself endowed with the Supreme Self;
through acts of self-surrender, one should desire the divine purity residing in the Supreme Self. (86)
Just as brass, through contact with gold, becomes similar to gold, so too does one whose body is like brass become like gold when valued at the price of gold. (87)
Through union with Hari, a person becomes golden and radiant;
likewise, all the sense organs [are purified] by the juices of the indravāruṇī plant.
O Lotus-born One, those honeyed offerings mixed with [other ingredients] and indeed offered to Hari become truly divine and eternal. (89)
Through union with Kṛṣṇa, one's own eternal true nature is realized;
through the beloved Kṛṣṇa, one attains immersion in eternal bliss. (3.53.90)
O Lakṣmī, in ancient times, thirteen sons of Māyā were indeed created by the Creator:
five Ākūtis, five Citayas, and also Mana. (91)
Likewise, the ego (ahaṃkāra) and the intellect (buddhi), impelled by the desire for progeny, were all told: "Create indeed offspring, though you yourselves possess invisible bodies. (92)
Then they did not welcome those words of the Supreme Lord;
having seen the defects in their own actions, they abandoned his command and their own duties.
Despising their actions, they indeed desisted from creation;
having abandoned wealth, virtue, and pleasure, they were truly inactive.
Desiring non-birth, they remained inactive and steadfast;
but Brahmā, having understood their intention, became enraged. (95)
He said to them: "Indeed, you have been appointed by me for the creation of progeny;
'Beget offspring and perform sacrifices,' thus were you addressed by me in the past. (96)
"Because you did not disregard my words and did not welcome progeny, I therefore always curse you: 'May you be devoted to ritual action! (97)
Thus cursed by Brahmā, they became devoted to ritual action;
those thirteen were always engaged in their own vast activities.
They proceed day and night, yet they never truly cease;
those gods are indeed called the Jayas, and all of them have diverse modes of activity. (99)
They alone are the Tuṣitas, the Bodhyas, and the Satyas;
they also exist as the Haris, the Vaikuṇṭhas, the Sādhyas, and the Ādityakas.
O Lakṣmī, one should always offer those [merits] to Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Lord;
for by that means, they become bestowers of liberation upon me, O Ādityas. (101)
For the offering to the Guru makes the rites of the gods virtuous;
it also effects the dedication of their modes of livelihood and their activities. (102)
Since I am your guru, you must perform [these rites] toward me; by that, they become divine for you.
All of them bestow the abode of Brahman. Thus has the secret been told to you. (103)

Thus ends the fifty-third chapter, titled "The Narration of the Secret Conduct of the Guru," within the *Vadhūgītā* of the Creator, in the third section, the *Dvāpara-santāna*, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*. 53.
Śrī Puruṣottama said: Listen, O Śrī Nārāyaṇī, to the supreme and most mighty power of the Guru, which is brilliantly radiant and the destroyer of great sins and even the most heinous crimes. || 1 ||
In the great sacred seat (pīṭha) of Jālandhara, in a region devoted to the service of slaves, a family of the Khaśa caste indeed resided in my city. || 2 ||
For there was a Khaśa named Viṣṇudāsa who was devoted to righteousness;
yet he would not offer [food] to Viṣṇu, nor would he offer it even to his guru. || 3 ||
There, Viṣṇudāsa’s guru, who was solely intent on liberation, did not consume food, clothing, or any fruit, nor even water at any time.
The sage named Sādhu was a bestower of liberation and an inspirer of devotion;
he bathed daily at the three periods of the day and worshipped the deities at the three times of the day.
His transformation is established in stability, free from the three qualities and the afflictions;
he always subsists on unasked-for food, leaves, and the like, and remains ever naked.
Having made his dwelling on the riverbank, he stays beneath a tree in a secluded place;
he constantly worships me, Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Person.
He is indeed patient with dualities, free from attachment and aversion,
effortless, utterly desireless, aged, and devoid of faults.
He who has mastered speech and he who observes silence both always conquer me;
for when those afflicted come to me for refuge in order to destroy their suffering.
Adorned with the virtue of helping others, he dispels the sorrows of those seeking refuge through blessings, gifts of water, and gifts of dust. (3.54.10)
People stand before him offering fruits, garments, sweet foods, and wealth; having honored him, they then depart.
This virtuous man neither touches nor even looks upon the goods;
yet other mendicants, or even animals, carry them off.
Free from delusion and free from the sense of "mine," he conducts himself without deceit;
such a one, the Khaśa, serves a guru who follows the dharma of the sages. (13)
Ramaṇī, the wife of Khaśa, served him with tasks such as sweeping, by offering leaves, flowers, and the like, and by massaging his feet and other services. || 14 ||
Khaśa had a daughter named Līlāvatī, who was auspicious; at twelve years of age, she was constantly engaged in the service of the holy man. (15)
She was devoted to the task of watering the flowering creepers for the sake of the gods,
and she was full of faith and devotion in welcoming and attending to her devotees.
And that girl, under the influence of ignorance, saw a female mouse with her young emerging from its hole while she was watering the trees. (17)
Out of childishness, that girl took those children and, having gone a great distance, cast away the infants, depriving them of their mother. || 18 ||
A female mouse, overcome with fear and staying within a heap of grass,
then cursed the girl as she was seizing her tiny young ones.
Just as my young children have fallen into misery when separated from me,
so may you, separated from your father, mother, and others, become one who suffers.
This terrible curse indeed arose from the mouse;
and on another day, the fruit of its ripening was experienced by the girl. (21)
Just as the maiden, having attended upon her teacher in the evening, was returning home,
a certain young Mleccha encountered her on the path and seized the girl.
Wailing piteously, the powerful one quickly led her into the forest;
from forest to another forest, he traveled through the night until he had reached a distant land.
That maiden Khaśī was made a slave in her own home by a Mleccha;
she was indeed made to drink liquor and likewise fed meat.
Likewise, sinful acts such as violence were repeatedly committed by him;
indeed, all manner of barbarian deeds were performed by that girl.
For she was a Mleccha woman and weak, and being unfamiliar with the forest path, she did not know it at all; she only constantly grieved for her home.
Then once, in the city, there occurred a festival for the Mlecchas born of a wedding;
at that time, female singers and courtesans arrived at the festival.
This very Khaśī, beautiful in form, looked upon the courtesans;
she offered betel-leaves in the service of a slave-girl during the dances and other performances. (28)
For, being employed by the Mleccha, she engaged in the service of a courtesan;
that courtesan asked her, "Daughter, where are your mother and father? (29)
Having heard Khaśī, he related his entire account;
then, perceiving her intention regarding the journey, he set his mind on abducting her. (3.54.30)
Then, having instilled confidence, he established a secret signal;
subsequently, after some time, in accordance with that signal, [he approached] the maiden.
For, having been led out from the house of a barbarian, the courtesan brought her to her own home;
thus the girl became the auspicious maidservant of the courtesan. (32)
Engaged in sexual intercourse and other such acts, she became devoid of dharma; under the influence of the courtesan, she committed great sins and even more heinous crimes.
Then, after some time, that courtesan indeed became ill;
afflicted by diseases of the abdomen and the organs, she even consumed medicines.
That courtesan did not indeed obtain health;
she lamented, "How might this disease consisting of fistula be removed from me? (35)
Then the daughter-in-law said: "I have a great master, a guru, who is capable of destroying disease; there is perfection of speech with him—go indeed there."
Having heard this and learned of the auspicious news concerning her teacher, the courtesan suddenly became ready, accompanied by her own wealth and ornaments. (37)
Taking other female servants, courtesans, household goods, and even men,
she crossed the Gaṇikā forest to where [the deity] shines resplendent.
The virtuous one arrived there at the riverbank with great devotion; Khaśī and Līlāvatī also became exceedingly joyful within their hearts. (39)
She bowed with devotion to the virtuous one as if she had reached her own father;
having prostrated before her guru as a god, she related her own story. || 3.54.40 ||
Then the virtuous man related the story of the courtesan, which was indeed for the purpose of destroying her disease; he then spoke of the fruit of karma.
Whatever was done by someone in the past, that very same thing is experienced by them;
O Līlāvatī, you separated the young mice from their mother. (42)
Then, at the time when the trees were to receive water, you were cursed by a female mouse;
consequently, you fell into the suffering of separation from your parents.
This courtesan suffers a wretched disease through sexual intercourse;
however, this is indeed the fruit of the service you previously rendered to me. 44.
He caused my attainment [of this state] once more under this very pretext;
moreover, this Gaṇikā became devoted to the service of guests. (45)
Through the yoga of you, my devotee, she has attained union with me;
for association with the virtuous leads one toward goodness, whereas evil company leads indeed to wickedness.
A wicked deed causes suffering, while a virtuous action brings happiness;
however, O daughter, association with the righteous arises only through merit, and not otherwise.
I shall indeed wipe away all your sins born of being a Mleccha, O daughter;
I shall also wipe away the sins of the harlot, O dear child.
Having constructed leaf-huts for their residence here in my presence, they indeed perform a vow right here for the sake of purifying the body. (49)
Thus addressed, they all constructed an auspicious leaf-hut on the ground beneath the tree and took up residence in its vicinity.
The sage, whose nature was dharma, gave them the vow of eating only once a day,
and during that vow, he had them consume the five products of the cow for three days.
Then, O Lakṣmī, that best of sages gave those auspicious mantras to them:
"Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa; obeisance to the Lord. (52)
Out of fear of Time, Illusion, evil karma, enemies, Yama, and treacherous friends,
one should wear the trident, fish, banner, bow, discus, and the svastika.
May Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa be my refuge forever;
I am eternally a devotee of Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, belonging to the lineage of Brahmā. 54.
"Anādi-Śrī-Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa is my Lord and my husband"—thus he gave the mantra into her ear and likewise placed water upon her hand. (55)
"Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Master; svāhā!
Having spoken thus, that sage Dharma released the water upon the ground. (56)
O Lakṣmī, at that moment a great wonder occurred there; listen to it:
from the bodies of Līlāvatī and those courtesans, [a light emerged]. (57)
From all sides, blue-colored crows emerged;
then owls emerged, and even mosquitoes emerged from there. (58)
And from that [place] also came Piśācas of hideous form and cruel appearance—mutilated, emaciated, hungry, weak, one-eyed, and lame. (59)
Then those afflicted with leprosy, the dull-witted, the blind, the foul-smelling, and those covered in filth—rich with blood and with all their limbs deformed—came forth. (3.54.60)
Seeing the sage naked and without shelter, Līlāvatī, Gaṇikā, and all the others wept and were filled with wonder.
Having bowed to their preceptor, the sage, they asked, "O Preceptor, who are these?
The Preceptor said, "O daughters, you truly possess all manner of sins."
By the bestowing of this mantra, these crows—which are indeed the sins born of association with outcastes—have been expelled from my body. (63)
These owls were indeed made into courtesans because of their committed sins; those mosquitoes were indeed made so because of the sins of drinking liquor. (64)
And those sinful piśācas who were eaters of your flesh have indeed all emerged from your bodies. (65)
O Sage, all those [trees] wept as they beheld these women; even their sins, O Lakṣmī, then made a prayer. (66)
"O Sage, we are all utterly destitute and deeply distressed; by all means, grant us liberation here through the gift of water. (67)
Having heard this, the sage washed his own right foot and cast it into them with his joined palms; the drops were indeed received by them.
Then all the yellow drops indeed satisfied the sins;
in this manner, the sage again cast another handful of water.
Then they assumed divine forms, just like the gods;
then he offered a third salutation with joined palms toward the deity.
Instantly, all the three-eyed Gaṇas became bearers of tridents;
even the sinful ones became Puṇyajanas by the thousands. ||71||
All of them, auspicious and possessing divine forms though having human shapes, took the sage’s command and, having bowed, departed for the Himalayas. (72)
Then they all went to Meru and indeed became holy beings;
through the power of that very saint, they all became renowned as hosts of gods.
Then those courtesans, freed from sin and the like, became like goddesses with divine forms; he gave them water for their feet.
Having drunk the water from the feet of the sage, the courtesan became free from disease;
others as well, having drunk that water, had their worldly attachments destroyed. (75)
Then all the yoginīs became like virtuous wives;
the diseases, having quickly emerged, bowed down and departed for Kailāsa.
For those courtesans were indeed virtuous women, and they all undertook the initiation;
at that time, the merchants there likewise took up the initiation of the virtuous.
Hare Kṛṣṇa, Hare Viṣṇu, Hare Nārāyaṇa, O Lord!
O beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, Sovereign of the Imperishable, All-pervading One! ||78||
Thus, united there in that hermitage, they performed worship;
and Līlāvatī’s parents, having recovered their daughter, were filled with happiness.
Indeed, Kamala and Bhakta became devoted through the majesty of their guru;
there, those two Khaśas received the initiation of a holy man from that true guru.
News of the nature of the destruction of sins spread in every direction;
then, men came in a state of agitation for the sake of destroying their own sins. 81.
Men and women received the Śrī Vaiṣṇava initiation from the sage; having prepared them and liberated them, he sent them to the Imperishable (Akṣara). 82.
He sent his disciples and their disciples with a message;
by the mere will of the sage, celestial chariots arrived from the sky of consciousness.
Accompanied by their attendants and indeed joined with the forms of Viṣṇu, they arrived and, having ascended those very forms, went to the supreme abode. ||84||
By the power of their guru, the courtesans and others became residents of Vaikuṇṭha;
likewise Līlāvatī, her five friends, and others as well. (85)
Thousands of such [beings] existed in my abode, Vaikuṇṭha, O Śrī Hari;
she is that very Līlāvatī who is now the daughter of the King of Kāśī. (86)
And here resides your sister, the beloved wife of a Brahmin;
she is a courtesan named Suśīlā, your friend here, O daughter of the ocean. (87)
Thus, by my yoga with Śivarājñīśrī, the sage Dharma became devoid of qualities (nirguṇa); and through that yoga, men and women likewise became devoid of qualities. 88.
Those who worship Me out of desire, anger, fear, greed, or delusion, they are born indeed devoid of qualities; they are truly liberated, there is no doubt. (89)
I uplift my devotees, the virtuous, and those who are my gurus;
even those who are sinful and of wicked conduct become purified through their connection with the guru.

Even those who dwell in the sacred abodes are born [as such]; how much more so for me, who have surrendered all my possessions to my guru and who serve him as if he were a sacred pilgrimage site? 9.1.
Those who have attained full faith in the Guru proceed to the supreme state.
The Guru is God, the Guru is Kṛṣṇa, and the Guru is indeed the purifying initiation. (92)
She for whom Hari is considered the guru, the vow, the gift, and the supreme goal,
crosses even the ocean of worldly existence through the power of that great sacred ford.
He indeed goes to the supreme bliss, the imperishable and eternal abode;
this divine dwelling of mine is the highest of all abodes and is dear to me. 94.
The state that bestows all satisfaction and fulfills all desires does not lack anything there; one enjoys pleasures together with me. (95)
Whether they be brides, widows, or even those who are childless and without refuge, by reaching the supreme Guru-tīrtha, they are liberated from the ocean of worldly existence. 96.
From reciting this, from hearing it, from remembering it, and even from speaking of it, enjoyment, liberation, a divine state, and the attainment of the [divine] abode arise. (97)
For those with desires, there is the attainment of heaven; for those free from desire, there is liberation;
and for those who desire me, there is the attainment of me, the Supreme Person who bears the Śārṅga bow. ||98||

Thus ends the fifty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Attainment of the Status of Brahma’s Consorts by Līlāvatī, Suśīlā, and Others through the Yoga of the Great Sage Ṛṣidharma at the Sacred Site of the Guru, and the Dissolution of Their Sins," in the *Vadhūgītā* within the third section, the *Dvāparasantāna*, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Puruṣottama said: Listen, O Śrī Nārāyaṇī, to another most purifying narrative,
which consists of the sacred ford of the Guru, which uplifts all and removes all sins.
In the city of Upaleṣṭā in Saurāṣṭra,
there was a virtuous woman named Rakṣā, a Cāṇḍāla woman who was a devotee of Hari and the wife of Sumara.
Indeed, she dwelt with her family in the city Malāpahāriṇī; because she removes impurities, she remains impure during the day.
Then, having bathed at midday and purified his own hands,
he went to his own home, which had been constructed amidst the trees.
Having prepared her own *roṭaka* and fed it to her husband Hari, she then gives some to the dog and eats herself; thus, the virtuous woman possesses the excellent quality of contentment.
Remaining in her home, she constantly reflected upon her own condition:
"How indeed have I become a dog-eater's daughter even here among human beings?"
Poverty persists at all times, as does servitude;
there is constant removal of filth and perpetual impurity. (7)
At every step there is contempt and perpetual untouchability;
though the human nature remains within me, my life is that of a beast. (8)
Food is seen but not obtained, nor is it flavorful;
garments are wretched, and no adornment is found.
The house is indeed splendid, yet there is no wealth to be enjoyed; there is neither honor nor fame. Fie upon this life born of sin! (3.55.10)
There are no vehicles or mounts, nor are there vessels for the elements;
there are no ornaments, and even sweet food does not exist. (11)
There is no wealth nor any coinage; there is no beautiful couch;
and indeed, there is never any hope for gold in a dream.
"Thus all my deformity and likewise my impurity are known to me;
indeed, there is but one auspicious quality found in me, born as I am in the lineage of a dog-cooker. (13)
Because another man is untouchable, there has never been any touch of him for me;
my devotion to my husband is always innate and more venerable than anything else.
Even those of my own kind exist far, far away in other cities;
there is no union with those men, nor even the touch of me.
Thus, I possess this vow, virtue, and merit which always bestow heaven; therein also exist freedom from pride, dispassion, and the absence of affliction. (16)
A river lies at my side, so I bathe daily;
I always dwell in the forest like a forest-dweller, yet I maintain a household. (17)
There is no fear of thieves for us, nor is there any fear of kings;
devoted to my service, I sleep happily with my husband. (18)
Sometimes, by the power of my fortune, I obtain the sight of the virtuous who travel along the path; yet, the sight of the sun is always present for me.
Until midday, my activity consists of removing impurities;
beyond that, my cessation occurs for half the day and during the night. (3.55.20)
Indeed, for the sake of especially worshipping the names of the Supreme Lord, I have the time and such benefits as well. (21)
When a great festival has commenced in a village, whether for a divine or a human purpose,
one also obtains the purifying grace that pertains to both gods and men.
Even in that regard, my human birth has borne fruit;
for even though I am an outcaste, my character is indeed supreme through my devotion to my husband.
Furthermore, the cohabitation of other women—whether they be men's wives or commoners—with people in the midst of a crowd or in a village is seen to be destructive of virtue. (24)
Where men and women dwell together in close proximity,
there indeed dharma is destroyed by the power of place and time.
For married women, contact with another man as well as frequenting him in private is a destroyer of dharma and leads to hell. (26)
Indeed, for those women of such a kind who cause the intermixture of castes, there is no hell today; for them, there is no hell thereafter.
That which is brought about by unrighteousness here may indeed occur in another birth;
however, for me, who have taken the form of a dog-eater's wife, hell is manifest right here.
But by the power of dharma alone, there is indeed no hell after death;
therefore, for women who are devoted to their offspring, there exists an excellent destination that is most superior. (29)
Lack of prosperity leads to dispassion, while prosperity indeed leads to bondage;
freedom from worldly attachment leads to the next world, while kindness indeed leads to bondage.
I wander like a virtuous woman free from bondage, though I am a dog-eater;
I roam from street to street like a chaste wife devoted to her husband. (3.1)
My state remains fearless, rich in happiness, and free from disease;
I cleanse the pits of impurity and I also attain detachment.
Indeed, all people in the world cleanse their own impurity day after day;
everyone, having risen in the morning, washes away their own filth.
Indeed, women with children wash their infants even when they have been placed in the middle of the house, in the midst of clothes, or upon the bed. (34)
Those like me indeed remove all the impurities of the ignorant;
likewise, there exists no distinction between me and them regarding the purification of those impurities. (35)
Indeed, all outcasts (śvapacas) are [only] concerned with removing the impurities from their own bodies;
therefore, my preeminence alone remains unassailable among the outcasts. (36)
The king would be constantly a partaker of suffering, and the queen even more miserable than he, being perpetually confined by guards within a palace resembling a prison. (37)
The noble merchants travel covered by cloth canopies;
even the merchants themselves do not go outside without fear unless accompanied by soldiers. (38)
Thus submerged in suffering, they experience hell directly;
what indeed is the difference between them and the dog-cookers here? (39)
Moreover, this demoness of craving cuts their hearts to pieces;
diseases, the manifest messengers of Yama, wither both their wealth and their bodies. (3.55.40)
Wealthy people are born with their servants dependent on them, and their servants' servants in turn;
dependence on others and hope for others—these two are hells residing within the householder. (41)
Independence and freedom from hope—these two heavens are already within my own hands.
Blessed am I, though a dog-cooker's wife; I am pure, being devoid of such faults.
A life connected with heaven leads to heaven even at its end;
like a doe in the forest, one obtains food consisting of fruits and leaves. (43)
Siṃhikā obtains food consisting of meat even in the great forest;
the merchant’s wife obtains food that is delicious yet fraught with disease. (44)
The dog-cooker woman receives food that is dry yet strength-giving;
blessed am I, this dog-cooker woman, endowed with great happiness. (45)
The king, the queen, and others likewise, during the final portion of their lives.
Those who have renounced the world become forest-dwellers for the sake of attaining liberation. ||46||
In the forest, I see them all, free from attachment to worldly enjoyments;
I am blessed by birth as well, since I have become a female ascetic like them.
I am always a female renunciant, always one for whom her husband is a deity, and I am always endowed with virtuous conduct, even as a low-caste woman of auspicious nature. (48)
"Aha! I have no bondage, nor do I have any rejection of the Dharma;
I shall practice here in the village that which is appropriate for my birth and brings about welfare. (49)
The virtuous, possessing the knowledge of Brahman, draw out the stains of sin from the hearts of the wicked by means of imparting instruction.
I shall expel from this pit the outcaste woman, who is defiled by her actions and ignorance and stained by impurity and sin, by means of providing her with service to my body.
Since the removal of impurity must be performed equally for both, I shall indeed become a female renunciant, just like one who has renounced all action. (52)
In this world, there are auspicious gurus who destroy impurity;
by destroying the impurity of ignorance, they illuminate true wisdom. (53)
Having become my own heavy [nature], I cast off even the impurity of grief;
and having myself become my own heavy [nature], I move about stainless.
"Oh, what fortune! Oh, what fortune! Though I am a dog-eater among humans, I am always happy compared to others by the grace of Hari. (55)
I have no obstacle to my fruit that arises from association with many;
nor do I have any destruction of dharma born of association with many. (56)
Even without a forest, dwelling in a forest brings me happiness;
even apart from the life of a wandering mendicant, my inner peace always abides within me. (57)
I am blessed; I am a vessel of merit and a supreme vessel of happiness, for I enjoy every pleasure bestowed by my own offspring. (58)
That house where there is suffering and dejection for both men and women, and which is a constant source of suspicion—that indeed is the Raurava hell. (59)
In whosever home there may be love and joy for both men and women,
as well as freedom from fear— that indeed is the state of Indra’s heaven.
Such a heaven as that exists right here in this house of the outcaste woman;
these trees are my garden, and this river is mine. (61)
"Your goodness stands supreme over all, bestowing liberation upon me;
therefore, I, though a dog-eater's wife, am blessed and endowed with every fortune. (62)
For the virtuous yogi who is thus engaged and proceeds by the path of the side-glance, there indeed arises the vision of Brahman.
By the name of the great Siddha, the Lord Caitanyaśīla, protection quickly went toward the virtuous man and stood upon his path. (64)
From afar, with palms joined and face bowed, she paid homage to the holy man.
The holy man said: "O you who are ever peaceful, may you become possessed of liberation. (65)
Having thus become a divine goddess, always be beloved by Brahmā; be a devotee of Hari, a virtuous woman, and a servant of the holy. (66)
Having spoken thus, Caitanyaśīla went to the bank of the Bhadrāvatī river and sat down for a moment at the foot of a tree far away.
Then, having gone to the river water and bathed, he performed the worship of Hari;
and having offered fruit, water, and sugar to Hari, he— ||68||
There, the sage granted his grace to the dog-cooker who had come there;
she too, having received his grace, reported it to her husband. (69)
Then, considering his own fortune to be supreme, he ate the remainder;
thereafter, the holy man took up residence for the night beneath the tree.
Seeing that the cold oppressed him, that outcaste woman gave him wood for the purpose of kindling a fire; the virtuous man then kindled the fire. (71)
He also rotated his rosary and performed worship, chanting:
"O Hari, Kṛṣṇa! O Hari, Viṣṇu! O Hari, Nārāyaṇa, Lord! (72)
The saintly one performed the kīrtana of the holy Name with the sounding of cymbals, [invoking] the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the glorious Puruṣottama. (73)
The outcaste woman, having come with her husband to the vicinity of the tree,
sat at a distance and performed that kind of worship.
And at the conclusion of her worship, she, filled with humility, asked that holy man:
"From where have you come, O holy one, and where is your permanent residence? (75)
"And where have you come from? Is all well in every respect? The virtuous man replied, "I have come from the abode of Hari, from a very great distance. (76)
My residence is with Śrī Hari, and I am proceeding toward Śrī Hari;
by the grace of my guru and the sacred fords, all is well in every respect. (77)
Rakṣā said: "O holy one, what indeed is the auspicious 'Great Holy Place' (gurutīrtha)?
O Sage, please tell me out of compassion that by which all may become well. (78)
The saintly one said: "Viṣṇu is the guru; Brahmā is the guru; Hara is the guru.
Hari, the Lord, is the guru; the saintly one is the guru; the mother, husband, and father are all gurus. (79)
The Guru is the bestower of knowledge and the remover of sin; the Guru is great.
The Guru is the bestower of liberation, and one's own Self is the supreme Guru.
The inner self of the guru is Śrī Hari, the Supreme Lord;
by taking refuge in Him, there is the destruction of sins and even eternal liberation. ||81||
Even one of evil conduct—a dog-cooker, a dog-eater, or even one who consumes liquor and meat, and indulges in sexual intercourse and wine—[is purified]. (82)
Even one who has committed the most grievous of great sins is purified by taking refuge in the Guru;
neither vows, nor sacred fords, nor any other atonement is superior to that. (83)
He by whom the grace of the guru has been obtained is instantly liberated from bondage;
he should receive from the guru the supreme purifying mantra of Hari’s name. (84)
Having drunk from the lotus-feet of the Guru, having meditated upon the form of the Guru of Gurus, and having served the Guru as a deity, one should propitiate him at that very moment. ||85||
By surrendering everything one possesses, one may immediately attain liberation;
the virtuous person is a boat, the Guru is a boat, Hari is a boat, and the husband of a chaste wife is a boat. (86)
"Knowledge is my boat, supreme devotion and taking refuge are my oars; protection is my sail.
She asked that holy man, "Grant me refuge! (87)
"Give the mantra to my outcaste wife and to my outcaste husband.
Caitanyaśīla first caused her to drink that auspicious [water]. (88)
Having poured his own water from his feet into that water of Śrī Hari,
and having made it pure and sanctifying, he then imparted the mantra.
Oṃ, salutations to Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa; salutations to the Lord.
The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa is my Lord and my husband. (3.55.90)
Hare Kṛṣṇa, Hare Viṣṇu, Hare Nārāyaṇa, O Lord!
Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, Śrī Puruṣottama! (91)
Thus the virtuous one gave the mantras to the outcaste woman and the outcaste man;
he caused them to perform worship, and from then on for half the night.
Both husband and wife then massaged the feet of the holy man;
indeed, through that service to the saint, his status as a Cāṇḍāla was dissolved. (93)
Until morning, they performed the massaging of his feet;
then in the morning, Hari arrived, resplendent in a divine celestial chariot.
Accompanied by his foremost attendants and adorned by Rādhā, Lakṣmī, and others, Hari said to the protectors of the virtuous: "Remember me as your followers. (95)
"All three of you are my devotees who have attained a divine state;
purified by me through the guru and the sacred ford, ascend this celestial chariot."
Having been addressed thus, those three bowed and, casting off their bodies upon the surface of the earth, became divine attendants, as did their attendants of similar kind. (97)
Then, having become divine and four-armed, they remained in that celestial chariot and went with Hari to Vaikuṇṭha, the supreme liberation.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, this Guru-tīrtha is indeed instantly purifying even for women who are impure and whose conduct is equal to that of outcaste dog-cookers. 99.
It bestows liberation and is supreme; therefore, one should serve a guru.
By reading and hearing this, both worldly enjoyment and liberation shall be attained in this very life.

Thus ends the fifty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Attainment of Liberation by Sumara’s Wife Rakṣāśvapacī, Together with Her Husband and the Guru, through the Power of the Guru Tīrtha Caitanyaśīla," within the *Vadhūgītā* of the third section, the *Dvāpara-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇī said:
O Blessed One, Lord of the gods of gods, tell me the reason why the supreme holy place of the Guru has attained the status of being the most excellent of all. || 1 ||
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
The purification of the earth is by wind alone; the purification of the body is by water;
the purification of the mind is by dispassion; and the purification of the self is through discrimination.
Discrimination is the knowledge of reality, and that indeed cannot be attained without a guru;
because you quickly bestow illumination, you are considered the supreme guru.
Just as a lamp becomes the source of illumination even among hundreds of thousands of people in darkness, so too is the Guru a lamp. || 4 ||

Just as a boat is the means of crossing for many aquatic creatures despite their presence in the ocean, so too is the Guru the savior of embodied beings despite their presence in the ocean of the world. || 5 ||
Just as there is no end to the stars in the sky, yet the moon is their illuminator;
so too, there is no end to human beings, yet the true guru is the giver of light to them.
Just as there is never the destruction or disappearance of the night by other planets,
so too there is no removal of ignorance without a true guru.
Water, sacred fords, the earth, worship, sacrifice, vows, and shrines—
indeed, it is said that in ancient times these sacred sites were brought into existence solely by the True Guru.
The sacred site of the form is known as the image, while the sacred site of knowledge is the book;
indeed, both have arisen solely from the True Guru and not otherwise.
All the gods derive their power from the guru; likewise, mantras derive their power from the guru;
yoga also derives its power from the guru; therefore, the guru is a sacred ford (tīrtha) even greater than that.
Through my yoga, my greatness increases and is revealed;
moreover, through association with me, one becomes filled with wonder.
Attachment to me, affection for me, devotion to me, and service to me—
by whomsoever this is performed for me alone, their status as a guru is eternal.
Since I am the eternal Guru, the Lord possessed of beginningless knowledge, therefore,
through my yoga, the state of being a Guru is eternal for the devotee.
By association with a valuable object, even a worthless thing becomes valuable;
just as a cow accompanied by her calf and milk is always of great value. (14)
A jewel created by knowledge becomes highly valuable;
even a diamond that possesses purity is reckoned as being of great value. (15)
Just as brass becomes highly valuable through contact with gold, so too a maiden who has chosen a husband is honored and esteemed as very precious in this world. (16)
All servants, when joined with a king, indeed become worthy of royal value;
likewise, O beloved, even a vessel filled with goods becomes valuable.
Thus, one who is devoted, endowed with devotion, especially united with me, and possessed of a state of purity, becomes of great value. || 18 ||
A contented servant indeed performs the work for the subjects immediately;
moreover, filled with haste, he causes it to be done immediately through the king's door. (19)
Indeed, the king’s puppet does not perform the work of the subjects, nor does the puppet cause the work to be performed with haste. (3.56.20)
Likewise, my servants are devoted to me and are protectors of those who have come for refuge;
they perform the duties of those seeking refuge even with great haste. 21.
"Indeed, on this earth, virtuous men are my spiritual preceptors in the form of pure consciousness;
likewise, the servants who carry out the king's business are his very embodiments of consciousness.
Having spoken thus, he laughed and accepted their service and so forth.
Having given gifts, they indeed perform the desired recitation of the mantra for embodied beings. ||23||
Since the gurus are the support for those living beings who have come for refuge, I have indeed offered my own station to the gurus; likewise, my authority is theirs.
They shall become worthy of worship in the world like me, for they are indeed Nārāyaṇas;
just as I am, so too are they, for they are the promoters of devotion to me. ||25||
Therefore, those gurus are supreme; the highest sacred ford consists of the guru himself, for they quickly effect the washing away of sins through the granting of water. ||26||
They swiftly destroy ignorance through the imparting of mantras;
moreover, by means of their blessings, they burn away [the obstacles to] great prosperity such as heaven and the like. //27//
Through their grace, they swiftly send one even to the state of liberation; at times, they effortlessly cause a vision of themselves to appear to me here quickly. ||28||
O Lakṣmī, by my grace, the vision of my divine form resides within their hearts;
therefore, virtuous people are always my most excellent gurus.
Through devotion, they indeed become for me the most excellent Supreme Lords;
I shall now describe that devotion by which they are truly most excellent.
Service to the guru, the gods, and the perfected sages; association with the saintly; and devotion to virtuous activities—this, in my view, is another form of devotion. (31)
Service to my portions and to my gurus is another form of devotion to me;
it is considered by me to be eternally the bestower of liberation. (32)
Having attained the divine essence of Brahman and having drunk that which is filled with bliss, the devotees, whose enjoyment is centered on Brahman, become eternally satisfied. ||33||
And they become flooded with the essence of Brahman, having the form of the Imperishable;
just as fire entering fire, so does the self enter the Supreme Self. (34)
One should always mutter the mantra "Hare Hare," which is named *brahmarūpakaraṃ*; [one should realize]:
"I am the supreme light of Brahman, devoid of the principle of Māyā. (35)
I am Brahman, the supreme light, possessing knowledge for the sake of liberation;
the Blessed Lord, the Supreme Person, is attainable through devotion enriched by knowledge. (36)
I, the Supreme Lord, am indeed attainable through meditation, worship, recitations, proper hymns of praise, observance of vows, service, and loving devotion. (37)
The remembrance of Hari’s discipline is the root of great welfare, the source of a continuous stream of merit, and the sweet fruit of life. (38)
Service accompanied by affection should be understood as devotion, which is the most abundant means of practice;
those devotees are intent upon my service with undivided thoughts. (39)
Shedding tears out of great joy, their hair standing on end, my Vaiṣṇavas are always devoted to the activities of Kṛṣṇa and are ever affectionate toward me. 3.56.40.
Hearing the imperishable syllable of Brahman and the Supreme Brahman, and chanting the Bhāgavata, the best of Vaiṣṇavas should proclaim it with devotion, preceded by prostrations. (41)
He who possesses affection for his devotees, who rejoices in the worship of his devotees, and who is delighted by hearing the songs of his devotees—he indeed is considered the best of devotees. (42)
He who has surrendered his entire being with devotion to Kṛṣṇa, having taken refuge in a true guru, is indeed a great devotee (mahābhāgavata). ||43||
If one worships me directly and likewise subsists upon Viṣṇu,
being endowed with manifold devotion, then even if he be a Mleccha, he is indeed a Vaiṣṇava.
He indeed is the most excellent sage and devotee; he goes to the supreme goal.
To him gifts should be given, from him they should be received, and he is to be honored just like Hari. 45.
Even a Cāṇḍāla who is a devotee of the Blessed One purifies by his very nature;
one who is my devotee is not a Cāṇḍāla, for he is a divine attendant of mine.
Show compassion to one who has sought refuge and who entreats you, saying, "I am yours.
One should grant fearlessness to all beings; this is the vow of Hari. 47.
One who knows the Vedas and Vedānta is superior to thousands of performers of mantra-sacrifices;
one who is a devotee of Viṣṇu is distinguished above all those who possess the specialized knowledge of the Vedānta.
Those who are single-mindedly devoted go to the supreme state with divine bodies;
Viṣṇu is equal to them through their exclusive devotion, for Viṣṇu is solely intent upon his devotees.
Those devotees who are single-mindedly devoted are considered the best among ten million Brahmins;
for they are dear to me, indeed most dear even among all things that are dear.
The great devotees of the Lord, being saintly and virtuous,
are considered always to be far superior to ten million brahmins and even to hundreds of millions of brahmins.
The Brahmins are the teachers of the worlds;
among Brahmins who perform Vedic sacrifices, the virtuous are considered the teachers of all Brāhmaṇas. (52)
Those Brahmins who were immersed in household life resorted to cremation grounds;
those virtuous ones who were absorbed in Brahman attained the supreme abode.
Those whose devotion is always unwavering even in times of adversity, and who possess that supreme, ever-abiding love for Kṛṣṇa-Viṣṇu; ||54||
My devotee who remembers Viṣṇu does not remain far from my heart;
even one with firm devotion, though bound by ropes and snares, binds me to himself.
He who bears devotion toward Viṣṇu has accomplished everything;
he alone is truly a perfected soul by whom I, his beloved, have been won over. (56)
Even those who have performed sacrifices of the foremost rites and have reached the further shore of the Vedas do not attain that supreme state which the best of sages attain.
"Whoever in this world is a Vaiṣṇava, even if they follow false conduct or belong to no stage of life, purifies all the worlds, just as I myself, the Blessed Lord, do. (58)
Even those who are cruel, evil-minded, and devoted to sinful conduct go to my supreme abode if they are solely devoted to Nārāyaṇa. (59)
Firm devotion to Nārāyaṇa that is always unswerving—that alone grants eternal happiness; what is heaven compared to its presence? (3.56.60)
Even after wandering repeatedly and on all sides within the great ocean called saṃsāra,
if Kṛṣṇa is somehow attained, one should grasp him by his own hand and hold fast.
He who does not hear of the divine qualities of Śrī Hari, the Supreme Soul,
should be known as deaf in this world, or else as one whose ears are ever filled with sin.
If, when the name of Viṣṇu is chanted, there is no bristling of the hair on one's body,
then even if he be a king or handsome in form, he should indeed be known as a corpse.
For men, women, and even those with neuter bodies who possess devotion and whose minds are fixed upon me, liberation is certain to occur.
He spoke to the Yamas who held nooses in their hands: "I am indeed the Lord, King Yama;
do not bring the Vaiṣṇavas here, but only the sinful ones who are not devotees of Viṣṇu. (65)
Even if one of wicked conduct worships me while remaining established in me, he is indeed a saint; liberated, such a teacher is superior to ten million Brahmins.
Indeed, all the most exalted dharmas of the Bhāgavatas dwell within him;
likewise, O lotus-born one, every kind of peace dwells there.
And what account can be made of his virtue, wealth, and pleasure?
Liberation is his constant servant, and liberation rests in his very hand. (68)
Whether they be illusions or the products of illusion, the worlds, sovereign powers, and spiritual accomplishments do not at all obstruct me, the yogin, even while being experienced. (69)

What is the use of sacrifices, what use of vows, what use of gifts, or what use of other means of merit, for him in whom love for Hari has arisen and by whom the Lord is worshipped through that? (3.56.70)
O Kamalā, I am not so pleased by other unguents, lamps, and the like, nor by sandalwood, perfumes, and ornaments, as I truly am by the offering of love.
Of the poisonous tree of saṃsāra, there are indeed two fruits comparable to nectar:
supreme devotion to me, Kṛṣṇa, and association with my devotees. (72)
Since I, the Lord who bestows liberation, am attainable through devotion by means of leaves, flowers, fruits, water, wealth, food, and ornaments, one should abide in that devotion. (73)
The ancestors clap their hands and the grandfathers dance, saying:
"Someone born in our family who is devoted [to us] will deliver us from the state of the departed. (74)
Even those who have taken refuge in me, though they are devoid of meditation and knowledge,
transcend death and go to my supreme state.
The person who bows to the Lord of Śrī, Puruṣottama—the cause of liberation, without beginning or end—becomes worthy of homage by all the world. (76)
One should always bow with devotion, using the mind joined with the body, to that Lord Hari, Viṣṇu, who is the treasury of bliss and resides within.
One should bow down to that beloved Supreme Lord, the witness of all, who dwells within and beholds the auspicious and inauspicious of all beings. 78.
Even a salutation offered with ease to the wielder of the discus (Cakrapāṇi) becomes the destroyer of the ropes of the snares of saṃsāra. ||79||
Even a prostration performed with devotion toward the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, who possesses the form of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, purifies even an outcaste. (3.56.80)
Having prostrated like a staff upon the ground, one should perform the salutation with joy;
by even a single prostration, one goes to my supreme abode. (81)
O Lakṣmī, by means of salutation, my liberation is indeed eternal;
I, Kṛṣṇa, truly deliver the one who bows from the ocean of worldly existence.
Whether sitting or lying down, or standing anywhere at all, the wise person should always recite the mantra: "Namo Nārāyaṇāya. (83)
The name "Nārāyaṇa" is worthy of my tongue;
nevertheless, contentious people perceive me as belonging to Yama's abode.
Vyāsa and others, as well as Śaṅkara and others, turn back from their efforts of intellect while praising the Supreme Lord; there is no end to my qualities. (85)
Even if one cries out "Nārāyaṇa" repeatedly against one's will,
the girdle has been fastened by him for the journey toward liberation.
Even in a dream, the chanting or hearing of the name of Śrī Hari leads to liberation; what then to speak of doing so while awake in this world?
"Salutation to the beloved Kṛṣṇa, salutation to Śrī Hari, and salutation to the Lord"—by speaking thus, one shall attain the path of liberation. (88)
Indeed, for those traveling a long distance set upon the path leading to the abode of Śrī Hari, there shall be the destruction of all impurities through the chanting of the names of Hari. (89)
O Lakṣmī, the chanting of the names of Śrī Hari is in every way the provision for the journey;
even women who are very modest remain within the home like brides.
By chanting "Kṛṣṇakānta, O Hari," people become liberated and go to the divine abode;
for him on whose tongue-tip the two syllables "Ha-ri" reside, [liberation is certain]. 91.
Having crossed the ocean of saṃsāra, she will go to my state, even though she was pervaded by a thousand misdeeds and devoid of righteous actions. (92)
Desiring purity and liberation found by taking refuge in me, she—though remaining hidden—should attain me by becoming devoted solely to my name. 93.
O beloved, for me, the propitiation of Śrī Hari, who is dear to the entire world, is the essence within this worthless saṃsāra, and it is in every way pleasing to women. 94.
One should offer flowers, water, and likewise fruit with a feeling of devotion toward my heart;
by that, the gods are worshipped by me, and the circle of liberated ones is honored. 95.
Neither mother, nor father, nor even kinsman does that which I do when I, the Lord, am satisfied and honored by service. (96)
O Lakṣmī, I am indeed propitiated by a woman who observes the conduct of her caste and stage of life; that alone is the path that brings me satisfaction. 97.
Indeed, I am to be propitiated by all who are endowed with wealth, sovereignty, and majesty, as well as by lineage and faith, and possessed of loving devotion. 98.
Without devotion, without affection, without love, and without meditative cultivation, I do not attain clarity; I am possessed by the hunger for such realization. 99.
Those of the past and even those of the more distant past have gone to my supreme imperishable state;
let those of the most ancient times who went there with devotion, as well as women, likewise go there.
In this way, virtuous people always protect me— who am Kṛṣṇa in form, the Lord of Śrī, the Master, and the Inner Self— within their hearts.
By my yoga alone, those who are peaceful, truthful, and virtuous, as well as the virtuous women belonging to the circle of gurus, are considered by me to be the most excellent of all. 102.
Those who are of my nature, whose very form is mine, and who are not inferior to me—such men are indeed Nārāyaṇas;
for all virtuous people who possess faithful wives are my incarnations.
All virtuous women who descend [into this world] for my sake truly become my gurus; through their yoga, they bestow mantras and even liberation.
Thus, O Nārāyaṇāśrī, the preeminence of the Guru indeed exists eternally;
I am the Guru and the Guru is I—there is not even the slightest difference here. (105)

Thus ends the fifty-sixth chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Reason for the Guru’s Being the Supreme Form of Śrī Hari," within the *Vadhūgītā* of the Third Section, the *Dvāpara-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Śrī Nārāyaṇī, to this essence of all the Vedas:
the Supreme Lord is indeed to be worshipped, for He is the goal to be attained through every means of spiritual practice. 1.
Through gifts, sacred fords, austerities, sacrifices, and acts of service to others, the Supreme Self is to be propitiated; Narayana is to be realized.
Sixty thousand and sixty hundred sacred fords (tīrthas) indeed reside within the feet of the devotees of Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. || 3 ||
Of all penances, austerities, and vows without exception,
the remembrance of Kṛṣṇa is the supreme among them all.
For those people and likewise for women who desire the burning away of their sins,
the supreme atonement is the remembrance of me, Śrī Hari.
Even meditation for a single moment upon Śrī Hari, the Supreme Soul, surely bestows heaven; however, constant meditation grants liberation.
Those men and women who, in the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, are solely devoted to Nārāyaṇa— whatever their mental dispositions may be— they are liberated, without a doubt.
Whether rising, falling, walking, speaking, or entering [a place],
as well as eating or drinking— he who remembers me, Kṛṣṇa, is indeed liberated.
In every case, one’s conduct in one’s own respective duty should be based on the refuge of Acyuta;
for by that, all such action becomes free from the gunas and bestows liberation.
Meditation is declared to be the supreme dharma; austerity is supreme, as is the supreme vow.
Purity is supreme, and meditation upon Hari is supreme; therefore, one should become absorbed in that meditation.
There is no higher object of meditation than Viṣṇu, nor anything higher to be sung about or attained than him;
therefore, one should perform meditation upon Viṣṇu, the Lord Hari, and contemplate him within the heart. (11)
Even that which is difficult to attain, supreme, and beyond the range of the mind—
Hari, when meditated upon here, being pleased, indeed bestows it.
Even if performed through negligence, meditation upon Kṛṣṇa, mindfulness of Him, or an act of salutation,
when accomplished, bestows the eternal state of the Supreme Brahman.
Indeed, there is nothing else equal to meditation for purifying sin;
the remembrance of Hari is the burner of the seed of future bodies.
The perfected accomplishment of meditative absorption indeed bestows concentration.
Having attained concentration, one attains liberation here. || 15 ||
When Viṣṇu is established within one's own heart, the sins of devotees are indeed burnt away from their very root, and the self becomes liberated Brahman. 16.
Just as gold becomes truly stainless through contact with fire, so indeed does the soul of a devotee become established in the abode of Brahman through union with Hari. (17)
Whatever sin is dissolved by a thousand baths in the Gaṅgā and ten million baths at Puṣkara,
that very sin perishes when Hari is remembered.
Whatever sin is dissolved by thousands of breath-control exercises (prāṇāyāma), that very sin is destroyed for the meditator upon meditating on Hari in a mere moment. (19)
Sin, Time, Illusion, Death, and the servants of Yama—even these do not exist for him who possesses the Supreme Person. (3.57.20)
That lunar day, that day and night, that astrological conjunction, and that moon—indeed, the omen and the ascendant are auspicious wherever Hari is remembered. (21)
That is indeed loss, that is disease, and that is injury and poverty, in which moment Kṛṣṇa Hari is not remembered in the home—O Keśava! (22)
In whosever home Hari resides, for him there is always the Satya Yuga;
in whosever home Hari is not present, other ages prevail in that house.
He in whose heart Kṛṣṇa does not reside, nor Hari in his thoughts,
and who has no image of Him in his home— his house is but a cremation ground.
Before him, behind him, within, and in his very faculties, Govinda indeed shines forth; for the Imperishable Abode truly surrounds him on all sides.
He whose mind is fixed on Vāsudeva during the acts of eating and drinking possesses the indestructible abode, which is firm and eternal.
Even while performing the duties of a householder and even while immersed in worldly affairs,
one who dedicates those actions to Keśava cuts through the illusion of human existence.
When Śrī Hari resides in the heart, obstacles depart far away, even Time abandons its crest-lock, and Death does not come within one's sight. (28)
One should meditate upon Nārāyaṇa, Viṣṇu, that Kṛṣṇa, in all undertakings;
for him there is gain, for him there is victory, in whose heart Janārdana resides.
Even for swarms of insects and birds who possess the grace of Śrī Hari, there is attainment of the world of Brahmā; how much more so, then, for those who serve Hari?
The shade of the Nārāyaṇa tree is neither too cold nor does it cause distress;
it soothes the southern gate and should be resorted to by those seeking happiness. (3.1)
Whether speaking, standing, or performing other actions according to his own will, he who does not forget Hari is indeed considered a perfected yogi (siddhayogī). ||32||

Hari should always be meditated upon by a virtuous woman in the form of her guru, her husband, or the sun—youthful, wearing ornaments and fine garments, and more beautiful than ten million gods of love. (33)
Indeed, there is no purifier equal to meditation for the destruction of sin;
even an outcaste (śvapaca) becomes pure, as does one who eats the food of an outcaste.
He in whose living soul there is devotion to Viṣṇu, and in whom Viṣṇu resides as his own self,
delivers tens of millions of those who have come to him for refuge from the cycle of worldly existence.
That is true knowledge where the Lord of Lakṣmī is known; that is the true story where Mādhava appears;
that is the true action which is for the sake of Keśava; and that is true service which is for the Lord of Śrī.
That is a true tongue which praises Hari; that is a true mind which meditates upon the Lord;
and those are true hands which are devoted to the service of Hari and likewise to the service of the virtuous. (37)
Prostration before Kṛṣṇa is the fruit of the head; mindfulness is the fruit of the intellect;
worship of Hari is the fruit of the hands; and devotion to Hari is the fruit of the mind. (18)
The fruit of speech is the hymn to Hari; the fruit of sight is the vision of Hari;
the fruit of the skin is the touch of Viṣṇu; and the fruit of the body is service to Him. (39)
The fruit of all offerings is prosperity, but for the living being, liberation is the fruit;
even a heap of sin as vast as the world and its beyond is destroyed.
Merely by remembering Śrī Hari, a person becomes a virtuous soul;
whatever action they perform—whether good or bad, auspicious or inauspicious—it [becomes pure]. (41)
Whether it be for one’s own sake or for the sake of others, whether it be voluntary or involuntary—having surrendered all of this to Nārāyaṇa, the agent is not defiled by it. 42.
The king is the refuge of the kingdom, and parents are the refuge of the child;
dharma is the refuge of all mortals, and Hari is the refuge of everyone. (43)
Those who always bow to, remember, and worship me—the Lord—are themselves the very form of sacred pilgrimage sites; they are inseparable from me and bestow liberation.
O Lotus-born One, I consider even a Śūdra who is a devotee of the Blessed Lord, or a Niṣāda, or a dog-cooker (outcaste), or even a courtesan or an executioner, to be superior indeed. (45)
Seeing a mountain ablaze with fire, deer and other animals flee;
seeing people set ablaze by me, those whose hearts are filled with evil flee.
For whatever one's degree of faith may be, one's accomplishment shall indeed be of that same measure;
herein, a special grace becomes the bestower of fruit that is never-ending.
There is no end to this clarity of devotion, nor is there any limit to its fruit;
in that regard, there is indeed no restriction whatsoever concerning Hari.
The gracious Lord, the Sovereign, is satisfied with mere water;
He, the Master, bestows the ocean of nectar—who indeed has a master? 49.
By giving a kiss to the King, a female companion obtains half his throne;
likewise, by giving it to Hari, she attains my imperishable state.
Thus, O Śrī Nārāyaṇī, you are the sovereign lady together with all the brides;
you have been offered along with them, for I am he and you are Hari himself.
If anyone, even while worshipping, does not cross over the cycle of worldly existence—which is difficult even for the gods to traverse—it is due to the lack of grace from Hari-Kṛṣṇa. 52.
One should always meditate upon and worship Viṣṇu, who resides within one's own self—the Lord Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa; by that, one shall be liberated from bondage.
By constantly meditating upon Viṣṇu—the creator of all bodies, the delight of all knowledge and the mind, the omnipresent true Guru—one is liberated. 54.
Meditating upon me—who transcend all abodes yet abide in all abodes, who am the cause of all incarnations, and whose very nature is that of the one who incarnates—one is swiftly liberated. 55.
Meditating upon me as Kṛṣṇa, the beginningless Kṛṣṇa, Nārāyaṇa, and Narāyaṇa—the very essence of Vāsudeva and the rest—one is swiftly liberated. (56)
Meditating upon me—the vastness beyond primordial nature, the Puruṣa, the Supreme Person, the Lord of all lords, the Beloved—he is completely liberated. 57.
Meditating upon me as the golden Mahāviṣṇu, as Vairāja Viṣṇu, and as the very nature of the inner self, one is instantly liberated.
It has been meditated upon by the liberated ones and their consorts, by the lords and their goddesses, and even by the incarnations and the gods; having meditated upon it, one is liberated.
Whosoever among embodied beings desires liberation from the bonds of saṃsāra is completely liberated by praising, meditating upon, and worshipping me, Hari.
O Lakṣmī, strength is eternally attainable for me, who manifest in all incarnations;
I have taken refuge in the Lord of the Imperishable—what can death do to me? ||6 1||
I have taken refuge in the Supreme Lord, who dwells within and bears the conch, the discus, the mace, and the lotus; what can death do to me? (62)
I have taken refuge in Him who is endowed with the fish, trident, banner, bow, svastika, discus, and arrows, and who bears the Śrīvatsa mark; what can death do to me?
I have taken refuge in Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the beloved husband, the son of Śrī Kambharā, born of Gopālā; what can death do to me?
I have fully taken refuge in the Lord who is beloved by Brahmā’s wife, the Lord who is beloved by Hari’s wife, the husband of Satī, and the Lord of Śrī; what can death do to me?
I have taken refuge in the Lord of Rādhā, Lakṣmī, Ramā, and Padmāvatī; I am the consort of Māṇikī—what can death do to me?
I have taken refuge in the Lord of Śiva, the husband of Lakṣmī who removes the suffering of Kamalā, the consort of Nārāyaṇa; what can death do to me?
I have taken refuge in the Lord of Divyādevī, the Lord of Kīrā, the Lord of Kāmodakā, and the Sovereign of Suśīla; what can death do to me?
I have taken refuge in Līlāvatīkhaśīnātha, the husband of the courtesan Huṇḍikā, the lord of Haṃsikā; what can death do to me? (69)
"I have taken refuge in the lord of Aśokasundarī, the husband of Vikalendumatī, the king of the Bhillas; what can death do to me? (3.57.70)
I have taken refuge in Hari, my beloved, the Lord who is the protector, wisdom, peace, and faith, and whose nature is liberation; what can death do to me? (71)
I have taken refuge in Kṛṣṇa, Rāma, Rāmakṛṣṇa, Nārasiṃha, Janārdana, and the King of Kings; what can death do to me? (72)
I have taken refuge in my Lord Vārāha, Vāmana, Viṣṇu, Mādhava, Keśava—the most beloved of the beloved; what can death do to me? (73)
I have taken refuge in Kapila, Hari, Vāsudeva, Janārdana, Śiva, and the Lord of the Imperishable; what can death do to me?
I have taken refuge in the eternal, supreme Lord Kṛṣṇa, who has infinite heads, the source of Brahman; what can death do to me? (75)
Standing by the side of Hari, I eternally drink the nectar of love for Him;
I have taken refuge at the feet of Hari—what can death do to me? (76)
I drink that sweet, fragrance-filled nectar born of Hari’s betel;
having surrendered to him, what can death do to me? (77)
I constantly savor the grace known as the nectar of immortality;
having attained the essence of the lips, what can death do to me? (78)
Having attained rest in Śrī Hari, I carry great bliss;
having taken refuge in Him who dwells within, what can death do to me? (79)
I have attained imperishable strength and have reached eternal bliss;
I have taken refuge in the one Self—what can death do to me? (3.57.80)
Having attained the bliss of identity with Him, enjoying the secret joy, and having entered into that very state, what can death do to me? (81)
I have taken refuge in that Lord by whom Death’s father, Mahākāla, was created and under whose control I am; what will Death do to me? (82)
Thus, my beloved, who has attained intoxication from the illustrious Hari, serves me fearlessly and enjoys all my happiness. (83)
She is blessed, she has achieved her purpose, and she abides in all happiness;
her life is fruitful—she who praises the Supreme Person. (84)
Oṃ, salutations to you who dwell in the imperishable; salutations to you who are served by the liberated.
Oṃ, salutations to you, the Lord of lords; salutations to you, the Lord of incarnations. (85)
Oṃ, salutations to the Lord of the Liberated and salutations to the Lord of the virtuous.
Oṃ, salutations to the Lord of the Imperishable and salutations to the Lord of the female Liberated ones. ||86||
Salutations to you, O Supreme Bliss; salutations to you, O Supreme Imperishable.
Salutations to you, O Eternal Omniscient One; salutations to you, O Giver of Knowledge and Liberation. ||87||
Salutations to you who dwell within the self; salutations to you, O Supreme Person!
Salutations to you, Nārāyaṇa, whose form is the inner self of all. ||88||
