Salutations to you, O son of Kambharā; salutations to you, the husband of Gopālā.
Salutations to you, O Lord of Śrī; and salutations to you, Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. ||89||
Salutations to you who dwell in the Kuṅkumavāpī lake, who recline upon the ocean,
who are the sovereign lord of Brahmapriyā, and who are beloved by Haripriyā.
Victory to you, the witness of the true universe! Victory to you, the bestower of all human goals!
Victory to you, who are known through the Vedānta! Victory to you, O beloved, the captivator of the mind! 9.1
Victory to you, O subtle consciousness-bliss! Victory to you, O stainless mind! Victory to you, O Lord! Victory to all! Victory to you, the eternal peace! 92
You are my guru, O Hari, you are my beloved; you are my master and my sovereign lord.
You are my dharma, knowledge, and the rest; you are Viṣṇu, the bestower of liberation upon me.
You are the Lord, you are the deliverer, you are the protector, and you are the destroyer;
you are prosperity, you are nourishment, you are fortune, you are radiance, and you are Māṇikī.
You are the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*), you are the Supreme Lord; you are the sacrifice, you are the consumer of oblations (*hutāśana*).
This entire universe is your form; you are the Supreme Brahman, you are the Sovereign. (95)
O Puruṣottama, the inhabitants of heaven worship your form which consists of incarnations; they do so in their worship, adoration, drinking, and eating.
O Lord of Gods, you ought to forgive that which was done by me and what was not done;
I am unable to always perform worship correctly—forgive me. (97)

O Puruṣottama, whatever recitations, fire-offerings, and so forth have been performed by me—whether they were deficient or complete, and whether they were impossible to accomplish—considering them as my own, O Lord, accept me. 98.
O Lord, day and night, at the twilights, and in all circumstances, my devotion to you is indeed unwavering; my stability rests in the pair of your feet. ||99||
Thus, O Nārāyaṇī, worship me, your Lord, with devotion through this hymn;
if you desire my bliss, serve the Teacher of the World with devotion.
One who recites this hymn at dawn while remembering Puruṣottama shall attain heaven, liberation, prosperity, and all desires. (101)
One desiring a son obtains sons; one who is bound is released from bondage. A woman seeking a daughter obtains a daughter, and a daughter obtains a virtuous husband.
The sick person is freed from disease, the poor person obtains wealth;
the wise man gains the memory of past lives, and the seeker of knowledge acquires wisdom. 103.
Even one who is base becomes foremost, even an evil man becomes the best of the virtuous,
and even a rogue becomes truthful in speech— he who praises Puruṣottama.
Even those virtuous ones who are excluded from all religious duties are considered true practitioners, provided that every action they undertake is performed with Hari in mind. 105.
No impurity exists for her who possesses devotion to the Supreme Lord;
she whose mind, speech, body, and all her possessions are here offered to Hari.
By always propitiating Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the bestower of happiness,
a man, a woman, or even a eunuch attains their heart's desire in this world.

Thus ends the fifty-seventh chapter, titled "The Demonstration of the Hymn of Total Surrender and Other Devotions to Śrī Hari, the Object of Meditation," within the *Vadhūgītā* of the third section, the *Dvāpara-santāna*, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Contemplating, "I am Brahman, the supreme light, Viṣṇu himself," O Nārāyaṇī, a human being indeed becomes liberated while living in this world. || 1 ||
The power of devotion, when accumulated while living, truly bestows joy;
and one endowed with such devotion attains liberation, without a doubt. (2)
He whose mind is attached to Viṣṇu perceives only Viṣṇu;
meditating on Viṣṇu, he gives up his life-breaths and goes to that supreme state. || 3 ||
By propitiating Hari, noble women, having reduced their sins to ashes,
become absorbed in Hari and, like the beloveds of Brahmā, attain the supreme goal.
For just as fire is seen through churning, so indeed is Hari seen through contemplation;
He is perceived right before the range of one's senses, and liberation is considered to be right here.
The Vedas know that Person who is of the nature of consciousness and beyond darkness;
for the sake of liberation from this "I-am-ness," there is no other path to freedom.
When all one's own states of being are offered unto the Supreme Lord,
then one attains immortality, remaining as the imperishable even while living.
"I am Brahman, the supreme light, existing entirely beyond the reach of Māyā"—by realizing the Supreme Self in this way, one should take refuge [in Him] and become a partaker of liberation. (8)
Recollection, worship, and prostration performed with devotion each bestow a fruit greater than that of a horse sacrifice.
In former times, there was indeed a brahmin named Kauśika who was solely devoted to me; he was constantly engaged in singing the Sāman hymns accompanied by the rhythmic clapping of his hands.
Whether at meals, on seats, or in bed; in business or in recreation, he was constantly and repeatedly singing only my own deeds.
Having reached the temple in the presence of the Supreme Lord,
she sang there of Hari, accompanied by rhythm, syllables, and tempo.
Seeing him there singing, distinguished by the application of melodic modulations (*mūrchanā*) and notes (*svara*), and differentiated by the various intervals (*śruti*), the Brahmin named Padma—
For Kauśika remained singing while giving food for the sake of alms;
and that one named Padma remained listening and constantly gave alms.
Then, indeed, Kauśika had many disciples;
all of them, accompanied by the Kauśikas, sang in the temple of Viṣṇu. || 15 ||
In that very temple, a Vaiśya named Mālava was devoted;
together with his wife, he constantly offered a row of lamps to Hari. || 16 ||
Having smeared the entire area of Hari’s field with cow dung,
she remained there with her husband, well-pleased, listening to the most excellent singing.
Thus, that devoted wife, performing worship, adored Mādhava;
and other Brāhmaṇas skilled in singing came from Kuśasthalī. || 18 ||
Fifty of them indeed entered the temple of Hari for the purpose of singing;
they also provide nourishment for the singing of Kauśika.
For those who know the true principles of the science of singing were listening and dwelling there;
indeed, those who knew the truth of singing had assembled thus in the palace. (3.58.20)
His singing there was indeed renowned;
having heard it, even the King of Kaliṅga then [heard] the fame of that master of song.
He arrived, offered his salutations, and thereafter spoke:
"Let all those who are skilled in song come to my palace."
"Let Kauśika also come to my great abode;
let Kauśika and the others perform my song in my abode. (23)
Let all my subjects also listen to my beautiful songs;
I shall give them excellent rewards and wages as well. (24)
"Gold, diamonds, and silver—these five qualities shall be yours in abundance.
Hearing that, Kauśika spoke slowly to King Kaliṅga.
"O Great King, my tongue does not praise anything other than Hari, nor does my speech, nor my mind; even Indra does not praise anything else, nor shall he ever speak of it. (26)
And others, including all the disciples of Kauśika, spoke likewise;
so too did Vasiṣṭha, Gautama, Hari, and Sārasvata. (27)
Citra, Citramālya, and Śiśu likewise said:
"We do not [know] any man or deity distinct from the Blessed Ones. (28)
"We shall sing, nor shall we ever cease singing, of Hare alone;
and likewise those who were Śrāvakas have also become Vaiṣṇavas. (29)
There they said to the king, "O King, we are indeed Vaiṣṇavas; for our bodies, senses, mind, intellect, ego, and self-attributes belong to Viṣṇu. (3.58.30)
Those devoted to Viṣṇu and intent on no other do not associate even by mistake with one who is not a Vaiṣṇava, even if that person serves a Vaiṣṇava.
O King of kings, these ears indeed hear the deeds of Viṣṇu and his devotee, but never those of anyone else.
We hear only the fame of Hari’s singing and no other praise;
we speak with you as if merely engaging in ordinary conversation with others.
We do not touch anything other than Vaiṣṇavas—neither water, nor land, nor the insentient, nor the sentient;
we do not speak of anyone other than Vaiṣṇavas, nor do we even look upon one who is not a Vaiṣṇava.
"We do not accept water, food, or anything else from anyone who is not a Vaiṣṇava at any time;
if such things should happen to be obtained, we consume them only when they have been offered by a Vaiṣṇava. (35)
Hearing that, the king became enraged and said, "These men are insulting me; they must be forced to sing, and let them sing! (36)
"Let my learned servants indeed proclaim my glory"—
having heard this command, those Vaiṣṇavas of firm vows [acted accordingly].
At that time, the king did not speak at all, but commanded his own servants;
by the king's command, the servants began to sing of his own glory.
Then those Vaiṣṇavas and others, wishing to protect the king's reputation, quickly covered their ears with their fingers and other means. ||39||
Then the king, greatly incensed, banished them from his own country;
the singers, abandoning him, went indeed toward the northern direction.
Singing the name of Śrī Hari, hearing of the Supreme Lord, and causing others to hear of Nārāyaṇa-Kṛṣṇa, those men indeed [attain their goal]. 41.
They went to the Himalayas for the sake of coolness, and thereafter they met their end.
Viṣṇu, having arrived, said: "Come after me. 42.
"O sirs, you are indeed my devotees who have renounced their lives for my sake.
Having spoken thus, the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu led them to the supreme heaven.
Honored by the gods and others, and saluted by the ancestors, those twice-born ones went swiftly to the world of Brahmā in a mere moment. (44)
Then, seeing Kauśika and the others, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds,
went forth to meet them and honored them with a welcome as was appropriate.
Then the blessed Lord Viṣṇu, the supreme master Vāsudeva, taking his own dependents with him, went swiftly to the world of Viṣṇu.
In that Vaikuṇṭha, Viṣṇu Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Lord, is indeed served by liberated souls, Siddhas, devotees of Viṣṇu, and his personal attendants. ||47||
By those who were like Nārāyaṇa, divine, auspicious, bearing four arms, endowed with the marks of Viṣṇu, radiant, and stainless; ||48||
He shines resplendently, being served on all sides by Sanaka and others, Nārada and others, and celestial women, within that place enclosed by a thousand doors.
In a divine, auspicious, and stainless jeweled celestial chariot, a thousand yojanas in extent and variegated in appearance, Hari sat upon a throne supported by elephant figures.
Then the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the glorious Puruṣottama,
Lord Hari Nārāyaṇa, beheld Kauśika and the others.
Indeed, he became of a single form and sat upon a divine elephant throne;
with great affection, he said, "O Kauśika," and likewise offered him a welcome.
At that time, there was a cry of victory from the devotees, sounding like a roar from the abode;
the Blessed One said, "Let my devotees dwell in Vaikuṇṭha."
They were intent on hearing my glory, experts in the true meaning of song, and singers of the exposition of the *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*. ||54||
"May these devotees, who worship no other deity, dwell near me;
may they become my eternal attendants here in my abode. (55)
Kauśika, Mālava, and also Mālavī, Padmanetraka, as well as all the other singers who serve me in song. ||56||
"Let them sing and dwell with me forever;
let Kauśika indeed provide my singing accompanied by instrumental music. (57)
"May this Mālava, together with his wife, create a garland of lamps;
may this Padmākṣa become my lord of wealth, indeed a bestower of food. (58)
"Indeed, all those honored by the worlds have attained my presence. While Viṣṇu was speaking thus, they all arrived there in an instant. ||59||
She knew the true qualities of the lute, was proficient in the science of instrumental music,
and the goddess possessed a gentle, slow smile and was charming with her sweet-toned words.
Adorned and singing, Lakṣmī, embraced by Viṣṇu,
was surrounded on all sides by thousands of crores of her own female attendants.
There, the great and virtuous Sarasvatī was remembered by the wielder of the Śārṅga bow;
she arrived accompanied by musical instruments and adorned with every kind of ornament.
Rādhā, Ramā, Kamalā, Māṇikī, Śrī, Satī, as well as Padmāvatī, Haṃsī, Mañjulī, and Sadguṇā; ||63||
The goddesses Gaṅgā, Durgā, and Savitrī, along with Sāvitrī, Virajā, and the Apsarases known as Nārāyaṇīs, indeed arrived there. (64)
Then Urvaśī and the others—skilled in the arts of song, dance, and graceful play—[namely] Menakā, Sahajanyā, Parṇinī, and Puñjikasthalī; ||65||
Kṛtasthalī, Ghṛtācī, Viśvācī, Pūrvacittikā, Anumlocā, Pramlocā, Manuvaṃtī, and Sukeśikā. ||66||
Arūpā, Subhagā, Bhāsī, Haṃsā, Sūtā, Sarovatī, Kāmalī, Abhayā, Haṃsapādī, Sumukhī, and Dayā. (67)
Anapāyā, Aruṇā, Varāmbā, Vimanuṣyikā, Asiparṇā, Miśrakeśī, Śucikālambuṣā, and Ramā. (68)
Mārīcī, Ādrikā, Vidyutparṇā, Tilottamā, Jayā, Kṣemā, Rambhā, Lakṣmaṇā, Asitā, Manobhavā, and Ambikā. (69)
Subāhvī, Supriyā, Puṇḍarīkā, Surasā, Prabhā, Ajagandhā, Sudatī, Subhujā, Śāntikā, and Himā. (3.58.70)
The goddesses Muktā, Haimī, Puṣpā, Campā, and Sāvitrī arrived,
as did the Gandharvas remembered by Nārāyaṇa—
namely Nārada, Parvata, Viśvāvasu, and Vareṇyaka. (71)
Vasuruci, Suruci, Varutha, and Dāruṇa; Haṃsa, Jyotiṣṭama in the middle, Ācāra, and likewise Tumburu. (72)
Subāhu, Hahā, Hūhū, Parjanya, Kali, Śāliśiras, Citraratha, Bhīma, and likewise Prayuta. (73)
Arkaparṇa, Parṇavān, Sūryavarcas, Dhṛtarāṣṭraka, Gomān, Suparṇa, Varuṇa, Ugrasena, and Bhīmaka. ||74||
These and others, accompanied by musical instruments and the like, arrived there;
and the Gandharva Tumburu was commanded by me to be present there.
O Lakṣmī, seeing you as the singer, he does not see either you or me beyond that;
seated there, he [perceives] according to his capacity, accompanied by various modulations (mūrchanās). 76.
Delighted, he sang in melodious tones and played upon the lute;
having sung an excellent song, the Supreme Lord was propitiated.
He gave divine jewels, ornaments, and garments, all of priceless value, to Tumburu; and Tumburu was then filled with joy.
There, Tumburu was praised by Hari and took the lead;
many other Gandharvas sang as well, each according to his strength.
According to their knowledge and according to their practice, they sang with instrumental sounds and melodies; they too indeed received excellent rewards there.
Nevertheless, that reward was not equal to Tumburu;
then all the Apsarases began to sing, employing the finest musical instruments.
Then the goddess Lakṣmī sang, and Sarasvatī likewise sang;
they both thought, "We have received the highest reward. (82)
Urvaśī sang beautifully, a song that causes delight to all;
the others also sang according to their ability, accompanied by dance. (83)
Then the Blessed Lord Śrī Hari and I became pleased;
I bestowed upon him diamonds, gems, garments, ornaments, and beautiful garlands. (84)
Then everyone, both male and female, was completely satisfied, and Nārada sang aloud;
he also gave him an excellent reward as a prize.
Nārada was not satisfied with Tumburu’s singing because it was slightly deficient; since it was not perfect even in its execution, he experienced distress.
Thereupon, he fell into reflection, his inner self becoming overwhelmed with grief.

"When shall I, having performed a song that is the most supreme among all the supreme, receive an excellent reward from the presence of Hari? That best [reward] was obtained by Tumburu; fie upon me, the deluded and senseless one! || 87-88 ||
Reflecting thus, the brahmin sage Nārada engaged in ascetic penance for a thousand divine years while remembering Śrī Hari.
Then he mastered every art of song even from Tumburu;
having learned everything from Tumburu, he sang it before Nārāyaṇa.
During the time of many Manvantaras, the Supreme Person, the Lord Hari Nārāyaṇa, being pleased, bestowed all auspicious things upon him;
he made his reward excellent and equal to that of Tumburu.
Thus indeed was she the wife of Nārāyaṇa, the maidservant of the illustrious Blessed One.
Just as Lakṣmī made a total surrender for the sake of Hari,
and as did Tumburu, and Nārada,
and also the brahmin Kauśika, and the twice-born Padmākṣaka.
And just as Mālavī was the wife and Mālava was the husband, so it was likewise. || 94 ||
Just as other singer-brahmins have offered [themselves] unto Hari, so too should the offering of everything be made unto Janārdana, the Supreme Lord. (95)
The functions, activities, and actions of the senses must be performed solely for my sake; by that, I am always pleased. (96)
Beholding, listening, touching, singing, dancing, and laughing for my sake must indeed be performed with devotion. (97)
Food, water, clothing, a house, a bed, a seat, a vehicle, a mount, a garden, or land should be given to my devotees. (98)
It should be given according to one's ability; it arises as a source of satisfaction for me.
That indeed yields the fruit of both worldly enjoyment and liberation; of this there is no doubt. (99)
O Lakṣmī, by merely hearing, reflecting upon, or even causing others to hear this, one shall indeed obtain a fruit equal to that of Nārada; there is no doubt in this matter.
People shall obtain a fruit equal to Lakṣmī in the form of a woman, equal to Sarasvatī in the form of a daughter-in-law, and equal to a singer; of this there is no doubt. (101)

Thus ends the fifty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Supremacy of the Vaiṣṇavas through the Example of the Singers Kauśika and Others," within the *Vadhūgītā* of the third section, the *Dvāparasantāna*, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇī Śrī said: O Nārāyaṇa, O Hari, O Beloved, O Lord of Śrī, O Supreme Lord!
By what yoga did Nārada indeed obtain the science of song?
O Śrī Narāyaṇa, tell me this ancient tale of a previous kalpa: at what time did he attain equality with Tumburu?
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Śivārājñī-Śrī, to that auspicious narrative in detail;
from that point onward, Nārada departed from Vaikuṇṭha.
Dejected and holding his breath, remembering the greatness of Tumburu,
he performed penance for a thousand years and thereby became a mass of ascetic power.
Then he heard an incorporeal voice in the sky:
"O Nārada, for what purpose do you perform this difficult penance? (5)
Go and see Ulūka, if your mind is intent on singing;
he is indeed renowned as Gānabandhu on Mount Mānasottara.
"Go quickly and behold him; you shall become a master of song.
Thus addressed, Nārada went swiftly to Gānabandhu.
Assuming any form at will, the bird, whose voice was as sweet as that of Kāma and who surpassed even the gods,
taught the art of singing to other birds and even to embodied beings.
Then the Gandharvas, Kinnaras, Yakṣas, and hosts of Apsarases sat down all around Gānabandhu.
Having mastered the science of song and being instructed by that bird,
they then sang there in succession with voices of sweet resonance.
Beholding the sage Nārada, Gānabandhu said:
"Salutations to you, O tiger among sages; welcome to you, and my greetings."
For what purpose has the Blessed One come here—out of compassion, by chance, or perhaps to grant me a meritorious vision? Tell me, what may I do for you?
Then Nārada said to him: "Listen, O Owl, to the truth as it is;
I shall tell you of a most wonderful event that occurred to me in the past."
In a past kalpa, during that bygone age, I went into the presence of Hari, eager there to perform a song.
Accompanied by Lakṣmī, Viṣṇu summoned Tumburu;
having set me aside, he joyfully listened to the sublime song.
Therefore, afflicted by extreme suffering, I went to perform penance [to learn] the majesty of the yoga of singing concerning the greatness of Viṣṇu.
After that, I indeed performed severe penance with full intention;
at the end of a thousand divine years, I addressed you with words from the sky.
I heard the name of Gānabandhu; if you have the inclination, go to him.
If your mind is set upon singing, then behold Ulūka without delay. 1.8.
Thus impelled, I have come here into your presence;
therefore, regarding me as your disciple, please instruct and protect me. 19.
Having heard this auspicious and most wonderful song centered on devotion to Viṣṇu, the learned Gānabandhu spoke to Nārada.
In a former kalpa, there was a king renowned as Bhuvaneśa;
he performed thousands of Aśvamedha sacrifices and ten thousand Vājapeya sacrifices.
With ten million times a hundred billion cows, with ten million crores of golden lotuses, and with parārdhas of garments, chariots, elephants, maidens, and horses; || 22 ||
Having bestowed gifts upon the virtuous brahmins, he protected the earth;
and day and night, he caused his own fame to be sung even by singers.
Those who do not sing, he seizes and imprisons in a jail; "He who does not perform my song is to be put to death"—such is his decree.
"Let women and men constantly sing my praises;
let the assemblies of Sūtas and Māgadhas sing my songs repeatedly. (25)
Having thus commanded, that king indeed protected his own kingdom.
In the empire of that monarch, there was one renowned as Harimiśra.
There was a brahmin who was a devotee of Viṣṇu; having reached the sandy bank of a river, he sang songs of praise to the auspicious image of Śrī Hari.
Having worshipped him and offered the food oblation, he gave water and sang with great affection, accompanied by rhythmic beats, vocal registers, and melodic timing.
Then a spy, acting on the king’s command,
arrived and ordered him to sing the fame of the king.
That Vaiṣṇava brahmin also did not accept his words;
then the spies, having seized that brahmin, brought him into the presence of the king.
Having brought him, the king informed [the queen] and rebuked that brahmin;
he then banished him from the kingdom, having seized all his wealth and possessions.
The Brahmin went into the depths of the forest and worshipped Śrī Parameśvara;
meanwhile, the king, due to the exhaustion of his lifespan, succumbed to the law of time.
Wherever he went in that world, there he fell into the Kumbhīpāka hell;
overcome by hunger and thirst, he was tormented by insults.
Having experienced various kinds of sufferings, he thereafter ascended to heaven;
however, the food and nectar-like water that he obtained there in the celestial chariot— || 34 ||
Only that which is seen arises and dissolves at the moment of perception;
thus, for the king and the deity, there exists neither drink nor food. (35)
Distressed by this, he lamented even for me who had gone to heaven:
"Hunger and thirst arise here; food and drink, once touched, dissolve away. (36)
"What evil have I committed, the fruit of which is now being experienced?"—as he was reflecting thus, a voice from the sky indeed arose. (37)
O King, out of ignorance and delusion, you have committed a great sin against a brahmin named Harimiśra, who was devoted to Kṛṣṇa and a singer of His praises.
He inflicted a severe punishment upon him for failing to sing for you;
his wealth was seized by you, and he was banished from the kingdom. (39)
Afflicted by hunger and thirst, he is indeed performing austerities in the forest;
this devotee of Hari, O King, has been made deeply distressed by you.
O King, by that sin, your food and drink shall dissolve;
all your acts of charity, sacrifice, and so forth, shall become fruitless. ||41||
Since you caused Harimitra—who was devoted to Hari, accompanied by song and instrumental music, and singing praises of the Lord—to become distressed; ||42||
Even your heavenly realm is lost; go to a mountain cave and dwell there eating dust for as long as a manvantara shall endure.
"You shall become an insect named Kardamī; then, after a period of time, having fully experienced the fruit of your sin, you will attain human birth. (44)
Thus that king, indeed fallen from heaven, came to Koṭara;
born in the mud, he became Kardama upon the watery ground.
"I was an owl there as well, and I went there for the sake of inquiry.
When questioned by me, he related the account of his former deeds."
He declared that the fruit of betraying a devotee of the Blessed One is being devoured by mud;
having said this, I then emerged from his cave.
Having seen from afar in the path of the sky a celestial chariot accompanied by attendants and filled with song, wherein dwelt the Brahmin Harimitraka.
Being praised by gods and attendants as well while in his celestial chariot, that glorious one went to the world of Viṣṇu; he too was beheld by me. (49)
The merit of singing the praises of Hari leads to a true destination toward Vaikuṇṭha;
by the power of that sovereignty, my mind has been drawn hither. (3.59.50)
Then, for the sake of the science of song, I sat down with the Kinnaras;
thus, through my application to singing, sixty thousand years passed for me.
My tongue attained clarity, and thereafter I practiced singing;
even after that, for a long time, I practiced singing again and again. ||52||
Engaged in the practice of singing, ten Manvantaras passed;
formerly, I was the preceptor of song for both the Gandharvas and their women. (53)
In a previous kalpa, I was the teacher of all the Kinnara singers, of all human women, and likewise of the Apsarases.
Then, O Nārada, the assemblies of singers who are present here now approached me, their teacher. ||55||
But those disciples of mine, along with their disciples and grand-disciples, exist as branches joined in thousands, forming lineages, sub-lineages, and successive descendants. (56)
"O Nārada, the science of singing cannot indeed be attained through austerity alone;
therefore, being perfected through sacred learning, receive the art of singing from me. (57)
Thus addressed, O Lakṣmī, Nārada prostrated and paid homage to me;
then, following the sequence of instruction, he learned singing there from an owl.
In conversation, in the company of women, in song, in gambling, in eating, in legal affairs, in the acquisition of wealth, and in income and expenditure for one's own sake; (59)
A person who has cast aside shame attains victory, whereas one possessed of shame certainly does not;
[victory is not won] by being contracted, hidden, or by means of veils such as clothing and the like.
Indeed, one should never sing while making gestures with the hands, with the mouth wide open, or by means of protruding the tongue. (61)
One should not sing with the arms raised, nor with the gaze directed upwards in any way;
likewise, one should not sing while looking at one's own limbs or while staring at another person.
In the case of a collision, as well as during rising or when the hand is placed on the hip, [the practice] is not recommended;
likewise, there may be a decrease in vigor, anger, or trembling, whereas mindfulness occurs elsewhere. (63)
O Great-minded One, these forms of rhythmic beating are not suitable for the application of song;
O Sage, it is impossible to coordinate the ensemble of beats with only one hand. (64)
One who is afflicted by hunger, afflicted by fear, or likewise afflicted by thirst,
should never practice the yoga of singing, nor ever in the darkness.
And other such things as these, which cause negligence and laziness, must certainly not be done by a wise singer on the stage. (66)
Having thus mastered the training according to the prescribed method, the sage Nārada likewise practiced divine song for a thousand years. 67.

Then, endowed with all perfections, he was accomplished in singing, instrumental music, and the like; he was proficient in the lute and other instruments, and was a knower of the distinctions of all musical notes.
And thirty-six million, eight hundred thousand—that best of sages understood the variations of the vowels through their combinations. (69)
Then the hosts of Gandharvas and likewise the Kinnaras,
together with the sages, became filled with joy.
Having attained unsurpassed song, the sage said to Gānabandhu:
"Having approached you, you have indeed become a master of melody. (71)
"O Guru, what may I do for you in the worship of you, my teacher?
Then Gānabandhu replied: "Indeed, on the day of Brahmā..."
"Grant me this boon: that fourteen Manus there, as well as myself, shall perish; for I desire this reward. (73)
"O Nārada, as long as this life of mine shall endure, and as long as my supreme welfare remains, may this desired object of my mind be fulfilled here through this sacrificial fee. (74)
Then Nārada said to him, "Let it be so;
furthermore, in another kalpa, you yourself shall become Garuḍa."
"May it be well with you, O one of great wisdom; may the auspicious vehicle of the Blessed One [protect] you.
Having said, "I shall depart; salutations to you," the illustrious Nārada went away. (76)
O Lakṣmī, in Vaikuṇṭha, the abode of Nārāyaṇa where I dwell,
he performed singing before me with many beautiful melodies.
Having heard that, I said to him who was indeed perfected in song:
"O Nārada, even now you are not superior to Tumburu in songs. (78)
"Once you have approached Gānabandhu and become a knower of the meaning of song, you will indeed be distinguished; then Mādhava too will be pleased. (79)
When I am to be born upon the earth as a human being who has descended [to it],
you should then approach me and cause [the task] to be performed exactly as it ought to be.
Then I shall make you, observer of the great vow, accomplished in song,
equal to Tumburu and even endowed with superior excellence.
For that duration, train yourself as is appropriate and according to the rule within the wombs of gods and gandharvas; may it be well with you, O Surāṣṭraka! (82)
Having heard the words of Nārāyaṇa and having bowed to Hari, Nārada took his lute upon his shoulder and wandered through all the worlds.
Having reached the assembly hall, Nārada beheld the regions of Varuṇa, Yama, Agni, Indra, Kubera, Vāyu, and likewise Īśāna.
Singing praises of Hari while being perfectly skilled in playing the lute,
he was honored here and there by hosts of Gandharvas and Apsarases.
Having reached the world of Brahmā, he spent the night lasting for a kalpa;
then, at dawn, once again in this kalpa, he was in the abode of the Unborn (Brahmā) in the world of Brahmā.
And the two Gandharvas Hāhā and Hūhū, experts in song and instrumental music—the divine singers of Brahmā who are ever intent upon singing—[were there]. (87)
There, having approached those two while singing praises to the Lord Hari, and having received his reward, he bowed down to the Grandfather (Brahmā). ||88||
He wandered according to his desire and went to the house of Tumburu;
taking up a lute there, he sang and also practiced.
Furthermore, Nārada learned from Tumburu all seven notes—beginning with Ṣaḍja—which are considered to exist there as kalpas of sound. (3.59.90)
Nārada also learned the seven musical notes along with their qualities;
however, at the time of singing, when joined with the lute, the qualities of the notes indeed [manifested]. (91)
The strings did not at all reach their appropriate places of origin;
then, once again, at the horse-saddle lake in the hermitage of Lomaśa.
When he had finished his song, I, Śrī Narāyaṇa,
spoke to you, O Lotus-born one, my beloved who possesses an eternally divine form.
"Teach Sarasvatī, Avadā, and indeed Nārada;
then, regarding the union of lute and song, say 'So be it'. Thereafter—
Laughing, you taught Lakṣmī and Sarasvatī;
thereafter, indeed, you performed a song in the presence of those dear to Brahmā.
"O Sage, although you were singing, you did not indeed know the musical scale.
Then Nārada, having obtained the musical notes and the application of the strings, [proceeded]. 96.
Having been summoned, I was taught the unsurpassed art of singing;
thereafter, O best of sages, I attained a superiority over Tumburu.
Then, having approached and prostrated before me repeatedly, he danced;
thereupon I said to Nārada, "You are omniscient; come into my presence."
Sing with the yoga of knowledge; and Nārada sang as well. Being pleased, I granted him my eternal presence here in this imperishable syllable.
That sage Nārada resides in the field of Kuṅkumavāpī,
having received an excellent reward bestowed by the Gracious One.
By me alone has the preeminence of Tumburu also been bestowed;
then, after some time, Nārada shall sing in the house of Kṛṣṇa.
O wives of Brahmā, this sequence of songs of the sage has been declared here to you; one who sings according to this sequence shall attain the same world as me (sālokya).
Devoted solely to Nārāyaṇa in deed, thought, and speech, one approaches Me by singing and listening; that indeed is considered the supreme song.
"O noble one, this owl is actually Garuḍa, residing at Lake Aśvasaras;
he is my attendant, a singer and a friend to music. (104)

Thus ends the fifty-ninth chapter, titled "The Narration of Garuḍa and Nārada’s Acquisition of Instruction in Singing," within the *Vadhūgītā*, in the illustration of the preeminent devotee, in the third section, the *Dvāpara-santāna*, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
The illustrious Śrī Nārāyaṇī said:
Those who are called Vaiṣṇavas are those who are solely devoted to Nārāyaṇa;
they are the Bhāgavatas and Sāttvatas who have surrendered their entire being.
O Lord, tell me what are the characteristics of those [men] and of them [women];
O Blessed One, O All-pervading Hari, what do you do with them?
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Nārāyaṇī Śrī, you who are the very embodiment of my devotee; hear this purifying account of my love, which conveys the state of identity with Me.
Wherever a devotee dwells, there I am always present;
I alone am the supreme deity for them and for them.
When Hari is being glorified, there constantly arises a frequent horripilation;
likewise, trembling, perspiration, and drops of water are seen upon the eyes. || 5 ||
Upon seeing men or women who are devoted to me, he whose heart immediately becomes filled with affection— such a person is indeed a Vaiṣṇava.
A virtuous woman should not cover herself with another garment, nor should she be dependent on another;
upon seeing a Vaiṣṇava or Sāttvata, she should stand before him with love.
Just as he performs prostrations and other marks of reverence toward Śrī Kṛṣṇa, so too,
upon seeing a male or female devotee, the devotee should quickly bow down to that devotee or devotee.
He who is my soul and my devotee, and that beautiful woman who is my devotee,
obtains victory throughout the three worlds, in all abodes and creations.
Without shame she attends upon me, having cast aside her wicked suitors;
she gives everything for my sake—truly he is a Vaiṣṇava, and she is a Vaiṣṇavī.
Even when hearing harsh words spoken at some point by one who is devoted,
he attains joy therein and does not indeed give way to anger.
One should accept only the merit with patience, preceded by a prostration;
she who is a Vaiṣṇava woman is indeed a Vaiṣṇava, endowed with divine vision and being virtuous.
She who indeed carries all things, such as perfumes and flowers, upon her head,
considering them all to belong to Hari— she is truly a Vaiṣṇavī.
In my field, he performs only auspicious deeds day and night;
full of affection, he serves me, the virtuous, and my devotees. || 14 ||
One who constantly worships my image with all types of offerings through action, mind, and speech is considered by me to be the most excellent devotee. 15.
In times of disease, hardship, or calamity, as well as in the face of obstacles and distress,
let there be honor for my service, for the company of the virtuous, and for the saints themselves.
And he who performs service day and night toward the temple, toward the virtuous, toward the wives of devotees, and also toward his gurus; || 17 ||
Likewise, [he performed] auspicious service for those dear to Brahmā, consisting of the provision of food, clothing, and water, as well as the washing of garments. (18)
[He performed] the rites consisting of smearing, washing, consecrating, and sweeping,
as well as the cleansing of vessels and the tending of cows and buffaloes.
He performed service for guests who had arrived, service consisting of providing food and drink,
service by massaging the feet, and service in the form of rubbing the limbs.
And [he should perform] the giving of herbs and so forth, taking the form of gathering wood, according to his capacity, as is appropriate, and in accordance with his caste and stage of life. ||21||
Whoever performs service— the activity of a servant or the excellent service of a male or female slave—
and whoever shows honor, he likewise shall perform the state of servitude.
For whomsoever Nārāyaṇa is the supreme goal, and for whomsoever He is their very all; for whomsoever He is the ultimate refuge of the virtuous, and for whomsoever He is their very all. (23)
For the sake of dharma and for the sake of liberation, they even gave away their entire possessions;
indeed, those two were supreme devotees of Nārāyaṇa.
He who constantly performs all services for the sake of food for a devotee of Viṣṇu according to his ability is indeed the best of Bhāgavatas. ||25||
Whatever food a devotee devoted to Nārāyaṇa eats, he eats from the very mouth of Hari;
indeed, Hari himself is satisfied.
The man or woman who worships the devotees of Viṣṇu with devotion, indeed like Viṣṇu himself,
attains proximity to Viṣṇu and eternal liberation.
A devotee of Viṣṇu excels over thousands of other devotees;
a devotee of Hari excels over thousands of devotees of Viṣṇu. (28)
A devotee of Hari is of the nature of Brahman and shall go to the abode of the Supreme Lord;
indeed, he is the sovereign of devotees unto me, whose very form is that of the Incarnate. (29)
"In this very place, O Lakṣmī, I shall always provide protection for her while she is alive and after she has been liberated; listen now to this supreme account of my devotee. (3.60.30)
Cidambarā became the queen, the sovereign consort of King Jiṣṇu;
she was devoted to me in the region of Godala in Saurāṣṭra. ||3 1||
For Jiṣṇuśakti, having met his end through devotion, went to my abode known as the Imperishable;
and Rājñī ruled the kingdom. (32)
Devoted, intent on Brahman, equal to a goddess, and endowed with purity, she rises in the morning and [worships] me, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the supreme among men. (33)
He constantly worshipped the Supreme Lord, the Lord of the Imperishable, the Lord of Śrī, the Most Excellent Person, through the actions of speech, mind, and body.
The offering of food, worship, the giving of water, the presentation of flower garlands, the grinding of perfumes and other substances, and the preparation of incense materials. ||35||
She herself performed the smearing of the ground as well as the cooking of the sacrificial offerings, for she was the very embodiment of all devotion and wonder. (36)
The auspicious Cidambarā constantly speaks with her voice the word "Nārāyaṇa," and repeatedly utters "Anādi-Śrī-Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa. (37)
For ten thousand years, she, with her inner self devoted to that [task],
constantly worshipped me as Kṛṣṇa with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
He constantly gratified other auspicious devotees of Viṣṇu, the great Bhāgavatas,
with gifts, honors, worship, wealth, and jewels.
Then, on one occasion, after her worship, that queen fell asleep at the end of the night on the twelfth lunar day; and Puruṣottama appeared visibly before her.
"O Lakṣmī, I myself became endowed with all splendor;
he accepted in its entirety the worship performed by her in her dream. (41)
The signs given by me are indeed a garland of tulasī on the neck, and likewise a beautiful saffron tilaka-moon upon the forehead. (42)
There was collyrium upon her eyes, earrings upon her ears,
a lotus garland upon her neck, and the marks of weapons upon her arms.
O Lakṣmī, I then became marked with lines of the conch, discus, mace, and lotus, as well as a tilaka; at that very moment, she indeed became invisible.
She quickly became wide awake and beheld her body marked [with the signs];
overcome by great wonder, she was filled with joy. || 45 ||
She has become a great devotee of the Lord and likewise a great follower of the Sātvata path;
she has surrendered her entire being for my sake, and the splendor of her kingdom exists for my sake alone. (46)
Therefore, that virtuous woman, whose entire being was dedicated to me, who embodied great dispassion, and who was solely devoted to the Supreme Lord, took refuge in me. (47)
Constantly devoted to the holy life (brahmacarya) and dedicated to the company of the virtuous, she always conducts herself like a chaste woman, having abandoned attachment to sense objects. 48.
Indeed, she remained like a servant-girl who has surrendered her very self;
then, after some time, I arrived there to test her.
Having indeed fashioned my own Garuḍa to be as inconceivable as Airāvata,
I myself became Śakra and approached the queen’s palace.
"I am Indra; may it be well with you. What boon shall I grant you?
As the lord of all heaven, I have come to you to bestow heaven itself. (5.1)
Take either the most excellent heaven or the supreme station of Mahendra;
let the sky be your slave, and let the earth always be your slave.
"Accept the kingdom, O fortunate lady; cast away widowhood!
Accept this supreme and auspicious good fortune that shall endure for the duration of a Manvantara. (53)
Do not waste this divine body, so delicate and fit for enjoyment;
having obtained it by chance, be happy, O beautiful woman.
Without a lover, the world is always harsh and indeed scorched for women;
therefore, O lady of merit, accept me as your beloved, your most handsome lover. (55)
Having heard this, Citāmbara said: "I bow to the yogi Indra;
let there be salutation to the deity for me. O deity, do not see any fault in me. (56)
This human body always contains a divine, radiant essence;
yet the human womb is a formidable destroyer of the status of Indra.
O best of gods, do not set your mind upon this human state, which is a gateway to the destruction of merit.
Do not be thus consumed by my curse; show me forbearance.
"O Lord of the Gods, having received worship and salutation, you may depart;
for the deities of the Rājasika nature are indeed naturally prone to women.
It is not surprising that they desire women there, but it is simply that this does not please me."
I do not rule the kingdom on this earth with you in mind.
"I shall not take what has been given by you; go, O Indra, to your own abode.
Nārāyaṇa is my lord; indeed, I worship that beloved one. (61)
"Go, O Indra; do not cause the destruction of my intellect here.
I shall become a servant of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
Upon hearing this, the Lord Indra withdrew his form as Indra.
He himself became one whose hands bore the Śārṅga bow, the discus, the mace, and the lotus.
Upon Garuḍa, I, the Lord Hari, accompanied by Lakṣmī and Śrī, became manifest before her; she praised me and bowed down to me. (64)
Be gracious, O Lord of the lords of the gods, O Lord of the lords of lords, Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, Śrī Puruṣottama! 65.
You are the beginningless Lord, the Protector, the Master, the Beloved, and the Consort of Śrī;
you are the immeasurable, all-pervading Viṣṇu, Govinda, the lotus-eyed one.
Lord of the beloved of Brahmā, Lord of the beloved of Hari, Supreme Sovereign;
I have taken refuge in You, O Govinda, O beloved Lord of Godāvarī. 67.
Without you, I do not desire even sovereignty, heaven, or supreme happiness;
there is no other refuge for me but you—you alone are my shelter. (68)
You are the Indra of truth, you are the Great Indra, and you are the Indra of the self, O Supreme Lord;
indeed, I worship You as the true Indra of all my senses.
I bow to You, the Lord of my life; I bow to You who abide within;
I bow to You, seated upon the couch of bliss, the yogi of the supreme fourth state.
Having heard that praise, I said to her: "What do you desire in your heart?
I shall grant all of that to you; speak, for you are my supreme devotee. (71)
"I am always fond of devotion; whatever you desire, I shall grant it.
Having heard this, Citambara said, "My mind and heart are eternally [fixed] on You."
May you, the Lord, the beloved of the Beloved, who are devoted solely to the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, abide within my heart. 73.
Just as you, O Hari, abide as the Lord who knows the inner self of all,
so too do I become, O Kṛṣṇa, one whose being is centered in your inner self.
Out of compassion for you, I shall protect the earth as long as it endures;
and having performed a Vaiṣṇava sacrifice, I shall gratify the deities.
I shall protect the Vaiṣṇavas; may you dwell in my home. You abide as my beloved; always be my protector. (76)
Or else, having led me to Your own abode, make me another Lakṣmī;
O Gopāla, O Protector of Ramā, wander as You please toward the realm of consciousness.
O Lakṣmī, as soon as I heard what Cidambara had said, my mace— endowed with the splendor to annihilate all things— was surrendered by me to him.
She is the protector of the kingdom, the destroyer of enemies, and the one who walks by one's side;
she whose very form consists of thousands upon thousands of maces.
At the time of battle, they indeed arise as destroyers of curses, diseases, and enemies;
having given her [the boon], the compassionate Lord returned to His own abode.
She too, being greatly delighted, protects the kingdom of Godala.
He established all the social classes on the path of dharma, each engaged in their respective duties. ||8 1||
In every house he caused devotion to the illustrious Pauruṣottama to be practiced;
in every house Hari resided, and in every house there was the chanting of the Vedas.
The daughter of the king caused the sound of Hari’s name and the sound of sacrifice to be heard in every city,
and she performed Vaiṣṇava sacrifices.
In the city of Cidambara and in the land of Śāstrī, the earth yielded its essence;
the subjects were free from disease, possessed even of their grass, and lived without affliction. (84)
The land shall be free from famine and other calamities, filled with auspicious and great festivals;
there shall be no untimely death, nor shall disease or mental anguish exist.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, that queen indeed established a Vaiṣṇava kingdom, and she protected the virtuous in their dwellings throughout every place. (86)
The virtuous were fully honored by her with water, garments, and food;
and truthful, chaste women were constantly protected and served by her. (87)
The cows were protected by that virtuous woman, and likewise, the helpless were nurtured;
every morning and evening, she performed my worship. (88)
Maṇḍalīs were also established, accompanied by devoted women, [chanting]:
"O Hari, Kṛṣṇa! O Hari, Nārāyaṇa! O Śrī Puruṣottama! (89)
"O Hare, O Lord of Lakṣmī, O Lord of Rādhā, O Lord of the beloved of Brahmā!"—in this manner, she caused my kīrtana to be performed everywhere. (3.60.90)
In that manner, she caused delightful food-distributions to be established;
she had water-stations constructed and provided shade from trees.
He caused dharma-halls to be built, and likewise he caused cow-pens to be built; he caused schools to be built, and likewise he caused schools for the knowledge of Brahman to be built. ||92||
She also established irrigation works and canals for the prosperity of agriculture;
furthermore, she constructed the temple of Cidambara at the site of Kuṅkumavāpikā.
Behold my temple here; it shines like a peak of the sky.
For every morning, that queen bathes and then worships me. (94)
Indeed, he constantly attends the assembly of those who possess the knowledge of Brahman;
there, Godalāyana always engages in discourse concerning Brahman. ||95||
He performs the recitation of the Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā;
thereafter, the chanting (kīrtana) takes place, and after that, the ritual dismissal (visarjana). ||96||
For the virtuous and the chaste, association with the good arises as auspicious;
indeed, service to those devoted to the character of Brahman becomes pleasing to the heart. (97)
"For in her kingdom, all five sacrifices are performed constantly.
Thinking thus, she carries out the administration of the kingdom for me. (98)
Divine, equal to divine nectar, the sky of consciousness, and beloved of Hari—having obtained Hari as her husband and lord, she took recourse in a state of dispassion. ||99||
May they worship that Blessed One, the Lord of Life, the Supreme Sovereign;
may they proceed to the eternal abode and attain supreme joy.
In this way, that virtuous woman, possessing a divine body, caused all her subjects to hear this constant instruction, which yields the certain fruit of merit. || 101 ||
I always provide protection for such devotees;
I grant them residence by my side as well as service at my feet.

Thus ends the sixtieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Marks of a Great Bhāgavata Devotee, the Testing of Queen Citrāmbā, and Her Devotion," within the *Vadhūgītā* of the third section, the *Dvāpara-santāna*, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Nārāyaṇī Śrī, to how the protection of your devotee was likewise accomplished by the mace;
I shall tell you that great and wonderful account. (1)
Once, a Rākṣasa named Bhadraka, who made his dwelling in the ocean,
heard and learned that the kingdom of Godala and the five surrounding provinces belonged to a woman.
Desirous of making his own wife Cidambārā [his], that Rākṣasa,
assuming a form at will, became a deluder of hundreds of kings.
Having become a youth, exceedingly charming, well-nourished, and resplendent with beauty,
he had fashioned a Vaiṣṇava tilaka by the virtuous Rākṣasas.
Accompanied by prepared Brahmins and adorned with the attire of a traveler,
he, endowed with royal splendor, arrived at the city named Godalā.
Having learned of the queen's situation, that devotee of Viṣṇu assumed the form of a Rākṣasa and dwelt in the garden where she was suffering from illness.
The king went to the royal palace and beheld the beautiful queen;
having recognized him, the queen honored the nobleman with a welcome and other courtesies.
Then, infatuated by passion, he begged the queen for the kingdom;
the queen quickly forbade him from going outside the realm.
The Rākṣasa also quickly gave orders,
and having bowed to his own people and led them away, he then proceeded swiftly toward the ocean.
Arriving alone at another time during the night, he approached the queen;
lifting her up as she lay there, he carried her upon his shoulder into the sky.
The Rākṣasa departed swiftly when the queen awoke;
then that virtuous lady saw the Rākṣasa in the sky carrying her away.
She remembered that Kaumodakī mace, and the mace immediately came before her;
then, commanded by the queen, it indeed stood ready for protection.
And indeed, in order to slay the Rākṣasa, that terrifying mace flew up into the sky and fell upon the shoulder of the demon.
Again and again, repeatedly, he struck at the various limbs of Bhadraka— on his head, the back, the arms, the thighs, and the feet.
He too struck the Rākṣasa, who, being hit, fell upon the earth and became unconscious near the garden of his seat. || 15 ||
Taking the mace with her and remembering me, the Supreme Lord, she abandoned the Rākṣasa while he still possessed life and returned to her own abode. || 16 ||
The Rākṣasa departed for his own abode in the midst of the ocean;
having heard of the protection of the queen, the subjects were then immersed in joy.
Eagerly, the subjects honored the queen with blessings;
having performed worship to Hari, the queen then performed worship to the mace (Gadā). 18.
Thus was the protection provided for the queen by the mace against the Rākṣasa at that time;
yet the Rākṣasa, in turn, returned after some interval accompanied by his army.
Prepared to bring back that queen and reclaim his own kingdom,
he surrounded the city with many divisions of his army and let out a roar.
He caused battle-instruments to be sounded through the path of the sky;
the queen praised me, Kṛṣṇa, and worshipped my mace with sandalwood pastes.
Thereafter, she chose protection by means of foods, necklaces, perfumes, and other such things;
then, rising from her own place, she instantly appeared in the sky.
In an instant, she became endowed with the brilliance of ten million suns and fires;
emitting tongues of blazing flame, she roared again and again.
Making the two worlds (heaven and earth) resound, she shone forth bringing victory;
she quickly advanced against Bhadraka’s auspicious army.
That mace, through the deluded Māra, slew Bhadraka;
thereafter, like one who is deluded, the Goddess of the Mace slaughtered the army.
The army of the Rākṣasas was broken and the Rākṣasa himself fainted;
he fell upon the earth, and at that moment, the mace became silent.
The Rākṣasa, having protected his life, fled;
the remaining army scattered, and there was a cry of victory for the woman.
That mace became quiet and, having returned to its place, became motionless;
the queen worshipped it according to the prescribed rites and likewise offered food offerings and other gifts.
Then, after some time had passed, many sea-born rākṣasas gathered together and held a consultation for the sake of regaining their kingdom and queen.
Others were experts in missiles and weapons; others were knowers of illusions and mantras; there were also those skilled in invisibility as well as those capable of assuming many forms.
Accompanied by thousands of powerful Rākṣasas and Rākṣasīs, and equipped with all the implements for battle, they arrived at the city of Godalā.
Desiring victory, the Rākṣasas roared through the path of the sky;
they raised shouts of battle and repeatedly sounded their kettledrums.
They sounded conch shells and played battle-instruments; they then uttered shouts of "kilakila" and performed the slapping of arms.
Having heard these terrifying cries of the rākṣasas, the subjects trembled, and the royal armies as well trembled greatly upon the earth.
Pradhāna and the others went to King Nṛpa and informed him of the severe calamity—the Rākṣasas' desire for battle. || 35 ||
The queen rose quickly, bathed, and worshipped the mace;
she honored it with incense, lamps, excellent food offerings, and the waving of lights. ||36||
Then that heavy mace, having assumed the form of a divine woman, the mistress of battle,
and being endowed with all missiles, weapons, and the like, spoke.
"I am the power of the Bhagavatī, appointed by the Supreme Soul, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, for the sake of your protection. (38)
Today, having granted battle three times to this offender who has approached him, he shall indeed bring about the destruction of his life through various means.
"I shall do this for you, O Great Queen; salutations to you, may there be well-being and auspiciousness for you.
Having spoken thus, the mace Raṇeśvarī, endowed with all powers, [then acted].
From his own body, he brought forth well-nourished warriors who were intolerant of battle;
he then joined all of them, those lords of the quarters who possess the power of moving through the sky.
Having equipped their armies with missiles and weapons,
those Rakshasa forces indeed took flight into the sky and launched their attack.
The Rākṣasas and hosts of Rākṣasīs, exceedingly fierce, also fell,
[struck] by weapons, maces, staffs, javelins, and iron balls.
With bundles of grass, stones, earth-clods, spears, javelins, trees, iron arrows, shafts, bolts, swords, crescent-headed arrows, and balls; ||44||
Then, seeing the exceedingly swift array of the Rākṣasas,
the lords of maces, who were fierce in battle, rushed forth through the sky.
Urged on by the goddess Gadā, the heroes struck down the Rākṣasas with weapons, missiles, iron balls, maces, javelins, and other such arms. ||46||
They struck one another with various kinds of weapons;
those fierce ones killed [their foes] and divided the Rākṣasas into two groups.
From the neck, from the shoulders, from the waist, from the hands, and likewise from the thighs,
they tore apart and destroyed the asuras.
Indeed, those lords of maces crushed the fierce rākṣasas, causing them to fall from the sky to the earth, deprived of their lives. 49.
Seizing the Asuras by the neck with both hands, they sucked them dry;
and perceiving fire, the lords caused the Rakshasas to blaze.
A great slaughter indeed occurred among the Rākṣasas who fell to the earth;
then that Bhadraka employed an illusion that restored the Rākṣasas to life.
He brought back to life the Rākṣasas, who were experts in all weapons and missiles;
rising up again and again, they repeatedly struck down the soldiers led by Gadeśvara.
Indeed, [he created] illusory elephants, camels, crocodiles, tigers, bears, lions, fish, śarabhas, leopards, and the foremost of serpents. ||53||
Having created by means of their illusory power (*māyā*) spirits, ghosts, demons, mountains, lightning, soldiers, and clouds of stone, they struck down the lords.
They raised up a rain of wind and likewise created a rain of dust;
they also produced a rain of fire and likewise created a rain of stones.
They brought down a great rain of locusts, a shower of scorpions, and a rain of serpents, lizards, and iguanas. ||56||
They unleashed a rain of poison and likewise a rain of blood;
with streams of hot water, they brought suffering upon the people.
Then they produced a rain of mud, a rain of elephants,
a rain of trees, and also a rain of lions.
There, the Rākṣasas discharged a shower of fires and a shower of Rākṣasas— a terrifying downpour of all kinds.
They also unleashed a rain of weapons capable of piercing the body;
thus did those rākṣasas wage a battle of such a destructive nature.
Brahmajit, Kratujit, Devāntaka, Narāntaka, Kumbhagarta, Śaṅkuraśmi, Ayomukha, and Śatāhvaya; ||6.1||
Indrajit, Ekacakra, Prāpaṇa, Puruṇḍaka, Cūrṇanābha, Asiloman, Kumbhāmāna, and Mahodaka. ||62||
Śvalabha, Tālaketu, Savyāsivya, Supuñjika, Kālanābha, Yajñaha, Śrāddhāda, and Vajraha; ||63||
Vidyutputra, Rasana, Vapāśa, and Raktakarṇaka; those with round eyes and tawny hair, those with eight fangs and large bellies.
They had thick heads and short shanks, with copper-colored eyes and hair standing upright;
they had sunken eyes, long tongues and lips, and drooping eyebrows and thick noses.
There, these hosts of Rākṣasas were slain with maces—
namely the Rākṣasīs Vikacā, Brahmadhānā, Ālambikā, and the others.
Struck by maces and clubs raised up by mace-wielders on the battlefields,
those armies of mace-bearers [saw] me, Nārāyaṇa, Kṛṣṇa, Hari, the Lord.
Falling again and again upon the heads of the rākṣasas,
they then crushed the skulls and chests of those demons.
"We shall forever slay all rakṣasas so that they go to the abode of Yama;
we, who are called Saṃkarṣaṇa, swear that they shall never rise again. (69)
Having spoken thus, the goddesses of the battlefield then struck with their maces,
and the hosts of rākṣasas met their ultimate destruction.
By means of his illusory power (māyā), all the rains were dissolved into the sky;
the earth became entirely covered with the corpses of the hosts of rākṣasas.
Bhadraka rushed forward to seize the battle-lord’s mace;
as he charged, a hundred maces appeared all around him.
He killed Bhadraka on all sides with the deluded Māra,
causing him to bleed profusely and vomit blood as well.
With his head shattered and his chest broken, Bhadraka fell to the ground crying out in distress;
he met his death, as did the other rākṣasas who were there.
Abandoning the battle, they fled by the hundreds;
yet the maces, falling upon their backs, struck them down as if granting them life.
Deprived of life, they fell down with their hands and knees outstretched;
with their bellies gaping open, they met their end.
Not even a single one remained; the entire army of a hundred thousand foremost Rākṣasas met its destruction, struck down by the mace.
Then the queen remembered her husband Nārāyaṇa, saying, "Indeed, he is I;
for the sake of purification and for the sake of the lives of the subjects on the fields of battle. (78)
Then, O Lakṣmī, I quickly offered that nectar of the water from my feet into the unfathomable pitcher whose nature is the sky of consciousness. ||79||
For the sake of reviving the subjects, she performed a consecration upon the earth by way of the sky, saying:
"May these subjects of mine, though dead, come back to life."
Thus, whatever offspring were conceived there at that time in battle,
they were forcibly brought to their death in the midst of the earth.
Then all those bodies of the Rākṣasas were restored to life, like those awakened from sleep, by means of maces and fire.
O Lotus-born One, it was indeed by my will that they were reduced to ashes there;
thus, having waged a supreme battle and slain the Rākṣasas, the maces [were destroyed].
The mistresses of the battlefield arrived before me at the palace of the queen;
their blessings having been magnified, they were urged to grant their boons. (84)
Those maidens indeed chose me, the Supreme Lord, as their husband;
and Cidambārā too, along with the Raṇeśvarīs, was filled with joy. 85.
Then, together with them, she honored me with an excellent garland;
indeed, a thousand Raṇeśvarīs chose me as their boon.
Likewise, the Gadeśvaras chose the delightful granting of boons;
and the Pārṣadas, being firm in their resolve, [chose] to be in my abode, saying, "So be it. (87)
All the attendants who were accepted went to my imperishable abode;
likewise, O Lakṣmī, the mistresses of battle and my other beloveds went to the supreme, imperishable realm. (88)
And those Muktānikās indeed abide in the supreme abode;
Cidambarā also is my devotee to Gadeśvara, the yogin. (89)
Having given my entire kingdom to my gentle devotee, who was a personal attendant (pārṣada), he departed for my supreme and transcendent abode, the imperishable realm.
King Gadeśvara, devoted to celibacy and adhering to the Vaiṣṇava dharma, ruled the kingdom for one hundred thousand years.
Having caused devotion toward me to arise, having made the subjects truly Vaiṣṇava,
and having performed sacrifices, offerings, and other rites, you shall satisfy the gods and the ancestors.
